text:
U.S. Rep. Kristen McDonald Rivet (D-Bay City) at a June 6, 2025 town hall in Lansing. | Kyle DavidsonAs the dust of election season settles across the country, the representative from Michigan’s politically purple 8th Congressional District has raised her hand to lead House Democrats’ frontline efforts at expanding their majority in 2028.
As first reported by The Washington Sun, U.S. Rep. Kristen McDonald Rivet (D-Bay City) sent out a letter on Thursday calling on her colleagues to elect her as the next “Battleground Leadership Representative.”
McDonald Rivet is serving her first term in the U.S. House after previously serving in the Michigan Senate. McDonald Rivet helped Democrats retain control of Michigan’s 8th District during her 2024 campaign, and recently won reelection against retired GM engineer Thomas Smith, who dropped out of the Republican primary weeks before he was selected to represent the party in the general election.
In a copy of the letter shared with Michigan Advance, McDonald Rivet congratulated her colleagues on their hard-fought victories in 2026, before looking ahead to 2028. 
“Our reward is a new set of challenges: the final two years of the Trump presidency, a 2028 cycle sure to bring plenty of landmines, and, most importantly, the responsibility to make good on our promises in the 120th Congress,” McDonald Rivet said. “To succeed, our caucus must look to the members who made this majority possible to help shape how we lead.”
2026-11-05 McDonald Rivet Battleground Leadership Representative Letter
 
McDonald Rivet, who serves as the freshman leadership representative for the New Democrat Coalition and vice chair of the Majority Democrats political action committee, noted she had spent her career running in political battlegrounds and was one of the candidates who helped deliver Michigan Dems their razor-thin 20-18 majority in the state Senate.
“We cannot squander the opportunity to deliver on the promises that brought us into the majority – people are hungry for results, and it’s our job to meet the moment,” McDonald Rivet said. “I would be honored to serve as your Battleground Leadership Representative, work alongside each of you to make the most of this moment, and help turn the hopes of the people who sent us here into real results.”
If elected, McDonald Rivet would succeed Rep. Susie Lee (D-Nev.), who created the battleground leadership role in 2022.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Most of CT turned more blue Tuesday. How did your town change?
description: Big blue shifts in House and Senate districts across Connecticut led to Democratic majorities the state hasn't seen in years, or ever.
text:
Voters in Connecticut, like the rest of the country, sent a loud message Tuesday that something had to change.
That sentiment trickled down to General Assembly races, resulting in the Connecticut GOP’s worst performance in the state House since 1974 and the worst ever in the state Senate.
Lamont also rode the blue wave, managing to increase his margin over Republicans by about 5 percentage points compared to 2022, with around 60% of the overall vote this year.
But it was a different story with General Assembly races, where Democrats picked up substantial portions of the vote in nearly every town.





Across all state Senate races, Democrats performed 11 percentage points better than in 2024, leaving Republicans with only three state senators, all in west-central Connecticut. 

Fairfield saw the largest shift, with Rob Blanchard increasing the town’s Democratic share by 35 percentage points, flipping Tony Hwang’s former district from red to blue. Eastern Connecticut saw staunch increases in Democratic support, and Woodstock, Newtown, New Hartford, Groton and Easton saw their Democratic margin increase by more than 25 percentage points since 2024.
Democrat support in the state House of Representatives increased by a thunderous 10-percentage-point margin. Stonington swung by 30 points, flipping the 43rd district, with North Stonington and Coventry also raising their margin by 25 percentage points.

name: WyoFile
title: Insurance cost hikes, fewer Medicare options add to Wyomingites’ healthcare struggles
description:
UnitedHealthcare ends a supplemental Medicare plan in Wyoming while people insured on the ACA marketplace see premiums jump again. 
The post Insurance cost hikes, fewer Medicare options add to Wyomingites’ healthcare struggles appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
After Stacey Mittelstadt retired from teaching in Wyoming, she and her husband, a retired Casper firefighter, found health insurance plans on the Affordable Care Act marketplace. It seemed to be the cheapest and best option to tide them over until they could enroll in Medicare, she said. 
But when ACA enhanced tax credits expired at the end of 2025, plan premiums jumped dramatically — and Wyoming customers experienced the highest price hikes in the country. Suddenly the cheapest ACA option for the Mittelstadts came with monthly premiums of $3,100, she said, which was too much. The Lander couple left the marketplace, but weren’t satisfied with a non-mainstream option that ultimately didn’t provide great coverage.
When 2027 ACA plan enrollment opened Nov. 1, Wyoming residents discovered that costs will again see double-digit percentage jumps, adding to the sticker shock that drove enrollees like the Mittelstadts to drop their plans last year. This time, the couple’s cheapest option for an ACA plan would cost more than $3,300 in monthly premiums, Mittelstadt said. 
“So if I’m paying my monthly payments of $3,300, and I don’t use the insurance … I’ve spent nearly $40,000 a year,” she said, and that doesn’t even factor in a $23,000 deductible. “It’s just crazy.”
It’s another example of fluctuating costs and market conditions that make healthcare affordability a huge challenge in Wyoming. Many residents on private plans offered through employers have also seen premium costs rise in recent years. The problem has become acute enough that the Legislature created a task force this year to tackle insurance affordability. 
This graph from KFF shows monthly premium cost trends for Affordable Care Act insurance plans in Wyoming. (KFF)
Coverage choices are also getting winnowed; UnitedHealthcare is ending its supplemental Medicare Advantage program in Wyoming at the end of the year, which means its customers have to shop for and switch plans. 
These are symptoms plaguing the entire healthcare system, an insurance executive said.  
“Like healthcare organizations across the country, insurers are also facing rising medical costs, increased utilization, changing federal requirements, and ongoing workforce challenges,” said Connie Trowbridge, president of WyoBlue Advantage, a company created in partnership with Blue Cross Blue Shield of Wyoming. “These factors don’t just affect one type of coverage. They impact the entire healthcare system and ultimately influence premiums across both the individual and Medicare markets.”
The Medicare market
Mike Garduno of Casper realized something was going to change with his UnitedHealthcare Medicare Advantage plan around September, when he started getting calls from insurance agents trying to enroll him in a new plan, he said. 
The 63-year-old has lived with multiple sclerosis since his early 20s. He worked for four decades before retiring and going on disability. 
When he called UnitedHealthcare customer service, he said, it seemed like the agent had been advised not to disclose the company’s plan to end its Medicare Advantage plan in Wyoming until later in October. But Garduno was able to confirm that the only way it would be available to him come 2027 is if he moved to Colorado. 
That’s because UnitedHealthcare is withdrawing the remainder of its Medicare Advantage plans from Wyoming. The company, like many major American insurers, has been shuttering plans it deems unprofitable; it began phasing out Medicare Advantage from several Wyoming counties last year and will pull the remainder by year’s end.  
Medicare Advantage plans are offered by private insurance companies as an alternative to original Medicare. Customers often choose them because they include extra benefits related to things like dental coverage or prescription drug coverage. 
A UnitedHealthcare spokesperson told WyoFile the company has equipped affected customers with information on next steps. 
This Oct. 16, 2012, file photo, shows a portion of the UnitedHealth Group Inc.’s campus in Minnetonka, Minn. (AP Photo/Jim Mone, File)
“UnitedHealthcare is making targeted changes to its individual Medicare Advantage offerings for 2027 to help ensure long-term sustainability for the members we serve,” Jessica Kostner wrote in an email. “Some of these changes include plan closures and market exits, and individuals impacted should have received a CMS-required notice in early-October, including guidance regarding their options and next steps.”
Customers can visit Medicare.gov to view their plan options for 2027, she said.
People like Garduno don’t have to move out of state, said Tisha Tuttle, with the Wyoming State Health Insurance Information Program. The federally mandated program helps seniors and others on Medicare understand their rights and navigate healthcare. 
“That does create quite the change, but it also gives those individuals losing that plan kind of this golden opportunity,” she said. “When they lose that plan or any plan through no fault of their own, they have guaranteed issue into any plan of their choice. Whether that be another Medicare Advantage plan or going back to original Medicare, they have that opportunity.”
For the more than 7,000 Wyoming residents Tuttle believes will lose their UnitedHealthcare plans, there are Medicare Advantage plans available through BlueCross Blue Shield’s WyoBlue Advantage. Humana also offers plans in some Wyoming communities. Original Medicare is another option. 
Customers have until Feb. 28 as a final deadline to choose a plan, Tuttle said, but if they take medications, they should find a plan before the end of December so they have coverage in January. 
Still, finding a new plan is a headache for Garduno. He felt that the rug was suddenly pulled from under him, he said, and he wished the company gave him notice earlier. The news created a lot of stress for him, and for a person living with MS, stress can exacerbate the condition.
ACA costs 
The Affordable Care Act marketplace, created in 2010, is available to people who don’t qualify for Medicaid and don’t have insurance through an employer. 
Congress created the Enhanced Premium Tax Credit during the COVID-19 pandemic to make marketplace insurance more affordable. That program provided subsidies that drastically reduced premium costs. For some low-income customers, monthly premiums went to $0.  
The program helped contribute to an all-time low in America’s uninsured rate, health advocates say. But they were not cheap — and fiscal conservatives argued they were unsustainable. Congress extended the credits in 2022, but did not extend them again in 2025. As a result, plan costs shot up. 
The 2027 enrollment period opened this week. It’s the annual window when individuals and families can sign up for ACA health insurance, adjust plans or cancel coverage.
Individual plans vary based on factors like household size and income. But in Wyoming, the average lowest-cost Bronze Premium is $875, while the average lowest-cost Silver Premium is $1,190 and the average lowest-cost Gold Premium is $1,076, according to KFF. Those are among the highest prices in the nation. 
Cheyenne resident Jason Mincer’s premiums will be nearly $1,500 starting in January. Along with worrying about his own financial impacts, Mincer sits on the board of Healthy Wyoming, a nonprofit that works on healthcare affordability and access. 
Healthy Wyoming Executive Director Jenn Lowe discusses health care access issues during a forum Sept. 4, 2025 in Lander. (Katie Klingsporn/WyoFile)
“As a board member for Healthy Wyoming, I am equally concerned that hard working people in Wyoming are going to drop their health coverage because they cannot afford it, leading to premature death and needless health problems for so many of our neighbors,” he told WyoFile.
ACA enrollment in Wyoming fell from 46,643 in 2025 to 37,643 in 2026, a drop of 9,000, according to the Wyoming Department of Health. 
When Mittelstadt asked an insurance broker for advice navigating the Lander couple’s situation, the broker said her options include: make less money, go without health insurance, pay the $3,300 a month or go back to work. 
The couple is on Wyoming retirement fed by pensions they earned. Making less isn’t really an option. And though they are healthy, Mittelstadt said, they don’t want to gamble with no coverage.
Instead of going back to the marketplace, they have joined a Health Ministry, which relies on a pool of patients — often affiliated by religion — to help one another pay for healthcare. 
“So basically we’ll just be uninsured,” she said. “And then it’s a health share where you submit your bills and other people help you pay them.” They’ll forgo things like yearly health checks that could come with unexpected costs, she said. 
Both are 57 years old, which means they are years away from qualifying for Medicare. Between now and then, Mittelstadt said, “I’m hoping something changes at some point.”
The post Insurance cost hikes, fewer Medicare options add to Wyomingites’ healthcare struggles appeared first on WyoFile .

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: Deep drought fueling White Mountains forest fire that has reached historic scale
description: On Thursday night, while crews from across the country battled a wildfire in the dense woods of the White Mountain National Forest, residents of nearby communities and officials with the U.S. Forest Service crowded into the Shelburne Town Hall. The blaze, which according to officials grew to a peak of nearly 1,000 acres since it […]
text:
A large wildfire in the White Mountain National Forest is burning through leaf litter on the ground. It is unlikely to kill or remove leaves from trees, U.S. Forest Service officials said on Thursday. (Photo courtesy Gorham NH Fire and EMS/U.S. Forest Service)On Thursday night, while crews from across the country battled a wildfire in the dense woods of the White Mountain National Forest, residents of nearby communities and officials with the U.S. Forest Service crowded into the Shelburne Town Hall.
The blaze, which according to officials grew to a peak of nearly 1,000 acres since it began on Sunday but was reduced to 856 acres as of Thursday night, is highly unusual for the region.
“We’re not used to fires of this size here in New England. This is, unofficially, the largest fire in the White Mountain National Forest’s history since its creation,” said Derek Ibarguen, forest supervisor.
Drought conditions during the last two years have made the forest much more flammable than it would be under average conditions, said Ryan Hughes, incident commander with the Forest Service, during the meeting.
Shelburne area residents asked about danger to their homes during a question-and-answer session with the U.S. Forest Service on Thursday, Nov. 5. A wildfire burning a few miles from the Maine border is one of the largest in the history of the White Mountain National Forest, and a first in recent history, officials said. (Screenshot)
About 40% of New Hampshire, including much of Coös County, is currently experiencing moderate drought, according to the U.S. Drought Monitor. Last year saw drought conditions stretch from what became New Hampshire’s driest summer on record into the winter.
At the site of the Wild River fire, which is burning just miles from the Maine border and downtown Shelburne, moisture that would ordinarily keep fire from spreading through leaf litter and the ground is depleted, Hughes said.
“That (moisture) is just not there this year,” he said. 
The near-annual cycles of intense drought that have affected New Hampshire in the past decade are linked to climate change, which is causing increasingly intense weather. That includes longer stretches of the hot, dry days that contribute to drought conditions.
In the decades before the White Mountain National Forest was created, large forest fires frequently tore through the region, often due to large-scale timber harvests that left piles of dry, flammable fuel throughout the forest and introduced spark-making machinery and trains to the forest.
Drought raises the stakes of New Hampshire’s relationship to fire

The creation of the national forest and changes in logging practices brought an end to that period. But now, New Hampshire’s relationship to fire seems to be changing again. With drought increasingly common, some researchers worry that climate change is making wildfire a more urgent threat to New Hampshire and the Northeast. 
At the community meeting on Thursday night, one attendee described seeing ash floating through the air downtown.
“I thought I was seeing things,” he said. “…That’s not good.”
Androscoggin District Ranger Josh Sjostrom said the fire was unlike what he had seen in the region before.
“We’re not really accustomed to this. I grew up here in Shelburne, and to imagine this happening 20 years ago could be jarring,” he said. 
Other residents asked officials whether evacuations would be necessary and whether any structures were threatened.
As of Thursday night, the fire was about two miles from the nearest private land, and the Forest Service did not believe any structures were in danger, Hughes said. 
Several teams of wildland firefighters, smoke jumpers, aircraft operators and engine crews were making progress on the fire, he said. But he stressed that certain weather conditions would need to be met before the fire could be fully extinguished,
“Just to be brutally honest with everybody, it’s so much ground to cover and so much challenging terrain that it’s going to take a season-ending event,” he said, like multiple inches of rain or a snowstorm, before the fire is fully out. 
Forest Service firefighters from around the nation will remain in the area indefinitely, Sjostrom said. 
“They’ll be around for a while, so welcome them into our community, because they’re going to be here to keep this in check,” he said.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri to pay $150,000 to settle lawsuit over prisoner’s death by suicide
description: Missouri must pay $150,000 to the mother of a man who committed suicide in a Southeast Missouri prison, a Mississippi County judge ruled Friday. Jahi Hynes was 27 when died April 4, 2021, at the Southeast Missouri Correctional Center in Charleston. His mother, Willa Hynes, sued the Department of Corrections, three of the agency’s corporate […]
text:
The Missouri Department of Corrections has settled a wrongful death lawsuit with Willa Hynes, mother of Jahi Hynes , who hanged himself the day after he was placed in administrative segregation on April 3, 2021 (Getty Images).Missouri must pay $150,000 to the mother of a man who committed suicide in a Southeast Missouri prison, a Mississippi County judge ruled Friday.
Jahi Hynes was 27 when died April 4, 2021, at the Southeast Missouri Correctional Center in Charleston. His mother, Willa Hynes, sued the Department of Corrections, three of the agency’s corporate contractors and 15 individuals in 2024 after forcing the release of records about her son’s death from the department.
In the settlement, the department does not admit any liability for Jahi Hynes’ death and Willa Hynes agreed to drop her claims against all the defendants, including the private contractors.
Associate Circuit Judge Blake Pearson approved the settlement in a brief hearing that came 10 months after the previous judge in the case sanctioned the department and threw out its defense for repeatedly violating court orders to produce records
Under the terms of the settlement, Willa Hynes will receive about $80,000 and her attorneys will receive $60,000 plus the expense of litigation.
“She’s had to wait a long time to get here, and had to fight hard to get here,” attorney Steve Groves said. “But we’re glad the case got resolved, so Miss Hynes can finally get some peace.”
The lawsuit alleged that corrections officials and contract medical personnel ignored Jahi Hynes’ mental health needs and disregarded department rules for the safety of people in administrative segregation.
Jahi Hynes was placed in administrative segregation on April 3, 2021, after allowing the food port door in his cell to strike the hand of a corrections officer, causing minor injuries, and blocking the port with his mattress. 
The next day, he hanged himself with a bedsheet.
Hynes’ death is one of more than 630 in department custody from 2021 to 2025, according to records compiled by the Missouri Justice Coalition. The department has been reluctant to release records on the deaths, which reached a record of 139 in 2024.
The highest profile case is the death of Othel Moore on Dec. 8, 2023, in the Jefferson City Correctional Center. Three former corrections officers face criminal charges for assault, with two also charged with second degree murder and the third charged with involuntary manslaughter. Charges against two corrections officers were dropped after they were filed in June 2024.
A hearing is scheduled for Monday in Jefferson City to set a trial date for the three charged in Moore’s death.
The Sunshine Law violations in Hynes’ case cost the department $60,000. The sanctions that removed the department’s defense did not strike the defenses of the individual plaintiffs or the department’s medical contractor.
When the settlement was reached, both sides initially sought to block the terms of the agreement, and the amount paid to Willa Hynes, from disclosure. The motion initially asked Pearson to remove the filings about the settlement and Willa Hynes’ affidavit accepting from the record and to keep the amount confidential.
The Independent objected to those actions in a letter to Pearson. Missouri court rules do not provide for the removal of records in a case but do allow them to be sealed if the plaintiff has sufficient reason.
The Missouri Sunshine Law has a blanket ban on confidential settlement payments.
The parties engaged in new negotiations after receiving the letter. All the settlement documents were placed in the court records and all are public.
The settlement’s statement about liability in the case is a blanket release.
“No actions taken by the parties hereto, or any of them, either previously or in connection with this agreement shall be deemed or construed to be an admission of the truth or falsity of any matter pertaining to any claim or defense alleged in the pleadings filed on behalf of the parties in the lawsuit, or an acknowledgment by any of the parties hereto of any liability to the other parties or to any person for any other claim, demand, or action, all liability being expressly denied by the parties,” it states.
Willa Hynes’ affidavit affirms that she is Jahi Hynes’ only living relative and that she is “satisfied my attorneys have fully investigated the facts and circumstances of his death” and that she accepts the settlement.
“I believe,” the affidavit states, “the terms of the settlement and distribution are fair and reasonable and should be accepted.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: OK, Democrats, now do something
description: Hakeem Jeffries and Chuck Schumer, before you get comfortable: we didn't send you there to protect the majority. We sent you there to use it.
text:
Democrats across this country knocked on doors this fall. They made the phone calls, stood outside supermarkets handing out flyers, went door to door and on Tuesday it paid off. In January, Democrats will run the House and the Senate. They won in Kansas, for heaven’s sake.
That’s worth celebrating. It’s also worth worrying about because we’ve been here before.
In 2009 we had Barack Obama in the White House, a big House majority and, for a few months, 60 votes in the Senate. We’d done the same work to get there. Then our own leadership talked itself out of most of what we’d been promised. The public option went first. By 2010 the majority was gone and it took us years to get it back.
So to House and Senate Majority Leaders Hakeem Jeffries and Chuck Schumer, before you get comfortable: we didn’t send you there to protect the majority. We sent you there to use it. Do something, and I don’t mean something with a small s. I mean Something with a capital S. Here’s what I’d like to hear at your first press conference.
Say out loud that what has happened in Gaza is genocide, and that it has to stop now, ceasefire or no ceasefire. Then back it up with the one tool Congress actually has, which is money. No more American funding for the bombs, the bulldozers or anything else being used against civilians there.
Then do something nobody in Washington seems willing to do. Namely, apologize. On February 28, the first day of the war with Iran, an American strike hit an elementary school in Minab. More than 100 children were killed, along with their teachers. The administration has never owned it, and the Pentagon still hasn’t released its findings. Congress can’t speak for the President, but it can speak for the American people. Pass a resolution apologizing to those families on our behalf, then subpoena the investigation and put it out in the open. I know how that will play on cable news. I don’t care. Any parent in America would want somebody to say they were sorry.
At that same press conference, take care of our own. Announce that every family who lost a service member in the war with Iran will be assigned a personal advocate, one person whose only job is to walk them through the benefits, the paperwork and the bureaucracy and to get them whatever they need. And announce that every servicemember wounded in that war will be treated by the best medical specialists in the world, with the government paying whatever it costs, for as long as it takes. Whatever anyone thinks of the war, the people we sent to fight it should never have to fight us for their care.
While you’re issuing subpoenas, finish the job on the Epstein files. Congress passed a law a year ago ordering their release. What we got was millions of pages with whole sections blacked out and no real explanation. Protect the victims’ names and release everything else. Then make sure the Justice Department pursues criminal charges against anyone the files show abused children, no matter how rich or connected they are. If that can’t happen in this country, nothing we say about the rule of law means much.
After that comes the domestic agenda people actually voted for. Put universal health care on the floor and make every member go on record. Do something real about student debt, and about the system that keeps creating it.
And deal with the money. AIPAC and the network of PACs around it have had a hold on both parties for a long time. This summer Leader Jeffries opposed cutting military aid to Israel only weeks after his fundraising committee took a record earmark from AIPAC. I don’t think he’s a bad man. I think he’s a careful one, and careful isn’t what this moment needs. Leader Jeffries, stop dodging the question. Say Democrats won’t take that money anymore and go first. The rest of the caucus will follow you, or they’ll have to explain why not.
Yes, Trump still has the veto. Fine. Make him use it. Make him veto health care and debt relief and let every Republican go home in 2028 and explain why they sided with him.
The folks in Kansas and Texas and Ohio who gave us a chance this year don’t owe us anything. They’ll give us two years, maybe. We did our part. Now do yours.
Joseph Luciano lives in Bridgeport.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: The view from under the Blue Wave
description: An unpopular war, presidential antics and voters struggling to get by all fueled this political massacre.
text:
In a massacre that would embarrass Genghis Khan, the Democrats obliterated Republicans in the midterm elections. 
At the time of this writing, the Democrats have picked up seven Senate seats giving them a total of 54. Two races, Alaska and Mississippi, are too close to call, but odds are they will both go Democratic. In the House the Democrats have already won 30 seats and political pundits believe this number could climb to 46. Thus, the Democrats will have about 260 to 175 majority.

Joseph Bentivegna MD

Traditional Republican states such as South Carolina, Ohio, Kansas and Iowa elected Democratic senators. And the liberal wish of turning Texas blue finally came true, as the incumbent Republican governor was vanquished and the open Senate seat was won by Democrat James Talerico by 12%. The State House also flipped to the Democrats as did all the constitutional offices.
In my home state of Connecticut, elected Republicans in our General Assembly and Senate are rarer than Ivory-billed Woodpeckers. Eight Senate seats were lost and now the Democrats have a 33-3 majority! The Governor, the Senators, constitutional officers and the members of Congress are all Democrats.
How did this happen?
The invasion of Iran was a disaster. With neither the consent of Congress nor the American people, President Trump decided he was going to bring peace to the Middle East by neutering Iran. But he had no plan.
Only regime change is going to change Iran’s policies, and this is not possible without an armed insurgency by Iranians, American ground troops or the use of nuclear weapons.
The result, the clever Iranians looked at American polls, blocked the Strait of Hormuz and caused gas and diesel prices to skyrocket. Hello Democrats.
People are tired of President Trump’s antics. The inflationary tariffs were bad enough, but having his family promote cryptocurrency scams while his son-in-law Jared Kushner is extorting foreign leaders to invest in his hedge fund is a bit much.
And why insult Canada by saying it should become our 51st state while imposing lumber tariffs that increased housing costs? And sucking up to the barbarian Putin has accomplished nothing. The federal deficit is higher than ever. So much for fiscal conservatism.
President Trump has lost his juice. The conventional wisdom was that either Vice President J.D. Vance or Secretary of State Marco Rubio would be the presidential nominee and if Trump choose one of them, the other would bow out. This has been thrown out the window. It may well be that both Vance and Rubio are too tainted by Trump and Republicans will look at more electable candidates such as Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis or Nikki Haley.
Trump was not the only issue. Seventy percent of the American people believe America is on the wrong tract. This number is consistent no matter what party is in the White House.
We once had a country in which a man could support a family on one income. Now you can barely do it on two incomes. Young people are refusing to marry because they can’t afford to. Neither party has any concrete solutions to high housing, health insurance and car prices. Taxes are too high but cutting them is politically impossible, especially with our massive $40 trillion deficit.
This Blue Wave makes it easier for Republicans to win the White House in 2028. Americans love divided government since it prevents the extremes of either party from imposing their will. The Democrats have relatively large majorities in the House and Senate, and many voters do not want to see an unchecked Democratic president, especially if the Democrats nominate a socialist such as U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (AOC).
Israel will have to fight harder for its existence. Even prominent Jewish politicians such as Bernie Saunders and Jamie Raskin have embraced the Palestinian cause, and Democratic rallies are replete with Palestinian flags. The swing state of Michigan just elected a Democratic Senator, Abdul El-Sayed, who is openly hostile to Israel’s existence. Unless President Trump by some miracle can turn the war around with Iran, Israel may soon find itself abandoned by the American political class.
But as bad as this election was for Republicans, it is not without precedent. The Democrats lost 63 seats during the Clinton presidency in 1994 and 54 seats during the Obama presidency in 2010 – more than the Republicans lost this cycle. Yet both Clinton and Obama won reelection easily. And there is no better street fight than Donald Trump, even when he is a lame duck. It would be foolish to count him out.
But if this election shows anything, America is an unhappy country in spite of our affluence. People find happiness in faith, family, friends and financial security. The pollical, economic and cultural changes of the past two generations have made this possible for fewer people.
Joseph Bentivegna MD is an ophthalmologist in Rocky Hill.

name: Source New Mexico
title: Conservation groups say proposed mining along New Mexico-Arizona border threatens wildlife crossing
description: A coalition of conservation groups is asking the Bureau of Land Management to scrutinize a proposed copper mining operation along the New Mexico-Arizona state line that they say would threaten an important wildlife crossing.
text:
A coalition of conservation groups said a proposed copper mining operation along the New Mexico-Arizona state line could imperil an important wildlife crossing for Mexican gray wolves (pictured), black bears and desert bighorn sheep. (Photo courtesy U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service)A coalition of conservation groups is asking the Bureau of Land Management to scrutinize a proposed copper mining operation along the New Mexico-Arizona state line that they say would threaten an important wildlife crossing.
Curiosity Exploration LLC earlier this year filed a permit application with the New Mexico Energy, Minerals and Natural Resources Department and sent a notice of intent to begin exploratory mining to the BLM.
The proposed site is near the Peloncillo Mountains, which run along the New Mexico-Arizona state line in Hidalgo County, New Mexico, and Cochise County, Arizona. The area is home to mountains known as “sky islands,” due to their rich, biodiverse ecosystems that tower above the region’s predominantly parched desert landscape.
A group of conservation groups — including New Mexico Wild, the Chiricahua Regional Council and the Sky Island Alliance — last week co-signed a letter to BLM officials, asking them to require an extensive environmental review of the proposal under the National Environmental Policy Act.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The Bureau of Land Management did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The conservation groups contend that the area is among the most important wildlife corridors in the Southwest. New Mexico’s Wildlife Corridors Action Plan identifies the region as particularly important to desert bighorn sheep, which are “especially vulnerable” to habitat disruptions caused by nearby highways such as Interstate 10. The plan calls for building highway overpasses and underpasses for desert bighorn sheep, black bears and Mexican gray wolves to safely traverse the area.
“Other impacts to the Peloncillos, like the border wall and I-10, can be mitigated one day and might not be as permanent,” New Mexico Wild community organizer Luke Koenig said in a statement. “But once you turn a portion of one of the West’s most important wildlife corridors into a giant hole in the ground, you’ll never get it back.”
Dirk Sigler, president of the resident’s watchdog group Chiricahua Regional Council, in a statement said that the corridor is “a stepping stone along an ancient pathway that’s been used by wildlife for millennia.”
“What would you rather see at your doorstep — a desert bighorn sheep or an open pit mine?” he asked.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: New limits on federal student loans steer borrowers toward private lenders
description: Private lenders are helping students make up the difference between program costs and the amount they can borrow from the federal government.
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — New limits on federal student loans filled Chloe Frabotta with anxiety as she began studying in New York City to become a physician assistant.
The changes that took effect this fall include caps on loans for particular programs as well as limits on the amount parents can borrow to pay for their children’s schooling. Up until weeks before Frabotta, 25, started her program, it was up in the air whether it would count as a “professional” program with higher loan limits.
Amid the uncertainty, she borrowed around $6,000 in federal loans for her first trimester, taking out private loans for the rest with her mother as a cosigner.
“At least in my circles a lot of people were like, ’I guess that’s what I’m going to have to do, and I’m going to try to make it work,’” Frabotta said.
Students have been turning to private lenders to make up the difference between the cost of their educational programs and the amount they can borrow from the federal government, which offers more flexible repayment terms, the possibility of forgiveness after 10 years in public service, and — for many — lower interest rates.
It’s showing up in banks’ bottom lines. Private lender SoFi reported in late October that student loan originations hit $2.9 billion in the third quarter, nearly doubling from a year earlier. Days earlier, Sallie Mae, which controls more than half of the private student loan market, said graduate loans were up 119% year-over-year.
Trump’s ‘Big Beautiful Bill’ put new caps on student loans
President Donald Trump’s “Big Beautiful Bill” slashed the amount new graduate students can borrow. Programs designated as professional degrees face federal student loan caps of $200,000, while other graduate programs are capped at $100,000. Previously, graduate students had been able to take out federal loans up to the full cost of their degree.
For new borrowers, the changes include an overall lifetime borrowing cap of $257,500 and limits to the amount parents can borrow to pay for their children’s schooling.
[RELATED: Blumenthal, CT nurses decry reduced loan caps for advanced degree programs]
When all the changes are fully phased in, more than half a million borrowers are going to need to borrow an extra $20,000 a year from somewhere other than the federal loan program, estimated Jordan Matsudaira, the director of the Postsecondary Education & Economics Research Center at American University. The hardest-hit students are in expensive programs like medicine, law and dentistry, an analysis by the center found.
The Trump administration has argued the new limits will curb “excessive borrowing” and force schools to evaluate their costs. Since the loan caps took effect, at least 40 schools have cut the cost of at least some programs, according to the conservative American Enterprise Institute.
But critics say most colleges cannot afford to lower tuition and have raised concerns that the changes will add hurdles for students from poor families.
After being denied by several private lenders, 25-year-old Darian Bogie started a crowdfunding campaign to raise some of the tens of thousands that federal loans didn’t cover for his first year of dental school at Howard University. Donations totaling around $76,000 poured in — something he described as “beautifully overwhelming.”
“It was really my absolute last option,” he said.
Students with limited credit histories often rely on family to cosign their loans. But Bogie’s father, a sanitation worker, paid out of pocket for everything until last year, and didn’t have a strong credit history either.
Colleges are stepping in to help
At South Carolina Student Loan, graduate student borrowing increased 400% this year as it rolled out more options to help students. Some schools, like the law school at the University of Kansas, got into the lending game, too. So far, it has approved eight loans, with more in process.
Steven Freedman, associate dean of admissions at the University of Kansas School of Law, said the loans are important to help provide access to all students.
“Now, frankly, private banks get to choose who goes to law school,” he said.
At Lewis & Clark College, a private liberal arts school in Portland, Oregon, the student aid office has been seeing more private student loans. Its graduate school of education and counseling also began offering a new scholarship this fall for students in financial need because of the loan caps.
Anastacia Dillon, associate vice president for financial aid, described the changes as “really disruptive.”
The private loan market boomed in the 1990s and early 2000s during an era of loan limits. After Graduate PLUS, a federal program, extended how much students could borrow up to the full cost of attendance, private lending began to collapse. But critics argue that Graduate PLUS ushered in new problems, contributing to high default rates because students were borrowing more than they could repay.
Some groups predicted the new loan caps could lead to large numbers of borrowers being denied loans from traditional lenders. But students on the whole appear to be finding ways to finance their education, even if they are turning more to private lenders, said Marc Schoonover, general manager of the lender ELFI.
“What we’re hearing and seeing now is that the number of students who truly can’t find an option is a lot smaller than many initially feared,” Schoonover said during a media call organized by the National Council of Higher Education Resources.
Students struggle to understand changes
A legal fight over which graduate programs would be deemed professional — and therefore eligible for larger loans — extended until just days before the new rule was set to take effect. Ultimately, students pursuing graduate degrees in nursing, physical therapy and several other fields were deemed eligible to take out higher federal student loan amounts — at least for now — after a federal judge blocked part of a Trump administration rule that held them to lower limits.
The last-minute changes caused schools to delay delivering financial aid packages, Jon Witter, the CEO of Sallie Mae, said on an earnings call with investors. He said the peak lending season extended into October as a result.
People pass the Weill Cornell Medicine center in New York on Sept. 26, 2019.  Credit: Mark Lennihan / AP File Photo
Dr. Robert Harrington, dean of Weill Cornell Medicine and provost for medical affairs of Cornell University, said the school received dozens of calls from confused students and their families.
Frabotta’s physician assistant program was ultimately deemed professional and eligible for up to $50,000 annually in federal loans. But she decided to borrow just a fraction of that from the federal loan program, fearful of other changes that might be in store.
“This is what I want to do, so if this is the means of how I get there, then if I have to sacrifice at some point,” she said.
Madison Jessen, another first-year Weill Cornell Medicine physician assistant student, said the uncertainty around loan caps prompted her to use most of her savings to pay for her first semester out of pocket. Jessen said she has several younger friends who had planned to go to PA school but pivoted when the loan caps took effect.
That’s Harrington’s biggest fear.
“What we don’t want to see,” said Harrington, himself a first-generation college graduate, “is our programs just becoming the purview of people whose family can afford to pay that bill.”

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Commentary: Dear Democrats: Make civility great again. Please.
description: I’m a Gen Xer. We were brought up on Sesame Street and Mr. Rogers, in a world that taught us that no matter what our differences, we had a basic responsibility to be decent and civil and fair to other people. Kind, even. Certainly not ugly or mean.  I’ve always thought of that as an […]
text:
(Photo by Leontura/Getty Images)I’m a Gen Xer. We were brought up on Sesame Street and Mr. Rogers, in a world that taught us that no matter what our differences, we had a basic responsibility to be decent and civil and fair to other people. Kind, even. Certainly not ugly or mean. 
I’ve always thought of that as an American value. But the last decade has tested that sorely, especially the last couple of years. 
I’m not just talking about edgelords and bigots spouting off on social media to get attention. I’m talking about the overt racism, sexism, homophobia, corruption and — maybe most of all — stunning lack of empathy or accountability we’re seeing every day from people in high places being paid with our taxpayer dollars. 
It’s not just name-calling, either. Shooting American citizens in the streets. Deporting grandmas and little kids. Terrorizing communities. Cutting food aid and medical care for low-income people to pay for tax cuts for the wealthy. Firing high-ranking officials because they’re black or female. Leaving disaster victims without help. 
The cruelty, as they say, is the point. It always has been, and it’s getting worse. 
In the meantime, an astonishing number of other people in high places — people whose job in part was to act as guardrails against this — have done nothing to stop it, or worse yet, have actively abetted it. 
I initially thought the huge turnout against President Donald Trump this week was about gas prices. On reflection, I think it’s too big to be just that. You don’t get a wave like that because voters are just mad about the economy. 
The last time we saw something this big was in 1974, when voters were viscerally morally repulsed by what they saw unfolding in the Watergate scandal and the Vietnam War. Their repudiation of it was historic. Maybe that’s what’s happening this time, too.
Maybe Americans, at least some of them, are fed up with cruelty and self-dealing. Maybe they don’t recognize their country anymore. Maybe they’re tired of bigots and bullies and an aspiring strongman willing to sell out our closest allies for a good deal on some real estate and a gilded ballroom.
The voters have given Democrats a chance to do better. So prove it. Go high. Make civility and decency great again. I bet a lot of voters will thank you for it.

U.S. Rep. Jeff Hurd, a Grand Junction Republican, speaks at a roundtable discussion on energy policy on May 27, 2026, at the Guzman Energy office in Denver. (Photo by Lindsey Toomer/Colorado Newsline)Republican U.S. Rep. Jeff Hurd of Grand Junction defeated Democratic challenger Dwayne Romero to win a second term in the House of Representatives, a lone bright spot for the Colorado GOP in the midst of a “blue tsunami” that saw Democrats triumphant across the state and country.

As of 9:40 a.m. on Friday, Hurd led in the 3rd Congressional District race with 49% of the vote, ahead of Romero’s 47%. The Associated Press called the race at 9:24 a.m. on Friday
With incumbent Rep. Lauren Boebert still slightly trailing Democratic challenger Eileen Laubacher Friday in the state’s 4th Congressional District, Hurd could be the only Republican member of Colorado’s eight-member U.S. House delegation to win election in 2026. GOP incumbent Reps. Jeff Crank and Gabe Evans also lost in the 5th and 8th districts, respectively.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The 3rd District is Colorado’s largest congressional district by area, stretching from the greater Pueblo area across the San Luis Valley and much of the Western Slope.
In 2023, Hurd, an attorney, was recruited to run for Congress in a primary challenge against Boebert, who had come within 600 votes of losing the 3rd District to Democratic challenger Adam Frisch a year earlier. Months later, Boebert moved across the state to run in the more heavily Republican 4th District instead. Hurd went on to win the 3rd District GOP primary and defeat Frisch in the 2024 general election.
As the most moderate of Colorado’s four House Republicans, Hurd pitched himself to 3rd District voters as a “voice of independence,” highlighting disagreements with Trump over his denial of disaster aid and a February vote against some of the president’s tariffs. That vote led Trump to briefly pull his endorsement from Hurd and back a primary challenger, before he reversed himself a month later and endorsed Hurd again.
Romero, an Army veteran and small business owner, launched his campaign relatively late in the 2026 election cycle, and won a head-to-head Democratic primary over financial executive Alex Kelloff.
Romero charged Hurd with being a “rubber-stamp vote” in favor of Trump’s agenda, including Republicans’ 2025 tax and spending law, which included steep cuts to Medicaid that are expected to hit particularly hard in rural areas like the Western Slope.
For much of the 2026 campaign, Hurd and his supporters, including several deep-pocketed Republican super PACs, had massively outspent Romero and Democratic campaign groups in the 3rd District race. But Romero benefited from a late infusion of $2.5 million in outside spending on his behalf by the House Majority Project, the main Democratic House super PAC, beginning in the final week of October.

title: Commentary: Bigotry against Somali Minnesota voters was a losing strategy
description: President Donald Trump has called Somali Americans “garbage.” He’s said they are “low IQ” but somehow also the “number one buyers of Mercedes-Benz and BMWs.”  This was not surprising, if you know Trump’s history. The Nixon administration successfully sued Trump and his father — Trump is a nepo baby, bigly — for systematically discriminating against Black and[...]
text:
Voters in the Cedar-Riverside neighborhood cast their ballots during the midterm elections Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026 in Minneapolis. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)President Donald Trump has called Somali Americans “garbage.” He’s said they are “low IQ” but somehow also the “number one buyers of Mercedes-Benz and BMWs.” 
This was not surprising, if you know Trump’s history. The Nixon administration successfully sued Trump and his father — Trump is a nepo baby, bigly — for systematically discriminating against Black and Puerto Rican renters as part of their vast outer borough real estate operations. 
Now, he is the government, and he sent 3,000 armed, masked, ill-trained immigration agents here with an unclear objective, so they roamed the Cedar-Riverside neighborhood, routinely racially profiling people, demanding their papers. Nearly 84% of Somali Minnesotans are citizens as of 2023, and they responded this election season with stoicism — and power — by going to the polls in huge numbers.
According to data compiled by retired journalist David Brauer, the heart of Cedar-Riverside in Ward 6 saw turnout that surpassed 2024, an unusual outcome given the typically greater intensity of presidential elections. In precinct 3, turnout was 135% of 2024, yielding an extra 548 votes. In precinct 9, turnout was 125% of 2024, yielding an additional 336 votes.  
And based on Reformer interviews with voters conducted by our contributor Atra Mohamed, we can be certain what motivated these voters. 
Halima Elmi, 53, a healthcare worker and mother of four, said during Operation Metro Surge she and her daughter went to a rental car company and encountered ICE agents in the parking lot. Masked men jumped out of a black van, grabbed them and pushed them in. She said they didn’t even give them a chance to produce their documents. “We screamed, and the rental car staff who were expecting us came and told them this was private property and that they were not allowed to pick up people here. In the meantime, we produced our passports, and they finally left us alone.” 
Elmi spent a lot of time volunteering this fall, taking people to the polls, she said.
Najma Tohu, 28, an entrepreneur and Whittier neighborhood resident, called Trump’s comments “a disgrace.” 
“Somali people have jobs and businesses and pay taxes like anyone else, and for him to say that we don’t work and live off government resources is a lie and disrespectful,” she said.
Faduma Abdi, 40, a mother of three who lives in the Cedar-Riverside neighborhood and works at a nursing home, said she previously voted to fulfill her civic duty, but Tuesday she voted to fight back against Trump by voting for every Democratic candidate on the ballot.
“Trump targeted us, and now we have the opportunity to fight back. He called us ‘garbage.’ And that’s not acceptable,” Abdi said.
Hibo Muse, 28, is a healthcare worker and Cedar-Riverside resident who voted for Trump in 2024. This year, she voted all Democratic-Farmer-Labor.
“I regretted voting for him. I feel as though I’m part of all the pain and suffering that Trump caused,” Muse said.
She said she wants candidates in office who respect and treat all Americans equally.
Trump’s hateful rhetoric, which his followers parroted, didn’t help Minnesota Republicans break their two-decade losing streak in statewide races. And every Minnesota House district voted more blue than in 2024. 
I’m sure it was mostly driven by the cost of food and fuel, and the naked corruption of the Trump administration and their cronies, but forgive my idealism if I also believe that Minnesotans also sought to send a message against his bigotry. 
The looting of the pandemic-era food relief program known as Feeding Our Future and some of our Medicaid programs is a big deal, which is why the Reformer has reported on it, and it’s why I editorialized on the issue beginning in 2023, when I could sense the Democratic establishment was negligent in confronting it. We were the first outlet I’m aware of, in 2024, to publish a piece by a Somali Minnesotan about the uncomfortable fact that nearly all of the people convicted in the Feeding Our Future scandal were of East African descent. If the Walz administration and the Legislature had fixed the problem sooner, that may have prevented it from becoming fodder for racist demagoguery. 
But that doesn’t change the fact that you don’t judge an entire community on the actions of a few, as most of us learned in elementary school. 
And, it was a little hard to take MAGA’s concerns about fraud seriously when KARE 11 reported last month that the Trump administration paid private prison operator CoreCivic $495 million for the Appleton prison — after the company offered to sell it to the state just a year prior for $75 million. CoreCivic gave $500,000 to Trump’s inaugural committee. 
The word “garbage” is an apt descriptor, but not of my Somali neighbors.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Mississippi GEAR UP programs help students navigate paths to college
description: Shannon Tatum, media manager for student publications at Jackson State University, asks students questions about storytelling during the GEAR UP writing workshop at the university on Thursday, Oct. 29, 2026.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Like some middle schoolers, La’David Hall never thought about going to college. Back then, anything beyond high school wasn’t part of his plan. 
That changed when Hall, a seventh grader at the time, heard a career coach speak at an assembly about careers in nursing, engineering, teaching, law and medicine. 
“We never really had people talk to us about our futures or careers,” said Hall, now a junior at  O’Bannon High School in Greenville. “I remember leaving school that day curious and thinking like, “‘Yeah, I can see myself doing any of those things.’” 
The 2021 event marked the start of Delta State’s participation in Gaining Early Awareness and Readiness for Undergraduate Programs, or GEAR UP, a federal, grant-funded program that aims to help students attending high-poverty schools prepare for education and careers after high school. 
Students participate in the GEAR UP writing workshop at the university on Thursday, Oct. 29, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
The program is one example of efforts across Mississippi to help disadvantaged students in rural areas navigate higher education and careers after high school.
The U.S. Department of Education awarded Delta State a $15 million grant to prepare students across the Mississippi Delta for college through programs and resources including summer camps, mentoring, academic support and trips to the Cleveland campus. 
In 2019, before Delta State earned a federal GEAR UP grant, Mississippi State University was awarded a $28 million GEAR UP state grant to work with Greenville, McComb and Meridian school districts. Two years later, completed applications for the Free Application for Federal Student Aid, known as FAFSA, increased by about 4% among the participating high schools.
Only about 73.4% of Mississippi’s graduating high school seniors completed FAFSA applications in 2025, according to estimates from the National College Attainment Network, a national organization that advocates for federal and state policy issues around college affordability and support services. Completing the federal application is considered a key indicator that a student will enroll in college. 
Now, Jackson Public Schools is also participating in GEAR UP. In August, JPS officials announced the district secured a $10.67 million GEAR UP federal grant. The grant will go toward serving 2,000 middle schoolers across six schools — Blackburn, Brinkley, Cardozo, Kirksey, Lanier and Peeples — over seven years. JPS is partnering with local colleges and universities, museums and education-based organizations to provide mentoring, summer camps, career exploration programs and parental college financial guidance workshops. 
Instructors guide students through a writing activity during the GEAR UP writing workshop at the university on Thursday, Oct. 29, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
About 52% of JPS graduating senior class of 2025 enrolled in college, said Jana Williams, the district’s college and career readiness manager. Supporting the participating middle schools with graduation-based career coaches will help students envision opportunities beyond high school and provide guidance on the academic and financial steps needed to pursue them, she said. 
“It’s about exposure,” Williams said, “seeing their eyes open up and providing them the  opportunity to learn more about college.” 
Helping students see higher education as a viable option
When the Delta State program began, about 43% of students surveyed in Delta communities believed they could attend college, said Sha’Ketta Davis Drungole, executive director of the university’s Mississippi Delta GEAR UP Partnership. Now, program data indicate that 64% of students plan to attend. 
“I have seen growth and development in the way they present themselves, the way they talk about college or careers in their thought processes, the way they engage with each other as students,” Drungole said, “and it’s just really heartwarming to see.”
Delta State’s GEAR UP program has served more than 4,600 students and provided 88,500 hours of services including parent workshops, teacher training and college visits to students, Drungole said. 
The program also provides staff and advisers to offer training for teachers in Delta-area school districts and to help students understand how to apply for college and how to transition to college after high school. 
Laura Miller, English instructor and coordinator of First-Year Writing, right, and Ebony Lumumba, department chair and associate professor of English, speak to students during the GEAR UP writing workshop at the university on Thursday, Oct. 29, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi TodayStudents participates in a writing activity during the GEAR UP writing workshop at the university on Thursday, Oct. 29, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi TodayStudents participates in a writing activity during the GEAR UP writing workshop at the university on Thursday, Oct. 29, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Glenda Lollis-Hawkins said her daughter Laroya, a senior at Cleveland Central High, has gained money management skills such as budgeting through attending GEAR UP summer camps. The program also offers parents access to resources that help with financial aid applications and understanding college admissions. 
“GEAR UP not only educates the child but [also] the parent about the importance of advancing your career past high school,” Lollis-Hawkins said.
“GEAR UP’s workshops help me parse through the important information,” she said. “They let us know about the ACT, the deadlines and finances when it comes to college.” 
Uncertain federal funding for GEAR UP may put such programs at risk. The Trump administration has proposed budgets that would eliminate funding for GEAR UP, but Congress has pushed back and rejected the request. 
Funding for the program is not guaranteed even if states or school districts were previously awarded grants, said Brandi Lyndall, director of college access strategy and statewide outreach at Get2College, a college access program of Woodward Hines Education Foundation.
For now, the program is helping Mississippi students and their families prepare for higher education. 
Craig Meyer, associate professor of English and director of Jackson State University’s writing program, speaks to students during the GEAR UP writing workshop at the university on Thursday, Oct. 29, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Hall, the O’Bannon High School student, said his curiosity led him to ask his parents questions about college. He wanted to know how to apply. He also asked his mother how she got her nursing degree and her master’s degree in social work. Hall’s father, who did not attend college, encouraged him to keep up with his studies.  
Hall has attended science and entrepreneur summer camps at Mississippi Valley State University over the past few summers. He has toured Mississippi State University’s campus in Starkville. He has also talked with his high school advisers about applying to college. He is now looking beyond his hometown for potential careers such as becoming a teacher, mortician or funeral director. 
“It’s just a new world out there for me,” Hall said.

title: Delaware 5Ks turn fitness into a force for good this weekend
description: From helping children play sports to supporting families facing illness and hardship, Delaware’s weekend races give walkers and runners a chance to improve their health while helping their neighbors. WILMINGTON, Del. — Getting healthy and giving back to the community can go hand in hand this weekend as Delaware hosts a series of 5K races and walks benefiting[...]
text:
Image was created on 11/6 using AI
From helping children play sports to supporting families facing illness and hardship, Delaware’s weekend races give walkers and runners a chance to improve their health while helping their neighbors.
WILMINGTON, Del. — Getting healthy and giving back to the community can go hand in hand this weekend as Delaware hosts a series of 5K races and walks benefiting charitable organizations across the state.
From Wilmington to Lewes, events scheduled for Saturday, Nov. 7, and Sunday, Nov. 8, will bring together runners, casual walkers, families and volunteers to raise money for causes ranging from childhood epilepsy and rare diseases to youth athletics and support for first responders.
And participants don’t have to be experienced runners to make a difference.
A 5K covers 3.1 miles, a manageable distance for many recreational walkers. At a comfortable walking pace, most people can complete the course in about 45 minutes to an hour.
For those looking to become more physically active, a community 5K can provide extra motivation. It offers a specific goal, an opportunity to exercise with friends and family, and the satisfaction of knowing that participation helps support a worthwhile cause.
The benefits extend well beyond the finish line.
Many Delaware charity races help nonprofit organizations raise money, introduce their missions to new supporters and recruit volunteers. For participants, they offer an opportunity to turn a healthy weekend activity into a contribution to the community.
Here are several opportunities to get moving for a good cause this weekend, along with a preview of the annual Bishop’s 5K, now called the Igniting Hope 5K, later this month.
Saturday, Nov. 7: Four ways to get moving
Nicola Pizza 5K Run/Walk — Lewes
The fourth annual Nicola Pizza 5K Run/Walk begins at 8 a.m. at Nicola Pizza in Lewes.
The event benefits the Warrior Weekend Program, which supports military veterans. Participants will follow a course through the Five Points area and onto the Georgetown-Lewes Trail before gathering for a post-race celebration.
Organizers welcome both runners and walkers, making it an opportunity for families and friends to enjoy exercise while supporting veterans.
Seashore Striders
Delaware Dash for Rare — Wilmington
The second annual Delaware Dash for Rare begins at 9 a.m. at Kelly’s Logan House in Trolley Square.
Organized in support of the National MPS Society, the event raises awareness and money for individuals and families affected by rare diseases.
Participants can choose a 5K race, a 1-mile walk or a virtual option. The shorter distance provides an accessible way for people who may not be ready for a full 5K to participate in the fundraising effort.
Make Today Count 5K — Newark
The Make Today Count 5K begins at 9 a.m. at Canal Little League on Glasgow Avenue.
The race supports the JB12 Foundation, established in memory of Jack Birch to help children participate in sports regardless of their families’ financial circumstances.
Proceeds help cover registration fees, uniforms, equipment, camps and other athletic expenses.
The event’s message connects two aspects of physical fitness: encouraging adults to exercise while making it possible for more children to enjoy organized sports. Casual walkers are welcome.
Harvest Hustle 5K — Camden-Wyoming
One of Delaware’s longtime fall races returns for its 20th anniversary at 10 a.m. at Fifer Orchards.
The Harvest Hustle benefits the American Cancer Society of Delaware and is held in memory of Patricia Vincent and Shelly Eckert.
The course takes runners and walkers through the countryside surrounding the farm, including a stretch through the apple orchard.
Participants and their families also receive admission to Fifer’s U-Play and corn maze, making the fundraiser an opportunity for a family outing.
Sunday, Nov. 8: Walking together for others
Walking Beside Kaden 5K Run/Walk — Newark
The Walking Beside Kaden 5K begins at 10 a.m. at Autumn Arch Beer Project on Pencader Drive.
The event supports Kaden Dennis, a young child whose experience with epilepsy inspired his family to create a fundraiser benefiting the Epilepsy Foundation of Delaware.
The organization provides awareness, advocacy and resources for individuals and families affected by epilepsy.
The race includes a dedicated competitive walking division, giving walkers an opportunity to participate without running. Teams and individual participants also can raise additional money for the cause.
Jack o’ Lantern Revenge 5K — Wilmington
The Jack o’ Lantern Revenge 5K begins at 10 a.m. at Kelly’s Logan House in Wilmington.
The race benefits the Trauma Survivors Foundation, which supports people affected by traumatic experiences, including first responders and health care workers.
The organization also uses proceeds to support its annual Thanksgiving meal for police officers and other first responders working on the holiday.
The event welcomes runners and walkers of different ages and abilities and concludes with a community celebration in Trolley Square.
Looking ahead: Bishop’s 5K returns with a new name Nov. 21
The charitable running season continues Saturday, Nov. 21, when the Diocese of Wilmington hosts its annual Bishop’s 5K, now renamed the Igniting Hope 5K.
The event will take place from 9 to 11 a.m. at Saint Mark’s High School in Pike Creek, with registration beginning at 8 a.m.
Organized to benefit Catholic Charities of the Diocese of Wilmington, the race supports programs that provide food, emergency shelter, housing assistance, counseling and other services to individuals and families experiencing hardship.
The organization serves communities across Delaware and Maryland’s Eastern Shore.
Last year’s Bishop’s 5K attracted 260 participants, raised nearly $30,000 and collected 75 pounds of donated food for people in need.
This year’s organizers are encouraging families, businesses, churches, schools and community groups to form teams. The event includes activities for children, food and refreshments.
Registration is $40 for adults and $25 for participants 18 and younger, with adult pricing scheduled to increase after Nov. 10. Walkers are welcome.
Participants are also encouraged to bring nonperishable food donations to support Catholic Charities’ hunger relief programs.
The race offers another example of how a community fitness event can help an organization provide assistance long after participants cross the finish line.
A small commitment can make a difference
For Delaware residents who have been thinking about becoming more active, participating in a charitable 5K can be a practical first step.
Walking regularly can improve cardiovascular fitness, support healthy weight management and help reduce stress. Participating with friends or family members can also provide encouragement to maintain an active lifestyle.
And unlike some competitive sporting events, many community 5Ks emphasize participation and charitable support as much as finishing times.
Whether someone runs the entire course, walks with friends or volunteers along the route, the weekend offers opportunities to improve personal well-being while helping others.
For Delaware’s nonprofit organizations, that combination of exercise, generosity and community involvement is what makes a charity 5K about much more than a race.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Former WV US Sen. Rockefeller, ‘a compassionate, decent, and true leader,’ dies at 89
description: Jay Rockefeller, a former West Virginia governor and a five-term U.S. senator representing the state, died Friday at the age of 89.
text:
Sen. Jay Rockefeller (D-WV) speaks during a news conference about preserving Medicaid funding during the "fiscal cliff" negotiations at the Dirksen Senate Office Building on Capitol Hill December 11, 2012 in Washington, DC. The legislators were joined by representatives from major unions and policy organizations in calling on the White House and Congressional negotiators to protect funding for Medicaid, a health program for people and families with low incomes and resources.  (Photo by Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)Jay Rockefeller, a former West Virginia governor and a five-term U.S. senator representing the state, died Friday at the age of 89. 
A native of New York and heir to the Rockefeller family fortune, Rockefeller first came to West Virginia as an anti-poverty worker in 1964. He was elected to the House of Delegates in 1966 and to secretary of state in 1968, according to his biography with the National Governors Association.
Rockefeller was first elected governor in 1976 and served until 1984. He went on to serve in the U. S. Senate from 1985 until 2015, spending most of his tenure as junior senator under the longserving Robert C. Byrd. 
As a senator, Rockefeller was a lead author of the Children’s Health Insurance Program, a joint state and federal program that provides healthcare to low-income children. He championed the 2010 Affordable Care Act, which expanded healthcare to millions of low-income people. 
Former U.S. Rep. Nick Joe Rahall, a Democrat, served in Congress alongside Rockefeller. He said Rockefeller was a leader in expanding access to healthcare and helping West Virginians affected by violent floods. 
“I just cannot thank him enough for his decades and decades of service to our people in West Virginia, to our nation, and indeed to all of humankind,” Rahall said. “Jay was a compassionate, decent and true leader of this nation, and his works, his many deeds, will stand on the top of our highest mountains in West Virginia forever.” 
Wes Holden worked for Rockefeller in the Senate as his director of constituent services, where he helped West Virginians with a litany of problems, from shoring up a creekbank behind someone’s house to pulling strings to get people on organ transplant lists. 
“The thing that I loved about him, he gave me free rein and allowed me to do things he was unaware of, and he trusted me that much, and I didn’t have a leash on me,” Holden said. “And he only found out about it after it made the press or some sort of thank you letter. So I will always appreciate that.” 
In a statement Friday, West Virginians for Affordable Health Care called Rockefeller a “steadfast champion of accessible, affordable health care.”
“Sen. Rockefeller understood that access to quality, affordable health care is fundamental to the strength and well-being of our families and communities,” Executive Director Ellen Allen said in the statement. “He devoted much of his life to making sure that children, working families, seniors, and some of our most vulnerable neighbors were not left behind. His commitment to West Virginia was evident in the way he listened to people, understood their struggles, and carried their concerns into the halls of government. 
“His legacy will live on in the countless lives made better by his service and his unwavering belief that every West Virginian deserves the opportunity to live a healthy life,” she said. 
Andy Richardson, a former Charleston city councilman, was a liaison for Rockefeller’s campaign at the West Virginia University campus during his successful gubernatorial run in 1976. Richardson was a freshman at the university at the time. Volunteering for Rockefeller’s campaign was his first foray into politics, he said. 
“He was a younger candidate, and I think that it is natural for young people to connect with young people,” Richardson said. “So I think that that was an important part of it. And I think that in West Virginia became less of a factor as time went on. 
“The luster of that Rockefeller name was attractive to a lot of people as I think back on it,” he said. “But for a person that had such affluence, being a northeastern blue blood, he honestly could also be very down to earth, and people like that.”
Richardson remembered Rockefeller as a friend and a “tremendous advocate” for the state. 
Several of West Virginia’s elected officials shared tributes to Rockefeller Friday morning. Gov. Patrick Morrisey said Rockefeller’s legacy will live on in West Virginia history. 
“From his early work in some of our state’s most disadvantaged communities to his efforts to strengthen healthcare, protect coal miners and their families, and support our veterans, Sen. Rockefeller demonstrated a deep commitment to the people of West Virginia,” Morrisey said. “His work helped shape our state and left a lasting mark on the lives of generations of West Virginians.” 
Sen. Shelley Moore Capito, R-West Virginia, shared her condolences on social media. 
“He was always a true gentleman who treated me with respect, kindness, and encouragement,” she said. “Over the years, we developed a wonderful friendship that transcended politics, and I will always be grateful for that.” 
Sen. Jim Justice, R-West Virginia, also remembered Rockefeller’s contributions. 
“His years of dedicated service as Governor and Senator truly reflect the love he had for his great state,” he said. “Sen. Rockefeller worked hard for West Virginians and made a difference in countless lives.” 
Del. Mike Pushkin, chair of the West Virginia Democratic Party, noted that Rockefeller didn’t have to devote his life to public service. 
“Jay Rockefeller was born into one of the wealthiest and most privileged families in American history. He could have spent his entire life enjoying every comfort and opportunity that wealth could provide,” Pushkin said in a statement. “Instead, he chose a different path. He came to the hills of West Virginia as a young VISTA volunteer, saw the struggles of working families firsthand, and made it his life’s mission to do something about them.”
Rockefeller was more than a statesman. He also had a bit of a jokester side to him, as Rahall and Holden recalled. 
Holden said he remembered in the later part of his career being texted a photo of a tree by Rockefeller, who was riding in a car with staff. The senator wanted to know what type of tree it was. 
“Who am I going to call for what’s what?” Holden recalled saying to himself.   
So he called a garden and found out. When he replied to Rockefeller 10 minutes later, Holden said the boss wasn’t surprised at all. 
“He was just wanting to show this other person that I was the go-to guy to get things done,” Holden said. 
During campaign season, Rahall said Rockefeller would stay at his house from time-to-time. In the mornings, the two candidates would stop at a gas station to get a cup of coffee. 
“He didn’t have any money,” Rahall said, with a laugh. “He never carried money around with him. It was always up to me to pay the bill.” 
Rockefeller leaves behind his wife Sharon, four children and nine grandchildren.
