name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Idaho’s abortion bans remain intact after Prop 1’s defeat. Idahoans respond with relief, dismay.
description: The failure of Idaho’s proposed abortion rights initiative Proposition 1 in Tuesday’s general election was met with celebration and concern as the state’s abortion ban remains fully in place.  Idaho voters rejected the ballot measure with 55.94% of the vote, according to the unofficial statewide results. Election officials will certify results by Nov. 24.  “[...]
text:
A “Stop Prop 1” sign leans up against the wall during a GOP election night watch party on Nov. 3, 2026, in Boise, Idaho. Voters soundly defeated a measure that would have restored access to abortion in the state, a sharp contrast with 2026 general election outcomes in three other states that expanded or enshrined abortion rights. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)The failure of Idaho’s proposed abortion rights initiative Proposition 1 in Tuesday’s general election was met with celebration and concern as the state’s abortion ban remains fully in place. 
Idaho voters rejected the ballot measure with 55.94% of the vote, according to the unofficial statewide results. Election officials will certify results by Nov. 24. 
Dorothy Moon, chairwoman of the Idaho Republican Party, addresses partygoers at the Idaho Republican Party’s general election watch party on Nov. 5, 2024, in Meridian. (Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)
“We defeated Prop 1, and that was the biggest issue facing our state,” Idaho GOP Chairwoman Dorothy Moon told the Idaho Capital Sun in a phone interview. 
Idaho’s result contrasted with Missouri, Nebraska, Nevada and Virginia, where voters approved ballot initiatives to protect abortion or rejected a measure to reinstate an abortion ban, Stateline reported. 
The Idaho initiative’s supporters expressed concern about healthcare access in the state as many physicians say the abortion ban limits their ability to perform their job. 
“I think that Idaho failed its communities in pushing to change restrictions that affect all of us,” said Dr. Jessica Evans-Wall, a Treasure Valley emergency medicine physician. “What I see in the emergency department is that these bans on providing healthcare don’t just affect patients who are pregnant and their families, they affect our whole community.” 
The proposed measure would have repealed Idaho’s strict abortion laws, legalizing the procedure up to fetal viability or in cases of emergency and enumerated rights related to access to reproductive healthcare. Under Idaho’s laws, physicians face felony prison sentences and licensing penalties if they perform nearly any abortion, with exemptions to protect the life of the mother in cases of rape and incest in the first trimester with a police report.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
 Idaho GOP, religious groups strongly opposed proposition 

The Idaho Republican Central Committee vocally opposed Prop 1, and county party central committees spent campaign funds to oppose it. Opponents formed Stop Prop 1 in response to the initiative proposal. 
Moon, the Idaho GOP chair, said the initiative was likely a motivating factor for many Idahoans to show up to the polls Tuesday. 
“All the churches jumped on board. Every demographic jumped on board to make sure that we do not allow abortion on demand in this state, so I think that that was the driving issue,” Moon said. 
A number of elected Republicans also spoke against the ballot measure. 
“We are so grateful to Idahoans for resoundingly defeating Prop 1,” Idaho state House leaders said in a written joint statement. “Idaho voters held the line against the extreme abortion agenda, against the lies and deceptions of the Prop 1 campaign, and proved once again why Idaho values are second to none. We are a pro-life state. We have been since our beginnings as a territory. And, thanks to the people of Idaho, we will remain so. God bless our great state.”
Blaine Conzatti is the president of the Idaho Family Policy Center. (Photo courtesy of the Idaho Family Policy Center)
The Idaho Family Policy Center helped author a bill allowing families of aborted fetuses to sue abortion providers for a minimum of $20,000 and has supported Idaho’s felony abortion ban. 
“As we proved last night, a broad majority of Idaho voters support our pro-life laws, including our Heartbeat law and the Defense of Life Act,” said Idaho Family Policy Center President Blaine Conzatti. “This is what happens when Christians speak out and get engaged — WE WIN.” 
The Salt Lake City-based Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, and Roman Catholic Diocese of Boise strongly opposed the initiative and made large donations to groups to oppose it. Conzatti, president of Idaho Family Policy Center, also served as a leader of Stop Prop 1. 
The Arlington, Virginia-based national advocacy group Susan B. Anthony Pro-Life America President celebrated Idaho’s rejection of the measure Wednesday in a press release. 
“We are incredibly grateful for Stop Prop 1 and all who stood up to defend the unborn,” President Marjorie Dannenfelser said. “This is a hard-fought win and an example to pro-life voters, candidates and elected officials across the country.” 
 Prop 1 supporters concerned about women’s healthcare access under Idaho’s existing laws 

Melanie Folwell, lead organizer for the ballot initiative in Idaho to restore abortion access, speaks to supporters at the Idaho Capitol in July. The nonprofit she leads, Idahoans United for Women and Families, is suing the state over a final segment of ballot language that will also appear in the statewide voter pamphlet. (Photo by Kelcie Moseley-Morris/Stateline)
The lead organizer behind Prop 1, Melanie Folwell, told the Sun in an email, “We’re encouraging Idahoans to reach out to their lawmakers, particularly those politicians who encouraged voters to reject Prop 1 and wait for a legislative fix, and demand needed exceptions in the coming session.” 
Many Idaho physicians have said the lack an exemption in Idaho’s abortion ban to protect the mother’s health may impede them from providing abortions in cases of emergency. 
Evans-Wall, the emergency medicine doctor, said she has seen more patients end up in the ER for non-life-threatening issues because they haven’t been able to access routine care from an OB-GYN.  
A 2025 study found Idaho had lost 35% of its OB-GYNs since 2022, when the U.S. Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade and Idaho’s criminal abortion law went into effect. That study has been challenged by the Idaho Family Policy Center, which sued over access to documents related to the study’s underlying data in July. 
“I’m seeing that our overcrowding has been affecting our entire communities and our ability to take care of everyone, not just our patients who are pregnant,” Evans-Wall said. 
She said she and other colleagues are also worried about continued problems recruiting and retaining new doctors to the state. 
The Idaho Medical Association did not take a position on Prop 1, but IMA CEO Susie Keller told the Idaho Capital Sun she has concerns related to access to healthcare. 
“Idaho’s abortion ban has negatively impacted the physician workforce and caused Idaho to lose 1/3 of our practicing Ob/Gyn’s,” Keller said in an email. “The ban prevents Idaho women from getting the care they need for pregnancy complications that threaten their health. This current environment is unsustainable, and I do fear that more physicians will choose to leave our state. IMA will continue to ask the legislature to pass a health exception to the abortion ban to bring more stability and consistency for Idaho patients.” 
Planned Parenthood Alliance Advocates, the advocacy arm of Planned Parenthood, bemoaned Tuesday’s election result. 
“Idaho’s abortion ban remains in place, and so does the harm it causes,” said Idaho State Director Mistie DelliCarpini-Tolman and CEO of Planned Parenthood Alliance Advocates Jennifer M. Allen in a joint, emailed statement.  “Across our state, people with life-threatening conditions are being denied abortions while politicians deny it’s happening, ob-gyns are leaving the state, and Idahoans are being denied the right to make the pregnancy decisions that are right for themselves and their families without political interference.”
 Some Idaho faith groups mourned Prop 1’s failure 

Many members of Interfaith Justice Idaho, progressive religious groups and churches in Idaho, supported Prop 1. 
The Rev. Josh Lee talks to a reporter at Boise’s First Congregational United Church of Christ on February 3, 2025. (Otto Kitsinger for Idaho Capital Sun)
“I feel really hopeful for the rest of the country, but then fairly discouraged by the results here in Idaho,” said the Rev. Josh Lee, a spokesperson for Interfaith Justice Idaho and senior pastor at Boise First United Church of Christ.
Lee said he can understand why people would choose against abortion for religious reasons, but that “I don’t think that those religious convictions should be forced upon anybody else.” 
“And that seems to be the position of many on the conservative right in Idaho,” Lee said, “is to try to legislate their religious beliefs into law, and in doing so, disregarding the fact that not everybody aligns with them.” 
A group called Catholics for Choice also expressed disappointment in Tuesday’s result for Prop 1 and condemned the Catholic Diocese of Boise’s involvement in its opposition. 
“Our hearts go out to the more than 110,000 Idahoans who signed to put this on the ballot, and to the organizers, partners, and advocates who worked hard to fight for the abortion access everyone deserves,” said Caitlin Borgmann, Catholics for Choice co-president for programs and development. “We stand with all the pro-choice Catholics who shared their stories and resisted the clergy’s abuse of power.”  
Idaho Capital Sun reporter Kyle Pfannenstiel contributing to this report

name: WyoFile
title: Wyoming to investigate claims Rocky Mountain Power dodges industry requests for more electricity
description:
The utility says it is beholden to regulations ensuring that speculative clients don't spike rates for existing customers.
The post Wyoming to investigate claims Rocky Mountain Power dodges industry requests for more electricity appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
The state will investigate allegations that Rocky Mountain Power is slow or unwilling to accommodate requests from existing and prospective customers who want large amounts of new electrical power.
The three-member Wyoming Public Service Commission — which holds authority over monopoly utilities like Rocky Mountain Power to provide reliable, lowest-cost services — voted unanimously Oct. 29 to “direct the company to provide relevant information and take such other action as the public interest may require.”
It is not yet clear what actions the commission might take if the investigation reveals shortcomings in the utility meeting its legal obligations in Wyoming. The commission is still finalizing the investigation order, an official told WyoFile.
What many in Wyoming see as a slow, years-long response to “large load” requests is due to a complex set of state and federal regulations, according to the company. The rules, along with Rocky Mountain Power’s own mission, are intended to protect against speculative investments so they don’t fall on the backs of existing customers to pay for if plans don’t pan out, Rocky Mountain Power President Dick Garlish told the commission.
Rocky Mountain Power President Dick Garlish, left, visits with customers during a customer meeting in Casper on Aug. 27, 2024. (Dustin Bleizeffer/WyoFile)
“We’re not going to do any deal for [just] any reason,” he said. “We take our responsibilities as a regulated monopoly seriously, and we care about our customers — existing and future.”
The decision to launch an investigation feels punitive, Garlish added, because no customer requesting power has filed a formal complaint. 
“I don’t see the reasonable, probable cause, or even a reasonable suspicion,” he told the commission. “We’ve been nothing but candid and forthright in this venue and in the legislative venue and with our customers, so it feels unnecessarily burdensome and punitive.”
Launching the investigation is not a condemnation of Rocky Mountain Power, Commission Deputy Chairman Chris Petrie said.
“I think that this situation, because of the persistent complaints in the public about the company’s handling of such matters, requires us to resort to this investigation process in order to obtain assurance.
“We have our obligation,” Petrie added, “to see that safe, adequate and reliable service at just and reasonable rates is available throughout the service territory of Rocky Mountain Power.” 
Persistent complaints
The move to investigate Rocky Mountain Power comes amid unprecedented, skyrocketing demand for electricity in Wyoming and across the nation. 
Driven primarily by the buildout of artificial intelligence computing, U.S. utilities say they’re fielding requests that would double or triple current electrical generation capacity, the Associated Press reported last year.
A Microsoft data center in Cheyenne’s Business Parkway on June 8, 2026,. (Ryan Dorgan/WyoFile)
In the Equality State, data center proposals from just two developers would require more than twice the state’s existing electrical generation capacity of 11,800 megawatts. Rocky Mountain Power — the largest regulated electric utility in Wyoming — says it has studied 83 requests for additional power during the past decade and served 24 of those to the tune of 258 megawatts. It has also evaluated some 4,300 megawatts-worth of “large load” requests, defined as more than 20 megawatts.
One megawatt is enough to power about 750 homes.
Yet Rocky Mountain Power’s response to new power requests continually comes before legislative committees, including from the long-existing trona and soda ash industry. Industry spokeswoman Jody Levin told a panel of lawmakers in May that trona expansion plans were delayed because the utility allegedly concluded that the soonest it could provide a significant boost in electrons to the industry is seven years out.
“Seven years is a de facto no,” Levin said. “That isn’t a reasonable timeframe.”
“Testimony before multiple legislative committees from industry and other entities have highlighted the issues that exist in acquiring timely and reliable access to power in southwest Wyoming,” Wyoming Mining Association Executive Director Travis Deti told WyoFile this week. “We will be monitoring this closely.”
A data center in Casper, June 2025. (Dustin Bleizeffer/WyoFile)
Many of the large electricity requests Rocky Mountain Power receives, Garlish told commissioners last week, come from “entrepreneurial” hopefuls, and many of their projects fall by the wayside for lack of financing, long permitting times and myriad other reasons apart from securing electrical power.
“Nobody wants to land a large-load deal in our service territory more than I do,” Garlish said. “But it has to protect existing customers. We won’t sign a deal that puts existing customers at risk. Growth needs to pay for growth. We have an obligation, just like you do, to protect our existing customers and protect our existing systems.”
The company is spending $80 million on initiatives to meet rising demand, he added.
The reason that no customers — prospective or existing — have filed a formal complaint against Rocky Mountain Power is because they are beholden to the utility, according to an attorney representing the Wyoming Industrial Energy Consumers group, which consists of oil and natural gas refineries, trona and other industrial customers of Rocky Mountain Power.
“They have to work with the incumbent utility,” Holland and Hart attorney Austin Jensen told the commission. “It is not good for business to call your only option before the commission [forcing them to undergo] a formal complaint process.”
Wyoming lawmakers, prompted by both entrepreneurial and existing industries in the state, have contemplated potentially tweaking regulations to allow for third-party power producers as an alternative to relying on established utilities. It’s an idea that Rocky Mountain Power has opposed.
Commissioners said they will investigate Rocky Mountain Power’s responses to large electricity requests dating back to January 2022.

name: WyoFile
title: Why do we think that?
description:
Columnist David Romtvedt asks us to consider our strongest opinions and what shaped them.
The post Why do we think that? appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Why do we like some things and dislike others? Where does our taste in music, art, books, architecture, movies and just about everything come from? Why do some of us feel lost if we can’t see water from our front window while others long for the mountains? Do any of us prefer the landlocked flatlands? Oops, my mistake revealing my opinion. Opinions. Where do we get them?

Opinion

“What’d’ya think?” I asked a bookseller friend about a novel I’d just read. “You think it’s any good?” The bookseller looked around the shop, waited for what seemed a long time, and answered, “I’m not so interested in having opinions anymore.”
How about politics? How do we become liberal or conservative? What opinions shaped the votes we cast in the general election? Are some of us born longing for change, excited about the possibility of the new, while others of us are born more cautious, concerned that in changing things we may make them worse?
I noticed that my daughter seemed to have a clear personality from the moment she was born. Did I? Or was my experience more important in shaping me? I’ve been powerfully influenced by my white working-class background. My father was a laborer who saw the union as the sole defender of the little guy against the bosses — the rich and powerful. I carry a bit of him inside me and share his views. But he was a harsh father, physically and verbally cruel. I would not be the father he was. Still, the man could really work. The factory or loading dock left behind, he spent hours tending his flower beds or building a cabinet. Unlike the jobs he hated, his personal work at home soothed him. Now I get up from my desk and find solace in the same work — the garden, the sauna I built during the COVID lockdown.
We often embrace what we’re taught growing up. But we resist what we’re taught, too. I have a friend who was raised in a Seventh-day Adventist family that ate no meat and neither smoked cigarettes nor drank alcohol. My friend had a happy childhood in a loving family, but when he went away to college, the first thing he wanted was a double cheeseburger and a beer. He took up smoking unfiltered Camels. Later, he abandoned his rebellion and went back to the food and drink he’d grown up with at home and in the church.
Sometimes what adults teach children feels wrong to us from the get-go and our resistance permanently shapes us. In my Arizona high school of 2,400 students, about half were Anglo-American and half Mexican-American. To graduate from high school, we had to complete two years of a foreign language. We could choose from French, German, Latin, or Spanish, except that native Spanish speakers were not allowed to study Spanish. The teachers suggested that these students already knew Spanish and were simply being lazy. This ignored the fact that many came from homes with parents who could speak Spanish but could neither read nor write it. Spanish-speaking students weren’t allowed to use their first language on the school grounds where their entire education had been administered to them in English. If they were caught conversing in the forbidden tongue, they were sent to language detention — a room where one sat in silence for 30 to 60 minutes.
I was pretty blind to this, but the day I graduated, my eyes opened. I vowed that I would learn to speak, read and write Spanish. I traveled and worked in Mexico, Central America, Cuba, Argentina and Spain. I began to play the Tejano conjunto polkas and música norteña rancheras that I’d ignored as a teenager in favor of top-40 English-language rock and roll. I worked at the University of Iowa’s International Writing program as a translation assistant for poets from Colombia and Costa Rica. I taught literary translation at the Universidad de Chihuahua. My work, my musical and literary interests, my longing for travel, my politics, my sense of self and community — all have been shaped by bilingual and bicultural experiences that were denied to me while growing up in a bilingual and bicultural community. Even if I was slow in coming to see it, the difficulties many of my Mexican Spanish-speaking classmates’ families faced were a lot like those faced by my white English-speaking family.
In Harper Lee’s novel “To Kill a Mockingbird,” the character Atticus Finch counsels his young daughter, saying, “You never really understand a person until you consider things from his point of view, until you climb inside of his skin and walk around in it.” I’ve tried to understand what it feels like to walk around inside someone else’s skin. Still, I wonder — how are we to sort out what we’re born with and what we make from the world we inhabit? How do we form the opinions to which we cling for dear life?

title: Grizzly bear deaths in Yellowstone region climb to modern record high for third-straight year
description: This story was first published by WyoFile on Oct. 30, 2026. With weeks left to go before many grizzly bears den up, it’s already the bruins’ deadliest year in the Greater Yellowstone Ecosystem in modern times, surpassing records set in 2024 and 2025. Historically, regional grizzly bear death counts have been higher. For example, biologist […]
text:
A grizzly bear crosses the road in Yellowstone National Park by LeHardy Rapids in 2017. (Photo by Kimberly Shields/National Park Service)This story was first published by WyoFile on Oct. 30, 2026.
With weeks left to go before many grizzly bears den up, it’s already the bruins’ deadliest year in the Greater Yellowstone Ecosystem in modern times, surpassing records set in 2024 and 2025.
Historically, regional grizzly bear death counts have been higher. For example, biologist Frank Craighead tallied 120 of the large carnivores that perished in 1972, the year after Yellowstone National Park closed the last of its garbage dumps that scores of bruins depended on for food.
Over the decades that followed, wildlife managers and landowners went to great lengths to reduce conflicts. At the same time, grizzly mortality rates plummeted as the population recovered and bears spread out geographically — expanding their range until 2021 when it began to slowly recede.
Wildlife managers call the uptick in bear fatalities somewhat predictable and not a cause for alarm, but the numbers of grizzlies that have died the last three years have each set a modern record. As of Oct. 21, 81 known grizzly bears died in the calendar year, according to a database maintained by the Interagency Grizzly Bear Study Team. And there’s at least one additional mortality that hasn’t been logged yet, bringing the count to 82, according to Wyoming Game and Fish Department Large Carnivore Supervisor Dan Thompson.
(Graph by Tennessee Watson/WyoFile, with assistance from AI)
This year’s total mortality tops past highs set in 2025 (74), 2024 (72) and 2021 (70). Although this year was a record, the surge in conflicts and related deaths for grizzly bears paled in comparison to the “unprecedented” conflict-ridden year for black bears in Wyoming and neighboring Rocky Mountain states.
“I don’t have conflict numbers yet, but it was just a more prominent [year] with black bear conflicts, definitely, than grizzly bears,” Thompson said.
In 2026, grizzly bears in the Yellowstone region predictably died from the full spectrum of causes. The majority, about 65% of the 81 deaths logged so far were human-caused — a dynamic that is the norm.
Grizzly bear managers break causes of death into nine categories. Higher-than-average causes in 2026 are listed below:

Cattle/livestock depredation: 27 grizzlies (1.6X higher than average)
Accidental: 12 grizzlies (2X average)
Natural: 11 grizzlies (3.6X average)
Illegal poaching: 6 (3X average)

Remaining causes — those that are undetermined, from human-bear site conflicts and “human removal,” self-defense killings or mistaken ID incidents from black bear hunters — either occurred at below average rates this year or haven’t yet been calculated.
Interagency Grizzly Bear Study Team leader Matt Gould told WyoFile in an email that the variations in causes of death occur every year and are “natural and often substantial.”
“Drawing major conclusions from a single year is difficult,” Gould said. “That’s why the long-term monitoring conducted by [the study team] is essential for understanding drivers of population dynamics as they relate to sources of mortality.”
Grizzly bear 399 and her four yearling cubs emerge from their den, walking from Jackson Lake Lodge to Signal Mountain Lodge on April 15, 2021 in Grand Teton National Park. The famous female grizzly died in a vehicle strike three years later. This year at least 10 grizzlies have died in bear-vehicle collisions. (Photo courtesy of Ryan Dorgan)
Wyoming Game and Fish’s Thompson noted some silver linings to the rough year for grizzly bears. For one, he said, adult female bears — the reproducers and important drivers of the population — fared relatively well, especially in the ecosystem interior zone known as the “demographic monitoring area.”
“Literally one female had been killed in an agency action in the DMA,” Thompson said. “I think that’s relevant because people think we’re just murdering bears left and right, but that’s not necessarily the case.”
Still, it was a rough year overall for grizzlies inside the 19,278-square-mile DMA, which is the area where wildlife managers estimate the population. The deadliest year for grizzlies inside that interior zone took place in 2025, when 54 known bruins perished. But this year isn’t far off, with 48 mortalities so far.
Another bright spot, according to Thompson: The grizzly bear population has so far absorbed the deaths without declining.

“There’s enough recruitment in the population going on that it compensates for this level of mortality,” he said. “We forget that there are over 300 bears born in the ecosystem every year.”
The now-record counts of grizzly deaths might end up becoming the norm as grizzly densities grow along the ecosystem periphery, Thompson said, though it’s too early to say.
“Maybe this is kind of where we’re at proportionally,” Thompson said. “I still am not worried about the population, whatsoever.”
Former Grizzly Bear Recovery Coordinator Chris Servheen agreed. The nearly 400% occurrence of natural bear-on-bear deaths in the Yellowstone region this year is “interesting,” he said.
“Grizzly bears are self-regulating,” Servheen said. “At higher densities, they tend to have lower subadult survival rates, because males are killing them. Over time, as the population increases in density, the growth of the population will slow because of those adult males and that higher mortality rate among subadults. That’s probably what we’re seeing.”
High mortality numbers alone don’t mean much in regards to the health of the population, he said.
“The key is the trajectory of the population,” Servheen said. “If we saw the trajectory change and start to decline, then I would be really worried about these numbers.”
So far, that’s not the case.
A grizzly bear killed by hunter gunfire in the Aspen Creek drainage west of Cody, Wyoming, in 2014. Grizzly bears have died at a record high rate so far in 2026. Some 17 deaths are being investigated, which means the bears were likely killed in self-defense. (Photo courtesy of the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service)
Grizzlies have recovered enough since hitting a low a half-century ago that the ecosystem’s tri-state managers in Wyoming, Montana and Idaho are anticipating a third attempt at “delisting” bears from their threatened status under the Endangered Species Act. In the meantime, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service is finalizing a rule that gives the states more management latitude.
Courts have reversed past attempts to delist grizzlies. In 2007, a ruling rejecting delisting hinged on how the decline of whitebark pine — its seeds are a major grizzly food source — would impact the species. In 2017, state jurisdiction was overturned days before the first hunting season in four-plus decades. The court cited concerns about genetic diversity and what happens when population numbers are “recalibrated” by scientists changing the way they count bears.
Recent high grizzly bear mortality figures likely won’t factor much into the delisting decision. Nevertheless, it “doesn’t benefit” states’ argument for more control, said Servheen, who’s been a leading voice against delisting. His chief concern is that anti-predator state politicians influence grizzly bear management, putting the species at risk.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Blue Huntsville: Democrats see major gains in Rocket City after years of effort
description: Alabama Democrats hoped to make gains in the Rocket City in Tuesday’s election, and they did.  Despite significant fundraising differences, two seats in the state Senate and one in the House flipped in Democrats’ favor, while Democrats closed the gaps in others. Democrats also won the Madison County Sheriff’s Office and two contested judicial races. […]
text:
Big Spring International Park in Huntsville is seen on Oct. 11, 2026. Alabama Democrats Tuesday flipped three Legislative seats in Madison County and saw other down-ballot successes. (Ben Sessoms for Alabama Reflector) 


Key Points:

Alabama Democrats flipped four Legislative seats on Tuesday, three of which were in Madison County where the party was focusing its efforts.


The Madison County delegation has a constantly changing constituency due to Huntsville’s industry, which leads to many “independent thinkers” and will likely require the Republican delegation to remain moderate.


Madison County’s shift towards Democrats may be more permanent than the rest of the state’s shift due to Democratic holds.




Alabama Democrats hoped to make gains in the Rocket City in Tuesday’s election, and they did. 
Despite significant fundraising differences, two seats in the state Senate and one in the House flipped in Democrats’ favor, while Democrats closed the gaps in others. Democrats also won the Madison County Sheriff’s Office and two contested judicial races. Democratic gubernatorial nominee Doug Jones won 58% of the vote in Madison. 
Violet Edwards, a Madison County commissioner and the Democratic nominee for state auditor, said in a phone interview Thursday that having a strong top of the ticket and Madison County natives – like herself and Democratic nominee in Alabama’s 5th Congressional District Andrew Sneed – helped in down-ballot races.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“Our county party did a great job of engaging the community,” she said. “I’m hearing a lot of people say that it was a fluke. That because the ticket of change existed, that really helped Madison County. I think that did help, but we have to prove that it wasn’t a fluke.”
Alabama Democrats had long hoped for gains in Huntsville, whose growth has brought in residents from blue and purple states and whose demographics are friendlier to the party than the rest of the state. 
But for years, Republicans held the delegation despite state Senate races in the county that were more competitive than most, due in part to Democratic candidates struggling to raise money. 
But in 2024, Democratic nominee Marilyn Lands, emphasizing reproductive rights after the Alabama Supreme Court temporarily made IVF unavailable in the state, won House District 10 with about 62% of votes, giving Democrats their first net gain in the Alabama Legislature in over 20 years. 
She held her seat on Tuesday with 60% of votes. 
“I checked her race, and she was reelected by about the same margin. It was really comfortable,” said J. Miles Coleman, associate editor of the Center for Politics, in a phone interview Thursday. “I thought that said something about how maybe these shifts are a little enduring.”
Lands said Thursday that voters in Madison County are thoughtful, and don’t always vote along party lines. 
“I’ve always had a significant amount of Republican support for a number of reasons. I’ve lived here forever, I know so many people, and I’ve focused so much on issues that really are not partisan,” she said. “Maternal health and mental health and public education; those things are not partisan issues.”
Alabama Democrats see opportunities to pick up legislative seats in Huntsville

‘Seeing the opportunity’
House Minority Leader Anthony Daniels, D-Huntsville, said in a phone interview Thursday that he thinks the momentum in Madison County will continue with Senate Minority Leader Bobby Singleton, D-Greensboro, elected Alabama Democratic Party Chair in August.
“I think we’ll see more gains, more opportunities. You see a lot of excitement, so you’ll see more qualified people want to run for office in future years,” Daniels said. “Seeing the opportunity to sweep the countywide offices in Madison County also sends a strong message, and I think that that will continue to happen.”
With Huntsville’s growth, economy and influx of government workers and defense contractors, Daniels said there is less apathy among voters.
“It was a top-down and bottom-up meeting in the middle approach. I don’t think that there’s one person that can receive the ultimate credit for being able to deliver the votes or the turnout,” he said.
After Tuesday, Republicans and Democrats each hold four seats in Madison County in the House, and Democrats hold both Huntsville-area Senate seats. Voters also chose Democratic candidates in some down-ballot races. 
House Minority Leader Anthony Daniels, D-Huntsville laughs on the Alabama House floor on April 9, 2026. (Andrea Tinker/Alabama Reflector)
The two Democratic candidates running for District Court Judge in places 4 and 5 beat their respective Republican rivals by 54% and 53%. Democrat Brett Jones won election as Madison County Sheriff, getting 53% of the vote. Jeff Taylor, a Democrat, won Madison County Tax Collector with 53% of the vote.
The Democratic nominee for Madison County Schools Superintendent lost, getting 47% of the vote against Republican Keith Trawick. Democratic Austin Jones also lost a school board race to Republican Brian Brooks by 41 points. 
Although the partisan makeup of the state legislature remains largely unchanged, Daniels said Democrats will continue to work with Republicans to move the state forward. 
He said the minority party will focus on affordability through the next quadrennium. Daniels sponsored an overtime tax exemption in 2023, but it expired in 2025. It was not extended because Republican leadership said it was a larger than expected impact to the Education Trust Fund. 
Republican leadership in October promised to eliminate the state grocery tax, which has been reduced over the last three years. Democratic lawmakers have also advocated for the elimination of the state sales tax on food for years. 
“They talk about grocery taxes. The grocery taxes are one thing, but the cost of groceries is another. Being able to try to make a proposal on something right before an election just did not sell to the voters. It didn’t seem to,” Daniels said. 
Rep. Parker Moore, R-Hartselle, said in an interview Thursday that affordability, rural health and mental healthcare will be top-of-mind for him.
“We’ve got to continue to look at ways that we, on a state level, can continue to try to make things more affordable for the average Alabamian,” Moore said. “Continuing to look at cutting the additional 2% of the grocery tax and and look at ways that we can continue to lower that tax burden and put more money back into the hands of the citizens of our state.”
‘A new age’
Jackson Hannan, data and technology chair of the Madison County Democratic Executive Committee, said in a phone interview Thursday that the county has entered a “new age.”
“The shifts that we saw in Madison County are stunning, not just in their breadth but in their depth. I personally did not see Democrats almost sweeping the countywide contests,” he said.
Although Hannan is still gathering and analyzing data, he hypothesizes that the changes in Madison County were due to persuasion, while shifts in more rural areas of the state were due to dips in turnout. 
Democratic turnout soars across Alabama in midterm election

While statewide Democratic vote totals nearly doubled on Tuesday, Republican turnout decreased by about 8%, according to election data.  
“The vast majority of the shift can be attributed to a national environment that is just absolutely corrosive and toxic for Republicans, especially in the South. Southern Republicans were hit by a multitude of issues,” Hannan said. “Their rural voters did not come out, but further, the rural white voters swung an unprecedented amount back towards Democrats.”
Allison Montgomery, a new Democratic representative for House District 25 and the first openly transgender lawmaker in Alabama, said in a statement Thursday that her grassroots campaign focused on her goals, and voters are “tired of yes-men and ‘business as usual’ governance.”
“I think a lot of folks running under the Republican Party have lost the trust of the people because the Republican party as a political force has shown itself to be lacking integrity in the ways that it operates and devoid of care in the way that it governs,” she said.
Jared Sluss, a new Democratic representative for Senate District 7, said in an interview Wednesday that voters were ready for a change.
“The goal isn’t just to flip seats, to flip them blue just for the sake of doing it, but the goal is to flip seats so that we actually have politicians on both sides of the aisle that deliver real things,” he said. “Wherever we can find a point of agreement that is going to benefit people’s lives. We have to deliver on that because that’s how we get real change that benefits people, and that should be the goal of any public servant.”
Paths for Republicans
Rep. James Lomax, R-Huntsville, stands on the floor of the Alabama House of Representatives on April 8, 2026 at the Alabama Statehouse in Montgomery, Alabama. (Brian Lyman/Alabama Reflector)
Hannan also said most Madison County Republicans are more moderate than the rest of the state party, which helped Moore and Reps. James Lomax and Rex Reynolds, both R-Huntsville, keep their seats. A message seeking comment from Reynolds was left Thursday.
Lomax, in House District 20, said his work will stay the same for the next quadrennium, even though the local delegation has changed.
“That just means that we’re going to have to be more cognizant, work together. We’re going to need to take that into account and build some bridges to be able to work together, because at the end of the day we have to take care of the people in Madison County. That’s what we’re elected to do,” he said. 
During the campaign, Republican Gov.-elect Tommy Tuberville said that the fast-growing region embraces “socialist, Communist nonsense.” Lomax said those comments did not impact his campaign, although he criticized them.
“I was able to run my own race. I think that’s the most important thing,” he said Thursday. “One of the things that so many people told me, even while I was out waving a sign at the polling precincts on the day of the election, is ‘We just like the way you work with other people and you are able to get things done.’”
Moore, in House District 4, said he will continue to be active in his community.
Rep. Parker Moore, R-Hartselle, speaks to staff on the floor of the Alabama House of Representatives on April 8, 2026 at the Alabama Statehouse in Montgomery, Alabama. (Brian Lyman/Alabama Reflector)
“One of the things we are experiencing is with people moving in, they’re bringing different perspectives, different ideas, different ways of life that we haven’t necessarily had here in our state,” he said. “Diversity and culture is a good thing, but we have to be cognizant of who we are, where we’ve come from, and continue to all work together for the betterment of our communities in the regions of our state where we represent.”
Coleman said that Madison County’s constantly changing constituency will likely require Republicans there to be more moderate than the rest of the state.
“You have this influx of new people, it is also more work to constantly be introducing yourself to new constituents as well,” he said.
During the 2026 legislative session, Republican leadership pushed a bill that would have required voters to register with a political party in order to cast a ballot in a primary election. It did not receive a vote in the Senate largely due to a lack of support from north Alabama Republicans. 
Lomax said that Tuesday’s results proved that there are independents in Alabama. 
“There’s a lot of independents in, not just Madison County, but the entire state of Alabama,” he said. “Alabama fared better than a lot of other states, but there are just a lot of people that are very independent minded. So I think we need to be cognizant of that. Period.”
Montgomery isn’t D.C.
Although Republicans do not need Democratic votes in the Legislature due to the supermajority, the two parties often work together. Lomax and Lands said on Thursday that Montgomery and Washington, D.C., are different. 
“I think that’s so important when people want to get so polarized with politics, especially on the national level, and that’s why they’re so sick of Washington D.C.,” Lomax said. “Here in the state of Alabama, in the Legislature, you have to be able to work with people, people you don’t agree with, people that are in the opposite party, and if you’re able to get things done, that means that you’re willing to do that.”
Both Lands and Daniels said they would stand with Montgomery in the face of any attacks due to her identity. In 2024, the Legislature passed a law defining biological sexes. In 2022, it passed a law designating bathroom use based on biological sex in public K-12 schools. Montgomery’s Republican opponent and Republican leadership in weeks leading up to the election attacked Montgomery for being transgender.  
Daniels said he would take any disrespect toward Montgomery personally. 
“If Allison Montgomery is not treated and respected, then that’s disrespect to my entire caucus,” Daniels said. “I condemn any mistreatment, whether it’s Allison Montgomery or whether it’s a person based upon their race, sexual orientation, or creed. I don’t care who they are, as long as they can deliver for our state and for their district.” 
Lands was hopeful. 
“I know how I was welcomed into Montgomery by folks on both sides of the aisle, and I feel like the same thing is going to happen for Allison,” she said. “I always try to share with people one thing I think people don’t understand because they think what happens in Montgomery parallels D.C., but it doesn’t.”
Montgomery said she will “work as hard for them as I am for anyone, because we all have the same needs.”
“I hope that all of us in the Legislature can work together to better understand those needs and find ways to materially address them,” she said.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Commentary: Stockard on the Stump: Blackburn camp nearly wrote losing playbook
description: And the band played on and on … It seemed they would play the entire Merle Haggard box set before U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn came out and claimed victory Tuesday night in Tennessee’s gubernatorial race. No doubt, folks in the Blackburn camp were getting antsy as the vote differential with Democrat Jerri Green ran between […]
text:
Gov.-elect Marsha Blackburn held her first press conference after winning her Nov. 3, 2026 election the next day, with outgoing Gov. Bill Lee. (Photo by John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)And the band played on and on … It seemed they would play the entire Merle Haggard box set before U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn came out and claimed victory Tuesday night in Tennessee’s gubernatorial race.
No doubt, folks in the Blackburn camp were getting antsy as the vote differential with Democrat Jerri Green ran between 2 and 6 percentage points, winding up at a resounding 2.5-point margin for the Republican nominee in the reddest state in the country.
Blackburn could blame independent David Hatley for stealing 9% of the vote, but those weren’t votes for the upper East Tennessee hot tub mogul — who flushed $12 million down the toilet — as much as they were votes by Republicans who weren’t exactly enthused with Blackburn. That’s putting it kindly.

SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 
When Blackburn finally saw there weren’t enough votes left in Shelby County to push Green past her, she emerged with other victorious folks at The Pinnacle in Nashville, such as U.S. Rep.-elect Johnny Garrett of Goodlettsville, U.S. Rep. Chuck Fleischmann of Chattanooga (trying to garner Blackburn’s U.S. Senate seat), and Senate Majority Leader Jack Johnson (still counting votes in the Tennessee Senate speaker’s race). 
We had been promised they would speak. But alas, time was running short.
In what might have been her most conciliatory statement ever, Blackburn said she realized every Tennessean didn’t vote for her but that she would be a governor for every Tennessean.
In fact, she received 45.5% of the vote, less than a majority and hardly a mandate, to Green’s 43%, according to the Secretary of State’s unofficial results. That’s 957,136 for Blackburn, 902,953 for Green and 195,564 for Hatley, who merely gave Republicans who don’t like Blackburn a chance to vote for a conservative. Former Lipscomb professor Lauren Pinkston didn’t even pick up the 2% she projected, coming in at 1.25%, 26,200 votes.
U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn, who won the Tennessee governor’s race in a narrow victory, embraces conservative talk show host Clay Travis at her Nov. 3, 2026 Election Night party. (Photo by John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)
Election party emcee Clay Travis, a lawyer-turned-conservative radio host, claimed that while it was a rough night nationwide for Republicans, “it hasn’t been a tough night for the great state of Tennessee.” 
At least not until you look at the facts.
Democrats picked up six state House seats, the largest pickup in three decades. And even after Republican lawmakers tried to fix the election by splitting Memphis’ majority Black congressional district, the GOP barely won those races and jeopardized Republican U.S. Rep. Scott DesJarlais, who is looking for 280 votes in what appears to be a loss to Democrat Victoria Broderick. She has claimed victory, but he hasn’t conceded.
After squeaking past Green, Blackburn bragged about a grass-roots campaign that ignored the media and focused on regular folks. Readers might recall she told NewsChannel5 she talks to Tennesseans every day as she refused for the umpteenth time to take a reporter’s questions.
Realists might say her campaign people wrote the book on how to darn near lose a race that shouldn’t be close. 
For instance, Blackburn depended on dark-money groups to attack Hatley, refused to debate her opponents, never sought the backing of primary rivals, state Rep. Monty Fritts and U.S. Rep. John Rose, and pretty much rested on her laurels as a career politician who encouraged people to throw rocks at the state Capitol during the income tax debate a quarter century ago.
She was fortunate that the Democratic Party never really got behind Green or spent heavily to elect her. TV viewers saw a barrage of anti-Hatley ads and a few Blackburn spots with former swimmer Riley Gaines fretting about transgender athletes but nothing positive about Blackburn and hardly anything about Green.
Presser with outgoing  Governor Bill Lee and incoming Governor Marsha Blackburn.

Photographs by John Partipilo/Tennessee LookoutCommissioner of Economic and Community Development Stuart McWhorter, right, will serve as director of Gov.-elect Marsha Blackburn's transition team. At left is former CoreCivic CEO Damon Hininger, thought to be a leading candidate to take Blackburn's soon-to-be-vacant U.S. Senate seat. (Photo by John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)
In her victory speech, Blackburn conceded that she realizes Tennesseans are hurting economically, though she failed to mention the pain stems from President Donald Trump’s policies. And she threw out words such as workforce development in a press conference with Gov. Bill Lee Wednesday, as well as affordable housing and workforce housing, which apparently are supposed to excite liberals and the unwashed masses.
Blackburn’s also broaching the idea of property tax breaks for seniors and young homebuyers, which sounds great but will put her in direct conflict with local governments that depend on that revenue to operate. Besides, Tennessee already has tax relief programs for seniors.
In a state known for moderation, she also continued Tuesday night to hammer socialists, communists and Islamists, none of whom hold much sway in these parts. Blackburn kept up the tough-on-crime tack too.
“We’re going to hunt down and we are going to prosecute these child predators, and if they molest and rape our babies, they need the death penalty,” she said, adding her administration will make that a priority.
That also sounds grand. But Tennessee has a law authorizing the death penalty for aggravated child rape. It runs counter to U.S. Supreme Court precedent.
Maybe the state legislature can fix that too.
Blackburn did promise reporters during her press conference that she would be keeping them busy. To be sure, she took more questions from different outlets Wednesday than she did for an entire year.
Chuck Blackburn, Gov.-elect Marsha Blackburn’s husband, listens to her first gubernatorial press conference on Nov. 4, 2026. (Photo by John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)
Voucher roadblock
Blackburn keeps dancing around a major expansion of the state’s private-school voucher programs but clearly wants to do something. 
The state has one for low-income students in Nashville, Memphis and Chattanooga and a separate one for everybody else that can be expanded by 5,000 students every year, depending on the number of applications and legislative funding. 
It’s so popular that even some Republicans call it a “giveaway.”
During her victory speech, Blackburn fell back on one of her talking points, saying the state needs “to expand educational opportunities for every child so parents don’t have to win the lottery in order to have a say in their child’s education.” We’re guessing that means expanding vouchers, which are costing the state upwards of $300 million already.
The blue wave they say didn’t hit Tennessee caused a problem, though. Democrats flipped six state House seats, and several reliable GOP voucher votes lost in primaries. In light of those changes, they’ll be lucky to keep the so-called Education Freedom Scholarship alive, much less twist enough arms to expand a program that hands out about $7,500 a year to kids, regardless of family income, for private-school enrollment.
Rejuvenating the conflict
Nashville Mayor Freddie O’Connell, who has been navigating a mine field in the Republican-controlled legislature for several years, said this week he was “proud” to have directed more than $125,000 from his leadership PAC to back Democratic candidates and protect voting rights.
“For years, the Republican supermajority has interfered in local decisions, from attempting to seize control of airport authorities in Nashville and Chattanooga to dictating the size of our Metro Council,” O’Connell said. (The Tennessee Supreme Court recently ruled in favor of the state on those battles, cutting Nashville’s city council in half.)
But that didn’t keep O’Connell from saying those types of state moves caused “confusion and costly legal fights.” 



Quotation







For years, the Republican supermajority has interfered in local decisions, from attempting to seize control of airport authorities in Nashville and Chattanooga to dictating the size of our Metro Council.


– Nashville Mayor Freddie O'Connell


Republican lawmakers have been going after O’Connell almost since he took office, yet he’s been meeting regularly with Lee to find some sort of common ground. After all, he points out, Nashville is the state’s “economic engine,” and he’s looking to work with “anyone” at the Capitol who’s committed to moving the city forward economically.
Considering his backing of Democratic candidates, it’ll be interesting to see if anyone wearing red will give him a call. Blackburn laid down a bit of a gauntlet this week, saying she will not allow any sanctuary cities, even though the legislature banned those in 2018, (O’Connell wasn’t thrilled with a state-federal immigrant roundup in South Nashville) and giving hope to Lower Broad bar owners that the state will rescue them from higher Metro property taxes. 
We wonder when O’Connell will have his first meeting with Blackburn and whether they’ll both emerge unscathed.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: NC’s new constitutional amendments pose financial dilemmas for state, local lawmakers
description: North Carolina voters who delivered a blue wave for Democrats Tuesday also overwhelmingly approved two constitutional amendments that will impact taxes for years to come. The first amendment, approved by 62% of voters, caps state income tax rates for individuals and corporations at 3.5%. The second amendment, which 60% of voters approved, requires the state [...]
text:
North Carolina voters overwhelmingly passed three constitutional amendments on Nov. 3, 2026 to authorize lawmakers to impose limits on local governments’ power to raise property taxes, cap the state income tax, and require photo ID for all voters — not just those voting in person. (Photo: Clayton Henkel/NC Newsline) North Carolina voters who delivered a blue wave for Democrats Tuesday also overwhelmingly approved two constitutional amendments that will impact taxes for years to come.
The first amendment, approved by 62% of voters, caps state income tax rates for individuals and corporations at 3.5%. The second amendment, which 60% of voters approved, requires the state legislature to limit increases in local property taxes, reducing the money communities can raise for schools, infrastructure and other needs.
Alexandra Sirota (Photo: NC Budget & Tax Center)
Alexandra Sirota, director of the North Carolina Budget & Tax Center, said Wednesday that the outcome of the constitutional amendments was deeply disappointing for the future of the state.
“We know that people were voting out of concern for rising costs, and we know that one of the best ways for our state leaders to address those rising costs is to fund programs and services that make life more affordable,” said Sirota. “Unfortunately, the tax amendments that passed put in place real limits on future policymakers’ ability to adjust their revenue to the needs of the moment.”
Sirota said the amendments don’t alter the need for increased investments in childcare, housing, and transportation infrastructure. The property tax measure also doesn’t offer any specifics about how the limit should work.
“It really is going to be up to state legislators to craft the exact language and the exact limit that they want to place on local governments,” Sirota said.
 Amendments could hamstring local governments 
Sirota said the proposed property tax limit could affect communities’ ability to upgrade infrastructure through future bonds, fill the gap when the federal government cuts food assistance, or put more money into public education.
This week the State Board of Education released a new report that detailed $18 billion in school facility needs over the next five years for the state’s 115 school systems.
Local governments often use property taxes to fund school capital projects. The newly passed constitutional amendment could limit that.
“What’s most important in this policy development is going to be having the time to really carefully consider how this gets implemented so that local governments are able to keep up with the rising costs they’re being asked to take on,” said Sirota.
New leadership, new ideas 
Rep. Deb Butler, D-New Hanover, said there’s no doubt that the amendments will present new challenges for legislators who now have to decide  how to structure limits on local property taxes without adversely affecting local government services.
Rep. Deb Butler, D-New Hanover (Photo: NCGA)
“Those are going to be some constraints that we’re going to have to work within,” Butler told NC Newsline.
Butler is a senior member of the House Finance Committee who has expressed interest in taking the reins of the committee when Democrats take control of the House in January.
“That’s of course the decision of the Speaker,” said Butler. “But I’ve been working on some ideas about how we generate more revenue, how we get rid of some of these ‘favorite son’ exemptions and how we level the playing field with corporations.”
Butler said the key will be to find a way to create new revenue for North Carolina without hurting small businesses or individual taxpayers.
 Limiting state revenue growth 
Under the state income tax amendment voters approved, the state’s maximum income tax rate is 3.5%. North Carolina’s personal income tax rate currently stands at 3.99%. It’s slated to fall to 3.49% in January, and fall again to 3.24% in 2030 .
North Carolina’s current corporate income tax rate of 2% is scheduled to reach zero by 2030.
The Budget & Tax Center says that as soon as 2028, the state is projected to face real financial challenges if the schedule of rate cuts continues.
“I think the biggest thing that state legislators are going to need to do is stop those scheduled rate cuts to make sure we at least hold the line on funding people’s priorities,” Sirota said.
The State Board of Education released a new report this week that detailed $18 billion in school facility needs over the next five years for the state’s 115 school systems. (Image: Adobe Stock)
In the new school facility needs report, the most common justifications reported for future expenditures are to resolve repairs or deferred maintenance. Plumbing, HVAC, and electrical needs account for $2.8 billion or 30% of all reported renovation needs at the state’s existing schools, according to the Department of Public Instruction.
Sirota notes that the failure to keep up with maintenance needs can often result in greater expense for costly HVAC repairs or mold remediation.
“Those costs need to be met with revenue,” said Sirota.
Sirota said difficult choices lie ahead. She says millionaires are already not being asked to pay their fair share. With the new income tax cap, future lawmakers may need to turn to raising sales taxes or fees, which would be a bigger financial burden on middle- and low-income households.
Some Democrats have suggested repealing the state’s opportunity scholarship program as one source of revenue.
The Republican-controlled legislature earmarked $705 million in its most recent budget for the Opportunity Scholarship Program in 2026-27, with plans to increase that appropriation to over $800 million annually by 2030.
Butler said she’ll leave it up to others in her caucus to determine how to deal with vouchers.
“That is a big source of revenue that needs to be reevaluated,” said Butler.
 Luxuries and loopholes 
Butler said there should be some agreement on easy reforms like removing luxury tax caps in North Carolina.
“In North Carolina, you can buy a $100 million dollar aircraft or yacht, and you pay a tax with a cap of $1,500,” said Butler. “That’s just not right.”
Butler said the next legislature should also revisit the “Blue Ridge exemption,” a property tax loophole for affordable housing that is being used by corporate for-profit developers while costing local governments tens of millions of dollars each year.
Bill to close property tax loophole advances in NC House committee

A bill to close that loophole passed the N.C. House in May, only to languish in the Senate.
“I think there’s a better, fairer way to do that that would generate revenue,” she said.
Butler said as a minority member, she’s had plenty of time to ruminate on some ideas. With a new House Speaker and a new crop of incoming lawmakers, she’s hoping for time to discuss them.
“If I’ve learned anything watching these current leaders, it’s that you don’t do anything in a rushed fashion,” said Butler. “I think about HB2 or the classroom size bill, or any number of things that they’ve gone after at breakneck speed.”
“I’d rather get it right the first time,” Butler said. “These are big changes and you don’t want to do anything that’s going to have unintended consequences.”

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Jefferson County sees a blue splash in midterm election
description: Having voted nearly straight ticket Republican in 2024, Jefferson County replaced three of four Republican incumbents in the House of Delegates with Democrats.
text:
Democrats Regina Dyer (from left to right), Jenny Thacker and Lucia Valentine beat out Republican House of Delegate incumbents Del. Wayne Clark, Del. Chris Anders and Del. Bill Ridenour on Tuesday. The three women will head to Charleston in January for their first legislative session to represent Jefferson County, West Virginia. (Submitted photos)There are swing counties. 
And then there’s Jefferson County. 
At least that’s what a Republican friend once remarked to John Doyle, a former Jefferson County delegate and member of the county’s Democratic Executive Committee, over lunch. 
On Tuesday, Jefferson County — located at the easternmost tip of the Eastern Panhandle — swung again. Having voted nearly straight ticket Republican in 2024, the county replaced three of four Republican incumbents in the House of Delegates with Democrats. 
Two county commissioner seats, both held by Republicans, were also won by Democrats. And both Democratic challengers in the midterm election carried the county. 
The county is also where now Gov. Patrick Morrisey, a Republican, moved in the mid-aughts. 
Doyle, reached by phone on Wednesday morning, said he expected to see some seats flip, but did not expect the blue wave to crest on the shores of the Potomac and Shenandoah rivers. 
Local issues surrounding the Valley Link transmission line project, data centers and a proposed bottling plant drove the election, Doyle said. 
“On all three of those issues, you had voters that were outright opposed, others just seriously suspicious of what was going on and they did not believe that the legislators or the county commissioners were giving them all the information,” Doyle said. “I really think the election coalesced around transparency and accountability.” 
Steven Roberts, the chairman of the Jefferson County Republican Executive Committee, said he believes national issues surrounding affordability, particularly the price of gas, led Jefferson Countians to vote Democratic. But those local issues also played a factor — and the local Republican ticket wasn’t in agreement on how to handle them. 
“Even though we like to really try to push forward and go into free market values, how that’s interpreted a lot of times is across the spectrum,” he said. “We had candidates that were for some of those issues and against some of those issues and across the board.” 
Over the last two decades, Jefferson County voters have shifted the pendulum between the two parties dramatically. In 2008, President Barack Obama won the county, as did nearly every Democrat on the ballot. 
Democrat dominance weakened over the next decade — the county voted around 60% for Morrisey’s first run for state attorney general — until a full flip towards Republican politics in 2016, the first year President Donald J. Trump won the White House. 
Roberts said Jefferson County encapsulates a trend seen in “purple” — neither solidly Republican nor Democratic — areas of the country. 
“That’s the nature of purple, and that’s the nature of modern politics right now,” he said. “It’s on both sides of the spectrum. There is a lot of frustration and anger that builds up once a sitting party has been there for a little bit.” 
Over the years, Jefferson County has transformed from a rural, agricultural based county where apple trees and bean fields lined the roads to a bedroom community for workers who commute to the Washington, D.C. area. 
“That growth tends to come in waves,” Doyle said. “You’ll have a period of a half a dozen years where there’s this wave coming over the Blue Ridge into Jefferson County, and then for a few years it will slow down and be merely a ripple, and then it’ll pick up again. Each wave brings a different group of newcomers with different ideas.” 
Winning elections is one thing — the task now, for the both the newly elected Democratic delegation and commissioners, is to govern. 
“In the Democratic Party it’s a fairly easy thing to be against everything,” Roberts said. “One of the real problems that the Democrats are going to have in the future is that they really don’t have any plan. All they have a plan to do is to run against the issues of Republicans because of some of the complex and sometimes dynamic issues that are not easy to address.” 
Doyle, who Jefferson County voters in the past had placed in office and tossed him out, said the newly elected need to be in tune with the needs of the constituents. 
“If someone is elected to either county commission, state legislature, whatever, it is important to understand the nature of the county, and a lot of people who are elected don’t,” Doyle said. “If you understand it can swing violently the other way at any time, you have a better chance to hold your seat and withstand that swing.”

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: Diesel tax breaks make limited impact as prices remain high
description: Moves to provide help for farmers, truckers and others hit by high diesel fuel prices are having a limited effect in North Dakota. For some farmers, loosening up restrictions on the use of lower-taxed diesel came too late and was complicated by farming in two states following different sets of rules. North Dakota on Sept. […]
text:
Trucks fill up with diesel fuel in Casselton, North Dakota on Oct. 1, 2026. (Photo by Jeff Beach/North Dakota Monitor)Moves to provide help for farmers, truckers and others hit by high diesel fuel prices are having a limited effect in North Dakota.
For some farmers, loosening up restrictions on the use of lower-taxed diesel came too late and was complicated by farming in two states following different sets of rules.
North Dakota on Sept. 29 announced it would allow expanded use of a lower-taxed diesel. The cheaper diesel, which is dyed red, is normally only allowed in tractors, combines and other off-road field equipment. Gov. Kelly Armstrong’s order allows red diesel for hauling grain on highways and for other on-road agricultural jobs.
But highway use only accounts for about 5% to 15% of a typical farm’s diesel use, said Matthew Gammans, assistant professor in NDSU’s Department of Agribusiness and Applied Economics. Far more diesel is used in field equipment that could already use the cheaper fuel. 
“The issue is that the share of diesel that’s actually used on the road relative to in the field is just so small that these policies are just not able to make a big dent,” Gammans said. 
Farms in two states
North Dakota charges a tax of 23 cents per gallon on regular diesel fuel but only 4 cents per gallon on red-dyed diesel, potentially saving farmers19 cents per gallon with the cheaper diesel until the order expires Nov. 30.
Similar to the North Dakota exemption, President Donald Trump on Oct. 5 issued an order allowing dyed diesel on the highways and a deferment on federal taxes on diesel for the rest of the year. The federal tax is 24 cents per gallon. 
But Minnesota has not signed on to the federal exemption, keeping the dyed diesel ban on roadways in place. 
Ben Bakko farms at Walcott in southeast North Dakota but also farms land on the Minnesota side of the Red River. 
Bakko was already done harvesting soybeans by the start of October and only had a small number of acres of corn left to harvest, he said. He didn’t want to risk a fine by using dyed diesel on Minnesota highways, so he kept clear diesel in his trucks until he finished harvesting sugar beets in Minnesota.
He moved on to his beets in North Dakota and finally was able to haul with the cheaper diesel. 
It takes more truckloads to haul a field of sugar beets than corn, he said, so he was grateful for the tax break.
But Bakko said it doesn’t come close to making up for the more than $2 per gallon price increase from last fall’s harvest. 
The average price for a gallon of diesel in North Dakota on Thursday was at $6.04 per gallon, about 22 cents below the national average but about $2.52 cents above a year ago, according to AAA. 


Harvest progress
As of Sunday, corn harvest in North Dakota was 76% complete, compared to the five-year average of 69%, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture.
Soybean harvest was  96%, compared to the five-year average of 91%
Sugar beet harvest was complete and sunflowers were 61% harvested. 


Bakko, who burns through about 30,000 gallons of diesel each year, mostly in the fall, is skeptical about seeing any break in prices soon.
“This diesel problem, these prices, are not going to go away by the end of the year,” he said. “I’m kind of wondering if they’re just going to reissue all this again next year.” 
Savings and losses
The fuel tax breaks were spurred by a spike in diesel prices just as harvest was ramping up, in part because of an attack on a key Mideast pipeline in September. The U.S. war with Iran and other global conflicts have restricted fuel shipments since February. 
North Dakota Tax Commissioner Brian Kroshus said the exemption would provide “a little bit of relief” but said the price of oil needs to come down to help farms with diesel and other energy-intensive expenses, such as fertilizer and farm chemicals. 
“The real solution to this isn’t through executive orders but seeing the price of oil moderate,” Kroshus said.  
The state Department of Transportation receives about $5.4 million per month from diesel tax revenue, according to the Governor’s Office. 
Kroshus said the Tax Department did not have a forecast for how tax revenue might be affected. 
Gammans, in a report published last month, estimated that corn and soybean farmers in the state could save up to $850,000 this fall because of North Dakota’s emergency order. 
The red-dyed diesel is usually delivered in bulk to farmers, who fill up large fuel tanks on their farms. Some farms would not have the ability to fuel tractors and trucks with their on-farm storage, further limiting the benefit.
Record diesel prices hit North Dakota farmers at the wrong time

Calvin Benson, director of public policy for the North Dakota Farm Bureau, said the tax breaks are “not a world-changing thing,” but show that the governor and president are aware of the challenges that farmers are facing. 
He said the longer-term solution that might come out of the fuel situation is policies that might help bring more diesel refining to the United States, making it less dependent on foreign sources. 
The federal exemption applies to all trucks, not just those involved in farming. 
How many truckers are switching to dyed diesel also is unclear. 
Normally, if a truck is inspected and the fuel is red, the operator faces a penalty. 
The North Dakota Motor Carriers Association advised its members that not all states may  honor the federal enforcement exemption.  It also notes that dyed diesel is not readily available and the dye may linger in a truck’s fuel system, potentially exposing the truck to enforcement of the red-dye ban when the order expires. 
The trucking association also said that while it is unlikely, any deferred diesel taxes could still be collected.
Federal payments
The price surge prompted another round of aid payments to farmers under the Harvest Fuel Relief program. The U.S. Department of Agriculture has made $8 billion available to compensate farmers for high diesel prices, but it has not announced how it will be distributed. 
Gammans has looked at scenarios for calculating the payments and said USDA could follow a formula similar to the farm bridge payments announced last year by the Trump administration. Or, Gammans said, USDA could come up with a new formula that factors in average fuel consumption for different crops. 
Gammans said a formula more tied to fuel use could mean more money for southern states that grow rice and cotton, with less money for states that grow wheat, such as North Dakota. 
“Cotton and rice are extremely fuel intensive, and they’re not grown in North Dakota, right? So if you reward proportional to fuel, you’re going to send a lot more money to the South,” he said.
Gammans said he expects an announcement this month.
Reach North Dakota Monitor deputy editor Jeff Beach at jbeach@northdakotamonitor.com

description: Switzerland-based manufacturing company ABB will invest $50 million into an expansion in Selmer, marking the company’s second expansion in McNairy County since last year. The move will add a projected 227 jobs, the Tennessee Department of Economic and Community Development announced Thursday. ABB will build a new 120,000-square-foot Industrial Connections & [...]
text:
ABB Industrial Connections and Solutions announced a second expansion in Selmer on Thursday, Nov. 5, 2026. The company will build a 120,000-square-foot facility next to its recently completed 325,000-square-foot manufacturing facility in McNairy County. (Photo: Courtesy ABB Industrial Connections and Solutions)Switzerland-based manufacturing company ABB will invest $50 million into an expansion in Selmer, marking the company’s second expansion in McNairy County since last year. The move will add a projected 227 jobs, the Tennessee Department of Economic and Community Development announced Thursday.
ABB will build a new 120,000-square-foot Industrial Connections & Solutions facility alongside its recently completed 325,000-square-foot manufacturing facility at the Selmer/McNairy County North Industrial Park. The larger manufacturing hub was part of ABB’s first Selmer expansion announced in March 2025, a $76 million investment projected to create 50 jobs. The company received a $500,000 grant from the state for that expansion. As of April, Industrial Connections & Solutions reported 33 net new jobs, adding to the company’s 191 existing employees.
It’s not yet clear what incentives the state offered for the expansion announced Thursday.
ABB will begin relocating about 90% of its equipment and employees to the recently completed manufacturing hub in 2027. The company will relocate its remaining employees and equipment from its current location on 4th street to the new 120,000-square-foot facility in the second half of 2027. The facility will manufacture electrical distribution systems and other electrical products, according to a TNECD news release.
Upon completing the expansion, ABB will employ more than 1,500 people at its Tennessee locations in Selmer, Portland, Athens, Memphis and Mount Juliet.
The state has poured nearly $1.4 million into the 39-acre Selmer/McNairy County North Industrial Park through site development grants to make the site more palatable for business investments. That includes a $500,000 grant in 2024 for engineering studies and a nearly $898,000 grant in 2022 for property grading and access road construction.
