name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: ‘He could barely hear me’: Deacon recounts Indiana death row inmate’s final hours
description: Jeffrey Weisheit’s spiritual adviser said prison staff kept him outside the condemned man’s cell during their final hours of prayer together, then allowed him only a few minutes at Weisheit’s side in the execution chamber early Thursday. Deacon Brian Nosbusch, who had ministered to Weisheit for about 13 years, described struggling to communicate through thic[...]
text:
Deacon Brian Nosbusch speaks outside the Indiana Government Center in Indianapolis on Oct. 19, 2026. Weisheit’s longtime spiritual adviser urged clemency ahead of the scheduled Nov. 5 execution. (Photo by Casey Smith/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Jeffrey Weisheit’s spiritual adviser said prison staff kept him outside the condemned man’s cell during their final hours of prayer together, then allowed him only a few minutes at Weisheit’s side in the execution chamber early Thursday.
Deacon Brian Nosbusch, who had ministered to Weisheit for about 13 years, described struggling to communicate through thick glass before being separated from him for roughly 90 minutes on Wednesday night. When prison staff brought him into the execution chamber, Weisheit was already strapped to a gurney with intravenous lines in his left arm.
Nosbusch said the execution appeared “calm.” But he left Indiana State Prison troubled by the restrictions on their time together and how little of the process anyone outside the execution team could see.
Former Rep. Andrew Ireland, a Republican death penalty supporter, also called Thursday for greater transparency in the process.
Death row inmate Jeffrey Weisheit (Photo courtesy the Indiana Department of Correction)
“My prayer was through that window,” Nosbusch told the Indiana Capital Chronicle of their hours outside the chamber. He leaned toward a small opening in the glass to speak and pray with Weisheit.
“He could barely hear me, and I had to sit outside the cell,” Nosbusch continued.
His account offers a closer look at an execution that other witnesses could see for only three minutes through a small, tinted window. Still unknown are when Indiana began administering pentobarbital, how much was used and what happened before witnesses were allowed to look inside.
Hours after the execution, Gov. Mike Braun defended carrying out Weisheit’s sentence but suggested that state lawmakers could examine Indiana’s execution secrecy provisions and difficulties acquiring lethal injection drugs.
“When it comes to even the transparency, that evidently is engulfed in our own code, that might be worthy of a legislator looking at,” Braun said Thursday morning.
The Department of Correction also released a temperature log Thursday showing six of seven recorded readings below the log’s stated target range of 68 to 77 degrees Fahrenheit in the days preceding the execution.
DOC had not yet provided the Capital Chronicle with an updated inventory log showing how much pentobarbital was used for Weisheit’s execution, however.
Weisheit was pronounced dead at 12:45 a.m. Central Standard Time for murdering 8-year-old Alyssa Lynch and her 5-year-old brother, Caleb, in a 2010 house fire near Evansville. Their mother, Lisa, was working overnight and had left the children in his care.
Victims were also allowed up to five witnesses in a separate room but their identities are protected.
Braun denied clemency Monday. His office did not publicly announce a decision on the attorneys’ separate requests for a temporary reprieve and an independent investigation of Indiana’s lethal injection procedures and drug procurement before the execution.
Praying through glass
Nosbusch, a Catholic deacon in the Diocese of Gary, said he visited Weisheit about twice a month for years and increased those visits to three times a week during his final month.
They talked about reconciliation, forgiveness and anger. They prayed for Weisheit’s parents and sister, for the children he killed and for the children’s mother and family.
About three months before the execution, Nosbusch said, a priest visited the prison to baptize and confirm Weisheit and give him Holy Communion.
Nosbusch had also served as spiritual adviser to Roy Lee Ward, whom Indiana executed in October 2025. During Ward’s final evening, he said, he was permitted to sit inside the holding cell with him.
He expected similar access Wednesday.
Indiana executes Jeffrey Weisheit for 2010 murders of two children

Instead, after arriving at the prison around 6 p.m., Nosbusch said a masked staff member told him he had not been informed that the deacon could enter Weisheit’s cell. Nosbusch said his requests to contact a supervisor did not resolve the issue.
Nosbusch said he had called the prison’s new warden, Erik Kruper, several times beforehand to clarify arrangements for the execution. He did not know why staff had not received instructions allowing him inside Weisheit’s cell.
He sat outside the glass, leaning toward a small opening to make himself heard. He could pass Communion through the opening and hold Weisheit’s hand, but said the arrangement made conversation and prayer difficult.
Nosbusch said prison staff stood nearby talking and repeatedly went in and out of the room, making it harder to hear Weisheit or have a private exchange.
“It was not personal,” Nosbusch said. “It was not anything.”
He said Weisheit tried to reassure him as he grew frustrated.
“Jeff calmed me down,” Nosbusch recalled. “He said, ‘Brian, don’t worry about it. It’ll be fine.’”
Nosbusch said he plans to write to prison leadership after taking more time to reflect. He wants to explain why he found their final hours together disappointing and ask for greater consideration of the spiritual adviser’s role.
At about 11 p.m., staff moved Nosbusch into another room at the state prison, he said. He waited there until approximately 12:30 a.m., wondering at times whether the governor might have granted a reprieve.
Nosbusch did not see Weisheit being moved into the chamber, restrained or fitted with intravenous lines.
Once brought inside, he said, he immediately began the prayers and Gospel reading he had prepared. He placed a hand on Weisheit’s shoulder and later touched his hand.
Nosbusch estimated he was in the chamber for six minutes at most.



Quotation







It was not personal. It was not anything.


– Deacon Brian Nosbusch


He said he saw two intravenous lines in Weisheit’s left arm but did not examine the right. Weisheit had told him beforehand that he intended to keep his eyes closed, Nosbusch said, and the deacon said he did not see him open them.
Nosbusch described a slight movement of Weisheit’s head when he touched his shoulder, followed by stillness. Toward the end, he said, Weisheit’s hand felt cold and his lips appeared to be turning blue.
Nosbusch was escorted from the chamber before DOC’s reported time of death and did not witness the official pronouncement.
“But it was very peaceful — very peaceful, from what I saw,” Nosbusch said.
He remained in the chamber only briefly after the witness room blinds closed.
“I was in there about a minute longer, so I prayed again and blessed him,” Nosbusch said. “And that was it. Then they took me out.”
The Capital Chronicle’s reporter, who witnessed Weisheit’s execution, saw no visible movement during the three-minute viewing period. The blinds opened at 12:34 a.m. and closed at 12:37 a.m., eight minutes before DOC’s reported time of death.
DOC spokesperson Noelle Russell declined to provide a detailed execution timeline early Thursday morning, citing security concerns, but said the process begins shortly after midnight and proceeds slowly to ensure nothing is rushed. Asked whether Weisheit showed any reaction suggesting complications, Russell said, “Not at all.”
“I am told he did not move at all,” she said.
Indiana does not guarantee journalists access to executions. The Capital Chronicle, which is challenging those restrictions alongside other news organizations, was the only media outlet to witness Weisheit’s execution. Its reporter attended via Weisheit’s personal witness list.
New storage records — and more questions
The November temperature log DOC provided Thursday lists a desired range of 68 to 77 degrees Fahrenheit — the same recommended storage range listed in prescribing information for Nembutal, the brand-name pentobarbital product.
The state received six 50-milliliter vials of pentobarbital on Oct. 29.
Its seven entries run from Nov. 1 through the morning of Nov. 4. Readings range from 65 to 68 degrees, with only one — the evening entry for Nov. 2 — reaching the stated range.
Story continues below.
20261104121633961_Redacted
 
Nembutal’s prescribing information also permits brief temperature excursions between 59 and 86 degrees.
All seven readings fall within that broader interval. But the twice-daily entries do not show how long temperatures remained below 68 degrees, and the log does not indicate whether those conditions affected the drugs’ quality.
The Capital Chronicle was still awaiting an updated drug inventory to determine how much pentobarbital was used in Weisheit’s execution as of late Thursday. Earlier inventory records obtained by the newsroom have documented the state’s purchases, use and destruction of execution drugs.
Dr. Jonathan Groner, an emeritus professor of clinical surgery at Ohio State University’s College of Medicine, said the limited viewing period left important questions about the procedure unanswered.

“When pentobarbital is properly administered as an IV bolus, it should cause rapid unconsciousness — 30 to 60 seconds,” Groner told the Capital Chronicle.
Groner did not attend the execution. Neither the witnesses’ observations nor Nosbusch’s account make clear when the drug was administered or whether Weisheit was conscious while witnesses could see him.
Weisheit’s attorneys had sought testing and storage records before the execution, raising concerns about the Indianapolis pharmacy they identified as the supplier, Pharmaneek Inc. The pharmacy is on probation and faces further disciplinary proceedings. Those proceedings do not establish that the execution drugs were contaminated or ineffective.
The Indiana Professional Licensing Agency confirmed Thursday that Pharmaneek’s disciplinary hearing has been postponed to Dec. 14 after its new counsel requested a continuance last week because of a scheduling conflict.
Before the execution, DOC said it remained confident in its ability to carry out the sentence humanely. The attorney general’s office likewise expressed confidence it could proceed safely and lawfully. Both cited state confidentiality law in declining to discuss supplier information.
Braun signals possible legislative review
Asked Thursday morning whether lawmakers should revisit capital punishment, Braun said the three executions carried out during his administration involved clear cases and lengthy court proceedings.
“I think going forward with it made perfect sense,” Braun said. “I think most Hoosiers would agree with it.”
He said the death penalty was not a particularly high priority but could be examined, including the transparency restrictions written into state law.
“But I think here, the way that drug is acquired certainly looks like it’s not easy, and the whole discussion probably needs to be looked at more broadly, and we’ll see where that goes,” Braun said.
The discussion would return to a Legislature changed by Tuesday’s election, which defeated two Republicans who approached capital punishment from different directions but supported greater scrutiny.
Gov. Mike Braun speaks to reporters at the Statehouse Thursday, Nov. 5, 2026. (Photo by Mackenzi Klemann/Indiana Capital Chronicle.)
Ireland, R-Indianapolis, who lost his reelection bid Tuesday night, additionally called attention Thursday to the Legislature’s failure to pass execution transparency language.
“One regret this last legislative session was not getting our death penalty transparency language passed,” he wrote.
Ireland said supporting capital punishment should also mean allowing reporters to observe whether executions are carried out lawfully, rather than requiring news organizations to sue for access.
Rep. Bob Morris, R-Fort Wayne, who also lost Tuesday, has been a vocal Republican opponent of capital punishment and sought more transparency around execution procedures.
After unsuccessfully seeking repeal in 2025, Morris introduced legislation this year that would have required execution teams to consist of volunteer legislators and made their names public records.
Lawmakers also considered expanding the methods Indiana could use to carry out death sentences. A House firing squad bill fell short in a narrow 48-47 vote in January, failing to secure the required 51 votes. A separate Senate proposal stalled without a committee vote.
Despite those unsuccessful efforts, DOC confirmed to the Capital Chronicle in June that the new prison in Westville was designed to accommodate both lethal injection and firing squad executions. The agency declined to provide design details, citing security concerns.
Indiana currently authorizes only lethal injection.
Groner said the public has an interest in understanding how the state carries out death sentences.
“If capital punishment is portrayed as a public good, then the public should be allowed to know how executions are performed,” he said.
For Nosbusch, the immediate concern is continuing a ministry that has taken him inside the prison for more than two decades. He intends to keep visiting men on death row and in protective custody.
After leaving the prison early Thursday, he sat in his car to gather his thoughts, then stopped for coffee before driving home.
Nosbusch described Weisheit as a friend. Accompanying him through the execution was difficult, he said, but he was grateful he had been there.
“It makes it hard,” he said. “But I’m so glad I did it.”

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Democrat Mat Anderson wins WV House District 50 seat, formerly held by Pritt
description: A Democrat will fill the West Virginia House of Delegates seat formerly held by disgraced former Republican lawmaker Elliott Pritt.
text:
Democratic candidate Mat Anderson won House District 50 Tuesday night, beating out independent candidate Tom Louisos, Constitution Party candidate Stacey L. Hensley and two write-in candidates, Republican William Jennings Vest and independent Eric Walton. (Submitted photo)A Democrat will fill the West Virginia House of Delegates seat formerly held by disgraced former Republican lawmaker Elliott Pritt.
Mat Anderson won House District 50 Tuesday night, beating out independent candidate Tom Louisos, Constitution Party candidate Stacey L. Hensley and two write-in candidates, Republican William Jennings Vest and independent Eric Walton. 
Anderson pulled in more than 51% of the votes cast in the general election.  
“We’ve been running this race — I think we just finished our 14th month of campaigning, so we have excitement,” Anderson said Thursday. “It’s an honor to be the next delegate of House District 50. I know that the last couple of seat sitters haven’t been pristine people, so our whole job is to show what good leaders look like with this house seat flip.”
Pritt resigned from office in July and withdrew from the district 50 race after he was arrested on federal charges for allegedly enticing a minor. Pritt was a public school teacher. According to the criminal complaint, the family of a 15-year-old female reported that the child had been sexually abused by Pritt. Pritt is scheduled to enter a guilty plea to charges next week. 
The Republican Party was not permitted to fill the vacancy on the general election ballot created by Pritt’s withdrawal due to a 2024 state election law. House Bill 4350 prohibits political parties from replacing a nominee late in the election process. The Republican-sponsored legislation went into effect last year.
Pritt was first elected as a Democrat to the House in 2022. He switched to the Republican Party in 2023. 
Prior to Pritt, District 50 was held by former delegate Austin Haynes, who faced allegations of sexual harassment and misusing his position in a 2023 lawsuit.  
In all, 12 seats in the House of Delegates will flip from red to blue this January after Tuesday’s election. Eight of the 12 new Democrats in the House are women. Republicans will still have control of both the House and Senate.
Anderson, a special education teacher and small business owner, said Thursday that during the campaign he knocked on around 2,400 doors, talking to voters. Most shared concerns about cost of living issues, he said. 
Anderson said the campaign process was “the honor of my lifetime.” Most voters were receptive to talking, he said. 
“I just can’t thank everybody enough for coming out to vote,” Anderson said. “This isn’t how I wanted my race to go, but we just plowed forward and we did what we knew how to do, and that was campaign.”

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico observers report ‘generally smooth’ 2026 election
description: The 260 certified observers enlisted to watch key steps of New Mexico’s 2026 general election said the process went “smoothly overall,” according to a news release this week from Observe New Mexico Elections, though a small number of voters seeking to register and vote on Tuesday faced delays.
text:
Observe New Mexico Elections, a nonprofit election monitoring group, said in a news release Nov. 4, 2026, that the 2026 general election in New Mexico went “generally smoothly.” (Photo by Matt Mondschein/Source NM)The 260 certified observers enlisted to watch key steps of New Mexico’s 2026 general election said the process went “smoothly overall,” according to a news release this week from Observe New Mexico Elections, though a small number of voters seeking to register and vote on Tuesday faced delays.
Observe New Mexico Elections, a nonprofit group funded by the Carter Center, which former President Jimmy Carter founded, has sent hundreds of observers to monitor the last five New Mexico elections. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Observers watched statewide this year during voting machine and equipment certification, poll worker training, early voting, absentee ballot processing and Election Day monitoring. The group’s aim was to watch every early voting location in the state at least once, as well as be in 50% of statewide polling places in each county and all of Bernalillo County’s polling places on Election Day, the group’s co-leader Carmen Lopez told Source NM in a pre-election interview last week.
In addition to Observe New Mexico Elections’ observers, five other groups deployed hundreds of watchers throughout the state on Election Day, and the United States Department of Justice sent approximately 10 monitors to observe Bernalillo County polling places on Tuesday. 
In a news release Wednesday, Lopez said observers saw strong voter turnout and smooth voting processes across the state.
“Initial feedback from ONME observers shows that the General Election ran smoothly overall, with a handful of polling sites impacted by delays in the same-day voter registration system,” she said. “In addition, poll workers in flood-affected areas sought creative solutions to keep the lines moving.”
San Juan County and others in northern New Mexico have been recovering from widespread flooding that damaged thousands of homes in the days leading up to Election Day. 
According to unofficial results from the Secretary of State’s Office, San Juan County voters turned out at a lower rate than in the last midterm election. In 2022, roughly 51% of voters cast ballots; this year, a little less than 45% of voters turned out. 
Statewide, Observe New Mexico Elections has repeatedly noted delays in recent elections with same-day registration, which enables voters to register to vote at a polling place and cast ballots afterward, once the Secretary of State’s Office has processed their applications.
Bernalillo County expecting 10 USDOJ monitors on Election Day

On Tuesday, the group said delays or system shutdowns affected same-day voters in a small number of locations, but the observer group received “positive reports about the creativity of poll workers in high turnout areas by shifting resources between polling locations” to address the issue, Lopez said. 
Lindsey Bachman, the secretary of state’s communications, legislative and executive affairs director, did not immediately respond to Source NM’s request for comment.
The Secretary of State’s Office, in a news release Tuesday night, celebrated what Secretary of State Maggie Toulouse Oliver said was a “safe, secure, and accessible general election in New Mexico.” On Thursday, the state’s Office of Cybersecurity announced that the state’s electronic election networks and systems stayed secure throughout the election, thanks to months of planning between the office and other state agencies.
“New Mexicans cast their ballots with confidence, and they had every reason to,” New Mexico Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham said in a statement. “Our agencies, election officials and partners spent months preparing for every scenario so voters never had to wonder whether their vote was safe. That is the strong foundation we’ll hand off to the next administration.”
Like it does after every election, Observe New Mexico Elections will send out a full, comprehensive report on New Mexico’s election processes in the coming weeks. The group will also send observers to witness the ballot certification process beginning soon.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Vandalia Health, osteopathic school to reopen labor, delivery services at Greenbrier Medical Center
description: Greenbrier County families will again have access to labor and delivery services through an agreement between Vandalia Health and the West Virginia School of Osteopathic Medicine.
text:
Greenbrier Valley Medical Center in Ronceverte, West Virginia, closed its labor and delivery room this spring. Officials announced Thursday it would reopen through an agreement between Vandalia Health and the West Virginia School of Osteopathic Medicine. (Photo by Chris Jackson for West Virginia Watch)Greenbrier County families will again have access to labor and delivery services through an agreement between Vandalia Health and the West Virginia School of Osteopathic Medicine, officials announced Thursday.
Greenbrier Valley Medical Center closed its labor and delivery room in April as it transitioned to being a critical access hospital. A spokesperson for Vandalia Health said at the time the hospital had tried unsuccessfully for two years to recruit a physician for the delivery room.
Gov. Patrick Morrisey announced Thursday that the school and Vandalia Health will establish an Academic Integration Agreement that calls for the hospital to reopen obstetric services at Greenbrier Valley Medical Center. The governor made the announcement at the West Virginia School of Osteopathic Medicine in Lewisburg, West Virginia.
Under the agreement, WVSOM will become Vandalia Health’s primary academic affiliation, with implementation beginning in phases on July 1, 2027, a news release says.
Morrisey also announced that the state will allocate $4 million in Rural Health Transformation Programs funds to establish the state’s second freestanding birthing center and address complex labor and delivery births.
“We are restoring essential healthcare services to the Greenbrier Valley by reopening labor and delivery at Greenbrier Valley Medical Center,” Morrisey said in the news release. “This historic partnership between two of West Virginia’s leading healthcare institutions, combined with a nearly $4 million investment, will build a stronger, more sustainable maternal healthcare system that serves mothers, babies, and families for years to come.”
Greenbrier County isn’t the only part of the state that’s had a shortage of maternity care. According to a 2024 report from the March of Dimes, about half of the 55 counties in West Virginia are “maternity care deserts,” compared with 32.6% in the United States. Twenty-two percent of West Virginia women have no birthing hospital within 30 minutes, compared to 9.7% in the rest of the country, the report says.
The planned reopening will restore local access to deliveries requiring hospital resources, including C-sections, epidurals, and care for higher-risk pregnancies, the governor’s office said.
“The challenge of providing OB/GYN and maternity healthcare in rural areas is not just a Greenbrier Valley issue. According to the federal Government Accountability Office (GAO), more than half of rural counties do not have a hospital that provides these services,” WVSOM President James W. Nemitz said in a news release. “WVSOM is honored to participate in this effort to resolve that issue for our region. What an appropriate use of Rural Health Transformation Program funding. We are proud of Dr. Drema Hill’s involvement and look forward to working with the other partners and Gov. Morrisey’s team.”

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: New Oklahoma schools chief preparing for ‘behemoth’ challenge of education turnaround
description: OKLAHOMA CITY — The work of Oklahoma’s top education official has already begun for state Superintendent-elect Robert Franklin. By late Wednesday afternoon, not even 24 hours since being elected Tuesday, the longtime educator from Sand Springs had spoken with a local district superintendent about preparations for the state’s new literacy law and exchanged me[...]
text:
State superintendent candidate Robert Franklin speaks at a campaign event in Edmond on Aug. 3, 2026. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY — The work of Oklahoma’s top education official has already begun for state Superintendent-elect Robert Franklin.
By late Wednesday afternoon, not even 24 hours since being elected Tuesday, the longtime educator from Sand Springs had spoken with a local district superintendent about preparations for the state’s new literacy law and exchanged messages with Gov.-elect Mike Mazzei, all amidst a marathon of media interviews.
Once he’s sworn into office in January, Franklin, 67, will be responsible for what he described as a “behemoth” task of turning around Oklahoma’s bottom-ranking reading and math scores. He called the work ahead “encouraging” and “daunting.”
“It’s an all-hands-on-deck kind of moment,” Franklin said. “We’ve got a lot of work to do.”
Despite facing skepticism within the state GOP, Franklin received broad bipartisan support, particularly from fellow educators. 
He defeated Democrat Jennettie Marshall 66% to 34% and was one of two candidates for statewide office to win all 77 counties of Oklahoma, general election results show. The other, Republican state Treasurer-elect Cindy Byrd, did not have a Democratic opponent.
Franklin promised a distinctly different vision and demeanor from former state Superintendent Ryan Walters, who was elected in 2022. Walters made headlines throughout his tenure for hyper-partisan rhetoric and numerous controversies before he resigned in September 2025.
State Superintendent Ryan Walters speaks during an Oklahoma State Board of Education meeting April 24, 2025, in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)
Gov. Kevin Stitt appointed Superintendent Lindel Fields and a “turnaround team” to lead the Oklahoma State Department of Education over the final 15 months of Walters’ term. Fields set out to quiet the turmoil by making the Education Department boring again. 
Franklin similarly promised to focus on students and schools, not partisan politics. He said voters, even those who were “somewhat dismissive” of his candidacy, realized “we’re all after the very same thing” of supporting children and young people.
“I think there is a mindset out there that says we don’t have to be ugly and politically divisive to lean in and support the work of schools, and that’s what I’m sensing from most folks,” he said. “And when you walked away from some of those meetings, even when it was complicated, people would say, ‘Well, I may not agree with everything that you said, but I do agree with the work at hand.’”
Franklin will take over an Education Department that’s been in transition for the past year. He said it’s unclear how many of Fields’ “turnaround team” wish to remain with the agency long term, but he intends to meet with the administration to find out.
In a statement through his communications office, Fields, who did not run to stay in office, said he and his staff “intend to do all that’s possible to ensure a smooth, uneventful transition.”
“Robert Franklin comes into this role as a highly-qualified educational leader,” Fields said. “He’s excited and as someone I’ve known for many years, I know his heart and I know he has great plans for education in Oklahoma. He’s ready to hit the ground running.”
State Superintendent Lindel Fields, left, stands with Gov. Kevin Stitt, right, during an Oklahoma State Board of Education meeting May 21 at the state Capitol in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)
Franklin also will step into office midway through the rollout of a major literacy law. 
The new Strong Readers Act, signed into law this spring, will require more academic interventions, like small-group tutoring and summer programs, for children scoring behind their grade level in reading. 
Starting in the 2027-28 school year, third graders who score below a basic reading level on state tests and fail a second assessment will have to repeat the grade, unless they meet limited criteria for an exemption.
Franklin said he plans to bring educators and experts to the table to develop a game plan before the high-stakes testing begins. The Education Department can help allocate resources, provide professional development and open regional centers to serve local schools while teachers and district leaders do the heavy lifting of educating children, he said.
He told Oklahoma Voice he’ll look at reversing a Walters-era rule that entwined a school’s academic results with its state accreditation, which Franklin said “conflates things” intended to be separate. The rule recently caused accreditation downgrades for dozens of school districts that had low math and reading scores.
Franklin said he also would push to change Oklahoma’s methods of student assessment from once-a-year exams to benchmark tests given incrementally through the school year — a plan that would require federal approval.
Tackling Oklahoma’s teacher shortage and adding behavioral health specialists in schools have been major campaign priorities, as well.
Robert Franklin files to run as a Republican candidate for state superintendent on April 1 at the state Capitol in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)
The next weeks and months for Franklin will center on establishing the right staffing and structure at the Education Department, he said, while building relationships across the state, particularly with Oklahoma legislators and the next governor.
Improving reading scores has been a major priority of Mazzei’s gubernatorial campaign. The governor-elect has given vocal support for the strict new reading law, and he pledged to hire a statewide literacy director to focus on its implementation.
“Let me just say that fixing our schools isn’t a Republican or Democrat issue,” Mazzei said during a news conference Wednesday. “It’s about giving every child in Oklahoma the opportunity to succeed.”
Franklin said he expects he and Mazzei have similar goals.
“He may see a particular tact that goes a little off course from what I’m thinking, but at the end of the day, I bet you a dollar to a donut, we’re going to be in complete accord with our outcomes that we want to achieve,” Franklin said. “And so, that’s going to be the discussion of how can we do that efficiently and effectively.”

title: Third major US offshore wind farm is now fully operational
description: This story was originally published by Canary Media. Read the original version here. text:
The service vessel ECO Edison sails toward the Revolution Wind project near New England. (Photo by Ørsted)This story was originally published by Canary Media. Read the original version here.
The offshore wind farm Revolution Wind is completely up and running — despite the Trump administration’s repeated and ongoing efforts to halt development of the $6.2 billion project.
On Thursday, the Danish energy giant Ørsted said its 704-megawatt wind farm near Connecticut and Rhode Island began ​“generating up to its full capacity” in October. Revolution Wind began producing smaller amounts of power in the spring, and the company installed the last of 65 turbines in September.
The project is the third U.S. utility-scale offshore wind farm to reach full commercial operations, after South Fork Wind near New York and Vineyard Wind near Massachusetts.
“Revolution Wind will provide enough electricity to power the equivalent of more than 350,000 New England homes, strengthening the region’s supply of affordable, reliable energy,” Ørsted said in an emailed statement after its quarterly earnings call. The company is selling the carbon-free electricity to three utilities in the area: Rhode Island Energy, Eversource Energy, and United Illuminating. 
America’s once-burgeoning offshore wind industry has weathered a series of political attacks since President Donald Trump took office in January 2025. Before his second administration began, BloombergNEF projected that the U.S. would build 39 gigawatts of offshore wind by 2035. Now, it expects just 5.9 GW to come online — an amount that reflects the handful of projects that were already completed or under construction at the start of last year.
Despite the diminished pipeline, the carbon-free energy source is still expected to help keep household utility bills in check across the U.S. Northeast, experts say. Revolution Wind and the country’s other completed projects have already played a key role in reducing grid stress during extreme weather events this year.
“Revolution Wind will provide an essential boost of utility-scale electricity to the power-hungry Northeast, delivering a substantial new source of generation, diversifying supply, and strengthening electric reliability for decades,” said Hillary Bright, executive director of offshore wind advocacy group Turn Forward, in a Thursday statement.
Ørsted hit its power milestone despite being forced to halt construction twice last year.
In August 2025, the Interior Department issued a stop-work order for Revolution Wind, due to unspecified national security threats. That order was tossed out by a federal judge one month later. But in late December, the administration issued new stop-work orders to all five offshore wind projects then under construction. Judges struck those orders down one by one — but not before developers had lost huge sums of money and nearly missed key project deadlines. 
Revolution Wind still isn’t fully out of Trump’s crosshairs. 
In October, the Interior Department asked a federal court for permission to reevaluate the agency’s 2023 approval of the wind farm’s construction and operations plan. While the move didn’t immediately affect the project’s activities, experts said it adds uncertainty around what is now a fully operational installation.
Meanwhile, Ørsted said it’s making progress on another offshore wind development, Sunrise Wind. The developer on Thursday said it has finished installing all of the wind-turbine foundations for the 924-MW project off the coast of Long Island, New York. That installation is expected to be fully operational in the second half of next year.

title: Van Epps secures reelection to Tennessee’s Congressional District 7 seat
description: Republican Matt Van Epps secured reelection to Tennessee’s 7th Congressional District, outperforming Democratic candidate Darden Copeland at the polls by just over 2 percentage points. The Associated Press called the race for Van Epps Thursday morning.  “I believe in showing up, getting to work, and delivering results. The people of Tennessee believe the sam[...]
text:
Matt Van Epps, photographed at his December 2025 special election victory celebration, secured his first full term in Congress with a narrow win in the midterm elections on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)
artipilo/Tennessee Lookout)Republican Matt Van Epps secured reelection to Tennessee’s 7th Congressional District, outperforming Democratic candidate Darden Copeland at the polls by just over 2 percentage points.
The Associated Press called the race for Van Epps Thursday morning. 
“I believe in showing up, getting to work, and delivering results. The people of Tennessee believe the same,” Van Epps wrote in a statement early Wednesday morning. “While our team took some losses tonight, I remain dedicated to the things that make America the greatest country on Earth — faith, family and freedom.”
Van Epps first secured the seat in a special election to replace former U.S. Rep. Mark Green in December 2025, besting Nashville Democratic state Rep. Aftyn Behn by 8.8 percentage points.
Tennessee’s Republican supermajority redrew the state’s congressional districts in May in hopes of creating higher odds for Republican candidates to win all nine of the state’s U.S. House seats. The new boundaries lessened the District 7’s Republican lean.
Copeland came within roughly 5,200 votes of claiming the seat, which was considered a solid Republican district going into Election Day. 
While Republican candidates won the governor’s seat, U.S. Senate and all but one of Tennessee’s nine U.S. House seats, voter margins in all of Tennessee’s counties shifted toward Democrats compared to the 2024 presidential election, AP data shows.
Copeland performed best in the half of Davidson County that falls within the newly drawn district, getting 67.4% of the votes to Van Epps’ 31.3%, according to The Associated Press.
Van Epps performed better in the seven other counties that make up the district. But in Montgomery County, Copeland wasn’t far behind with 46.3% of the vote to Van Epps’ 51.8%.

name: VTDigger
title: Apparent election ploy to oust Chittenden County state’s attorney fails
description:
Sarah George was among the county law enforcement officials across Vermont who won four-year terms on Tuesday.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Apparent election ploy to oust Chittenden County state’s attorney fails.
text:
Chittenden County State’s Attorney Sarah George speaks during closing arguments in Chittenden Superior criminal court in Burlington on Monday, Sept. 21, 2026. Jason Eaton faces charges of attempted second-degree murder in the shooting of three Palestinian students. Pool photo by Paul Heintz/Boston Globe

An incumbent won reelection over an opponent who said he didn’t even want the job.
In Chittenden County — the state’s most populous — Sarah George, the incumbent state’s attorney who ran in the general election with the nomination of the Democratic and Progressive parties, prevailed for a third, four-year term. 
George won 50,635 votes, besting Republican challenger Jace Laquerre, who collected 27,591 votes, according to unofficial results from the Vermont Secretary of State’s Office.
“This campaign was about what justice should look like: fair, smart, and free from fear,” George wrote in a social media post Wednesday. “That means standing up for victims, holding people accountable, and pursuing solutions that make our community safer.”
Laquerre, a software engineer who isn’t an attorney, pledged that, if elected, he would resign, creating a vacancy that would be filled by a governor’s appointment and who would serve out the remaining term in office.

READ MORE

The unconventional move sought to get George out of office by Laquerre and others critical of George’s criminal justice reform efforts. 
George faced a stronger challenge in the Democratic primary in August from Bram Kranichfeld, who currently serves as the Franklin County state’s attorney. Kranichfeld decided against running for the Franklin County post this year, opting instead to compete for the state attorney  position in Chittenden County where he resides.
In Franklin County, Zach Weight, a Washington County deputy state’s attorney who earned the Democratic and Republican party nominations in the August primary, finished Tuesday with 11,615 votes, winning over John Lavoie, an independent, who had 7,843 votes, according to the unofficial results. 
Lavoie had previously served as the county’s state attorney following his election in 2022 to the post. However, he resigned in the face of a legislative impeachment investigation a year later, prompted by a report detailing harassment and discrimination by him against his employees.
In Grand Isle County, incumbent State’s Attorney Douglas DiSabito, who won the Democratic and Republican primaries in August, was challenged by independent Joshua Martin. 
DiSabito had faced a drunken driving charge this spring that was eventually deferred to a court diversion program, ending prosecution for the charge.
In voting Tuesday, DiSabito easily won reelection to a fourth term with 2,981 votes compared to 1,019 votes for Martin, according to the unofficial results. 

READ MORE

Those were among the voting results Tuesday night from the contested elections for the 14 county state’s attorneys and 14 county sheriffs in Vermont.
In contested sheriff races, Claude Weyant, a Democrat, with 18,976 votes, finished ahead of Richard King, a Republican and lieutenant in the Windsor County Sheriff’s Department, who had 7,436 votes, according to unofficial results.
Weyant, the chief deputy of the Windsor County Sheriff’s Department, has been running the day-to-day operations of the office for the past several months. 
Sheriff Ryan Palmer stepped back from overseeing the day-to-day operations of the department earlier this year after his arrest on charges, including lewd and lascivious conduct. He has pleaded not guilty to the charges and did not seek reelection. 
In Franklin County, Chad Miles, a Republican and a captain in the department, won election to his first term as sheriff with 10,397 votes. Andre LaBier, who ran in the general election as a Democrat after failing to gain the Republican nomination in the August primary, had 9,929 votes, according to the unofficial results.
John Grismore, the incumbent Franklin County sheriff, did not seek reelection. He had his law enforcement certification revoked in 2023 over a use-of-force policy violation. 
Grismore had also been criminally charged in connection with that incident for allegedly kicking a person in custody. After two mistrials with jurors were unable to reach unanimous verdicts, the prosecutor dropped the case.
In the only other contested county sheriff race, Sean McRae, a Democrat, prevailed with 8,609 votes in Orange County, finishing ahead of Jacob Held, a Republican, with 5,316 votes, according to unofficial results.
Incumbent Orange County Sheriff George Contois did not seek reelection.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Kansas’ rate of children without health insurance tops national average for second year
description: Kansas' rate of uninsured children surpasses the U.S. average for the second consecutive year with 8.5% of Kansans under age 18 without access to coverage.
text:
Erica Andrade, president and CEO of El Centro, says Medicaid and CHIP, which is specifically designed to deliver health coverage to children, have been configured to deter enrollment. A new report says the portion of uninsured Kansas children increased for the second consecutive year. In this Oct. 8, 2024, image, Andrade speaks during a news conference in Kansas City, Kansas. (Photo by Tim Carpenter/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — More government red tape, the demise of COVID-19 benefits and anxiety about immigration crackdowns factor into a surge to 8.5% in the portion of Kansas children without health insurance in 2025.
It was the second consecutive year the American Community Survey published by the U.S. Census Bureau reported children younger than 19 who reside in Kansas were more likely to go without health insurance than children nationwide. The rate of uninsured children in Kansas climbed from 5.2% in 2022 to 7% in 2024, when the U.S. rate of children without health insurance stood at 6%. Nationally, the uninsured rate for kids bumped up to 6.2% in 2025.
Erica Andrade, president and CEO of the nonprofit El Centro, which focuses on improving lives of Latino residents in the Kansas City area, said some people assumed the rising percentage of children without health coverage in Kansas was because of the failure of Medicaid and the Children’s Health Insurance Program. CHIP is the joint state and federal initiative offering coverage to children in families earning too much to qualify for Medicaid but not enough to afford private insurance.
“They say, ‘Well, the system is broken,’ ” Andrade said during a forum Thursday hosted by the nonpartisan Kansas Health Foundation. “No, the system’s working perfectly fine. The system was designed to keep people from using public benefits.”
Andrade said aggressive immigration enforcement operations ordered by President Donald Trump prompted some parents in Kansas who knew their children qualified for Medicaid or CHIP to voluntarily disenroll or not apply for preventative health care services serving young people. One in four children living in the United States have at least one foreign-born or immigrant parent.
“We also serve a lot of mixed-status householders,” Andrade said. “Because of fear … people actually come in to decline, to withdraw, knowing their kids were eligible. We’ve had a few families that have asked to do that proactively just because of the fear and knowing what this possibly could mean for their families.”
Anne Dwyer, a research professor at Georgetown University’s Center for Children and Families, said Medicaid and CHIP enrollment fell nationally in 2025 and that preliminary data suggests the same transpired during the first half of 2026. The latest report says nine states, including Kansas shifting from 7% in 2024 to 8.5% in 2025, experienced meaningful escalation in the percentage of children without insurance, she said.
“Kansas did experience a statistically significant increase in the rate of uninsured children along with other states. Kansas is definitely notable, but it’s not alone,” Dwyer said. “Some children might be finding coverage elsewhere.”
Dwyer said shrinking enrollment in Kansas and other states was tied to escalating amounts of government red tape, the Trump administration’s decision not to embrace federal protections on coverage for children, parental confusion about work reporting requirements and the pending program cuts imposed by Congress and Trump.
Complicating the task of securing health insurance for children has been unwinding of COVID-19 policies that automatically sustained health coverage for U.S. children during the pandemic. In addition, there have been increases in health insurance premium rates for employer-sponsored policies and options in the Affordable Care Act Marketplace.
Sonder Crane, a pediatric physician in Manhattan and president of the Kansas chapter of the American Academy of Pediatrics, said uninsured children were more likely to miss out on preventative health care checkups that could catch illnesses early when maladies could be treated more effectively and less expensively. The lack of regular access to medical care among children promoted inconsistent vaccinations, he said.
“That is basic care that everybody should have accessible to them,” Crane said.
Crane said the growing health insurance problem in Kansas was also associated with parents who didn’t speak English as their first language, a wave of retirements among family physicians and the lack of easy geographic access to doctors for families residing in rural areas. Some patients in her Manhattan clinic drive an hour each way for routine appointments, she said.
In Kansas, the portion of uninsured children younger than 6 advanced from 3.7% in 2022 to 7.2% in 2024, federal reports said. The change in Kansas’ 6-18 age group was less severe, moving from 5.8% in 2022 to 7% in 2024.
The government reporting shows ethnic distinctions in terms of access to health insurance in Kansas. The rate of Hispanic children without coverage went from 8.6% in 2022 to 16.2% in 2024, while rates for Black children ticked up from 5.7% to 9.8% in that period. The percentage of white children in Kansas without health insurance increased from 6.8% in 2022 to 7.9% in 2024.
Kaci Cink, a senior analyst at the Kansas Health Institute in Topeka, said behind each insurance statistic were families grappling with medical challenges.
“These disparities raise important questions about why some populations are more likely to be uninsured than others,” she said.

title: Several Maine towns approve data center moratoriums on local ballots
description: After Gov. Janet Mills vetoed a temporary statewide data center moratorium earlier this year, voters in several Maine towns approved local ordinances this week.  Voters in Peru, a town in Oxford County, approved a 180-day moratorium on data center development and permitting. The local ballot question received 578 votes in support and 182 against, according [[...]
text:
An Amazon Web Services data center is shown situated near single-family homes. Some local and state officials across the country want to halt development of the facilities. (Photo by Nathan Howard/Getty Images)After Gov. Janet Mills vetoed a temporary statewide data center moratorium earlier this year, voters in several Maine towns approved local ordinances this week. 
Voters in Peru, a town in Oxford County, approved a 180-day moratorium on data center development and permitting. The local ballot question received 578 votes in support and 182 against, according to local results on the town website. 
Wiscasset voters also approved a measure to temporarily stop the town from accepting, processing, reviewing or approving applications for new or expanded data centers. Unless lifted earlier or extended, it would expire six months after enactment.
The Wiscasset moratorium got 1,363 votes in favor and 713 against. 
In York County, voters in Wells were asked if they want a 180-day moratorium on development of data centers 100,000 square feet or larger. Residents were resoundingly in favor of the measure, with 5,818 yes votes and 1,282 no votes. 
But not every moratorium was successful. In North Berwick, a ballot question that would have created an outright ban on data centers larger than 25,000 square feet failed. The measure got 738 votes in support and 1,698 votes against.

title: Tennessee voters adopt three constitutional amendments
description: Tennessee voters on Tuesday soundly approved three constitutional amendments that limit access to bail, expand victim rights and prohibit a statewide property. The vote counts for all three ballot initiatives on the ballot this year cleared the threshold set by the state to amend the state’s constitution: a majority vote in favor of the amendment […]
text:
Tennessee voters approved three constitutional amendments to limit access to bail, expand victim rights and bar statewide property taxes.  Pictured: Voters line up in a Clarksville poll during the last day of the early voting, Oct. 29. 2026. (Photo by John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)Tennessee voters on Tuesday soundly approved three constitutional amendments that limit access to bail, expand victim rights and prohibit a statewide property.
The vote counts for all three ballot initiatives on the ballot this year cleared the threshold set by the state to amend the state’s constitution: a majority vote in favor of the amendment that numerically surpasses half the total votes cast in the governor’s race. An estimated 1.2 million votes were cast for governor Tuesday, and each amendment garnered enough “yes” votes to pass, according to unofficial results by the Tennessee Secretary of State.
The amendments:
Amendment 1 allows a court to order pre-trial detention of a defendant without bail before trial if accused of a series of offenses. 
The offenses include crimes punishable by the death penalty, second degree murder, aggravated child rape, aggravated rape, grave torture, or any crime for which a convicted person would be required to serve 85% of their sentence — a criteria imposed on the most serious offenses. 
Judges have discretion: they are not required to deny bail for the charges, but they are mandated to provide a public record of their reasons for setting or denying bail for the offenses
The amendment passed 67% to 33%, according to unofficial vote tally by the Secretary of State. 
Amendment 2 prohibits the Tennessee General Assembly from imposing a state property tax. 
Tennessee has not had a statewide property tax since 1949, when the Legislature repealed one. 
The measure passed by a 67% to 33% margin, according to unofficial results. 
Amendment 3 creates new constitutional rights for crime victims. 
They include the right to fair treatment; to be informed about and participate in the parole process; to be protected from harassment, intimidation, and abuse; and to be informed of the minimum sentence the convicted criminal will serve and their scheduled date of release. 
Victims will also have the right to their own safety, their family’s safety and the public safety taken into account before a decision is made to release an individual convicted of a crime. They will have the right to be informed of a perpetrator’s release date and to have their safety, their family’s safety, and the public’s safety taken into account before any decision is made to release the convicted criminal.  
The amendment passed 76% to 24%, according to the unofficial vote results.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Arkansas Democrats say they have more leverage on budget after midterm results
description: Breaking Republicans’ supermajority in the Arkansas House will give Democrats more leverage to influence policy, including upcoming budget discussions, party leaders said Thursday.  Republican Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders, who won reelection Tuesday, will present her proposed balanced budget to lawmakers Friday morning. Arkansas Democrats flipped 11 legislati[...]
text:
Arkansas House Minority Leader Andrew Collins gives his party's assessment of the just concluded legislative session. Behind him are (left-right) Reps. Stephen Magie of Conway, Tippi McCullough of Little Rock, Jessie McGruder of Marion, Ashley Hudson of Little Rock and Jay Richardson of Fort Smith. (Photo by Sonny Albarado/Arkansas Advocate)Breaking Republicans’ supermajority in the Arkansas House will give Democrats more leverage to influence policy, including upcoming budget discussions, party leaders said Thursday. 
Republican Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders, who won reelection Tuesday, will present her proposed balanced budget to lawmakers Friday morning.
Arkansas Democrats flipped 11 legislative seats — 10 in the House and one in the Senate — during the midterm election. Republicans will have a 70-30 majority in the House during next year’s legislative session, so Democratic support will be needed for certain funding legislation.
With Arkansas Republicans’ House supermajority lost, a changed dynamic

Appropriations bills, which authorize government agency spending, require a three-fourths vote in the House and Senate. The only exception is the public schools appropriation, which requires a simple majority.
During a virtual call with reporters Thursday, House Minority Leader Andrew Collins said just because Democrats have more leverage doesn’t mean the party’s going to hold up appropriations bills.
Collins said Democrats will continue challenging policies they disagree with and looking for common ground with Republicans. 
“But if we continue to see some of the extreme legislation and bad policies come down that we have seen in the last few sessions, we’re not going to shy away from being vocal about that,” he said. “If that means contentious, that means contentious, but we have to stand up for the people we represent.”
During Sanders’ first term, controversial legislation that passed with only Republican support included a bill that created the state’s school voucher program and another that prohibits K-12 students from using bathrooms that do not match their gender assigned at birth.
Northwest Arkansas Democrat Rey Hernandez will become one of the House’s newest members after defeating Republican Rep. Rebecca Burkes on his third try for the House District 11 seat. 
As a Latino, veteran, senior citizen and cattle rancher, Hernandez said he’s looking forward to providing “representation for the minority populations that are hardworking Arkansans that need a voice in government.” 
Democrat Rey Hernandez speaks with guests at the annual Chickin, Peelin’ and Politickin’ event in downtown Springdale Oct. 6, 2022. (Photo by Antoinette Grajeda/Arkansas Advocate)
House District 11 includes portions of Benton and Washington counties, which will be represented by five of the 10 new Democratic House candidates. The Democratic Party of Benton County said in an emailed statement that voters sent a clear message that “the status quo will no longer be accepted.”
“In an election full of historic victories, we are proud to have flipped four state house seats and four justice of the peace seats,” the release said. “Every Democratic candidate who ran in Benton County demonstrated strength and a clear vision for the kind of Arkansas they hope to help create.”
Sanders’ spokesperson Sam Dubke said Wednesday that Arkansas remains a very conservative state with large Republican majorities in the Legislature.
“Governor Sanders will continue her focus on education, public safety, and tax cuts, but also looks forward to working with members of both parties when priorities align, like she has on free school breakfast, phone-free schools, and other bipartisan issues,” Dubke said.

name: Michigan Advance
title: MPSC sets December deadline for decision on Consumers Energy dam sales
description: Consumers Energy, one of the state’s largest energy utilities, has once again asked Michigan energy regulators to delay their decision on whether to approve a sale of 13 hydroelectric dams located throughout the state. While the Michigan Public Service Commission’s three members unanimously approved Consumers’ request to delay decision-making during their Th[...]
text:
Foote Dam in Iosco County, one of 13 hydroelectric dams proposed for sale by Consumers Energy. (Photo from Consumers Energy)Consumers Energy, one of the state’s largest energy utilities, has once again asked Michigan energy regulators to delay their decision on whether to approve a sale of 13 hydroelectric dams located throughout the state.
While the Michigan Public Service Commission’s three members unanimously approved Consumers’ request to delay decision-making during their Thursday meeting, Chair Dan Scripps stressed that this would be the final extension, unless a majority of the parties in the case agree to another.
“Any settlement agreement must be filed by 5 p.m. on Dec. 9, 2026, and any further extension of the waiver of the statutory deadline would require a stipulation from a majority of the parties to the proceeding that must be filed on that same date,” Scripps said.
If the parties do not reach a settlement, the commission will issue a final order at its Dec. 17 meeting, Scripps said.
Consumers Energy filed its first request to delay the commission’s decision on Sept. 8, stating it felt they could come to a constructive solution regarding some of the concerns raised by the parties opposing the sale.
However, the company’s call for a compromise was met with skepticism by multiple environmental and conservation organizations opposing the sale. Daniel Abrams, a senior associate attorney at the Environmental Law and Policy Center, wrote in opposition to the request, stating “This is not a case in which the parties are fully and deeply engaged in ongoing negotiations that are close to resolution.”
That skepticism had not faded when the company filed its latest request on Tuesday.
While Consumers Energy Attorney Bret Totoraitis said the company believes “there continues to be opportunity for a constructive settlement solution in this case that addresses the concerns raised during the course of the proceeding and wishes to continue to engage in negotiations to achieve such a solution,” Abrams disputed that assessment. 
Michigan AG urges state regulators to reject Consumers Energy dam sale

“Simply put, this case is not going to settle,” Abrams wrote in his response on behalf of Michigan Trout Unlimited, the Michigan Steelhead and Salmon Fishermen’s Association, Great Lakes Council of Fly Fishers International, Anglers of the Au Sable and the Michigan Hydro Relicensing Coalition.
Consumers Energy announced it had found a buyer for the collection of dams in 2025.
Under the conditions of the sale, Confluence Hydro – a subsidiary of Hull Street Energy, a Maryland-based private equity company – will purchase the dams for $1 each and enter a contract with Consumers Energy to provide them with power from the dams for 30 years.
However, several parties, including Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer and Attorney General Dan Nessel, have raised safety concerns around selling the dams, which were built between 1906 and 1935, to an out-of-state private equity company.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“These dams are powerful, and they can be dangerous when they’re not maintained,” Nessel told Michigan Advance in an Oct. 21 interview. “So any sale that takes 13 dams in Michigan out of the hands of a well-funded and highly regulated public utility, and then gives it to the interests of out-of-state private equity, we think, should be looked at very carefully and candidly, very skeptically.”
In a letter to the public service commission, Whitmer argued that the deal around the sale “lacks firm, enforceable protections to ensure the dams will be properly maintained and safely retired when they are no longer economical to operate.” 
“It does not require Hull Street Energy, the parent company, to cover all future repair, accident, environmental, and decommissioning costs, nor does it require adequately funded reserves to cover those expenses,” Whitmer wrote.
If it is unable to move forward with the sale, Consumers Energy has said the dams will be decommissioned, sparking concerns among the communities who use the waterways created by these dams.
However, Nessel told Michigan Advance that Consumers cannot make that decision on its own. 
“It would require entirely separate and lengthy cases before the MPSC, and the local communities get to have a say in that,” Nessel said. “But that wouldn’t be the case if they’re sold off to private equity.”
In an email following Thursday’s commission meeting, Consumers Energy Media Relations Manager Brian Wheeler told the Advance the company appreciates the commissioners’ decision to establish a timetable to reach a settlement.
“We understand the desire for communities and our coworkers to resolve this sale,” Chris Fultz, Consumers Energy’s senior vice president of electric supply said in a statement. “Today’s MPSC ruling keeps us on that path toward an agreement that will be a win for our customers, Michigan and the communities we care about.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: DeSoto County elects its first Black judges
description: Voters on Tuesday, Nov. 6, 2026, elected John Hughes as its first Black circuit judge and Gwen Baptist as its first chancery judge in DeSoto County. The election came months after a failed federal lawsuit tried to halt voting from subdivisions created last year through redistricting efforts carried out by the state Legislature. Additionally, lawmakers added [...]
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
DeSoto County voters elected the first Black circuit and chancery court judges to newly created positions from last year’s redistricting efforts. 
John Hughes, a Southaven attorney and Walls Municipal Court judge, received 61% of the vote to become a circuit court judge and Gwen Baptist, a Southaven attorney, received 51% of votes, to become a chancery judge, according to unofficial results. 
On Wednesday morning, both recognized how their wins made history and thanked supporters. 
Hughes said it was humbling to be both the first Black municipal judge and circuit judge to be elected in DeSoto County. 
“All citizens deserve a court that balance(s) fairness with the temperance of justice and compassion, when within reason,” Hughes wrote on his campaign Facebook page. “I am proud to be your humble public servant and neighbor.”
The circuit court is responsible for felony criminal prosecutions, which includes trials and sentencing. It also handles civil claims over $200 and hears appeals from the county and justice courts. 
Throughout her campaign, Baptist shared her family’s generational roots in DeSoto County and her connection to land, including a few videos of her on family land. In a message to supporters after Election Day, she said her father and grandfather had to conduct legal business outside the courthouse during the state’s Jim Crow era, but the win gives her the privilege to walk through the doors and serve from the bench.
“This victory is both a profound professional honor and an opportunity to honor my father, recognize the sacrifice of those who came before me and carry forward their legacy through service,” she wrote on Facebook.
The chancery court is responsible for wills and estates; adoption, child custody and divorce; and guardianships and conservatorships. The court can also approve final domestic abuse protection orders. 
The only countywide Black official in DeSoto is Sheriff Thomas E. Tuggle II, who was elected  in 2023. 
The milestone comes several months after a federal lawsuit challenged the creation of the majority Black subdistricts that eventually elected Baptist and Hughes.  
Last year, lawmakers redrew state court districts using the most recent 2020 U.S. Census data. In DeSoto County, one of the fastest growing counties in the state, lawmakers created the two majority Black subdistricts in parts of Horn Lake and Southaven. Black residents make up over a third of the county’s population. 
U.S. District Judge Sharion Aycock on Aug. 13 denied efforts by four DeSoto County residents, including county Supervisor Robert Foster, to prevent subdistrict of voters from electing the two countywide judges.
Foster argued that a small section of voters discriminated against white residents and that voting should be opened across the entire county. In her ruling, Aycock said the evidence presented at trial did not clearly point to race as the justification for the drawing of the judicial maps.
In the DeSoto case, Aycock ruled that just because race was referenced when the Legislature created the subdistrict and statistics show that it created a majority-Black subdistrict, it didn’t necessarily mean it was an unconstitutional gerrymander. 
She also noted that Rep. Dan Eubanks, a Republican from Walls, had testified that the Legislature added one circuit court judge and one chancery judge because the county needed help with the case backlog that stemmed from its growing population. 
Foster filed the lawsuit after the U.S. Supreme Court ruling in Louisiana v. Callais struck down a portion of the Voting Rights Act of 1965 that enabled the drawing of majority-minority districts. In Callais, the high court rejected Louisiana’s second majority Black congressional district, finding it relied too heavily on race and calling it an “unconstitutional gerrymander.”
That ruling has led to worries that Republican-led states would try to eliminate majority Black and Latino electoral districts. Some state lawmakers have called for the state’s only majority-Black congressional district to be eliminated.
Republican states including Mississippi began redistricting efforts after the Callais decision. The state Senate formed a redistricting study committee that traveled across the state to hear from residents about redistricting. 
Redistricting is also expected to be taken up during the 2027 legislative session that starts in January. 
DeSoto County previously faced a lawsuit that alleged its 2022 electoral map diluted Black voting power in county office elections and called for creation of majority-Black districts. In June, a federal judge dismissed the lawsuit, finding the plaintiffs didn’t provide enough proof that maps were drawn to intentionally dilute Black voting power.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: I-195 to close overnight Friday to demolish East Providence bridge
description: Despite heavy rain in the weather forecast, a stretch of Interstate 195 in East Providence is scheduled to close in both directions overnight Friday as crews demolish the Potter Street Bridge. The Rhode Island Department of Transportation (RIDOT) plans to close I-195 near the Taunton Avenue exit at 10 p.m. Friday, with all lanes expected […]
text:
Traffic on I-195 West at Exit 2B in East Providence is shown on Thursday, Nov. 5, at 3:53 p.m. (Photo via Rhode Island Department of Transportation Camera)Despite heavy rain in the weather forecast, a stretch of Interstate 195 in East Providence is scheduled to close in both directions overnight Friday as crews demolish the Potter Street Bridge.
The Rhode Island Department of Transportation (RIDOT) plans to close I-195 near the Taunton Avenue exit at 10 p.m. Friday, with all lanes expected to reopen by noon Saturday. The demolition is part of the state’s ongoing Washington Bridge rebuild project, which is expected to be complete by November 2028.
Over the next 12 to 18 months, RIDOT plans to rebuild the Potter Street Bridge to accommodate a wider highway corridor and additional travel lanes on I-195 West. 
The closure will require I-195 East traffic to detour at Exit 1D, Warren Avenue, and follow Warren Avenue for  1 mile to the on-ramp to return to I-195 East. Traffic on I-195 West will detour at Exit 2, Broadway, to Warren Avenue for approximately ¾ of a mile to the on-ramp toward I-195 West, which is being temporarily opened to be used for this detour.
Interim Department of Transportation Director Robert Rocchio said the lowest traffic volume of the week occurs during the closure hours and expressed hope that the public has more flexibility to avoid traveling in the area.
“We’re counting on at least 30% of the traffic that typically drives over 195 at this location to divert,” Rocchio said at a noon press conference Friday at the department’s headquarters. “If they don’t, it’s going to be significant congestion so we need the public’s help. We apologize for any convenience this causes you.”
East Providence Mayor Bob DaSilva said 30 extra police and traffic control personnel will be working along Warren Avenue corridor to keep traffic from side roads from interfering with traffic. An extra rescue will be on service during the closure hours as well, DaSilva said.
The mayor called the work a “necessary inconvenience” but said local businesses along Warren Avenue may benefit from the increased traffic flowing by.
“Communication has been very good. DOT went out there and leafletted the whole area, neighborhoods, homes, businesses,” DaSilva said. 
The National Weather Service has issued a flood watch for Rhode Island from 4 a.m. Friday through 10 a.m. Saturday. Approximately 2 to 4 inches of rain could fall across the region, with a low risk of isolated areas receiving 5 to 6 inches.
Excessive runoff could cause flooding in rivers, streams and other low-lying areas, particularly in urban areas where storm drains and ditches may become clogged with leaf debris.
RIDOT spokesperson Charles St. Martin wrote in an email Thursday the department is still moving forward with the demolition.
“Typically, heavy rain does not affect demolition activities,” St. Martin wrote.
DaSilva said the rain will help minimize noise and dust from the demolition work.
