title: Flores selected as new Nevada Senate majority leader
description: Democratic State Sen. Edgar Flores was selected as the next Senate Majority Leader, the Nevada Senate Democratic Caucus announced Thursday.  Flores, an immigration attorney, was first elected to the state Senate in 2022 and previously served in the Assembly.  “Our state faces urgent challenges, and working-class Nevadans are counting on us to deliver real so[...]
text:
Democratic state Sen. Edgar Flores. (Photo: Trevor Bexon/Nevada Current)Democratic State Sen. Edgar Flores was selected as the next Senate Majority Leader, the Nevada Senate Democratic Caucus announced Thursday. 
Flores, an immigration attorney, was first elected to the state Senate in 2022 and previously served in the Assembly. 
“Our state faces urgent challenges, and working-class Nevadans are counting on us to deliver real solutions from expanding access to affordable housing and health care to investing in our neighborhood public schools and making sure our economy works for everyday people,” Flores said in a statement. “I am excited to get to Carson City and work with our colleagues in the Assembly and Governor-elect Aaron Ford to build a Nevada where every community has the resources and opportunities to thrive.”
He will replace current Nevada State Senate Majority Leader Nicole Cannizzaro, who won her race to be Nevada’s next attorney general.
Flores won his general election bid, which was uncontested. He earlier had faced a tough primary election this year against North Las Vegas City Councilman Isaac Baron. 
The election centered around failed efforts by state lawmakers to massively expand the state’s existing film tax credit program, which Cannizzaro supported, Flores opposed. 
The $1.8 billion subsidy would have been tied to a planned film and production studio in the Summerlin neighborhood of Las Vegas. Legislative staff warned the proposal would lead the State of Nevada’s general fund off a fiscal cliff.
The proposal died in the Senate, falling short by just one vote.
Labor unions warned those opposed to the bill that there would be political consequences and Laborer’s Local 872 funneled a combined $20,000 to Barron’s campaign to unseat Flores.
Flores beat Barron with nearly 55% of the vote.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: MWRA pulls largest water transfer request in history after drawing backlash from Quabbin communities
description: The MWRA’s request landed the agency in even more hot water among Quabbin communities, which mobilized to kill the proposal.
text:
THE STATE’S BIGGEST drinking water provider has nixed a groundbreaking request to draw an additional 20 million gallons of water per day out of the Quabbin Reservoir in a nod to the outrage it prompted within central Massachusetts communities. 
The Massachusetts Water Resources Authority, which serves 61 municipalities mostly in and around Greater Boston, had pursued its plan — by far the largest withdrawal request in its history — in order to meet growing demand from new communities like Weymouth and Wayland looking to join the system.  
But in addition to the size of its proposal, which totaled 10 percent of average annual demand, the agency faced fierce backlash for the process it deployed to win approval from state regulators at the Water Resources Commission. The proposal added fuel to an escalating feud with the small rural towns surrounding the Quabbin and their representatives on Beacon Hill.  
Water transfers like the one the MWRA pitched here are governed by the 40-year-old Interbasin Transfer Act, in which state officials ensure that the move is environmentally sound and meets demonstrated need for both what’s known as the donor basin, the resource sending water elsewhere, and the receiving basin, or the area taking in more water. 
Yet for the first time in state history, the MWRA sought the greenlight from state regulators on its donor basin proposal separately, before any receiving basin requests that may come in the future in an effort to streamline the process and cut red tape. If advanced, the MWRA could have had donor basin approvals in hand by the time new communities attempt to receive the water and join the system. 
“It is clear that the use of that regulatory option added to confusion and concern, rather than allaying it,” Stephen Estes-Smargiassi, MWRA’s interim executive director, wrote in a letter to the Water Resources Commission on Thursday.  
Estes-Smargiassi said the agency will “commit” to returning to the traditional process under the law, in which donor basin and receiving basin analyses are considered simultaneously.  
But the decision may not kill the underlying drive to win approval for future requests to support system expansion.  
Jonathan Gulliver, who was recently named the agency’s full-time executive director, supports withdrawing the request and “pursuing a more focused submission that addresses the demonstrated needs of the communities currently seeking admission to the MWRA system,” according to the letter.  
The MWRA’s request landed the agency in even more hot water among Quabbin communities, which mobilized to kill the proposal.  
Those small towns themselves don’t drink water from the reservoir, creating a cruel irony as private and municipal wells near the largest water body in the state dried up and towns instituted water restrictions during recent years’ record drought while MWRA customers faced few limits. 
Plus, these communities are barred from developing — and therefore taxing — large sections of land around the reservoir to protect the water source from which they don’t benefit. The glaringly little state compensation they do receive for stewarding that land has further laid bare the intense fiscal shortfalls those towns confront as they cut public school workers, consolidate emergency services, and navigate local water crises of their own that in some cases render municipal buildings unusable.  
To these towns, the MWRA’s water transfer request could feel more like an end run to expedite its expansion efforts in the eastern part of the state than a legitimate push to reduce bureaucracy.  
Sen. Jo Comerford, who represents the Quabbin towns at the State House and is spearheading legislative reforms to boost payments to these communities and grant them a permanent seat on the MWRA board, said in a statement that the agency’s decision to pull back its transfer request is a “powerful recognition of the significant concerns” the towns raised. 
“Arm in arm with statewide partners, constituents and the state legislative delegation showed up, raised our voices, and made clear that regional equity, the voices of watershed communities, and a shared potable water future must be centered in all decisions involving the Quabbin Reservoir,” Comerford said. 
Gov. Maura Healey, who won a second term Tuesday, sided with the Quabbin communities’ concerns earlier this year — even though the MWRA argued the transfer request would help meet ambitious state housing goals that Healey has stressed are necessary to tackle a sweeping affordability crisis.
“Every day, these watershed communities provide an invaluable public service to the communities served by the MWRA system,” Healey wrote in a letter to the agency. “They continue to help protect the watershed’s natural resources while navigating infrastructure constraints, including limitations on their own water supply and economic development.” 
Even with this transfer request off the table, Gulliver will step into the top spot at the MWRA in January amid major expansion plans and continued discontent from the communities surrounding the agency’s main water source.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: War, high prices, typical midterm backlash spurred NJ GOP losses, party says
description: Republicans took a drubbing nationally and lost two of their three New Jersey House seats Tuesday. Now they're asking why.
text:
Republicans took a drubbing nationally and lost two of their three New Jersey House seats Tuesday. GOP officials say high prices and the Iran War are to blame. (Photo by Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder)New Jersey’s top Republican party official said a dour national political climate and economic fallout from the Iran War helped seed the party’s broad losses Tuesday, but she said it is too soon to chart the GOP’s course into the future.
The electoral losses cost New Jersey Republicans two of their three House seats and cemented for national Democrats their largest congressional majorities in nearly 20 years.
“I would say that it’s, No. 1., you have the midterm backlash, which is normal, and then on top of that, you have a war, you have high gas prices,” said Republican State Chair Christine Hanlon, who is also Monmouth County clerk. “I don’t think it’s too difficult to look at what was going on, to come up with the reasons why people were not happy.”
Democrats must deliver on their affordability promises

On Tuesday, Democrats swept congressional races across the country. They won at least 54 seats in the Senate and have claimed at least 247 seats in the House, a feat not seen since a wave of Democrats entered Congress on President Barack Obama’s coattails in 2008.
New Jersey Republicans’ losses included House seats held by Reps. Tom Kean Jr. and Jeff Van Drew, as well as losses further down the ballot, including for county offices in Monmouth, Cumberland, and Morris counties.
Republicans had been bracing for Kean’s loss to Democrat Rebecca Bennett but were stunned when Van Drew was ousted by Zack Mullock, the Democratic mayor of Cape May City.
Sen. Jon Bramnick (R-Union), a frequent and longtime critic of President Donald Trump, said Trump’s brand is corrosive in New Jersey, adding that Republicans need to return to moderation and fiscal conservatism. Trumpism “just doesn’t work in New Jersey,” he said.
“Stop making excuses. Stop blaming fraud in voting and start to accept the fact that you win when you follow traditional Republican values,” he said.



Quotation







Right now, we’re at the point of not being a viable entity, and we can’t let that happen.


– Ocean County Republican Chair George Gilmore


Bramnick has for years sparred with Trump allies in New Jersey over whose brand of Republicanism is more favored in the Garden State.
The president’s allies were sure they won that argument in 2024, when Trump came closer to winning New Jersey in that year’s presidential election than any other Republican in decades, but the following year the party’s Trump-supporting gubernatorial candidate lost in a landslide.
Hanlon acknowledged decisions made in Washington, D.C., had a “real impact” on New Jersey’s races but said Republicans need to regroup first before looking forward. The state party had limited success getting its own messaging out, she conceded.
“Our legislators have been banging the drum,” she said, adding, “We’ve been trying to have a New Jersey message, and it kind of gets drowned out in the national. “
Ocean County Republican Chair George Gilmore likewise acknowledged Trump contributed to Tuesday’s results, but said the GOP needs to do a better job of matching candidates to districts and financially supporting its office seekers.
Further, the disparate Republican campaign arms need to better coordinate their plans and spending, both to keep hold of GOP ground that has progressively shrunk over the last two years and bolster Republican organizations whose control has waned in counties like Bergen and Somerset.
“What I want to see is progress all the way around, in the Senate, in the Assembly, in the state committee, and among the county chairs to work together to make the Republican Party viable again,” Gilmore said. “Right now, we’re at the point of not being a viable entity, and we can’t let that happen.”
For Bramnick, the path forward is a clean break with Trump, even if that split proves electorally costly for members in heavily Republican districts, like those based in Ocean County or the state’s northwest.
“They have to get over self-preservation and start thinking about the Republican Party as a whole in New Jersey,” Bramnick said. “I don’t know how you do that. People have to be selfless, and they have to say, ‘Look, here are the results. Stop.’”
The Republican Party has limited time to find its path forward. Every seat in the New Jersey Legislature — that’s 40 in the State Senate and 80 in the General Assembly — is up for a vote next year. Democrats, who control the Senate 25-15 and the Assembly 57-23, have controlled the Legislature for more than two decades.
Bramnick’s anti-Trump stance has already drawn a 2027 primary challenge from Peapack-Gladstone Councilman Conor Sweeney. Bramnick represents the 21st Legislative District.
Gilmore said Republicans need to adapt their candidates to the districts they are running in, warning that Sweeney could win that primary but could cost Republicans the district’s Senate seat in the general election.
The 21st is a suburban district long targeted by Democrats. Last year, Democrats ousted Republican Assembly members there, marking Democrats’ first win in the district since 1989.
“Don’t tell me there’s going to be some miracle wave that comes into everybody’s mind and in Bramnick’s district they’re going to vote conservative next year,” Gilmore said. “It’s not going to happen, so why set yourself up for failure?”

name: Maine Morning Star
title: Former Republican senator and tribal ambassador to lead Pingree’s transition team
description: Governor-elect Hannah Pingree announced leaders of her transition team Thursday as she prepares to take over the Blaine House, including former Republican state Sen. Roger Katz and former Penobscot Ambassador Maulian Bryant. Katz and Bryant will serve as co-chairs of Pingree’s transition committee and help identify candidates to hire for her cabinet. Their a[...]
text:
Maulian Bryant speaks at a rally on Indigenous Peoples’ Day at the Maine State House in Augusta on Oct. 9, 2023. (Photo by Jim Neuger/ Maine Morning Star)Governor-elect Hannah Pingree announced leaders of her transition team Thursday as she prepares to take over the Blaine House, including former Republican state Sen. Roger Katz and former Penobscot Ambassador Maulian Bryant.
Katz and Bryant will serve as co-chairs of Pingree’s transition committee and help identify candidates to hire for her cabinet. Their appointment may signal how Pingree intends to deliver on her campaign promises to work across the aisle and prioritize tribal sovereignty.
Both “bring the experience and judgment I want at the table as we build this administration,” Pingree said in a statement. She added that she will look for leaders who “put results first and reflect the best of Maine: integrity, accountability, public service, and shared optimism about improving the lives of Maine people.”
The transition team announcement does not mention Katz’s party affiliation. When asked about it, Pingree spokesperson Mary-Erin Casale said, “former state Senator Katz and the governor-elect have a long-standing relationship.” 
“She’s proud to have him on her team,” she added.
It’s unclear if Katz still identifies as a Republican. In 2024, he co-chaired a “Republicans for Harris” coalition, endorsing former Vice President Kamala Harris over President Donald Trump. His association with Pingree goes back much further: in 2014, they started a TV show together to discuss topics from welfare reform to gun control.
Pingree was endorsed by the Wabanaki Alliance, which Bryant leads as executive director. In October, she was among the tribal leaders who said that they are optimistic about the future of the relationship with the state. Outgoing Gov. Janet Mills, also a Democrat, had opposed sweeping change, though Pingree has committed to restoring full sovereignty. 
“No more compromises,” Bryant said during the alliance’s annual gathering last month. “We’re going for it.”  
The governor-elect’s professional staff transition team will be led by co-directors Scott Ogden and Karen Geraghty. Ogden, who served most recently as former deputy chief of staff to Mills, will coordinate “personnel decisions, legislative and policy agenda development, stakeholder engagement, and day to day operations,” the statement said.
Geraghty, former mayor of Portland who led philanthropy at Planned Parenthood of Northern New England, will direct planning of the inaugural event in January 2027.
“This transition team brings the energy, experience, optimism, and determination we need to tackle the challenges ahead,” Pingree said in a statement. “We’re ready to get things done to improve the lives of Maine people at an urgent moment.”

text:
"I Voted" stickers, designed by New Hampshire fourth and fifth graders, line the railings outside Webster Elementary School in Manchester. (Photo by Maya Mitchell/New Hampshire Bulletin)In these first days of a new political era, the simplest explanation for what transpired on Election Day is also the most common one: The American people have rejected the Trump administration’s Iran war, and they are sick of getting squeezed by the price of gasoline, groceries, healthcare, childcare, housing, college, and on and on.
If that is in fact what spurred the American rebuke of the Republican Party this week, from coast to coast and up and down ballots, this was a largely reactionary election. A potential blip, but a profound one nonetheless.
I wonder, though, whether the shift in New Hampshire runs deeper. It’s possible that voters delivered a verdict not only on war and high prices but also on two core tenets of modern American conservatism: one, that in order for most to prosper some must be made to suffer; and, two, that making sure the rich get ever-richer serves the best interests of families and the working classes.
It’s possible that the people have had enough of cruelty, enough of the greed-fueled myth of trickle-down economics. 
Over the past decade, New Hampshire Republican legislative majorities have frequently practiced each of those forms of exploitation. With their policies, they have helped drive this callous era by painting bull’s-eyes on the backs of immigrants, poor people, LGBTQ+ people, public school teachers, medical professionals, and others. They have also exerted downward pressure on low- and middle-income New Hampshire residents through tax cuts and repeals, universal school vouchers, an embarrassing pittance of a minimum wage, and fresh burdens on low-income Granite Staters, among countless examples.  
For years, the rhetoric and behavior of New Hampshire’s Republican legislative leaders have been at odds with the New Hampshire I experience daily, the New Hampshire where I grew up. Because this is not a cruel state filled with uncharitable people, I have spent a good part of my adult life wondering why so many cruel and uncharitable people were elected to pass cruel and uncharitable bills — all while ignoring the state’s fundamental challenges.
My hope is that Tuesday marks the end of broad bewilderment.
The responsibility on the soon-to-be Democratic legislative majorities in the State House is undoubtedly enormous. They are being asked not only to take New Hampshire in a new direction but to simultaneously seek opportunities to work with Republican Gov. Kelly Ayotte, who survived her party’s bloodbath and will now serve a second term.
There are a lot of areas for cooperation between the Legislature and the governor’s office, and I suspect that a majority of New Hampshire residents would like to see plenty of it. 
Despite Ayotte’s narrow and rigid perception of what gives New Hampshire its imagined advantage over New England neighbors, she seems sincere in her desire to ease housing and childcare burdens, and each is a good place to start in a budget year. If U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders can envision avenues of cooperation with President Donald Trump, I’m confident Democratic leaders in New Hampshire can find common ground with the more moderate Ayotte. 
They will, of course, have to go around her at times, and they’re already eyeing a couple of spots to do just that. Cannabis should be legal in a state that has no moral qualms about promoting gambling and lining its highways with liquor stores, and so Democrats should force the issue. (Not for nothing, I would encourage Ayotte to ask her police officer friends who poses a greater public safety risk in general, a drunk person or a stoned person.) Democrats should also restore the Interest and Dividends Tax — the repeal of which almost exclusively benefited the top 20% of income earners — and direct that revenue toward investments in childcare, affordable housing, and countless other areas of structural crisis.
And, should the New Hampshire Democratic Party finally see fit to encourage a robust gubernatorial primary in 2028 rather than appointing a nominee, maybe the state can at long last find a candidate willing to address its greatest challenge: a thoroughly broken and inequitable school funding system.
If the people of New Hampshire are truly sick of high property taxes, while also recognizing that destroying public education is no kind of solution, they’ll have to rise above this state’s entrenched political myopia. They’ll have to raze New Hampshire’s monuments to economic myth — if for no other reason than to have long-delayed revenue conversations that place living people over rote ideology.
It’s doubtful those meaningful conversations will take place in earnest anytime soon, but Tuesday certainly felt like a step in the right direction.
New Hampshire voters set out to hire builders this week, so let the building begin.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Sixth measles-associated death in Pa. recorded in Jefferson County
description: The state Health Department on Wednesday confirmed that an unvaccinated person in Jefferson County who tested positive for measles has died. It’s the second death related to the highly contagious virus in the county.
text:
The measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine, administered in two doses, is 97% effective. (Photo by Courtney Bell/Oklahoma Voice)Pennsylvania recorded its sixth measles death of the year as the outbreak that has sickened nearly 1,500 mostly unvaccinated people grows.
The state Health Department on Wednesday confirmed that an unvaccinated person in Jefferson County who tested positive for measles has died. It’s the second death related to the highly contagious virus in the county. 
Citing the privacy of the deceased person and their family, the department said it would not release any other details that could identify them. Jefferson County Coroner Greg Furlong said he also could not release information about the person.
Another death in Franklin County reported by that county’s coroner as a possible measles case does not meet the criteria to be considered measles-related, state health officials said. 
A University of Utah clinic in Salt Lake City displays a sign warning about measles last year.  (Photo by McKenzie Romero/Utah News Dispatch)
To be considered a result of measles, a death must occur within 30 days of symptoms beginning with clinical evidence of a measles infection and a positive test. The death must also not be attributable to unrelated causes such as a motor vehicle accident. Other factors including whether a person was exposed to a confirmed measles infection and supporting medical records are also considered.
The department said it is working with coroners across the state to improve communication and refine reporting standards as the outbreak continues.
Measles is a highly contagious respiratory virus that can cause serious long- and short-term complications including pneumonia and swelling of the brain. The measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine, administered in two doses, is 97% effective. 
Among the 1,467 cases recorded in Pennsylvania, only five people who are fully vaccinated have been infected, the Health Department said.
State health center staff have provided more than 6,800 MMR vaccinations at pop-up vaccination clinics in the affected communities. The department also reported a surge in vaccination by health care providers, with 61,000 doses administered in October, compared to 25,000 in a typical month. 
The MMR vaccine is available by contacting a health care provider, a pharmacy, county or municipal health department, DOH State Health Center, Federally Qualified Health Centers (FQHCs), or a Vaccines for Children (VFC) program. 
People who may have been exposed to measles and have symptoms should contact their doctor or call the Department of Health at 877-PA-HEALTH.

name: National
title: Young home shoppers still priced out without help, according to survey
description: The age of the typical first-time homebuyer last year remained stuck at a historic high of 40 years old as younger people continue to get the worst of brutally high prices and interest rates in much of the country. That’s according to new data from the National Association of Realtors, and it’s the second year […]
text:
A workman paints a door at a house under contract in Nanuet, N.Y. New York was ranked last and Indiana first among states for affordability and home building by a realtors.com report this year. (Photo by Tim Henderson/Stateline)The age of the typical first-time homebuyer last year remained stuck at a historic high of 40 years old as younger people continue to get the worst of brutally high prices and interest rates in much of the country.
That’s according to new data from the National Association of Realtors, and it’s the second year in a row that the median price of first-time buyers was 40, after being as low as 28 years old in 1991. 
An increasing number of first-time homebuyers are using all cash rather than taking a mortgage, and those are even older, typically 54, said Jessica Lautz, the association’s deputy chief economist and vice president of research. Cash purchases are usually because of inheritances or other family help. 
“That’s actually 1 in 10 first-time buyers, so we’re really seeing that generational transfer of wealth,” Lautz said of cash offers. Repeat homebuyers also remained at a median 62 years old, also an all-time high, according to the report. 
First-time homebuyers face hurdles despite gradual improvement

The Bay Area near San Francisco is an area where prices are still escalating because of the AI boom, Lautz said, though some Rust Belt areas and states building a lot of housing are seeing more reasonable prices. 
A realtor.com report in June ranked Indiana, Iowa, South Carolina, Texas, North Carolina and Nebraska highest for affordability and homebuilding rates, based on prices compared to income and new building permits. 
At the bottom: New York, Massachusetts, Rhode Island, Hawaii and California. 
Including cash sales is one reason the National Association of Realtors’ survey of homebuyers found a higher median age than other surveys, such as the New York Federal Reserve Bank’s review of mortgage applications, Lautz said. 
The Federal Reserve pegs the median age at 33 for first-time buyers for the first six months of 2026, said Yanling Mayer, a research economist for the Texas Real Estate Research Center at Texas A&M University. That’s about the same as in 2019, while the Realtors’ association survey — which includes cash purchases —  recorded a jump from 33 years old in 2019, to 40 for the past two years. 
“We’re certainly not brushing aside the challenges facing first-time homebuyers,” Mayer said. “Are they finding other means to achieve home ownership? Help from family, help from friends?” 
There were several surveys last year that generally showed first-time buyers at between 35 and 40 years old and getting older, said Eric Finnigan, vice president of demographics research for John Burns Research and Consulting.
“The answer is probably somewhere in the middle,” Finnigan said.
Stateline reporter Tim Henderson can be reached at thenderson@stateline.org.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Former Hinds DA Jody Owens sentenced to 41 months after pleading guilty to corruption
description: Former Hinds County District Attorney Jody Owens in June 2026.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
A federal judge sentenced former Hinds County District Attorney Jody Owens to 41 months in prison, nearly two years to the day after federal prosecutors brought bribery charges against him, former Jackson Mayor Chokwe Antar Lumumba and former Jackson City Councilmember Aaron Banks.
Owens must also pay a fine of $100,000 and serve three years probation, U.S. District Judge Daniel P. Jordan III ruled Thursday afternoon. 
The judge called his decision “somber” and said he believed Owens still had a bright future. 
“I actually think the future you have in front of you is better than the one that you were going down,” he said.
Banks was expected to be sentenced later Thursday afternoon, while Lumumba’s sentencing will conclude later this month.
Other Jacksonians ensnared in the case have yet to be sentenced, including former Jackson City Councilmember Angelique Lee and Owens’ cousin, Sherik “Marve” Smith.
Lumumba attended Thursday’s hearing to register objections to his presentencing report, which judges use to help determine what punishment a defendant gets.
The judge had previously set Nov. 20 for the conclusion of the former mayor’s sentencing hearing but on Thursday foreshadowed that Lumumba could spend between 37 and 46 months in prison.
Former Jackson City Councilmember Aaron Banks heads into the Thad Cochran U.S. Courthouse for his sentencing hearing, Thursday, Nov. 5, 2026, in Jackson. Credit: Vickie D. King/Mississippi Today
Federal prosecutors indicted Owens, Lumumba and Banks on Nov. 7, 2024, after years of investigating suspected wrongdoing in Jackson. Mississippi Today previously reported that the capital city caught the attention of federal authorities during a yearslong conflict between Lumumba and the Jackson City Council over the selection of a garbage collection vendor. 
No charges ever arose from that matter. Instead, the U.S. Department of Justice launched a sting operation in 2023 and deployed two undercover FBI agents to pose as out-of-state real estate developers seeking to build a convention center hotel in downtown Jackson. 
Former Jackson Mayor Chokwe Antar Lumumba enters the Thad Cochran U.S. Courthouse for a sentencing hearing, Thursday, Nov. 5, 2026, in Jackson. Credit: Vickie D. King/Mississippi Today
Owens wound up going into business with them, serving as an intermediary to Lumumba, Banks and other Jackson officials, according to the federal indictment. 
The DA was a registered agent for the developers’ company in Mississippi, organized a Fort Lauderdale, Florida, fundraiser for Lumumba on their behalf, and used his campaign account to pay off Lee’s campaign debt to a local printing company, allegedly in exchange for her future vote.
Owens also hired Banks’ daughter for an internship at the DA’s office that prosecutors allege was funded by the purported developers.
Owens, whose family has helped develop parts of southern Hinds County, was elected district attorney in 2019.
Banks, who was deemed indigent by the federal judge, represented Ward 6 in south Jackson from 2017 to 2025. A political organizer, he started working for the city during Lumumba’s father’s mayoral administration in 2013.
Owens, Banks, Lumumba and their attorneys sat together on the right side of the courtroom. The gallery was sparse, and Lumumba’s supporters left shortly after the judge took the former mayor’s objections to the presentencing report.The proceedings began with lengthy arguments over the defendants’ presentencing reports from Lumumba and Banks. Presentence reports are sealed, but arguments over the information included in the document for each defendant showed the facts of the case remain murky. 
Despite having pleaded guilty over the summer, the three former Jackson officials and a federal prosecutor appeared at times to be relitigating the exact nature of their scheme. 
As Jordan evaluated Lumumba’s objections, the judge noted the mayor had taken a $50,000 bribe from Owens in exchange for moving up the city’s bid deadline. 
“The ask was to move the date of the RFQ,” Jordan said, referring to so-called requests for quotations, which is part of the project bidding process. 
Not so, responded Dave Fulcher, the federal prosecutor leading the case. 
“That is a strawman that has been set up by Lumumba’s counsel,” he said. “The bribery scheme was not, ‘We need him to move the RFQ.’ The bribery scheme was, ‘We need him involved.’”

name: Delaware
title: Important games across the state in Delaware High School Football’s penultimate weekend
description: The penultimate week in Delaware High School Football’s regular season begins this weekend (November 6 and 7) with critical matchups across the DIAA’s three classifications.   The Delaware High School Football postseason is fast approaching with only two weeks of regular season competition remaining. There are only a couple opportunities for teams on the pla[...]
text:
Smyrna sophomore, Terrell Ingram, runs the ball against Red Lion in the Eagles first game of the season. Photo credit: Dave Reeder
The penultimate week in Delaware High School Football’s regular season begins this weekend (November 6 and 7) with critical matchups across the DIAA’s three classifications.
 
The Delaware High School Football postseason is fast approaching with only two weeks of regular season competition remaining. There are only a couple opportunities for teams on the playoff bubble to earn their way into the state tournament and only a couple shots for teams trying to win their district and a top-seed in the postseason. 
With that being said, here are a few games throughout the state to keep an eye on:
Class 3A:
Smyrna vs Dover @ Dover at 6:00 p.m. on Friday, November 6
The Eagles are currently 3-0 in the Class 3A District Two standings and can win the district with a win against the Senators. Cape Henlopen and Caesar Rodney are both 2-1 in District Two, but Smyrna defeated both of them this season, giving the Eagles the tiebreaker should they all have the same record at the conclusion of the regular season.
Middletown vs Hodgson @ Middletown at 7:00 p.m. on Friday, November 6
Middletown’s win over Salesianum last week put the Cavaliers in the top spot of the Class 3A District One standings. The Cavaliers are undefeated in district play and have two more games against district opponents this season — Hodgson and Appoquinimink. The Cavaliers’ will most likely have to clinch the District One title when they face the Jaguars on November 13, but there is a chance they clinch the district this weekend. Middletown would need to win on Friday and Appoquinimink to lose on Saturday against William Penn. The Cavaliers hold the tiebreaker over Salesianum.    
Class 2A:
Archmere vs Tower Hill @ Tower at 6:00 p.m. Friday, November 6
The Auks and Howard Wildcats are both 3-0 in Class 2A District One. The Tower Hill Hillers sit behind them in the standings at 2-1 and could play an integral role in how the district shakes out. 
Should Tower Hill defeat Archmere on Friday, the Hillers would own the tiebreaker over the Auks. The Wildcats have already defeated the Hillers this season and Archmere and Howard play each other on November 14 during the regular season’s final week. All three of the teams could end the regular season with a 4-1 district record in which case the determination of who wins the district would come down to a series of tiebreakers that includes head-to-head matchups, overall winning percentage and fewest points allowed per game. With a win and a pair of Wildcats losses, Tower Hill could win the district outright. 
Archmere will not be able to clinch the district this week no matter the outcome of this week’s games. 
Odessa senior Thomas Ngateh leaps into the air and focuses on catching the ball for an interception against the Newark Charter Patriots earlier this season. Photo Credit: Dave Reeder
St. Mark’s vs Odessa @ Odessa at 7:00 p.m. on Friday, November 6
The Spartans own a Class 2A District Two record of 2-1 tied with Delaware Military Academy and a game behind the district leader Red Lion Christian Academy. The Red Lions lead the district with a 3-0 record. The Spartans and Red Lions play each other in the final week of the regular season.
Similarly to the scenario in Class 2A District One, should the Spartans win their next two games and finish with a 4-1 record alongside DMA and Red Lion there would be a three-way tie for the district winner. DMA defeated St. Mark’s earlier this season and Red Lion defeated DMA last week. Red Lion’s remaining schedule includes Polytech and St. Mark’s. DMA finishes the season with games against Milford and Odessa. 
The district champion will come down to the results of the final week of the regular season.
Lake Forest vs Woodbridge @ Lake Forest at 7:00 p.m. on Friday, November 6
The Lake Forest Spartans currently lead the Class 2A District Three standings with a 3-0 district record and 7-1 overall record. The Spartans have a chance to clinch the district title if they win their matchup against the Blue Raiders on Friday and Indian River is defeated in its week nine game against Delmar. Should Indian River win in this scenario, the district would come down to the final game of the regular season when Lake Forest plays Indian River.
There is also a scenario in which Woodbridge comes out atop the district three standings. The Blue Raiders would have to win both their games against Lake Forest and Sussex Tech and the Indians would have to lose one of their next two games. Sussex Tech could win the district with a pair of Lake Forest losses and a pair of wins against Laurel and Woodbridge.  
Class 1A:  
Concord vs John Dickinson @ Concord at 10:30 a.m. on Saturday, November 7
The Concord Raiders and Brandywine Bulldogs are tied for the top spot in the Class 1A District One standings with 3-0 district records. Dickinson remains a game behind the pair with a district record of 2-1, the lone loss to Brandywine. Neither the Raiders nor Bulldogs can clinch a district crown during this weekend, but Dickinson could fall out of the race with a loss to the Raiders. A Concord win would make their game against the Bulldogs in week ten the deciding game.
Should Dickinson defeat Concord and win its week ten matchup against AI duPont, the Rams could force a three-way tie for first place. In that scenario, Concord would need to beat the Bulldogs in week ten and the Bulldogs would need to win against McKean this weekend.
Charter School of Wilmington vs Christiana @ Charter School of Wilmington at 11:00 a.m. on Saturday, November 7
The Forces are currently second in the Class 1A District Two standings with a district record of 2-1. Conrad leads the district with an undefeated district record and two more games left on their schedule. Should Conrad win and the Forces lose to Christiana, the Red Wolves would win the district this weekend. A Forces win would make their game against the Red Wolves in week ten the deciding game in the district. 
Newark Charter senior Cayden Anderson leaps over the defender to make the catch in Newark Charter’s game against Seaford. Photo Credit: Dave Reeder
Newark Charter vs St. Andrew’s @ St. Andrew’s at 1:00 p.m. on Saturday, November 7
The Patriots are undefeated both overall and in district play this season and have a chance at winning Class 1A District Three title with a win on Saturday afternoon. The Saints could make the race interesting if they defeat the Patriots. 
A win would put St. Andrew’s ahead of Newark Charter in the standings with a 3-0 record and a week ten matchup against Seaford to close out the regular season. Should the Saints win and the Blue Jays lose to Early College, the Saints would win the district this weekend. 
If the Blue Jays and Saints win this weekend, their matchup in week ten would be crucial in deciding the victor of the district.

name: Washington State Standard
title: Albertsons must pay $900M for role in WA opioid crisis, judge rules
description: SEATTLE — Grocery giant Albertsons must pay Washington state $900 million for its pharmacies’ role in fueling the opioid epidemic, a judge ruled Thursday. Washington Attorney General Nick Brown said this is believed to be the largest verdict in state history. It came after a 9-week trial before King County Superior Court Judge Janet Helson. […]
text:
Washington state Attorney General Nick, alongside attorneys from his office, speaks to reporters outside the King County Courthouse after a $900 million verdict against Albertsons for its role in fueling the opioid crisis on Thursday, Nov. 5, 2026, in Seattle. (Photo by Jake Goldstein-Street/Washington State Standard)SEATTLE — Grocery giant Albertsons must pay Washington state $900 million for its pharmacies’ role in fueling the opioid epidemic, a judge ruled Thursday.
Washington Attorney General Nick Brown said this is believed to be the largest verdict in state history. It came after a 9-week trial before King County Superior Court Judge Janet Helson.
Washington has now won nearly $2.2 billion for state and local governments in numerous cases against drug manufacturers and distributors in recent years. The money goes toward resources to prevent drug abuse and overdoses. But it’ll take a while for the $900 million to reach Washington, as Albertsons can appeal Helson’s verdict.
The state alleged Albertsons, which owns Safeway and Haggen and runs more than 200 pharmacies in Washington, dispensed 641 million opioid pills between 2006 and 2022. Many of those prescriptions had red flags that should’ve been investigated before distributing the pills, according to Brown’s office.
“This is a victory for the people of the state of Washington,” Brown told reporters after the verdict. “It is a victory that affirms that when corporations put safety measures at risk, when they do not prioritize their customers, when they are focused not on safety, that they will be held accountable.”
Albertsons filled prescriptions more than 6.5 million times without showing that pharmacists had confirmed doctors wrote them for legitimate medical purposes, according to the state. 
This led to them being diverted for illicit use as an epidemic roared across Washington, and the nation. Here, opioid overdoses have claimed tens of thousands of lives.
Albertsons has been defending against similar claims across the country. In April, the grocery chain agreed to pay $774 million to settle numerous other lawsuits filed across the country. 

SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 
In a statement, Albertsons said it was “disappointed by the court’s ruling and respectfully disagrees with its conclusions.” 
“We are reviewing the decision closely and will evaluate all available options, including appeal,” the company said. “We are proud of our pharmacists and their dedication to the patients and communities they serve, and we will continue to support our customers and communities across Washington through responsible pharmacy operations.”

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Straight-ticket ballots reach 70% of all Alabama votes; Democrats increase share
description: More than 70% of Alabama voters cast straight-ticket party ballots on Tuesday, a record that also featured a higher percentage of those votes going to Democrats. The Secretary of State’s Office published a news release Thursday that said almost 1.2 million of the nearly 1.7 million votes were straight ticket. Of those, about 645,000, 54%, […]
text:
Campaign signs line the driveway to the entrance of a polling place on Tuesday, November 3, 2026, in Millbrook, Alabama. The Alabama Secretary of State's Office Thursday said more than 70% of ballots cast on Tuesday were straight ticket. (Ralph Chapoco/Alabama Reflector) (Getty images)More than 70% of Alabama voters cast straight-ticket party ballots on Tuesday, a record that also featured a higher percentage of those votes going to Democrats.
The Secretary of State’s Office published a news release Thursday that said almost 1.2 million of the nearly 1.7 million votes were straight ticket.
Of those, about 645,000, 54%, voted straight-party ticket for Republican candidates. Almost 550,000, about 46%, went to Democrats.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
In 2022, about 947,000 of the 1.4 million votes cast that year (66.5%) were straight-ticket. But about 649,000 of those (68.4%) went to Republicans, while just over 298,000 (31.5%) went to Democrats.

As of 2026, Alabama is one of six states to offer straight-ticket voting on the ballot along with Indiana, Michigan, Kentucky, Oklahoma, and South Carolina, according to the Election Lab at MIT.
Messages were sent to Sen. Bobby Singleton, D-Greensboro, and Republican Party Chair Scott Stadthagen Thursday seeking comment.
Critics of straight ticket voting say that it allows more extreme candidates to be elected more easily and does not motivate voters to be more informed about the candidates. Democratic gubernatorial nominee Doug Jones made ending the practice  part of his campaign.
Black Belt counties, most of which lean Democratic, led in use of straight-ticket ballots. Almost 90% of ballots cast in Greene County (3,216 of more than 3,600) went straight ticket, with 87% going to Democrats. In Sumter County, 86% of ballots cast were straight ticket, with 83% of those going to Democrats. Perry County saw 80% of its ballots marked straight ticket, and 85% went to Democrats.
Republican candidates were the ones to benefit in the two other counties.
In Escambia County in south Alabama, more than 7,800 of the 9,800 votes cast (80%) were straight ticket; of those, 64.7% went to Republicans. About 3,600 of the 4,500 votes (80%) cast in Lamar County in northwest Alabama were straight-ticket; over 3,000 of those (84%) went to Republicans.
Etowah County had the lowest percentage of voters who cast a straight-party ticket at 54%. Cherokee County had the second-lowest total at 55%. That is followed by Choctaw and Washington counties, both at 57%. Lee County was at 61%.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico Rep. Reeb backtracks on resignation from Legislature
description: New Mexico state Rep. Andrea Reeb, a Republican, announces she's staying in the Legislature after all, after announcing resignation in October.
text:
After announcing her resignation on Oct. 15, 2026, state Rep. Andrea Reeb (R-Clovis) said on Nov. 5 that she would be staying in the state Legislature after all. (Photo by Danielle Prokop for Source NM)New Mexico state Rep. Andrea Reeb (R-Clovis) on Thursday announced she would not be resigning from the state Legislature after all.
Reeb announced her resignation from the state House of Representatives on Oct. 15 following a ruling by a federal judge that her role in the House represented a conflict with her work as a special prosecutor in the involuntary manslaughter case against Alec Baldwin.
In a statement accompanying her resignation, Reeb said she “respectfully” disagrees with the Court “but I respect our Constitution and the institutions that uphold it.” As such, she said she was resigning to continue her work as a special prosecutor and resigning, effective immediately.
In the weeks since, according to a news release, Reeb said “constituents, local leaders, and fellow lawmakers” urged her to stay.
Voters reelected Reeb in Tuesday’s election for House District 64 in an uncontested race.
“I have been humbled by how many people called, wrote, and stopped me in town to ask me to come back,” Reeb said in a statement. “The voters re-elected me knowing exactly what had happened. They made their wishes clear, and I couldn’t ignore that. The people of District 64 asked me to serve, and I’m going to. I’m ready to get back to work for them.”
According to a news release, Reeb will continue working as a special prosecutor work through the end of the year while “transitioning her pending cases to other attorneys.” In January, she will join the law firm of Payne, Powell, Truitt, and Chandler as a partner, “resolving the conflict ahead of the legislative session.”
At the time of her resignation, Reeb noted that she had “relied” on guidance from both the State Ethics Commission and the New Mexico Attorney General to continue serving in both roles.
State Rep. Andrea Romero (D-Santa Fe), with whom Reeb serves on a special investigatory committee examining Jeffrey Epstein’s activities in the state, also cited Attorney General Raúl Torrez’s opinion when she was criticized for taking a job in Carmack-Altwies’ office while serving in the Legislature. She subsequently resigned after Torrez issued a letter that his 2024 opinion had “been read more broadly than intended.”
Reeb’s resignation last night prompted a valley of criticism between Republican and Democratic state House leadership.
This is a developing story.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Lincolnites favor changing timing of city elections, limiting terms of City Council members
description: LINCOLN — Voters in Nebraska’s capital city widely favored ending off-year elections after 2029 and limiting Lincoln City Council members to two consecutive four-year terms. Lincoln voters saw five city charter amendments on their ballot. Of those, the conservative-led Good Government Lincoln campaign and the blue leadership of the city of Lincoln proposed c[...]
text:
Voters fill out ballots and check in with election workers at a polling place in Lincoln, Nebraska, Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. Tables and voting booths fill the room as neighbors exercise their right to vote. (Photo by Michelle Montenegro/Nebraska News Service)LINCOLN — Voters in Nebraska’s capital city widely favored ending off-year elections after 2029 and limiting Lincoln City Council members to two consecutive four-year terms.
Lincoln voters saw five city charter amendments on their ballot. Of those, the conservative-led Good Government Lincoln campaign and the blue leadership of the city of Lincoln proposed competing ideas around whether to change Lincoln’s practice of holding municipal elections in every odd year or whether to place term limits on Lincoln City Council members.
A fifth question, from Good Government Lincoln, sought to allow voters in the 3-mile boundary outside Lincoln city limits, the extraterritorial zoning jurisdiction, to vote in municipal elections.
Then-state Sen. Tony Fulton of Lincoln. He is now a lead sponsor on the Good Government Lincoln campaign. (Courtesy of Unicameral Information Office)
The city of Lincoln initially refused to place the three Good Government Lincoln petitions on the Nov. 3 ballot. The campaign was wrapped up in allegations of fraudulent signature collection on a first batch of petitions this summer, and seven out-of-state circulators were arrested. However, the campaign regrouped and submitted new signatures in mid-August.
The city argued the measures needed to instead appear on May 2027 city ballots.
Nebraska Attorney General Mike Hilgers, a former Lincoln state senator who now lives in Lincoln’s ETJ, took city officials to the Nebraska Supreme Court. He prevailed, and the justices ordered the city to place all measures on the Nov. 3 ballot. The Supreme Court ordered Lincoln officials to pay the state $9,150 in costs from the litigation.
City officials went on the offensive with two alternative proposals. Under the Nebraska Constitution, if two conflicting measures pass, the one with the most affirmative votes, regardless of the winning percentage, wins.
Mixed election results
The latest election results are as of 3:15 a.m. Wednesday, Nov. 4. The Lancaster County Election Commission has approximately 6,000 early vote ballots to count on Friday, and 3,000 provisional ballots will be processed Nov. 13. It’s unclear how many of those are from voters within Lincoln city limits, the only Lancaster County voters who could vote on the measures.
For moving election dates, both versions passed, but voters favored the city’s alternative of Ballot Question 3, to end off-year elections after 2029, compared to Good Government Lincoln’s Ballot Question 2, to end off-year elections after city elections in 2027.




The city’s alternative had 56,308 positive votes to Good Government Lincoln’s 50,950 votes.
Under the city’s proposal, four district-bound City Council members and the mayor elected in 2027 would serve through 2030, and three at-large council members elected in 2029 would serve through 2032. 
Under Good Government Lincoln’s proposal, a term for anyone elected in 2027 would end at the end of 2028, and previous council members elected in 2025 would serve through 2030.
Lincoln Mayor Leirion Gaylor Baird, a chief opponent of Good Government Lincoln, was elected in 2019 and 2023. She has not yet announced whether she’ll run in 2027. Lincoln mayors are limited to three four-year terms. She backed the two city alternatives.
Voters also passed both versions of the term-limit proposals. The Good Government Lincoln proposal, Ballot Question 4, had nearly 6,000 more affirmative votes. It would limit City Council members to two consecutive terms. The city’s alternative, Ballot Question 5, would have allowed council members to serve three consecutive four-year terms instead, similar to the mayor.




Term limits would count for any terms that begin in 2027 or at future city elections.
Finally, voters appear likely to reject Good Government Lincoln’s Ballot Question 6 to allow non-city residents to vote in municipal elections, excluding bonds, beginning next year. As of the Wednesday results, about 48% of voters favored the measure.


Sponsor, Lincoln mayor weigh in
Former state Sen. Tony Fulton of Lincoln, a sponsor behind Good Government Lincoln, told Nebraska Public Media that the campaign “defined the terms of the playing field for Lincoln’s future.”
“We’re grateful to every Lincolnite who signed a petition, knocked on a door or voted for our proposals,” Fulton, a former state tax commissioner, said in a statement. “Because of you, our city elections will be normalized, and our city council will be subject to term limits.”
Lincoln Mayor Leirion Gaylor Baird speaking at a press conference in downtown Lincoln on Sept, 14. 2026 (Juan Salinas II/Nebraska Examiner)
Just before 6 p.m. Wednesday, Gaylor Baird wrote in a Facebook statement to thank Lincoln voters for supporting the city’s alternative on the timing of elections while rejecting the proposal to allow non-city residents to vote in city elections.
The mayor said the voters’ actions “demonstrate that our community values sensible, effective, and ethical leadership.”
“While powerful political interests spent more than a million dollars in an attempt to manipulate our local elections for their own gain, Lincoln voters proved they can make their own decisions about what’s best for our city,” Gaylor Baird said in her campaign post.

title: Budget challenges remain, says KY Chief Justice in annual address
description: FRANKFORT —  Kentucky’s Administrative Office of the Courts is operating with 86 fewer people in management, Supreme Court Chief Justice Debra Hembree Lambert said in her State of the Judiciary address Thursday.  The budget passed by the General Assembly in 2026 underfunded some court operations, Lambert previously said. As a result, she rearranged staff pos[...]
text:
Supreme Court Chief Justice Debra Hembree Lambert delivers the 2026 State of the Judiciary address. Nov. 5, 2026. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Sarah Ladd). FRANKFORT —  Kentucky’s Administrative Office of the Courts is operating with 86 fewer people in management, Supreme Court Chief Justice Debra Hembree Lambert said in her State of the Judiciary address Thursday. 
The budget passed by the General Assembly in 2026 underfunded some court operations, Lambert previously said. As a result, she rearranged staff positions, focusing cuts to management-level positions. 
“Ultimately only 11 employees were separated under the reorganization,” Lambert told members of the judiciary committee Thursday. 
“The state of Kentucky’s judiciary is strong because of the men and women who serve it,” she said, “but sustaining that core strength requires us to confront the very real pressures of staffing, compensation, facilities and technology.” 
During the 2027 legislative session, she said, the Kentucky Judicial Commission on Mental Health will recommend two policies: 

Improve crisis transportation options for people experiencing mental health emergencies. 
Allow children in out-of-home care who reach recommitment age (18 years old) to seek continued assistance from the Cabinet for Health and Family Services without having to obtain a court order. 

These recommendations, Lambert said, “grew from gaps identified by the people and agencies working with these issues.” 
The court system in Kentucky is also working to repair outdated infrastructure in judicial buildings across the country using money allocated in the 2024 session, Lambert said, and has approved 446 projects so far, allocating roughly $32 million out of the $47 million available. 
KY specialty courts safe, but staff positions cut in ‘challenging times’ for justice system

“That designated support is helping us replace aging roofs, electrical systems and heating and cooling equipment, so these buildings can continue to serve their communities without interruption,” she said. 
During the next budget cycle, in 2028, Lambert asked lawmakers to consider allotting funds for staff attorney wage increases. Staff attorneys, she said, are bringing in salaries 25% below the comparison market.
“We all are having difficulties hiring and keeping staff attorneys,” Lambert said. “Most of us can tell about frequently losing staff to the other branches and also to the private sector. The reality just is that we struggle to recruit and retain the people we need to do our vital work for the citizens.”

title: Ohio Gov. DeWine does not plan to sign anything into law that would limit the governor’s authority
description: Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine has begun talks with Governor-elect Amy Acton about her administration, saying “we want to be helpful.” He also indicated that he does not support any attempt by lame-duck Republican supermajority lawmakers to dramatically change the powers of governor before January. The DeWines had Governor-elect Acton and her husband Eric over at […]
text:
Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine gives the State of the State address in the Ohio House chambers at the Ohio Statehouse on Wednesday, March 12, 2025 in Columbus, Ohio. (Pool photo by Samantha Madar, Columbus Dispatch.)Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine has begun talks with Governor-elect Amy Acton about her administration, saying “we want to be helpful.” He also indicated that he does not support any attempt by lame-duck Republican supermajority lawmakers to dramatically change the powers of governor before January.
The DeWines had Governor-elect Acton and her husband Eric over at the Ohio Governor’s residence Wednesday night.
“It’s in everyone’s interest that the new administration be successful, that they get things done,” DeWine told reporters at a post-election results conference Thursday morning. 
“We’re going to do everything we can, and that would have been true whether it was Vivek Ramaswamy or Governor-elect Acton. … What I started to do with her is here’s what I know. Here’s what my experiences have been. Here are some difficult things. Here are things that, I think, as I look at the trajectory of Ohio, I think is going to be challenging.”
Ohio Democrats broke the Republican supermajority in the Ohio House, limiting the lawmakers’ ability to override vetoes from Acton. Political analysts expect Ohio Republican lawmakers to try to push proposals that could limit the governor’s authority.  
“I don’t think any governor is going to approve anything, whether Democrat or Republican, that would dramatically change the powers of the governor,” DeWine said.
“I don’t think that’s appropriate. I have no idea if they are going to do that.” 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Acton previously served on DeWine’s cabinet as Ohio Department of Health director from February 2019 to June 2020.  
Acton will take office as Ohio governor on Jan. 11 and she named John Haseley as her  transition chair. Haseley has previously worked with members of the Ohio Democratic Party including Ted Strickland, John Glenn, and Dick Celeste. 
“We govern in this state from the center-right and the center-left, and I have every expectation that Governor-elect Acton will do the same, and she will be consistent with that long, long tradition of Democrats and Republicans in the state of Ohio who govern either from the center-left or the center-right,” DeWine said.
“Predictability, stability, is really one of the strengths that we have as a state.” 
DeWine hopes Acton will continue the science of reading with more reading coaches, the OhioSEE Program, the Governor’s Merit Scholarship, and the Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library. 
“We must continue to invest, frankly, in our greatest asset. And our greatest asset is our children,” DeWine said. 
“If you look at (Acton’s) speech she made on election night … She certainly talked about children. She talked about H2Ohio. Now I will say this: Vivek Ramaswamy, when I talked to him, he had expressed that he would try to continue those issues as well. She’s got to govern, and she’s got to face the challenges that she faces. All I can do is talk about what I think is in the best interest in the state of Ohio. Investing in children is absolutely the best money we can spend.”
Ohio governor-elect Amy Acton looks on during a rally on April 28, 2026 in Cincinnati, Ohio. (Photo by Jon Cherry/Getty Images.)
DeWine declined to say if Ramaswamy’s controversial ad featuring Acton’s estranged mom impacted other Ohio Republicans in Tuesday’s election. 
“I’m not going to get into micromanagement and dissect campaigns,” he said. 
Following a national trend, Ohio Democrats won several races both at the state and federal level.
Democrat Sherrod Brown will going back to the U.S. Senate, Allison Russo was elected Ohio Secretary of State, John Kulewicz will be Ohio’s Attorney General, Seth Walsh was elected Ohio Treasurer, Justice Jennifer Brunner retained her seat on the Ohio Supreme Court and Marilyn Zayas was elected to the Ohio Supreme Court. 
DeWine called Tuesday’s election a “mighty wind that came across not just Ohio, but across, of course, the whole country.”
“Sometimes there is a mighty wind out there, and no matter what you do, there’s nothing you can do in that campaign to win. This is something that happens every once in a while. And this mighty wind really took it away from many candidates who, in a normal year, would have won.” 
DeWine said he expects Ohioans to hear from Republican U.S. Sen. Jon Husted again. Husted lost to Brown and was formerly DeWine’s lieutenant governor. 
When asked if Husted will run for governor in 2030, DeWine said “I’m not going to get into that.” 
DeWine, who has about 65 days left in office, said he has a list of things he hopes to see the legislature do during lame duck, but has not yet talked about those with Ohio House Speaker Matt Huffman and Ohio Senate President Rob McColley. 
“There’ll be certain things we’ll be trying to get done,” he said. “I’m sure they’ll have things that they want to get done. I hope we can reach some consensus about things that we both can support.”
DeWine said he is focused on highway safety and passing the primary seatbelt law, which allows law enforcement to pull over and ticket a driver or passenger for not wearing a seat belt. Currently in Ohio, law enforcement officers can only cite drivers for not wearing a seat belt if they are stopped for a different traffic violation.
“We know that Ohio still lags behind in regards to seatbelt use, we know the primary seatbelt law will increase that use,” he said.
“Ninety percent put on a seatbelt. Yet 60% of the fatalities in the state come from people who do not have a seatbelt. So that tells you the magnitude of having that seatbelt on. We can protect our lives. We can keep families from mourning young ones, mourning their father, their mother.” 
He said there are other things too, but quickly followed up by saying “I won’t reveal my whole list today.”

name: Michigan Advance
title: Commentary: Mike Rogers never understood Michigan — but Michigan voters understood him
description: There is a reason Republicans haven’t won a U.S. Senate race in Michigan since the last century.  The state is politically competitive, culturally diverse and home to an electorate that doesn’t fit neatly into the narrow partisan boxes that have come to define Republican politics. Mike Rogers is simply the latest Republican to learn that […]
text:
Republican U.S. Senate nominee and former U.S. Rep. Mike Rogers and speaks during a rally with Vice President JD Vance on Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026 at CHI Aviation in Howell, Mich. (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance)There is a reason Republicans haven’t won a U.S. Senate race in Michigan since the last century. 
The state is politically competitive, culturally diverse and home to an electorate that doesn’t fit neatly into the narrow partisan boxes that have come to define Republican politics. Mike Rogers is simply the latest Republican to learn that lesson the hard way…twice.
Election cycle after election cycle, Michigan Republicans have put forward candidates who seem to be running congressional campaigns designed to win purposely drawn districts with a relatively uniform group of voters. 
But Michigan is not a congressional district. It is a diverse state, incorporating everything from major cities like Detroit, Flint and Grand Rapids to the suburbs of Oakland and Kent counties to the wide-open rural expanses up north. The political priorities and experiences of these communities vary considerably.
And that’s the point. Winning statewide in Michigan requires building a coalition broad enough to reflect that diversity. Rogers never seemed particularly interested in doing that.
Trump invokes anti-Muslim rhetoric to attack El-Sayed at Michigan rally supporting Rogers, James

Instead, his campaign sought to exploit divisions among Black and Jewish Democratic voters, often in ways that were harmful, inflammatory and deeply cynical. Though Rogers denied his Muslim Brotherhood line of attack against El-Sayed was based on his faith, he helped unleash a wave of outright Islamophobia that was not only disgusting, but also a profoundly misguided political strategy.
Attempting to turn a candidate’s Muslim faith into a liability might energize a segment of the Republican base, but it does little to persuade the broad cross-section of Michigan voters necessary to win a U.S. Senate seat.
That miscalculation reflects something deeper about Rogers and his political experience.
I reported on Rogers throughout the entirety of his congressional career, largely defined by the security of representing the same mid-Michigan district in which he grew up. The only congressional election that appeared to seriously test him was his first in 2000, which he won by just 111 votes. Redistricting the following year made the seat safe for Republicans by adding a GOP-leaning part of Oakland County. After that, Rogers went on to serve six more terms in Congress, never facing any real reelection challenge.
There is a significant difference between winning repeatedly in a safely Republican congressional district and building a statewide political coalition. Rogers spent much of his career doing the former. Both of his Senate campaigns suggested he never quite learned how to do the latter.
When Rogers decided against seeking reelection in 2014, it appeared he might be headed for something considerably bigger. As chairman of the powerful House Intelligence Committee, he had developed a national profile and established himself as a prominent voice on national security. His name was frequently mentioned in national political circles, and a future in the White House did not seem out of the question.
But the Republican Party was about to meet a transformative force that few, Rogers included, anticipated: Donald Trump.
Trump’s rise in 2015 remade the party, reshaping its political priorities, its rhetoric and its expectations of elected officials. Rogers initially appeared to resist that transformation.
Republican U.S. Senate nominee Mike Rogers, right, speaks at a rally hosted by President Donald Trump, left, on Sunday, Oct. 25, 2026 at McMorran Place Sports & Entertainment Center in Port Huron, Mich. (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance)
During Trump’s first term, he was, at times, a relatively moderate Republican voice willing to offer criticism of the president and the direction of his party. He openly contradicted Trump’s approach toward Russia in 2018, criticized Trump for trying to interfere with the results of the 2020 election and committed perhaps the greatest apostasy in MAGA world: condemned Trump after Jan. 6 (on CNN no less) for contributing “to violence at the Capitol to try to overturn an election.”
Eventually, though, Rogers seemed to get the memo that opposition to Trump was a dead-end in Republican politics. So when he decided to return from his new home in Florida for his first run at U.S. Senate in 2024, principled opposition gave way to accommodation. Rogers abandoned much of that independence and climbed aboard the Trump Train, seemingly convinced that aligning himself with the president was the surest route back to elected office.
But he made that transition too late to become a natural part of Trump’s political movement and too completely to retain the independence that once distinguished him. He has spent much of the time since trying to catch up, clinging to the caboose of a political train that has moved well beyond the Republican Party he once represented.
His 2026 Senate campaign brought those contradictions into sharp focus. Rather than offering a vision broad enough to appeal to Michigan’s diverse electorate, Rogers leaned into the divisive politics that have become the currency of the national Republican Party. He treated Michigan as though it were another safely Republican congressional district, where appealing to the base and attacking the opposition might be enough.
It wasn’t.
Michigan voters have consistently demonstrated that statewide success requires something more than partisan loyalty and culture-war rhetoric. It requires an understanding of the state’s communities, a willingness to reach beyond the political base and a recognition that voters are not simply interchangeable pieces in a national partisan, and frankly bigoted, strategy.
Mike Rogers had decades in politics to learn that. His Senate campaign demonstrated that he never did.

name: Mississippi Today
title: What to know as open enrollment begins for ACA plans: higher costs, fewer options
description: Pages from the U.S. Affordable Care Act health insurance website healthcare.gov are seen on a computer screen in New York on Tuesday, Aug. 19, 2025.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Tens of thousands of Mississippians covered by Affordable Care Act marketplace health insurance will face higher premiums and fewer options during this year’s open enrollment period, experts say. 
This is the second consecutive year of double-digit premium increases nationally. The average benchmark premium will rise 23% in Mississippi in 2027, according to KFF data. Last year the state saw a 37% increase in the average premium. 
Many marketplace customers are eligible for income-based subsidies that are expected to help shield them from premium increases. In 2027, the income range for a single person to qualify is roughly $16,000 to $64,000 annually. 
But even those that qualify already face significant premium increases after enhanced subsidies that made insurance more affordable for more than 22 million Americans expired in December 2025. A large share of Mississippians switched to plans with higher out-of-pocket-costs last year after those subsidies expired. 
“It’s the same story we had last year,” said Michael Minor, who leads the Hernando-based Get Covered Mississippi, a statewide, faith-based coalition that helps connect Mississippians to health insurance options. “People are already struggling.”
Open enrollment began Sunday and will continue through Jan. 15. 
Nationally, average premiums will increase 13%. Health insurance plans across the board are seeing rates rise due to inflation and increasing healthcare costs, said Matthew McGough, a policy analyst at KFF. 
Marketplace premium costs are also affected by the downstream effects of the expiration of subsidies that made health insurance more affordable for customers, McGough said. Because more enrollees, and especially healthier people, dropped their coverage, the remaining group of people is smaller, sicker and more costly to insure. 
McGough said he expects marketplace enrollment to continue to decline into 2027. 
“To what extent, I think that remains to be seen,” he said. 
Mississippians will also see fewer options when they shop for plans. Two insurers previously offering plans on the state’s marketplace will not offer plans in 2027: Cigna Healthcare and Molina Healthcare. Three plans, UnitedHealthcare, Oscar Health and Ambetter from Magnolia Health, will continue offering coverage. 
The more limited options for coverage comes at the same time as a temporary freeze on new broker registrations as a part of a federal anti-fraud crackdown and decreased funding for navigators who provide assistance to people shopping for and enrolling in health coverage through the marketplace.
“Together, consumers are potentially going to have less choice and a more difficult time finding avenues to sign up,” McGough said.
Some lawfully present immigrants will lose eligibility for federal financial assistance for marketplace plans in 2027, including refugees and asylees without a green card and people on work visas, among others. Others, including lawful permanent residents, or “green card” holders, will still be eligible for subsidies. 
Declining marketplace enrollment in Mississippi
When Congress first authorized expanded subsidies for marketplace plans in 2021 during the COVID-19 pandemic, Mississippi was one of the states that benefitted the most from the increased federal support, in part because state lawmakers, for over a decade, have chosen not to expand Medicaid. 
Marketplace enrollment peaked in 2025 with over 300,000 people enrolled in plans statewide. 
With the enhanced subsidies, marketplace premiums for people renewing their coverage in 2026 more than doubled on average, according to KFF. Mississippi saw one of the steepest declines in coverage. 
Mississippi Insurance Commissioner Mike Chaney said enrollments have since dropped by half. He said as of Oct. 28, enrollments fell to 135,000 people among the three insurers that will continue to offer plans next year. He said the two plans leaving the marketplace next year have few remaining beneficiaries.
Mississippi’s declining marketplace rolls may also have been impacted by federal efforts to eliminate fraud. 
The Trump administration in September cancelled 315,000 “unauthorized” policies covering more than 760,000 people nationwide, claiming fraud and improper enrollment. A small number of people were errantly disenrolled and later reinstated. 
Marketplace insurers reported that over 2,500 members were disenrolled in Mississippi, said Beth Reiss, communications director for the Mississippi Insurance Department.
