name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri childcare subsidy waitlist grows as providers struggle to fill classrooms
description: Missouri childcare providers have classrooms sitting empty and parents eager to fill them. But with funding stretched thin, the state isn’t approving most new applications for subsidies that would make those openings affordable. There were 11,618 children on the waiting list for Missouri’s childcare subsidy program on Oct. 5 — more than a third of […]
text:
Children play at Kids in Christ Academy in Kansas City with teacher Heather Malone on Oct. 23 (Steph Quinn/Missouri Independent).Missouri childcare providers have classrooms sitting empty and parents eager to fill them. But with funding stretched thin, the state isn’t approving most new applications for subsidies that would make those openings affordable.
There were 11,618 children on the waiting list for Missouri’s childcare subsidy program on Oct. 5 — more than a third of all children eligible for assistance — according to the Department of Elementary and Secondary Education.
The department established the waiting list after demand increased by 19% between January 2025 and late February, exceeding the amount of money appropriated for fiscal year 2026.
No children have been moved off the list since it started March 1.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The program helps cover the cost of childcare for families earning no more than 150% of the federal poverty level. That’s $40,980 for a family of three, or the equivalent of one person earning $19.70 per hour for a year of full-time work. Families are responsible for paying a sliding scale rate based on their monthly income.
The average annual cost of childcare for an infant in Missouri is $13,780, according to Child Care Aware of Missouri. For a 4-year-old, it’s $9,568. 
For families on the waiting list, that means finding a way to pay for care themselves — or going without it.
Christina Puckett, owner of Kids in Christ Academy in Kansas City, which serves 84 children ages six months through preschool, told The Independent she tries to help when she can.
Even before the waitlist, Puckett said, some families receiving subsidies struggled to pay their sliding scale rate.
“The struggle was there before the waiting list,” Puckett said.
Now families ask Puckett if they can enroll their children at Kids in Christ and pay out of pocket until the department begins processing applications on the waiting list.
Puckett said she gives discounts “just to help some parents because they can’t afford that.”
“I have them text me, ‘Can I bring my kid in? I just want to pay you,’” Puckett said. “Well, I know they can’t afford to pay me, so then what do I do?”
Despite the growing waiting list, the department is not requesting additional funding for the program in fiscal year 2028.
Its budget request of $287.6 million would maintain an increase of about $139 million in state funding included in the current budget to replace federal funding that accumulated while COVID-19 relief funds were still flowing. But it would omit $17.2 million restricted by Gov. Mike Kehoe in June in the current budget.
A statement released by the department indicated requesting additional funds “was not feasible” because of state budget constraints.
The statement said the department plans to begin processing waitlisted applications when monthly subsidy payments consistently fall below $28 million — the amount available per month in the current state budget.
The department met that benchmark in September, the most recent month with published data, spending $26.9 million on subsidy payments. 
But subsidy payment totals increased in four of the seven months since the waiting list started, peaking at $30.2 million in August compared to $27.1 million in March.

Higher utilization of childcare in the summer could be one reason for the increases, according to the department.
“At any one time, several thousand children already have approval to access childcare, but are not currently utilizing the service,” the statement said.
The statement also pointed out that while the total number of children receiving subsidies has decreased since March, the number of children who have entered the program because they are in the custody of the Missouri Children’s Division has continued to rise.
Children in foster care are not subject to the waiting list, and the department reimburses providers at a higher rate for their care — 100% of the rate determined in an annual market rate survey instead of 65% for most preschool and school-age children. 
The current budget law for the department also directed the Office of Childhood — the agency within the department that administers the subsidy program — to meet with a stakeholder group and recommend changes to payment structures to “balance rates, availability and quality” and “improve access to low-income families and address childcare availability shortages.” The law gave the Office of Childhood a Nov. 1 deadline to report the group’s recommendations to the governor’s office and the chairs and ranking members of the House Budget and Senate Appropriations committees.
According to the department, as the group looks for ways to address the waiting list, they have considered “information on rate enhancements, (provider) base rates, and the sliding‑scale fees paid by families.”
 Weighing options

Casey Hanson, deputy director of Kids Win Missouri, told The Independent providers who serve a high percentage of children receiving subsidies are facing losses from the waiting list.
As children receiving subsidies start kindergarten, providers are left with vacancies they can’t fill.
“They have parents that can come into those slots, but if they’re parents that rely on subsidy, then they’re not able to fill them,” Hanson said. “There’s a lot of providers that have classrooms sitting empty, and their subsidy receipts are way less than they’re used to.”
Christy and Paul Prevo, owners of Tiger Tots Child Development Center and Tiger Tots Academy of Early Learning in Columbia, told The Independent they are serving about 50 fewer kids than in previous years because of the waiting list. 
“We have about 15 students that, if they received subsidy today, they would be here tomorrow,” Christy Prevo said.
Both Tiger Tots locations serve more than 50% subsidy-eligible families: about 55% at one location and close to 75% at the other. Together, the two locations serve more than 300 children.
Kids climb on the playground at Tiger Tots Child Development Center in Columbia, Missouri on Oct. 28 (Steph Quinn/Missouri Independent).
The waiting list is also affecting the centers’ ability to staff their classrooms.
Christy Prevo said a teacher with three children on the waiting list quit because childcare took so much out of her paycheck that it didn’t make sense to keep working — even with a discount.
Puckett estimated that about 85% of the children at Kids in Christ Academy receive subsidies. Eighty-four children currently attend the academy, which has a capacity of 108.
While there’s no shortage of parents looking for childcare, Puckett said she has to be careful not to accept too many families paying out of pocket to avoid losing a 30% rate enhancement she receives for being accredited and because more than 50% of the children her academy serves qualify for subsidies.
Puckett said the rate enhancement allows her to attract highly qualified staff and pay them competitively.
“I’ve got a teacher here who has a bachelor of education,” Puckett said. “Instead of working in a school district, she wanted to work for me.”
If the state eliminated the 30% boost, Puckett said, “I don’t know where I’d be.”
Rate enhancements also help providers serve children with special needs.
Christy Prevo said Tiger Tots can hire staff with the skills to care for children with special needs because of the rate enhancement.
“My understanding is families were having much difficulty finding a place for a special needs child because there was no extra incentive to do that for centers,” Christy Prevo said. “…And having the state say this is important to us that these students also have a place to be—I feel very strongly about both of those rate enhancements.”
Lawmakers proposed a $51.5 million cut in March that would have eliminated rate enhancements, but the funding was restored in the final version of the budget.
Paul Prevo said the state should consider lowering rates for providers and use the savings to open up spots on the waiting list. That would allow providers to fill vacancies, he said.
“Instead of only being at 50% capacity, now you’re at 75% capacity,” he said. “The increase in the number of students you have would also help offset any of the losses from the lower rate.”
But Puckett said she worries the department will reduce rates because providers “are already underpaid.”
She said it takes all the funding she currently receives to pay staff well.
“They’ve got to live and survive just like those parents,” Puckett said.
The department plans to implement an excessive absence policy to ensure that families approved for the program are using their subsidy. Families with too many unexcused absences could lose eligibility for the program after receiving warnings from the department. Training for department staff and providers on the new policy will begin in November, according to the department.
Paul Prevo said that if the excessive absence policy opens up subsidy spots, it could help move people off the waiting list at no cost to the state.
“I would love to open up those spots for eight to 10 more students to be here that are waiting to be here,” he said. “The funds would be going toward people who are working families who are utilizing it.”
Hanson said the growth of the waitlist points to a mismatch between Missourians’ childcare needs and the resources available to fund them.
“The waitlist is evidence that we have a much greater demand than we’re able to afford as a state right now.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: Mississippi lawmakers hear testimony amid debate over statewide kratom ban
description: Kratom products are seen at Vape Plus in Byram, Miss., on Feb. 12, 2025. In 2025, a bill passed by the Mississippi House of Representatives restricted kratom purchases to those 21 and older and prohibit synthetic kratom products.
text:
Lawmakers on Wednesday considered steps to further restrict kratom, a debate reignited by the recent deaths of two University of Mississippi students who were found near suspected kratom derivatives.
Members of the House Drug Policy Committee, led by Rep. Beth Waldo, a Republican from Pontotoc, heard testimony from state health officials, law enforcement officers and doctors as well as Mississippians who have used kratom. Several health and law enforcement officials advised legislators to classify all forms of kratom and its synthetic derivatives as controlled substances. 
In doing so, they echoed the mother of Robert Strang, one of the two University of Mississippi students who died in September. She blamed her son’s death on failed enforcement of federal drug regulations and implored lawmakers to ban the substances. 
“My position is clear. All kratom products need to be banned,” Rebecca Strang of Atlanta told lawmakers Wednesday. 
Over 5 million Americans have used a kratom product in their lifetime, according to a recent study from the Journal of Addiction Medicine. Derived from a tropical evergreen tree native to Southeast Asia, kratom leaf herbal products and concentrated or synthetic kratom-derived products are widely sold in gas stations and tobacco or vape shops.
Critics of kratom argue that it is a highly addictive and dangerous drug that produces stimulant- and opioid-like effects, and that synthetic kratom products are difficult to regulate. But advocates argue it can be an effective tool for treating opioid use disorder, chronic pain and depression.
In August, the Department of Justice announced the temporary emergency scheduling of some potent kratom-related compounds. The action did not apply to traditional botanical kratom. 
As of January, 30 states had laws regulating kratom or its components. Six states, including Alabama, Arkansas and Louisiana, classify the substance’s primary chemical compounds as controlled substances, resulting in kratom products being banned. 
More than 30 counties and cities in Mississippi have restricted or banned the product.
Mississippi restricted kratom purchases to people ages 21 and older and prohibited sales for potent kratom extracts in 2025. The bill, authored by Rep. Lee Yancey, a Republican from Brandon, and signed into law by Gov. Tate Reeves, instituted fines for people under 21 who buy or possess kratom and retailers that sell it to them.
But several speakers on Wednesday told House members the law did not go far enough to protect the public. 
Oxford Police Chief Jeff McCutchen, who also serves as the president of the Mississippi Association of Chiefs of Police, said the law was not sufficient because it sets low fines — up to $1,000 for selling a restricted product — and requires law enforcement officers to test products for compliance.
“The law is set up for us to fail,” McCutchen said. 
Col. Phillip Pope, the director of the Mississippi Bureau of Narcotics, agreed, adding that to enforce the law, officials must buy the products from gas stations and send them to laboratories for testing using taxpayer dollars. 
State health officials, including State Health Officer Dr. Dan Edney, who has a subspecialty board certification in addiction medicine, and Dr. Tom Recore, the Department of Mental Health’s medical director, have recommended scheduling kratom as a controlled substance. 
Philip Chamblee, the executive director of the Mississippi Petroleum Marketers and Convenience Stores Association, said the organization’s board voted unanimously last week to support a statewide ban on the sale of all kratom products. 
Some speakers argued that lawmakers should consider the distinction between natural forms of kratom and more potent synthetic derivatives. 
Sheldon Bradshaw, an attorney representing Botanicals for Better Health and Wellness and former chief counsel for the Food and Drug Administration, said natural forms of kratom have been unfairly associated with the University of Mississippi student deaths. 
He said synthetic kratom derivatives often market themselves to suggest they are natural products. 
“The snake oil salesmen want people to believe they’re kratom, but they’re not kratom,” Bradshaw said. 
During the hearing, Sherry Owings, 63, of Mississippi, said she began using kratom after struggling with chronic pain and the side effects of prescription medications. She said kratom has improved her quality of life. 
“I don’t want to go backwards,” she said, advocating regulation and transparency about the ingredients in kratom but urging lawmakers not to restrict natural forms of the substance.  
Officials said more Mississippians are seeking help for kratom addiction.
Wendy Bailey, the executive director of the Mississippi Department of Mental Health, said the agency’s helpline has received a sharp increase in calls over the last two months from callers experiencing addiction to kratom.
Among those calls, she described one man struggling to manage withdrawal symptoms and a nurse who began taking kratom for fatigue before losing her job due to her addiction. 
“I think we have the opportunity to approach this from a public policy perspective,” Bailey said.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Incoming bipartisan coalition of the Alaska Senate announces key leadership
description: Anchorage Republican Cathy Giessel will be the next Alaska Senate President for the upcoming 35th Alaska State Legislature, according to an announcement from a bipartisan coalition of senators on Wednesday. Giessel showed a comfortable lead with 61% of the vote in her bid for re-election, as of Wednesday afternoon results, and has served in the […]
text:
The Alaska State Capitol is seen during the last week of the 2025 session on May 19, 2025. (Photo by Corinne Smith/Alaska Beacon)Anchorage Republican Cathy Giessel will be the next Alaska Senate President for the upcoming 35th Alaska State Legislature, according to an announcement from a bipartisan coalition of senators on Wednesday.     

Senate Majority Leader Cathy Giessel, R-Anchorage, is seen during an at ease on the Senate floor on May 7, 2026. (Photo by Corinne Smith/Alaska Beacon)
 

Giessel showed a comfortable lead with 61% of the vote in her bid for re-election, as of Wednesday afternoon results, and has served in the Senate since 2011. She previously served as Senate President from 2019 to 2022, and as Senate Majority Leader and chair of the Senate Resources Committee from 2023 to 2026.
The bipartisan Senate coalition, first formed in 2022 under Kodiak Republican Gary Stevens, is moving to form the Senate Majority coalition in the next Legislature. But its membership and numbers are not confirmed as thousands of votes are still being counted by the Alaska Division of Elections, and winners choosing which caucus to join. 
The majority coalition must have at least 11 members to be a majority in the 20 member chamber. Final election results are scheduled to be certified on Nov. 25. 
In an interview, Giessel said the top priorities for the next Senate will include public education funding, reviving a public pension system, election reform measures and energy.
While Alaska state revenues have seen a surge with the high price of oil, Giessel said the bipartisan Senate leadership will take a “balanced” approach to state spending.
“We are aware that there is going to be excess funding or excess revenue, but we are not going to go on a spending spree. This is something that we all agree on. This is going to be constrained. We’re going to be focusing on the priority budget items first,” she said. 
Giessel said the coalition has not formally spoken with the Democratic gubernatorial frontrunner Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins yet, but meetings would likely begin later this month. 
The coalition named Senator-elect Louise Stutes, a Kodiak Republican, as Senate Majority Leader. Stutes is a first-time candidate for the Senate representing the district which includes Kodiak Island, the southern Kenai Peninsula and Prince William Sound communities, but she has served in the Alaska House since 2015. She has so far received 48.6% of the vote, as of Wednesday afternoon, a significant lead over Republican Heath Smith with 39.7%. 
Another senator-elect that is still unconfirmed is Dillingham independent and House Speaker Rep. Bryce Edgon. He has been appointed as co-chair of the powerful Senate Finance Committee.     

Rep. Bryce Edgmon, I-Dillingham, is seen during debate on the operating budget on Apr. 13, 2026. (Photo by Corinne Smith/Alaska Beacon)
 

As of Wednesday afternoon, Edgmon received 36.1% of the vote to represent one of the state’s largest districts that extends from Western Alaska to the Aleutian Islands. He led Republican Darren Deacon who got 26.8%, and Democrat Wissilie Guy who received 24.8%. Many absentee-in-person and by-mail ballots from the rural region have yet to be counted.  
Anchorage Democrat Bill Wielechowski, who ran unopposed, will be the Senate Rules Chair. He has served in the Senate since 2007, and has chaired the Rules Committee since 2023. 
Juneau Democrat Jesse Kiehl, who was not up for re-election this year, will be co-chair of the Senate Finance Committee, of which he has been a member since 2023. He was first elected to the Senate in 2018. 
Wielchowski said in a statement with the announcement the team has experience representing communities across the state as well as working together and across party lines. 
“This is the message that Alaskans have continued to send us to address the many needs for a stronger Alaska future,” he said. “This coalition will continue to focus on lowering costs for families, ensuring Alaska receives its fair share for our resources, election reform, and making sure that every community across the state, urban and rural, has a seat at the table.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Offshore Revolution Wind development is now fully operational
description: Revolution Wind reached full commercial operation off the coast of Rhode Island in October, developer Ørsted told investors on Thursday.
text:
Revolution Wind reached full commercial operation off the coast of Rhode Island in October, officials with Danish offshore wind developer Ørsted said in a call with investors on Thursday.  
Work began on the 704-megawatt project in 2023, and its turbines began producing power for the New England energy grid earlier this this year. 
But construction on the $6 billion project was twice interrupted by stop-work orders from President Donald Trump’s administration, which has sought to dismantle the nation’s burgeoning offshore wind industry. 
Officials with the U.S. Department of Interior said Revolution Wind and other projects under development along the Atlantic Coast had the potential to interfere with military radar — arguments that were rejected by a federal judge who allowed work on the projects to continue.
Revolution Wind’s 65th and final turbine was installed in September. On-shore assembly work took place at the State Pier in New London. 
In a statement, the company said Revolution Wind is “generating up to its full capacity,” but did not provide further details about its output.
Revolution Wind is supported by power-purchase agreements with utility customers in Connecticut and Rhode Island. For Eversource and United Illuminating customers, that price is set at $99 per megawatt-hour, recovered through the public benefits charge.
When operating at full capacity, the project can produce enough electricity to power roughly 350,000 homes. 
Officials at the Connecticut Department of Energy and Environmental Protection have calculated that Revolution Wind will help save customers roughly $500 million annually starting in 2028, due primarily to the project’s competitiveness with other, more expensive forms of electricity. 
“This is an important milestone which provides much needed new energy generation to customers at a time when demand is rising,” Eversource spokesman William Hinkle said in a statement. 
The Trump administration has not let up on its efforts to scuttle Revolution Wind, even as the project neared total completion. In October, attorneys for the Interior Department sought permission from a federal judge to rescind prior approvals for the project’s construction plan.
That request remains pending before U.S. District Court Judge Royce C. Lamberth in Washington D.C., who has twice sided with developers in lawsuits against the Trump administration.
Ørsted is continuing development of another offshore project, Sunrise Wind, from the State Pier in New London. That project is about 60% complete, according to the company’s third quarter report.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Southeast Alaska port development named for Frank Murkowski
description: The Republican trio served together in Congress for more than two decades, and while the Anchorage port is named for the late Rep. Don Young and the Anchorage airport is named for the late Sen. Ted Stevens, their congressional colleague, Sen. Frank Murkowski, is more at home in Southeast. The Wrangell borough assembly on Oct. […]
text:
Wrangell, Alaska is seen from the window of Alaska Airlines Flight 64 on Monday, Sept. 12, 2022. At bottom is the tip of the airplane's wing. (Photo by James Brooks/Alaska Beacon)The Republican trio served together in Congress for more than two decades, and while the Anchorage port is named for the late Rep. Don Young and the Anchorage airport is named for the late Sen. Ted Stevens, their congressional colleague, Sen. Frank Murkowski, is more at home in Southeast.
The Wrangell borough assembly on Oct. 27 voted unanimously to name the former 6-Mile sawmill property, which the borough is developing as an industrial site, as the Frank H. Murkowski Deepwater Port of Wrangell, Alaska.
Murkowski got his Alaska start in Southeast in Ketchikan and Wrangell 70 years ago before moving into politics and public service in Juneau and Washington, D.C.
In introducing the naming resolution at the Oct. 27 assembly meeting, Borough Manager Mason Villarma spoke to Murkowski’s long-term contributions to the state and the community, adding, “he has been an advocate of the site for a long, long time.”    
Gov. Frank Murkowski, a Republican, who served from 2002 to 2006.. (Photo provided by the Alaska State Library Historical Collection)

The assembly last month adopted an ordinance, setting out requirements for naming public property after an individual. The port is the first use of that new ordinance.
“That’s very thoughtful of them,” Murkowski said in an interview the day after the assembly vote, though he noted, “That Polish name doesn’t sound very Southeast.”
Talking about the borough’s big plans for the property, he said: “Hopefully, all the things we hear are going to happen out there happen.”
The municipality purchased the 42 acres more than four years ago for $2.5 million, looking to develop and lease out the acreage for industrial tenants. The aim is to replace some of the jobs and economic activity lost in town when the mill and logging industry started shutting down in the 1990s.
Alaska Marine Lines is working to move its barge landing and freight operations to the property; Tideline Construction runs its scrap metal recycling and Southeast Alaska construction business from the site; and the borough is working with JAG Marine Group, the Ketchikan shipyard operator, to look for state and federal funding to build a multi-hundred-million-dollar large-scale shipyard to work on government vessels.
Villarma noted that the U.S. Economic Development Administration has awarded Wrangell about $30 million toward site work — utilities and roads — to prepare the former mill property for use as a deepwater industrial port.
“This couldn’t come at a most opportune time for us,” he told the assembly. “And I think it’s going to help attract investment to the site and create some additional buzz.”
Murkowski is 93 years old. He and his wife, Nancy, spend their summers in Wrangell. He came to Southeast with the U.S. Coast Guard in the mid-1950s and then went into banking and managed the National Bank of Alaska Wrangell branch from 1963 to 1966 and served on the school board.
He was named commissioner of the Alaska Department of Commerce and Economic Development in 1966, then returned to banking until his election to the U.S. Senate in 1980.
He left the Senate in 2002, winning election as governor and serving one term.
And although he questioned whether his Polish name fits in Southeast, the Murkowski Port is not alone. There is an island in Southeast, Kosciusko Island, just north of Prince of Wales Island, named in 1879 after Polish citizen Tadeusz Kościuszko, who fought in the American Revolutionary War as a volunteer engineer, according to the Dictionary of Alaska Place Names published by the U.S. Department of the Interior.
This story is republished from the Wrangell Sentinel.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: NC Democrats will have more power next year, but must first face a GOP-controlled lame duck session
description: Next year, North Carolina Democrats will have more political power than they’ve had since 2010, with a commanding majority in the House and the governorship. As anticipated, Rep. Robert Reives, D-Chatham, who has led the House Democrats since 2021, announced he would seek the House speakership.  “I will be running for Speaker of the House […]
text:
“We’ve got providers that are trying to figure out how they’re going to keep their doors open during Christmas,” House Democratic Leader Robert Reives, D-Chatham, told reporters at a press conference on Nov. 17, 2025. “Yet we’ve got folks that will not sit down and have a conversation about passing a budget for North Carolina, like 49 other states have done.” (Photo: Galen Bacharier/NC Newsline)Next year, North Carolina Democrats will have more political power than they’ve had since 2010, with a commanding majority in the House and the governorship.
As anticipated, Rep. Robert Reives, D-Chatham, who has led the House Democrats since 2021, announced he would seek the House speakership. 
“I will be running for Speaker of the House and will seek the support of my caucus at our organizational meeting and the support of the full House on January 13,” Reives said in a statement. 
He thanked candidates who agreed to run, and vowed, “Democrats will fight for the policies that put us in this position.”
Though the House will vote on House Speaker candidates next year,  Gov. Josh Stein and state Democratic Party Chair Anderson Clayton are already referring to Reives as “Speaker-elect.”
House Speaker Destin Hall, R-Caldwell, congratulated Reives and the Democratic House caucus on Tuesday night, saying he looked forward to working with Reives when Democrats take control of the House. 
Unofficial results show Democrats winning 71 seats to Republicans’ 48, with one unaffiliated winner. In five districts, the leader appears to have won by less than 1 point, placing those races in recount territory. 
After years pushing back against policies they oppose, House Democrats will have the chance to set the agenda. 
Over the years, Democrats have voted against rollbacks of environmental protections, Republican power grabs, and mandatory law enforcement cooperation with ICE, among other policies. 
Are limits on private school vouchers possible?
One issue that unites returning veterans and newly-elected Democrats is the position that public school funding is too low.
In a news release Tuesday night, the N.C. Association of Educators cheered the Democrats’ new House majority. 
“North Carolina voters sent a clear message: our public schools are not for sale,” NCAE President Christina Cole said in a statement. “For years, legislative leaders have handed out corporate tax cuts and private school vouchers while our classrooms went without.”
NCAE will hold every legislator accountable for fully funding public schools, the statement said. 
In recent years, House Democrats have denounced the expansion of the state’s private school voucher program. Over time, Republicans erased income caps on vouchers, so well-off families now receive taxpayer subsidies for private school tuition. 
At a news conference today, Stein said spending on vouchers should be up for discussion next year. Stein says he supports parents who think private schools are best for their children, but he says the state doesn’t have enough money to pay for a universal voucher program and properly fund public schools at the same time. 
“Do we really want these scarce dollars for education to go away from a public school kid, taken out of that public school kid’s backpack, and put into the bank account of somebody who’s doing pretty well, sending their child to an unaccountable private school, whose child was never in public school?” he asked. 
“We don’t have enough dollars invested in public education today to be taking $750 million a year away. We’re 50th in the nation in terms of what we invest on a per-child basis in our public schools. That’s an embarrassment.”
The state budget for vouchers is set to increase from $700 million next year to $825 million in 2032.
A last meeting before the GOP loses control of the House 
Before Democrats take control of the House, Republicans are set to return to Raleigh for a lame duck session. 
In past lame duck sessions, Republicans stripped power from Democratic governors and other Democratic officials.
Democrats appear to win the NC House majority and gain seats in the Senate

For example, in December 2024, knowing that House Republicans would lose their supermajority in a month and Stein was preparing to move into the Executive Mansion, the legislature transferred power to appoint the state Board of Elections from Stein to Republican Auditor-elect Dave Boliek. 
In December 2016, after Roy Cooper won the governorship, the legislature passed a law expanding the state Board of Elections and limiting Cooper’s appointments to the board. That law was invalidated by state courts. 
Another law passed during the 2016 lame duck session reduced political appointee positions in cabinet departments from 1,500 to 300, limiting the jobs Cooper and his department heads controlled. That bill also required the state Senate to confirm the governor’s cabinet appointees. Republicans had won supermajorities in both chambers in the 2016 elections. 
Stein said Wednesday that he didn’t know what bills Republicans have planned for Nov. 16, when the legislature is scheduled to return. 
“If they do come back, what they need to do is learn the lesson of the election last night, which is don’t do politics, don’t engage in gamesmanship,” Stein advised. “Focus on issues that make a difference, whether it’s driving down costs that families are experiencing or whether it’s keeping people safe.”

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Massachusetts should not settle for half-measures on children’s online safety
description: Children deserve to get through their most sensitive years before encountering a product built to profit from vice and vulnerability.
text:
THIS FALL, a six-member conference committee will decide whether Massachusetts joins the international movement to restrict children’s access to social media.  
The committee is reconciling a House bill on student mental health that would prohibit children under 14 from holding social media accounts. Separately, the Senate has passed a bill restricting the addictive design features that keep children compulsively engaged. Taken together, the two proposals point toward a stronger policy: Massachusetts should prohibit children under 16 from holding accounts on platforms that employ predatory design features. 
In Massachusetts, more than one in three high schoolers report sustained sadness or hopelessness. Pediatric behavioral health boarding in Massachusetts emergency departments remains six times higher than before the pandemic. A mounting body of evidence suggests social media is not incidental to this public health crisis, but rather a significant contributor. 
Even Meta no longer pretends its product is safe for children. In August, facing testimony that its internal culture made child safety “practically impossible,” the company agreed to pay up to $17 billion to 52 attorneys general and to limit teenagers to two hours a day on its platforms.  
But a daily allowance of an addictive product is still a choice to subject children to harm. Massachusetts should not settle for simply regulating the dose. 
The damages of the modern internet extend well beyond mental health. The share of Massachusetts fourth-graders scoring below the basic level in reading has nearly doubled since 2011, from 17 percent to 32 percent, while longitudinal research finds that earlier social media use harms later language and math performance.  
In-person socialization among young Americans has fallen to a 21-year low, while nearly four in 10 young children spend an hour or less playing outside on weekdays. American children now experience an indoor, phone-based childhood, sedentary and solitary. 
What passes for social media today is increasingly neither social nor interactive. Across major social media platforms, entertainment consistently ranks among teens’ leading reasons for use. Algorithmically served short-form videos are interspersed with ads for online gambling and promotions for weight-loss supplements, alongside AI-generated explicit sexual material. 
Children deserve to get through their most sensitive years before encountering a product built to profit from vice and vulnerability. 
Prohibiting account creation for children under 16 protects them through much of adolescence, a second major window of heightened brain plasticity after early childhood in which experience can shape development well into adulthood. Age restrictions on addictive products have a proven track record of reducing consumption at the population level, even with imperfect enforcement. Social media is an addictive product unfit for developing minds, and it should be regulated accordingly. 
Restrictions on addictive design features of social media platforms remain an important safeguard, but they reach only the minors a platform has already identified and place regulators in the position of repeatedly deciding which practices warrant intervention and how each should be regulated. By defining covered platforms according to the design features they deploy rather than the content they host, lawmakers can make access to children conditional on the product a company builds. 
Platforms that redesign their products around safer forms of interaction can become eligible to serve children under 16. The law thereby creates an incentive not merely to comply with individual restrictions, but to build a safer product. 
Relying solely on parental controls fails the children most in need of protection. Parents without graduate degrees are far less likely to impose screen-time limits, while about four in 10 parents say it is hard to manage how much time their teen spends on their phone. A patchwork of household rules inevitably protects children unevenly; a statewide default ensures protection does not depend on parents’ time, technical fluency, or resources. 
The constitutional case for restricting minors’ access to social media is getting stronger by the day. In June, a federal appeals court rejected a facial challenge to an Ohio law requiring parental consent before children under 16 can join social media platforms defined by features such as profiles, friend networks, and feeds of user-generated content. In April, the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court ruled unanimously that Section 230, a crucial provision of a 1996 federal communications statute, does not shield platforms from claims targeting those same kinds of engineered design features. That gives lawmakers a path to regulate social media by product design rather than content. 
Civil liberties advocates have warned that age checks will require invasive ID collection, threatening online anonymity. But Apple and Google are already deploying device-level age assurance that can signal whether a user falls above or below an age threshold without disclosing a birthdate or ID. When a child’s age is affirmed by a parent rather than estimated from their face or behavior, the system avoids the estimation failures inherent to age-estimation systems. 
This will be remembered as the year the world drew a firm line on social media. Over the past year, Australia, Britain, France, and Denmark have all moved to restrict social media for young teenagers, and 20 countries have now acted or begun drafting similar laws. The recent settlement could produce billions in additional obligations if state legislatures bind Meta’s rivals to equivalent rules. An overwhelming majority of Americans support requiring age verification and parental consent for social media. 
Massachusetts currently leads the nation on many traditional measures of child well-being. Beacon Hill now has the opportunity to set the standard on the challenge that will define childhood in the 21st century by enacting the strongest children’s online safety law in the nation. Parents, educators, and children across the Commonwealth deserve nothing less. 
Matthew Allaire, a senior majoring in political science at Macalester College, is executive director of Commonwealth IRL, an advocacy organization working to curtail the influence of addictive and persuasive technology on young people.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: On Election Day in Lawrence, political corruption, low voter turnout, and uncontested races converge
description: Lawrence voters, candidates, and civic organizations alike grappled Tuesday with the city’s recent political scandals, historically low turnout, and uncontested races as they tried to mobilize residents and make political change in the city. Though the city's voter turnout rate increased slightly this election, the city still has a long way to go.
text:
NOT MANY POLITICAL CAMPAIGNS are born in a bar a month before Election Day, but Diego Leonardo’s decision to run for state office certainly wasn’t the most striking news to come out of Lawrence this year.  
In September, the 34-year-old college professor and biotech company owner stopped by Sazón Perú, a Peruvian restaurant and bar, to grab a drink. There, he watched the local evening news being broadcast on multiple TVs.  
On one was a segment detailing Mayor Brian DePeña’s arrest after federal prosecutors in August charged him with fraud and money laundering.  
On another, there was a segment covering the 11-count indictment of state Rep. Francisco Paulino, a Democrat representing Lawrence and Methuen, who was also arrested and charged in August with eight counts of wire fraud and three counts of money laundering.  
Both men have pleaded not guilty.  
“I thought, ‘Wow, it’s so embarrassing to live here. What are we doing?’” Leonardo recalls.  
The city of 90,000 is no stranger to political corruption scandal.  
Since the end of 2023 alone, a city councilor was charged with and pleaded guilty to voter fraud, DePeña’s former chief of staff was sentenced for transporting and possessing child pornography, and Attorney General Andrea Campbell launched a criminal investigation into allegations of secret audio recording inside Lawrence City Hall. More than a decade ago, William Lantigua was also shrouded in scandal throughout his time as mayor.  
Lawrence City Hall. (Hallie Claflin/CommonWealth Beacon) 
That night earlier this fall, Leonardo struck up a conversation with other bargoers about corruption in Lawrence and the city’s historical lack of competitive elections. Some said they wouldn’t waste their time voting this year. 
That’s when Leonardo, an immigrant from Guatemala, asked if they would vote for someone like him. They said they would.  
“The next day, I called some community leaders and said, ‘What do you think about me running?’” Leonardo said. “They said, ‘Yeah, next year we definitely need somebody.’ And I was like, ‘Not next year — now.’”  
Though he was already months past the April 28 deadline to submit nomination papers, meaning his name couldn’t appear on the November 3 ballot, Leonardo, an independent, charged ahead with a write-in campaign for 16th Essex District state representative, the seat currently held by Paulino.  
Diego Leonardo holding flyers for his write-in campaign on Election Day, Nov. 3, 2026. (Hallie Claflin/CommonWealth Beacon) 
City Councilor Celina Reyes, who defeated the indicted representative in the September Democratic primary, won the seat by a large majority on Tuesday. Leonardo, who ran without a campaign team and a source of funding, knew his bid was a long shot. 
But running any non-incumbent campaign, write-in or not, is no easy endeavor in Lawrence. The city typically has one of the lowest turnout rates in the state.   
“It’s worthwhile giving options to the community,” Leonardo said. “I think one thing my candidacy brought is hope.”  
In the 2022 midterms, the city of Lawrence had the lowest voter turnout rate in Massachusetts at just under 22.8 percent. That number is even more striking when compared to more affluent communities like Mount Washington and Alford, which had the highest turnout at 75.7 and 73.3 percent, respectively.  
This year, the city’s turnout landed at 25.6 percent, according to unofficial results. The modest increase represents progress, though the city still has a long way to go.  
Statewide turnout numbers won’t be finalized and reported for a few weeks — but Chelsea, Lowell, and Springfield, which saw the state’s fourth, third, and second lowest turnout rates in 2022, on Wednesday were reporting roughly 33.6, 26.5, and 28.4 percent turnout respectively, according to unofficial results.
Lawrence voters, candidates, and civic organizations alike grappled Tuesday with the city’s recent political scandals, historically low turnout, and uncontested races as they tried to mobilize residents and make political change in the city.   
Lawrence voters cast their ballots at South Lawrence East Elementary School on Nov. 3, 2026. (Hallie Claflin/CommonWealth Beacon) 
“When government cannot be trusted, it gives folks a reason to say participating is pointless,” said Julio Mejia, executive director of the Merrimack Valley Project. “It deepens the distrust, it drives people away from the system, and it overshadows the community when Lawrence is being defined by headlines and controversies.” 
But Mejia also said an opening for accountability has been created in Lawrence.  
“There has been this call for us to create a pathway from that frustration, from that mistrust in government, to participation,” he said.  
Gateway Cities like Lawrence — generally some of the state’s most disadvantaged and ethnically diverse urban communities — consistently have some of the lowest voter turnout rates in Massachusetts. In 2022, nine of the 10 municipalities with the lowest turnout in the state were Gateway Cities.  
The phenomenon is hardly unique to Massachusetts. A 2023 report published by the Pew Research Center found that 2022 voters were whiter, older, and more educated than nonvoters, and research consistently finds higher turnout among voters with higher incomes. That discrepancy translates to more affluent people and communities having more of a say in who gets elected. 
“The people who are least likely to vote are often the people who are most affected by decisions made through policy,” Shanique Rodriguez, executive director of the nonprofit Massachusetts Voter Table.  
Lawrence voters face a litany of barriers when it comes to voting, including language and translation challenges, a lack of transportation, and economic insecurity. Nearly 83 percent of city residents are Hispanic or Latino, nearly half its population is foreign-born, and 78 percent speak a language other than English at home.  
Downtown Lawrence, Nov. 3, 2026. (Hallie Claflin/CommonWealth Beacon) 
“We are a community with people of color, immigrants, and folks that work multiple jobs, and there is an economic cost to voting,” Mejia said.  
Around 18 percent of Lawrence residents live below the poverty line, which is nearly twice the statewide average of just under 10 percent. The city’s median household income is $60,000, less than 60 percent of the state’s $104,000.  
Those with lower incomes are less likely to own a home and more likely to rent, meaning they also tend to move more frequently than homeowners. This often disrupts voter registration and can impact how attached someone feels to the community where they live, and how likely they are to vote. Around 72 percent of Lawrence households rent, while 28 percent own homes.  
“Low voter turnout is not necessarily evidence that residents don’t care about the city,” Mejia said. “It reflects a combination of structural barriers, limited political engagement, and a lack of confidence that participation and voting would lead to change.” 
Voter registration reports filed by Secretary of State Bill Galvin’s office show that more than 50,000 people were registered to vote in Lawrence this election, the highest that number has been in any election in well over a decade.  
Unofficial election results show that nearly 560 write-in votes were cast in the 16th Essex District on Tuesday, which was more than three times as many seen in other state legislative districts. Reyes, the only candidate on the ballot, received around 4,250 votes, while nearly 900 voters left the contest blank.  
Leonardo holds a flyer encouraging voters to write his name on the ballot. (Hallie Claflin/CommonWealth Beacon) 
Leonardo stands with his family outside of a school on Election Day. (Hallie Claflin/CommonWealth Beacon) 
Outside an elementary school on Tuesday, Leonardo’s supporters held signs and handed out flyers alongside Reyes’s supporters.  
“It’s encouraging. It brings more people out to vote, and it brings another option for people,” City Councilor Gregory Del Rosario said of Leonardo’s run, even as he held a campaign sign for Reyes. “When people are running unopposed, it leads voters to believe there will be no chance.”  
Supporters of Celina Reyes hold campaign signs outside of a school on Election Day. (Hallie Claflin/CommonWealth Beacon) 
State Sen. Pavel Payano, a Democrat representing Lawrence, ran uncontested in the 1st Essex District, as did state Reps. Estela Reyes and Frank Moran in the 4th and 17th Essex districts. Several other races, including the district attorney’s office, were also uncontested.  
The recent headlines about Mayor DePeña’s arrest and the indictment of Rep. Paulino have in some ways reinforced a reputation for lawlessness that some say Lawrence does not deserve.  
“Corruption in politics has been there forever. It’s a nationwide crisis, and you see it at all levels of politics,” Del Rosario said.  
DePeña, who has refused to resign, held signs throughout Lawrence on Tuesday urging people not to sign a citizen-led petition to recall him. Organizers have 30 days to collect signatures from at least 15 percent of registered voters, which is more than 7,000 signatures in Lawrence. 
Meanwhile, residents like Juan Tejada and Altagracia Mayi camped out under a curbside tent on Election Day and gathered signatures to oust the embattled mayor. To them, the charges against DePeña birthed a deep sense of betrayal in the community that left some voters jaded, even though the mayor was not on the ballot.  
Lawrence residents collected signatures on Election Day for a citizen-led petition to recall Lawrence mayor Brian DePeña, who was arrested in August after federal prosecutors charged him with fraud and money laundering. (Hallie Claflin/CommonWealth Beacon) 
“We are Dominican just like him. It’s like — why are you doing this to your own people?” Tejada said. “When you have people in office like that, it’s like, ‘Why would I go and vote? It’s going to be the same.’ That’s what people think.”  
As Leonardo put it: “Corruption starts to corrupt the whole system.” 
Even those who did show up to vote in Lawrence agree.  
“A lot of things going on are unsavory … It’s all just so close to home, and it’s much more sobering when it’s that close to you,” 21-year-old voter Gianmarcus Marrero said as he left his polling site on Tuesday. “Corruption leads to voter turnout being low. You see this going on for so long, and you become numb to it. You start to think, ‘What’s one vote of mine going to do?’ But we shouldn’t normalize these things.” 
A 21-year-old voter, Gianmarcus Marrero, stands outside of his polling place at South Lawrence East Elementary School on Election Day. (Hallie Claflin/CommonWealth Beacon) 
Getting more people to the polls surely won’t guarantee scandal-free mayors and representatives in Lawrence, but could it, at the very least, increase public scrutiny of office seekers?  
Lawrence voters like Janelle Nutter are still holding out hope.  
“It’s scary, because these are people put in a position where we should be able to trust them,” she said as she left the polls on Tuesday. “But you still put your vote in and pray for a change — pray for something better.” 
Mejia said when the public’s trust in democracy is shaken, what they need are not reasons to be cynical but rather meaningful ways to demand transparency and integrity from their elected officials. 
The Merrimack Valley Project’s nonpartisan civic engagement work includes door-to-door outreach, phone calls, and resource-building. The organization has also held candidate forums and public assemblies in an effort to engage residents in local elections.  
“We need change,” Shaneka Rodriguez, another Lawrence resident, said outside of her polling place. “I don’t think a lot of people here realize that they can make a difference. I see so many people who have opinions, but the numbers don’t show those opinions.” 
Other local nonprofits like Lawrence Community Works tabled outside rent-restricted housing developments on Tuesday, encouraging voters to head to the polls and study up on the flurry of ballot questions. Still, many residents told the organization they weren’t voting, either because they couldn’t get to the polls or simply didn’t want to. 
Lawrence Community Works staff speak with a potential voter on Election Day outside of an affordable housing property at 50 Island Street. (Hallie Claflin/CommonWealth Beacon) 
“Lawrence can take its power back when the people who live, work, worship, and raise their families here recognize that their voice can actually shape the future of the city,” Mejia said. “If we have that larger vision, we’ll be able to build a community powerful enough to hold leaders accountable and set priorities, but also shift this narrative that Lawrence doesn’t vote or is not engaged.”  
But he said it’s about more than just getting people to the polls. It’s about engaging them beyond the voting booth and encouraging them to participate in public meetings or organize with their neighbors.  
Or run for office themselves, as Leonardo learned. 
“If you don’t get into politics, politics gets into you,” Leonardo said.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: What SC voters had to say about the midterm election
authors: Skylar Laird, Jessica Holdman, Katharine Wilson
description: At polling places across the state, voters said they were supporting Annie Andrews, the Democrat who won a seat in the US Senate.
text:
U.S. Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.) waves bye to supporters during an election night GOP watch party on Nov. 3, 2026, in Columbia, South Carolina, after she concedes her loss in the U.S. Senate race. (Photo by John A. Carlos II/Special to the SC Daily Gazette)Ahead of the vote-counting for Tuesday’s historic election in South Carolina, SC Daily Gazette reporters headed to the polls to hear what mattered most to voters.
The election brought record-high turnout for a year without a presidential race on the ballot. Democrat Annie Andrews achieved a major upset by turning a U.S. Senate seat in South Carolina blue, while Republican Alan Wilson clinched his bid for the Governor’s Mansion. In the Lowcountry, Democrat Nancy Lacore declared victory in the 1st District, while other congressional incumbents held onto their seats.
Here’s what some of the voters told the Daily Gazette about their decisions.
In Columbia
Among the more prominent vote-casters Tuesday was outgoing South Carolina Gov. Henry McMaster, who cast his ballot Tuesday morning at the Lourie Center in Columbia.

Gov. Henry McMaster and first lady Peggy McMaster leave the polling place after voting Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026, at Lourie Center in Columbia, S.C. (Photo by Katharine Wilson/SC Daily Gazette)

Asked about the state’s tight U.S Senate race between Andrews and Darline Graham, the younger sister of the late U.S. Sen. Lindsey Graham, the GOP governor predicted Darline Graham would win.
The night’s events proved McMaster wrong.
“You never know how the voters are going to react, but South Carolina traditionally is a conservative state,” McMaster told reporters early in the day. “Ms. Andrews, according to what I’ve read, is quite far from the conservative side. That’s a big plus for Senator Graham. I think she will prevail.”
South Carolina’s longest-serving governor in state history will depart in January after a 10-year tenure. McMaster said the transition will be smooth, as “that’s the easiest thing in the world to do.” The governor said he still has work to do in his remaining days, but his office will help the winning candidate learn the role.
Governor-elect Alan Wilson walks on stage at the GOP election night party at the State Fairgrounds in Columbia, South Carolina, on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by John A. Carlos/Special to the SC Daily Gazette)State Sen. Mike Reichenbach, the elected lieutenant governor, addresses supporters at the GOP election night party at the State Fairgrounds in Columbia, South Carolina, on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by John A. Carlos/Special to the SC Daily Gazette)Governor-elect Alan Wilson addresses supporters at the GOP election night party Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by John A. Carlos II/Special to the SC Daily Gazette)Roxanne Wilson and U.S. Rep. Joe Wilson look on as their son, governor-elect Alan Wilson, addresses supporters at the GOP election night party Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by John A. Carlos II/Special to the SC Daily Gazette)South Carolina Governor Alan Wilson thanks supporters during an election night GOP watch party on Nov. 3, 2026, in Columbia, South Carolina. (Photo by John A. Carlos II/Special to the SC Daily Gazette)
 
“We will cooperate with whomever wins in any of these offices, whatever they want to know from us, we’ll give you,” McMaster, the former state attorney general, said about all of the statewide offices on the ballot.
Also in Columbia, the price of groceries and gas drove a lot of voters to the polls.
“Prices are way too high, and it has to change,” said Nyquobi Ross, a 22-year-old freelance writer in Columbia. “My pockets cannot handle this.”
Throughout the early afternoon, a steady stream of people voted at the county election office, a barrier-free voting location for people throughout the county.
Deanthony Franklin, a 19-year-old musician, voted for the first time Tuesday. He usually doesn’t pay much attention to politics, but when he noticed his grocery bill and gas bill rising, he felt he needed to participate, he said.

South Carolina Education Superintendent Ellen Weaver speaks to supporters during an election night GOP watch party on Nov. 3, 2026, in Columbia, South Carolina. (Photo by John A. Carlos II/Special to the SC Daily Gazette)South Carolina's next comptroller general, Mike Burkhold, speaks to supporters during an election night GOP watch party on Nov. 3, 2026, in Columbia, South Carolina. Behind him are Superintendent Ellen Weaver, Secretary of State Mark Hammond, Treasurer Curtis Loftis, and soon-to-be Agriculture Commissioner Cody Simpson. (Photo by John A. Carlos II/Special to the SC Daily Gazette)State Treasurer Curtis Loftis speaks to supporters during an election night GOP watch party on Nov. 3, 2026, in Columbia, South Carolina. (Photo by John A. Carlos II/Special to the SC Daily Gazette)South Carolina Secretary of State Mark Hammond speaks to supporters during an election night GOP watch party on Nov. 3, 2026, in Columbia, South Carolina. (Photo by John A. Carlos II/Special to the SC Daily Gazette)Cody Simpson, the soon-to-be commissioner of agriculture, speaks to supporters during an election night GOP watch party on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026, in Columbia, South Carolina. (Photo by John A. Carlos II/Special to the SC Daily Gazette)South Carolina's next lieutenant governor, state Sen. Mike Reichenbach, speaks to supporters during an election night GOP watch party on Nov. 3, 2026, in Columbia, South Carolina. (Photo by John A. Carlos II/Special to the SC Daily Gazette)U.S. Sen. Darline Graham gives a concession speech Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026, at the State Fairgrounds in Columbia.  John A. Carlos II/Special to the SC Daily Gazette)

Franklin wants President Donald Trump out of office, he said. Without the president on the ballot, he voted for every Democrat.
“You’ve got to do something,” Franklin said. “You can’t just sit around and expect change to come overnight.”
For Zai Shiver, education was the biggest issue. A former educator, the nearly-60-year-old wants to see more funding go toward the state’s public schools.
Shiver declined to say who she voted for but noted she did want to see change in the state Department of Education.
In that election, Superintendent Ellen Weaver won re-election over Democrat Sylvia Wright.
“Definitely there need to be some major changes to better educate the children, to give them supplies that they need, to deal with their home lives and issues that they may have with their home lives,” Shiver said about her vote.

Campaign signs line the roadway around the State Fairgrounds in Columbia, S.C., where GOP nominees and their supporters gathered for an election night watch party Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by John A. Carlos II/Special to the SC Daily Gazette)South Carolina Republican Party Chairman Drew McKissick addresses the crowd at the GOP election night watch party on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026, at the Moore Building on the South Carolina State Fairgrounds in Columbia. (Photo by John A. Carlos II/Special to the SC Daily Gazette)Supporters gather at a GOP election night watch party on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026, at the Moore Building on the South Carolina State Fairgrounds in Columbia. (Photo by John A. Carlos II/Special to the SC Daily Gazette)Supporters gather at a GOP election night watch party on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026, at the Moore Building on the South Carolina State Fairgrounds in Columbia. (Photo by John A. Carlos II/Special to the SC Daily Gazette)

Richland County, which includes the state capital, is a blue county in a red state.
In Lexington
Across the river in Lexington County, which is Graham’s home and a Republican stronghold, the Gazette expected responses to be different. But the only voters who would talk to Gazette reporters also expressed frustrations with Graham.
Griffin Archer said his top priority while voting in West Columbia was to keep Graham from winning.
“She’s completely unfit for office,” the 23-year-old civil engineer said. “She has no qualifications. And I don’t think her deceased brother was doing a very good job, anyway.”
At the Saxe Gotha Presbyterian Church in Lexington, voters had no line around 3 p.m.
Kelly Council, a College of Charleston student, said she travelled back home to vote for Andrews.
“I saw what was happening with Darline Graham, and she just seemed like she was put into a position rather than actually working to fight for it,” Council said.

David Terry votes Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026, at Saxe Gotha Presbyterian Church in Lexington. (Photo by Katharine Wilson/SC Daily Gazette)

David Terry, also from Lexington, said he could not in good conscience vote for any of the U.S. Senate candidates. In the governor’s race, he said he “unfortunately” voted for Wilson.
“I wish the Wilsons would quit running, too,” Terry said. “We need a lot of new people all over the place.”
Khalil Smith, a 24-year-old security guard, said he voted for all Democrats because he wanted to vote for change.
“I’m not going try to sway people in one direction. I think if you have the right to vote, you should vote. It does count,” Smith said. “You might not think it does, but it most definitely does.”
Charleston area
Keisha Pinckney, 39, cast her ballot at West Ashley High School on Tuesday for Andrews, though she had some reservations about the former pediatrician.
“She wasn’t my first choice, but she became my only choice,” said the stay-at-home mom and substitute teacher.
Pinckney said she was more excited about Democratic Rep. Jermaine Johnson’s bid for the Governor’s Mansion. She said his message, advocating for improvements to the state’s schools and roads, rang true for her.
Lori Spillers, who moved to West Ashley from Michigan more than 30 years ago, said she felt a bit uninformed about the statewide candidates.
“All I heard in the news was about Darline Graham and Annie Andrews, and I thought they were both horrible candidates,” the 56-year-old nurse said.
Even the candidates for governor, she said, she hadn’t heard much about, though she ultimately voted for Attorney General Alan Wilson.
“I guess because I feel like South Carolina has done really well with the Republican governor, so I just voted for the Republican,” she said. “Hopefully that’ll continue South Carolina on the track it’s been on.”

Dr. Annie Andrews celebrated with supporters in downtown Charleston Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026, as the Associated Press declared her the winner of South Carolina's U.S. Senate Race. To her left is Jaime Harrison, former chairman of the Democratic National Committee, who lost his own bid for Senate against the late Sen. Lindsey Graham in 2020. (Photo by Jessica Holdman/SC Daily Gazette)Dr. Annie Andrews celebrated with supporters in downtown Charleston Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026, as the Associated Press declared her the winner of South Carolina's U.S. Senate Race. (Photo by Jessica Holdman/SC Daily Gazette)Former Democratic National Committee and state Democratic Party Chair Jaime Harrison takes the stage at the Annie Andrews watch party at the Charleston Marriott on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Jessica Holdman/SC Daily Gazette)South Carolina Democratic Party Chairwoman Christale Spain, left, celebrates with Jaime Harrison, former chairman of the Democratic National Committee, in downtown Charleston Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Jessica Holdman/SC Daily Gazette)

In particular, she pointed to South Carolina’s economic strength as a positive.
John and Mari Shine, of North Charleston, both voted straight Democratic tickets.
But it was the Senate race they were watching most closely.
“Polls have been wrong, but if everything aligns like they’re predicting, then we’re hoping to have a celebration tonight,” said John Shine, a 45-year-old screenwriter.
“We need change. Something needs to happen,” his wife added.
The 49-year-old accountant said she saw the ads against Andrews calling “radically left.”
“And I was like, oh, that sounds good to me,” Mari Shine said. “I just want a strong middle class and for everyone to be treated fairly.”
“The demonization of everything that is even moderate at this point has pushed middle America so far to the right that it’s no longer accurate anymore,” he husband added.
Thomas Maltese cast his ballot at the North Charleston Sports Complex for Andrews too.
“I’m really hoping to see if we can turn South Carolina blue,” the 43-year-old software engineer said.
Hoping, he said, but not getting his hopes too high in the ruby red Palmetto State. For Andrews, anyway, he got his wish.
Maltese, who grew up in New York but has lived in South Carolina for the last 14 years, calls himself an independent. He said Andrews’ policies align more with his political beliefs.
“I feel like Annie has battled harder for it instead of just being given it,” he said of Andrews vs. Graham.
Tre Tailor, emcee of Rep. Jermaine Johnson's election night watch party; Rep. Gilda Cobb-Hunter of Orangeburg; Roshanda Pratt, who works for Johnson's campaign; and Tawana Allen look at results as Johnson pulls ahead with a big drop of votes from Richland County. The room erupted in cheers and all stood as the votes came in Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Skylar Laird/SC Daily Gazette)Barbara Pickens, a 72-year-old from Columbia, celebrates after the Democratic nominee for governor, state Rep. Jermaine Johnson, briefly pulls ahead in the results, waving a flag with "Clyburn" across it. Pickens, who is retired, volunteers with various Democratic groups, including the Richland County Democrats. (Photo by Skylar Laird/SC Daily Gazette)Keon Washington, who wrote Johnson's campaign song, and Mamacita Thomas, who organized in Spartanburg County for Johnson, watch with smiles as Jermaine Johnson concedes in the governor's race Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026, at Brookland Baptist Church in West Columbia. (Photo by Skylar Laird/SC Daily Gazette)A video thanking Rep. Jermain Johnson played at his election watch party at Brookland Baptist Church in West Columbia, S.C. "You made South Carolina your home," read the video, which included clips from the campaign trail and messages from his family members. It ends with "Thank you, Jermaine." (Photo by Skylar Laird/SC Daily Gazette)Rep. Jermaine Johnson and his running mate Sam Skardon look on at their crowd of supporters at Brookland Baptist Church in West Columbia, S.C., on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Skylar Laird/SC Daily Gazette)State Rep. Jermaine Johnson concedes in South Carolina's governor's race at his watch party at Brookland Baptist Church in West Columbia, S.C., on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Skylar Laird/SC Daily Gazette)
At the watch parties
At Johnson’s watch party, at Brookland Baptist Church in West Columbia, spirits stayed high throughout the night, even when Johnson trailed Wilson.
Musical group John Lakin and Friends sang to a crowd of more than 100, sometimes passing the microphone around the room. People stood and clapped along to songs, and dancing broke out later in the evening.
Johnson briefly pulled ahead of Wilson after a large drop of Democratic votes from Richland County. Shouts interrupted a speech by Rep. Gilda Cobb-Hunter, an Orangeburg Democrat, and the crowd erupted into cheers.
Tre Tailor, the event’s emcee; Rep. Gilda Cobb-Hunter; Roshanda Pratt, who works for Johnson’s campaign; and Tawana Allen embraced at the front of the room, watching the results on a large screen at the front of the room.
“I feel confident. I feel positive,” said Allen, a 66-year-old retiree who has lived in Columbia for about 30 years. “The whole day, I’ve felt positive, and I just think, hey, South Carolina needs to change.”
Allen remembers when Jim Hodges, the last Democrat to be governor, was in office. She’s spent the two decades since then hoping another Democrat might win, she said.
Similar celebrations took place across the state, at Andrews’ party at the Charleston Marriott downtown in Charleston. People sang along to “Carolina on My Mind” and cheered when results showed Andrews ahead.
Bill and Susan Taylor, of Chapin, made the drive down to celebrate.
“We love Annie,” Susan Taylor said. “She’s amazing.”
Lisa Izzo, a longtime friend of Annie Andrews, cheers as results come in showing Andrews in the lead for the U.S. Senate race Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026 at the Charleston Marriott in downtown Charleston. (Photo by Jessica Holdman/SC Daily Gazette)Lisa Izzo, a longtime friend of Annie Andrews, cheers as results come in showing Andrews in the lead for the U.S. Senate race Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026 at the Charleston Marriott in downtown Charleston. (Photo by Jessica Holdman/SC Daily Gazette)Lisa Izzo, a longtime friend of Annie Andrews, turns to celebrate with her friend Karen Hollings, also of Charleston, as results come in showing Andrews in the lead for the U.S. Senate race Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026 at the Charleston Marriott in downtown Charleston. (Photo by Jessica Holdman/SC Daily Gazette)Linda Carlson, left, and Melissa Davis, both of Mount Pleasant huddle over their phone screen watching results pour in at the Annie Andrews watch party at the Charleston Marriott on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Jessica Holdman/SC Daily Gazette)Bill and Susan Taylor, of Chapin, cheer numbers coming in for Democrat Annie Andrews at her election night watch party at the Charleston Marriott in downtown Charleston on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. The couple made the drive down to celebrate. "We love Annie. She's amazing," Susan Taylor said. (Photo by Jessica Holdman/SC Daily Gazette)Bill and Susan Taylor, of Chapin, and Sue Kreines of Ladson, cheer numbers coming in for Democrat Annie Andrews at her watch party at the Charleston Marriott in downtown Charleston, S.C., on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Jessica Holdman/SC Daily Gazette)State Democratic Party Chair Christale Spain talks to other supporters of Annie Andrews at her election night watch party at the Charleston Marriott in downtown Charleston on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Jessica Holdman/SC Daily Gazette)
People mingled and chatted at the State Fairgrounds, where most of the statewide Republican candidates gathered to watch results come in. But the mood there was more somber than celebratory for most of the night.
As the results came in, Dawn Pierce of Lexington County said she was “a little nervous,” but added that it was great to be at the event to see people and celebrate.
People at the GOP election night party at the State Fairgrounds in Columbia, S.C., watch former Gov. Nikki Haley talk about the midterms as results start coming in Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by John A. Carlos II/Special to the SC Daily Gazette) Supporters gather at a GOP election night watch party on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026, at the Moore Building on the South Carolina State Fairgrounds in Columbia. (Photo by John A. Carlos II/Special to the SC Daily Gazette)Supporters gather at a GOP election night watch party on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026, at the Moore Building on the South Carolina State Fairgrounds in Columbia. (Photo by John A. Carlos II/Special to the SC Daily Gazette)Supporters gather at a GOP election night watch party on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026, at the Moore Building on the South Carolina State Fairgrounds in Columbia. (Photo by John A. Carlos II/Special to the SC Daily Gazette)Lexington Council Member Ron Williams talks to people at an election night watch party for The GOP OP election night watch party on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026, at the Moore Building on the South Carolina State Fairgrounds in Columbia. (Photo by John A. Carlos II/Special to the SC Daily Gazette)
