title: How did California’s gerrymander work out? Better than Texas’
description: To win control of the U.S. House, Democrats needed to secure at least 218 seats. By Wednesday night, the party won at least 240 — picking up more than two dozen additional seats, and flipping the Senate too. A year ago Democrats were far less confident they could pull off the blue wave. Back then, […]
text:
Gov. Gavin Newsom meets with attendees during a campaign event on Proposition 50 in Los Angeles on Nov. 1, 2025 Photo by Ethan Swope, AP Photo




To win control of the U.S. House, Democrats needed to secure at least 218 seats. By Wednesday night, the party won at least 240 — picking up more than two dozen additional seats, and flipping the Senate too.
A year ago Democrats were far less confident they could pull off the blue wave. Back then, Texas Gov. Greg Abbott — at the urging of the Trump administration — carried a gerrymander to create five more Republican districts in his state. It threatened to stack the deck against Democratic gains.
Gov. Gavin Newsom counter-punched with his own bid to draw five more seats for California Democrats, Proposition 50. 
In the end, however, it wasn’t necessary — and some Prop. 50 critics say it did a disservice for democracy in general.
As CalMatters’ Maya C. Miller and Nadia Lathan explain, at least five of California’s nine-member Republican delegation suffered losses. It’s not clear yet whether California Democrats could have gained those seats anyway without the gerrymandering, but the party would have had enough to flip the House regardless.
Meanwhile, the partisan redistricting didn’t work out so well for Texas: GOP lawmakers drew five Republican-leaning seats and lost all but one of them.
Prop. 50 proponents say the measure was a unifying force for California Democrats and voters who wanted to mobilize against President Donald Trump. But in passing the measure, some critics say, California paid a steep price. It temporarily dismantled its independent redistricting commission, which is considered the “gold standard” for drawing voting maps. 
The move set a “very, very dangerous” precedent that prioritized party loyalty over legal norms, said Mike Madrid, co-founder of the Lincoln Project and an anti-Trump Republican who opposed Prop. 50.

Madrid: “What they were literally saying is, ‘Let’s undo democracy to protect democracy.’ There’s something very Orwellian about it.”

Read more.
More election fallout: The likely failure of Prop. 40 means Californians won’t impose a new tax on billionaires. The passage of Prop. 42, meanwhile, puts up a new obstacle to any future wealth tax. Read more. 



More ways to get CalMatters: We have an app, available for iPhone and Android. You’ll get a notification each morning about the day’s top stories, and you’ll be the first to know about breaking news. We can also send you text alerts on our latest investigations, political coverage and more. Sign up here.

Other Stories You Should Know


What will Becerra do?


Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra speaks during an election night watch party in West Sacramento on Nov. 3, 2026. Photo by Fred Greaves for CalMatters




During his victory speech in West Sacramento Tuesday, Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra told the audience, “You have now entered the Becerra era.” But what would a Becerra era look like given that the Democrat has remained relatively mum on his policy stances?
As CalMatters’ Jeanne Kuang explains, there are some hints we can glean from that illuminate his position on taxes, immigration and other concerns. Though he opposed the billionaire tax, for example, he’s not against all new taxes. He supports the idea of taxing corporations whose workers are paid so little they qualify for public benefits, or potentially ending tax credits to those companies.
Becerra also seeks to reverse restrictions to Medi-Cal that forced tens of thousands of immigrants who are in California illegally off the program. Newsom last year began rolling back some immigrant health coverage amid a budget deficit and unexpectedly high healthcare costs.
But in an interview with KQED published Monday, Becerra said that “anyone who works hard in California should have access to the healthcare they need for themselves and for their family … and that includes undocumented (immigrants).”
Read more.



New deadline for phasing out gas-powered water heaters


Water heaters on display at a Lowe’s hardware store in Fresno on May 19, 2025. Photo by Larry Valenzuela, CalMatters/CatchLight Local




You have another year to buy a gas-powered water heater if you live in the Bay Area. That’s the main takeaway from regulators’ decision to delay their plan to curb pollution by phasing out those appliances, writes CalMatters’ Alejandra Reyes-Velarde.
On Wednesday the Bay Area Air District voted to delay until January 2028 a rule requiring most property owners to replace gas water heaters with models that emit no nitrogen oxides, typically electric heat pumps. Regulators also added exemptions to the rule, including low-income owners and owners whose mortgage and property tax payments total to at least 28% of their income.
Though adopting the rule would reduce health risks, such as asthma, and save millions of dollars in healthcare costs, regulators cited the high cost of complying as part of the reason for amending it.

John Gioia, Bay Area air regulator and Contra Costa County supervisor: “We need to do this in a way that respects that lower-income residents may not be able to afford it. We need to figure out how to help them.”

Read more.



And lastly: The one county struggling to count votes


Shasta County Clerk and Registrar of Voters Clint Curtis at an elections office in Redding on Nov. 3, 2026. Photo by Salvador Ochoa for CalMatters




Though Shasta County voters in June ousted Registrar of Voters Clint Curtis in his bid to secure another term, the longtime election denier still had to oversee Tuesday’s election before he leaves office in January. It didn’t go very smoothly: Reports of overflowing ballot boxes, staffing shortages, computer hiccups and other troubles resulted in the county reporting initial results more than two hours later than the rest of the state. Read more from CalMatters’ Ryan Sabalow.






California Voices
CalMatters columnist Dan Walters: The election set the state for yet another confrontation between pro- and anti-tax advocates, and the rejection of Prop. 40, the most notable tax measure, handed the anti-tax faction a win.
California Voices editor Yousef Baig: In the end, Prop. 40 opponents’ empirically baseless fears of billionaire migration and lost tax revenue were more persuasive than the realities of an unequal economy and the chance for voters to send a message.

text:
Wilmington Friends and Delaware Military Academy play in the first round of the 2026 DIAA Division Two Field Hockey State Tournament. Photo Credit: Ryan Colasanti
The first round of the 2026 DIAA Division Two Field Hockey State Tournament concluded with all but one of the higher seeds moving on to the quarterfinal round.
 
WILMINGTON, Del. — Wilmington Friends defeated Delaware Military Academy, 5-2, on November 4, during the first round of the 2026 DIAA Division Two Field Hockey State Tournament.
The Quakers scored three goals in the first half while controlling most of the action on their offensive end of the field. 
Sophomore Tillie Hopkins started the scoring with a backhand shot to the back left of the cage with nine minutes left in the first quarter. The Quakers scored twice in the second quarter on goals from freshman Palmer Jenney and sophomore Ava Clothier and entered halftime ahead, 3-1. The Seahawks one goal came from junior Elena Sheets in the first quarter.
Friends scored two more goals in the second half, both in the fourth quarter. 
Senior Schuyler Hopkins scored her first goal of the playoffs on a ball that bounced around near the front of the cage. The ball bounced out of the scrum of players fighting for possession and right to Hopkins near the middle of the cage. Hopkins fired and scored giving Friends a 4-1 advantage. Freshman Peyton Galbraith gave the Quakers a 5-1 lead with her score off a penalty corner assisted by her sister, senior Keeley Galbraith. The Quakers finished the game with 18 shots, 17 penalty corner opportunities and five goals scored by five different goal scorers.  
“We try to look up before we shoot and find the best option and I think that’s kind of what we’ve been teaching for a few years now,” Wilmington Friends head coach Scott Clothier said postgame. “Rather than just relying on one player that can be easily defended we try to dish the ball around, look up, get our head up and just find that open player.” 
Sheets scored DMA’s second goal with a little less than three minutes remaining in the game, scoring both of the Seahawks goals. DMA senior Rebecca Wolhar played a strong game in goal, saving 13 of Friends’ 18 shots.
“The girls executed the gameplan, which has been our gameplan since really August until today, and I thought DMA played really well. Their defensive unit played strong, their goalie had some great saves, but ultimately I think we wore them down a little bit there,” Clothier said.

title: Commentary: Healthcare workers must stand up to ICE
description: Federal officials allege that on May 28th, 2026, a nurse at Trinity Health Ann Arbor helped a patient who had been detained and injured by ICE to escape custody. The state is now charging this nurse, Chloe Renee Freeman, with a federal misdemeanor. As ICE, DHS, and other arms of state violence increase their systematic […]
text:
A man identified only as 'OBP' in federal court records is pictured in surveillance footage as he leaves Trinity Health Ann Arbor on May 28, 2026. A nurse from the hospital, Chloe Renee Freeman, has been charged by authorities with "Instigating or Assisting
Escape of Person Under Arrest, a misdemeanor offense." (Photo is a screenshot from the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Michigan)Federal officials allege that on May 28th, 2026, a nurse at Trinity Health Ann Arbor helped a patient who had been detained and injured by ICE to escape custody. The state is now charging this nurse, Chloe Renee Freeman, with a federal misdemeanor.
As ICE, DHS, and other arms of state violence increase their systematic assault on immigrant communities, Freeman’s alleged actions exemplify what solidarity from the medical field can and should look like.
Under the current ICE siege, hospitals have become battlegrounds. Immigration agents often brutalize their targets, then bring them to emergency departments on their way to detention centers. This means that hospitals are often the first point at which people are disappeared into ICE custody. Once inside the emergency room, agents use pseudonyms to obscure the location of detained migrants; they deny patients visits with their community or lawyers; they physically restrain and surveil migrants; they harass and threaten staff.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
These acts of violence are not only deeply immoral, they are also often illegal, violating migrant patients’ rights to care and to privacy.
Once transported to detention centers, patients are subjected to severe medical neglect that can be life-threatening. They not only lack access to medication, medical professionals, disability accommodations, and other forms of treatment, but also lack clean air, food, water, adequate clothing, and access to hygiene. Temperatures are dangerous high or low, and raw sewage and dangerous insects abound; staff are physically and verbally violent.
ICE detention is unsafe for anyone, much less patients who have been injured by ICE or who have any sort of illness, chronic condition, or disability. These concentration-camp-esque conditions have contributed to 52 deaths in ICE detention so far between January 2025 and June 2026.
Healthcare workers have a moral and professional duty to protect our patients. Complicity in ICE’s kidnappings is a violation of our mandate to do no harm. Healthcare workers who take action in solidarity with detained migrants, as Freeman is alleged to have done, exemplify courage and moral clarity.
These workers often act in defiance of a workplace culture which demands compliance with state violence and which capitulates to ICE, even when not legally required. But they are not alone. They are part of a rich history of healthcare workers declining to adhere to immoral laws, from doctors who participated in the Underground Railroad to underground abortion practitioners to healthcare workers providing gender affirming care despite criminalization. Today, resistance to ICE’s occupations of our hospitals and emergency rooms is everywhere.
When healthcare workers are willing to take action in solidarity, hospitals can also be spaces where kidnapped migrants are reappeared. For example, in LA and St. Paul, medical staff connected detained migrants in their care to legal resources. They kept these patients in their respective hospitals, instead of releasing them into ICE custody. Attorneys were able to fight for these patients’ release from ICE custody, and in both cases they were returned to their communities without entering a detention center.
Nessel praises ruling temporarily blocking Trump administration from sharing health data with ICE

Organizing collectively can lead to even bigger wins, such as a May 2026 policy passed in L.A. to expand protections against ICE for hospital patients and staff.
As healthcare workers, we stand with Chloe Renee Freeman, and with all care providers who are penalized for protecting their patients. Freeman’s experiences shed light on the broader failures of our healthcare and legal systems, which surveil patients, criminalize their care, and punish providers for protecting their patients.
We call on the federal government to drop Freeman’s charges. We call on Michigan’s Department of Licensing and Regulatory Affairs (LARA) not to punish Freeman or anyone else accused of non-cooperation with ICE. And more broadly, we call on our fellow healthcare workers to stand in solidarity with our patients by working towards systemic change within medicine in the following ways:

End police and ICE presence in and near healthcare facilities
End medically unnecessary information gathering, documentation, and surveillance
Stop calling police or ICE on patients
Stop providing or sanctioning substandard and/or coercive care in prisons, jails, detention centers, and other facilities
Stop punishing healthcare workers for refusal to participate in systems of harm

We must resist turning our hospitals and clinics into prisons, our nurses into jailors.
If you are a healthcare worker, there are several ways to get involved supporting Chloe Freeman and fighting for immigrants. You can support Chloe by signing our letter of support here. Or get involved with your local ICE rapid response group – many immigrant rights organizations have connections with various local rapid response networks.
If you want to work specifically within the medical system, Beyond Do No Harm is a group of healthcare workers working to interrupt criminalization in southeastern Michigan; you can contact them here.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: New study says river diversions key to restoring coastal swamp forests in Louisiana
description: Coastal swamp forests in Louisiana, facing rapid sea level rise, land subsidence and lack of fresh sediment from rivers, are particularly hard to protect and restore. A new study from the Louisiana Universities Marine Consortium suggests that river diversions can restore sediment and support the root growth needed for these forests to remain healthy.
text:
Trees in Bayou Pierre on Saturday, Oct. 31, 2026. (Photo by Piper Hutchinson/Louisiana Illuminator)Coastal swamp forests are perhaps one of the most iconic Louisiana wetlands. They are made up of mainly Cypress and Tupelo trees, supporting a wide range of ecosystem benefits, such as habitat for native species, carbon storage and storm surge protection for the coast. 
But these types of forests in Louisiana, facing rapid sea level rise, land subsidence and lack of fresh sediment from rivers, are particularly hard to protect and restore. A new study from the Louisiana Universities Marine Consortium suggests that river diversions can restore sediment and support the root growth needed for these forests to remain healthy. 
The trees and shrubs of coastal swamp forests are used to growing within water-heavy soils, the roots essentially binding together the fabric of Louisiana’s coast. When healthy, these forests can maintain themselves by collecting sediment spread by rivers and tides and building their roots into thick woven networks below ground. 
That natural process has become hindered by sea level rise and changes to the ways the Mississippi and Atchafalaya rivers carry much needed sediment. Because of that process changing, the study found that another factor is playing a key role in the declining health of these forests — too much water. 
“We have this weird situation in Louisiana where we have too much water because of the submergence, but we don’t have enough of the right water, which is seasonal river water pulses,” said Ken Krauss, executive director of science at LUMCON and author of the study published in the academic journal Forest Ecology and Management. 
Too much salty water can cause these roots to die. Sea levels are rising along Louisiana’s coast, moving further north through natural and manmade navigational channels carved throughout the wetlands. Dams, channels and levees higher up on the Mississippi River have reduced the amount of sediment carried down to Louisiana swamps, starving the swamp forests of the sediment it needs. 
The study found that these factors paired together with cypress and tupelo roots submerged in water for too long a time period deeply affects the health of these forests. The amount of healthy roots in the coastal swamp forests sites studied “was influenced by flooding as much as by salinity,” with less salty areas that had deeper and longer flooding still showing lower amounts of root growth, similar to the effect that salt has.
This has big implications for what kind of restoration these wetlands need, said Krauss. 
“Restoration-wise, we need to find a way to reconnect rivers with the forested wetlands,” he said. 
The study concluded that building back these roots in coastal swamp forests is critical to maintaining their health as sea levels continue to rise.
“With that river water will actually come sediment deposition, and that will help maintain the forested wetland,” added Krauss. 
Several areas in Louisiana’s Coastal Master Plan that are working to do just that, such as the Davis Pond river diversion project in Luling and the Maurepas Swamp diversion near Garyville. Krauss said that putting more emphasis on diversion projects such as these, particularly upriver in the coastal zone, will build more resilience into these vulnerable wetland forests.  
“In time, salinity is gonna kind of overwhelm a lot of these swamp forests,” he said. “The idea is that what can we do now to extend the life of these systems and in some places armor it such that we can sustain it.”

name: California
title: Democrats’ blue wave beat Texas’ GOP gerrymanders. Did California even need Prop. 50?
description: Democrats notched big wins across the country, even in deep red districts that Republicans in Texas, Florida and North Carolina had gerrymandered to benefit their own party. That begs the question — did California really need to toss aside its independent redistricting commission?
text:
In summary
Democrats notched big wins across the country, even in deep red districts that Republicans in Texas, Florida and North Carolina had gerrymandered to benefit their own party. That begs the question — did California really need to toss aside its independent redistricting commission?


California Democrats went all in on redistricting last year in a rebuke of President Donald Trump’s call for Republicans to gerrymander red states and preserve their U.S. House majority. 
Ultimately, though, it appears such a gamble wasn’t even necessary. 
The “blue tsunami” that engulfed the country was enough to sweep away Republicans in ruby-red districts that Trump won by double digits two years ago as Democrats improved on their 2024 margin by a stunning 15 percentage points. 
At least five of California’s nine-member Republican delegation were among the political casualties. 
It’s not clear yet whether California Democrats could have picked up those seats under the old district lines drawn by the state’s independent redistricting commission, known as the gold standard for map drawing.
“There was no need to undermine the work of independent redistricting when there has been so much good work done to improve representation,” said Carah Ong Whaley, executive director of the group Better Choices for Democracy, which opposed Proposition 50, the voter-approved measure to temporarily suspend the commission and redraw the maps to oust five Republicans. 
She said it was party elites with large public platforms, led by Gov. Gavin Newsom, who drilled into voters’ psyches that California voters would suffer from Texas’ “rigging” of the midterm elections. 
“It wasn’t that a lot of voters all of a sudden organized and said, ‘We need to get back at Texas,’” Ong Whaley said. “It was party elites telling voters they shouldn’t take this.”
‘People were despondent about Trump’
Still, the party faithful are adamant that Prop. 50 was a crucial unifying force for California voters who felt helpless in the face of a mercurial second Trump administration.
“It gave Democrats and voters an opportunity to do something and to realize that they, in fact, did have power to act,” said Rep. Zoe Lofgren, who leads the California Democratic delegation, in an interview with CalMatters Wednesday. “People were despondent about Trump.”
At first, Lofgren said, the delegation hoped that the mere threat of California redrawing its own districts would be enough to call Trump’s bluff. She said Newsom wrote a letter to Texas Gov. Greg Abbott — who lost his own reelection bid Tuesday night — and proposed a detente: If you stop your gerrymandering, we’ll stop ours. Texas forged ahead.
Gov. Gavin Newsom meets with attendees during a campaign event on Proposition 50 in Los Angeles on Nov. 1, 2025 Photo by Ethan Swope, AP Photo
The energy from the Prop. 50 win, along with off-year victories in New York City’s mayoral race and gubernatorial contests in New Jersey and Virginia, helped propel Democrats out of the political wilderness, said Paul Mitchell, who drew the new maps. 
“That victory put wind in the sails for a lot of folks who went on to help create this blue tsunami,” Mitchell said. “It was the only way the Democrats were fighting back.”
In addition to ousting five Republicans, the maps were also drawn to shore up support for incumbent Democrats in Southern California swing districts. Mitchell estimated that protecting those members in one of the most expensive media markets in the country freed up more than $100 million that the cash-strapped party could spend in newly competitive districts elsewhere.
But critic Mike Madrid said it was unethical to try to save democracy and preserve good governance by actively dismantling the voter-created redistricting commission designed to keep map drawing out of the hands of partisan operatives and lawmakers. 
“It’s like a textbook warning of what the founders were concerned about when they warned about political parties,” said Madrid, co-founder of the Lincoln Project and an anti-Trump Republican who opposed Prop. 50. He called the move to prioritize party loyalty over democratic norms a “very, very dangerous” precedent.
“What they were literally saying is, ‘Let’s undo democracy to protect democracy,’” Madrid said. “There’s something very Orwellian about it.”
‘Can all meet in one car’
Tuesday’s blue tsunami dealt a seismic blow to California’s Republican delegation, which is expected to drop from nine to just four or even three members. 
The handful who survived were in solidly red districts that shielded them from voters’ fierce pushback elsewhere.
Prop. 50 packed conservative voters into just a few reliably Republican districts, including those of Central Valley Rep. Vince Fong and Sierra Nevada Rep. Tom McClintock, whose races were called shortly after polls closed Tuesday night. In Southern California, two incumbents were still duking it out for the state’s last safe Republican seat.
“I guess the good news is that they can all meet in one car,” quipped longtime Republican consultant Jon Fleischman of the waning California GOP delegation.
Fong defeated Democratic challenger Sandra Van Scotter with 63% of the vote as of Wednesday in a district with a 20-percentage-point Republican voter registration advantage.
Campaign spokesperson Ryan Gardiner declined to make Fong available for an interview or comment on Republicans tumultuous losses elsewhere. In a statement, Fong said he would “continue fighting to lower costs, protect our communities and deliver critical investments for our region.”
To the northeast, McClintock’s victory over Democrat Michael Masuda was a narrower but comfortable lead with 56% of the vote as of Wednesday.
Jon Huey, a campaign manager for McClintock, declined an interview request from CalMatters and did not respond to questions about the GOP’s losses but  McClintock signaled in a statement that perhaps his Republican colleagues had acquiesced to Trump too much.
“The American people spoke loudly and clearly that they are hurting and angry about the economic impact of the war in Iran and the tariffs on their quality of life,” McClintock said in a statement. “Congress has surrendered too much of these responsibilities to the executive branch and it is time for Republicans and Democrats alike to restore the constitutional balance.”
Rep. Ken Calvert, who moved to run in Orange County’s 40th Congressional District after his Inland Empire district was redrawn, was leading with about 54% of the vote against Republican colleague Rep. Young Kim Wednesday.
Meanwhile, Mojave Desert Republican Rep. Jay Obernolte was hanging on for his political life against Tessa Lynn Hodge, a Democrat, in a race that wasn’t even considered competitive before Election Day. On Wednesday, Obernolte was leading with 51% of the vote.
“Everyone else was caught in the blast zone,” GOP strategist Rob Stutzman said.
Coming out of a ‘massacre’
Tuesday’s results could spell more trouble for congressional Republicans in future elections. National party leaders will have even less of an incentive to invest in California candidates if there are simply fewer of them.
Trump’s botched redistricting maneuver in red states and his failure to respond to California’s gerrymander ultimately left the California delegation out to dry, Stutzman said.
The National Republican Congressional Committee, the fundraising arm responsible for electing House Republicans, will likely focus on competitive seats in North Carolina, Texas and Florida going forward, he said.
“It’s a complete disaster, and these California Republicans just got the worse end of the stick.”
NRCC spokesperson Christian Martinez did not immediately return a phone call, voicemail and text message requesting comment Wednesday.
The few remaining GOP members are unlikely to challenge the president despite his all-time unpopularity, Fleischman said.
“None of them are mavericks,” he said. “I don’t see our four most conservative Republicans from California bucking the president and bucking House leadership.”
Next steps for Democratic gerrymandering
As part of their promise to win over voters for the mid-decade redistricting last year, California Democrats promised to roll back the new House maps ahead of 2030 and pass legislation to ban gerrymandering. 
The ball is now in their court, said Ong Whaley. “They promised it was just this one time.” 
Lofgren, who has repeatedly introduced legislation aimed at banning mid-decade redistricting and establishing independent commissions in each state, said she was optimistic that a Democratic-controlled Congress would be open to ending partisan gerrymandering. 
“Congress has the right to legislate on this,” she said. “The idea that this will be bipartisan, I’m skeptical because of their prior actions. But we’ll see.”

name: California
title: New deadline for phaseout of gas water heaters gives Bay Area homeowners one more year
description: Up to half of Bay Area households can skip electric water heaters under an updated rule by air regulators. Residents not exempt have one more year to comply.
text:
In summary
Up to half of Bay Area households can skip electric water heaters under an updated rule by air regulators. Residents not exempt have one more year to comply.


Bay Area air regulators voted 16-1 Wednesday to delay the state’s first phaseout of gas water heaters by a year and let up to half of property owners who replace one skip the switch to electric heat pumps. 
The rule, adopted in 2023, does not require anyone to replace a working water heater. But starting in January 2028, a year later than planned, most Bay Area property owners replacing a gas water heater will have to install a model that emits no nitrogen oxides, typically an electric heat pump.
Low-income owners, those who spend heavily on housing, and homes with tight spaces or outdated electrical systems can apply for exemptions.
The vote is the latest sign that California is easing off on its push to cut pollution from home appliances, one of the largest sources of smog-forming emissions. 
Last year, Southern California air regulators rejected a plan to phase out gas water heaters and furnaces, and the California Air Resources Board has backed away from requiring all new space and water heaters sold to be zero-emission by 2030.
Supporters say the Bay Area is different. Regulators built in years to review the rules before they took effect, and SPUR, a Bay Area urban policy nonprofit, says the exemptions largely match what environmental groups asked for to address property owners’ concerns, even if they go further than advocates would have liked. 
In an email, an air district spokesperson said the just-passed water heater rule would prevent up to 16 premature deaths and 21 new asthma cases annually, and avoid $90 million in healthcare costs. But staff also estimate the exemptions could put roughly half of the rule’s originally projected pollution cuts out of reach.
A heat pump water heater costs about $3,500 more to install than a gas model, according to the air district. Heat pump water heaters use roughly a third to a quarter as much energy as standard gas models, but because electricity often costs more than gas in California, savings on utility bills are smaller. 
Property owner groups say the rules will become a financial burden to many residents. 
“The proposed mandate really doesn’t take into account all the nuances that have to be factored in when you look at many of the multi-unit buildings in the Bay Area that were built in the ’60s and ’70s, and even much earlier,” said Joshua Howard, executive vice president of local public affairs for the California Apartment Association.
Some board members agreed. Ray Mueller, a San Mateo County supervisor, said he wished the board could repeal the rule entirely. Shamann Walton, a San Francisco County supervisor, voted no after speaking about affordability concerns. Benicia Mayor Steve Young abstained. 
But board member John Gioia, a Contra Costa County supervisor who voted to delay the rule, said the amendments address affordability concerns. 
“We need to do this in a way that respects that lower-income residents may not be able to afford it. We need to figure out how to help them,” Gioia said. “And let’s face it, the exemptions are big enough to drive a truck through.” 
Who’s exempt
Under the amended rule, people with incomes at or below 80% of the area median, or who are enrolled in programs such as Medi-Cal or CalFresh, can avoid installing an electric water heater and instead install a gas one. So can people whose mortgage and property tax payments add up to at least 28% of their gross income. The air district estimates about 20% of Bay Area households qualify.
Homes with physical barriers, such as a cramped closet, a low ceiling or an electrical panel too small to handle a heat pump, get a one-time exemption, covering an estimated 20% of installations. People can continue to buy water heaters 30 gallons or smaller, about 10% of sales, because no zero-emission models of that size are available in the U.S.
Larger water heaters, common in apartment buildings and businesses, now have until 2033 instead of 2031. 
Statewide efforts
The state Air Resources Board, which once aimed for all new space and water heaters sold in California to be zero-emission by 2030, has scaled back its plans. 
At a December 2025 workshop, air board staff proposed instead capping sales of gas models and creating a credit system that would let manufacturers switch to zero-emission equipment more slowly. 
The air board is “continuing to meet with interested parties to understand their feedback and evaluating potential revisions,” to the rules, said spokesperson Lindsay Buckley. 
Still, the state backed the Bay Area’s rule. In a letter to the board, an agency official said the rule “contributes to California’s broader strategy to reduce building-sector emissions while delivering public health, clean air, environmental justice, and climate benefits.” 
In Southern California, the South Coast Air Quality Management District proposed rules last year that would have set rising targets for manufacturers to sell more zero-emission appliances, with fees on gas models. It backed down under pressure from the Trump administration. 
Advocates say that makes the Bay Area’s rule, even scaled back, a rare step forward.
“The state and the Bay Area are doing a great job of trying to push things forward in a more challenging environment,” said Tony Sirna, deputy policy director of environmental group Evergreen Action. “We’re pedaling just as hard, but we’re facing headwinds, and so we are making slower progress than we would have otherwise.” 
The cost of switching 
The air district estimates up to 120,000 Bay Area households replace a water heater each year. 
A consultant for the district estimated the amended rules will cost those households about $372.8 million a year, after accounting for about $60.8 million in energy bill savings. Howard, of the apartment association, said the district “needs to recognize the true cost of the mandate.”
Adam Pearce, president of the California Rental Housing Association, said the newly-passed rule does not  fix property owners’ concerns, and just “kicks the issue down the road.” 
“We’re not against clean air and healthy living. Certainly providing quality housing coincides with all of that,” he said. But forcing change isn’t the answer, Pearce added. “They would get a lot more buy-in over time if it was incentive-based.”
Advocates say incentives can help close the gap. The Bay Area will receive about $55 million a year in heat pump incentive funds over the next few years, according to SPUR estimates, said Sam Fishman, a policy manager for the group.
“These rules are a really big deal,” Fishman said. “They are a strong market signal that can ramp up demand for heat pumps in California, show that they work, and build demand both from consumers, from contractors, from manufacturers at every level of the supply chain.”

name: California
title: California billionaires faced down a tax and won new protections for their wealth
description: California billionaires put Prop. 42 on the ballot to counter a proposed wealth tax. It passed, creating a new obstacle to future wealth taxes.
text:
In summary
California billionaires put Prop. 42 on the ballot to counter a proposed wealth tax. It passed, creating a new obstacle to future wealth taxes.


The proponents of a California billionaire tax didn’t just lose their campaign to impose a first-in-the-nation tax on wealthy people’s assets. They also appear to have lost a campaign that will make it harder for them to try again in the future. 
Proposition 42, which prohibits new taxes on personal property such as business holdings, intellectual property and financial assets, is leading by a wide margin at 54% with nearly 60% of anticipated votes counted. It was one of two measures that tech billionaires placed on the ballot in an effort to cancel out the wealth tax. 
Its apparent passage puts proponents of Proposition 40 — who have vowed to keep pushing for a tax on the wealthiest residents — at an immediate disadvantage. 
The nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office says Prop. 42 will make it harder for state lawmakers to raise taxes in the future and potentially reduce state revenue, though it’s hard to say how much.
And for the many California Democratic leaders who said they wanted the wealthy to pay more taxes but didn’t like how Prop. 40 was written, Prop. 42 will prevent them from considering a differently written asset tax.
Proponents of Prop. 42, including the public safety unions California Professional Firefighters and Peace Officers Research Association of California, promoted it in digital ads and mailers as a way to protect pensions and retirement accounts from future taxes, though it was primarily bankrolled by billionaires to the tune of $159 million. Even Gov. Gavin Newsom endorsed it.
“These Californians backed the strongest protections available to protect their hard-earned life savings from double taxation,” said Nathan Click, a spokesperson for the Yes on 42 campaign.
Billionaire tax proponents, primarily the Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, said the argument was misleading: Prop. 40 never targeted ordinary retirement savings, with the exception of Roth IRA accounts with more than $10 million in them. 
Tax proponents have vowed to try again, despite the roadblock now in their way with Prop. 42, saying on Tuesday night they had started a movement to put the idea of taxing billionaires on the national agenda. 
“We’re going to call out these economic royalists. We’re going to tax them the way they need to be taxed, and we’re going to invest in Medicare for all and free childcare,” said Rep. Ro Khanna, a Santa Clara Democrat who was a lead supporter of the measure.
Prop. 42 bans any new wealth tax, whether created by state law or by a constitutional amendment, which voters must approve. But the ban isn’t permanent: voters could undo it by passing another ballot measure later.
“That’s not set in stone,” said Lorena Gonzalez, president of the California Labor Federation. “We have the ability to change things.” 
But despite supermajorities of Democrats in both houses of the state Legislature,  lawmakers have never seriously considered taxing assets. In a handful of times progressives have tried to do so since 2020, the proposals never even made it out of a committee.
California has faced four consecutive years of deficits despite revenue growth, leading to healthcare cuts, suspended payments to schools and tax increases. Federal cuts to Medicaid will also put pressure on Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra from patient advocates and health workers who say the state should backfill the losses. Becerra has said he’s open to new taxes, but he opposed the billionaire tax.
Some Democratic legislators have repeatedly argued that the Legislature should raise revenue by closing corporate tax loopholes and other tax measures, though Republican lawmakers argue that out-of-control spending is the issue. 
Senate Budget Committee Chair John Laird, a Santa Cruz Democrat, said he’d never imagined a scenario where Prop. 42, designed solely to offset the billionaire tax measure, would pass on its own.
Laird said he does not expect an immediate effect on the state budget.
“We will want to just drill down to see if it has any unintended consequences on the budget, but I think we still have to make that determination,” he said Wednesday.
Click said Prop. 42 is narrowly tailored and leaves lawmakers and voters plenty of other tax revenue options to choose from, such as taxes on business sales, corporate income, healthcare providers and insurance.
“Existing funding for schools, public safety, roads, healthcare, etc. is untouched by this measure.”
Kayla Kitson, senior policy analyst at the California Budget and Policy Center, raised concerns about a different section of Prop. 42 — one that bans lawmakers from applying any new taxes retroactively, unless the state needs the money to deal with a budget emergency. 
It is common for state and federal lawmakers to adopt a new tax and backdate it to the beginning of a tax year, she noted. The practice helps prevent tax evasion before a new tax takes effect and helps the state raise money quickly in a pinch, she wrote in a September blog post. 
Under Prop. 42, the state could miss out on at least several months of tax revenue in a future scenario, she said.

name: California
title: California’s election featured a big showdown over taxes. Wealth tax defeat was the biggest
description: California voters have long rejected raising taxes — or tried limiting them — via the ballot box. Propositions 40 and 42 keep up that trend.
text:
California adopted the initiative system — allowing proposed laws to bypass the Legislature and be placed on the ballot via petition — in 1911, but until the 1970s it was scantily used.
Since 1971, no year has passed without at least a few and sometimes dozens of measures being filed, records from the Secretary of State’s office show. The most was in 2005, when 109 ballot proposals were cleared for signature gathering.
Since 1911, a total of  2,194 measures have gained permission to circulate petitions: 410 qualified for the ballot and, not counting this year’s crop, just 141 survived to become law. 
Despite the less than 30% rate of success, the initiative process has evolved into a powerful tool for changing governmental policy. Sometimes even the threat to qualify an initiative can force the Legislature to act.
Proposition 13, the iconic 1978 measure to limit property taxes and make enactment of other taxes more difficult, stands as the ultimate example of that power. However, this year’s ballot offered a measure, Proposition 40, that would rival Prop. 13 in impact.
The votes in Tuesday’s election are still being counted, but Prop. 40, which would impose a 5% tax on the wealth of California’s billionaires, was consistently running behind by roughly 5 percentage points as votes were being tallied Wednesday.
Pre-election polls had indicated Prop. 40, which enjoyed popularity earlier in the year, had dropped into negative territory.
In a sense, its apparent failure should not be surprising.
It was placed on the ballot by the Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West to improve financial support for medical services that faced cuts in both federal and state funds.
The union said the one-time tax could raise as much as $100 billion, but its campaign for the measure was relatively weak, while the billionaires targeted by Prop. 40 pumped several hundred million dollars into a massive media campaign against it.
Prop. 40 also suffered from deep divisions within the Democratic Party and within the labor union community, the latter because most of the revenues would have gone to healthcare, rather than being shared with other services, such as education.
Dave Regan, the pugnacious leader of SEIU-UHW, vowed to try again if the Legislature “fails to deliver a real solution” to healthcare support. 
“That’s not a hypothetical. That’s our plan,” Regan said.
Tuesday’s election was a double-barreled loss for Regan. By a huge margin, voters also rejected his Proposition 44, which would have required clinics serving low-income patients to spend 90% of their annual revenue on patient care.
Moreover, voters appear to have approved Proposition 42, a measure placed on the ballot by Prop. 40’s wealthy opponents to counter the wealth tax. It places a prohibition of taxing personal wealth into the state constitution.
By prohibiting some taxes, Prop. 42 is, in effect, a win for the state’s tax limitation advocates — the same groups that backed Prop. 13  about 48 years ago and have jousted with unions and other pro-tax forces ever since.
Prop.  42 partially offsets voters’ rejection of Proposition 43, which would have made passage of local government taxes more difficult, and their approval of Proposition 3, which makes a temporary hike in income taxes on high-earning Californians, first approved in 2012, permanent.
Putting all of these issues together, Tuesday’s election was another in a long string of ballot measure confrontations between pro- and anti-tax advocates — with rejection of Prop. 40, the biggest of the bunch, giving the anti-tax faction a win on points.
Had Prop. 40 passed, it would have, like Prop. 13 in 1978, fueled a national taxation battle. Taxing personal wealth has become a holy grail goal for the Democratic Party’s uber-progressive wing.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Trans sports bans get voter approval in 4 states
description: Arizona, Colorado, Nebraska and Washington are on track to pass or have passed restrictions to transgender athletes’ participation in sports.
text:
Four states — Arizona, Colorado, Nebraska and Washington — are on track to pass or have passed measures to restrict transgender athletes’ participation in sports, a key policy focus of the Trump administration. 
Colorado, Nebraska and Washington’s measures were ballot initiatives, while Arizona reached the ballot by way of the legislature.  
Although there were sweeping Democratic wins in Republican strongholds Tuesday, GOP-backed proposals are winning over voters in various parts of the country.
Arizona’s initiative, which was garnering approximately 59% support late Wednesday, expands existing restrictions on transgender athletes to include private athletic associations and prohibits schools and athletic organizations from allowing individuals to use bathrooms, locker rooms and other private spaces designated for a sex different from the one recorded on their original birth certificate.
Colorado’s Proposition 134 was passing with 52% of the vote. The measure would require school athletic teams from elementary school through college to be designated for male, female or coeducational participation and require students to compete according to their biological sex. Nebraska’s measure is an amendment to the state constitution, which now prohibits students of the male sex from participating on teams designated for girls’ and women’s teams. 
Washington’s initiative will prohibit transgender girls from competing in girls’ K-12 sports and require healthcare documentation verifying sex eligibility for students seeking to participate on female teams. The state interscholastic athletics association reported knowing of only about 10 transgender athletes participating statewide each year.
According to Ballotpedia, 29 states had laws, regulations or interscholastic rules limiting or banning participation on female school sports teams to students of the female sex. 
This story was first published Nov. 4, 2026 by Stateline.

name: Washington State Standard
title: Ferguson lays out wishlist for Congress after ‘breathtaking’ midterms
description: With Democrats now poised to retake both chambers of Congress, Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson wants action in the other Washington.  Speaking to reporters Wednesday, the first-term Democratic governor appeared jubilant about the results. Even with the defeat of an initiative to repeal the high-earners income tax he signed, the state faces a budget shortfall wi[...]
text:
Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson discusses the midterm election results on Wednesday, Nov. 4, 2026, in Olympia. (Photo by Jake Goldstein-Street/Washington State Standard)With Democrats now poised to retake both chambers of Congress, Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson wants action in the other Washington. 
Speaking to reporters Wednesday, the first-term Democratic governor appeared jubilant about the results. Even with the defeat of an initiative to repeal the high-earners income tax he signed, the state faces a budget shortfall with a number starting in “b,” Ferguson said, while declining to share how many billions of dollars his budget team is expecting.
He’s hoping for some federal mitigation. So he’s got his list of priorities he wants the new Democrat-ruled Congress to deal with. He doesn’t need to check it twice, as Ferguson has been discussing all of these issues for over a year. 
First is healthcare. Republicans in Congress last year dealt a major blow to federal Medicaid spending, which means hundreds of thousands of low-income Washingtonians could potentially lose their coverage. They also let federal subsidies for health insurance purchased through the Affordable Care Act exchange expire, raising premiums. 
Various changes to federal Medicaid funding will mean the state taking on new costs that dent the budget here. 
Sen. Patty Murray, a Washington Democrat, said last week that reversing these spending cuts is a priority for her. Murray is poised to be one of the most influential senators in Washington, D.C.
Second is immigration. President Donald Trump has pushed a growing crackdown on people here without legal status.
“Some sanity around immigration enforcement would be nice,” Ferguson said. “What’s going on with ICE is deeply un-American. ICE is completely and totally out of control, and something just has to be done.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
And third are Trump’s tariffs on imports from other countries. Washington, bordering Canada, is a state especially dependent on trade. 
Ferguson also hopes the sudden cuts to grant funding by the Trump administration cease with a Democrat-held Congress. 
The tsunami, as Democrats are calling Tuesday’s results, is exceeding even their wildest hopes, as voters rebuke the president’s war in Iran and its effects on gas prices and other policies. 
“Sort of breathtaking the breadth and width of the tsunami,” Ferguson said, citing wins in states Democrats thought they’d never achieve, like U.S. Senate and governor in Texas.
In December, Ferguson will propose his first two-year budget, which will be colored by a forecast of the state’s revenue later this month. This spending plan will face a “short-term challenge,” he said, but the income tax money will start arriving to state coffers in 2029, so long as it withstands a court challenge. 
He sees “a true light at the end of the tunnel” starting in 2029 for Washington’s fiscal stability after Tuesday’s results. 
In the next legislative session starting in January, the state House will likely feature a two-thirds supermajority of Democrats, which gives them the ability to pass bonds and advance constitutional amendments without Republican help. The state Senate’s majority also could widen, but not enough to earn that overwhelming power. 
With a supermajority comes the ability to override a governor’s veto, like the one he continues to promise for any lowering of the million-dollar threshold for the income tax. 
But Ferguson believes, with a smile on his face, “they would never do that to me.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: Winning Black candidates make history in races for governor
description: Democratic gubernatorial candidate Nevada Attorney General Aaron Ford speaks at an election night event Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026, in Las Vegas.
text:
Five Black governors will serve at the same time for the first time in America’s history. Hours after Black governors-elect on opposite sides of the political spectrum became firsts, two more wins followed, and an incumbent won reelection. 
Georgia Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms became the first Black woman elected governor in American history. Republican Byron Donalds has become Florida’s first Black governor in his state. Democrats David Crowley in Wisconsin and Aaron Ford became the first Black governors of their states. And Wes Moore easily won a second term as Maryland’s governor. 
Georgia Democratic gubernatorial candidate Keisha Lance Bottoms speaks at an election night event, Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026, in Atlanta. (AP Photo/Brynn Anderson)
Before Tuesday night, only three Black candidates had been elected governor – and they’d all been Black men and Democrats. 
This year’s gubernatorial pool was politically diverse, and all the candidates wanted the focus to be on their policies, not their identities, as they made history.
Incumbent Maryland Gov. Wes Moore, who was reelected Tuesday, joined the ranks of Black governors in 2022, following in the footsteps of Virginia’s Doug Wilder and Massachusetts’ Deval Patrick. Wilder was elected Virginia’s first Black governor in 1989. Patrick was elected in Massachusetts in 2006 and reelected in 2010.  
Earlier this year in response to the redistricting battles across the country, Moore told Capital B, “It’s the greatest form of political redlining we’ve seen in generations, where we are intentionally trying to disenfranchise Black voters and trying to minimize Black leadership in a way that frankly we have not seen since Reconstruction.”
After Democrats made history in several states and retook Congress, from the Mid-Atlantic to the South to even the West Coast, five of the eight Black gubernatorial candidates will head to the governor’s mansion in 2027.
Republicans
Byron Donalds in Florida
U.S. Rep. Byron Donalds was elected Tuesday to replace outgoing Gov. Ron DeSantis.
“We have won a massive victory,” Donalds told supporters at an election night event after The Associated Press called the race in the GOP primary in August.
Donalds defeated David Jolly, a Republican-turned-independent-turned-Democrat. The Brooklyn, New York, native has represented Florida’s 19th District in the state’s southwest since 2021. 
Republican gubernatorial candidate Rep. Byron Donalds, R-Fla., celebrates at an election night event with his wife Erika Donalds on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026, in Hollywood, Fla. Credit: AP Photo/Rebecca Blackwell
Florida A&M students grilled the gubernatorial candidate during a town hall meeting. He has referenced his time at the HBCU from 1996 to 1999, even though he didn’t graduate from the school. Donald’s campaign focused on the economy, healthcare, law and order, education and affordability.
Lisa Demuth in Minnesota
Democratic U.S. Sen. Amy Klobuchar defeated Republican state House Speaker Demuth in a race shaped by a widespread fraud scandal in state government, according to The Associated Press. Demuth was elected to the Minnesota House of Representatives in 2018. It was the first all-woman major-party race for governor in Minnesota history. In September, Demuth joined a growing number of Republican candidates calling an end to the war in Iran. 
Demuth’s campaign has focused on education, affordability, public safety and fraud prevention. Despite frequent portrayals of Minnesota as unique or among the worst in the nation at preventing fraud from government programs in recent years, data shows otherwise.
John James in Michigan
The Republican congressman had called himself the “only candidate for governor who is a true outsider to Lansing,” the state’s capital city. Early Wednesday, AP projected he’d been defeated by Democrat Jocelyn Benson, Michigan’s secretary of state.
James became the first Black Republican elected to Congress when he was elected to represent the state’s 10th Congressional District in 2022. He voted to pass the One Big Beautiful Bill Act and anti-abortion legislation. He’s also co-sponsored bipartisan legislation that supports the Great Lakes and nuclear prevention. James continues to face ethical complaints from constituents who allege he misused taxpayer money to fund his gubernatorial campaign. In 2026 the claims were dismissed, finding “no reasonable justification.”
Democrats
Keisha Lance Bottoms in Georgia
The former Atlanta mayor defeated wealthy Republican businessman Rick Jackson on Tuesday. A recent Atlanta Journal-Constitution poll had Jackson and Bottoms in a statistical dead heat. Bottoms was the second Black woman in state history to run for governor on a major party ticket. Stacey Abrams became the first in 2018 when she launched the first of her two historic bids. 
In recent ads from Jackson’s campaign, Bottoms has been accused of abandoning Atlanta, but she served her full term and chose not to seek a second term to focus on her family. She campaigned on education, housing, healthcare, and helping farmers and small businesses.
David Crowley in Wisconsin
Democrat Crowley defeated Republican Congressman Tom Tiffany, according to AP. Crowley’s campaign focused on “lowering costs for working families” and bringing more jobs to Wisconsin. The county executive’s win over Trump loyalist Tiffany marks the first time in Wisconsin’s 178-year history that Democrats will hold the governor’s office for more than eight consecutive years. 
Wisconsin Democratic gubernatorial candidate David Crowley speaks at an election night event Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026, in Milwaukee.  Credit: AP Photo/Nam Y. Huh
“Because of you all, a boy facing eviction will now live in the governor’s mansion,” Crowley told cheering supporters in Milwaukee, just a couple of miles from where he grew up.
Aaron Ford in Nevada
The Democratic attorney general defeated Republican incumbent Joe Lombardo in the key battleground state. Nevada will play a critical role in the next presidential election.
Ford has served as the state’s top prosecutor since 2019. Throughout his campaign, he described growing up in poverty and going to school hungry. He explained how he became a math teacher before earning his law degree, and highlighted efforts to fight the Trump administration.
“This campaign didn’t happen by accident,” Ford said at a watch party on Tuesday, AP reported. “It happened because of faith, because of family, because of hard work, and because the people of Nevada decided that our best days are still ahead of us.”
Jermaine Johnson in South Carolina
Johnson, a representative in the South Carolina House, was defeated by Republican Alan Wilson, who is the state’s attorney general.
His campaign has focused on his work advocating for better infrastructure, broadband access, and medical access for rural communities, among other issues. 
Wes Moore in Maryland
The incumbent won a second term. Most polls showed him with a considerable lead over Republican Dan Cox. Cox had been critical of Moore’s support for changing the state constitution, which currently requires congressional districts to be contiguous and follow natural boundaries.
“This is outrageous. This is not democracy. Marylanders should not surrender their protection of community boundaries under our own state constitution,” Cox said. 
Maryland Gov. Wes Moore speaks to reporters outside the Silver Spring Civic Building for the first day of early voting in the 2026 midterm race, Thursday, Oct. 22, 2026, in Silver Spring, Md.  Credit: AP Photo/Allison Robbert
In an interview with Capital B about redistricting earlier this year, Moore said, “I will never move on from fighting for our democracy, and it is something that I know is going to be a long-term fight.”
Capital B is a local and national nonprofit news organization that produces in-depth journalism on topics of crucial importance to Black people across the country, such as politics, health, criminal justice, the environment, and rural issues.

name: Missouri Independent
title: ‘We’ve got to listen’: Missouri Republicans confront fallout from historic election losses
description: After losing 16 Missouri House seats Tuesday in their worst election since Watergate, Republicans are questioning whether their own legislative agenda helped drive voters away. Some blamed national political headwinds and low Republican turnout. Others pointed directly to a string of unpopular proposals pursued by their own party. “We need to focus on the bu[...]
text:
State Rep. Darin Chappell of Rogersville, right, speaks Wednesday with state Rep. John Simmons of Washington and state Rep-elect Tony Lovasco of Wentzville after being selected House Majority Leader (Rudi Keller/Missouri Independent).After losing 16 Missouri House seats Tuesday in their worst election since Watergate, Republicans are questioning whether their own legislative agenda helped drive voters away.
Some blamed national political headwinds and low Republican turnout. Others pointed directly to a string of unpopular proposals pursued by their own party.
“We need to focus on the business of the people, and quit pursuing what I would call just personal pet projects of individual legislators, and do what people want done,” said House Speaker Pro Tem Chad Perkins of Bowling Green.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
In the 99 seats contested by both parties this year and in 2024, Democrats gained more than 12 percentage points. In the seats they flipped, the margin shifted an average of 21 points in favor of the Democratic candidate.
Democrats defeated 10 incumbent Republicans on Tuesday, bringing the total of new members of both parties to 64 and ending 14 years of GOP supermajorities in the House.
On Wednesday, the diminished caucus selected state Rep. Darin Chappell of Rogersville as House majority leader for the coming session. Chappell, who has been an outspoken advocate of cutting state spending, is the uncle of popular singer Chappell Roan.
Chappell was re-elected Tuesday with 70% of the vote in the 137th District in Greene County. The margin narrowed by 15 percentage points from his 2024 election.
Chappell will lead House Republicans as they try to recapture districts lost this year and defend others — 17 Republicans won by fewer than 10 percentage points.
“We’re in a total reassessment,” Chappell said in an interview with The Independent.
House Republicans will pursue policies enhancing liberty, security and prosperity, Chappell said.
“If we need to change course on specific issues, we will,” he said. “We absolutely will.”
In the 1974 election, just a few months after the resignation of President Richard Nixon, Republicans lost 17 seats in the Missouri House. That year, as in this, Democrats benefited from a political backlash against Republicans.
But some lawmakers say Missouri Republicans added to their burdens by pushing an unpopular agenda. Every major policy initiative put before voters by Republicans since Gov. Mike Kehoe was sworn in last year has gone down to defeat. 
Constitutional amendments to replace the income tax with sales tax and make it harder to pass constitutional amendments by initiative lost by historic margins in August. A proposal to ban almost all abortions failed Tuesday despite the personal involvement of Kehoe’s wife, Claudia. and voters rejected a Republican-backed congressional redistricting plan. 
The income tax amendment was dead the day lawmakers voted to put it on the ballot, Perkins said.
“We all knew how doomed it was before it ever got started,” he said. “We’ve got to stop doing that. We have to stop doing stuff like that.”
Democrats mainly won new seats in suburban areas adjacent to districts they already hold. But they also won seats they were not expected to take in Jefferson City and Cass County.
The election “was a disaster,” said state Rep. Jeff Vernetti of Camdenton.
“The voters have spoken, and we’ve got to listen to our districts and move forward as one,” Vernetti said. “Obviously, the messaging of the last several years ended up costing us 16  seats.”
The losses left Republicans without the two-thirds majority needed to override a veto or enact legislation that takes effect immediately without Democratic support.
Republicans will hold 95 seats, their lowest total since 2008. Republicans have held the House majority since 2002.
State Rep. Tim Taylor of Bunceton, who won re-election in the 48th District with 65% of the vote, said the unpopular income tax proposal hurt Republicans. Taylor has worked for the past two years to overhaul property taxes.
Voters can understand how they would benefit from a focus on property taxes,Taylor said. Republicans would have won favor with the public by addressing the issues of rapidly rising tax assessments, he said.
“That particular subject covers everybody, regardless of political affiliation, whether you’re a voter or not a voter,” Taylor said. 
Secretary of State Denny Hoskins, who visited with Republicans as they gathered, said voters are souring on the GOP.
“This is a wake up call for us as Republicans,” Hoskins said. “There’s plenty of blame to go around.”
Hoskins was one of the most vocal defenders of the plan to redraw congressional districts to favor Republicans. The issue of redistricting is not dead, he said, because of a U.S. Supreme Court decision changing the interpretation of the 1965 Voting Rights Act.
“It may be forced on their hands because right now the 2022 map, according to the U.S. Supreme Court, is unconstitutional because it includes a majority-minority district,” Hoskins said. “These new state reps may not have a choice.”
The U.S. Supreme Court did not rule Missouri’s 2022 congressional map unconstitutional. Its April ruling struck down a Louisiana congressional district drawn predominantly on the basis of race, while a separate September ruling allowed Missouri to use its 2022 map in Tuesday’s election.
Israel Baeza of Sedalia, who was elected to the House with 63% of the vote in the 52nd District, said the election returns sent a clear message. His 28% margin was down from the 49% victory for Republicans in 2024.
Democrats flip 16 Missouri House seats, ending Republican supermajority 

“This is a good reminder that people send us here to get things done,” Baeza said. “People have been speaking loud and clear that they want us to focus on issues that affect their pocketbooks.”
Matt Sergent of Knob Noster won the 57th District with 73%. His margin of 46% was down from a 62% margin in the district in 2024.
He said a data center in Benton County is a major issue in his district.
Voters are generally angry at the government, Sergent said.
“They’re upset with Washington for sure, and that trickles down to the state level,” he said. “They think that we’re doing something because Washington’s doing it. It’s happening up there, so it must be happening here.”
Alex Riley, the Republican from Springfield who will be House Speaker next year, said the national trend to Democrats was the dominant factor on Tuesday.
“It was a blue tsunami that impacted the entire country, so it’s hard to point fingers and say it’s because Missouri Republicans worked on a particular issue or passed a particular issue,” Riley said.
For some Republicans, the defeats on Tuesday were more about who didn’t vote than who did. 
“Republicans didn’t show up yesterday,” Perkins said.
There is no one factor that accounted for the defeats, Perkins said.
“If yesterday taught us something, it’s that there’s enough blame to go around,” he said.
Republicans had a huge cash advantage, outraising Democrats by $10 million for House races. At the beginning of 2024, House Republicans chose Axiom Strategies to guide its campaign efforts, dropping the consultant who had engineered the supermajority. That change is not the reason Republicans had a bad night, Vernetti said.
“It’s on every single thing top to bottom,” he said. “You can’t blame the consultants. You can’t blame the governor or Trump. You can’t. We’ve got to look in the mirror.”
Taylor said he won’t alter his views or change his approach because of the election. And, he said, it might make the caucus more cohesive.
“People do better in smaller groups,” he said. “They work better, and they’re more focused on things.”

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Commentary: Democrats must deliver on their affordability promises
description: Voters have swung between Trump and Democrats in just two years. If Democrats don’t deliver, they may swing back to the GOP in 2028.
text:
Reps. Rob Menendez, Analilia Mejia, and LaMonica McIver share a moment outside the federal courthouse in Newark on Nov. 4, 2026. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)Democrats are understandably giddy about an Election Day that saw them winning in places the GOP hasn’t lost in generations.
Allow me to be a wet blanket.
Just two years ago, Donald Trump rode a wave of voter anger over high prices to recapture the White House by promising to lower costs on day one.
On Tuesday, some of the very voters who gave him a second chance at the presidency delivered a stinging rebuke because many of them remain angry about high prices.
The big message for Democrats from Tuesday’s results is that they’d better not waste a single day, because if they don’t deliver, the pendulum may swing back in the GOP’s direction two years from now.
Some of the victorious Dems say they got the message.
“You have to deliver. And what you tell people you’re going to do, you have to do,” Rep. Rob Menendez told me in Newark Wednesday morning.
Menendez had no GOP challenger to worry about this year, because Hudson County’s Republican Party appears to have given up trying to win there. But he worked his tail off for his colleagues, including Rep.-elect Rebecca Bennett, who ousted GOP Rep. Tom Kean Jr. in one of New Jersey Democrats’ biggest Election Day wins.
Menendez was in Newark Wednesday to join activists crowing about the election results. He danced a jig of glee at the mention of Democrat Zack Mullock’s stunning win in the heavily Republican 2nd District.
Also on hand was Democratic Rep. Analilia Mejia, who won reelection in a romp Tuesday. Mejia said voters have watched their elected leaders “nibbling around the edges” of the cost-of-living crisis instead of acting boldly to address affordability. That’s why they swung from Trump to Democrats in just 24 months, she said.
“It’s not that they’re fickle, it’s that they didn’t see a result. They have eyes and they have ears,” she said.
What those eyes and ears saw over the last two years was a president enacting tariffs that made costs higher and starting a war in Iran that led to skyrocketing gas prices, not to mention focusing heavily on building a grand ballroom for himself and putting his picture on every piece of public property he could find, including money.
Rep.-elect Adam Hamawy, who won New Jersey’s 12th Congressional District on Tuesday, speaks outside the federal courthouse in Newark on Nov. 4, 2026. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)Rep. LaMonica McIver speaks outside the federal courthouse in Newark on Nov. 4, 2026. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)Rep. Analilia Mejia speaks outside the federal courthouse in Newark on Nov. 4, 2026. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)Rep. Rob Menendez speaks outside the federal courthouse in Newark on Nov. 4, 2026. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)Darionah Scott holds poodle Mocha, 2, while she chants outside the federal courthouse in Newark on Nov. 4, 2026. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)Mocha, 2, attends a rally outside the federal courthouse in Newark on Nov. 4, 2026. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)Reps. Rob Menendez and LaMonica McIver share a moment outside the federal courthouse in Newark on Nov. 4, 2026. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)Rep. Analilia Mejia fixes Rep. LaMonica McIver’s necklace as Rep. Rob Menendez watches outside the federal courthouse in Newark on Nov. 4, 2026. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)
At Trump’s first post-election press conference — one other presidents have used to express humility about their party’s losses and pledge that they’ve heard the message voters sent — the president touted his various vanity projects. The voters said, we need lower costs! Trump responded, look at my pretty ballroom!
Menendez told me he believes there’s a chance Trump will work with the new Congress on issues like elder care and child care.
“I think he wants to salvage whatever he can, and if that means making deals with Democrats, he will,” Menendez said.
I have my doubts. For Democrats’ sake, they’d better find a way to deliver on their affordability promises regardless. Considering the actions of our seesawing electorate in the last two cycles, voters are tired of waiting for change. They’re demanding it now.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Commentary: Missouri’s CAFO policy is built to multiply pollution, not prevent it
description: Missouri’s refusal to establish setback spacing requirements between concentrated animal feeding operations, to CAFOs. isn’t just a bureaucratic oversight — it’s a structural failure that guarantees cumulative pollution. Our laws treat each CAFO as if it exists in isolation, but rural communities live with the reality of multiple industrial barns clustered t[...]
text:
(Photo by Kent Becker, U.S. Geological Survey)Missouri’s refusal to establish setback spacing requirements between concentrated animal feeding operations, to CAFOs. isn’t just a bureaucratic oversight — it’s a structural failure that guarantees cumulative pollution.
Our laws treat each CAFO as if it exists in isolation, but rural communities live with the reality of multiple industrial barns clustered together, all potentially draining into the same creeks, the same wells, and the same air column.
A single large CAFO can produce more manure than a small city. When two or three facilities operate side by side with no spacing requirements whatsoever, their waste streams can overlap. Yet the state reviews each permit separately instead of asking the obvious question: What happens when all that waste enters the same watershed? Rural Missouri already shows the consequences: increasing nitrate levels in private wells, persistent phosphorus pollution in streams, and industrial odors so strong that nearby residents cannot open their windows.
Missouri’s list of impaired waters has grown from 24 streams in 2002 to 549 in 2026. Of these, 215 were added after local control was removed in 2020 by SB391. Nearly half are impaired by e-coli or nutrients, potentially linked to CAFO waste and runoff.
The absence of setbacks is a likely accelerant. It allows industrial barns to stack like freight containers, concentrating millions of gallons of manure and wastewater in tight clusters. Regulators may insist each facility “meets its permit,” but permits don’t account for the combined load of multiple CAFOs operating in the same drainage area. Rural residents aren’t living next to one operation: they’re living next to the accumulated waste of an entire cluster.
A new trend is making the problem even worse: CAFOs are deliberately building barns just under the permit threshold to avoid regulation altogether. By staying a few animals below the number that triggers a state operation permit, operators side-step engineering reviews, public notice requirements, and even basic environmental safeguards. These “permit‑exempt” barns still produce enormous quantities of manure, yet they operate with virtually no oversight.
This loophole has become a strategy. Instead of one fully regulated barn, companies build two or three unregulated barns — each technically below the threshold but collectively producing the same waste load as a major CAFO. And because Missouri has no setbacks for Class II operations, these barns can be placed right next to each other, creating a de facto industrial complex with none of the protections that would normally apply.
The problem doesn’t stop at the property line. Missouri also refuses to regulate exported chicken litter — the waste hauled off‑site and spread on fields miles away. This creates a second layer of cumulative impact. A CAFO can legally export thousands of tons of manure into a watershed already saturated by neighboring operations, and regulators will still claim “no violation” because each facility’s paperwork looks clean.
This is the core failure: Missouri regulates CAFOs as isolated units, but pollution behaves as a single, combined system. Without setbacks, without spacing, without limits on exported waste, and without closing the permit‑exempt barn loophole, the cumulative burden grows heavier every year.
Setbacks cannot solve every problem, but they acknowledge a basic truth: closely clustered CAFOs create cumulative pollution beyond any single permit’s control.
