name: WyoFile
title: Incumbents on both sides of the aisle defend seats in key legislative races
description:
Another educator will replace longtime Rep. Harshman. House District 11 turned blue. 
The post Incumbents on both sides of the aisle defend seats in key legislative races appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
The Wyoming Legislature’s balance of power was largely determined in August’s primary elections, when voters resoundingly rejected the hard-right Wyoming Freedom Caucus in favor of more moderate Republican candidates. But a handful of races still posed uncertainty ahead of Tuesday. Here’s how those races panned out.  
Rep. Posey keeps House District 33, one of the Legislature’s few swing districts.
Democrat Rep. Ivan Posey defended his seat for House District 33 against his opponent, Republican Justin Morgan. Posey, an Eastern Shoshone educator, has represented the district since 2024.
A member of the House Transportation Committee and chairperson of the Select Committee on Tribal Relations, Posey said in response to WyoFile’s candidate questionnaire that his biggest concerns are rising costs and access to healthcare, education and young people leaving the state.
Stretching across Fremont County, House District 33 encompasses the Wind River Indian Reservation towns of Fort Washakie, Ethete and Arapahoe, as well as the small non-tribal communities of Atlantic City, Crowheart and Hudson. Over the years, its representation has flipped back and forth between Democrats and Republicans, as well as enrolled tribal members and white ranchers.
Costello will replace longtime Rep. Harshman in House District 37.
Republican Brian Costello, a Casper educator and coach, will be House District 37’s new representative after longtime Republican Rep. Steve Harshman decided to run for state superintendent of public instruction. 
Harshman has represented Natrona County’s House District 37 since 2003, including two terms as speaker of the House. The district spans Casper Mountain and several west-side neighborhoods, including Wolf Creek and Valley Hills. Costello faced Democratic candidate Betsy Erickson, also an educator, in the general election. 
Born in Kemmerer and raised in Big Piney, Costello said in his response to WyoFile’s candidate questionnaire that he would prioritize local control, supporting schools and businesses, protecting public lands and creating opportunities for young people to build lives in the state. 
House District 23 keeps a Democrat. 
Democrat Rep. Liz Storer defended her House District 23 seat against Republican Shannon Brennan. Storer, who has represented the district since 2022, has largely focused on abortion rights, tourism and tax reform. 
(Storer is the president and CEO of the George B. Storer Foundation, a financial supporter of WyoFile. The foundation has no role in WyoFile’s editorial content.)
Since 2015, voters in Teton County, one of Wyoming’s two blue bubbles, have sent a Democrat to Cheyenne to represent its northern half, including Teton Village, an eastern section of Wilson, as well as the communities of Kelly, Moran and Moose.
Rep. Sherwood also defended her House District 14 seat. 
Democratic Rep. Trey Sherwood also defended her seat in House District 14, which spans northern Laramie and the Albany County communities of Rock River and Bosler. Sherwood has represented the area since 2020. She faced Republican candidate Emily Study in the general election.
As a lawmaker, Sherwood rose through the ranks of the minority party, while focusing on housing, supporting rural schools and suicide prevention. Most recently, she served as the sole Democrat on the House Appropriations Committee — the Legislature’s panel responsible for crafting the state’s budget bill.
House District 11 turns blue.
Democrat Britney Tennant, who runs the Cheyenne Animal Shelter, defeated Republican Dan McIntosh and Libertarian Ryan Shollenberger in House District 11’s three-way race, according to Laramie County’s unofficial results.
Tennant is set to replace Republican Rep. Jacob Wasserburger, who didn’t run for reelection after serving one term representing the central Cheyenne district. 
House District 11’s boundaries shifted significantly during the Legislature’s 2022 redistricting process. Years before then, several Democrats represented the district. But for the last decade, it has favored Republicans.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Idaho voters turned out at high rates to vote in midterm election. Some waited hours to vote.
description: In Idaho’s general election on Tuesday, some voters were voting hours after polls had closed in the state’s second most populated county. Voting bled into Wednesday. The last voter in Canyon County cast their ballot at 12:20 a.m., Idaho Secretary of State Phil McGrane said in an interview Wednesday morning.  In Idaho, polls close at […]
text:
An election worker speaks to a voter in South Hills Middle School gymnasium on Election Day in Twin Falls, Idaho, Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Andrew Eakin for the Idaho Capital Sun)In Idaho’s general election on Tuesday, some voters were voting hours after polls had closed in the state’s second most populated county.
Idaho Secretary of State Phil McGrane, a Republican, attends a GOP election night watch party on Nov. 3, 2026, in Downtown Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)
Voting bled into Wednesday. The last voter in Canyon County cast their ballot at 12:20 a.m., Idaho Secretary of State Phil McGrane said in an interview Wednesday morning. 
In Idaho, polls close at 8 p.m. local time. But voters can still cast votes if they are in line by the deadline. And in Canyon County in southwest Idaho, some voters waited in lines for more than four hours, McGrane said. The lines there, driven by high turnout and long ballots, were one of his biggest challenges of the night.
“The interesting thing, both visiting with the poll workers and watching some of the news outlets that visited out there, the voters were really patient, really kind, very determined to want to be able to cast their vote. I think it was incredible just to see the sense of community out there,” McGrane said. “Regardless, I think we owe it to the voters, and we’ve certainly heard some feedback just in terms of how frustrating that was. We want to make sure the voting process goes smoothly.”
The lines were a sign of a bigger trend. 
In Tuesday’s general election for statewide offices, congressional seats, legislative seats and ballot measures, including an abortion ballot initiative, Idaho voters turned out at high rates. A midterm record high of 731,980 voters cast ballots, based on initial voter turnout data from the Secretary of State’s Office. Overall, it seems likely that registered voters turned out in the high 60% range to vote in the election, McGrane said. 
Besides the long lines in Canyon County, the day was fairly smooth, he said. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
 Abortion ballot initiative drove voter turnout, experts say

Proposition 1, a ballot initiative that sought to repeal Idaho’s near-total abortion ban, seemed to drive many voters to the polls. Nearly 99% of voters cast ballots in that race — more than any statewide ballot measure. Voters rejected it, with nearly 56% voting no, according to unofficial election results. 
“I do think the fact that more ballots were cast on Prop 1 than any of the other statewide races indicate that it was driving some people to the polls, particularly to vote on that issue,” Boise State University political scientist Jaclyn Kettler said in an interview.
The drive to turn out was likely twofold, she said: Voters tend to care deeply about abortion and reproductive healthcare issues, and there was active campaigning from both sides.
But the blue wave in midterms across the country — where Democrats secured control of both chambers of Congress, and won control of some state legislatures and most governorships — didn’t extend to Idaho. Republican incumbents in all statewide offices and the state’s congressional delegation all easily secured reelection. Kettler wasn’t surprised.
“Idaho is a solidly Republican state. We don’t tend to see too many competitive races” in the general election for statewide races, she said. “ … It’s just solid enough Republican that it’s hard for even a blue wave in other areas of the country to have too much influence, especially for those statewide races.”
Still, Democrats saw some success in Idaho as they picked up six seats in the state Legislature, which remains under Republican supermajority control. In those wins, Democrats secured full control of three swing districts.
Tuesday’s election results in Idaho won’t become official until they are certified by the State Board of Canvassers on Nov. 24. Within the next week, McGrane said his office will conduct a random draw to determine which counties will undergo post-election audits. 
 How did voters turn out in Idaho’s general election?

Initial state data shows that about 69% of registered voters turned out to vote in Tuesday’s election. On paper, that would eclipse the state’s 2018 midterm elections, when more than 66.5% of voters turned out when no incumbent ran for governor and a Medicaid expansion ballot initiative was up for a vote. 
First-time voter Abigail Strand registers to vote during the general election on Nov. 3, 2026, at Borah High School in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)
But McGrane expects this year’s voter turnout rate to drop while his office processes at least 43,000 voters who registered at the polls on Election Day.
About 290,000 of the more than 731,000 ballots cast in Tuesday’s election came through absentee and early voting, according to the Secretary of State’s Office. That is 100,000 more of those voting types than in 2022, the state’s last election for statewide offices, according to the state election agency. 
At the county level, turnout varied widely — up to as high as nearly 85.1% in rural Butte County in eastern Idaho, where less than 1,400 ballots were cast, down to as low as 56.8% turnout in Madison County in eastern Idaho, the early results show. In Ada County, the state’s most populated, more than 232,000 voters cast ballots at a turnout rate of nearly 74.6%.
Even though some races saw political control flip, McGrane said he doesn’t expect any races will be close enough to trigger an automatic recount. 
 In Canyon County, election officials evaluating if they have enough polling places

By peak voting time, after 5 p.m. Mountain time, McGrane was warning about delayed election results from Canyon County, which had long lines. 
Many other counties, he said Wednesday morning, had absorbed their lines. But Canyon County had three polling places with “excessively long lines.”
Late in the night, around 1:30 a.m., McGrane said he went out and visited a polling place there. Then he took a one-hour nap on a couch in his office in downtown Boise around 4 a.m., and got back to work. Canyon County officials didn’t finish reporting election results until around 10 a.m., local officials said.
Canyon County Clerk Jess Urresti, the local election official, could not be immediately reached for comment midday Wednesday. McGrane said he and the clerk believe that: “no voter should have to wait that long.”
“We’re going to be working very hard to make sure that that doesn’t happen again,” McGrane said. 
The line to vote at Middleton Middle School snaked through the gymnasium, through the foyer and out the door, as voters waited up to an hour to cast their ballots in Idaho’s May 2022 primary election. Voters again faced long lines and wait times during the 2026 general election.(Photo courtesy of Becky Swain)
The county’s director of constituent services, Steve Cushman, said the clerk and the local election team had left for rest after a long night. 
Cushman said part of the reason for the county’s long lines was limited space in some polling locations and a high number of voters turning out. About 79,000 of the county’s more than 119,000 registered voters turned out for this election. That made for a nearly 66% turnout rate for Canyon County, which is slightly below the statewide rate.
After this election cycle, he said local officials are evaluating if the county has enough voting locations. The county is up to 51 precincts, an increase from a steep decline during the pandemic, Cushman said. Before then, he said the county had 64 precincts.  
“That’s something they’re definitely going to evaluate to see how we can get some more locations,” he said.
Long ballots played a role too, he said. His own ballot was four pages long. That means voters might need more time in the booths, he said.

name: WyoFile
title: Wyoming voters dodged a big-time bullet by defeating Prop 1
description:
If the state had approved a 50% residential property tax cut, it would suffer a major loss of essential services, columnist Kerry Drake opines.
The post Wyoming voters dodged a big-time bullet by defeating Prop 1 appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Wyoming didn’t catch any part of that mighty blue wave that washed over much of the country in Tuesday’s midterm election, but I don’t think anyone seriously thought it would.

Opinion

It did, however, dodge a major bullet by rejecting a dud of an idea that would have resulted in major cuts to essential services throughout the state. Wyoming communities could not have absorbed that much pain.
The Equality State did what it’s done in most elections for years: send an all-Republican congressional delegation back to Washington, D.C., elect a slate of GOP state officeholders and put Republican supermajorities in both houses of the Legislature.
But in one vital nonpartisan area, Wyoming voters came together and scored a smashing victory over an attempt to cut most residential property taxes by a whopping 50%.
If the Proposition 1 initiative had passed Tuesday, opponents said Wyoming could have lost $125 million a year or more in property tax revenue, resulting in major cuts to essential services, including law enforcement, fire protection, emergency medical services, hospitals, schools, roads and bridges.
And that revenue would have just disappeared; the initiative didn’t provide any means to replace it. During previous legislative discussions about either cutting property taxes by 50% or eliminating them altogether, some lawmakers had proposed increasing the state sales tax to “backfill” the lost revenue.
Fortunately, Prop 1 failed. According to unofficial final results, 58% of voters opposed or didn’t vote on Prop 1, while a total of 42% backed the measure. If a voter left the question blank, it was counted as a “no” vote.
This misguided idea was the brainchild of three people: Brent Bien, who was endorsed by the Wyoming Republican Party but finished third in this year’s GOP gubernatorial primary; his former campaign manager, Rich Weber, and ex-Wyoming Republican Party state committeewoman Cheryl Aguiar.



Two years ago this trio began a movement to get the massive tax exemption on the ballot for the 2024 election. While they failed to collect enough signatures to make the deadline, Secretary of State Chuck Gray certified the initiative for 2026 after his office verified more than 30,000 signatures of registered voters in January 2025.
It was a stunning accomplishment, the first citizen’s initiative to be placed on a Wyoming ballot in 30 years. One of the reasons for the extreme dry spell is because the state has such a high bar for ballot initiatives, which must obtain signatures equal to 15% of the votes cast in the previous general election’s U.S. House race.
Moreover, the signatures must come from registered voters in at least two-thirds of the state’s 23 counties, which is 16 counties.
The Legislature has rejected attempts to lower the bar, obviously because lawmakers want to make the laws, and not turn that power directly over to voters. 
In the case of the long-winded “People’s Initiative to Limit Property Tax in Wyoming Through a Homeowner’s Property Exemption,” it initially appeared to many political observers as one issue that had a great chance of passing.
Within a few months after its ballot certification, I heard of — but did not specifically see — polling data that found more than 80% of the state’s likely voters viewed the initiative favorably. I didn’t doubt it.
For people who understood what a dangerous impact such action could have on property tax revenue that goes directly to local governments, special districts and public schools, it appeared potentially devastating.
One of the reasons is because lawmakers in the far-right Freedom Caucus had seemingly convinced the public that passing tax cuts was imperative due to major tax increases that had swept through much of the state.
As home values rose, residential property taxes during the COVID-19 pandemic in 2022 increased by an average of 16%, compared to prior years when annual hikes were 3% to 4%. During the same time of double-digit property tax increases throughout the state, Teton County — the wealthiest county in the nation — saw a 36% increase due to skyrocketing house values.
Some Freedom Caucus members in the House and their Senate allies claimed some homeowners would lose their property unless the Legislature provided some so-called “tax relief.” They made this claim without producing any real-life examples of anyone that would happen to, but the narrative was quickly ingrained by politicians and their constituents as gospel.
In the 2024 election, the Freedom Caucus saw enough members elected to take control of the House. The leadership immediately went to work on bills to cut residential property taxes.
One new law capped the annual increase at 4%. A tax rebate program was expanded. For homeowners of more than 25 years, a temporary 25% tax cut was passed, then made permanent.
These measures had started to work. At the same time, the rapid increases in home values began to subside. Meanwhile, the Freedom Caucus had clearly lost the support of voters in the Aug. 18 Republican primary, as it was booted out of House control and its much-ballyhooed attempt to take over the Senate fizzled.
The cries for property tax cuts died too. Two months before Tuesday’s general election, the Joint Revenue Committee said no to a proposed bill to eliminate residential property taxes that it had approved the previous year. In 2025, the bill died when the House ran out of time to consider it.
The panel’s decision came amid the release of new data showing that the majority of Wyoming homeowners did not take advantage of the 25% property tax cut that the Legislature had approved without any income restrictions.
Clearly, the ballot initiative would have only paved the way for the rich to get richer, while people who owned modest homes would receive a small tax cut.
People had stopped coming to legislative committee meetings demanding that property taxes be cut. During the Joint Revenue Committee’s meeting on sponsoring a bill to let voters amend the Wyoming Constitution by eliminating residential property taxes and a companion measure to backfill it with higher sales taxes, no one spoke for or against the measure.
That particularly pleased Rep. Liz Storer, D-Jackson, who asked the panel, “What is the purpose of these bills, and why would we take the time to continue to move them forward, also given that I do not think they will be met with success in the next Legislature? So help me understand your reasoning.”
No one could.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Commentary: Is it time to rethink Idaho’s involvement with DOE’s Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus?
description: Gov. Brad Little proudly announced in July that the Idaho National Laboratory had been selected by the Trump administration as one of five finalists for designation as a Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus.  We were told that if the state was picked as one of the three NLICs, there would be massive financial investment and jobs […]
text:
U.S. Department of Energy Secretary Chris Wright (center) visits the Idaho National Laboratory in December 2025. (Photo courtesy of Sarah Wood/U.S. Department of Energy)Gov. Brad Little proudly announced in July that the Idaho National Laboratory had been selected by the Trump administration as one of five finalists for designation as a Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus. 
We were told that if the state was picked as one of the three NLICs, there would be massive financial investment and jobs galore at INL. The only catch was that INL had to take and store one third of the country’s nuclear waste. Little promised that storage at INL would not be permanent. 
There was a short timeline to compete with the other finalists because a binding host agreement with the feds needed to be finalized by Sept. 30. That deadline has come and gone, but we’ve heard practically nothing about the matter since then.
We do know that the Trump administration filed a troubling lawsuit against Idaho on Sept. 11, claiming INL’s water right should not suffer if there was a water shortage in the vicinity. The shortage would be visited upon farmers, fish producers and other water right holders.
Idahoans must – once again – fight off a serious federal water threat

Word about the lawsuit was for some reason kept under wraps by the governor, attorney general and other state elected officials. The reason for the secrecy is mysterious and concerning. The federal lawsuit is without legal merit, although the lawsuit may have been an indication that Idaho is under serious consideration for NLIC designation.
But then an interesting story popped up from Oak Ridge, Tennessee. The Nuclear News reported that Tim Walsh, an assistant secretary of the U.S. Department of Energy, was in Oak Ridge on Oct. 27 to announce a $15 billion nuclear project there, which happens to be another NLIC finalist. 
The project will provide 10,000 construction jobs and many permanent jobs. Participating companies and projects were disclosed. One might wonder whether this announcement means that Oak Ridge has been selected as an NLIC. If not, how does this comprehensive “nuclear energy hub” differ from an NLIC?
Mr. Walsh said that the only thing lacking at Oak Ridge for NLIC designation was where the nuclear waste would be permanently stored. “The last component that we need to solve is really a final repository for the spent nuclear fuel,” he said. 
So, the DOE contemplates that a NLIC designee will need to permanently store its one-third share of the country’s nuclear waste or find another jurisdiction that will. That should be a definite no-go for the state of Idaho. Most of us don’t want a permanent nuclear waste storage site anywhere in the state.
I do not believe we have been informed about the companies and projects that have been lined up for the INL. Idahoans should be told what is being contemplated for INL so that we are not being asked to buy into a pig in a poke. It would be of great interest to see what the needs might be for water and electric power for the various projects because neither are in plentiful supply in the vicinity.
In his initial proposal to the DOE, the governor says on page 14: “Idaho is prepared to identify sources of readily accessible on-site water supplies capable of meeting industrial-scale needs, including cooling systems for reactors and reprocessing facilities.” 
However, it is not clear where those sources are in that water-short area. The wording – “industrial-scale needs” – implies a lot of water. The governor has yet to reveal those “readily accessible” water supplies, perhaps because they do not exist.
Similarly, we don’t know where the electricity will come from for any new projects. It is contemplated that data centers will be part of the NLIC. Since the centers would be on federal land, they would not be subject to state laws. Any data centers should be required by any binding agreement with DOE to furnish their own needs for water and power in an environmentally responsible manner. 
Above all else, state officials should remove the shroud from this entire project. The public has a right to know what our government is proposing as inducements to get the NLIC designation. 
How will the project impact Idahoans and exactly what benefits will it produce? What will be the monetary benefits to, or burdens upon, the state? 
The failure of our officials to reveal the federal attack on Idaho’s control of water resources on federal land is not encouraging. We have a right to be informed about such troubling developments.
There should be public hearings and opportunities for input by Idahoans before any binding plan is locked in by the negotiators. The planning and implementation should be conducted transparently, instead of behind closed doors. 
This is a representative democracy. Our elected leaders should respect that and act accordingly. The people deserve nothing less.

title: Tennessee judge extends block on immigration checks in HIV/AIDS program
description: A Nashville judge on Wednesday continued to block the Tennessee Department of Health from demanding proof of citizenship or immigration status from HIV-positive individuals who are enrolled in a safety-net healthcare program.  Chancellor I’Ashea Myles’ extension of a temporary restraining order, first issued Oct. 21, prevents the state from imposing immigrat[...]
text:
A Nashville judge on Wednesday extended her temporary order preventing Tennessee health officials from imposing immigration and citizenship checks on people receiving services through the federally-funded Ryan White HIV/AIDS program. Pictured: Historic Metro Nashville Courthouse (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)A Nashville judge on Wednesday continued to block the Tennessee Department of Health from demanding proof of citizenship or immigration status from HIV-positive individuals who are enrolled in a safety-net healthcare program. 
Chancellor I’Ashea Myles’ extension of a temporary restraining order, first issued Oct. 21, prevents the state from imposing immigration status checks in the Ryan White HIV/AIDS program until at least next week, as she weighs arguments for a longer injunction. 
The order also applies to a companion program called Housing Opportunities for People with AIDS. The programs, which provide federal funding to every state, have served as the cornerstone of the U.S. government’s response to HIV/AIDS for more than 30 years. 
In a four-hour hearing Wednesday, an attorney for Nashville CARES argued state officials are wrongly demanding agencies that serve patients in the programs amend their contracts to reflect Tennessee law requiring anyone seeking public benefits be lawfully present in the United States. 
Lawsuit: Tennessee to impose immigration checks in HIV/AIDS safety-net program

The demand conflicts with federal law and the rules set for the federally funded HIV/AIDS programs, and it’s contrary to the public health goal of the programs, argued Brant Harrell, an attorney with the Tennessee Justice Center representing Nashville CARES, one of Tennessee’s largest providers of HIV/AIDS services. Harrell noted that the second Trump administration has imposed no such requirements.
The 2026 state law invoked by the Health Department in October to require the immigration checks re-incorporates language that has been on the books in Tennessee for 14 years, raising questions about why the state is now requiring the contract changes, Harrell noted. (The 2026 law adds provisions that require the reporting of applicants for public benefits who cannot verify their citizenship or lawful status to a state immigration enforcement division and introduces criminal penalties for failure to verify patient status.)
“The department makes no attempt to deny increased transmission of disease,” as a result of the new directive, Harrell said. “The department’s actions endanger public health. That’s not disputed by the department.”
Assistant Attorney General Andrew Grams, representing the Health Department, argued the case didn’t belong in court at all. Grams called it a contract dispute.
Grams said the state was not forcing Nashville CARES nor any participating agency to amend their contracts to require immigration status verification. Instead, he said, the state was “making offers” and “giving the options” to amend their contracts. 
The Health Department intends to impose immigration checks on patients in the programs with or without the cooperation of local agencies that directly serve them, Grams noted. 
Nashville judge temporarily blocks immigration status checks in HIV/AIDS program

“At the end of the day, if a recipient refuses, the department has to do verification,” he said.
Several Tennessee agencies that serve HIV/AIDS patients have already agreed to update their contracts to reflect the new immigration status checks, Grams said. 
Grams said that the program is one of many the Health Department is now seeking to impose the verification requirements on.
“The department has many, many other programs it is working through,” he said. 
Should Myles issue an injunction against the HIV/AIDS program verification, Grams asked that Nashville CARES be required to produce a $450,000 bond.
Myles said she would render a decision by next week on whether to issue an injunction preventing the state from going forward with the immigration status checks while the legal challenge continues.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Democratic turnout soars across Alabama in midterm election
description: Alabama Democrats Tuesday nearly doubled their midterm turnout from four years ago and saw their percentage of the vote increase in all 67 counties.  According to the Alabama Secretary of State’s office, voter turnout Tuesday was 43.9% with 1.7 million ballots cast. That’s up from 38.9% turnout and 1.3 million ballots cast in 2022.  In […]
text:
Voters stand in line at Messiah Lutheran Church in Montgomery, Alabama on Nov. 3, 2026. (Andrea Tinker/Alabama Reflector)Alabama Democrats Tuesday nearly doubled their midterm turnout from four years ago and saw their percentage of the vote increase in all 67 counties. 
According to the Alabama Secretary of State’s office, voter turnout Tuesday was 43.9% with 1.7 million ballots cast. That’s up from 38.9% turnout and 1.3 million ballots cast in 2022. 
In contrast to 2022, when many Democratic statewide candidates were unknowns and newcomers to politics, the party had a prominent gubernatorial candidate in former U.S. Sen. Doug Jones and a favorable national environment. National issues such as the war in Iran and affordability also influenced voters across the state.
“I have a wife and two kids, trying to make a living,” said Michael Simmons, a voter in Prattville on Tuesday. “(Since) this president came into office, it has been rough. The food prices, the gas prices, just being able to afford everyday living is hard.”
Over 800,000 Alabamians voted for Democratic gubernatorial nominee Doug Jones, nearly doubling the 413,000 people who cast ballots for 2022 Democratic nominee Yolanda Flowers. Montgomery County, considered critical to the fortunes of Jones and U.S. Rep. Shomari Figures, D-Montgomery, who won re-election on Tuesday, saw turnout rise to 50.3% with over 80,000 Democratic votes cast, a 39% increase over 2022.     


David Hughes, a political science professor at University of Louisiana at Lafayette, called the results “incumbency backlash” in an interview Wednesday afternoon.
“Voters are not happy with the status quo at the moment,” Hughes said. “They’re not happy with the cost of living. They’re not happy with healthcare, which is associated with cost of living, but not exactly the same because we’ve seen issues with insurance, particularly things like Affordable Care Act subsidies and premiums that people are paying both for public options and private options.”
Hughes also added that despite the high turnout and Jones’ performance in the election, “there’s not enough anger there to sweep Republicans out of office” in Alabama.
Jefferson County, another mostly Democratic county, saw Democratic votes go from 197,600 votes in 2022 to 247,600 on Tuesday, a 25.3% increase.
Several blue counties saw gains in the Democratic turnout cast in Tuesday’s election. Wilcox County had the highest voter turnout reported for the election at 62.1%, up from 46.8% in 2022.
Alabama Democratic Party Chairman Bobby Singleton, D-Greensboro, said in an interview Wednesday morning that the increased turnout is due to the slate of candidates this election cycle and the investments in those candidates.
“The party was now beginning to support our candidates like we’ve never been able to support candidates before, and so we had a lot of small things that came together in a short period of time since August that gave us some momentum to take this to the level that we were,” he said. 


Madison County, where both parties focused their efforts, saw three Legislative seats flip while turnout surged, going from 39.1% turnout with 121,000 ballots cast in 2022 to 47.7% turnout with 160,900 ballots cast Tuesday. Democratic votes in Madison more than doubled, from about 42,000 in 2022 to 92,000 on Tuesday. The county, home of Huntsville, has long been a target of the Democratic Party.
“We knew and saw (Madison County) over the last three or four years that it was (beginning) to be more and more purple because of the government move and all of the major companies that are going up there and the education level of people,” Singleton said. “Tuberville didn’t make it any better with the rhetoric that he has in terms of divisiveness, calling them Communists up in that area and uneducated, and so I think that all of that resonated with (them. And) the shutdown of the government when a lot of those contractors in Huntsville area lost their jobs. I think all of that bottled up over the last couple of years, and people were just tired, and so they wanted change.”
Hughes said the reason for an uptick in Democratic turnout in Madison County is because of the education status of voters in the region and because “Republicanism has evolved into something in 2026 that doesn’t reflect what attracted these people to the Republican brand in the 1980s.”
“That is low taxes, free trade, maintaining America’s position as a global hegemon, preferably as the only superpower in the world. You know that the current Republican administration has not been doing that,” Hughes said. “They’ve been raising taxes via tariffs, they have been starting wars, they have been making you know the United States’ position as a global hegemon questionable as they’ve retreated from issues like the Ukraine war. So there’s just a lot of dissatisfaction amongst more affluent white voters, and where they tend to be located are places like Madison County.”
Republican votes fell by about 75,000 over 2022, a nearly 8% decrease.
In 2022, 31,800 votes in Tuscaloosa county were cast for Ivey, compared to 28,800 votes cast for Tuberville on Tuesday. In Mobile, 63,600 voters cast a ballot for Ivey compared to 57,600 for Tuberville.
Despite the gains made by the Democratic Party, Republicans still won elections in all statewide and a majority of Legislative offices, though often by reduced margins over 2022. 
“Despite the best efforts of Democrats and their willing accomplices in the liberal media to claim that a massive blue tidal wave was heading for Alabama, the political waters across our state remained bright red once the ballots were counted,” Alabama Republican Party Chairman Scott Stadthagen, R-Hartselle, said in a statement Wednesday morning.
Shelby County, a usually solid Republican county, saw a decrease in Republican ballots cast, losing 2,600 Republican votes during this year’s election cycle. In 2022, 51,200 votes were cast for Ivey while in 2026 48,600 votes were cast for Tuberville. Jones won 43% of the vote in the County.
Lee County, Tuberville’s home county, saw a slight uptick in Republican votes, going from 27,242 in 2022 to 27,989 on Tuesday. Tuberville narrowly carried the county.

title: North Carolina seeks $40 million to help schools cover rising fuel costs
description: Transportation spending for school districts has nearly doubled this school year as diesel prices have reached record highs. Now, the North Carolina Department of Public Instruction is asking lawmakers for a one-time $40 million fund to help districts cover the additional costs. Between August and the beginning of October, school districts in the state spent[...]
text:
North Carolina school buses are ready to roll out for the start of the 2025-26 school year. (Photo: NCDPI) Transportation spending for school districts has nearly doubled this school year as diesel prices have reached record highs. Now, the North Carolina Department of Public Instruction is asking lawmakers for a one-time $40 million fund to help districts cover the additional costs.
Between August and the beginning of October, school districts in the state spent $17.1 million on 3.8 million gallons of diesel fuel. That’s nearly double the $8.6 million they spent for 3.6 million gallons during the same period last school year, according to data DPI presented to the State Board of Education on Wednesday. Districts also spent $8.6 million on 3.7 million gallons during the same period in the 2024-25 school year.
“We were seeing that school districts are spending about twice as much on fuel in the first couple of months of the school year as they were in the previous two school years, even though they bought the same amount of gallons,” Geoff Coltrane, DPI’s senior director of government affairs and strategy, told board members. 
The money would help districts cover fuel costs above the roughly $3 per gallon included in their transportation funding allocation. It would be distributed to school districts and charter schools based on need, Coltrane said.
Diesel prices in North Carolina hit a record average of more than $6 per gallon earlier this fall, putting so much pressure on school transportation budgets that some district leaders said they may be forced to make cuts elsewhere or use money from their reserves.
NC Gov Stein signs gas tax holiday into law

Last month, the General Assembly suspended the state’s motor fuel tax, including the tax on diesel, through Nov. 30. But the suspension doesn’t help school districts because they’re already exempt from fuel taxes.
The department has already begun sharing the request with lawmakers and legislative staff, Coltrane said. DPI did not provide an estimate of how much individual districts could receive.
Democrats won control of the state House in Tuesday’s midterm elections for the first time since 2010, while Republicans retained a narrow majority in the Senate.
The proposal was part of a broader package of budget priorities DPI presented to the State Board of Education. The department plans to submit its recommendations to the state budget office by early January for consideration in the governor’s budget.
Among the other requests, DPI is seeking $300 million in each year of the two-year budget to help school districts buy new literacy and math instructional materials aligned with recently adopted standards. The department is also asking for $115 million to help districts replace student devices, after a report found that many districts don’t have enough money to replace them.
DPI is also seeking $117 million to increase funding for needs-based school construction grants, and another $25 million for school repairs and renovations. The department wants to increase funding for school health personnel by 20%, which it estimates could help districts hire about 700 additional counselors, nurses, social workers and psychologists.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Arkansas economic development proposal sponsors regroup after close loss at the ballot box
description: Following the narrow defeat of a ballot measure that would have allowed the creation of local economic development districts Tuesday, Issue 3 supporters said they’re going to take time to analyze election results and consider ways to move forward.  “We’re not giving up. We’re just going to regroup and figure out another game plan,” said […]
text:
Voters cast their ballots at the Pulaski Heights United Methodist Church in Little Rock, Arkansas, on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Katie Adkins/Arkansas Advocate)Following the narrow defeat of a ballot measure that would have allowed the creation of local economic development districts Tuesday, Issue 3 supporters said they’re going to take time to analyze election results and consider ways to move forward. 
“We’re not giving up. We’re just going to regroup and figure out another game plan,” said Randy Zook, president and CEO of the Arkansas State Chamber of Commerce and the Associated Industries of Arkansas. 
Zook also chairs Arkansans For Strong Communities, a ballot question committee that backed Issue 3. The proposed measure would have amended the Arkansas constitution to permit lawmakers to create programs, loans and grants using public money for the purpose of economic development. 
The Legislature would have been given the authority to pass laws allowing local governments to create economic development districts where incentives like tax rebates could be negotiated to attract new business to a designated area. 
Supporters said Issue 3 was needed to make Arkansas more competitive with other states by allowing cities and counties to offer economic incentives to spark economic growth in smaller communities. 
Arkansans approve 3 of 4 proposed ballot measures

Opponents argued the measure would grow government and could harm Arkansans who were being asked to approve a program whose rules have yet to be outlined.
Zook said he respects the decision of voters, who rejected Issue 3 with 50.7% of votes, according to results from the secretary of state’s office. However, Zook noted that 41 of Arkansas’ 75 counties voted in favor of the measure, which means “there’s significant support for doing what we wanted to do,” he said. 
While Arkansas has “very robust economic incentives” at the state level to attract industry, Zook said Issue 3 was a tool for local communities aimed at quality of life issues like attracting retail facilities and supporting development of rundown properties. 
This type of tool is needed in the Delta where communities are losing population due to a lack of amenities, he said. 
Zook said supporters will do some “real in-depth research” about what might be done, which could include less comprehensive and highly targeted proposals.
“The goal remains the same — help people be in a position to attract what it takes to keep a healthy community,” he said. 
Monette Mayor Bob Blankenship supported Issue 3 and following its defeat said his “sleepy little town” in northeast Arkansas will continue focusing on things like water infrastructure to be prepared for when economic development opportunities do arrive.
Located between Jonesboro and Blytheville in Craighead County, Blankenship said Monette is growing thanks to its proximity to the burgeoning steel industry in Mississippi County. Blankenship said he’d like to offer residents more amenities to keep them in town, such as a sitdown restaurant, which Monette currently doesn’t have. 
“Our hands are tied as far as doing the tax breaks that the (Issue) 3 was going to help on, but we can offer it in our own little way and hopefully that’ll work,” he said. 


Let us know what you think...


 

Senate President Bart Hester, a Cave Springs Republican who also backed Issue 3, said there have been no discussions about lawmakers referring a similar measure to voters in the future. Hester and Democratic Sen. Clarke Tucker appeared in a video touting the measure as something conservatives and progressives could support.
The proposed constitutional amendment, one of four measures on the November ballot, was referred to voters by the Legislature through a resolution sponsored by Republicans Sen. Jonathan Dismang and Rep. Howard Beaty. 
Northwest Arkansas, a rapidly-growing region that Hester represents, doesn’t need Issue 3 to help spur economic development, but other parts of the state do, he said. Hester said the measure would have made a big difference in border towns like Texarkana, and he hates to lose the opportunity to compete with neighboring states that do offer these types of incentives.  
“We knew it was the right thing for Arkansas, the voters felt differently and the voters rule,” he said.
Arkansas Explained: What are the incentives for West Memphis’ possible superproject?

Hester said conservative friends opposed to Issue 3 argued the state just needs to create a great tax and regulatory environment that encourages businesses to pick Arkansas over incentives they would receive elsewhere. Arkansas will continue to work on that, he said. 
“Issue 3 was just another tool in the toolchest,” Hester said. “So we’ll just continue to double down on cutting corporate income tax, cutting personal income taxes.”
Republican Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders, who won reelection Tuesday, has said she wants to continue cutting taxes in her next term. Hester said Wednesday that he plans to file a tax cut bill during next year’s legislative session. 
“Over the past four years, Governor Sanders has cut taxes four times, lowering the income tax by 25%, slashed red tape, attracted billions of investment to Arkansas, and helped create 75,000 new jobs,” Sanders’ spokesperson Sam Dubke said in an email. “The Governor will use the same playbook to continue to grow our economy and keep costs low for working Arkansas families.”
Hester also touted the governor’s executive order to speed up permitting for economic development projects.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: School meals focus shifts to North Dakota Legislature after Measure 2 defeat
description: An attempt to guarantee free school meals to K-12 students narrowly failed at the ballot box Tuesday, but the issue isn’t going away in North Dakota.  Supporters and opponents of Measure 2, the defeated constitutional amendment, are looking ahead to next steps. Nearly 51% of voters rejected the measure, while about 49% supported it, according […]
text:
Students eat lunch at Roosevelt Elementary School in Bismarck on Nov. 2, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)An attempt to guarantee free school meals to K-12 students narrowly failed at the ballot box Tuesday, but the issue isn’t going away in North Dakota. 
Supporters and opponents of Measure 2, the defeated constitutional amendment, are looking ahead to next steps. Nearly 51% of voters rejected the measure, while about 49% supported it, according to complete but unofficial results.
Sen. Paul Thomas, R-Velva, said Wednesday he thinks there is unanimous support in the state for the core principle of ensuring no child goes hungry. 
“Nobody in North Dakota feels or has any belief that a child should ever not be fed,” said Thomas, who opposed the initiated measure but supports legislative action. “This really isn’t a partisan Republican-Democrat divided issue.”
Voters defeat free school meal ballot measure in North Dakota

An advocate for free school meals in the Legislature said she plans to introduce legislation in 2027 to accomplish what Measure 2 failed to do. 
Rep. LaurieBeth Hager, D-Fargo, the sponsor of a free school meals bill that failed to advance in 2025, said she plans to introduce similar legislation again to require all K-12 schools to offer breakfast and lunch to students at no cost. 
“It’s equalizing the kids. We don’t charge them differently for books. We don’t charge them differently for using the buses,” Hager said. “It’s part of the school day and part of the learning experience.”
Hager said she believes the fact that Measure 2 was a constitutional amendment likely scared off voters who are otherwise supportive of providing free school meals to K-12 students.
“If the powers that be think this needs to be in statute instead of in the constitution, then we will get it done that way,” Hager said. “The fight continues.”
Opponents of the measure, including Gov. Kelly Armstrong, criticized putting school meals in the constitution. The program was estimated to cost $124.3 million to $134.3 million every two years starting in 2027-29. Critics said mandating that spending in the constitution would tie lawmakers’ hands during lean budget years.
Armstrong said Wednesday he doesn’t anticipate a large push by Republican lawmakers to revisit a universal school meals program.
“I just think it’s a little harder politically today than it would have been even six months ago,” he said.
Rep. Mike Nathe, R-Bismarck, said voters rejected Measure 2, and he questioned why state lawmakers would consider going against the voters’ wishes.
“The people of North Dakota spoke. They rejected Measure 2, and we have to respect that,” Nathe said. “But that does not mean we can’t work around the edges a little bit and kind of make some things better.”
Nathe sponsored a school meal bill in the January special session that aimed to head off a constitutional ballot measure. House lawmakers approved the bill, but it lost in the Senate by two votes.
Thomas said he does not support a statutory free school meals bill like Hager’s proposal, but the senator said the election result shows voters expect lawmakers will continue working on the issue.
“They want us to continue working on some of the shortcomings of current policy,” Thomas said.
Thomas is working on policy ideas he plans to introduce in the legislative session that begins in January. His bill is being drafted and he plans to gauge his colleagues’ interest when the Legislative Management committee meets next week. 
Other lawmakers, including Rep. Chuck Walen, R-New Town, have said they plan to propose alternative solutions on school meals. Sen. Michelle Axtman, R-Bismarck, said the issue has not been “put to bed,” and expects to make progress during the session.
“I think we’ll find a way to maximize federal dollars and be very strategic and problem-solving to come up with a solution that makes more sense than the measure did,” Axtman said in an interview Tuesday night.
North Dakota families can face debt collections if they can’t afford school lunch

While North Dakota lawmakers have voted against free school meal bills, they have adopted other proposals including an anti-lunch shaming bill in 2023. However, more than two dozen school districts reported in a survey that they refer families to collection agencies for unpaid lunch debt.
Legislators also have slightly expanded how many students qualify for free and reduced lunch through the federal program. In 2025, lawmakers earmarked $6 million to raise the income level used to determine families’ eligibility. 
About $2.5 million of that funding was spent in the first half of the 2025-27 budget cycle, said Lynelle Johnson, director of the Office of Child Nutrition and Food Distribution for the North Dakota Department of Public Instruction. The funding has helped about 3,000 students who would not have otherwise qualified under the federal free and reduced lunch income eligibility requirements. 
“That additional expanded eligibility is very appreciated,” Johnson said.
Robin Nelson, chair of Together for School Meals, said many North Dakotans gave their “time, energy and heart” to the Measure 2 campaign because they saw a need in their schools and communities. 
“We wish we could have given North Dakota families better news. They are why we took on this effort, and they remain our concern as we consider what comes next,” Nelson said. 
Amy Jacobson, the group’s spokesperson, said members of the coalition are going to take time to digest the results and consult with stakeholders before they make any decisions on what they will focus on moving forward. 
“Families are still stretching their budgets, and children still need meals to get through the school day ready to learn,” Jacobson said.
North Dakota Monitor reporter Jacob Orledge can be reached at jorledge@northdakotamonitor.com. Monitor reporter Michael Achterling can be reached at machterling@northdakotamonitor.com.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Democratic women gain 8 seats in the House, moving the needle in the male-dominated chamber
description: Democratic women made strides in West Virginia on Election Day, winning eight seats in the House of Delegates.
text:
After Tuesday's midterm election, 19 women will be in the West Virginia House of Delegates next year. (Photo by Perry Bennett/West Virginia Legislative Photography)Democratic women made strides in West Virginia on Election Day, winning eight seats in the House of Delegates.
West Virginia’s Legislature has the fewest number of women lawmakers, with just 12 Republican and Democratic women serving in the House.
In 2027, that number will grow to 19.
Del. Kayla Young, D-Kanawha, is one of only two Democratic women serving in the statehouse. That number has gone up after the midterm election on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Perry Bennett/West Virginia Legislative Photography)
“I am so excited for the breadth of representation for women that we are going to have in the West Virginia House,” said Del. Kayla Young, D-Kanawha. “We’re going to have so many new women — 10 Democratic women and nine Republican women.”
“I think people know that women get things done,” she added.
While the GOP maintains firm control of the House, the Democratic caucus added 12 new members after election results thus far. The House Democratic Caucus will go from the current nine to 21 in 2027.
On the left side of the House floor, where the minority caucus sits, most of the new faces will be female.
Democrat Marisa Jackson defeated incumbent Del. Walt Hall, R-Kanawha, in District 58. (Submitted photo)
Marisa Jackson, a Democrat in St. Albans, is familiar with the Legislature after advocating for her two children with disabilities. She defeated incumbent Del. Walt Hall, R-Kanawha, in District 58.
Jackson acknowledged she is joining a still predominantly male Legislature.
“I feel this deep sense of duty to do my best, to represent people,” she said. “Women are half the population, and we deserve to have female voices representing us in the Legislature. We understand issues in a different way men may not understand, so we can bring a different perspective when we’re making laws affecting people.”
Democratic women picked up three seats in West Virginia’s Eastern Panhandle: Jenny Thacker won the race for District 100, Lucia Valentine won in District 97 and Regina Dyer won in District 99.
Thacker, a retired ocean cartographer for the National Oceanic Atmospheric Administration, said it’s “fantastic” that more women won seats in the statehouse.
Women tend to focus on issues like healthcare, education and childcare more than male legislators, she said.
“Women need more healthcare, and we need different healthcare than men do,” Thacker said. “Education. And not that men don’t care about their children’s education, but women tend to be much more front line with education, caring for foster kids, caring for the childcare issues. There a lot of women wind up getting stuck staying home because they can’t find childcare.”
Democrat Karen Stakem won the District 5 race in the Northern Panhandle over Republican Beth Hinebaugh. The seat was formerly held by Democrat Shawn Fluharty, who lost his bid for the state Senate Tuesday to incumbent Republican Laura Wakim Chapman.
“I think it’s great that we picked up seats in general because I believe in balance,” Stakem said Wednesday. “I believe having two different sides makes for better policy, and we haven’t seen that in recent years having a super majority. So I’m excited there’s going to be more balance back in the Legislature.”
Stakem, a small business owner and mother of three, said her priorities in the Legislature are bringing good jobs to the state, improving quality of life and making things more affordable.
She also hopes that having more women in the Legislature will lead lawmakers to focus on public education.
West Virginia’s public school funding woes are expected to dominate the 2027 legislative session, which will begin in January. Lawmakers are considering how they could change the state’s school funding formula in light of the declining enrollment.
Thacker, a first-time candidate, said the current Legislature hasn’t paid attention to what people in Jefferson County wanted on issues like data centers. Thacker said many residents in her district worry that the area is developing too fast, and that there’s not enough water for people, let alone data centers.
“There are issues that are very specific to our county that run the gamut. They’re not Republican issues. They’re not Democrat issues. They’re not national issues. They are our issues, and we need to focus on those. And that’s what I’ve been doing,” Thacker said.
Jefferson County sits across the state border from Loudoun County, Virginia, which has one of the highest median incomes in the country. Public teachers living in Jefferson County drive to work in Virginia, where they can earn more money, she said.
“I’m hoping that we can get a locality pay that isn’t just for the Eastern Panhandle, but a locality pay for every county that’s higher than average cost of living,” Thacker said. “Because our cost of living here, a typical house in this area is like $400,000. There are parts of West Virginia where you can buy a house for $40,000. You know, one tenth of what it costs here. And yet, we all have the same base pay scale wherever we are in West Virginia. That doesn’t work.”
Lawmakers have floated the idea of locality pay for teachers in the past, but measures haven’t made it to the governor’s desk.
Other Democratic women who won House races on Tuesday are: Linda Longstreth in Marion County; Olivia Miller in Monongalia County; and Shannon Welsh in Harrison County.
In a statement Wednesday, Del. Mike Pushkin, chair of the West Virginia Democratic Party, said he’s proud that eight of the 12 newly elected Democrats in the House are women, who will make up nearly half the caucus.
“These victories are a testament to the strength, determination, and leadership of women across West Virginia who stepped forward to fight for their communities and bring a fresh perspective to the Legislature,” Pushkin said.
Del. Anitra Hamilton, D-Monongalia, and Young both were unopposed this year and will return to the House.
Across the nation, a record number of women ran in state legislative races this year.
“I think people want to see change. Women want to be represented by women,” Young said. “I think we’re finally seeing the tides turn after redistricting and after 10 years of President Trump. We’re starting to see the light at the end of the tunnel.”

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Alabama scheduled to execute death row inmate for 1991 murder of couple
description: Alabama is scheduled to execute a death row inmate Thursday for his role in the murders of a couple in Gadsden in 1991. Michael Shannon Taylor, 54, is set to be put to death by lethal injection for the deaths of Ivan and Lucille Moore during a robbery. Taylor would be the third person executed […]
text:
Michael Shannon Taylor is seen in this undated photo. Taylor is scheduled to be executed on Thursday for the murders of Ivan and Lucille Moore during a robbery of their home in Gadsden in 1991. (Alabama Department of Corrections)Alabama is scheduled to execute a death row inmate Thursday for his role in the murders of a couple in Gadsden in 1991.
Michael Shannon Taylor, 54, is set to be put to death by lethal injection for the deaths of Ivan and Lucille Moore during a robbery.
Taylor would be the third person executed in Alabama this year. Jeremy Tremaine Williams was put to death in August. Jeffery Lee was executed in September.
Ivey also commuted the death sentences of Charles “Sonny” Burton in March and Toforest Johnson in October.
According to court documents, Taylor was absent without leave from the Navy when he received a ride from Ivan and Lucille. He asked to use the couple’s telephone inside their home when Taylor beat them to death.
Taylor filed two appeals in state court Tuesday. The first is a request for a stay of execution with the Alabama Supreme Court. He also filed an appeal with the Alabama Court of Criminal Appeals after the Etowah County Circuit Court ruled against him last week.
In his appeal, Taylor alleges that the state is violating its own law if it executes him by lethal injection because the Alabama Legislature passed a bill in 2018 that authorized execution by nitrogen gas. Federal courts in June ruled in response to a suit from Lee that Alabama’s nitrogen gas protocol violated Lee’s Eighth Amendment right against cruel and unusual punishment.
A subsection of the 2018 state law states that “if electrocution or nitrogen hypoxia are held unconstitutional, the method of execution shall be lethal injection,” according to the appeal filed by Taylor.
The law also states that “if lethal injection is held unconstitutional or otherwise becomes unavailable, the method of execution shall be by nitrogen hypoxia.”
“Thus, unavailability is a trigger only for replacing lethal injection,” Taylor’s appeal said.
Lethal injection is not an option for the state since it is “unavailable” because he chose to be executed by nitrogen gas and that execution method is still allowed, according to Taylor’s appeal.
Lee made a similar argument to Taylor’s but ultimately lost his challenge to the state’s decision to use lethal injection. U.S. District Judge Emily C. Marks declined to block that method, citing the situation had changed.
Neither the Alabama Supreme Court nor the Alabama Court of Criminal Appeals had ruled on Taylor’s request by Wednesday afternoon.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Virginia voters split on 1% sales tax for school construction
description: On Election Day, out of 47 Virginia localities, about 30% authorized their governments to collect a 1% sales tax to address rising school construction costs, while about 70% did not.  In June, state lawmakers authorized localities, pending voter support, to raise revenue for school construction and modernization with a 1% sales tax. The state estimates […]
text:
An early view of the school construction work in Halifax County. (Photo courtesy of Halifax County Public Schools)On Election Day, out of 47 Virginia localities, about 30% authorized their governments to collect a 1% sales tax to address rising school construction costs, while about 70% did not. 
In June, state lawmakers authorized localities, pending voter support, to raise revenue for school construction and modernization with a 1% sales tax. The state estimates over 1000 school buildings are more than 50 years old, and would take $25 billion to rebuild or improve. 
House Education Committee Chair Sam Rasoul, D-Roanoke, and Sen. Jeremy McPike, D-Prince William, proposed the idea last January. Both measures were ultimately added to the state’s budget.
“School construction is a critical need,” said McPike ahead of the results. “This is a direct question to the voters in the form of a referendum, and it’s up to the voters to decide how they want to fund school construction.”
Tuesday’s results are expected to help 14 localities move the needle on school modernization, while leaving questions about the 33 that rejected the opportunity and what comes next.

Rasoul said the idea was to help address billions in school construction needs in the commonwealth. But citizens have raised concerns about tax increases, a point former Gov. Glenn Youngkin raised in previous years
Mecklenburg, one of the nine localities with state-approved authority, has not put the matter to voters since receiving authorization, largely because it opposed raising taxes, according to Board of Supervisors’ records in 2021. 
Mecklenburg estimated it would need about $6 million per year in debt payments to move forward with new school construction, which ultimately dampened interest in adding the option to ballots. 
In addition, the county had already invested in newer additions to the three elementary schools. 
No action has been taken since former state Sen. Frank Ruff successfully proposed the change in 2020.
In 2019, Halifax County became the first locality to receive authority from the state, which is required since Virginia is a “Dillon’s Rule” state, meaning local governments can only exercise powers granted by the state legislature. 
Localities can adjust property tax rates, but they need General Assembly approval to change sales taxes.
With the election’s results, the list has grown from the original nine — city of Danville and the counties of Charlotte, Gloucester, Halifax, Henry, Mecklenburg, Northampton, Patrick and Pittsylvania — to 23 locations.
Rasoul acknowledged that, while he championed the bill, it is not a long-term solution to the state’s school construction needs. Additional support, particularly at the state level, will be necessary to help struggling school divisions, he said.
“This isn’t going to be able to build all the schools that need to be built,” Rasoul said. “So there’s a lot more that needs to be done … even at the state level to help struggling school divisions.”
McPike said upcoming discussions with his colleagues on the Commission on School Construction and Modernization should focus on analyzing the referendum results once they are available, evaluating long-term funding structures for school construction and reviewing stabilized projections over time.
The commission and all state lawmakers will return to Richmond on Jan. 13, 2027 to discuss future legislation and budget amendments.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Public hearings for the NextEra-Dominion merger have begun. Here’s what you need to know.
description: Public hearings in the case to decide the fate of the proposed merger between Dominion Energy and Florida-based NextEra Energy begin this week at the State Corporation Commission. The $67 billion all-stock deal would create the largest regulated utility in the world.  In the months preceding the hearings, scores of lawmakers, consumer advocates and citizens [...]
text:
Dominion Energy offices in Richmond, Va. (Photo by Parker Michels-Boyce for the Virginia Mercury)Public hearings in the case to decide the fate of the proposed merger between Dominion Energy and Florida-based NextEra Energy begin this week at the State Corporation Commission. The $67 billion all-stock deal would create the largest regulated utility in the world. 
In the months preceding the hearings, scores of lawmakers, consumer advocates and citizens have strongly opposed the proposal, with leaders at the top level of state government pushing for more time to review the case.
As public testimony gets underway Thursday, here are the key details of the case so far.
The proposal: original and revamped versions
NextEra owns the traditional utility Florida Power and Light Company as well as the unregulated NextEra Energy Resources, which constructs and operates large scale energy infrastructure. If NextEra acquires Dominion, it would create a combined portfolio of over 10 million customers, 110 gigawatts of power, and a connection queue of 130 GW.
In the joint proposal’s latest filing, the companies laid out a deal that included a bill credit totalling about $10 monthly on the average residential customer’s bill, for four years total. 
The revised offerings also include job protection for Dominion employees for five years, the promise to build an office building in downtown Richmond and various workforce development investments and weatherization programs totaling up to $200 million.
NextEra shareholders will own 74.5% of shares and Dominion shareholders will own 25.5%, if the merger is approved.
Dominion has assured regulators that the utility would remain its own entity that is still beholden to Virginia state laws, including the Virginia Clean Economy Act and its mandate that Dominion be carbon-free by 2045, with some exceptions.
In a July interview with the Mercury, Dominion’s vice president of corporate affairs and communication Bill Murray said that the merging of the companies would expand the energy infrastructure buying power, a cost-cutting maneuver.
Buying in bulk would bring down the price of infrastructure needed in the buildout to meet the power demands that are growing in both the utilities’ territories, he said.
“It’s not a matter of we threw our hands up and said ‘we can’t do this, somebody, please, merge with us,’” Murray said. “But doing it together… at a one-notch credit rating upgrade, financing it more efficiently. That’s a benefit to customers.”
This is not the first iteration of the proposal. The first version of the deal was filed over the summer and included bill credits for just two years. Dominion customers in the GS5 rate class, largely data centers, would have been able to cash in on the credits, too. 
But the updated version redirects the savings GS5 customers would have realized in order to extend the credit for residential customers. 
In his testimony, Dominion CEO Bob Blue stated the companies “believe(d) that their original bill credit allocation proposal is fair and reasonable,” but they offered the alternative plan as a way to ease concerns.
Another aspect of the merger case that prompted public concerns and led some lawmakers to raise questions of ethics: SCC Chairwoman Kelsey Bagot used to work for NextEra. 
Bagot worked as an attorney for the utility for two years until 2024 when she was appointed to the commission, which led to her resignation of the post.
Sen. Scott Surovell, D-Fairfax, he stated in an Aug. 12 letter to Bagot that “several members of the General Assembly and other third parties that have raised questions about your continued participation as a commissioner in this matter due to your prior employment by NextEra Energy especially in light of your prior recusal in a prior NextEra Energy case.”
In a response letter, Bagot stated that she will not be recusing herself from the merger case, despite stepping back during previous NextEra related cases. 
Bagot said she consulted legal counsel and determined that her involvement in the merger case did not violate the Canons of Judicial Conduct.
“As has been demonstrated by long-standing historical Commissioner practice, mere work history with a regulated entity has not served as a categorical basis requiring recusal,” Bagot wrote.
Pre-filed arguments against the merger
Virginia law is at the center of the case, and is a key consideration for commissioners. 
The Utility Transfers Act states:
The commissioners will base their decision on whether “adequate service to the public at just and reasonable rates will not be impaired or jeopardized” by approving the merging of the two companies .
In the initial review of the proposal, SCC staff made a slate of recommendations regarding whether the two companies have met their burden of proof that the merger would protect ratepayers. Staff determined that they had not. 
“The Merger Commitments and Supplemental Merger Commitments of the Petitioners are not sufficient to ensure that (Dominion) will maintain the resources to provide adequate service to its customers post-Merger,” staff testimony stated, adding that NextEra’s “unregulated, competitive business” exposed Dominion to additional risks.
That unregulated business is the NextEra Energy Resources (NEER) branch of the company. The energy infrastructure value is closely tied to the market value of power. As power demands grow, so does the cost of electricity, leading to which means more profits for these unregulated companies.
While the commissioners are not bound to staff’s recommendations, they are taken into careful consideration.
In their filing, the consumer advocacy group Clean Virginia echoed staff’s concerns about the high-risk aspect of the unregulated portion of NextEra’s investments and how it is a wholly different system than Dominion’s traditional regulated utility model.
Staff created a list of over 100 requirements and conditions that they felt would protect Virginia ratepayers if the merger were allowed to move forward. 
Dominion’s president should remain a Virginia resident, SCC staff recommended, and the company should maintain separate bank accounts and financing arrangements.
Another condition would bar NextEra Energy Transmission from owning any future transmission projects in the Dominion zone of regional grid operator PJM. 
Dominion and NextEra have accepted a number of those policy recommendations from SCC staff and the Attorney General’s office. They did reject some aspects, including a rate freeze and certain ring-fencing protection plans.
In expert testimony filed on behalf of Gov. Abigail Spanberger and Chief Energy Officer Josephus Allmond, the governor’s administration called for expanded benefits and protections for rate payers. 
Increasing customers’ bill credits to $29 monthly is chief among their recommendations, along with a base rate freeze for six years.
They also suggest formulating a new, separate subsidiary to oversee building zero-carbon energy generation serving large data centers, which would be financially walled off from the rest of customers.
“A $10 monthly bill credit does not provide much confidence when Dominion has already petitioned the Commission to recover more than $10 per month in fuel-related costs this year alone,” said Robert McCann in his testimony for the governor.
The governor also wants to tie Dominion executives’ bonuses to ratepayer affordability, efficiency measures, and clean energy investment benchmarks. Her recommendation only allows 50% of the compensation to be tied to shareholder benefits.
The concerns laid out in SCC staff’s recommendations mirror those of Lt. Gov. Hashmi, who formally opposed the merger last month. 
After hosting a statewide listening tour, Hashmi said the overwhelming sentiment from Virginians is that they were not convinced the merger would bring down their utility bills, which have increased in recent years. 
If the merger succeeds, NextEra would take over the utility company supplying power to the most data centers in the nation. 
Dominion’s interconnection queue, the time it will take to bring power to any one data center project, stretches about seven years. Amazon and Google are participating in the merger case as intervenors. They have some of their own recommendations on policies that could be changed to help with bringing power to projects and the grid sooner.
“(Dominion’s) large-load interconnection study process is not keeping pace with demand. The current batch process produces project-by-project upgrade solutions whose costs are borne broadly by customers,” Cameron Brooks said on behalf of Amazon Data Services in prefiled testimony. 
“The Company faces a capacity shortfall, yet customers willing to fund, source, enable, or already control new capacity at their own expense have no pathway to receive credit for that capacity.” 
NextEra’s past raises concerns
In the months leading up to the beginning of the hearings, lawmakers dug into NextEra’s past business dealings. The utility has made multiple failed attempts to acquire other utilities across the nation.
Hawaiian regulators determined that NextEra’s attempt to take over Hawaiian Electric Companies was not in the public interest. In Texas, the company’s effort to take on Oncor was determined to be a risk for ratepayers due to NextEra’s hefty debt. That deal did not have tangible benefits for ratepayers, regulators said.
This summer, Virginia legislators learned from industry experts that the proliferation of data centers in Virginia is an attractive draw for companies like NextEra, who want to capitalize on the buildout of the energy infrastructure needed to support them.
Clean Virginia, who is also an intervenor in the merger case, successfully petitioned to include details of a $150 million settlement over whether the company lied about its involvement in political interference schemes in Florida to be in the case’s evidence. 
Requests for more time
While the General Assembly does not get to weigh in on whether the merger should be approved or not, lawmakers have tried to extend the amount of time the SCC could have to review the case. 
Legislators called on Spanberger to convene a special session in order to pass a policy that would allow for the SCC to extend their six-month review period. The governor declined that request, noting that she already took action by intervening in the case. 
When the revamped proposal was filed, Attorney General Jay Jones called for the clock to be reset on the six-month countdown when the SCC must make a determination on the merger. The commission has not yet ruled on this request.
That deadline remains at Jan. 11. The first public hearings have already begun in person across the state, which is a rare move by the commission. 
Telephonic public testimony begins Nov. 5, with the final in person hearing scheduled in Richmond at the SCC the same day. The evidentiary portion of the case will begin Nov. 17.
