title: Eight municipalities vote to cap rent increases on mobile home lots
description: Voters in eight Maine municipalities approved referendums on Tuesday to help stabilize the cost of rent for mobile home lots.  Affordability is a concern for people in various types of housing across Maine, as a massive shortage in supply confronts stagnant wages, high building costs, and an influx of residents in part due to an […]
text:
Urban Grove, a manufactured home community in Saint Anthony, Minnesota,, Tuesday, Feb. 24, 2026. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)Voters in eight Maine municipalities approved referendums on Tuesday to help stabilize the cost of rent for mobile home lots. 
Affordability is a concern for people in various types of housing across Maine, as a massive shortage in supply confronts stagnant wages, high building costs, and an influx of residents in part due to an increase in remote workers.
While mobile home residents often own their physical homes, they have to rent the underlying land, leaving them vulnerable to skyrocketing monthly lot rents, especially when corporate or out-of-state investors buy parks. 
“Mobile home owners across Maine have been squeezed by corporate park owners who buy up parks, jack up the rents, and let maintenance fall by the wayside,” Joe Hupperich, organizing director for the Maine Labor Climate Council, said in a statement. 
“Residents of the parks are mostly seniors or people who are otherwise on fixed incomes, who are left struggling to make up the money. Tuesday’s results send a clear message that Mainers believe the people who own their homes deserve stable, predictable housing costs.”
Augusta, Eliot, Standish, Oakland, Wells, Farmington, Jay and Wiscasset each passed lot rent stabilization measures on Tuesday. Many of these limits were based on a framework created by a state working group as a result of a law passed in 2025.
Augusta, Eliot and Standish capped annual lot rent increases at either 3% or the rate of inflation, whichever is lower. Oakland capped the annual increase at 5%, while Farmington capped increases at 3% for occupied lots and 5% for vacant lots. Wells passed an annual increase limit at the rate of inflation plus 1%, and Jay limited most increases to the Northeast Consumer Price Index. Wiscasset passed a temporary 180-day ban on lot rent increases exceeding 3%.
“This win belongs to every neighbor in the community who showed up,” Lynzy Kosmes, a resident organizer from a Wells mobile home park, said in a statement. “Nobody just handed us this.”

name: Maryland Matters
title: Harford County pursues Penman in court, even as councilman prepares to exit job
description: Aaron Penman's days as Harford County councilman are numbered, but that isn't stopping the county from trying to get the Supreme Court of Maryland to reverse the ruling that restored the Republican lawmaker to the council this year.
text:
The term of Harford County Councilmember Aaron Penman (R) ends in a month, but the county is appealing a decision that let Penman, a sheriff's deputy, return to the panel.  (File photo by Bryan. P. Sears/Maryland Matters)Aaron Penman’s days as Harford County councilman are numbered, but that isn’t stopping Harford County Executive Bob Cassilly from trying to reverse the ruling that restored his fellow Republican to the council this year.
The county Wednesday asked the Supreme Court of Maryland to overturn an April ruling by an Appellate Court of Maryland panel that reinstated Penman, almost two years after he was removed by a lower court that said he could not serve on the council while employed as a county sheriff’s deputy.
Harford County Attorney Jefferson Blomquist argued the high court should rule on the issue even though Penman will only be on the court until Dec. 7, when the new council is sworn in. Penman did not run for reelection this year.
“No, it does not become moot because to become moot, it has to be incapable of repetition,” Blomquist said in response to justices’ questions. “Clearly this is not a situation that’s capable of repetition.”
The legal issues, Blomquist said, are of great public importance.
County Charter eligibility provisions “provide for the checks and balances and the separations of power that allow our government to function as a republic or as a democracy,” he said during arguments Wednesday.
But Cassilly, who has feuded with Penman and his boss, Sheriff Jeff Gahler, as well as the outgoing council president, is not relenting in his pursuit of a ruling that is both against the councilman that also might clarify his county’s charter.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
Wednesday’s appeal is one of two before the Supreme Court of Maryland involving Penman and potential conflicts between his elected position and day job. The court is set to hold arguments in March on a case involving Penman and the Harford County Ethics Commission.
Cassilly in 2022 refused to swear in Democrat Jacob Bennett to the council, saying the charter banned Bennett because he was also a middle school science teacher.
The state’s highest court ultimately ruled in favor of Bennett, ruling that county charter eligibility provisions were wrongfully applied to Bennett because “a county board of education does not have a particular character as State, county, hybrid, or independent entity.” A school board can have the character of any of those entities — the definition is dependent on the situation, the court wrote.
Cassilly later used the same charter language — and the county ethics commission — to deny Penman a seat on the council. In both the Bennett and Penman cases, the same circuit court judge ruled in Cassilly’s favor.
Penman was off the council for roughly 18 months as he appealed. In April, the Appellate Court of Maryland ruled that while the position of sheriff is a constitutional office, it’s role as a state or county government entity is trickier.
“In the absence of clear textual guidance or definitive legislative history, we must apply the presumption favoring eligibility,” Judge Jeffrey Geller wrote for the panel.
“In this case, a county council member who also serves as a deputy sheriff, and the sheriff who employs them, both ultimately answer to the voters,” Geller wrote. “When statutory text leaves the question open, the ultimate judgment belongs not to this Court, but to the ballot box.”
The court remanded the case back to Harford County Circuit Court, where a new judge specially appointed to the case restored Penman to his job.
In the meantime, because of the initial ruling, Penman opted to not seek re-election, instead backing Alison Imhoff, the social worker who had been appointed to fill his then-vacant seat.
Justin DeMichael, who is one of two attorneys representing Penman, told the high court Wednesday there are similarities between Bennett’s and Penman’s jobs. In both cases, the school system and sheriff’s department are independent agencies and not necessarily within county government.
“I think they are definitely unique in how they are created,” DeMichael argued. “I think if you do an analysis of the sheriff’s office, it creates the same contextual issues that were present in Bennett.”

name: Maryland Matters
title: Political notes: Jawando transition, Black Caucus’ new director, Blueprint rallying
description: Montgomery County Executive-elect Will Jawando unveils a talent-heavy transition team, the Legislative Black Caucus convenes, the same week it gets a new executive director, and advocates line up support for the Blueprint for Maryland's Future, in political notes.
text:
Montgomery County Councilmember Will Jawando at an event June 1 at Zinnia Restaurant in Silver Spring. (File photo by William J. Ford/Maryland Matters)Montgomery County Executive-elect Will Jawando (D) announced a transition steering committee Wednesday, about 17 hours after the polls closed, that will draw on former White House talent and current state and local officials.
“Our Moment Montgomery” calls on every resident to be involved in making the county better. Among those on the steering committee are Karine Jean-Pierre, the White House press secretary for President Joe Biden (D), and Shalanda Young, who was the first Black woman to lead a Cabinet agency as director of the White House Office of Management and Budget.
Others on the eight-member committee include County Councilmember Kristin Mink (D), former County Councilmember and school board member Nancy Navarro, and former Executive Vice President of Marriott International Kathleen Matthews.
Jawando, who spoke for about 40 minutes Wednesday before taking questions from reporters, also named chairs and co-chairs of a dozen policy committees.
They include Del. Jheanelle Wilkins (D-Montgomery), who will help lead “A Government that Works for All” committee, charged with exploring “stronger independent oversight, transparent budgeting, and ways to reduce the influence of private money.” One thing Jawando would like to see the General Assembly change is the ability for local jurisdictions to charge different tax rates.
“A data center should [not] pay the same tax rate as a single-family home, or that a mansion should pay the same rate as a condo,” he said. “We need that flexibility, especially if they’re going to pass on cost to us.”
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
Another committee will focus on protecting immigrants’ rights and exploring ways to expand language access and improve trust with county government. One of the co-chairs will be Alex Vazquez, the Maryland organizing director at We Are CASA.
Jawando said the committees will start next week, with community workshops throughout the county starting the week of Nov. 30. He will sworn in as executive exactly one week later, on Dec. 7.
Jawando, who got 78% of the vote over Republican challenger Esther Wells in unofficial results, said he plans to be “your county executive, too,” for the 20% that didn’t vote for him, and for those who didn’t vote.
“This transition is open to each and every resident of Montgomery County,” he said. “Bring your ideas and your concerns. Our doors are open, and we’re going to work every day to earn your trust.”
Black Caucus weekend
Fresh off the election, the Maryland Black Caucus Foundation, the nonprofit fundraising arm of the Legislative Black Caucus of Maryland, is rolling into its 31st legislative weekend.
Caucus members will moderate virtual panels Friday on topics such as environmental injustice, health disparities and civil rights in the world of artificial intelligence. One topic that could be a hot-button issue in the 2027 legislative session is education: The state faces a projected $3 billion budget gap next year, according to the Maryland Associations of Counties (MACo), and about $1.8 billion of that is tied to the Blueprint for Maryland’s Future education reform plan. Fiscal 2028 is the first year in which Blueprint costs will exceed dedicated revenues.
Other speakers Friday include Maryland Agriculture Secretary Kevin Atticks; Nicole Earle, who became the first Black woman in June to chair the Maryland Racing Commission; and Robin Williams, international vice president with the United Food and Commercial Workers International Union (UFCW).
Del. N. Scott Phillips (D-Baltimore County) at a September news conference in support of Question 3 . (Photo by William J. Ford/Maryland Matters)
A “business over breakfast” event will be held Saturday at Maryland Live! featuring Del. N. Scott Phillips (D-Baltimore County), the caucus chair, Sen. Shaneka Henson (D-Anne Arundel), first vice chair, and Del. Karen Toles (D-Prince George’s), second vice chair.
Henson, who became the first Black official elected to the Senate from Anne Arundel County, will be one of three Black women in the Senate in January, with Sen. Mary Washington (D-Baltimore City and Baltimore County) and Sen.-elect Tiffany Alston (D-Prince George’s). When Sen.-elect Malcolm Ruff (D-Baltimore City) is sworn in, Black senators will account for half of the 34 Democratic members in the Senate.
A Saturday night gala at Maryland Live!, “Standing Strong for Injustice, Equity and Democracy,” is scheduled to feature Gov. Wes Moore (D), who easily won reelection for a second term Tuesday.
Change in leadership
The foundation event comes the same week that MJ Browning started as executive director of the Legislative Black Caucus. Browning takes over for Ufuoma Agarin, who became director of external affairs with the Maryland Office of the Public Defender last month, after working as the caucus’ executive director since the 2023 legislative session.
“For much of my tenure, I was a staff of one, and I worked fiercely because I genuinely cared about getting the work done and supporting each of you well,” Agarin wrote in a letter to the caucus. “Whether it was preparing for a meeting, responding to a last-minute request during session, organizing an event, advancing our legislative priorities, working with our community partners, or simply making sure a member had what they needed, I always wanted you to know that you had someone in your corner.”
Bring your voice
The Blueprint Coalition, a group of nonprofit organizations, community leaders and education advocates who support the Blueprint plan, will continue its statewide community sessions with a virtual one at 6:30 p.m. Nov. 16.
The coalition has held community sessions in Montgomery, Prince George’s and Howard counties. The discussion not only focus on the Blueprint, but also ways to improve overall public education.
Strong Schools Maryland, the grassroots organization that advocates education equity in the state and a member of the coalition, will also hold a virtual session at 6:30 p.m. Dec. 9. That particular discussion will help parents, students and community leaders advocate before lawmakers when the 2027 session convenes in Annapolis.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Opinion: Does the Republican Party speak for the entire state of Kansas? Not after that thumping, it doesn’t.
description: If any one statement sums up the colossal miscalculation underlying Kansas Republicans’ historic wipeout Tuesday night, it’s a single social media post from Senate President Ty Masterson. You might remember Masterson as the GOP leader who hoped to succeed Democrat Laura Kelly as governor. He ran against fellow state senator Cindy Holscher, who appeared poise[...]
text:
GOP nominee for governor Ty Masterson addresses the crowd at a GOP watch party Nov. 3, 2026, in Wichita, where he says the race is too close to call. (Photo by Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)If any one statement sums up the colossal miscalculation underlying Kansas Republicans’ historic wipeout Tuesday night, it’s a single social media post from Senate President Ty Masterson.
You might remember Masterson as the GOP leader who hoped to succeed Democrat Laura Kelly as governor. He ran against fellow state senator Cindy Holscher, who appeared poised for victory Wednesday after a hard-fought race. In the post, Masterson urged patience as election officials audited ballots in coming days but also edged toward a concession.
That’s not all he said, though.

Last night was a difficult night in Kansas and around the country. But I’m grateful to the hundreds of thousands of Kansans who stood with us, and to every volunteer who gave their time to this campaign.
The first count does not seem to be going our way, but the margin is narrow enough that Kansas law calls for another look, and we’ll let that process finish. Every Kansan deserves to know the result is right.
Whatever the outcome, the fight for lower property taxes, safer communities and better schools doesn’t end tonight. I’ll keep working for those things no matter what, and I’ll work with anyone who wants to get them done.
— Ty Masterson (@TyMastersonKS) November 4, 2026

The Senate president describes the election in black-and-white, good-versus-evil terms. This Manichaean viewpoint allows for no subtlety, no persuasion, no essential humanity. You were either for Masterson or against him.
Look at his first sentence: “Last night was a difficult night in Kansas and around the country.”
Difficult for who, exactly?
Sure, it may have been difficult for Republican candidates and their supporters. But that’s the way elections work. One side wins and one side loses. What’s more, if a majority of voters selected Democrats rather than Republicans to represent them in Kansas and across the nation, where’s the difficulty?
Masterson implies that Kansas and the Republican Party have some sort of inseparable bond, that a political movement’s setback means a setback for the region. That’s nonsense. Kansas simply made a different choice.
That’s not “difficult.” That’s the essence of representative democracy, and it ought to be celebrated by winners and losers alike.
In my first column after U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall’s loss to Democrat challenger Adam Hamilton, I noted how Marshall’s embrace of similar divisive rhetoric proved toxic as the American people turned against President Donald Trump. Our country may face overwhelming challenges, and we may disagree with one another heartily, but we do reserve the right to change our minds.
Those asking tough questions of Marshall at an Oakley town hall on March 1, 2025, are just as much “real Kansans” as anyone else — Republican, Democrat, Libertarian, Green, independent or devotee of the Flying Spaghetti Monster.
Masterson doesn’t seem to believe that Democrats are real Kansans.
Back in 2018, he denied that Kelly had a mandate as governor, telling Associated Press legend John Hanna that “it’s the legislative elections that are the more indicative of what is going on in the state.”
Well, now that Democrats have won a whopping 57 seats in the Kansas House, does Masterson still believe that? Or was his purpose to never credit his opposition with any claim to guiding this incredible state? (I don’t know why I even bother to phrase those sentences as a rhetorical questions. Those with eyes can see the answers.)
Here’s what Hamilton had to say, as a matter of contrast: “This election is a rebuke of unkindness and cruelty in Washington.”
Kansas includes an incredible diversity of people with a range of beliefs. On Tuesday night, some celebrated while others wept. Most, I suspect, simply went to bed and dreamed of a better world.
Politicians who hope to serve this evolving oasis of Midwestern good sense should embrace them all.
Clay Wirestone is Kansas Reflector opinion editor. His first book, “Opinionated: Kansas Journalists Who Proved Why Commentary Matters — Then and Now,” was published in September 2026 by the University Press of Kansas. Through its opinion section, Kansas Reflector works to amplify the voices of people who are affected by public policies or excluded from public debate. name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Victorious Wisconsin Democrats lay out their plans
description: Following Democrats’ resounding victories in Wisconsin Tuesday night, Gov.-elect David Crowley and Democratic legislative leaders spent Wednesday talking about preparing to work for Wisconsinites, though the specifics are still being worked out.  Crowley said as he begins putting together a transition team and cabinet he wants it to be representative of the [...]
text:
Gov.-elect David Crowley and Lt. Gov.-elect Sarah Godlewski address media Wednesday after winning the 2026 election. (Photo by Isiah Holmes/Wisconsin Examiner)Following Democrats’ resounding victories in Wisconsin Tuesday night, Gov.-elect David Crowley and Democratic legislative leaders spent Wednesday talking about preparing to work for Wisconsinites, though the specifics are still being worked out. 
Crowley said as he begins putting together a transition team and cabinet he wants it to be representative of the entire state, not just Madison and Milwaukee. He emphasized that he is committed to hearing from people with diverse viewpoints across the state as he begins that work. 
“While we witnessed major victories in the state Legislature last night, I am committed to bringing people together from across the political spectrum and all across this state. We’re going to listen to every region … every community. We’re going to make decisions that are based on what’s best for everyone here in the state of Wisconsin, and we are going to measure our success on whether life gets better for all families in this great state.” 
Crowley told reporters on Wednesday afternoon in Milwaukee that affordability and healthcare are his top priorities, but he didn’t provide specifics about the legislation he wants to see on his desk soon after he takes office. 
“You’re asking me about the legislative process. I think it is extremely important that you talk to the legislative leaders,” Crowley said. “I look forward to working with them about what our priorities are going to be. We are less than 24 hours of knowing that we won this race right now. I think all of us are basking in the fact that we won, we have the Democratic trifecta, and we know that the hard work is going to begin today.”
Over the course of the campaign, Democrats and Crowley said that if elected they would address an array of issues including lowering costs, improving education and healthcare accessibility. 
Assembly Democratic Leader Greta Neubauer (D-Racine) told reporters on a call that legislators needed a chance to connect with Crowley and their Senate colleagues while working to build their governing agenda. She said addressing the costs working families face is the first priority. She said some proposals include providing free school meals to all students and addressing housing costs, healthcare and childcare. 
“We do have a big list, and we are going to be ambitious,” Neubauer said. “We recognize this is a huge opportunity. Wisconsin on a new course; we are going to be busy. We’re going to be busy for two years getting all these things done.” 
Neubauer said the Assembly will have several options for addressing healthcare. She said lawmakers will explore a public option as well as regulations on prescription drugs and other costs. She said taking the federal Medicaid expansion is complicated given recent changes made by the Trump administration, including work requirements and changes to the federal funding mechanism. 
“It’s a shame that Wisconsin has not done that up to this point,” she said. “We are going to be working very closely with the administration to figure out the best way to expand access to affordable healthcare for Wisconsinites, even given the Trump administration’s efforts to cut access and raise costs.” 
“We know that Wisconsinites are struggling to afford access to quality healthcare, and that is going to be a key priority for us,” she added.
Senate Democratic Leader Dianne Hesselbein (D-Middleton) said in a statement on Wednesday that the Democratic majority was elected to invest in public schools, lower property taxes, stand up for Wisconsin workers and protect freedoms, including the right of women to make their own healthcare decisions.  
“The people of Wisconsin have placed their trust in Senate Democrats, and we’re not going to take it for granted,” Hesselbein said. “We are ready to breathe new life into the ‘Wisconsin Idea’ and ensure that everybody in Wisconsin, no matter your race, gender, who you love, or where you live, has a fair shot at the American dream.”

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Majority of Indiana school referendums pass
description: Hoosiers supported a majority of referendums for public K-12 schools Tuesday despite widespread concern about property taxes in what was a record year for referendums. The Indiana School Boards Association found voters supported 27 of the 39 referendums on the ballot this year, or about 70% passage rate. ISBA Director Terry Spradlin described it as […]
text:
A school bus sits waiting for Indiana students on Aug. 6, 2026. (Photo by Niki Kelly/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Hoosiers supported a majority of referendums for public K-12 schools Tuesday despite widespread concern about property taxes in what was a record year for referendums.
The Indiana School Boards Association found voters supported 27 of the 39 referendums on the ballot this year, or about 70% passage rate.
ISBA Director Terry Spradlin described it as a paradox: In an election dominated by angst about the cost of living, many Hoosiers were still willing to pay more in property taxes to support their public schools.
“That’s quite a testament,” he said. “It really does signify that Hoosiers and voters and citizens really do believe in the power of public education.”
Where referendums failed
Twelve referendums failed Tuesday, including renewals for the Anderson, Franklin, Decatur, Sheridan and Smith-Green school districts.
The next chance for districts to seek a referendum won’t come until November 2028 due to referendum rule changes enacted through property tax reform legislation last year, which limit referendums to General Elections of even years when turnout is generally higher.
Budget cuts are anticipated in the interim.
“Without this funding, our district will face difficult decisions regarding the necessity to cut over $8 million from our budget by 2028,” Scott Collins, superintendent of the Metropolitan School District of Decatur Township south of Indianapolis, said in message to parents Tuesday.
District leadership will meet with the school board in the coming months to evaluate its financial situation, Collins wrote. The process will likely include staffing and programming cuts.
“We recognize the difficult financial decisions ahead and the significant challenges they present,” he wrote. “We remain committed to fiscal responsibility and transparency while working to limit the unavoidable impact on students, classrooms and educational services.”
In a statement Wednesday, Anderson Superintendent Joe Cronk said the incoming school board and superintendent will have to address the district’s budget shortfall in the months ahead after the renewal levy failed.
“There will be difficult decisions, and I do not have all the answers this morning,” he wrote. “Those decisions deserve careful thought, honest discussion, and a clear understanding of how they affect our students and staff.”
Indiana superintendents say they’re cutting jobs because of property tax reforms

Spradlin said there was no discernible demographic or regional trend behind the referendum losses.
In Johnson County, voters supported the referendum for Clark-Pleasant Community Schools but not the neighboring Franklin Community Schools.
Referendums for Indianapolis Public Schools and MSD of Washington Township passed, yet failed in nearby Decatur Township.
Five of the six referendums on the ballot in Hamilton County passed, with Sheridan Community Schools losing a $2.9 million operating ask.
Tuition boost?
The ISBA intends to push for a 6% minimum increase in state tuition support for public K-12 schools in the next biennial budget, which would restore K-12 funding to 2024 levels at a time when state revenues have outperformed forecasts, Spradlin said.
Lawmakers increased K-12 tuition support by 5% in the 2026-27 budget, but individual school districts received lower amounts due to enrollment factors.
Still, Spradlin said the cost of non-discretionary expenses like fuel, utilities, bus replacements and employee health insurance has far exceeded inflation, with many districts reporting health insurance increases in excess of 10%.
“Those kinds of things are outside the control of a CFO or superintendent,” he said.
House Democrat Leader Rep. Phil GiaQuinta — fresh off picking up 16 seats in the Indiana House — said one area his caucus will focus on is increased funding for public education. He said when he first arrived at the General Assembly in 2018, schools received upwards of 4% to 5% each year in new funding. But under the Republican supermajority that has dropped to 1% to 2% for schools in his district.
The midterm elections delivered unexpected leadership shakeups, with voters ousting Rep. Robert Behning, the House Education Committee chair.
Democrats will likely gain at least one new member on the committee too after they gained enough seats to break the GOP supermajority, which would grant the party more influence over education policy.

title: Commentary: Wisconsin’s blue wave and the post-Trump era
description: The depth and breadth of Republicans’ stunning losses in Tuesday’s blue wave are still coming into focus. Unprecedented Democratic wins in red states including Texas, Kansas, South Carolina and possibly Mississippi ushered in a new era. Democrats won big majorities in the House and Senate. They gained control of governorships and legislative chambers across [...]
text:
Blue wave (Getty Images Royalty free)The depth and breadth of Republicans’ stunning losses in Tuesday’s blue wave are still coming into focus. Unprecedented Democratic wins in red states including Texas, Kansas, South Carolina and possibly Mississippi ushered in a new era. Democrats won big majorities in the House and Senate. They gained control of governorships and legislative chambers across the country, including in Wisconsin. 
Perhaps most dramatic was what didn’t happen. Menacing threats of armed federal agents at the polls melted away as Republicans crumbled. President Donald Trump accepted the results. So did Wisconsin’s Republican gubernatorial candidate Tom Tiffany, who voted against certifying the 2020 presidential election, but who conceded early and graciously this week.
Fear itself was vanquished on Tuesday. The dread of an authoritarian government poised to crush dissent with coercion and violence yielded to ordinary citizens voting, by the millions, to oust a self-dealing, out-of-touch party led by a malignant narcissist busy enriching himself at the people’s expense.
Just days before the election, voting rights groups in Wisconsin sent a letter to Attorney General Josh Kaul urging him to provide additional guidance to election workers in case federal agents showed up to seize ballots and tamper with election results.
Instead, voting went smoothly and the results, a massive rebuke to President Donald Trump and his party, now stand.
The lesson of the 2026 midterms was that regular people are not powerless in the face of this aggressive, anti-democratic regime. There is still time and hope left for our country. 
That, more than any particular surprise win, was the biggest thrill of the night.
In Wisconsin, Democrats took over both houses of the Legislature and David Crowley celebrated a convincing, historic win as the state’s first Black governor. Jan. 6 rallygoer and MAGA blowhard U.S. Rep. Derrick Van Orden was shown the door. The 2026 change election also swept away incumbent U.S. Rep. Bryan Steil, who lost to Mitchell Berman in the 1st Congressional District. As Erik Gunn and Heather Asiyanbi report, Berman broke Steil’s four-term winning streak and Republican control of the district stretching back more than three decades, through the Paul Ryan era. 
Berman represented the mood of the country’s fed-up electorate. An emergency room nurse dismayed by seeing patients who could not afford health insurance, he took on the smooth-talking, well heeled Steil on his support for Medicaid cuts, tariffs and his record of coddling the very wealthy and corporations, voting in lock-step with President Donald Trump. Corruption and the abandonment of regular working people were the themes of the 1st District race and of the midterms generally. Not, as Republicans hoped, trans people, “woke” politics and a debate about the decorative aesthetics of the Cheesecake Factory.
It turned out people were too fed up to be distracted from their own very real struggles by these culture war topics. Nor were they dissuaded by the massive infusion of cash from billionaires Elon Musk, Dick and Elizabeth Uihlein and Diane Hendricks.
There will be plenty more struggle ahead. But it’s a good time to bask in the glow of the complete rout of fear, hate and division as our inevitable national political atmosphere. 
In Wisconsin, Democrats set an example for what it means to overcome division. Francesca Hong, after narrowly losing the primary on a progressive, democratic socialist platform, worked hard to help elect Crowley — despite the hard feelings among many of her supporters who felt he big-footed her by getting back in the race after dropping out and narrowly winning with Gov. Tony Evers’ endorsement.
Angela Lang, founder and director of Black Leaders Organizing for Communities, told Isiah Holmes at Crowley’s joyful, raucous victory party that Crowley’s personal history — being evicted along with his parents, who struggled with poverty and addiction when he was a child — and his efforts as Milwaukee county executive to do right by people who have also struggled, moved her.  “I’ve always been nervous. Because sometimes Wisconsin doesn’t always do the right thing. But I always knew it was possible and I’m glad to know that the rest of Wisconsin felt it was possible, too,” she said.
So much is possible if the majority of us unite against the corrosive politics of the Trump era and look out for our shared interests.
This week, it became suddenly clear that a bad era is coming to an end, and a new era of possibility is dawning.

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Commentary: Bookman: Here’s why the midterm election blowout is actually good for Republicans
description: Tuesday night was a great night for the Republican Party. I’m dead serious. The GOP needed to be slapped across the face and told to snap out of it. It needed to be kicked in the butt, and kicked hard. The party that once liked to think of itself as the grownup party needed to […]
text:
Congressman Mike Collins addresses supporters on Wednesday, Nov. 4 after losing his run for U.S. Senate. Collins lost to U.S. Sen. Jon Ossoff by 18 percentage points. Ross Williams/Georgia RecorderTuesday night was a great night for the Republican Party.
I’m dead serious.
The GOP needed to be slapped across the face and told to snap out of it. It needed to be kicked in the butt, and kicked hard. The party that once liked to think of itself as the grownup party needed to be sent to its room without supper and have its car keys and phone taken away.
Well, courtesy of the American voter, that’s what it got.
The breadth and scale of the GOP’s repudiation was as awe-inspiring as it was deserved. Here in Georgia – until recently a deep-red state – it lost the U.S. Senate race by 18 points. Voters who hadn’t elected a Democrat to a constitutional office during a regular election in decades elected 10 of them, from governor through school superintendent and public service commissioner. The margin in some of those races was double digits, and none was smaller than seven points.
Eight of those incoming constitutional officers, including our new governor, will be Black women. Welcome to the new Georgia, y’all.
Democrats who had dared to dream really big, who had dared to believe that maybe they could regain control of the state House of Representatives, appear to have achieved that goal easily. If that chamber flips, they will now have the votes to elect yet another Black woman, Carolyn Hugley, as House speaker.
And while no Democrats had openly dreamed of taking the heavily gerrymandered state Senate, they fell just short of doing that also.
Of course, great, sudden and somewhat unexpected success comes with its problems. In this case, Georgia Democrats have been handed the full burden of governance, and they’re out of practice and don’t have an experienced bench. Some of the people swept into office this week by the blue tsunami are going to have a steep learning curve, and mistakes will be made. To be honest, they were elected not because of who they are, but because of who they are not. They now have a great opportunity to shine on their own merits.
Hire smart, honest people to help you; don’t surround yourself with sycophants and hangers on; rely on the career professionals in state government, most of whom are competent and mission-committed. Be humble in service. 
Republicans have an entirely different sort of problem. This is not a “we’ll get ‘em next time” election. The margins are too big to be dismissed so easily, and a look beneath the hood makes it even more troubling.
According to NBC exit polling, Republicans got 14% of the vote from Georgians aged 18-29, and just 26% of the vote among those 44 and younger. That’s the future electorate of Georgia.
Among voters of color, Republicans got 13% of the vote, in a state where white people are already a minority. Among the 71% of Georgia voters who were not white evangelicals, Republicans got 26%. Georgia Republicans have built their party on a narrow base, and structures built on a narrow base have a tendency to topple.
Racial purity, ideological purity, religious purity …. you can’t build a lasting democratic majority around an obsession with purity. The numbers just don’t work.
And then there’s the matter of Donald Trump.
Over the past decade, Republicans in Georgia and other states have built their political identity around Trump, and this week voters across the country made it clear that they repudiate that style of leadership and politics. If GOP strategists try to explain away this week’s catastrophe as something temporary, as a function of gas prices for example, they ensure that their time in the political wilderness will be long.
This didn’t happen because gas is $4 a gallon instead of $3.25 a gallon. It goes much deeper. In service to Trump, Georgia Republicans and their counterparts in Washington have run off most of the competent party leaders who had the intelligence and spine not to kneel to the worst instincts of this president. That will make it difficult to rebuild the party into the conservative counterweight that the state and the country need it to be.
But in the wake of Tuesday’s nightmare, outgoing Gov. Brian Kemp immediately announced that he would not call an emergency legislative session, declining to use the GOP’s last remaining days in power to undermine and sabotage the incoming Democratic administration.
“The voters of our state have spoken,” Kemp said. “As long as I’m governor, we will always respect the results of secure, accessible, and fair elections, and also abide by the laws and constitution of our state.”
That’s how a grownup acts.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Queer Michigan history was made in the midterms this year
description: As Democrats nationwide and across Michigan celebrated historic victories in the 2026 midterm elections, history was also made by a number of LGBTQ+ Michiganders.  Among them was state Sen. Jeremy Moss (D-Bloomfield), who was elected to the state’s 11th Congressional District, becoming the first openly gay member of Congress from Michigan. Joanna Whaley also[...]
text:
LGBTQ+ flags fly at the Michigan Capitol near the state Senate building during Michigan Pride in Lansing on June 26, 2022. (Photo by Laina G. Stebbins/Michigan Advance)As Democrats nationwide and across Michigan celebrated historic victories in the 2026 midterm elections, history was also made by a number of LGBTQ+ Michiganders. 
Among them was state Sen. Jeremy Moss (D-Bloomfield), who was elected to the state’s 11th Congressional District, becoming the first openly gay member of Congress from Michigan. Joanna Whaley also made history, becoming Michigan’s first openly transgender state legislator when she was elected to Michigan’s 2nd House District.
“I’ve always said, you can’t be what you can’t see,” Moss said in an interview with Michigan Advance. 
“I think it’s important for all of us to be in the rooms where decisions about us are being made, and again, I’m a representative from my neighborhood. I’m a representative from my community. I’m a representative from my district, and I also happen to be gay,” he continued. “I’m shaped by everything that my neighbors are shaped by. But I also have a story to tell about how policy decisions impact LGBTQ people, and that’s the important dynamic here. We’re just as ingrained in Michigan as anybody else is.”
Senate Regulatory Affairs Committee Chair Jeremy Moss (D-Southfield) hears testimony on a bill cutting back on incoming changes to Michigan’s earned sick time law during a Feb. 11, 2025 meeting. | Kyle Davidson
Whaley similarly said that she believes that when people — including transgender folks in Michigan looking to her — see someone like themselves in government, it will inspire them to believe that they, too, can lead.
“We do that by leading with competence and using our skills, not because of who we are, but because we want to serve,” Whaley said. “And if they feel like their government is going after them and attacking them, then that’s their call to be in the room.”SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Whaley faced a campaign eligibility complaint during the primary from her Democratic opponent, Frank Liberati, and again faced transphobic attacks in the general election cycle from Republican Ron Kokinda, who she defeated by a 24-point margin on Tuesday.
Whaley and her campaign — which was not focused on her transgender identity, but on affordability and accountability for her Downriver district — were able to overcome those types of attacks twice, which Whaley said makes her believe that the messaging attacking her for her gender identity did not resonate with voters, in her district or elsewhere nationwide.
“I think our community and the state in general has finally said we reject culture war crap. They want politicians who are going to do the work and show up for them,” Whaley said. “This election cycle, from the U.S. Senate down into our race, were some of the most vile, disgusting political attacks I think I’ve ever seen in my lifetime. I am really proud of our community for sifting through the junk and listening for the substance.”
State Rep.-elect Joanna Whaley, who will be representing Michigan’s 2nd House District after winning in Tuesday’s election. (Photo courtesy of Joanna Whaley)
Moss, who was the first openly gay member of the Michigan Senate and one of the first openly gay members of the Legislature, said that Whaley’s election is important because, while he has worked hard to advocate for trans Michiganders and their needs, he is not part of that community. As anti-trans attacks and rhetoric escalate nationwide, “for the very first time in the Michigan legislature, every piece of the community has representation,” he said.
Moss also shared a similar sentiment to Whaley about how much Michiganders actually care about culture war issues like transgender girls participating in sports. 
“I really, truly don’t know any family in this district that sits at the dinner table lamenting about a trans athlete. I don’t,” he said. “They do lament over the grocery bills. They do lament about gas prices. They do lament about access to healthcare should they need it. That’s what real people are talking about. So, I’d love to cut through the chaos of Trump’s administration and really deliver for people back home.”
Moss and Whaley are not alone in making history for queer Michiganders in government.
State Rep. Jason Hoskins (D-Southfield), who was elected to fill Moss’s now-vacant seat in the state Senate, becomes the first openly gay Black member of the Michigan Senate, having previously been the first out person of color elected to the Michigan Legislature while serving in the state House. 
State Rep. Jason Hoskins (D-Southfield), speaking at a Lansing press conference to announce the reintroduction of the Michigan Voting Rights Act. May 19, 2026 | Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance
“That’s another segment of our community that needs a voice, that needs representation. So everybody is bringing their unique experiences even from within the community to be able to make sure all of our challenges are being addressed,” Moss said of passing the baton to Hoskins.
Joseph McClusky, who was elected to Michigan’s 86th House District on the west side of the state, is the first openly LGBTQ+ person to represent that district — flipping it blue after being held by Rep. Nancy DeBoer (R-Holland), who as a city council member in Holland voted against anti-discrimination laws protecting LGBTQ+ people.  
And other LGBTQ+ state representatives, both new and incumbents, saw success on Tuesday — Pride Source reported that every LGBTQ+ incumbent in the Michigan Legislature won their reelection campaign. 
Chris Gilmer-Hill, Mike McFall, Laurie Pohutsky, Noah Arbit, Jason Morgan and Emily Dievendorf will all serve in the Michigan House of Representatives as openly LGBTQ+ members, bringing the total number of openly LGBTQ+ state legislators in Michigan to nine.

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Georgia Democrats ride national blue wave into power in history-making election
authors: Maya Homan, Alander Rocha, Ross Williams
description: Within an hour of polls closing Tuesday, it was clear that Democrats had made a strong showing and that U.S. Sen. Jon Ossoff would be re-elected by a large margin. But what unfolded after that far exceeded what even the most optimistic Georgia Democrat could have imagined. By about 9 p.m., it became apparent that […]
text:
Georgia governor-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms celebrates her electoral victory in Atlanta on Nov. 3, 2026. Ross Williams/Georgia RecorderWithin an hour of polls closing Tuesday, it was clear that Democrats had made a strong showing and that U.S. Sen. Jon Ossoff would be re-elected by a large margin.
U.S. Sen. Jon Ossoff speaks to supporters in Atlanta Tuesday night after winning reelection. Julia Beverly for the Georgia Recorder
But what unfolded after that far exceeded what even the most optimistic Georgia Democrat could have imagined.
By about 9 p.m., it became apparent that not only would former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms become Georgia’s first Democratic governor since Roy Barnes left office in 2003 but that the entire slate of Democratic statewide candidates would share in the victory, flipping offices like agriculture and insurance commissioners that had been considered relatively safe for Republicans. House Democrats are also poised to take control of the state House of Representatives for the first time in more than two decades.
“I’ve been at these elections a lot of times when we went home crying, and so it was hard for me to believe when the results came in as early as they did,” House Minority Leader Carolyn Hugley, who could be in line to be the chamber’s next speaker, told reporters Wednesday. “I’m like, OK, is that really real? And then they kept coming, kept coming, kept coming. So it was overwhelming. I was so very excited.
“We’re excited not only for the Democrats, but for the people of Georgia, because this shows people that elections matter and that your voices can be heard and your votes will matter,” she added.
What happened on Tuesday will be discussed by Georgians for years – and shape the state’s future for generations, starting by transforming the state government next year. As the dust settles in the aftermath, here are five of the biggest initial takeaways from a historic election.
How far did the blue wave reach?
Democrats have a lot to celebrate, with victories this year far exceeding the traditionally blue stronghold of metro Atlanta.
Georgia governor-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms celebrates her victory on Nov. 3 in Atlanta. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder
Bottoms made gains across middle and southwest Georgia, winning over a majority of voters in eight counties where voters picked Republican Gov. Brian Kemp in the 2022 midterms: Burke, Clay, Fayette, Houston, Jefferson, Peach, Sumter and Washington.
Emory University political science professor Andra Gillespie said that Democratic candidates made strides with many key groups, including independents and white voters in the state.
“The national mood was sour, and Democrats were able to ride that wave in places that we didn’t expect,” she said. “But I think it remains to be seen whether or not voters who were dissatisfied with Trump are going to stick with Democrats.”
But Georgia Republicans did have one bright spot in all the election news, managing to hold on to their nine seats in the U.S. House even as a number of congressional seats across the country flipped Democratic. But Gillespie noted that the margins of victory in many House districts were much tighter this year than they normally are, signaling widespread dissatisfaction with GOP leadership.
“I think Republicans should heed the margins and recognize that there was discontent in their districts even when they won, and that voters in their districts contributed to the Democratic sweep of the statewide offices,” she said.
The energy benefited down-ballot Democrats too, bringing a wave of new lawmakers to the Legislature and changing the balance of power.
Even before the polls closed, some conservative voters said they felt the tide changing. Joel Pirtle, a 50-year-old IT manager from Henry County who voted for Collins and Jackson, said that he would not be surprised if Democrats managed to flip his state representative’s seat, which is currently held by Republican state Rep. Noelle Kahaian. Kahaian did end up losing her seat to truck driver Mishael White, who is a Democrat, by nearly 8 points, according to unofficial results from the secretary state’s website.
“I’m seeing Georgia going more and more Democrat, so I would not be surprised if it does. I don’t necessarily agree with it, but we’ll see what happens when it does. If it works out, great. If it doesn’t, then we’ll vote again,” Pirtle said.
Trump was on the ballot
President Donald Trump gestures to the crowd at a rally in Dalton on Friday, Oct. 16, 2026. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder
In the weeks leading up to the election, Trump made stops across the country, including in Georgia, where he held two rallies last month calling on the GOP faithful to vote as if he were on the ballot.
His intention was to fire up low propensity voters who support Trump but inconsistently turn out to support other Republican candidates.
He may have achieved the opposite. Many Democratic and independent voters who were interviewed at the polls said they were encouraged to get out and vote in opposition to Trump.
Woodstock retiree Judi Smith, who is 74, said she voted for Ossoff and Bottoms because she said she wanted to send a message to the Trump administration.
“I just want Trump and all of those people out of office,” she said.
“Everything about Trump, all of those people, all of that corruption, it just needs to be over and done with,” she added. “And all of the hatred that they have sown in this country, it’s just horrible.”
Voters in Henry County who backed Democrats said that a change of party control was overdue. Keisha Thompson, a 48-year-old federal employee who saw many of her former colleagues lose their jobs due to funding cuts from the Trump administration, said she had a simple goal.
“We just need to make some change. We need to change it from whatever color it is to blue,” Thompson said.
Trey Hood, a political science professor at the University of Georgia, said that Democrats outperformed Republicans because of what he called a “national repudiation of Trump.” He said they tied current economic issues like high gas prices due to the war in Iran to the White House.
Some Republican voters said Trump had no influence on their decisionmaking.
“It’s got nothing to do with Trump,” said Brad Baldwin, a 65-year-old retiree in Henry County who voted straight Republican. “No, no, no. I vote for a guy I want to vote for. I don’t care if he likes Trump, hates Trump. I can’t wait for Trump to get out of office just so people will shut up about it.”
Split-ticket voters were not a significant factor
Gov. Brian Kemp speaks in Roswell on Oct. 27, 2026. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder
During the 2022 midterm elections, Georgians chose Kemp, a Republican, and U.S. Sen. Raphael Warnock, a Democrat, during the same election, largely thanks to independent and split-ticket voters who helped both candidates across the 50% minimum threshold amid tight electoral margins.
But this year, split-ticket voters weren’t the tiebreaking force they had been in 2022, with independents breaking “very hard for the Democrats this election cycle,” Hood said.
“There’s hardly any roll off if you go downballot, down the constitutional offices in Georgia. I mean, the margin is almost the same. So it was just people checking the Democratic box all the way down the ballot,” Hood said.
Ossoff, who was running as an incumbent, won with nearly 60% of the vote, according to unofficial results from the secretary of state’s office. Bottoms received more than 54% of the vote, numbers that Gillespie said signal widespread enthusiasm among Democratic base voters and gains among demographics that have tilted towards Republicans in recent elections.
“The reason why [Democrats] won this time is they were able to get over the hump with white voters in ways that we have not seen them do, even in the elections of Joe Biden, Raphael Warnock and Jon Ossoff in previous cycles,” Gillespie said.
That’s not to say that every voter cast their ballot along party lines, though. Jordan Fuller, a 36-year-old tech support worker in Union City, said he doesn’t vote consistently for either party. He cast his vote for Ossoff and the Republican nominee for governor Rick Jackson this year, citing his disapproval of Bottoms’ mayoral record.
“I’ve already experienced Keisha,” he said. “She was the mayor of Atlanta, and I’m not much of a fan of how she handled some things.”
But other independent voters turned away from Republican candidates altogether. Gillespie said the data shows Democrats overperforming among independent voters in this election cycle.
Steve Bigler, a Gwinnett County voter, said he has voted for candidates of both parties throughout his life, but he went into this year’s election hoping to enact some guardrails against Trump’s policies in the federal government.
He supported both Kemp and Warnock in 2022 and would have voted for Kemp again if that was an option. But he said Jackson’s early campaign ads, including one where he warned that immigrants who broke the law would end up “deported or departed,” made him uneasy.
“I believe in supporting law enforcement and all that,” Bigler said. “But come on, let’s just get a little humanity into our politics.”
Conrad Gill, another Gwinnett County resident, chose Ossoff in the Senate race and voted for Bottoms in the governor’s contest, fearing that Jackson would be too closely tied to Trump and his policies.
“I was leaning toward Jackson until the ad came out about his affiliation with Trump and his statements about ‘he’s going to be Trump’s man, he’s going to be Trump’s best friend as a governor’ and all of that,” Gill said. “I didn’t want to vote for him based on that because I don’t think Trump is doing a good job. I don’t think he’s honest. I don’t think he’s fair. I think he’s very corrupt.”
But Gillespie said it remains to be seen whether this year’s midterm election results were an outlier or part of a larger political realignment within Georgia.
Future support from independent voters, she added, will likely depend on “whether or not [Democrats] are going to deliver on the policy promises that they [made], and whether or not they’re going to look like they can govern effectively. If they don’t govern effectively, then what I suspect is that independent voters could possibly defect.”
What’s next for the parties?
Georgia GOP chairman John McKoon speaks at a rally in Dalton on Friday, Oct. 16, 2026. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder
Outgoing Georgia Republican Party Chair Josh McKoon said that in the short term, the state party will help Republican state Rep. Mike Cheokas keep his seat in a runoff.
But in the long term, the plan is to do a thorough review of the election results to develop a platform that better resonates with voters ahead of 2028, when he feels prospects for Republicans will be “very positive.”
While Democrats ran on making life more affordable for Americans, McKoon thinks that Democrats will “pursue a far-left agenda that is totally out of touch with where most Georgians are.”
“I think there’s going to be a lot of anger with national Democrats by the time 2028 rolls around here at the state level,” McKoon said.
Georgia Democratic Party Chair Charlie Bailey speaks at an event marking the third anniversary of the Dobbs decision. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder
He hopes that when 2028 comes around, voters will be ready to “take a fresh look at Republicans and probably realize there is a reason that Republicans have run this state for two decades.”
House Minority Leader Carolyn Hugley, who is in line to become the next speaker, said House Democrats plan to stick to the pocketbook issues that she acknowledged is ushering her party into power, at least for now.
“What Georgia citizens have told us is affordability is the number one issue. And so you can expect the issues that we put forth in this first legislative session are going to be focused on meeting that challenge of affordability,” Hugley told reporters this week.
For his part, Democratic Party of Georgia Chair Charlie Bailey said he hopes to use the wins in Georgia to boost the state’s importance in the eyes of national Democratic groups and PACs.
“We will certainly be making the argument, as we have been for at least as long as I’ve been chair, that we have to expand into the South if we’re going to be a truly national party with a national, governing majority,” Bailey said in a Zoom call with reporters Wednesday. “We are the ultimate battleground in Georgia, but we’ve got to kind of lock it down here, you know?”
To do so, Bailey said Democrats will expand into year-round organizing in Georgia for the first time.
“That’s going to take a lot of resources, and we’ll be leaning on our partners to send those resources down here, and I’m optimistic we’ll get some takers,” he said.
Georgia Recorder Editor Jill Nolin contributed to this report.

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Parts of law that supported Ohio’s six-week abortion ban struck down by judge
description: A Franklin County judge yet again ruled other provisions of a law that included Ohio’s former six-week abortion ban can not be enforced. The ban on abortions at six weeks, also called the “Heartbeat Ban,” was already blocked from enforcement, which the Ohio Attorney General’s Office chose not to fight on appeal. As Franklin County […]
text:
Stock photo from Getty Images.A Franklin County judge yet again ruled other provisions of a law that included Ohio’s former six-week abortion ban can not be enforced.
The ban on abortions at six weeks, also called the “Heartbeat Ban,” was already blocked from enforcement, which the Ohio Attorney General’s Office chose not to fight on appeal. As Franklin County Common Pleas Judge Christian Jenkins put it in his newest court decision, the ban on abortion when cardiac activity is detected “has gone the way of the dodo.”
But Jenkins’ newest court order added to the already struck-down abortion ban, saying all the measures of the Senate bill that were written alongside the ban are unconstitutional and can’t be used individually.
The six-week abortion ban has been a point of contention in the state for several years, partly because it’s been in court essentially since it was enacted in 2019. When the first lawsuit came about, Roe v. Wade’s legalization of abortion nationwide was still in effect. But once the U.S. Supreme Court overturned the decision in 2022, Ohio Attorney General Dave Yost quickly moved to get the law out of its legal limbo, which a federal court agreed to do.
A few months later, the law was back in court, first with the Ohio Supreme Court, and then in Franklin County Common Pleas.
Jenkins ruled against the state in Oct. 2022, and the state appealed to the Ohio Supreme Court.
But as the state’s highest court considered the appeal, a constitutional amendment protecting abortion rights was passed by 57% of Ohio voters in 2023. The Ohio Supreme Court dismissed the appeal due to “a change in the law,” and sent the case back to state court.
This time, Jenkins permanently blocked most of the law, saying one part of the law was unconstitutional, and “most of the provisions … are unconstitutional in their own right,” adding that the provisions of the bill couldn’t be separated from each other.
When the state appealed that decision to the First District Court of Appeals, the Ohio Attorney General’s Office said they wouldn’t fight the striking down of the six-week abortion ban, but argued the other elements of the law should remain viable.
Included in the law were requirements that medical professionals report tests for cardiac activity to the Ohio Department of Health, along with any actions they believe are exceptions to the six-week ban.
The appellate court ruled that the Franklin County court had the authority to block multiple statutes in the same bill, against the state’s arguments. But it upheld the attorney general’s claim that the state court should not have considered the constitutionality of the other provisions of the six-week ban law before considering whether they could stand on their own as separate laws.
With the case returning to Franklin County, Jenkins now had to rule on whether the provisions that were alongside the six-week abortion ban could be used as their own measures.
In his Oct. 29 decision, Jenkins found that the other parts of the law are “the same species” as the six-week abortion ban, “and for that reason, they cannot survive.”
“These measures were passed alongside the six-week ban to make it difficult, or impossible, to obtain abortion care in Ohio by placing providers at risk of criminal prosecution as well as professional and financial ruin,” Jenkins wrote.
The judge went on to say the other provisions “were enacted to enforce, document, and define the six-week ban,” and without them, the other measures can’t be read as the legislature wrote them.
“They require every physician who performs an abortion to record whether the patient’s health was a reason for it, and they make a physician who fails to keep that record subject to discipline by the State Medical Board,” Jenkins wrote.
If the provisions were allowed to stay in place, Jenkins said physicians could still face prison time for conducting abortions “to which the patient now has a constitutional right.”

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Indiana executes Jeffrey Weisheit for 2010 murders of two children
description: The Indiana Capital Chronicle was the only media outlet to witness the execution. This story will be updated with observations from inside the prison. MICHIGAN CITY — Indiana executed Jeffrey Weisheit early Thursday for murdering 8-year-old Alyssa Lynch and her 5-year-old brother, Caleb, in a 2010 house fire near Evansville. Weisheit was pronounced dead at [[...]
text:
Jeffrey Weisheit answers questions during his Oct. 16, 2026, clemency hearing at the Indiana State Prison in Michigan City. (Screenshot from livestream)The Indiana Capital Chronicle was the only media outlet to witness the execution. This story will be updated with observations from inside the prison.
MICHIGAN CITY — Indiana executed Jeffrey Weisheit early Thursday for murdering 8-year-old Alyssa Lynch and her 5-year-old brother, Caleb, in a 2010 house fire near Evansville.
Weisheit was pronounced dead at 12:45 a.m. Central Standard Time at the Indiana State Prison in Michigan City, according to a release from Department of Correction.
Indiana Department of Correction says the execution process started shortly after midnight, and that Weisheit had no final words. His final meal was barbecue ribs from Texas Corral and Mountain Dew.
Gov. Mike Braun denied clemency on Monday, rejecting Weisheit’s request for life without parole. His lawyers separately sought a temporary reprieve and an independent investigation of Indiana’s lethal injection procedures and drug procurement.
Braun’s office did not publicly announce a decision on the reprieve request or comment on it before the execution. But they did release a statement after Weisheit’s death.
“Jeffrey Weisheit’s case has been heard and reviewed numerous times by both state and federal courts, including the Indiana Supreme Court, since his conviction in 2013. These reviews have never resulted in an overturned sentence,” the governor said. “The State Parole Board issued a unanimous recommendation to deny Weisheit’s final appeal for clemency and that his execution proceed as scheduled. Today, Weisheit’s sentence has been carried out as ordered by the court.”

Attorney Joe Perkovich speaks at the Indiana Statehouse on Wednesday, Nov. 4, urging Gov. Mike Braun to halt Jeffrey Weisheit’s execution and order an independent investigation of Indiana’s execution practices. (Photo by Casey Smith/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
The Indiana Supreme Court voted 3-2 Wednesday to deny Weisheit’s emergency request to stop the execution while he challenged the drugs and lethal injection procedures in Marion Superior Court. His attorneys alleged improper drug procurement, inadequate storage safeguards and insufficient qualifications for staff placing IV lines. A supplemental filing also alleged that the pharmacy supplying the drugs contributed $5,000 to Attorney General Todd Rokita’s campaign in June while on probation.
The court questioned why Weisheit’s lawyers waited until hours before the execution to seek a stay. His attorneys said they could not have filed sooner because they had only recently learned the supplier’s identity and when DOC obtained the drugs.
Chief Justice Loretta Rush and Justice Christopher Goff dissented, saying they would grant a 10-day stay for immediate submissions on the drugs’ formulation, expiration, storage and testing, along with the timing of the defense’s disclosures and filings and whether Weisheit had exhausted available remedies.
At a Statehouse news conference Wednesday afternoon, defense attorney Joe Perkovich urged Braun to intervene and said the legal team would continue pursuing questions about the drugs.
“This will not be resolved by simply taking his life,” Perkovich said.
Attorney General Todd Rokita said “this case stands as a clear affirmation that those who commit the most heinous crimes against the most vulnerable will be held fully accountable under Indiana law. My thoughts and prayers remain with the families of Alyssa and Caleb. Nothing can ever bring their children back, and the pain of this loss will never fully leave them. Yet, hopefully, with this justice being done, they may find some measure of peace.”
Outside the prison, the Diocese of Gary organized a Wednesday night prayer vigil. The Indiana Abolition Coalition, Death Penalty Action and other opponents remained in the prison parking lot through the execution. A separate protest was scheduled late Wednesday outside Braun’s Indianapolis residence.
Pharmacy linked to Indiana execution drug invoice faces possible suspension

Weisheit’s legal team also sent the Indiana Board of Pharmacy a letter Wednesday asking to address its Nov. 9 disciplinary hearing involving Pharmaneek Inc., the Indianapolis pharmacy the identified as Indiana’s execution drug supplier.
Pharmaneek is on probation and faces possible emergency suspension over alleged violations of restrictions on compounding, the preparation of customized medications. The board has not ordered suspension in that proceeding.
The hearing was moved from Oct. 5 to Nov. 9 after the pharmacy’s newly retained attorney requested additional preparation time. Perkovich questioned that timing in Wednesday’s letter, pointing to DOC’s Sept. 25 invoice for the $275,000 drug purchase and an inventory entry recording delivery Oct. 29.
The board did not respond Wednesday to the Capital Chronicle’s questions about the pharmacy’s role, the hearing’s postponement or whether Weisheit’s attorneys would be permitted to speak at the upcoming meeting.
Perkovich said Wednesday that the defense still had not received testing results or temperature records for the newly acquired drugs. Similar public records requests from the Capital Chronicle had not yielded those documents as of late Wednesday, either.
DOC and the attorney general’s office previously defended the state’s preparations, saying they were confident the execution could be carried out lawfully. The attorney general’s office also expressed confidence it could proceed safely. Both agencies declined to discuss supplier information, however, citing state confidentiality law.
