name: Florida Phoenix
title: Commentary: Here are the messes the next Florida governor needs to clean up
description: Dear Governor-elect Donalds: Congrats on your historic win! Feel free to continue celebrating for (checks watch) the next 24 hours. Then you better buckle up. What’s that, sir? What am I holding? Oh, this is your official Gubernatorial Mop and Bucket. Turns out being governor of Florida these days is like being the new janitor […]
text:
Toxic algae bloom taints the St. Johns River thanks to its excessive pollution. DeSantis promised to fix this problem but failed to do so. (Photo courtesy St. Johns Riverkeeper)Dear Governor-elect Donalds:
Congrats on your historic win! Feel free to continue celebrating for (checks watch) the next 24 hours. Then you better buckle up.
What’s that, sir? What am I holding?
Oh, this is your official Gubernatorial Mop and Bucket.
Turns out being governor of Florida these days is like being the new janitor at the elementary school. There are LOTS of nasty messes you need to clean up.
I know you were endorsed by your two Republican predecessors, but you don’t have to copy them.
Gov. Fuller Warren via Florida State Archives
I’m not going to say Rick Scott and Ron DeSantis were the worst governors ever. That dubious distinction belongs to a dimwitted Democrat, Fuller Warren, who before his 1948 election thought the job would be all ceremonial duties like ribbon-cuttings. Then he discovered the state was broke and he was expected to do something about it.
“He was surprised to find … that the position was much more complex than he had envisioned,” historian David Colburn wrote.
The big flaw with Scott and DeSantis wasn’t not knowing what the job entailed. The problem was that neither ever cared much about one of the state’s most important issues, the environment.
Florida’s natural bounty is a big tourism attraction. It draws tons of people willing to spend billions of dollars to go hiking, kayaking, horseback riding, biking, birding, or fishing.
The environment is also pretty important for the continued quality of human life in this state. If you don’t believe me, try drinking a glass of bright green algae blooms.
Conservation used to be a conservative cause. Jeb Bush launched the Florida Springs Initiative, and Charlie Crist tried to buy out an entire sugar company to help the Everglades.
Scott and DeSantis paid lip service to Florida’s waters and wildlife. Scott even cosplayed as a park ranger — the least convincing performance since Jim Carrey pretended to be Clint Eastwood. Alas, their actions never matched their words.
So now it’s up to you, sir, to clean up what they left behind. For your benefit, I’ll run down the most immediate crises and suggest fixes. To create this list, I called on a number of experts.
Let’s start with the toughest problem: Water pollution.
 Taking care of business
Water defines our life here in Florida. We’ve “surrounded on three sides” by it, as humorist John Keasler joked.
And yet our state government has treated our waterways the way a dog treats a hydrant.
Florida is the No. 1 state for polluted lakes. A pollution-fueled algae bloom killed off so much seagrass in the Indian River Lagoon that more than 1,000 manatees starved to death. Florida’s longest river, the St. Johns, is coping with steadily increasing pollution from septic waste and biosolid dumping.
As if that’s not bad enough, our largest body of water, Lake Okeechobee, has been named the dirtiest lake in the United States. Things have gotten so bad there that Bass Masters removed Lake O from its Top Ten Bass Lakes in the country.
When DeSantis was first elected in 2018, Floridians were concerned about toxic algae blooms that lasted so long we called it “the Summer of Slime.” Scott had been so negligent about the problem, people heckled him as “Red Tide Rick.”
DeSantis swore he’d fix it. He said he’d appoint a panel of scientists to tell him what to do. He appointed the panel — then he and the Legislature failed to follow most of the scientists’ recommendations.
Instead, DeSantis cut a deal to pay millions of dollars to an Israeli company that dumps a hydrogen peroxide mix into algae-tainted waterways. Then the algae comes back and the Israelis have to do it over.
Even the head of the Israeli company thinks this is futile.
“DeSantis’ fight against algal blooms in Florida will fail,” he wrote on X, back when it was just plain Twitter. “There is no question that preventing raw sewage and runoffs from spilling into waterways must be addressed.”
You, as our new governor, need to do better. You made a major misstep on this issue in 2024. I’m praying you learned your lesson, because EVERYONE I talked to named poor water quality as the state’s biggest issue.
Elizabeth Fleming via Defenders of Wildlife
Even Elizabeth Fleming of Defenders of Wildlife said in an email that the top issue is “poor water quality management across the state” involving urban and agricultural runoff, because it “can cause fish kills and die offs of manatees, dolphins, seabirds and other wildlife and cause respiratory discomfort in people.”
The passage of Amendment 3 means local governments will be severely hampered in cleaning up their own pollution problems. They will look to the state for help, especially when it comes to our beaches.
Katie Bauman via Surfrider International
“Florida needs the next governor to focus on statewide water quality improvement and public health,” said Katie Bauman of Surfrider International, which promotes healthy beaches. “This means addressing the gaps and inconsistencies in the Florida Healthy Beaches Program, the state program responsible for monitoring fecal indicator bacteria in coastal waters and informing the public for safe recreation.”
You may be thinking that only a nincompoop would oppose warning people about poop at the beach. But as Bauman reminded me, two years ago DeSantis, with only the flimsiest of excuses, vetoed a bipartisan bill updating this program,
Estus Whitfield via Florida Conservation Voters
How can you bring water pollution under control? I asked Estus Whitfield, who advised five Florida governors from both parties on environmental issues. He said the key is getting the Department of Environmental Protection to go back to actually, you know, protecting the environment.
Even when the Legislature specifically ordered the DEP to set new standards to clean up Florida’s springs, the agency dragged its feet like a mopey teen who doesn’t want to leave the mall.
“The DEP just doesn’t take care of business,” Whitfield told me. “They take care of the big donors’ business.”
I’d recommend you find that list of scientific recommendations in DeSantis’ waste basket, uncrumple it and start making those things happen. Then pick a DEP boss who’s willing to make the polluters stop fouling the waterways, no matter how much they howl.
Speaking of people howling, let’s talk about the Everglades.
“Alligator Alcatraz” when it was open, via Florida Division of Emergency Management
 Guarded by gators
In June 2025, Attorney General James Uthmeier — the mastermind behind the Hope Florida scandal and the political guru who ran the DeSantis presidential campaign into the ground — unveiled his latest brainstorm.
Florida would build a massive immigrant detention center in the middle of Big Cypress National Preserve and then pretend the inmates were being guarded by the gators.
“You don’t need to invest that much in the perimeter,” Uthmeier said at the time. “People get out, there’s not that much waiting for them other than alligators and pythons.”
His boss DeSantis gave it the green light without first checking its environmental impact, which left a lot of environmental groups howling.
After less than a year, the camp shut down, thanks to the $1.2 billion cost to the taxpayers. It’s not cheap to make people live in tents in the Everglades.
“Alligator Alcatraz will likely turn out to be the single most expensive immigration detention center in the history of the United States,” WFOR-TV reported.
Eve Samples via Friends of the Everglades
While Uthmeier raked in big bucks for his successful political campaign, his project gouged out a deep wound in the Glades, one that still needs to be repaired. To Eve Samples, executive director of Friends of the Everglades, that repair needs to be extremely high on your priority list.
The cleanup should focus on removing “more than 20 acres of new asphalt and heaps of trucked-in fill with invasive plants that have taken root,” Samples told me. “Remove the asphalt, eradicate the invasive vegetation and restore the land.”
If you’re surprised that DeSantis would treat the Everglades this cavalierly, remember that he also tried to build golf courses in a state park — which brings us to the next crisis.
 Parks and wreck
Both DeSantis and Scott — other than his stint as “Ranger Rick” — had little love for our state parks. Scott even tried selling some of them off!
Both of them also tried to add golf courses to these green spaces. Apparently, they believed Alan King in the movie “Sunshine State” when he described a Florida golf course as “nature on a leash.” They didn’t realize that this would be wrecking the parks.
You see, Florida parks are wildly popular even without any 18-holers. More than 28 million visitors hit the 176 state parks every year, generating $3.6 billion in direct economic benefits to the surrounding local communities.
In fact, the most popular Florida park is Honeymoon Island, by DeSantis’ hometown of Dunedin. I wonder if he’s ever been — with or without his white go-go boots. I bet he hasn’t or he wouldn’t have tried to build pickleball courts in that park.
Yet our duly elected do-nothings have repeatedly failed to spend enough money to fix up the facilities. The list of repairs is a long one, too, according to the DEP’s own report from last year.
“Florida state parks face $759 million backlog of needed repairs, state report finds,” said the headline on a Tampa Bay Times story. That includes visitor centers, cabins, pavilions, boardwalks, fences, restrooms, boat ramps — you name it.
I asked former Florida State Parks director Eric Draper, a Florida native who was in charge from 2017 until 2021, what the next governor should do. He strongly recommends tackling that parks backlog.
Eric Draper via subject
“When as director I visited parks, conversations with the volunteers and the managers started with requests for funds to fix facilities,” Draper recalled. “Managers put me in their rustiest truck for tours of leaky roofs, crumbing paths, and closed bathrooms. It was frustrating to not be able to get the money from the state budget to fund the repairs.”
Mry advice is to hold a press conference at Jonathan Dickinson State Park in Hobe Sound, the park that DeSantis tried to give golf courses. Hold up the DEP report and say you’re committing yourself to a four-year program of addressing every item.
Then every year after, hold another press conference at a different park to outline what you’ve done and what you’re going to do.
That’s a good segue to my final recommendation, this one on land-buying.
 Not easy being green
Florida once had a magnificent program for preserving environmentally sensitive land. It was the envy of the nation and strongly supported by the voters.
But it’s not easy being green, as we learned from Kermit the Frog. In the past year, the Florida Forever program has been battered by a couple of big problems.
One was that our Legislature decided that it would devote ZERO dollars to the Florida Forever land-buying program. Instead, it sent millions to a program to buy conservation easements on farmland.
Remember that land bought with Florida Forever funds can be used by the PUBLIC, while farms protected by an easement remain PRIVATE.
Then devious politicians in the Legislature steered the state to squander some of its remaining conservation cash on 4 acres of land in Destin that no agency had put on any land-buying list.
DeSantis could have objected, but he didn’t. He and the Cabinet voted unanimously to spend $83 million on the property, which was owned by one of his campaign contributors. That was 10 times what the buyer had paid.
One expert told me then that $83 million would have bought 25,000 acres of land sold outright — a much better deal than the 4 acres.
This is why several experts, including Fleming and Whitfield, singled out Florida Forever as another top priority for you.
Urge the Legislature to pass a law that forbids the kind of financial finagling that DeSantis & Co. pulled on that Destin deal, then vow to put at least $100 million into land-buying every year, not conservation easements.
All right, sir, those are the immediate priorities. Get these all taken care of, and then we can talk about (lowering voice to a whisper) how climate change is sending us big rain-bombs and king tides that flood our cities. Maybe with DeSantis gone, we can finally discuss that.
As this stuff continues, that mop will definitely come in handy.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Whither goest thou, Democrats?
description: The Blue tsunami was not a confirmation of the Democrats’ platform but a refutation of the GOP’s. And so, this is a time of reckoning.
text:
OK, Democrats. Where do we go from here?
Now that the real patriots have stormed the Capitol in the only legal, strategic, and peaceful way allowed in a democratic republic, it’s time for some soul-searching. By all means, take a minute to revel in the victory, to exclaim over the unexpected turns (I see you, Texas!), to breathe huge sighs of relief, and perhaps to weep with joy that sanity prevailed Tuesday night. 

Christine Palm

Those of us who have not recognized our own country for years have heard a loud knock and, with amazement, see on our doorstep a beloved old friend we thought had been lost in a deep snowstorm.
But, let’s not pretend the Blue tsunami was a confirmation of the Democrats’ platform; rather, it was a refutation of the GOP’s. And so, this is a time of reckoning.
We must ask ourselves: what will we do with all this power?
First, we must resist the urge to “move on.” The Trump era has not left us sad the way the death of a dog does. It has not left us shaken the way a car accident does. It has not set us back the way a cancer diagnosis does. Instead, it has shaken our very identity, and most damagingly, robbed an entire generation of hope.
So, just as we did after after World War II, we must have our own Nuremberg moment. If we — and the world — are to regain faith in our institutions, and in particular the Judicial Branch, we must push for accountability. If it means jail time, so be it. Forgiveness is noble, (and may come eventually) but far too many people — indeed entire nations and economies — have suffered for us to move on easily.
Second, we must get a real plan. Not just a message that pushes back on the misogyny, racism, homophobia and incompetence of Trump and his minions. An actual plan of our own. And it must be ambitious, unified and grounded not only in equity and compassion, but also in real understanding of why we lost our base in the first place.
Finally, we must listen to young people when they say they want us to be bold. Along with the GOP, the notion of moderation got a real drubbing in the mid-terms. Contrary to the way the professional Democratic machinery would have us believe, centrists, on the face of it, are not more electable than candidates like Zoran Mamdani, who has inspired millions with his candor, vision and practical solutions to ease people’s suffering. Candidates too eager to compromise have been shown to be uninspiring at the polls. Current Affairs Magazine debunks the notion that Democratic voters want someone who walks proudly down the center of the aisle.  
So, will our Democratic leaders in Connecticut take a page from the national trend toward elected officials who are not afraid to take bold stands? Here in Connecticut, the General Assembly Democrats have made their supermajority a super-super one. The plethora of new, diverse faces is exhilarating. But will business be run any differently? Will the House and Senate leadership continue to allow the ever-diminishing minority of GOP members filibuster, defuse, dissemble, waste time, and mischaracterize and water down bills?
Or will they listen to voices like that of Julie Donato, a sophomore at the University of Connecticut, who texted me early this morning: “For the first time since I’ve been old enough to understand our government, I feel hope. I can only imagine what this bold new wave will bring, but I’m determined to be part of it — I’m determined to do my part  in helping our country become a place I’m actually proud to talk about again.”
Christine Palm, who served three terms in the Connecticut General Assembly, is founding director of The Active Voice, a leadership development program for young environmentalists.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CCSU’s fresh start: Forget the past, remember your friends
description: At Central, shared governance apparently means being invited to speak, then finding out what happened after everyone stopped listening.
text:
Welp. The accountability turnstile has clicked again.
Central Connecticut State University has discovered a remarkably efficient approach to institutional reform. When a president resigns amid allegations of bullying, intimidation, and retaliation, replace her, promise to listen, and announce a fresh start. The investigation? Unfinished. The employees who raised concerns? Still waiting. The university? Already moving forward.
And if a senior position opens up, why not call an old friend?
Interim President Kimberly Kostelis succeeded Zulma Toro after serving five years as her provost. The old administration has left the building. Except, of course, for the people still running it.
In an October 19 WFSB interview, Kostelis spoke warmly about listening, rebuilding community, hearing quieter voices, and putting students first. All admirable sentiments. But when asked about the terminated investigation and whether those who filed complaints deserved closure, she defended the Connecticut State Colleges and Universities (CSCU) system’s decision to end it and emphasized the importance of moving forward.
Kostelis didn’t end the investigation. But she chose to defend the decision. An odd way to begin a new era of accountability.
Family therapists have a term for harmony maintained by avoiding painful truths: pseudomutuality. Add a little collective denial, and suddenly the family’s darkest secrets become less troubling than the person who insists on bringing them up.
Everyone smiles for the family photograph. Nobody asks why Aunt Accountability is locked in the attic.
Kostelis wasn’t an outsider brought in to clean house. She helped lead Central during the very years now under scrutiny. What complaints reached her office? How were they handled? And what responsibility, if any, does she acknowledge for the workplace culture she helped oversee?
Curiously, Kostelis seems willing to revisit another Toro-era initiative: Central’s proposed polytechnic designation. Apparently, looking backward is perfectly acceptable when university branding is on the table. Workplace accountability, however, is a renovation best left unfinished.
Then came the appointment of Tracey Matthews as interim provost.
Matthews has substantial academic and administrative credentials. She also has a longstanding professional relationship with Kostelis. The two coauthored a textbook, and in its preface Matthews recalled: “I had the privilege of having Dr. Kimberly Kostelis as my graduate assistant.”
The former graduate assistant became a colleague, coauthor, interim president, and eventually the person who appointed her former supervisor to Central’s highest academic office.
Higher education calls this professional networking. At Central, the academic buddy system apparently comes with executive placement services.
Knowing someone, of course, doesn’t prove favoritism. Which is precisely why a transparent appointment process and meaningful shared governance matter.
Central’s Committee on Appointments and Personnel first met on October 20. That afternoon, members interviewed Matthews and recommended considering additional candidates. Kostelis supplied materials from 11 applicants in an ongoing associate vice president search. Committee members identified two possibilities, interviewed one on October 22, and remained willing to interview the other if contact could be made.
Members had reservations about Matthews but considered her appointable and preferable to the second candidate interviewed.
In other words, faculty did their jobs. They interviewed candidates, weighed qualifications, raised concerns, and offered recommendations.
Democracy had been served. Or at least the consultation box had been checked.
On October 23, without further consultation or notification to the committee, Matthews’s contract was prepared, sent, and signed. Committee members learned this only on October 28, after coming across an October 20 news report stating that Matthews had announced her resignation from Jacksonville State the previous day at an Academic Affairs committee meeting.
October 19. A full day before Central’s faculty committee first met.
That timeline raises some obvious questions. Had Matthews already received assurances about the position at Central? Or had she independently decided to leave Jacksonville State? The resignation announcement doesn’t tell us. What we do know is that she publicly announced her departure before Central’s faculty consultation even began.
So what happened to Kostelis’s much-publicized commitment to shared governance?
Faculty were consulted, yes. But they were left out when it mattered most. No final discussion. No notification that a contract had been signed. No explanation until committee members went looking for one.
At Central, shared governance apparently means being invited to speak, then finding out what happened after everyone stopped listening.
To be clear, shared governance doesn’t mean faculty appoint the provost or get veto power over the president’s decisions. But surely it should mean good-faith consultation, transparency, and some basic respect for the people asked to participate.
Otherwise, why bother? Faculty get speaking parts while administrators write the ending.
It’s a strange opening act for a university promising to change its leadership culture. The interim president publicly champions transparency and shared governance, then appoints a longtime professional associate through a process that leaves faculty wondering whether the decision had already been made before they entered the room.
A fresh start, apparently, doesn’t require fresh habits.
And this is where Kostelis’s interview and the appointment become especially revealing. Taken together, they suggest a troubling approach to leadership: Listen to employees, but don’t revisit the investigation. Consult faculty, but don’t necessarily tell them when the decision is made. Promise change, but steer clear of the uncomfortable questions that might actually require it.
None of this proves wrongdoing. But Central’s fresh start is beginning to look an awful lot like painting over cracks and declaring the building repaired.
Listening isn’t the same as answering. Consultation isn’t necessarily shared governance. And moving forward isn’t the same as making things right.
Dysfunctional families can be remarkably good at keeping up appearances. Everyone gathers around the dinner table. Everyone agrees things are better now. And anyone who dares mention what happened last year is accused of ruining the evening.
At Central, the table is set. The guests already know one another. The investigation has disappeared from the menu. And faculty are left wondering whether dinner was ordered before they arrived.
“Together, we will move forward,” Kostelis promised.
Apparently, the CCSU family’s fresh start begins by making sure nobody opens the attic door.

title: Alaskans approve largely meaningless noncitizen voting ballot measure
description: Partial election results Wednesday afternoon show Alaska voters overwhelmingly approving Ballot Measure 3, which would add a new state law prohibiting noncitizens from voting in Alaska. A different Alaska law already prohibits noncitizen voting, as does federal law. When enacted, Ballot Measure 3 will not change existing practice, according to an analysis by[...]
text:
Voters are seen on the first day of early in-person voting in the midterm elections at a polling site in Juneau on Oct. 19, 2026. (Photo by Corinne Smith/Alaska Beacon)Partial election results Wednesday afternoon show Alaska voters overwhelmingly approving Ballot Measure 3, which would add a new state law prohibiting noncitizens from voting in Alaska.
A different Alaska law already prohibits noncitizen voting, as does federal law. When enacted, Ballot Measure 3 will not change existing practice, according to an analysis by the Alaska Department of Law.
The department said in October that “the bill proposed by (the ballot measure) would not change the qualifications to vote.”
With 399 of 400 precincts reporting results at 1:09 p.m. Wednesday afternoon, 69.6% of participating voters were in favor of Ballot Measure 3. 
Sponsors of the initiative, a trio of Republican former Alaska state legislators, thanked voters in a press release on Tuesday night after initial reporting from the Division of Elections showed strong support for the measure.
Former House Speaker Mike Chenault of Nikiski and former state senators John Coghill of Fairbanks and Josh Revak of Anchorage sponsored the initiative as the group Alaskans for Citizen Voting. They say current state law is unclear and should be updated to clarify that only U.S. citizens may vote.
“Alaskans have spoken clearly,” said Coghill, the measure’s primary sponsor, in the statement. “The passage of Ballot Measure 3 affirms the importance of citizenship as a fundamental qualification for voting in our elections. We are grateful to the thousands of Alaskans who signed petitions, volunteered their time, and helped bring this important question before the voters.”

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Arkansas election shows shift in Democrats’ favor, but far short of other states’ gains
description: After losing her bid for U.S. Senate, Arkansas Democrat Hallie Shoffner had a message for the national party. “Just because a state is considered unwinnable does not mean its people are unworthy,” Shoffner said in her concession speech Tuesday night in Little Rock. Shoffner’s 12-point, nearly 105,000-vote loss to incumbent Republican U.S. Sen. Tom Cotton […]
text:
Hallie Shoffner prepares to deliver her concession speech to supporters at the Mosaic Templars Building in Little Rock, Arkansas on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by John Sykes/Arkansas Advocate)
After losing her bid for U.S. Senate, Arkansas Democrat Hallie Shoffner had a message for the national party.
“Just because a state is considered unwinnable does not mean its people are unworthy,” Shoffner said in her concession speech Tuesday night in Little Rock.
Shoffner’s 12-point, nearly 105,000-vote loss to incumbent Republican U.S. Sen. Tom Cotton came as Democrats won congressional seats and governor’s races by sizable margins nationwide.
Other states went blue after years and even decades of Republican dominance, but “in Arkansas, we had something of a red wall,” said John Davis, a University of Arkansas associate professor of political science who has studied the state’s shifts in political power.
Democrats have not won a statewide or U.S. House race in Arkansas since 2010. Three of the state’s four Republican congressmen defeated Democratic challengers Tuesday, and central Arkansas’ U.S. Rep. French Hill led Democrat Chris Jones by more than 4,000 votes as of Wednesday evening, though The Associated Press had not yet called the race.
Jones indicated Wednesday he was waiting to see if provisional ballots could close the gap, declaring “we are not done yet” in a Facebook post. 
But AP voter data shows an electoral shift toward Democrats in all 75 counties, two years after Republican President Donald Trump won 64% of Arkansas’ vote.


AP graphics may not be republished.
“Homegrown, high-quality candidates” like Shoffner and Jones contributed to Democrats’ down-ballot gains, said Jay Barth, a Hendrix College professor emeritus of politics.
“In some places, especially rural areas, it was a slightly demobilized Republican electorate, and then in urban and suburban areas, I think [Democrats] had a little bit more of a true blue wave,” Barth said.
 Democrats’ pickups concentrated in 3 counties

Democrats flipped 11 state legislative districts, the party’s biggest gain in the General Assembly in more than two decades. Republicans have held supermajorities in both chambers of the General Assembly since 2016, and the Democrats broke the House supermajority needed to pass most budget bills by winning 10 seats.
The pickups were concentrated in Benton, Washington and Pulaski counties, the state’s three most populous. Democrats also gained one House seat each in Conway, Jonesboro and the Delta.
The party also retained legislative seats by larger margins than its 2024 wins. Rep. Diana Gonzales Worthen of Springdale received more than twice as many votes as her Republican challenger, two years after flipping Arkansas’ only majority-Latino district.
At the time, Gonzales Worthen’s 2024 win was Democrats’ first net gain in the statehouse in 20 years. Democrats have said repeatedly since then that they hoped to capitalize on their growing momentum.
The Senate will keep its Republican supermajority after Democrats gained one seat in northern Pulaski County.

Democrats see rare signs of hope in solidly red Arkansas’ midterms


 Republicans lose ground in northwest Arkansas

Cotton is the U.S. Senate’s third-ranked Republican, and he will lose his Intelligence Committee chairmanship in January since Democrats took control of the chamber.
He won his first U.S. Senate term in 2014 when he unseated Democratic then-Sen. Mark Pryor by more than 144,000 votes. Cotton easily won reelection in 2020 without a Democratic opponent.
But Cotton’s 6,000-vote margin over Shoffner in Benton County, formerly a Republican stronghold, exemplified the party’s loosening grip on Arkansas, Barth and Davis said.
Trump won Benton County with 62% of the vote in 2020 and 2024. This year, Cotton won roughly 51% of the county’s vote.
Democrats flipped four Benton County state House seats, including one that bleeds into Washington County, where the party already holds a few legislative seats. The party made both state and local gains there, winning an 8-7 majority on the Washington County Quorum Court.
Washington County voted for Democrat Robb Ryerse over Republican U.S. Rep. Steve Womack, who won the county in 2024. Womack won reelection Tuesday with nearly 28,000 fewer Benton County votes than his 2024 win.
Northwest Arkansas’ shift away from Republicans in federal races “softened the margins for victory” down the ballot, “largely due to a really impressive ground game for Democrats,” Davis said.

Arkansas Sen. Tom Cotton, along with his family, takes the stage at the Republican Watch Party to thank his supporters on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026 in North Little Rock, Arkansas. (Photo by Katie Adkins/Arkansas Advocate)

Statewide, Shoffner received a greater percentage of the vote against Cotton than either Democratic opponent of Arkansas’ other Republican U.S. senator, John Boozman, who won reelection by 24 percentage points in 2016 and 34 percentage points in 2022.
A first-time candidate and sixth-generation Arkansan, Shoffner built her campaign on her decision to close her family’s soybean farm last year under financial strain she attributed to Trump’s tariffs. She portrayed Cotton, who declined to debate her twice, as uninterested in everyday Arkansans.
Shoffner attempted to appeal to Republicans, independents and non-voters, saying Arkansans “don’t have to change your party to change your senator.” Cotton and his allies spent millions on ads portraying Shoffner as soft on immigration.
Jones and Shoffner both attempted to tie their opponents to Trump, whose approval rating in Arkansas and nationwide has declined. 
The rising cost of living fueled Trump’s unpopularity, and Arkansas Democrats prioritizing “kitchen table issues” above its opposition to the president was a good messaging strategy, Little Rock state Sen. Clarke Tucker said.
“Republican attempts to paint and define Democrats as extremists failed in large part because voters understand that Democrats care about affordability for working families, a successful economy [and] the price at the gas pump,” said Tucker, who unsuccessfully challenged Hill in 2018.
 ‘Dust your boots off’

National Democrats poured money and attention into red states that flipped federal seats but invested much less in Arkansas, even though Shoffner’s campaign received some national media attention.

Democratic congressional nominee Chris Jones expresses appreciation to supporters alongside his wife, Jerrilyn Jones, during an election night watch party in Little Rock, Arkansas on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by John Sykes/Arkansas Advocate)

The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee directed fundraising efforts to Jones in October. Barth said the effort “probably could have paid off” if it had happened earlier in the race.
Jones also received former Vice President Kamala Harris’ endorsement. Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg and former Massachusetts U.S. Rep. Joe Kennedy III campaigned for Jones on the ground in central Arkansas, and Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker spent money on ads supporting Jones’ bid.
Hill has not made any public statements since polls closed Tuesday night.
If Hill wins, it would be his narrowest margin of victory in his seven congressional elections, even after Republican state lawmakers redrew the 2nd District in 2021 to favor their party. Hill’s closest race before Jones was his 2018 victory over Tucker by nearly 16,000 votes.
Jones first ran for office in 2022 when he lost the governor’s race to Republican Sarah Huckabee Sanders, who was reelected Tuesday. He was far from the only Arkansas Democrat to run for at least the second time.
Seven of the 11 Democrats who flipped state legislative seats had run in the same district or region before, with some unseating Republicans who previously beat them. Repeat candidates have the advantage of familiarity regardless of party, Tucker said.
“I think one message to the [Democratic] candidates who got close would be to take a week off and catch your breath, dust your boots off, and get ready to go start hitting the streets again,” Tucker said.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Sen. Justice, mulling WV governor run, will soon be in Senate minority caucus after election results
description: Sen. Jim Justice, R-W.Va., wasn’t on the ballot this election, but the blue tsunami that blew out midterm elections will put him in the minority party in the Senate.
text:
Gov. Jim Justice addresses state lawmakers Jan. 8, 2025, for the last time as governor. Justice, a Republican who has spent two terms as the state's chief executive. (Photo by Will Price /West Virginia Legislative Photography)Sen. Jim Justice, R-W.Va., wasn’t on the ballot this election, but the blue tsunami that blew out midterm elections will put him in the minority party in the Senate.
Democrats ousted Republicans and seized control of the U.S. Senate on Tuesday night.
Republicans’ nearly two-year control of the federal government since President Donald Trump’s return to the White House will come to an end in January when the 120th Congress gavels in.
Justice, a friend and ally of Trump, said Tuesday was “a tough night for Republicans.”
“We lost some really good senators whom I’ve gotten to know and think the world of over the last two years,” Justice told West Virginia Watch in a statement. “Since the day I came to Washington, my goal has been to do what’s right for West Virginia and get things done for the American people.”
“Now, I have my conservative values, and I’m not going to back down from those, but I’ve always said that you can stand firm in what you believe and still be willing to reach across the aisle,” he continued. “At the end of the day, the voters sent us here to deliver results, and that ought to be our number one priority, regardless of which party we belong to.”
Justice, who is in his first term in the U.S. Senate, has already floated the idea of running again for West Virginia governor, likely challenging Gov. Patrick Morrisey for the GOP nomination.
The decision could come after the midterm elections, Justice said. 
Justice was an ultra-popular governor in West Virginia from 2017 to 2025.
Recent tax liens and financial troubles at The Greenbrier resort, now only partially owned by the Justice family, haven’t really dulled his popularity in the Mountain State. 
Justice, 75, has served in the U.S. Senate since 2025. 
Trump recently signed Justice’s bill, the “Hershel ‘Woody’ Williams National Medal of Honor Monument Location Act,” into law. It’s the first piece of legislation by Justice to clear Trump’s desk. 
Republicans currently control a six-seat majority of 53 seats in the Senate, while Democrats hold 47.
Thirty-three of the 100 U.S. Senate seats were up for election on Tuesday night.
The stunning Senate upset on Election Day included states that Trump had won by double digits in 2024, signaling voters’ stroke rebuke to the president’s policies. 
Incumbent Sen. Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., won her reelection bid on Tuesday, and will begin her third term in the Senate in 2027.
She is currently fourth in the Senate Republican majority leadership while the GOP has control of the Upper Chamber. 
Justice attended Capito’s election night watch party in Charleston, remarking on their teamwork and work in Washington, D.C.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Dems flip seats in Montana Legislature
description: Montana Democrats flipped two seats in the state Senate in the midterm election, giving the party 20 members in the upper chamber, the highest number it’s had there since 2019. Republicans will have a 30-to-20 advantage in the 2027 Legislative session and a majority in the House as well, though it likely will be slimmer […]
text:
The Montana Senate is seen during the Wednesday, February 12, 2025 session. (Nathaniel Bailey for the Daily Montanan)Montana Democrats flipped two seats in the state Senate in the midterm election, giving the party 20 members in the upper chamber, the highest number it’s had there since 2019.
Republicans will have a 30-to-20 advantage in the 2027 Legislative session and a majority in the House as well, though it likely will be slimmer in the lower chamber once the final results are tabulated. 
Even late Wednesday, the Montana Secretary of State’s Office reported that only 78% of the precincts in the Treasure State were completely counted.
In Senate District 10, Margaret Mitchell, a Democrat, flipped a seat previously held by Jeremy Trebas who ran unsuccessfully for the Montana Public Service Commission. With all precincts in the Great Falls district reported, Mitchell took 3,701 votes to Republican Jessica Drydahl’s 2,832, a 14-point win in a seat the Democrats will hold for the next four years.
Margaret Mitchell (Photo courtesy of Margaret Mitchell campaign).
Mitchell plans to be a voice on bills dealing with the tech industry and related issues. She said the Legislature needs more engineers. Mitchell was formerly an executive at American Express. She’s a mom, grew up in Great Falls and graduated from Montana State University, where she’s now an adjunct professor teaching about blockchain.
“This will be new to me,” Mitchell said. “I’m going to put my nose to the grindstone to learn very quickly how to be effective.”
In order for Democrats to flip more seats, they need to deliver on promises and come to the Legislative session with solutions, she said. She also added that a split government could lead to solutions-oriented work for Montanans. 
“It was a common theme when I was at the door, that people want us to work across the aisle and work with each other for Montana,” Mitchell said. “I think focusing on the things that really matter to Montanans and will affect their lives is what’s going to make the difference. And when they see Democrats being effective and focusing on the things that are most important to them, we will gain their trust.”
Meanwhile, further south, Scott Rosenzweig flipped a seat for the Democrats in Senate District 29, which previously had been held by John Esp of Big Timber. The seat includes the Treasure Valley from Livingston to Gardiner, and north to Clyde Park, as well as part of Bozeman. 
With 12-of-15 precincts fully reported, Rosenzweig had 56% of the votes to Republican Jason Gunderson’s 44%. Rosenzweig said the ballots left were all in Gallatin County and he expected them to break largely for him.
Despite relatively small gains for the Democrats, Rosenzweig said he woke up to a much different political climate.
“I personally feel like even though the Democratic Party didn’t win any majority, I feel like I woke up in a much more committed purple state,” Rosenzweig said Wednesday.
Scott Rosenzweig is pictured. (Courtesy Scott Rosenzweig)
He, too, said he’s interested in tech legislation and is vehemently opposed to the concept of a sales tax. Capital gains changes are on his to-do list as well. Hotel taxes need to increase, he said, and vowed to address infrastructure issues in rural tourist hotspots.
The district is partially in Park County and partially in Gallatin County. Gardiner is one of the entrances to Yellowstone National Park.
“I have two counties, one of them is large and relative to the other, economically successful,” Rosenzweig said. “The other is very sparsely populated and suffers a burden of tourism infrastructure upkeep costs and gets nothing from the state in support.”
Republicans in the Montana Legislature appeared to be relatively calm about the election results in the Treasure State. 
Sen. Greg Hertz, in a statement, said that state Republicans outperformed their counterparts in other states around the nation. Hertz is chair of the Montana Republican Legislative Campaign Committee and is from Polson.
  Montana House results 

Montana Republicans were expected to keep at least 55 seats in the Montana House. Republicans had 58 House seats during the 2025 Legislature. House Democrats held all 42 seats going into election night, and gained at least one and potentially as many as three.
Hertz added that the redistricting in 2023 played a part for Montana Democrats during the midterm elections.
“Ironically, the Democratic-backed 2023 legislative redistricting map helped preserve Republican majorities. By creating relatively few competitive districts, the map insulated Republicans from significant losses even in a strong Democratic election year,” Hertz said in a statement. “The results demonstrate the unintended consequences of partisan redistricting.”
The contested House races include House District 4, where Paul Koch held a 500-vote lead over Republican Shaun Pandina. None of the five precincts in that race have been fully counted.
In House District 20, Democrat Steve Keller beat Melissa Nikolakakos by 46 votes with all three precincts fully reporting. 
Rep. Curtis Schomer, a Republican in House District 48 looking for reelection, had a 15-vote lead over Democrat challenger Tucker Colvin. The three precincts in that race have not been fully reported.
And in House District 57 — Rosenzweig’s former seat — Democrat Becky Edwards appeared to be on the way to a win over Republican Bob Crank. 
With around 85 total seats, Montana Republicans will also be well short of a supermajority, which in Montana would be 100 total seats between the House and Senate.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: ‘Blue tsunami’ hits Utah: House Republicans on pace to lose 17 seats, breaking supermajority
description: By the time Utah’s election night results were posted at 9 p.m. Tuesday, it was already clear that Democrats were sweeping the nation in a scathing rebuke to President Donald Trump and the Republican Party.  Though margins indicated Democrats here were performing far better than they usually do, Utah’s congressional races largely came down as […]
text:
Lawmakers work in the House Chamber at the Capitol in Salt Lake City on the final night of the legislative session, Friday, March 6, 2026. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)By the time Utah’s election night results were posted at 9 p.m. Tuesday, it was already clear that Democrats were sweeping the nation in a scathing rebuke to President Donald Trump and the Republican Party. 
Though margins indicated Democrats here were performing far better than they usually do, Utah’s congressional races largely came down as expected. Rep. Ben McAdams overwhelmingly won the state’s new Democratic-leaning congressional district that turned blue after an anti-gerrymandering lawsuit resulted in new, court-ordered boundaries. And Utah’s other three red districts were unsurprisingly won by GOP incumbents, Reps. Blake Moore, Celeste Maloy and Mike Kennedy. 
Utah Legislature 2026 election night results: Here’s who is on track to win and lose

But what wasn’t expected in mostly Republican-controlled Utah came down the ballot. 
Eric Biggart — a longtime Democratic strategist in Salt Lake County who is a member of the Utah Democratic Party’s executive committee and chair of LDS Democrats — said disbelief initially washed over him as he scrolled down, down, down through the state legislative race results. 
There weren’t just a handful of Democratic candidates beating Republican incumbents and in the lead to flip open seats previously held by the GOP supermajority, as Utah Democrats had hoped for in a best-case scenario. Rather, they were leading in far more. 
“There was never a world where we were looking at double-digit (wins) being on the table this year,” Biggart told Utah News Dispatch Wednesday morning. He said they had hoped for maybe four to seven seats — but in the teens? That was unthinkable. 
Yet as of Wednesday morning, unofficial election results show Democrats are in the lead to pick up 15 seats in the Utah House, and unaffiliated candidates are slated to take two. Republicans are on track to lose 17 seats. In the Senate, Republicans are poised to lose two seats to Democrats.
Election results are preliminary, with thousands more still needing to be tallied. But to political pundits, aside from a couple of races with razor-thin margins, the results are likely to hold. 
That puts Republicans on pace to lose their two-thirds, veto-proof supermajority in the House. They’re projected to still have a simple majority, 38 of the House’s 75 seats. And the Senate will still be controlled by a GOP supermajority, with 20 seats to Democrats’ eight. 


 










View this post on Instagram






















 
A post shared by Eric Biggart (@ericbiggart)



But for a state that hasn’t seen a House chamber without a GOP supermajority since 1993 — and no recent memory of Democrats sweeping that many seats in a single election year — it’s extraordinary. 
Biggart said he and other Utah Democratic strategists have spent years trying to carve a path toward breaking the supermajority, but they expected it to take eight or 10 years — not all in one election.
The “blue tsunami” washing over the nation made landfall in Utah, Utah Democratic Party Chair Brian King said Tuesday night. Political pundit Taylor Morgan agreed, but he said he hadn’t expected the way it seeped down into local legislative races. 
“I was absolutely shocked. I was flabbergasted, blown away,” Morgan, a political consultant with the lobbying and public affairs firm Morgan & May, told Utah News Dispatch on Wednesday. 
He said he expected Democrats to do well in Salt Lake County — but what he didn’t expect was that phenomenon to be so widespread in counties up and down the Wasatch Front, the Wasatch Back and beyond. 
“Goodness gracious,” he said. “Look at Davis County. Look at Weber County. They’re both blue. Utah County results are blue in so many ways.” 
And Morgan said he didn’t expect so many voters who weren’t Democrats “to turn out to vote and intentionally vote for the Democratic candidates down ballot to punish the Republican party.”
“This is the first time in my lifetime that a national election wave has also taken over the Utah ballot like this,” Morgan said. “It is frankly unprecedented.” 
Morgan’s firm built a website to track the results and their impact on the balance of power in the Utah Legislature. He told Utah News Dispatch he expects most Democrats to keep their leads as vote tallies are finalized in coming weeks. 
What happened? To both Biggart (a Democrat) and Morgan (a Republican), it wasn’t just Utahns fed up with Trump and an energized Democratic base. It was also Utahns of other political stripes — even some Republicans — having yearslong, mounting frustration with how the Republican-controlled Utah Legislature has handled redistricting, ballot initiatives, unions and other issues, along with an ongoing wave of outcry over data centers and development. 
“That combined with a general repudiation of the Republican Party, because of Donald Trump, I think that caught up with Utah legislative Republicans,” he said. 
To Biggart, the blue wave was fueled “50-50” by Trump and a frustration with Utah Republican legislators. 
“Data centers and gerrymandering and Amendment B and Amendment D before that, all these tricks and power grabs, have weighed on people,” Biggart said. “We’ve reached a point where Democrats are organized. And we’ve knocked literally hundreds of thousands of doors and sent hundreds of thousands of texts to a degree we’ve never done before.” 
Democrats, Biggart said, “ran a professional, world-class campaign for these candidates in these targeted races. And it worked.” And he said the results show Utah independents and even some Republicans “have just had it.” 
“The Trump effect,” he said, was “a nice kicker at the end.”
Senate Majority Leader Kirk Cullimore, R-Draper, speaks during a media availability with senate leadership at the Capitol in Salt Lake City on the first day of the legislative session, Tuesday, Jan. 20, 2026. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)
Another powerful Senate Republican on track to lose his seat
When one of Utah’s most powerful Republicans, Senate President Stuart Adams, lost his primary election to GOP challenger Stephanie Hollist, apparently that was just the beginning. 
Now Adams’ No. 2, Senate Majority Leader Kirk Cullimore, was trailing his Democratic challenger, Shana Anderson, by nearly 14 percentage points as of Wednesday. 
It was an upset in Sandy, Highland and Alpine areas making up Senate District 19 that perhaps only Anderson herself saw coming. 
(Photo courtesy of Shana Anderson)
“I keep hearing people say how surprised they are, but I actually was not surprised at all,” Anderson, a U.S. Army veteran and stay-at-home mom who lives in Sandy, told Utah News Dispatch Wednesday. “I’ve been out there talking to voters, and I knew where everybody was at.” 
She’s not claiming victory yet, noting there are still votes to be tallied. But she said she was happy to see “voters coming out and letting their voices be heard.” 
Cullimore did not return a request for comment Wednesday. Anderson said she hasn’t heard from him, and he hadn’t called her to concede. 
Anderson’s experience on the campaign trail reflected Biggart and Morgan’s takeaways. She said she heard from a lot of people “upset with the Trump administration,” but also many who were directly frustrated with Cullimore’s track record, especially when it came to supporting school voucher programs or anti-public union legislation. 
“I had volunteers coming out of the woodwork from all different angles because of what he’s been doing,” Anderson said. “And I honestly think he had no idea that people were paying attention. And people would try to reach out to him, but he would not listen or respond to them.” 
Largely, Anderson said the perception she heard from her district’s voters was that Cullimore “has not been doing the job” representing their interests. 
“He’s been working for people in power, people with money, and special interests. And he’s not been working for the people in his district,” she said. “It wasn’t even a heavy lift, to be honest.” 
How will this shake up the Legislature? 
To Morgan, Cullimore’s likely loss and Democrats’ gains in the House will send reverberations through the halls of the Utah Capitol. 
Before the election, Cullimore and Sen. Evan Vickers, R-Cedar City, were in a tight race to replace Adams as the next Senate president. Now that race — which will be decided in a closed caucus meeting Friday night — has a new, giant question mark over it. Will Vickers take it? Or will a different candidate swoop in to run in Cullimore’s place? 
End of the Adams era: A look at Utah’s outgoing Senate president and what’s next

“That election has been shaken up completely,” Morgan said. 
And because the House is slated to lose so many Republicans and get so many new Democratic faces, Morgan expects even House Speaker Mike Schultz might be in for a shakeup. 
“Speaker Mike Schultz has lost 15 members of his caucus, some of whom will be really devoted to Speaker Schultz,” Morgan said. “Will now Speaker Schultz face a challenger within his caucus for the speakership because of what happened?” 
Additionally, Morgan wondered if House Democratic leadership might see some changes due to all the new members. 
Committee assignments, chair positions and policy priorities are all influenced by who is in House and Senate leadership, so the implications run deep, Morgan said. 
To Biggart, the political aftershock of this year’s elections will energize Democrats in Utah like never before — and he expects it to open the floodgates for more candidates willing to run now that they’ve seen what’s possible in traditionally red Utah. Now that it appears the House supermajority has been cracked, Biggart said that will open the floodgates. 
“It’s at that point where people really start to believe, where people start to donate, start to knock on doors, start to make those text messages to their friends and family,” Biggart said. “Because when it’s on the margins and it feels real, all of a sudden it becomes a lot easier to do.”

name: Maryland Matters
title: Moore wants new congressional maps for Maryland after Question 3 victory
description: Gov. Wes Moore (D) said Wednesday that he wants to see new congressional maps for Maryland after the General Assembly convenes in January and that he is "ready to engage" with lawmakers on the subject of redistricting.
text:
Maryland Gov. Wes Moore (D) said Wednesday he wants the General Assembly to move forward on new congressional maps after the passage Wednesday of Question 3, Maryland's redistricting-focused ballot question. (Photo by Christine Condon/Maryland Matters)Gov. Wes Moore (D) said Wednesday that he wants to see new congressional maps for Maryland after the General Assembly convenes in January and that he is “ready to engage” with lawmakers on the subject of redistricting.
The remarks came as part of the governor’s victory lap Wednesday, the day after “historic” wins by Democrats in elections nationwide and Maryland voters’ approval of Question 3, which loosens restrictions on redistricting in the state.
Moore invested significant political capital on the question, which passed with 60% of the vote just weeks after polls showed that voters were skeptical.
“Two weeks ago, everybody said that Question 3 was done,” Moore told reporters outside of Mount Vernon’s Ceremony Coffee Roasters, the day after his reelection. “I am very proud to say that, in a loud and resounding fashion, Question 3 passed in Maryland, and we made sure that Maryland could help to meet the moment.”
Meeting the moment, to Moore, should come in the form of new maps that would give Democrats the advantage in all eight of the state’s congressional districts come 2028— in response to the GOP-led effort to draw district lines in its favor leading up to Tuesday’s midterms. Republicans currently hold just one of those eight seats, the 1st District where eight-term GOP Rep. Andy Harris was reelected Wednesday.
Maryland Gov. Wes Moore (D) told reporters Wednesday that he wants to see lawmakers move forward with new congressional maps after the passage of Maryland’s redistricting-focused Question 3. (Photo by Christine Condon/Maryland Matters)
“Donald Trump is not done. He has already been very clear about his intention to go after additional states,” Moore said. “The courts have spoken, the people of Maryland have spoken, and it is time to make sure that Maryland does meet this moment.”
Legislative leaders Wednesday welcomed the passage of Question 3 and said they look forward to working with the governor on redistricting. But it did not appear to be on the top of anyone’s list of priorities.
House Majority Leader Del. David Moon (D-Montgomery) said he believes the legislature should take up other, more pressing, issues first in January, especially given that new congressional maps couldn’t be used until 2028 anyway.
“It would be, I think, a big misread to make mapmaking the first priority of the legislature,” Moon said. “The first priority of the legislature is going to be work on the top concern of Marylanders and that continues to be healthcare access and affordability.”
Maryland House Speaker Joseline Peña-Melnyk (D-Prince George’s and Anne Arundel), who campaigned for Question 3, was noncommittal Wednesday, saying through a spokesperson she was “very pleased that the voters had their say and approved Question 3.”
“Question 3 does not require new maps to be drawn but ensures Maryland is on even ground with other states moving forward,” the spokesperson said. “We welcome the opportunity to continue conversations with the Governor and the Senate President to determine the best approach for our state. The House has met this moment before and we will be ready again when it’s necessary.”
Question 3 clarifies that requirements for electoral districts that are compact and contiguous apply only to General Assembly districts, after a 2022 court decision said those restrictions should apply to congressional districts as well. It also states that the neither the state constitution nor the Declaration of Rights govern congressional redistricting, and grants the Supreme Court of Maryland original jurisdiction to review the state’s redistricting plans.
Months of congressional redistricting fights end with win for Question 3

The House of Delegates passed a new map during this year’s General Assembly session, but the Senate declined to take it up. Maryland Senate President Bill Ferguson (D-Baltimore City) resisted redistricting for much of the year, publicly sparring with Moore and citing potential legal concerns with drawing new maps that could fall in the courts.
Ferguson reversed course after the U.S. Supreme Court “gutted” the Voting Rights Act, and agreed to an August special session where lawmakers pushed Question 3 on to the ballot.
Ferguson said in a statement Wednesday that he was pleased with passage of the ballot question, which “gives Maryland clear legal standards for redistricting.”
“I’ll be discussing any next steps with my Senate colleagues and other state leaders,” his statement said. “We will certainly take into account the results of how mid-cycle redistricting efforts played out across the country and any further actions other states may pursue. Regardless, lowering costs, growing our economy, and protecting programs Marylanders rely on will remain our top priorities.”
The map previously approved by the House earlier this year could provide a template for the future. That map swept across the Chesapeake Bay, connecting Maryland’s rural and red Eastern Shore with blue strongholds in Annapolis and Columbia. It also divided parts of Baltimore City into three different districts, and divided Democratic counties Montgomery and Prince George’s.

Sen. Clarence Lam (D-Anne Arundel and Howard), who has long supported redistricting, said he agrees with the governor that new maps are necessary, because more red states will attempt mid-decade redistricting in an effort to improve their electoral outcomes in the future. And future years may not be as good for the Democrats as this year was, meaning Republicans could find more success in gerrymandered districts.
“We have massive tailwinds — tailwinds that we will perhaps never again see in our lifetimes,” Lam said. “That tailwind will not be present in 2028.”

Lam said he does not think the House map passed earlier this year will be the final map, since it could have diminished Black representation in Maryland’s congressional delegation by dividing heavily minority districts.
“It may be a starting point for discussion, but I think there’s some genuine considerations,” Lam said. “There have been  some concerns from colleagues to not break up Baltimore City to the degree that it was broken up before. There are also some concerns of not losing African American representation in our federal delegation.”
Moon believes the legislature can approach the district lines with a fresh set of eyes, given the approval of Question 3.
“We can operate with a little bit of a clean slate of mind here, because the constitutional amendment that just passed has the effect of alleviating, I believe, any concerns about potentially having a map struck down in court,” Moon said.

name: Washington State Standard
title: 4 takeaways from Washington’s election tsunami
description: Tuesday’s blue wave could remake the political landscape of Washington state. A likely supermajority in the state House. A shocker in the 5th Congressional District. A walkover in the 3rd District. An emphatic affirmation of an income tax. These are signs of where the wave crested in a blue state. Voters responded to the second […]
text:
People cheer "working people standing strong, millionaire tax all day long," at an election night event in Seattle, Washington, after results showed voters rejected an initiative that would have nixed an income tax on high income earners. (Photo by Jacquelyn Jimenez Romero/Washington State Standard)Tuesday’s blue wave could remake the political landscape of Washington state.
A likely supermajority in the state House. A shocker in the 5th Congressional District. A walkover in the 3rd District. An emphatic affirmation of an income tax. These are signs of where the wave crested in a blue state. Voters responded to the second term of The Donald, a period featuring a war in Iran, surging gasoline and diesel prices, tariffs, and less federal aid for health care and social services.
But the leftward trend didn’t carry over to a conservative-backed initiative to bar transgender girls from girls’ sports in public schools. 
Over 2 million ballots have been counted. Hundreds of thousands remain to be tallied in the coming days. 
Here are four takeaways from Tuesday’s results.
GOP sings the blues
Republicans in the state House woke up Wednesday – presuming they went to bed — to see at least 13 seats they now hold could be lost to Democrats depending on those future counts.
That would be a third of their caucus. It would mean Democrats attain a supermajority, meaning they can pass bonds, override vetoes by a governor, and advance constitutional amendments without any of their votes. 
GOP leaders knew, based on primary results, their four incumbents in southwest Washington were in trouble and the party’s grip on a seat in a blue-turning district in Pierce and Kitsap counties was slipping. 
On election night the scenario worsened. Democrats also led races for four more Republican-held seats, including two in the Yakima Valley, one in the Cascades-straddling 12th District and another in the Puyallup-area 25th District. Republicans are barely ahead in four other contests.
“This is a low point for the Republican party,” GOP campaign consultant Alex Hays said.
The wave carried Democratic U.S. Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez to an unexpectedly easy win over a formidable foe in state Senate Republican Leader John Braun. She claimed victory Tuesday night when she had 55% of the vote. AP called the race early Wednesday. In contrast, her first win in 2022 went to a recount and in her re-election she finished with just under 52%.
Imagine eastern Washington’s surprise when the wave crossed the Cascades into the 5th Congressional District, putting the re-election of Republican U.S. Rep. Michael Baumgartner in jeopardy. 
This is reliable Republican terrain. Yet Baumgartner is only up a percentage point on Carmela Conroy, his Democratic challenger. Two years ago, he defeated her by 21 percentage points. 
Where do Republicans go from here? Leadership changes in the House caucus and the state party could be on the horizon. 
Taxing the rich paid dividends
Washington voters have been asked numerous times over the past century to allow an income tax. Each time, they’ve said no. Tuesday was different, as Initiative 645 to repeal the high-earners income tax passed this year was failing by a wide margin. 
Will this win embolden Democratic state lawmakers to feel voters could be okay with them eventually lowering the tax threshold below $1 million? Gov. Bob Ferguson, a Democrat, has vowed to veto such legislation if it reached his desk. 
Winning at the ballot was the first battle. A legal fight is next; the state Supreme Court is expected to be called on to decide the tax’s constitutionality. The membership of that court will be different from today as a result of the election.
Voters filled five of the state high court’s nine seats. Those races received much more attention and money than usual, with the prospect of the income tax legal scrap looming. They served as a statewide proxy battle between Democrats and Republicans, with each political party backing a slate. 
Four candidates backed by Democratic forces are leading. A fifth, appeals court Judge Ian Birk is trailing King County Superior Court Sean O’Donnell in a race that will take a few days to decide. O’Donnell had the support of Republican forces, including the state party, but also a distinguished list of Democrats such as former Gov. Christine Gregoire.
This duel had all the strains of a contest for a partisan office, sowing interest in whether whoever wins might play a decisive role in a future income tax ruling.
Ahnaleigh Wilson, 17, of Eastmont High School, left, and Frances Staudt, 17, of Tumwater High School, right, are high school athletes who supported INitiative 638 to ban transgender girls from girls sports in public schools. Here they are recognized at Let’s Go Washington’s election night party on Nov. 3, 2026, in Redmond, Washington (Photo by Ryan Berry/Washington State Standard)
Sports are personal, not partisan
Early results show voter decisions on Initiative 638 to ban transgender girls from girls’ sports were not driven by one’s political ethos or the partisan currents.
It passed in 36 of 39 counties. It failed in King, Jefferson and San Juan counties, all home to large numbers of liberals.
Even in King, tens of thousands of people who voted to preserve the millionaire’s tax also voted for the ban. In Clark County, 61% voted for Gluesenkamp Perez and 60% voted for the ban, which was vociferously supported by Braun.
This looks to be a case where individuals understood the initiative and individuals had strong views. It wasn’t a trick question and had received lots of coverage with recent high-profile examples of transgender students competing in school sporting events in Washington.
A legal challenge to the initiative is expected.
Brian Heywood, founders of Let’s Go Washington, takes a moment alone as he watches results come in during the group’s election night party on Nov. 3, 2026, in Redmond, Washington. (Photo by Ryan Berry/Washington State Standard)
Whither Let’s Go Washington
Since Brian Heywood registered Let’s Go Washington as a political committee in 2022, he’s used his money and mouth to make it a relevant force in state politics. Five of its 10 initiatives have made it into law though Democratic lawmakers subsequently found ways to neuter two and the courts tossed another.
Tuesday they lost a big one, Initiative 645 and passed a big one as well, Initiative 638. 
Setbacks are hard. For Heywood it’s costly. The hedge fund manager has invested millions of dollars into the effort to redress what he sees as overreach in fiscal and social policy by the ruling Democratic majority. His foes hope he’s tiring and will stop. 
On Tuesday night, in front of the committee’s supporters and volunteers, Heywood didn’t sound like a millionaire throwing in the towel. He emphasized that the issues they tackle aren’t partisan but grounded in  common sense.
“We’ve tried to give a voice to those who feel like Olympia stomped on them, won’t listen to them, and they’re up against the machine,” he said. “We built an infrastructure that I think can do something that is meaningful in this state and should give people a reason not to give up.”
Translated: Let’s Go Washington isn’t going anywhere.
Andrew Barrett contributed to this report.

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Kemp won’t call Georgia lawmakers back to redraw maps or to curb executive powers
description: Outgoing Republican Gov. Brian Kemp announced Wednesday that he would not call a special session to push new political maps and curb the executive powers of future state leaders after the Democratic sweep in the 2026 midterms. “The voters of our state have spoken. As long as I’m governor, we will always respect the results […]
text:
Gov. Brian Kemp speaks on Sept. 3, 2026, at the state Capitol in Atlanta. Rocha/Georgia RecorderOutgoing Republican Gov. Brian Kemp announced Wednesday that he would not call a special session to push new political maps and curb the executive powers of future state leaders after the Democratic sweep in the 2026 midterms.
“The voters of our state have spoken. As long as I’m governor, we will always respect the results of secure, accessible, and fair elections, and also abide by the laws and constitution of our state,” Kemp said in a statement Wednesday morning. “I will not be calling a special session of the Georgia General Assembly in order to curtail executive branch powers or debate redistricting changes.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Kemp had called a special session earlier this year partly to redraw Georgia’s maps for the 2028 election after a U.S. Supreme Court ruling weakened key protections under the Voting Rights Act. Republican leaders ultimately decided against pursuing redistricting during the summer session, but they were widely expected to revisit it after the election. Kemp’s announcement Wednesday puts an end to that speculation. 
But Kemp also didn’t rule out calling a special session before Democrats take charge of most of the state’s government next year. The governor said in a statement that there are “budgetary issues that may need to be addressed before the convening of the regular session in January.”
“My office will continue to monitor and evaluate this situation and keep our partners in the General Assembly apprised of the state’s fiscal outlook in the days to come,” Kemp said.
What that means is unclear.
“Maybe it makes sense for the governor to warn that they did approve legislation that is very costly and that there wasn’t really a plan to pay for, and that is a problem that we need to address but not something that I think we need a special session for,” said Danny Kanso, vice president of public policy at Georgia Budget and Policy Institute.
Kanso was referring to an income tax cut package that the Legislature approved earlier this year. The measure cut the state’s income tax rate to 4.99% this year, down from 5.19%, and it continues to trim it over time to 3.99% if certain economic conditions are met, among other changes. Kanso called it “one of the most reckless and fiscally irresponsible pieces of legislation enacted.”
The head of the governor’s Office of Planning and Budget said in May that the bill created a $1.3 billion hole in the state’s budget. Kemp made about $300 million in cuts to help cover part of that gap.
The state currently has a surplus of $8.7 billion in rainy day funds, according to an October annual report from the State Accounting Office, down from $14.6 billion as of January.
Governor-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms, the former mayor of Atlanta, speaks to a crowd of supports at her campaign’s field office in southwest Atlanta on Nov. 4, 2026. Alander Rocha/Georgia Recorder
Governor-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms, the former mayor of Atlanta, said at a press conference Wednesday afternoon in southwest Atlanta that she had a conversation with Kemp earlier, but that the governor didn’t specify what those budget issues were.
“He just mentioned that there were some priorities that he had, which I respect,” Bottoms said. “There’s one governor at a time, so as the person who will be the governor through the first part of January, that’s certainly his prerogative to call a session to try and deal with some of those budgetary issues that he believes need to be dealt with in a special session. And again, whatever that may be, we’ll see it when it happens.”
House Minority Leader Carolyn Hugley, who could be in line to be Georgia’s next speaker, downplayed any legislative budgetary changes Republicans may do in a special session at a press conference Wednesday. The budget process is underway now, with the governor typically presenting their budget proposal in January and lawmakers leaving their imprint on the spending plan before it goes back to the governor’s desk.
“We look forward to what he is proposing, but I’m sure Gov. Bottoms will look at that and reformat that budget to match her policy objectives, and then the House will do as it always does, go to work on that budget,” Hugley said.
Democratic state Sen. Josh McLaurin, the lieutenant governor-elect, and Senate Minority Leader Harold Jones answer questions at a press conference at the state Capitol in Atlanta on Nov. 4, 2026. Alander Rocha/Georgia Recorder
Democrats did take comfort in Kemp saying he won’t pursue redistricting or curbing executive power. Democratic state Sen. Josh McLaurin, the lieutenant governor-elect, said at a press conference Wednesday afternoon that Republicans walked back their efforts to redistrict over the summer after intense backlash and that Tuesday night’s results indicated voters will continue to “resist a similar move to redraw the maps.”
“I would say that the resounding rejection of MAGA politics that you saw last night did not invite much adventurism by the Republican majority to keep drawing those maps,” McLaurin said.
Bottoms said she is “just grateful (Republicans) will not be touching the powers of the governor.”
