name: Arkansas Advocate
title: With Arkansas Republicans’ House supermajority lost, a changed dynamic
description: When Arkansans went to bed Tuesday night, Republicans were beginning to see the full scale of what amounted to historic losses. The blue wave didn’t upend statewide and federal offices or flip legislative chambers in Arkansas as it did in Texas and North Carolina. But it did break the status quo, with Republicans losing the […]
text:
Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders speaks after the conclusion of the 2026 fiscal session on April 29, 2026, with Senate President Pro Tempore-designate Breanne Davis (left) and House Speaker Brian Evans (center) listening. (Photo by Ainsley Platt/Arkansas Advocate)When Arkansans went to bed Tuesday night, Republicans were beginning to see the full scale of what amounted to historic losses.
The blue wave didn’t upend statewide and federal offices or flip legislative chambers in Arkansas as it did in Texas and North Carolina. But it did break the status quo, with Republicans losing the supermajority in the House for the first time in a decade. 
Democrats picked up at least 10 seats in the House, concentrated in Benton, Washington and Pulaski counties; plus one seat in the Senate, where Republicans still have a supermajority. Democrats saw increases in support in every county in the state in U.S. Senate and gubernatorial races, even as they lost to Republican incumbents.
The gains in the Legislature mean it will be difficult for Republicans to pass most budget bills along strictly party lines.
Appropriations bills, which authorize state agency spending, require a three-fourths vote for approval. Without a 75-vote supermajority in the House, Republicans will need Democrats for must-pass spending measures. 
That gives Democrats more leverage in discussions on the future of Arkansas’ Medicaid expansion program, school vouchers and other policy priorities that require taxpayer dollars.
It could also complicate passage of Republican Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders’ agenda next year — though she said in a statement that she looks forward to working with both parties “when priorities align.” 
Sanders has already faced discontent on both sides of the aisle with the growing cost of the voucher program — one of her signature legislative achievements in her first term — and her attempts to build a new prison. 
“Arkansas remains one of the most conservative states in the union, with wide Republican majorities in both chambers of the legislature,” said Sam Dubke, Sanders’ spokesperson.
Democrats made gains across the state Tuesday, but especially in populous Benton, Washington and Pulaski counties — though Republican House Speaker Brian Evans appeared to downplay the significance of the gains.
“The makeup of the House will be a little different in 2027 as compared to what it was in January of 2025. That could change some of the dynamics of the session,” Evans said. “What we have here is 100 people who represent 100 diverse districts across the state, and we all know what the issues in our state are,” such as Medicaid and maternal health.
Speaking to the Arkansas Advocate in his office at the Capitol, Evans acknowledged the legislative reality that losing 10 seats creates for his party going into next year. Still, the Cabot lawmaker said when it comes to “good policy,” Democrats and Republicans “typically do find common ground.” Republicans still hold a solid majority in the House to pass non-appropriations bills.
“We saw people all across the country that are not happy, whether they’re Republicans, or Democrats, or independents, or any other party,” Evans said. “They are not happy, in their household, where our economy is, and they took their voice to the polls and they looked for change.”
But former Republican Gov. Asa Hutchinson, Sanders’ predecessor, said the losses could not go ignored by the state party.
“I think it’s a reminder that we need to make sure that it’s an Arkansas-oriented campaign,” said Hutchinson, who challenged Trump for the GOP nomination for president in 2024. “The national implications of Donald Trump’s negatives impacted it all the way down to the (justice of the peace) level in our state.”
Hutchinson said that effective fiscal lawmaking during next year’s session will require bipartisanship.
“It’s going to be a different type of session,” Hutchinson said. 
Robert Coon, a Republican campaign consultant and strategist, agreed with Evans’ assessment on affordability. Coon also attributed the losses in traditionally Republican territory to the northwest region’s growing population and independent voters forgoing their usual affiliation with the state GOP — as well as a deeply unpopular president.
“Tip O’Neill famously said ‘All politics is local,’ but this– it’s not,” Coon said. “When the president is immensely unpopular, and that’s what people are paying attention to, that is going to have an effect downstream.”
Coons said Democrats should still be cautious about using their newfound leverage too liberally. 
“You can easily overplay that,” he said.

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: After staggering legislative upset, Democrats and Republicans process a new reality in Concord
description: Rep. Alissandra Murray long assumed Democrats would take back the New Hampshire House this year. But it wasn’t until the Manchester Democrat saw the results of their own race Tuesday that they realized how big a night might lie in store.  Murray’s purple, two-seat district is typically shared with a Republican. But as the results […]
text:
Voters cast their ballots at Winnisquam Regional High School in Tilton during the Nov. 3, 2026, midterm elections. (Photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)Rep. Alissandra Murray long assumed Democrats would take back the New Hampshire House this year. But it wasn’t until the Manchester Democrat saw the results of their own race Tuesday that they realized how big a night might lie in store. 
Murray’s purple, two-seat district is typically shared with a Republican. But as the results came in, it became clear no Republican would be winning the second seat. 
Then came the reports from Rochester of Democratic gains in Republican areas. 
Then the trickle of defeats of well-known Republican lawmakers — from Reps. Ross Berry of Weare to Kristin Noble of Bedford. 
Then the news that Republican House Speaker Sherman Packard lost his seat by 0.6%.
“I honestly was speechless for a couple hours,” Murray said Wednesday. 
By Wednesday morning, House Democrats looked set to not just take back the chamber but to clear a two-thirds supermajority; a preliminary estimate by the House clerk counted 291 Democrats, 108 Republicans, and one independent representative, though those totals could change after recounts. 
Senate Democrats were on track to win either 15 or 16 seats in the 24-seat Senate, pending a potential recount in District 8, which was narrowly won by Republican Jim Creighton. And Democrats won all five seats on the Executive Council, wiping out Republicans’ current 4-1 majority. 
In a span of hours, the staggering scale of victory changed how Murray and other Democrats are looking at the next two years.
“I hadn’t filed any of my legislation during the first filing period (in September) because I wanted to know the context of the State House before I decided what legislation I wanted to prioritize,” Murray said. “And these results completely changed what I thought was possible.”
From left, Rep. Laura Telerski, of Nashua; Senate Minority Leader Rebecca Perkins Kwoka, of Portsmouth; House Democratic Leader Alexis Simpson, of Exeter; and New Hampshire Democratic Party Chairman Ray Buckley hold a press conference to denounce the Republican budget June 26, 2025. (Photo by Ethan DeWitt/New Hampshire Bulletin)
Still processing
Democratic and Republican lawmakers are still processing the significance of Tuesday night’s seismic upheaval, which saw Republican Gov. Kelly Ayotte keep her seat but Democrats reverse six years of Republican legislative majorities.
“I did not expect a historic majority like this,” said House Democratic Leader Alexis Simpson, who announced Wednesday she would mount a campaign to become House speaker next session. “We have never had this many Democrats elected.” 
In interviews and statements, Republicans have run the gamut of emotions, from despair over the direction of the state to exasperation at President Donald Trump and national forces like higher gas and food prices, to open frustration with New Hampshire Republican leaders.
Democrats are elated, but appeared to still be considering the implications of the win. Simpson and Senate Minority Leader Rebecca Perkins Kwoka said Wednesday they were still taking in the size of the majorities and assessing their legislative priorities. 
“We’ll think about that as we’re getting our agenda together,” said Perkins Kwoka, a Portsmouth Democrat who could be Senate president when the new Legislature takes power next year.  
“But in general, we have brought what we view as common-sense solutions over the last two years, and those are not yet lost,” she added, mentioning efforts to lower housing costs, childcare costs, and property taxes. “So those are the ideas we’re certainly going to start with.” 
Perkins Kwoka said the Democratic caucus will meet soon to assess its priorities and strategy given the large majority. 
Simpson, of Exeter, echoed that response.
“It really doesn’t change our agenda,” she said of the House Democratic supermajority. “We were focused on a future where we lead with integrity and life is affordable, not just for us, but also for our kids, for our neighbors’ children.”
But Murray, a longtime member of the House Criminal Justice and Public Safety Committee, has some specific ideas of what Democrats can aim for with their new majorities. Murray hopes to reverse a recent Republican law allowing landlords to evict tenants without a specific cause, advance LGBTQ+ protections, push for more aggressive housing, and potentially restore the interest and dividends tax, which Republicans repealed in 2021. 
The Democratic majorities could also give Democrats and libertarian-leaning Republicans a long-sought goal, Murray says: a cannabis legalization bill that can survive Ayotte’s veto. 
“I see a lot of us really going to bat for that,” Murray said. “And I know that she’s not interested in having that conversation, but we’re going to bring it to her because that’s what the people want us to do.”
Republican frustrations
The Democratic victories swept away a number of long-serving Republicans in both chambers, and prompted a cascade of social media posts from Republicans diagnosing the losses.
Among the notable House casualties were Reps. Berry, Noble, Erica Layon of Derry, Sam Farrington of Rochester, and Jennifer Rhodes of Winchester. 
Republican Sens. Tim Lang, of Sanbornton, James Gray of Rochester, Dan Innis of Bradford, Denise Ricciardi of Bedford, Kevin Avard of Nashua, Tim McGough of Merrimack, and Victoria Sullivan of Manchester also lost their seats.
“The voters have spoken, and I respect their decision,” Packard said in a statement reacting to his loss. 
“I’m looking forward to some well-earned time off,” he added. “But first, I’m committed to ensuring a smooth and orderly transition for whoever is chosen to lead the House in a new term.”
On the social media website X, some Republicans pointed to national economic factors animating voters.
“Omg how did we ever lose?” wrote Berry alongside a picture of a gas pump with a $125.42 bill. 
Rep. Mike Belcher, a Wakefield Republican who kept his seat, argued voters had rejected Republicans’ calls to “rationally accept short-term financial pain” to support the war in Iran.
But other Republicans thought New Hampshire leaders shared the blame.  
Late Tuesday night, Rep. David Lundgren paced in the lobby of the Artisan Hotel at the Tuscan Village in Salem — the site of Ayotte’s results party — calling up fellow House members one by one.
“Did they get you too?” he asked one colleague.
Lundgren, a Londonderry Republican, served last session as part of the town’s seven-member group of Republicans that included Packard and former New Hampshire Republican Chairman Wayne MacDonald. 
On Tuesday night, Democrats pushed out all Republicans in Londonderry except Lundgren, who hung on by fewer than 200 votes. 
Now the lone survivor, Lundgren said House Majority Leader Jason Osborne and other top Republicans bore responsibility. 
“Personally I thought we’d lose the House,” he said. “And it’s because of the extreme far right in leadership.”
Lundgren pointed back to a more collegial time years ago when Democrats and Republicans sat interspersed in the House chamber, a practice that ended in 2017, when House Speaker Shawn Jasper separated the chamber by party. 
“I went (to the House) to begin with 20 years ago to build bridges,” he said. 
To Lundgren, a cascade of harsh, pugilistic rhetoric against Democrats from Republican leaders in the last decade hurt the party’s leadership. “I just didn’t like the way they ran the show,” he said.
House Republican leaders’ uncompromising tactics did not just extend to Democrats, Lundgren said. They were also directed at members of their own party. “We used to make a joke that Democrats never fight with each other,” he said. “Republicans are ready to cut people’s throats.” 
Now, Lundgren is worried House Democrats might turn those same tactics against House Republicans. He has already noticed that where many House Democrats were once open to friendly conversations with Republicans, that amiability has decreased.
“If you take today’s Democrats and try to have a discussion, they talk over you,” he said. “They don’t listen to you.” 
Republican Sen. Bill Gannon of Sandown, who won his reelection, also took issue with some of the bombastic rhetoric from leaders in the House. He took particular issue with a monthslong campaign by House Republicans to champion school district tax caps as a way to punish Democrats for overspending. 
“We come out too hard,” Gannon argued Tuesday night. 
Sen. Daryl Abbas, a Salem Republican who also won reelection, was less critical. The Senate is more decentralized on messaging than the House, and the Republican candidates who lost each ran hard-fought campaigns, Abbas argued. 
Instead, Abbas had a different conclusion from the election. New Hampshire Democrats who won majorities on the issue of affordability should be careful what they wish for, he said.
“Anyone who’s campaigning that they’re going to lower your fuel costs, that they’re going to lower your property taxes, they know damn well that they can’t deliver on that,” he said. “Do you think if we could lower the cost of fuel, we wouldn’t have already done that?”
Gov. Kelly Ayotte addresses supporters in Salem, an hour before the Associated Press declared she had won reelection, Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Ethan DeWitt, New Hampshire Bulletin)
Democrats vs. Ayotte
The strong majorities give Democrats significant influence over the state’s two-year budget, which must be passed by July 2027. They could also allow Democrats to advance constitutional amendments to the 2028 general election ballot, which require 60% support in both the House and Senate to appear on the ballot. 
How Democrats wield that power — and how aggressively they approach their relationship with Ayotte — remains to be seen. 
They could attempt to negotiate with Ayotte. Without a 16-seat veto-proof majority in the Senate, they would need the support of the governor or at least one Republican senator to get anything passed into law. 
If Democrats wanted to be aggressive, they could attempt to use the state budget, which must be approved by both the House and Senate, and the governor. 
In recent years, conservative Republicans have attached legislation to the state budget to force a moderate governor to accept policies they might otherwise veto. Most notably, in 2021, Republican lawmakers used the budget to force into law a 24-week abortion ban and a “banned concepts” teaching restriction law. Then-Gov. Chris Sununu had publicly opposed both policies before they passed, but signed the budget enacting them anyway, arguing it was necessary for stability.
On Wednesday, neither Simpson nor Perkins Kwoka commented directly on how forcefully they would use their majorities. 
“I think that for the good of government being a place where problems can get solved, it’s important to run the chamber in a way that allows for full discussion, that rewards hard work and compromise,” said Perkins Kwoka. 
But Simpson noted that whatever happens during budget negotiations, the scale of her caucus — which could be 291 members — meant Democratic leadership would have to be careful to listen to all members in their tent.
“What’s most important to us is that the people who are elected to represent their communities are listening to one another within our caucus, and that our legislation that we file and our agenda that we pursue reflects that,” she said.
For her part, Ayotte did not mention the legislative results during her brief remarks Tuesday night. In a statement Wednesday, the governor did not mention the Democratic victories. 
“I promise to work tirelessly to ensure that we defend the New Hampshire Advantage and keep working to solve our housing crisis, make childcare more affordable, and bring down energy prices,” Ayotte wrote Wednesday.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Arkansas accuses prediction market, online gaming platform of operating illegal gambling
description: Arkansas filed lawsuits Wednesday against online prediction market Kalshi and an Australian company operating an online “sweepstakes casino,” accusing them of running illegal gambling operations. Attorney General Tim Griffin filed the lawsuits against Kalshi and VGW, an online gaming platform that features such games as Chumba Casino, LuckyLand Casino, Lucky[...]
text:
(Getty Images)Arkansas filed lawsuits Wednesday against online prediction market Kalshi and an Australian company operating an online “sweepstakes casino,” accusing them of running illegal gambling operations.
Attorney General Tim Griffin filed the lawsuits against Kalshi and VGW, an online gaming platform that features such games as Chumba Casino, LuckyLand Casino, LuckyLand Slots, and Global Poker.
The lawsuit against Kalshi, filed in Independence County, is the latest in a wave of actions states have taken accusing the online prediction market operator of skirting anti-gambling laws.
“It doesn’t take a genius to understand that wagering money on whether the Razorbacks win or lose is gambling,” Griffin said in a news release. “And gambling on an unregulated platform is squarely prohibited by Arkansas law.”
A spokesperson for Kalshi did not immediately respond to an email late Wednesday afternoon.
In the complaint, Griffin’s office accuses Kalshi of operating a “pocket-sized bookie” and ignoring the legal restrictions for casinos and sports betting in Arkansas by allowing users as young as 18 years old to wager real money on sporting and entertainment events.
“This action seeks to hold Kalshi accountable for operating outside the bounds of Arkansas law while exposing Arkansas consumers to the very harms that Arkansas’ gambling laws were enacted to prevent,” the lawsuit said.
Kalshi leads prediction markets’ $3 million effort to fight off state regulations

In the Kalshi suit, Griffin asked a judge to declare that the company violated the state’s deceptive trade practices act and to award restitution. 
Griffin’s office made similar complaints against VGW in a lawsuit filed in White County over the company operating websites that allow consumers to play slot machines, blackjack, poker and other casino games for real money. 
VGW did not immediately respond to an email seeking comment Wednesday.
According to Griffin’s lawsuit, VGW’s sites allow users to wager “Sweeps Coins” that can ultimately be redeemed for cash, similar to poker chips.
“While masquerading as a free sweepstakes, defendants accepted money from Arkansans, provided them the means to gamble, and paid out winnings in cash and other prizes,” the lawsuit said.
VGW has faced complaints from other states and earlier this year paid $8 million to New York regulators following a cease-and-desist letter from that state’s attorney general.
Griffin’s suit against VGW seeks to have civil penalties levied against the company and for it to pay restitution to consumers.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Iowa’s voter turnout broke records for midterm elections
description: Iowa voters broke midterm turnout records in the general election Tuesday, with more than 1,380,528 residents casting their ballots. Iowa Secretary of State Paul Pate told reporters Wednesday the 2026 general election was “the largest midterm in three decades here in Iowa” in voter turnout. This year’s election fell slightly short of the turnout in […]
text:
Iowa Secretary of State Paul Pate held a news conference Nov. 4, 2026 discussing voter turnout in the 2026 midterm elections. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)Iowa voters broke midterm turnout records in the general election Tuesday, with more than 1,380,528 residents casting their ballots.
Iowa Secretary of State Paul Pate told reporters Wednesday the 2026 general election was “the largest midterm in three decades here in Iowa” in voter turnout. This year’s election fell slightly short of the turnout in 1990 — a year when 63.47% of registered voters cast ballots, in comparison to 2026, when preliminary reports show a participation rate of 63.34%. But it surpassed the previous record for the most votes cast, beating the total of 1,329,930 votes during the 2018 midterms.
The 2018 and 2026 election cycles share similarities, coming as midterm cycles during President Donald Trump’s first and second terms in office, and resulting in major Democratic victories across the state.
Democrats clawed back power in many races in Iowa in the 2026 midterm election. Voters elected Rob Sand as governor, according to preliminary results, as well as Josh Turek as U.S. senator. Three of the state’s four congressional districts will be represented by a Democrat in January, a major shift from Iowa’s current all-GOP federal delegation. Democratic challenger Nate Willems also defeated incumbent Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird for the statewide elected office, and Taylor Wettach was leading in the open race for auditor.
Pate, who won his own reelection campaign as an incumbent Republican, said Tuesday’s results are a reflection both of national trends that favored Democrats this election cycle, as well as high engagement among Iowa voters. Though there were Democratic victories, Pate said some of Iowa’s election results show that voters were not necessarily voting one party in the election, as Republicans retained majorities in both state legislative chambers.
“You didn’t see a big ticket thing here,” Pate said. “I don’t think it was a Democrat wave or a Republican wave. This was a wave based on the candidates and their messaging. So we’ll watch and see how it unfolds over the next two years.”
In addition to high turnout overall, Pate said Iowa saw a major rise in early voting this election cycle, particularly for in-person early voting, rather than mailed absentee ballots. He said he believed higher early voting rates were in part driven by concerns about the voting process in 2026. President Donald Trump had moved earlier this year to restrict mail ballots sent through the U.S. Postal Service, and some were concerned about the deployment of U.S. Department of Justice election monitors on Election Day — but he also said he expects to continue to see high early turnout.
Moving forward, Pate said he was advocating for lengthening the early voting window by five days, a move he said was necessary to give county auditors needed time to prepare mailed absentee ballots.
But he also said there were several internal and logistical changes he and county auditors plan to work on to prevent hourslong lines some early voters faced when they went to cast their ballot before Nov. 3. These changes could include adding more satellite voting locations.
“The (early voting) trending is definitely there, and I think it’s gonna be here for a while,” Pate said. “So again, we’ll be having a lot of conversations. I will be visiting with the auditors to discuss what things we should do to improve the process. That will be starting yet in December, so we’re ready for the Legislature in January, if we need to change new laws to allow us to do it.”

First lady Melania Trump greets student presenters at the Presidential Artificial Intelligence Challenge National Champion Awards on June 9, 2026, on the Blue Room Balcony of the White House.(Official White House photo by Andrea Hanks)First lady Melania Trump will attend LSU’s football game Saturday to announce an endowment to the university that will support students from the foster care system. 
Trump said she will launch the “Fostering the Future” campaign during the Tigers’ matchup against the Alabama Crimson Tide. It features a $5 million permanent endowment for LSU to fund scholarships. 
“Every young person deserves the opportunity to build a bright future, and this $5 million investment helps make that possible for students who have experienced foster care,” state Department of Children and Family Services Secretary Rebecca Harris said in a statement. “I’m grateful to first lady Melania Trump and LSU for investing in Louisiana’s children and creating opportunities that can make a lasting difference in their lives. This is what it looks like when we come together to put children first.”
LSU Chancellor Jim Dalton has been a vocal proponent of fostering and is a foster parent himself, according to a DCFS social media post earlier this year. 
Some 4,300 children are in the state foster care system, according to DCFS figures. Nationally, 20% to 30% of foster youth head directly to college after graduating high school, according to the Annie E. Casey Foundation. The rate increases past 60% when counting those who enroll later.
LSU spokeswoman Meg Sunstrom said fans should plan ahead for increased traffic and security for the 2:30 p.m. kickoff.

title: Indiana House Republicans pick new leader after big election losses
description: The Republican lawmaker who led the Indiana congressional redistricting push last year was picked Wednesday as the next leader for the state House of Representatives. A drastically reduced Republican House majority elected Rep. Ben Smaltz of Auburn as speaker-elect — a day after House Speaker Todd Huston lost reelection and Democrats picked up an apparent […[...]
text:
Rep. Ben Smaltz, R-Auburn, speaks with reporters after his selection as Indiana House speaker-elect during a private meeting of House Republicans at the Statehouse on Wednesday, Nov. 4, 2026. (Photo by Tom Davies/Indiana Capital Chronicle)The Republican lawmaker who led the Indiana congressional redistricting push last year was picked Wednesday as the next leader for the state House of Representatives.
A drastically reduced Republican House majority elected Rep. Ben Smaltz of Auburn as speaker-elect — a day after House Speaker Todd Huston lost reelection and Democrats picked up an apparent 16 seats in the chamber.


Senate leadership change
Indiana Senate Republicans confirmed their pick of Sen. Chris Garten as the chamber’s next president pro tem — a day after Democrats chopped five seats from the GOP’s majority.
Republican senators had endorsed Garten in August as their pick to replace Sen. Rodric Bray as the chamber’s top leader.
An announcement from Senate Republicans said Garten’s selection on Wednesday was unanimous. The private vote followed Garten, of Charlestown, winning election on Tuesday to a third term.
Republican senators also voted to make Sen. Tyler Johnson of Leo the new majority caucus chairman. He replaces Sen. Travis Holdman, who was defeated in the May primary.


That election outcome ends the two-thirds supermajority House control Republicans held since the 2012 elections and reduces what was a 70-30 GOP margin to an expected 54-46.
Smaltz emerged from a 3-½ hour private meeting of House Republicans indicating they would still set the legislative agenda.
“We have a good working relationship with the Democrats. I always have had that,” Smaltz told reporters. “We’re still in the majority. We’re still going to operate like a body in the majority.”
Smaltz called Tuesday’s election results “terribly disappointing” for legislative Republicans and pointed to “a lot of national headwinds that we are dealing with.”
“We’re going to be committed to doing what we are sent here to do,” he said. “We’re sent here by the Hoosiers that want a better life, that want things to be affordable, and that want high-paying jobs, that want a strong economy. And we’re going to focus on that.”
Along with Smaltz in top House positions, Rep. Matt Lehman of Berne will continue as majority leader. Rep. Jake Teshka of North Liberty was picked as majority caucus chair, replacing Rep. Greg Steuerwald of Avon after he also lost his reelection bid.
House Democrats were jubilant with their sizable gains, which gave them their most House seats since they lost the majority with the 2010 elections.
Democratic Leader Phil GiaQuinta of Fort Wayne said Wednesday they would now have “more leverage” on legislation and hoped to see Republicans reaching across the aisle rather than working “on the extremes.”
“When it comes to figuring out ways to lower costs for utilities, healthcare, funding of our schools, and things like that, I do think that we’re going to work together to get that stuff done,” he said. “I also think it’s probably, frankly, a wake-up call that this is what Hoosiers want. So it’s time to come together to work to get things done.”
Smaltz is poised to be formally elected as speaker during the Legislature’s Organization Day on Nov. 17 ahead of the next session beginning in early January.
The House speaker presides over the chamber’s floor sessions, but also appoints committee chairs and leads the party’s legislative agenda.
House Democrat Leader Phil GiaQuinta, of Fort Wayne, speaks to reporters on Nov. 4, 2026, at the Indiana Statehouse after major wins for his caucus. (Photo by Niki Kelly/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
Smaltz was first elected to the House in 2012 — so he has never served in the chamber without a Republican supermajority allowing them to take action even if  Democrats were not present.
Smaltz was a top lieutenant to Huston as the House Rules Committee chair for the past four years. He previously spent six years as leader of the House Public Policy Committee, which prominently handles gambling and alcohol-related legislation.
Smaltz was in the middle of last year’s Republican push to follow President Donald Trump’s call for mid-decade congressional redistricting in hopes of improving the GOP’s chances of holding its U.S. House majority.
He was the House author of the bill redrawing Indiana’s congressional maps that included carving up two Democratic-held districts with the aim of engineering a 9-0 Republican sweep of the state’s seats.
He acknowledged the proposed districts as “politically gerrymandered” as the plan cleared the House over unanimous Democratic objections.
The proposal failed in the Senate, leading to Trump supporting a political revenge campaign against Republican senators who voted against the plan. 
Smaltz said Wednesday that the success of cooperation rested with the Democrats.
Rep. Joanna King speaks on the phone in the Indiana Statehouse before a private meeting of the House Republican caucus on Wednesday, Nov. 4, 2026. (Photo by Tom Davies/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
“That’s going to be up to them,” he said. “I mean, they’re going to have to accept us for who we are and we’re going to accept them for who they are.”
When asked whether congressional redistricting could return as an issue for the next legislative session, Smaltz replied: “I’m not sure that’s an issue that’s important to Hoosiers right now, and we’re focused on doing what’s important for them.”



Legislative flips
Democrats have gained at least 16 Indiana House and five Indiana Senate seats from preliminary election tallies.
If those results hold, Republican majorities would fall to 54-46 in the House and 35-15 in the Senate.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Former Arkansas Gov. Asa Hutchinson: Election shows consequences of ‘chaos’ under Trump
description: Former Arkansas Gov. Asa Hutchinson said Wednesday that Republicans’ widespread losses in the midterm elections show that the party needs to get back to focusing on issues that matter to voters. Hutchinson, a Republican who served two terms as governor and unsuccessfully ran for the GOP presidential nomination in 2024, said his party needs to […]
text:
Former Arkansas Gov. Asa Hutchinson attends the Republican Watch Party on Tuesday, November 3, 2026 in North Little Rock, Arkansas. (Photo by Katie Adkins/Arkansas Advocate)Former Arkansas Gov. Asa Hutchinson said Wednesday that Republicans’ widespread losses in the midterm elections show that the party needs to get back to focusing on issues that matter to voters.
Hutchinson, a Republican who served two terms as governor and unsuccessfully ran for the GOP presidential nomination in 2024, said his party needs to understand voters’ frustration with the “chaos” that’s being created by President Donald Trump. Republicans need to show a level of independence from Trump, Hutchinson said.
“(The election) shows that there’s an independent streak among the voters and the Republican Party has lost its identity to a certain extent,” the former Republican governor and congressman told the Arkansas Advocate in a phone interview. “The Republican Party has always been trusted on economic issues, on crime and security and on America leading national defense issues. And we’ve lost the confidence of the voters on some of those issues.”
Democrats won control of the U.S. House and Senate and a majority of governorships in Tuesday’s election, in what was widely seen as a rebuke to Trump.
Hutchinson said Trump hurt the party with his fixation on things like the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, building a new 250-foot triumphal arch in Washington and complaints about not winning the Nobel Peace Prize rather than focusing on issues like diesel fuel prices.
“When President Trump is right on policies such as securing the border, he ought to be supported on it,” Hutchinson said. “But you know the chaos and the concentration on issues that are not important to average Americans has consequences, and that’s what we see in the election results.”
In Arkansas, Democrats did not claim the governor’s office or a U.S. Senate seat. But the party broke Republicans’ House supermajority for the first time in a decade.
Hutchinson said his successor Republican Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders’ victory in the political environment was a “significant affirmation” but said the Democrats’ gains show both parties will have to work together.
“You can’t pass appropriations bills without some Democrat support, so it’s going to be a different type of session,” Hutchinson said. “I hope that it keeps Arkansas different from Washington, D.C.-style politics.”

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Democrats claim supermajorities in Colorado state House and Senate
description: Democrats will hold supermajorities in both chambers of the Colorado Legislature after they flipped one seat in the state Senate and up to six in the state House, according to preliminary election results and statements by Democratic state leaders. Democrats expect to have a 24-11 majority in the Senate and a 49-16 majority in the […]
text:
Outgoing Colorado House Speaker Julie McCluskie, surrounded by other Democrats in the Colorado Legislature, speaks during an election night watch party at Mission Ballroom in Denver on Tuesday. (Photo by Andrew Fraieli/Colorado Newsline)Democrats will hold supermajorities in both chambers of the Colorado Legislature after they flipped one seat in the state Senate and up to six in the state House, according to preliminary election results and statements by Democratic state leaders.
Democrats expect to have a 24-11 majority in the Senate and a 49-16 majority in the House. Combined with a Democratic governor, that gives the party a lot of power to enact its agenda.
Douglas County Democrat Kevin Leung declared victory on Wednesday afternoon in Senate District 30 when he led incumbent Republican Rep. John Carson with 52.5% of the vote. The Associated Press had not called the race by the time of publication. Republican-backed groups spent millions of dollars to defend the district, especially in October as the race narrowed.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“Outside groups spent millions trying to keep this seat, but our volunteers kept showing up,” Leung said in a statement. “To everyone who gave up a Saturday to walk one more block, and to every neighbor who opened the door and heard us out, thank you. You won this race.”
Democrats also maintained seats and beat heavily-funded Republicans in other Senate districts. Aaron Gutierrez beat Republican Dana Charles with 54.4% of the vote in Pueblo’s Senate District 3. Sen. Janice Marchman of Loveland defeated former Republican Sen. Rob Woodward in Senate District 15 by 16 points. And, though the AP has not officially called it, Sen. Tony Exum looks likely to beat Republican Levon Stilson in the Colorado Springs-based Senate District 11. Exum had 61% of the vote as of Wednesday afternoon.
In a Facebook post, Charles said she congratulated Gutierrez and wrote that she has “every confidence that he will remain committed to putting Pueblo at the forefront, and I look forward to helping him in any way I possibly can.”
Three flips
In the House, Democrats were on track to flip six seats as of Wednesday afternoon. That includes races that brought a lot of attention and money, such as a rematch in a Weld County district, and two seats in Colorado Springs that flew mostly under the radar.
The party won back three seats that Republicans flipped in 2024. Democrat Jillaire McMillan beat Republican Rep. Dan Woog in Weld County’s House District 19 with almost 60% of the vote. In House District 16, Steph Vigil won back her seat against Republican Jill Haffley with 57.3% of the vote. And in House District 50, former Greeley City Council member Tommy Butler has 60% of the vote and is poised to defeat Republican Rep. Ryan Gonzalez. The AP has not called that race.
“My team and I are going to try to get a little rest tomorrow, perhaps, and then we have work to do for the upcoming legislative session. Thank you, thank you, thank you to this beloved community — I’m excited to get back in there,” Vigil posted on Facebook on election night.
From left, Colorado state Reps. Naquetta Ricks, Gretchen Rydin, and Monica Duran, listen to speakers during an election night watch party for Democrats at Mission Ballroom in Denver on Tuesday. (Photo by Andrew Fraieli/Colorado Newsline)
Gonzalez also weighed in, posting on X, “Mr. President, you would be more effective if you would just shut the f*** up.” While President Donald Trump was not active in Colorado’s statehouse races, he was outspoken in many of the races that ended up going to Democrats on Election Day and told voters to act like he was on the ballot.
Democrats also look likely to flip House District 51, with former Loveland Mayor Jacki Marsh leading Republican Amy Parks by about 5 points. In House District 15 in Colorado Springs, unofficial results show Democrat Jeff Livingston ahead of Pricilla Tiegen by about 600 votes. Whoever wins will replace outgoing Republican Rep. Scott Bottoms, one of the most conservative members of the Legislature, who lost a primary run for governor this year. Democrat Michelle Tweed is leading Republican Brenda Miller 50.7% to 49.3% in House District 21, which is currently represented by Republican Rep. Mary Bradfield of Colorado Springs.
Leadership elections
The new Democratic caucuses in each chamber will select their leadership this week. As a supermajority — with at least two-thirds control — the party can put constitutional amendments on the ballot and override vetoes from the governor if they are united. That sets Democrats up to try again on bills outgoing Gov. Jared Polis has vetoed, including labor union election reform and creating a civil cause of action against federal immigration agents. It also further dilutes Republican membership on the committees that bills must pass through before getting a floor vote.
“In Colorado, Democrats get things done,” House Speaker Julie McCluskie, a Dillon Democrat who is term-limited and won’t be returning to the Legislature next year, said at the Colorado Democratic watch party Tuesday night. “We have secured a future where everyone can realize their Colorado dream.”

title: Democrats will retain control of Maine Legislature, expanding power in House
description: Democrats will retain their trifecta of control in Augusta for another term following victories in several legislative districts previously held by Republicans. The party’s victory is part of a national wave of candidates gaining power in areas previously held by Republicans in response to economic woes and President Donald Trump’s declining popularity. Thou[...]
text:
Maine House of Representatives Speaker Ryan Fecteau addresses supporters at the Democrat's election night watch party in Portland. (Photo by Jim Neuger/ Maine Morning Star)Democrats will retain their trifecta of control in Augusta for another term following victories in several legislative districts previously held by Republicans.
The party’s victory is part of a national wave of candidates gaining power in areas previously held by Republicans in response to economic woes and President Donald Trump’s declining popularity.
Though not all races have been called as of 6 p.m. Wednesday, Democrats have secured a majority by winning in at least 18 Senate races and 79 in the House of Representatives, according to The Associated Press. 
A Maine Morning Star analysis of results from the Bangor Daily News — which gathered totals from municipalities and partnered with Decision Desk HQ to make the calls — found several House and Senate districts where Democrats had captured seats formerly held by Republicans. A couple districts were also flipped by Republicans and independents.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
That included 10 districts in the Maine House of Representatives — including in Sanford, Windham and Auburn — that Democrats are on track to win, nine of which have been called by the BDN. Republicans captured one seat in Lewiston, and Clinton Collamore, a former Democratic state representative, will likely turn his Waldoboro-area district from Republican to independent. 
At a Democratic victory party in Portland, House Speaker Ryan Fecteau highlighted the Auburn seat, called for Democrat Pamela Hart and previously held by Republican Rep. Laurel Libby, who rose to national prominence after she was punished by Fecteau for doxxing a transgender high school athlete on her legislative social media account. Libby chose not to run for re-election, focusing instead on her conservative advocacy organization, Lead Maine.
“I’ll be the first to welcome Laurel Libby as having to be represented by a Democrat now,” he said. “I just want Laurel to know she’s going to be represented really well, and that’s because when Democrats get elected, we serve everyone.”
Legislative Republicans did not respond to a request for comment.
Senate Democrats flipped four seats, beating two incumbent GOP senators: Scott Cyrway from Benton and Bruce Bickford from Auburn. Both were among the most hotly contested races with the most outside spending. Independent Sen. Rick Bennett, who ran for governor, will be replaced by Democrat Elizabeth Bosworth, turning a district that Bennett held for several years before he unenrolled from the Republican Party in 2025. 
On Wednesday morning, several Southern Maine legislators joined incoming Democratic Gov. Hannah Pingree at a press conference in Portland, during which she highlighted the work they aim to tackle together. 
“Legislating is a team sport, and you have to work together with a group of people to get things done,” said Democratic Rep. Traci Gere from Kennebunkport. “And we’re so lucky now… to have more numbers, more people to work on that team.”
Gere, who co-chaired the Legislature’s Housing and Economic Development Committee, said she particularly appreciated Pingree’s experience and commitment to working on affordable housing. 
“When you look at the affordability issues, housing costs make up the majority of everyone’s budget,” she said. “If we can really address housing costs, that will help relieve pressure for families all across the state.”
Sen. Jill Duson from Portland said maintaining the legislative majority  “is an opportunity and a challenge.” 
“The important thing for us to do right away is figure out how we’re going to govern, how we’re going to bring it home for Maine people,” she said.
“I’m just so damn excited and nervous because we got a big job ahead of us, but we’ll work together and make it happen.”
Pingree and the Democrat-led Legislature face a projected gap of more than $1 billion in the first two-year budget that they may be tasked with closing. Republicans had tried to make growth of the state budget a campaign issue, but Democrats pushed back, noting that it has corresponded with the state finally meeting its statutory obligations, including municipal revenue sharing to lower tax rates and funding 55% of education, as well as reducing the number of uninsured people.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Commentary: Nerding the numbers: These 7 parishes propelled Julia Letlow to victory
description: There are two things I look forward to ahead of Election Day, and both involve an intense passion for fine details. One is the obligatory newsroom pizza binge, and God help the soul who takes liberties with ordering. It’s not the time to go rogue with an artisan crust or bespoke toppings. The other eagerly […]
text:
U.S. Sen.-elect Julia Letlow, R-Baton Rouge, speaks with reporters at her victory party Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026, at the University of Louisiana at Monroe. She narrowly defeated Democrat Jamie Davis. (Photo by Julie O'Donoghue/Louisiana Illuminator)There are two things I look forward to ahead of Election Day, and both involve an intense passion for fine details.
One is the obligatory newsroom pizza binge, and God help the soul who takes liberties with ordering. It’s not the time to go rogue with an artisan crust or bespoke toppings.
The other eagerly anticipated element is a post-election, nerd-mode exploration of the numbers behind the results. Each election cycle births enough data to sustain weeks of analysis from geeks like me.
For the purposes of this breakdown, we’re going to drill down into how Republican U.S. Sen.-elect Julia Letlow eked out a win against the aggressive ground game of Democrat Jamie Davis. Her 25,857-vote margin of victory, less than 2% of the total vote, hinged on strong performances in the following parishes:
St. Tammany
Most people sleep on the fact that St. Tammany, a dependable Republican base for decades, is the state’s fourth-most populous parish. Letlow received 63% support here, almost 64,000 votes. That was 26,000 more than Davis. 

Davis’ biggest win margins

Orleans: 101,879
East Baton Rouge: 43,639
Caddo: 12,833
Jefferson: 9,739
St. John the Baptist: 6,674



It’s also not far off what GOP U.S. Sen. John Kennedy received in his home parish for his 2022 re-election bid. Kennedy exceeded 68,000 votes to win outright in an open primary against a weak field.    
Tuesday’s total for Letlow was also considerably higher than what Republicans in the 2023 governor’s race pulled from St. Tammany. That ballot featured frontrunner Jeff Landry and two GOP candidates from the parish — state Sen. Sharon Hewitt and Treasurer John Schroder — and all three combined received about 16,000 votes less than Letlow did this week.
Livingston
The ninth largest parish in the state also has a strong conservative track record in elections, and it provided Letlow with one of her largest margins of victory on the night — 73%. She came close to beating Davis by 20,000 votes here. 
By comparison, Landry received 68% support in Livingston when he won the governor’s race outright in the October 2023 open primary.
Lafayette 
Landry easily carried his home parish in 2023 with 61% support, totaling more than 35,000 votes. Even though Letlow only received 55% of the vote Tuesday, her vote total was more than 8,000 more than the governor’s count three years ago. 
She also collected 3,000 more votes than all Republicans in the most recent governor’s race combined.
Ouachita
The Monroe-area was Letlow’s longtime home before she moved her family last year to Baton Rouge, parts of which were added to her 5th Congressional District in a 2024 redrawing. Most of her academic career before entering politics was spent at the University of Louisiana at Monroe.
Those roots proved valuable on Election Day, when Ouachita Parish delivered 25,451 votes for Letlow. Davis trailed her by 4,600. 
Calcasieu
One of Letlow’s more resounding wins was in Calcasieu Parish, where she pulled in 59% of the vote. Davis finished nearly 11,000 votes behind her. 
The 33,195 votes Letlow garnered were 11,000 more than Landry received in 2023, when Lake Charles attorney Hunter Lundy, an independent, was in the governor’s race. 
Vermilion
Vermilion is a rather small parish that’s been making a lot of big news. SpaceX is moving ahead with plans for a $100 billion spaceport on Pecan Island, and this was the first major election involving a candidate with President Donald Trump’s backing. That’s notable because Trump, as recently as Monday, claims to have recommended a Louisiana location to Elon Musk for his next launch facility.  
If you’re to read anything into the Senate race results, it’s that Vermilion voters seem to be on board with their Republican leaders’ vision for the parish. Of their more than 17,000 ballots, 12,500 went to Letlow.
Jefferson
Yes, Letlow finished behind Davis in Louisiana’s second largest parish with 46% of the vote. But the more than 60,000 votes she received there helped eat away at the advantage her opponent posted in some of the state’s Democratic strongholds.  
Letlow’s losing total in Jefferson was fifth best among Republicans in statewide elections who have won the parish since 2019.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: ‘Too close to call’: Kansas secretary of state, attorney general candidates wait for final tallies
description: TOPEKA — Kansas attorney general and secretary of state candidates are waiting for counts of provisional and mail-in ballots, as winners in the races remain undecided Wednesday. Democrat Chris Mann claimed victory over Republican incumbent Kris Kobach in the attorney general race. The two were 11,597 votes apart, with Mann in the lead, as of […]
text:
Democrat Chris Mann, shown here at an August 2026 event in Olathe, claimed victory in the race for attorney general against Republican incumbent Kris Kobach but the race hasn't officially been called.  (Photo by Anna Kaminski/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — Kansas attorney general and secretary of state candidates are waiting for counts of provisional and mail-in ballots, as winners in the races remain undecided Wednesday.
Democrat Chris Mann claimed victory over Republican incumbent Kris Kobach in the attorney general race. The two were 11,597 votes apart, with Mann in the lead, as of Wednesday afternoon. 
“To those who didn’t vote for me, I look forward to earning your trust in the months ahead,” Mann wrote in a Facebook post. 
Kobach’s campaign has not issued a statement or responded to questions. He attended a GOP watch party Tuesday in Topeka but stayed less than an hour in the public area and didn’t reappear for statements throughout the evening, as other candidates did.
Democrat Jennifer Day and Republican Pat Proctor are 10,477 votes apart in the race for secretary of state, with Proctor leading.
“As of this morning, this race remains too close to call,” Day wrote in an email. “There are still provisional ballots and advance mail ballots being processed and counted across Kansas, and we owe it to every eligible voter to make sure their vote is counted.”
Day said she knew the race was going to be competitive, and that she will follow the process.
“This is about the integrity of our elections and making sure every Kansan has a voice,” she said.
When asked via text if he could answer questions about the race, Proctor responded: “Not for you!” 
Proctor has consistently refused to answer Kansas Reflector questions. He did not respond to a question about whether he would continue that policy if he is elected to become the secretary of state.
The state took the next step in its post-audit election process, selecting one federal, one legislative, one county and the constitutional amendment race to be audited in each county, according to the Secretary of State’s website. 
The county election office randomly selects 1% of precincts to be audited for each race, and ballots will be hand counted to ensure the vote is accurate. 
Six races in the state will be audited because the vote count is close, including governor, attorney general; secretary of state; and House districts 27, 40 and 117, Secretary of State Scott Schwab said at a news conference Wednesday.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Early ranked choice results indicate Republicans Tilton, McCabe trail in Alaska legislature races
description: Incumbents Sen. Cathy Tilton, R-Wasilla, and Rep. Kevin McCabe, R-Big Lake, led in first-choice election results Tuesday night, but preliminary results from ranked choice runoffs show them trailing challengers in their hotly contested Matanuska-Susitna Borough legislative races. Rep. Elexie Moore, R-Wasilla, trailed in first-choice election results but a Wed[...]
text:
Voters mark their ballots on Election Day, Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026 at the University of Alaska Anchorage. (Photo by Loren Holmes/Alaska Beacon)Incumbents Sen. Cathy Tilton, R-Wasilla, and Rep. Kevin McCabe, R-Big Lake, led in first-choice election results Tuesday night, but preliminary results from ranked choice runoffs show them trailing challengers in their hotly contested Matanuska-Susitna Borough legislative races.
Rep. Elexie Moore, R-Wasilla, trailed in first-choice election results but a Wednesday morning ranked choice tabulation performed by the Alaska Beacon using Division of Elections data shows her leading by six votes.
In all three races there are early and absentee ballots left to be counted, which could change the analysis.
Using RCTab, an open-source analysis and auditing tool, the Beacon analyzed a data file showing how district voters ranked the state House and Senate candidates.
Under Alaska’s election system, if no candidate for an office has more than 50% of the vote, ranked choice voting is used to elect a winner. 
The candidate with the fewest first-choice votes is eliminated, and people who voted for them have their votes redistributed to their second choice. The process repeats until only two candidates are left, and the person with the most votes wins.
Several legislative races in the Mat-Su had four candidates, increasing the likelihood that no one would top the 50% threshold. 
Results from rural Alaska — where most election precincts count ballots by hand, making immediate ranked choice tabulation impossible — were too incomplete to verify an accurate leader in those races on Wednesday.
As many as 60,000 early and absentee ballots remain uncounted statewide, and the current leaders may change as more votes are counted.
In Senate District M, where Tilton is running for a full term after being appointed to the seat by Gov. Mike Dunleavy this year, she had 33.4% of first-choice votes in ballots counted by 2:45 a.m. Wednesday. Her closest challenger was Republican Ryan Berry with 32.5%. 
Democratic candidate Pat Chesbro was third with 28.3% and Republican Zane Vrvilo was fourth with 5.5%.
Tilton has served in the House since 2015, and was appointed to the Senate seat vacated by Shelley Hughes, who resigned to run for governor. 
While the Division of Elections will not publish an official ranked choice tabulation until Nov. 18, it did publish data that allows Alaskans to perform their own analysis.
The Beacon’s analysis found that enough Chesbro and Vrvilo voters picked Berry as an alternate to give him a win over Tilton.
In the data published by the Division of Elections early Wednesday, he leads 51.7% of the vote to Tilton’s 48.3%.
In House District 30, where McCabe is seeking re-election, he had 38.4% of the vote while Republican challenger Doug Massie had 35.8%. Democratic candidate Sandra Loomis had 25.4%.
When Loomis is eliminated and her supporters’ votes are redistributed, Massie takes the lead with 50.6% of the vote. 
In Wasilla’s House District 28, Republican challenger Stephen Wright led Republican incumbent Rep. Elexie Moore in a three-way race that also featured Democratic candidate Kit Kennedy.
When Kennedy is eliminated and her votes are redistributed, Moore takes a six-vote lead over Wright.
In other multicandidate races, the ranked choice runoff doesn’t change the Republicans in the lead. In Eagle River, Republican Rep. Jamie Allard leads in both the ranked choice runoff and in first-choice votes. In Palmer, Republican Rep. DeLena Johnson does as well.
Rep. Garret Nelson, R-Sutton, leads a four-way race in House District 29 in both first-choice votes and the ranked choice runoff there.
In the race to replace Sen. Gary Stevens, R-Kodiak, current Republican Rep. Louise Stutes, R-Kodiak, leads in both first-choice votes and the ranked choice runoff.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: North Dakota’s historically low voter turnout attributed to lack of competitive races
description: Voter turnout in North Dakota’s general election sagged to a low point of just under 40%, a dismal showing political observers connect to uninspiring races, voters’ busy lives and enough political fatigue for some to sit this one out. About 39.8% of eligible voters cast ballots, the lowest general election turnout in the last 50 […]
text:
Jamie Macias votes during the national midterm election at the El Zagal Shrine Hall in Fargo, North Dakota, on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Dan Koeck/For the North Dakota Monitor)Voter turnout in North Dakota’s general election sagged to a low point of just under 40%, a dismal showing political observers connect to uninspiring races, voters’ busy lives and enough political fatigue for some to sit this one out.
About 39.8% of eligible voters cast ballots, the lowest general election turnout in the last 50 years, according to Secretary of State Michael Howe’s office.
“There’s no sugar-coating it: 40% turnout is not something that we want. We want to figure out anything we can to get that number higher,” Gov. Kelly Armstrong said Wednesday.
Voters defeat free school meal ballot measure in North Dakota

The ballot had no real competitive elections or compelling candidates, said Mark Jendrysik, professor of political science and public administration at the University of North Dakota. Even the two ballot measures weren’t enough, he said. 
Measure 1, to require 60% voter support to change the state constitution, was somewhat technical, and Measure 2, for free K-12 school meals, just didn’t capture people’s imaginations, Jendrysik said.
Ballot measures don’t drive turnout the way candidates do, said Armstrong, a former state GOP chair.
Howe attributed the low voter turnout to a lack of passion for any particular statewide candidate or competition on the ballot. He said he thought turnout might reach 46%.
“I did not think it would be this low,” Howe said.
People in other states were passionate about candidates and issues leading to high turnout often motivated by fear, anger and frustration, Howe said. Those are emotions he said he did not sense among constituents about North Dakota state officials while he was campaigning.
Voters approve North Dakota governor’s first appointees, reelect all Republican incumbents

It was clear Republicans would sweep statewide offices, and their Democratic challengers just didn’t have compelling personalities or the resources to compete, Jendrysik said.
“When you have a one-party state like this, you just reduce the incentive for people to come out to vote, and I think that’s what happened,” Jendrysik said. Democrats struggle to compete and even recruit candidates in rural areas, he said.
Former Democratic lawmaker Josh Boschee’s mayoral win in Fargo in June might be the Democrats’ highlight of the year, but Fargo is growing and becoming different from North Dakota in that Democrats have more appeal there, Jendrysik said.
Democrats are closing the gap on Republicans in North Dakota based on Tuesday’s results, said Bismarck-Mandan Democratic-NPL Director Bob Valeu. Though the national trend favored Democrats, North Dakota remains a tough landscape due to legislative redistricting “extremely” favoring Republicans and a decades-long GOP “lockdown on governance in the state as a political party,” he said.
“I believe politics is a marathon, not a sprint, and when things start to really change in North Dakota from an economic reality and it hits home with working families, I think voters are going to recognize that the Democratic Party has something to really offer them,” Valeu said.
Barely 40% voter turnout is awful, former Republican Gov. Ed Schafer said.
“It worries me because we’re supposed to be a government by the people, and people can’t bring themselves to vote before they go to work or vote at 7:30 at night or after dinner. They just don’t do it, and I’m very disappointed. I’m not sure what the answer is,” Schafer said.
Perhaps loyal Republican voters fed up with the Trump administration simply stayed home, he said. Maybe the ultraconservative takeover of some GOP legislative districts led some Republicans to sit it out because of intraparty disagreements or “participation fatigue,” he said.
New faces, new leaders and a few more Democrats will shape North Dakota’s next Legislature

North Dakota keeps electing Republicans, probably because there is “no reason to vote for a change in political philosophy at leading the state,” Schafer said. North Dakota’s economy is good, unemployment is low, the state is putting money into property tax breaks and social services, he said. 
In some ways, North Dakotans don’t have many excuses not to vote, said Cody Schuler, advocacy manager for the American Civil Liberties Union of North Dakota. Voting is made to be easy in North Dakota, which doesn’t have voter registration and allows voters to bring updated address information for outdated IDs to the polls, he said.
But people also are busy with their own lives, and unless they are passionate about an issue or a candidate, it’s easy to forget to vote, Schuler said. He pointed out that North Dakota’s ballot had no U.S. Senate race, leaving the state’s sole House seat at the top of the ticket in a year that also had no presidential or gubernatorial race.
“Unless there is something that sparked you to go, it can be easy to put it on the back burner, to forget,” Schuler said.
Howe said his office will continue its civic engagement initiative to educate the public about voting and elections in North Dakota, such as visiting schools and other organizations.
“We want to assist any way we can in getting the word out about how to vote, when to vote, why to vote, all of it,” Howe said.
The June primary – a decisive election for Republicans who often go on to win the general election – saw just under 21% turnout.
North Dakota Monitor reporter Michael Achterling contributed to this report.
Reach Monitor reporter Jack Dura at jdura@northdakotamonitor.com.

text:
Drone footage shows flooding in Bluff, Utah, on Monday, Nov. 2, 2026. (Video by Raini Pachak/Bluff Community Foundation)Voters in San Juan County were dealing with the aftermath of devastating flooding as they made plans to cast their ballots on Election Day. But, with expanded options made available through an emergency declaration to allow electronic voting, a couple of hundred voters received accommodations to vote.
Utah Election Director Ryan Cowley, said 244 people were able to cast their ballot through the emergency system the lieutenant governor’s office had announced Monday. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“There’s some pretty catastrophic flooding in several areas down there that impeded people’s ability to get to the polling places and out of their homes,” Cowley said. “The system worked really well.” 
Utah activates emergency electronic voting in San Juan amid devastating floods

There are 8,095 registered voters in San Juan County, according to statistics updated by the state on Monday, but turnout numbers for the area are still unavailable as a small crew works on counting the ballots.
Statewide, Cowley said, turnout was at about 42% on Wednesday morning. The elections office expects final numbers to be in the 60% to 65% range. 
“San Juan very well would likely be in that same range, but I can’t necessarily project that specifically for them,” Cowley said. 
The electronic system is designed for military and overseas voters, as well as for people with disabilities, he said. Voters receive access to a portal, and they are able to receive a ballot, fill it out and submit it electronically. 
After the proclamation was issued Monday afternoon, Utah elections officers sent emails, spread the word through the media, and county officials announced it through their social media channels, Cowley said.
“I feel like we definitely provided the opportunity, and hopefully we got the word out to as many people as we could. It’s hard in a situation like that because it’s so close to the election where it was basically the day before, but I think we got the word out the best we could to voters,” he said. “And the fact that 244 were able to take advantage of that, I think, is a pretty cool thing.”

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: NJ governor warns gas companies of sanctions for importing Russian diesel
description: Gov. Mikie Sherrill told 12 fuel companies that operate ports or terminals in New Jersey that buying or unloading Russian diesel is illegal.
text:
A gas station on Broadway in Newark shows diesel fuel at nearly $6 a gallon on Nov. 4, 2026. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)Gov. Mikie Sherrill has warned 12 energy companies that operate out of private ports and terminals in New Jersey that buying or unloading imported Russian fuel violates federal law, with lawbreakers facing millions of dollars in penalties.
Congress banned Russian fuel imports in April 2022 in response to Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. But fuel prices have skyrocketed since President Donald Trump launched his war against Iran, so he made a deal last month with Russian President Vladimir Putin to buy potentially millions of tons of oil. Administration officials soon after lifted sanctions on Russian diesel exports.
A bipartisan group of senators objected to the move as illegal, and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky blasted it as a “weak decision,” predicting it would do little to bring down fuel prices.
But multiple oil tankers loaded with Russian diesel already are on their way to the East Coast. So Sherrill sent a letter Monday to gas companies that operate ports and terminals in Perth Amboy, Bayonne, Linden, Carteret, Port Reading, and Sewaren alerting them of the Russian Oil Act’s prohibition on Russian diesel exports. The ports and terminals regulated by the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey didn’t get the letter because they handle cargo, not petroleum products.
Neither Trump nor any administration officials have the authority to waive the act’s sanctions without certifying that Russia has agreed to withdraw from Ukraine or congressional review, Sherrill wrote.
“These actions are illegal, in part, because Vladimir Putin continues to engage in an illegal war of aggression against Ukraine,” she wrote. “Further, the U.S. is currently engaged in hostilities with Iran, whose military is responsible for the killing of 23 service members and wounding dozens of others. In purchasing oil from Russia, a known supplier and financial supporter of Iran, Donald Trump is providing funding for a country that is engaged in hostilities with America, up to and including killing American soldiers.”
Gov. Mikie Sherrill talks about the results of Tuesday’s midterm elections outside Small World Coffee in Princeton on Nov. 4, 2026. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor)
Talking with the press Wednesday about Tuesday’s election results, Sherrill tied Trump’s Russian diesel deal to the routing Republicans suffered in the midterm elections, saying companies considering violating the law for profit should recognize the shifting political winds.
“Not holding corporations accountable, allowing people to break the law, and thinking you’re going to have the cover of Trump and MAGA Republicans, that is not the case anymore, and people are on notice,” Sherrill said.
Besides, the Russian Oil Act carries a five-year statute of limitations, and Trump will be out of office in two years, meaning he’ll be powerless to protect lawbreakers, she added.
A White House spokesperson said allowing the U.S. to accept diesel from Russia is consistent with similar actions previously taken by the Office of Foreign Assets Control and is “in compliance with all applicable laws.”
Sherrill advised the companies to turn away any tankers looking to unload in their ports.
“Any effort to profit from the illegal trade in Russian fuel will be met with harsh penalties,” she wrote in her letter.
State officials are now examining “every legal and regulatory tool” to prevent the fuel from making its way into the U.S. through New Jersey’s shores, she added.
“The answer cannot simply be that the president of the United States can break the law and nobody can hold him accountable,” Sherrill said Wednesday.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Congressman-elect Forstag says fight for working Montanans just beginning
description: Sam Forstag, Montana’s soon-to-be first Democratic U.S. Representative in three decades, said on Wednesday that winning his election was just the beginning of the fight for working-class Americans.  He is going to Washington, D.C., to fight “so that every person in this country and this state can afford to work one good job and afford […]
text:
Scenes from the a watch party for Sam Forstag, Democratic candidate for Montana’s western congressional district, for the 2026 midterm election at the Florence Building in Missoula on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. (Ben Allen Smith/Lee Enterprises)Sam Forstag, Montana’s soon-to-be first Democratic U.S. Representative in three decades, said on Wednesday that winning his election was just the beginning of the fight for working-class Americans. 
He is going to Washington, D.C., to fight “so that every person in this country and this state can afford to work one good job and afford the basics, a roof over our head, healthcare that actually gets care when you need it, childcare and dignified retirement,” Forstag said in his first press conference as representative-elect.
“And to make sure that our public lands agencies that have underwent full-scale assault over the course of the last one-and-a-half, two years, are being rebuilt by people who actually know what it’s going to take and who actually know what it’s like on the ground to be doing that work,” he said.
Forstag, a Missoula smokejumper and former union leader, declared victory over Republican Aaron Flint on Tuesday in Montana’s western congressional district. 
Flint conceded, although the Associated Press had not called the race, even by late Wednesday afternoon. 
Addressing reporters at the Missoula County Courthouse on Wednesday afternoon, Forstag outlined a handful of priorities he wants to focus on in Congress that largely mirrored his campaign rhetoric — making everyday life affordable for Montanans and protecting public lands. 
He also acknowledged the historic nature of his victory. It came as part of a nationwide wave of Democratic wins that political analysts described as a rebuke of the Trump administration. 
“We have not had a Democrat elected to the United States House from western Montana since 1994, when Pat Williams was last sent to Congress 32 years ago, the year that I was born,” Forstag said. “And those are big shoes to fill.”
While Forstag will be part of the largest Democratic house majority since 2008, he said it’s important to craft bipartisan legislation that can withstand the “political whipsaw.”
He said his first call, after speaking with Flint, was to Montana’s other congressman, Republican Troy Downing, to congratulate him on reelection and start discussing ways to work together. 
In particular, he mentioned the River Runs Through It Act, introduced earlier this year and sponsored by Downing and retiring Republican Rep. Ryan Zinke, who had endorsed Flint.
Forstag described the act, a large-scale proposal to expand wilderness areas and prioritize forest management in the state, as a good place to start working together.
He said partisanship is part of the reason the government doesn’t work well. 
“I don’t care who’s going to get the credit for actually passing legislation to make sure we’re building affordable housing, making the reforms we need to do so, legislation to save our sawmills or improve land management,” Forstag said. “All I care is that we get bills passed into law because people are suffering and drowning in costs out there. 
“So, well, if we got to give the president credit for signing a bill into law, by all means, that is how we get desperately needed aid and relief to Montanans who’ve been waiting far too long.”
Forstag will be the only Democrat in Montana’s federal delegation, and the only elected Democrat in the state in an office higher than the Legislature. 
He said that Montana needs to rebuild the Democratic Party so that people are excited to engage with it. 
“I think we saw a lot of that last night. We saw hundreds of people who were hopeful and happy to be at a political event. That’s not a common thing today in Montana,” he said. 
He added that one of the most common things he heard on the campaign trail was surprise at the turnout of young voters. 
“That is the way it ought to be,” he said. “Politics should be a place that you can feel hopeful about the prospect of our politics, our government actually improving our life on a material basis.”
Forstag said staffing up offices across western Montana would be a priority to ensure constituents have access to staff and services when they need them. 
He also committed to holding regular town halls while in office and regularly returning to the district to engage with Montanans. 
Forstag will be sworn into the seat in January.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Sen. Riebe resists calls to resign over harassment, discrimination allegation
description: Sen. Kathleen Riebe is resisting Senate Democrats' calls for her to resign based on findings of a review that have not been made public.
text:
Sen. Kathy Riebe, D-Cottonwood Heights, works on the Senate floor at the Capitol in Salt Lake City on the final night of the legislative session, Friday, March 6, 2026. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)A state lawmaker says she won’t step down as fellow Senate Democrats call on her to resign and allege an independent inquiry found “a pattern of conduct towards others that was likely motivated by race, national origin, or ethnicity.” 
Sen. Kathleen Riebe, of Cottonwood Heights, said in a statement Wednesday that she disputes the characterization, hasn’t seen the investigation and wasn’t asked to provide a response.
Utah Senate Democrats call for Sen. Riebe to resign after harassment, discrimination investigation

“I am not resigning,” Riebe said in the prepared statement. “Fair process matters. Voters have entrusted me with public office four times, and I have important work ahead on behalf of my constituents.”
Her colleagues announced less than an hour before polls closed on Election Day that they had voted to remove Riebe from their caucus and were calling on her to resign. 
The independent review, which has not been made public, followed a complaint alleging workplace discrimination and harassment, according to the joint Tuesday statement from Senate Minority Leader Luz Escamilla, Minority Whip Karen Kwan, Sen. Jen Plumb, Sen. Stephanie Pitcher and Sen. Nate Blouin.
“It also revealed statements concerning employment decisions involving individuals based on their sexual orientation or other protected characteristics,” the senators said. 
Riebe said she has requested a copy of the report and its findings and will seek an opportunity to respond. 
“I was elected as a Democrat, remain committed to Democratic values, and am confident that this matter can be addressed fairly and responsibly,” Riebe said Wednesday. 
She went on to say that “across Utah and the country last night, voters sent a loud message: they expect their elected officials to focus on getting work done. I will continue doing that work for my constituents. We have a great deal to accomplish together, and that is where my focus will remain.”
A Senate spokesperson declined to release the investigation’s report Tuesday, citing “the confidentiality of those involved.”
Riebe, an educator, was first elected to the state Senate in 2018 after serving on the Utah State Board of Education. Earlier this year, she ran to represent Utah’s newly drawn 1st Congressional District before dropping out to endorse Ben McAdams. Her current Senate term runs through Jan. 1, 2029.
