name: VTDigger
title: In a ‘blue tsunami,’ how did Republican Gov. Phil Scott win another term?
description:
“He's created a category of one, you know? And Democrats are willing to pull the lever for him even as they vote blue across the ballot,” said Senate President Pro Tempore Phil Baruth.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  In a ‘blue tsunami,’ how did Republican Gov. Phil Scott win another term?.
text:
Gov. Phil Scott the Associated General Contractors facility in Montpelier on Tuesday, November 3, 2026. Photo by Andy Duback/VTDigger
There are just two Republican governors, as it stands, who serve alongside a state legislature controlled by Democrats. One of them, Gov. Joe Lombardo of Nevada, was ousted Tuesday night amid a “blue tsunami” of Democratic gains across the country.
But the other, Vermont’s GOP Gov. Phil Scott, defied the national trends — again.
Scott overcame a well-funded challenge from Amanda Janoo, a Democrat who also had the backing of the Vermont Progressive Party, to win 52.6% of the vote to Janoo’s 45.6%, according to The Associated Press. He is now set to serve a sixth two-year term, something no other governor has done in the modern history of the state.
At the same time, Scott’s six-point margin of victory is the narrowest of any race he’s run for governor. His push to get more Republican lawmakers elected down the ballot this year could hardly have fallen flatter: Democrats flipped enough GOP seats in the state House and Senate to regain the supermajorities they enjoyed several years ago. And his choice for lieutenant governor, the Republican incumbent John Rodgers, was ousted by a whopping 25 points by a Democrat, former Lt. Gov. Molly Gray.  
So, how did Scott do so well Tuesday while so many others in his party faltered? 
‘A category of one’
Tuesday’s election proved that while voters were eager to reject Republicans in an election widely viewed as a referendum on President Donald Trump, many Vermonters don’t see Scott in Trump’s light. There is little doubt that Trump’s unpopularity gave Janoo a boost in a year when Democratic voters were eager for change. But “people don’t regard Phil Scott as a Republican” all that much, said Senate President Pro Tempore Phil Baruth, D/P-Chittenden Central. 
“It’s like they have a separate category in their mind of the Scott Republican,” Baruth, who did not run for reelection this year, said Wednesday. He described that brand as moderate on wedge issues like gun control but critical of Trump’s foreign policy. 
“I just think he’s created a category of one, you know? And Democrats are willing to pull the lever for him even as they vote blue across the ballot,” Baruth said. 
Of all the state Senate districts — which roughly correspond to county boundaries — Scott performed best in Franklin County, where he won about 68% of the vote, according to a VTDigger analysis of unofficial results. At the same time, Democrats flipped a number of GOP-held Vermont House seats there, results show. 
Statewide, Janoo scored about 141,000 total votes. That’s about 50,000 fewer than Gray, the Democratic lieutenant governor-elect, and 57,000 fewer than U.S. Rep. Becca Balint, D-Vt., who also won her race Tuesday, noted Chris Graff, a longtime and former Vermont political journalist for the AP. 
“So there was a conscious decision on the part of people who were voting for Democratic candidates up and down the line not to vote for Amanda,” Graff said. 
Scott made a point this fall that he has been talking about affordability — the central issue of this year’s campaign, in Vermont and around the country — for far longer than most other candidates. Janoo argued Scott’s plans for addressing affordability, namely cutting taxes and state regulations, would not help. But even if voters agreed with her, they might not have blamed Scott for their cost of living woes, which are more easily assigned to factors outside the state’s control, such as the war in Iran. 
Voters appeared to reward Scott’s leadership on state-level issues above all else, said Senate Minority Leader Scott Beck, R-Caledonia, in a statement Wednesday. 
“Governor Scott’s victory reflects a clear message from voters: Vermonters want practical leadership focused on solving problems, not partisan politics,” Beck said. “Throughout his tenure, Governor Scott has consistently demonstrated an ability to bring people together, manage taxpayer dollars responsibly, and keep Vermont moving forward during challenging times.”
Incumbency vs. inexperience
It was always going to be an uphill battle for any Democrat to unseat Scott, who has long polled as the most popular governor in the country. That was certainly the case for Janoo, an economist who had never run a political campaign before and had no name recognition at the start of the year.
Only twice in Vermont’s history has an incumbent governor lost a bid for reelection, with the most recent case in 1962. And of Vermont’s 22 governors who served over the past century, all but two were previously lieutenant governor or in the state Legislature, according to Graff. Scott served in the Senate and as lieutenant governor. Some voters, Graff said, may have liked Janoo’s ideas but questioned her ability to implement them.
At the same time, Janoo’s lack of specificity on how some of her proposals would be funded — possibly a result of running for office the first time — left her open to political attacks, said Matt Dickinson, a political science professor at Middlebury College. Janoo ran on raising taxes on high-income earners and luxury second homes to pay for free primary healthcare and other public services. But when pressed, she said that many details of her proposals would need to be fleshed out after she was elected. 
That proved to be an easy target for Scott, Dickinson said, who has spent years building his political brand around not raising taxes. The governor may well have clinched the race, Dickinson said, in his closing statement of the last debate of the campaign on WCAX last week, when he characterized Janoo’s platform as “free this, free that.” 
“When we hear about hundreds of millions of dollars in new promises, you need to ask yourself, ‘Who’s going to pay for that?’” Scott said. “Spoiler alert, I’ve seen this movie before. And the answer is: You do.”
That was one of the few times during a civil and respectful campaign that Scott attacked Janoo directly, Dickinson noted. At the same time, though, Scott also benefited from an outside group — a political action committee — taking aim at Janoo on his behalf. 
The Republican Governors Association poured $950,000 into a pro-Scott super PAC, which is legally barred from coordinating with Scott’s campaign, in the final weeks of the race. The PAC ran ads questioning Janoo’s experience and even quoting her opponent in the Democratic primary, Aly Richards, seeming to criticize her ideas as unrealistic. 
Scott told reporters last month that he would have preferred no outside spending in the race on his behalf. But the reality was that “somebody was doing his dirty work for him,” Dickinson said. 
The value of the outside spending “wasn’t the money itself. It was the ability to go negative in a way that effectively raised concerns about how, A, Janoo could pay for this, and B, whether Janoo was prepared to be governor,” Dickinson said. 
The outside spending also helped counter the fact Janoo raised more money than Scott over the last two months of the race. Over the full campaign, Janoo raised just over $1 million, which is more than any Scott challenger since the governor’s first bid for the office in 2016. Scott, by comparison, raised just shy of $720,000 by Election Day. 
A disparate map
Janoo won the Democratic primary in part by running up large vote totals in the state’s population center, Chittenden County.
Tuesday, she outperformed her primary margin of victory in the county’s deep-blue heart of Burlington and Winooski. But she couldn’t score enough votes in surrounding suburbs — Shelburne, Williston, Colchester — to overcome Scott’s support there. Those so-called “ring towns” tend to be communities that match Scott’s politics well, said Baruth, the Senate president: socially liberal but more fiscally conservative. 
Janoo did well in some other blue pockets of the state, including the areas around Brattleboro and Montpelier. But she couldn’t replicate the same success in a broader pattern of communities that gave her the win in August, according to Graff. 
“Phil picked up support sort of here and there, but all across the state,” he said. “He just never stopped getting votes.” 
With Democrats doing so well in downballot races in many of those same communities, how far the governor’s support will take him once the Legislature resumes its work in January remains to be seen, Dickinson said. Scott has routinely cast blame on the Democratic supermajority that was in place several years ago for some of the state’s current woes, including affordability concerns.
“His support dropped, you know, 20 percentage points or more depending on where you were,” Dickinson said. “Some Vermont voters said, ‘Yeah, you’ve been talking about affordability all the time. But things still aren’t affordable, so maybe we should look the other way.’”
Baruth said he thinks there is a limit on Scott’s power for the next two years while an unpopular Republican is still president.
“I don’t know that it’s possible so quickly to gin up the boogeyman of the supermajority again when you’ve still got Trump in the White House,” Baruth said. “Everybody now sees that Donald Trump was crazy, is crazy and will be crazy.”

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Governor-elect Klobuchar promises to transform state government, grow economy
description: Amy Klobuchar held her first press conference as Minnesota’s governor-elect Wednesday to outline her vision for the state, which includes auditing state government to eliminate the defrauding of government programs, and growing the state’s workforce and economy. Klobuchar, who will become Minnesota’s first woman governor when she takes the oath in January, t[...]
text:
Sen. Amy Klobuchar delivers a speech as she announces that she is the governor-elect at the DFL watch party during the midterm elections Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026 in St. Paul, Minnesota. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)Amy Klobuchar held her first press conference as Minnesota’s governor-elect Wednesday to outline her vision for the state, which includes auditing state government to eliminate the defrauding of government programs, and growing the state’s workforce and economy.
Klobuchar, who will become Minnesota’s first woman governor when she takes the oath in January, thanked Minnesotans for their support and said she will work hard to transform the state.
“Whether I or not I got your vote, I will do my best for you. I will work my heart out for you. Nobody will work harder,” Klobuchar said at a press conference in St. Paul’s historic James J. Hill Center.
Klobuchar will have 60 days before her January inauguration to staff her office, draft a two-year budget that includes her promise of no new tax hikes and turn her campaign talking points into legislation.
She announced the membership of her 14-person transition team, which will be chaired by Cindy Jesson, former Minnesota Department of Human Services commissioner and former appellate judge. Jesson worked on Gov. Mark Dayton’s transition team.
Members of the transition team include Doug Baker, former EcoLab CEO and former executive committee member of the Minnesota Business Partnership, which lobbies for the state’s biggest companies; Miguel Pozo, a trial attorney and former head of the Hispanic National Bar Association; Justin Buoen, a longtime Klobuchar advisor who ran her 2020 presidential campaign; and Rose Sullivan, Klobuchar’s former Senate chief of staff.
Klobuchar’s transition will have $162,000, according to state statute, with which to staff a transition team, rent out office space and recruit new employees. She launched a transition website on Wednesday where people can submit forms if they would like to work in her administration.
Klobuchar noted that members of the transition team are volunteers and may not necessarily serve in her administration once she takes office.
She also answered media questions for the first time since her election win.
Asked for more details about her audit of state government, Klobuchar said she will appoint an independent “senior leader” to conduct an audit of every state agency. That person will coordinate with the new state inspector general, the Office of the Legislative Auditor and Minnesota Management and Budget, the state’s budget agency, to identify fraudulent activity.
Klobuchar said she will also direct agencies to create a process for reporting fraud and better work with whistleblowers.
The audit will not only flag fraud, she said, but it will also point out areas where she could cut the budget. Minnesota’s spending is rising faster than revenue, creating a structural imbalance beginning in July. If Klobuchar refuses to raise taxes, she may have to cut spending. Unlike Washington, where Klobuchar has served for 20 years, state government is constitutionally banned from the kind of deficit spending that is routine in the nation’s capital.
Klobuchar reiterated that she will not raise taxes and noted that the state’s financial outlook could be better than forecasters predicted earlier this year. The state has consistently reported monthly revenue higher than what was forecast, and state officials will offer another forecast early next month.
Klobuchar has until the third Tuesday in February to craft a two-year budget and submit it to the Legislature, according to state statute.
Regarding Klobuchar’s own U.S. Senate seat, if she resigns before her inauguration, Gov. Tim Walz would appoint her successor. An early resignation and appointment would give the successor more seniority than the large incoming freshman class. Even if Klobuchar were to resign early, Walz can and most likely would defer to Klobuchar, who would then appoint her own successor.
Asked when she planned to resign, Klobuchar remained tight-lipped, as she has since she announced her campaign earlier this year.
“The decision has to be made pretty much before I get in the governor’s office or around that time, so stay tuned for that,” Klobuchar said. “I will do right by the state of Minnesota with that person.”

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico Democrats expand state House majority following ‘historic blue wave’
description: New Mexico legislative Democrats unseated four incumbent Republicans on Tuesday, with leaders crediting the national  “historic blue wave” for expanding the party’s already sizable majority in the state House of Representatives.
text:
New Mexico Democrats flipped four state House of Representatives seats from Republicans following the general election on Nov. 3, 2026, increasing their already significant majority. (Photo by Danielle Prokop/Source NM)New Mexico legislative Democrats unseated four incumbent Republicans on Tuesday, with leaders crediting the national  “historic blue wave” for expanding the party’s already sizable majority in the state House of Representatives.
Incumbent state Reps. Catherine Cullen (R-Rio Rancho), Rebecca Dow (R-Elephant Butte), Tanya Mirabal Moya (R-Los Lunas) and Luis Terrazas (R-Silver City) all lost their general election matchups against Democrats. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
As a result, Democrats will hold 47 of 70 House seats when the new legislative session begins on Jan. 19 for a 60-day session. Democrats also kept their 10-seat majority in the state Senate, after incumbent Sen. Rex Wilson (R-Ancho) defeated Democratic challenger William Neil Griffin, an attorney in Ruidoso.
New Mexico House Speaker Javier Martínez (D-Albuquerque), in a statement celebrating the results Wednesday, credited the gains to both the national fervor that won Democrats control of Congress on Tuesday, along with state Democrats’ delivery of “real results that are making life better and more affordable for families across our state.”
New Mexico, he said,“serves as an example for the rest of the nation on how to lead. We’ll carry the energy and momentum from tonight with us into the Roundhouse this January as we continue to show other states the way forward.”
In the case of House District 39, Democrat Raul Turrieta, a four-time county assessor, beat incumbent Terrazas by 53% to 47%. 
Turrieta told Source NM on Wednesday that he attributed his victory to being a well-known local and running a good campaign, but also to the “blue wave.”
“The Democrats really came out,” he said. “We raised enough money to be comfortable to do what we had to do, but mainly the blue wave. Let me tell you, man, that thing really took me over the top.”
‘It represents hope’: New Mexico Democrats cement control following historic blue wave

Terrazas, in a text message Wednesday to Source NM, thanked his supporters and said it is now time for “our community to continue working together.”
Democrat David Mooney, in House District 38, beat incumbent Republican Rebecca Dow by 53% to 47%. Dow previously held the seat between 2016 and 2022 before returning to represent the district in 2025, and fighting a legal ballot in the spring to appear on the primary election ballot. 
Mooney ran as a write-in candidate in the June primary after no other Democrat stepped up to challenge her. The race marked his first foray into running for elected office. 
Mooney told Source NM on Wednesday that his victory shows that Democrats can compete in rural districts like District 38, which covers parts of Doña Ana, Sierra and Socorro counties, but has more Democrats registered than Republicans. Mooney said his message helped spur Democrats to the polls.
“I came into the race absolutely as an underdog, but I have truly believed for years that folks could win in more rural districts like House District 38 if they just actually run on a campaign standing up for working folks and against corporations and special interests in our politics,” he said.
Mooney said one of his main priorities in January will be advocating for a data center moratorium of at least 18 months and a law requiring all new data center developments to be approved only if a majority of affected community members approve them. Data centers are proposed or in progress in each of the three counties covered by the district, he said. 
“I think that will do a lot to restore trust in the community about developers coming in,” he said of requiring a referendum on new developments. “I do think that’s going to be a hard fight.”
In addition to Turrieta and Mooney, the Democrats who flipped Republican seats are Rickie Allen Gonzales II in District 7 and Chriselle Martinez in District 57. Gonzales defeated Mirabal Moya by 52% to 48%, and Martinez defeated Cullen by 54% to 46%. 
Gonzales and Martinez could not be reached for comment Wednesday. 
In all but the District 57 race, registered Democrats outnumbered Republicans in the districts they flipped on Tuesday. Democratic House leaders, in their statement Wednesday, thanked those Democrats for voting to send more Democrats to the Roundhouse. 
“Our communities showed up at the ballot box and sent Democrats back to the Roundhouse with an even stronger majority, so we can build on our progress in the upcoming session and beyond,” House Majority Whip Day Hochman-Vigil (D-Albuquerque) said in a statement.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: US Reps. Hudson and McDowell concede races in 2 of NC’s most stunning election upsets
description: Two Republican members of North Carolina’s congressional delegation acknowledged Wednesday there was no path to victory in their respective districts after Tuesday’s midterm elections. Both were in districts widely considered to be safe Republican seats and were not expected to lose their 2026 reelection bids. Congressman Richard Hudson, chair of the Nationa[...]
text:
Rep. Richard Hudson, 9th Congressional District incumbent and National Republican Congressional Committee chairman, left, appears to have narrowly lost his seat to Democrat Richard Ojeda, right. (Photos courtesy of campaigns) Two Republican members of North Carolina’s congressional delegation acknowledged Wednesday there was no path to victory in their respective districts after Tuesday’s midterm elections. Both were in districts widely considered to be safe Republican seats and were not expected to lose their 2026 reelection bids.
Congressman Richard Hudson, chair of the National Republican Congressional Committee, officially conceded his bid for reelection to Democrat Richard Ojeda.
Strong Democratic turnout flips at least 5 US House seats across North Carolina

“Last night, the voters of North Carolina’s 9th District made their choice, and I respect it,” wrote Hudson in a statement released Wednesday afternoon. “God is sovereign over my life, and He has a plan for all of us.”
Hudson, who has represented the district since 2013, trailed Ojeda, a former West Virginia state representative and veteran, by just over 6,000 votes. In unofficial results with all precincts reporting, Ojeda won 51% of the vote to Hudson’s 49%.
Hudson said it was the honor of his life to represent the 9th district and have the privilege of being Fort Bragg’s congressman.
“In the words of Ronald Reagan: we lost a skirmish, but the battle goes on,” Hudson wrote.
Ojeda said voters in the district viewed Hudson as being more focused on running the Republican money machine for the NRCC than local needs.
“This win belongs to every teacher, every nurse, every veteran, every family at Fort Bragg and every working person who’s sick and tired of watching the billionaire class take everything,” Ojeda said in a statement.
Donald Trump and Addison McDowell pose for a photo in 2023. (Photo: McDowellfornc.com/)
Joining Hudson in conceding on Wednesday was Republican U.S. Rep. Addison McDowell in the 6th Congressional District. He lost to Democratic High Point Mayor Cyril Jefferson.
McDowell said he recognized the frustration of voters in the current political climate.
“I urge my fellow conservatives not to back down,” McDowell wrote. “Now is the time to stand taller, dig in, and join me in rebuilding the values and principles that have always made our communities strong.”
Hudson and McDowell’s concessions come as fellow Republican U.S. Rep. Virginia Foxx tries to hang on to her seat in North Carolina’s 5th Congressional District. Foxx trails Democratic challenger Chuck Hubbard by just 99 votes. She said Wednesday that overseas and provisional ballots have yet to be counted and she would not concede until all eligible votes had been counted.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Ranked choice voting may help Republican US Sen. Dan Sullivan, analysis finds
description: This article is developing and may be updated. If Republican U.S. Sen. Dan Sullivan wins re-election, Alaska’s ranked choice runoff system may deserve part of the credit. Early Wednesday morning results published by the Alaska Division of Elections show Democratic challenger Mary Peltola leading Sullivan by 626 first-choice votes, but according to preliminar[...]
text:
Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska, waves signs on Election Day, Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026 in Midtown Anchorage. (Photo by Loren Holmes/Alaska Beacon)This article is developing and may be updated.
If Republican U.S. Sen. Dan Sullivan wins re-election, Alaska’s ranked choice runoff system may deserve part of the credit.
Early Wednesday morning results published by the Alaska Division of Elections show Democratic challenger Mary Peltola leading Sullivan by 626 first-choice votes, but according to preliminary data published at 2:45 a.m. by the Alaska Division of Elections, Sullivan will gain hundreds more redistributed votes than Peltola if the race goes to a ranked choice runoff.
That scenario may change. The Division of Elections said Wednesday morning that 20,000 early votes remain uncounted, and as many as 40,000 absentee ballots may still need to be counted and added to the 215,341 votes already recorded by early Wednesday morning.
Under Alaska’s election system, if a general election candidate has more than 50% of the first-choice votes, they win outright, without a need to use ranked choice voting.
A Peltola win would help Democrats expand their control of the U.S. Senate, while a Sullivan win would at least mildly limit Democratic gains in the Senate during this week’s midterm elections.
Using RCTab, an open-source analysis and auditing tool, the Alaska Beacon analyzed a data file showing how 204,530 Alaskans ranked the four candidates for U.S. Senate as of Wednesday morning. 
Sullivan would gain 2,728 votes when Republican challenger Gerald Heikes and independent Dan J. Sullivan are eliminated.
Peltola, meanwhile, would gain 1,868 votes from the same eliminations.
These figures come with major caveats. 
The cast vote record doesn’t include ballots cast on Election Day at the 131 voting precincts without ballot scanners. Those precincts are primarily in rural areas that favor Peltola. 
Altogether, about 11,000 ballots listed in the state’s first-choice results Wednesday morning are not included in the cast vote record.
The record also doesn’t include the early and absentee ballots that haven’t been counted at all.
Despite those gaps, the cast vote record does illustrate voting trends, including the way Heikes voters preferred Sen. Dan Sullivan as an additional choice.
Election Day figures show Dan J. Sullivan is the first candidate eliminated, and of 3,426 votes for him in the cast vote record, 991 would be distributed to Peltola. Sullivan would get 560 and Heikes would get 627. Another 608 would be dropped because of misvoting or because the voter picked no other candidate.
That result indicates little, if any, voter confusion between the incumbent Republican senator and Dan J. Sullivan, who was listed as Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. on the ballot.
Members of the Republican Party in Alaska and nationally have claimed without evidence that a Peltola victory would be fraudulent because of confusion.
A federal judge dismissed a lawsuit filed by the U.S. Department of Justice about the issue; that decision is now on appeal to the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals.

name: Michigan Advance
title: As voters task Dems with delivering affordability, Hines keeps her family close to heart
description: After Election Day delivered major gains for Democrats across the country, party leadership and their newly-elected members are pledging to deliver on the mandate that Republicans promised voters in 2024: lowering costs and delivering economic relief.  Among those candidates is U.S. Rep.-elect Christina Hines (D-Warren), who flipped Michigan’s 10th Congressi[...]
text:
Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer and Democratic Congressional candidate Christina Hines take questions from the press following a campaign launch in Rochester, Oct. 28, 2026. (Photo Kyle Davidson/Advance)After Election Day delivered major gains for Democrats across the country, party leadership and their newly-elected members are pledging to deliver on the mandate that Republicans promised voters in 2024: lowering costs and delivering economic relief. 
Among those candidates is U.S. Rep.-elect Christina Hines (D-Warren), who flipped Michigan’s 10th Congressional District, currently held by U.S. Rep. John James (R-Shelby Township), who opted against seeking reelection to run for governor, which was unsuccessful, as he lost to Democrat Jocelyn Benson. 
Made up of Rochester and Rochester Hills in eastern Oakland County, and the southern portion of Macomb County, which has long been defined by the blue-collar workers who call it their home, Michigan’s 10th District was a major target for Democrats and Republicans.
While Hines and her Republican opponent, Michael Bouchard Jr., each campaigned on lowering costs, voters elected Hines, a former prosecutor, to succeed James in Congress.
Speaking with Michigan Advance Wednesday, Hines said her district’s residents were concerned about how expensive life can be while heading into the polls.
Christina Hines, the Democratic nominee for the 10th Congressional District, addresses supporters and Democrats at a rally featuring former President Barack Obama at Cass Technical High School on Oct. 24, 2026, in Detroit, Mich. (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance)
“Whether it’s healthcare, gas, groceries, whatever it is, people need some relief and they need some change,” Hines said. “And so I think that that’s what they were voting for certainly here in our district.”
As Democrats pledge to deliver the relief Americans are seeking, Hines said her perspective as a working mother of three is more in line with the residents of her district than members of Congress.
“I talk about how there’s more millionaires in Congress than there are moms, and that is so different, right?” Hines said. “Like many people in Congress don’t have to think about, ‘Oh my gosh, it just took me $90 to fill up my minivan, and how is that going to impact my grocery budget?’”
For that reason, Hines said she will always be focused on lowering costs, noting that if more members of Congress had the experience of an ordinary working life, it would be a very different place.
When asked if there was one central issue she would address in her first term if given the opportunity to deliver a solution, Hines pointed to healthcare. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“I’m hearing just heartbreaking stories from people all over this district that cannot afford the care that they need,” Hines said, noting that her mother was chronically ill when she was growing up, and that she had been on Medicaid before.
“Every single American should have access to quality, affordable healthcare and I will genuinely work with anyone and create any type of plan and review any type of plan to make that happen,” Hines said. 
In addition to the key issues around affordability, Hines said she would also like to take a look at regulations around big tech and AI. In addition to her perspective as a parent, she also pointed to her experience as a former child abuse prosecutor, where she’d seen the ways social media can harm children’s mental health.
“So far we’ve had a Congress that has really failed to put any guardrails up to keep our community safe,” Hines said, noting her excitement to begin working putting those regulations in place.
“We’ve got a lot of younger people, a lot of parents that are coming in,” Hines said in reference to her fellow newly-elected members of Congress. “I bet that we can find some really great bipartisan approaches here to protect families.”

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Democrats say they have flipped Georgia’s state House; some races are still unsettled
description: With just a handful of races left to be called a day after Tuesday’s midterm elections, Democrats appear poised to take control of the Georgia state House of Representatives, ending more than two decades of Republican control of the chamber. Democrats needed to flip control of 10 seats to control 91 seats in the 180-member […]
text:
House Minority Leader Carolyn Hugley with members of the House Democratic Caucus celebrating their apparent win of the House majority Nov. 4, 2026. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder.With just a handful of races left to be called a day after Tuesday’s midterm elections, Democrats appear poised to take control of the Georgia state House of Representatives, ending more than two decades of Republican control of the chamber.
Democrats needed to flip control of 10 seats to control 91 seats in the 180-member chamber, and party leaders expressed confidence they will narrowly exceed that margin when all the votes are counted.
“Georgia voters have made their voices heard, and history has been made,” said House Minority Leader Carolyn Hugley of Columbus. “The Georgia House Democratic Caucus has indeed achieved this majority, and this victory represents more than just a change in the numbers. It’s a testament to the power of unity, determination, political courage and an unwavering commitment to the people of Georgia.”
As of 5 p.m. on Wednesday, only six races were still undecided.
House Speaker Jon Burns, a Newington Republican, said the ballot counting wasn’t over yet. But he also indicated Republicans will carry on fighting for conservative priorities if they become a minority party.
“While a few key seats remain within the recount margin, we still have a strong, resilient, and committed caucus,” Burns said in a statement. “Our dedication to protecting Georgia’s conservative values has not — and will not — change. We will continue showing up for the job we were elected to do each and every day — defending our future, uplifting our neighbors, strengthening opportunity, and keeping Georgia the great state we all know and love.”
The apparent victory would give Democrats the ability to pass bills out of the chamber without Republican support, but that’s not all. Democrats will have the opportunity to elect a House speaker and to appoint members to House committees, giving them power over what bills even get a hearing.
Georgia state Rep. Mary Margaret Oliver, a Decatur Democrat, stands behind Gov. Brian Kemp during signing ceremony for the amended budget on March 3, 2026, at the state Capitol in Atlanta. Alander Rocha/Georgia Recorder
“I can list for you 25 things that I’ve introduced that never got a hearing, and times are going to change,” Rep. Mary Margaret Oliver, a Decatur Democrat who has served in the House since 2003, told reporters Wednesday.
Hugley, who has served since 1993, indicated that she will seek the speaker’s gavel. She would be both the first Black person and the first woman elected to that role.
“I’ve been a member of this body for 34 years,” Hugley said. “And I love the House, and I respect and honor its traditions, and I believe it’s important for us to make sure that everyone is treated with courtesy and respect.”
“I’ve served under every speaker since Tom Murphy,” she added, referring to the Democratic speaker who served for 28 years until 2002. “So I kinda know what speakers are supposed to do.”
Speaking to reporters Wednesday, Hugley said the Democratic majority will focus on affordability, but she declined to discuss specifics, saying she would hold space for governor-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms to have a say in the party’s priorities.
Georgia governor-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms celebrates her victory on Nov. 3 in Atlanta. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder
“Let’s not jump ahead of her agenda right now, but know that we will be working on all those things you heard us talk about in the campaign,” Hugley said.
House Democrats will have an ally in the governor’s mansion – Bottoms is set to become the first Democratic governor since 2003, but dealing with the Senate will be more complicated.
Democratic state Sen. Josh McLaurin is set to lead the Senate as the incoming lieutenant governor, but the chamber is expected to retain a slight Republican majority.
Here’s the latest on the races set to determine the shape of Georgia’s House of Representatives.


Confirmed Democratic gains

Educator Cynthia Starke-Jones defeated Rep. Joseph Gullett of Dallas to represent House District 19
Grant administrator Elisa Lassiter defeated Rep. Kimberly New of Villa Rica to represent House District 40
Clinical therapist Danielle Bell defeated Rep. Don Parsons of Marietta to represent House District 44
Attorney Adam Cleveland defeated Rep. Scott Hilton of Peachtree Corners to represent House District 48
Former CDC public health professional Beth Fuller defeated Rep. Deborah Silcox of Sandy Springs to represent House District 53
Truck driver Mishael White defeated Rep. Noelle Kahaian of Locust Grove to represent  House District 81
Nonprofit CEO Michelle Kang defeated Rep. Matt Reeves of Duluth to represent House District 99
Arbitrator and former state Rep. Farooq Mughal defeated Rep. Sandy Donatucci of Locust Grove to represent House District 105
Retired U.S. Army Command Sergeant Major Renita Duncan defeated Rep. Bethany Ballard of Warner Robins to represent House District 147
Tradesman David Dillie defeated Rep. Bill Hitchens of Rincon to represent House District 161
Attorney Stephanie Burgess defeated Rep. Ron Stephens of Savannah to represent House District 164

Confirmed Republican gains

Small business owner Mack “Dutch” Guest IV defeated Rep. Eric Gisler of Watkinsville to represent House District 121

Still pending 

Republican Rep. Jordan Ridley of Woodstock is leading Democrat James “JL” Shade, a corporate legal professional in House District 22
Republican Rep. Matt Dubnik of Gainesville is trailing Democrat Scott Soracco, a retiree, in House District 29
Republican state Rep. Soo Hong of Lawrenceville is trailing Democrat Chris Luchey, a sports agent, in House District 103
Republican transportation company owner Trey Sheppard is leading Democratic certified public accountant Tyrone Evans in House District 128. The incumbent, Democratic Rep. Mack Jackson, did not seek re-election.
Republican Rep. Mike Cheokas of Americus is headed to a runoff with Democrat Ethan Wolfe, a retired military officer, in House District 151 after neither candidate managed to secure a majority of the vote in a three-way contest with independent candidate Travis Lockhart.
Republican state Rep. Gerald Greene of Cuthbert is trailing Democratic contractor Harry James in House District 154

Georgia Recorder Editor Jill Nolin contributed to this report.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT Dems preview agenda after blue wave swamps U.S. Congress
description: CT's delegation prepares to gain significant influence with new committee roles. They want to strike a balance on oversight and priorities.
text:
After a GOP wipeout in elections across the country, Democrats in Connecticut outlined a vision of how they’d like to use their new majorities in Congress and specifically their newfound authority across several congressional committees.
Democrats stormed back into power, regaining control of both the U.S. House and the U.S. Senate after making major gains in some of the reddest parts of the country. That will give them a large but also ideologically diverse coalition of Democrats who want to play a role in setting the party’s agenda.
Members of Connecticut’s delegation all drove home the same point: Democrats will need to take a two-pronged approach when they return to the majority. The party will have the delicate balance of pushing back on President Donald Trump through oversight efforts and tackling policies in the hopes of directly addressing voter concerns that led to their electoral success.
The 2026 midterm was a change election — some longtime incumbents lost in the primaries, including in the Connecticut General Assembly, and then voters sent a rebuke to Trump and Republicans, who have controlled all levers of power in Washington for two years.
Connecticut Democrats argue they can’t squander the opportunity afforded by Tuesday night’s wins.

U.S. Rep.-elect Luke Bronin speaks during a post-Election Day news briefing at the state Capitol in Hartford on Wednesday, Nov. 4, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / ct mirror

“If we want last night’s election to be remembered as more than a historic backlash to a corrupt president, then we need to get to work, solving problems that the American people desperately want us to see us solve,” said U.S. Rep.-elect Luke Bronin, the newest member of the congressional delegation, who unseated a longtime lawmaker in the August primary for the 1st District.
For Bronin, that means accountability as it relates to corruption and self-enrichment related to the administration while pursuing legislation to ban members of Congress from trading stocks and “serious” efforts on campaign finance reform.
Bronin was joined by a couple of his new colleagues in the congressional delegation at a Wednesday press conference outside of the state Capitol, who echoed sentiments about how Democrats in Washington need to navigate.
“We need to get to work not only saying no to Trump,” U.S. Sen. Richard Blumenthal said, “but positively yes to programs that cut costs to everyday Americans on healthcare, on everyday needs of people’s livelihood and lives and, of course, hold Trump accountable and fighting corruption.”
Democrats view their newfound power as much-needed oversight of the Trump administration, which some argue the party didn’t do enough of the last time they held majorities in Congress.
“Congress has the responsibility to conduct oversight. And I think part of the problem with the moment that we are in right now is that when we had the opportunity to enforce some of these regulations, to close some of the loops and gaps that we had seen, we didn’t do as much as we could,” U.S. Rep. Jahana Hayes, D-5th District, said Wednesday.
“We will also be legislating, but we have a responsibility to subpoena people and bring them in and peel back some of the layers of what has been happening because, again, people showed up because they were upset.”
In the lead-up to Tuesday’s elections, members of Connecticut’s delegation started to sketch out what Democrats’ return to power could look like from some of the highest echelons in Congress.
Nearly all of the Democrats will vie for the top spot on their committees, likely giving Connecticut’s delegation significant influence in the new session next year.
Their committees have different jurisdictions and roles, but Connecticut’s lawmakers see a throughline in the work for next year: a focus on oversight of the White House.
U.S. Rep. Rosa DeLauro, D-3rd District, hopes to reclaim the gavel of the House Appropriations Committee. She led the influential panel in 2021, but when Democrats lost the House majority two years later, she became the ranking member and has served in that role since.
The Appropriations Committee crafts spending bills, allocates money and funds the federal government. DeLauro’s leadership role on the committee comes at a time when there has been a major strain between the executive and legislative branch regarding federal funding. 
DeLauro, 83, currently doesn’t face any challengers for the leadership position. She has said she hopes to restore education and job opportunities that could help address the higher cost of living and restore her committee’s authority on grants and other funding.
DeLauro has also said she envisions handling some oversight “in my lane” by taking a look at where federal dollars are flowing and whether some money “has been transferred illegally.”
U.S. Rep. Jim Himes, D-4th District, is angling for the top spot on the House Intelligence Committee. 
Himes’ job as ranking member places him in the “Gang of Eight,” a group of the Republican and Democratic leaders in the House and Senate plus the chairs and ranking members of both intelligence committees.
The House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence has oversight over U.S. intelligence agencies as well as some issues concerning the Pentagon and other government agencies. As a likely chairman, Himes, 60, has previewed congressional oversight as a main objective.
The congressman has already issued warnings to defense companies about cooperating with congressional oversight, specifically on a potential investigation into corporate donations for the construction of the White House ballroom. But if he gets the chance to become chair, he said, he’s cognizant he’ll need some amount of buy-in from Republicans during such a polarized time.
U.S. Rep. Joe Courtney’s work on the Seapower Subcommittee has a lot of crossover with the defense industries that power much of Connecticut’s workforce and economy, especially in his 2nd District.
Some of Courtney’s focuses will be on the Department of the Navy, submarine programs and the AUKUS agreement between the U.S., U.K. and Australia that will have to meet deadlines on the delivery of Virginia-class submarines.
Courtney, 73, also sees opportunities for oversight, whether that’s on the Air Force One plane gifted by Qatar as well as the White House’s battleship proposal. He also believes oversight over the war in Iran and U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth’s tenure will be “front and center” for the full House Armed Services Committee.
Hayes would be a newcomer to leadership on the House Education and the Workforce Committee. So far, Hayes and Oregon Rep. Suzanne Bonamici are challenging the current top Democrat on the panel, U.S. Rep. Bobby Scott of Virginia.
Education is one of her top priorities, especially as a former teacher in Waterbury, and she’s cited concerns about the administration’s efforts to dismantle the U.S. Department of Education. She currently serves as the ranking member of the House Agriculture’s Subcommittee on Nutrition and Foreign Agriculture.
“I start tomorrow running for chair of Education and Workforce, because that to me is a big priority, but we have a budget that expires on Dec. 12,” Hayes said at Tuesday’s election night party in Waterbury. “I’m hoping we can do some negotiating on these big cuts in the ‘One Big Beautiful Bill.'” When asked about Trump’s veto powers, she said, “I don’t concern myself too much with what Trump says. We have the votes.”
Hayes has she’d prioritize trying to rescind cuts to Medicaid and the federal nutrition program known as SNAP that the law will enact through changes like new work requirements. Nearly 63,000 residents in Connecticut have so far lost SNAP benefits since eligibility changed as a result of H.R. 1. Medicaid changes are coming in January.

Attendees applaud for U.S. Sen. Richard Blumenthal during a post-Election Day news briefing at the state Capitol in Hartford on Wednesday, Nov. 4, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

Blumenthal said he plans to serve as chairman of the Homeland Security’s Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations — a role he previously held when Democrats were in the majority — as well as the top spot on the Senate Veterans’ Affairs Committee.
Blumenthal, who signaled he’ll run for a fourth term in 2028, said he spoke Wednesday morning with Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer, who is likely to return as majority leader next year. Blumenthal said he’ll support the New York Democrat for that role.
“I don’t think people understand the kind of weight that our delegation brings. We’re going to have at least two major chairman in the House and hopefully a third,” Blumenthal said, referring to Hayes’ run for committee chair. “Person per person, we’re going to be in a position to get results for the people of Connecticut.”
U.S. Sen. Chris Murphy currently serves as the top Democrat on the Senate Appropriations subcommittee that deals with funding for the U.S. Department of Homeland Security. When asked a couple of months ago if he would stay in that role or look to become chair, Murphy was uncertain and said, “there will be a lot of movement.” He is currently recovering after his hospitalization due to a stroke.
Tuesday’s elections cemented Democrats’ ironclad grip on federal races after they swept all five U.S. House races. Republicans in Connecticut have been locked out of Congress since 2009 after Chris Shays lost reelection to Himes.
Connecticut GOP Chairman Ben Proto is looking to the national party to help fund and sustain long-term party building. Republican congressional candidates in Connecticut had all bemoaned the lack of resources and financial support from the GOP at all levels.
“There was a time, not all that long ago, where the New England Republicans were dominant, and there’s been a shift. I understand that,” Proto said Tuesday night. “I think in order to make New England again a player at the federal level, those entities are going to have to invest — again with time, resources, human resources, dollar resources, professional work, ground-building work, grassroots work.”
When asked about whether Republicans’ messaging needs to change, Proto gave some indications of what they might need to do.
“I don’t know that the messaging has to change. I think that the messaging has to improve. I think the messaging has to be more personal. I think we have gotten caught up way too much in the consultant class in the Republican Party,” Proto said. “And we’ve lost the ability to just have conversations.”
Even with big majorities next year, Democrats will still need to contend with a president who can wield a veto pen. And they’ll need to negotiate with Republicans who will still have some leverage on must-pass legislation like government funding.
But Bronin argues that will show where Republicans are as Democrats look to build momentum into 2028.
“If the man in the White House vetoes those things,” Bronin said, “then it will be more evidence that he doesn’t give a damn about what the American people want.”
CT Mirror reporter John Moritz contributed to this story.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Idaho voters nominate lever-action rifle ‘that Won the West’ to be state’s official gun
description: In a non-binding vote, Idaho voters nominated a lever-action rifle, dubbed the “Gun that Won the West” to be the state’s official gun. The gun, the Winchester Model 1873, had the backing from about 31% of Idaho voters, the highest share of any of the guns on the ballot in Tuesday’s general election, according to […]
text:
The Idaho Legislature unanimously approved placing the non-binding poll of state guns on the ballot through House Bill 932 this year. (Yves Adams/Getty Images)In a non-binding vote, Idaho voters nominated a lever-action rifle, dubbed the “Gun that Won the West” to be the state’s official gun.
The gun, the Winchester Model 1873, had the backing from about 31% of Idaho voters, the highest share of any of the guns on the ballot in Tuesday’s general election, according to unofficial results from the Idaho Secretary of State’s Office at 12:30 p.m. Wednesday. All of Idaho’s 44 counties were reporting election results by then.
A digital representation of a Winchester 1873. (Photo courtesy of Robert Logan/Idaho Secretary of State’s Office)
The vote tees up a decision by the Idaho Legislature to potentially join 10 other states that have official state guns. Idaho, a Republican supermajority-controlled state, has strong protections for gun ownership — such as not requiring permits for concealed carry in city limits. 
None of the six guns — placed on the ballot in a unanimous vote by the Legislature — received a majority vote. 
Here’s how all the guns on the list fared with voters this year:

Winchester Model 1873 “Gun that Won the West” (.44-40): 31.1% of the vote, or 164,394 votes.
Winchester Model 1894 (.30-30): 25.32% of the vote, or 133,859 votes. 
1873 Colt Single Action Army Revolver, or “Peacemaker,” (.45 Colt): 15.26% of the vote, or 80,699 votes.
Remington Model 700 bolt-action rifle (.30-06): 12.45% of the vote, or 65,818 votes.
Colt M1911 .45 automatic Colt pistol (.45 ACP): 8.78% of the vote, or 46,405 votes.
M1 Garand rifle (.30-06): 7.09% of the vote, or 37,500 votes.

None of the guns on Idaho’s ballot have developmental ties to the state, unlike the official guns in some other states, like Utah.
If Idaho declared a state gun, the recognition would grow the list of officially declared state symbols, like the state flower, the syringa; the state gem, the star garnet; or the state amphibian, the Idaho giant salamander.
House Majority Leader Jason Monks, R-Meridian, said in an interview last month that he pushed to put the question on the ballot to help drum up voter turnout. The measure, called an advisory question, had the lowest share of ballots cast of any of the statewide ballot measures. 
About 70% of voters cast votes in the race for the state gun, out of the more than 731,000 of voters who turned out to the polls for this election, unofficial election results show. Nearly 99% of voters cast votes on Proposition 1, a ballot initiative — which voters rejected — that sought to repeal Idaho’s near-total abortion ban. About 97% of Idaho voters cast ballots on each of the constitutional amendments: A successful one to declare English as the state’s official language, and a failed one that would’ve revoked voters’ powers to legalize marijuana and other drugs.
Idaho voters turned out to vote at high rates this year in a midterm election, when voters tend to vote less. About 69% of the state’s registered voters cast ballots, early data show. But election officials expect the turnout rate to drop several points as they factor in voters who registered to vote on Election Day.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Commentary: The ‘blue tsunami’ brings a ripple of hope to South Dakota Democrats
description: By the time Tuesday’s “blue tsunami” washed in from the coasts and reached South Dakota, it was a ripple. State Democrats added four legislative seats, moving from eight to 12. It was the first time in 16 years Democrats have gained ground in the 105-member Legislature. Otherwise, South Dakota stayed Republican red as another 16-year […]
text:
Attendees at the South Dakota Democratic Party's election night watch party on Nov. 3, 2026, in downtown Sioux Falls applaud a national news outlet's call that Democrats won control of the U.S. House. (Photo by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)By the time Tuesday’s “blue tsunami” washed in from the coasts and reached South Dakota, it was a ripple.
State Democrats added four legislative seats, moving from eight to 12. It was the first time in 16 years Democrats have gained ground in the 105-member Legislature.
Otherwise, South Dakota stayed Republican red as another 16-year streak persisted: It’s been that long since Democrats won a race for a statewide office, and they lost all those races again Tuesday.
Further blunting Democratic enthusiasm is the sobering realization that Tuesday’s 49% turnout was the worst for any South Dakota general election since at least the 1960s. It could thus be said that historically depressed levels of voter enthusiasm are necessary for Democrats to make even meager gains in the Mount Rushmore State. That’s not exactly a solid base for further Democratic success.
Or, maybe it is.
Democrats gain seats in South Dakota Legislature for the first time since 2008

Before Tuesday, it seemed possible there would never again be good news for South Dakota Democrats. Their yearslong slide had shown no signs of abating.
It began in 2008 while Democrats were briefly riding high. Their voter registrations within the state reached a peak of more than 200,000. A Democrat, Barack Obama, won the presidency. Two members of the state’s three-member congressional delegation were Democrats — Rep. Stephanie Herseth Sandlin and Sen. Tim Johnson — and both won reelection. In the Legislature, Democrats jumped from 35 to 39 seats.
Yet the seeds of Democratic demise had already been planted with Johnson’s suffering of a cerebral arteriovenous malformation in 2006 and the financial crisis that Obama inherited when he took office.
Johnson won reelection in 2008 while enduring stroke-like symptoms that he never fully overcame, and he decided against running for reelection in 2014, opening the door for Republican Mike Rounds to win the seat. Johnson died 10 years later. Meanwhile, backlash against the federal government’s bailout of big banks gave rise to the tea party movement and turned the tide against Democrats nationally.
Amid all that came the unforeseen, politically rocket-fueled rise of Republican Kristi Noem, starting with her 2-point victory over Herseth Sandlin in 2010.
We all know what Noem went on to do as a U.S. representative, governor and member of President Donald Trump’s Cabinet. Herseth Sandlin became president of Augustana University in Sioux Falls and has never been heard from politically again.
Since 2008, Democrats have lost every statewide race. Trump has won South Dakota three times. Democratic voter registrations have plummeted, falling behind the collective number of people registered as independent, as a member of a minor party or as nothing at all. Democrats’ eight-member legislative delegation this year was their smallest since 1953.
Then came Tuesday, with dire national circumstances that have traditionally created political opportunities. Among the five Democrats who’ve been governor of South Dakota, two won election during the Great Depression and one was elected during the Vietnam War and Watergate scandal.
What the country faces now is not Vietnam or Watergate, but it’s bleak: 7% mortgage rates, $6 diesel, $4 gas, tariff-caused disruptions to the farm and ranch economy, and out-of-control health insurance premiums, among other problems, many of which can be pinned on Trump.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
For a path forward, Democrats can seek inspiration from another period that produced a Democratic governor. That was a 1958 victory by Herseth Sandlin’s grandfather, Ralph Herseth, amid a renaissance led by a young dynamo named George McGovern. He took over the state party as executive secretary in 1953 when there were two Democrats in the Legislature. Six years later, McGovern was in the U.S. House (on his way to the U.S. Senate and the 1972 Democratic presidential nomination), while Herseth was in the Governor’s Mansion and Democrats had a majority in the state Senate.
McGovern’s rebuild wasn’t magic. It was grinding, day-to-day candidate and voter recruitment, retold in great detail in the many books by and about him.
This year, by South Dakota Searchlight’s count, Republicans had already won 52 of the seats in the Legislature before the election, thanks to a lack of Democratic candidates in various parts of the state. Yet a cluster of Democrats sprouted in Sioux Falls like a stubborn weed in the state’s Republican garden, rising up to win 10 seats in that metro area.
Therein lies an opportunity to turn those candidates into more candidates, spreading out from Sioux Falls and growing Tuesday’s ripple, if not into a tsunami, at least into a wave that a few more people can surf.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: DeSantis wants special session to implement ‘taxpayer bill of rights’
description: One of the last actions Gov. Ron DeSantis wants done before leaving office in January is to implement a “taxpayer bill of rights” via a special legislative session, he said Wednesday. He established that expectation during a news conference following passage Tuesday of Amendment 3. The specific date for the session is up to the […]
text:
Gov. Ron DeSantis hosted a news conference at the Florida Capitol following the 2026 elections, on Wednesday, Nov. 4, 2026. (Photo by Jay Waagmeester/Florida Phoenix)One of the last actions Gov. Ron DeSantis wants done before leaving office in January is to implement a “taxpayer bill of rights” via a special legislative session, he said Wednesday.
He established that expectation during a news conference following passage Tuesday of Amendment 3.
The specific date for the session is up to the two chambers of the Legislature, he said. But, when asked before the election, incoming legislative leaders were non-committal on an Amendment 3-focused special session. Neither chambers responded to requests for comment Wednesday afternoon.
“That has to be done by January 1, and we will do it by January 1,” DeSantis said.
The amendment takes effect Jan. 1, but the first two years of its property tax exemption are set in the Florida Constitution already. The amendment allows legislators to eventually expand homestead exemptions to the full value of homes.
Tax shift?
DeSantis wants a special session, in part, to prevent local governments “from doing an end-run around the amendment and taxing them in other ways.”
Lawmakers skeptical of the amendment and local leaders from around the state questioned how governments will function with the decreases in revenue, and some insisted that shifting taxes, perhaps through fee-based government, could be the only way to maintain services.
Former state Sen. Jeff Brandes, who has rallied hard against Amendment 3, questioned the governor’s approach. He serves as president of the nonpartisan Florida Policy Project.
“I don’t know how [DeSantis] would exempt non-ad valorem taxation, or try to prevent some other type of fee shift. [Local governments] have all these statutory fees available to them,” Brandes told the Phoenix Wednesday. “I just don’t understand where he’s going, because so many have already built this into their system.”
Brandes sees no need for a special session.
“I don’t think there’s any reason that the Legislature should go back into special session under a DeSantis administration,” Brandes said, going on to say that an implementing bill for Amendment 3 can be the first bill of the 2027 session.
“Understand, many legislators are reading this amendment for the first time and trying to understand what it really does now. They didn’t think it was going to pass,” Brandes said.
Legislators “are going to have to build an entire process” for cities that operate under Amendment 3 to consolidate into counties — particularly counties that aren’t interested in absorbing cities.
To do a special session, Brandes said, “you’re going to be basically putting out a skeleton, an outline, and then you’re going to be filling in the holes for the next five years.”
“None of this is going to go smoothly,” he said.
“The cities and counties, before they were concerned; now they’re terrified and the Legislature itself is terrified,” Brandes said.
Legislative leaders dubious
On the “Between the Lines with Dara Kam” podcast, recorded and published before the election, the two incoming legislative chamber leaders didn’t sound committed to a special session before January.
“We in the Senate believe a lot of it in what we did was self-executing. However, there may be some implementation language we need to put around it — we do understand that,” Senate President-Designate Jim Boyd said on the podcast. “Personally, I believe that it can wait until we reconvene in January. I think the new administration ought to have a say in that.”
House Speaker-Designate Sam Garrison told Kam that Amendment 3 “will dominate the upcoming session, and not be something that can be rolled out and just implemented in three days. This is a very, very complicated issue.”
“I personally am of the belief, I’d rather be right than be quick,” Garrison said at the time, prefacing that comment by saying, “I don’t want to pre-judge it because I’m a big believer of you play the hole you’re on.”
The amendment was the only one of three on the ballot to garner more than 60% support from voters, the threshold required to pass state constitutional amendments.
Property tax slash crosses approval threshold on election night

The amendment will increase the homestead exemption for non-school taxes from $50,000 per year to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028.
At full implementation, state economists estimate Amendment 3 could reduce local revenues by as much as $12 billion annually.
The amendment did not receive 60% in any individual county among the five least populated counties in the state. Rural counties voiced concern they would not be able to function in a world in which Amendment 3 passed.
In Liberty County, the least populous in the state, the amendment received near 58%. In the next least populated counties, Franklin and Lafayette, the amendment received 47% and 57% support, respectively.
DeSantis said he wants to work with legislators to create a fund for smaller counties to ensure they can pay for core needs.
The amendment, DeSantis said, “that’s going to be such a breath of fresh air for people.”
“I’m glad that since I was involved with this, I want to make sure that we land it right,” DeSantis said.
Lawmakers will be in Tallahassee for a mostly ceremonial organizational session the week of Nov. 30.

title: Democrat Jessica Killin in 5-point lead over Rep. Crank in Colorado Springs district
description: Democrat Jessica Killin as of Wednesday afternoon had a 5-point lead over Republican U.S. Rep. Jeff Crank in the congressional district that’s centered on Colorado Springs. Killin had about 51% of the vote over Crank’s 46% as of 3:20 p.m. Wednesday. These are preliminary figures and can change. The Associated Press estimated 80% of votes […]
text:
Democrat Jessica Killin, pictured at her election night watch party on Tuesday, has a 5-point lead over incumbent U.S. Rep. Jeff Crank, a Republican. Voters of the 5th Congressional District, centered around Colorado Springs, have never sent a Democrat to Congress. (Photo courtesy of Jessica Killin's campaign)Democrat Jessica Killin as of Wednesday afternoon had a 5-point lead over Republican U.S. Rep. Jeff Crank in the congressional district that’s centered on Colorado Springs.
Killin had about 51% of the vote over Crank’s 46% as of 3:20 p.m. Wednesday. These are preliminary figures and can change. The Associated Press estimated 80% of votes were counted since polls closed Tuesday. 
Her lead in a district that has only sent Republicans to Congress shows that voters are fed up with having a representative focused on hyperpartisanship and not constituents, she said, adding voters are also struggling to afford daily necessities like gas, groceries and healthcare. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“People are sick and tired of the chaos and the corruption and lawlessness in Washington,” Killin told Newsline. “They want someone who’s going to be accountable and accessible, and who’s going to show up and listen and also focus on delivering real results for this community.”
Crank’s campaign did not respond to Newsline’s request for comment on the state of the race.
The 5th District is the only district in Colorado that has never sent a Democrat to Congress. National Democrats named the district as a top priority to flip this election.
Crank is a first-term member of Congress who won his seat in 2024 after former Republican Rep. Doug Lamborn retired. He won the seat with about 54.7% of the vote, continuing the perfect record of the district electing a Republican representative. 
Killin, an Army veteran former chief of staff to second gentleman Doug Emhoff, has drawn massive support from national Democrats who saw her candidacy as an opportunity to flip the 5th District seat. 
While Killin said it’s important to provide oversight and hold members of the Trump administration accountable, constituents care more about reversing the policies that have harmed them over the last two years, she said. That includes scaling back tariffs, working to make healthcare more affordable, incentivizing new housing in El Paso County and taking back the war power authority of Congress, she said. 
“I think what people really want is a Congress that actually delivers legislation and policies that make an impact on people’s lives,” Killin said. 
She wants to see ethics reform to restore integrity and trust in government, she said. People are unhappy that politicians focus too much on partisanship and not on public service, she said.
Killin said she would support House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries to be speaker of the House. 
The AP has not yet called the race. Killin said she had not spoken to Crank.

name: National
title: Trans sports bans get voter approval in 4 states
description: Voters in four states — Arizona, Colorado, Nebraska and Washington — are on track to pass or have passed measures to restrict transgender athletes’ participation in sports, a key policy focus of the Trump administration.  Colorado, Nebraska and Washington’s measures were ballot initiatives, while Arizona reached the ballot by way of the legislature.   Althou[...]
text:
Ahnaleigh Wilson, 17, of Eastmont High School, center, and Frances Staudt, 17, of Tumwater High School, right, speak with the media about Initiative 638 at Let’s Go Washington’s election night watch party Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026, in Redmond, Wash. (Photo by Ryan Berry/Washington State Standard) Voters in four states — Arizona, Colorado, Nebraska and Washington — are on track to pass or have passed measures to restrict transgender athletes’ participation in sports, a key policy focus of the Trump administration. 
Colorado, Nebraska and Washington’s measures were ballot initiatives, while Arizona reached the ballot by way of the legislature.  
Although there were sweeping Democratic wins in Republican strongholds Tuesday, GOP-backed proposals are winning over voters in various parts of the country.
Arizona’s initiative, which was garnering approximately 59% support late Wednesday, expands existing restrictions on transgender athletes to include private athletic associations and prohibits schools and athletic organizations from allowing individuals to use bathrooms, locker rooms and other private spaces designated for a sex different from the one recorded on their original birth certificate.
Colorado’s Proposition 134 was passing with 52% of the vote. The measure would require school athletic teams from elementary school through college to be designated for male, female or coeducational participation and require students to compete according to their biological sex. Nebraska’s measure is an amendment to the state constitution, which now prohibits students of the male sex from participating on teams designated for girls’ and women’s teams. 
Washington’s initiative will prohibit transgender girls from competing in girls’ K-12 sports and require healthcare documentation verifying sex eligibility for students seeking to participate on female teams. The state interscholastic athletics association reported knowing of only about 10 transgender athletes participating statewide each year.
According to Ballotpedia, 29 states had laws, regulations or interscholastic rules limiting or banning participation on female school sports teams to students of the female sex. 
Stateline reporter Robbie Sequeira can be reached at rsequeira@stateline.org.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Wallingford to conduct ‘discrepancy recount’ after running out of ballots
description: The town of Wallingford will conduct a “discrepancy recount” on Friday following potential ballot mishandling.
text:
The town of Wallingford will conduct a “discrepancy recount” on Friday following potential ballot mishandling.
Joan Ives-Parisi, Wallingford’s Republican registrar of voters, told Connecticut Public on Wednesday that the town ran out of ballots on Election Day.
“We just had a record turnout for the gubernatorial, which we were happy to see because we want people to vote, but it did cause a shortage of ballots,” Ives-Parisi said.
Per state contingency procedures, election officials then printed new ballots, which the secretary of the state’s office advised to be segregated and counted by hand. Instead, Ives-Parisi said, 100 of them went through a tabulator.
Secretary of the State Stephanie Thomas said a town running out of ballots was not too unusual.
“It’s fairly common, but these were mistakenly run through the tabulator,” Thomas told Connecticut Public’s The Wheelhouse on Wednesday morning. “This is why I’m always like, it’s great we have paper ballots, so the only delay is they now have to hand count.”
Ives-Parisi said she agreed when the secretary of the state’s office recommended a recount.
“We want to put the voters in Wallingford… at ease that their ballots were all counted properly, and their votes went where they should,” Ives-Parisi said.
Ives-Parisi said there would have been a recount anyway due to close margins in the state Senate District 34 race between Republican incumbent Paul Cicarella and Democratic challenger Brandi Mandato. The results of that race could determine whether Democrats enjoy an historic state Senate majority of either 32-4 or 33-3.
“We may have a little bit of time to wait, but it’s not like we won’t know the results,” Thomas said.
“This is exactly why Connecticut uses paper ballots. We don’t guess. We check,” Thomas said in a statement about the incident. “We’re committed to ensuring every ballot is counted fairly and accurately.”
This story was first published Nov. 4, 2026 by Connecticut Public.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Blackburn won’t address U.S. Senate appointment
description: Gov.-elect Marsha Blackburn refused to say Wednesday whether she will appoint a former private prison executive to the U.S. Senate seat she is set to vacate. Asked by a Lookout reporter whether she would name Damon Hininger, the one-time president and CEO of Tennessee’s private-prison company, CoreCivic, to replace her, Blackburn said, “We’ll have conversati[...]
text:
U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn, left, who is now governor-elect, joined outgoing Gov. Bill Lee for a joint press conference on Nov. 4, 2026, as Blackburn outlined her priorities. (Photo by John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)Gov.-elect Marsha Blackburn refused to say Wednesday whether she will appoint a former private prison executive to the U.S. Senate seat she is set to vacate.
Asked by a Lookout reporter whether she would name Damon Hininger, the one-time president and CEO of Tennessee’s private-prison company, CoreCivic, to replace her, Blackburn said, “We’ll have conversations about the Senate at a later date. … Not a conversation for today.”
Blackburn didn’t say Wednesday whether she still plans to appoint her replacement or whether she would select someone other than Hininger.
Nevertheless, Hininger, who stepped down from the post with Brentwood-based CoreCivic at the end of 2025, attended a joint press conference between Blackburn and Gov. Bill Lee Wednesday morning at the State Capitol, just a few hours after Blackburn captured the governor’s race in a 2.5-percentage point victory over Democrat Jerri Green.
Hininger said afterward he attended the press conference because he’s been friends with Blackburn and Lee for more than 20 years each and wanted to show them support but acknowledged he is “absolutely” interested in the U.S. Senate seat. He has attended several other events involving Blackburn in recent weeks, as well, including a visit by President Donald Trump to Clarksville.
“It’s been on my heart for probably a decade to serve the state in some capacity,” Hininger said.
Damon Hininger, former CEO of private prison company CoreCivic, attended the Nov. 4, 2026 join press conference between outgoing Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee and Gov.-elect Marsha Blackburn. Hininger is interested in filling the U.S. Senate vacancy created by Blackburn’s resignation to serve as governor. (Photo by John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)
In April, Hininger launched an organization called “Believe in Tennesssee.” A press release announcing the venture described it as a “conservative non-profit organization focused on keeping Tennessee the best place to raise a family and grow a business.” A search of the IRS website found no listings for the group. 
Hininger also launched a personal website, damonhininger.com, which features photos of his family and a listing of his community service. The home page labels Hininger “Believer. Husband. Father. Servant leader. Tennessee conservative.”He didn’t know whether Blackburn and Lee would be working together to decide who makes the appointment but acknowledged. “I’m sure they’re talking about it, but I have no inside knowledge on that,” he said.
Hininger added that he wants to show respect for Blackburn’s timetable on making the decision and how she approaches the matter.
Other potential candidates are former Knox County Mayor Glenn Jacobs, who served as Blackburn’s gubernatorial campaign treasurer, U.S. Rep. Tim Burchett of Knoxville, U.S. Rep. Chuck Fleischmann of Chattanooga and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, the latter two of which are considered outside contenders.
Blackburn said during the August primary she would choose her replacement if elected governor rather than leaving the selection to Lee. The matter raised state and federal constitutional questions because the governor makes the appointment and no public official has held a U.S. Senate seat and governor’s office simultaneously.
If Blackburn steps down from her Senate seat before she is inaugurated on Jan. 17, 2027, the appointment would fall to Lee.
Waiting until mid-January could cause problems for the appointee because the U.S. Senate makes decisions on committee assignments early in January.
Lee has declined to talk about Blackburn’s desire to appoint her replacement, saying in August, “We’ll take governors one at a time, and I don’t give advice to the next governor.”
Blackburn and Lee started the transition of the governor’s office Wednesday and announced that Deputy Gov. Stuart McWhorter is chairing the team.
Lee has not addressed the matter, even though a Lookout reporter asked him to clarify his previous statement after a recent press conference.
