name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Advocates push state to hold public hearing on opioid settlement spending
description: Advocates are pushing the state to hold a public hearing on the use of opioid settlement funding after reports about questionable spending.
text:
Harm reduction advocates staged a die-in at the Trenton Statehouse on Monday, June 30, 2025, after legislators — fearing federal Medicaid cuts would hurt hospitals — decided to divert $45 million in national opioid settlement funds to four of the state's largest hospitals. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor)Advocates for people whose lives have been battered by addiction want New Jersey officials to host a hearing on the use of opioid settlement funds in the wake of reports that money is being squandered by some local governments on community events or police programs that do little to address the problem.
The New Jersey Harm Reduction Coalition joined 50 treatment and advocacy organizations and 100 individuals in a request Tuesday urging the state Department of Human Services to schedule a public hearing to gather input on state oversight of the settlement money.
Jenna Mellor, the coalition’s executive director, said the state has the power to better protect these critical funds.
“It’s time for the state to step up and get a handle on these settlement funds. This public hearing request makes clear that people all over the state care about how these dollars are spent, and they want the state to lead,” she told the New Jersey Monitor.
New Jersey is set to collect $1.1 billion through 2038 from drug makers, distributors, and pharmacies as part of a series of multistate lawsuits. Half is controlled by the state and the rest is distributed to participating towns and counties.
The state has spent more than $100 million to expand access to treatment, housing, and other services, including harm reduction work to distribute the opioid-reversal agent naloxone, or Narcan. But a government watchdog flagged questionable spending among some municipalities, state lawmakers diverted $45 million from the fund for hospital aid, and recently released reports show counties and towns spent millions from the settlement to fund concerts, parties, and police equipment.
“We have more than enough evidence that local governments need clear guidance, and without that, millions of dollars are getting wasted at best, and going towards punishing people who need care at worst,” Mellor said.
The request comes just weeks after advocates told lawmakers that greater oversight and stricter guardrails are needed to protect this funding.

A state panel made up of treatment experts, prevention advocates, and people with first-hand addiction experience issued a strategic spending plan in 2025 that recommended the settlement dollars be invested in things like housing, treatment programs, family support services, and harm reduction. State allocations have largely followed this model and advocates say local governments should do the same.
“The use of opioid settlement funds has significant consequences for people and communities across New Jersey. These funds represent an opportunity to address the harms of the overdose crisis, support evidence-informed services, and invest in the community-based organizations that work directly with people affected by substance use,” the letter says.
The Department of Human Services did not comment on the request.

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Colorado Gov.-elect Phil Weiser names transition team to face ‘challenges on many fronts’
description: Colorado Gov.-elect Phil Weiser said Wednesday he has a “very long reading list” as he prepares to take office in the coming months — including a controversial budget proposal released this week by outgoing Gov. Jared Polis. Weiser, Colorado’s Democratic attorney general, defeated Republican Victor Marx by a landslide in the governor’s race Tuesday, leading [...]
text:
Gov.-elect Phil Weiser, Colorado's Democratic attorney general, spoke to reporters at a press conference on Nov. 4, 2026. (Photo by Chase Woodruff/Colorado Newsline)Colorado Gov.-elect Phil Weiser said Wednesday he has a “very long reading list” as he prepares to take office in the coming months — including a controversial budget proposal released this week by outgoing Gov. Jared Polis.
Weiser, Colorado’s Democratic attorney general, defeated Republican Victor Marx by a landslide in the governor’s race Tuesday, leading a Democratic ticket that tightened its grip on the levers of state government amid a “blue tsunami” of positive results for the party nationally.
He will be inaugurated as Colorado’s 44th governor on Jan. 12, 2027. On Wednesday he named a roster of well-known Democratic figures to lead his transition team between now and then, including former Interior Secretary Ken Salazar, former Gov. Roy Romer and former Denver Mayor Federico Peña, all of whom were named honorary co-chairs of Weiser’s transition.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“We’ve got challenges on many fronts,” Weiser said in a press conference Wednesday near the state Capitol in Denver. “I believe that one of the most important things I’m going to need to do is to build a team worthy of meeting these challenges.”
Those challenges include a state budget that could be in for another round of painful cuts when the Legislature, where Democrats on Tuesday captured supermajorities in both chambers, convenes next year. Polis on Monday released his final budget request as governor, initiating a process that will be completed by Weiser and the Legislature’s Joint Budget Committee, with a final vote typically held in late March.
Democrat Phil Weiser elected Colorado governor

Polis’ proposal includes a strict growth cap on the state’s safety-net Medicaid program, which would mean hundreds of millions of dollars in cuts to existing services as healthcare costs continue to soar. Healthcare advocates slammed the plan, which they said puts “the health of vulnerable Coloradans at risk.”
“There’s a Medicaid commission right now that is analyzing these issues from all sides. I’m very much looking forward to that conversation,” Weiser said. “It is obvious that there has been real growth, and there has to be the type of scrutiny that is happening, and we will continue that.”
He spoke as unofficial results showed Colorado voters approving Proposition NN, a referred measure to increase K-12 education funding by about $500 million a year by raising the state’s constitutionally-mandated revenue growth cap, potentially alleviating some budgetary pressure. The results of Amendment 87, a graduated income tax measure that would raise $2 billion a year by hiking taxes on incomes over $500,000, remained too close to call Wednesday.
‘Adjustments’ for anti-LGBTQ+ measures
Weiser signaled a willingness to back legislative changes to a pair of anti-trans ballot initiatives that appeared on track to pass by slim margins. Proposition 134, which to prevent transgender children from participating in school sports, and Proposition 135, which would prohibit health care professionals from knowingly performing any surgery on a minor “for the purpose of altering biological sex characteristics,” were both backed by anti-LGBTQ+ organization Protect Kids Colorado.
“We’re going to have to take a look at these anti-trans measures, and what adjustments are necessary and appropriate,” Weiser said. “I will say, for example, I don’t believe it would be acceptable for Colorado to have every student athlete have to go through full-body examinations or other invasions of privacy.”
Also on the governor-elect’s to-do list, he said, was to take up recommendations from a “competitiveness council” convened by Polis this year to address a state business climate that conservative lobby groups say is holding Colorado back economically.
“We should be open to asking: Can we create more targeted laws? Can we remove unnecessary and cumbersome restrictions?” Weiser said. “That dialogue that I’ve been having with the business community will continue.”
Landslide victory
Election results Wednesday showed Weiser winning 61% of the vote in the governor’s race, holding a 27-point lead over Marx, a first-time candidate and ministry leader from Colorado Springs.
It’s the most lopsided result in a Colorado governor’s race since former GOP Gov. Bill Owens’ blowout reelection victory in 2002, and is set to be one of the five largest winning margins in a governor’s race in state history.
Marx, who failed to pick up endorsements from many prominent Colorado Republicans — some of whom backed Weiser instead — did not hold an election-night watch party and had not released a public statement on his loss as of midday Wednesday. Weiser said Marx called him to concede the race around 9:30 p.m. Tuesday.
“He congratulated me on my victory, and he said he was praying for me and for Colorado,” Weiser said. “I told him I appreciated it. It was a very cordial conversation.”

title: Iowa Republicans’ legislative majorities shrink in 2026 elections
description: Though Iowa Republicans suffered serious losses in Tuesday’s midterm elections, the party appears to have kept control of both chambers at the Iowa Legislature. However, these Republican majorities are smaller than previous years. In the Iowa Senate, Republicans currently hold a 32-17 majority, with one vacancy — already a decrease from the GOP supermajority[...]
text:
The Iowa State Capitol as seen April 8, 2026. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)Though Iowa Republicans suffered serious losses in Tuesday’s midterm elections, the party appears to have kept control of both chambers at the Iowa Legislature.
However, these Republican majorities are smaller than previous years. In the Iowa Senate, Republicans currently hold a 32-17 majority, with one vacancy — already a decrease from the GOP supermajority elected to the chamber in 2024.
Democrats flipped two GOP seats in special elections: Sen. Catelin Drey, D-Sioux City, won a special election in September 2025 to represent Iowa Senate District 1 after Sen. Rocky De Witt, R-Lawton passed away in June 2025, and Sen. Mike Zimmer, D-DeWitt replaced Lt. Gov. Chris Cournoyer in Senate District 35 through a January special election victory.
Drey survived her first general election, defeating Republican Christopher Prosch Tuesday with 57.4% of the votes, according to preliminary results. But Zimmer was not reelected to serve a full term, as Republican Joe Stutting is set to take the seat with a lead of 51.9% to Zimmer’s 48.1%.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Iowa Senate Democratic Leader Janice Weiner recognized Zimmer’s efforts in the district despite the election loss.
“Senator Zimmer once again overperformed the 2024 Democratic vote margin of his district,” Weiner said. “This was a direct result of his hard work to represent his constituents and work in a bipartisan way to deliver for eastern Iowa.
But Senate Majority Leader Mike Klimesh said Prosch’s victory — and the retention of many seats currently in GOP control — showed the strength of Senate Republicans’ message. Klimesh said “Iowa Senate Republicans continue to be a bright spot in difficult election years,” as the party saw major losses in federal and statewide races.
“Iowa Senate Republicans talked to voters about our historic accomplishments and our vision for jobs, affordability, and common sense and the voters responded, taking out a Democrat incumbent,” Klimesh said. “We are happy to see continued successes with voters and the agenda Republicans delivered for the last several years.”
The current vacancy in the Iowa Senate has existed since June after Iowa Sen. Julian Garrett, R-Indianola, died following a battle with cancer. The winner in the general election race to fill the Senate District 11 seat has not yet been called. As of 4 p.m. Wednesday, Republican Hollie Arlene Zajicek leads with 59.2% to Sinikka Waugh at 40.8%, with 67% of votes counted.
Another still uncalled race was in Iowa’s Senate District 47, where results show Democratic challenger Nikhil Wagle leading with 50.2% of the vote to incumbent GOP Sen. Scott Webster with 49.8%. The AP estimates 99% of votes have been counted, showing Wagle with a 151-vote lead.
If Wagle retains the lead, it could mean Senate Democrats flipped two seats in the chamber, as the AP called the race for Democratic Iowa Rep. Heather Matson in Senate District 21 against Republican John Hollinrake. The seat is currently held by Iowa Sen. Mike Bousselot, R-Ankeny, who had initially run in another district before ultimately ending his campaign to work in the private sector.
Weiner said these results show that voters want changes in how the state government operates.
“Today, voters made their voices heard and resoundingly rejected another decade of one-party rule in Iowa, which has left too many Iowans feeling like their voices aren’t being heard,” Weiner said in a statement. “That isn’t healthy for our state, and it isn’t how Iowa is supposed to work. These results are a reminder that Iowa deserves a government focused on getting back to the basics: making sure families can afford the essentials, fully funding our public schools, protecting our water, and finally confronting Iowa’s cancer crisis.”
Weiner’s comments echo those of Democratic Gov.-elect Rob Sand. As he celebrated victory Tuesday night, he said his win meant “balanced government has been restored.” Sand said Democrats and Republicans will be forced to reach compromises in a divided government in 2027, and said he looked forward to working with state lawmakers “on the same common sense ideas and solutions that we advocated for throughout this campaign” come January.
But Republican state leaders like House Speaker Pat Grassley have already laid out plans to push back against “radical” policies proposed by Sand or Democrats.
“Governor-Elect Sand ran as a moderate,” Grassley said in a statement. “Now, we’ll find out if he was being genuine. If Sand brings forward sensible policies that make Iowa a better place to live, work, and raise a family, House Republicans stand ready and willing to work with him to accomplish that shared mission.
“But rest assured, if he tries to enact the same radical left agenda that we’ve seen democrats champion across the country, then our caucus will stand strong as a firm firewall. We will not allow Iowa to follow the failed path of neighboring states like Illinois or Minnesota. Iowans expect accountability, and we intend to deliver it.”
House Republicans maintain a majority after the 2026 general election, but the party has lost its 2024 supermajority hold on the chamber. Republicans entered Election Day with a 66-33 majority.
The chamber also had a vacancy, as Iowa Rep. Jon Dunwell, R-Newton, resigned from his seat in September after Gov. Kim Reynolds appointed him to serve on the Iowa Utilities Commission. Dunwell, who had already announced he would not seek reelection, had his House District 38 seat filled by Republican Matthew Oleson in the general election, according to preliminary results showing Oleson defeating Democrat Brad Magg.
Grassley said House Republicans’ agenda allowed the caucus to “maintain a strong majority after what was obviously a tough night for Republicans nationwide,” but GOP numbers in the chamber still took a hit. The AP had not called eight Iowa House races as of 3 p.m. Wednesday, but Democrats appeared to have picked up 11 seats in the chamber.
This includes the defeat of several Republican incumbents. In the Des Moines metro alone, Democrat Tom Walton unseated Rep. David Young in House District 28, Heather Sievers defeated Rep. Bill Gustoff in House District 40, former state Rep. Molly Buck won against Rep. Ryan Weldon in House District 41.
Democrats also took House District 43, a seat currently represented by Rep. Eddie Andrews, who did not run for reelection as he competed to become the GOP gubernatorial nominee. Democrat Jill Alesch will fill the seat with her win against Republican Nicole Hasso. One of the races not yet called by the AP is House District 46, but with 99% of votes counted, Democrat Amy Newton Rosenow leads with 50.7% against Rep. Dan Gehlbach with 49.3%.
This trend continued statewide, according to preliminary results.

Democrat Mike Tupper defeated Rep. David Blom in House District 52.
Democrat Jacob Welper won against Rep. Christian Hermanson in House District 59.
Democrat Matt Robinson defeated Rep. Jennifer Smith in House District 72.
Democrat Randy Meier defeated Rep. Thomas Determann in House District 69.
Incumbent Rep. Mark Cisneros was defeated by Democrat Nick Salazar in House District 96.
Democrat Jennifer Kirkman unseated Rep. Matt Rinker in House District 99.

Iowa House Democratic Leader Brian Meyer said his caucus “delivered the biggest electoral gains in a generation, sending a clear message that our state is ready for bold, balanced leadership.”
“I am incredibly proud that we picked up House seats all across Iowa, confirming that when Democrats fight for every Iowan, we win,” Meyer said Tuesday. “The momentum is on our side, and tonight’s results lay the foundation leading into 2028 and beyond. With a stronger caucus than we’ve seen in years, Iowa House Democrats are ready to get to work with Governor-Elect Sand, stand ready to stop any veto efforts, and fight for every Iowan, because tonight shows that when we fight for every Iowan, we win.”
The remaining six uncalled races are seats that are expected to stay aligned with current party control.

In House District 21, incumbent GOP Rep. Brooke Boden has a 59.1% lead against Democratic challenger Spencer Waugh at 40.9%, with 65% of votes counted.
Incumbent Republican Rep. Samantha Fett leads with 57.9% to Democrat Rory Taylor’s 42.1% with 66% of votes counted in House District 22.
Rep. Daniel Gosa, an incumbent Democrat, is leading with 58.9% in House District 81 against GOP challenger Dillon Fillion with 99% of votes counted.
In House District 94, Rep. Mike Vondran, an incumbent Republican has a lead at 50.8% against Democrat Karen Roebuck at 49.2%, with 99% of votes counted.
House District 97 is currently represented by Rep. Ken Croken, a Democrat who was defeated in the June primary by Adam Peters. Peters holds a general election lead at 69.4% to Republican Charlie Helmick at 30.6% with 99% of votes counted.
Democratic Rep. Monica Kurth announced in 2025 she would not seek reelection in House District 98. With 99% of votes counted, Democrat Andrew Fitzgerald leads with 60.6% against Republican Nathan Ramker at 39.4% in the race to fill her seat.

title: Oklahoma’s next governor discusses transition plans
description: OKLAHOMA CITY – Gov.-elect Mike Mazzei on Wednesday announced that his brother will chair his transition team. Dan Mazzei, a structural engineer who has worked on political campaigns, will lead efforts to put together Mike Mazzei’s incoming administration ahead of his swearing in as the state’s 29th governor on Jan. 11.   “We ran a lean, […]
text:
Mike Mazzei, center, gives the OK sign on Nov. 3, 2026, as he stands next to his brother, Dan Mazzei, right, and other family members during his watch party in Tulsa after winning the general election for Oklahoma governor. (Photo by Ace Cuervo/For Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY – Gov.-elect Mike Mazzei on Wednesday announced that his brother will chair his transition team.
Dan Mazzei, a structural engineer who has worked on political campaigns, will lead efforts to put together Mike Mazzei’s incoming administration ahead of his swearing in as the state’s 29th governor on Jan. 11.  
“We ran a lean, scrappy campaign with a small team,” said Mike Mazzei, who loaned his campaign a record $13 million. “Now it is time to build an administration of top notch Oklahomans, efficiency experts, and subject matter experts who want to improve the lives of everyday Oklahomans.”
He encouraged those who are interested to submit a resume to mikeforok.com.
“We’re looking for talented, hardworking people who share our commitment to serving Oklahomans and delivering results,” Mike Mazzei said.
Mike Mazzei, a Republican, on Tuesday defeated Democrat Cyndi Munson and three independents to become the state’s next governor. 
He garnered nearly 52% of the vote to Munson’s nearly 46%, according to the Oklahoma State Election Board.
Mike Mazzei said he looks forward to working with Gov. Kevin Stitt, who is in his final months of a second term, on a smooth transition. Stitt cannot run again due to term limits.
Mike Mazzei, who served as budget secretary under Stitt, would not say if he planned to retain any members of Stitt’s administration.
Mike Mazzei, a financial planner from Tulsa, said he wasn’t going to make any personnel announcements at this time, but expects to make some announcements fairly soon.
Mike Mazzei said he will be working with House Speaker Kyle Hilbert, R-Bristow, and Senate Pro Tem Lonnie Paxton, R-Tuttle, on “some priorities, so we can have a very effective first 100 days.”
He also expects to create an office of State Finance and Fiscal Responsibility to address funding issues involving state agencies, including food stamps and Medicaid.
He plans to require state agencies every 90 days to provide financial reports that compare budgeted expenses to actual expenses.
Mike Mazzei said now that the election is finished he will be taking a few days off.
“My wife and I are headed to an undisclosed location for a couple of days because my wife’s birthday is Saturday and I promised her a beach house somewhere in North America,” he said.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Rhode Island’s congressional delegation prepares for more influence in Washington
description: U.S. Rep. Gabe Amo was an 18-year-old field organizer for Sheldon Whitehouse’s first U.S. Senate campaign in 2006 when he celebrated inside Providence’s Biltmore Hotel as Democrats won back both chambers of Congress. Two decades later, Amo returned to the same hotel Tuesday night celebrating another Democratic takeover of Congress — one that will put […]
text:
Rhode Island’s congressional delegation — U.S. Sens. Jack Reed and Sheldon Whitehouse, and U.S. Reps. Seth Magaziner and Gabe Amo — expect to have a more prominent role in Congress as Democrats take control of both chambers. (Photos by Alexander Castro and Ken Castro/Rhode Island Current; collage by Alexander Castro/Rhode Island Current)U.S. Rep. Gabe Amo was an 18-year-old field organizer for Sheldon Whitehouse’s first U.S. Senate campaign in 2006 when he celebrated inside Providence’s Biltmore Hotel as Democrats won back both chambers of Congress.
Two decades later, Amo returned to the same hotel Tuesday night celebrating another Democratic takeover of Congress — one that will put him and Rhode Island’s other House member in the majority for the first time in their careers. 
“This is seismic,” Amo said in an interview outside L’Artisan Cafe in Providence’s Wayland Square Wednesday morning. 
Amo was first elected to Congress in a 2023 special election a year after his colleague, U.S. Rep. Seth Magaziner, was elected, just as Republicans were taking control of the House. 
Despite their relatively short tenures, both could find themselves among the more senior members of the House Democratic caucus next year when a large group of new Democrats arrives, Adam Myers, a political science professor at Providence College, said.
“There’s no doubt that the state’s profile on Capitol Hill will be greatly enhanced starting next year,” Myers said in a phone interview.
Magaziner said he hopes the new majority will move quickly to address voters’ concerns about the economy and the conduct of the Trump administration.
“I don’t think the message should be that Democrats won big because people love Democrats and think that we’re awesome,” Magaziner said in a phone interview. “They were trying to send the message that they expect us to bring change to Washington.”
Both of Rhode Island’s congressional representatives identified lowering costs as a priority for the incoming Democratic majority, pointing to reversing President Donald Trump’s tariffs and restoring enhanced Affordable Care Act tax credits that lapsed last year. 
“The first thing we have to do is stop the bleeding,” Amo said. “The status quo cannot exist and I’ll do everything I can to push us to a future where everybody in our country gets to live with dignity.”
Myers cautioned that delivering on the affordability agenda may prove more difficult, noting that many of the economic pressures facing voters are beyond Congress’ direct control especially as the president may veto much of the Democratic agenda.
Trump told The New York Times Tuesday he was willing to work with Democrats as they made gains across the country. But he also posted an image to his Truth Social account of a red baseball cap with the word “VETO” emblazoned on it.
“We can’t have that instability, that lack of predictability,” Amo said. “The expectation from the American people is that we deliver and I’m going to do everything to get that done.”



Quotation







I don’t think the message should be that Democrats won big because people love Democrats and think that we’re awesome. They were trying to send the message that they expect us to bring change to Washington.


– U.S. Rep. Seth Magaziner, D-Rhode Island's 2nd Congressional District


Magaziner sees at least one area of bipartisan agreement that Trump may not be able to stop: banning members of Congress and the president from trading stocks. He said the proposal likely has enough support to pass with a veto-proof majority.
“The momentum behind this issue is really at a fever pitch,” he said. 
More stature in the Senate
The shift in Congressional power could be even more consequential for Rhode Island’s two senators, who are among the most senior Democrats in the chamber and are expected to take the helm of influential committees.
U.S. Sen. Jack Reed, who was easily reelected to a sixth term Tuesday, told Rhode Island Current he anticipates he will reclaim the chairmanship of the Senate Armed Services Committee, where he is the top Democrat.
“We’ll have to wait for the formal vote,” he said in a phone interview. “But that’s my expectation.”
Reed said he expects the committee to conduct a broad review of the administration’s military operations in Iran and their global consequences, as well as its actions in the Caribbean, where he cited attacks on civilian vessels.
He also wants to scrutinize the administration’s financial ties to private industry, including stock purchases by officials, and reassess the threats facing the United States.
On domestic policy, Reed said Democrats should move quickly to restore the enhanced Affordable Care Act tax credits that help people buy insurance through the federal marketplace and replace funding cuts from Medicaid. He warned that the cuts could further weaken Rhode Island’s already strained health care system.
“Our health care system in Rhode Island is dysfunctional at the moment,” Reed said.
Whitehouse, who was elected to a fourth term in 2024, is expected to become chair of the Senate Judiciary Committee, succeeding retiring ranking member Sen. Dick Durbin of Illinois, his office confirmed Wednesday.
Myers said Whitehouse’s expected chairmanship could give Rhode Island’s delegation an especially prominent role in shaping the Senate’s response to the Trump administration, particularly through the committee’s authority over federal judicial nominations.
“He’s going to be leading one of the most important committees in the Senate,” Myers said.
Rhode Island’s junior senator appears ready to use that position to challenge the Trump administration and the federal judiciary. In a statement Wednesday celebrating Democrats’ victories, Whitehouse criticized what he called a Supreme Court “captured by the billionaire class” and a Justice Department that has “gone rogue.”
“We are ready for the hard work ahead to fix what’s badly broken and set a course for a new, brighter future for the country,” Whitehouse said.

name: VTDigger
title: Hunting is part of who we are as a state
description:
From grouse walks in October to quiet hours in a deer stand, hunting season carries generations of Vermont tradition, family bonds and community.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Hunting is part of who we are as a state.
text:
Dear Editor,
I adore Vermont in the fall. As mornings turn crisp, leaves begin to change and fall, and days grow shorter, a familiar feeling of anticipation stirs in my heart. It is not just the anticipation of my favorite holidays — Thanksgiving and Christmas — that I look forward to. It is also the season that comes first: hunting season.
For me, hunting season begins at the end of September. On a sun-drenched October afternoon, I love nothing more than simply going for a walk in the woods with my shotgun, hoping to flush a grouse. These outings are also opportunities to scout for deer sign, find game trails and identify where I might place my deer stand later in the season. Sometimes alone, sometimes with a good friend, they offer an opportunity for tranquil reflection, communing with nature and taking in the beautiful Vermont landscape.
As autumn progresses, I look forward to deer season, when I will track deer through the snow or spend quiet hours in my stand. My wife affectionately calls this “meditation for men,” although nowadays I deeply appreciate the many women who have come to love the sport as well. There is something profoundly restorative about spending hours in the woods away from the distractions and demands of everyday life.
To us rural Vermonters, tradition matters. I began hunting with my family as a child. It was a lesson in respect for nature, collaboration, patience and, importantly, the safe handling of firearms. I loved hunting with my brother or a neighbor, and while our family never had a deer camp of our own, I always enjoyed visiting friends whose families did.
Then, as now, community mattered. Not just the community of friends and family enjoying the sport together, but the wider community as well — game suppers, buck pool and sharing stories about the one that got away. These traditions have been woven into the fabric of rural Vermont life for generations. They connect us to the land and remind us of the importance of family, friendship and shared experience.

READ MORE

Hunting is part of our culture, and I am proud to have raised my boys with that experience. While my youngest would prefer simply to enjoy the fruits of our labor, my eldest is a hunter, and I treasure the time we have spent together in the woods — teaching him to read sign, move quietly and safely, and respectfully take game. 
There’s a saying that “men make friends facing the same way,” and my hunting experience has certainly borne that out, both with my sons and with some of my closest friends. There is a special bond that comes from sharing a cold morning in the woods or simply sitting quietly and enjoying one another’s company.
In today’s modern world, where so much of rural Vermont’s culture and traditions seem increasingly under threat, I believe it is important that we remember what makes our state special. Hunting is more than the pursuit of game. It is a connection to our land and the generations who came before us.
Not everyone will choose to hunt, and that’s perfectly fine. But I hope we can continue to respect and preserve this important part of Vermont’s heritage, and ensure that future generations have the same chance to experience it.
For that, and for so much more, I am grateful for hunting season.
Shawn TesterLyndonville, Vt.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Once again, the Democratic blue wave misses Florida
description: Tuesday night saw the near virtual destruction of the Republican Party power structure in this country. Except in Florida. Democrat David Jolly lost to Republican Byron Donalds by 1.3% in the race for governor. The races for attorney general, chief financial officer, and agriculture commissioner all went to the Republican incumbents by similarly close margin[...]
text:
Democratic gubernatorial candidate David Jolly with his wife Lauren while addressing a crowd at the Tampa Convention Center on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Mitch Perry/Florida Phoenix)Tuesday night saw the near virtual destruction of the Republican Party power structure in this country.
Except in Florida.
Democrat David Jolly lost to Republican Byron Donalds by 1.3% in the race for governor. The races for attorney general, chief financial officer, and agriculture commissioner all went to the Republican incumbents by similarly close margins. And Angie Nixon, the Democratic candidate for Senate, lost by 3 points to Republican Ashley Moody, 51%-48%.
However, the Democrats did net 15 seats in the state House and one in the state Senate, moving them out of their superminority status in the state Legislature. The House District 33 seat is now in the recount process, with Democratic candidate Dan McDow ahead. Currently, the House Democratic Caucus is at 49 members. If McDow wins, the Democrats will have 50 members to the Republicans’ 70 in the 120-member House.
Some analysts say the blue wave, or tsunami, did hit Florida, noting that approximately 68% of registered Democrats voted statewide, compared to 63% of Republicans, according to the Fresh Take Florida Project. That’s the highest turnout for a midterm election for Democrats in living memory, said Matt Isbell, a Democratic data consultant.
Republican Byron Donalds celebrates his win in the Florida governor race on Nov. 3, 2026, flanked by his wife, Erika, and running mate Bryan Ávila. (Photo via Donalds Facebook page)
“A blue wave did hit Florida,” said University of Central Florida political science professor Aubrey Jewett, noting not only the wins in the state House but also how the Democrats staved off the Ron DeSantis’ redistricting map, specifically drawn to allow Republicans four more seats in the state’s 28-member congressional delegation.
Instead, Democrats appear to have won all four, including Darren Soto in Florida’s 9th Congressional District, which voted for Donald Trump by 18 percentage points in 2024. (Soto leads Republican Dan Green, 50.26% to 49.74%, a race so tight that the Associated Press has not yet called it).
Isbell says Florida Democrats overall overperformed Tuesday, especially with independent voters and even some “soft Republicans.”
So why did Florida Democrats not win statewide when Kansas Democrats and Texas Democrats did? Isbell believes that’s because of the Republicans’ 11-point lead in voter registration, which Jewett calls their “insurance policy.”
Massively outspent
Following Jolly’s narrow loss, don’t overlook is how massively outspent he was. The Donalds campaign raised nearly $174 million, while Jolly’s campaign took in less than $28 million. During a campaign event in Tampa in late September, Jolly said he needed the national Democratic Party to start spending money on his behalf, arguing the only way he could lose was if national Democrats “chose to take a pass on Florida like they have in the past 10 years.”
Speaking to reporters on a remote conference call Wednesday morning, Florida Democratic Party Chair Nikki Fried acknowledged that, “for years, Florida has been written off by people who believe this state is no longer competitive and too expensive.”



Quotation







It is not about spending in Florida. It is about investing early in Florida the infrastructure that is necessary to win the third-largest state.


– Nikki Fried, Florida Democratic Party chair



	“Well, I hope that they are paying attention this morning,” she said. “Because what we saw last night should send a very clear message to our national Democratic Party and our partners: Florida is worth investing in.”
Noting Democrats’ wins in the Legislature, Fried said, “We demonstrated what can be accomplished with very limited resources.”
“Florida Democrats are looking at the results across the country and can only imagine what kind of a day we would be having if we had sustained national support and the investment this state deserves,” she said. “It is not about spending in Florida. It is about investing early in Florida the infrastructure that is necessary to win the third-largest state.”
Isbell noted that the national Democratic Party and its political committees that fund races pulled out of Florida after 2018 and 2020 election cycles, and voter registration efforts since then have fallen off a cliff. Only 67% of eligible adults are registered to vote in Florida, the fourth worst registration rate in the country, he said.
“That’s because we as Democrats of Florida have a couple of coins and a shoestring to try to register people in a state where if you make mistakes with forms you can be hit with lawyer fees and all of this other crazy stuff. And the Republicans, who have more money than God, have been able to at least sustain their level,” he said.
Limits on voter drives
In 2023, the Florida Legislature passed SB 7050, a law that imposed new regulations on the activities of third-party voting registration organizations. Under that law, those groups must re-register with the state before each election cycle to collect voter registration forms, and they have a shorter time to return forms to the county supervisors of elections, with a penalty of $50 per late day, up to $2,500 per application.
Meanwhile, during a press conference in Tallahassee Wednesday, Gov. Ron DeSantis said it would be an understatement to call the electoral earthquake that took place Tuesday simply a “wave.”
“It’s the political equivalent of a meteor strike that went all around the United States,” he said — adding that the one state able to “hold the line and withstand that was right here in the free state of Florida.”
The reason for that, DeSantis said, was that Republicans in Florida had built a record of achievement and trust from voters “that even in the worst situation that you can imagine politically, we were able to hold the line and prevent the worst from happening here.”
Specifically, the governor cited Central Florida Republican state Sen. Jason Brodeur’s loss to Democrat John Lowndes in the Senate District 10 race by 10 points as an example of how no Republican was safe from the national headwinds against the GOP. “That wasn’t a reflection of him. He got caught up in a wave,” he said.
In addition to the recount in the Florida House District 33 seat, Fried noted that the race in Florida’s 27th Congressional District between Republican incumbent Maria Salazar and Democrat Eliott Rodriguez was headed for an automatic machine recount. The latest totals have Salazar up 50.23% to Rodriguez’ 49.77%, within the 0.5% margin that triggers a recount.
Salazar won the seat in 2024 by 20 points. “The voters have spoken loud and clear all over District 27 and the rest of my country, that my party — my Republican Party — needs to course-correct on the economy and on immigration,” said Salazar, according to WLRN Public Media.
With additional reporting from Jay Waagmeester.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Pearson accepts loss in U.S. District 9 race, but says ‘Tennessee politics will never be the same’
description: Democratic state Rep. Justin J. Pearson conceded the race to represent Tennessee’s 9th Congressional District Wednesday after coming in roughly 1.1% behind his Republican opponent. State Sen. Brent Taylor tallied roughly 2,500 more votes than Pearson in a district redrawn to give Republicans their best chance at flipping the longtime Democratic seat that for[...]
text:
MEMPHIS, TN -- Rep. Justin J. Pearson speaks during his Election Night Watch Party at the Power Center in Memphis.  (Photo by Brad Vest for Tennessee Lookout)Democratic state Rep. Justin J. Pearson conceded the race to represent Tennessee’s 9th Congressional District Wednesday after coming in roughly 1.1% behind his Republican opponent.
State Sen. Brent Taylor tallied roughly 2,500 more votes than Pearson in a district redrawn to give Republicans their best chance at flipping the longtime Democratic seat that for decades encompassed Shelby County. 
The Associated Press has yet to call the race as of 3:30 p.m. Wednesday.
As the Tennessee Secretary of State finalized the race’s unofficial results late Tuesday night, Pearson told a crowd of supporters at the New Direction Christian Church’s Power Center in Hickory Hill that he would wait until all ballots were counted.
Supporters had waited for more than three hours, refreshing results pages with bated breath, at times erupting in cheers when Pearson pulled ahead in the district designed by Tennessee Republicans for a Democratic loss.
Taylor claimed victory just after 11 p.m. 
MEMPHIS, TN – Rep. Justin J. Pearson turns to his wife, Oceana Pearson, during his Election Night Watch Party at the Power Center in Memphis.(Photo by Brad Vest for Tennessee Lookout)
“What I will tell you, without a shadow of a single doubt, is that together we changed history,” Pearson told supporters in his election night speech. “Tennessee, and Tennessee politics, will never be the same again. Together, we have made history in a district that they drew to gerrymander us into oblivion.”
Pearson will continue to serve Memphis in his role as District 86’s state representative. 
In a Wednesday statement, Pearson said his campaign had accomplished what he set out to do.
“Every single county in our district swung between 10 and 30 points toward Democrats, inspired by our vision to get big money corruption out of politics, stop billionaires from building toxic data centers in our backyards, and take on politics as usual in both parties,” Pearson stated.
“For the first time in decades, many people feel seen and believe Tennessee can be changed for the better,” he stated. “And we all learned that we have more in common than we could have ever imagined.”
Pearson secured about 85% of the vote in the redrawn district’s portion of Shelby County, and nearly 55% of the vote in a sliver of Rutherford County in Middle Tennessee, according to results data compiled by the Associated Press. While Taylor prevailed in rural West and Middle Tennessee counties, Pearson still claimed double-digit percentages in each. In the 9th District’s portion of Williamson County, a Republican stronghold, 38.1% of the votes went to Pearson compared to Taylor’s 60.4%.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Voters in two South Dakota counties reject local sales taxes for property tax reductions
description: Voters in South Dakota’s Brown and Codington counties rejected new half-percent county sales taxes Tuesday, voting down plans their county commissions had proposed to lower homeowners’ property taxes. Brown and Codington were the first counties where voters weighed in on the new taxes. The decisions come after a string of county commissions approved local sa[...]
text:
A Minnehaha County property tax bill delivered in early 2026. (Photo by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)Voters in South Dakota’s Brown and Codington counties rejected new half-percent county sales taxes Tuesday, voting down plans their county commissions had proposed to lower homeowners’ property taxes.
Brown and Codington were the first counties where voters weighed in on the new taxes. The decisions come after a string of county commissions approved local sales taxes for homeowner property tax reductions. At least seven other counties have adopted a sales tax without putting it to voters or being subjected to a referendum.
State lawmakers and Gov. Larry Rhoden gave counties the authority during this year’s legislative session to implement their own sales taxes for the first time in state history, with proceeds going toward lowering homeowners’ property taxes. Counties are limited to a half-percent tax. Lawmakers and the governor also decided to use proceeds from next year’s increase in the state sales tax rate, from 4.2% to 4.5%, to reduce property taxes for homeowners statewide. 
4 South Dakota counties will vote in November on new sales taxes to lower property taxes

Brown County commissioners chose to put the tax on the ballot, while Codington County residents gathered petition signatures to force a vote. In Brown County, 56% of voters opposed the tax. In Codington County, 60% did, according to unofficial results from the Secretary of State’s Office.
Shelly Alvine, a Codington County resident, helped lead the petition drive and called the result a “nice outcome.”
Alvine said voters were “voting with their pocketbook” as inflation strains household budgets, and she called the rejection “decisive.” Renters, she added, wouldn’t have benefited from lower property taxes while paying higher sales taxes.
“If you could look a person in the eye and ask them for $50 to pay for your property tax, that’s what you’re asking them to do with this sales tax,” Alvine said.
Alvine said the results should give other counties reason to pause before pursuing their own sales taxes. Voters in Clay and Charles Mix counties will decide on theirs in special elections Nov. 17.
“I think that’s a good reason for the Legislature, before passing off their decisions on South Dakotans and the counties, to look for other ways to make property tax relief more equitable,” Alvine said.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: With Democrats taking control of Congress, Stein hopes for more Western NC recovery funds
description: North Carolina will send more Democrats than Republicans to Congress next year.
text:
Gov. Josh Stein addresses reporters after the 2026 midterms on Nov. 4, 2026. (Photo: Christine Zhu/NC Newsline)North Carolina Gov. Josh Stein is hoping the newly-elected Democratic majorities in Congress will move more quickly than Republican incumbents have to send hurricane recovery funding for Western North Carolina, he told reporters Wednesday. 
A blue tsunami hit the Tar Heel State Tuesday night as Democrats coasted to victory in the U.S. Senate and flipped at least five seats in the U.S. House. At the state level, unofficial results show Democrats winning a near-supermajority in the North Carolina House and gaining seats in the Senate.
Nationally, Democrats flipped both chambers in Congress. By winning North Carolina and six other seats, Democrats stand to hold at least 54 seats in the U.S. Senate, while Republicans have 44. Races in Alaska and Mississippi are yet to be called, although Democrats narrowly lead in both. In the U.S. House, Democrats also won a sizable majority. 
North Carolina will send more Democrats than Republicans to Congress next year. Former Gov. Roy Cooper, who was serving at the time the storm hit in 2024, is among the new faces heading to Washington in January. 
“Senator-elect Cooper understands very well the needs of Western North Carolina,” Stein told reporters outside the Executive Mansion in Raleigh on Wednesday. “His voice will be loud and important, and I am eager to work with him.”
Republicans currently hold a 53-47 majority in the U.S. Senate. North Carolina’s GOP senators, Ted Budd and Thom Tillis, have pressed Washington for more Hurricane Helene aid, but Congress hasn’t delivered.
The federal government has provided about $11 billion towards recovery funding from Helene. 
“It sounds like a lot until you realize the damage was $60 billion,” Stein said. “I want this Congress to act before the year ends, but if this Congress doesn’t, I’m going to work with Senator-elect Cooper to make sure that people of Western North Carolina are supported.”
Stein said Democrats flipped the North Carolina House “in dramatic fashion.”
Looking ahead at the 2027 legislative session, the governor said his priorities are making the right investments in the budget, supporting the recovery and economic development of Western North Carolina, and setting conditions for continued economic success.
He said he’s eager to work with Rep. Robert Reives, D-Chatham, and Sen. Sydney Batch, D-Wake, who are expected to become House Speaker and Senate Democratic leader, respectively. The caucuses will hold leadership elections in the upcoming weeks.
“There is a lot that’s going right for North Carolina,” Stein said. “I want to make sure that we continue that momentum so that more people can actually feel the real benefits, the tangible benefits of this economic growth.”

name: Michigan Advance
title: Lawrence says Democrats must deliver bold change after election victories
description: After declaring victory in a hard-fought battle for Michigan’s most competitive swing district, U.S. Rep.-elect William Lawrence reconvened with his supporters and members of the media to celebrate his victory and reaffirm his commitment to promises he made along the campaign trail. Standing outside his campaign office in Lansing, Lawrence offered his thanks[...]
text:
Congressman-elect William Lawrence outlines his priorities for serving in the U.S. House while speaking with reporters outside his campaign HQ in Lansing, Nov. 4, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance)After declaring victory in a hard-fought battle for Michigan’s most competitive swing district, U.S. Rep.-elect William Lawrence reconvened with his supporters and members of the media to celebrate his victory and reaffirm his commitment to promises he made along the campaign trail.
Standing outside his campaign office in Lansing, Lawrence offered his thanks to family members, staff, campaign supporters and U.S. Rep. Tom Barrett (R-Charlotte) who currently represents the district.
“I was thankful to get a phone call from him last night and have a conversation with him where he congratulated and conceded the race, and I expressed my readiness to work with him on the transition and I thanked him directly for his service,” Lawrence said.
The Associated Press called the race for Lawrence at 2:05 p.m. on Wednesday, with unofficial results showing Lawrence with 51% of the vote and Barrett with 47.7%.
The soon-to-be freshman representative reiterated his belief that “Washington’s priorities are all upside down,” and emphasized that there is much to be done over the next decade to deliver economic security, restore law and order, address worsening climate change and bring peace to the global stage.
“We’re not going to get it all done over the next few years, but I’m excited to get to work with some very specific priorities,” Lawrence said, pointing to constituent services, ending foreign wars and accountability for big tech as his main concerns.
U.S. Rep.-elect William Lawrence (D-Lansing) speaks with reporters the morning after the election, Nov. 4, 2026 (Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance)
Shortly after speaking with reporters, Lawrence joined members of the Congressional Progressive Caucus’s Political Action Committee on a press call where they laid out their goals for the remaining two years of President Donald Trump’s administration. 
Rep. Greg Casar (D-Texas), the caucus chair, said Tuesday’s election delivered big wins for progressives, with the caucus set to grow its ranks by 25 members. He noted that even candidates who did not campaign as progressives campaigned on issues that progressives have championed for decades, including opposition to big money in politics, ending foreign wars, standing up to political corruption and delivering healthcare reforms. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
However, Casar emphasized that Democrats cannot remain idle in the next two years.
“Last night was not a sign that all of Democrats’ problems are solved,” Casar said. “The election is not an endorsement of returning to the status quo or tinkering around the edges. This is a message that people in this country are mad as hell, and are giving Democrats a shot to show them we can do something about it. And so it’s our turn to take them up on that opportunity.”
Maxwell Frost, the co-chair of the caucus’s political action committee underscored Casar’s point, noting that “especially over the last decade, voters will give you power and take it away just as quickly as they gave it to you.”
Heading into the 120th Congress, Casar emphasized that the Congressional Progressive Caucus and its more than 100 members would be a crucial governing partner in Congress, noting that they hold a productive relationship with U.S. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), who will likely be elected the next Speaker of the House.
Congressman-elect William Lawrence
“Leader Jeffries has said this election is a mandate for bold change, and the progressive caucus is ready to be the energy behind delivering these results,” Casar said.
In addition to delivering economic security and anticorruption measures, Lawrence said House Democrats will also need to set its foreign policy straight.
“People in my district are tired of these endless wars,” Lawrence said. “We’ve seen one war after another. We’re throwing good money after bad – trillions each year – and we are not any safer or more secure or more prosperous than when these forever wars began. People across the political spectrum are ready for a change.”
Casar also stressed that Democrats’ newly won majority in Congress is not for one day, or 100 days but 100 weeks.
“Every single week, we should now be sending a bill to Donald Trump’s desk that is overwhelmingly popular with the American people, that cracks down on corporate greed, that cracks down on price gouging, that cracks down on big money in politics,” Casar said. “We won such a big victory last night that we’re not going to settle for one progressive bill on the first day.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT Dems say blue wave presents opportunities — and challenges
description: CT Democrats celebrated Gov. Ned Lamont's landslide reelection and Republicans' stunning General Assembly losses.
text:
Connecticut Democrats gathered Wednesday to celebrate Gov. Ned Lamont’s landslide reelection and Republicans’ stunning General Assembly losses as an affirmation of them and a repudiation of President Donald Trump that comes with opportunity and challenges.
Basking in sunshine outside the state Capitol, Democrats assessed what message voters intended in giving the Democratic governor an 18-percentage point win over Ryan Fazio while making the GOP an endangered species in Hartford with a legislative drubbing of historic dimensions.
“I think the message yesterday was loud and clear. People are fed up with what’s going on in Washington, D.C., and the dysfunction there, and they’re having a hard time getting by,” Lamont said. “And I like the fact that people had some confidence in the state of Connecticut and how we’re managing through these very complicated times.”
Was it truly a mandate, given the results reflected similar losses rung up Congress and state capitals across the U.S., including Austin, Texas? 
“I think it’s a plea,” Congressman-elect Luke Bronin said. “It’s a plea by the American people for leadership that focuses more on making their lives better and less on making some leaders’ friends richer. It’s a plea for leadership from the White House to Congress to state houses across the country that focuses on fixing the things that feel broken in this country.”
Other Democrats nodded when Bronin said voters will expect them to deliver solutions.
Barring changes in recounts, Democrats gained eight seats in the Senate to win a majority of 33-3 in the Senate and picked up 14 in the House to swell their majority to 116-35. The GOP’s House results were the worst since the post-Watergate debacle of 1974; the Senate was the worst ever.
Sen. Rob Sampson, R-Wolcott, explains his gun control objections to an empty gallery and nearly empty Senate in May, 2026. Credit: mark pazniokas / CT Mirror
“Make no mistake, the election results are a reaction to the chaos in Washington rather than an endorsement of the policies of Democrats in our General Assembly,” said House Minority Leader Vincent J. Candelora, R-North Branford, who was unopposed for reelection.
Senate Minority Leader Stephen Harding, R-Brookfield, who was among the casualties Tuesday night, said the national wave that flipped control of the U.S. Senate and U.S. House to Democrats and gave Democrats a majority of governorships was greater than anything the GOP could offer in defense.
“It has absolutely nothing to do with me or Vin or Steve and the state of the Republican Party in Connecticut,” said Ben Proto, the state chair of the Republican Party.
Senate Democrats are set on Thursday to vote for Senate Majority Leader Bob Duff of Norwalk as the next Senate president pro tem and Sen. Gary Winfield of New Haven as successor to Duff as majority leader.
Duff said the Democrats’ success were due to more than the blue wave. 
“We targeted every Republican seat but two, and the two we didn’t were in firm Republican hands,” Duff said.
The only Republican victors were Sen. Eric Berthel of Watertown, Sen. Henri Martin of Bristol and Sen. Rob Sampson of Wolcott. Sen. Paul Cicarella of North Haven lost a close race that faces as recount.
House Democrats are committed to reelecting House Speaker Matt Ritter of Hartford and House Majority Leader Jason Rojas of East Hartford.
In a press conference in his office and then at a unity event outside the Capitol on Wednesday, the governor said Democrats could claim a mandate, albeit one enmeshed in national politics. 
How he define it to the new lawmakers?
“I would tell them, look where we were eight years ago. Look where we are today,” Lamont said. “I think people feel pretty good about the direction we’ve gone, how we’ve been able to get our fiscal house in order. That has also allowed us to get resources to make some significant new investments that we weren’t able to do in the 2010s.”

title: Center for Intellectual Freedom director finalist rejects job offer
description: The Iowa Board of Regents’ selection to lead the Center for Intellectual Freedom at the University of Iowa has rejected the role, leaving the center without a director for the near future. Carson Holloway, chair of the University of Nebraska at Omaha’s department of political science and interim chair of the philosophy department, was selected […]
text:
Panelists speaking Dec. 6, 2025, at the Center for Intellectual Freedom at the University of Iowa, from left, are center Interim Director Luciano de Castro, U.S. Assistant Secretary for Postsecondary Education David Barker, state Rep. Taylor Collins, state Sen. Kerry Gruenhagen and Regent Christine Hensley. The center is still without a director after selected candidate Carson Holloway rejected the offer for another position. (Photo by Brooklyn Draisey/Iowa Capital Dispatch)The Iowa Board of Regents’ selection to lead the Center for Intellectual Freedom at the University of Iowa has rejected the role, leaving the center without a director for the near future.
Carson Holloway, chair of the University of Nebraska at Omaha’s department of political science and interim chair of the philosophy department, was selected by the board Oct. 20 out of three finalists to serve as director for the center for intellectual freedom.
In an email sent to Regent Christine Hensley, chair of the board committee overseeing the center, Holloway said he’s decided to take another job offer for a tenured professor position at the University of Florida.

“I believe strongly in the Center for Intellectual Freedom’s principles and mission, and it would have been my honor to be the Center’s leader,” Holloway said in the email. “I came away from my interview and our interactions incredibly impressed by everyone’s commitment to making the Center a success.”
Iowa Board of Regents Senior Communications Director Josh Lehman said in an email the director search is still ongoing, as Iowa law requires the center’s advisory council conduct a national search to fill the position. Closed-session meetings are being tentatively planned to look at other applicants, he said.
The center for intellectual freedom committee, composed of Hensley and regents Robert Cramer and Steve Lacy, is currently overseeing the center, Lehman said in an email. Hensley will lead a discussion about the center director position at the board’s Nov. 11-12 meeting in Ames.
Holloway would have succeeded former center interim director Luciano de Castro, whose last day was Oct. 22. Before his time leading the center was done, de Castro submitted the center’s annual report to the General Assembly, alleging unlawful actions by university and board staff to control the center’s operations.
De Castro refused to comment on Holloway’s selection, but said in an email potentially working with the center in the future depends “to a large extent, on the decisions of the new leadership.” He added that currently “the prospects do not look good.”

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Republicans blame Trump and national environment on their sweeping losses in Wisconsin
description: WAUSAU — Wisconsin Republicans started the evening on Tuesday feeling optimistic.  Attendees at Republican Tom Tiffany’s election night party in Wausau chatted while holding old fashioneds and napkins that declared: “You betcha we’re celebrating!” Tiffany arrived at the party around 7 p.m., taking pictures and shaking hands with attendees. The celebratory vi[...]
text:
“I mean, it's clear voters have said, ‘You're the party in power, and we're gonna try something different,’” Republican Tom Tiffany said. (Photo by Baylor Spears/Wisconsin Examiner)WAUSAU — Wisconsin Republicans started the evening on Tuesday feeling optimistic. 
Attendees at Republican Tom Tiffany’s election night party in Wausau chatted while holding old fashioneds and napkins that declared: “You betcha we’re celebrating!” Tiffany arrived at the party around 7 p.m., taking pictures and shaking hands with attendees.
The celebratory vibe didn’t last long as a blue wave swept across the nation and Wisconsin Tuesday evening. Tiffany was defeated by Gov.-elect David Crowley. Democrats won control of the state Senate and Assembly, ousted Republican incumbent Treasurer John Leiber and defeated Jay Schroeder, the Republican candidate for secretary of state who ran on a promise  to take over elections in Wisconsin. 
Wisconsin Republicans’ inability to buck national trends was foreshadowed a couple of hours before polls closed when Republican Party of Wisconsin Chair Brian Schimming told reporters that U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany had run a good campaign, but they were watching turnout. 
“We’re getting different signals around the state about turnout. We’re kind of watching that. I believe big turnout helps Republicans and helps Tom Tiffany,” Schimming said. Republicans have struggled in statewide races during years that President Donald Trump hasn’t been on the ballot as some of his supporters don’t turnout for midterm or spring elections. “I’m conscious of the fact that it’s an off year.” 
According to the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel, preliminary turnout was about 56% across the state and there was high turnout in the blue stronghold of Madison, which saw about 79% turnout, and Milwaukee, which saw nearly 71% turnout. 
A little before 10 p.m., Tiffany took the stage to concede Gov.-elect David Crowley, who will serve as Wisconsin’s first Black governor. He told reporters he had called Crowley beforehand and congratulated him. He said the night didn’t turn out as he’d hoped.
“I wanna congratulate David Crowley on his victory. While we have our differences, we both love this great state and I wish him and his family the very best as he prepares to serve as Wisconsin’s next governor.” 
When one attendee tried heckling Crowley, Tiffany shut it down, telling the crowd “We’re gonna be magnanimous.”
Asked what led to the loss, Tiffany did not mention President Donald Trump, instead blaming himself for not delivering the Republican message well enough. He also pointed to the price of gas and other high costs. 
“I mean, it’s clear voters have said, ‘You’re the party in power, and we’re gonna try something different,’” Tiffany said. “Now, there’s going to be a new party in power here, and they’ll have to deliver.” 
Tiffany and Republicans in the state Assembly and Senate tried to distance themselves from the unpopular president throughout their campaigns, but it was a difficult task, as Trump remained a constant in the campaign. As Democrats sought to tie their opponents to Trump, Trump highlighted his endorsement of Tiffany throughout the campaign, including on Election Day when Trump wrote in a post on X that Tiffany has “always been at my side.”
Over the course of the campaign, Trump’s popularity fell significantly across polls conducted by Marquette Law School. In October just ahead of Election Day, 61% of Wisconsinites said they disapproved of the job he was doing. 
Republican Treasurer John Leiber, who lost reelection by 4 points to Democrat Yee Leng Xiong, told WisPolitics that he doesn’t see a “future for the Republican Party with Trump in it.”
Two Republicans who serve in the state Legislature — and will now serve in the minority for the first time in their tenure — also pointed to the national environment. Republicans there will be disempowered for the first time in 16 years. They won just 15 seats in the Senate and 46 seats in the Assembly on Tuesday. 
Rep. Karen Hurd (R-Withee), who won reelection easily to her red district, told the Examiner that Republicans were conscious of how the federal government could affect Republican chances in the state. 
“What happens at the federal level has not just a trickle-down effect, but a flood effect on what’s happening in our state elections, and we knew that,” Hurd said. “We were doing our very best to say, ‘Separate us from the federal… We’re worried about schools and universities and roads. We don’t have anything to do with the war in Iran. We don’t have anything to do with the gas prices or with the price of eggs.” 
“It’s very hard for people to separate that,” she added.
Sen. Mary Felzkowski (R-Tomahawk) told the Examiner a little bit before Democrats declared victory in the state Senate that it was an “uphill battle going into this” and there were “a lot of national headwinds for Republicans.”  
Republicans will have to work to have an influence on Wisconsin policy from a disempowered position for the first time in over 16 years. 
Felzkowski noted that there are only two Republicans, Rep. Jeff Mursau and Rep. Dan Knodl, who have ever served in the minority.
“No one else has ever served in the minority, so this is a learning curve for all of us,” Felzkowski said. 
Felzkowski said Republicans in the Senate will choose their leadership next week and Assembly Republicans will choose theirs the following week. Both leadership positions are open as Assembly Speaker Robin Vos (R-Rochester) and Sen. Devin LeMahieu (R-Oostburg) both decided against running for reelection. Vos wrote in a post on X reacting to the Democratic wins that he knows that over the next two years “Republicans will stand firmly with the taxpayers and job creators who built Wisconsin’s success.” 
“Conservatives will offer constructive alternatives, demand accountability, and make sure voters can see the difference between growing government and growing opportunity,” he said. “The next two years will test our resolve. They will also clarify the choice ahead.”
Both Felzkowski and Hurd said they look forward to working with Crowley in office. Felzkowski said she would work well with Crowley, noting they worked together on Act 12, a 2023 law that overhauled local government funding and allowed Milwaukee County to raise its sales tax. The law became a point of attack for Republicans during the campaign as they alleged Crowley would raise taxes as governor. 
However, Felzkowski also said that if Republicans had held control of the Legislature, they would have been able to keep Crowley in check. A Democratic-led Legislature, she said, will mean “the brakes are off.”
“We are gonna go so far left. Crowley himself came right out and said, when he beat Francesca Hong, my platform’s not much different to hers, and she’s a Democrat socialist so we’ll see what happens,” Felzkowski said. “I think it’s a sad day for Wisconsin.”

name: VTDigger
title: Republican incumbent state senator from Rutland County arrested last week loses reelection bid
description:
It was one of several legislative races across Rutland County that Republicans lost. 
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Republican incumbent state senator from Rutland County arrested last week loses reelection bid.
text:
Sen. Terry Williams, R-Rutland, center, on the first day of the legislative biennium at the Statehouse in Montpelier in Jan. 2023.  File photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
An incumbent Republican Rutland County state senator arrested last week on a charge of domestic assault has lost his bid for reelection, ousted by an independent candidate who served in the state Senate over 30 years ago. 
Republicans also suffered setbacks in House districts in Rutland County, with four seats flipping to Democratic candidates. 
Sen. Terry Williams, from Poultney, had been running for his third two-year term. Last Wednesday, Williams was in court pleading not guilty to a misdemeanor charge accusing him of striking a woman in the face during an argument.
Williams finished in fourth place with 11,175 votes Tuesday in the race for three Rutland County state Senate seats, according to unofficial results from the Vermont Secretary of State’s Office.
Incumbent Sen. Brian Collamore, R-Rutland, bested the four-person field with 15,731 votes, earning another two-year term in office. He has served as a Rutland County senator for the past 12 years.
Collamore was followed by challenger David Wolk, an independent and former Castleton University president who previously served in the state Senate as a Democrat from 1988 to 1992, with 14,329 votes Tuesday.
Incumbent Sen. David Weeks, R-Rutand, earned the third Rutland County state Senate seat and his third two-year term with 13,301 votes, according to the unofficial results. 
Despite his loss, Williams earned the most votes in Benson, Middletown Springs, Pawlet and his home town of Poultney. Wolk led the pack in Rutland City, Killington and Chittenden. 
“I am especially proud that I carried my towns in Western Rutland County. It has been one of the greatest honors of my life to represent the good people of these communities in the Vermont Senate,” Williams wrote in a Facebook post on Wednesday regarding his defeat. 
Williams did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Wednesday.
Republicans Collamore, Weeks and Williams also appeared on the ballot as Democrats having won as write-ins during the August primary with no Democratic candidates running.
The three incumbent Republicans engaged in a hard fought race, and it was a disappointment for Vermont Republicans that the national blue wave seeped into Vermont’s local and countywide political outcomes, Steven Thompson, chair of the Rutland County Republican Party, said on Wednesday. 

READ MORE

“We got pretty all beat up,” Thompson said. “I think Washington spilled over into Vermont as it spilled over into a lot of other states.”
While not beneficial for Williams’ odds, Thompson said he is unsure if the allegations against Williams had a huge bearing on the outcome of his race. He added that he thought Wolk was a strong and well-known candidate and he hopes the independent will work together with the two reelected Republicans. 
A nonpartisan independent, Wolk said in an interview with VTDigger last month that he plans to caucus with the Democratic or Republican party during discussions of public policy issues, but will not caucus with either party during political strategizing meetings.  
The Democratic Party in Vermont won back its supermajority in both the state Senate and House of Representatives, after a red wave broke the supermajority in 2024. 
In the historically Republican “red” Rutland County, the Democratic Party maintained its sole House seat representing Rutland-6, previously occupied by longtime legislator Mary Howard. Chris Siliski, the Democratic House candidate for Rutland-6, won with 735 votes, against Republican Cindy Laskevich. 
Rutland County Democratic candidate Jeff Haylon picked up the Rutland-9 House seat, representing Brandon, winning against Republican candidate Aida Neilson after her husband Rep. Todd Neilson, R-Brandon, stepped down from that seat.
Some Democratic candidates running for House districts comprising municipalities straddling Rutland County and other counties also won this time around. 
Democratic candidate Jonathan Hescock gained the Addison-Rutland House seat, against Republican Jim Casey. Democrat Phoebe Tucker won the Rutland-Windsor seat against the Republican Kevin Winter. Former Representative Mike Rice won back the Bennington-Rutland House seat he lost two years ago against incumbent Sandra Pinsonault.
Rutland County Democrats’ Chair Thomas Fagan said that he is glad to see “new blood” in the legislature and more balanced political representation in the House coming out of Rutland County. The Democratic candidates that won ran strong campaigns and were able to channel the national energy that favored Democrats candidates this time around, Fagan said. 
Thompson is “scared to death” by the return of a Democratic supermajority, but he hopes that the newly reelected Republican Gov. Phil Scott can find common ground with the Democratic Party, he said. He hopes “we don’t go backwards” on land use planning and climate policy issues that he believes would take a toll on affordability for Vermonters, he added. 
“We’re going to have to see what the leaders of the House and Senate have for us, and you know, try to work with them the best we can to impact change,” Thompson said. 
Fagan said that it is important that the Democratic Party still works with Gov. Scott despite the supermajority, or likely “next round it’ll switch back.”
