name: California
title: California has one ballot-counting trouble spot. It’s the one run by an election denier
description: The only California county having problems counting ballots is Shasta, which has an election office run by Clint Curtis, one of Trump’s election deniers.
text:
In summary
The only California county having problems counting ballots is Shasta, which has an election office run by Clint Curtis, one of Trump’s election deniers.


In the end, it wasn’t shady bogeymen stuffing ballot boxes or federal agents who caused disruptions on election night in the rural Northern California Republican stronghold of Shasta County. 
It was the seeming incompetence of Clint Curtis, the county’s election-denying elections chief who’s soon to be unemployed.Journalists, including CalMatters’ reporting partner Shasta Scout, have reported numerous problems with the vote count in Shasta County, a 2.5-hour drive north of Sacramento. They reported overflowing ballot boxes, staffing shortages, workers putting ballots in the wrong bins, computer hiccups and voters arriving at their polling places to find signs saying the location had been moved.
Most counties dropped initial results right after 8 p.m. when the polls closed, but Shasta didn’t report any until around 10 p.m. since elections officials hadn’t set up their computer system properly, leaving it as the only county in the state that on Wednesday morning hadn’t finished counting ballots from those who voted in person. 
A reporter for the Shasta Scout asked Curtis Tuesday night why the extra staffers he claimed to have hired over recent months didn’t pick up the ballots from drop boxes. Curtis himself left the election office to grab ballots when he should have been overseeing the count.
“Because I’m stupid,” Curtis told Shasta Scout. “So when I see it needs to be done, I just do it myself.” Curtis did not immediately respond to an interview request from CalMatters Wednesday.
The problems in Shasta County are an outlier in California. No major issues were reported in California’s other 57 counties, despite pre-election worries that the Trump administration might try to interfere with the vote count after federal officials made unprecedented threats to California election workers. 
Curtis brought FBI to Shasta County 
Because of Curtis, it appeared this fall that Shasta County could become Ground Zero in President Donald Trump’s war on blue state elections as his prosecutors sought to prove Trump’s longstanding claims that Democrats are rigging elections against him.
Curtis, a longtime election denier, made outlandish claims that nefarious actors had stuffed drop boxes with fake ballots in the June primary. He lost his bid for a full term in that election.
Curitis reduced the number of ballot drop boxes in Shasta County from 13 to four last year. Then, after the June election, Curtis claimed a plot was afoot to stuff ballot boxes after he and his team found ballots they claimed had paper that looked, felt and smelled funny.
His claims caught the attention of top law enforcement officials in Trump’s administration.
Officials sent a team of FBI agents to the county elections office in September carrying bolt cutters to get into a room holding old ballots that Curtis had padlocked and thrown away the key. Curtis said the agents didn’t seize any ballots.
The status of the federal investigation in Shasta County is unclear. The U.S. Department of Justice has not acknowledged there is an investigation.
Curtis’ replacement takes over in January
Curtis, a minor celebrity among the election deniers in Trump’s MAGA movement, had never had an official role in elections before the far-right members who controlled the Shasta County Board of Supervisors in 2025 appointed him.
Curtis, an attorney and former Democratic congressional candidate in Florida and California, lost the June primary to Joanna Francescut, a former Shasta County elections official who helped run the elections office before Curtis fired her.
Francescut will take over in January.

name: WyoFile
title: Wyoming Republicans strike defiant tone as Democratic sweep of Congress ushers in a new era
description:
After Senate victory, Harriet Hageman described the fight against the Democrats’ agenda as a ‘battle for the future of this nation.' Reckoning with the loss, others blamed Trump for blowing a ‘golden opportunity.’ 
The post Wyoming Republicans strike defiant tone as Democratic sweep of Congress ushers in a new era appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
WASHINGTON—The midterm election blowout delivered a new era in Washington, with Democrats in Congress eager to meet voter demands for change while Republicans watched their majorities evaporate after a revolt against President Donald Trump and his party in power.
Democrats ousted Republicans from coast to coast, with many surprising places in between, in a decisive rejection of unified GOP control for the promise of something different for the country. Their majorities will be padded by unusually wide margins in both the House and the Senate.
The blue wave did not sweep through Wyoming, which elected two Trump loyalists to Congress: Harriet Hageman to the Senate and Chuck Gray to the House. Posting to social media as it was becoming clear that Democrats would enjoy a historic victory, Hageman struck a defiant tone.
“We are about to engage in a battle for the future of this nation, and as we all recognize, the looming fight with the left is about much more than just policy differences,” she wrote. “It’s about the very survival of this country as it has been and as we know it. Are we a capitalist nation, or will we slide precipitously into communism? The left hates our founding principles of freedom, just as they hate our strength and prosperity. A strong United States of America embarrasses them, so they aim to tear it all down. And I aim to stand in their way.” 
The staggering results are setting up a starkly divided government, with an emboldened Congress poised to reassert itself as a coequal branch when Democrats take over in the new year. They are ready to launch a 100-day agenda to lower the costs of gas, groceries and healthcare and conduct vast oversight and investigations into Trump and his administration, with impeachment an option.
“We hear you,” said House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York, who would make history as the first Black speaker of the House if his colleagues elect him to the job when the new Congress begins on Jan. 3, 2027.
Jeffries called the election a “stunning rebuke of MAGA extremism” and “a great victory for the American people.”
Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer acknowledged the political reality that voters may have been more willing to reject Trump’s party than to embrace the Democrats.
“Many of the folks who voted for us yesterday are still skeptical, and that’s OK,” the New York senator said Wednesday at the Capitol.
He said the history-making scale of his party’s wins — picking up long-shot Senate seats in South Carolina, Texas and Kansas — creates “the opportunity to prove ourselves worthy of their trust.”
All told, the results present a fundamental reshaping of power in Washington, with new openings and challenges for governing. The tally was bewildering for the scope of Democratic gains and the depth of Republican losses, which indiscriminately wiped out GOP firebrands, moderates and veteran conservatives nationwide. The swelling majorities, with some races still too early to call, underlined a deep sense of voter anger and concern over the economy and the state of democracy.
Republican primary candidate for U.S. House of Representatives Bo Biteman talks during a forum on Thursday, July 23, 2026, at Casper College. (Dan Cepeda for WyoFile)
State Sen. Bo Biteman placed the blame for that anger solidly on Republicans generally and Trump specifically.
“Turns out starting a war nobody wanted, sky high inflation, trading America First for Israel First, covering up the Epstein scandal and breaking every single campaign promise doesn’t win you elections! I saw this coming a mile away,” he wrote in a social media post. “The GOP deserved every bit of this ass kicking. The problem is that the American people will continue to suffer because of it. 
“President Trump had a golden opportunity to be one of the greatest Presidents in history but he blew it,” Biteman continued. “Republicans in Congress had a golden opportunity to finally deliver on their promises that won them huge electoral victories and they blew it.”
Trump acknowledges the impact of the Iran war
Trump struck a conciliatory tone, suggesting he could work with the Democrats, but he also warned of gridlock ahead as he threatened to use the power of the presidential veto to strike down their agenda.
“I don’t want to be just sitting there for two years vetoing everything,” he told Politico.
Later, he acknowledged the Iran war impacted the midterm elections, suggesting voters were frustrated by surging gas prices that have been a byproduct of the 8-month-old conflict.
President Donald Trump speaks with reporters as Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., from left, Sen. John Barrasso, R-Wyo., and Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., listen on Capitol Hill, Wednesday, June 24, 2026, in Washington. (AP Photo/Jacquelyn Martin)
“The Iran thing we had to do, and we continue to do it,” Trump told reporters.
He said he was not considering replacing Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, despite voter dissatisfaction with the war, saying Hegseth was “doing a great job.”
Vice President JD Vance, often eyed as Trump’s likely successor at the White House, pointedly blamed the president’s war in Iran for Republicans’ midterm wipeout.
Democrats vow a 100-day agenda and investigations of Trump
House Democrats are planning to quickly launch efforts to reverse Trump’s GOP cuts to the Affordable Care Act and Medicaid healthcare programs. They’re also ready to dive into a robust oversight agenda too, as Jeffries says, “hold the crooks accountable.”
The top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, Rep. Robert Garcia of California, issued a one-sentence warning: “Lawyer up.”
Sen. Ron Wyden, the top Democrat on the Senate Finance Committee, issued his own one-word missive: “Subpoenas.”
Democrats will be under pressure to quickly show that they have solutions for voters’ anger and frustration over high prices, the war in Iran and unease about the direction of the country. About 7 in 10 voters nationally say Congress is not doing enough to provide checks and balances on the presidency, according to The AP Voter Poll.
Hageman pledged to push back against the Democratic agenda.
“Wyoming has a great deal at stake in the coming years as we know the forces of the left will stop at nothing to prevent us from safely accessing our own natural resources,” she wrote on social media Tuesday evening. “Wyoming leads the nation in coal production, has the most uranium reserves, and is prominent in oil and natural gas as well. We must defend America’s energy independence and block all efforts to punish the lawful production of domestic energy. Not only does our economy depend on it, so does the very existence of the United States of America.”
Former President Donald Trump embraces Harriet Hageman at a “Save America” rally in Casper May 28, 2022. (Natalie Behring)
Sen. John Barrasso also vowed to fight for the Republican agenda, while also saying it was important to listen to the message sent by voters. 
“There are clear lessons to be learned from the results. First, we should listen to what voters unmistakably said last night,” he wrote on social media. “Their priorities must always come first. Our job is to forcefully act on them. Senate Republicans have an opportunity and obligation to show our voters that we are fighting for them.
“In the Senate, we will aggressively oppose terrible ideas that drive our country toward the socialism Democrats embraced. Our commitment is to common sense. And our focus should not waiver from the top priority of driving down prices that have remained stubbornly too high.”
The Wyoming Republican Party, which saw its own preferred candidates lose in key races during the August primary, encouraged the state’s congressional delegation to fight back against the Democratic agenda.
“Wyoming is sending its best to help President Trump fight back against the liberals who are hell-bent on destroying this country,” the party wrote in a statement distributed Wednesday morning. “Our Wyoming Republican Party Platform aligns perfectly with this fight to preserve the character and well-being of our nation. 
“Going forward we will work tirelessly to ensure all who are elected under the Republican banner support that fight here in Wyoming too as they uphold their promises to support our platform and serve the people that put them in office.”
For Jeffries and his leadership team, it will be their first time in the majority, managing a class of newcomers including a handful of far-left democratic socialists.
With the majority in the 435-member House growing well past the 218 needed and the Senate Democrats holding at least 54 of 100 seats in that chamber, Jeffries and Schumer will have room to maneuver.
House Speaker Mike Johnson of Louisiana will not seek reelection as House Republican leader, according to two people familiar with his decision, setting up a potentially brutal leadership battle following the party’s trouncing by the Democrats. The people who told The Associated Press about Johnson’s decision insisted on anonymity to disclose it.
Vance cites the Iran war for Republicans’ losses
For Republicans, their shriveled numbers quickly launched a reckoning of their own, as they try to figure out what went so uniformly wrong.
In a lengthy online post, the vice president seemingly sought to distance himself from election results seen as a referendum on Trump that featured big Republican losses across the country.
“The reason we lost is the war,” Vance wrote, adding, “If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that’s at least honest.”
A lame-duck session and leadership elections await Republicans
Republicans may be anxious during the post-election lame-duck sprint to accomplish as much as possible in their remaining weeks in power. But hopes for another GOP-only priority package like their big tax breaks and spending cuts bill seem dim as defeated lawmakers prepare to go home at the end of the year.
Conservatives have also eyed the opportunity for Trump to nominate more judges or even a justice to the Supreme Court while Senate Republicans still hold a majority to confirm the picks.
And the government could be headed toward a federal shutdown next month if Congress fails to pass a funding bill to keep operations running.
In the weeks ahead, the parties will hold internal leadership elections.
Associated Press writers Tom Beaumont, Joey Cappelletti, Jill Colvin, Kevin Freking, Mary Clare Jalonick and Will Weissert contributed to this report.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: John Deere plans to phase out Ottumwa, Clarion factories
description: John Deere factories in Ottumwa and Clarion are set to be phased out over next two fiscal years as the company looks to “optimize” manufacturing and “improve operational efficiency” according to a Wednesday announcement from the company.  The company also plans to move small planter production from a facility in Moline, Illinois, to a John […]
text:
The John Deere manufacturing facility in Ottumwa, pictured, is slated to close along with a facility in Clarion, the company announced. (Photo via Google Earth)John Deere factories in Ottumwa and Clarion are set to be phased out over next two fiscal years as the company looks to “optimize” manufacturing and “improve operational efficiency” according to a Wednesday announcement from the company. 
The company also plans to move small planter production from a facility in Moline, Illinois, to a John Deere production facility in Paton, Iowa, in the next fiscal year. 
A spokesperson with the company said Wednesday that at “normal production volumes” approximately 300 people would be impacted by closures, though he said Deere is currently operating “far below normal production volumes due to the downturn in the ag economy.” 
“Specific employment impacts will depend on future business conditions, production volumes, and staffing needs,” Dustin Lemmon, the spokesperson, said. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
A news release from the company said it “continually evaluates its manufacturing footprint” as technology, customers and markets evolve. 
“That work includes streamlining operations, expanding capacity where it creates the most value, advancing automation and modern manufacturing technologies, and leveraging strategic sourcing to improve flexibility and cost competitiveness,” the news release said. 
As part of that evaluation, the company has decided to relocate windrower and round baler production from Ottumwa Works to the Des Moines Works facility. Windrow production is expected to transition by the end of fiscal year 2027 and round baler production by the end of fiscal year 2028, when Deere also plans to close the Ottumwa factory.  
Deere laid off workers from facilities across the state, including at the Ottumwa facility, in 2025 but at the end of October, the company announced that “all employees previously on layoff in Waterloo, the Quad Cities, Ottumwa, and Dubuque” had been asked to return to work. 
The City of Ottumwa said in a Facebook post Wednesday that the decision was “not something anyone in Ottumwa wants.” The city estimated closing the Ottumwa plant would have a payroll loss of more than $30 million.
“John Deere has been part of Ottumwa and a piece of our identity for a long time,” the social media post read. “We want to thank John Deere for the investment they have made in Ottumwa for so long. We appreciate all that they have done for our community and for the commitment they are making in helping Ottumwa through this transition and in locating a future company to Ottumwa.”
The social media post from the city also said the John Deere Foundation has “affirmed” its commitment of nearly $1 million to support Ottumwa and Clarion over the next three years.
Deere to end production in Clarion
The production of Hagie STS sprayers at the Hagie Manufacturing plant in Clarion will move to a Deere factory in Thibodaux, Louisiana. 
According to Hagie’s website, Deere acquired ownership of the Iowa-founded company in 2020. Hagie started making personnel carriers and self-propelled sprayers in the mid 1940s. 
The news release from Deere said it plans to end manufacturing operations at the Hagie factory in Clarion by fiscal year 2029. 
In addition to the changes in Iowa, Deere said it will move production of sugar cane harvesters from its plant in Thibodaux, Louisiana, to a facility in Catalão, Brazil. Deere said the move puts production of the machinery “closer to the largest concentration of customer demand.” According to the news release, the Louisiana facility manufactured around 35 sugar cane harvesters annually for market in the U.S.
Lemmon said affected employees at the Deere facilities will receive “timely information as plans are finalized.” 
“Deere will provide comprehensive transition support for employees at impacted facilities, which may include internal transfer opportunities, retraining assistance, retention offers, relocation assistance, severance benefits, and career-transition support,” the spokesperson said.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico Forward Party candidates lose Election Day races, promise more campaigns in 2028
description: Three New Mexico candidates running for office with the state’s newest minor political party lost their races Tuesday evening, but New Mexico Forward Party officials say they’ll continue to field candidates in the next election.
text:
Former presidential candidate Andrew Yang and New Mexico Forward Party Chair Bob Perls stood outside the Roundhouse on April 10, 2026, to announce the creation of the New Mexico Forward Party. The party’s candidates lost their races in the Nov. 3, 2026, general election, but Perls said he intends to field more in the 2028 election. (Photo by Joshua Bowling/Source NM)Three New Mexico candidates running for office with the state’s newest minor political party lost their races Tuesday evening, but New Mexico Forward Party officials say they’ll continue to field candidates in the next election.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The centrist New Mexico Forward Party ran candidates for the Public Education Commission and for magistrate judgeships in Santa Fe and Luna counties. Other candidates seeking to run for U.S. Senate and Office of the State Auditor did not gather enough signatures to qualify for Tuesday’s general election ballot and lost subsequent legal challenges to gain ballot access.
Former presidential candidate Andrew Yang co-founded the national Forward Party in 2022 with former Republican New Jersey Gov. Christine Todd Whitman. The Forward Party’s tenets include treating “everyone with dignity and respect.”
Despite the party’s losses Tuesday, Chair Bob Perls in a statement said the candidates’ presence on the ballot signaled a growing appetite among voters to move away from the two-party political system.
“The two major parties are satisfying their donors and pandering to their voting base rather than building broad-based governing coalitions to solve our wicked-complex problems,” he said.
Prior to Election Day, the New Mexico Forward Party endorsed four candidates seeking public office: Republican James “Jim” Ellison for state treasurer; incumbent Democrats Kathleen Cates and Meredith Dixon for the state House of Representatives; and independent Zachary Withers for the state House of Representatives.
Cates and Dixon won their reelection bids, according to results from the New Mexico Secretary of State’s Office.
Perls said that Forward Party officials will focus on fielding candidates for the state Legislature in the 2028 election cycle.
“Half of all state representatives had no competition this election cycle. This is no way to run a democracy,” he said. “Voters need choices and desperately want something and someone thinking beyond the vise grip that the two legacy parties have on political thought and political candidates today.”

name: Michigan Advance
title: Benson promises bipartisan approach as she prepares to take office with Democratic trifecta
description: At her first press conference as Governor-elect, Jocelyn Benson repeatedly emphasized the importance of working with legislators across the aisle to deliver on her campaign promises of lowering costs and increasing wages — even as she will be governing alongside a large Democratic trifecta in the Legislature.  Benson won the governor’s race Tuesday as Democr[...]
text:
Governor-elect Jocelyn Benson spoke to reporters the morning after winning the gubernatorial election, telling reporters that her agenda for the first 100 days would be rolled out soon. (Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance)At her first press conference as Governor-elect, Jocelyn Benson repeatedly emphasized the importance of working with legislators across the aisle to deliver on her campaign promises of lowering costs and increasing wages — even as she will be governing alongside a large Democratic trifecta in the Legislature. 
Benson won the governor’s race Tuesday as Democrats made gains across the country, including in Michigan, where they flipped a number of seats in both the state House and Senate, retaining their majority in the latter and regaining it in the former. 
“Voters in Michigan spoke loud and clear. They want leaders who will work together to lower their costs and grow our economy,” Benson said, noting that specific plans for her first hundred days in office would be announced soon. “That is my focus, and as well as improving our public schools. And so you can expect to see some specific things that we’re going to start working on that we’ll be able to announce more in the weeks ahead. That hopefully will enable us to hit the ground running.”
Governor-elect Jocelyn Benson and her lieutenant, Winnie Brinks, spoke to reporters the morning after winning the gubernatorial election. (Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance)
Benson referenced a few specific policies that she intends to put in place, all of which align with past campaign statements on the issues, including voluntarily making the governor’s office subject to public records requests and evaluating different ways to reduce the gas tax.
But despite entering the position on Jan. 1, 2027 with her party in control of both legislative chambers, as well as both the attorney general’s office and that of secretary of state, Benson repeatedly emphasized the need to work across the aisle. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“We do have a historic trifecta that we’re excited about because I’m going to Lansing not to play political games but to get things done. And I believe with this trifecta, you will see a number of leaders committed to that,” Benson said. “But in addition to that, every voice will have a place around our table.”
She said that the results of Tuesday’s election in Michigan showed that the people had an appetite for elected leadership who “will work for the citizens and not Donald Trump.”
“Michiganders have given us a clear mandate to work for them, to lower costs, to grow our economy, to improve our public schools, and get things done,” she said. “And we will meet that mandate working hand in hand with our legislative leaders and everyone in the Legislature on both sides of the aisle, frankly, from day one.” 
Lt. Governor-elect Winnie Brinks, the outgoing Senate Majority Leader, agreed, citing her own time as a legislator.
“I know how this works,” she said. “Real progress doesn’t come from one office or one party alone. It comes when people sit down at the same table and focus on what works for the families that we serve. I’m ready to partner with anyone in either party, in either chamber, to get things done for Michigan and turn Governor-elect Benson’s agenda into real results for people.”
Lieutenant Governor-elect Winnie Brinks spoke to reporters the morning after Democrats won the gubernatorial election. (Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance)
Michigan Democratic Party Chair Curtis Hertel, speaking to reporters after Benson and Brinks’ press conference, said that he had been told that the Democratic majorities in the Legislature were the largest since 1978.
“We had just great candidates that worked across the state and did that work on the ground,” he said. “Lots of exciting things in the Legislature, and it gives us that opportunity to have a majority that can get big things done for people and make Michigan a place where people can afford to raise a family again, which I think is the most important thing.”
Hertel was less gracious to the Republicans as they face losses in the midterms, though he did note his own experience working across the aisle when he was a state legislator.
“I do believe in being a gracious winner,” Hertel said. “But on the opposite side of that, Mike Rogers ran what I think is one of the most racist, Islamophobic, terrible campaigns that I’ve ever seen. It should be offensive to anybody that that was even possible. That was a campaign out of some past time in America where I think we were a much more hateful place, and so, I do find a little joy, I will say, in rejecting that.”
Benson noted that U.S. Rep. John James (R-Shelby Twp.), her Republican opponent in the governor’s race, had called her earlier that day to concede the race. In a video posted to social media, James also said that he had called her to congratulate her on a win. 
“The constituents that I have had the privilege of representing, thank you,” he said. “I’ve always said that when service calls, we have an obligation to answer, and sometimes it calls us home. So, I look forward to getting back to my first and most important titles, that being husband and dad. But regardless, I’m never going to relent in working with anyone and everyone for a greater, more prosperous, and a more free Michigan.”

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Commentary: The GOP gerrymander didn’t work. And it hurt Tommy Tuberville.
description: The Alabama Legislature could try to redraw Alabama’s 2nd Congressional District again. If Republicans are unhappy with Shomari Figures’ decisive victory Tuesday, they can change the borders. The U.S. Supreme Court said this spring that the Legislature can do anything it wants with congressional districts. So long as they’re “political gerrymanders,” of cour[...]
text:
U.S. Rep. Shomari Figures, D-Mobile, leaves the lectern after speaking to an Alabama Senate committee on May 7, 2026 at the Alabama Statehouse in Montgomery, Alabama. The Alabama Legislature this spring redrew the 2nd Congressional District, represented by Figures, to favor a Republican. Figures won re-election to the seat on Tuesday. (Brian Lyman/Alabama Reflector)The Alabama Legislature could try to redraw Alabama’s 2nd Congressional District again.
If Republicans are unhappy with Shomari Figures’ decisive victory Tuesday, they can change the borders. The U.S. Supreme Court said this spring that the Legislature can do anything it wants with congressional districts. So long as they’re “political gerrymanders,” of course. Don’t explicitly say you’re trying to mute the voice of Black voters. Just blurt “Democrats,” and you’ll be fine.
So have at it. Draw more of Elmore County (73% white) in and more of Montgomery County (59% Black) out.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
But after Tuesday, they should seriously reconsider.
The main reason, of course, is the blatant racism. Alabama Republicans in the last several years, like many of their peers in Congress and the federal government, brazenly pursued policies to dilute Black voting power.
They’ve criminalized some forms of absentee ballot assistance, citing a dubious claim that it could result in fraud. (In the process, a federal judge had to order the state to let blind, illiterate or disabled voters get help with their ballots.)
And two years ago, when Alabama elected two Black U.S. representatives to Congress for the first time in history, state Republican officials didn’t accept the popular will. They continued to pursue a lawsuit to eliminate one of those voting districts.
The U.S. Supreme Court, which stopped the creation of a near-majority Black district months before the 2022 midterms, eagerly allowed the state to destroy it within an even shorter timeframe in 2026. Silencing Black Alabamians meant far more than consistency or orderly election administration.  
But if you’re a Republican watching what all that wrought, you may want to consider the tactical problems.
The Republicans’ major mistake was assuming they could repress Black voters without pushback. Black voters quickly disabused them of that idea.
All five days of the May special legislative redistricting session featured protests. And because Republican lawmakers were still tied up in litigation over the maps, they could say nothing in defense of their moves, ceding the stage to Black voters and Democrats.
When Republicans passed the maps, Black voters helped drive a surge of Democratic voting in the May 19 primary.
And they came out on Tuesday. In majority-Black Montgomery County, turnout increased 39% over 2022. In Jefferson County, about 42% Black, turnout jumped 25%.
Then there was Figures himself.
At the start of his time in the U.S. House, Figures lived in Mobile, a city his mother Vivian has represented in the Alabama Senate for nearly 30 years and his father Michael represented before his death in 1996. The new district lines cut Figures out. Perhaps the GOP thought Figures would retire from the House or try running in the 1st Congressional District, which includes Mobile.
Figures, though, moved to Montgomery and waged a fierce campaign. He used his incumbency to amass a large war chest as Republicans spent weeks campaigning ahead of an Aug. 11 primary.
When the general campaign began against Rep. Rhett Marques of Enterprise, the Republican nominee, Figures showed he could give as good as he got. Marques and Republicans called Figures a socialist. Figures attacked Marques over his 2019 vote to raise the gas tax — a measure supported by most lawmakers. President Donald Trump called Figures a “communist.” Figures took the opportunity to attack Marques over the gas tax again. A barrage of ads attacking Marques, some from PACs funded by Illinois Gov. J.B. Pritzker, tore at the Republican nominee for weeks.
Figures proved to have political discipline and skills like his parents. Once Montgomery County reported Tuesday night, the race was over.
The Republican gerrymander had another effect.
The Wiregrass runs through the 2nd Congressional District. It’s considered one of the most reliably Republican areas in the state. A GOP nominee who can run up the score there should be in good shape.
Unless you’ve mobilized almost every Black voter to come out to the polls. That sank Marques and sent fallout beyond the district. Black voters held down GOP margins throughout the Wiregrass. Kay Ivey got 77% of the vote in Houston County in 2022; Tommy Tuberville on Tuesday got 63%. Ivey got 78% of the vote in Dale; Tuberville got 67%. Ivey got 59% of the vote in Barbour County; Democrat Doug Jones won it with 52% of the vote on Tuesday.
If you’re looking for reasons why the Jones/Tuberville battle was close, that was a big one. Legislative Republicans managed to damage a key GOP base.
There is nothing stopping Republicans from going after the 2nd Congressional District again.
But they may want to pause before they do. Because the attempt to grab one U.S. House seat almost cost them a lot more.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Dems oust five Oklahoma Republican incumbents
description: OKLAHOMA CITY — While failing to win any statewide races on Tuesday, Oklahoma House Democrats saw their biggest caucus gains in over 20 years. Democrats not only maintained their existing seats, but gained six more in the state House by ousting five Republican incumbents and winning one other open seat previously held by the other […]
text:
The Oklahoma House legislative chamber sits empty. (Photo by Kyle Phillips/For Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY — While failing to win any statewide races on Tuesday, Oklahoma House Democrats saw their biggest caucus gains in over 20 years.
Democrats not only maintained their existing seats, but gained six more in the state House by ousting five Republican incumbents and winning one other open seat previously held by the other party.
After experiencing a technical issue Tuesday night, Comanche County election officials manually tallied ballots through Wednesday afternoon before determining that a Democrats also picked up a Lawton-area seat where an incumbent was not running. 
House Minority Leader Melissa Provenzano, D-Tulsa, said her caucus knew there was a need for the Democratic Party to focus on solutions for working families, so this election they honed in on finding candidates who aligned with solving these issues.
She said there’s excitement mixed with disappointment over Tuesday night’s outcomes. Nationally, Democrats made huge gains in other states winning governorships, statewide offices, and congressional seats. Oklahoma didn’t see a similar blue wave as the GOP continued its dominance.
House Minority Leader-elect Melissa Provenzano, D-Tulsa, speaks on the House floor of the state Capitol in Oklahoma City on June 26, 2026. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)
But Provenzano said Oklahoma Democrats are celebrating their gains in the state House. 
“I think there’s just a lot of joy right now,” she said of Tuesday night’s outcome. “I know that the results nationwide are very exciting, but I know our state level results are also a little bit sad because we didn’t get the ones we wanted there.”
With 75 members, House Republicans are expected to retain their super majority, but Provenzano said having 26 members gives Democrats “more sway” when it comes to things like veto overrides. 
Democrat Joe Watkins won House District 75, which includes parts of Tulsa and Broken Arrow, over incumbent Republican Rep. T.J. Marti. 
Watkins, of Tulsa, said he’s still in shock after his win but he’s excited to work on housing and food insecurity, affordability issues and improving public education. He celebrated the news with his wife at a watch party in Tulsa. 
“The campaign is not my bread and butter, that’s not what I’m in it for,” he said. “I’m not comfortable with campaigning. But doing the actual work, that starts now, is what I’m most excited about.”
In House District 83, Democrat Dalton Gau bested incumbent Republican Rep. Eric Roberts to represent northwestern Oklahoma City near Lake Hefner. 
Gau, from Oklahoma City, wrote that he will fight for better schools, a more inclusive economy and greater privacy for Oklahomans’ data as a state representative.  
Democrat Jeffrey Perez was elected over Republican Rep. Tammy West to represent House District 84, which includes much of Bethany and parts of Oklahoma City and Warr Acres. 
The Bethany resident said he was at a loss for words and cried when he heard he’d won the House seat. 
“I knew that the national sentiment would help us a lot in this race,” Perez said. “But seeing it in person throughout the course of the campaign, it’s been an eye opening experience to see how many Oklahomans want change. And I’m just grateful to be the one that they chose.”SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
He said he wants to focus on improving public education and teacher pay. 
Democrat Tegan Malone, of Midwest City, ousted incumbent Rep. Max Wolfley. She’ll represent House District 95, which includes Midwest City, Moore, Oklahoma City, and Tinker Air Force Base. 
“Running for office three times has taught me a lot about perseverance, community, and never giving up on something you believe in,” she wrote. 
Finally, Chaunté Gilmore beat Republican Rep. Marilyn Stark in House District 100, which includes Bethany, Oklahoma City and Warr Acres. 
Gilmore, of Oklahoma City, said she’s the first African American to represent House District 100. 
“This seat belongs to HD100,” she wrote. “Every door knocked, every conversation, and every vote brought us here. I will show up and fight for our students, seniors, and working families.”
Democrat Kathy Suttles also won the Lawton-area House District 64 race, which was previously held by Rep. Rande Worthen who did not seek reelection. 
Democrats though were unable to oust incumbent Rep. Danny Williams, R-Seminole, who a House committee found had sexually harassed multiple women. The House Rules Committee recommended he not seek reelection, be formally reprimanded by the full chamber, be stripped of his committee membership and leadership positions, lose access to House staff and attend workplace harassment training. 
Williams is also under investigation by the state Ethics Commission for a variety of allegations, including that he misused his office for personal gain.
It was not immediately clear how the committee’s recommendations would impact Williams after his reelection.

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Colorado voters reject measures requiring mail-ballot ID numbers, ICE cooperation
description: Colorado voters on Tuesday rejected a ballot measure that would have required them to put part of their Social Security number or other identifying information on mail-in ballots. The Associated Press said at 10:18 p.m. on Election Night that Amendment 84 failed. As of midday Wednesday, 63.4% of voters were against the measure. The numbers […]
text:
Voters cast ballots in the Adams County Government Center, Brighton on Tuesday. (Photo by Andrew Fraieli/Colorado Newsline)Colorado voters on Tuesday rejected a ballot measure that would have required them to put part of their Social Security number or other identifying information on mail-in ballots.
The Associated Press said at 10:18 p.m. on Election Night that Amendment 84 failed. As of midday Wednesday, 63.4% of voters were against the measure. The numbers in this story are current as of 1:20 p.m. on Wednesday. 
Colorado voters would have needed to write the last four digits of their Social Security number, Colorado driver’s license or identification card on their mail-in ballot envelopes under the constitutional amendment. It was backed by the Coalition for American Prosperity and Growth, and supporters said it would encourage election security by making sure every ballot belongs to the right voter. 
But groups including the League of Women Voters and Colorado Common Cause said it wasn’t necessary for voter verification, and people could be wary of having their ID numbers so visible.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
It is 1 of 6 measures with definite results so far as counties continue processing ballots. Voters also approved Proposition 133 to require life sentences for child sex trafficking crimes and Proposition NN to redirect more tax revenue to public education, according to The Associated Press. 
They rejected other constitutional amendments to require coordination with immigration enforcement, enshrine the right to buy and sell natural gas, and create a new right to hunt and fish in the state.
Colorado voters had 14 ballot measures to decide this year, one of the highest number of questions put to voters in the last five decades. Nearly all were citizen-led initiatives that garnered enough petition signatures to make it onto the ballot.
A handful of this year’s measures were brought by Advance Colorado, a conservative “dark money” group that doesn’t disclose its donors. Republicans have increasingly relied on ballot measures to promote policy ideas in the state, as their influence in statewide offices and at the state Legislature dwindles under Democratic control. 
Most of the Advance Colorado measures are on the path to defeat.
A right-leaning group, Protect Kids Colorado, pushed three ballot measures this year. The group was founded by an anti-trans activist from Larimer County, and this is the first election cycle it ran propositions. All three of those measures were winning as of Wednesday at noon. 
Constitutional amendments require 55% of the vote to pass, while statutory measures need a simple majority.
Amendment 81
Amendment 81 was backed mainly by Advance Colorado. It would have expanded Colorado’s local law enforcement’s role in immigration enforcement and require local police to notify U.S. Department of Homeland Security if they charge someone known to be “not lawfully present” in the country, or if “the status of the person’s lawful presence is unknown” and the person has a previous violent criminal conviction or felony conviction.
Colorado’s Democratic-led Legislature has passed a handful of laws limiting state and local law enforcement’s cooperation with federal immigration enforcement. 
The amendment was opposed by a coalition of district attorneys in the state. 
The AP said at about 1 p.m. Wednesday it failed, when 55% of voters were against it. 
Amendment 82
Amendment 82 would have enshrined the right to buy and sell natural gas in the state’s constitution, and it came amid growing state policies that limit the use of natural gas. Phasing out natural gas aligns with Colorado’s climate goals, and some cities like Denver have passed ordinances requiring new commercial buildings to use electric space and water heating. 
This was an Advance Colorado ballot measure. 
The AP said the amendment failed when 53.9% of voters were opposed.
Amendment 84
Under Amendment 84, Colorado voters would have needed to write the last four digits of their Social Security number, Colorado driver’s license or identification card on their mail-in ballot envelopes under the constitutional amendment.
The AP said the amendment failed.
Amendment 83
Amendment 83 proposed a constitutional right to hunt and fish in the state. Proponents said it would protect hunting from wildlife advocacy efforts, while opponents worried the language could undo bans against such methods as steel leghold traps and luring bears. The amendment was championed by the out-of-state organization International Order of T. Roosevelt in Wisconsin.
The Colorado Parks and Wildlife is in charge of regulating hunting in the state. It has 11 members appointed by the governor and confirmed by the state Senate. 
Twenty-four states have a similar constitutional amendment, with Florida voters most recently approving the language in 2024. 
Voters rejected it, and the AP declared it defeated when 55.2% of the vote was against it. 
Amendment 85
Amendment 85 seeks to make Colorado’s ballots easier to read by requiring questions to be written at an eighth-grade reading level. It was put on the ballot by Advance Colorado, and supporters said it would increase understanding in elections. 
The amendment did not define what an eighth-grade reading level actually means, so stakeholders worried that vagueness would make it difficult to actually implement. 
There are about 50.8% of the votes in favor of Amendment 85 so far, below the required 55% threshold.
Amendment 86
Amendment 86 was a response to the rush of states that redrew their congressional district lines this year to give one political party an advantage. It would require any mid-decade redistricting to be approved by the state’s independent redistricting commission and the Colorado Supreme Court. Redistricting typically happens the year following a census. 
Earlier this year, a Democratic-aligned group tried to get a ballot measure approved to allow mid-decade gerrymandering, but a court blocked it. Advance Colorado backed Amendment 86 in response to that attempt. 
About 53.4% of the vote so far is against the amendment. 
Amendment 87
Amendment 87 would amend the Taxpayer’s Bill of Rights to create graduated income tax rates, so the rate increases with income levels. Individuals and companies making more than $500,000 per year would see their income tax rate rise, maxing out at 8.4% for people making over $1 million, while those making less will see it drop. It was backed by Protecting Colorado’s Future, a coalition of progressive and liberal advocacy groups.
The amendment faced a last-minute court challenge by a person who claimed paid signature gatherers did not properly register with the state. Denver District Court and the Colorado Supreme Court both decided it should stay on the ballot. 
A bit over 50% of voters approved the amendment so far.
Proposition NN
Proposition NN asked voters to raise the limit the state can keep under TABOR and send that money to public K-12 education. It was the only ballot measure referred to voters by the state Legislature. The Colorado Education Association led the campaign for Proposition NN and argued that while it wouldn’t fully close the state’s education funding gap, it would get spending closer to the true cost of educating students today. 
Conservatives were against the proposition and saw it as an attack on TABOR. 
According to the AP, it passed with 55.4% of the vote.
Proposition 132
Proposition 132 would make it a felony to manufacture, distribute or sell a list of synthetic opiates, including fentanyl, and imposed an eight-year mandatory minimum sentence. That would be a significant increase of current criminal penalties. It also would remove a provision in state law that gives immunity to felony prosecution for those offenses to people who report an overdose to authorities. 
It was backed by Advance Colorado and other conservative activists and politicians, including Republican District Attorney George Brauchler. A coalition with groups like ACLU of Colorado, Colorado Criminal Justice Reform Coalition and the Signal Behavioral Health Network were opposed to the proposition. 
It is currently passing with 52.7% of the vote. 
Proposition 133
People convicted of child sex trafficking will receive a life sentence without parole under Proposition 133. Child sex trafficking is already a felony in Colorado. The AP called the race around 9 p.m. on Election Day. About 62% of voters were in favor of the measure.
The proposition also expands the definition of human trafficking of a minor for sexual servitude to include trading anything of monetary value to buy or sell sexual activity with a minor.
The measure was backed by Protect Kids Colorado. Supporters saw the stronger penalty as a deterrent. Opponents, such as the Colorado Coalition Against Sexual Assault and the Colorado Organization for Victim Assistance, said the measure could inadvertently imprison victims who can be pressured into helping their own traffickers target more people. 
Proposition 134
Protect Kids Colorado backed Proposition 134 to require student athletes to play on sports teams that correspond to their sex assigned at birth, so a transgender girl would be excluded from playing on a girls sports team. Schools would need to adopt a policy that classifies teams as male, female or co-ed. Transgender students would be able to play on co-ed teams. 
There are 27 states that ban trans girls from competing in girls sports.
But Colorado is generally considered one of the most trans-friendly states. Groups like One Colorado, the Bread and Roses Legal Center and Rocky Mountain Equality campaigned against the proposition. 
Around 52.4% of votes approve the measure so far. 
Proposition 135
The third measure backed by Protect Kids Colorado would ban surgeries on minors “for the purpose of altering biological sex characteristics.” It defines those surgeries as treatment related to the child’s “perception” of sex or gender. 
Those surgeries are rare for transgender youth in Colorado and across the country and Children’s Hospital Colorado and UCHealth, two major providers of gender-affirming care in the state, have never performed surgeries for transgender minors. It is more common for those patients to undergo gender-affirming care like puberty blockers, counseling and social transition. 
The proposition is passing so far with 51.9% of the vote.
Proposition 136
Proposition 136 was Advance Colorado’s answer to Amendment 87, the graduated income tax measure. It would cap the state’s income tax at the current 4.4%. It was losing with 52.7% of votes against it as of Wednesday afternoon. 
Proposition 137
Proposition 137 would divert some existing sales tax revenue from sporting goods to wildlife mitigation and land protection. The measure would reduce taxpayer refunds in some years. The race is still very close with 50.3% in favor.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: ‘Wow. Just… wow’: Political scientist Chris Cooper on North Carolina’s historic 2026 midterms
description: Tectonic. Generational. A Blue-nami. A bloodbath. Just a few of the terms out there today as people in North Carolina, around the country — and around the world — try to make sense of what just happened in American politics. North Carolina had arguably one of the biggest shifts in the country — our […]
text:
Western Carolina University political science professor Chris Cooper 
Tectonic. Generational. A Blue-nami. A bloodbath. Just a few of the terms out there today as people in North Carolina, around the country — and around the world — try to make sense of what just happened in American politics.
North Carolina had arguably one of the biggest shifts in the country — our U.S. House delegation went from 4 Democrats and 10 Republicans to potentially 10 Democrats and 4 Republicans, depending on the fate of longtime Republican congresswoman Virginia Foxx, who is currently 99 votes behind her Democratic challenger Chuck Hubbard. This is in unofficial results with provisionals and military votes still to come.
The state House saw a similar flip. Democrats now appear to have a working supermajority, rather than a superminority, In the Senate, Republicans seem to have held onto a slim 26-24 majority – if Republican senator Danny Britt survives a likely recount in his very tight race.
And yet, voters also passed three constitutional amendments supported by Republicans.
NC Newsline Editor Laura Leslie sat down Wednesday with Western Carolina University political science Professor Chris Cooper, who’s been slicing and dicing the data behind the votes.
Click here to listen to the full interview with Western Carolina University political science professor Chris Cooper.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Kansas Democrats in line to pick up 20 seats in House, wipe out Republican supermajority
description: Kansas House Democrats are on the cusp of claiming 20 more seats, which will leave Republicans with a 68-57 advantage. It's smallest GOP edge since 1992.
text:
Kansas House Majority Leader Chris Croft, an Overland Park Republican, appears to be the biggest loss among GOP candidates in Tuesday's election as Democratic candidates seize 20 additional seats. In this April 9, 2026, image, Croft works with colleagues on the House floor. (Photo by Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — Voters in Kansas forced recalculation of partisan math in the Kansas House as Democrats flipped as many as 20 seats and crushed the Republican supermajority that allowed one-party domination of public policy debates for the past 16 years.
Unofficial results from Tuesday indicated Republicans absorbed losses in 15 House districts that voted for President Donald Trump two years ago in the presidential race. If preliminary counts were to hold, Republicans would retain a majority in the House, but the GOP advantage would shrink to 68-57. It would be the smallest working margin for House Republicans since 1992.
The blue wave that filtered to down-ballot races in the Kansas Legislature took out Republican House Majority Leader Chris Croft, an Overland Park Republican. He fell to Democrat Megan Phillips, also of Overland Park, by a margin of 51% to 49%. Croft was among contenders to become House speaker.
Croft’s loss in a district Trump carried by 6.1 percentage points in 2024 was in line with the evolving electoral landscape in Johnson County. Republicans were poised to surrender at least 10 House seats in the populous county in the Kansas City metro.
On Wednesday, Secretary of State Scott Schwab said his office would perform close-race audits of results in three House districts.
Schwab’s review would begin with the District 27 battle between Democrat Sara Kiewiet of Overland Park and incumbent Republican Sean Tarwater of Stilwell. At this point, Kiewiet had a 41-vote edge over Tarwater, who was in line to seek a role in GOP House leadership.
The secretary of state planned to review results in the 40th District involving Democrat Mika Stilwell and incumbent Republican David Buehler. In that Lansing showdown, Buehler was ahead with 3,806 votes to Stilwell’s total of 3,739. The other review would take place in District 117. Democrat Brandon Holland of Baldwin City held the edge at 6,566 votes to incumbent Shawnee Republican Adam Turk’s 6,433.
House Minority Leader Brandon Woodard, a Lenexa Democrat who didn’t have a Republican opponent, said fundraising, candidate recruiting, get-out-the-vote efforts and policy positions on the cost of living, public education and healthcare contributed to the surge among Democrats. The results demonstrated Kansans were convinced the state deserved better outcomes in the Kansas House, he said.
“This wave of victories is not only a testament to the devotion of our caucus and candidates, but of the dedication of Kansans to our state,” Woodard said. “By picking up this unprecedented number of House seats, we have effectively shattered the Republican supermajority and restored balance to the Kansas Legislature.”
Woodard said he had an uncomfortable front-row seat to the work of Republican House leaders who placed “divisive culture wars ahead of issues that matter the most to Kansas families” and advocated policies “designed to advance an extreme political agenda at the expense of everyday Kansans.”
During the 2026 legislative session, House Republicans dictated to Democrats during floor debates by virtue of their 88-37 advantage. With that two-thirds majority, Republicans in the House could disregard Democrats when voting to override vetoes by Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly or when considering whether proposed amendments to the Kansas Constitution went on statewide ballots.
The addition of Democrats to the House meant they would be assigned more seats on budget and policy committees and had an opportunity to block Republicans from compelling middle-of-the-night debates on controversial legislation.
Jason Probst, a Hutchinson Democrat, prevailed in a rematch against Republican Rep. Kyler Sweely, who defeated Probst in 2024. On Tuesday, Probst earned 53% of the vote against Sweely’s 47%.
“There was a moment last night where I looked out at all the people who came out to support me,” Probst said. “I took a deep breath, and I looked at all their faces. I looked in their eyes. I wanted to remember the emotion of two years ago, feeling so alone, looking out at a room full of people who had put so much time and energy into supporting me — only to have to tell them that I had failed. To feel that I had let them all down, that I had let my community down.”
Probst said the election was a first step in the process to create a political system that effectively served Kansans. He said worthwhile change would “require all of us to move from the established habits of old and demand something new.”
Rep. Adam Smith, a Weskan Republican who didn’t have an opponent in the Tuesday election, said he hadn’t planned to seek reelection until Senate President Ty Masterson, the GOP nominee for governor, blamed him for the Legislature’s inability to make meaningful progress on property tax reform.
“I may not even run in ’28,” Smith said. “I wasn’t going to this year until a certain someone decided to blame me for everything wrong with property taxes.”
As Smith considered his 100% approval rating among western Kansas voters, he shared a tongue-in-cheek idea about deriving a payback on behalf of Kansans who endured an avalanche of political advertising.
“I’m thinking we should have a surcharge/tax on political advertising that goes into a fund that is then 100% directly sent back to each homeowner in the form of a property tax rebate,” he said.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Iowa public universities report $9.5B in revenues, identify future fiscal challenges
description: Iowa’s public university system saw a combined total of $9.52 billion in actual revenues for fiscal year 2026, according to a report the Iowa Board of Regents will receive next week. The board released its fiscal year 2026 comprehensive fiscal report, detailing revenues and expenditures for Iowa’s public universities and their units, ahead of its […]
text:
Two of Iowa's public universities saw revenue increases in fiscal year 2026, which helped offset costs in other areas. (Photos by Brooklyn Draisey/Iowa Capital Dispatch. Logo via Iowa Board of Regents)Iowa’s public university system saw a combined total of $9.52 billion in actual revenues for fiscal year 2026, according to a report the Iowa Board of Regents will receive next week.
The board released its fiscal year 2026 comprehensive fiscal report, detailing revenues and expenditures for Iowa’s public universities and their units, ahead of its Nov. 11-12 meeting at Iowa State University. It also lists “headwinds impacting higher education” and how state universities are preparing.
Tuition continues to make up the majority of operating revenues across the University of Iowa, Iowa State University and University of Northern Iowa, making up 63.1% where state appropriations accounted for 30.5% and indirect cost reimbursements making up 5%. Total operating revenues for fiscal year 2026, excepting University of Iowa Hospitals and Clinics, reached $1.937 billion.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
When compared to the board-approved fiscal year 2026 budget from July 2025, the report stated revenues were 1% over budget and expenses were 0.6% under budget.
“Overall, strong enrollment growth drove increases in tuition and fee revenue,” the fiscal report stated. “The Universities also realized indirect cost recovery and investment income that exceeded budgeted expectations.”
Challenges in higher education
The report identified both state and federal policy changes that could potentially impact Iowa’s public universities, including the passage of the Income Tax Rate Reduction and Exemptions Act and the Individual Income Tax Rate Act by the Iowa Legislature.
These changes to tax policies have “resulted in reduced state general fund receipts,” the report stated, and they could hurt funding of public higher education and other services while lowering taxes for Iowans.
“Without the identification of alternative revenue sources, the decline in state tax revenues increases uncertainty regarding future state support for Iowa’s Regent universities,” the report stated.
Changes to student financial aid options will impact low-income students and those in high-cost programs, the report stated, potentially leading to students deciding to not enroll or drop out. The federal government is contemplating changes to the Pell Grant program for low-income students. Iowa’s universities enroll around 13,715 students who receive grant funding.
The Grad PLUS loan was also eliminated and borrowing caps implemented, which the report stated “disproportionately affects students in high-cost programs” like law, medicine and dentistry. More than 6,250 graduate and professional students enrolled in Iowa’s public institutions who have federal student loans.
Fewer students graduating high school in the next few years could also pose a problem for universities, the report stated. The enrollment cliff won’t impact Iowa so much but it will hit other states from which Iowa universities draw students, like Wisconsin and Illinois.
Inflation and federal research spending shifts are also ongoing issues and ones the board has addressed in previous discussions.
“Revenue diversification across tuition, research funding, philanthropic support and private partnerships provides a buffer against volatility in any single area,” the report stated.
University of Iowa
The UI saw both tuition and fee revenues exceed their budgets by 0.5% in fiscal year 2026 due to higher enrollment than what was projected, totaling more than $3 million. Other increased revenue came from indirect cost reimbursement and interest.
Expenses were also 0.2% over budget, driven by “higher-than-expected building repair costs” reaching nearly $20 million more than expected. Salaries made up 65% of expenditures but were 0.7% below budget. More than 20% of tuition revenue went to financial aid provided by the university, totaling $122.7 million.
UI Athletics saw ticket sales exceed budgets across all sports as well as conference revenue and “novelty revenue,” due to College Football Playoff and royalty income.
Iowa State University
ISU’s operating budget also exceeded its budget, by 1.6% totaling $13.2 million, driven by tuition revenue from 285 extra students who weren’t expected. “Conservative budgeting amid the dynamic federal funding environment” led to indirect cost reimbursement revenues being 12.4% higher than budgeted, the report stated, and differences in the fiscal years for ISU and the federal government led to 9.9% more federal funding for the Agricultural Experiment Station and Coop Extension.
Conversely, general fund operating expenses for the Ames university were down by 1.3% in fiscal year 2026, with big variances between expected and actual costs.
“Professional and scientific supplies, building repairs, and rental expenses were under budget by 24.7%, 23.5%, and 10.1%, respectively, reflecting cost efficiencies and expenditure management efforts,” the report stated. “State auditor expenses were under budget by 6.9% due to the timing of ongoing audit work.”
Expenses for utilities and equipment, however, were higher than projected by 24.5% and 18.2%, caused and offset by shifts in funding between restricted funds and the general fund. Student financial aid expenditures also exceeded the budget by 5%, alongside increased enrollment and shifts in student residency.
ISU Athletics revenues and expenditures both exceeded the budget by $4.4 million, the report stated, while fiscal 2026 revenues and expenses totaled $145.6 million. Less cash reserves were used for athletics than originally planned due to the revenue increases.
“Strong competitive performance drove significant gains across several revenue categories, including football, men’s basketball and women’s basketball ticket sales, as well as fundraising, premium seating and postseason revenues,” the report stated. “Additional positive variances were realized through increased multimedia rights revenue, higher licensing income, and stronger auxiliary revenues.”
Personnel costs and additional capital renewal investments drove increased expenses, the report stated, though the athletics department enacted “targeted cost-saving measures” to offset them.
University of Northern Iowa
UNI was the only state university to see revenues come in under budget targets in fiscal year 2026 — a $1.1 million shortfall the report stated “was covered by the enrollment contingency budget.” While the Cedar Falls university’s investment income budget was unchanged, it ended up exceeding the budget due to strong performances in the equities market, the report stated.
Other budget variances for the university included higher supply costs from changes in the UNI Foundation, decreased utility costs due to good weather and a $2.3 million increase in building repairs for deferred maintenance, paid for with surplus utility funds.
UNI Athletics planned out its fiscal year 2026 budget in response to a board audit and with the goal of balancing the budget by fiscal year 2028, the report stated. Revenues came in at $2.76 million below the board-approved budget due to shortfalls in support from the Missouri Valley Conference and NCAA, athletic marketing, football and support from alumni and the UNI Foundation.
Expenses also came in at $2.56 million over the budgeted amount, driven by administration bonuses and increased costs in men’s basketball and event operations.
To balance the budget, the report stated UNI is “pursuing new revenue and cost-management opportunities” through new group ticket sales and licensing vendors, updating donor giving levels for annual funds, new partnerships and contracts and right-sizing scholarship budgets.
“These efforts are intended to improve financial predictability and position athletics to achieve the internal audit target of a balanced budget by FY 2028,” the report stated.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: The Ocean State’s version of a blue wave: 10 Republicans left in the legislature
description: Democratic dominance of the Rhode Island General Assembly deepened Tuesday night, after five incumbent lawmakers — four Republicans and one independent — were ousted by challengers from the left. The results leave just 10 Republicans in the 113-member legislature, down from 14. That includes two GOP members of the 38-person Senate, and 10 out of […]
text:
Republicans five-term Sen. Thomas Paolino, left, deputy minority leader, of Lincoln, and six-term Sen. Elaine Morgan, right, of Hopkinton, now deputy minority whip, both lost their seats in the Rhode Island Senate to Democratic challengers in Tuesday's election. (Photo by Alexander Castro/Rhode Island Current)Democratic dominance of the Rhode Island General Assembly deepened Tuesday night, after five incumbent lawmakers — four Republicans and one independent — were ousted by challengers from the left.
The results leave just 10 Republicans in the 113-member legislature, down from 14.
That includes two GOP members of the 38-person Senate, and 10 out of 75 in the House. And there’s still one independent, as former Republican darling Allan Fung, now disaffiliated and at odds with GOP leaders, won his wife’s old House seat in Cranston.
But don’t mistake a handful of upsets for a harbinger of change on Smith Hill. Excluding open seats, 95% of state lawmakers who won Tuesday are incumbents. Reelection was all but guaranteed for most due to the absence of serious opponents — or any at all.
“There’s no sea change in Rhode Island state government based on these results,” said Adam Myers, associate professor of political science at Providence College. “Republicans were already a non-factor. Essentially, now, they’re going to be even less of a factor.”
The absence of change in the legislature stands in stark contrast to Congress as Democrats flipped at least 30 Republican-held seats, notching enough victories to control both chambers. 
Yet, the Ocean State’s few progressive pickups could stem from the same national rebuke of Trump that led to Democratic victories nationwide, Myers said. 
“The fact that this happened in very different parts of the state, everywhere from Woonsocket, to Cranston, to Exeter, suggests to me that the best way to explain it is, these were nationalized races,” Myers said. “Voters in Rhode Island were primarily acting on, or responding to, national changes.”
Rep. Jon Brien, a Woonsocket independent, left, lost his District 49 House seat to progressive Democrat Veronicka Vega in Tuesday’s general election. (Left photo by Alexander Castro/Rhode Island Current. Right, courtesy photo)
Woonsocket’s about-face
Perhaps the clearest example was in Rhode Island’s House District 49 where independent Rep. Jon Brien lost to progressive-backed Democrat Veronicka Vega by nearly 5 points. 
Brien, a former Democratic state representative from Woonsocket who became an independent before his second, non-consecutive legislative career began in 2022, espoused conservative stances on taxes, the Israel-Hamas War and COVID-era public health rules. And Woonsocket voted for Trump in 2024 — the first time the northernmost city backed a Republican presidential candidate since Ronald Reagan in 1984.
“As the lone independent in the House, I couldn’t help but get swept up in a confluence of political events that seemingly affected elected leaders across the country,” Brien said in an email. “It seems that this election cycle was less about the candidate and more about the candidate’s ideology.
Vega, 26, was a first-time candidate who put her personal story of facing homelessness, poverty and food insecurity — and the social safety net programs that helped support her — at the heart of her campaign. She was backed by the Rhode Island Working Families Party, Reclaim RI and Affordable RI, among other progressive groups.
To Dan Denvir, co-chair of Reclaim RI, Vega’s victory shows voters’ appetite for progressive politics extends beyond Providence.
“There are poor and working-class families all over this state who oppose MAGA extremism and the corporate Democratic politics that allowed MAGA extremism to happen,” Denvir said. 
Vega did not immediately respond to requests for comment Wednesday.
Across the state in Senate District 34, voters also moved left in electing Democratic challenger Samantha Wilcox over 12-year Republican incumbent Sen. Elaine Morgan.
Richmond Town Council President Samantha Wilcox, center, defeated six-term Republican Sen. Elaine Morgan for the Senate District 34 seat in Tuesday’s general election. At left is Lynn Gamwell and at right is Hayden Kendall, her campaign manager. (Photo by Deb Carney
Wilcox, 37, a paralegal and Richmond Town Council president, didn’t think her victory meant anything about a progressive shift in the rural, western district spanning parts of Charlestown, Exeter, Hopkinton, Richmond and West Greenwich.
“We canvassed thousands of doors, regardless of political party,” Wilcox said. “That’s what our district was looking for, someone who listens to both sides.”
Limitations on solar development on rural land, property taxes and housing were what voters wanted to talk about, not political party, Wilcox said.
Morgan did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Four’s a crowd 
The Senate GOP also lost 10-year incumbent Sen. Thomas Paolino, who was defeated by Democrat Nelly Burdette in a four-way race with two independent candidates. The number of names on the ballot — the most of any state legislative race — likely contributed to Paolino’s loss, Myers said.
Indeed, the 2,000 votes combined for the two independents, Jina Petrarca and John Barr II, is four times the 500-vote margin between Burdette and Paolino, according to preliminary, unofficial results Tuesday night.
Paolino also pointed to the split as the reason for his loss.
“I don’t believe the results are indicative of what 57% of District 17 wants,” Paolino said in a text message Wednesday morning.
He did not call Burdette to concede because he said he did not have her number.
But Denvir with Reclaim, which helped canvas for Burdette, argued that the two independents, both of whom ran for and held office before as Democrats, likely siphoned votes away from Burdette, rather than Paolino.
Burdette, a Ukrainian refugee, clinical psychologist and first-time candidate, said she began canvassing the district in April, well before any of her opponents. The Working Families Party also supported Burdette.
Party ideology came up much less than concerns over healthcare access and energy bills, Burdette said.
“People liked that I was part of the community, not from the political world,” Burdette said Wednesday.
However, Senate Minority Leader Jessica de la Cruz warned of the consequences from an even more imbalanced legislature.
“Rhode Islanders are already struggling with some of the highest electricity costs in the country, an increasingly unaffordable cost of living, and a state government that continues to spend more while delivering too little,” de la Cruz, a North Smithfield Republican, said in a statement. “The last thing taxpayers need is even less scrutiny of the decisions being made on Smith Hill.”
Former Republican turned independent Allan Fung, right, won the Cranston House District 15 seat away from Rep. Christopher Paplauskas, left. (Courtesy photos)
The Fung factor
A three-person competition for Cranston’s House District 15 may have also helped Fung defeat freshman Republican Rep. Chris Paplauskas, Myers said. The race, which also included Democrat Colleen Crudele, grew contentious in the final weeks before the election, driven by a rift between the Fungs and Cranston Mayor Ken Hopkins, for whom Paplauskas works as chief of staff. Fung’s wife, Barbara Ann Fenton-Fung ran and lost to Hopkins in the 2024 mayoral primary. Her mayoral campaign opened up the legislative seat, which Paplauskas won by 26 votes in 2024.
