Fung served 12 years as city mayor, and has run twice for governor and once for U.S. Congress, all as a Republican. He disaffiliated this spring, prompting criticism from state party officials including House Minority Leader Mike Chippendale.
“It will be interesting to see how a man who once thought himself gubernatorial and congressional material will operate as but one of 75 in a room that doesn’t embrace independence and rejects disloyalty,” Chippendale, a Foster Republican, said of Fung. 
Chippendale, too, blamed national sentiment for GOP losses.
“Rhode Islanders were beaten over the head, day after day and hour after hour, with ads about Donald Trump,” he said. “One might think Trump was running in every RI race. Even after all those ads, I’m still waiting to hear what the Democrats who ran them intend to do about the electric bill, the shortage of primary care doctors or the cost of buying a home in this state.”
A second freshman GOP representative, Richard Fascia of Johnston, also lost his reelection campaign to Democrat Edward Stravato.



Quotation







“The fact that this happened in very different parts of the state, everywhere from Woonsocket, to Cranston, to Exeter, suggests to me that the best way to explain it is, these were nationalized races. Voters in Rhode Island were primarily acting on, or responding to, national changes.”


– Adam Myers, associate professor of political science at Providence College


 Stravato, 40, a lawyer and small-business owner, credited his “old school” campaign — heavy on handwritten letters with little-to-no social media presence — for his victory.
“I think it speaks more to our campaign than it does a blue wave,” said Stravato.
The district spanning Johnston and Cranston backed Trump in the last three elections. Stravato said he identifies as a moderate Democrat, “not a liberal.”
Stravato said Fascia had called him to congratulate him earlier Wednesday morning.
Fascia did not immediately respond to requests for comment. 
Almost no luck for The League of RI Businesses 
Conservative political group The League of RI Businesses notched one victory from its efforts to put more “business-minded” candidates in the legislature. League-backed Republican Michael Riley defeated Democrat Shaina Smith in the open House District 42 seat, which includes all of Scituate and a piece of Cranston. Riley will succeed Republican Rep. Robert Quattrocchi, who chose not to run for reelection after 10 years in office.
Dave Levesque, co-founder of The League and owner of Brewed Awakenings coffeehouses, said he was disappointed but not surprised by The League’s low success rate among its endorsed legislative candidates.
“We’ve learned a lot of lessons,” Levesque said, citing the need for better vetting of candidates, and being more selective in the process.
The League bypassed the $2,000 per candidate per year donation limit in state law by setting up a political action committee for every city and town in the state. Levesque acknowledged that campaign finance strategy might have worked better if money was spent on advertising and outreach, rather than poured into candidates’ campaign accounts directly.
“It’s not just about money, you need a strong ground game,” Levesque said.
He was unbothered by the prospect of campaign finance reforms championed by lawmakers and good government groups like Common Cause Rhode Island seeking to prevent The League from leveraging multiple PACs to donate more money to candidates.
“There’s ways around it,” Levesque said. “That’s the least of what we have to worry about. The problem now is, what’s going to happen in the General Assembly? What bills and laws are they going to pass that make Rhode Island not as business-friendly as it needs to be?”
Democrat Angela Coburn, right, with supporter Betsy Alexander, left, campaign outside Greenbush Elementary School in West Warwick on Tuesday, Nov. 3. Coburn defeated Republican Lawrence Almagno Jr. for the open House District 27 seat vacated by Pat Serpa, who held the seat for 20 years. (Photo by Laura Paton/Rhode Island Current)
Open seat races 
Other open seat races decided Tuesday include:

Providence House District 7: Democrat Amy Santiago defeated Republican Chris Ireland.
Providence House District 12: Democrat Arlette Hidalgo ran unopposed.
Warwick House District 22: Democrat Zak Pereira defeated Republican Barbara Quigley.
Warwick House District 23: Democrat William Muto defeated Republican Dana James Traversie.
West Warwick/Coventry/Warwick House District 27: Democrat Angela Coburn defeated Republican Lawrence Almagno Jr.
North Kingstown House District 31: Democrat Jim Sheehan ran unopposed.
North Kingstown House District 32: Democrat Robert Craven Jr. ran unopposed.
Barrington/Warren House District 67: Democrat Nicole Jellinek defeated independent Joseph DePasquale.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Democrat flips state education board seat but GOP maintains majority control
description: TOPEKA — A Democrat in eastern Kansas flipped a state education board position previously held by a conservative Republican, shifting the board’s makeup to four Democrats and six Republicans. Four Republicans were elected Tuesday to the remaining open seats on the Kansas State Board of Education, which oversees Kansas public schools. The winners filled five [...]
text:
From left, Republican Amy Cawvey, Democrat Amy Diediker, Republican Destry Brown, Republican Jean Clifford and Republican Alana McWilliams won election to the Kansas State Board of Education. (Kansas Reflector composite from photos submitted by the candidates)TOPEKA — A Democrat in eastern Kansas flipped a state education board position previously held by a conservative Republican, shifting the board’s makeup to four Democrats and six Republicans.
Four Republicans were elected Tuesday to the remaining open seats on the Kansas State Board of Education, which oversees Kansas public schools. The winners filled five open seats on the 10-member board after current seat holders declined to run for reelection.
Amy Diediker, a Democrat and former elementary school teacher from Olathe, won a small eastern district near the Kansas City metro that has been held by Republican Michelle Dombrosky since 2019. Diediker leaned into defending public schools during her campaign.
“I think that there’s been a lot of work on the other side to undermine public education,” Diediker said.
 
Northeastern district
The northeast Kansas district elected Republican Amy Cawvey of Lansing, who beat her Democratic opponent Jennifer Lloyd by 10 percentage points.
Cawvey, the Kansas chair of the National School Boards Coalition, celebrated her win from Leavenworth at a Republican watch party. 
“I attribute this victory to voters who are ready to see real improvement in Kansas education,” Cawvey said in a text message to Kansas Reflector. “Kansans understand that simply pouring more money into education without seeing improved student outcomes is not the answer.”
During her campaign, Cawvey said she wanted to audit school’s special education spending records. But literacy is her main priority, she said.
“First, we must confront the literacy crisis facing Kansas students,” she said. “Far too many children are not reading at grade level, and that should concern every Kansan.”
 
Southeastern district
Republican Destry Brown of Fort Scott won the southeast district with 69% of votes, while Democrat Heather Guernsey lost by 37 percentage points.
Brown recently retired after serving 42 years as the Fort Scott school district’s superintendent and has worked in five different Kansas school districts. 
While campaigning, Brown and Guernsey agreed on multiple issues. They both said discussions of topics such as race and gender belong in classrooms and that the state board should set curriculum guidelines, not the Legislature. 
In the 2026 session, the Legislature attempted to impose an annual fitness test, a citizenship test, daily recess, and lessons on “the negative impacts of communist, fascist and socialist regimes and ideologies.” 
Brown said he thinks voters were drawn to his experience and his perspective on local control. His next step, he said, is to prepare.
He said he planned to “listen and learn and figure out what I need to do to get ready to start serving on the board.”
 
Western district
Republican Jean Clifford of Garden City will represent the board’s largest district. She earned 73% of votes and her opponent, Democrat Lorie Wood, lost with 27%.
Clifford, a retired Air Force attorney, served one term on the board from 2019-2023 and has served on her local school board.
She said voters elected her for her experience and interest in raising academic performance. 
“I believe the message that resonated most with voters was my focus on student achievement and outcomes,” she said in a text message to Kansas Reflector. “I also think voters understood that my strong background and experience in education and having lived in western Kansas for over 30 years and raised my family here showed that I had a deep understanding of the issues we have in education in rural Kansas.”
 
Eastern district
An eastern district that covers much of Johnson and Miami counties, elected Diediker, the Democrat who flipped a seat currently held by a Republican, and she earned 55% of votes over Republican Jim McMullen.
Diediker has never held or run for public office before. She worked as an elementary school teacher for seven years and more recently has volunteered around her community, including for the Johnson County Democratic Party. 
She said voters responded to her support for public schools.
“I think people were ready for a champion for public education and someone who would be a fierce supporter of public schools,” she said.
Leading up to the election, Diediker has said she wants to focus attention on middle and high school grade levels and promote bipartisan communication between state bodies. 
McMullen, a Johnson County attorney, served on the Blue Valley School Board from 2021 until he lost reelection. The board stripped his vice president role in 2022 over anti-trans social media posts. 
 
Central district
Republican Alana McWilliams of Abilene will represent central Kansas. She won 63% of votes and her opponent, Democrat Ann Zimmerman of Salina, lost with 37%.
McWilliams is an education advocate and founder of Designed to Learn, a Wichita-based reading tutor center for students with learning disabilities. 
Her campaign focused on advocating for improving Kansas public school’s reading curriculum. 
She previously said she homeschools her three children — two of whom have dyslexia — because public schools didn’t adequately teach them reading skills or accommodate their learning differences. 
“At nearly every forum and event, I heard the same concerns,” she said. “Parents know something isn’t working for their kids. Teachers want better tools and support in the classroom.”

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Republicans sweep State Board of Education races; nonpartisans win 2 NU Regents seats
description: LINCOLN — Nebraskans chose five new faces for the State Board of Education and University of Nebraska Board of Regents in seven races across the state Tuesday. Conservatives are on the verge of flipping a key seat and shifting the ideologically 4-4 State Board of Education red. The NU Board of Regents is set to shift […]
text:
The 2026 candidates for Nebraska State Board of Education, left, and University of Nebraska Board of Regents, arranged by district. (Photos courtesy of the candidates/campaigns | Nebraska Capitol photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — Nebraskans chose five new faces for the State Board of Education and University of Nebraska Board of Regents in seven races across the state Tuesday.
Conservatives are on the verge of flipping a key seat and shifting the ideologically 4-4 State Board of Education red. The NU Board of Regents is set to shift more blue and purple.
Seven seats were up across the two eight-person boards, of which five had no incumbent running. Four were for the State Board of Education, where members serve four-year terms and oversee the Nebraska Department of Education. Regents, by contrast, serve six-year terms. Neither position includes a salary.
Both the State Board of Education and NU Board of Regents are officially nonpartisan, meaning candidates’ party affiliation doesn’t appear on the ballot. New board members take office Jan. 7.
State Board of Education
In Douglas County, Republican Lou Ann Goding led registered nonpartisan Sherrye Hutcherson for the Omaha-based District 8. Incumbent Deb Neary of Omaha, a Democrat, decided not to seek reelection and endorsed Hutcherson.
Goding led Hutcherson by 1,883 votes, or 2.4%, as of 6 a.m. Wednesday. Goding has declared victory in the race.


In an Oct. 8 pre-election interview, Goding recalled her service on the Omaha Public Schools Board of Education, where she was selected as president and vice president at a time when Republicans were a minority on the board. She said she always thoroughly researches what’s best for students and brings people together.
“I showed that I was fair and independent when it came to what was the right thing to do for students, and that that was where my focus was,” Goding said. 
State Board of Education President Elizabeth Tegtmeier of North Platte ran unopposed for the board’s District 7 in western Nebraska. Incumbent Sherry Jones, a Republican like Tegtmeier, ran against Democratic challenger Grady Erickson for the Grand Island-based District 6. Jones defeated Erickson by 16,131 votes, or 24.4%, as of 6 a.m. Wednesday morning.
For the board’s District 5 in southeast Nebraska, Republican Angie Eberspacher of Beaver Crossing defeated Democrat Michaela Conway of Crete. Incumbent Kirk Penner of Aurora, a Republican, decided not to seek reelection and endorsed Eberspacher.
Eberspacher led Conway by 9,300 votes, or 11.4%, as of 6 a.m. Wednesday. Conway has conceded and congratulated Eberspacher.


If the unofficial results hold, the State Board of Education would be 5-3, with a majority of Republicans.
The State Board of Education has set various priorities through 2030. These include improving 3rd grade reading proficiency to 75% on state assessments, 8th grade math proficiency to 80% on state assessments and math and reading proficiency of high school juniors to 71% and 73%, respectively, on the ACT. Other goals include reducing chronic absenteeism by 50%, halving the number of unfilled and vacant teacher positions and improving graduation rates to 94%.
NU Board of Regents
For the NU Board of Regents, two incumbents decided not to seek reelection — Regent Tim Clare of Lincoln for NU Regents District 1 (he was first elected in 2008) and Regent Jack Stark of Omaha for NU Regents District 2 (he was elected in 2020). 
Regent Joel Makovicka of Omaha, who was appointed to NU Regents District 4 in February, did not run in a special election for a four-year term. He succeeded former NU Regent Elizabeth O’Connor of Omaha, who was reelected to a second term in 2024. She resigned in January as she faced a felony charge of driving drunk and causing serious bodily injury connected to a May 2025 crash. She pleaded guilty and was sentenced to one year in prison in August.
Clare, Stark and Makovicka are all Republicans. O’Connor is a Democrat. The board currently consists of seven Republicans and one Democrat.
In Lincoln’s District 1, registered nonpartisan Brent Comstock defeated Dr. Jeremy Hosein, a Republican, and will succeed Clare. Comstock led by 9,895 votes, or 14.3%. Hosein has conceded and congratulated Comstock, who celebrated his victory, too.


For District 2, which is split between Douglas and Sarpy counties, registered nonpartisan Elizabeth Butler leads Republican Jill Wolfe of Elkhorn to succeed Stark, by 7,810 votes, or 9.5%. Butler declared victory after noon Wednesday. Wolfe had not yet made a public post as of 1:30 p.m. Wednesday.


And in the special election to finish O’Connor’s initial term, former University of Nebraska-Lincoln student Regent Justin Solomon leads former first lady Susanne Shore by 11,477 votes, or 22.2%. Both are Democrats. Solomon declared victory at 10:30 p.m. Tuesday. Shore had not made a public post as of 1:30 p.m. Wednesday.


NU Regent Barbara Weitz, the board’s only current Democrat, had donated more than $121,000 supporting Comstock, Butler and Shore.
If the unofficial results hold, the NU Board of Regents would be 4-2-2, still with a majority of Republicans but split with two Democrats and two registered nonpartisans.
The regents have had to navigate slowing state investments into the NU system in recent years, and nearly all regent candidates say they want to be more active in connecting with faculty, staff, students, policymakers and community members. Multiple candidates have identified restoring trust within the NU community as a top goal.
The State Board of Education meets nearly every month, with the final meeting of the year scheduled for Friday. Regents meet every other month, with the final meeting of 2026 on Dec. 4.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: What will Pennsylvania Democrats do with a trifecta in Harrisburg?
description: Roughly 12 hours after winning 26 seats in the Pennsylvania Senate, thus clinching a Democratic trifecta in state government, a crowd of party members stood on the Capitol steps to celebrate “a very good day” following a successful midterm election.  “It is now the obligation of all of my colleagues to recognize that with this […]
text:
Rep. Malcom Kenyatta (D-Philadelphia) said a Democratic trifecta in Harrisburg would mean a body "where we stand unequivocally with organized labor" at a Capitol celebration on Nov 4, 2026. (Photo by Whitney Downard/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)Roughly 12 hours after winning 26 seats in the Pennsylvania Senate, thus clinching a Democratic trifecta in state government, a crowd of party members stood on the Capitol steps to celebrate “a very good day” following a successful midterm election. 
“It is now the obligation of all of my colleagues to recognize that with this honor comes tremendous responsibility to govern well, to govern thoughtfully, to govern pragmatically,” said House Majority Leader Matt Bradford (D-Montgomery). “This is an opportunity that we will not fail. We cannot fail.”
The atmosphere was joyous as leaders detailed their plans for a unified General Assembly where both chambers have a Democratic majority for the first time since 1993. In an unproductive legislative session, speakers pinned the blame squarely on the current GOP majority in the Senate.
Rep. Greg Scott (D-Montgomery) holds up a homemade sign vowing to increasing the state’s minimum wage. (Photo by Whitney Downard/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)
“Far too often, hundreds of our bills got stuck in a drawer over in the Senate,” said House Speaker Joanna McClinton (D-Philadelphia). “Voters in the commonwealth of Pennsylvania have decided that we should go in a different direction … and we can’t wait to deliver.”
Her caucus holds 111 seats out of 203, according to The Associated Press, “a mandate to respond to the needs of this hour,” McClinton continued. The Senate will now have 26 Democrats, a one-seat majority. 
Increasing the minimum wage — currently at the federal minimum of $7.25/hour — to $15 is a top priority, alongside codifying access to reproductive healthcare. Various leaders mentioned increasing pay for home health workers, continued investments in public education, establishing paid family leave, healthcare affordability and guardrails around data centers.
“We’re going to get them to the governor’s desk because there’s so much that’s been bottled up for so many years that we’re going to do,” Senate Minority Leader Jay Costa (D-Allegheny) said. 
 Looming agenda items in 2027

In campaign messaging, Senate Republicans painted themselves as a bulwark against Democrat’s uncontrolled spending, consistently pushing to spend less in the commonwealth’s annual budget. 
”Elections bring both victories and setbacks, but our responsibility to the people of Pennsylvania doesn’t change. We have work to do, and we will take the time to analyze these results, strengthen our organization, and ensure we are prepared for the challenges ahead,” said Pennsylvania GOP Chairman Greg Rothman in a statement.
Rothman is also a state senator from Cumberland County.
But Costa said lawmakers would be “thoughtful” about the budget, even if Democrats no longer had to compromise “in places where we really didn’t want to.” 

Gov. Josh Shapiro cruises to a second term in Pennsylvania


“We are going to be fiscally responsible, fiscally conscious,” Costa said. “We recognize that we have limited resources in the commonwealth, and we have to be thoughtful in what we do. And we’re going to make sure that we’re being thoughtful going forward because you know we don’t want to just have a majority for two years — we want to stick around a little while.”
Also on the radar: drafting a sentencing structure for felony murder and tackling skill games. 
In two separate decisions, the Pennsylvania Supreme Court ruled that the state’s mandatory life sentence for felony murder was unconstitutional and that skill games fell under the state’s gambling laws. 
Justices gave legislators 120 days to draft new laws to comply with the rulings, but the General Assembly missed both deadlines. 
House Speaker Joanna McClinton introduced Sen. Jay Costa, pictured above, as “the next president of the Senate.” Costa is currently Senate Minority Leader. (Photo by Whitney Downard/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)
County judges currently have no minimum or maximum guidance for sentencing those convicted of felony murder, a charge levied when someone dies — intentionally or not — during the commission of another felony. 
And state police confiscated tens of thousands of skill games machines, working with small business owners to remove the unauthorized gaming terminals from gas stations, grocery stores and fraternal clubs around the state. 
Bradford previously said that lawmakers’ last-minute deal on skill games fell through when Senate Republicans failed to muster enough support.
“The House has shown a way forward. The Senate has not,” Bradford said Wednesday. “Obviously, there’s new leadership and we are very excited for the new management in the Senate.”
Costa said that neither topic was a partisan issue, though a sticking point in prior negotiations was whether taxes on skill games would go toward transit or stay in the state’s general fund. He vowed that mass transit would be “a conversation we’re going to have early on,” as the state’s largest system in Philadelphia faces a looming deficit. 
“The felony murder ruling, I think, is something we just got to come together on,” Costa added. “It’s not a Democrat or Republican issue. It’s something we have to work together on to get something done, and I think we will.” 
The current legislative session ends on Nov. 30.
Newly elected members of the House and Senate will be sworn in on Jan. 5.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Dems expanded the map across the nation and in Kentucky for future elections, Beshear says
description: Tuesday was a good night for Democrats and an extremely good night for Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear.  Leading up to midterm elections, Beshear had a spotlight trained on him as the Democratic Governors Association chair, campaigning across the country in races that ultimately led to Democrats flipping five seats, and so now controlling at least […]
text:
Kentucky Governor Andy Beshear talks after Democrat Zach Dembo’s Sixth Congressional District win against Ralph Alvardo, at the Central Bank Center in downtown Lexington, Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Brian Simms for Kentucky Lantern)Tuesday was a good night for Democrats and an extremely good night for Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear. 
Leading up to midterm elections, Beshear had a spotlight trained on him as the Democratic Governors Association chair, campaigning across the country in races that ultimately led to Democrats flipping five seats, and so now controlling at least 28 governorships. He also supported some candidates back in Kentucky, like Zach Dembo, the congressman-elect in the 6th Congressional District who flipped the seat after Republican U.S. Rep. Andy Barr held the seat for 14 years. 
Beshear, a two-term governor thinking about a possible run for president in 2028, told the Kentucky Lantern Wednesday afternoon that the results expanded the national map for Democrats in ways “some people thought was impossible” in states like Iowa, Ohio, Alaska and Texas. He also called it a “team effort” as Democrats had strong candidates this cycle and good leadership at DGA giving support. 
“Whether it’s me or not, the Democratic nominee will be able to run on the best map in decades because of my work and the work of the DGA,” Beshear said when asked what Tuesday’s wins mean for 2028. “We now have a Democratic governor in every current battleground state, and we have shown that the right candidate can win in places like Ohio and Iowa.”
Beshear added that he was proud that the “map has fundamentally changed,” because “Democrats have to win in 2028.” 
“(Vice President) JD Vance could be a worse president than even Donald Trump, and now being able to run in a much more favorable map just gives Democrats that (much) bigger of an opportunity,” the governor added.  
As for the Kentucky inroads, Beshear praised those candidates and said he thinks people could see a difference between Democratic candidates and the policies of Trump, which he said led to higher costs. 
Zach Dembo and his wife, Lindsey, celebrate his win in the 6th District Congressional race on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Brian Simms for Kentucky Lantern)
“I think one of the things that people said very loud and clear last night is they want to like their neighbor, and they’ve had Donald Trump trying to turn them against their neighbor,” the governor said. “We’ve had a Republican supermajority often saying the same things here in Kentucky, and we’re taught to love our neighbor as ourselves, and we can disagree with them politically, but governing from a place of cruelty or division is wrong, and the American people sent a strong message about that.” 
Beshear predicts a good future for Kentucky Democrats once he leaves office at the end of 2027. He said both high-profile Democrats running to succeed him, Lt. Gov. Jacqueline Coleman and former adviser and state Rep. Rocky Adkins, “are great candidates.” He also highlighted Democratic leaders in the General Assembly and its new members. Beshear also anticipated “more energy” for recruiting Democrats to contest legislative races next cycle. 
“I think now that we have won in some of these places that we can expand our map. I am proud of how the party has operated in that it focused,” Beshear said. “We had not netted a legislative seat in 10 years, and so being very focused on a couple of races, making sure that would happen, meant we did pick up those seats, and we won a few more too.”
‘Running as Mr. Nice’
However, not everyone agrees on how much credit Beshear should get. Tres Watson, the former spokesperson for the Republican Party of Kentucky said a handful of seat flips in the Kentucky General Assembly was “all national” as a reflection of Trump and the GOP brand, not because of Beshear. 
“He’ll try to take a victory lap on it,” Watson said, calling Beshear “a complete failure” when it came to moving seats in past election cycles. In 2024, Kentucky Democrats did not change their overall numbers in the Kentucky House and Senate and Republicans’ supermajorities remained strong. 
Beshear did have one falter in Kentucky’s Court of Appeals race. Fayette Circuit Court Judge Lucy VanMeter defeated Court of Appeals Judge Will Moynahan in the 5th Appellate District. Beshear had appointed Moynahan to the bench in 2025 and was involved in fundraising for him. 
Meanwhile, state Rep. Adam Moore, a Lexington Democrat who was endorsed by Beshear for reelection, said Beshear “has been a great standard bearer of what a Kentucky Democrat is.” Moore said he faced “running against the label of being a Democrat” in Kentucky while being tied to national figures like Presidents Joe Biden and Barack Obama. Beshear being shown as someone who “puts those kitchen table issues forward,” like healthcare access and affordable housing, counteracts that, Moore continued. 
“That is the message, and that is what Kentuckians need to see from us, and I think him leading the way on that helps us make those inroads. And it’s not overnight, but I mean, seven flips last night in the House is a big step forward,” Moore said. 
Al Cross, a longtime political columnist and reporter, said he didn’t see that Democrats in Kentucky had a clear, “real effort to recruit candidates” for 2026 races. More than half of the legislative races on the ballot had uncontested elections. 
“The gains it made last night were gains that would have eventually been made anyway, and thanks to the national tsunami, they were probably greater than expected,” Cross said. “It’s almost a mirror image of what happened 10 years ago when the Republicans got five or six more seats than they expected because of the Trump tsunami in Kentucky.”
Yet, Cross said the national results for Democrats are to Beshear’s advantage should he run for president. Beshear-like Senate candidates such as James Talarico in Texas and Adam Hamilton in Kansas showed themselves to be candidates that “want to end the drama, to end the hate and the cruelty and the division.” 
“They want a conciliatory president. They want a president who stands up for things, but they don’t want a nasty president,” Cross said. “They want a nice president, and Andy Beshear is running as Mr. Nice.”

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Alabama Democrats flip four legislative seats in 2026 midterms
description: Alabama Democrats flipped four legislative seats in Tuesday’s midterm elections, while a Senate race in northeast Alabama between a conservative independent and a Republican incumbent was too close to call on Wednesday.  Although Republicans maintain control of all constitutional offices and a supermajority in both chambers, the flips came amid a major shift[...]
text:
Construction of the new Alabama Statehouse as seen on July 29, 2026, in Montgomery, Alabama. Legislators are expected to occupy the new building in time to verify November's election results. Alabama Democrats flipped four legislative seats on Tuesday, and one race between a conservative independent and an incumbent Republican is too close to call. (Anna Barrett/Alabama Reflector)Alabama Democrats flipped four legislative seats in Tuesday’s midterm elections, while a Senate race in northeast Alabama between a conservative independent and a Republican incumbent was too close to call on Wednesday. 
Although Republicans maintain control of all constitutional offices and a supermajority in both chambers, the flips came amid a major shift toward the Democratic Party. Ballots cast for Democratic candidates increased in all 67 counties on Tuesday, according to election data, and represented one of the best nights for legislative Democrats in decades.
The party focused most of its efforts in Madison County, where one House and two Senate districts flipped. Allison Montgomery defeated incumbent Rep. Phillip Rigsby in House District 25, becoming the first openly transgender representative in Alabama. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
As of Wednesday morning, Montgomery got 12,456 votes (53.2%), and Rigsby got 10,929 votes (46.7%), according to the Alabama Secretary of State’s office.
Montgomery’s campaign focused on improving public education and healthcare access. Rigsby and Republican leadership in weeks leading up to the election attacked Montgomery and Terri Osborne, a Democratic State House candidate in south Alabama, for being transgender. 
Rigsby’s reelection campaign focused on building on his first term, infrastructure and healthcare access.
Messages seeking comment from Montgomery and Rigsby were left Wednesday morning. Rigsby outraised Montgomery by a ratio of 21 to 1. According to campaign finance records, Rigsby raised almost $242,000 in cash and spent about $246,000. Montgomery raised about $11,400 in cash and spent about $19,600. 
In another Huntsville-area state Senate seat, voters chose Democratic nominee Jared Sluss over incumbent Sen. Sam Givhan in Senate District 7. Sluss got 30,255 votes (50.5%), and Givhan got 29,678 votes (49.5%), according to unofficial returns.
Similarly to his Democratic colleagues, Sluss campaigned on affordability, healthcare access and public education. He said in a phone interview Wednesday afternoon the goal is not to flip the supermajority in the State Legislature, but to deliver to the people.
“I think it is a strong indicator that people are hungry for change. I think people want politicians who are going to deliver results and ultimately view their role as public servants versus theoretical policies,” he said.
At 29, Sluss will be the youngest member of the Alabama Senate. 
Givhan conceded in a statement posted to social media Wednesday morning. 
“We knew there were political headwinds in this cycle and I ran a positive, results-oriented campaign because I thought it was the right thing to do,” he said. “While I received many bipartisan compliments on my ads, regrettably, I came up a bit short last night. Of course, I will second-guess myself on strategy as I dive into the results, but now is the time for rest and reflection.”
According to campaign finance records, Givhan also had a cash advantage over Sluss. Givhan reported more than $704,000 in cash donations to Sluss’ $62,200. Givhan spent nearly $978,000, and Sluss spent about $45,500.
In a wide-open State Senate seat in Huntsville, voters chose Democratic nominee Rudolph Valentino Drake over Republican John Roberts in Senate District 2. Sen. Tom Butler, R-Madison, decided not to seek re-election. 
Drake had 34,585 votes (55.9%), and Roberts had 27,130 votes (43.8%), as of Wednesday morning. 
Drake campaigned on the rising cost of living, infrastructure and funding public education. Roberts prioritized workforce development, improving infrastructure and economic development in his campaign. 
According to campaign finance records, Roberts also had a significant cash advantage. He raised more than $843,000 and spent more than $775,000. Drake raised about $4,400 and spent about $22,000. 
Drake declined to comment on Wednesday. In a statement posted to social media Wednesday morning, Roberts thanked supporters. 
“It has been a privilege to meet so many people across Madison and Limestone counties, and I’m thankful for the friendships we’ve made along the way,” Roberts said. “While this campaign has come to an end, I look forward to finding other ways to serve and make a difference in our community.”
Further south, voters chose Democratic nominee Nell Brown over Republican incumbent Leigh Hulsey of Helena in House District 15 in Shelby and Jefferson counties. Brown got 11,042 votes (51.2%) to Hulsey’s 10,516 votes (48.8%), according to unofficial results. 
In a post on Facebook, Brown wrote, “Thank you, District 15. We did it.” 
A message seeking comment from Hulsey was left Wednesday afternoon. 
Hulsey also significantly outraised Brown in cash contributions. Hulsey reported about $206,000 in donations to Brown’s $11,000. 
In a northeast State Senate seat, an independent conservative Jesse Battles currently has a narrow lead over incumbent Sen. Andrew Jones, R-Centre, in Senate District 10. Battles was removed from the Republican primary ballot before launching his independent campaign in April.
As of 11:16 a.m., Battles had 20,341 votes (49.85%), and Jones had 20,289 votes (49.72%), according to the Secretary of State’s office. 
Battles declared victory Wednesday morning in a statement posted to social media. 
“Northeast Alabama is my home, and representing the people and communities I love is an honor I will never take for granted,” he said. “Thank you to everyone who believed in us, stood beside us, and bubbled in Jesse Battles! I promise to work hard, listen, and fight for the people of this district.”
Jones on Tuesday night posted that the margin was within the threshold for an automatic recount, and did not concede. Under state law, that margin is less than one half of one percent.
“Tuesday night’s vote margin appears to be within the threshold for an automatic recount. Additionally, it is my understanding that there are a good number of provisional ballots still to be reviewed,” he said. “The principle of “one person, one vote” has always been the backbone of our democratic system. I ask for your patience as every vote is counted and as we ensure that no mistakes were made.”
Jones raised nearly $1.5 million to Battles’ $158,000. 
Unless Jones concedes and provides a waiver to the Secretary of State, a recount will be conducted within 72 hours of the election’s certification. Battles was ahead by 52 votes as of early Wednesday afternoon.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: US Rep. Virginia Foxx says vote count isn’t over as she trails Dem in NC’s 5th District
description: Republican U.S. Rep. Virginia Foxx trails her Democratic challenger by just 99 votes – less than 1% – in North Carolina’s 5th Congressional District, leaving one of the state’s closest congressional races undecided following Tuesday’s midterm elections.  With all 230 precincts reporting, unofficial results after Election Day show Democrat Chuck Hubbard recei[...]
text:
Republican Congresswoman Virginia Foxx and Democrat Chuck Hubbard. (Photos via House.gov and Hubbard campaign)Republican U.S. Rep. Virginia Foxx trails her Democratic challenger by just 99 votes – less than 1% – in North Carolina’s 5th Congressional District, leaving one of the state’s closest congressional races undecided following Tuesday’s midterm elections. 
With all 230 precincts reporting, unofficial results after Election Day show Democrat Chuck Hubbard received 48.7% of the vote, while Foxx won 48.66%. Libertarian candidate Robert Luffman has about 2.64% of the vote, according to the North Carolina State Board of Elections.
Foxx, 83, said Wednesday that the counting process is not over, pointing to overseas and provisional ballots that have yet to be counted. Military and overseas ballots are accepted if they arrive by Nov. 12.
She said more than 1,000 provisional ballots were cast in the 2024 elections, and Republicans gained enough votes from those ballots to pass the current margin.
“Free and fair elections are a cornerstone of our healthy republic,” Foxx said. The voters exercised their American rights and cast their ballots. I am so grateful for all those who took the time to vote in this election.”
Foxx has represented the district since 2005, winning 11 consecutive general elections in the district. She defeated Hubbard in 2024 by a much larger margin, winning about 60% of the vote. 
Strong Democratic turnout flips at least 5 US House seats across North Carolina

The 5th district stretches across northwestern North Carolina, including areas like Watauga County and Boone, and has historically favored Republicans. It’s long been considered one of the state’s safest GOP seats.
Hubbard, 64, also acknowledged the close margin in a statement that claimed victory in the race. 
He said he was proud to have been selected by voters and looked forward to working on issues including Hurricane Helene recovery and lowering costs for families in his district. 
“Last night’s results came out extremely close, which means we will have to fight for this seat,” Hubbard said. “I trust the Board of Elections to complete their work correctly and fairly.”
The race could be decided through a recount. State law allows a candidate in a non-statewide race to request a recount when the margin is less than 1% of the total votes cast.
County election boards need to complete their canvasses before the results can be certified. The county canvasses are scheduled to be finished by Nov. 13 in North Carolina. After that, the losing candidate can request a recount.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Oklahoma City man accused of sending threatening letters with white power to election officials
description: OKLAHOMA CITY — An Oklahoma City resident has been arrested following accusations that he sent more than 700 threatening letters to officials around the country.  Robin Patrick Martin, 67, is charged in the U.S. Western District of Oklahoma with mailing threatening communications and with conveying false or misleading information and hoaxes. He’s accused of [...]
text:
A photo of a threatening letter sent to the Oklahoma State Election Board in Oklahoma City. (Provided by FBI affidavit)OKLAHOMA CITY — An Oklahoma City resident has been arrested following accusations that he sent more than 700 threatening letters to officials around the country. 
Robin Patrick Martin, 67, is charged in the U.S. Western District of Oklahoma with mailing threatening communications and with conveying false or misleading information and hoaxes. He’s accused of sending packages with white powders, threatening messages and letters to election officials, members of Congress, pollsters, media organizations and the FBI in 2024 and 2026. 
On Oct. 13 the State Election Board in Oklahoma City received a letter containing white powder, and offices at the state Capitol were evacuated, according to the criminal complaint. 
Martin is being represented by federal public defenders. His attorney, Kiefer Rose, did not return a phone call seeking comment as of publication. 
The case is being investigated by the FBI, the United States Postal Inspection Service, the U.S. Capitol Police, the Oklahoma City Police, and the Texas Department of Public Safety.
A photo of the back of a threatening letter sent to the Oklahoma State Election Board in Oklahoma City. The message, written in invisible ink, reads, “Stay on the right side of history, your life might depend on it!” (Provided by FBI affidavit)
FBI Special Agent David Cole wrote in an affidavit that the FBI and U.S. Postal Service identified suspicious packages sent to election officials in all 50 states in 2024 with a return address for the “United States Traitor Elimination Army.” They included messages only seen under ultraviolet light, white powdery substances and three-page letters titled “DECLARATION OF WAR,” according to the affidavit. 
These packages were followed by more than 700 mailings sent in 2026 with a return address of “DSA NEW YORK NY,” according to the affidavit. FBI field offices determine these mailings all appear to be associated with the same sender, according to the affidavit, which includes an image of the October package sent to the Oklahoma State Election Board. 
Investigators have not found evidence linking the DSA, or Democratic Socialists of America, to the letters, and the organization no longer uses the address allegedly used by Martin, according to the affidavit. The DSA is the largest socialist political organization in the U.S. 
Members of the Democratic Socialists of America reported to investigators that they were also receiving emails from a “George Livingston” who outlined an “ambush” planned for Nov. 3 as a member of the United States Traitor Elimination Army and warned people that voting in the midterm elections would be considered treason, according to the affidavit. 
Investigators found that the language in the emails is consistent with the messages on envelopes sent to officials in October and tied the email to a phone number and cellphone purchased by Martin at a Walmart in Oklahoma City, according to the affidavit. Investigators also allege he purchased ingredients that can be used to make invisible ink at Walmart. 
The threatening mailings were deposited at U.S. Postal Service locations in OKC, northern Texas and San Antonio between Oct, 9 and 13, according to the affidavit, and investigators tracked Martin and his vehicle to those locations. 
The suspicious powders that have been tested have been yeast or flour, according to the affidavit.

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Ohio Democrats break Republican supermajority in the Ohio House
description: Ohio Democrats broke the Republican supermajority in the Ohio House, limiting the lawmakers ability to override vetos from incoming Democratic governor Amy Acton.  Ohio voters elected 42 Democrats and 52 Republicans to the Ohio House, according to unofficial election results. Five of the races were too close to call as of Wednesday afternoon.  “It is […]
text:
The Ohio Statehouse. (Photo by Megan Henry/ Ohio Capital Journal) Ohio Democrats broke the Republican supermajority in the Ohio House, limiting the lawmakers ability to override vetos from incoming Democratic governor Amy Acton. 
Ohio voters elected 42 Democrats and 52 Republicans to the Ohio House, according to unofficial election results. Five of the races were too close to call as of Wednesday afternoon. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“It is pretty earth-shattering for the general operations of the assembly,” said University of Cincinnati Political Science Professor David Niven. 
“(Ohio Republicans are) quite used to getting their way, and even though Republicans will maintain a majority, they’ve lost their ‘we can do anything we want’ majority.”
A supermajority is 60 or more seats in the Ohio House and 20 or more seats in the Ohio Senate. Republicans have held a supermajority in the Ohio House since 2013.  
“When you have one party that is simply unaccountable to any other check or balance, it means that they can do whatever they want, and that’s particularly been the case for the Republican legislature,” said University of Akron political scientist David Cohen.
“This was just an enormous event for Democrats to be able to break that stranglehold that they have on the legislature.” 
Republicans will have to work with Democrats to pass legislation, the political analysts said. 
“It provides an opportunity for the legislature and the governor to work together, but it will take goodwill and hard work, and it won’t be easy,” said Common Cause Ohio Executive Director Catherine Turcer. 
Republicans at the Statehouse are not used to having to work with Democrats, Cohen said.
“It’s not something that they really want to do, but it’s something that they’re going to be forced to do if they want to have to be able to to get legislation passed and laws on the books,” he said. 
Niven anticipates Acton and the Republican lawmakers will disagree on school funding and vouchers.
“I don’t think there’s a middle ground on that one,” he said. “That’s a philosophical difference, and I don’t know that there’s any way that they’re going to come together.”
The rest of the General Assembly before Acton takes office in January is going “to be fairly unpleasant,” Turcer said. 
“Legislative leaders are likely going to push proposals that could limit the authority of the governor,” she said. 
“There are things like executive agencies under the purview of the governor who end up making a lot of administrative rules, and the legislature could claw back some of that agency rulemaking and put the control in their own hands.” 
Ohio House races 
Republicans currently hold a 65-34 majority in the Ohio House, but some Republican incumbents lost to their Democrat challengers in Tuesday’s election, according to unofficial results. 

Democrat Megan Coy defeated incumbent state Rep. Mike Dovilla, R-Berea. 
Democrat Rose Lounsbury defeated state Rep. Andrea White, R-Kettering. 
Democrat Shelby Kimball defeated state Rep. Brian Lorenz, R-Powell. 
Democrat Krista Allison defeated state Rep. Jim Thomas, R-Plain Township. 

Democrats picked up a handful of seats in open districts that are currently held by Republicans. 

Democrat Noah Spinner won Ohio’s 31st district, which is currently held by state Rep. Bill Roemer, R-Richfield.  
Democrat Samantha Salamon won Ohio’s 35th district, which is currently held by state Rep. Steve Demetriou, R-Bainbridge Twp. Demetriou lost his bid for election for the Ohio Senate. 
Democrat Daquan Neal won Ohio’s 39th district, which is currently held by state Rep. Phil Plummer, R-Dayton. 
Democrat Mike Baker won Ohio’s 52nd district, which is currently held by state Rep. Gayle Manning, R-Avon. Manning won her seat in the Ohio Senate. 

A few races with Republican incumbents were too close to call as of Wednesday afternoon. 
State Rep. Haraz Ghanbari, R-Perrysburg, has a slight lead in a tight race with Democrat Richard Rettig and state Rep. Cindy Abrams, R-Harrison, has a small lead against Democrat Jonathan Bradner, as of Wednesday afternoon. 
Democrat Tom Herner had a slight lead over state Rep. Tom Young, R-Washington Twp., as of Wednesday afternoon. 
Republican Edward Schimmel and Democrat David Fournier were nearly tied for Ohio’s 44th district, which is currently held by Josh Williams, R-Sylvania Twp., as of Wednesday. 
“We didn’t just break the supermajority — we shattered it,” Ohio House Minority Leader Dani Isaacsohn, D-Cincinnati, said Tuesday night. 
“This means that we have the opportunity to actually govern in Ohio. It’s not enough that Dr. Acton is our next governor. We have flipped these seats so that Dr. Acton can govern when she’s in.”
Ohio House Speaker Matt Huffman, R-Lima, said he’s seen similar political cycles in 2006 under President George W. Bush and in 2012 under President Barack Obama. 
“Despite that national trend, Republicans have maintained a strong majority in the Ohio House, positioning us to advance the priorities we believe will best serve the people of Ohio over the next two years,” Huffman said in a statement to the Ohio Capital Journal.
Ohio Senate races 
The supermajority remains in the Ohio Senate as 22 Republicans and 11 Democrats were elected Tuesday, according to unofficial election results. 
Ohio Democrats did pick up two seats as Democrat Stacie Baker beat incumbent state Sen. Michele Reynolds, R-Canal Winchester, and Democrat Mike Roberto beat Republican state Rep. Steve Demetriou for Ohio’s 27th district, which is currently held by Republican state Sen. Kristina Roegner. 
“The people of Ohio have spoken, and it’s clear that they are ready for change,” Ohio Senate Democratic Leader Nickie J. Antonio, D-Lakewood, said in a statement.

title: General election voter turnout declines in Oklahoma
description: OKLAHOMA CITY — Oklahoma voter turnout has fallen from the previous two major election years, despite key statewide races appearing on the ballot Tuesday. Just over 45% of the state’s 2.46 million registered voters participated in the 2026 general election, the Oklahoma State Election Board reported. Oklahoma’s 1.3 million registered Republicans outnumber th[...]
text:
Voters fill out ballots for the general election at the Millwood Field House on Tuesday in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Emma Murphy/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY — Oklahoma voter turnout has fallen from the previous two major election years, despite key statewide races appearing on the ballot Tuesday.
Just over 45% of the state’s 2.46 million registered voters participated in the 2026 general election, the Oklahoma State Election Board reported. Oklahoma’s 1.3 million registered Republicans outnumber the 627,500 Democrats by nearly 2-to-1, according to Election Board data released this month, and another 500,000 voters are registered as independents.
Tuesday’s turnout saw a decrease from the last time governor, lieutenant governor, attorney general, state superintendent and other statewide offices were up for election in 2022, when slightly more than 50% of registered voters cast ballots.
Buoyed by a presidential race, the 2024 general election drew more than 64% of registered Oklahoma voters.
About 1.11 million voters cast ballots in this year’s race for governor, electing Republican Mike Mazzei over Democrat Cyndi Munson and three independents. 
Mazzei won with 52% of the vote while Munson carried 45%. 
Other statewide elections received slightly fewer votes than the governor’s race.
In 2022, when Gov. Kevin Stitt won reelection, 1.15 million Oklahomans cast ballots in the gubernatorial race. Stitt could not run again this year because of term limits.
State questions on the November ballot received far more participation than those up for a vote in June and August.
One million Oklahomans voted Tuesday on State Questions 845 and 847, rejecting both. SQ 845 would have made changes to the Judicial Nominating Commission, and SQ 847 would have limited the growth of property taxes.
In the June primary election, a ballot measure to raise Oklahoma’s minimum wage received about 630,000 votes and ultimately failed. Even fewer people voted on state questions during the August runoff election.

title: Nebraska Legislature Republican supermajority will end; Democrats could pick up three seats
description: OMAHA — A 33-seat Republican supermajority in the Nebraska Legislature will end come 2027 as Democrats and a Democratic-endorsed nonpartisan led in three key districts by Wednesday afternoon. Twenty-five seats were before voters Tuesday, including a special election for a two-year term in the officially nonpartisan Legislature. Republicans gained 33 of 49 se[...]
text:
The 2026 candidates for the Nebraska Legislature arranged by district. (Photos courtesy of the candidates/campaigns | Nebraska Capitol photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)OMAHA — A 33-seat Republican supermajority in the Nebraska Legislature will end come 2027 as Democrats and a Democratic-endorsed nonpartisan led in three key districts by Wednesday afternoon.
Twenty-five seats were before voters Tuesday, including a special election for a two-year term in the officially nonpartisan Legislature. Republicans gained 33 of 49 seats in spring 2024 when a Democratic labor leader switched parties. But come Jan. 6, when the new Legislature convenes, that streak will end.
Riepe: ‘It was a true honor’
The New York Times has called one flip: Democrat Christy Knorr of Omaha has won over state Sen. Merv Riepe of Ralston. By 1:30 p.m. Wednesday, Knorr, a hospice nurse, led Riepe, a former hospital administrator, by 1,313 votes, or 11.3%, for Legislative District 12.
The 2026 candidates for Legislative District 12, state Sen. Merv Riepe of Ralston and Christy Knorr of Omaha, in the district on Oct. 8, 2026. (Photos by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Knorr and her campaign did not immediately respond to a request for comment Wednesday morning.
Riepe, 84, was first elected to the Legislature in 2014. He lost in 2018 but returned in 2022. He became more moderate in his return and was often a central figure on contentious issues.
In a call Wednesday with the Nebraska Examiner, Riepe noted headwinds for Republicans nationwide, particularly anger against President Donald Trump and voters’ frustration at promises he made and bad appointments that “cascaded down” for Democratic successes. 
“It was a true honor, and I will always be a better person for having done it,” Riepe said of his service. “I hope that I maybe made one little slight change someplace along the line.”


Unofficial results
Based on unofficial results as of 1:30 p.m. Wednesday, another Democrat and one registered nonpartisan led in two key races in Douglas County against Republicans:

Registered nonpartisan Cindy Maxwell-Ostdiek of Omaha led incumbent state Sen. Brad von Gillern of Elkhorn by 292 votes, or 1.7%, for Legislative District 4.
Jess Goldoni of Omaha led Taylor Royal of Bennington by 367 votes, or 2.4%, for Legislative District 18. State Sen. Christy Armendariz of Omaha decided not to seek reelection.

State Sen. Brad von Gillern and Cindy Maxwell-Ostdiek are facing off again to represent west-central Douglas County’s Legislative District 4. They are pictured in Omaha in early October 2026. (Photos by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Royal has conceded and congratulated Goldoni. Maxwell-Ostdiek, in a post at about 12:30 a.m. Wednesday, said the race was too close to call. Von Gillern had not yet made a social post as of 1:30 p.m. Wednesday.
The Douglas County Election Commission has not yet said how many early-vote ballots are left to be counted Friday, or how many provisional ballots will be processed next week.
In Sarpy County, two other races are also too close to call, according to The New York Times, one being with Republican state Sen. Rick Holdcroft of Bellevue. He leads Democratic challenger Darin Tompkins of Papillion by 736 votes, or 4.5%. Tompkins has conceded and congratulated Holdcroft.
And in nearby Legislative District 14, Bill Bowes of La Vista, a Republican, leads SuAnn Witt of Papillion, a Democrat, by 231 votes, or 1.5%. Speaker John Arch of La Vista is term-limited after two four-year terms. Witt has conceded and congratulated Bowes.


A shifting Legislature
The New York Times has not called those four races, nor two other races in central and southeast Nebraska.
For Legislative District 38 in central Nebraska, the race to succeed term-limited state Sen. Dave Murman of Glenvil, Sutton Mayor Tim Anderson is ahead 410 votes, or 2.6%, over GROW Nebraska CEO Janell Anderson Ehrke of Orleans. Anderson claimed victory in the race Wednesday morning.
The 2026 candidates for Legislative District 18, from left: Jess Goldoni of Omaha and Taylor Royal of Bennington. State Sen. Christy Armendariz of Omaha declined to seek reelection. (Photos courtesy of the candidates/campaigns | Nebraska Capitol photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
In Lincoln and part of Cass County, Republican Dean Helmick of Plattsmouth led Democrat Caitlin Knutson by 960 votes, or 5.3%, for Legislative District 2. State Sen. Rob Clements of Elmwood, chair of the Legislature’s Appropriations Committee, was term-limited after serving 10 years. Neither Helmick nor Knutson has yet posted statements on the race results as of 1:30 p.m. Wednesday.
Thirty-three Republicans, 15 Democrats and one progressive, registered nonpartisan currently compose Nebraska’s Legislature. 
The “officially nonpartisan” moniker means a candidate’s party doesn’t appear on the ballot for the seat, and lawmakers don’t organize by party in the legislative chamber. Some votes can land along party lines, or urban-rural divides, and it takes 33 votes to overcome a filibuster and 30 votes to override a gubernatorial veto or change legislative rules.
Should unofficial results hold, the legislative partisan structure would change to 30 Republicans, 18 Democrats and one registered nonpartisan.
Three incumbent senators and one new face ran unopposed: state Sens. Barry DeKay of Niobrara, Teresa Ibach of Sumner and Danielle Conrad of Lincoln. Dawson Brunswick will succeed term-limited state Sen. Mike Moser. Both are from Columbus.
Of the other 21 seats, 12 pitted a Republican against a Democrat, four had Republicans facing a nonpartisan candidate, two featured two Republicans, two had two Democrats and one was between a Democrat and a nonpartisan.
More than $9.5 million had been raised heading into the election, according to late campaign filings available as of election weekend. Candidates had together spent more than six figures in 17 of the 25 races by mid-October.


The 2027 legislative session
One of the biggest hurdles for lawmakers to tackle in 2027 will be closing a projected budget deficit that state forecasters estimate could be as high as $1.2 billion by mid-2029.
Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen greets State Sen. George Dungan of Lincoln on the final day of the 2026 legislative session. April 17, 2026. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Riepe said a concern he has is the knowledge and skill level of new senators, particularly with the budget. He added: “I wish the state well because it’s going to be an interesting session.”
Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen of Columbus won reelection. He said early Wednesday at his election night watch party that he didn’t yet know what the legislative breakdown would look like but that a top priority would be balancing the budget. He and dozens of legislative candidates have said addressing property taxes remains a top priority, too.
Von Gillern, current Revenue Committee chair, had been eyed as the frontrunner for speaker of the Legislature in 2027. State Sen. Mike Jacobson of North Platte, who easily won reelection Tuesday, had wanted the Revenue Committee chairship.
Depending on the conclusion of LD 4, Jacobson has said he could step up for speaker. State Sen. Kathleen Kauth of Omaha has also expressed interest in running for the role.
Lawmakers are paid an annual salary of $12,000. They can serve two four-year terms in a row (voters widely rejected a proposal Tuesday to expand the limit to three consecutive terms).

name: National
title: Voters reject most big tax overhauls, with a few notable exceptions
description: Despite the blue wave that swept the nation on Tuesday, voters were more cautious about making sweeping changes to their taxes. Most states with tax policy on the ballot saw voters reject large-scale change, though some passed smaller changes or reined in officials’ ability to make changes. “Even though there are big political shifts on […]
text:
Voters fill out ballots for the midterm election at the Millwood Field House on Tuesday in Oklahoma City. Oklahoma voters rejected measure that would have capped annual increases in property taxes, one of a number of tax-related measures that were on the ballot in multiple states.  (Photo by Emma Murphy/Oklahoma Voice)Despite the blue wave that swept the nation on Tuesday, voters were more cautious about making sweeping changes to their taxes.
Most states with tax policy on the ballot saw voters reject large-scale change, though some passed smaller changes or reined in officials’ ability to make changes.
“Even though there are big political shifts on the federal level, people are generally feeling the same about taxes as they always have,” said Janelle Fritts, senior policy analyst at the Tax Foundation, a nonpartisan analysis and research organization.
One of the biggest examples: California’s much-discussed billionaire wealth tax looked likely to fail, with a ‘no’ vote of more than 55% by Wednesday morning. Proposition 40 is a measure no other state has tried: a one-time 5% tax on billionaires’ net worth to raise tens of billions to close budget holes in the state’s Medicaid, food assistance, education and other programs.
Opposition, led by California billionaires including Google co-founder Sergey Brin, raised more than $379 million to defeat the measure, outspending its supporters more than 250-1, The Washington Post reported.
But the campaign spending alone may not have fully accounted for its failure, Fritts said.
“The specific proposal had a lot of really strange structural issues,” she said, noting that it would have retroactively applied to any California resident who was a billionaire as of Jan. 1, 2026, and that it taxed everything a billionaire owned — from cars and yachts to art and collectibles — some of which could be difficult to place a value on.
“When people started understanding what was really in the bill, I think that was a deterrent,” she said. She expects it could influence similar efforts in other states to tax the wealthy.
Proponents of California’s billionaire wealth tax have already promised to try again.
Washington state voters appeared to be choosing to keep the state’s new millionaire tax, as a ballot initiative to repeal it was failing 58% to 42% by Wednesday morning. Earlier this year, Washington’s Democratic-led state legislature created a 9.9% tax on annual incomes above $1 million. The repeal measure, which failed to garner support in the state’s population centers, was a political victory for its champion, Democratic Gov. Bob Ferguson, according to the Washington State Standard.
“Washingtonians understood one thing,” Ferguson told a gathering hosted by a campaign opposing the measure, the Washington State Standard reported. “We’re not going to give tax breaks to millionaires when we can use those dollars to make life more affordable for working families all across the state.”
In Colorado, a sweeping income tax change remained too close to call Wednesday, though ‘yes’ votes had a slight lead. Amendment 87, if it passes, would hike taxes on the state’s highest-income households, and cut taxes for nearly everyone else by replacing the state’s flat 4.4% tax.
A ballot measure that would block Amendment 87 appeared short of the majority needed to pass, while a legislatively-referred measure to raise the revenue the state is allowed to keep appeared likely to pass.
Property tax wins, losses
Voters in Florida showed an appetite for change, overwhelmingly approving a constitutional amendment that will make one of the most significant alterations to their property taxes in decades.
Amendment 3 will gradually reduce Floridians’ property taxes — aside from those that benefit public schools — by increasing the state’s homestead exemption. That will let homeowners cut their property tax bills by exempting a bigger share of their home’s value from taxation.
The state GOP endorsed the amendment, but other groups — including law enforcement, child welfare advocates and municipal government officials — say it would blow a massive hole in local governments’ budgets. Florida’s state and local coffers could take a hit of up to $12 billion each year beginning in 2031, according to state projections.
“It will be a pretty big challenge for local governments,” Fritts said. “They’re going to have to shift a lot of things around.
“Not a lot of other states were willing to take as big a swing on property taxes as Florida,” she said.
Oklahoma voters rejected a measure that would have capped annual increases in property taxes. The state legislature proposed the initiative to address rising costs, but critics said it would hurt funding for public schools and other services. The state estimated local governments would have lost nearly $46 million in property tax revenue in the first year, had it passed.
Oklahoma House Speaker Kyle Hilbert, a Republican, said Tuesday night that the vote showed that Oklahomans “don’t want to see changes to property taxes, and so moving forward, we’ll take that into consideration,” the Oklahoma Voice reported.
In Wyoming, voters defeated a property tax cut initiative that would have exempted half of a primary residence’s assessed value from being taxed. Had it passed, Proposition 1 could have decreased the state’s annual property tax revenues up to $124.8 million, WyoFile reported. The initiative was opposed by a variety of groups including state hospital and education associations, as well as some Republican and Democratic officials.
Reining in government power
In North Carolina, voters approved both tax-related constitutional amendments.
The most controversial, which passed with 60% of the vote, will cap how much cities and other local governments can grow their revenue. It was a priority for Republican leadership focused on addressing constituent complaints over rising prices.
But critics say the new limits could torpedo local budgets, forcing local governments to cut services including public safety, libraries, parks and education, NC Newsline reported.
North Carolinians also approved a new maximum state income tax rate of 3.5% in a Republican-backed constitutional amendment that caps the rate for personal and corporate income taxes. Critics have said it will cement tax cuts that mainly benefit the wealthy and corporations.
An Iowa constitutional amendment to make it harder for state legislators to tinker with taxes looked as though it would pass. The GOP-backed measure would require a two-thirds supermajority of state lawmakers to raise personal or corporate income taxes.
The Iowa Capital Dispatch reported that Republican supporters argued the restriction was needed to preserve tax policies including 2025’s 3.8% flat-rate income tax.
But critics said it would lock in unsustainable tax cuts that mostly benefit Iowa’s wealthier households and could push the state to raise other taxes when it needs revenue, such as sales tax increases that have a bigger impact on low- and middle-income families.
In Massachusetts, a ballot measure that would change how the state’s tax revenue limit is calculated was still too close to call as of Wednesday morning. Current state law caps how much tax revenue the state can keep each year, and any extra beyond the cap is refunded to taxpayers as credits. But if voters approve the ballot measure, taxpayers would be more likely to get money back in a given year. Proponents say it would slow down state spending, while opponents have said it leaves less money available for public services.
Stateline reporter Anna Claire Vollers can be reached at avollers@stateline.org.

title: Which Senate and governors races are still uncalled by The Associated Press
description: Fall leaves begin to surround the U.S. Capitol on Election Day, Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026, in Washington.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
WASHINGTON — Just a handful of races for Senate and governor have not yet been called by The Associated Press as of noon Eastern time on Wednesday.
The narrow margins come as Democrats flipped seats in places Republicans comfortably won two years ago, securing control of both chambers of Congress.
In the House, 59 races where party control of the seat is at stake have yet to be called.
The AP does not make projections and will only declare a winner when it’s determined there is no scenario that would allow the trailing candidates to close the gap.
Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Scott Colom is greeted by supporters during his election watch party at the Ice House in Jackson on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
In Mississippi’s Senate race, Democrat Scott Colom has a lead of few dozen votes over Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith. Mississippi does not have an automatic recount process, but a challenger can seek a court order for one.
LIVE: 2026 Mississippi election results
Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, left, chats with supporters at her watch party held at the Sheraton Flowood The Refuge Hotel & Conference Center, Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026, in Flowood. Credit: Vickie D. King/Mississippi Today
The Associated Press has also not called Alaska’s Senate contest between incumbent Republican Dan Sullivan and Democrat Mary Peltola, who has a 626-vote lead over Sullivan with an estimated 74% of votes counted. Under Alaska law, if neither candidate gets more than 50% of the vote then it goes to ranked-choice tabulation.
Also in Alaska, Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins has a 20 percentage point lead over Republican Bernadette Wilson in Alaska’s governor’s race. Kreiss-Tomkins had 49.2% of the vote with an estimated 74% of the ballots counted.
Like the Senate contest, the governor’s election advances to another round if no candidate gets more than 50% of the votes.
In Kansas, Democrat Cindy Holscher has less than a percentage point lead over Republican Ty Masterson in the Kansas governor’s race. Holscher’s 5,557 vote lead with an estimated 98% of votes counted comes after Democrat Adam Hamilton became the first member of his party to win a Senate seat in nearly a century.
Both Holscher and Masterson serve in the state Senate, where the Republican serves as its president.
