name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Burgin council members paid a price for their data center support. They weren’t the only ones.
description: Joe Monroe knew he had a good shot at winning as a write-in candidate, yet he also realized it was going to be an “uphill battle.”  But when he went to the Mercer County courthouse Tuesday night to check the results for the Burgin mayoral race, he had won handily, with 75% of the vote […]
text:
More than 100 people packed inside the engine bay of Burgin's fire department for the September special meeting. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Liam Niemeyer)Joe Monroe knew he had a good shot at winning as a write-in candidate, yet he also realized it was going to be an “uphill battle.” 
But when he went to the Mercer County courthouse Tuesday night to check the results for the Burgin mayoral race, he had won handily, with 75% of the vote over his opponent, George Hensley, a sitting city council member. He won 273 write-in votes over Hensley’s 91 votes. 
“I didn’t realize it would be by that kind of margin,” Monroe told the Lantern. “I’m thinking it probably had to do something with the data center.”
The small Mercer County city of Burgin, with a little more than 1,000 people, has been embroiled in prior months leading up to the election over a proposal to annex property into the city for a hyperscale data center. Officials with the local school district touted the potential boon of tax revenue the data center could bring, while residents with the community group We Are Mercer County packed city council meetings with a range of concerns, including environmental impacts. 
While Monroe, appointed interim mayor earlier this year, won his election, other incumbents on the Burgin city council did not. The Burgin city council and mayoral races were among a number of elections for local and state elected office across Kentucky where the politics of data centers — and their relative unpopularity with the public — could have played an outsized role in ousting incumbents and pushing new people into office. 
Monroe said there are four new members elected to the Burgin city council. One of them is Bethany Corea, a former volunteer firefighter and a volunteer with the community group “We Are Mercer County” that’s raised strong concerns about the potential impacts of a hyperscale data center. The top vote-getter for the city council was Melinda Wofford, who walked out of a city council meeting to prevent a vote that would have advanced consideration of the data center.
“Some of the other council members that got beat didn’t follow what the voters were saying. They just didn’t listen to them,” Monroe said. “The ones that got in that were elected, the four new ones, they listened to the people, and they let the people be heard.”
Hensley, the city council member who lost to Monroe, told the Lantern he believed Monroe’s comments were “bullcrap” and suggested that people outside of Burgin had conducted a door-knocking campaign to oppose him. Hensley had supported annexation efforts connected to the data center and opposed a recent move by the city to implement planning and zoning regulations, a move also connected to the local data center debate. 
“I wish now that we could have had the data center. I really do,” Hensley said. “I don’t see Burgin surviving too many more years without some kind of income.” 
Data center influence
Elsewhere in Kentucky, other incumbents lost in races where data centers became a prominent talking point. 
In Mason County, where the technology company Meta is planning to build a hyperscale data center campus, Democratic Mason County Judge-Executive Owen McNeill lost reelection to Republican Eric Bach. McNeill was a big backer of the economic development potential of the data center campus, citing millions of dollars in tax revenue and jobs the county would receive. McNeill and other members of the fiscal court had signed non-disclosure agreements, which generally require the signee to not reveal specific information on a project.
McNeill had won a four-year term to his seat by about a nine-point margin in 2022 but lost the seat by about 26 points on Tuesday, according to unofficial results. McNeill and Bach did not respond to text messages and voicemail messages Wednesday requesting an interview. 
In state legislative races, candidates who attacked their opponents in attempts to tie them to the unpopularity of data centers also won races. 
Democrat Jennifer Hardin defeated House Majority Whip Jason Nemes in a very tight election after Hardin attacked Nemes over being a primary sponsor of a bill, House Bill 775 in 2025, that expanded to all counties a sales and use tax break for data center equipment. Nemes had responded in a Facebook post that “there are lies and misleading ads of statements taken wildly out of context” being “peddled” about him, arguing he wanted ratepayer protections against data center impacts.
In Northern Kentucky, Democrat Aaron Currin defeated Republican Rep. Stephanie Dietz, R-Edgewood, in a race where local Democrats put up a billboard that stated “REPUBLICANS SOLD US OUT ON DATA CENTERS.” Dietz had voted for HB 775 in 2025. 
And in Mercer County, Republican Rep. Kim King, R-Harrodsburg, fended off a challenge and a rematch by Democrat Katrina Sexton that saw Sexton essentially split the voters in Mercer County, according to unofficial results. 
Tres Watson, a former spokesperson for the Republican Party of Kentucky, told the Kentucky Lantern he believed the debate over data centers had a larger role in local races, including the Mason County judge-executive race, but that it was harder to pinpoint how influential they were in state legislative races. 
Watson said King’s past statements of wanting to respect local decision-making on weighing a data center got unfairly interpreted by anti-data center activists to mean she was for the data center. Members of We Are Mercer County have accused King of dismissing data center concerns, and a campaign ad for King had stated that she was “holding big tech and data centers” accountable. 
“As a member of the General Assembly, I think a lot of those members typically tend to basically say, ‘Well, I don’t want local government telling me how to do my job. I’m not going to tell local government how to do their job.’” Watson said. “Regardless of what the actual facts were or what her intentions were, it got taken to be a pro-data center position.” 
However, Elizabeth Fels-McDowell, a Lexington resident who started the Facebook group “No Kentucky Data Centers,” believes Kentucky voters awarded candidates who took stands for data center protections and against active proposals. 
She pointed to victories by Currin, Hardin and Rep. Adam Moore, D-Lexington’s victories, as evidence of that. Moore is drafting a bill to implement protections against data center impacts for next year’s legislative session. 
“I think that a lot of people in Kentucky are realizing that you can be a regular person with a family, with a job in Kentucky, and run for office to defend your community, to defend Kentucky families and farmers from out-of-control, unregulated development,” Fels-McDowell said. “I think people are realizing that the bar to clear to run for office is often really low.”

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Florida Legislature gets its first DSA member in Ashley Herrmann
description: During the just-concluded midterm elections, Republicans told Florida voters they were the only thing standing between keeping the “free state of Florida” free and having socialists and even communists take over the Sunshine State. “THE COMMUNISTS ARE COMING!” Moody pushed out on social media last week, retweeting a social media posting that asked for progre[...]
text:
Ashley Herrmann with Angie Nixon, from Herrmann's Facebook account.During the just-concluded midterm elections, Republicans told Florida voters they were the only thing standing between keeping the “free state of Florida” free and having socialists and even communists take over the Sunshine State.
“THE COMMUNISTS ARE COMING!” Moody pushed out on social media last week, retweeting a social media posting that asked for progressive canvassers to come to Florida to support Democrat Angie Nixon’s campaign for Senate.
Such messaging has been a staple for Republicans campaigning against Democrats in South Florida over the years, where the population includes people who fled authoritarian governments in Cuba, Nicaragua, and Venezuela.
Moody focused on Nixon, who joined the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) this summer, although she never received the group’s endorsement.
But there was a DSA-backed candidate on the ballot in Hillsborough County Tuesday — Ashley Herrmann — and she upset Republican incumbent Danny Alvarez in the House District 69 race, winning 52%-48%.
Herrmann, 36, qualified for the seat on the last day possible, June 12. She explained she ran because she saw that Alvarez was going to run uncontested, “and that didn’t sit well with me.”
She’s a climate activist who ran on a platform opposing data centers, holding developers accountable, and raising teacher pay.
On the campaign trail, Herrmann boasted she was the only candidate on the ballot in Florida who had been endorsed by the DSA. She joins St. Petersburg City Council member Richie Floyd as the only elected DSA-backed candidates serving in Florida politics.
She said she knocked on 30,000 doors in her campaign, and said voters were excited to greet her “and we came up with voting plans together.”
Although state House Democrats had a big night Tuesday, netting 15 seats, they’ll still be part of the minority party in that chamber when they convene in Tallahassee to reorganize the Legislature in the next few weeks.
“It’ll be tough with a lot of Republicans and some Democrats owned by corporate interests, but they have to deliver for voters as well,” she said. “We cannot remain 50th for teacher pay and continue to ignore the insurance housing crisis.”
Herrmann says she is willing to work with Republicans, and noted that, during the stormy weather Florida saw on election night, she and her campaign manager spent several hours with Republican Congressional District 14 candidate Mike Beltran directing traffic and helping cars get unstuck from the mud.
“I’ll also make sure the House minority acts like an opposition party fighting for the priorities of everyday working people,” she said.

name: Source New Mexico
title: Day after historic win, New Mexico Gov.-elect Haaland starts accepting resumes
description: The morning after her historic Election Day victory, New Mexico Gov.-elect Deb Haaland began recruiting “anyone who loves New Mexico and has what it takes to serve” to apply to work for her incoming administration.
text:
Democratic New Mexico Lt. Gov.-elect Stephanie Garcia Richard, left, and Gov.-elect Deb Haaland, right, address the media at Barelas Coffee House in Albuquerque on Nov. 4, 2026, about their priorities for their administration's transition and next year's legislative session. (Photo by Joshua Bowling/Source NM)The morning after her historic Election Day victory, New Mexico Gov.-elect Deb Haaland began recruiting “anyone who loves New Mexico and has what it takes to serve” to apply to work for her incoming administration.
Haaland, a former member of Congress and U.S. Department of the Interior secretary, defeated Republican challenger Gregg Hull, a former longtime mayor of Rio Rancho, in Tuesday’s general election race for governor, making her the first Native American woman elected to lead a state in U.S. history.
New Mexico elects Democrat Deb Haaland as first Native American woman governor in US

She and her running mate, Lt. Gov-elect Stephanie Garcia Richard, shook hands with New Mexico voters and spoke to reporters Wednesday morning at Albuquerque’s Barelas Coffee House, a frequent stop for politicians. Haaland said that she plans to speak with Democratic Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham, who called to congratulate her on her win Tuesday night, about the transition and noted that she has not yet made final decisions about who will serve in her cabinet.
Her campaign debuted a new website, haalandtransition.com, where prospective employees can upload their resumes and express interest in roles of all levels with her administration.
“We didn’t know we would win until last night when the results came in, and I am not the type of person to put the cart before the horse,” Haaland said. “We will absolutely start thinking about and looking at potential folks to fill those positions. I feel confident that we can find the right people to fill the right positions to help us move New Mexico forward.”
Garcia Richard said both she and Haaland have experience recruiting talented staffers, citing her experience as New Mexico commissioner of public lands and Haaland’s experience as U.S. Department of the Interior secretary.
“We’re going to rely on that experience,” she said.
Haaland said her top priorities upon taking office include signing a data center moratorium executive order, finding a new leader for the state’s troubled child welfare agency, addressing affordability, investing in education and public safety and bolstering the state’s first-in-the-nation universal childcare program.
“I feel ready to move our priorities forward for the people of New Mexico,” she said, adding that she is focused on “making sure that folks can pay their rent or mortgage and buy groceries in the same month.”
She said that using the 2027 legislative session to address the changing eligibility requirements for Medicaid, which are set to take effect in January and could remove coverage from nearly 90,000 New Mexicans, is also “top of mind.” On the campaign trail, she often promised to combat the Trump administration’s cuts to social services and to “work toward” a statewide public option for healthcare.
In her Tuesday evening victory speech, Haaland said her time in Congress combatting the first Trump administration prepared her to “do it again.” During her Wednesday morning visit to Barelas Coffee House, she reiterated that point.
“I’m willing to work with the administration to make sure that they live up to their obligations to New Mexico,” Haaland said Wednesday morning. “And I absolutely will speak to the attorney general if, in fact, those conversations aren’t successful. New Mexico deserves and requires funding from the U.S. government.”
New Mexico Governor-elect Deb Haaland shakes hands with customers at Albuquerque’s Barelas Coffee House on Nov. 4, 2026, the morning after making history as the first Native American woman in the nation to be elected governor. (Photo by Joshua Bowling/Source NM)

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Morrisey announces water filtration program for Southern West Virginia coalfields
description: Gov. Patrick Morrisey announced Wednesday the state will be investing $3.2 million into home water filtration systems in Mingo and McDowell counties.
text:
Gov. Patrick Morrisey announces a $3.2 million water filtration initiative to deliver clean, dependable drinking water to 5,000 households in McDowell and Mingo counties, in Welch, West Virginia on Nov. 4, 2026. (West Virginia Office of Gov. Patrick Morrisey video screenshot)Gov. Patrick Morrisey announced Wednesday the state will be investing $3.2 million into home water filtration systems in Mingo and McDowell counties. 
The initiative will cover 5,000 homes that rely on well-water or have no running water at all and consist of distributions of “countertop water purification systems,” testing for bacteria and other hygiene measures. 
The Morrisey administration will target $1.2 million of the federal Rural Health Transformation fund to 1,000 high priority households, which include homes with no running water, elevated amounts of bacteria in the water and homes with infants and seniors. 
The remaining $2 million will go to 4,000 additional homes. 
Morrisey said the initiative was born out of the listening tour he took in the coalfields in August and is just a step in solving the southern coalfield’s water crisis. He said he doesn’t want to see videos of dirty water coming out of faucets. 
“Like you, I get tired of it. I see some of the videos,” he told a crowd in Welch. “I don’t want to see those videos anymore. I want to know that I can look you in the eye and say 10,000 people are going to benefit from what we’re doing to address those very issues.” 
Residents in the southern coalfields have spent decades dealing with dirty and contaminated water. During the last legislative session, activists and lawmakers from the area pushed several funding packages for new water systems, but the Republican supermajority shot it down. 
Rep. Riley Moore, R-W.Va., who doesn’t even represent that part of the state, tried and failed to get more funding in the annual budget bill on the federal level. 
The Rev. Caitlin Ware is an organizer with From Below: Rising Together for Coalfield Justice, a group that has focused on advocating for clean water in the region. She said the announcement is a good step to immediately addressing the problem, but in her experience filters can be eaten up by water in the region within months of installation. 
“I’m curious to see how much it will cost the state extra beyond what’s announced, but it’s a start,” she said. “I can’t complain.” 
Distribution is expected to begin in February 2027. The state will be coordinating with the McDowell County Commission on Aging, food banks, churches, and volunteer fire departments.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Gov. Sherrill toasts Democratic victories and calls for change
description: New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill said Democrats' resounding midterm wins show voters want affordability and accountability.
text:
Gov. Mikie Sherrill approaches the press outside Small World Coffee in Princeton on Nov. 4, 2026, to talk about the results of Tuesday's midterm elections. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor)PRINCETON — One day after voters kicked close to two dozen Republicans out of Congress, Gov. Mikie Sherrill said Democrats must improve affordability and undo the cuts President Donald Trump made to Medicaid, food assistance, and other public welfare programs.
Sherrill, a Democrat who logged nearly four terms in the House herself before New Jersey voters elected her governor last fall, met with reporters Wednesday morning outside Small World Coffee to celebrate Tuesday’s election results, which will deliver control of Congress to Democrats in January.
Her coffee stop came just a month after federal eligibility rules for Medicaid narrowed, eliminating coverage for hundreds of thousands of people. Other changes are expected to cost Medicare billions a year. Both changes were part of a bill Trump signed last year and are expected to add up to over $1 trillion in federal cuts over the next decade.
Sherrill said those cuts, coupled with other Trump policies that cripple everyday Americans’ ability to afford healthcare, gas, groceries, and more, make affordability the top mandate for the next Congress.
Still, she conceded, congressional Democrats will have “a lot of No. 1 priorities.”
Accountability also must be one of their top tasks, she said. Sherrill said Democratic leaders should schedule hearings to hold the Trump administration accountable for its corruption, as well as its policymaking that hurts American citizens and helps America’s enemies.
“It’s kind of gone maybe under some people’s radar that the president of the United States wants to illegally have people buy Russian diesel — fund Russia, who’s funding Iran, who’s killing American service members. Unacceptable, and I think the Congress of the United States will really bring that out,” Sherrill said.
Sherrill had a hand in helping Democrats dominate in Tuesday’s midterms, with her political action committee, Mission to Deliver, supporting federal and state candidates around the country. That included Cape May Mayor Zack Mullock, a Democrat whose upset of four-term Republican Rep. Jeff Van Drew stunned many election observers. Sherrill headed to South Jersey twice this week, to stump for Mullock in Vineland Monday and join his victory party election night in Cape May.
“Just yesterday the New York Times had it listed as an easy pickup, an easy win for Van Drew. But we knew we could take it. The early-vote results were great,” Sherrill said Wednesday. “So it was an all-hands-on-deck effort. Everybody got involved.”
Trump and Vice President JD Vance on Wednesday largely blamed Republicans’ midterm losses on the war in Iran and its impact on gas prices. Trump was unrepentant, though, saying the war was “the only answer” to stop Iran from getting nuclear weapons.
Trump still has two years left in the White House, leaving some predicting gridlock during his lame-duck term. But congressional Democrats can use the leverage of the budget process to get some of their agenda passed, and the House has investigatory and subpoena authority too, Sherrill said.
Republicans should heed the lessons their drubbing offers, she added.
“Republicans have been incredibly unwilling to call Trump to account. They’ve been shockingly, egregiously in violation of their duty to the Constitution for the most part,” Sherrill said. “What they saw last night is that there is no path forward for them or for their party or for elections if they continue down this path. So I am hopeful that some of them will wake up, and if not for the country, then for their own electoral prospects, grow a spine and stand up to Trump and work with Democrats to get some of this done.”
Asked to respond, the White House referred to a message Trump posted on social media Tuesday night.
“I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE! Thank you for your attention to this matter,” the president wrote.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Senator-elect Peggy Flanagan calls for new leadership of Senate Democrats
description: Peggy Flanagan, in her first news conference since being elected to the U.S. Senate, hailed the new voices headed to Congress after Democrats won landslide victories across the country in Tuesday’s midterms. Voters elected at least 10 new Democratic senators, already the largest incoming class of elected first-time Democratic Senators in 40 years, with resul[...]
text:
Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan waves to supporters alongside her 13-year-old daughter Siobhan and her husband Tom Weber after the Senate race was called in her favor at the DFL watch party during the midterm elections Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026 in St. Paul, Minnesota. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)Peggy Flanagan, in her first news conference since being elected to the U.S. Senate, hailed the new voices headed to Congress after Democrats won landslide victories across the country in Tuesday’s midterms.
Voters elected at least 10 new Democratic senators, already the largest incoming class of elected first-time Democratic Senators in 40 years, with results from Alaska and Mississippi still outstanding. Many made history: Flanagan is the first Native American woman elected to the Senate, Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan the first Muslim and Chris Pappas of New Hampshire the first out gay man.
All those new voices need a new leader, Flanagan said.
“I am tremendously grateful for Chuck Schumer’s leadership … and I think it is time for new leadership,” Flanagan said, repeating a campaign promise to support an alternative.
She did not say who she thinks should replace Schumer, the soon-to-be 76-year-old senator from New York who has led the Democratic caucus in the upper chamber for the past decade and first arrived in Congress in 1981.
Flanagan rode a blue wave to victory with a batch of other new progressives including El-Sayed, Juliana Stratton in Illinois and Troy Jackson in Maine.
All are eager to push the party to use their new majorities in Congress to advance sweeping economic proposals: Medicare for All, universal childcare, raising the federal minimum wage.
Flanagan also said there’s opportunity to pass popular legislation with Republican support, which will generally be necessary to overcome the Senate filibuster, such as forcing an end to the war in Iran, banning prior authorization in health insurance, guaranteeing farmers the right to repair their equipment.
“We are going to pass some pretty bold legislation. If the president decides that he wants to screw over the American people and veto those bills. I guess that’s his choice,” Flanagan said.
Polls showed Flanagan in a tight race with Michele Tafoya, a retired sports broadcaster whom Republicans saw as their best chance in years of winning statewide. Unofficial results from the secretary of state, however, show her winning by 10 percentage points, nearly matching the margin of victory of moderate Gov.-elect Amy Klobuchar’s victory.
That will fuel Flanagan’s argument that Democrats must show they’re not just “nibbling around the edges” in order to continue building momentum to retake the White House in 2028.
She said Democrats also have a mandate to investigate the Trump family’s sprawling business empire that’s grown markedly since Trump took office in 2025, including crypto, international real estate and mineral deals, defense contracts and presidential pardons for campaign contributors.
And, she said, Democrats must hold the Trump administration accountable for its violent immigration crackdown that left two American citizens dead in Minneapolis.
“There’s a long list of things that this administration needs to answer for,” Flanagan said. “In Minnesota, Renee Good’s family and Alex Pretti’s family deserve justice.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Blumenthal signals another run for Senate in 2028
description: Blumenthal, 80, didn’t have a formal announcement. But he 'looks forward to being on the ballot in 2028' as he prepares to be in the majority.
text:
This story has been updated.
As Democrats were well on their way to securing majorities in Congress, U.S. Sen. Richard Blumenthal took the stage at Tuesday night’s election party in Hartford to strongly suggest, if not commit to, what he’s signaled for months: he plans to be on the ballot again in two years.
The 2028 campaign season has, essentially, already begun — mere hours after polls closed in the midterm elections. Democrats are already laying out their agenda for their new majorities in Congress for the last two years of President Donald Trump’s term. And the attention is quickly turning to who will lead both parties at the top of the ticket.
“We need to start working tomorrow toward winning our local elections in 2027, the building blocks so we will win in 2028 and put a Democrat in the White House as president,” Blumenthal said Tuesday night as Democrats in Connecticut and across the country claimed massive victories.
“I’m so proud to be your United States senator. Democracy is a fight. I am glad to be in this fight,” he continued. “I look forward to continuing to fight and work for the people of Connecticut to 2028 and beyond.”
Sen. Richard Blumenthal at an election night party at Dunkin’ Park in Hartford on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror
Blumenthal, 80, will need to decide whether to run again when his fourth term expires in two years. 
“I’m more excited and energized than ever. And I look forward to fighting and working for the people of Connecticut in this term through 2028 and beyond,” Blumenthal said Wednesday afternoon alongside other members of the congressional delegation and top state officials. “I don’t have a formal announcement today, but I look forward to being on the ballot in 2028 and continuing to serve the people of Connecticut.”
He wasn’t on the ballot this year, but the senior senator from Connecticut has an unrelenting work ethic whether he’s up for reelection or not. After the August primaries, he suggested he’s not slowing down and essentially echoed that message after Tuesday’s blue wave.
Blumenthal and his Democratic colleagues will enter the Senate next year back in the majority, with the likelihood of leadership roles on a couple of his committees.
Questions emerged about his political future after longtime U.S. Rep. John Larson’s primary defeat in August amid calls for generational change from younger challengers. If Blumenthal runs again and wins reelection to a six-year term, he would be about a month shy of his 83rd birthday when elected.
In his last race, Blumenthal easily won reelection in 2022 against Republican Leora Levy, who secured the nomination after a last-minute endorsement from Trump.
Blumenthal and Senate Democrats will return to power next year as the party reclaims majorities back in Congress. Connecticut’s delegation stands to gain influence next year if they win the gavel on House and Senate committees.
During this session of Congress, Blumenthal has been working on a number of issues, including some priorities that could slip into next year, like the Kids Online Safety Act, known as KOSA. He helped get one of the rare pieces of major bipartisan legislation through Congress: the Russia sanctions bill.
Blumenthal said he’ll make an 11th-hour push to try to get KOSA through Congress in the lame-duck session before the end of the year. 
Connecticut Attorney General William Tong renewed his push among his colleagues to urge Congress to pass the Senate version, which was co-authored with Blumenthal.
Looking to next year when Democrats are at the helm, Blumenthal said he plans to become the chairman of two committees he sits on: the Senate Veterans’ Affairs Committee and the Homeland Security’s Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations. The latter is a role he held when Democrats were in the majority.
As the top Democrat of that panel, he’s already wielded some of his investigatory power, including a recent investigation into a cryptocurrency firm and a series of public forums on U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s practices. But as a chair in the majority party, he and other Democrats will regain their subpoena power.
Following Connecticut’s primaries in August, Blumenthal wouldn’t divulge his future plans but had also signaled his intention to run again.
“Age is always a state of mind, not just a time of life,” Blumenthal said in an August interview with The Connecticut Mirror. “The energy and excitement are impressive, and I hope to carry it forward myself.”
“I have a campaign committee,”  he said at the time. “I haven’t announced anything. I’m raising money, but my focus is on November.”

Connecticut Attorney General William Tong speaks at Democrats’ election watch party in Hartford on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. Tong won reelection and had a film crew getting footage of his victory speech. Credit: Mark Pazniokas / CT Mirror

It’s unclear if Blumenthal would get a challenger if he runs for reelection. There’s a deep bench of Democrats in Connecticut who might want to pursue higher office and serve in Washington.
Tong, who had a film crew getting footage at Tuesday night’s election watch party, said his team was getting content of his victory speech to use for messaging on social media. He said it shouldn’t be interpreted as a preliminary step to run against Blumenthal for the U.S. Senate seat and said he doesn’t see himself mounting a challenge.
Incumbency didn’t stop Democrats from running against Larson, who sought a 15th term. Three challengers, including former Hartford Mayor Luke Bronin, announced they would run against a sitting congressman. Bronin went on to defeat Larson in the Aug. 11 primary and soundly defeated his Republican challenger on Tuesday night.
CT Mirror reporter Mark Pazniokas contributed to this story.

name: Mississippi Today
title: ‘An army of lawyers.’ Colom, Hyde-Smith camps monitor vote counting as nation watches
description: Keundra Friday prepares to cast her ballot at Briarwood Presbyterian Church in Jackson during the midterm elections on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Both Mississippi Senate candidates on Wednesday vowed to have people closely monitor final vote counting after neither was declared a victor on Election Day.
Legal challenges are possible, which would put Mississippi’s courts into uncharted territory and prolong a process that could take a week even without litigation to determine a winner.
2026 Mississippi midterm election results
And all eyes are on Mississippi to see if Democrat Scott Colom will pull off an historic upset over Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, and have the Magnolia State join a blue wave that swept out Republicans nationwide on Tuesday.
By Wednesday afternoon, Colom, a Democratic district attorney in north Mississippi led incumbent Hyde-Smith, a cattle farmer from Brookhaven, by fewer than 100 votes in incomplete and unofficial results.
Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Scott Colom speaks to his supporters during his election watch party at the Ice House in Jackson on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Many pundits are expecting a fierce legal battle over the final Mississippi vote count, whichever way it breaks. But this would be an unprecedented challenge. Mississippi has no automatic recount law or no process for a candidate to request one. A recount would happen only if a court ordered it. 
But the gap in the law goes further than recounts. State law contains no mechanism for contesting a U.S. Senate general election. The election code allows challenges to primary elections, including Senate primaries, but speaks only to countywide contests for general elections.
Colom said at a press conference Wednesday morning that his campaign had deployed attorneys across the state to monitor local election officials counting the remaining ballots and processing affidavit and absentee ballots that could arrive over the next week. 
“We will protect the process of this election,” Colom said. “We will protect the integrity of this election.” 
Ballots remained uncounted in Hinds County, the most populous area of the state and a Democratic stronghold, and in counties along the Coast where Hyde-Smith has maintained an edge. Thousands of affidavit and mail-in ballots also remain to be counted.
An affidavit ballot is Mississippi’s version of a provisional ballot, which is a vote cast by someone whose eligibility can’t be confirmed at the polls, such as when they lack photo ID or don’t appear on the voter rolls. These are set aside and counted only after election officials verify the voter’s eligibility.
Kelcy Higgins, a Mississippi-based political operative and community organizer and director of the Magnolia Project, called for volunteers to help with Election Day fallout.
Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, with her daughter Anna-Michael Smith, speaks to supporters during her watch party held at the Sheraton Flowood The Refuge Hotel & Conference Center, Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026, in Flowood. Credit: Vickie D. King/Mississippi Today
“The work of the 2026 election is not over,” Higgins said. “Affidavit ballots remain to be reviewed and counted across Mississippi’s precincts, and we must ensure that every eligible vote is properly counted. Mississippi needs election protection volunteers now to help protect the process and make sure every eligible vote is counted and no voter’s voice is left out.”
Marc Elias, a prominent longtime Democratic election lawyer, also declared on Wednesday morning that he was “leading the legal effort” to ensure Colom would emerge victorious from the legal fight.  
It could be a week before a winner is declared. State law allows for local election workers to receive and count mail-in absentee ballots until Nov. 10, as long as the ballots were postmarked by Election Day. 
Voters also have until Nov. 10 to return to their local election officials to complete casting an affidavit ballot, which is a vote cast by someone whose eligibility can’t be confirmed at the polls because they lack photo ID or don’t appear on the voter rolls. 
At a watch party on Tuesday evening, Hyde-Smith had all but declared victory.
“I assure you I will continue to be your U.S. senator.”
That was before Colom took a late-night lead. 
By late morning on Wednesday, shortly after Colom addressed reporters, her campaign manager Jake Monssen issued a statement thanking supporters and pointing out that thousands of ballots remained uncounted. 
“With the vast majority of Election Day ballots reported, the margin is measured in just dozens of votes,” Monssen said. “We have thousands of outstanding ballots, including affidavit and absentee ballots, which still must be processed and verified under Mississippi law. Our campaign is closely monitoring the remaining count. We remain confident that when every legally cast vote is fully and accurately counted, Mississippians will have reelected Cindy Hyde-Smith.”
Colom has not declared victory, but he said he believes the numbers show he’s on a path to winning. He also responded to Hyde-Smith’s near declaration of victory the evening before.
“Bless her heart,” Colom said.  
When asked if he was worried about Hyde-Smith and the GOP launching election lawsuits, Colom said he hopes that she “would understand the people of Mississippi have spoken.”  
“We have to accept the will of the voters,” Colom said. “It’s very clear that we’re going in a new direction. We’re prepared to litigate, though. We were prepared for this for months. We have an army of lawyers.”
The narrow margin in and of itself reflected what some onlookers called a “bluenami,” with Democrats notching stunning victories in Republican strongholds such as South Carolina and Texas.
Most forecasters had rated the Mississippi Senate race as safely Republican. But as results came in, it became clear the race would be anything but safe for the GOP, with Colom overperforming in many counties compared to Democrats in other recent races. 
A trove of national Democrats visited the state to stump for Colom in hopes that Mississippi could flip blue for the first time in over four decades. These included former Vice President Kamala Harris, former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigeig and around a dozen U.S. senators. 
U.S. Sen. Maria Cantwell of Washington was at Colom’s election night party and said she had been an early believer in Colom’s campaign. 
“He has focused this race on the things that people in Mississippi need to be successful,” Cantwell said. “Access to health care, affordable products like groceries and fuel. And he’s talked about Mississippi mattering on a larger scale. I’m excited for him.” 
Democrats have been dreaming of a political upset in Mississippi for years and seemed almost in disbelief at Colom’s watch party at the early election returns.
After having narrowly lost the governor’s race in 2019 and 2023, several Mississippi Democrats thought they would have a repeat of those races. But after Colom led in several bellwether areas like DeSoto, Lafayette and Madison counties, the room started to buzz. 
Wil Colom, Scott Colom’s father, approached Charles Taylor, the Mississippi NAACP chapter president, with a smile on his face and asked if he thought his son was trending in the right direction. 
“I’m cautiously optimistic,” Taylor told the elder Colom with a grin.

University of South […]
text:
Sioux Falls residents vote in South Dakota's general election on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)South Dakota’s general election voter turnout dropped to a historic low Tuesday, with 49% of registered voters casting a ballot.
Turnout is generally lower in non-presidential election years, according to data from the Secretary of State’s Office dating to 1964. The state’s previous low for a general election was 52% in 2010.
University of South Dakota political science associate professor Julia Hellwege called the 2026 turnout “exceptionally small.” 
“It means we as a people are losing our voice to be represented,” Hellwege said, “and our democracy relies on our engagement.”


This year’s top races — for governor and Congress — were not “highly competitive,” leaving South Dakotans of all political affiliations less interested in participating, Hellwege said.
Republicans who skipped the election may have been fatigued or figured they could “free ride” after a competitive primary in June and a runoff for the Republican nomination for governor in July, Hellwege said. Democrats may not have felt their votes mattered in a state dominated by Republican officials, she said, and independents may not have felt represented either. Complex ballot questions didn’t help, she added, saying that a lack of understanding about the proposed constitutional amendments may have kept some voters away.
Oglala Lakota County had the lowest turnout at 29%, followed by Corson at 33%, Ziebach at 36% and Dewey and Todd at 37% each. All five include tribal lands. Twenty-one of the state’s 66 counties reported turnout under 50%, including the two most populous, Minnehaha and Pennington.
Jones County had the highest turnout at 72%, followed by Harding at 66%, Sully at 62% and Grant and Haakon at 61% each.

title: UAW’s Shawn Fain: The 2026 election results were a case of the ‘many versus the mighty’
description: DETROIT — The political outreach efforts of Michigan’s labor movement played a significant role in the 2026 elections as Democrats helped elect candidates who put the plight of working people first in their campaign messages and policy planks, said UAW President Shawn Fain on Tuesday evening. In an interview with Michigan Advance, the leader of […]
text:
United Auto Workers President Shawn Fain speaks at the Michigan Democratic Party's election night watch party in Detroit on Nov. 5, 2024. (Photo by Andrew Roth/Michigan Advance)DETROIT — The political outreach efforts of Michigan’s labor movement played a significant role in the 2026 elections as Democrats helped elect candidates who put the plight of working people first in their campaign messages and policy planks, said UAW President Shawn Fain on Tuesday evening.
In an interview with Michigan Advance, the leader of one of the nation’s largest unions said the gains made in the Nov. 3 election — which saw several of the movement’s endorsed candidates sail to victory — were a testament to the on-the-ground efforts of labor over the past year, including its get out the vote effort within UAW’s own ranks.
“We mobilized our membership. We have 350,000 members here in Michigan, and over 200,000 voted early,” Fain told the Advance while he was watching election night returns at the Michigan Democratic Party victory event in downtown Detroit. “Our members have been out with 500,000 phone calls, 100,000 doors knocked on. We’ve seen double digit percentages of support. What that means for me, and working class Michiganders, is that we’re going to have people who stand behind working class people who are struggling to afford to live right now.”
Fain said the election, and its efforts in 2026, was a true case of “the many versus the mighty.”
“You had a lot of rich people who tried to inject a ton of money, outside groups who came to Michigan, to buy a seat, to buy these races,” Fain added. “Michiganders are smarter than that and they’re telling these people they’re not for sale.”
Michigan Democratic Party members and supporters watch election night returns on Nov. 3, 2026, at a watch party in Detroit, Mich. (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance)
Many of the UAW’s endorsed Michigan candidates won on Tuesday, including Governor-elect Jocelyn Benson, Secretary of State-elect Garlin Gilchrist, U.S. Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed, Attorney General-elect Eli Savit, and Michigan Supreme Court Justices Meghan Cavanagh and Noah Hood. The UAW had also endorsed Christina Hines, Sean McCann and Will Lawrence — all of whom were elected to congressional seats.
Fain said those gains have the potential to change or improve labor laws, as well as policies that address affordability, both here in Michigan and nationally. The focus on working people from several candidates, particularly from the El-Sayed campaign, showed Fain that the union had done what was necessary to elevate working class needs and issues to the very top of Democratic politics.
“We’ve served notice,” he said. “We’re done getting behind candidates just because of a party label. The days of just endorsing people are over. They’ve got to do the work, and we have expectations. We expect that they are going to be there for working class people. We laid that standard down back in 2023, and we’ve really focused our efforts here in 2026 to mobilize our membership and mobilize our people like we’ve never done in my lifetime, and you’re seeing the results of that tonight.”SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Now that Democrats control the whole of Michigan government, and also control both chambers of Congress, Fain said he wants them to focus on adequate wages, healthcare and retirement security. Any efforts to create an economic environment where people who are already working 12 hours a day, seven days a week and don’t have to work two or three jobs would also go a long way, he said.
“That’s not a life. Working class people deserve better,” Fain said. “We expect the Democratic Party to get back to their roots. Some of those Democrats forgot about that over the years. … Working class people are sending a message tonight that they are fed up with struggling to afford to live. If these candidates can get behind those issues, they’re going to be there for a long time. If they don’t, no matter which party they belong to, they’ll be out of the way the next round.”

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: Democrats poised to take all five NH Executive Council seats after dramatic election night
description: For years, New Hampshire’s Executive Council has been controlled by Republicans with a 4-1 majority, election after election. However, that changed Tuesday. The “blue wave” that brought Democrats big wins in Congress and the state Legislature also flowed to the Executive Council. That 4-1 Republican majority council is set to become a 5-0 Democratically cont[...]
text:
Executive Councilor Karen Liot Hill speaks during a Sept. 3, 2026, event at Planned Parenthood of Northern New England in Concord. (Photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)For years, New Hampshire’s Executive Council has been controlled by Republicans with a 4-1 majority, election after election.
However, that changed Tuesday. The “blue wave” that brought Democrats big wins in Congress and the state Legislature also flowed to the Executive Council.
That 4-1 Republican majority council is set to become a 5-0 Democratically controlled council next year after a shocking election result.
Melanie Levesque looks on during a Sept. 3, 2026, event at Planned Parenthood of Northern New England in Concord. (Photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)
As of midday Wednesday:

Luz Bay, a two-term state representative and Dover scientist, was beating incumbent District 1 Councilor Joe Kenney 52% to 48%, with 80% of precincts reporting.
Karen Liot Hill, previously the only Democrat on the council and the former mayor of Lebanon, beat out her Republican challenger Tobin Menard 65% to 35%, with 87% of District 2 precincts reporting.
Lisa Kennedy Sheldon, a Portsmouth nurse, earned roughly 52% of the vote in District 3 to incumbent Janet Stevens’ 48%, with 96% of precincts reporting.
Jim O’Connell, a former Manchester School Board member, earned roughly 54% of the vote as opposed to incumbent John Stephen’s 46%, with 97% of precincts reporting in District 4.
Melanie Levesque, a former state senator and representative of Brookline, earned roughly 54% of the District 5 vote to incumbent David Wheeler’s 46%, with 89% of precincts reporting.

The Executive Council is an elected body unique to New Hampshire. It serves as a check on the governor, approving or rejecting state contracts and vetting the governor’s nominees, including for the state Supreme Court and agency commissioners. It’s a little-known arm of government that holds immense power in the state.
Asked what a Democratically controlled council looks like, Liot Hill said “it looks like a Supreme Court that is going to have justices on it who are highly qualified and not embroiled in these ethical scandals that are plaguing the Supreme Court right now.”
Lisa Kennedy Sheldon attends a Planned Parenthood of Northern New England event in Concord on Sept. 3. (Photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)
There is currently a vacancy on the state’s highest court. The former chief justice, Gordon MacDonald, resigned after reporting from NHPR and an investigation from the judicial branch discovered a highly unusual personnel move he orchestrated to allow a close ally to collect nearly $50,000 in state funding. Gov. Kelly Ayotte, a Republican who weathered the blue wave Tuesday to win reelection, has yet to nominate his successor, though she may nominate someone before the new councilors are sworn in in January.
Another state Supreme Court justice, Anna Barbara Hantz Marconi, was convicted late last year of criminal solicitation connected to a conversation with then-Gov. Chris Sununu about an investigation into her husband, Geno Marconi. Prosecutors said she attempted to wield her influence as a justice to induce Sununu to intervene in a criminal investigation into whether her husband, the state port authority director, had illegally shared confidential records. 
“I think that there’s going to be an appetite for true accountability on the Supreme Court and at all levels of government,” Liot Hill said Tuesday night. I think that the people of the nation and of our state are showing that they want real accountability.”
Liot Hill stressed that the new council wouldn’t say no to federal funds “because of ideological agendas.” She said the council will likely approve contracts that Republicans on the council have recently rejected, including several Planned Parenthood contracts for services like cancer screenings, STD treatment, and contraception, and a childcare-related contract with Pyramid Model Consortium to provide early education for children with disabilities under the Granite Steps for Quality program. She also said the new council will be “holding the governor accountable.”
State Rep. Luz Bay attends an event at Planned Parenthood of Northern New England in Concord on Sept. 3. (Photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)
Bay said Tuesday night her first priority would be funding Planned Parenthood. Over the past five years, the Executive Council has repeatedly rejected contracts with the reproductive health organization and similar healthcare organizations. In addition to the cancer screenings, STD treatment and contraception that the organizations would’ve provided under the contracts, they also provided abortions. And although the contracts weren’t related to abortion, the conservatives didn’t want to do business with them. They argued that providing funds would help keep the lights on and pay other bills in buildings that provide abortions, even if the state funding wasn’t spent directly on abortions. The contracts, which were supported by then-Gov. Chris Sununu, also a Republican, became among the most contentious issues for the council. The Democratic candidates have signaled their desire to return to the topic.
Bay also suggested the council would take its duty as a check on the governor seriously.
“There is no rubber stamp for the governor,” she said. “It doesn’t really matter whether it’s Kelly or Cinde (Warmington, Ayotte’s campaign foe, who ultimately lost Tuesday). No rubber stamping. I’m gonna do the due diligence for every contract, for every appointment, for everything that goes through the council, there’s nothing that’s going to get rubber stamped.”
Bay and Levesque both also brought up judicial nominees and agency commissioner vetting.
“Good governance is a first priority to appoint judges and commissioners who are qualified, who are experienced, that follow the rule of law,” Levesque said. “That’s mostly with judges, but with commissioners, people that are experienced in their field, that are well respected by their peers, and have a history of making good judgments and good policy.”
Bay said the “baseline” for Supreme Court appointments is that “they should have bench experience.” Ayotte’s first appointment to the Supreme Court — Bryan Gould — was an attorney with deep GOP connections with no judicial experience when he was nominated. Her second, Daniel Will, was a superior court judge.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Spanberger saw a path to four House flips. Democrats have won two.
description: Just six months ago, Virginia Democrats hoped a new congressional map would help them capture 10 of the state’s 11 U.S. House seats. Instead, they went into Tuesday’s midterm election under the existing boundaries and flipped two Republican-held districts, with a possible third pickup still undecided Wednesday afternoon.  The results fell short of what Democ[...]
text:
Voters at the precinct inside Main Street Station in Richmond, Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Charlotte Rene Woods/Virginia Mercury)Just six months ago, Virginia Democrats hoped a new congressional map would help them capture 10 of the state’s 11 U.S. House seats. Instead, they went into Tuesday’s midterm election under the existing boundaries and flipped two Republican-held districts, with a possible third pickup still undecided Wednesday afternoon. 
The results fell short of what Democrats had sought through redistricting and landed at the low end of what Gov. Abigail Spanberger had suggested was possible even without new maps. In August, she told WTOP that strong turnout could help Democrats flip the 1st, 2nd, 5th and 6th districts. 
But when the dust settled, Democrats ousted Republican incumbents in the first two, trailed in the 5th and lost the 6th. 
Asked whether the time, money and political capital spent on redistricting had been a mistake, Spanberger acknowledged that the debate around new congressional lines had overshadowed parts of her affordability agenda during the General Assembly session earlier this year. 
But she still credited Democratic candidates and local party organizations for delivering two victories. 
“What I always knew would be the case is that we would flip seats in Virginia,” Spanberger told reporters on a Zoom Wednesday morning. “I’m proud of the fact that we flipped the 1st and the 2nd.”
Spanberger also pointed to Democratic gains in districts where Republicans won or remained ahead. She said every locality in the 5th, 6th and 9th districts had shifted toward Democrats compared with 2024, crediting candidates for listening to voters and addressing their concerns. 
Senate Majority Leader Scott Surovell, D-Fairfax, said he remained confident Democrat Tom Perriello would deliver a third pickup in the 5th District. Spanberger said the race was still too close to call. 
First-term U.S. Rep. John McGuire of Goochland, the Republican incumbent, declared victory at a watch party in Charlottesville late Tuesday night, while Perriello urged election officials to count every remaining ballot. The Associated Press had not called the race by Wednesday afternoon. 
Virginia Elections Commissioner Steve Koski cautioned that the state does not declare winners before results are certified, even as news organizations and analysts weigh whether to call close contests such as the one in the 5th District.
“From our perspective, all race results remain pending until final certification,” Koski said in a text message. 
The Virginia Board of Elections is scheduled to certify the results Dec. 7. 
Stephen Farnsworth, professor emeritus of political science at the University of Mary Washington, said Democrats had reason to celebrate their gains under the existing map. 
“A net gain of two seats is a good night for Democrats, and three seats would have been an exceptional night for Democrats,” he said. 
Farnsworth said President Donald Trump’s unpopularity and economic concerns hurt Republicans in competitive districts. Candidates who distanced themselves from the president risked alienating his supporters, while those who embraced him faced voters unhappy with his administration. 
 Where Democrats broke through

In the 1st District, Henrico County Commonwealth’s Attorney Shannon Taylor defeated Republican U.S. Rep. Rob Wittman of Westmoreland  51.04% to 48.72% out of roughly 406,300 votes cast, according to unofficial returns. 
Wittman had represented the district since 2007. Trump carried it in 2024, but Spanberger won 51% there in last year’s governor’s race.
In her victory statement, Taylor renewed her calls for congressional term limits and a ban on stock trading by members of Congress. 
“Tonight, we sent a message: people are sick and tired of the corruption and they are ready for change,” Taylor said. 
In the Virginia Beach-centered 2nd District, former U.S. Rep. Elaine Luria reclaimed a seat she lost to Republican Jen Kiggans in 2022. 
Luria won 53.06% to Kiggans’ 44.56% out of roughly 336,360 votes cast. Independents Matt Baker and Bishop Staten received 1.36% and 0.89%, respectively. 
Luria said in a statement Tuesday evening Hampton Roads voters wanted leaders willing to challenge Trump when his policies hurt Virginia. 
Democratic Party of Virginia Chair Lamont Bagby cited Luria’s work for military families and veterans during her previous two terms in Congress, along with her service on the House committee that investigated the Jan. 6 attack on the U.S. Capitol.
Former Republican Del. Tim Anderson of Virginia Beach pointed to the political climate in both elections. Luria lost in 2022 while Joe Biden was president, he noted, while Kiggans lost with Trump back in the White House. 
Anderson argued the backlash that helped Kiggans win four years ago worked against her Tuesday. 
Democrats also posted strong Election Day results statewide. U.S. Sen. Mark Warner won a fourth term with about 61% of the vote, defeating Republican Bert Mizusawa by roughly 22 percentage points. 
Voters also approved all three proposed constitutional amendments, protecting reproductive rights, guaranteeing marriage equality and automatically restoring voting rights after incarceration. 
 A third pickup remains in play

In the 5th District, McGuire led Perriello 50.22% to 47.98% out of roughly 360,200 votes cast, according to unofficial returns. Independent Cooke Harvey received 1.6%. 
“This was a tough race, but by the grace of God we won!” McGuire said in a statement. 
Perriello won the seat in a 2008 upset but lost his reelection bid two years later. Republicans have held it since, although the district’s boundaries have changed considerably. 
Trump carried the district by 12 percentage points in 2024, and McGuire won his first term by 15 points that year. 
The 5th District joined the 1st and 2nd as a focus of late Democratic campaign efforts, with Perriello trying to repeat his 2008 victory. 
Rick Buchanan, the outgoing 5th District Republican Committee chair and an outspoken McGuire critic, blamed the close result on the congressman’s failure to energize local Republicans and heal divisions within the party. 
“He will stand out on the side of a road behind a big sign and wave for hours, but he did not mend any fences,” Buchanan said in a phone interview. 
David Richards, a political science professor at the University of Lynchburg, attributed the tight race to Perriello’s strength as a candidate, McGuire’s campaign weaknesses and voters’ economic concerns and dissatisfaction with Trump.
Richards said Democrats would have trouble recreating those circumstances in 2028. 
“I think the 5th is stuck with McGuire for a while now, but the Republicans would do well to buy a little insurance and get someone in there who is a better candidate for 2028,” he said. “I expect a primary challenge against McGuire after this poor performance.”
 Will Democrats try to redraw the map again?

Virginia voters approved a congressional redistricting amendment in April, but the Supreme Court of Virginia struck it down in May, leaving the existing boundaries in place. 
The proposed map would have created 10 Democratic-leaning districts. Under the lines used Tuesday, Republican U.S. Rep. Ben Cline of Botetourt defeated Democrat Beth Macy in the 6th, another district Spanberger had identified as a potential pickup.
Asked Wednesday whether she would rule out another attempt at mid-decade redistricting, Spanberger described this year’s amendment as a temporary response to Republican-led map changes in Texas and other states. 
Farnsworth said Democrats were likely already preparing for the possibility of another amendment that could change congressional boundaries before the next presidential election. 
He said “2028 is a question mark, because we’re not even certain where the lines will be two years from now.”
