name: California
title: Las escuelas recibirán miles de millones en fondos con la aprobación de la Propuesta 3
description: La Proposición 3 hace permanente un impuesto sobre la renta para los ricos con el fin de financiar las escuelas primarias y secundarias y otros servicios.
text:
This article is also available in English. Read it here.
Las escuelas de California evitaron un fuerte recorte de ingresos el martes, después de que los votantes extendieran de forma permanente un impuesto sobre la renta para los ricos.
 La Proposición 3 , impulsada por el sindicato de maestros más grande del estado, fue aprobada con el 59% de los votos frente al 41% en contra. Esta medida convierte en permanente un impuesto sobre la renta para las personas con mayores ingresos, destinado a financiar las escuelas primarias y secundarias, así como otros servicios. Aprobado originalmente en 2012, el impuesto fue renovado en 2016 y estaba previsto que expirara en 2031.
 Los partidarios de la medida estaban entusiasmados el martes por la noche.
 “Los votantes de California reafirmaron la importancia de mantener la inversión en la educación pública”, dijo Debra Schade, presidenta de la Asociación de Juntas Escolares de California y miembro de la junta escolar de Solana Beach, cerca de San Diego. “Los estudiantes de California se lo merecen”.
Desde su aprobación inicial, este impuesto ha generado entre 5,000 y 15,000 millones de dólares anuales, hasta un 15% de los ingresos totales de las escuelas. Si no se hubiera renovado, las escuelas perderían ese dinero a partir de 2031 y probablemente tendrían que realizar importantes recortes presupuestarios.
La Asociación de Maestros de California ha impulsado con fuerza la aprobación de la medida, invirtiendo casi 60 millones de dólares en publicidad y enviando a sus miembros a visitar más de 200,000 hogares en todo el estado. El presidente del sindicato, David Goldberg, calificó la medida de “vital” para proteger las escuelas y los puestos de trabajo de los docentes.
 Goldberg declaró el martes por la noche que estaba contento, pero no sorprendido, de que la medida hubiera sido aprobada.
 “En términos prácticos, esto significa que tendremos financiación segura para las escuelas y los estudiantes no tendrán que temer que sus profesores sean despedidos”, dijo Goldberg. “En un nivel más profundo, demuestra que los californianos están dispuestos a asumir riesgos y apoyar la educación pública”.
El impuesto se aplica a las personas que ganan más de 371,000 dólares al año o a las parejas que ganan más de 743,000 dólares. Si se aprueba la Propuesta 3, estas personas seguirían pagando un impuesto sobre la renta del 12.3%, uno de los más altos del país.
 ¿Un engaño?
 Los opositores a la Proposición 3 afirman que el estado no puede seguir imponiendo impuestos indefinidamente a los residentes adinerados. Estos residentes, unos 200 de los cuales también podrían enfrentarse a un impuesto único del 5% si se aprueba la Proposición 40 , simplemente se mudarían a estados con impuestos más bajos, lo que supondría una importante merma en los ingresos fiscales estatales.
 Los opositores argumentan que el impuesto se concibió como una solución temporal para ayudar a las escuelas a superar la Gran Recesión, y que convertirlo en permanente equivale a un engaño. Asimismo, cuestionan la necesidad del impuesto, considerando la disminución de la matrícula y el aumento del gasto público en educación en los últimos años.
 Una vez recaudado el impuesto, el dinero se destina a la compleja fórmula de financiación escolar de la Proposición 98 del estado, que garantiza que el 40% de los ingresos estatales se destine a las escuelas. De ese dinero, el 89% se destina a las escuelas primarias y secundarias (K-12) y el 11% a los colegios comunitarios. Cualquier excedente generado por el impuesto se destina a un fondo de reserva. 
 Aumento de los costos, disminución de la matrícula
 California financia las escuelas en función del número de alumnos que asisten a clase cada día, una cifra que lleva disminuyendo aproximadamente una década debido a que las familias se marchan a estados menos costosos, la inmigración disminuye y las familias tienen menos hijos.
 Al mismo tiempo, las escuelas se han enfrentado a un aumento vertiginoso de los costos de los seguros y a costosas reparaciones en edificios antiguos, entre otros gastos. Si bien el estado ha incrementado la financiación escolar en los últimos años, los administradores escolares afirman que el dinero no ha sido suficiente para cubrir el aumento de los gastos.

name: California
title: Xavier Becerra será el próximo gobernador de California: cinco cosas que debes saber.
description: A diferencia de su predecesor, el gobernador electo demócrata Xavier Becerra ha hecho pocas promesas durante la campaña electoral y solo ha insinuado ciertas prioridades políticas.
text:
This article is also available in English. Read it here.
El gobernador electo de California, Xavier Becerra, tomará las riendas en un momento delicado para California.
Se enfrenta a la perspectiva de recortes más profundos en la sanidad federal, un aumento vertiginoso de los costos de los incendios forestales y una persistente crisis del costo de la vida. Sin embargo, muchos de los detalles de sus políticas aún se desconocen, ya que llevó a cabo una discreta campaña como demócrata en un estado tradicionalmente demócrata, promoviendo pocos programas y evitando comprometerse.
 Esto es lo que debes saber sobre los retos que abordará Becerra y cómo gobernará. 
Está abierto a nuevos impuestos
 Becerra se opuso a la propuesta de impuesto a los multimillonarios , argumentando que no cree que gravar los activos sea una forma estable de generar ingresos para el estado. Y si bien ha afirmado que cree que los ricos deberían pagar lo que les corresponde en impuestos, no ha respaldado explícitamente ningún nuevo impuesto sobre la renta.
 Sin embargo, ha dado a entender que apoya la idea de gravar a las empresas cuyos trabajadores reciben salarios tan bajos que califican para beneficios públicos, o incluso de eliminar los créditos fiscales para dichas empresas. El Departamento de Finanzas del estado está estudiando cómo sería ese tipo de impuesto y se espera que presente recomendaciones a los legisladores el próximo año.
También ha declarado que está considerando una propuesta controvertida para que el estado grave a los conductores con un impuesto basado en los kilómetros recorridos, como forma de financiar la reparación de carreteras y autopistas. El estado recauda estos fondos mediante los impuestos a la gasolina, pero se prevé que esta fuente disminuya en 31,000 millones de dólares durante la próxima década, a medida que más conductores adopten vehículos eléctricos.
 “No me complace decirle a la gente que los impuestos tienen un propósito”, dijo a los periodistas la semana pasada. “Creo que los usuarios deben pagar por las carreteras”. 
Grandes decisiones sobre el clima y la energía
 Becerra ha hecho hincapié en la necesidad de mantener la energía a precios asequibles mientras California continúa su transición hacia la energía limpia.
 Un programa que está impulsando proporcionaría a los hogares de bajos ingresos dos horas de electricidad gratuita al día durante el día, cuando la energía solar es abundante y el consumo es bajo. El programa, al que llama “hora de energía”, estaría limitado a los clientes de la compañía eléctrica que ya cumplen los requisitos para recibir programas de asistencia.
 Ha declarado que quiere “seguir avanzando hacia la energía limpia, pero mientras avanzamos en ese camino, debemos asegurarnos de estabilizar los precios”, incluso perforando más pozos petrolíferos en el estado, y decidirá si mantiene el plazo de 2030 de California para prohibir la venta de coches nuevos de gasolina en lo que respecta a la infraestructura de carga de vehículos eléctricos.
 También tendrá que enfrentarse a la presión de las empresas de servicios públicos de propiedad privada, que han estado presionando a los legisladores y al gobernador saliente, Gavin Newsom, para que reduzcan lo que deben pagar a las compañías de seguros y a las víctimas de incendios cuando sus equipos provocan incendios forestales destructivos.
 Si Newsom no resuelve el problema en los próximos dos meses, Becerra tendrá que ocuparse de él cuando asuma el cargo; hasta ahora se ha negado a tomar una postura, calificando el debate de “pelea campal” entre aseguradoras y empresas de servicios públicos. 
 Atención médica para inmigrantes indocumentados
 En 1993, cuando era congresista por Los Ángeles en su primer mandato, Becerra causó revuelo en el Capitolio al debatir con un veterano político demócrata sobre un plan para recortar los programas de asistencia social a los inmigrantes legales; se opuso a él. Ha declarado que buscará revertir las restricciones a Medi-Cal que dejaron fuera del programa a decenas de miles de inmigrantes indocumentados en California.
 La inmigración ha sido un tema clave a lo largo de su carrera. Como gobernador, ha prometido hacer cumplir las nuevas leyes estatales que buscan limitar el uso de la fuerza y las actividades de los agentes de inmigración en propiedades estatales.
 Newsom había ampliado gradualmente la cobertura sanitaria para inmigrantes a todos los adultos que cumplían los requisitos de ingresos, pero el año pasado comenzó a reducir parte de la cobertura en medio de un déficit presupuestario y unos costes sanitarios inesperadamente altos.
 “Mis valores y mis convicciones fiscales me dicen que cualquier persona que trabaje duro en California debería tener acceso a la atención médica que necesita para sí misma y para su familia, y que debería poder pagarla, y eso incluye a las personas indocumentadas”, dijo Becerra a KQED . 
Continuar con la moratoria de Newsom sobre la pena de muerte
 Newsom impuso una moratoria a la pena de muerte en 2019 al asumir el cargo, alegando su oposición moral a las ejecuciones, y durante su mandato comenzó a desmantelar el corredor de la muerte del estado en San Quentin. Desde entonces, los presos condenados a muerte han sido trasladados a otras prisiones.
 California no ha ejecutado a ningún recluso desde 2006. Newsom está considerando la posibilidad de conmutar las sentencias de muerte de más de 560 presos por cadena perpetua sin libertad condicional, pero incluso si no lo hace, no se espera que Becerra reanude las ejecuciones.
 Como fiscal general, Becerra defendió las sentencias de muerte y dijo que las apoyaba en principio, pero durante la campaña afirmó que mantendría la moratoria de California debido a la preocupación por los prejuicios raciales y las condenas injustas. 
Se autodenomina un “progresista pragmático”
 En un partido que atraviesa una crisis de identidad desde hace años sobre hasta qué punto debe inclinar sus políticas hacia la izquierda, Becerra opta por el cambio gradual en lugar de las grandes hazañas progresistas.
 Durante sus más de dos décadas en el Congreso, contó con el apoyo tanto de los defensores progresistas como de la cúpula demócrata establecida, y fue un estrecho aliado de la expresidenta de la Cámara de Representantes, Nancy Pelosi, aunque ambos tuvieron un momento tenso en 2009 cuando Becerra quiso que ella presionara más para incluir una opción pública en la Ley de Cuidado de Salud Asequible.
 Este año, se retractó de su antiguo apoyo a un sistema de salud de pagador único, diciendo que es una posibilidad remota para California, ya que es poco probable que la administración Trump le dé al estado permiso para implementarlo.
 Incluso antes de eso, afirmó que valoraba más la experiencia que las grandes promesas como Medicare para Todos. Como secretario de salud del presidente Joe Biden, por ejemplo, dijo que se centró en ampliar la cobertura.
 “Cuando ayudaba a Hillary Clinton en 2016, mis hijas querían votar por Bernie Sanders”, dijo en una entrevista. “Y yo les repetía: lo entiendo, lo comprendo. Quiero un sistema de salud universal… Pero tenemos que lograr resultados, y quiero a alguien que haya estado realmente involucrado en la situación”.

name: Source New Mexico
title: ‘It represents hope’: New Mexico Democrats cement control in New Mexico following historic blue wave
description: The historic wave of Democratic enthusiasm that wrested control of Congress from Republicans on Tuesday also cemented Democrats’ control up and down the ballot in New Mexico, where the party continues to hold all state and federal elected offices and expanded its hold in the state House of Representatives.
text:
Democrat Amanda López Askin, New Mexico’s newly elected secretary of state, told supporters Nov. 3, 2026, that her party’s resounding victory in New Mexico and across the country marks a return to “humanity and reason and compassion” in politics. (Photo by Leah Romero for Source NM) The historic wave of Democratic enthusiasm that wrested control of Congress from Republicans on Tuesday also cemented Democrats’ control up and down the ballot in New Mexico, where the party continues to hold all state and federal elected offices and expanded its hold in the state House of Representatives.
Incumbent Democrats retained their U.S. Senate seat and all three U.S. House seats, and new Democrats running for statewide offices successfully beat Republican challengers for offices including governor, secretary of state and land commissioner. Democrats also successfully secured second terms in races for attorney general, auditor and treasurer.
All those Democrats won their races by 10 percentage points or more. Democrats in the state House of Representatives also expanded their majority after defeating four incumbent Republicans. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
In New Mexico’s closely watched 2nd Congressional District race, incumbent U.S. Rep. Gabe Vasquez (D-N.M.) defeated Republican challenger Greg Cunningham with nearly 58% of the vote, despite the Republican National Congressional Committee targeting the race with fundraisers and donations, and outside donors promising to spend at least $10 million on the race. 
Vasquez, in a statement late Tuesday night touting his “double digits victory” against Cunningham, said the results are “a reminder that in America, the people — not political parties, big corporations, or special interests — have the power.”
Democrat Amanda López Askin, the Doña Ana County clerk who handily defeated Republican challenger Ramona Goolsby in the race for secretary of state, summed up the results in a speech to supporters Tuesday night in Las Cruces. 
“Not only is it a mandate, it represents hope. We can get out of this,” she said. “You know what this is? This is step one to 2028. This is step one of getting humanity and reason and compassion back into leadership in our country.”
Nearly half of the state’s registered voters had cast ballots by 9 p.m. on Tuesday, driven primarily by Democrats, who turned out at a rate of at least 62%, according to Secretary of State’s Office figures. That’s higher than 57% of registered Democrats who cast ballots in the 2022 midterm elections.
Republicans turned out at a rate of 53% this year, compared with 61% in 2022, according to Secretary of State’s office figures. 
The state’s overall turnout remained at slightly less than in the previous midterm elections in 2022, in which 52% of statewide registered voters cast ballots.
The shortfall appears to be a result of relatively low turnout by the state’s third major voting bloc: unaffiliated or Decline to State voters.
Those unaffiliated voters represent more than 28% of the state’s registered voters. But only about one-third of them cast ballots this year, according to Secretary of State’s Office figures.
Still, Democratic turnout, predominately in the state’s most populous counties, exceeded that of 2022, and contributed to the seismic Democratic victories locally and nationally. 
“With Democrats winning a majority in the U.S. House and Senate,” Vasquez noted Tuesday in his victory speech, “the time for real accountability and reform is finally here. The day of reckoning for the corrupt Trump administration has come.”
Source New Mexico freelance reporter Leah Romero contributed to this report.

name: Nevada Current
title: Benitez-Thompson makes history as first Democrat to win NV 2nd congressional district
description: In a development that was unthinkable at the start of the year — and that stands as testament to how deep the nation’s rejection of Donald Trump and his policies was in the midterm elections — Democratic former state legislator Teresa Benitez-Thompson defeated Republican David Flippo in Nevada’s second congressional district. No Democrat has ever […]
text:
Teresa Benitez-Thompson is the first Democrat to win CD2 since its creation after the 1980 Census. (Photo: Abra Richardson/Reno Gazette-Journal)In a development that was unthinkable at the start of the year — and that stands as testament to how deep the nation’s rejection of Donald Trump and his policies was in the midterm elections — Democratic former state legislator Teresa Benitez-Thompson defeated Republican David Flippo in Nevada’s second congressional district.
No Democrat has ever won the district since it was created after the 1980 Census.
With a nearly 7 percentage point lead as of Wednesday morning and an estimated 90% of votes counted, Benitez-Thompson declared victory.
“I am honored that Northern Nevadans have placed their trust in me to represent our home in Congress,” Benitez-Thompson said in a release. “Our region faces unique challenges that only someone with deep local roots and a genuine commitment to our communities can tackle. In Congress, I will fight every single day to protect our wallets, our water, and our way of life.”
“I’m especially grateful to our dedicated supporters, volunteers, and staff who worked tirelessly to make sure a Northern Nevadan actually represents Northern Nevada,” Benitez Thompson added.
Flippo started the year running in Nevada’s fourth congressional district, hoping to unseat Democratic Rep. Steven Horsford. But when Republican incumbent Rep. Mark Amodei announced in February that he was retiring, Flippo flipped to compete in the much more Republican-friendly CD2.
Both Amodei and Gov. Joe Lombardo had endorsed James Settelmeyer in the Republican primary. But Trump endorsed Flippo, and Flippo won.
Multiple Democrats had filed in the CD2 primary. After Trump’s endorsement of Flippo, Democrats, entertaining the prospect that a Democrat might actually win the district, coalesced around Benitez-Thompson.
Flippo’s candidacy almost immediately started to make news, and not in a positive way. He was hammered as an opportunist for switching districts. He came under fire for what critics called shoddy finance reports. And most damagingly, his campaign materials said he had been awarded a Bronze Star with valor while in the Air Force. Flippo was awarded a Bronze Star for merit, but not valor, and critics accused him of “stolen valor.”
After the primary Amodei barely hid his displeasure with Flippo and the nominee’s relative unfamiliarity with the district. Amodei ended up announcing that he couldn’t support the nominee, and said he had instead voted for the Independent American Party candidate.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Amy Eddy cruises to victory in Montana SupCo
description: Flathead County District Court Judge Amy Eddy will replace retiring Montana Supreme Court Justice Beth Baker after a commanding victory over fellow Flathead District Court Judge Dan Wilson.  The Associated Press called the race late last night, and vote counts at noon on Wednesday showed Eddy pulling 59.2% to Wilson’s 40.8%.  Wilson also ran unsuccessfully [[...]
text:
Flathead District Court Judge Amy Eddy announced her run for the Montana Supreme Court. (Contributed photo)Flathead County District Court Judge Amy Eddy will replace retiring Montana Supreme Court Justice Beth Baker after a commanding victory over fellow Flathead District Court Judge Dan Wilson. 
The Associated Press called the race late last night, and vote counts at noon on Wednesday showed Eddy pulling 59.2% to Wilson’s 40.8%.  Wilson also ran unsuccessfully for the state supreme court in 2024.
“It feels totally overwhelming,” Eddy told the Daily Montanan on Wednesday morning. “I’m a little bit in shock.”
The nonpartisan supreme court race had an overtly partisan flavor this year as Wilson was backed financially by the Montana Republican Party and spoke at GOP events. Eddy, while backed by liberal-leaning organizations, stayed away from partisan political events.
She said it was “really gratifying, frankly, that Montanans wanted to maintain this nonpartisan tradition that we have and rejected this overt partisan influence.”
Statewide, Montanans also overwhelmingly backed an initiative to enshrine nonpartisan judicial elections in the state constitution, making a 90-year state of affairs permanent. 
“In one way it doesn’t change anything. We had nonpartisan judicial elections, we just ran a nonpartisan judicial election,” Eddy said. “But more than anything, it signals to the legislators that the public is committed to nonpartisan judicial elections, and they wanted that question taken away from the legislature.”

In 2025, Republican legislators made multiple attempts to make judicial candidates run with party labels, saying it would help inform voters. 
Montana’s supreme court race was put to voters during the June primary with Eddy winning by 3 points — though with both candidates advancing to the general election, it was a low stakes contest. 
In Flathead County, Wilson won the primary vote by 10 points. On Tuesday, Eddy prevailed by 2 points.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Democrats flipped legislatures, won trifectas and toppled GOP supermajorities
description: In the midterm elections, Democrats seized more power over state governments than they've had in years, sweeping races up and down the ballot.
text:
Democrats seized more power over state governments than the party has had in years after the party swept races up and down the ballot in Tuesday’s midterm elections.
Republicans have held a majority of state legislatures and governorships since 2010. But that reign appears over as Democrats swept a majority of governorships and state legislative chambers.
Tracking from the Democratic Legislative Campaign Committee on Wednesday showed the party had flipped 12 chambers so far, winning the most chambers since 2008 and putting Democrats in control of more than half the nation’s state legislative chambers.
“With this sweep, Democrats have achieved their best performance since the Watergate scandal,” the committee, which works to elect Democrats at the state level, said in a news release Wednesday.
Unofficial results show Democrats will control the Arizona legislature for the first time in 60 years. Building off a historic sweep of statewide races, Democrats are poised to take control of the Texas House for the first time in over 20 years. In North Carolina, Democrats flipped several House seats held by influential, veteran Republicans to give the party control of the lower chamber for the first time since 2010.
“We have the power to make this state better,” state Rep. Robert Reives, who was introduced as the next House speaker, said Tuesday night.
Many legislative races had yet to be called by midday Wednesday. But the National Conference of State Legislatures said current results showed Democrats would secure new trifectas – control of both chambers and the governor’s office – in Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin. Democrats also broke Republican trifectas in Georgia, Iowa, Ohio and Texas.
Additionally, Democratic wins crushed GOP supermajorities in several states. In Florida, the loss of the Republican supermajority takes away the party’s power to override rules regarding procedure and debate and override the governor’s veto.
Democratic gains also ended supermajorities in the Indiana state House, the Kansas House, both of Missouri’s legislative chambers, the Ohio House, and the South Carolina House.
In a statement on Wednesday, the Republican State Leadership Committee, which works to elect Republicans at the state level, cited an “historically difficult political environment” facing the party.
“Democrats made state legislative races a national priority, pouring unprecedented resources into these contests because they understand the power state legislatures hold in shaping policy and building the pipeline for the next generation of leaders,” President Edith Jorge-Tuñón said in the statement. “In many key battleground states, the national political environment and the impact of top-of-the-ticket races significantly affected our candidates’ ability to defy historical trends.”
This story was first published Nov. 4, 2026 by Stateline.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Commentary: The rest of the country got a blue wave. Don’t ignore Arkansas’ blue ripples.
description: A red state governor and outspoken supporter of Donald Trump winning by double digits in a blue wave election that was a stinging rebuke of the president would be considered a bragging point for many Republicans. But Tuesday’s election in Arkansas instead dealt a setback to Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders that complicates her second-term agenda […]
text:
Voters cast their ballots at the Pulaski Heights United Methodist Church in Little Rock, Arkansas, on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Katie Adkins/Arkansas Advocate)A red state governor and outspoken supporter of Donald Trump winning by double digits in a blue wave election that was a stinging rebuke of the president would be considered a bragging point for many Republicans.
But Tuesday’s election in Arkansas instead dealt a setback to Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders that complicates her second-term agenda and 2028 political ambitions. The midterm results also offer hope for a Democratic Party that saw its ranks decimated in recent years in a state it had dominated for generations.
The blue tsunami that swept up the nation and handed Democrats control of the U.S. House, Senate and a majority of governorships mostly passed over Arkansas. Sanders and Sen. Tom Cotton, another national Republican considered to be eyeing the White House, fended off challenges with double-digit margins. Central Arkansas’ 2nd Congressional District, where Democrat Chris Jones hoped to unseat Republican Rep. French Hill, remained too close to call as of Wednesday morning with Hill holding a razor-thin lead.
Instead of a blue wave, Arkansas Democrats enjoyed a series of localized blue ripples that may fly under the national radar. But their implications are still significant for the state.
The biggest impact will be in the Arkansas House, where Democrats broke the supermajority that Republicans have held in the House for the past decade. It takes at least 75 votes in the 100-member House to pass most budget bills, and Republicans’ dominance meant that they didn’t have to worry about winning over Democrats to clear that hurdle.



Let us know what you think...


 


Democrats flipped 10 state House seats, giving them newfound leverage that could prompt new budget battles when the Legislature meets next year.
It comes at a particularly precarious time for Sanders, with a session where the future of the state’s Medicaid expansion is expected to be at the top of the agenda.
The Trump administration’s decision to not renew the program for another five years has created uncertainty for hundreds of thousands of people who rely on it for health coverage. It’s also worried medical providers who say the state’s hospitals already face significant strains.
The new legislative makeup could create an inverse of the dynamic that led to the first-in-the-nation hybrid program’s creation, a compromise crafted between the state’s Democratic governor and Republican lawmakers in 2013. 
Could Sanders, who has reveled in partisan skirmishes and frequently frames her divide with Democrats as “normal versus crazy,” be forced to find middle ground with a party she once vilified?
The picture gets even murkier for Sanders’ other policy priorities. Even before Democrats’ gains, the governor was forced to put her plans for a new 3,000-bed prison in Franklin County on hold after facing resistance from fellow Republicans. It’s hard to picture the project moving forward given the new House party breakdown.
And it opens the door for new funding debates over the school voucher program that was the central part of Sanders’ signature education law. Concerns about the program’s cost and impact on schools had come from some rural Republicans along with Democrats, and could become even louder next year.
The new dynamic comes days before Sanders appears ready to soft launch a potential 2028 presidential campaign, with a book set to be released Tuesday that feels like a precursor to a White House bid.
To be clear, Democrats still face challenges that can’t be ignored in Arkansas. Democratic nominee Hallie Shoffner’s loss to Cotton, who heavily outspent her in a Senate race that national Democrats mostly ignored, shows the party still faces serious resource gaps.
And Democratic state Sen. Fred Love’s performance in the governor’s race was better than expected given his lackluster fundraising but still underwhelming considering how much the Trump brand weighed down Republicans in other predominantly red states. 
And the party’s lack of candidates running in other statewide races for attorney general and lieutenant governor shows Democrats have work to do in building a bench for future elections.
Tuesday night’s election showed Democrats haven’t completely overcome those obstacles. But it also may have revealed that the gaps aren’t as insurmountable as they once appeared.

name: National
title: In blue wave, Democrats flipped legislatures, won trifectas and toppled GOP supermajorities
description: Democrats seized more power over state governments than the party has had in years after the party swept races up and down the ballot in Tuesday’s midterm elections. Republicans have held a majority of state legislatures and governorships since 2010. But that reign appears over as Democrats swept a majority of governorships and state legislative […]
text:
Indiana state Reps. Ed DeLaney, Cherrish Pryor, Phil GiaQuinta, Carey Hamilton, Vanessa Summers and Greg Porter declare that Indiana Democrats broke the House GOP’s supermajority on Tuesday night. Democrats flipped several legislative chambers and broke Republican supermajorities across the country. (Photo by Tom Davies/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Democrats seized more power over state governments than the party has had in years after the party swept races up and down the ballot in Tuesday’s midterm elections.
Republicans have held a majority of state legislatures and governorships since 2010. But that reign appears over as Democrats swept a majority of governorships and state legislative chambers.
Tracking from the Democratic Legislative Campaign Committee on Wednesday showed the party had flipped 12 chambers so far, winning the most chambers since 2008 and putting Democrats in control of more than half the nation’s state legislative chambers.
“With this sweep, Democrats have achieved their best performance since the Watergate scandal,” the committee, which works to elect Democrats at the state level, said in a news release Wednesday.
Unofficial results show Democrats will control the Arizona legislature for the first time in 60 years. Building off a historic sweep of statewide races, Democrats are poised to take control of the Texas House for the first time in over 20 years. In North Carolina, Democrats flipped several House seats held by influential, veteran Republicans to give the party control of the lower chamber for the first time since 2010.
“We have the power to make this state better,” state Rep. Robert Reives, who was introduced as the next House speaker, said Tuesday night.
Many legislative races had yet to be called by midday Wednesday. But the National Conference of State Legislatures said current results showed Democrats would secure new trifectas – control of both chambers and the governor’s office – in Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin. Democrats also broke Republican trifectas in Georgia, Iowa, Ohio and Texas.
Additionally, Democratic wins crushed GOP supermajorities in several states. In Florida, the loss of the Republican supermajority takes away the party’s power to override rules regarding procedure and debate and override the governor’s veto.
Democratic gains also ended supermajorities in the Indiana state House, the Kansas House, both of Missouri’s legislative chambers, the Ohio House, and the South Carolina House.
In a statement on Wednesday, the Republican State Leadership Committee, which works to elect Republicans at the state level, cited an “historically difficult political environment” facing the party.
“Democrats made state legislative races a national priority, pouring unprecedented resources into these contests because they understand the power state legislatures hold in shaping policy and building the pipeline for the next generation of leaders,” President Edith Jorge-Tuñón said in the statement. “In many key battleground states, the national political environment and the impact of top-of-the-ticket races significantly affected our candidates’ ability to defy historical trends.”

name: National
title: Voters back tougher crime penalties, reject marijuana rollbacks
description: Millions of voters in 11 states approved tougher criminal penalties and more bail restrictions in Tuesday’s midterm elections, while rejecting efforts to roll back marijuana legalization and expand cooperation with federal immigration authorities. The results reflected a mixed approach to criminal justice policy, with voters supporting harsher penalties for [...]
text:
Sheriff’s deputies walk past voting booths at San Francisco City Hall on Nov. 3, 2026. Voters across 11 states weighed in on criminal justice and drug policies Tuesday, approving tougher bail restrictions and criminal penalties while rejecting efforts to roll back marijuana legalization. (Photo by Benjamin Fanjoy/Getty Images)Millions of voters in 11 states approved tougher criminal penalties and more bail restrictions in Tuesday’s midterm elections, while rejecting efforts to roll back marijuana legalization and expand cooperation with federal immigration authorities.
The results reflected a mixed approach to criminal justice policy, with voters supporting harsher penalties for certain drug and human trafficking offenses and greater authority for judges to deny bail, even as they resisted other changes to state laws.
The measures were among 15 criminal justice and drug policy proposals on ballots in nine states, covering issues ranging from pretrial detention and crime victims’ rights to immigration enforcement and traffic cameras.
Voters expand bail restrictions
Voters in Indiana, Louisiana and Tennessee approved constitutional amendments expanding restrictions on bail.
In Indiana, 59% of voters supported a measure allowing judges to deny bail when evidence of guilt is strong and a defendant poses a substantial risk to another person or the community.
States put criminal justice, marijuana policies before voters in 2026

Louisiana voters approved a measure prohibiting post-conviction bail, which is sometimes referred to as an appeal bond, for people convicted of aggravated offenses against minors. 
Post-conviction bail allows a person who has been found guilty of a crime to remain free or be released from custody while they wait to be formally sentenced or while they appeal their conviction.
In Tennessee, voters expanded the list of offenses for which judges can deny bail, including charges of terrorism, second-degree murder and aggravated rape of a child.
Tennessee voters also approved a constitutional amendment expanding crime victims’ rights, including the right to receive notice of criminal proceedings, to attend hearings and to be heard during decisions involving defendants’ release, sentencing and parole.
Those outcomes continue a recent trend of voters supporting greater restrictions on pretrial release. In May, Alabama voters approved a similar constitutional amendment allowing judges to deny bail for defendants charged with certain violent offenses.
Tougher penalties gain support
Colorado voters approved two measures increasing criminal penalties for fentanyl offenses and child sex trafficking.
Proposition 132 increases penalties for certain fentanyl offenses, requires court-ordered treatment for some possession convictions and changes how drug possession is considered under the state’s habitual criminal law.
Proposition 133 requires life imprisonment without parole or release for people convicted of human trafficking of a child for sexual servitude.
But Colorado voters rejected Amendment 81, which would have required state and local law enforcement to notify federal immigration authorities after charging certain people who are unlawfully present in the country or whose immigration status could not be determined.
In Arizona, voters supported measures designating drug cartels as terrorist organizations under state law and restricting the use of photo traffic enforcement systems, such as stop sign and speed cameras.
Missouri voters narrowly approved a constitutional amendment establishing elected county sheriffs as the chief law enforcement officers in most counties and limiting the circumstances under which they can be removed from office.
Voting rights and pardons
In Virginia, 55% of voters approved a constitutional amendment automatically restoring voting rights to people with felony convictions after they complete their sentences, replacing a system that required a gubernatorial pardon or a successful petition for restoration.
Kentuckians overwhelmingly approved a constitutional amendment that will prohibit the governor from issuing pardons or commuting sentences during a period beginning 60 days before a gubernatorial election until five weeks after it.
Marijuana rollback efforts fail
While voters supported tougher criminal penalties, proposals affecting marijuana legalization were defeated. 
In Massachusetts, voters overwhelmingly rejected a measure that would have repealed much of the state’s law allowing licensed recreational marijuana sales. The outcome preserves a legal market approved by voters in 2016.
The proposal would have eliminated licensed recreational sales while continuing to allow adults to possess limited amounts of marijuana.
In Idaho, voters rejected a constitutional amendment that would have given state lawmakers exclusive authority to legalize marijuana, narcotics and other psychoactive substances.
The measure would not itself have legalized or prohibited marijuana. Instead, it would have prevented citizens from using the state’s ballot initiative process to legalize those substances.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: Nancy Lacore declares victory in flipping SC’s 1st District
description: Retired vice admiral Nancy Lacore claimed the win, albeit a narrow one, in South Carolina's coastal 1st Congressional District.
text:
Democrat Nancy Lacore declared victory Wednesday, Nov. 4, 2026, at her Mount Pleasant campaign headquarters in the race for South Carolina's coastal 1st Congressional District. (Photo by Jessica Holdman/SC Daily Gazette)MOUNT PLEASANT — Retired Vice Adm. Nancy Lacore claimed the win, albeit a narrow one, in South Carolina’s coastal 1st Congressional District.
“We knew it wouldn’t be easy, but we also knew that South Carolinians are frustrated, tired, and looking for some change,” Lacore said at her campaign headquarters in Mount Pleasant Wednesday, after ballot-counting issues delayed results from state election officials the night before.
The race appeared headed for an automatic recount, but by 2:11 a.m., the state Election Commission posted results to its website showing Lacore ahead by 1.01 percentage points, putting her just above the required recount margin under state law.
A little more than 3,300 votes separate Lacore from her Republican opponent, attorney and Charleston County Councilwoman Jenny Costa Honeycutt, according to unofficial results.
Libertarian Bill Reese received 1.6% of the vote. The district spans the lower part of South Carolina’s coastline, including all of Beaufort and Berkeley counties and most of Charleston County.
The delay involved ballots in Dorchester County. Officials had to manually rescan about 5,500 ballots due to a faulty memory stick from the voting machine, according to Kizzie Scott, executive director of the county board of voter registration and elections.
Scott said this issue is not unusual, and all the county’s ballots are now counted.
“This is nothing new. This is not just a Dorchester County thing. The stick can become faulty,” she said.
Lacore said she’s confident in the results, even as The Associated Press has yet to call the election in her favor.
Lacore’s win marks a major victory for Democrats in a seat that was supposed to be safe for Republicans.
Republicans held control of it for nearly 40 years until Joe Cunningham flipped the district in 2018. Cunningham narrowly lost two years later to Republican U.S. Rep. Nancy Mace, who gave up the seat this year for an unsuccessful bid for governor.
Then, after the 2020 census, legislators redrew the district to favor Republicans. Mace easily won reelection in 2022, when she defeated now-U.S.-senator-elect Annie Andrews by 14 percentage points. In 2024, Mace’s winning margin grew to 17 points.
Mace congratulated Lacore and “all of South Carolina’s newly elected officials” in a statement Wednesday.
“Serving the people of South Carolina is a tremendous responsibility,” Mace said. “I wish each of them success as they begin this next chapter of public service.”
Mace also promised a smooth transition as she leaves office in January and called her time in office “the honor of my lifetime.”
The only public statement Honeycutt has made is an early morning social media post thanking her supporters.
“My prayers now are for the Lowcountry, the state of South Carolina and our nation,” she wrote. “And my commitment to the people I love and the place I call home will never waiver.”
Lacore told reporters she received an email from Honeycutt’s campaign congratulating her and conceding. But Honeycutt’s campaign did not confirm any concession, instead telling the SC Daily Gazette they were still seeking more information from election officials. Lacore’s campaign did not provide the email.
Throughout the election cycle, polls showed the coastal district moving closer to the middle, until the nonpartisan Cook Political Report considered it a “toss-up” for Tuesday night.
Lacore, a political newcomer, pointed to her experience in government as qualification enough for Congress. She started her career as a Navy pilot, before joining the part-time reserve to raise her six children and work as a defense contractor. As head of the reserve, Lacore oversaw about 59,000 sailors and often worked with Congress for resources, including securing new airplanes, she previously said.
She moved to South Carolina last year, after Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth removed her from her job as chief of the Navy Reserve with no reason given several months prior. That move, which came as part of a larger pattern of the Trump administration targeting perceived critics of the president, drew national interest.
The 1st District was among at least 32 House seats Democrats picked up nationwide, guaranteeing the party more control of the chamber than the slim majority Republicans held.
“We have a majority in the House. We have a significant majority in the Senate as well. So, I think we’ll have some real power,” Lacore said. “Of course, the president will have the veto authority, but people are ready to make life better in the United States, and I think that’s very clear by the results that we saw from across the country.”

title: LePage declares victory in Maine’s 2nd District race
description: This is a breaking story that will be updated.  Republican Paul LePage declared victory in the election for Maine’s 2nd Congressional District on Wednesday afternoon, though outlets had not yet called the race. As of 2 p.m. Wednesday, LePage had secured 49.9% of votes and Democrat Matt Dunlap had 48.8% with 93% of results counted, […]
text:
Former Gov. Paul LePage, Republican candidate for Maine's 2nd Congressional District, speaks to reporters at Augusta City Hall on Oct. 22, 2026, after voting early in the November election. (Photo by Kaitlyn Budion/Maine Morning Star)This is a breaking story that will be updated. 
Republican Paul LePage declared victory in the election for Maine’s 2nd Congressional District on Wednesday afternoon, though outlets had not yet called the race.
As of 2 p.m. Wednesday, LePage had secured 49.9% of votes and Democrat Matt Dunlap had 48.8% with 93% of results counted, according to initial numbers from the Bangor Daily News, which gathered totals from municipalities and partnered with Decision Desk HQ.
The Associated Press, which also had not yet called the race, had LePage at 50% and Dunlap at 49.9% with 88% counted. 
The Secretary of State’s Office has not yet weighed in on the close race or said if a ranked-choice run off would be necessary. But with so few votes separating the candidates, a recount is possible.
Democratic U.S. Rep Jared Golden currently holds the seat, but announced last November that he would not seek reelection. LePage had already announced his campaign, and faced no Republican primary challengers. Dunlap had intended to challenge Golden, and went on to defeat three other candidates in a ranked-choice runoff in the June primary. 
Nationally, Democrats are poised to take over control of the U.S. House of Representatives and Senate after many previously Republican-held districts flipped in their favor in response to President Donald Trump’s declining approval.

description: Gov. Mike Braun signed executive orders Wednesday renewing Indiana’s fuel tax suspension for another 30 days. The orders suspend the state excise and usage tax on gasoline — worth a combined 64 cents per gallon in the month of November — and lift restrictions on untaxed diesel fuel for farmers and timber harvesters through Dec. […]
text:
Indiana fuel prices reached near $4 a gallon on Oct. 24, 2026. The gas cost includes a 60-cent reduction due to the suspension of related taxes by Gov. Mike Braun. (Photo by Niki Kelly/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Gov. Mike Braun signed executive orders Wednesday renewing Indiana’s fuel tax suspension for another 30 days.
The orders suspend the state excise and usage tax on gasoline — worth a combined 64 cents per gallon in the month of November — and lift restrictions on untaxed diesel fuel for farmers and timber harvesters through Dec. 4.
“Affordability is my top priority, and I’m using every tool available to help Hoosier families and farmers save money at the pump,” Braun said in a statement Wednesday. “We’re keeping these savings for Hoosier families and farmers in place for another month while protecting funding for our roads and infrastructure.”
Indiana’s average cost for a gallon of regular gasoline came in at $3.75 Wednesday — 37 cents below the national mark, according to AAA.
This is the final anticipated fuel tax suspension.
Braun first lifted the state’s 7% gasoline usage tax in April using an obscure energy emergency law. He renewed and expanded the order the following month to cover the state’s 37-cent-per-gallon excise tax, both of which remain suspended six months later.
Braun declared a separate energy emergency in late September lifting restrictions on untaxed diesel fuel, which is typically reserved for off-road vehicles like combines.
The emergency is set to expire Dec. 4.
The governor would need to declare a new emergency to continue the suspensions, but Braun previously told reporters he is unlikely to issue another emergency so close to a new legislative session that is to begin in early January.
The Indiana Department of Transportation projected in August the state would forgo $1.1 billion in revenue if Braun suspended the gasoline taxes through early December.
Braun told reporters in September the fiscal impact of the off-road diesel order would range from $1 million to $3 million.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Defendant asks US Supreme Court to halt attempted murder retrial in New Albany
description: This still from a video captures the moment when Lane Mitchell stabs Russell Rogers in the neck at the Tallahatchie Gourmet in New Albany , Miss., on Feb. 9, 2019. The photo is time stamped 21:18:27.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Less than six months before a scheduled retrial, attorneys for a north Mississippi man acquitted by a judge in 2023 for stabbing a customer in the neck at a New Albany restaurant are asking the U.S. Supreme Court to look at double jeopardy issues in the case. 
Attorneys for Lane Mitchell argue that another trial for attempted first-degree murder would violate the Fifth Amendment clause protecting defendants from being tried twice for the same crime. 
The legal team argues that Mitchell’s case is the proper vehicle for the high court to provide clarification and uniformity about a fundamental tenet of constitutional law. The Mississippi Court of Appeals issued a 5-4 ruling in July 2025 allowing Mitchell to be retried, which also found the acquittal was not based on the evidence.
“Clarification on this question is necessary to ensure that the constitutional finality of an acquittal does not vary with the vocabulary of the trial judge or the characterization supplied by a reviewing state court,” Mitchell’s attorneys wrote in the 93-page petition.  
The state waived its right to respond to Mitchell’s petition. 
The Supreme Court justices are set to consider Mitchell’s case at a Nov. 13 conference, a private meeting in which they vote whether to take on a case for review. Only a small fraction of certiorari writs are accepted by the court. 
Mitchell is set to be retried in March in Union County Circuit Court.
His attorneys ask whether the double jeopardy clause permits a second trial after the following circumstances unfolded during Mitchell’s trial:

A jury was sworn in.
Both sides rested their case.
The trial judge entered a judgment of acquittal based on constitutional violations determined by facts established at trial. 
The trial judge didn’t separately state the prosecution’s evidence was legally insufficient.

The victim, Tennessee resident Russell Rogers, was not present at trial. The week leading up to trial, attorneys from the defense and prosecution sent subpoenas to Rogers to come to court. 
Rogers’ father, who was appointed as his conservator after the stabbing, obtained an order from the Tennessee probate court to block the defense’s subpoena, stating that Rogers’ mental health from the attack made him incapable of testifying. 
 In court records, the defense team and Union County Circuit Judge Kent Smith said Rogers “appear(ed) to be intentionally unavailable” to testify at trial because of the conservator, who the court deemed part of the prosecution. 
The prosecution proceeded with the belief that Rogers would testify, even though he did not. Mitchell testified in his defense, and both sides rested. 
Before the case went to the jury for deliberation, Smith removed the case from the group, issuing an acquittal and dismissing the charge against Mitchell. The judge cited violations of his constitutional rights, including the Fifth Amendment and the Sixth Amendment right to confront an accuser: Rogers.  
“This procedural posture matters,” Mitchell’s attorneys wrote in the petition to the U.S. Supreme Court.
The attorneys argue also that the Mississippi Court of Appeals decision conflicts with how the U.S. Supreme Court, constitutional text, history and tradition consider acquittals final. 
After Smith dismissed Mitchell’s charge, prosecutors appealed. Before trial, the Mississippi attorney general’s office appointed prosecutors because the local district attorney recused himself. Those prosecutors argued that Mitchell’s acquittal would set a precedent of dismissing “every criminal cause when a recalcitrant victim refuses to appear at trial.”
The Mississippi Court of Appeals considered the trial court’s ruling a dismissal based on violation of the compulsory process rather than an acquittal that determined guilt or innocence, which got around double jeopardy concerns. A slim majority said the state had the right to appeal and Smith was incorrect to dismiss the charge, leading the court to reverse the acquittal and return the case to Union County for a new trial. 
From that ruling, Mitchell appealed to the state Supreme Court, arguing the state couldn’t appeal and retrial would violate double jeopardy protections. The court initially agreed to review the appeal, but this year the justices dismissed that review.
The case dates back to a Feb. 9, 2019, stabbing at the Tallahatchie Gourmet restaurant in New Albany. 
Rogers, a regular customer of the restaurant, had been there for several hours when then-18 year-old Mitchell arrived and joined his parents and their friends in the bar area. Witnesses testified about Rogers’ behavior earlier in the day and how he seemed to make a young waitress feel uncomfortable. 
Lane Mitchell, seen top center, holds a knife behind his back while looking at Russell Rogers, top left, as he talks to a waitress the night of Feb. 9, 2019 at Tallahatchie Gourmet in New Albany. Moments later, Mitchell stabbed Rogers three times in the neck, leading Mitchell being charged with attempted murder. At his 2023 trial, a Union County judge ordered an acquittal for Mitchell, finding that the victim’s absence in court was a violation of the defendant’s constitutional rights. The attorney general’s office, which prosecuted the case, is appealing the acquittal in the Court of Appeals.  Credit: Courtesy of Union County Circuit Court documents.
Video of the incident presented in court and included in court records shows Mitchell taking a knife from the bar and holding it behind his back as Rogers talked to a waitress. Mitchell’s father, who worked at the restaurant, talked with Rogers, who moved toward him. That prompted Mitchell to approach Rogers from behind and stab him in the neck three times. 
Mitchell testified at trial and argued in court filings that he believed Rogers had a gun and was going to harm his father. A gun was not found in Rogers’ possession.
Rogers’ injuries nearly killed him and resulted in a diagnosis of post-traumatic stress disorder and mental issues, which months later led to the appointment of a conservator, his father Bob Rogers. 
A civil lawsuit filed in 2020 led to years of litigation revolving around access to Rogers’ medical records related to the stabbing that were contained in the lawsuit. The lawsuit was settled the same year and a protective order was issued, directing confidential information and copies to be returned or destroyed.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Montanans overwhelmingly approve 3 ballot measures
authors: Micah Drew, Keila Szpaller, Jordan Hansen
description: What had been customary in Montana for nearly a century is now constitutional. On Election Day, Montanans made nonpartisan judicial races part of the state’s DNA by adding an amendment, Constitutional Initiative 132, to the state constitution which ensures those races stay that way, despite a recent push by the GOP to make them party-affiliated.  […]
text:
A No Kings rally attendee holds a Transparent Election Initiative sign during a No Kings event on Saturday, Oct. 17, 2026 at the Montana State Capitol in Helena, MT. (Jordan Hansen / Daily Montanan)What had been customary in Montana for nearly a century is now constitutional.
On Election Day, Montanans made nonpartisan judicial races part of the state’s DNA by adding an amendment, Constitutional Initiative 132, to the state constitution which ensures those races stay that way, despite a recent push by the GOP to make them party-affiliated. 
CI-132’s support hovered around a 35-point margin. The Associated Press called the race at 11:36 p.m., on Election Night, though final ballot tabulations were still ongoing late into Wednesday morning. 
“Montana citizens just took the historic step of enshrining their right to nonpartisan judicial elections into our Constitution,” said Caitie Butler, spokesperson for Montanans for Nonpartisan Courts, which ran the initiative. “For 90 years, Montanans have elected nonpartisan judges from local courts to the Supreme Court. Thanks to the overwhelming majority of Montanans voting yes on CI-132 we protected that tradition, ensuring judges can make decisions based on the law and the Constitution, not political parties and their money. 
“Together, we set an example for the country by affirming our Montana-made model of nonpartisan judicial elections.”
The initiative will add five words to Montana’s constitution, requiring that “judicial elections shall remain nonpartisan.” 
Montana’s district and state supreme courts have stymied many of the GOP-controlled legislature’s actions in recent years, overturning laws related to LGBTQ-rights, the environment and election access. In 2025, it was a stated goal of a conservative state senate majority and Republican Gov. Greg Gianforte to change how judicial races operated, including by trying to add partisan labels to candidates in the name of transparency for voters. 
Also on Tuesday, Montanans voted for a new member of the state Supreme Court, electing Flathead County District Court Judge Amy Eddy, who campaigned on the need for judges to stay impartial in their work. Her opponent, Dan Wilson, had an endorsement and campaign funding from the state Republican Party. 
Numerous former district and supreme court judges backed CI-132 including Pat Cotter, who served on the state supreme court bench for two eight-year terms. 
“Nonpartisan judicial elections keep all of our courts accountable to the people and the Constitution, and now Montanans have spoken loud and clear: keep politics out of our courts,” Cotter said in a statement. “We know Montanans want to keep their courts impartial.”
  Initiative to protect initiatives approved 

Montanans chose with 65% of the vote to protect the initiative process in the constitution.
With most precincts fully reporting Wednesday, 284,543 Montanans had said yes to the initiative, and 152,970 had said no.
The Associated Press called the race late Tuesday, according to results on the Montana Free Press.
CI-133 protects people’s right to propose laws through ballot measures and aims to prevent government interference in the process.
“These results show that Montanans support permanent protections for our ballot measure process,” said Montanans Decide campaign manager SK Rossi in a statement Wednesday. “Ballot measures are a part of what makes Montana, Montana – and despite attempts to weaken the process, everyday Montanans will continue to have a way to make their voices heard, hold government accountable, and vote directly on the issues that impact their lives.” 
CI-133 amends Article II of the state constitution to add the following language, in part:

        “The people have a fundamental right to exercise their powers of initiative and referendum under Article III and Article XIV. The government may not deny or burden this right unless justified by a compelling government interest achieved by the least restrictive means.”    
Opponents described the initiative as vague and unnecessary, and said it wasn’t clear how the courts would interpret the language.
But Montanans Decide, the coalition to protect the initiative process, said CI-133 was straightforward.
The measure “outlines clear requirements for impartial, predictable, open and timely processes for approving petitions and ballot statements, resolving legal challenges, gathering signatures, and verifying signatures,” Montanans Decide said in a news release. “The initiative prevents the government from taking sides on ballot measures and using taxpayer dollars to influence voters.”
Montanans across the political spectrum said they believe decisions about Montana’s future should belong to Montana voters, “not special interests or politicians in Helena,” Rossi said. “We are grateful to everyone who gathered signatures, knocked on doors, talked with their neighbors, and helped educate voters. Thank you for securing this right, now and for the future.” 
Montanans Decide pulled in at least $2.44 million for the initiative since December 2025.
Funders include American Opportunity Action, with a mission that includes holding government accountable to the people; The Fairness Project, which works to protect voter access to ballot measures; and the GI Social Welfare Fund, which includes a focus on voter rights.
The campaign earlier said the money was necessary “because of ongoing government interference in the initiative process,” including ones that result in legal battles.
  ‘The Montana Plan’ wins, too 

Montana voters also approved Initiative 194, which seeks to remove corporate spending from Montana politics.
Unlike the other two initiatives, it does not add anything to the state’s constitution. It instead utilizes the citizen’s right to propose state laws.
The vote received approval from 65% of voters in early returns, while 35% said no. Nearly 57% of the state’s ballots had been counted by 11 a.m. Wednesday. The Associated Press called the race early Wednesday morning.
Called “The Montana Plan,” the initiative is based upon the concept that corporations are regulated by states, and that Montana could limit corporate powers when it comes to contributing to elections, candidates and political parties.
The initiative was brought by the Transparent Election Initiative, a group seeking to remove “dark money” from politics. The initiative was fought by several groups, including the Montana Chamber of Commerce, the Montana Mining Association and the Montana Petroleum Association. The state Republican party also added opposition to I-194 to its party platform.
“We were up against some of the biggest special interests in Montana, and today, the people of Montana have won,” said Jeff Mangan, founder and president of the Transparent Election Initiative, in a press release. “They had high-powered corporate lawyers and powerful industry associations. We had hundreds of volunteers, small business owners, and Montanans who believed their elections should belong to them.”
Mangan also said in the release that TEI was prepared to “defend what Montanans voted for in the courts, in the Legislature and even by bringing this back to voters as a constitutional amendment in 2028.”
Government corruption was a major issue in Tuesday night’s midterm election and removing corporate from politics has gained significant traction since the 2024 U.S. Senate race in Montana. That year, Tim Sheehy flipped the seat for Republicans, and saw hundreds of millions of dollars in spending in the lead-up to the election.
“Montana just became the first state where the voters themselves said corporations don’t get to buy our elections,” said Russ Cleveland, Executive Director of Partnerships for TEI, in a statement. “Nobody in Washington did this for us. Folks stood outside grocery stores and at farmers markets with clipboards, sat at kitchen tables with their neighbors and talked about what kind of state they wanted to live in. People who don’t agree on much found out they agree on this, and that’s what won tonight.”
In a call on Wednesday, Cleveland added that TEI expects an injunction to be filed over the new law. The Legislature will also have an opportunity to change the law during the 2027 Session and Cleveland said the group was already gathering legislators friendly to their efforts.
This started back in July, he said.
“We’ve got bipartisan support across the board of people that are committed to keeping intact,” Cleveland said.

name: National
title: Idaho voters reject abortion ballot measure as Missouri, Nevada and Virginia back access
description: Nationwide results for abortion ballot initiatives on Tuesday night largely favored protecting access to abortion and other reproductive care, with the exception of Idaho, where a measure that would have restored access to abortion was soundly defeated. Idaho’s outcome stood in stark contrast to the other three ballot questions, with 56% voting against the a[...]
text:
A “Stop Prop 1” sign leans up against the wall during an election night watch party on Nov. 3, 2026, in Boise, Idaho. Voters soundly defeated a measure that would have restored access to abortion in the state, a sharp contrast with outcomes in three other states that expanded or enshrined abortion rights. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)Nationwide results for abortion ballot initiatives on Tuesday night largely favored protecting access to abortion and other reproductive care, with the exception of Idaho, where a measure that would have restored access to abortion was soundly defeated.
Idaho’s outcome stood in stark contrast to the other three ballot questions, with 56% voting against the approval of Proposition 1 and 44% voting in favor, nearly the inverse of Missouri’s outcome, where 55% of voters struck down an amendment that would have reinstated the ban that was overturned through a ballot initiative in 2024. 
Other abortion-related measures were on the ballot in Nevada and Virginia, two states where abortion is already accessible until 24 weeks and 26 weeks of pregnancy, respectively. Voters in both of those states passed constitutional amendments ensuring the right to abortion. 
The outcome in Idaho ensures the state’s abortion ban remains intact. The ban prohibits abortion at any stage of pregnancy with exceptions only for rape and incest in the first trimester and to save a pregnant patient’s life.
Blaine Conzatti, president of the Idaho Family Policy Center, the organization that helped craft the ban and campaigned against the initiative, said in a statement that “abortion advocates fundamentally misunderstood Idaho.”
“As we proved last night, a broad majority of Idaho voters support our pro-life laws,” Conzatti said. “This is what happens when Christians speak out and get engaged — we win.” 
Melanie Folwell, executive director of Idahoans United for Women and Families and lead organizer of the initiative, said in a statement that more than $1.3 million in donations from the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints and the Catholic Diocese of Boise fueled a disinformation campaign about what the law would do. 
Told her baby wouldn’t survive, she had to leave Idaho for an abortion. She’s sharing her story.

“We’re encouraging Idahoans to reach out to their lawmakers, particularly those politicians who encouraged voters to reject Prop 1 and wait for a legislative fix, and demand needed exceptions in the coming session,” Folwell said. 
A federal appeals court ruled on Oct. 30 that Idaho’s law does not include exceptions for a pregnant person whose physical or mental health is in jeopardy by continuing the pregnancy, a situation that Idaho doctors have repeatedly said puts them in a position to feel compelled to wait until a patient’s life is in danger before acting. 
A peer-reviewed study published in 2025 in JAMA showed 114 OB-GYNs left Idaho or stopped practicing obstetrics between August 2022 and December 2024, the first two years after the ban took effect. That number represents 43% of the 268 physicians practicing obstetrics statewide.
Several of those who left have said publicly that the ban made it more difficult to do their jobs without fear of criminal prosecution. Providers found guilty of violating the ban face up to five years in prison, the revocation of their medical license and up to $20,000 in civil penalties. Many doctors who have continued to practice obstetrics and gynecology in Idaho say the loss of those providers has increased their workload to a stressful and at times dangerous degree. 
In the months leading up to the vote, Idaho women shared their stories of needing to seek care in other states, including Utah, because of fatal fetal anomalies, along with others who said their care during a miscarriage was delayed, causing dangerous infections. 
With the failure of the ballot measure, pregnant patients who need an abortion will continue to need to seek care in other states. 
Dr. Caitlin Gustafson, a physician in rural Idaho and board president of the Idaho Coalition for Safe Healthcare, told Stateline she was deeply saddened by the results, but said the fight is “far from over” because she knows every community across Idaho is affected by the law. 
“The work ahead is to make sure that other aspects of reproductive healthcare can stay in place, that we can proactively protect IVF, contraception, and timely miscarriage care,” Gustafson said. “Because that was part of this effort too. We must protect all areas of reproductive freedom and privacy.  I remain committed to fight for women, families, and my medical colleagues who provide safe healthcare across Idaho.” 
Missouri defeats amendment despite heavy lawmaker involvement 
The Fairness Project, a national nonprofit organization that supports ballot initiatives on economic and social issues, funded efforts to defeat Amendment 3 in Missouri, where the legislature attempted to undo an initiative passed by voters in 2024. 
“Missouri is a shining example of politicians trying to take people’s rights away and voters taking them right back,” said Hannah Ledford, executive director of the Fairness Project, in an interview Wednesday. “It is so cool.” 
Ledford said the outcome in Idaho compared with Missouri wasn’t surprising, in part because Missouri’s measure was a defensive move against the legislature attempting to take a right away, while Idaho’s initiative was proactive and would grant rights. 
“The proactive question is just inherently more difficult than convincing voters to vote ‘no,’” Ledford said. 
According to the Missouri Independent, the Amendment 3 effort had significant and organized support from Republican lawmakers this time around, along with Gov. Mike Kehoe’s office and many of the state’s largest churches. It also would have added a constitutional amendment prohibiting gender-affirming care for minors, which is already state law. 
National anti-abortion leaders had pointed to Missouri’s amendment as a possible model for reinstating abortion bans in other states by pairing abortion restrictions with a ban on gender-affirming care.
“When Missouri wins, every other state will learn that these bad amendments can be reversed and undone. But if it loses, no other state will likely try this again for a long time, perhaps for a generation,” said David Bereit, executive director of the Virginia-based Life Leadership Conference, during a virtual fundraising event in October.
Virginia, Nevada enshrine constitutional right to an abortion 
Nevada voters easily passed the second round of the measure amending the constitution to include a right to abortion up to fetal viability, generally considered to be about 22 to 24 weeks of pregnancy. After that point, exceptions could be made to preserve a pregnant person’s life or health. About 63% of voters approved the measure. State law requires that constitutional amendments be passed by voters twice to take effect — it passed with 64% approval in 2024.  
In Virginia, voters approved the amendment that protects the freedom to make decisions about prenatal and postpartum care, birth control, childbirth, abortion, miscarriage management and fertility care. It also protects doctors, nurses and patients from being punished for those decisions and allows exceptions during later pregnancy for abortion if the pregnant patient’s health is at risk or the fetus cannot survive. The measure garnered 62% approval from Virginia voters. 
“Never again will our reproductive rights be a political football in Virginia,” said Han Jones, campaign manager for Virginians For Reproductive Freedom, on Tuesday, according to Virginia Mercury. “It takes multi-year concerted work, but as you can see in Virginia, it’s paying off.” 
Missouri Independent reporter Anna Spoerre and Virginia Mercury reporter Charlotte Rene Woods contributed to this report.
Stateline reporter Kelcie Moseley-Morris can be reached at kmoseley@stateline.org.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Legislators plan for 3.5% increase in tax revenue, keeping up with inflation
description: Gov. Tate Reeves, left, discusses proposed revenue estimates with Lt. Gov. Delbert Hosemann during a meeting of the Joint Legislative Budget Committee, Wednesday, Nov. 15, 2023, in Jackson.
text:
In the upcoming 2027 session, the Mississippi Legislature will have an additional $266 million to spend, an increase of 3.5% from last year’s estimate partially driven by changes in tax collections, wage growth and inflation.
Wednesday’s Joint Legislative Budget Committee meeting was just the latest step in the state budget process. The committee, which consists of state House and Senate members, and Gov. Tate Reeves adopted a revenue estimate of $7.8 billion for the next fiscal year, which begins July 1. The bulk of the money comes from state taxes, such as sales and income taxes. 
The revenue estimate, presented by Corey Miller, the state economist, is based on tax collections to date and state and national economic conditions. The estimate may be adjusted based on new data. Miller said the growth is good, given the inflation rate, which is about 3.4% this year.
Mississippi takes a conservative approach when it comes to budget estimates and in recent years has collected more than it estimated. 
Ahead of the upcoming session, the Legislature and the governor will each develop a proposed budget based on the revenue estimate for how to divide the money between state agencies. The Legislature will then pass a final budget during the session. 
During the COVID-19 pandemic, the state saw an increase in actual revenue collections of about 24% from 2020 to 2023. However, over the last few years revenue collections have barely changed, hovering around $7.6 billion, even as many agencies are requesting more funds.The approximately $5.65 billion collected in 2017 adjusted for inflation would be worth about $7.68 billion in 2026 dollars – a little more than last fiscal year’s revenue estimate of $7.53 billion.


The Legislature may need the additional revenue projected to be collected to offset budget pressures during the 2027 legislative session, which begins in January. The Division of Medicaid requested around $179 million more than last year, about a 15% increase year over year as it faces a budget deficit. The Mississippi Institutions of Higher Learning, which governs the state’s public universities, asked for an additional $93 million, although lawmakers discussed keeping the funding level at a recent budget meeting.
State revenue represents a portion of the state’s overall budget, which was about $28 billion last year. Mississippi is consistently one of the top 10 states most reliant on federal funding. Last year, over 40% of the state’s budget came from the federal government.
Miller said the revenue estimate was driven by expected growth in sales, corporate income and use tax revenues, as well as a slower than expected rate of decline in income tax collections. Historically, close to 70% of the state’s revenue comes from sales and income taxes. 
Sales taxes generate the most revenue for the state and are expected to make up around 40% of all state revenue this year. The state expects to collect more in sales taxes next year due to inflation – higher prices means the state collects more in sales taxes and continued wage growth. 
Personal income in Mississippi has grown by around 5% annually for the past three years, with a projected average of about a 3.8% annual increase over the next three years. 
This wage growth and larger number of people working in the state have resulted in a slower than expected decline in income tax revenue. In 2025, Mississippi voted to gradually eliminate the income tax, which used to make up about a third of the state’s revenue. Gov. Tate Reeves cautioned that this trend will not continue but remained optimistic about the state’s financial future.
“As the individual income tax rate continues to decline, the total dollars collected in income revenue, at some point we’ll roll over and we will start seeing declines there. But the good news is we were $5.8 billion total revenue seven years ago, we’re $7.8 billion in total revenue now,” Reeves said.
Reeves said that, by allowing more people to “keep more of their own money,” the state’s economy has grown resulting in more jobs and higher wages.
“I think Mississippi’s future is bright, and I think we can continue this economic growth,” Reeves said.

Democrats flipped four legislative districts in Ma[...]
text:
Democratic gubernatorial nominee Doug Jones speaks to 200 supporters at an Election Night gathering in Birmingham, Alabama on Nov. 3, 2026. Jones conceded the Alabama gubernatorial race on Wednesday in what became the closest contest for the office since 2002. (Andi Rice for Alabama Reflector)Democratic gubernatorial nominee Doug Jones Wednesday conceded in Alabama’s gubernatorial race in what became the closest contest for that office since 2002. 
In a statement Wednesday afternoon, Jones repeated that the objective of his campaign was not to win but to make gains across the state for Democrats. Democrats flipped four legislative districts in Madison and Shelby counties, and U.S. Rep. Shomari Figures, D-Montgomery, successfully fought a GOP attempt to gerrymander his district.
“While we came up short in this election, we accomplished so much together that I believe will bode well for Alabama in the future,” Jones said.
