As of Wednesday at 12:18 p.m., Tuberville received 872,561 votes (51.8%), and Jones got 806,253 votes (47.9%), according to unofficial results. Tuberville declared victory Tuesday with less than 70% of ballots counted. The Associated Press had not made a call in the race at the time, and Jones declined to concede, citing outstanding ballots were in Democratic-leaning counties like Jefferson, Greene and Tuscaloosa. 
A message seeking comment from the Tuberville campaign was sent Wednesday afternoon.
“But this campaign was never about me; it was always about giving the people of Alabama choices, fresh ideas, and hope for a better future. We brought new people into the political process and helped lay the groundwork for Democrats to compete in elections for years to come,” Jones said.
Tommy Tuberville wins Alabama governor’s race; Doug Jones does not concede

Ballots cast for Democratic candidates increased in all 67 counties on Tuesday, according to election data. Jones cited Figures’ win and broader improvements by Democratic candidates. 
“Local candidates across Alabama either won their races or finished stronger than expected,” he said. “Those are big wins. In districts that some people had written off as unwinnable, Alabama voters proved otherwise.”
Jones congratulated Tuberville on his win and offered him support in the “tough issues ahead.” State officials have repeatedly warned state agencies that fiscal year 2028 will be “challenging” and budgets will need to be conservative. The state’s two public employee insurance boards are seeking more funding and increasing premiums or direct costs amid rising healthcare costs. 
“The responsibility for Alabama’s future doesn’t rest with one person. It belongs to all of us. I encourage every Alabamian to stay involved, to hold our elected leaders accountable, and to make sure their voices are heard, not just on election day, but every day,” he said.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Mass. just tackled 9 ballot questions. Here’s where each landed, and what comes next.
description: Facing nine ballot questions, Bay Staters rejected efforts to throw out existing cannabis and gun laws, and to change an obscure tax cap law. They gave the green light to legislative transparency and Election Day voter registration while waving away a quest to replace party primaries with nonpartisan ones. A new state agency will now be allowed to unionize, [...]
text:
DEMOCRATS IN MASSACHUSETTS are cheering their party’s return to power, as a blue wave crashed around the country and claimed control of Congress. The state’s Democratic leadership swept back into office, with every major race called before midnight in Massachusetts.  
The real question was how voters would handle a record-tying amount of direct democracy at the ballot box.  
Facing nine ballot questions, Bay Staters rejected efforts to throw out existing cannabis and gun laws, and to change an obscure tax cap law. They gave the green light to legislative transparency and Election Day voter registration while waving away a quest to replace party primaries with nonpartisan ones. A new state agency will now be allowed to unionize, and there may be more money for conservation efforts in the next few years. 
With all but one of the measures decided, all but two of their outcomes official, and a slew of new policies heading into effect in the next few years, eyes are now on Beacon Hill and how legislators choose to respond to the will of the voters. 
Here’s how it all shook out:  
QUESTION 1 — Public Records — YES 
For the second cycle in a row, State Auditor Diana DiZoglio successfully pushed a ballot measure aimed at making the Legislature’s inner workings more accessible. Question 1, which the Associated Press called at about 11:40 p.m., makes the Legislature and the governor’s office subject to the public records law, with some exceptions to protect constituent privacy. 
With just over 80 percent of votes counted, the measure was leading by a staggering margin, 86 percent to 14 percent.  
The ballot measure was two things at once: a common enough “good government” reform where voters decided if their state lawmakers should follow the same laws as every city and town legislative body, and a follow-up to a ballot question voters overwhelmingly approved in 2024 to authorize the state auditor to probe the Legislature, which Beacon Hill leadership has forcefully opposed. 
“It’s a very difficult sell to make to anybody that the Legislature and governor shouldn’t be subject to the public records law,” Jonathan Cohn, policy director of Progressive Massachusetts, said in late September. “Straightforward good government questions will always resonate with voters.” 
Legislative leaders have said the measure raises serious separation of powers issues. In the coming weeks, they may surface legislation before January that could alter the newly passed public records law. 
Read more on the results from CommonWealth Beacon reporter Chris Lisinski. 
Auditor Diana DiZoglio testifies alongside members of her team at a Joint Ways and Means Committee hearing on February 11, 2026. Chris Lisinski/CommonWealth Beacon
QUESTION 2 — CPCS Union — YES 
There could soon be one more public sector union in town, after voters approved a ballot measure to allow employees at the Committee for Public Counsel Services to collectively bargain. The measure does not create a union automatically, but the employees are now empowered to form one and negotiate with the state over things like work conditions and hours. 
The Associated Press projected Question 2 would pass at about 12:30 a.m. on Wednesday. The yes side held a strong lead, of about 65 percent to 35 percent, with about 80 percent of votes counted on Wednesday morning around 8 a.m. 
Over 180 state agencies, including other employees in the court system, are allowed to collectively bargain. But CPCS employees like public defenders, secretaries, and social workers have long been left off the list. Beacon Hill leadership has shown little interest in legislation filed over several consecutive cycles that would have added CPCS to the list of public agencies whose staff is able to unionize and bargain. 
A Tufts Center for State Policy Analysis review of the question, which faced no formal opposition, found it would likely lead to improved pay, more consistent employment terms, firmer job security, a clearer process to express employee grievances, and a more robust voice in agency decision-making. But it could also complicate their ability to flexibly serve low-income clients and will likely affect how much the state relies on private-sector public defenders known as bar advocates.  
QUESTION 3 — All-party primaries — NO 
A measure that would have overhauled the state’s primary system went down in defeat, with the Associated Press calling the race at 1:47 a.m. on Wednesday. Had it passed, the ballot question would replace the current primary rules, where parties each hold separate primaries to determine which Democrat and Republican advance to the general election. Instead, all candidates would all face off in a single primary from which the top two would have advanced to the general election regardless of affiliation. 
The no side looked held 61 percent of the vote to the yes side’s 39 percent on Wednesday morning, around 8 a.m., with about 80 percent of all votes counted. 
One of the fiercest fights of the ballot season, the all-party primary question pitted both major parties and legislative leadership, along with some progressive groups and unions, against the advocates who pitched the question and the private equity executives pouring money into the effort. 
It’s a disappointing end for a well-funded operation helmed by Danielle Allen, a political scientist who ran for governor four years ago and touted the overhaul as a way to generate much-needed competitiveness. 
“When you throw grit into the gears of a political machine, the machine fights back,” the Coalition for Healthy Democracy, which led the charge for the measure, wrote in an emailed statement. “The people who benefit most from the way things are fought hard for this result.” 
Jordan Berg Powers, chair of the opposition campaign Voter Rights MA said the rejection was a sign of “grassroot power.” 
“We did not have millions of dollars in private equity money,” Powers said in a statement at 11 p.m. Tuesday. “But what we had mattered: community activists, labor unions, grassroots organizations, and elected officials united in a broad ideological coalition to say ‘no’ to billionaires buying our democracy.” 
Read more on the results from CommonWealth Beacon reporter Chris Lisinski. 
QUESTION 4 — Election Day Registration — YES 
This long-sought reform, allowing Bay Staters to register to vote on Election Day, was championed for almost a decade by Secretary of State William Galvin only to be met with shrugs on Beacon Hill. Galvin decided this cycle to pitch the idea directly to voters with a ballot question, circumventing the lack of movement in the Legislature. 
And voters signed on for the change, with the Associated Press calling it for the yes side overnight. Yes votes were leading 57 percent to 43 percent by Wednesday morning. 
Starting in 2028, Bay Staters will be able to register at their polling place on Election Day, then cast a ballot. For the next federal election — this time with the presidency on the line — it’s as simple as heading to a polling place, presenting proof of residency, and signing a written oath. But for next year’s municipal elections, the current deadlines will remain in place: Residents must register to vote or update their address at least 10 days in advance of the election. 
The coalition behind the Election Day registration measure, which includes Common Cause Massachusetts, the state’s League of Women Voters chapter, and the ACLU of Massachusetts, called the policy a “tried-and-true reform” and said “voters resoundingly support expanding access to the polls for every eligible citizen.” 
Read more on the results from CommonWealth Beacon reporter Chris Lisinski. 
Secretary of State William Galvin addresses reporters ahead of the 2026 primaries. (Photo by Jennifer Smith | CommonWealth Beacon)
QUESTION 5 — Tax Cap Change — NO (but not yet called) 
Proponents of Question 5, which would have led to more tax refunds under the existing law known as Chapter 62F, conceded defeat Wednesday morning. The race had not yet been called by the Associated Press as of midday, but the cadre of influential business groups said “voters have chosen to retain the existing law.” 
“That decision deserves respect, even as important questions remain about the growth of state spending, the cost of living and doing business, and Massachusetts’ ability to retain residents, jobs, and investment,” Taxpayers for an Affordable MA, the group pushing the question, said in a statement. 
Labor unions opposed the measure, arguing that forcing Beacon Hill to return money to taxpayers more frequently would eat away at the state’s ability to fund popular programs and services. 
“The people of Massachusetts chose to protect critical state funding for healthcare, education, housing, and local aid; not slash state spending to pay for occasional tax rebates,” said Harris Gruman, executive director of the SEIU Massachusetts State Council and a leader of the opposition campaign. “Despite not running any advertising until the final week of the campaign, our grassroots campaign of working people defeated the corporate lobby at the ballot.” 
As of 1:15 p.m. Wednesday, the measure was slightly but steadily trailing by about 52 percent to 48 percent. More than 93 percent of the votes had been tallied. 
The proposed tax cap change was one of two business-backed ballot measures this cycle that had been aimed at putting a lid on taxes but criticized by progressives and lawmakers as benefiting wealthy residents while making it harder for the state to fund its many social supports. The other measure was jettisoned by the state’s high court for an erroneous summary by the attorney general’s office.  
As Bay Staters struggle with high costs, Beacon Hill fretted that the tax cap change could pass, and lawmakers prepared legislation that could undercut it. Ultimately, it looks like they won’t need to pull that ripcord, but the proponents have signaled that they may be back at the ballot box soon enough. 
Colin Reed, spokesperson for the Mass Opportunity Alliance, said the group was disappointed by the apparent outcome, which “does not resolve the underlying questions about the cost of living and doing business in Massachusetts, or the loss of residents and economic opportunity.” 
Read more on the results from CommonWealth Beacon reporter Chris Lisinski. 
QUESTION 6 — Conservation Funding — YES 
Voters approved a measure that supporters say could steer $100 million annually from existing sporting goods sales tax revenues toward a new nature conservation fund. 
“The results of Question 6 confirm what we already knew: that protecting the outdoors has broad appeal,” Mass Audubon President David O’Neill said in a statement. “This is an historic night for the nature of Massachusetts.” 
By Wednesday morning, the yes side held a 61 percent to 39 percent lead, and the Associated Press had called the race. 
The measure, which was backed by environmental groups and endorsed by Gov. Maura Healey, faced no formal opposition but prompted gentle skepticism from some. Attracting substantial financial support from a few wealthy individuals, the question means the fund will be established to support clean drinking water, create and improve local parks, and protect wildlife habitats without raising taxes or levying a new one.  
Instead, future revenue from the sales tax already being collected from purchases of camping equipment, hunting and fishing gear, and golf clubs will boost the new fund. But it will happen only if lawmakers choose to allocate those funds, and some on Beacon Hill have warned about the ramifications of setting state spending decisions via ballot and taking money out of the General Fund during a time of fiscal constraints. 
The MassGOP suggested a no vote, the Massachusetts Democratic party recommended a yes vote, and it was the only question where Progressive Massachusetts said people should “vote how you want.”  
Supporters cheered the win on Tuesday night as an important signal that conservation efforts should not wait for an indifferent Legislature. 
“Massachusetts has been at the forefront of land conservation for generations, but for years we’ve underfunded nature,” said Katie Theoharides, president of The Trustees. 
Read more on the results from CommonWealth Beacon reporter Jordan Wolman. 
Katie Theohardies, president of The Trustees conservation organization and a former state environmental secretary, speaks at an Election Night event on November 3, 2026 hosted by supporters of a ballot question to earmark tax revenue for nature preservation. Chris Lisinski/CommonWealth Beacon
QUESTION 7 — Starter Homes — TBD 
By Wednesday afternoon, the lone ballot question whose outcome remained unclear was the one that involved the bête noire of the state’s affordability crisis: housing.  
The measure, if passed, would force municipalities to allow homes on smaller lots, preventing local governments from requiring more than 5,000 square feet and 50 feet of frontage to build a single-family home on lots served by water and sewer. Proponents said the large lot sizes now required in many municipalities were stifling new construction that could be more affordable to more households. 
This “Legalize Starter Homes” campaign sought to build on a recent trend of overriding local control on zoning rules, following on the heels of the MBTA Communities multifamily housing law and the statewide legalization of accessory dwelling units. Like those earlier laws, which Beacon Hill leaders and housing abundance groups say are essential to building the 222,000 units needed by 2035 to meet demand, opposition came from cities and towns that say they are best positioned to decide what housing fits their communities. 
Well into Wednesday, Question 7 remained too close to call, with the yes and no votes just 1 percentage point apart. 
QUESTION 8 — Recreational Marijuana Rollback — NO 
Legal recreational cannabis is staying on the books, after voters rejected Question 8.  
The measure, pushed by a group backed by the national anti-legalization organization Smart Approaches to Marijuana (SAM), would have dismantled the state’s recreational cannabis industry and created new penalties for possessing a certain amount of marijuana. Proponents said tax revenue from recreational marijuana sales does not make up for what they consider the associated economic and societal costs of legalization. 
The campaign was dogged early on by allegations with keep of fraudulent signature gathering, but the ballot law commission ruled against most of those claims, citing a lack of substantial evidence.  
Some voters still had the episode on their minds as they hit the polls. Outside a Somerville polling place Tuesday night, voter Jack Branigan voiced his strong opposition to the question for just that reason, citing what he called “pretty shady” tactics by signature gatherers early in the repeal campaign. 
“I signed a petition outside a supermarket, and the people who spoke to me just kind of gestured at some very vague, positive idea,” he recalled. “I signed it, not even thinking twice about it. More fool I — I later found out that was the group pushing to put the marijuana question back on the ballot.” 
The Associated Press called the question just before midnight, and voters on Wednesday were opting, by a three to one margin, to keep in place the current system — itself the result of a ballot measure 10 years ago. 
“Voters told an out-of-state effort that wanted to dismantle a decade of work and replace progress with restrictive policies, ‘No,’” said Stop the Repeal campaign chair Ryan Dominguez in a statement. “Massachusetts voters know that our safe, regulated cannabis market is working.” 
The recreational cannabis industry argued the consequences for a repeal would be disastrous. The industry employs tens of thousands of people in the state, and state regulators say Massachusetts has pulled in about $2 billion in tax revenue since legalization. 
New Dia dispensary in Fenway (Emily Glick/CommonWealth Beacon)
QUESTION 9 — Gun Law Repeal — YES (keeps the law) 
They may have some gripes with the Legislature, but Massachusetts voters were mostly happy with the firearm law it passed two years ago and turned aside an attempt by gun rights advocates to repeal it. 
Supporters of keeping the law in place celebrated victory around 10:45 p.m., as Ruth Zakarin, chair of the Yes on 9 campaign, described the outcome as a way to “protect the strong foundation that we have already built with this legislation and with the legislation that came before it.” Zakarin noted that Massachusetts has one of the lowest rates of gun violence in the country, but she said “they’re not low enough.” 
“Every shooting is a crisis and a call to action,” she said. “No family should be missing a family member at their dinner table, and no community should be left traumatized by gun violence.”  
The sweeping legislation enhanced requirements on training, licensing, and data collection, and created regulations for ghost guns and 3-D printed guns. Second Amendment groups quickly moved to repeal the law, arguing the legislation was an unacceptable intrusion from liberal lawmakers and violated their constitutional rights. 
The Associated Press called the question around 12:20 a.m. on Wednesday. As a repeal referendum, the yes and no votes were reversed. A yes vote meant keeping the law, and a no vote would toss it. Voters came down firmly on the yes side, with 67 percent in favor of keeping the law and 33 percent voting to repeal with about 82 percent of the votes tallied. 
Voters may have another repeal effort to look forward to in the near future, as opponents of a recently signed late-term abortion law say they have gathered enough signatures to trigger a referendum in 2028.

text:
Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Alani Bankhead stands during an election night party on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026 in Helena, MT. (Jordan Hansen / Daily Montanan)Alani Bankhead, the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate in Montana, congratulated Republican Kurt Alme in his U.S. Senate win in a statement Wednesday.
Bankhead, a military veteran, also thanked her supporters for the energy they brought to her campaign.
Alme declared a win late Tuesday, and independent candidate Seth Bodnar, who earned the second most votes, conceded just before midnight.
Bankhead said she’d never seen people work harder for something they believed in, and she thanked people who gave even $5 to show the campaign owed nothing to corporate and out-of-state money.
Bankhead’s campaign pointed out that “prominent Democrats” backed independent U.S. Senate candidates instead of a Democratic nominee in four states including Montana, and all lost.
“We ran on the belief that the Democratic Party is worth rebuilding, not abandoning,” Bankhead said. “We don’t fix the party by denouncing the party, or running from it. We fix the party by listening to the people.”
Bankhead said she would continue to work to elevate Montanans voices, and she encouraged Alme to answer to the people, not donors. Libertarian Kyle Austin also ran.
An email from her campaign said her website would soon post resources for supporters who want to get involved in their county party or run for local office.
“Thank you, Montana,” Bankhead said. “It has been a privilege.”

name: National
title: Voters in five states back bans on noncitizen voting while one state bucks trend
description: Voters in five states approved new citizenship voting requirements on Tuesday while Arizona voters rejected theirs. Proposals to explicitly bar noncitizens from voting were on the ballot this week in six states: Alaska, Arizona, Arkansas, Kansas, South Dakota and West Virginia. Arizona voters defeated Proposition 144, which would have mandated that only citi[...]
text:
A Star Wars-themed campaign sign opposing Proposition 144 at a Phoenix intersection. Arizona voters defeated Proposition 144, which would have mandated that only citizens could register and vote in Arizona elections. (Photo by Jim Small/Arizona Mirror)Voters in five states approved new citizenship voting requirements on Tuesday while Arizona voters rejected theirs.
Proposals to explicitly bar noncitizens from voting were on the ballot this week in six states: Alaska, Arizona, Arkansas, Kansas, South Dakota and West Virginia.
Arizona voters defeated Proposition 144, which would have mandated that only citizens could register and vote in Arizona elections.
Arizona’s measure was much broader than those in other states. The citizenship voting requirement was included in a more sweeping proposal that would have required government-issued ID to cast in-person and mail-in ballots, banned foreign contributions in elections, and allowed voters to have their ballots counted at their polling precinct on election day.
Opponents were surprised the measure was defeated, reported the Arizona Mirror. Republicans and other supporters said it would make state elections faster and more secure. But critics including voting rights groups worried it would lead to the end of no-excuse mail-in voting.
Federal law already bars noncitizens from voting in federal elections, and no state currently allows noncitizens to vote in statewide elections.
Most states, including Arkansas, Kansas and South Dakota, already have citizenship voting requirements in state law or their constitutions, making the ballot measures seem redundant at first glance.
But sponsors of the citizenship voting requirements — primarily Republicans — said they wanted to preemptively bar cities or other local governments from allowing noncitizens to vote in local elections, as municipalities in California, Maryland and Vermont have done. Legal experts say that some state laws that seem to require citizenship to vote can be interpreted to allow noncitizen voters in certain elections.
Voters in West Virginia overwhelmingly supported adding the amendment to the state constitution to bar noncitizens from voting.
The amendment “would ensure that no future legislature could just simply change the election law with only a bill,” said West Virginia state Sen. Patricia Rucker, a Republican who sponsored the legislation that proposed the amendment, in September.
Rucker said Tuesday that she was “proud that West Virginia’s voters chose to protect the integrity of our elections” by voting yes on the amendment, reported the West Virginia Watch.
Critics of Kansas’s newly approved ballot measure worry it could make it harder for people to legally vote in the future.
“The supermajority in our legislature has a documented history of attempting to restrict voting in various ways,” Amii Castle, a law professor at the University of Kansas, told the Kansas Reflector. “My concern is that they’re going to use that to justify or as a pretext to say, ‘Well, wait a minute. We amended our constitution. Now it says only citizens can vote, therefore, prove your citizenship. Bring your documents.’”
This year’s ballot measures are the latest in a flurry of similar initiatives in recent years: Between 2018 and last year, states put 15 citizenship requirement measures on their ballots and voters approved all of them.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Commentary: Editor’s Notebook: In a blue wave, one nonpartisan electoral victory that’s very good for democracy
description: The blue wave that swept America made Tuesday a very good night for university presidents and law firms and Haitian refugees and immigrants, and all the other people who have suffered the worst excesses of a vengeful President Donald Trump and his feckless administration.  That wave didn’t sweep Kentucky so much as splash it around […]
text:
Last March, CivicLex organized the first Civic Assembly in Lexington to review Lexington's merged government charter. (Photo courtesy Brandon Turner, Unsung Hero Media)The blue wave that swept America made Tuesday a very good night for university presidents and law firms and Haitian refugees and immigrants, and all the other people who have suffered the worst excesses of a vengeful President Donald Trump and his feckless administration. 
That wave didn’t sweep Kentucky so much as splash it around the edges; still, the flipping of the 6th Congressional District and nine Republican statehouse seats may put the GOP supermajority in a slightly less arrogant, slightly more conciliatory mood as the next General Assembly session approaches. Maybe they will stay away from culture wars and focus on affordability.
But something else happened Tuesday night in Lexington that’s very hopeful and very interesting. Three ballot amendments passed in a very commanding fashion.
The first would raise Urban County Council members’ salaries to Lexington’s average income of $59,987starting in 2031. Several retiring members said they could not afford the council’s nearly full-time work on a part-time schedule.
The second would require accountability for those council members to show up to meetings and do their jobs. That one passed by 94%.
And the third would require a review of the Lexington-Fayette Urban County Government’s charter every eight years.
But those amendments were put on the ballot through a process known as Civic Assembly. CivicLex, a journalism and civic education nonprofit in Lexington convened 30 people who represented Lexington’s demographics in age, income and political affiliation. Over nearly a month, they gathered and discussed what Lexington’s needs were. And 80 percent of them agreed on these three amendments. 
“I think it’s super exciting,” said CivicLex Executive Director Richard Young who helped lead the process with Deputy Director Kit Anderson. “We were blown away by the margins, especially on numbers two and three. Our assembly members were so over the moon about it.”
The process was long, about three years from the first discussion to the 35 hours of meetings that took place last March. 
“I think it’s proof that trying new processes and bringing citizens into decision making helps get policies that people want,” Young said. “It shows that alternative methods to what we traditionally do in our political life can really help people overcome differences and produce results that are compelling and popular.”
Young said he hopes other Kentucky communities will look into taking on problems with parts and pieces of the civic assembly process, particularly working with a group of people who match that community’s demographics.
“That helps mitigate things like political ideology, it brings a truly representative group of politically diverse people to the table, which is especially important in places like Kentucky,” he said. 
Lexington’s victories may be the first successful amendments by civic assembly in the country, although the process is being used elsewhere, and in other countries, like Ireland.
This election signaled that people all over this country are tired not just of Trump, but of partisanship, corruption and politics led by big money rather than citizens. Civic assemblies are an answer to those problems.
“People want to be involved, people want to have a say,” Young said. “The idea, ‘I could be a part of this decision making process’ speaks to people. It certainly did to our Assembly members, they feel their perspective and presence really mattered. And it really did.”

text:
Election Day, Nov. 3, 2026 in Maine: Jackie Sartoris, a Democrat running for reelection as Cumberland County district attorney, greets voters outside the polling station at Scarborough High School. (Photo by Jim Neuger / Maine Morning Star)Democratic incumbent Cumberland County District Attorney Jackie Sartoris defeated independent Stephanie Anderson, who previously held the role as a registered Republican.
Sartoris’ win mirrored many across the state and country Tuesday night, as Democratic victories delivered a rebuke of President Donald Trump and the GOP. 
Despite being outraised, Sartoris secured 66.92% of votes to Anderson’s 24.50%. 
“I’m humbled and grateful at the overwhelming support by Cumberland County voters of the progress we’ve made here in adopting pragmatic reform,” Sartoris said in a statement. “I promise to work for everyone to create a more just Cumberland County for all.”
Coming out of retirement to run, Anderson had argued Sartoris destroyed her legacy and endangered public safety. Meanwhile, Sartoris claimed a return to Anderson’s leadership would set the district back after she made major progressive changes. 
Sartoris was first elected in 2022. Anderson served as district attorney for 28 years, first elected in 1990. She is currently a town councilor in Cape Elizabeth. 
While Anderson was district attorney, she was known for her toughness. She established Maine’s first drug court, juvenile unit and domestic violence unit. 
Sartoris has broadened the use of restorative justice programs, worked through a backlog of untested rape kits, and publicly shared her willingness to prosecute illegal use of force by federal immigration agents. 
Some of that work has been opposed by police unions, which backed Anderson, along with several attorneys. Meanwhile, Sartoris was endorsed by several city councilors and Democratic state legislators, including Speaker of the Maine House of Representatives Ryan Fecteau, as well as former Democratic candidates for national and statewide office.

name: VTDigger
title: Vermont Conversation: ‘An incredible repudiation of Trump.’ Sen. Peter Welch on the 2026 Democratic tsunami.
description:
The Vermont senator said one of the election’s clearest messages was a demand for accountability from elected officials.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont Conversation: ‘An incredible repudiation of Trump.’ Sen. Peter Welch on the 2026 Democratic tsunami..
text:
U. S. Sen. Peter Welch, D-Vermont, speaks in Burlington on Election Night, Tuesday, November 3, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell, VTDigger

The Vermont Conversation with David Goodman is a VTDigger podcast that features in-depth interviews on local and national issues. Listen and subscribe for free on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, YouTube or wherever you get podcasts.
Landslide. Tsunami. Earthquake. Bloodbath. Wipeout. Massacre.
That is how mainstream news accounts are characterizing the results of this year’s midterm election, as Democrats led a historic rout of Republicans. Democrats are poised to retake control of both the U.S. Senate and House. The election marked a decisive rejection of President Donald Trump and his MAGA movement.
And with the election to the U.S. Senate of Troy Jackson in Maine and Chris Pappas in New Hampshire, the Boston Globe reports that “New England will not have a single Republican U.S. Senator for the first time since the founding of the Republican Party in the mid-19th century.”
U.S. Sen. Peter Welch, D-Vt., told me that the election was “an incredible repudiation of Trump” and said voters across the political spectrum united around concerns about affordability, government integrity and presidential overreach.
“This election was an opportunity for the American people to weigh in,” Welch said. “That arbitrary use of authority is something people really reacted to because it had real consequences in their lives.”
Welch pointed to widespread dissatisfaction with Trump’s tariffs, his administration’s handling of immigration enforcement, and the president’s decision to expand U.S. military involvement in Iran without congressional approval.
“People were appalled by the cruelty and the corruption of the Trump administration,” Welch said, arguing that voters ultimately rejected both the policies and style of Trump’s presidency.
The Vermont senator said one of the election’s clearest messages was a demand for accountability from elected officials.
“The most significant act of accountability is the American voters repudiating policies and actions and behaviors by incumbents,” Welch said. “The American voter did that on a massive scale.”
While Democrats celebrated major gains, Welch cautioned against interpreting the results as a broad endorsement of his party.
The vote “was not a big embrace of Democrats,” he said. “What Democrats have been given by the American people is an opportunity to earn their trust.”
That trust, Welch said, must be earned by addressing issues that cut across partisan lines, including healthcare costs, child care, fuel prices and economic insecurity.
“Families can’t afford healthcare. It’s a broken system. Families can’t afford childcare,” he said. “We have to approach this with humility and try to hear and act on what the American people said.”

READ MORE

Among the first priorities for the incoming Democratic majorities, Welch said, should be efforts to repeal Trump-era tariffs and reassert congressional authority over trade and war powers.
“The president doesn’t have authority unilaterally to impose taxes, and a tariff is a tax,” he said. “We’ve got a new majority in both houses, and we should act on it.”
Welch also called for legislation to curb immigration enforcement practices that he described as harmful and indiscriminate. Recounting a recent visit to a detention facility in St. Albans, he said several detainees he met had legal status, jobs and no criminal records.
“These mass roundups are absolutely unacceptable,” Welch said. “They’re violent. They’re cruel. They’re not only unnecessary, but they’re really harmful.”
At the same time, Welch urged Democrats to focus on governance rather than political retribution.
“There will be corruption investigations,” he acknowledged. But, he added, accountability should be “about making life better for everyday people, not a focus on corruption that is about vengeance and payback.”
The election also produced a series of historic gubernatorial victories by women, immigrants, Black candidates, Native Americans and Muslims, developments Welch described as evidence that voters were focused more on character and economic concerns than identity politics.
“People were colorblind in terms of their vote,” he said. “They were laser-focused on candidates who they believed would make their lives better.”
Does this election mark the end of the MAGA movement?
“Yes,” he said. “I think Trump is done in terms of an effective political spokesperson. His policies have collapsed, and the meanness of his policies have been revealed.”
Whether Democrats can translate their electoral triumph into legislative victories remains uncertain. Trump retains his veto power, and many of the party’s priorities will require bipartisan support. But after a stunning election night that reshaped American politics, Welch said voters have sent an unmistakable message.
“The American people,” he said, “rejected Trump and his corruption. That is the loudest and clearest message about the demand for accountability that can be given.”

description: Alabama Republicans won most statewide office contests Tuesday, though their margins were smaller than four years ago. Former Republican Party Chair John Wahl won the Lieutenant Governor’s race after he received 911,304 votes, about 54.3% of the electorate, according to unofficial results from the Alabama Secretary of State’s office. Former Rep. Phillip Ensl[...]
text:
A roll of "I voted" circular stickers. Republicans won most of the statewide offices during Tuesday's election, but Democratic nominees narrowed the voting gap from previous elections. (Getty)Alabama Republicans won most statewide office contests Tuesday, though their margins were smaller than four years ago.
Former Republican Party Chair John Wahl won the Lieutenant Governor’s race after he received 911,304 votes, about 54.3% of the electorate, according to unofficial results from the Alabama Secretary of State’s office. Former Rep. Phillip Ensler, D-Montgomery, garnered 765,203, about 45.6% of the total vote.
Lt. Gov. Will Ainsworth, a Republican, is term-limited and could not seek re-election; Ainworth won 83% of the vote in his campaign for a second term in 2022.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
A message was sent to Wahl Wednesday seeking comment.
Ensler thanked his supporters in a statement sent by email shortly after the race was called, telling them he was grateful for their support. He also said he closed the vote gap for the office.
“Our race shows that with sustained effort, dedicated organizing, and strong leadership, we can continue to move the needle and Democrats can eventually win in Alabama,” Ensler said. “I am not going to sugarcoat it. Tonight’s results are disappointing. But I am proud of the campaign we ran and the diverse coalition we put together.”
Wahl campaigned on the issue of affordability and said he supports eliminating the 2% grocery tax. Ensler said he also supports abolishing the sales tax on food but is also in favor of raising the minimum wage, expanding Medicaid and establishing a lottery in the state.
Young Boozer was elected to his fourth term as Alabama Treasurer after he received 917,177 votes, almost 55% of the electorate. Rosilyn Houston, the Democratic nominee, received 749,785 votes, 45% of the total.
A message was sent to Boozer Wednesday seeking comment. Boozer won about 84% of the vote against a Libertarian challenger in 2022.
Boozer touted his accomplishments while in office on his campaign website. He highlighted how he replenished the Alabama Prepaid Affordable College Tuition (PACT) college savings program that was in “crisis and near bankruptcy.” He also said he restructured the Treasurer’s office so that it does not cost anything from the General Fund budget.
A message was sent to Houston Wednesday seeking comment.
Houston focused on protecting the money of taxpayers and giving the public more information about how the state spends residents’ tax dollars. She also said she wants to enhance financial literacy in the state by engaging schools, churches and community centers.
Andrew Sorrell was elected to his second term as state auditor after he beat Madison County Commissioner Violet Edwards, the Democratic nominee. Sorrell received 918,666 votes, about 55.2% of the electorate while Edwards got 744,632 votes, 44.8% of the total. Sorrell, like Boozer, got 84% of the vote in 2022 against a Libertarian challenger.
Sorrell said he was humbled to be reelected for a second term but was disappointed in the results nationwide. He said he believed the results showed the electorate is pleased with the work he is doing.
“I think what Alabamians want is people who stick to their campaign promises, and not just campaign as conservatives but govern like conservatives,” he said.
Sorrell said on his campaign website that he will work with legislators to pass a bill that would allow the State Auditor’s Office to determine if there is negligent loss of state property. He would like to issue letters to those who are responsible for damaging state property to demand repayment.
He also said he will continue to appoint members to the board of registrars who vote regularly and believe in the integrity of elections.
A message was sent to Edwards Wednesday seeking comment.
Edwards campaigned on expanding access to the ballot box by appointing registrars who pledge to make it easier for people to register to vote, and to keep the board of registrars’ offices open during the same hours as county offices.
Caroleene Dobson, the 2024 GOP nominee for the 2nd Congressional District, won the election for Alabama Secretary of State after she beat Democratic nominee Wayne Rogers. Dobson garnered 909,477 votes or about 54.5% of the total. Rogers received 756,490 votes, 45.4% of the electorate.
Alabama Secretary of State Wes Allen, who won 66% of the vote in 2022, ran for the Republican nomination for lieutenant governor but lost to Wahl in a June runoff.
A message was sent to Dobson Wednesday seeking comment.
Dobson said on her campaign website that she wants to reduce fees on businesses and streamline services for people in Alabama. She also said she “will never back down from the liberal activist groups who want to undermine the security of our elections.”
Rogers thanked his supporters in an interview Wednesday.
“I had a lot more fun than I could have imagined out on the campaign trail meeting so many wonderful people in the state I love and the state I called home for my entire life,” he said.
Rogers campaigned on strengthening voting rights protections in Alabama.
He said he will continue to work to expand access to the ballot box.
“One thing that I will be asking legislators to put forward is to establish early voting in Alabama,” Rogers said. “I believe early voting is a popular issue among both Democrats and Republicans.”
Republican Greg Shaw won a seat on the Alabama Supreme Court against Democratic nominee AshLeigh Meyer Dunham. Shaw received 824,749 votes, about 58% of the total, while Dunham got 594,428 votes, 41.9% of the total.
Shaw sought reelection to the state’s highest court after he assumed office in 2009.
A message was sent to Shaw Wednesday seeking comment.
Shaw called himself a constitutional conservative on his campaign website. He said he will “protect and stand up for Alabama’s values and our people, and he will always apply the law as it is written.”
Dunham, a family attorney and Jefferson County Juvenile Court referee, said in an interview Wednesday that she beat her expectations when the results were finalized Tuesday.
“I was also told not to mention women’s issues and that the voter base would not listen to those,” she said. “I think that it showed that, by getting so much better than we expected, people do care about those things.”
In LePage v. Center for Reproductive Medicine, the Alabama Supreme Court ruled that frozen embryos qualify as children under the state’s Wrongful Death of a Minor Act. That ruling threatened in vitro fertilization in the state.
Republican Brad Mendheim, who won a full term in 2020, ran unopposed Tuesday and was reelected to another term on the Alabama Supreme Court.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Democrats gain seats in South Dakota Legislature for the first time since 2008
description: No Democrat won a statewide race Tuesday in South Dakota, but the party picked up four seats in the Legislature. Nationally, Democrats racked up historic gains. They retook control of the U.S. House of Representatives and Senate, and scored major state-level wins, including the governorship in Texas for the first time since 1994 and Iowa […]
text:
Shane Merrill, chair of the South Dakota Democratic Party, speaks at the party's election night watch party in downtown Sioux Falls on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)No Democrat won a statewide race Tuesday in South Dakota, but the party picked up four seats in the Legislature.
Nationally, Democrats racked up historic gains. They retook control of the U.S. House of Representatives and Senate, and scored major state-level wins, including the governorship in Texas for the first time since 1994 and Iowa for the first time since 2006.
Democratic gains in the South Dakota Legislature were historic in their own way. The addition of four Sioux Falls-area seats brings the total number of Democrats in the 105-member South Dakota Legislature to 12, marking the party’s best showing since the 2018 election, when 16 Democrats won seats.
Tuesday marked the first time South Dakota Democrats have gained legislative seats in a general election since 2008.
2026 South Dakota general election results

The Republican Party’s dominant position in the Legislature was assured before the polls opened Tuesday morning. Fifty-two seats were guaranteed for Republicans, due to a lack of opposition: 21 in the Senate and 31 in the House. 
During the 2026 legislative session, there were eight Democrats among the 105 lawmakers — three in the state Senate and five in the House of Representatives.
Next year, Republicans will have 33 seats in the Senate, and Democrats will have two. The House of Representatives will have 59 Republicans, 10 Democrats and one independent, Evangeline Poor Bear of Pine Ridge, who told South Dakota Searchlight she aligns with Republicans but ran as an independent because she missed a filing deadline. Nevertheless, she’s the first person elected as an independent to the Legislature since 2010.
Hailing from Sioux Falls
All incumbent Democrats on the ballot with hopes of returning to the Capitol in 2027 won their respective races.
All but two of the 12 Democrats elected on Tuesday were from the Sioux Falls area. Those two are incumbent Reps. Nicole Uhre-Balk of Rapid City and Eric Emery of Rosebud.
Uhre-Balk issued a news release Wednesday morning noting that she’s the first Democrat to be reelected in her district in 36 years. She and Emery are also the only South Dakota Democratic legislators residing west of the Missouri River.
The blue tsunami sweeps the US, as Democrats land huge gains in Congress

In the Sioux Falls area, Democratic Sen. Liz Larson was reelected, as was incumbent Rep. Kadyn Wittman. Rep. Erik Muckey ran for Senate, beating Republican Brenda Lawrence and holding a seat vacated by Democrat Jamie Smith, who narrowly lost a bid for Sioux Falls mayor earlier this year.
Democrat June Copperstad was elected to replace Muckey in the House.
District 10, where Larson serves, had been a split district with one Republican and two Democrats across both chambers. The Democrats now hold all three seats.
Districts 11, 12, 13 and 14 had been all Republican, but each will have a Democrat in the House in 2027: Sonja Mentzer in District 11, Stephanie Arne in District 12, Ali Rae Horsted in District 13 and Erinn Williams in District 14.
Horsted ousted Republican incumbent John Hughes, and Williams came in second in the District 14 House race for two seats behind incumbent Republican Taylor Rae Rehfeldt but ahead of Republican Tyler Tordsen, who served in the House from 2023 to 2024.
Recounts possible in several races
Democrat Aaron Matson was narrowly defeated in the Sioux Falls-area’s District 11 by Republican Senate President Pro Tempore Chris Karr in a race close enough for a recount if Matson requests one. Republican Kari Shanard-Koenders beat Democrat Joe Zweifel in District 12. That contest is also close enough for a recount.
Additional recounts are possible in District 3, where Democrat Erin Ronayne Rudner was edged out for a House seat by Republican Timothy Hanigan, both of Aberdeen, and in District 9, where Republican Megan Tschetter of Hartford narrowly beat Democrat Amanda Potter of Sioux Falls for a House seat.
Zweifel, who’s also deputy director of the South Dakota Democratic Party, told South Dakota Searchlight he’s still deciding if he’ll request a recount. So did Matson.
The rest of the losing Democratic candidates did not immediately reply to calls and text messages asking if they intend to request recounts.
Independents fizzle
Legislative races included an unusually high number of independent candidates. Eleven were vying for seats, and one was guaranteed a seat in District 27, where four independent candidates faced a single Republican for two slots.
Republican incumbent Liz May won that race, followed by Poor Bear, who outperformed the other three independents. 
The remaining independent candidates lost. They included Rep. Peri Pourier, who switched from Democrat to Republican in 2025 and ran for Senate as an independent in District 27. She lost to Anthony Kathol, a Republican who’d challenged her candidate nominating petitions all the way to the state Supreme Court. The court ruled that Pourier had qualified for the ballot on Monday, but she came in third, behind Kathol and Democrat Celestine Stadnick, in the race for the District’s single Senate seat.

Neal Tapio, a Watertown independent who’d formerly served in the Legislature as a Republican, came in third and lost his bid for a seat in the House. Another former Republican lawmaker, Bryan Breitling, ran unsuccessfully as an independent for a Senate seat in District 25.
Incumbent Republican Sen. Tom Pischke dropped out of that race this summer. He faces two felony charges for allegedly filling out candidate nominating petitions for county Republican party leadership positions without those candidates’ knowledge.
Bart Sample, the former Flandreau City Council member chosen by the Minnehaha County Republican Party to replace Pischke, won that Senate seat.

title: US Rep. Mike Flood narrowly wins reelection in 1st District House race
description: LINCOLN — Though results were too close to call Tuesday night, U.S. Rep. Mike Flood celebrated a narrow victory in his bid for reelection representing Nebraska’s 1st Congressional District Wednesday morning. Flood said the race was called in his favor moments before a press conference at the Nebraska Republican Party headquarters, and that his opponent […]
text:
U.S. Rep. Mike Flood proclaims victory in his bid for reelection to Nebraska's 1st Congressional District. Behind him (from left to right) are Nebraska Attorney General Mike Hilgers, U.S. Sen. Deb Fischer, U.S. Sen. Pete Ricketts, State Treasurer Joey Spellerberg and State Auditor Mike Foley. LINCOLN — Though results were too close to call Tuesday night, U.S. Rep. Mike Flood celebrated a narrow victory in his bid for reelection representing Nebraska’s 1st Congressional District Wednesday morning.
Flood said the race was called in his favor moments before a press conference at the Nebraska Republican Party headquarters, and that his opponent Chris Backemeyer called to concede earlier this morning. Unofficial results showed Flood leading with 50.1% of the vote to Backemeyer’s 46.4% as of 11 a.m. Wednesday.
“This seat belongs to the people that live here,” Flood said.
Backemeyer conceded in a Wednesday press release, saying that he was proud of his campaign, and that his supporters had sent a message that “the status quo isn’t good enough.”
Democratic canidate Chris Backemeyer converses with attendees during the Chris Backemeyer watch party at Bin 105 Quality WInes on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026, in Lincoln. (Photos by Emma DeShon)
“I know this is not the outcome we hoped for, but it has been the honor of my lifetime to be your nominee,” Backemeyer said in the release. “I will carry your stories and experiences with me every day.”
Flood praised Backemeyer’s campaign, saying he appreciated that his messaging focused on the issues and not “character assassinations.” He said he would work to earn the favor of voters who supported Backemeyer over him.
“I know today is a tough day,” Flood said to those who voted against him. “I’ll do my best to earn your trust.”
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
The slim margins in the 1st District race came as a surprise to some, after Flood comfortably prevailed in his 2024 reelection bid by a margin of about 20 percentage points. Flood said the difference seemed to stretch beyond the normal headwinds expected for midterm candidates aligned with the current president’s party, and attributed it to voters upset with the country’s ongoing affordability crisis.
Flood said it was tough to predict if the close results held any implications for future elections for the seat. He said the results of federal races often depend on the national mood at the time.
“It’s really, where is America at when the polls open?” Flood said. “So it’s hard to predict what that will look like in two years.”
While a collection of historically red states flipped blue in their congressional races, Republicans celebrated Nebraska holding up a “firewall” — using U.S. Sen. Pete Rickett’s term — that allowed most GOP incumbents to hold onto their seats.
U.S. Sen. Deb Fischer said she was thrilled by the results. Though she lamented Brinker Harding’s loss to Democrat Denise Powell in the 2nd District, Fischer said she was pleased that her remaining Republican colleagues would be returning to Washington, D.C. with her.
“Nebraska held the line,” Fischer said.

title: Walz concedes Nebraska governor’s race to Gov. Jim Pillen
description: FREMONT, Neb. — Former Democratic state Sen. Lynne Walz conceded the governor’s race shortly after 9:30 a.m. Wednesday to Republican Gov. Jim Pillen. text:
Democratic gubernatorial candidate Lynne Walz of Fremont, a former state senator, addresses supporters during her election night watch party on Nov. 3, 2026, in Omaha, Nebraska. (Photo by Chase Zagurski for Nebraska Examiner)FREMONT, Neb. — Former Democratic state Sen. Lynne Walz conceded the governor’s race shortly after 9:30 a.m. Wednesday to Republican Gov. Jim Pillen.
Walz, in a statement, said she called Pillen “to congratulate him on a hard-fought campaign and wish him well as he continues to serve Nebraska.” 
She gave a Republican gubernatorial candidate their toughest run since the 1990s — Democrat Ben Nelson unseated Republican Gov. Kay Orr in 1990 by just 4,030 votes, which Walz had sought to emulate. Nelson handily won reelection in 1994, and Republicans have won since 1998. He was elected to the U.S. Senate in 2000.
Pillen won in 2022 by 23 percentage points. As of 6 a.m. Wednesday, he led Walz by 11 points. The Associated Press called the race for Pillen just before 2 a.m. Wednesday.
“This isn’t the result we hoped for, but this campaign was always about bringing Nebraskans together, and that work doesn’t end today,” Walz said Wednesday morning. “Nebraskans will be watching to make sure our leaders in Lincoln deliver, and I’ll be right there with them.”
Nebraska Democrats have not won a statewide race since 2006, when Nelson won a second term in the U.S. Senate. 


Walz served in the Nebraska Legislature representing the conservative Legislative District 15. She defeated a Republican appointee in 2016 and won reelection in 2020. Both times, Dodge County heavily favored President Donald Trump.
In 2021, Walz, a former teacher, narrowly won the support of her colleagues to chair the Legislature’s Education Committee.
In her year of campaigning, Walz said, she and her running mate, Humboldt farmer Ben Steffen, an ex-Republican, spoke with Nebraskans of “all walks of life, and heard the same thing: families are working harder than ever before and are still falling behind.”
“That shared struggle is a reminder that what unites Nebraskans runs far deeper than anything that divides us, and it’s the foundation we’ll keep building on in the months ahead,” Walz said.
Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen wins reelection

Pillen, at his Lincoln watch party, praised his supporters and said he looks forward to his next four years. Nebraska bucked a blue wave nationwide, and Pillen said that “when Nebraska wins, we all win.”
“You chose a leader, not a politician, and I will never forget that trust,” Pillen told a cheering crowd in Lincoln.
National pundits, pollsters and figures, including Trump, Vice President JD Vance and Democratic Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, had not initially placed Nebraska on the map. But over time, Pillen and Walz faced a closer-than-expected matchup. 
The Republican Governors Association had given Pillen $2 million in the last month, and the Democratic Governors Association, which Beshear chairs, gave Walz more than $500,000.
Walz thanked her family, Steffen and his wife, and all campaign supporters. Walz said she and Steffen are proud of their campaign and “even prouder” of those who stood with them.
“The best days for Nebraska are still ahead of us,” Walz said. “Thank you, Nebraska, for opening your doors to me this year. My family and I are truly grateful.”

title: A shrinking state can’t afford to lose its top earners
description:
More taxes on ‘the rich’ will drive away the professionals Vermont most needs.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  A shrinking state can’t afford to lose its top earners.
text:
Dear Editor,
In his recent letter to VTDigger, Alan Turnbull proposes raising taxes on “the rich” to spare up to 90% of Vermonters from income taxes. Like most such proposals, Turnbull’s would hurt Vermont and Vermonters, not help. 
I support raising taxes on the wealthy — on a national level. I think it would be a major mistake to do so in Vermont. Vermont is already among the states with the highest tax burdens in the country. Unlike other very high-tax states, such as California, New York and New Jersey, Vermont simply doesn’t have many high-income individuals. It has the second-lowest population of any state and the smallest GDP. Importantly, rich people are generally much more mobile than the general population. People with the education, skills and traits that earn them a lot of money — think doctors, lawyers, engineers, entrepreneurs — can often choose where they live. And we certainly don’t have an overabundance of these professionals; just try getting a medical appointment in Vermont.
In Turnbull’s opinion, someone making $300,000 a year in Vermont should pay 9% to 13% in state income tax so that most Vermonters pay no income tax at all. 

READ MORE

Let’s take an example. According to Turnbull, there are just under 10,000 such households in Vermont. Despite Vermont doctor salaries being below the national average, a good portion of those 10,000 households are doctors; there are about 3,000 doctors in Vermont, including those in telemedicine. So, let’s say you’re a young doctor thinking about coming to Vermont — or even an established one — and you make $360,000 a year. By my estimates, assuming they were a single filer, this person would pay about $90,000 in federal income tax, another $18,000 in Social Security and Medicare taxes and over $26,000 in Vermont income and child care tax. A doctor would probably live in a nice house in a nice neighborhood, so at a rough guess they would pay another $18,000 a year in property tax.
The remaining $200,000-plus in income is still a lot, right? Sure. But that’s not the point. The point is this person is rational and can make and keep substantially more in another state. Maybe Vermont is so uniquely attractive that they would still choose to live here. But our tax picture certainly doesn’t incentivize it, and our demographic data confirms that people are not choosing Vermont, with consecutive declines in population over the past two years following the pandemic bump. Now apply this same thinking to any variety of high-income professionals and entrepreneurs and business owners. Vermont needs more of all these people, not fewer. Think about what the state will look like in 10 years with even fewer doctors and a more aged population. Will companies like BETA Technologies be able to compete for top talent so they can stay and grow in Vermont?
Vermonters need to stop focusing on zero-sum “tax the rich” thinking and look toward policies that grow the population and the economy.
Ali JaliliBurlington, Vt.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Blue wave washes over Michigan as Dems flip key congressional battlegrounds
description: The success of Democrats across the nation in Tuesday’s election manifested itself squarely in Michigan’s congressional delegation, which saw three districts change hands from Republicans to Democrats.  What had been a 7-6 GOP majority has now been reversed to a 9-4 Democratic advantage starting in 2027. Here are the unofficial results from the U.S. House […[...]
text:
A "Vote Here" sign on Nov. 3, 2026, outside of Bethlehem Lutheran Church in Lansing, Mich., one of several local polling places in Ingham County. (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance)The success of Democrats across the nation in Tuesday’s election manifested itself squarely in Michigan’s congressional delegation, which saw three districts change hands from Republicans to Democrats. 
What had been a 7-6 GOP majority has now been reversed to a 9-4 Democratic advantage starting in 2027.
Here are the unofficial results from the U.S. House races across Michigan’s 13 congressional districts:
 
1st Congressional District
Fending off a push from Democrats at the local and national level, U.S. Rep. Jack Bergman (R-Watersmeet) won a sixth term.
In a rematch against Traverse City Attorney Callie Barr, Bergman had won over 53.2% of voters when the Associated Press called the race at 1:09 a.m. Wednesday, while Barr received 44.7%.
 
2nd Congressional District
Emerging victorious against Marine Corps veteran Ben Ambrose, U.S. Rep. John Moolenaar (R-Caledonia) will serve a seventh term in the U.S. House of Representatives. 
According to unofficial results from the Associated Press at 10:45 p.m. Tuesday, Moolenaar received 62.9% of the vote, while Ambrose received 35.8%
 
3rd Congressional District
U.S. Rep. Hillary Scholten (D-Grand Rapids) has defeated former broadcast meteorologist Terri DeBoer, winning a third term as representative for Michigan’s 3rd Congressional District.
Unofficial results at 12:54 a.m. Wednesday showed Scholten with 57.3% of the vote while DeBoer received 41.2%.
 
4th Congressional District
Building on gains in 2022, Democrats have continued to make headway in Western Michigan as state Sen. Sean McCann (D-Kalamazoo) claimed victory Wednesday against U.S. Rep. Bill Huizenga (R-Holland Township) for his seat in Congress.
Who is Hakeem Jeffries? Meet the likely first Black speaker of the US House.

Unofficial results from the Associated Press, which finally called the race at 1:13 p.m. Wednesday, show McCann had 50.1% of the vote while Huizenga received 48.3%.
McCann will conclude his time in the state Legislature and serve as representative for the state’s 4th Congressional District, which includes Allegan and Van Buren counties, and portions of Ottawa, Kalamazoo, Calhoun and Berrien counties.
“I am honored and humbled that the people of Southwest Michigan have put their trust in me to represent and serve this amazing district,” McCann said in a statement. “Thank you to the voters, and to every volunteer and supporter who knocked on doors and made phone calls, talked to their neighbors, and helped out in ways big and small. I will be forever grateful for your support, because you are the heart and soul of this campaign. And thank you to Congressman Bill Huizenga for his years of service to our community.”
 
5th Congressional District 
U.S. Rep. Tim Walberg (R-Tipton) was easily reelected for a ninth term. Unofficial results show Walberg bested educator and labor organizer Christian Vukasovich with 64.4% of the vote, according to unofficial results shared by the Associated Press, which called the race at 11:11 p.m Tuesday.
 
6th Congressional District
Voters overwhelmingly reelected U.S. Rep. Debbie Dingell (D-Ann Arbor) for a seventh term. 
Dingell defeated her Republican challenger, Heather Smiley, with 71.8% of the vote according to unofficial results. Smiley received 25.8%.
 
7th Congressional District
In a tight race for Michigan’s politically purple 7th Congressional District, Lansing area political organizer William Lawrence declared himself the victor against incumbent Congressman Tom Barrett (R-Charlotte).
Return of the trifecta: Michigan Democrats reclaim full control of state government

Lawrence’s campaign shared their proclamation of victory at 2:49 a.m. Wednesday, though the Associated Press had not yet called the race. 
While Barrett was leading through most of the evening and into the night, Lawrence’s campaign began making gains in the early hours of the morning. 
Barrett departed his election night watch party at 2:39 a.m. without speaking to the media. As of 6:29 a.m., Lawrence was leading by 3.2 percentage points.
“We built an unprecedented movement here in Mid-Michigan, powered by thousands of volunteers, and we showed that you can beat an incumbent Republican without taking a dime of corporate PAC money,” Lawrence said in a statement. “We united people from every corner of this district – and found common ground in opposition to war and data centers, and in favor of good housing and healthcare, social security, jobs and education. Our people-powered movement took on the richest and most powerful people in the world, and we won.”
 
8th Congressional District
U.S. Rep. Kristen McDonald Rivet (D-Bay City) defeated retired GM engineer Thomas Smith, winning a second term in the House of Representatives. 
First elected in 2024, McDonald Rivet received 54.4% of the vote according to unofficial results shared by the Associated Press at 1:48 a.m. Wednesday, while Smith received 43%.
While the 8th Congressional District was a key target for Republicans and Democrats in 2024, Smith was never a serious threat to McDonald Rivet’s reelection chances, having won the GOP primary despite dropping out just weeks before. 
 
9th Congressional District
U.S. Rep. Lisa McClain (R-Bruce Township) will serve a fourth term in Congress, with unofficial results at 11:45 p.m. Tuesday showing she defeated CNC Machinist Ray Pooley with 61.7% of the vote. 
McClain serves as the U.S. House Republican conference chair.
 
10th Congressional District
In the early hours Wednesday morning, former prosecutor Christina Hines announced her victory over Army National Guard veteran Michael Bouchard Jr.
While Hines declared victory at 3:52 a.m., the Associated Press officially called the race shortly before 12:30 Wednesday afternoon with unofficial results showing Hines with 52.4% of the vote to 45.3% for Bouchard.
The district is currently held by U.S. Rep. John James (R-Shelby Township), who opted against seeking reelection to run for governor, which was unsuccessful, as he lost to Democrat Jocelyn Benson. Encompassing southern Macomb County, the district also includes Rochester and Rochester Hills in eastern Oakland County. 
A former prosecutor in Wayne and Washtenaw counties, Hines focused her campaign on bringing down costs, emphasizing that as a mother of three and a Macomb county resident, she understood the hardship families in the district are facing.
“This campaign started with a simple truth: that working families in our district are sick of being left behind by corrupt politicians in Washington and deserve someone who will actually put their needs first,” Hines said in a statement. “Over the last 18 months, I have been moved by the thousands of people who have told me their stories, shared their struggles, and demanded more from their leaders. Your words have stayed with me throughout this entire campaign and I will carry them with me to Washington.”
Hines’ win is one of three GOP-held congressional districts in Michigan to flip to Democratic control. Democrat William Lawrence declared victory in the 7th Congressional District early Wednesday over incumbent Republican Congressman Tom Barrett of Charlotte and state Sen. Sean McCann did the same against his opponent, incumbent Republican U.S. Rep. Bill Huizenga of Holland Township.
 
11th Congressional District
Michigan state Sen. Jeremy Moss (D-Bloomfield) emerged victorious against Troy Mayor Ethan Baker, receiving 59.6% of the vote, according to unofficial results shared by the Associated Press at 9:33 p.m. Tuesday. 
Moss, the state’s first openly gay state senator, will be Michigan’s first openly LGBTQ+ representative in Congress. He will succeed U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Birmingham), who unsuccessfully sought the Democratic nomination for U.S. Senate and then stunned Democrats when she endorsed Republican Mike Rogers just days before the election.
In a statement celebrating his victory, Moss said Michiganders need a Congress that can put a check on the president.
“I will work hard every day to lower costs, protect and expand our healthcare, dismantle ICE, and hold the Trump administration accountable,” Moss said.
 
12th Congressional District
U.S. Rep. Rashida Tlaib (D-Detroit) will serve a fifth term in Congress, easily defeating Republican James Hooper, who she previously faced in 2024.
Unofficial results from the Associated Press at 9:33 p.m. Tuesday, show Tlaib with 84.8% of the vote and Hooper with 12.7%.
 
13th Congressional District
State Rep. Donavan McKinney (D-Detroit) will succeed U.S. Rep. Shri Thanedar to represent Michigan’s 13th Congressional District. 
McKinney defeated Republican T.P. Nykoriak with 75.5% of the vote, according to unofficial results shared by the Associated Press, which called the race at 10:33 p.m. Tuesday.
Michigan Democratic Party Chair Curtis Hertel congratulated McKinney on his victory in a statement.
“As a labor organizer and state representative, Donavan has the values and experience we need to fight and deliver for Detroiters in the halls of Congress. His leadership will be key to making the wealthy pay their fair share, expanding access to healthcare and housing, and making sure every Michigander has a fair shot, no matter their zip code.”
The Working Families Party, a minor political party backing progressive candidates, also cheered McKinney’s victory.
“WFP champion Donavan McKinney defeated a sitting Congressman in the primary, despite millions in spending from corporate and crypto interests,” Branden Snyder, state director for the Michigan Working Families Party, said in a statement. “ Now he’s heading to Congress to fight for the community that raised him. We know that Donavan will fight with everything he has to protect the rights of workers and unions, stand up to corporate greed, and bring back investments to Michigan’s 13th Congressional District.”

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Commentary: Ohio voters show their frustration over corruption and cost of living
description: Amid interminable refreshes of Associated Press Ohio election projections Tuesday night and into late Wednesday morning, one thing repeatedly stuck out to me. It was the AP Voter Poll survey of Ohio voters. The AP Voter Poll is a survey of the American electorate conducted by SSRS for The Associated Press, ABC News, CBS News, […]
text:
The Ohio Statehouse. (Photo by Megan Henry/ Ohio Capital Journal)Amid interminable refreshes of Associated Press Ohio election projections Tuesday night and into late Wednesday morning, one thing repeatedly stuck out to me.
It was the AP Voter Poll survey of Ohio voters.
The AP Voter Poll is a survey of the American electorate conducted by SSRS for The Associated Press, ABC News, CBS News, CNN, FOX News Media, NBC News and Versant.
The survey looked at what Ohio voters prioritized on different issues.
The two that stick out by far above the rest are the cost of living and government corruption.
These are both well-worn topics here at the Ohio Capital Journal, where we have reported news stories and written commentary for seven years on rampant corruption and the struggle Ohio families are having to make ends meet.
After a historic election night in Ohio, alleviating these concerns of Ohio voters should be the primary goal and project of every elected official in the state.
Ohio voters proved this Election Day that politicians are far more obsessed with political labels and rank partisanship than normal everyday Ohioans. There’s a reason the vast majority of Ohioans are unaffiliated voters.
Like much of the country, everyday people in Ohio are pretty cynical and cautious about politicians of all types. For many years now, everyday people have suspected with good reason and ample evidence that our politicians have not been looking out for us, but for themselves, for their buddies, for the special interests.
What’s been left out of all the favors and back-scratching and handouts to big money interests are the interests of everyday Ohio families.
Folks aren’t asking for too much: They want safe neighborhoods, good schools, access to healthcare, and access to opportunity to earn a good living to support their families and live a dignified life.
In Ohio, many families feel that was all once possible, but no more. The rug has slowly been pulled out from under us.
Nearly half of Ohioans don’t make enough to be economically secure, the Urban Institute reported this year.
Over one-third of Ohioans do not make enough to afford basic expenses.
And 1 in 5 Ohio children continue to experience food insecurity.
Sharp increases in the price of gas and electric and heating bills have played hell on middle-class Ohio family budgets.
As Ohio families have struggled, we’ve seen countless corruption scandals at the local and state level where politicians take pennies on the dollar to give out public resources like candy to their donor networks.
The results of the 2026 Election in Ohio should not be read through a lens of hyper-partisanship.
The results of the 2026 Election in Ohio should be heard as a scream from struggling Ohio families that enough is enough and that it’s time, at long last, to put Ohio families first.
Political gamesmanship can not accomplish that amid a split state government.
The toxic, intoxicating distraction of partisanship will only destroy the opportunity and frustrate Ohio families further.
The only thing that can accomplish that is if our politicians hear that scream — that plea from Ohio families — and realize that their job is not to be a mindless team player for one political party or the other; their job is to do the hard work of compromise and coalition-building and lawmaking and governance that makes life better in tangible ways for all of the everyday people of Ohio.
A lot of people who’ve had their brains and hearts eaten away by the rot of partisan politics will try every trick right now to keep that ugliness going.
To paraphrase the bard, it is a tale told by an idiot, full of sound and fury, signifying nothing, and accomplishing nothing.
To accomplish something, to put Ohio families first, the mental and emotional adults of both parties will now need to step up.
