name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Contractor who hired Kosta Diamantis’ daughter gets probation
description: Antonietta DiBenedetto Roy was sentenced to two years' probation on Wednesday after admitting to bribing Kosta Diamantis.
text:
One of three school construction contractors who admitted to bribing Connecticut’s former deputy budget director, Konstantinos Diamantis, was sentenced to two years of probation in federal court in Bridgeport on Wednesday. 
Antonietta DiBenedetto Roy, the owner of a company called Construction Advocacy Professionals, previously admitted to paying Diamantis thousands of dollars and hiring his daughter so that her company could win contracts on school building projects that he oversaw. 
The charge that DiBenedetto Roy pleaded guilty to — conspiracy to commit bribery — could have carried a maximum sentence of up to 5 years in prison and 3 years of supervised release. The federal sentencing guidelines recommended that she serve between 2 to 2 1/2 years in prison.
But U.S. District Judge Stefan Underhill handed down a far lighter sentence for DiBenedetto Roy, which had been requested by her defense attorney and federal prosecutors. 
The sentence will mean that DiBenedetto Roy will be remain out of prison. The judge ordered her to obey a curfew for the first six months, however. 
Before the sentence was handed down, DiBenedetto Roy struggled through tears and told the judge that she was deeply sorry for taking part in the bribery scheme with Diamantis, who was convicted on 21 federal charges last year but fled to Greece before he could be sentenced earlier this fall.
“I’m ashamed and embarrassed to be standing in front of you today,” DiBenedetto Roy said. 
DiBenedetto Roy’s attorney, Craig Raabe, told the judge that his client has already faced significant damage as a result of her guilty plea and the corresponding news coverage surrounding the public corruption scheme. 
“She’s already paid a very serious price,” Raabe said, noting that her construction company has lost clients and work in the industry. 
Even more, Raabe argued that his client only became involved in the bribery scheme because of the pressure placed on her by Diamantis, who ran Connecticut’s school construction program for more than six years. Prior to her involvement with Diamantis, Raabe argued, DiBenedetto Roy was an upstanding citizen.
“She got sidetracked by getting into the vortex of Diamantis,” Raabe told the judge. 
When Assistant U.S. Attorney David Novick spoke, he reminded DiBenedetto Roy and the judge that the crime she pleaded guilty to was a serious offense. But he agreed that Roy should receive some leniency because of her cooperation with federal investigators and assistance in helping to convict Diamantis. 
DiBenedetto Roy testified for several hours last year during Diamantis’ criminal trial and told jurors that she hired Diamantis’ daughter and paid her bonuses in order to continue winning school construction contracts. She also explained how she delivered checks and cash to Diamantis.
Novick told the judge that his team may not have been able to convict Diamantis for that scheme without DiBenedetto Roy’s assistance. 
Underhill ultimately agreed with that point, and he said that DiBenedetto Roy should get credit for cooperating with the federal investigation and taking responsibility for her crimes. 
Before he sentenced DiBenedetto Roy, however, the judge acknowledged how serious her crimes were. 
“Public corruption is an evil that has to be rooted out,” Underhill said. “That’s what this larger case is all about.” 
Ultimately, Underhill laid the blame for the bribery scheme at the feet of Diamantis, who is facing seven years in federal prison if he is ever apprehended and returned to the United States. 
“It’s unfortunate that you did the right thing after doing the wrong thing,” Underhill told DiBenedetto Roy. 
DiBenedetto Roy is the first school construction contractor to be sentenced for conspiring with Diamantis. But she won’t be the last. 
Later this month, John Duffy and Sal Monarca, two masonry contractors who also testified against Diamantis, are scheduled to be in court to face their federal sentences.

name: VTDigger
title: Vermont Democrats make major Statehouse gains amid nationwide ‘blue wave’
description:
“We were confident we'd pick up seats,” said Vermont Democratic Party Chair Lachlan Francis. But “I certainly think it's safe to say we are surprised.”
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont Democrats make major Statehouse gains amid nationwide ‘blue wave’.
text:
The Vermont Statehouse in Montpelier in June 2026. File photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
Theo Wells-Spackman is a Report for America corps member who reports for VTDigger.
The Democratic “blue wave” felt across the country swept through Montpelier too on Tuesday.
Two years after the party saw its supermajorities shattered in both state legislative chambers with significant Republican wins, Democrats returned to a veto-proof majority in the Senate and substantially strengthened their control of the House. Progressive wins in the House combined with Democratic victories will at a minimum give the parties a joint two-thirds majority in the chamber, according to party leadership, with a number of races too close to call Wednesday morning.
“We were confident we’d pick up seats,” said Vermont Democratic Party Chair Lachlan Francis in an interview Wednesday. But “I certainly think it’s safe to say we are surprised.”
In the Senate, Democrats flipped at least four closely watched seats in Orange County, Addison County, Grand Isle County and the Chittenden-North District. Dave Wolk, an independent former Rutland County senator, will return to his old position after ousting embattled Republican Sen. Terry Williams.
Democrats currently hold 87 House seats to Republicans’ 56, with other parties making up the remaining seven seats, according to Ballotpedia. Tuesday saw Democrats flip at least 10 GOP seats, and at least six other such victories appeared likely Wednesday morning, with the Associated Press reporting 99% of votes counted.
Vermont Democrats’ wins came alongside historic gains for their party nationwide. Francis said the national political context played a major role in local results.
“I think the horrors of what we’ve seen from this federal administration absolutely motivated Democrats, independents and even some Republicans in Vermont to stand up and say that we need to do something different,” he said.
The energy of Democrat/Progressive Amanda Janoo at the top of the ticket, Francis added, was likely a key factor in the legislative victories despite Republican Gov. Phil Scott’s eventual win in that race.
Paul Dame, the state’s Republican Party chair, agreed. Anger at the Trump administration was likely the dominant factor in Tuesday’s legislative outcomes, he said.
“Pretty much all the gains that we had (the) last two years are essentially wiped out,” he said.
This story will be updated.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Indiana Republicans lose 2nd statewide office in comptroller race
description: Indiana Republicans lost a second statewide office with Democrat Jessica Bailey defeating incumbent Comptroller Elise Nieshalla.
text:
Democrats formally nominated Coumba Kebe, left, for state treasurer, and Jessica Bailey, right, for state comptroller, at the party's state convention on Saturday, June 6, 2026, in Indianapolis. (Photo by Mackenzi Klemann/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Indiana Republicans lost a second statewide office with Democrat Jessica Bailey defeating incumbent Comptroller Elise Nieshalla.
With 95% of the votes counted Wednesday, Bailey led by almost 45,000 votes — or 50% to 47%. Libertarian John Schick captured 3%.
The pickup comes alongside Democrat Beau Bayh’s win for secretary of state.
But while Bayh spent millions, Bailey spent only $169,000 this year according to the most recent campaign finance reports. Nieshalla spent about $290,000. These figures don’t include spending by the state parties on the overall ticket.
Bailey’s win could also aid Bayh’s planned audit of the Secretary of State Office because she would control many of the financial records in question.
Indiana State Comptroller Elise Nieshalla speaks during a news conference on July 15, 2026. (Photo by Tom Davies/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
The comptroller, formerly known as the state auditor, is responsible for accounting, disbursing and reporting how Indiana spends its $26 billion in annual state general fund revenues.
Nieshalla was appointed to the post by then-Gov. Eric Holcomb in 2023 after Comptroller Tera Klutz resigned.
“Through this election, Hoosiers have spoken, and I fully respect our democratic process. I have called Jessica Bailey to congratulate her and made a promise, that I also make to you: my office will ensure a smooth and professional transition in service to her and the great State of Indiana,” she said in a statement.
She also said it was a “tough night last night, not just here, but for Republicans across the country. It hurts, but we can’t let disappointment turn into retreat. Now is the time to evaluate what happened and why, and then get right back in the fight to keep our Republic free and Indiana strong — because the next election will be here before we know it.”
Bailey is finishing her second term as clerk of courts for Porter County, where she manages marriage licenses, traffic and criminal records and oversees county elections. She also spent six years as a member of the Porter Township school board.
The apolitical nature of the comptroller’s office is attractive to Bailey, who said she was inspired to seek the nomination to make Indiana’s transparency portal more accessible to the average Hoosier.
She also wants the three-member State Board of Finance — which authorizes loans, appropriations and transfers made between accounts that don’t require legislative approval —to engage in more public discussion.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: The budget dog bites back: Ousted House Finance chair spoils GOP vote in Wood County
description: Ousted House Finance Chair Vernon Criss appears to have handed his delegate seat off to a Democrat after launching a kamikaze-style write-in campaign in the GOP stronghold of Wood County.
text:
House Finance Chairman Vernon Criss, R-Wood, speaks about proposed amendments to the Senate’s budget bill on Feb. 25, 2026. (Photo by Perry Bennett/West Virginia Legislative Photography)Ousted House Finance Chair Vernon Criss appears to have handed his delegate seat off to a Democrat after launching a kamikaze-style write-in campaign in the GOP stronghold of Wood County. 
Democrat Dennis Rempel, a retired federal employee, defeated Republican nominee Charles Hartzog for the House District 12 race in Parkersburg. The victory is the first time Wood County has sent a Democrat to the statehouse since 2012. 
Rempel, a first-time candidate, is projected to beat Hartzog by 151 votes, according to Associated Press results as of Wednesday. The AP has not called the race, but shows 99% of the vote has been tallied. 
Both Rempel and Hartzog attribute the victory to Criss, R-Wood, launching a write-in campaign that garnered 261 votes. Libertarian Stephen Thomas Smith also pulled 215 votes. 
Both essentially watered down Hartzog’s base. 
Hartzog, a 24-year-old gas station clerk, beat Criss in the May primary after three super political action committees poured $145,000 into the race. Those super PACs — Sugar Maple PAC, the School Freedom Fund and Americans for Prosperity — are funded by out-of-state billionaires and are supportive of Gov. Patrick Morrisey. 
Criss drew the ire of the groups after he proposed legislation to cap payments from the Hope Scholarship, a program that uses taxpayer money for families to send their children to private schools or to home school them. 
He launched a write-in campaign in August, contending the closed Republican primaries had kept independent voters who would’ve supported him in the primary from showing up in May. 
Jason Huffman, executive director of Americans for Prosperity-West Virginia, said Criss’ write-in campaign was the deciding factor. 
“I think Republicans in that county can blame it all on Vernon Chris based on the amount of votes that probably would have gone to the Republican nominee if he had honored the will of the voters and decided not to run a foolish write-in campaign,” Huffman said. 
Criss, who headed up the power House Finance Committee and for a decade this go-around (he had a stint in the 1980s), garnered support from Republican mainstays, such as the state chamber of commerce and the West Virginia Home Builders Association for his long-shot write-in campaign. 
Criss ran a scorched earth campaign against Hartzog, from blocking campaign signs with his own to questioning if the nominee had a real girlfriend. He was accused of being a Morrisey toady and hinted at collusion with the super Pacs, which would be a violation of campaign finance law. 
Following the election, Criss purged most mentions of Hartzog from his campaign Facebook page. Criss could not be reached for comment Wednesday morning. 
Hartzog said other Wood County delegates who lost their seats in primary challenges didn’t react this way. 
“I can say it was deplorable,” Hartzog said. “I mean, it shouldn’t take a 24- year-old to tell a 72-year-old that he’s acting like a child. He lost the election. Scott Heckert moved on. Bill Anderson moved on. Why can’t Vernon? Because Vernon’s a child.” 
Hartzog threw a few elbows too.
For instance, he published a police blotter report from the local newspaper showing Criss’ wife had been charged with a DUI and obstructing an officer, both misdemeanors. The DUI was dismissed, but she pleaded guilty to the obstruction charge. 
The super PACs who had boosted Hartzog to a resounding victory in the primary didn’t show up in the general election. 
Huffman said for Americans for Prosperity-West Virginia, they had other races they needed to focus on, such as the close calls for Del. J.B. Akers, R-Kanawha, and Del. Margitta Mazzocchi, R-Boone. 
“You kind of have to make some trade-off decisions in terms of your resourcing, your time and bandwidth,” Huffman said. “And that one was not one that we considered to be hyper competitive in the general.” 
Hartzog said while the dispute between himself and Criss garnered some outsized attention, he believes that his political star is rising. 
“I defeated the House Finance chairman by a significant and wide margin. That was impressive as it is, and then I only lost by 151 votes out of 3,600,” he said. “That is a razor-thin margin. That is still impressive. I would say whenever l run again, I would hope that whoever runs against me takes that into consideration.” 
For his part, Rempel said he just focused on knocking on doors and talking to constituents. He focused his campaign on a winning issue for Democrats both statewide and nationally: affordability. 
“I tried to run a clean race, and there was a lot of discontent between a couple of them,” he said. “And you know, I just let that go.”

name: California
title: Xavier Becerra is California’s next governor: Five things to know
description: Unlike his predecessor, Democratic Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra has made few promises on the campaign trail and only hinted at certain policy priorities.
text:
In summary
Unlike his predecessor, Democratic Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra has made few promises on the campaign trail and only hinted at certain policy priorities. 


California Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra will take the reins during a delicate time for California. 
He faces the prospect of deeper federal healthcare cuts, skyrocketing wildfire costs and a persistent cost-of-living crisis. But many of the specifics of his policies are still unknown after he ran a quiet race as a Democrat in a safe blue state, promoting few programs and avoiding making commitments. 
Here’s what to know about what Becerra will tackle and how he’ll govern.
He’s open to new taxes
Becerra opposed the billionaire tax ballot proposition, saying he does not think taxing assets is a stable way to provide state revenues. And while he’s said he believes the wealthy should pay their “fair share” in taxes, he hasn’t explicitly endorsed any new income taxes. 
But he has signaled that he supports the idea of taxing corporations whose workers are paid so little they qualify for public benefits, or potentially ending tax credits to those companies. The state Department of Finance is studying what that kind of tax would look like and is expected to deliver recommendations to lawmakers next year. 
He has also said he’s considering a controversial proposal for the state to tax drivers based on their miles driven as a way to pay for road and highway repairs. The state collects that funding through gas taxes, but that source is expected to decline by $31 billion over the next decade as more drivers adopt electric vehicles. 
“I take no pleasure in telling people taxes are for a purpose,” he told reporters last week. “I believe that users should pay for (roads).”
Big decisions on climate and energy
Becerra has emphasized the need to keep energy affordable while California continues its clean energy transition. 
One program he’s pushing would give low-income households two hours of free electricity each day during daytime hours when solar energy is abundant and usage is low. The program, which he’s calling “power hour,” would be limited to utility customers who already qualify for assistance programs. 
He’s said he wants to “continue the path toward clean energy, but while we’re on that path we have to make sure we stabilize the prices,” including by drilling more oil in-state and will decide whether to keep California’s 2030 deadline to ban the sale of new gas cars on the state of electric vehicle charging infrastructure. 
He’ll also face pressure from investor-owned utilities that have been pushing lawmakers and outgoing Gov. Gavin Newsom to reduce how much they must pay to insurance companies and fire victims when their equipment sparks destructive wildfires.
If Newsom doesn’t resolve the issue in the next two months, Becerra will have to deal with it when he takes office; so far he’s declined to take a position, calling the debate a “food fight” between insurers and utilities.
Healthcare for undocumented immigrants
As a first-term congressmember from Los Angeles in 1993, Becerra caused a splash on Capitol Hill by arguing with an elder Democratic statesman over a plan to single out legal immigrants for social safety net cuts — he opposed it. He’s said he will seek to reverse restrictions to Medi-Cal that forced tens of thousands of immigrants who are in California illegally off the program.
Immigration has remained a key issue throughout his career. As governor, he’s promised to enforce new state laws that aim to curb immigration agents’ use of force and activities on state property. 
Newsom had expanded immigrant health coverage gradually to all income-qualifying adults but he began rolling back some coverage last year amid a budget deficit and unexpectedly high healthcare costs. 
“My values and my fiscal beliefs tell me that anyone who works hard in California should have access to the healthcare they need for themselves and for their family and they should be able to afford it, and that includes undocumented,” Becerra told KQED.
Continuing Newsom’s death penalty moratorium
Newsom placed a moratorium on the death penalty in 2019 when he took office, citing his moral opposition to executions, and during his terms he began to dismantle the state’s death row at San Quentin. Prisoners sentenced to death have since been moved to other prisons.
California has not executed any inmate since 2006. Newsom is considering whether to commute the death sentences of more than 560 prisoners to life sentences without parole but even if he doesn’t, don’t expect Becerra to resume executions. 
As attorney general, Becerra defended death sentences and said he supported them in principle, but said during the campaign that he would continue California’s moratorium over concerns about racial bias and wrongful convictions.
He calls himself a ‘pragmatic progressive’
In a party undergoing a yearslong identity crisis over how far left to push its policies, Becerra chooses incremental change over progressive moonshots. 
In his more than two decades in Congress, he had the ear of both progressive advocates and established Democratic leadership and was a close ally of former Speaker Nancy Pelosi, though the pair had a testy moment in 2009 when Becerra wanted her to push harder for a public option in the Affordable Care Act. 
This year, he backed away from his longtime support for single-payer healthcare, saying it’s a longshot for California with the Trump administration unlikely to give the state permission to launch. 
Even before that, he said he valued experience over grand promises like Medicare for All. As President Joe Biden’s health secretary, for example, he said he focused on expanding coverage. 
“When I was helping Hillary Clinton in 2016, my daughters wanted to vote for Bernie Sanders,” he said in an interview. “And I kept saying to them, I get it, I understand. I want Medicare for All … But we got to get (things) done, and I want someone who’s actually been in the thick of things.”

title: Pingree invites public to submit ideas for transition after election win
description: Fueled by little sleep, almost enough coffee and dozens of supporters touting “Governor-elect Hannah Pingree” signs, the second woman to serve as Maine’s chief executive celebrated her victory in Portland on Wednesday morning. While results are still coming in, The Associated Press reported as of noon that she secured 55.1%, with 91% of votes counted. […]
text:
Governor-elect Hannah Pingree with her daughter Elsie at the eastern promenade in Portland the morning after the Nov. 3 election. (Photo by Eesha Pendharkar/Maine Morning Star)Fueled by little sleep, almost enough coffee and dozens of supporters touting “Governor-elect Hannah Pingree” signs, the second woman to serve as Maine’s chief executive celebrated her victory in Portland on Wednesday morning.
While results are still coming in, The Associated Press reported as of noon that she secured 55.1%, with 91% of votes counted. Pingree is among at least 17 women that voters elected governor across the country Tuesday, a result she highlighted to cheers from the crowd.
“Last night we won, and we won big. And now I am ready to get to work, and I am not going to wait until January,” she said. 
But Pingree’s victory speech on Wednesday also focused on what comes next, highlighting the continuation of Democratic control in Augusta and the affordability challenges Mainers face that her administration will attempt to solve.
“A big majority is not a license to go it alone; it is a promise to get it done well,” she told the crowd gathered at Fort Allen Park. 
In victory speech, Pingree vows to fight for Maine

Pingree invited people to submit ideas through her transition website, which launched Wednesday morning and promised the process would be “open and transparent,” offering voters insight into “who’s helping us prepare, what we’re working on, and what decisions are being made.”
Pingree’s husband, Jason Mann, introduced her by recalling two qualities he said had defined her throughout the race: her empathy and her relentless work ethic.
“No one has ever outworked her, and no one ever will,” Mann said.
Pingree echoed that emphasis on hard work, crediting the people who knocked on doors, made calls, hosted events and helped build the campaign. She also thanked her predecessor, Gov. Janet Mills, saying the outgoing Democrat had led Maine through difficult times and given her opportunities to work on issues including healthcare and housing, which she intends to keep building on.
She also reiterated her central priorities from the campaign trail: housing that working families, young people and seniors can afford; accessible and affordable healthcare; and strong communities with good jobs, thriving small businesses and quality public schools.
“Maine sent a message to the whole country: We are ready to fix what is broken,” she said. 
To mitigate the impact of President Donald Trump’s policies on the state, Pingree said her administration will need to collaborate with Maine’s congressional delegation, including U.S. Senator-elect Troy Jackson and her mom, U.S. Rep. Chellie Pingree, who won her 10th term on election night.
“We need your help here in the state of Maine to turn around the healthcare and the food program cuts,” she said, addressing the delegation. “We need your help ending this war in Iran, these reckless tariffs that are raising prices, and we need heating oil relief. We need you as a partner with the state of Maine urgently.”

title: KY Dems capitalize on Trump’s bad image to flip US House seat, make legislative inroads
description: While Zach Dembo’s win in central Kentucky allowed the state to take a part in Democrats’ nationwide “blue tsunami,” part of that wave trickled down to the Kentucky General Assembly.  Nine Republican incumbents were ousted from their seats Tuesday evening, most with close margins in suburban areas of the state. Most of those lawmakers are […]
text:
Supporters of Zach Dembo, Kentucky Sixth Congressional District Democratic candidate, cheer while watching 2026 midterm election results at the Central Bank Center in downtown Lexington, Nov. 3, 2026.(Photo by Brian Simms for Kentucky Lantern)While Zach Dembo’s win in central Kentucky allowed the state to take a part in Democrats’ nationwide “blue tsunami,” part of that wave trickled down to the Kentucky General Assembly. 
Nine Republican incumbents were ousted from their seats Tuesday evening, most with close margins in suburban areas of the state. Most of those lawmakers are from areas surrounding the largest city in Kentucky, Louisville. Republicans still maintain a supermajority in the House and Senate. 
In a statement Wednesday morning after dust settled, Kentucky Democratic Party Chairman Colmon Elridge celebrated the seat flips and Democratic incumbents who maintained their seats. 
“Together, these leaders will rein in the GOP’s cruel, hyperpartisan supermajorities that have pushed Kentuckians to the side and taken corporate orders to kill popular, bipartisan bills on affordable housing, healthcare and data centers,” Elridge said. 
However, Tres Watson, a former spokesman for the Republican Party of Kentucky, said the midterms were a bad environment for Republicans and President Donald Trump.
“The people that we lost — both nationally and in the General Assembly here in Kentucky — we didn’t lose the hardcore MAGA people. We lost the center-right folks who were in competitive, potentially competitive districts, who weren’t Trumpers themselves, but they had that R behind their name, and that’s what that’s what people were mad at,” Watson said. “And because of the demographics of the districts, they were the most vulnerable to it.”
One incumbent Democrat, Rep. Adam Moore of Lexington, held his seat in the 45th House District with 54% of the vote over Republican challenger and former state Rep. Killian Timoney, who had 46% of the vote. Wednesday morning, Moore said the changes in the General Assembly for his caucus were because “Kentuckians are sick of a supermajority that just focuses on culture wars instead of bringing down costs for Kentuckians.” Moore pointed to mailers and attack ads within several of the statehouse races, including his own. 
“I think the mood today has to be celebratory, but also purposeful. We’re not going to go in there and say, ‘Hey, look at us. We have 26 seats now. We pass all the laws.’ … It’s the first time in a while that we have actually grown the Democratic caucus in Frankfort, and so that’s what we needed,” Moore said. “That was the giant step for Kentucky Democrats, but it’s only a small step in that direction towards getting back towards a majority.”
Flipping the 6th
Moore, whose state House district falls within the 6th Congressional District, said he did feel like that race influenced his. Dembo, the Democratic candidate there, won over Republican Ralph Alvarado by about 10 points Tuesday. The seat had been in Republican hands since 2012. 
“I think Zach Dembo was going to win regardless of who the Republican candidate was, but he won because of the national tide. Also, he is a great candidate, someone who has served in uniform, has served in the Beshear administration, has served as a prosecutor, and is now going to serve us in Congress,” Moore said. 
The lawmaker added that he viewed Alvarado as a candidate with “way too much baggage.” Dembo’s campaign repeatedly highlighted that Alvarado, a former state senator, was former Gov. Matt Bevin’s running mate in 2019. Gov. Andy Beshear, who endorsed and campaigned with Dembo this year, defeated Bevin. 
Speaking to the Kentucky Lantern at Dembo’s watch party Tuesday, Elridge called Alvarado “a uniquely bad candidate,” while Dembo was “a uniquely great candidate” and  connected with voters over “the frustrations that people in the district felt.” 
“I think his biggest misstep was that he ran,” Elridge said of Alvarado. “Now, I’m thankful for him that he ran. I think it was a great misstep that we capitalized on. But frankly, I also believe … we would have beat whoever they ran because the Republican Party right now has a Trump problem, and they are so beholden to him that no candidate that came out of that primary was going to abandon Trump and his policies.”
Trump endorsed Alvarado ahead of the May primary. 
Trey Grayson, a former Republican secretary of state, said Dembo “ran a really good campaign” and was bolstered by national Democratic support. The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee named the seat as a district in play and put the race on its Red to Blue program. Like Watson, Grayson also pointed to a bad national environment for Republicans heading into midterms. Grayson said Alvarado did run a good campaign in the 6th. 
Asked if Tuesday night signaled that Republican candidates need to pivot from Trump, Grayson said two narratives came up. Suburban and urban areas showed “a clear message from those voters about Trump,” but in rural Kentucky areas, Republicans continued to win. 
“The reality is that Trump’s a lame duck. He’ll be leaving office in two years. He’s likely going to receive or should receive a lot of political blame for what happened nationwide, and that’s going to weaken him,” Grayson said. “So, in some respects, the separation from Trump will kind of happen naturally, given all those factors. … When you try to attach yourself to the hip of Trump when it’s good, and then it’s hard to detach yourself from the same hip when all of a sudden it was bad.”

title: Dem challenger defeats Indiana House GOP leader in stunning upset
description: A virtual unknown has unseated one of the most powerful Republicans in Indiana elected office. text:
House Speaker Todd Huston stands atop the podium as the chamber chugs through remaining proposals on ate Thursday, April 24, 2025. (Leslie Bonilla Muñiz/Indiana Capital Chronicle)A virtual unknown has unseated one of the most powerful Republicans in Indiana elected office.
Democrat Lauren Cole, a clinical trial coordinator, defeated House Speaker Todd Huston 52% to 48%.
“This victory belongs to every person who believed in this campaign and helped make it possible,” Cole said on social media. “To the voters of District 37: thank you for trusting me to represent you. This campaign was always about putting people first, and that’s exactly what I intend to do.”
Democrat Lauren Cole (Courtesy photo)
House District 37 covers parts of Hamilton County. It’s among the more than a dozen seats to flip for Democrats so far, shattering the GOP’s 14-year supermajority in the House.
Cole ran on a platform of access to affordable healthcare, strengthening public school funding and investing in workers.
Huston, of Fishers, was first elected to the chamber in 2012. He has served as speaker since 2020.
His stunning defeat comes even though caucus leaders usually represent comfortably drawn districts.
“This was an incredibly challenging midterm election and ultimately the national headwinds were too difficult to overcome in a number of our races,” Huston said in a written statement. “We’re so proud of our team and all our candidates who stepped up to serve and spent countless hours in their communities, listening to voters and talking about the issues that matter to Hoosiers.”
He said he was disappointed by the results but was proud of the progress “we’ve made in Indiana to grow our economy, bring good-paying jobs to our state, lower taxes and create thriving communities where people want to live, work, start a business and raise their family. It’s been the honor of my life serving Hoosiers in Hamilton County and across our great state. I’m grateful for the opportunity and all that we’ve accomplished together.”

name: WyoFile
title: Wyoming soda ash producer to cut 350 jobs amid market pressure from China
description:
The layoffs will take place over the next two years, beginning in January, due to competition from China.
The post Wyoming soda ash producer to cut 350 jobs amid market pressure from China appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Wyoming trona miner and soda ash producer WE Soda will convert its Westvaco underground mining operation to in-situ solution recovery, a less labor intensive drill-and-pump method that will lead to 350 job cuts over the next two years.
Layoffs will begin in January, the company announced Wednesday morning.
“The [underground mining] transition will be carried out progressively over approximately the next two years,” the company stated in a press release. “This repositioning is necessary to strengthen the long-term competitiveness of the company’s Wyoming operations in response to the significant impact which low-cost Chinese soda ash exports have had on the pricing of American soda ash in export markets.”
Tata Chemicals workers observe a train being loaded with soda ash in southwest Wyoming. (Dustin Bleizeffer/WyoFile)
A United Steelworkers Local 13214 union representative posted on social media that WE Soda workers in Wyoming were “blindsided” by the news, and vowed to “protect as many jobs as possible.”
In addition to the job cuts from approximately 850 workers to 500 over the next two years, the operational transition will reduce soda ash production output by more than 1.5 million metric tons annually, “with a corresponding reduction in export sales that are no longer commercially viable,” the company said.
WE Soda CEO Alasdair Warren told WyoFile in September the greater trona and soda ash industry in southwest Wyoming is under pressure from a flood of Chinese soda ash, requiring producers here to find “efficiencies.”
“There’s a lot of headwinds,” Warren told WyoFile. “Historically, any downturn in the industry had typically been resolved as demand picked up over 18 months. We’re now in year four, and it looks like it’s going to roll on for at least another couple of years. This is a long downturn.”
Soda ash derived from trona is the state’s largest global export commodity, reaping an annual $1.3 billion, according to industry officials. Soda ash is used to make glass, myriad home products such as toothpaste, and industrial materials.
This is a breaking story and may be updated.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Who won Mississippi’s midterm Senate race? We may not know for a while
description: Natasha Harris holds a sign encouraging residents to vote during the midterm elections in Jackson on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Democrat Scott Colom was within striking distance Wednesday of pulling off an historic upset in Mississippi’s U.S. Senate race between him and Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, but the race remained too close to call.
As Mississippians woke up Wednesday morning and the nation turned its attention to the Magnolia State, a razor-thin margin separated Colom, a Democratic district attorney in north Mississippi, and Hyde-Smith. As of 9 a.m., Colom led by less than 100 votes in incomplete and unofficial results.

A legal fight is likely. Ballots remained uncounted in Hinds County, the most populous area of the state and a Democratic stronghold and counties along the Coast where Hyde-Smith has maintained an edge. Thousands of affidavit and mail-in ballots also remain to be counted.
The midterm race saw a massive turnout, with nearly 1 million people voting, rivaling presidential election turnout in Mississippi.
Colom addressed reporters at his campaign headquarters on Wednesday morning, saying that he has a clear path to victory.
“I’m very happy with where we stand,” Colom said. “I’m confident once the process lays out where the ballots are, we’re going to win, because the people of Mississippi turned out in historic numbers to make this race possible.” 
Colom said his campaign had deployed attorneys across the state to monitor local election officials counting the remaining ballots and processing affidavit and absentee ballots that could arrive over the next week.
“We will protect the process of this election,” Colom said. “We will protect the integrity of this election.” 
At a watcher party on Tuesday evening, Hyde-Smith’s all but declared victory. 
“I assure you I will continue to be your U.S. senator.”
That was before Colom took the lead. 
By late morning on Wednesday, shortly after Colom addressed reporters, her campaign manager, Jake Monssen, issued a statement thanking supporters and pointing out that thousands of ballots remained uncounted. 
“With the vast majority of Election Day ballots reported, the margin is measured in just dozens of votes,” Monssen said. “We have thousands of outstanding ballots, including affidavit and absentee ballots, which still must be processed and verified under Mississippi law. Our campaign is closely monitoring the remaining count. We remain confident that when every legally cast vote is fully and accurately counted, Mississippians will have reelected Cindy Hyde-Smith.”
It appeared many groups are gearing up for a fight. 
On Tuesday night, the state Democratic Party filed a court challenge claiming several precincts in DeSoto County had problems, including delayed openings, “extraordinary waiting periods” and a shortage of regular ballots and affidavit ballots.
LIVE: 2026 Mississippi election results
Kelcy Higgins, a Mississippi-based political operative and community organizer and director of the Magnolia Project, called for volunteers to help with Election Day fallout.
“The work of the 2026 election is not over,” Higgins said. “Affidavit ballots remain to be reviewed and counted across Mississippi’s precincts, and we must ensure that every eligible vote is properly counted. Mississippi needs election protection volunteers now to help protect the process and make sure every eligible vote is counted and no voter’s voice is left out.”
Colom, a district attorney in northern Mississippi, would be the first Democrat elected to the U.S. Senate since John Stennis in 1982. He would be the first Black person elected to the U.S. Senate from Mississippi since Reconstruction, when the state Legislature elected Hiram Revels in 1870 and Blanche Bruce in 1875.
Hyde-Smith is the first woman to be elected to federal office in Mississippi.
Most forecasters had rated the Mississippi Senate race as safely Republican. But on the issues defining the midterms in Mississippi and beyond, voters left little doubt it would be a referendum on President Donald Trump — on soaring consumer prices exacerbated by tariffs and his war with Iran.
Colom has campaigned hard, crisscrossing the state and receiving help from the national party. 
Dan Pffeifer, a political commentator and former senior advisor to President Barack Obama, said Colom “has run a campaign that is a model for Dems trying to flip very red states.”
Hyde-Smith, a Brookhaven cattle farmer, was first appointed to the Senate in 2018 to replace longtime Sen. Thad Cochran. She won two races against former U.S. Agriculture Secretary Mike Espy and early on appeared confident she would gain a third victory, in part from the continued endorsement of Trump. 
Hyde-Smith’s main campaign message was to label Colom an extremist, and the “most radical Senate candidate of our lifetime.” She attempted to label him as a puppet of far-left national Democrats, with a spokesman calling him a stooge of Schumer and to billionaire donor George Soros.

name: Delaware
title: Delaware GOP faces rebuilding challenge after election losses, fundraising struggles
description: Democrats’ new legislative supermajorities, a widening gap in statewide votes, and limited campaign resources leave Republican leaders confronting difficult questions about the party’s future. By George D. Rotsch, Delaware LIVE News DOVER, Del. — Delaware Republican Party Chairman Gene Truono is calling for unity, stronger candidate support and a reassessmen[...]
text:
Democrats’ new legislative supermajorities, a widening gap in statewide votes, and limited campaign resources leave Republican leaders confronting difficult questions about the party’s future.
By George D. Rotsch, Delaware LIVE News
DOVER, Del. — Delaware Republican Party Chairman Gene Truono is calling for unity, stronger candidate support and a reassessment of party operations following Tuesday’s election, which left Republicans without a statewide elected office and reduced their representation in the General Assembly.
The Nov. 3 results underscore the challenges facing a party that has struggled for years to compete statewide, particularly in heavily Democratic New Castle County, while relying increasingly on Sussex County and portions of Kent County for its electoral base.
Democrats won all five federal and statewide contests, captured three Republican-held House seats and secured more than two-thirds of the seats in both chambers of the legislature. The result gives Democrats the votes needed to approve constitutional amendments without Republican support, provided their members remain united.
In a statement Wednesday, Truono thanked Republican candidates and their families, volunteers and supporters but acknowledged the organizational challenges confronting the party.
“Every candidate faces unique challenges, from fundraising and organizing volunteers to communicating with voters,” Truono said. “While candidates are ultimately responsible for managing and running their individual campaigns, the Delaware Republican Party recognizes those challenges and remains committed to strengthening the resources, coordination, and support available to them.”
His remarks come as election results and campaign finance reports raise questions about whether the Delaware GOP has the financial resources, organizational reach and voter support necessary to compete more effectively.
Election results reveal the size of the challenge



Republican House seats   11  Down from 14

Statewide offices held        0   Five GOP losses

Registered Republicans    24.6%  Of Delaware voters


Sources: Unofficial Nov. 3 election returns and Delaware Department of Elections registration report, Nov. 1.

Republicans entered the election holding 14 of the 41 House seats. They will begin the next legislative session with 11, compared with 30 Democrats.
The GOP also will hold six of the 21 Senate seats, while Democrats control 15. That gives Democrats approximately 73% of House seats and 71% of Senate seats.
Three House races illustrate the Republican losses:




Kent County, District 34: Democratic challenger Annie Norman defeated Republican Rep. Lyndon Yearick, 4,905 votes to 4,755 — a margin of just 150 votes.






Sussex County, District 4: Democrat Gregg Lindner defeated Republican Dan Zitofsky, 8,039 votes to 7,658, capturing the seat being vacated by Republican Rep. Jeff Hilovsky.






New Castle County, District 9: Democrat Ayanna Khan-Flowers defeated Republican Jamar Money, 8,451 votes to 4,753, winning the seat being vacated by Republican Rep. Kevin Hensley.




Republicans did retain several competitive or open seats, including House districts 33, 38 and 41 and Senate District 15. Republican Mike Smith also won reelection in his Pike Creek-area district, while Republican Emily Thompson won the open Senate seat previously held by Dave Lawson.
The results leave Republicans with fewer legislators to influence policy, negotiate legislation or prevent Democrats from acting along party lines.
Republicans can still participate in legislative debates, negotiate with Democratic lawmakers and build coalitions on individual issues. But without sufficient votes to block constitutional amendments on their own, their influence will depend increasingly on public opinion and disagreements within the Democratic caucuses.
Statewide vote totals show a persistent Republican disadvantage
The results were similarly one-sided in statewide races. Democratic candidates received between 60% and 65% of the vote in each of the five federal and statewide contests.
Democratic U.S. Sen. Chris Coons won reelection with 63.6% of the vote against Republican Mike Katz, while U.S. Rep. Sarah McBride received 64.3% against Republican Joe Arminio.
In the open state treasurer’s race, Democrat Ted Lauzen defeated former Republican House Minority Leader Mike Ramone, 62.4% to 37.6%. Attorney General Kathy Jennings and Auditor Lydia York also won reelection.
Those figures suggest the GOP’s difficulties extend beyond individual candidates or particular campaigns. Republicans are attracting support beyond their registered voter base, but that support has not been sufficient to seriously challenge Democratic control of statewide offices.
Voter turnout increased, but Republicans failed to capitalize
Delaware’s statewide turnout increased to 47.5%, compared with 42.7% in the 2022 midterm election, according to unofficial results.
A total of 384,862 ballots were cast, up from 325,558 four years earlier.




Delaware midterm voter turnout



Despite the stronger participation, Republicans did not gain ground in the legislature or statewide offices.



Registration figures help explain the challenge. As of Nov. 1, Delaware had 333,488 registered Democrats, compared with 199,294 Republicans and 276,849 voters registered as unaffiliated or with other parties.
That gives Democrats a registration advantage of more than 134,000 voters. Republicans account for approximately one-quarter of the electorate, while more than one-third are not registered with either major party.

Source: Delaware Department of Elections, Nov. 1, 2026.
Republicans retain a registration advantage in Sussex County, where they outnumber Democrats 78,779 to 68,370. But in New Castle County, Democrats have more than twice as many registered voters as Republicans.
The GOP’s dependence on its Sussex County base presents a mathematical challenge. Winning strongly Republican districts is not enough to offset Democratic margins in the state’s most populous county.
Final turnout figures by party registration were not yet available Wednesday. Mid-afternoon Election Day data showed Democrats voting at a higher rate than Republicans, although those numbers did not represent final turnout.
Republicans have historically demonstrated an ability to turn out their registered voters at competitive rates. In 2022, for example, 52.1% of registered Republicans voted, compared with 42.6% of registered Democrats. That advantage in participation was not sufficient to overcome the Democratic registration lead.
Fundraising gap raises questions about party resources
Financial records indicate that the Delaware Republican Party also entered the final weeks of the election with substantially fewer resources than its Democratic counterpart.
According to Federal Election Commission filings covering Jan. 1, 2025, through Oct. 14, 2026, the Republican State Committee of Delaware reported approximately $556,572 in total receipts and $583,180 in expenditures.
The committee reported just $4,954 in cash on hand at the end of that reporting period, along with $11,000 in outstanding debt.
The Democratic State Committee reported approximately $1.52 million in receipts over the same period, nearly three times the Republican total.

Party committee receipts, 2025-26 cycle through Oct. 14




Federal Election Commission committee receipts, including transfers and other noncontribution income




FEC figures represent receipts, not exclusively donor contributions. They include transfers and other income, and do not encompass every state or local committee.

The money gap was even more pronounced in the federal campaigns.
In the U.S. Senate race, Coons reported raising approximately $7.69 million through Oct. 14, compared with about $190,000 reported by Katz through the same date.
In the U.S. House race, McBride reported raising about $5.56 million through Oct. 14, while Arminio reported approximately $12,300 through Sept. 30. The latter comparison uses the candidates’ latest available reports, which cover different ending dates.
Fundraising advantages do not guarantee electoral victories, and statewide party committee filings do not capture all fundraising by candidates, county organizations and outside groups.
Nevertheless, the differences demonstrate the scale of the financial challenge. Campaigns with limited resources face difficulties maintaining paid advertising, voter outreach, data operations and professional staffing across an election cycle.
Truono’s statement recognizes fundraising as a candidate responsibility while also acknowledging the need for stronger party assistance. It does not specify new fundraising commitments, staffing changes or financial targets.
Truono acknowledges divisions and looks to Democrats for lessons
Perhaps the most revealing portion of Truono’s statement is his recognition that Delaware Democrats have managed to coordinate electoral efforts despite significant disagreements within their own party.
“There are also lessons to be learned from our political opponents,” Truono said.
“Despite significant ideological and policy disagreements within the Democratic Party, including among progressive and Working Families Party-aligned candidates, Democrats have often demonstrated an ability to set aside public divisions and come together around shared electoral objectives.”
The comments follow a Democratic primary season in which progressive candidates defeated several incumbent lawmakers, creating differences within the party over its direction and leadership.
Those disagreements have not prevented Democrats from retaining statewide control, although the next General Assembly will test their ability to remain united on legislation and constitutional amendments.
Truono also acknowledged criticism within Republican ranks.
“We also recognize that there are differing opinions and constructive criticisms concerning the direction of our Party,” he said. “Those perspectives deserve to be heard respectfully.”
He urged Republicans to turn disagreements into solutions rather than allow internal disputes to overshadow shared objectives.
The statement, however, provides few specifics about how the GOP will change its operations. It does not identify organizational decisions that may have contributed to Tuesday’s defeats or establish measurable goals for improving future campaigns.
In a separate election-night interview with Delaware Public Media, Truono expressed disappointment that the party had failed to achieve its objectives in competitive legislative races. He said Republicans had hoped to gain House and Senate seats and expected to continue concentrating on local contests rather than statewide offices.
What comes next for Delaware Republicans?
Tuesday’s results offer evidence of both the GOP’s difficulties and the limits of Democratic dominance in certain parts of the state.
Republicans won several open legislative races, retained their advantage in Sussex County voter registration and remained competitive in some districts. The 150-vote loss in House District 34 and the 381-vote defeat in District 4 show that relatively small shifts in local elections can change legislative representation.
But the broader statewide picture is less encouraging for the party.
Republicans have not held a statewide elected office since 2018. They now face even smaller legislative minorities, a substantial disadvantage in registered voters and significant gaps in campaign fundraising.
The party’s challenges cannot be attributed entirely to internal disagreements or limited financial support. The results also raise questions about the appeal of Republican candidates and policies to unaffiliated voters and moderate Democrats, particularly in New Castle County.
For Republicans, improving campaign operations alone may not be enough. A significant change in electoral performance would also require building a broader coalition of voters.
For Democrats, their expanded majorities create additional responsibility for governing. The party will have the votes to advance major policy changes, but its increasingly diverse caucuses may not agree on every issue. Democratic leaders will also face scrutiny over the decisions they make with that authority.
Truono closed his statement by congratulating those elected and expressing a willingness to work constructively across party lines.
“This election presents an opportunity to reflect, listen, and build,” he said. “We remain committed to representing Delaware voters, strengthening our organization across all three counties, and advancing responsible government, affordability, accountability, and meaningful representation.”
Whether that reflection produces meaningful organizational changes remains to be seen.
For now, the election leaves the Delaware GOP with a clear set of challenges: fewer elected officials, a smaller voter base than its principal opponent and substantially fewer financial resources.
The question confronting Republican leaders is no longer simply how to compete in individual elections, but how to rebuild a party capable of competing consistently across Delaware.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Democrats flip six TN state House seats, as Mufreesboro area delivers blue wave
description: Tennessee Democrats flipped six state House seats during Tuesday’s election and nearly wiped out the existing Rutherford County delegation as three of five Republicans lost their races. Democrats still remain in the superminority in Tennessee’s state House, but the victory marked the first time the party has gained multiple seats in an election since 1996. [[...]
text:
Allie Phillips, photographed on Oct. 29, 2023, flipped a Clarksville state House district, defeating incumbent state Rep.Michael Lankford. (Photo by John Partpilo for Tennessee Lookout)iTennessee Democrats flipped six state House seats during Tuesday’s election and nearly wiped out the existing Rutherford County delegation as three of five Republicans lost their races.
Democrats still remain in the superminority in Tennessee’s state House, but the victory marked the first time the party has gained multiple seats in an election since 1996. Republicans will now hold 68 seats in the state House, down from 74; Democrats will have 31
Three rematches from 2024 — in Clarksville, Knoxville and Memphis — were top priorities this election cycle and all three Democratic candidates performed to plan, knocking out GOP incumbents.
Bryan Goldberg defeated state Rep. Elaine Davis in Knoxville, Jesse Huseth defeated state Rep. John Gillepsie in Memphis and Allie Phillips defeated state Rep. Michael Lankford in Clarksville.



Quotation







It’s a testament to the Republican supermajority agenda of cultural wars over affordability.They’ve neglected Rutherford for so long.


– Rep. Aftyn Behn, D-Nashville, on Democratic wins in Rutherford County


In Rutherford County’s mini-blue wave, Democrats flipped a trio of seats. Connie Casha defeated state Rep. Mike Sparks in Smyrna, Brett Windrow defeated state Rep. Robert Stevens in Smyrna and Owen Farnsworth defeated state Rep. Tim Rudd in Murfreesboro.
State Rep. Aftyn Behn, a Nashville Democrat, said the election was a “Murfreesboro miracle.”
“It’s a testament to the Republican supermajority agenda of cultural wars over affordability,” said Behn. “They’ve neglected Rutherford for so long.”
Republican support in Rutherford County cratered by nearly 19% from the 2024 Presidential election. President Donald Trump won the county in 2024 with 60% of the vote. On Tuesday, U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn received 41% of the county’s vote in the gubernatorial election.
Huseth and Phillips races drew the most attention from the party
Huseth and Gillepsie faced off in a district in the Memphis suburbs that was the only state House district held by a Republican that Democratic Vice President Kamala Harris won during the 2024 Presidential election, and which Huseth narrowly lost in the last election.
The Tennessee House Democratic Caucus poured $27,000 into Huseth’s campaign. Huseth said he focused more on the state budget this year, campaigning on issues like eliminating the state grocery tax and making Pre-K more accessible. 
Gillespie, an outspoken supporter of the Memphis Safe Task Force, ran on a platform of public safety and crime reduction. During his legislative tenure, Gillespie sponsored several crime-focused laws, including several that increased sentences for certain violent convictions and a controversial “truth in sentencing” law requiring certain convicted felons to serve their entire sentence without parole eligibility. 
Jesse Huseth, a Memphis businessman, defeated GOP Rep. John Gillespie in a rematch from 2024. (Photo by Karen Pulfer Focht for Tennessee Lookout)
He also worked with Republican  Sen. Brent Taylor of Shelby County to sponsor a bill that overturned a Memphis ordinance barring police from making “pretextual” traffic stops, or stops for minor violations that act as a “pretext” for further investigation. The Memphis City Council passed the ordinance after the beating and death of Tyre Nichols at the hands of Memphis police, who pulled Nichols over for reckless driving in January 2023.
Phillips also ran in 2024 against state Rep. Jeff Burkhart. Lankford was appointed to fill the vacancy created when Burkhart died in November  2025. Phillips made a national name for herself after she was forced to leave the state to terminate a nonviable pregnancy because of Tennessee’s strict abortion ban.
The Democratic victory in Clarksville continues the party’s strong showing in Montgomery County, which won the majority of the county’s commission seats in the August election for the first time since the body began holding partisan elections. 
In the state Senate, each party held its current slate of seats. Republicans hold a 27-6 advantage in the state’s upper legislative chamber.
State. Sen. Brent Taylor won both his U.S. House and state Senate races, so a special election will be needed to replace him. Republican Jimmy Matlock won the seat to replace outgoing Senate Speaker and Lt. Gov. Randy McNally. Matlock previously served in the state House from 2006 to 2018. 
The Tennessee Senate Republican caucus will hold a vote on Nov. 10 to pick its replacement for McNally, ahead of the legislative session. Whoever is chosen will also be second in line of succession for governor.
Cassandra Stephenson contributed to this report.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Charlie Christ wins the St. Petersburg mayoral race
description: ST. PETERSBURG — Charlie Crist is back in government, this time at the local level following his victory over incumbent Ken Welch Tuesday to become St. Petersburg’s next mayor. The former Republican governor-turned-Democratic U.S. House member won the nonpartisan race easily, 62%-38%. Speaking at his election party in downtown St. Pete, Crist said people cam[...]
text:
Charlie Crist (photo taken from his Facebook page).ST. PETERSBURG — Charlie Crist is back in government, this time at the local level following his victory over incumbent Ken Welch Tuesday to become St. Petersburg’s next mayor. The former Republican governor-turned-Democratic U.S. House member won the nonpartisan race easily, 62%-38%.
Speaking at his election party in downtown St. Pete, Crist said people came up to him on the campaign trail to ask why as a former governor he would run for mayor.
“Cause it’s home,” he said. “It’s [my] hometown. And you know, home is where the heart is.”
Crist is one of the rare public officials to become mayor of a city after leading a state as governor. The most notable member of that club is Jerry Brown, who became mayor of Oakland in 1998 after serving as California governor from 1974 through 1982. (He served as governor again between 2010 and 2018).
Another former governor-turned-mayor is John Carney in Delaware. He served as governor there from 2016 to 2024 and was elected mayor of Wilmington in November 2024.
Former New York Gov. Andrew Cuomo failed in his attempt to become mayor of New York City in 2025.
Crist’s victory marks another remarkable turn in a political career unlike anyone else in Florida politics. He has served on and off in public office going back more than three decades, representing both political parties. He was a Republican when he first won a seat representing parts of Pinellas and Hillsborough counties in the Florida Senate in 1992. He was reelected to that seat in 1994.
In 1998, he suffered his first defeat, losing badly to Democrat Bob Graham in a bid for U.S. Senate.  He rebounded, winning election as Florida education commissioner in 2000 (when it was still a statewide elected position), and then Florida attorney general in 2002.
In 2006, he became Florida’s governor, defeating Tampa-area Democratic U.S. Rep. Jim Davis. For the first three years of his tenure, he enjoyed high approval ratings. But his literal embrace of Democratic President Barack Obama and his economic stimulus plan put Crist on the wrong side with Republicans.
His plan to run as the GOP nominee for U.S. Senate in 2010 hit a buzzsaw when former Florida Speaker of the House Marco Rubio entered the race. Realizing he couldn’t beat Rubio in the Republican primary, Crist left the party and ran as an independent, losing in the general election to Rubio by nearly 20 points in a three-way race.
He was still a political independent when he spoke during the Democratic National Convention in North Carolina in 2012, announcing his endorsement of Barack Obama. Later that year, he became a registered Democrat.
In 2014, he was Democratic nominee for governor in Florida, losing by a single percentage point to Republican Rick Scott, 48%-47%.
In 2016, after congressional redistricting made the Pinellas County-based Congressional District 13 more Democratic-leaning, Crist took on then-Republican incumbent David Jolly and won a seat in Congress, where he served for six years.
In 2021, Crist announced he would run for governor as a Democrat against Republican Ron DeSantis. It did not go well, with DeSantis winning by 19 points in November 2022.
Following that defeat, Crist began spending significant time living in Minnesota with his fiancée, Chelsea Grimes. He moved back to St. Petersburg last year to qualify for the mayoral race,  announcing in the spring that he would challenge Welch, who was elected in 2021.
He immediately began raising large amounts of campaign cash and took in the most votes in the primary in August against five opponents, winning 35% of the vote. Welch came in second with 21%, separating the two to compete in the general election.
“This is a race that I think is the most unifying experience politically I’ve ever had,” Crist said Tuesday night. “As you know, it’s a nonpartisan race. And I can’t tell you how sweet that’s been. … Because, as you all know, it’s a little toxic out there, politically. But we have Republicans, we have Democrats, we have independents, we have Black, we have white, we have everything in this room, and it’s a great thing. St. Petersburg comes together.”
Crist will be sworn into office in early January.

name: WyoFile
title: Wyoming poised to welcome new major political party based on Bextel’s vote totals
description:
The Constitution Party is set to become the state’s third major party. 
The post Wyoming poised to welcome new major political party based on Bextel’s vote totals appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Wyoming is poised to recognize a new major party after Rebecca Bextel, a Constitution Party candidate for governor, secured approximately 16% of the vote, according to the secretary of state’s unofficial results in Tuesday’s general election. 
A minor party in Wyoming can elevate to major-party status if one of its candidates for governor, secretary of state or U.S. House collects at least 10% of the total vote for that office in the general election. 
The Constitution party will now join the Republican and Democratic parties with major status. That means it will nominate candidates through the primary election process rather than through party conventions. 
“Thank you to everyone who cast their vote for me yesterday,” Bextel said in a statement to WyoFile. “Nine weeks ago, I entered this race to fulfill a promise I made to the people of Wyoming: to give them a choice in this gubernatorial election. While the results were not what I had hoped for, it is clear that there are many misinformed voters still out there who blindly voted for an R, which is what the Democrats were counting on to get their guy in there!”

Constitution Party candidate Tamara Trujillo takes her opening stance on Wednesday, Oct. 14, 2026, during the Wyoming PBS secretary of state debate in Riverton. (Carl Cote/County 10)

No minor-party candidate has ever won a statewide elected office in Wyoming, but at least once before they’ve been able to garner the requisite support to upgrade to major-party status. 
That happened in 2014 when Constitution and Libertarian party candidates running for secretary of state earned the necessary votes. The status, however, was short-lived for both parties. Each dropped back down to minor status following the 2016 election cycle. 
This year, Shawn Johnson of Casper ran as a Libertarian candidate for congress, while three Constitution Party candidates also sought higher office including Rebecca Bextel of Jackson for governor, Tamara Trujillo of Cheyenne for secretary of state and Jeff Haggit of Mountain View for U.S. House. Only Bextel received the requisite 10% vote for major-party status, according to the unofficial results. 

Libertarian Candidate for Wyoming’s U.S. House seat Shawn Johnson fields a question a debate in Riverton on Thursday, Oct. 15, 2026. (Carl Cote/County 10)

Bextel and Trujillo are both former GOP members, while Johnson and Haggit have previously run for office with their current party affiliation. 
Haggit has served as chairman of the Wyoming Constitution Party and is currently vice chairman. 
Johnson served on the Casper City Council, a nonpartisan body, from 2014 to 2022 and was the city’s vice mayor in 2019. 
From 2023 to 2024, Trujillo, a Republican at the time, represented Cheyenne’s House District 44. 
In May, Bextel announced she would run as a third-party candidate for governor if Republican voters nominated Gillette Sen. Eric Barlow in the primary election. Before that, Bextel unsuccessfully ran for chairman of the Wyoming Republican Party on her fundraising chops. She was also at the center of the Checkgate controversy that dominated the 2026 legislative session which involved her handing out campaign checks to lawmakers on the House floor. 

Constitution Party candidate Jeff Haggit gives his closing remarks during the U.S. House debate on Thursday, Oct. 15, 2026, in Riverton. (Carl Cote/County 10)

Constitution Party Chairman Josh Shimkus previously told WyoFile he didn’t know Bextel before Checkgate, but recruited her in the months afterwards when he saw a potential ally for his vision for his party. 
“I was very interested in obtaining ‘Bextel bucks,’ as the press put it,” Shimkus said in May.
Political parties in Wyoming are not required to file campaign finance reports until Nov. 13. Meantime, Bextel amended her campaign finance filings on Oct. 29 to report more than $362,000 in donations from the Wyoming Constitution Party. 
In her original filings, Bextel reported raising a total of approximately $89,000. Soon after, Jackson Democratic Rep. Mike Yin filed a complaint against Bextel and other candidates regarding contributions to several gubernatorial campaigns allegedly exceeding the legal limit an individual can give to a statewide candidate per election. The secretary of state’s office is currently reviewing such complaints.
Bextel did not respond to WyoFile’s request for comment by publishing time. 
Wyoming’s election results are considered unofficial until they are certified by the state canvassing board next week.
The post Wyoming poised to welcome new major political party based on Bextel’s vote totals appeared first on WyoFile .
