name: California
title: Lo que sabemos sobre los resultados de las 14 propuestas electorales de California
description: Las 14 propuestas electorales de California incluyen un impuesto a los multimillonarios, la identificación de votantes, cambios en las elecciones revocatorias y un intento de acelerar la construcción limitando las evaluaciones ambientales.
text:
In summary
Las 14 propuestas electorales de California incluyen un impuesto a los multimillonarios, la identificación de votantes, cambios en las elecciones revocatorias y un intento de acelerar la construcción limitando las evaluaciones ambientales.


This article is also available in English. Read it here.Los votantes están decidiendo el destino de 14 propuestas estatales, incluido el polémico impuesto a los multimillonarios. Las campañas a favor y en contra de estas propuestas han gastado un total de casi mil millones de dólares, la mayor cantidad jamás invertida en medidas electorales estatales. Más allá del impuesto a los multimillonarios, los californianos se enfrentan a decisiones sobre una amplia gama de temas, incluyendo cómo se llevan a cabo las elecciones revocatorias, cómo acelerar el desarrollo limitando las evaluaciones ambientales y si el estado debería destinar más dinero a la vivienda y la investigación médica. Esta noticia se actualizará a medida que se conozcan los resultados de las elecciones. Propuesta 1: Esta medida autoriza al estado a endeudarse hasta $11.25 mil millones para la construcción y renovación de viviendas , principalmente para unidades de alquiler. Muchos promotores inmobiliarios y gobiernos locales que reciban el dinero deberán reservar una parte para viviendas asequibles para inquilinos de bajos ingresos o para viviendas especializadas para personas sin hogar. La medida fue aprobada con el 59% de los votos a favor del bono a las 23:00 horas. Propuesta 2: Los votantes decidieron permitir que el estado deposite más dinero en sus reservas , también conocidas como fondo de reserva. California tiene un sistema tributario bastante volátil que fluctúa según los ingresos de sus contribuyentes más ricos, pero las normas estatales de la década de 1970 limitan la cantidad de dinero que el estado puede ahorrar en años de superávit. La medida fue aprobada con el 60% de los votos a las 22:00 horas, según la agencia Associated Press. Propuesta 3 : Este impuesto sobre la renta para las personas con mayores ingresos destinaría más fondos a la educación primaria y secundaria. Aprobado inicialmente en 2012 como medida temporal, este impuesto, que afecta a las personas que ganan más de 360.000 dólares al año, se convertiría en permanente si los votantes aprueban la Propuesta 3. La medida fue aprobada con casi el 59% de los votos a favor a las 2:55 a. m. Propuesta 4: Esta medida permitiría a los gobiernos estatales y locales crear financiamiento público para campañas políticas , lo que, según sus defensores, podría ayudar a limitar el gasto político. Para aceptar fondos públicos para sus campañas, los candidatos generalmente deben aceptar ciertos límites de gasto. El "No" va a la cabeza, con casi el 52% de los votantes en contra a las 22:00 horas. Proposición 5 : En California, las elecciones revocatorias preguntan a los votantes si desean destituir al funcionario electo y a quién prefieren en su lugar. Esta medida establecería que las elecciones revocatorias solo pregunten si los votantes desean destituir al funcionario electo. Una segunda elección determinaría quién debería reemplazarlo. El "sí" va ganando por un estrecho margen a las 22:00 horas. Propuesta 37: Si se aprueba la Propuesta 37, el estado crearía un nuevo fondo que otorgaría préstamos a compradores de vivienda de clase media. Los compradores que se beneficien de este fondo devolverían el dinero al estado poco a poco. La medida fue aprobada con más del 61% de los votos a favor hasta las 22:00 horas, según la agencia Associated Press. Proposición 38: Esta medida destinaría 8.400 millones de dólares en fondos estatales a la investigación inmunológica, con una condición : aproximadamente la mitad del dinero iría a parar a una organización sin fines de lucro de tres personas, el Instituto de Inmunología e Inmunoterapia de California. Gary K. Michelson, cofundador del instituto, impulsó esta propuesta para que se incluyera en la boleta electoral. El "Sí" va a la cabeza , con el 57% de los votantes a favor a las 22:00 horas. Proposición 39: Esta propuesta electoral aumentaría los requisitos de identificación para los votantes de California. Esta campaña, financiada en gran parte por el multimillonario de Illinois Richard Uihlein, exigiría a los votantes del estado presentar prueba de ciudadanía en las urnas o escribir su número de Seguro Social u otro número de identificación oficial en las boletas de voto por correo. Según la Associated Press, la medida fracasará, ya que más del 60% de los votantes se oponen a ella a las 22:00 horas. Proposición 40: Este polémico impuesto a los multimillonarios impondría un impuesto único del 5% sobre el patrimonio neto de los multimillonarios. El sindicato de trabajadores de la salud que impulsó la medida afirma que recaudaría aproximadamente 100 mil millones de dólares en cinco años y ayudaría a los programas de salud con dificultades. Los opositores señalan que los multimillonarios ya pagan una gran parte de los impuestos estatales y temen que esto pueda provocar que abandonen el estado. El "No" va a la cabeza , con poco más del 56% de los votantes en contra a las 22:00 horas. Proposición 41: Creada por los opositores al impuesto a los multimillonarios, esta medida invalidaría la Proposición 40 al establecer normas más estrictas sobre los nuevos impuestos en California. Si se aprueban tanto la Proposición 40 como la Proposición 41, prevalecerá la que obtenga más votos. El "No" va a la cabeza, con casi el 53% de los votantes en contra a las 22:00 horas. Proposición 42: También impulsada por los opositores al impuesto a los multimillonarios, la Proposición 42 dificultaría que el estado imponga un nuevo impuesto sobre la riqueza, como las cuentas de inversión o los bienes personales, invalidando así el impuesto a los multimillonarios . Si los votantes aprueban tanto la Proposición 40 como la Proposición 42, ganará la que obtenga la mayor cantidad de votos. El "Sí" va a la cabeza, con más del 54% de los votantes a favor a las 22:00 horas. Proposición 43: Esta medida dificultaría la aprobación de las iniciativas tributarias locales impulsadas por los ciudadanos . Estas iniciativas solo necesitan la mayoría simple para ser aprobadas, pero si se aprueba la Proposición 43, necesitarían dos tercios de los votos. El "No" va a la cabeza, con más del 54% de los votantes en contra a las 22:00 horas. Proposición 44 : Si se aprueba la Proposición 44, las clínicas de salud tendrían que destinar al menos el 90% de sus ingresos anuales a la atención al paciente. La medida cuenta con el respaldo del mismo sindicato que propuso el impuesto a los multimillonarios, el Sindicato Internacional de Empleados de Servicios – Trabajadores Unidos de la Salud del Oeste. La medida fracasará, ya que más del 81% de los votantes se oponen a ella a las 22:00 horas, según la agencia Associated Press. Proposición 45: Los votantes decidirán si modifican la emblemática ley de evaluación ambiental de California, conocida como CEQA . Esta ley de 1970 exige que las agencias consideren el daño ambiental antes de construir, pero los promotores inmobiliarios afirman que a menudo se utiliza para retrasar proyectos de infraestructura y viviendas asequibles muy necesarios. El "No" va a la cabeza, con más del 54% de los votantes en contra a las 22:00 horas.

name: California
title: Es oficial: California elige a Xavier Becerra para reemplazar a Gavin Newsom.
description: El demócrata Xavier Becerra ganó fácilmente la contienda por la gobernación en el estado demócrata más poblado del país.
text:
In summary
El demócrata Xavier Becerra ganó fácilmente la contienda por la gobernación en el estado demócrata más poblado del país. 


This article is also available in English. Read it here.
Xavier Becerra es el próximo gobernador de California tras conseguir una victoria contundente que garantiza que los demócratas continúen su racha de 16 años controlando el estado.
 Con casi la mitad de los votos escrutados, el ex fiscal general y secretario de salud de EE. UU. obtuvo el 65% de los votos, mientras que el republicano Steve Hilton, ex presentador de Fox News y estratega político británico-estadounidense, obtuvo el 34% el martes por la noche. La Associated Press declaró a Becerra ganador.
 Será el primer latino en ocupar el cargo de gobernador en siglo y medio, y el primero en ser elegido para el puesto. En un discurso triunfal la noche de las elecciones ante sus seguidores en West Sacramento, les contó a la multitud que sus padres, inmigrantes mexicanos, llegaron a California con 12 dólares.
 “Mis padres eran obreros de la construcción y oficinistas, quienes ganaban cada dólar y ahorraban cada centavo”, dijo. “No me postulé para hacer historia. Me postulé para marcar la diferencia… para el próximo obrero de la construcción y oficinista que quiera comprar su propia casa”.
 Hilton reconoció su derrota aproximadamente una hora después del cierre de las urnas.
 “El cambio puede demorarse, pero el cambio llegará”, dijo a sus seguidores en el condado de Orange.
 La victoria de Becerra culmina un ascenso meteórico e inesperado para un político de carácter apacible y reacio al riesgo, que hace apenas ocho meses tenía tan poca intención de voto que se le presionaba para que abandonara la contienda.
 Pero cuando el principal aspirante demócrata en unas primarias muy concurridas se retiró en abril por acusaciones de agresión sexual, Becerra era el demócrata moderado al que los miembros influyentes del partido y los grupos de interés apoyaban con mayor fuerza. Para cuando él y el republicano Steve Hilton quedaron primero y segundo en las elecciones primarias de junio, ya se le consideraba el virtual próximo gobernador de California.
 Con una cómoda posición en las encuestas y enfrentándose a un oponente republicano al que fácilmente podría vincular con el presidente Donald Trump, Becerra evitó hacer promesas políticas radicales y, en cambio, se centró en su larga experiencia en el gobierno.
 Con la elección de Becerra, es improbable que el estado se aleje significativamente de las políticas del gobernador demócrata saliente, Gavin Newsom, incluyendo sus disputas de larga data con la administración Trump. Becerra ha manifestado su apoyo a los cambios que Newsom y la Legislatura, controlada por los demócratas, han implementado para acelerar la construcción de viviendas, y en general respalda la transición del estado hacia la energía limpia, pero también busca maneras de reducir los precios de la gasolina.
 Sin embargo, es probable que su estilo sea diferente al de su predecesor. El sello distintivo de Newsom era la ambición; llegó al poder hace ocho años con una larga lista de objetivos, como millones de nuevas viviendas y proyectos ambiciosos e innovadores como un sistema de salud universal, no todos los cuales logró. Becerra ha evitado tales promesas, limitándose a hablar en términos generales sobre la importancia de priorizar a las familias trabajadoras, y afirma que no quiere perder la confianza pública exagerando sus posibilidades.
 “Los californianos no esperan un milagro del gobierno”, dijo el martes por la noche. “Simplemente quieren un gobierno que funcione”. 
 El Partido Republicano veía sus mejores posibilidades con Hilton.
 Mientras tanto, Hilton desplegó una larga lista de políticas desreguladoras y, en ocasiones, excéntricas. Propuso recortes de impuestos, la abolición del Departamento de Vehículos Motorizados, la cancelación del proyecto del tren de alta velocidad y el fin de los objetivos climáticos del estado, en una agresiva campaña centrada en la reducción del costo de vida. Sin embargo, se enfrentaba a grandes dificultades al postularse como republicano en un estado tradicionalmente demócrata, en unas elecciones en las que se esperaba que los demócratas arrasaran en todo el país.
 Representaba la mejor esperanza en años para una victoria republicana. Recaudó más de 33 millones de dólares frente a los 38 millones de Becerra y basó su campaña en una serie de ambiciosas promesas para reducir costos mediante la eliminación de regulaciones e impuestos. Presentó a Becerra como la personificación del statu quo político californiano, alguien que tomaría decisiones que beneficiarían a influyentes grupos de interés, como los sindicatos.
 El martes por la noche, presentó su campaña como el inicio de un “movimiento popular por el cambio”. Su objetivo era romper la supermayoría demócrata en la Legislatura en 2028 y elegir a un gobernador republicano en 2030.
 “Nos enfrentábamos a una maquinaria que lleva mucho tiempo en el poder”, dijo. “Creen que son dueños de este estado”. 
El candidato a gobernador Steve Hilton habla con miembros de la prensa en su fiesta para seguir los resultados electorales en The Waterfront Beach Resort en Huntington Beach el 2 de junio de 2026. Foto de Jules Hotz para CalMatters
 Hilton tuvo dificultades para deshacerse del lastre que suponía el respaldo de Trump.
 Becerra recordó a los votantes en todo momento la vinculación de Hilton con Trump, y se presentó como un luchador que, al igual que Newsom, desafiaría decisiones en Washington como la agresiva campaña de deportación de Trump.
 Desestimó a Hilton por considerarlo poco serio y basó su campaña principalmente en su larga experiencia representando a Los Ángeles en el Congreso y desempeñando los cargos de fiscal general del estado y secretario de salud de los Estados Unidos.
 Las elecciones se producen en un momento especialmente delicado para California.
 La indigencia aumentó durante años y solo comenzó a disminuir nuevamente en 2025. Los incendios forestales han dificultado la contratación de seguros para propietarios de viviendas. La inflación, en gran parte atribuible a la guerra de Trump en Irán, los aranceles y la represión migratoria, ha incrementado el ya elevado costo de vida.
 El presupuesto estatal, siempre sujeto a las fluctuaciones del mercado bursátil, se ha vuelto particularmente dependiente de la suerte de la industria de la inteligencia artificial. Bajo la administración de Newsom, el estado ha implementado medidas regulatorias enérgicas para frenar el uso de combustibles fósiles que contribuyen al calentamiento global. Sin embargo, a pesar de las encuestas recientes que muestran que la mayoría de los californianos apoya la transición ecológica, menos personas están dispuestas a pagar precios más altos por la energía que hace una década.
 Además, la política liberal del estado a menudo lo ha puesto en el punto de mira de la administración Trump, que ha retenido fondos federales, ha cuestionado las políticas medioambientales de California y ha intentado intervenir en estas elecciones.
 Ambos candidatos reconocieron el martes por la noche que existe una preocupación generalizada de que el “sueño californiano” esté fuera del alcance de muchos y deba recuperarse. Hilton culpó a los intereses particulares que presionan para imponer demasiadas regulaciones; Becerra afirmó que las políticas ambientales del estado, los derechos LGBTQ+, las comunidades inmigrantes y el acceso a la atención médica estaban siendo atacados por la administración Trump.
 “Como gobernador, mi misión es sencilla: lograr una California que podamos costear y defender una California que no podemos permitirnos perder”, dijo.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Commentary: A disquiet follows West Virginia’s supermajority
description: On a night where shocking results dominated election-watching media, U.S. Sen. Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., having her re-election race insta-called was a reassuring respite of routine for a Republican Party having a terrible, horrible, no good, very bad night.
text:
The West Virginia state Capitol in fall 2021. (West Virginia Legislative Photography)On a night where shocking results dominated election-watching media, U.S. Sen. Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., having her re-election race insta-called was a reassuring respite of routine for a Republican Party having a terrible, horrible, no good, very bad night. 
The win for the fourth-ranking Republican in the Senate this midterm was only half the margin of the 40-point drubbing she delivered in 2020, but comfortable enough given the wider circumstances. Her nephew, Rep. Riley Moore, and his congressional compatriot Rep. Carol Miller both retained their seats in Washington, D.C. with little real electoral threat to their positions. While a blue tsunami created only the fourth double flip of the House and Senate in the post-WWII era nationally, West Virginia’s top-line races were never really in doubt.  
Nor was the GOP supermajority in state government. Republicans will still dominate the state Senate and House of Delegates by wide margins as the state political factions start gearing up for the simmering 2028 gubernatorial campaign that will rise to the boil with the midterms out of the way. Much attention, and a record amount of money, will be going to that endeavor forthwith. 
But there is movement in deep red West Virginia’s political waters, even if the various metaphors and nomenclatures regarding waves mostly missed the Mountain State this time. The West Virginia Democratic Party had its best night in a long, long time, gaining seats in the state Senate and, as reported by Henry Culverhouse, the potential for enough House of Delegate Democrats to perhaps prevent suspending the constitutional rule. While a small but meaningful procedural victory, such an ability to slow down the GOP super majority would be a welcome tool for a rebuilding Democratic Party looking for those first steps back to power. 
Del. Mike Pushkin, who was one of the winning House of Delegate Democrats and also leader of the state party, gave a Belichickian “tomorrow” when asked on West Virginia MetroNews when recruitment for further Democratic efforts would begin. He rightfully focused on the foundational parts of politics: recruitment, messaging, campaign infrastructure and contesting every race.
While nationally the Republican Party suffered defeats that felt more like punishment than politics, the West Virginia GOP was largely spared. For now. But the political waters are stirring. After a 2026 primary that was dominated by eye-popping spending, intraparty squabbling and embarrassingly low turnout, the discussion turned to Team Red’s growing numerical advantage in voter registration. But running in parallel to the GOP’s dominance is a steady increase in registered independents. Combined with Democratic Party voters and the smattering of others, the registration numbers mean that even while still dominant, there are more voters registered as something other than Republican in the state of West Virginia. While the GOP supermajority is not in danger, the foundations for electoral coalitions are there for possible erosion in coming cycles. 
Capito’s congressional win in 2000 was one of the waypoints in West Virginia’s electoral trip from cobalt blue to deep red. As one of the most powerful members of the U.S. Senate, she has definitely reached the political mountaintop; matriarch of a political dynasty and will hold her Senate seat until she decides she no longer wants it. While President Donald Trump’s 40 plus point victory is often cited as the high spot of West Virginia going red, Capito’s 2020 re-election that saw her clear 70 percent and dominate all 55 counties might be the most impressive win and margin of victory the state will ever see. The peak of the red wave she was, in many ways, the face of, and has now dominated West Virginia politics for nearly a generation. 
But all mountaintops are surrounded by downslopes, trees don’t grow to the sky and supermajorities are never permanent. The Republican Party in West Virginia would be wise to take stock of the respite they have against the political fortunes their party cohorts nationwide suffered through. While still rebuilding and finding their election legs, the Democratic Party in West Virginia is alive and making strides. The independent numbers in West Virginia are growing: Independents who are angry at the political parties and processes thereof and are determined to make it the problem of the in-power politicians if they are not better catered to. Closed primaries, national buzzwords and the culture war du jour are not likely to quell their feelings. 
Capito has a long-running interview line stemming from her early, historic successes in tough races that she was “Republican before being a Republican was cool” in the formerly heavily Democratic West Virginia. The quip works for the head of the Moore-Capito political dynasty, wielded by a master politician who hasn’t had a competitive race in over 25 years. But for other West Virginia Republicans who came to office when it was very cool to be a Republican, the future is going to require much more than just party labels, national endorsements, outside money and the political phrases that used to pay. The West Virginia GOP should look at its cohorts in Texas, in Iowa, in Kansas, and elsewhere after the 2026 midterm, and decide if that’s the road they want to travel. And adjust accordingly.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Trailing by less than 1%, Ty Masterson calls for ‘another look’ at results in Kansas governor’s race
description: TOPEKA — With Democrat Cindy Holscher holding a narrow lead in the Kansas governor’s race, Republican Ty Masterson said Wednesday the results warrant “another look.” Holscher declared victory, even though the race was too close to call, as election offices across the state braced for a hand count of ballots from 10% of the precincts […]
text:
GOP nominee for governor Ty Masterson talks with supporters at a GOP watch party Nov. 3, 2026, in Wichita, where he says the race is too close to call. (Photo by Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — With Democrat Cindy Holscher holding a narrow lead in the Kansas governor’s race, Republican Ty Masterson said Wednesday the results warrant “another look.”
Holscher declared victory, even though the race was too close to call, as election offices across the state braced for a hand count of ballots from 10% of the precincts in each county. An unknown number of late-arriving mail ballots and provisional ballots also could affect the total.
Holscher’s lead over Masterson grew from about 5,500 votes Wednesday morning to 7,045 votes Wednesday night, with 549,974 to his 542,929.
“The first count does not seem to be going our way, but the margin is narrow enough that Kansas law calls for another look, and we’ll let that process finish,” Masterson said. “Every Kansan deserves to know the result is right.”
Holscher issued a statement asserting she had prevailed.
“The people of Kansas made their voices heard, and I’m deeply honored by the trust Kansans placed in me to serve as your next governor,” Holscher said. “Whether I earned your vote or not, I will work for you.”
State law triggers a close-race audit of 10% of precincts per county when the margin between candidates is within 1%. In addition to the governor’s race, the margins for attorney general, secretary of state and three House districts require a close-race audit.
Bryan Caskey, the state elections director, said election officials must hand count the ballots from 10% of precincts and compare the results to the totals counted by machines. He said election offices would be working from Thursday into the weekend to complete the audit before Monday, when county commissions begin to certify results.
Past audits have confirmed election results in Kansas. Sometimes, Caskey said, the hand count will be slightly different because of something like a machine not counting an oval that wasn’t correctly filled in.
Masterson also would have until 5 p.m. Nov. 17, the day after county commissions must finish certifying results, to request a full recount.
Under Kansas law, the state will cover the cost of a standard recount, where ballots are run back through machines, if the race is within one-half of a percentage point. Masterson would have to pay for the cost of a hand recount, or if the margin is more than 0.5% and the outcome doesn’t change.
It wasn’t clear whether Masterson’s statement about taking “another look” referred to the close-race audit or his right to request a recount.
“He’s referring to the one in law,” said Garrett Henson, his campaign spokesman.
As of 7 p.m. Wednesday, Holscher’s margin was 0.64%. The margin could change, however. Mail ballots that were postmarked by Tuesday and arrive by Friday will be counted. And county commissions will have to consider provisional ballots.
“I believe it is premature to ask for a recount until after the county board of canvassers start certifying the results at the county level,” Caskey said. “There will be an increase in the number of votes that are included in the count because every county has provisional ballots, and so I believe that for a candidate request to recount, they should look at the best possible information they have, the conclusion of the post-election audits, and the review of provisional ballots.”
Caskey said the Secretary of State’s Office was trying to find out how many provisional ballots there were.
At his watch party Tuesday night in Wichita, Masterson told the crowd: “What I’m afraid is we’re gonna have lawyers involved in this thing.” Several in the crowd offered their assistance.
Masterson, of Andover, is president of the Kansas Senate. Holscher, of Overland Park, also serves in the Senate.
“Whatever the outcome, the fight for lower property taxes, safer communities and better schools doesn’t end tonight,” Masterson said in his early Wednesday statement. “I’ll keep working for those things no matter what, and I’ll work with anyone who wants to get them done.”
In declaring victory, Holscher thanked Masterson for his service to the state and congratulated him on running a hard-fought campaign.
“Throughout this campaign, I heard from people who want their leaders to put politics aside and work together to deliver on the things that matter most: strong public schools, lower costs for our families and farmers, and an economy where every Kansan can get ahead,” Holscher said.

name: California
title: Prop. 40’s failure points to the tax California already pays for its wealth: Politics overrun by money
description: The playbook for defeating the the billionaire tax was simple: Stoke economic fears and confuse Californians.
text:
California voters have done right by their local billionaires. They appear to have rejected the wealth tax.
With most ballots counted and almost six percentage points needed as of Wednesday morning, a political fight that garnered national attention has reached an unsatisfactory end for many Californians. In a moment of deep economic angst, as a populist backlash against tech companies and widening inequality grew louder, the ultrarich in California have won — again.
This should not be considered a shock. When Google co-founder Sergey Brin began mobilizing an opposition campaign to defeat Proposition 40, powered by an infinite war chest and not one but two poison-pill ballot measures to cancel it out, this seemed inevitable. Because for all the talk of California being a test case for wealth taxes, the truth is California already pays a tax for its wealth: Our political system is suffocated by money.
The initiative by SEIU-United Health Care Workers West would’ve imposed a one-time 5% tax on the assets that actually create excessive wealth, generating an estimated $100 billion to help backfill federal cuts to Medi-Cal. Since it targeted stocks, bonds and business holdings, it was seen as an act of war. Brin and his allies left nothing to chance, raising $379 million to fight it. 
We won’t need much analysis to identify what swayed voters. The playbook for defeating the tax was simple: Stoke economic fears and confuse Californians. 
Prop. 40’s authors may have even doomed their own campaign with an amendment provision that opponents seized on. If a supermajority — two-thirds of the Legislature — wanted to retool the tax, they could, so long as “the statute is consistent with and furthers the purposes of the 2026 Billionaire Tax Act.” Opponents created ads proclaiming politicians would use this clause to come after our retirement accounts.
It lit up social media. Some Californians are so cynical that they figured seven out of 10 state lawmakers would vote to extend a billionaire tax to people with fewer zeros and commas invested. It also made one of Brin’s countermeasures, Proposition 42, an easy sell. It would bar taxes on personal property and its passage would make it almost impossible to enact a similar tax in the future. It was ahead in the count Wednesday morning.
Ultimately the most persuasive reason to reject the tax was the possibility it would stifle innovation or scare off the companies that anchor the state’s economy. Even worse, it might chase away the owners and executives who control these market-making conglomerates — their tax dollars leaving with them. 
Gov. Gavin Newsom, a presumed contender for president, threw his support behind the “no” camp more than a year ago and started echoing this talking point shortly thereafter. He later said he would welcome a wealth tax at the federal level, even though we all know how that would go — even if it is the correct approach. 
Nevermind that the research on capital flight is largely settled. Earlier this year, I spoke with Cornell University sociologist Cristobal Young, who literally wrote the book on this (it’s called “The Myth of Millionaire Tax Flight: How Place Still Matters for the Rich”). Decades of research show that it is much easier for the ultrarich to threaten to leave than actually do it, Young said. Brin and Larry Page and Peter Thiel did flee, but they are outliers. Study after study, on wealth taxes domestic and abroad, consistently show that taxes don’t compel rich people to move, and certainly not enough to compromise a $300 billion state budget.
Still, their departure fueled a report by the Hoover Institution, a conservative think tank at Stanford University, which suggested California risked income tax losses and would receive far less than what was promised by Prop. 40’s proponents.
The Hoover report also presumed billionaires pay income taxes like everyone else. In 2021, ProPublica received a trove of IRS files on the richest people in America — many of whom would have been affected by Prop. 40. The investigative newsroom uncovered how the ultrarich artificially lower their income and instead derive their wealth through their investments. Billionaires exploit loopholes in the tax code to amass vast fortunes and pay the government as little as possible.
In most instances, their effective tax rate is lower than the people who work for them. Buy. Borrow. Die. That’s what they do.
The little they do pay — the Stanford economists said it was as much as $5.8 billion annually to California’s coffers — represents a fraction of the $123 billion in income taxes the state collects overall. 
A supporter holds a sign during a “Ballots Over Billionaires” rally at the Curran Theater in San Francisco on Oct. 3, 2026. Photo by Manuel Orbegozo for CalMatters
If voters weren’t worried Prop. 40 was a slippery slope or would sacrifice the state’s golden goose, then they subscribed to the myriad other critiques: It’s badly written. It’s only for healthcare. It’s socialism.
I didn’t like it, either — for a while. Then the Legislature kicked the can on fixing the state’s budget problem and swiftly killed a Citizens United reform proposed by Assemblymember Chris Rogers of Santa Rosa, mirrored after a novel law in Hawaii to curb political spending.
Suddenly the Prop. 40 battle became a much simpler feud between billionaires and everyone else in California. Opponents were spending hundreds of millions to fight a tax they could afford. Meanwhile, I’m trying to figure out if my wife and I can buy a home and pay for child care on two incomes.
The speed and scale of inequality is intensifying in California and nationwide. A majority of Americans believe billionaires are a threat to democracy, especially millennials and Gen Z. If corporations continue to flood the political sphere with limitless sums of money, the ballot box is one of the remaining places we can register our opposition.
Initial returns this week also suggest Proposition 4 could fail. This was a measure that would have reversed a 1988 ban on financing political campaigns with public dollars. It is the sort of policy that helps reduce the influence of money in politics and empower candidates who are not beholden to the donors that helped them get elected.
Instead, California has once again resurfaced the ironies that define this incredible state. We talk about progress but struggle to deliver it. We dislike what excessive wealth is doing to our state but avoid reining it in. We create world-changing technologies but oppose boundaries that ensure our safety.
California may have the biggest economy of any U.S. state, but that does not make it a lab for innovative policy. It simply means we are home to giant companies and smart people. The issues we like to boast about, such as environmentalism or civil rights, are rife with contradictions and trade-offs.
Prop. 40 should have never been considered a litmus test for wealth taxes. It should not discourage them, either. California voters have backed income taxes on millionaires and high-earners to fund mental health treatment and education over the last two decades. As Young, the Cornell researcher uncovered, those taxes didn’t cause an exodus. Proposition 3, which extends a tax for public school funding permanent, officially passed early Wednesday morning.
If there is a glimmer of hope, it is that Brin and other billionaires stepped into the sunshine. The record spending and attack ads and political gamesmanship was done out in the open. Many Californians took notice, whether they backed Prop. 40 or not.
The state’s billionaires may have avoided this wealth tax, but voters won’t forget how some of the richest people on the planet behaved when fairness was on the ballot.

The Health Literacy Council’s program “Establishing Equity Through Literacy,” centers on helping everyone gain the knowledge needed to make informed health decisions. Greg O’Neill, co-chair of the Health Literacy Council of Delaware, accepts the proclamation in June 2025. 
For Delawareans, Health Literacy is practical: clearer information, greater understanding and a stronger foundation for making health decisions.
By John Riddle, Contributing Journalist, Delaware LIVE
A healthcare decision can begin with a question. But when the answer comes wrapped in unfamiliar terms, complicated instructions or confusing paperwork, understanding what to do next can become a challenge of its own.
The Health Literacy Council of Delaware wants to help change that.
Formed in 2022, the council brings together healthcare leaders, community partners and advocates with a shared goal: making health information and healthcare easier for Delawareans to understand.
Its vision, “Establishing Equity Through Literacy,” centers on helping everyone gain the knowledge needed to make informed health decisions. Its work includes advocating for education and policy changes, strengthening partnerships and encouraging clearer communication throughout the healthcare system.
For Greg O’Neill, co-chair of the Health Literacy Council of Delaware, collaboration is an important starting point.
“Delaware has strong momentum around health literacy, bringing together healthcare systems, community organizations, and public health leaders around a shared goal: making health information and healthcare easier to understand for everyone,” O’Neill said.
Turning that momentum into lasting improvements requires more than distributing information. The council’s strategies address how health information is developed, shared, taught and supported across the state.
One priority is creating policies and guidelines that provide ongoing support for health literacy programs. Another involves engaging healthcare and government leaders to encourage consistent practices throughout Delaware.
The council also promotes health literacy campaigns that reach public and private audiences, emphasizing the importance of helping people understand information that affects their health.
Clear materials are another focus. The council helps leaders identify and use health information that is accessible, accurate and easy to understand. Its education goals include incorporating health literacy into school lessons and professional training programs.
Together, those efforts aim to make understandable communication a regular part of healthcare and community education.
Still, measuring progress presents a challenge.
“We still have work to do as health literacy has yet to be built into the systems that we use to measure progress,” O’Neill said.
The council is developing proposals to build on existing data, gather testimonials and highlight community needs. Those efforts could help document experiences while providing a clearer picture of where additional support is needed.
Building the organization itself also takes time.
“Like any new organization, HLCD is still working on building our network, solidifying stakeholder commitments, and raising awareness about the size of the health literacy issue,” O’Neill said.
Much of that work depends on people contributing their time and expertise alongside other responsibilities.
“The majority of the work comes through hours of volunteer time from leaders around the state and most of the work is grant funded so in that sense HLCD is like any small non-profit enterprise working for the public good,” he said.
Competing demands in healthcare delivery, changes in health communication and evolving community needs add to the challenge, according to O’Neill. Those pressures reinforce the council’s case for investing in health literacy, even as they make securing attention and resources more difficult.
The council’s approach places responsibility on organizations and leaders as well as the people seeking information. Making healthcare easier to understand requires examining the messages people receive and the systems they must navigate.
For Delawareans, the goal is practical: clearer information, greater understanding and a stronger foundation for making health decisions.
For the council, the next steps involve expanding partnerships, strengthening support and finding better ways to demonstrate progress.
Its work begins with a straightforward idea: health information can serve people better when they can understand it. Bringing that idea into everyday practice is the mission connecting the council’s volunteers, healthcare partners and community advocates across Delaware as they work toward lasting improvements in health communication.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Mississippi Medicaid won’t confirm if it will use federal grant to pay for doulas next year
description: Kashuna Watts at the Mississippi State Capitol, Friday, Oct. 30, 2026, in Jackson. Watts started the Professional Association of Mississippi Doulas in 2023.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Mississippi Medicaid has not yet confirmed whether it will begin reimbursing for doula services next year, despite receiving a federal grant that requires it to do so. 
Mississippi, along with Idaho and North Dakota, is one of three states that have not implemented or taken steps publicly toward covering the cost of doulas through Medicaid, according to the National Health Law Program. 
Doulas are nonmedical professionals who provide emotional, physical and informational support during pregnancy, childbirth and the postpartum period.
In 2025, the federal government awarded 15 states, including Mississippi, a grant to improve maternal healthcare for women enrolled in Medicaid. The Transforming Maternal Health Model gives eligible state Medicaid agencies up to $17 million over 10 years to bolster their maternal health workforce. Guidelines from the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, the agency distributing the grant, say states receiving the federal funding must begin doula reimbursement by the end of 2027. 
“There is significant evidence that incorporating doula services in a patient’s care team can improve outcomes across a range of conditions and circumstances,” the guidelines read. “Therefore, participating state Medicaid agencies will be required to cover doula services by the end of Model Year 3 under the TMaH Model.”
Amy Chen, a senior attorney at the National Health Law Program, said she learned through conversations with people at the Mississippi Division of Medicaid that they are “exploring avenues” to provide funding for doula coverage, but they have established no definitive course of action. 
Medicaid spokesperson Matt Westerfield did not answer questions about the state’s plan for Medicaid reimbursement of doulas. Mississippi Today followed up with him six times between Oct. 22 and Nov. 2. 
In one of the poorest states in the nation, more than half of births are covered by Medicaid. Those mothers rarely have access to doulas, because of Mississippi’s reimbursement policies. 
The Mississippi Division of Medicaid is located in the Walter Sillers Building, seen here on Monday, Oct. 16, 2023, in Jackson, Miss.  Credit: Eric J. Shelton/Mississippi Today
Meanwhile, Mississippi infants die at a rate nearly twice the national average. In 2024, Black infants died at nearly three times the rate as white ones in Mississippi, according to the state’s 2025 infant mortality report. The state earned an F grade in its latest report card from the March of Dimes, a national nonprofit aimed at improving the health of mothers and babies. For years, the group has urged Mississippi to expand reimbursement options for doulas. 
Honour McDaniel Hill, who directs the Infant and Maternal Health Initiatives for March of Dimes, said she believes the growing movement and evidence behind doula care make it a safe investment. 
“You’ve got a bunch of states who are doing it, so you’re not doing it alone,” McDaniel Hill said. “It’s an opportunity to join in on something that has shown to improve mom’s experiences, improve mother-baby bonding and being able to have a healthy pregnancy and birth.”
Part of the success of doulas is that mothers confide in them more than doctors, said Kashuna Watts, a Jackson-based doula and founder of the Professional Mississippi Association of Doulas. Watts said doulas tend to spend more time with women and focus on building trust.
“When you pick up a client, you serve that client during pregnancy, birth and postpartum,” Watts said. 
That continuity of care can be lifesaving, Watts said. She recalled a first-time pregnant woman she cared for earlier this year. That mother called Watts experiencing hand pain and headaches – symptoms she “didn’t want to worry the doctor with,” according to Watts. But Watts recognized those symptoms as warning signs of preeclampsia, a life-threatening condition related to high blood pressure, particularly during and after pregnancy. Within minutes, she said, she made sure the mother got to the hospital. 
“If she hadn’t gone to the hospital, she would have had to have an emergency C-section,” Watts said, referring to a cesarean section. Instead, doctors stabilized her blood pressure and she gave birth without complications, Watts said. 
Doulas aren’t interested in taking the place of medical providers, Watts said. Instead, she said they’re interested in filling in gaps in care, providing women with information and connecting them to doctors and resources. 
“If every mother had access to a doula,” said Watts, “I know that not only would our maternal mortality rate drop, but (the) infant mortality rate would drop, also.”
Efforts to expand access
Rafia Tchatikpi was 21 when she first gave birth. She said doctors told her she needed a C-section because her baby was large. After the surgical birth, Tchatikpi said, she found out her daughter weighed only six pounds. 
That is common, and research suggests many women nationwide undergo C-sections unnecessarily. Studies show that only one in five U.S. women who were told their babies might be large actually delivered infants weighing more than eight pounds, 13 ounces – the standard definition of a large infant. 
Tchatikpi believes if she had a doula by her side and advocating for her at the hospital when she gave birth for the first time, she may not have ended up with a C-section. 
“My mom passed away on my 21st birthday, so I had to go through that pregnancy alone,”  Tchatikpi said. “I was just becoming an adult, I had no idea about any of the birth process.”
Studies show receiving continuous care from a trained doula throughout pregnancy and labor significantly reduces the risk of undergoing a C-section. The problem isn’t unique to Mississippi. But it is worse in Mississippi, where 38% of births are surgical. The state has recorded the highest rate of C-sections overall and particularly among first-time mothers – and experts say hospital culture often makes a difference in shaping those trends. 
When Tchatikpi arrived in Mississippi in 2020, she was surprised at the dearth of maternity care – especially after just completing a doula certification program in California. 
Now, Tchatikpi hopes to be part of an effort to change that. In 2027, Tchatikpi will begin teaching doula work to other Mississippians through a new doula certification program at Sisters in Birth, a Jackson-based women’s health clinic. 
Clinic founder Getty Israel said the 10-month program costs $2,100 per person. Israel said the course aims to take a more comprehensive approach to doula training in which students will also learn the fundamentals of public health. That’s especially important in Mississippi, Israel said, where sexually transmitted diseases and chronic conditions, such as diabetes and obesity, remain maternal health challenges. 
Rebuilding maternity care in the state demands more than expanding the doula workforce and reimbursing for doula services, Israel said. Israel said she has tried for nearly six years to open the state’s first birth center, a home-like, non-hospital healthcare facility for childbirth. Israel said she has run into myriad policy obstacles. Despite growing evidence that midwife-led birth centers improve outcomes for mothers and infants, Mississippi remains one of 10 states with no centers. 
A birth center may have made a difference for Tchatikpi, who delivered two of her six children at home in Mississippi. She said she would have preferred to use a birth center, but given the choice between the hospital and her home, Tchatikpi chose her home. 
“No one wants to do it on their own, but it was something I felt I had to do because I was so traumatized with the doctors and their way of doing things,” said Tchatikpi, who is Black. 
While Tchatikpi isn’t sure whether race played a part in her traumatic hospital birth, the majority of Black Americans said they had negative experiences with doctors, according to a poll from the Pew Research Center. 
For Tchatikpi, investing in maternity care reflects the spirit of what Mississippi should stand for. Tchatikpi, whose mother was from Mississippi, said she always loved the welcoming nature of the state. But she believes Mississippi’s maternal-infant health woes directly contradict that value. 
“What hospitality can we say we’re giving if we’re letting our most vulnerable members of our society – which is infants, babies – have a poor start in life?” Tchatikpi said. “We’re letting their mothers suffer.”

name: VTDigger
title: Barre voters approve school district budget on fourth attempt
description:
The $56.6 million budget approved Tuesday notably makes cuts to open staff positions and facilities expenses while maintaining funds for sports. The district is the last in the state to approve an annual spending plan. 
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Barre voters approve school district budget on fourth attempt.
text:
The Barre City Elementary and Middle School seen on Tuesday, August 8, 2023.  File photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

BARRE — Voters in the Barre Unified Union School District approved an annual spending plan for the district on their fourth attempt Tuesday. 
The district was the last in the state to approve a budget, which allocates $56.6 million this school year. Residents across Barre Town and Barre City previously voted down three costlier proposed spending plans. 
Notably, the district’s new budget approves cuts to office staff, open positions and facilities expenses. It spares cuts to winter sports and after school activities, which board members previously said might be on the chopping block after the last budget failed in September. 
Across both municipalities, 58% of voters approved the latest spending plan, according to totals from Barre Town’s website and Barre City’s clerk.
The drawn-out process of approving the district’s budget is notable because the district has among the lowest rates of per-student spending in the state. Still, voters rejected a $57.8 million budget on Town Meeting Day and have rejected two smaller proposed budgets since then. 
When students went back to school without a voter-approved budget for the district, board members said the district had to take out a line of credit, a measure expected to cost the district up to $22,000 in monthly interest payments. 
This story will be updated.

title: Contest for Hinds County district attorney heads to runoff
description: Gwen Agho, left, and Darla Palmer will face off during a Dec. 1 runoff to become the next Hinds County district attorney.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
The race for Hinds County district attorney is heading to a runoff between Darla Palmer and Gwen Agho after none of the five candidates in Tuesday’s special election won a majority of the votes. 
The runoff, scheduled for Dec. 1, will decide who will finish the term of former District Attorney Jody Owens, who left office over the summer after pleading guilty to a federal corruption charge. He is scheduled to be sentenced Thursday.
Palmer led the pack with roughly 27% of the vote, while Agho finished second with roughly 23%, according to unofficial tallies from the Hinds County elections office.
The winner of the special election will serve through January 2028 and take over the job from interim District Attorney Brad McCullouch, who was appointed by Gov. Tate Reeves. 
Palmer, 59, a private defense attorney, twice unsuccessfully challenged Owens for DA. She ran on the campaign slogan that asked, “Are you ready to feel safe?” She touted during the race that she was the only candidate who had never worked in the Hinds DA office. 
Palmer was the only candidate of the five who did not file a campaign finance report by the Oct. 27 deadline. As of election night, she still had not filed the mandatory preelection disclosure, according to the secretary of state’s website. 
Agho, 37, has spent nearly her entire career as a prosecutor for the Hinds DA office, which she joined in 2016 under former DA Robert Shuler Smith. She has argued that her familiarity with the office has given her insight into its many problems. 
The next district attorney will inherit an office facing significant challenges, including a backlog of criminal cases that has contributed to crowding at the troubled Hinds County Detention Center, which remains under federal oversight under a consent decree.

title: Jackson voters overwhelmingly reject measure to boost tourism tax
description: A sign welcomes in audience members during Visit Jackson's State of Tourism address on Tuesday, Oct. 13, 2026.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Jackson voters soundly rejected a ballot measure on Tuesday that would have boosted taxes on restaurant checks and hotel bills, dealing a financial blow to the city’s tourism agency that had counted on tax proceeds to bridge a sizable gap in its budget.
The referendum garnered 46% of the vote – far short of the required 60% to win passage.
Had it passed, taxes on restaurant bills would have risen from 1% to 1.5% and hotel stays from 1% to 2%. The additional revenue would have benefited Visit Jackson, the city’s tourism office. 
A reaction from Visit Jackson officials was not immediately available, but a spokesperson previously told Mississippi Today she hoped voters would be sympathetic to the agency’s financial challenges.
“We’ve done a lot with what we have been given, and we will continue to do the work that will help improve the quality of life for our citizens and that will still make us a welcoming and sort of destination for visitors,” Visit Jackson spokesperson Yolanada Clay-Moore had said.
Visit Jackson has operated on a $5.4 million budget for the past two years, which included about $1.7 million a year from the COVID-era American Rescue Plan Act. 
Those funds stopped after the 2026 fiscal year, leaving a hole in the agency’s budget.
Even if the boost had been ratified, Jackson’s higher tourism taxes would have kept the city’s rates lower than surrounding suburbs. Ridgeland, Flowood and Brandon all have a 10% restaurant tax and 9% lodging tax when combined with the state’s sales tax, according to the Mississippi Department of Revenue. Neighboring Madison only observes the state’s required 7% sales tax.
The referendum’s failure means Visit Jackson will have to continue relying on the city’s current 1% flat tax, which has been in place since 1983.
The increased tax rate would not have fully fixed the agency’s budget gap. Visit Jackson estimated a $1.2 million budget increase this fiscal year if the tax were able to be implemented by February, leaving a shortage of $500,000.
The agency wanted to campaign for increased tourism earlier, Clay-Moore said, but was put on hold because of the pandemic and the arrival of temporary federal aid.
While there is no plan to fully fix the hole left by the ARPA funds, Clay-Moore said the agency would be able to operate with the funds it receives.

description: Renee Shaw, one of the most well-known moderators and journalists at Kentucky Educational Television for nearly three decades at the public television network, will lead the public media organization as its new executive director and CEO.  In a Wednesday press release, KET announced Shaw as its new executive director and CEO where she will lead […]
text:
Renee Shaw will now be the CEO and executive director of KET.  (Photo courtesy of KET)Renee Shaw, one of the most well-known moderators and journalists at Kentucky Educational Television for nearly three decades at the public television network, will lead the public media organization as its new executive director and CEO. 
In a Wednesday press release, KET announced Shaw as its new executive director and CEO where she will lead all of KET’s services, including cultural and historical programming and resources for classroom education. The announcement comes just days after the network announced that its former longtime leader Shae Hopkins had died. 
“KET has been such an important part of my life, and it is an incredible honor to have the opportunity to lead an organization that means so much to Kentucky,” Shaw said in a provided statement. “Throughout my career, I’ve had the privilege of listening to Kentuckians and sharing their stories. Although we all are dealing with heavy hearts right now after the passing of Shae Hopkins, I look forward to building on the strong foundation she and others helped build and working alongside our talented staff and partners to ensure that KET continues to inform, educate and connect people across the Commonwealth for generations to come.”
During her previous time at KET, she served as moderator and host of “Kentucky Tonight” along with coverage of elections, forums and other issues. She helped expand programming, including “Kentucky Edition”, while serving as the network’s director of public affairs, according to a KET press release. 
She has also been recognized with a number of awards and accolades for her journalistic work, including three Ohio Valley Regional Emmy awards and induction into the Silver Circle of the National Academy of Television Arts and Sciences, the Kentucky Journalism Hall of Fame and the Kentucky Civil Rights Hall of Fame.
A search committee made a recommendation Wednesday to name Shaw as the network’s leader, according to the KET release. 
Dan Griffith, the chair of the Kentucky Authority for Educational Television, in a provided statement said Shaw “brings to this role an extraordinary understanding of Kentucky, a deep commitment to public service and a genuine appreciation for the important role KET plays in the lives of people across the Commonwealth.
“I have no doubt Renee will proudly take the torch from Shae and continue building on her great work,” Griffith said.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Commentary: Blue wave changes Kentucky’s political landscape, raises questions
description: This column was originally published in the Northern Kentucky Tribune. Tuesday’s blue tsunami that gave Kentucky one more Democratic congressman, two more Democratic state senators and eight more Democratic state House members raises at least two questions: Would Gov. Andy Beshear have won the race for U.S. senator, and does the Democratic surge give that […[...]
text:
Kentucky Governor Andy Beshear, left, talks after Democrat Zach Dembo’s Sixth Congressional District win against Ralph Alvardo, at the Central Bank Center in downtown Lexington, Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Brian Simms for Kentucky Lantern)This column was originally published in the Northern Kentucky Tribune.

Tuesday’s blue tsunami that gave Kentucky one more Democratic congressman, two more Democratic state senators and eight more Democratic state House members raises at least two questions: Would Gov. Andy Beshear have won the race for U.S. senator, and does the Democratic surge give that party more hope of electing a Democrat to succeed him next year?
To both questions, the initial answer seems to be “Yes, but.”
Given Beshear’s persistent popularity and President Trump’s record unpopularity, I think the Democratic governor would have beaten U.S. Rep. Andy Barr for the seat of retiring U.S. Sen. Mitch McConnell. That would have been ironic, since McConnell won the third of his seven terms by beating Beshear’s father in 1996. More importantly, it would have given the state its first Democratic senator since Wendell Ford retired in 1998.
Yes, but. Beshear said he didn’t want to be a senator, and if you take him at his word, people shouldn’t run for offices that they don’t really want, but see as a useful steppingstone to higher office – in this case, the presidency. If you were more cynical and skeptical, you might say that Beshear merely said he didn’t want to be a senator because he knew the race would be too risky.
If Beshear had run and lost, it would have killed his presidential ambitions. If he had run and won, he would have had to manage two challenging and conflicting enterprises: being a presidential candidate and a freshman senator, a job that includes compiling a voting record that could have been used against him. If he had run for senator, Republicans would have used against him his shortcomings as governor, and that wouldn’t have done his presidential ambitions any good.
That logic, of course, is all about Beshear’s self-interest, not the interests of his party, which he has done little to serve as governor. Once he was re-elected in 2023, he had an obligation to help rebuild his party at the legislative and local level, but he doesn’t seem to have done much of anything for it. Instead, he largely invested his political committee’s money in politicizing races for nonpartisan judgeships, helping get a friend elected to the state Supreme Court in 2024 but losing in Tuesday’s election a Court of Appeals Judge he appointed. A better bet would have been legislative races, in which Democrats probably could have gained even more seats with more Beshear money.
Now the parties turn to next year’s statewide elections, led by the race for governor, in which two Beshear lieutenants, Rocky Adkins and Lt. Gov. Jacqueline Coleman, want the Democratic nomination. The party’s Tuesday successes will stir more interest in its May 18, 2027, primary, and that will carry over to the general election. But likely Republican nominee James Comer will campaign on the failings of the Beshear administration, such as the abysmal juvenile-justice system.
On the other hand, the Democratic nominee will likely use against Comer his lack of action, as chairman of the House Committee on Oversight and Reform, against Trump’s blatant corruption. That wouldn’t have mattered under the status quo ante of a year ago, but Trump has fallen from favor and voters have begun to contrast their struggles with his gold-plated family and administration – and rightly assign him blame for the economic impact of tariffs and the Iran War. Comer will have to offer a platform wholly of his own; the Trump train is no longer an adequate vehicle, and may actually be one to avoid.
Trump accelerated Kentucky’s conversion to a Republican state, to the point that the GOP now has a plurality of registered voters. It lacks a majority, because an increasing number of Kentuckians are independents, registered with no major party or with minor parties. Tuesday’s election showed that Kentuckians continue to be capable of voting independently.
Some people who chose U.S. Rep.-elect Zach Dembo over Republican Ralph Alvarado in the 6th District also voted for Barr over Democrat Charles Booker, and some who voted for Barr also picked Louisville-area Democrats who defeated Republican state Sens. Lindsey Tichenor, an extremist, and Julie Raque Adams, a moderate. Adams got into trouble by starting a nonprofit “dedicated to training Republican women to seek and hold public office” that did little in the last three years except collect money from groups with interests before the legislature and pay Adams $80,500, as reported by Tom Loftus in the Kentucky Lantern.
Adams lost to Sarah Cole McIntosh and Tichenor lost to Christian Furman in suburban districts, like those where Democrats also gained eight House seats – including the one of GOP Whip Jason Nemes of Louisville. It wasn’t just a blue wave, but the lack of a red tide; Republican turnout seemed depressed in Kentucky, as it was nationally. Many Republicans are through with him.

Under Article XVI of the Delaware Constitution, an amendment must receive votes from two-thirds of all members elected to each chamber. Democrats will have enough seats in the [...]
text:
DOVER, Del. — Delaware Democrats will hold more than two-thirds of the seats in both chambers of the General Assembly, according to unofficial results from Tuesday’s midterm election.
Under Article XVI of the Delaware Constitution, an amendment must receive votes from two-thirds of all members elected to each chamber. Democrats will have enough seats in the new General Assembly, which convenes in January, to give final approval to eight proposed amendments without Republican support.
Democrats gained three House seats and received the most votes in all five federal and statewide races. Turnout was 47.5%, up from 42.7% in the 2022 midterm.
All 530 election districts had reported by 3 a.m. Wednesday. The state also listed absentee ballot tabulation as done in all three counties. The Department of Elections cautions that those county updates do not necessarily mean every ballot has been counted. Results remain unofficial until the state certifies them.

What it means for the Constitution
The Delaware Constitution is the state’s highest law. An amendment must pass twice: once in one General Assembly and again in the next one, after an election. Amendments passed this way become part of the Constitution without going to voters.
The 153rd General Assembly passed eight proposed amendments once. They cover topics including early voting, absentee voting, marriage and the death penalty. The 154th General Assembly will decide whether to give them final approval. If Democrats vote together, they would have enough votes to pass the amendments without Republican support, and Republicans would not have enough votes to block them. Democrats could spare no more than two votes in the House and one in the Senate.
Where the House changed
Three House seats held by Republicans went to Democrats. No seat held by a Democrat went to a Republican.

House District 34, Kent County: Democrat Annie Norman received 4,905 votes to 4,755 for Republican Rep. Lyndon D. Yearick, a 150-vote margin. It was the closest House race in the state, and Rep. Yearick was the only incumbent state legislator who lost Tuesday.
House District 4, Sussex County: Democrat Gregg Lindner received 8,039 votes to 7,658 for Republican Dan Zitofsky, a 381-vote margin, for the seat Republican Rep. Jeff Hilovsky is leaving.
House District 9, New Castle County: Democrat Ayanna Khan-Flowers received 8,451 votes to 4,753 for Republican Jamar Money, for the seat Republican Rep. Kevin Hensley is leaving.

Republicans kept the other open seats they held: House districts 33, 38 and 41, and Senate District 15, the seat Republican Sen. Dave Lawson is leaving. Table 3 has those results.
The statewide picture
In this midterm, with no presidential race on the ballot, the Democratic candidates in the five federal and statewide races each received between 60% and 65% of the vote. U.S. Sen. Chris Coons received 63.6%, U.S. Rep. Sarah McBride 64.3% and Attorney General Kathy Jennings 63.6%. In the open race for state treasurer, Democrat Ted Lauzen received 62.4% to 37.6% for Republican Michael Ramone. Auditor Lydia York received 60.4%.
Registered Democrats make up 41% of Delaware’s registered voters, registered Republicans 25% and everyone else 34%, according to the state’s Nov. 1 registration report. Democrats will have 73% of the seats in the House and 71% in the Senate.
