name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Minnesota Democrats secure majorities in state House and Senate
description: The Democratic-Farmer-Labor Party will take control of both chambers of the Minnesota Legislature after riding a national wave of anti-Trump fervor that swept the country Tuesday. With Democrat Amy Klobuchar’s victory in the governor’s race, Minnesota will again have a DFL trifecta after two years of shared control with Republicans. While the exact margin of[...]
text:
Attendees celebrate as Sen. Amy Klobuchar takes the stage to announce that she is the governor-elect at the DFL watch party during the midterm elections Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026 in St. Paul, Minnesota. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)The Democratic-Farmer-Labor Party will take control of both chambers of the Minnesota Legislature after riding a national wave of anti-Trump fervor that swept the country Tuesday.
With Democrat Amy Klobuchar’s victory in the governor’s race, Minnesota will again have a DFL trifecta after two years of shared control with Republicans. While the exact margin of victory wasn’t clear by Wednesday morning, the party is expected to secure larger majorities than those that comprised the 2023-24 trifecta.
By 8 a.m., The Associated Press had called 34 Senate races in favor of Democrats, securing at least a one-seat majority in the chamber with the results in nine races still outstanding. Democrats lead in five of those races.
In the House, Democrats flipped several seats, and The Associated Press had called 72 races for the DFL, four more than the 68 they needed for a majority. Democrats were leading in five of the 12 races yet to be called.
“Minnesotans put their trust in us to fight for them,” Senate DFL Campaign Chair Nick Frentz said in a statement early Wednesday. “Much of that trust was built because we knocked on their doors, we answered their calls and we stood up for them in the face of harm coming from Washington.”
The DFL picked up seats in both chambers in metro suburbs and Greater Minnesota alike, giving them a strong mandate to continue Minnesota’s tradition of robust investments in education, health care and social services. Republican Reps. Aaron Repinski of Winona and Jeff Dotseth of Kettle River lost to DFL challengers. In the Senate, Democrats ousted Sen. Jim Abeler of Anoka and also won Maple Grove’s historically red District 37, long held by Sen. Warren Limmer, who is retiring.
State Rep. Brad Tabke, DFL-Shakopee, won his seat by more than 14 percentage points. Two years ago, he won by only 14 votes. 
Once Democrats finish celebrating, they’ll soon face reality: The 2027-28 Legislature will face an uphill battle to pass ambitious progressive legislation, given that Klobuchar has promised voters no new tax increases. The state is spending more money than it’s bringing in, and federal funding cuts to safety net programs will place additional pressure on the budget. 
Meanwhile, some of Minnesota’s most important institutions, which are also feeling the impact of federal cuts and policy changes, will be clamoring for cash from the state: universities, school districts, local governments and food banks, among others. The rising cost of healthcare means the state will pay more to insure its more than 50,000 employees and take care of the more than 1.2 million low-income and disabled Minnesotans enrolled in Medical Assistance, Minnesota’s version of Medicaid.
It’s a stark departure from the 2023-24 legislative session, the last time Democrats held both chambers and the governor’s office. Then, the DFL walked into budget negotiations with a $17 billion surplus and the political will, including from Gov. Tim Walz, to spend it and even raise taxes on metro residents for housing and transportation.
That historic session led to major investments in housing, education, transportation, tax credits to low-income families, free school meals and more.
During her victory speech, Klobuchar cautioned that some of her decisions may not be popular, including with members of her own party in the Legislature.
“Spoiler alert: You may not like every single thing I do,” Klobuchar said.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Rhode Island inspector general finalist withdraws after landing Washington job
description: Gov. Dan McKee now has to choose between two finalists to become Rhode Island’s first inspector general after a third candidate accepted another job on the West Coast. Stuart Robinson, one of three finalists recommended to McKee in September, withdrew from consideration Oct. 15, after being confirmed as first inspector general for King County, Washington. […[...]
text:
Stuart Robinson, director of investigations for the Palm Beach County Office of Inspector General, sits in the audience during interviews for Rhode Island’s first inspector general on Sept. 24, 2026. At right is Steven Krueger, first assistant inspector general for the city of New Orleans. Robinson withdrew his name from consideration for the job. (Photo by Christopher Shea/Rhode Island Current)Gov. Dan McKee now has to choose between two finalists to become Rhode Island’s first inspector general after a third candidate accepted another job on the West Coast.
Stuart Robinson, one of three finalists recommended to McKee in September, withdrew from consideration Oct. 15, after being confirmed as first inspector general for King County, Washington. The county announced his appointment to a five-year term on Oct. 6
Olivia DaRocha, a spokesperson for McKee’s office, confirmed the withdrawal in an email to Rhode Island Current and provided a copy of Robinson’s accompanying message.
“As expected, I was just confirmed as the inspector general for King County Washington, and therefore I will be removing my name for consideration as the Rhode Island inspector general,” Robinson wrote.
The two remaining finalists are David Harper, who has served as inspector general for the U.S. Capitol Police since February 2024, and Jim Kirdar, assistant inspector general for investigations for the Capitol Police since April 2025.
The commission recommended all three finalists to McKee, with the caveat that the governor should not make a final selection until the candidates completed background checks by the Rhode Island State Police.
Lt. Col. Erik Yanyar, a State Police spokesperson, told Rhode Island Current the background checks are expected to be completed by the end of November. 
Robinson was director of investigations for the Palm Beach County Office of Inspector General since November 2017. His resume notes he led more than 50 completed and publicly reported investigations involving a county with a $9.6 billion budget and 39 municipalities, including cases involving multimillion-dollar vendor overcharges and more than 36 grant and assistance fraud matters.
Robinson was one of five candidates interviewed Sept. 24 at the State House by the Inspector General Independent Advisory Commission, a five-member panel tasked with conducting a nationwide search for Rhode Island’s first inspector general, an office created to root out waste and improve government efficiency.
The inspector general may serve for five years and be eligible for reappointment for one term of the same duration. The annual salary range for the position is between $175,000 and $225,000.

name: Michigan Advance
title: McCann declares victory against Huizenga, delivering Michigan’s 4th Congressional District for Dems
description: Building on gains in 2022, Democrats have continued to make headway in Western Michigan as state Sen. Sean McCann (D-Kalamazoo) claimed victory Wednesday against U.S. Rep. Bill Huizenga (R-Holland Township) for his seat in Congress. Unofficial results from the Associated Press, which has yet to officially call the race, showed that as of 9:45 a.m., […]
text:
State Sen. Sean McCann (D-Kalamazoo) is joined by U.S. Sen. Gary Peters, at left, during a  stop in Kalamazoo of the "Sick of It! Fix Health Care Now" bus tour on Oct. 20, 2026. (Campaign photo)Building on gains in 2022, Democrats have continued to make headway in Western Michigan as state Sen. Sean McCann (D-Kalamazoo) claimed victory Wednesday against U.S. Rep. Bill Huizenga (R-Holland Township) for his seat in Congress.
Unofficial results from the Associated Press, which has yet to officially call the race, showed that as of 9:45 a.m., McCann had 50.3% of the vote while Huizenga received 48.2%.
Return of the trifecta: Michigan Democrats reclaim full control of state government

If confirmed, McCann will conclude his time in the state Legislature and serve as representative for the state’s 4th Congressional District, which includes Allegan and Van Buren counties, and portions of Ottawa, Kalamazoo, Calhoun and Berrien counties. The win would be at least the third Michigan congressional district to flip to the Democrats, following wins by William Lawrence in the 7th District and Christina Hines in the 10th District.
“I am honored and humbled that the people of Southwest Michigan have put their trust in me to represent and serve this amazing district,” McCann said in a statement. “Thank you to the voters, and to every volunteer and supporter who knocked on doors and made phone calls, talked to their neighbors, and helped out in ways big and small. I will be forever grateful for your support, because you are the heart and soul of this campaign. And thank you to Congressman Bill Huizenga for his years of service to our community.”
While the nonpartisan Cook Political Report initially rated the district as a likely win for Republicans, its rating gradually shifted to “toss-up,” meaning either party has a good chance of winning. 
During a canvass launch organized by McCann’s campaign five days before Election Day,  U.S. Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Holly), said a Democratic victory in the 4th Congressional district would signal that “when Democrats compete, they win,” reflecting on U.S. Rep. Hillary Scholten’s 2022 win in the neighboring 3rd Congressional District, previously considered to be a conservative stronghold.
“This victory belongs to the people all across Southwest Michigan, and it’s the people that I will work every day to serve – to take on the corruption and policies shortchanging our families, and work with anyone to make life better and protect the American Dream for our children. Michigan families deserve nothing less, and I look forward to getting right to work for the people of this district,” McCann said.

name: VTDigger
title: First in their families: Five first-generation students share their stories
description:
National First-Generation College Celebration Day is November 8. Meet five Vermont students who are the first in their families to pursue college and hear more about the dreams that motivate them and the persistence that carries them forward.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  First in their families: Five first-generation students share their stories.
text:
What does it mean to be a first-generation student? Technically, a first-generation student’s parents or guardians have not yet completed a four-year degree from a college or university. First-generation students may face barriers to attending college, like financial and time pressures related to caregiving or employment. And they may need additional support to successfully navigate the application and financial processes, as well as the academic system. 
Despite these challenges, being first generation builds resilience, fosters leadership, and motivates students to succeed. National First-Generation College Celebration Day is November 8, a day that commemorates the signing of the Higher Education Act of 1965 and the creation of the federal financial aid programs that turn the dream of education after high school into a possibility for so many. 
VSAC and colleges and universities across Vermont are celebrating our first‑generation students’ contributions to their communities and recognizing the work still to be done to break down barriers to first‑generation student success. A few first-generation students from around Vermont shared their experiences with us. 
“You can do anything—but you can’t do everything.”
Ailyn Langley participated in VSAC’s GEAR UP college and career readiness program in high school, and she began working with VSAC outreach counselor Kassidy Moore at the end of her junior year. Narrowing her interests and selecting schools to apply to was a journey, but whenever she made a college list, Dartmouth College was on it. Thinking back to the moment she found out that she was accepted to Dartmouth, Ailyn says it felt a little surreal.
Now Ailyn is in her second year at Dartmouth. A first-generation student, she tapped resources offered by Dartmouth to help provide additional guidance and support to students whose parents did not graduate with a four-year degree. 
The director of the Dartmouth first-generation office helped her get oriented during her first year, she noted. “He always says, ‘You can do anything—but you can’t do everything at Dartmouth.’ It kind of helps narrow my focus a bit,” she explained. 
Ailyn said Dartmouth’s community contributed to her successful transition to college, and she especially appreciated the support system the first-generation office provided. “The director has a tissue box in his office signed by everyone who’s cried in there. There are a lot of names. You can get so overwhelmed in college, but that helps you know it’s normal to feel that way,” she said.
 “Having that person who could explain it and believed I could do it—that changed everything.”  
Tasha Gallup was wrapping up high school, and she knew she wanted to go to college. But she also faced the reality that her family couldn’t afford to help her. 
When she first told her mother she wanted to go to college, Tasha says that her mom said: “We can’t afford that. It’s not going to work.” Tasha notes, “I was dashed but I was heated. I wanted to do it, so I was going to do it.”
She met with Clark Amadon, an outreach counselor working in VSAC’s Talent Search program at the time. Clark began helping her figure out what might be possible.
“I told Clark the truth. I said my parents couldn’t afford it. I was ready for him to say goodbye. Instead, he said, ‘Okay, if your parents can’t do this, there are other options. There are steps along the way.’ And I started to see it could be attainable.”
When her financial aid package arrived, she was excited and apprehensive. She remembers, “it was so exciting to see that financial aid package. It felt like a true success when I had the realization that my goal of getting to college, being there, was going to happen.”   
Tasha also recalls what it felt like to sign that first promissory note. “I took it so seriously when I signed that note. That meant a lot. My mom was nervous. She said, ‘This is for real. You have money on the line. If you’re going to do this, do this.’ I was committed. I had to get myself into a career field that could substantiate the obligation of what that loan meant.”
Tasha not only earned her bachelor’s degree, but years later she also earned a master’s degree, which allowed her to become a physician assistant. Looking back, she is clear that the help she got from VSAC mattered. “Clark helped me understand the steps I needed to take to secure financial aid. He came to the house, sat down with my parents, and helped us with the paperwork. Having that person who could explain it and believed I could do it—that changed everything.”  
“If more education gets me to my goal, that’s what I’ll do.”
“I always knew I wanted to go to college,” Hadley Kistler said. “And my family is really supportive of that.” In 2025, Hadley’s family moved, and she transferred to St. Johnsbury Academy. She’s been working with Trish Turner, an outreach counselor in VSAC’s GEAR UP college and career readiness program, ever since. Hadley’s goal is to get into a competitive academic program and become an early childhood educator. 
“Trish has helped me understand when deadlines are, when grants are open, what scholarships might be good for me. Sometimes I struggle with deadlines and she’s great about helping me with remembering them,” Hadley noted.
Hadley knows she wants to earn her bachelor’s degree. It’s not only a requirement for early childhood education, but an opportunity for her to be the best teacher she can be in the field. If finances, life, and time allow, she’d like to go further to her master’s degree or beyond. “If more education gets me to my goal, that’s what I’ll do,” Hadley said.
“My parents and I had so many questions.”
Patrick Dillon is nailing his education goals. But just a few years ago, he didn’t picture himself going on to college after he graduated from Fair Haven Union High School. Even when he enrolled in Dual Enrollment his junior year, then signed up for Early College his senior year, he figured he was getting a few college credits under his belt “just in case”—but he probably wouldn’t go any further, he thought. 
While still in high school, Patrick participated in VSAC’s GEAR UP college and career readiness program, and Rachel Casey was his VSAC outreach counselor. As Patrick started thinking more seriously about college, Rachel started meeting with his parents too. “The college stuff didn’t make sense to them, so Rachel helped me and my parents understand it… Rachel’s explanations of how everything worked were so helpful. My parents and I had so many questions,” he says.
Despite his initial indifference about continuing to college after high school, Patrick says his perspective began to shift when he stepped into his Early College classes at Vermont State Castleton. The campus felt different than he expected—more personal, with details that made him feel acknowledged, and memorable professors who made him feel included. 
As his interests developed, earning a psychology degree at Vermont State Castleton stood out as both a meaningful and practical option. Now in his third year of college, Patrick is studying to become a psychiatric registered nurse, as well as working as a crisis recovery specialist and psychology tech. “The experiences I’ve had inspire me,” he notes. 
“I kept asking for help along the way and she kept encouraging me. It was hard, but she kept telling me it would be worth it.”
Neema Isadore is the middle child of five siblings. A 2026 graduate of Winooski High School, she started at Saint Michael’s College this fall.
Neema has known she wanted to go to college since she started high school. But the path was challenging; Neema was born in Burundi. She came to Vermont when she was in the seventh grade, speaking Swahili and Kirundi. As she got used to a new community and a new school, she was also learning a new language; then, halfway through high school, she experienced a traumatic brain injury.
Neema persisted, keeping her eyes on her goal. While at Winooski High School, she joined VSAC’s GEAR UP college and career readiness program, which, among other support, helped her visit several colleges. When she toured Saint Michael’s College, she says that she felt immediately connected to the school, the professors, and the campus. 
She worked with her VSAC GEAR UP outreach counselor, Stevya Mukuzo, on her applications and her financial aid forms. “I struggled a lot because English isn’t my first language,” Neema noted. “But Stevya was helpful, making sure my mom and I knew what we were doing. I kept asking for help along the way and she kept encouraging me. It was hard, but she kept telling me it would be worth it. And now it is and I really appreciate that.”
Neema was delighted to receive a full-tuition scholarship from Saint Michael’s College. She is also leveraging additional scholarships and grants, which will help cover some of her other expenses. “It was a happy moment,” she said, when she got the news about her scholarship. “Not everyone gets that opportunity and I was so excited and surprised. My family is very proud,” she added.

The Vermont Student Assistance Corp. was created by the Vermont Legislature in 1965 as a public nonprofit agency. We advocate for Vermont students and their families to ensure that they have the tools they need to achieve their education and training goals. We create opportunities for all Vermont students, but particularly for those—of any age—who believe that the doors to education are closed to them. Growing families save for education with VT529, Vermont’s official 529 savings program. To help Vermonters plan and pay for college or job training, our counselors work with students in nearly every Vermont middle school and high school, and are also available to work with adults. Our grant, scholarship, and workforce development programs create opportunity, help students re-skill or learn new skills, and grow the economy. VSAC’s loan, loan refinance, and loan forgiveness programs provide competitive education financing to students and families. Find us at www.vsac.org or visit Facebook, Instagram, or LinkedIn.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  First in their families: Five first-generation students share their stories.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Voters subject governor and Legislature to public records law, but there’s no guarantee lawmakers will comply
description: All eyes will now turn to the House and Senate, where negotiators need to decide in the next eight weeks whether to follow through on an earlier proposal to substitute their own idea for public records access for the version that four out of five voters embraced.
text:
ALL EYES, especially those that want to pry, now turn to the Legislature. 
Massachusetts voters on Tuesday gave overwhelming approval to a ballot measure subjecting the House, Senate, and governor’s office to the state’s public records law. There’s just one catch: In the remaining eight weeks between the election and the start of the next lawmaking term, Democrats who control the Legislature might erase what voters decided in a landslide. 
Although lawmakers have been openly grousing about the measure for months, they opted not to mount a formal opposition campaign, and few voters were swayed by legislative complaints about its constitutionality. The measure wound up smashing its way to victory. With about 80 percent of votes counted, the “yes” side led 86 percent to 14 percent. 
By the time every ballot is counted, it could wind up a significantly larger margin of victory than the 2024 ballot question allowing the state auditor to probe the Legislature, a thematic predecessor that led directly into the records campaign. 
It’s at once a signal that voters are eager for more transparency, a rebuke of the Democratic supermajority’s opacity, and a reflection that the idea — extend an existing law to parts of government that do not currently follow it — was a simple pitch hard to rebut on the campaign trail.  
Auditor Diana DiZoglio, who led the charge for the 2024 measure and was the most prominent backer of the latest push to expand the public records law, said the vote sends “a loud and clear message to Beacon Hill that we’re not giving up and we’re not going away.” 
“Time will tell how this plays out but it’s really important that we all stay alert and vigilant in the coming days and call our legislators to tell them it’s time to stop playing games,” she said in a statement, calling the margin a “tremendous victory.”  
“Now there is more work to be done to make sure they don’t break the law or overturn it,” DiZoglio added. 
Question 1 wasn’t the only ballot measure for which the Legislature set a lame-duck trap. But following Tuesday’s results, it’s the only one that might be sprung. 
Lawmakers had also been weighing action to make tax refunds under the existing law known as Chapter 62F less likely, essentially offsetting Question 5, which sought to make those rebates more common. But voters rejected the measure, which was backed by several influential business groups, and the campaign conceded shortly before 8 a.m. Wednesday. 
“Voters have chosen to retain the existing law,” Taxpayers for an Affordable MA, the group pushing the question, said in a statement. “That decision deserves respect, even as important questions remain about the growth of state spending, the cost of living and doing business, and Massachusetts’ ability to retain residents, jobs, and investment.” 
Labor unions opposed the measure, arguing that forcing Beacon Hill to return money to taxpayers more frequently would eat away at the state’s ability to fund popular programs and services. 
“The people of Massachusetts chose to protect critical state funding for healthcare, education, housing, and local aid; not slash state spending to pay for occasional tax rebates,” said Harris Gruman, executive director of the SEIU Massachusetts State Council and a leader of the opposition campaign. “Despite not running any advertising until the final week of the campaign, our grassroots campaign of working people defeated the corporate lobby at the ballot. Wealthy CEOs and investors spent millions of dollars this election cycle in a blatant attempt to buy themselves multiple tax cuts, and that money was completely wasted.” 
At this point, it’s essentially a certainty that the governor’s office will be more forcefully required to comply with the existing public records law — which includes exemptions for categories such as personnel rules and investigatory materials — after governors in both parties have deemed themselves not covered on a case-by-case basis. The outlook for the House and Senate is an open question. 
In the summer, the House and Senate each approved bills that would subject the governor’s office to the existing records statute, and create a new framework for their own members. Their proposals would codify access to some legislative documents, replacing a status quo in which the Legislature is entirely exempt from the public records law, but would make less information available than the ballot question does. All correspondence would remain private under the Legislature’s approach, for example, while the ballot measure subjects most emails to public release. 
Crucially, both versions of the legislation included language declaring that it would map out the only way the public could acquire House and Senate records — a clause that legal experts suggest could supersede any law enacted at the ballot box. 
Legislative leaders shuttled the House and Senate versions of the bill into a conference committee, a private negotiating panel tasked with finalizing a compromise text, where it’s sat unfinished since the end of July. Any accord will now emerge after voters made their decision. 
Once a conference committee produces a deal, the text is final. Lawmakers can only approve or reject the entire bill, not amend it further. So if the negotiating panel embraces the controversial change, rank-and-file Democrats could be expected to fall in line and hand the political football to Gov. Maura Healey, who on Tuesday won her own reelection to another four-year term. 
Gov. Healey celebrates her 2026 election night win. (Emily Glick/CommonWealth Beacon)
Late last month, Boston 25 reporter Kerry Kavanaugh asked Healey if she would veto a records bill from the Legislature that affects the ballot question’s outcome. The governor answered with a single word: “Yes.” 
House and Senate Democrats wield sizable enough majorities on paper to override any gubernatorial veto. 
Aides to the chairs of the conference committee, Rep. Alice Peisch and Sen. Cynthia Creem, could not be reached immediately early Wednesday morning. 
Beacon Hill’s intervention could risk drawing the ire of voters, but none of the Legislature’s 200 lawmakers face reelection for another two years — and most go unopposed anyway. 
Democratic lawmakers have been clear they dislike both ballot measures. The tax cap changes, they say, would inject uncertainty into the state budgeting process at a time when federal funding cuts are already pushing Massachusetts into a precarious position. Legislative leaders also acknowledge there is public appetite for more transparency, but they contend the ballot question as drafted would violate the constitutional separation of powers because the secretary of state, who is a member of the executive branch, would need to enforce its provisions against the legislative branch. 
“While I agree that we should update the public records law, there are things in that ballot [question] that I would argue make it almost impossible for me to do my job,” Sen. Cindy Friedman, a top Senate deputy, told CommonWealth Beacon last month. “If I want to fix that, I have to then take that ballot initiative once it passes, if it passes, I then have to change it. And then what happens is all those people start screaming, ‘You’re not following the will of the people.’” 
“So I’m stuck in a very difficult situation because it’s my job to make law. That’s what you elected me to do,” she added. 
Any action to limit the scope of the voter-approved public records expansion could exacerbate an already-tense political battle. 
Two years ago, 72 percent of voters backed a ballot measure explicitly empowering the state auditor to audit the Legislature. Top House and Senate Democrats resisted compliance for the better part of two years, saying the measure was unconstitutional but declining to ask a court to issue a decisive ruling. 
A lawsuit attempting to unjam the gears is slowly advancing through Superior Court after an initial skirmish before the state’s highest court. DiZoglio, who has repeatedly clashed with lawmakers after previously serving in both chambers, lead the campaign for the records question and pitched it as a follow-up to the 2024 vote. 
She’s pledged to pursue legal action if the Legislature curtails the scope of the ballot question.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: SC Democrats flip 10 state House seats, undoing GOP supermajority
description: South Carolina’s GOP no longer enjoys a supermajority in both chambers following Democratic upsets in the state House.
text:
Scenes from the South Carolina House of Representatives chamber on Tuesday, March 29, 2022. (Travis Bell/STATEHOUSE CAROLINA)COLUMBIA — South Carolina’s GOP will no longer rule with supermajority power in both chambers following Democratic upsets in the state House.
Democrats managed to flip 10 seats across the Palmetto State on Election Day, according to unofficial results from the state Election Commission, though one of those will require an automatic recount under state law.
An 11th Republican seat also remains in question as Simpsonville Rep. David Vaughn’s 42-vote win over Democrat John MacCarthy also heads to a recount.
The flips erase gains from the last two election cycles. The GOP first took two-thirds control with the 2022 election.
“It sends a message to the Republican-led General Assembly,” South Carolina Democratic Party Chairwoman Christale Spain told the SC Daily Gazette Tuesday night. “This is from the national level all the way down back home at the Statehouse. We’re primed. The infrastructure is built. We’re ready to start really competing all across the state.”
Spain also said she thinks it “brings the temperature down in the chamber” after an unsuccessful, last-minute attempt to redraw South Carolina’s congressional map ahead of the midterms.
“It is a mandate that Democrats are not going to take it,” Spain said.
A statement from House Republican leadership took on a confident tone, despite the losses, as the party still holds 79 out of 124 House seats.
“Voters have given us the opportunity to continue delivering results and that’s exactly what we intend to do,” Rep. Brandon Newton, R-Lancaster, said in a statement.
“We have important work ahead of us and we look forward to getting back to work,” Speaker Murrell Smith said in a statement.
Half of the flips were in the Lowcountry.
Incumbents who lost included:

Rep. Daniel Gibson, a commercial pilot and two-term incumbent from Greenwood
Rep. Lucas Atkinson, a consultant from the Pee Dee first elected in 2016
Rep. Fawn Pedalino, a Realtor from Turbeville, who in 2022 flipped the Clarendon County seat long considered a Democratic stronghold
Rep. Jackie Terribile, a marketing consultant and freshman from the Charlotte suburb of Fort Mill
Rep. Brandon Cox, a U.S. Air Force veteran and two-term House member from Goose Creek
Rep. Greg Ford, a U.S. Air Force veteran from Summerville narrowly elected in a January special election to replace the late Rep. Chris Murphy following his resignation
Rep. Harriet Holman, a U.S. Army veteran from Ridgeville, who in 2024 ousted Democratic Joe Jefferson to flip the seat
Rep. James Teeple, a child care center operator and U.S. Navy veteran from Johns Island first elected in 2024 after former Rep. Matt Leber successfully ran for state Senate
Rep. Bill Hager, a retired engineer from Hampton, who flipped the seat in 2022

It also appears likely that recently elected Majority Leader Micah Caskey, a West Columbia attorney, also will lose to Democrat Joe Madge by just over 100 votes. With a margin of less than 1%, state election officials will have to recount to verify the results.
Voters first elected Caskey to the seat a decade ago.
In three other Lowcountry races, Republican incumbents Sylleste Davis, Gary Brewer and Jordan Pace, who leads the ultra-conservative House Freedom Caucus, eked out wins and narrowly avoided mandatory recounts. Each one by less than 400 votes.
Democrats’ largest margin among the flipped seats was in Greenwood and McCormick counties, where healthcare administrator Jumelle Brooks beat out Gibson by nearly 10 percentage points.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Democrats set to win majority of governorships for the first time in 16 years
description: Democrats could control majority of governor’s offices for the first time in 16 years after the GOP racked up major losses across the country.
text:
Democrats are poised to control the majority of governor’s offices for the first time in 16 years after the GOP racked up major losses across the country.
Democrats flipped governorships in Iowa, Ohio, Georgia and Texas and defended competitive races in Maine and Wisconsin, according to unofficial results from The Associated Press and Decision Desk HQ.
Midterms are always tough for the party that holds the White House, but high prices and growing disapproval of President Donald Trump delivered even stronger than expected results for Democrats Tuesday.
“It’s a blue wave that was bigger than anyone had expected, and it’s having consequences across the country, including here in Texas,” said Mark Jones, a political science professor at Rice University in Houston. “Overall, Donald Trump has single-handedly turned many red states blue — or at least purple.”
By late Tuesday, Democrats had won races for attorney general and lieutenant governor for the first time in decades and were well on their way to flipping the Texas House.
“One of the real questions will be what do Democrats do with this power, and will they be able to retain it,” he said. “This has effectively opened a door for Democrats across the country.”
Gubernatorial races proved historic for both Democrats and Republicans on Tuesday with the election of the nation’s first Black woman governor and the first Black Republican governor.
But the Democratic party made major gains coast to coast, particularly in reliably conservative states, that could reshape state policy for years to come.
In Iowa, the election of Democrat Rob Sand ends more than a decade of Republican control of the legislature and the governor’s office.
In Ohio, Democrat Dr. Amy Acton’s win marks the first time in 20 years that Ohio voters have selected a Democrat to lead the Buckeye State.
Former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms will become Georgia’s first Democratic governor since 2002. 
While governors were on ballots in 36 states, the nonpartisan Cook Political Report with Amy Walter only identified a dozen races for governor as competitive. Those included: Alaska, Georgia, Florida, Iowa, Kansas, Michigan, Nebraska, Nevada, Ohio, Oregon, Texas and Wisconsin.
Republicans have controlled a majority of state governments since 2010. Before Tuesday’s election, Republicans boasted a 26-24 gubernatorial advantage over Democrats. But the GOP’s state legislative advantage was even stronger, with Republicans controlling 28 state legislatures and Democrats controlling 18 with divided control of chambers in three states, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures.
By 12:30 a.m. Wednesday, Democrats had notched  major legislative wins. Democrats broke the GOP supermajority in Florida, flipped control of the Wisconsin state Senate and flipped the North Carolina state House.
In Pennsylvania, Democrats won the GOP-held state Senate, seizing  a trifecta – control of the governor’s office and both chambers of the legislature – in Harrisburg.
“Tonight’s earth-shattering victory is undeniable proof that voters are fed up with the MAGA agenda,” Heather Williams, president of the Democratic Legislative Campaign Committee, said in a news release.
In Arizona, Democrats declared victory in a yearslong effort to win control of the legislature, proclaiming that Republicans would be in the minority at the state Capitol for the first time in 60 years.
This story was first published Nov. 4, 2026 by Stateline.

name: California
title: What happened in the California election while you were sleeping
description: The blue tsunami was bigger than almost any Democrat could dream up. Democrats not only reclaimed control of the House by a decisive margin, but they flipped the Senate too, claiming seats in deep red states like Kansas, South Carolina, and Texas. That gives the party a powerful check on President Donald Trump in his […]
text:
U.S. Rep. Robert Garcia speaks during a press conference at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C. on April 10, 2025. Photo by Kayla Bartkowski, Getty Images




The blue tsunami was bigger than almost any Democrat could dream up.
Democrats not only reclaimed control of the House by a decisive margin, but they flipped the Senate too, claiming seats in deep red states like Kansas, South Carolina, and Texas. That gives the party a powerful check on President Donald Trump in his final two years in office.An Associated Press poll released Tuesday showed many voters disapproved of the president and also faulted Congress for not doing its job.
Now some California Democrats will wield gavels as they kick off investigations into the administration when they take the majority in January.
Rep. Robert Garcia of Long Beach had a two word message to Republicans: “Lawyer up.” The second-term Democrat is on track to lead the House Oversight Committee, which can be used to investigate just about anything in government.
Sen. Alex Padilla, the top Democrat of the Senate rules committee, and Rep. Pete Aguilar of San Bernardino, the chairperson of the House Democratic Caucus, would also likely gain more sway in Congress to challenge Trump.
On the social media site X, both of them signaled they planned to check the president. Padilla posted an image of a blue wave and mocked Trump’s recent rallies where he urged his supporters to vote as if he was on the ballot.
“America: HEARD LOUD AND CLEAR,” Padilla wrote. 
Aguilar, meanwhile, wrote “House Republicans’ days of rubber stamping Trump’s reckless agenda are coming to an end.”
Amid concerns by Democrats that Trump would challenge the results of the midterm elections, the president said Tuesday in an interview with The New York Times that he would accept the results and that he looks forward to working with Democrats.
To see how California’s congressional races are going, check out our rundown here from CalMatters’ Maya C. Miller.



Thank the independent CalMatters journalists who routinely help millions of Californians every election. Plus, help our 501(c)(3) nonprofit newsroom continue holding lawmakers, state agencies and institutions accountable every day of the year. Please give.

Other Stories You Should Know


California’s next governor


Governor-elect Xavier Becerra speaks during an election night watch party in Sacramento on Nov. 3, 2026. Photo by Fred Greaves for CalMatters




With Democrats outnumbering Republicans in California two-to-one, Democrat Xavier Becerra’s win wasn’t nearly as surprising as the sweeping changes coming to Congress. 
As CalMatters’ Jeanne Kuang explains, for months polls showed Becerra with a double-digit lead against Republican Steve Hilton. Media outlets declared Becerra the winner minutes after polls closed. By Tuesday night he secured at least 64% of the votes and will be California’s first elected Latino governor.

Becerra: “Tonight I have a message for all those who have been made to feel afraid. There’s a new sheriff in town. … If anyone wants to come after California or any one Californian, they better be ready for a fight.”

But Hilton didn’t go down without a fight: He had raised more than $33 million (Becerra raised $38 million) while campaigning on ambitious pledges such as $3.00 gas, abolishing the DMV and slashing taxes.

Hilton: “This isn’t the best year to be running for office as a Republican when we see what’s going on around the country. … The change we hope for may be delayed, but the change is coming. Our fight goes on and I’ll be there with you.”

It’s been a long time since a Republican won statewide office in California, and that trend appears likely to continue. Democratic candidates claimed all but one statewide elected position last night, writes CalMatters’ Jocelyn Wiener.
Two statewide positions are still undecided — superintendent and insurance commissioner. The Democratic-backed candidate for superintendent has a big lead, and two Democrats are facing off for insurance commissioner. Jane Kim is leading Ben Allen in the race for insurance commissioner.



What we know about all 14 propositions


Attendees stand next to a “Tax the Ultra-Rich Now” bus parked in San Francisco on Oct. 3, 2026. Photo by Manuel Orbegozo for CalMatters




Proposition 40, which would be a first-in-the-nation wealth tax, is falling short with only 44% of the vote as of Tuesday night, reports CalMatters’ Kristen Hwang. Though a handful of Bay Area counties are in favor of the one-time tax, dozens of others across California appear on course to reject it. 
Meanwhile, only one of the two billionaire-backed measures that would nullify Prop. 40 are above water: Prop. 42, which would ban new taxes on personal assets, is leading with 55% of the vote. The other, Prop. 41, which would impose limits to certain new state taxes, is trailing with just 48%.
As for the other measures:

Prop. 1, the $11.25 billion housing bond, passed.
Prop. 2, which allows the state to save more in its rainy day fund, passed. 
Prop. 3, which would make permanent an income tax for high earners, passed.
Prop. 4, which lift a ban on public financing for political campaigns, is trailing with 48% of the vote.
Prop. 5, which would change how recall elections work, has a slim majority with 50.3% of the vote.
Prop. 37, which creates a loan program for homebuyers, passed.
Prop. 38, which would fund immunology research, is leading with 56% of the vote.
Prop. 39, which would have required voter ID, failed.
Prop. 43, which would make it harder to pass citizen-driven local tax measures, is trailing with 45% of the vote.
Prop. 44, which would have required health clinics to spend more on patient care, failed.
Prop. 45, which would lift some environmental review requirements for development, is trailing with 46% of the vote.




Trouble brews down-ballot for GOP


Lawmakers gather on the Assembly floor at the state Capitol in Sacramento on Aug. 31, 2026. Photo by Fred Greaves for CalMatters




From CalMatters politics reporters Nadia Lathan and Kate Wolffe:
As Democratic upsets swept across the nation, Republican headwinds trickled down the ballot in California. Early returns Tuesday night had GOP candidates in toss-up legislative races struggling to fend off their Democratic challengers.
That means Democrats are likely to keep their supermajorities in both the Assembly and the Senate. 
In the Sacramento area, retired school superintendent Amy Slavensky, a Democrat, was leading with 53% of the vote against Republican incumbent Assemblymember Josh Hoover hours after polls closed. 
Other Republican incumbents in competitive races, including Assemblymembers Jeff Gonzalez, Greg Wallis and Leticia Castillo, were trailing their Democratic competitors. 
Democrats led in four open seats Republicans were targeting. In Fresno, county Supervisor Brian Pacheco, a Democrat, had 63% of the vote in his race against Republican Mike Murphy, the former Merced Mayor. Republicans were hoping to flip the seat.
Democrats supported by tech and business interests were also faring well Tuesday night. Grow California, a billionaire-backed independent expenditure committee, put millions behind senate candidate Sara Hernandez and assembly candidate David Penaloza. Both ended the night ahead of their more progressive opponents, although the races were too close to call.






California Voices
CalMatters columnist Dan Walters: When it comes to the state budget, Becerra faces a stark choice as the next governor: Continue the deficit spending or adopt a face-the-music attitude that could entail spending reductions and tax increases.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Jake Johnson declares victory in potentially huge upset in MN’s 1st Congressional District
description: Jake Johnson, a former high school math teacher who campaigned on lowering costs and working-class concerns, held a razor-thin lead in unofficial results early Wednesday against Republican U.S. Rep. Brad Finstad, in what would be a major upset in Minnesota’s 1st Congressional District.  The difference between the two candidates is just over 300 votes out […]
text:
Jake Johnson, DFL candidate for Minnesota's 1st Congressional District, answers questions at an “extra credit” town hall in Harmony, Minn. on Sept. 26. (Photo by Maya Betti/Minnesota Reformer)Jake Johnson, a former high school math teacher who campaigned on lowering costs and working-class concerns, held a razor-thin lead in unofficial results early Wednesday against Republican U.S. Rep. Brad Finstad, in what would be a major upset in Minnesota’s 1st Congressional District. 
The difference between the two candidates is just over 300 votes out of more than 325,000 cast, which means a recount is likely.
Johnson would be the first Democrat to represent the southern Minnesota district since Gov. Tim Walz left Congress in 2019.  
“I’m ready to get to work bringing down costs, taking on corruption and investing in small towns across southern Minnesota. Whether you voted for me or not, I work for you now,” Johnson said in a statement early Wednesday.
The win would mark a significant shift in a district that President Donald Trump carried by nearly 12 percentage points in 2024. 
The district runs the length of southern Minnesota from Wisconsin to South Dakota and includes Rochester, Mankato, Winona and many rural communities. 
Johnson, 43, built his campaign around affordability, drawing on his own experience growing up in a working-class family in Stewartville. 
Before he left his job to campaign full time, Johnson was a math teacher of 20 years at Rochester Public Schools. 
Over the summer, Johnson traveled nearly 20,000 miles across all 21 counties in the district in a beat-up minivan, holding town halls to meet with voters in person. In October, he announced a “Receipts Tour,” collecting residents’ receipts to document rising costs and pledging to bring them to Washington if elected.  
His election underscores a changing district: Rochester is growing quickly with highly skilled immigrants and other highly educated workers for the Mayo Clinic and the ecosystem that’s grown up around it. They lean Democratic and showed their growing electoral power this year. 
Finstad, 50, a fourth-generation farmer from New Ulm, won the seat in a 2022 special election. He went on to win the general election that year by more than 11 percentage points, and again in 2024 by 17 points. 
In Congress, he has largely worked in agricultural policy, pushing for legislation to expand crop insurance and reduce costs for farmers. 
Throughout the campaign, Johnson worked to draw a sharp contrast between his own 21-county town hall tour and Finstad’s low-profile, TV-dependent campaign, arguing Finstad had become out of touch with his constituents. 
Johnson will enter Congress as Democrats take control of the House after a generational victory that saw the party carrying districts in deep red areas across the South and Midwest. 
Johnson has criticized tariffs that raise prices for farmers and everyday people and opposed cuts to programs such as Medicaid and the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP. 
He has also called for a moratorium on data centers and an end to the war in Iran.
Johnson has pledged to continue holding his town halls in every county, in every term he serves in Congress.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Rural microtransit is a lifeline. Massachusetts should help it reach more people.
description: We need to change how we judge whether transportation is working. Ridership matters, but it cannot be the only measure.
text:
IN PARTS OF rural Massachusetts, buying a gallon of milk can require a nine-mile trip. A doctor’s appointment or workplace may be much farther away, with no direct bus route to get there. For someone who cannot drive or does not have access to a car, going about daily life can depend on whether a ride is available. Too often, it isn’t. 
These residents often depend on rural microtransit, flexible, on-demand public transportation services, which use vans or other small vehicles to fill in transportation needs in rural areas where fixed-route bus service is sparse or non-existent.  
To understand both the human and economic impact of rural microtransit, Transportation for Massachusetts commissioned three reports from the UMass Amherst Donahue Institute. The reports focus on three community-based microtransit programs: the South County Connector in the Berkshires, Hilltown Community Development Corporation’s transportation services in Western Massachusetts, and Helping Our Women on the Outer Cape. 
The Donahue Institute looked at how each service operates, the trips it provides, and the communities it serves, and spoke with local providers and partners. Across the three programs, they found $24.6 million in economic benefits from service provided between 2022 and 2025. Depending on the program, every dollar invested produced between $8 and $23 in benefits for state and local economies. 
In 2025 alone, the three programs provided 26,887 one-way trips, connecting people to health care, jobs, groceries, senior services, and other essential destinations. 
For Grace, a Helping Our Women client, microtransit meant being able to travel from Truro to Hyannis every day for four weeks during cancer treatment. The service made sure she could get to the lifesaving care she needed. 
Grace’s experience reflects a broader challenge in communities where distances are long and transportation choices are few. On the Outer Cape, a round trip by bus from Provincetown to Hyannis for medical care can take as long as six hours. In the Hilltowns, even a trip to the grocery store can take 45 minutes. 
When people think about public transportation in Massachusetts, they often think first of the MBTA. But outside its service area, many residents rely on regional transit authorities serving large, spread-out regions. Fixed-route buses may run infrequently, travel only along major roads or require several connections. 
Microtransit is one way to fill those gaps. For its grant programs, Massachusetts follows the federal definition of microtransit as a technology-enabled service that uses multi-passenger vehicles to provide on-demand trips with routes generated in response to riders’ needs. Trips can be scheduled by phone, online, or through an app. 
These programs are not a replacement for fixed-route buses, rail, or paratransit. They work alongside them, reaching people and places a traditional route cannot. 
Each program shows what these services make possible in different parts of rural Massachusetts.  
The South County Connector provided 21,924 trips in 2025, including more than 6,000 trips to work, and generated approximately $16.5 million in economic benefits. Hilltown CDC provided nearly 14,000 trips between 2022 and 2025, with nearly three-quarters of its 2025 trips going to medical appointments, and generated nearly $4 million in benefits. Helping Our Women provided more than 3,600 trips for women with chronic or serious health conditions and generated approximately $4.2 million in benefits. 
We are seeing similar results in other parts of rural Massachusetts. A 2025 Donahue Institute analysis found that the Quaboag Connector, which serves 10 towns in Worcester, Hampshire, and Hampden counties, generated nearly $45 million in economic benefits, or almost $11 for every dollar invested. 
For people with few other ways to get around, these services are lifelines. They are also essential public infrastructure, helping residents stay healthy, keep working, manage daily life and remain independent. The benefits do not stop with riders. Local employers, health care providers and communities benefit too. 
Yet many programs are struggling to meet the need that already exists. Providers in all three regions reported shortages of drivers and vehicles, limited scheduling availability and more requests than they could accommodate. On the Outer Cape, limited volunteer capacity can make urgent rides difficult to arrange. In the Hilltowns, eligibility rules prevent some younger residents from using services even when they have no other way to reach work. 
The challenge is no longer proving that microtransit has value. It is giving successful programs the stability and capacity to serve the people already asking for rides. 
Massachusetts is beginning to respond. The state has committed $15 million through two supplemental budgets to the Microtransit and Last-Mile Transit Grant Program, supporting services operated by regional transit authorities, municipalities and community organizations. 
That is real progress, but someone who depends on a ride for dialysis, cancer treatment, work, or groceries needs to know the service will still be there next year. Providers need reliable, multiyear funding to keep drivers, maintain vehicles, expand hours and meet growing demand. 
The state should provide that funding, particularly where transportation gaps are greatest. It should help providers add drivers, vehicles, and service hours while strengthening connections among community-based services, regional transit authorities, health care organizations, and existing transportation networks. 
As microtransit grows, Massachusetts also needs a clearer picture of where services exist, where gaps remain and how successful programs can be funded over the long term.  
State Reps. Tricia Farley-Bouvier and Todd Smola, along with Sens. Julian Cyr and Jo Comerford, have proposed creating a statewide commission to study existing and emerging microtransit services and their funding. Such a commission could improve coordination and help develop a statewide strategy that still allows communities to design services around local needs. 
We also need to change how we judge whether transportation is working. Ridership matters, but it cannot be the only measure. A rural service covering hundreds of square miles will never carry the same number of people as a subway line or urban bus route. Its value should also be measured by whether it helps people reach health care and work, lowers household transportation costs, serves communities with few alternatives, and provides trips that otherwise would not happen. 
Rural residents and providers already know what a reliable ride makes possible. Now state leaders have the numbers to match their experience. Massachusetts should build on what is working and give these services the support they need to reach more people. 
Reggie Ramos is executive director of Transportation for Massachusetts. Gwynne Guzzeau is the executive director of Helping Our Women.

title: Clark County approves quicker, easier short-term rental application process
description: The Clark County Commission on Tuesday unanimously approved new rules attempting to simplify the short-term rental application process amid an ongoing federal court case.  The commission first adopted an ordinance in 2022 seeking to rein in short-term rentals, which critics warned had become oversaturated with corporate out-of-state investors who bought up a[...]
text:
Clark County Government Center (Photo: Jeniffer Solis/Nevada Current)The Clark County Commission on Tuesday unanimously approved new rules attempting to simplify the short-term rental application process amid an ongoing federal court case. 
The commission first adopted an ordinance in 2022 seeking to rein in short-term rentals, which critics warned had become oversaturated with corporate out-of-state investors who bought up affordable housing stock.
The process the county initially set up to apply for a license led to a backlog of applications and prompted a U.S. District Court last December to impose an injunction on efforts to regulate the industry.   
The Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals in October ruled the district court’s injunction was “unnecessarily broad” and ordered the lower court to narrow its scope.
The ordinance approved Tuesday by the county, which requires in-person appointments for new short term rental applicants, is a response to federal court rulings, said Jeff Rogan, the deputy district attorney with Clark County. 
The changes address the concerns of the court and allow people with “a meaningful opportunity to apply for a short-term rental license and to have their applications processed in a reasonable time,” he said.
With new procedures in place, Rogan hoped the district court would “lift that injunction or at least narrow it down, so we can continue to enforce our short-term rental ordinance.”
“The court did say that short-term rentals still may be regulated despite the concerns the court had with our process,” he said. “We’re keeping those regulations today.”
The ordinance requires new applications for short term rentals to be received by appointment rather than applying online. 
Dec. 15 is slated to be the first day applicants can schedule an appointment, which will be available starting Jan. 5, 2027. 
State lawmakers first passed legislation in 2021 that required municipalities to develop short term rental regulations. 
When Clark County adopted its first ordinance in 2022, there was a backlog on processing applications, Rogan said. 
“The bill itself had an effect of opening licensing all at one time, and we knew that there was a large demand for these licenses,” he said. “And because it opened at one time, we received an influx of a large number of applications.”
What was supposed to be about a six-month application period “turned into about a 10- or 11-month application period where people submitted it and they waited before we even reviewed it,” he said. “We’re getting rid of that.”
The county is implementing a rolling application period that will remain open instead of a lottery system. 
The ordinance also imposes a 14-day deadline for applicants to respond to requests for additional information and to schedule an inspection.
Under the previous procedure, an application wouldn’t be approved until the fees were paid after a final inspection, which slowed down the process, Rogan said.
Instead the county is “going to approve or deny the application at the time that they pass their fire inspection” and the license itself won’t be administered until all fees have been paid, he said. 
If an applicant for a short term rental is denied, they have 30 days to appeal. The county is considering a separate ordinance seeking to shorten the appeal period to 14 days. 
“A person who is denied an application has a right to an appeal, and we have to honor that,” Rogan said. “We can reduce some of those timelines.”

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: New nature conservation fund wins voter approval, setting stage for funding fight
description: Passage of the ballot question now means a new nature conservation fund will be established to support clean drinking water, create and improve local parks, and protect wildlife habitats without raising taxes or levying a new one.
text:
MASSACHUSETTS VOTERS approved a ballot question that would steer sales tax revenue already being generated from sporting goods toward a new nature conservation fund. 
Question 6, which passed with around 60 percent of the vote, was spearheaded by environmental advocacy groups like The Trustees, Mass Audubon, The Nature Conservancy, and Conservation Law Foundation. Gov. Maura Healey and former Gov. Deval Patrick endorsed the measure.  
“This is our one and only home,” Katie Theoharides, who is president and CEO of The Trustees and served as energy and environmental affairs secretary under former Gov. Charlie Baker, said in a victory speech Tuesday night. “It is the place we live. It’s what we’re going to give to our children. This matters.” 
Passage of the ballot question now means a new nature conservation fund will be established to support clean drinking water, create and improve local parks, and protect wildlife habitats without raising taxes or levying a new one. Instead, future revenue from the sales tax collected from purchases of camping equipment, hunting and fishing gear, and golf clubs will boost the new fund. 
Although the measure faced no formal opposition, some on Beacon Hill have warned about the ramifications of setting state spending decisions via ballot and taking money out of the General Fund during a time of fiscal constraints.  
There’s also no guarantee that passage of the question will automatically lead to the outcome proponents sought. Even though supporters estimate $100 million per year will be generated for the new fund — other calculations put that number much lower — lawmakers could either choose not to allocate money to the new fund or simply deduct what they would have otherwise provided for nature conservation in the budget, leading to few, if any, new net additional dollars for the cause.  
The Boston Globe’s editorial board endorsed a “no” vote for precisely those reasons.  
But proponents maintained that a stable source of funding to protect nature is critical to keep the state on track to conserve 30 percent of land by 2030 and guard against budget cuts that often fall hardest on environmental, restoration, and conservation programs. Healey’s fiscal year 2027 budget cut funding for the Department of Conservation and Recreation by nearly 4 percent. 
And they argued that going before voters, in a rebuke to Beacon Hill, was their best bet for action.  
The Yes on 6 campaign was able to generate more than $4 million in contributions, including $800,000 from one donor alone, to send a message to the State House that more needs to be done to keep pace with one of the nation’s fastest-growing outdoor recreation economies, despite the initiative’s lack of teeth.  
Supporters recognized in the immediate aftermath of their ballot victory that more needs to now be done to secure the additional funding sought for conservation. 
“We have to fight to lock in the money that we secured in this fight,” said Brad Campbell, president of Conservation Law Foundation.

title: Alaska Democrats flip at least two Republican state House seats and grow coalition control
description: The “blue wave” that marked national results during Election Day appears to have washed into the Alaska House of Representatives as well. According to preliminary election results updated early Wednesday morning, independent and Democratic lawmakers are leading in 23 of the House’s 40 seats. Independents and Democrats won 19 seats in the 2024 elections. Many[...]
text:
Genevieve Mina, D-Anchorage, waves a sign on Election Day, Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026 in Midtown Anchorage. (Photo by Loren Holmes/Alaska Beacon)The “blue wave” that marked national results during Election Day appears to have washed into the Alaska House of Representatives as well.
According to preliminary election results updated early Wednesday morning, independent and Democratic lawmakers are leading in 23 of the House’s 40 seats. Independents and Democrats won 19 seats in the 2024 elections.
Many votes remain uncounted, including thousands of early and absentee ballots that could change the results in districts where all precincts have reported Election Day results.
Since 2024, the House has been controlled by a 21-person coalition that includes 16 Democrats, 3 independents and 2 Republicans, and Election Day results indicate that coalition is likely to grow, even if no Republicans choose to join. 
The 20-person state Senate has been controlled by a 14-member coalition for the past two years, and preliminary election results indicate that coalition is likely to continue as well, with coalition-minded senators either being elected or re-elected. 
Democrat Cliff Groh waves signs on Election Day, Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026 in Midtown Anchorage. (Photo by Loren Holmes/Alaska Beacon)
Democrats flip two Republican state House seats in Anchorage
Former Democratic state Rep. Cliff Groh will return to the Alaska House after defeating Republican Dan Sager in the House district covering Anchorage’s Government Hill and Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson.
Republican Rep. David Nelson did not seek re-election, leaving the seat open. Groh previously represented the district but was defeated by Nelson in 2024. The district’s large military population does not usually vote in midterm elections, which causes its state House representation to regularly flip between Republican and Democratic control.
Elsewhere in Anchorage, Democratic candidate Denny Wells has defeated Republican incumbent Rep. Mia Costello after unsuccessfully challenging her in 2022 and 2024. With all six precincts reporting results, Wells has 52.4% of the vote for House District 15, which covers the Campbell Lake and Jewel Lake area of Anchorage.
Independent leads narrowly in Republican House district
Democratic-backed independent candidate Joy Beth Cottle leads Republican candidate Harmony Tomaszewski by 43 votes out of 6,601 counted so far in House District 34, which covers northern Fairbanks.
Some absentee and early votes remain uncounted.
House District 34 voted strongly for Republican President Donald Trump in 2024 and re-elected state Republican Rep. Frank Tomaszewski by a wide margin over Cottle in that year, but Tomaszewski declined to run for re-election and instead ran for the state Senate seat being vacated by Sen. Robb Myers, R-North Pole.
Myers announced his retirement close to the election filing deadline, which deterred other candidates from running for the office. It also deterred candidates from running against his wife Harmony, who had inside knowledge of the upcoming state House vacancy and filed to replace her husband.
Rep. Bryce Edgmon, I-Dillingham, is seen during debate on the operating budget on Apr. 13, 2026. (Photo by Corinne Smith/Alaska Beacon)
Southwest Alaska state House seat undecided
With Speaker of the House Bryce Edgmon, I-Dillingham, vacating his state House seat to run for Senate, House District 37 had four candidates vying to replace him.
As of Wednesday morning, that race remained unresolved. With 22 of 35 precincts reporting results, Democratic candidate Evelynn Trefon had 36.4% of the vote, followed by Republican Brenda Wilson with 33.7%, independent Mark Smith with 22.6% and independent Cade Woods with 6.8%.
The district went for Trump in 2024, and the winner of the state House race will be decided by a ranked-choice runoff. 
If Wilson wins, it likely will be the only district to flip to Republican control in this election.
Eagle River state House seats undecided
Both of Eagle River’s state House seats were undecided early Wednesday morning. In House District 24, where Republican Rep. Dan Saddler retired after a long tenure, Republican Ken McCarty leads fellow Republican Gina Wall by just 16 votes out of 6,729 cast. The margin could change as more absentee and early votes are counted.
The race for House District 23 is headed to a ranked choice runoff, as incumbent Republican Rep. Jamie Allard has 38.1% of the vote. Behind her are Democratic challenger Jim Arlington with 28.5%, Republican candidate Ruby Jones with 26.4%, and Democratic candidate Lee Hammermeister with 6.8%. 
Speaker of the House Cathy Tilton, R-Wasilla, speaks Thursday, April 27, 2023, at a news conference in Juneau. (Photo by James Brooks/Alaska Beacon)
Tilton in close four-way race
Sen. Cathy Tilton, R-Wasilla, was one of the longest-serving Republican members of the state House when Gov. Mike Dunleavy appointed her to fill a Senate vacancy last year.
But late in her first senatorial election campaign, several local residents accused her of having a predatory relationship with a teenager in the 1990s, and an anonymous website accused her of grooming the teenager for sex. After the Anchorage Daily News covered the allegations, Tilton denied any criminal conduct.  
With all precincts in Senate District M reporting results Tuesday night, Tilton had 33.4% of the vote, followed by Republican challenger Ryan Berry with 32.5%. Democratic candidate Pat Chesbro was third with 28.3% and Republican Zane Vrvilo was fourth with 5.5%.
The race is almost certain to be decided by a ranked choice runoff. 
Democratic votes will decide ranked choice runoffs in the Mat-Su
The Matanuska-Susitna Borough had several legislative races stocked with candidates, and preliminary Election Day results showed most will be headed to ranked-choice runoffs.
In Senate District O, where Sen. George Rauscher, R-Sutton, is running for election after being appointed by Gov. Mike Dunleavy to fill a vacant seat, Rauscher has 43% of the vote compared to 30.7% for Republican challenger Ryan Sheldon and 26% for Democratic candidate Peter Bauer.
Longtime Republican Rep. DeLena Johnson, R-Palmer, is in a close three-way race. She has 36.7% of the vote, while independent challenger Steve Merritt has 32.6% and Republican Michael Bowles has 30.4%.
Incumbent House District 28 Rep. Elexie Moore, R-Wasilla, is trailing a more conservative Republican, Stephen Wright. Moore has 35.2% of the vote to Wright’s 37.4%. Democratic candidate Kit Kennedy has 26.9%, meaning Democratic votes will decide the district when the ranked choice runoff takes place.
Rep. Garret Nelson, R-Sutton, was appointed by Gov. Mike Dunleavy and is running in his first election campaign. He has 35.7% of the vote, ahead of fellow Republican Steve Menard with 33.7%, Democrat Kimberly Slone with 18.8% and independent Jessica Kusner-Kalarchik with 11.7%. The ranked choice runoff will decide the race.
And in House District 30, incumbent Rep. Kevin McCabe has 38.4% of the vote while Republican challenger Doug Massie has 35.8%. Democratic candidate Sandra Loomis has 25.4%, meaning that Democrats’ second-choice votes are likely to decide the ranked choice runoff. 
Lyman Hoffman’s successor still uncertain
The race to replace Sen. Lyman Hoffman, D-Bethel, the longest-serving member of the Alaska Legislature, remained uncertain early Wednesday morning, with only 37 of 57 precincts reporting results from Senate District S in southwest Alaska.
Speaker of the House Bryce Edgmon, I-Dillingham, led a four-candidate race with 30.4% of the vote, followed by Republican Darren Deacon with 28%. Democrat Wassilie Guy was fourth with 25.2% and independent Rick Robb of Bethel had 16.1%.
The race is almost certain to be decided by a ranked-choice runoff.
Bethel House race unresolved
The race for House District 38, covering Bethel and parts of the Yukon delta region, remained undecided early Wednesday morning but likely to remain in Democratic control. 
With 15 of 22 precincts reporting results, incumbent Democratic Rep. Nellie Unangiq Jimmie led former Democratic Rep. CJ McCormick, whom Jimmie defeated in 2024. Jimmie had 35.5% of the vote, and McCormick had 32.1%.
Republican candidate Willy Keppel was third with 22.5%, and independent Joseph Amik was fourth with 9.7%. 
A ranked choice runoff likely will decide the result.
Kodiak/Southern Kenai Peninsula/Prince William Sound
In Senate District C, which covers Kodiak, the southern Kenai Peninsula and Prince William Sound, incumbent Sen. Gary Stevens, R-Kodiak, retired after serving as Senate President.
With all precincts reporting results, Rep. Louise Stutes, R-Kodiak, leads the race to replace him. She has 48.1% of the vote, followed by Republican Heath Smith with 39.4% and Republican Carrie Harris with 11.6%.
Stutes has been a member of the House’s coalition majority for several years and is expected to join the Senate’s coalition if elected. Smith said he would not join the Senate coalition.
If no candidate has at least 50% of the first-choice votes, a winner will be chosen through the ranked choice runoff.
Stutes is vacating the House District 5 seat, where independent candidate Kathy Simpler is leading Republican Sheldon Prout. Simpler, who is expected to replace Stutes in the House coalition, has 55.9% of the vote, with 11 of 12 precincts reporting results.
Senate District C’s other half is House District 6, where Republican incumbent Rep. Sarah Vance has 51.3% of the vote against independent challenger Brent Johnson.
Johnson had more votes than Vance in the primary, but Vance reversed the result in the general election.
Anchorage Senate
All four incumbent Anchorage senators on the ballot won re-election by healthy margins Tuesday night. Republican Sen. Cathy Giessel and Democrats Elvi Gray-Jackson, Löki Tobin and Bill Wielechowski will each return to the Capitol in January.
Tobin and Wielechowski ran unopposed.
Southeast Alaska
Election Day wrought no changes in Southeast Alaska’s legislative contingent. Republican Sen. Bert Stedman, R-Sitka, was unopposed for re-election, as was Rep. Sara Hannan, D-Juneau. Sen. Jesse Kiehl, D-Juneau, was not up for election this year.
In Ketchikan, Republican Rep. Jeremy Bynum won re-election against independent challenger Grant EchoHawk, and in Sitka, independent Rep. Rebecca Himschoot defeated Republican Kenny Skaflestad and undeclared candidate Alston Evans.
In Juneau, Democratic Rep. Andi Story beat Republican challenger Annette Kreitzer of Haines.
Kenai Peninsula
Similarly, there were no changes on the Kenai Peninsula either. Republican Rep. Justin Ruffridge defeated Democrat Kate Veh in House District 7, and Republican Rep. Bill Elam earned 76% of the vote against two independent candidates in House District 9. Republican Sen. Jesse Bjorkman was not up for election this year.
