text:
Katherine Robertson, Deputy Attorney General and Republican runoff candidate for Attorney General, speaking with voters at the Shelby County Republican Party runoff candidate forum May 26, 2026, in Pelham, Alabama, at the Pelham Civic Complex. (Anna Barrett/Alabama Reflector)Republican nominee Katherine Robertson led the race for Alabama attorney general late Tuesday night.
As of 11:08 p.m., Robertson, chief counsel in the AG’s office, received 854,919 votes (56%) in unofficial returns. Democratic nominee Jeff McLaughlin, a former state representative from Guntersville, garnered 673,380 votes, almost 44%.
The numbers were taken from the Alabama Secretary of State’s website. The Associated Press had not called the race as of late Tuesday evening.
A message was sent to the Robertson campaign Tuesday evening seeking comment.
Robertson will succeed Alabama Attorney General Steve Marshall, who has held the office since 2017 and was term-limited. Marshall sought the Republican nomination for U.S. Senate earlier this year but finished third in the primary.
Robertson highlighted endorsements she received from Second Amendment rights groups such as the National Rifle Association on her campaign website. She also posted endorsements from the Coosa, Tuscaloosa and Madison sheriff’s offices.
A message was sent to the McLaughlin campaign Tuesday evening seeking comment.
McLaughlin did not have a significant campaign presence until September when his website went online. On it, McLaughlin pledged to address corruption and to hold state officials accountable. He also promised to protect consumers in Alabama and equally apply justice in the state, “protecting the rights of every Alabamian and refusing to use the office to settle political scores.”
In an interview in September, McLaughlin said he would use the authority of the office to help ensure that consumers in Alabama will pay the lowest power rates possible.
Robertson defeated Alabama Supreme Court Justice Jay Mitchell for the Republican nomination in June.
The Republican nominee held a major cash advantage in the race. Robertson raised a total of $4.4 million for the primary and general elections this year and spent a total of $5.3 million through Friday, according to the Alabama Secretary of State’s Office. McLaughlin raised just under $51,000 and spent about $45,000.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri Republicans suffer biggest electoral setback in a generation
description: Republicans still control Missouri politics. But after Tuesday’s election, their grip on state government looks considerably less secure. Democrats ended Republican supermajorities in both legislative chambers, picked up 16 Missouri House seats and ousted a seven-term Republican congresswoman. Voters rejected a renewed abortion ban, defeated a congressional [...]
text:
By a preliminary count, Democrats won 68 of the 163 Missouri House seats, a gain of 16 from 2024 (Getty Images).Republicans still control Missouri politics. But after Tuesday’s election, their grip on state government looks considerably less secure.
Democrats ended Republican supermajorities in both legislative chambers, picked up 16 Missouri House seats and ousted a seven-term Republican congresswoman. Voters rejected a renewed abortion ban, defeated a congressional map backed by President Donald Trump and imposed new restrictions on lawmakers’ ability to overturn citizen initiatives.
The results raise questions about how a Republican Party accustomed to overwhelming legislative majorities will govern when lawmakers return to Jefferson City in January — and whether Tuesday represents a temporary backlash or something more enduring.
By a preliminary count, Democrats won 68 of the 163 Missouri House seats, a gain of 16 from 2024. That leaves Republicans with 95 seats, their lowest total since the 2008 election, when they won 89. Democrats flipped 16 Republican-held districts while Republicans failed to capture a single Democratic seat, despite Republican House campaigns raising $17.7 million compared with $7.1 million for Democrats.
Missouri voters reject Amendment 3, preserving abortion rights approved in 2024

In the Senate, Democrats won the two seats needed to end another Republican supermajority. State Rep. Betsy Fogle captured a Springfield-based district Republicans had held for more than 80 years. In eastern Jackson County, state Rep. Keri Ingle defeated House Speaker Jon Patterson.
Republicans can still write budgets, pass legislation and set the agenda without a single Democratic vote. But they can no longer override vetoes or make most new laws take effect immediately through emergency clauses without help from across the aisle.
The geography of the victories challenged assumptions about where Democrats can compete. The party won three House seats in St. Charles County, where it had gone two decades without a House victory, and captured an open seat in Cass County. In Cole County, home of the state Capitol, Democrat Suzanne Luther defeated Republican Shane Kampeter by just 189 votes.
Republican losses extended to Congress, where Democrat Fred Wellman defeated seven-term U.S. Rep. Ann Wagner in suburban St. Louis. Wellman won St. Louis County by 14 points and cut Wagner’s margin in St. Charles County from roughly 16,000 votes in 2024 to about 4,000.
His victory gave Missouri’s bitter redistricting fight an unexpected ending, at least for now. Trump and Republican lawmakers sought new congressional boundaries that could produce a 7-1 GOP delegation. A referendum campaign and court rulings kept the existing 6-2 map in place for Tuesday’s election. Voters then rejected the proposed replacement through Proposition A, 62% to 38%, and elected a 5-3 delegation under the old lines.
The ballot measures showed how consistently Missourians have broken with the Republican Legislature. Two years after narrowly approving constitutional abortion protections, they rejected an attempt to repeal them. Amendment 3, which would have restored a ban on most abortions, received about 44% support despite an organized campaign backed by churches and Republican officials, including Gov. Mike Kehoe. His wife, Claudia, was the campaign’s treasurer.
That followed overwhelming defeats in August for two other Republican priorities: an amendment making citizen initiatives harder to pass and another allowing lawmakers to replace Missouri’s income tax with expanded sales taxes. Kehoe made the income tax plan a centerpiece of his agenda and called the 2025 special session that produced both the initiative measure and the congressional map. Each effort has now failed at the ballot box.
Missouri voters reject Trump-backed congressional map, dealing GOP redistricting defeat

On Tuesday, voters went further, approving Amendment 6 with roughly 60% support. It requires extraordinary legislative majorities and another statewide vote before lawmakers can change voter-approved initiatives or revive laws rejected by referendum. Legal challenges remain possible. But three months after more than 80% of voters rejected making initiatives harder to pass, a clear majority voted to make them harder for lawmakers to undo.
Eight years ago, the last national Democratic wave left Missouri’s Republican legislative supermajorities intact. Voters raised the minimum wage, rejected right-to-work and approved the Clean Missouri ethics and redistricting overhaul. But they also ousted Democratic U.S. Sen. Claire McCaskill and reelected Wagner.
This time, opposition to Republican policies coincided with significant losses for Republican candidates.
Missouri was also part of a national backlash. Democrats captured control of Congress, with Senate breakthroughs in traditionally Republican states including Texas and Kansas. Next door in Iowa, Republicans lost three of four U.S. House seats. That broader wave complicates any claim that Missouri’s results were driven primarily by disputes with state lawmakers.
Nor was Tuesday a wholesale rejection of Republicans. State Auditor Scott Fitzpatrick won reelection, though by roughly three points after winning by nearly 22 in 2022. Republicans retain the governorship and both legislative chambers, and Democratic gains were concentrated largely in cities and suburbs rather than rural Missouri.
One election cannot establish a lasting realignment. But the consequences are immediate: Kehoe and Republican lawmakers return in January facing falling revenues, pressure on school and healthcare budgets and an electorate newly willing to deny them seats as well as policy victories.
For years, Republicans could assume that losing a ballot measure did not necessarily threaten their grip on power. Tuesday offered the clearest evidence yet that the two can no longer be treated as separate questions.

text:
Voters cast their ballots on the first day of early voting at the Hillary Rodham Clinton Children’s Library in Little Rock, Arkansas on Monday. In Arkansas and five other states, voters are considering ballot measures that would make it clear that only U.S. citizens may vote.  (Photo by Ainsley Platt/Arkansas Advocate)Ohio Democratic candidate for attorney general John J. Kulewicz holds a narrow lead in the race against Ohio Republican Keith Faber.
With 102,148 provisional ballots outstanding, and 100% of precincts reporting in unofficial results on the Ohio Secretary of State website, Kulewicz is winning the race with 2,285,117 votes, or 50.31%, compared to 2,256,710 votes, or 49.69%, for Faber.
Republican Keith Faber and Democrat John Kulewicz faced off to become the state’s chief law enforcement officer and legal counsel.
Faber took the role of state auditor after being a legislator in both the Ohio House and Ohio Senate. He also served as the Senate president during his legislative tenure.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Kulewicz has spent 40 years as part of the law firm Vorys, Sater, Seymour and Pease, LLP. He also sits on Upper Arlington City Council. He campaigned on the idea that the state was looking for a change in the attorney general’s office, just as they are looking for change in other statewide offices. He told the Capital Journal before the election that he’d heard from people who believe “36 years of almost uninterrupted one-party rule has gotten us nowhere.”
Both vowed to enforce state laws to the highest degree, including investigations of elder abuse, human trafficking, and cybercrime.
Faber stood against sanctuary cities and emphasized the need for local law enforcement to work with federal immigration enforcement.
“Where you have problems is when local communities decide they want to be a sanctuary community, and they don’t cooperate with federal law enforcement, that leads to all sorts of potential conflicts,” Faber said in a Youngstown Press Club debate.
Kulewicz said he would do what was required under federal law when it came to immigration enforcement, but would prioritize local issues “to the extent that (enforcement) is discretionary.”
Both candidates said they would get the trial related to Ohio House Bill 6’s energy bailouts, and the leaders of FirstEnergy back in the courtroom after the previous case ended in a hung jury.
The previous person elected to the post, Republican Dave Yost, resigned in June to join a conservative non-profit law firm.

The Ohio Treasurer keeps track of the state’s investments and financial accounts, amounting to $280 billion. The office established programs for small business loans and homebuyer savings, and keeps records on government salaries, revenue, and spending.

What he doesn’t support is using state money for projects like entertainment venues and sports stadiums.
Edwards also spoke against the decision of a plan from state lawmakers to use the state’s unclaimed funds account, saying it was “very negative, what was done in the budget, and I can tell you, if I was finance chair, it wouldn’t have happened.”
A lawsuit was filed after the budget was passed with the measure in place, and a temporary block has been placed on it as the lawsuit continues.

name: WyoFile
title: Sheriff’s office cites Shoshoni mayor with unlawful contact after heated confrontation with mayoral candidate, police chief says
description:
Police kept the two separated until a sheriff’s deputy arrived. Amid allegations of electioneering and chest bumping, Mayor Joel Highsmith said he didn’t “knowingly touch” the candidate.
The post Sheriff’s office cites Shoshoni mayor with unlawful contact after heated confrontation with mayoral candidate, police chief says appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
The Fremont County Sheriff’s Office cited outgoing Shoshoni Mayor Joel Highsmith with unlawful contact Tuesday following a heated confrontation with mayoral candidate and councilmember Jordan Whitener over an electioneering allegation, according to Shoshoni Police Chief Christopher Konija. 
Whitener allegedly confronted Highsmith in his office at the Shoshoni Town Hall Tuesday morning after Highsmith accused him of electioneering at the Shoshoni Senior Center polling place earlier in the day, Konija told WyoFile, adding that the allegation was “unfounded.” Highsmith, however, said in a call with WyoFile that he had “never accused” Whitener of electioneering. “There was a concern, but he wasn’t,” Highsmith said, declining to elaborate. “I’m satisfied he was not.” 
Whitener didn’t respond to WyoFile’s inquiry before publishing time. 
Konija said the election-related concern apparently stemmed from Whitener talking to voters across the street from the Shoshoni Senior Center polling place after they had already voted, although he emphasized that he didn’t witness this first-hand.
After Whitener appeared at his office, Highsmith said he called police to get the council member “removed.” “I felt that Councilman Whitener was disrupting the town business, and I wanted him to leave,” Highsmith said. 
Konija and two other officers responded, according to the police chief. Before they arrived, Konija said the mayor allegedly “made physical contact several times,” including alleged “chest-bumping.” 
Shoshoni police chief Chris Konija, who doubles as the town clerk, takes a call from a local resident who had some questions about the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development’s rental housing assistance (Section 8) program. (Mike Koshmrl/WyoFile)
Because the incident involved the mayor and a city council member, creating a conflict of interest for the police department, the Fremont County Sheriff’s Office “immediately” took over the investigation, according to Konija. (WyoFile called the Fremont County Sheriff’s Office for comment but was transferred to Konija.) The police chief said he and the other officers kept the men separated until a sheriff’s deputy arrived. 
Following the incident, the Fremont County Sheriff’s Office cited Highsmith for unlawful contact, a misdemeanor offense punishable by a $750 fine and up to six months in jail. Highsmith said he was asked if he wanted to press charges against Whitener. 
“Other charges could have been brought. I chose not to,” the outgoing mayor said. 
Highsmith said he didn’t “knowingly touch” Whitener. “My stomach might have touched him,” the mayor said. “I’m a little overweight, so that’s the thing that sticks out the most … I’m a short, fat man.” 
The mayor added later in a text message that Whitener “came into town hall as the aggressor.” Noting his age and various physical ailments, Highsmith asserted that he poses “no physical threat” to the council member. 
Highsmith, who ran for an at-large Fremont County School District 24 seat after losing his primary reelection bid for mayor, said his court date is in early December. (Konija also ran for one of four school board seats in that district.)

title: Democratic candidates hold leads in both Ohio Supreme Court races
description: Ohio Democratic incumbent justice Jennifer Brunner and Democratic challenger Marilyn Zayas hold leads over their Republican opponents in unofficial results from the Ohio Secretary of State’s website. Two slots for the Ohio Supreme Court were open, one currently filled by Republican Justice Dan Hawkins, and the other by the only currently statewide elected De[...]
text:
The Gavel outside the Supreme Court of the State of Ohio. (Photo by Graham Stokes for Ohio Capital Journal. Republish photo only with original article.)Ohio Democratic incumbent justice Jennifer Brunner and Democratic challenger Marilyn Zayas hold leads over their Republican opponents in unofficial results from the Ohio Secretary of State’s website.
Two slots for the Ohio Supreme Court were open, one currently filled by Republican Justice Dan Hawkins, and the other by the only currently statewide elected Democrat, Justice Jennifer Brunner.
Brunner faced Republican opponent and former Franklin County Common Pleas Judge Colleen O’Donnell. O’Donnell spotlighted her time as an immigration judge in Texas as part of her campaign, a time in which she said she never granted asylum for those who were in her courtroom.
With 102,148 provisional ballots outstanding, and 100% of precincts reporting in unofficial results on the Ohio Secretary of State website, Brunner has 2,324,212 votes, or 51.37%, to 2,200,021 votes, or 48.63% for O’Donnell.
Zayays has 2,307,346 votes, or 51.01%, to 2,215,728n votes, or 48.99% for Hawkins.
O’Donnell also aligned with the many Republican judges she defeated in the primary in supporting “originalism” as the method for interpreting the state constitution during supreme court cases.
“I do not take the view that the Constitution, for example, is a living, breathing document, and so I honor both substantive and procedural judicial restraint,” O’Donnell told the Capital Journal in May.
The former common pleas and immigration judge served in the Ohio Attorney General’s Office, clerked for a federal judge and worked in private practice before being appointed to serve as judge in the Franklin County Common Pleas Court. After she left the post in 2023, she served as a federal immigration judge in Laredo, Texas.
She is also the daughter of retired Ohio Supreme Court Justice Terrence O’Donnell.
Brunner has been on the bench since 2021, and has been the sole Democrat on the bench since her colleagues Michael Donnelly and Melody Stewart were defeated in 2024. Since she started on the bench, the court has seen the chief justice change from Maureen O’Connor to Sharon Kennedy, and considered cases on topics ranging from redistricting, data centers, and education, to abortion, victim’s rights, and gender-affirming care.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
A state law passed in 2021 required supreme court races to include partisan labels on ballots, something Brunner sued to repeal in 2023. The lawsuit is still ongoing in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Ohio, and cites the state’s judicial conduct code in arguing judicial candidates are not allowed to participate in political or campaign activities that go against judicial independence or impartiality.
Brunner told the Capital Journal before the election that she sees it as a First Amendment issue which causes voters to assume she agrees wholesale with the Democratic platform.
“And I’m not in in a position to say, ‘well, it’s more nuanced here,’ or ‘no, it’s not the same here,’ or even ‘yes, it is the same,’ because I’ve got the code of judicial conduct,” Brunner said in August.
First District Court of Appeals Judge Marilyn Zayas is no stranger to campaigning for a seat on the supreme court, but as the campaign moved past the primaries, she said she felt a different energy in the 2026 election.
“I’m seeing how we are losing faith in our court because of politics, and politics has no place in our Ohio Supreme Court,” Zayas said at the Ohio Democratic Party’s primary event in May.
Hawkins was elected in 2024, taking over for fellow Republican Justice Joe Deters, who chose not to run for re-election, but to run for the seat that was held by Justice Melody Stewart. He previously served on the Franklin County Court of Common Pleas. He also spent more than a decade as a trial prosecutor, and a decade as director of Franklin County’s Special Victims Unit.
On social media, he campaigned with the idea that there would be no special treatment or “gray areas” in his method of judging.
“The moment justice becomes selective it stops being justice,” a post on his Facebook page stated. “That is a line this court will never cross while I’m on the bench.”

title: ‘Not the end of the fight’: Green strikes positive tone in concession to Blackburn
description: As the night wore on in Chattanooga and election results poured in, a crowd of supporters at Jerri Green’s watch party cheered each time the screen displayed a lead for the Democratic gubernatorial candidate over her Republican opponent, U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn. In the end, ultimately, Blackburn prevailed with 45.4% of the vote to Green’s […]
text:
"This was just one battle for our state and it was not the end of the fight," said Democratic gubernatorial nominee Jerri Green, conceding the race to U.S.Sen. Marsha Blackburn on Nov. 3, 2026, in Chattanooga. (Photo by Ben Sessoms for Tennessee Lookout)As the night wore on in Chattanooga and election results poured in, a crowd of supporters at Jerri Green’s watch party cheered each time the screen displayed a lead for the Democratic gubernatorial candidate over her Republican opponent, U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn.
In the end, ultimately, Blackburn prevailed with 45.4% of the vote to Green’s 43.1%, according to unofficial final results from the Tennessee Secretary of State on Tuesday night. But the Democrat urged her supporters to maintain enthusiasm and to keep fighting for what fueled a near shocking upset in what, historically, has been a deep red state.
“Tonight isn’t the result we wanted. I understand and I know that this hurts. Because I know how much each and every one of you has put into this campaign,” Green said in her concession speech. “It’s okay to be disappointed. It’s okay to breathe for what could have been. But tomorrow, we have to get back up. We have to dust ourselves off. We have to get back to work.”
Green stressed that the issues that led so many to her campaign — opposition to school vouchers, the lack of rural healthcare, money in politics — are grievances that would not disappear after the election.
“These aren’t abstract political debates,” Green said. “These are people’s lives. These are our neighbors, our families and our communities. And there are lives on the line.”
“While we may be sad, as the other side may celebrate, let us remind them of something,” she continued. “This was just one battle in the future for our state, and it was not the end of the fight.”
Following a race in which every county in the state swung left, including five that flipped to Democrats from the 2024 presidential race — Rutherford, Knox, Montgomery, Madison and Hamilton — Green insisted this would not be the end for her in Tennessee politics.
“Tonight, I didn’t win for you. But I want you to know that I’m not going anywhere, that you aren’t going anywhere, that we aren’t going anywhere,” she said. “We’re not backing down, and we’re not done fighting.”

text:
Image courtesy of the Food Bank of Delaware


Food Bank Launches Thanksgiving Food Drive as Families Face Rising Costs
NEWARK AND MILFORD, Del. – With Thanksgiving approaching and household budgets stretched by the cost of everyday necessities, the Food Bank of Delaware is asking Delawareans to help neighbors put a holiday meal on the table.
The organization’s annual Thanksgiving Food Drive invites individuals, businesses, schools, and community groups to donate food, organize collections, or contribute financially. Thanksgiving donations are requested by noon Friday, November 13, 2026.
According to Feeding America estimates cited by the Food Bank, approximately 157,000 Delawareans, including 42,000 children, face food insecurity. The cost of groceries, housing, and other essentials continues to force families to make difficult spending decisions.
The Food Bank’s pantry traffic indicates that demand for assistance remains high. Visits to its Healthy Pantry Centers in Newark and Milford increased 22% during the summer compared with the same period last year. September 2026 visits increased 15% compared with September 2025.
“For many families, Thanksgiving is a time to gather with loved ones and enjoy a special meal. But for neighbors already struggling to afford groceries and other basic necessities, putting a holiday meal on the table can feel out of reach,” said Cathy Kanefsky, President and CEO of the Food Bank of Delaware.
“No family should have to choose between paying a bill and celebrating Thanksgiving together. With the generosity of our community, we can help ease that burden and make the holiday a little brighter.”
Requested donations include holiday staples and everyday essentials:

Canned vegetables and fruits
Canned gravy and cranberry sauce
Instant mashed potatoes and stuffing mix
Canned meats and soups
Cornbread and biscuit mix
Frozen turkeys
Baby diapers and formula
Cereal
Peanut butter and jelly

Donations may be delivered to the Food Bank’s facilities at 222 Lake Drive in Newark or 102 Delaware Veterans Blvd. in Milford. Frozen turkeys must be delivered directly to one of the warehouses.
Although the Thanksgiving announcement lists a noon deadline on November 13, regular Friday donation hours at both locations end at 11:30 a.m. Donors should plan accordingly. Donations received after the Thanksgiving deadline will be distributed throughout the remainder of the holiday season.
New this year, a virtual food drive offers another way to participate. Supporters can fill an online shopping cart with needed items and make a tax-deductible monetary donation. Participants can also create personalized fundraising pages and invite friends, relatives, and coworkers to contribute.
Community members interested in organizing a collection can contact Aaron Stone at astone@fbd.org.
For more information about donating, hosting a food drive, or participating online, visit the Food Bank of Delaware’s food drive page.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Commentary: West Virginia’s doctors and federal workers fear the paper trail
description: Along Interstate 79 in North Central West Virginia, two kinds of workers carry a quiet fear about their own mental health. One group is the physicians, nurses and other clinicians who keep the state’s hospitals and clinics open. The other is the federal workforce in Clarksburg, home of the FBI’s Criminal Justice Information Services Division, […]
text:
Some healthcare and  federal employees believe that getting medical help for stress, depression or burnout could put their job credentials at risk. (Photo by Olga Pankova/Getty Images)Along Interstate 79 in North Central West Virginia, two kinds of workers carry a quiet fear about their own mental health. One group is the physicians, nurses and other clinicians who keep the state’s hospitals and clinics open. The other is the federal workforce in Clarksburg, home of the FBI’s Criminal Justice Information Services Division, which the FBI describes as the largest division in the bureau.
Both groups depend on a credential: a medical license in one case, a security clearance in the other. And both tend to believe that getting help for stress, depression or burnout could put that credential at risk.
I am a licensed clinical social worker. I want to describe what that belief costs West Virginia, and why it is often more fear than fact.
The doctors West Virginians depend on
Physicians across the country worry about how mental health care might affect their license. In a national sample of 5,829 physicians published in Mayo Clinic Proceedings in 2017, nearly 40% said they would be reluctant to seek formal care for a mental health condition because of concerns about repercussions to their medical licensure.
In West Virginia, that fear has company. In a small town, the local counselor may also treat the doctor’s patients. The physician who is the only one for miles cannot easily sit in a waiting room. So many simply keep working, carrying the weight of a stretched health system on their own sleep, families and health.
The cleared workforce
People who hold security clearances face a parallel worry: that seeing a therapist will cost them their eligibility. The federal background form, Standard Form 86, says plainly that mental health treatment and counseling, “in and of itself,” is not a reason to deny or revoke eligibility, and that seeking care “may contribute favorably” to decisions. Its questions focus on court orders, hospitalization and a short list of serious diagnoses, not routine counseling.
Many cleared workers have never read that language. Some prefer to work with a clinician who knows the process, such as a psychologist experienced with security clearance questions, because they want someone who can speak to their specific concern.
Hiding is a calculation, everywhere
The pattern is not unique to medicine or federal work. In a 2026 CEREVITY review of law firm partners, covering 305 equity partners and senior counsel who sought therapy through the CEREVITY network, 67% said they had hidden mental health strain from their firm. People whose careers depend on being seen as reliable make the same decision again and again: say nothing, keep performing, deal with it later.
Later usually means a crisis. By then, the strain has moved into relationships, drinking and health, and recovery is harder.
What would help in West Virginia
Much of the fix is clear information.
Hospital systems and medical groups can tell their clinicians, in plain language, what the state’s licensing process does and does not ask about mental health, and can offer at least one confidential counseling option outside the hospital’s own systems.
Federal employers and contractors in the Clarksburg area can put the Standard Form 86 language in front of their staff, and security officers can say out loud that counseling is not a disqualifier.
Leaders in both worlds can say, without details, that they have used care themselves.
And individuals can use telehealth to see a licensed clinician outside their own town and professional circle, which removes the waiting room problem entirely.
West Virginia cannot afford to lose the people who keep its health care running or the federal professionals who work in Clarksburg. Helping them seek care early, without fear for their credentials, is one of the least expensive ways to keep them.
If you or someone you know is in crisis, call or text 988 at any hour.
Disclosure: The author is a co-founder of CEREVITY, a private-pay therapy network that provides confidential care to professionals.

text:
Voters mark their ballots during the first day of early voting in Bismarck, North Dakota, on Oct. 22, 2026. Experts and voting rights advocates are bracing for the potential of federal influence over the results of next week’s midterm elections. (Photo by Jack Dura/North Dakota Monitor)Republican Frank LaRose holds a lead over Maple Heights Mayor Annette Blackwell in the race for Ohio Auditor, according to unofficial results on Tuesday night.
With 102,148 provisional ballots outstanding, and 100% of precincts reporting in unofficial results on the Ohio Secretary of State website, LaRose is winning the race with 2,310,105 votes, or 50.79%, compared to 2,237,955 votes, or 49.21%, for Blackwell.
The Auditor of State is the chief compliance officer for Ohio, conducting performance audits on state entities, local governments like cities and townships, and school districts around the state. The auditor has the power to designate fiscal watches and emergencies for entities who don’t receive clean financial audits. In times when the redrawing of state voting district maps occurs, the auditor has a seat on the Ohio Redistricting Commission as well.

Democratic Maple Heights Mayor Annette Blackwell leads one of the cities who faced fiscal emergency while current auditor Keith Faber led the office. She said her experience bringing the city back from the emergency gave her perspective she planned to use in leading the office.
Her campaign focused on enhancing the role of the office through the use of recommendations for struggling municipalities, and support for those entities as they go through the audit process.
She also said financial modeling needs to be upgraded to allow the state and it’s local governments to better predict their future under lower support from the local government fund, and tax incentives brought in to appeal to industries like data center developers and other large companies.
Republican Ohio Secretary of State Frank LaRose campaigned for the move to auditor on a platform of accountability, affordability, and transparency. As part of his plan for office, he pledged both to harness the power of artificial intelligence for use within the auditor’s office, and to keep watch over AI’s potential to cause problems for local governments and the agency itself.
He acknowledged public trust in governmental institutions is “at an all-time low,” and pushed for more programs to identify public corruption, including an “Ohio Taxpayer Fraud Bounty Program” to encourage public reports of corruption.

title: PEIA finance board to hold public hearings about proposed rate increases for the 2028 fiscal year
description: The finance board of the West Virginia Public Employees Insurance Agency will host a series of public meetings around the state this month about proposed rate increases for fiscal year 2028, which begins in July.
text:
The Public Employees Insurance Agency is proposing increasing premiums again for the 2028 fiscal year. (Photo by Lori Kersey/West Virginia Watch)The West Virginia Public Employees Insurance Agency finance board will host a series of public meetings around the state this month about proposed rate increases for fiscal year 2028, which begins in July 2027. 
PEIA is proposing a 2% aggregate premium increase for state workers and employers as well as a $2.50 increase in the employer administrative fee for state agencies
For non-state employees, PEIA is planning a 4% aggregate increase for the gold, silver and bronze plans.
The non-state gold HDHP plan will have a 24% premium increase, in order to “properly price the Plan’s risk according to its historical performance and reduce its Medical Loss Ratio into alignment with the rest of PEIA’s Plans,” according to PEIA. The gold HDHP plan has about 5,000 policyholders, according to PEIA.
In addition, non-state agencies will have an employer administrative fee increase of $2.50.
Medicare and non-Medicare retirees will not have premium increases in fiscal year 2028, according to PEIA’s proposal. 
Also this year, PEIA will require all participating non-state employers to have at least half of their employees enrolled in a PEIA health plan by June 30, 2027. 
PEIA premiums have increased by higher amounts in recent years. Last year the PEIA finance board approved a premium hike of 3% for employees, employers and retirees for the 2027 fiscal year, which began in July. 
The year before that, rates increased by 14% for state employees and by 16% for local government employees. Retirees also saw a 12% increase in premiums.
The finance board is expected to meet again Dec. 3. 
Registration for each of the public hearings will begin at 5:30 p.m. The public meetings will take at 6 p.m. on the following locations and dates:

description: Democrat Victoria Broderick claimed victory in Tennessee’s 4th Congressional District late Tuesday after unofficial election results showed her with a razor-thin margin of victory to flip a reliably Republican seat occupied by U.S. Rep. Scott DesJarlais since 2011. DesJarlais had not conceded defeat as of midnight in a race that separated him from Broderick [...]
text:
Democrat House candidate Victoria Broderick claimed victory over incumbent GOP Rep. Scott DesJarlais in Tennessee's 4th Congressional District Tuesday (Photo: Courtesy of Tennessee Democratic Party)Democrat Victoria Broderick claimed victory in Tennessee’s 4th Congressional District late Tuesday after unofficial election results showed her with a razor-thin margin of victory to flip a reliably Republican seat occupied by U.S. Rep. Scott DesJarlais since 2011.
DesJarlais had not conceded defeat as of midnight in a race that separated him from Broderick by fewer than 300 votes, according to unofficial totals reported by the Secretary of State. Broderick received 48.87% of the vote to DesJarlais’ 48.73%, according to the unofficial results. 
Broderick, 34, is a tech support worker and member of the Tennessee Democratic Party executive committee, who campaigned on affordability. She described herself as “a working-class mom from rural Tennessee” and said she was in the race “because we deserve better than being treated like an afterthought.” She lives in Lincoln County with her husband and two sons.
Broderick ran against DesJarlais in 2024, losing by more than 40 percentage points. Since then, a redistricting process by Tennessee Republicans rejiggered the 4th district in east Tennessee to include a portion of Nashville.
Broderick won only two of the 11 counties that make up the district — Davidson and Rutherford. The counties are the two most populous in the district.

title: Dominion-NextEra accept some proposed protections in merger case, rejects rate and staffing freeze
description: In the final days before the Dominion Energy and NextEra merger case is set to begin at the State Corporation Commission, the companies are responding to a list of recommendations and conditions that staff members at the SCC and the Attorney General’s Office laid out as critical changes needed before commissioners approve the merger. The […]
text:
State Corporation Commission building in downtown Richmond. (Photo by Shannon Heckt/Virginia Mercury)In the final days before the Dominion Energy and NextEra merger case is set to begin at the State Corporation Commission, the companies are responding to a list of recommendations and conditions that staff members at the SCC and the Attorney General’s Office laid out as critical changes needed before commissioners approve the merger.
The all stock trade of the two companies is valued at $67 billion and would create the largest regulated utility in the country. In pre-filed testimony for the case, SCC staff suggested that the companies had not met their burden of ensuring “that adequate service to the public at just and reasonable rates will not be impaired or jeopardized by granting the prayer of the petition” as mandated by the Utility Transfers Act. 
Dominion CEO Bob Blue stated in his rebuttal testimony that “while the standard does not have a “net benefit” demonstration requirement as may exist in other jurisdictions, I likewise believe that it is not a weak burden. It is a reasonable one. Virginia…allows these types of corporate transactions to go forward so long as there is assurance that the essential functions of the public utility will not be compromised.”
The two companies were given a slate of policy changes that both the SCC and Attorney General’s staff said would create reasonable protections for ratepayers in the case of bankruptcy, protect people currently employed by Dominion, and ensure rates won’t spike if the merger is approved. Dominion and NextEra accepted a number of the recommendations, but did reject some or offered alternatives.
Chief among the recommendations that the petitioners rejected were the suggestions to freeze rates for three years, to keep the current staffing for 10 years, and to only implement separating finances and resources, otherwise known as ring-fencing, in specific “trigger events.” The companies also rejected the suggestion that if the combined companies would downsize their current Virginia offices they would need SCC approval. 
The two companies did accept several recommendations that ranged from allowing Dominion to be the entity to determine how it will meet load growth demand. Staff also recommended that “(Dominion) establish a bankruptcy remote Special Purpose Entity (SPE) to serve as (Dominion’s) direct parent and sole shareholder,” in the case of bankruptcy. This means a separate legal entity would insulate the parent company from financial risk by taking over resources, projects, or shares of the company. However, the joint petitioners amended that proposal to mean the separate entity would be assigned those resources only in specific cases, such as a rating drop of two credit ratings.
The discrepancy between what was rejected or amended by the company from the list will be litigated in the full case before the commissioners. 
The overall proposal for the deal remains the same heading into the evidentiary portion of the case which includes: maintaining a bill credit of about $10 a month for the average residential customer, keeping current staff numbers for five years, building an office building in downtown Richmond, and investments in weatherization and workforce development.
The list of recommendations made by Gov. Abigail Spanberger and Chief Energy Officer Jospehus Allmond were not addressed in the rebuttal by the two companies. Some of their requests included increasing the monthly bill credit to $29, freezing base rates for six years, and formulating a new separate subsidiary for building zero-carbon energy generation to serve large data centers. 
Blue stated in his rebuttal that some of those issues do not belong in the merger case and should be litigated in a biennial rate case for the company instead — and should not be a basis for the merger to be denied by the commissioners.
“The proposed transfer of control is not due to be denied simply because various Intervenors’ “wish lists,” which I alluded to above, have not been satisfied,” Blue’s Nov. 2 testimony reads. “While those “asks” may be (and in many cases have been) a permissible proposal in a biennial review or other Commission proceeding, they simply are not a basis to assert that the Joint Petitioners have failed to demonstrate that NextEra’s combination with Dominion will not impair or jeopardize adequate service at just and reasonable rates.”
Public testimony will begin on Nov. 5 both telephonically and in person. The evidentiary portion of the case is set to begin on Nov. 17.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Amid national blue wave, Idaho Democrats could gain a handful of legislative seats
description: As the nation experienced a blue wave in congressional midterm elections across the country, Democrats in Idaho could pick up a handful of seats in the state Legislature.  Based on unofficial, incomplete election results early Wednesday, the potential gains position Democrats to boost their 15-member presence in the 105-member state Legislature by four seats[...]
text:
Voters cast their ballots in the general election on Nov. 3, 2026, at Borah High School in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)As the nation experienced a blue wave in congressional midterm elections across the country, Democrats in Idaho could pick up a handful of seats in the state Legislature. 
Based on unofficial, incomplete election results early Wednesday, the potential gains position Democrats to boost their 15-member presence in the 105-member state Legislature by four seats. With very few precincts counted as of 3 a.m. Wednesday in Bannock County, Democrats were leading in two other races in eastern Idaho’s Legislative District 29.
But in a deep red state, Republicans still hold supermajority control of both chambers of the Legislature — and maintain control of all seven statewide constitutional offices and the state’s four congressional seats.
The results of Tuesday’s election, published by the Secretary of State’s Office, are unofficial and preliminary. Results will not become official until they are certified by the Idaho State Board of Canvassers on Nov. 24. 
In Tuesday’s election, Democrats were on track to have success in flipping seats in the state’s few competitive legislative districts in west Boise, the Magic Valley in central Idaho, and potentially Pocatello in eastern Idaho.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
 Where Democrats could pick up seats in the Idaho Legislature

Idaho voters reject abortion rights initiative Prop 1

In west Boise’s Legislative District 15, Democrats appeared on track to pick up two seats. 

Democratic challenger Jae Etchart was leading over Republican incumbent Rep. Dori Healey for one of the district’s seats in the Idaho House of Representatives. Etchart had 53% of the vote, or about 10,700 votes, over Healey’s nearly 47% of the vote, or roughly 9,500 votes. That’s based on unofficial results at 2:24 a.m. with 20 precincts reporting.
In the district’s state Senate race, former Boise School District Trustee Nancy Gregory was leading against Republican candidate Desi Burbank for a seat left vacant by Republican Sen. Codi Galloway, who did not seek reelection. Gregory led with roughly 54% of the vote, or about 11,000 votes, over Galloway’s nearly 46% of the vote, or almost 9,300 votes. That’s based on results at 2:24 a.m. with 20 precincts fully reporting.
The district’s lone incumbent Democrat, Rep. Steve Berch, was in a healthy lead against Republican challenger Steve Keyser. Berch led with nearly 58% of the vote, or more than 11,800 votes, over Keyser’s 42% of the vote, or nearly 8,600 votes. That’s based on results at 2:24 a.m. with 20 precincts reporting.

In central Idaho’s Legislative District 26, Democrats were also leading in two legislative races that would represent progressive pickups if results hold. 

In the district’s House Seat A race, Democratic candidate Anita Janis was leading incumbent Rep. Mike Pohanka, R-Jerome. Janis had received 49.5% of the vote, or nearly 8,100 votes, and Pohanka had received almost 45% of the vote, or roughly 3,400 votes. A third candidate, independent Bella Schiffler, had received 5.5% of the vote, or about 900 votes. That’s based on results at 2:24 a.m. with 5 of 33 precincts fully reporting, and 27 precincts partially reporting. 
In the district’s House Seat B race, Democratic candidate Kevin Marsh was leading Republican Lyle Johnstone in the race for the vacant legislative seat held by retiring Rep. Jack Nelsen, R-Jerome. Marsh had received 57.8% of the votes, or 9,350 votes, over Johnstone’s 42% of the votes, or about 6,800 votes. That’s based on results at 2:24 a.m. with 5 of 33 precincts fully reporting, and 27 precincts partially reporting. 
In the district’s Senate race, incumbent Democratic Sen. Ron Taylor, R-Hailey, was leading Republican challenger Bryan Hyde and independent Shaila Tate. Taylor had 55% of the vote, or nearly 9,000 votes, compared to Hyde’s nearly 39.6% of the vote, or about 6,450 votes. Tate received nearly 5.3% of the vote, or about 860 votes. That’s based on results at 2:24 a.m. with 5 of 33 precincts fully reporting, and 27 precincts partially reporting. 

In Bannock County’s Legislative District 29, Democrats led two legislative races:

In a House race there, incumbent Republican Rep. Dustin Manwaring was trailing in his re-election bid to Democratic challenger Mary Shea. Shea led with nearly 62.3% of the vote, or almost 3,300 votes, over Manwaring’s 37.7% of the vote, or almost 2,000 votes. That’s based on results at 2:24 a.m. with none of 31 precincts fully reporting. 
In the district’s other House race, former Democratic state Rep. Nate Roberts was leading over Republican challenger Jennifer Miles. Roberts had 61.75% of the vote, or 3,266 votes, over Miles’s 38.25% of the vote, or 2,023 votes. That’s based on results at 2:24 a.m. with none of 31 precincts fully reporting.  The seat is held by Republican Rep. Tanya Burgoyne, who lost her primary election.

A North Idaho race to unseat a Republican state lawmaker was tight.
In Legislative District 6, incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Foreman faced a close challenge from Democratic opponent Robin Weldy. Foreman led with 57.4% of the vote, or about 14,600 votes, to Weldy’s nearly 42.6% of the vote, or nearly 10,800 votes. That’s based on unofficial results at 2:24 a.m. with seven of 54 precincts fully reporting.
Poll workers help voters cast their ballots in the general election on Nov. 3, 2026, at Borah High School in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)
 After a primary that ousted nine incumbent Republicans, the Legislature is set to change

Regardless of Tuesday’s election results, the Legislature was set for significant turnover. After a primary election where nine Republican incumbents lost, fifteen legislative races had no incumbents running for re-election. 
But a few of them had familiar faces running, such as Scott Herndon, a former Republican state senator who was leading in his bid to regain his seat in Legislative District 1, and Roberts, a Democrat who previously held his legislative seat in Pocatello. Herndon led with 57.27% of the vote, or 14,838 votes, over independent Steve Johnson, who had 42.73% of the vote, or 11,069 votes. That’s based on unofficial results at 2:43 a.m. with 34 precincts fully reporting.
One House seat, in District 24, had a Republican vying for the office for the first time, Chance Requa, who faced no challenger. 
Thirteen incumbents — largely Republicans — ran unopposed in the general election, including Republican Reps. Jordan Redman, from Coeur d’Alene, and Rep. John Shirts, from Weiser who just became Idaho’s top federal prosecutor.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Return of the trifecta: Michigan Democrats reclaim full control of state government
description: DETROIT — Michigan will have a new Democratic Party majority in the state Legislature after Tuesday’s election, according to unofficial returns. The party and its top incumbent officials in the state Legislature declared victory on Wednesday morning after it became clear that they would have a new trifecta, as Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson was […]
text:
State Rep. Ranjeev Puri (D-Canton) steps to the podium in Detroit with Senate Majority Leader Winnie Brinks (D-Grand Rapids) after Democrats retook the majority on the Michigan House and retained control of the Senate. Puri is likely to be the next Speaker of the House, while Brinks was elected at lieutenant governor earlier Wednesday, Nov. 4, 2026. (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance)DETROIT — Michigan will have a new Democratic Party majority in the state Legislature after Tuesday’s election, according to unofficial returns.
The party and its top incumbent officials in the state Legislature declared victory on Wednesday morning after it became clear that they would have a new trifecta, as Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson was also elected to the office of governor on Nov. 3.
As of early Wednesday morning, Michigan Democrats have secured 19 seats in the state Senate while the Republicans secured 14 seats, the Associated Press reported.
The AP also reported that the Democrats secured 51 seats in the state House, compared to the 43 seats that GOP secured on election night.
Those unofficial returns show that the balance of power in the legislative branch will return to where it was in 2023 and 2024, when the party held both chambers of the Legislature and the governor’s office.
Democrats’ main priority was protecting their state Senate majority and preventing it from falling into Republican hands in a demonstrably favorable year for the party. Democrats also aimed to capitalize on their momentum in 2026 to retake the House.
With a Democratic wave cresting in Michigan on Tuesday, the party achieved both victories.
“Since winning back the majority for the first time in nearly 40 years in 2022, we knew we would have a new mission in 2026 – defending and expanding that majority. And today, Senate Democrats have done just that,” Senate Majority Leader Winnie Brinks said in a statement. “This newly expanded majority will allow Senate Democrats to reach new heights.”
Brinks will join Benson in the executive office as the lieutenant governor-elect. In that role, she will still retain a top leadership position in the chamber she is now leaving, as the lieutenant governor is the president of the Senate and breaks ties, if needed.
“I look forward to working with our new caucus as Lieutenant Governor to drive costs down and wages up throughout this great state,” Brinks said.
Senate Majority Leader Winnie Brinks (D-Grand Rapids) steps to the podium in Detroit after Democrats retook the majority on the Michigan House and retained control of the Senate. Puri is likely to be the next Speaker of the House, while Brinks was elected at lieutenant governor earlier Wednesday, Nov. 4, 2026. (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance)
Michigan Senate Democrats must also choose a new leader going into the 2027 legislative session.
Current House Minority Leader Ranjeev Puri (D-Canton) is the likely pick for House speaker now that Democrats have also taken back the state House. He will replace current Republican House Speaker Matt Hall (R-Richland Township), if elected to the position by his caucus as expected.
Puri said what Michigan experienced on Tuesday night was not a “blue wave,” but a “tsunami.”
“For the last two years, I served in the Michigan House as a minority leader, and I watched the institution be driven into the ground,” Puri said at the Democrats’ watch party in Detroit. “I watched healthcare be ripped away from our sick. I watched food and benefits taken away from our needy, and I watched tax cuts to billionaire corporations. The people of Michigan spoke up tonight and said that they’ve had enough, and they delivered a House Democratic majority.”
Puri will become the first Indian American and Sikh speaker of the Michigan House.
State Rep. Ranjeev Puri (D-Canton) speaks to supporters in Detroit after Democrats retook the majority on the Michigan House and retained control of the Senate. Puri is likely to be the next Speaker of the House. Nov. 4, 2026. (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance)
Following the momentous win, state Rep. Jason Morgan (D-Ann Arbor), said the victory was the culmination of intense focus on the issues of affordability and the damage that they said the Republicans had done to their gains during the last Democratic trifecta. Morgan added that Republicans in Washington, D.C. also had a hand to play in creating the environment that made 2026 such a favorable year for the opposing party.
“The hard work for us was just showing the people of Michigan that we will actually make their lives better. We will make their lives more affordable. We will create opportunity, and we will make our state better for the long term,” Morgan told Michigan Advance. “And I believe that people saw that, and they also looked at Washington D.C. and realized that everything Donald Trump was doing was hurting their daily life. 
Morgan said he was “extremely excited about what we can do over the next years to make life better for every Michigander.”
Brinks on Wednesday morning said that the Senate’s top priority would be to push for a Michigan Voting Rights Act, which they have had in mind through the period of divided government from 2025 and 2026.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Morgan said that the House’s first priority was to focus on making life more affordable for for Michiganders — at the rest would fall into place. That includes potential Freedom of Information Act reform to extend the law to the governor’s office and the Legislature, and other accountability issues. But affordability would come first.
“Government transparency, ethics, and accountability, those are critical … but the most important thing that I’ve heard consistently from voters while knocking doors all over the state of Michigan is that people need life to be more affordable,” Morgan said. “That’s what we’re focused on as priority number one.”
Michigan Democratic Party Chair Curtis Hertel said that, “when Democrats are in power, we make progress for working people.”
“With our last trifecta, we restored workers’ rights, cut taxes for families, fed kids at school, and lifted tens of thousands of children out of poverty,” Hertel said in a statement. “Now, we will continue that critical work. With the leadership of Governor-Elect Benson and the future leaders of the state legislature, we will keep building toward a Michigan where every person has a chance to thrive.”

text:
Indiana Lt. Gov. Micah Beckwith preaches at Faith Baptist Church in Elkhart on July 26, 2026. (Photo from public livestream)In the run-up to this week’s midterm election, it was not uncommon to hear Indiana political figures attack Muslims. 
Indiana Attorney General Todd Rokita announced his office would investigate two groups for connections to terrorism. The groups, the Council on American-Islamic Relations and Students for Justice in Palestine, support Muslim causes.
Lt. Gov. Micah Beckwith called Islam a “demonic death cult” and suggested public calls to prayer should be banned in Indiana.
A relatively new political group, Save Heritage Indiana, promoted mass deportation at an August rally hosted in Fishers, Indiana. 
Our local news media have important choices to make when xenophobic speech peppers our information feeds. Journalists must decide what to report on and how to add context. Simply repeating shocking and offensive claims like these runs the risk of giving them more power than they deserve. 
I looked closely at how Indy newsrooms performed when they faced these decisions. It’s clear that the editors and reporters serving the Indy market are making thoughtful choices as they approach statements that are designed to promote fear and stoke hate. Local news outlets also reported on the community response to these ideas, which included condemnation and counter demonstrations. This added context is key in providing news consumers a complete view of their own communities.
Politicians “other” foreign-born citizens to cast them as un-American
Xenophobic speech, or speech that seeks to vilify, humiliate, dehumanize and incite hatred against people based on their perceived foreignness, nationality or migrant status tends to ramp up during election season. These recent attacks – on immigrants, Muslims, and other non-Christian faiths – are designed to make groups of people appear un-American.

In early October, Indiana Attorney General Todd Rokita singled out the Council on American-Islamic Relations and the National Students for Justice in Palestine, suggesting that they should be investigated as “terrorist supporters.” 

Beckwith took aim at Muslims this summer, saying that the Muslim call to prayer, or Adhan, was “not part of American culture or history.” He has also agreed with Rokita on designating CAIR and NSJP as terrorist organizations, and on the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks, he shared a video of a person falling from a burning World Trade Center Tower and said in the caption: “Never forget what Islam wants to do to the American way of life.” The Indiana Citizen reported on his comments, which he posted on X.
(Courtesy banner)
The Indiana Citizen also reported on Beckwith’s May 21 appearance on an online conservative talk show during which he said that people should be given “permission to hate again.” 

In its story, the Citizen sought comment from Muslim civil rights advocates and U.S. Rep. André Carson, who represents Indiana’s 7th Congressional District and is one of a handful of Muslims in Congress. 

For the most part, Indianapolis media is doing a good job of not amplifying these comments and instead bringing context and showing the community’s reaction.

IndyStar assigned its coverage to its First Amendment issues reporter, Cate Charron, whose role is to report on threats to the five freedoms — speech, religion, press, assembly and petition. She aptly tackled the topic by reporting on the “politician-led Islamophobic surge” of policies and remarks, reaction from Indy’s Muslim community, expert testimony on the historical intent of the Founding Fathers, and data from reports and Pew Research Center studies on Islamophobic incidents and discrimination.

IndyStar also published opinion columns condemning the attacks, including by staff columnist James Briggs and these guest columnists. 

Both columns described how Beckwith was flat-out wrong about the U.S. Constitution and suggested that his provocative claims are more about his own political ambitions. The Constitution prohibits the government from establishing a national religion and protects all faiths from government interference. All of this context gives readers a chance to analyze the merits and intent of Beckwith’s speech, as well as Rokita’s investigation. 

The Indiana Citizen, which is a nonpartisan platform aimed at increasing Hoosiers’ civic engagement, did additional reporting. Journalist Sydney Byerly examined the history of Muslims in the United States. In doing so, she refuted Beckwith’s assertion that Muslims are not a part of America’s history and culture. 

TV news station WTHR fact-checked Beckwith’s claims that the Muslim call to prayer is publicly broadcast outside Indiana mosques to the community. Public radio station WFYI talked to pro-Palestine groups about their reaction to Attorney General Rokita’s call for the investigation, which they referred to as a “publicity stunt.”

This reporting by Indy news outlets gave the public context and added depth to stories, instead of merely repeating the statements of elected officials.
The press is getting wise to the way political speech can manipulate and misinform 
In her 2025 book on “otherness,” Angie Chuang examines how the news media have historically responded to political efforts to exclude some Americans from “fully belonging to American identity.” 

Throughout the book, “American Otherness in Journalism: News Media Representations of Identity and Belonging,” Chuang describes example after example where journalists have failed to identify the racist behavior of politicians in the name of “objectivity.” By contrast, when I asked her to look at how Indy news media have performed over the past couple of months, she was pleased.
“The local reporting on anti-Muslim attacks in Indianapolis, particularly the Lieutenant Governor’s Islamophobic speech and its potential incitement of other hateful acts, has been robust and contextualized,” Chuang told me. “Unlike the news events I highlight in my book, in which Trump’s insertion of racially coded statements hijacked the narratives of events like the Unite the Right rally in Charlottesville, the coverage in Indianapolis has prioritized the voices of community members and organizations like CAIR—and called out Beckwith’s hateful statements for what they are.”

Chuang notes in her book that the press sometimes struggle to identify political speech and actions as racist or discriminatory. In fact, at times newsrooms can sugarcoat racist ideology with more palatable descriptions, like “alt-right,” a term that took hold during President Donald Trump’s first term. 

In 2017 the Associated Press advised newsrooms to avoid using the term “alt-right,” saying that it was “a euphemism to disguise racist aims.” Instead, the AP advised newsrooms to use specific wording and terms like “racist,” “white supremacist” or “neo-Nazi” when describing the Unite the Right Charlottesville protestors. 

By not precisely describing the ideology behind Unite the Right as racist, Chuang argued that news media enabled Trump “to underplay the role of race and racism” of the rally.
Lack of context and depth of reporting harms communities
There is a danger in simply repeating racist political rhetoric and hoping that the audience will recognize it for what it is. It makes the statements sound normal. 

I’m grateful that Indy journalists don’t do this. Instead, they fully examine each argument, exposing the weaknesses and flaws. 

The people who are most harmed by these attacks tell me they appreciate that journalism has evolved. And they want even more of it.

The Indy Public Editor is a grant-funded pilot project run by the Poynter Institute. This column is edited by Kelly McBride and copy edited by Lauren Klinger. The project is managed by Nicole Slaughter Graham with support from Amaris Castillo.

“I would like the press’ curiosity and more of their input,” said Jordan Esparza-Kelley, communications coordinator for CAIR-Chicago, one of the organizations that state Attorney General Rokita wants to investigate. “Don’t be a stenographer for these politicians. Like I said, follow the thread; let’s ask ‘why’ a couple more times.”

Rupal Thanawala, president of the Asian American Alliance in Indy, also notes the danger of amplifying hate speech without adding analysis: “I think giving people that media platform is also wrong. You want to talk, just talk to the wall and be done with it. But, we are giving them the mouthpiece.”
Thanawala is worried that the rhetoric already emboldens people to act out and say offensive things to the community through the comments section on news stories’ social media posts.

“Everybody’s so uncomfortable and everybody’s even worried about backlash,” she said. 

Just this past September, community fears led leadership at Alhuda Islamic Center of Indiana in Fishers to add security and police patrols to the mosque during daily prayers. 

When powerful politicians attack Muslims or immigrants, the press have many choices about how to respond. There are consequences for the community that come with how the media respond. When the news media handle inflammatory rhetoric poorly, they risk spreading hate and inspiring violence. When they ignore it, they risk misrepresenting politicians and further marginalizing minority groups.

When they handle it responsibly, their reporting equips people with the knowledge they need to see through fear-mongering and manipulation. We should expect journalists to give this value-added perspective to their reporting. It is refreshing to see Indy newsrooms get it right in this situation.

name: Nevada Current
title: Lombardo falls to Ford as Republicans nationwide suffer historically brutal election
description: Nevada Democratic Attorney General Aaron Ford squashed the reelection bid of Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo, part of a drubbing suffered by Republicans nationwide. The Associated Press called the governor’s race for Ford shorty before 2 a.m. Wednesday. The Lombardo camp’s massive fundraising edge combined with incumbency gave the appearance early that Ford mig[...]
text:
Aaron Ford addressing a Democratic watch party Tuesday night. (Photo: April Corbin Girnus/Nevada Current)Nevada Democratic Attorney General Aaron Ford squashed the reelection bid of Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo, part of a drubbing suffered by Republicans nationwide.
The Associated Press called the governor’s race for Ford shorty before 2 a.m. Wednesday.
The Lombardo camp’s massive fundraising edge combined with incumbency gave the appearance early that Ford might have trouble mounting a competitive race. But as has been the case for Republicans up and down the ballot nationwide in 2026, the Republican governor’s ties with Trump effectively saddled him with Trump’s economy.
Early in the year Lombardo’s campaign and its related political action committees, which heavily outraised and outspent the Ford effort from the start, spent lavishly on ads labeling the Democrat “High-flying Aaron Ford” for multiple trips Ford took in his capacity as attorney general. 
More recently, the Lombardo camp criticized Ford for placing the clemency bid of a Nevada inmate, who was convicted of voluntary manslaughter in the shooting death of a pregnant woman and her baby, on the state Pardons Board agenda, portraying the move as Ford coddling a criminal. 
But Ford’s campaign and its related PACs took advantage of the voter displeasure with Trump economic policies, frequently tying Lombardo to Trump, connections that were often accompanied by the word “affordability.”
Those dots were easier for Ford to connect after Lombardo appeared next to Trump on stage in Las Vegas in August and defended the president’s penchant for “taking care of his billionaire friends.”
Both campaigns scrambled to navigate the public backlash to data centers. Both candidates had a history of supporting state tax breaks to attract data centers, positions both of them would revise in an effort to match public sentiment.
Ford addressed supporters at a Democratic watch party in downtown Las Vegas late Tuesday night, saying that the election “was about whether working people in Nevada have a government that works for them” and “whether Nevadans, not billionaires, not special interests, not politicians, decide what happens in the Silver State.”
His speech was interrupted by the release of early election results showing him ahead of Lombardo.
Earlier in the evening, Lombardo had addressed his own supporters and attempted to strike an upbeat tone.
“There’s a lot of things going on in the world, right, out of our control,” Lombardo said. “Who gives a crap what’s going on in the rest of the world? We are worried about Nevada, right? I think we’ve done a great job. I think we’ve done a fantastic job.”
Shortly after making those remarks, Lombardo left the building, a supporter telling the crowd that no results in the race were expected until Wednesday morning.
Arguably the most memorable line uttered by a Nevada politician in 2026 was “I’m Joe Lombardo,” declared by Lombardo in a traffic stop that was caught on camera, and in which the officer who had pulled Lombardo over for failing to stop at a red light let the former sheriff go without a ticket.
This article has been updated with comments from Ford.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Harris holds on against spirited challenge from Schwartz; other House members cruise to wins
description: Republican Rep. Andy Harris held off a surprisingly tough challenge from Democrat Dan Scwhartz in the 1st District Tuesday, the closest House race in Maryland where the other seven incumbents in the state's delegation all cruised to reelection wins.
text:
U.S. Rep. Andy Harris, R-1st District, at a candidate forum in Cambridge, Maryland, on Oct. 13, 2026. (Photo by Danielle J. Brown/Maryland Matters)Dan Schwartz, the Democrat challenging Republican Rep. Andy Harris, opposed the question on congressional redistricting that was on this year’s ballot, arguing that the best way for Democrats to take back the 1st District is not through redistricting but to win it “fair and square.”
That win did not come Tuesday.
In unofficial returns, Harris had 150,615 votes to 119,088 for Schwartz. That’s a 55% to 44% advantage over Schwartz, a first-time candidate who quit his job to run full time in the deep-red district that covers the Eastern Shore and spills over into eastern Baltimore County.
As of 11:15 pm, Schwartz had not conceded, waiting for official outlets to call the race. But when he addressed supporters shortly after 10 p.m., he acknowledged that the numbers weren’t “looking great.”
But with early projections indicated Democratic control of the U.S. House of Representatives, Schwartz said Republicans like Harris will have less influence in Congress.
“Big wins all over this country and in some places we didn’t expect,” he said at Cult Classic Brewery on Kent Island. “We don’t know what’s going to happen here — numbers aren’t looking great — but if Andy Harris pulls this thing, he’s going to run a diminished Freedom Caucus that will have no power in Washington.”
The Associated Press called the race for Harris shortly before midnight.
Dan Schwartz talks with supporters ahead of election results at Cult Classic Brewery on Kent Island. (Photo by Danielle J. Brown/Maryland Matters)
In a state where Democrats have a 2-1 registration advantage over Republicans, District 1 is a GOP stronghold. Republicans account for 42% of registered voters in the district to 32% for Democrats and the remaining 26% unaffiliated or members of smaller parties, according to state data from mid-October.
Harris, running for his ninth term, has been unbeatable in the district, with his closest challenge coming in 2022, when he won by 11 percentage points. Because of that, Democrats have been pushing Question 3, a proposed constitutional amendment that would remove most restrictions on drawing congressional maps — and make it easier to target Harris.
Question 3 was widely unpopular on the Eastern Shore, with Schwartz saying he would vote against it. But it was winning by a comfortable 60%-40% margin in early returns Tuesday.
Because it is a safe seat, the 1st District is usually an afterthought in Maryland elections. But it got unusual attention because of the focus on Question 3 — easily the highest profile issue on the ballot this year — and a viral video of Harris berating a student reporter after the only debate in the campaign last month.
For other members of Maryland’s congressional delegation, the election was essentially settled in the Democratic primary, which chose nominees to run in districts that are largely safe for Democrats.
Maryland Del. Adrian Boafo, D-Prince George’s, emerged from a field of 24 Democrats in the 5th District Democratic primary in June to win the nomination to succeed longtime Rep. Steny Hoyer, a Democrat who’s held the seat for more than 40 years. Boafo, a former aide to Hoyer, was helped enormously by an endorsement from the retiring Hoyer.
Boafo had a comfortable 68%-31% lead Republican nominee Chris Chaffee in unofficial results in the 5th District.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
The other high-profile primary race was in the 6th District, where freshman Rep. April McClain Delaney held off a multimillion-dollar challenge from businessman David Trone, who held the seat before making an unsuccessful run for the U.S. Senate nomination in 2024. Trone, who has a history of self-funding, poured at least $25 million into the primary, and McClain Delaney loaned her campaign at least $7.2 million on her way to a 44% to 37% primary win over Trone.
On Tuesday, McClain Delaney held a 56%-41% lead over Republican nominee Robin Ficker, a perennial candidate. Green Party nominee Moshe Y. Landman had just under 3% of the vote in the unofficial results.
In other House races:
District 2: Freshman Rep. Johnny “Johnny O” Olszewski Jr., D-2nd District, the former Baltimore County executive, was leading with 62% of the vote over Republican nominee Dave Wallace, a businessman.
District 3: Rep. Sarah Elfreth, D-3rd District, the third freshman in the Maryland delegation, also appeared headed to reelection, grabbing 65% of the vote over the GOP nominee, Air Force veteran Berney Flowers.
District 4: Rep. Glenn Ivey, D-4th District, appears headed to a third term, with 89% of the vote to 6% for perennial Republican candidate George McDermott and 4.5% for Green Party nominee Sam Husseini.
District 7: Rep. Kweisi Mfume, D-7th District, who served five terms in the House in the last century, appears on his way to reelection to a fifth term again, with 83% of votes to Republican Scott M. Collier’s 17% votes with all precincts reporting.
District 8: Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-8th District, appears to be heading for a sixth term in the Democrat-safe Montgomery County seat. In a rematch from 2024 against Republican Cheryl Riley and Green Party candidate Nancy Wallace, Raskin had 83% of the vote to Riley’s 16% and Wallace’s 1% .

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Opinion: US Sen. Roger Marshall lost his seat long before Kansans kicked him out. He just didn’t realize it.
description: U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall officially lost his seat to the Rev. Adam Hamilton on Tuesday night as part of a resounding repudiation of Republicans across the United States. But Marshall actually lost that seat 20 months ago, when he clashed with everyday Kansans at a March 1 town hall meeting in Oakley. Facing tough questions […]
text:
Republican U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall delivers his concession speech alongside his wife, Laina, at the Nov. 3, 2026, GOP watch party in Wichita. (Photo by Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall officially lost his seat to the Rev. Adam Hamilton on Tuesday night as part of a resounding repudiation of Republicans across the United States.
But Marshall actually lost that seat 20 months ago, when he clashed with everyday Kansans at a March 1 town hall meeting in Oakley.
Facing tough questions from an audience fed up with President Donald Trump’s Department Of Government Efficiency, Marshall left the meeting early. For the rest of 2025 and all this year, he avoided further public events. Oh, he would show up for photo opportunities, but Marshall had apparently had it with his constituents. (Town halls, he claimed, could lead to violence.)
That wasn’t all, though. Marshall’s apparatchiks apparently felt the need to blame those who made their boss look bad.
His chief of staff Brent Robertson, blasted the following vitriolic statement:
“Democrat operatives who couldn’t place Oakley, Kansas on a map before today sabotaged a local town hall — even still, Senator Marshall stayed and answered every question that was asked for 45 minutes. Real Kansans overwhelmingly support President Trump’s DOGE initiative, shrinking the size of the federal government, and firing career bureaucrats. Local Oakley citizens had no clue who these people were and were embarrassed by the behavior. Senator Marshall is to be commended for staying as long as he did.”
“Real Kansans,” huh?
I think “real Kansans” had something to say on Tuesday to night to Marshall — and to Robertson, whom the senator still managed to thank in his deer-in-the-headlights concession speech.
That’s the kind of rhetoric made all too familiar by Trump and his Make America Great Again Acolytes. Marshall arrived in Washington, D.C., alongside Trump, and he seldom let a millimeter of daylight shine between him and the president.
That slavish devotion earned him favor. Not for nothing did Trump visit Kansas twice in recent weeks. Not for nothing did Vice President JD Vance make two stops of his own.
But this attachment to the man and his style left Marshall flat-footed when it came to actually interacting with — actually listening to — his constituents. Those who dared to question Republican policies were, as Robertson claimed, embarrassing. The real, true, conservative Kansans would support the senator no matter what.
Marshall genuinely seemed to be confused!
“I’ve never seen such hatred coming out of people’s mouths at President Trump and his agenda,” he said last year. “I don’t know why people are upset that the borders are safe and the price of gas and groceries are down and the economy’s looking better.”
He still seemed bewildered last night, admitting in his concession speech that “I don’t have any answers.”
Real Kansans had an answer. And that was voting for a new senator — one who might actually stop and listen.
Clay Wirestone is Kansas Reflector opinion editor. His first book, “Opinionated: Kansas Journalists Who Proved Why Commentary Matters — Then and Now,” was published in September 2026 by the University Press of Kansas. Through its opinion section, Kansas Reflector works to amplify the voices of people who are affected by public policies or excluded from public debate.
