title: In Michigan’s 10th Congressional District, Hines claims victory
description: In the early hours Wednesday morning, former prosecutor Christina Hines announced her victory over Army National Guard veteran Michael Bouchard Jr. While the Associated Press had not officially called the race when Hines declared victory at 3:52 a.m., unofficial results at 4:01 a.m. showed Hines with a 5.5 percentage point lead over her Republican opponent. [...]
text:
Former prosecutor and Democratic congressional candidate Christina Hines in Rochester, Oct. 28, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance)In the early hours Wednesday morning, former prosecutor Christina Hines announced her victory over Army National Guard veteran Michael Bouchard Jr.
While the Associated Press had not officially called the race when Hines declared victory at 3:52 a.m., unofficial results at 4:01 a.m. showed Hines with a 5.5 percentage point lead over her Republican opponent.
The district is currently held by U.S. Rep. John James (R-Shelby Township), who opted against seeking reelection to run for governor, which was unsuccessful, as he lost to Democrat Jocelyn Benson. Encompassing southern Macomb County, the district also includes Rochester and Rochester Hills in eastern Oakland County. 
A former prosecutor in Wayne and Washtenaw counties, Hines focused her campaign on bringing down costs, emphasizing that as a mother of three and a Macomb county resident, she understood the hardship families in the district are facing.
“This campaign started with a simple truth: that working families in our district are sick of being left behind by corrupt politicians in Washington and deserve someone who will actually put their needs first,” Hines said in a statement. “Over the last 18 months, I have been moved by the thousands of people who have told me their stories, shared their struggles, and demanded more from their leaders. Your words have stayed with me throughout this entire campaign and I will carry them with me to Washington.”
If confirmed, Hines’ win would be at least the second GOP-held congressional district in Michigan to flip to Democratic control. Democrat William Lawrence declared victory in the 7th Congressional District early Wednesday over incumbent Republican Congressman Tom Barrett of Charlotte.
In a statement shared to social media, Bouchard congratulated Hines on her victory, offering his assistance as she steps into the role of the 10th Congressional district’s next representative. 
“I got into this race because I love this country,” Bouchard said. “America is the greatest country that has ever existed and election results going to the other party, do not diminish America’s shine. I will endeavor to ensure we remain that beacon on the hill throughout the world. Our promise is not political, it is in you. It is in freedom and our democracy.”
This is a developing story and will be updated as more information becomes available.

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Ohio Democrats flip two US Congressional districts. Delegation stands at 7-7 with 1 race undecided
description: All five Ohio Democratic incumbents held their U.S. Congressional district seats Tuesday while Democratic challengers have flipped at least two and maybe three Republican seats. According to Associated Press projections, Ohio Democratic candidate Brian Poindexter won Ohio’s 7th Congressional district, beating incumbent Republican U.S. Rep. Max Miller, and De[...]
text:
The U.S. Capitol on March 3, 2026. (Photo by Jennifer Shutt/States Newsroom)All five Ohio Democratic incumbents held their U.S. Congressional district seats Tuesday while Democratic challengers have flipped at least two and maybe three Republican seats.
According to Associated Press projections, Ohio Democratic candidate Brian Poindexter won Ohio’s 7th Congressional district, beating incumbent Republican U.S. Rep. Max Miller, and Democrat Don Leonard defeated Ohio Republican incumbent U.S. Rep. Mike Carey. 
Decision Desk HQ projects that Democratic challenger Kristina Knickerbocker also defeated Ohio Republican incumbent U.S. Rep. Mike Turner, while the DCCC congratulated her and she gave a victory speech, the Dayton Daily News reports.
As of 4 a.m., Knickerbocker had 149,024 votes, according to unofficial results from the Ohio Secretary of State’s website, compared to 144,086 for Turner, a difference of 4,938 votes.
Results will remain unofficial until they are certified by election officials later this month.
Nationally, Democratic candidates flipped control of the U.S. House in the Midterm elections Tuesday night.
Miller, who has served in Congress since 2023, is under investigation by the House Ethics Committee for allegations he “may have engaged in domestic violence and abuse or illegal drug use.”
Allegations of domestic violence against Miller caused several prominent Republicans to call for his resignation over the summer — a movement led by Miller’s ex-father-in-law, U.S. Sen. Bernie Moreno. Miller denies the allegations against him.
Ohio’s 15th Congressional district
Ohio Democrat Don Leonard beat incumbent Ohio Republican U.S. Rep. Mike Carey for Ohio’s 15th Congressional district.
Leonard previously taught regional and city planning at Ohio State University and Carey has served in Congress since 2021.
Ohio’s 1st Congressional District 
Democratic U.S. Rep. Greg Landsman won Ohio’s 1st Congressional District, beating Republican Eric Conroy, the Associated Press projected Tuesday.
Landsman has served in Congress since 2023. 
Ohio’s 13th District 
Ohio Democratic U.S. Rep. Emilia Sykes won Ohio’s 13 Congressional District, beating Republican Carey Coleman, the Associated Press projected Tuesday.
Sykes has served in Congress since 2023. 
“It is my great honor to be re-elected to represent my community,” she said in a statement. 
“I will continue to fight to bring down costs and keep more money in your pockets, address the corruption in Washington that is making politicians rich while Ohioans suffer, and overturn policies that are stripping healthcare and food benefits away from kids and the elderly.”
Ohio’s 10th Congressional District
Ohio’s 10th Congressional district race between incumbent Ohio Republican U.S. Rep. Mike Turner and Democrat Kristina Knickerbocker was too close to call late Tuesday night. 
Turner has served in Congress since 2003, and Knickerbocker is an U.S. Air Force Veteran and oncology nurse practitioner.
Ohio’s 9th Congressional District
Ohio’s 9th Congressional District race between incumbent Democratic U.S. Rep. Marcy Kaptur and Republican Derek Merrin was too close to call as of late Tuesday night. 
Kaptur has represented Ohio’s 9th congressional district since 1983 — making her the longest-serving woman in congressional history.
Merrin served four terms as an Ohio state representative for the Toledo district from 2016 to 2025. He lost a close race to Kaptur during the 2024 election.
Ohio’s remaining congressional districts
Republican Ohio U.S. Reps. Dave Taylor, Jim Jordan, Bob Latta, Michael Rulli, Warren Davidson, Troy Balderson, and David Joyce all won their races. 
Democratic Ohio U.S. Reps. Joyce Beatty and Shontel Brown both won their races.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: GOP solicitor wins job as SC’s attorney general
description: David Stumbo will become the state's top prosecutor after 14 years of overseeing criminal cases in rural counties.
text:
Eighth Circuit Solicitor David Stumbo officially launched his bid for South Carolina attorney general Tuesday, Sept. 16, 2025. (Photo provided by Stumbo campaign)COLUMBIA — South Carolina’s 8th Circuit solicitor will become the state’s top prosecutor after winning election Tuesday.
David Stumbo, the chief prosecutor for four rural counties, had 52% of the votes over Democrat Richard Hricik, a Mount Pleasant attorney, according to the State Election Commission’s unofficial results.
Stumbo has spent the past 14 years overseeing cases in Abbeville, Greenwood, Laurens and Newberry counties. He will replace Alan Wilson, who left the office he’s held since January 2011 to run for governor.
As attorney general, Stumbo will become responsible for representing the state in all appeals of criminal convictions, including death penalty cases. The office also oversees the State Grand Jury and task forces dedicated to prosecuting human trafficking and child sexual abuse cases.
The retrial of Alex Murdaugh, whose conviction of killing his wife and son was overturned earlier this year, also falls to the attorney general’s office.
Before being elected solicitor, Stumbo worked in private practice. During a three-way GOP primary, he billed himself as the most conservative candidate.
Hricik ran unopposed to become the Democratic nominee. He signed up because no other Democrats had, he previously told the Daily Gazette.
Originally from Ohio, Hricik moved to South Carolina in 1997 to teach at Charleston Southern University before starting his law firm. He still teaches part-time at the Charleston School of Law and online for his alma mater, William & Mary Law School.
Hricik, who accepted no donations and took out a single loan for his campaign, primarily represents people in personal injury and wrongful death cases. He is not a criminal prosecutor, though he said that shouldn’t matter.
The last Democrat elected attorney general was Thomas Medlock, who held the office from 1983 until 1995.

Nevada’s three Democratic U.S. representatives all sailing to reelection


By Hugh Jackson - Wednesday November 4, 2026 12:53 am





Nevada’s three Democratic congressional incumbents were each on their way to comfortable victories over their Republican challengers early Wednesday morning.
Dina Titus, the dean of Nevada’s congressional delegation, was seeking her seventh term as the representative for Nevada’s 1st Congressional District, which includes the Las Vegas Strip. She was running against Republican state Sen. Carrie Buck. As of early Wednesday morning with 65% of the vote reporting, Titus led Buck with with 60% of the vote compared to Bucks 37%. 
Susie Lee was reelected to a fifth term in Nevada’s 3rd Congressional District. Since the district, which covers Henderson and edges of the Las Vegas metro area up to Summerlin, was formed following the 2000 Census, it has been perennially viewed as the most competitive House district in the state. But a Republican hasn’t won it since 2014. She defeated Republican video game composer Marty O’Donnell. As of early Wednesday morning Lee had declared victory with 68% of the vote to O’Donnell’s 38%.
Steven Horsford was reelected to his fifth consecutive term in Nevada’s 4th Congressional District. The lion’s share of registered voters in the district live in northern portions of Clark County, including Mesquite. The district also covers Nye, Esmaralda, and Mineral counties, along with portions of Churchill, Lyon, and Lincoln counties. Horsford also served as the district’s congressman after the 2012 election, the first since the district was created after the 2010 Census. He was defeated in 2014, but won the seat back in 2018. Horsford defeated Republican Lincoln County businessman and rancher Cody Whipple. The Associated Press called the race in Horsford’s favor shortly before 1 a.m. Wednesday morning.

Nevadans enshrine abortion rights in state constitution


By April Corbin Girnus -  12:18 am





Nevadans once again voted to enshrine the right to an abortion in the state constitution.
Nevadans For Reproductive Freedom declared victory on election night, shortly after polls closed.
Early returns showed Question 6 at around 63%, about the same percentage of support it saw two years ago when it was first approved by voters. It had to pass the second time to be adopted in the state constitution.
Abortion in Nevada is currently legal up to 24 weeks after the start of the pregnancy and after 24 weeks if a physician believes the pregnant person’s life or health is at risk. Those protections were put in place via a citizen-driven referendum passed by voters in 1990 and would require a direct vote of the people to change.
That is a fairly high bar to overcome, but given the onslaught of attacks on reproductive rights across the nation under the Trump administration, advocates want the bar to be even higher.









As Republicans get pummeled nationwide, Lombardo urges supporters to remain upbeat


By Jeniffer Solis - Tuesday November 3, 2026 10:11 pm





As Democrats swept gubernatorial races across the country and Nevada waited for results, Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo struck a positive note at his Election Night watch party. Long lines in Washoe and Clark counties meant no election results had been released in Nevada more than three hours after polls closed, but Lombardo reassured Republican voters that Nevada would buck the national blue wave.
“I want everybody to stay upbeat. I want everybody to stay positive,” Lombardo said in brief remarks at the election party in Las Vegas. 
Lombardo recalled his 2022 victory, when his race against former Gov. Steve Sisolak was not called until three days after the election. 
“I don’t want anybody in this room to have their head down currently, okay? Because we have no idea what’s going to happen,” Lombardo said. “If you remember, four years ago, we had our heads down, and what happened? We won, right? We won.”
Lombardo acknowledged the blue wave across the country, but said he believed Nevada would buck the national trend.
“We are going to be the unique state in this national picture because we’re going to be successful here in a couple hours,” Lombardo said. 
“There’s a lot of things going on in the world, right, out of our control,” Lombardo said. “Who gives a crap what’s going on in the rest of the world? We are worried about Nevada, right? I think we’ve done a great job. I think we’ve done a fantastic job.”
Lombardo told voters not to be discouraged by early vote counts in Nevada, noting that Republicans turn out in larger numbers on Election Day which are counted later. 
“I don’t want anybody to lose any enthusiasm when the first dump comes…and it doesn’t look good, right? It doesn’t matter. Republicans come late to the process. They come late to the process, and we still have no idea what the nonpartisans are going to do in this endeavor, and I anticipate success. I anticipate success, and I want everybody to remain upbeat,” Lombardo said. 
By 10:45 p.m., Lombardo had left the building. Dr. Tony Alamo announced that Lombardo left because there was nothing to report Tuesday night and results likely would not be known until Wednesday or later.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Handful of legislative seats up for grabs, but General Assembly overall unchanged
description: Sen. Shaneka Henson (D-Anne Arundel) survived a bitter campaign that split the party, to become the first elected Black senator from Anne Arundel County and Democrats appear to have picked up two seats in the House of Delegates in legislative races Tuesday.
text:
Democratic candidate Chuck Cook gives a few remarks Tuesday night during an Election Night watch party with Anne Arundel County Democrats. Cook unseated Republican Del. Stuart Schmidt Jr. in District 33B, one of two Democratic pickups in the House Tuesday. (Photo by William J. Ford/Maryland Matters)The balance of power in the Maryland General Assembly will not change as a result of Tuesday’s voting, with Democrats all but guaranteed to maintain firm control of both the Senate and House of Delegates.
But a handful of seats were in play from both parties, in both the House and Senate. While no senator was unseated, despite come close calls, it appears the Democrats may have picked up two seats in the House.
The most contentious was the race for the District 30 Senate seat, where Sen. Shaneka Henson (D-Anne Arundel) faced a robust challenge from former Anne Arundel County Councilmember Jessica Haire, a Republican. With all 42 precincts reporting, however, Henson had about 57% of the vote to Haire’s 43%.
“Obviously, I’m disappointed to see that voters could be so deceived by a campaign of such obvious lies and deception,” Haire said in a text message Tuesday night. “I’m grateful to all the volunteers across party lines who put so much time and effort into our campaign — a campaign based on ideas to strengthen our communities!”
Henson, who was appointed to the seat in 2025, was running to become the first elected Black senator from Anne Arundel County. But her potentially historic campaign was dogged by attacks from some fellow Democrats, who were unhappy with Henson’s votes against some reproductive rights and LGBTQ+ rights bills.
Haire, meanwhile, challenged Henson’s ethics, pointing to a letter from the Joint Committee on Legislative Ethics from 2024, when Henson was still in the House. It urged Henson to apologize to the public and to legislative leaders for her involvement as a delegate in funding requests for a religious organization to which she belonged.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
Still, Haire faced an uphill climb in a district Democrats have held for at least 44 years. And the Maryland Democratic Senate Caucus Committee sought to keep it what way, sending a reported $488,399.10 of in-kind contributions to Henson’s campaign.
Democrats also dredged up an incident from 2022, when Haire ran unsuccessfully for county executive. She was criticized then for contracting with Rory McShane, a Republican consultant whose firm was associated with the neo-fascist and racist group The Proud Boys. Haire said at that time she ended her association with the group when she found out about the connection.
Two other Anne Arundel races were in the spotlight, including the race for the District 31 seat left open by the retirement of Sen. Bryan Simonaire (R-Anne Arundel). Republicans appeared to be on their way to retaining that seat, however. With all 46 precincts reporting, Del. Nic Kipke (R-Anne Arundel), who was elected to the House in 2006 and who served as minority leader between 2013 to 2021, had 57% of the vote to Democrat Brent Mulrooney’s 43%.
The same cannot be said for District 33B, where first-term Del. Stuart Schmidt (R-Anne Arundel) was unseated by Democratic challenger Chuck Cook, a senior adviser to Maryland Secretary of Housing and Community Development Jake Day. Schmidt, part of the informal “basketball caucus” of members who play during the 90-day session, had 48% of the vote to Cook’s 52% in unofficial results.
In District 38B on the Lower Shore, which Vice President Kamala Harris (D) carried by 7 points in the 2024 presidential election, another Republican freshman appears to have been ousted. Del. Barry Beauchamp (R-Lower Shore) was trailing Wicomico County Councilmember Josh Hastings, a Democrat, with all 21 precincts reporting. Hastings had 58% of the vote to Beauchamp’s 42%.
A national political entity called the American Future PAC, which is connected to the internet gaming industry and supports Democratic legislative candidates, spent at least $202,630 to defeat Beauchamp and an additional $38,687 to boost Hastings.
Democrats appeared to hold on to an open seat in Southern Maryland. District 29B, a Democratic seat in St. Mary’s County sandwiched between two Republican subdistricts, was widely seen as a possible pickup for the GOP when Del. Brian Crosby (D-St. Mary’s) said he would not run for reelection. But Democrat Adrianne Mathis cruised to a comfortable 57-43 win over Republican BJ Hall in the district.
And Republicans managed to hold onto two Senate seats, one open and one occupied by what was thought to be an entrenched incumbent.
In District 42, Democrats were not able to capitalize on the retirement of Sen. Chris West (R-Baltimore and Carroll), with GOP nominee Kevin Ford, a local business owner, getting 58% of the final vote to 42% for Democrat Stephanie Popescu, a public school teacher.
And in one of the closest legislative races of the night, Sen. William G. “Bill” Folden (R-Frederick) was able to come from behind in early returns and notch a 52-48 win over Democratic challenger Lara Westdorp to retain seat that covers most of Frederick County outside the city of Frederick.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen wins reelection
description: Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen won reelection Tuesday in a winding year that gave a Republican gubernatorial candidate their toughest run since the 1990s.
text:
Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen thanks supporters after declaring victory in his reelection bid to lead the Cornhusker State on Nov. 4, 2026, in Lincoln, Nebraska. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen won reelection Tuesday in a winding year that gave a Republican gubernatorial candidate their toughest run since the 1990s.
The Associated Press called the race just before 2 a.m. Wednesday. Pillen, who became governor in 2023, defeated former Democratic state Sen. Lynne Walz by more than 48,000 votes, with 50.4% of the vote to Walz’s 42.6%. He defied a blue wave nationwide while still running in a closer race than in 2022, when he won by a margin of 23%.
Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen talks with reporters after declaring victory in his reelection bid to lead the Cornhusker State on Nov. 4, 2026, in Lincoln, Nebraska. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Former state Sen. Brett Lindstrom of the new America First Party earned 4.4% of the vote. Rick Beard of the Legal Marijuana NOW Party earned 2.6% of the vote.
“You chose a leader, not a politician, and I will never forget that trust,” Pillen told a cheering crowd in Lincoln.
Walz had hoped to repeat the 1990 upset where Ben Nelson unseated then-Gov. Kay Orr by just 4,030 votes, a 0.7% margin.
National pundits, pollsters and figures, including President Donald Trump, Vice President JD Vance and Democratic Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, had not initially placed Nebraska on the map. But over time, Pillen and Walz faced a closer-than-expected matchup. 
The Republican Governors Association had given Pillen $2 million in the last month, and the Democratic Governors Association, which Beshear chairs, gave Walz more than $500,000.


‘Everything is trending upward’
Pillen credited his victory with bringing people together, including those who had never been to similar political events before.
Lt. Gov. Joe Kelly speaks at an election night watch party for Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen, his running mate, on Nov. 3, 2026, in Lincoln, Nebraska. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Throughout the night, Lt. Gov. Joe Kelly, who agreed to join Pillen for another four years, repeatedly took the stage to encourage voters to be patient and to say that the campaign remained confident the night would end their way.
Just before 8:30 p.m., Kelly said the results, which had Walz with a widening margin above Pillen, were still “very encouraging, very positive” and above campaign projections. Around 10:20 p.m., Kelly said things still looked good even if some national races “might be startling” to some of the “good Republicans in this room.”
“We have now gone ahead in the race. Everything is trending upward, and the bar is still open,” Kelly said just before 11:15 p.m. to a cheering crowd and hoots and hollers.
Pillen during his victory speech acknowledged “a lot of tough stuff” going on nationwide. He said it was important that conservatives unite and build relationships so they can run government like a business. He credited Nebraskans for his win.
“When Nebraska wins, we all win,” Pillen said.
‘We’re all still Nebraskans’
Walz told a crowd of supporters in Omaha just before 11 p.m. that when she set out across Nebraska to listen about a year ago, from everywhere she went she heard the same thing: “Government is not working for people anymore. That’s the spirit I am asking for tonight.” 
Democratic gubernatorial candidate Lynne Walz of Fremont, a former state senator, addresses supporters during her election night watch party on Nov. 3, 2026, in Omaha, Nebraska. (Photo by Chase Zagurski for Nebraska Examiner)
She told supporters to go home, get rest and when every vote is in, “we’ll have more to say.”
“Be patient. Be kind to each other,” Walz said. “And to the folks on the other side who are waiting up, just like we are: tomorrow morning, we’re all still Nebraskans.” 
Pillen said he hadn’t heard from Walz before he took the stage shortly after 12:10 a.m.
A ‘challenging’ election year
The race had also been complicated by the late addition of Lindstrom, an ex-Republican who had initially run for Nebraska’s 2nd Congressional District until suspending his campaign in January. He later dropped his party registration and ran petitions this summer to become a nonpartisan gubernatorial candidate. His campaign got ensnared in a web of allegedly fraudulent signature collections that initially took down a separate Lincoln petition campaign. 
In total, seven out-of-state circulators were arrested in the case.
The 2026 candidates for Nebraska governor and their respective running mate. Top left is incumbent Republican Gov. Jim Pillen and Lt. Gov. Joe Kelly, top right is former Democratic state Sen. Lynne Walz and Ben Steffen, bottom left is Legal Marijuana NOW’s Rick Beard and Keenya Barnes and bottom right is former state Sen. Brett Lindstrom and Michael Picard of the America First Party. (Photos courtesy of the candidates/campaigns | Nebraska Capitol photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Lindstrom found a “pirate ship” he was looking for to revive his bid: the America First Party, one of two new political parties that emerged this summer, too. Some Republicans had feared the label could mislead voters and pull votes from the GOP.
The new Nebraska Working People Party did not run a gubernatorial candidate.
In addition, a new political action committee had popped up in the last month to support Beard, labeling him the “real progressive” in the race. The main funder of the new PAC, Nebraskans for Cannabis Future, had previously only donated to Pillen and other Republican-aligned groups.
Beard had told the Nebraska Examiner last week that he suspected the move was meant to hurt Walz and that he had no knowledge of or involvement in the latest PAC effort.
Pillen said 2026 presented a “challenging year” for the state, “especially for all of us here that still hold high expectations for how government should work.”
“The political garbage, the sham parties, the dirty tricks, the dark stunts that were unprecedented, a historic amount of dark liberal money poured into Nebraska from outside of our state, trying to divide us and manipulate us,” Pillen said. “I am very, very, very proud that our campaign avoided all that garbage.”
An agricultural governor
Pillen had faced pushback over how his handling of Nebraska’s budget and how state agencies under his purview handled an emergency no-bid contract with a bioeconomy consultant and lobbyist whom Pillen was familiar with. On Friday, law enforcement said Pillen’s office “was not implicated in any criminal wrongdoing.”
Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen, center, with first lady Suzanne Pillen, poses with his reelection campaign team on Nov. 4, 2026, in Lincoln, Nebraska, shortly after declaring victory. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
The governor had told the Examiner last week that Republicans and commonsense Nebraskans knew  how “critical” the election was, at all levels, “to keep far-left radicals from gaining a foothold in our state.”
Walz had faced criticism over her familial ties to Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz — a distant cousin through marriage — and over legislative votes Pillen said went against Nebraska values.
The former lawmaker had pitched a different message, seeking to travel the state, hear Nebraskans’ ideas and bring people together with kindness. She often leaned into the biblical instruction to “love thy neighbor” regardless of who they are or what differences they may have. 
Lindstrom had pitched a middle-ground political alternative, while Beard leaned into a state-run medical cannabis program and a desire to get money out of politics.
The next legislative session
State Sen. Mike Jacobson of North Platte speaks at an election night watch party for Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen on Nov. 3, 2026, in Lincoln, Nebraska. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
State Sen. Mike Jacobson of North Platte took the stage before 9 p.m. and repeatedly praised Pillen and Kelly for their record, particularly around agriculture.
“People ask what he knows about agriculture. He’s forgotten more about agriculture than his opponents know,” Jacobson said of Pillen.
“I can tell you that I am feel privileged to work with him because, having also grown up on a farm and having still stayed involved in farming, it’s not an easy path forward, and he understands that.”
Jacobson appears to be a frontrunner to be the next speaker of the Legislature; state Sen. Brad von Gillern of Elkhorn, the current Revenue Committee chair, continues to trail his challenger, Cindy Maxwell-Ostdiek of Omaha.
A teary-eyed Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen watches as his grandchildren speak in favor of his reelection bid during an election night watch party on Nov. 3, 2026, in Lincoln, Nebraska. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Pillen heads into an increasingly tough legislative session where Republicans appear likely to lose their 33-seat supermajority (the number needed to overcome filibusters, such as on party-line votes). The state also faces a projected $1.2 billion deficit through mid-2029. 
Pillen has denied that Nebraska faces a “budget crisis” as all three of his opponents had said, and he said it’s time that Nebraskans shed their political “sweaters.” The governor has long said his priorities are “kids, taxes, agriculture and values,” and he’s said finding a “solution” to Nebraska’s property tax crisis will remain top of mind the next four years, as will balancing the budget. The legislative session begins Jan. 6.
‘You keep working’
Pillen’s seven grandchildren took the stage just before 10 p.m. Each read from a slip of paper thanking their grandpa and “our Jim.” The children said they’ve seen just how much Pillen loves Nebraska and how seriously he takes the responsibility.
One said that the governor didn’t work to win an election but that he believes in his work. A teary-eyed Pillen watched from the crowd.
“That might be the biggest lesson he has taught us: When you are given an opportunity, you don’t just sit back and enjoy it,” one of Pillen’s grandchildren said. “You go to work, and even after you succeed, you keep working. You work harder. You try to leave things better than you found them. And if there is more work to be done, you don’t ever quit. We are so proud of you.”
Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen hugs one of his granddaughters during his election night watch party on Nov. 3, 2026, in Lincoln, Nebraska. Seven of his grandchildren took the stage to praise their grandfather. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Nebraska Examiner senior reporter Cindy Gonzalez and UNO student journalist Chase Zagurski contributed to this report.

text:
Democratic Congressional candidate William Lawrence announces his final push to mobilize voters as he stands outside of U.S. Rep. Tom Barrett's (R-Charlotte) former office in Lansing on Oct. 27, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance)In a tight race for Michigan’s politically purple 7th Congressional District, Lansing area political organizer William Lawrence has declared himself the victor against incumbent Congressman Tom Barrett (R-Charlotte).
Lawrence’s campaign shared their proclamation of victory at 2:49 a.m., though the Associated Press had not yet called the race. 
While Barrett was leading through most of the evening and into the night, Lawrence’s campaign began making gains in the wee hours of the morning. 
Barrett departed his election night watch party at 2:39 a.m. without speaking to the media. At 2:40 a.m., Lawrence was leading by 2.2 percentage points.
“We built an unprecedented movement here in Mid-Michigan, powered by thousands of volunteers, and we showed that you can beat an incumbent Republican without taking a dime of corporate PAC money,” Lawrence said in a statement. “We united people from every corner of this district – and found common ground in opposition to war and data centers, and in favor of good housing and healthcare, social security, jobs and education. Our people-powered movement took on the richest and most powerful people in the world, and we won.”
Prior to his run for Congress, Lawrence had co-founded the Sunrise Movement, a youth-led climate action group which helped shape President Joe Biden’s climate policies. Lawrence also advocated for housing reforms as a founder of the MI Rent is Too Damn High Coalition.
If official results declare him the victor, Lawrence will serve as the U.S. representative for the state’s 7th Congressional District, which includes Clinton, Shiawassee, Ingham and Livingston counties and parts of Eaton, Genesee and Oakland counties.
Prior to Barrett winning the seat in 2024, the district had been represented by Democrat Elissa Slotkin, who ran for and won a U.S. Senate seat that same year.

name: Washington State Standard
title: Washington voters backing initiative to keep transgender girls out of girls’ sports
description: The only state ballot measure that will likely pass in Tuesday’s election is the one that would prohibit transgender girls from competing in K-12 girls’ sports. It’s a major loss for the progressive left. As of Tuesday night, Initiative 638 leads with nearly 57% of the total votes counted thus far.  “To every female athlete […]
text:
Ahnaleigh Wilson, 17, of Eastmont High School, center, and Frances Staudt, 17, of Tumwater High School, right, speak with the media about Initiative 638 at Let’s Go Washington’s election night watch party Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026, in Redmond, Wash. (Photo by Ryan Berry/Washington State Standard)The only state ballot measure that will likely pass in Tuesday’s election is the one that would prohibit transgender girls from competing in K-12 girls’ sports. It’s a major loss for the progressive left.
As of Tuesday night, Initiative 638 leads with nearly 57% of the total votes counted thus far. 
“To every female athlete who wondered whether her voice mattered: tonight, Washington heard you,” Brian Heywood, founder of the political organization backing the measure Let’s Go Washington, said in a statement. “Five years from now, I hope girl athletes don’t know this fight took place, because that will mean that boys know their place is not in girls’ sports.”
Members of the opposition campaign, No Hate in Washington State, called out Let’s Go Washington and Heywood, a hedge fund manager, for using the measure as a means to “distract from the real issues.”
“We look forward to the ballot returns over the next few days and are hopeful that Washington voters will also reject I-638, the attempt to scapegoat a handful of vulnerable trans children,” Libby Watson, campaign manager, said in a statement. 
Approximately 10 Washington students have disclosed being transgender to the Washington Interscholastic Activities Association, but the initiative would affect all girls who wish to participate in K-12 sports. 
As it is, the measure requires students in K-12 sports to undergo a physical examination. The measure adds a requirement for medical professionals during those exams: verifying a student’s sex assigned at birth. 
School boards, or other school governing entities, would be required to create the rules on what sex verification would look like. It would rely on “one or more” of the following methods: “the student’s reproductive anatomy, genetic makeup, or normal endogenously produced testosterone levels,” according to the initiative.
Some school districts have backed the measure. Earlier this year, the Mead School Board unanimously passed a resolution supporting the initiative.
“We’ve consistently recognized the inherent biological and physiological differences that give male athletes a competitive advantage in most sports,” said Michael Cannon, school board director. “This has been an issue that has always had majority support.”

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Pete Ricketts claims victory over Dan Osborn in US Senate race still being counted Tuesday night
description: Nebraska Sen. Pete Ricketts declares victory over registered nonpartisan Dan Osborn in the bitter Senate race.
text:
Nebraska Sen. Pete Ricketts declaring victory in senate race in Omaha on Nov, 4. 2026. (Juan Salinas II/Nebraska Examiner)OMAHA — Nebraska Republican U.S. Sen. Pete Ricketts declared victory in his reelection bid over registered nonpartisan Dan Osborn Tuesday, even as results from the race were still coming in. 
As of 1:30 a.m. Wednesday, a winner of the race had not been called by The Associated Press, and only 78 percent of votes had been counted, but Ricketts held a 34,000-vote lead over Osborn, 49.6% to 44.4%, respectively.
As it stood based on unofficial results available early Wednesday, Osborn, a former union leader, appeared to have improved on his performance compared to his 2024 challenge of U.S. Sen. Deb Fischer, which he lost by 6 percentage points.
“The Democrat Social America found out tonight that socialism does not work in Nebraska,” Ricketts told the audience at his watch party. “They came here with their fake labels, their fake candidates, thinking that they could just come in here and fool Nebraskans … They had nothing but contempt for us, but we showed them that Nebraskans will not be fooled by the socialists.” 
The Ricketts campaign and national Republicans have spent a year and a half painting Dan Osborn as a Democrat, despite his nonpartisan status. The race has heavily focused on Osborn’s independence, as Osborn often had to play defense against controversies amplified by Ricketts and Republicans, including multiple audio leaks. 
Ricketts thanked his campaign for tracking Dan Osborn, as they were “able to expose” Osborn as “the fraud that he is.”
“While we’re not going to go into the names of the people who were there tracking him, they played a pivotal role in this,” Ricketts said.
The Senate race has had twists and turns, with lawsuits, candidates and new political parties facing allegations of being spoilers, and candidates suspending their campaigns to support Osborn. The race had a lot of mudslinging and negative ads. 
Though Osborn told the audience at his Omaha watch party Tuesday night that things didn’t look good for his campaign, he said there was a “5% chance” he could win, depending on the next batch of votes in more urban areas of the state. 
“Depending on how it turns out … I would just urge Sen. Ricketts to take care of the Coalition of the people here tonight,” Osborn said. “We might not have won this election tonight; we must continue to demand better from our government.”

Osborn added, “Unfortunately, money won.” 
Candidates running with two new political parties received a combined total of 6 percent of the vote, according to preliminary results early Wednesday morning. Working People Party’s Robin Richards received 2.6 percent of the vote, while America First Party’s Chuck Conboy got 1.2 percent of the vote.
Legal Marijuana NOW’s Mike Marvin, who suspended his campaign but was still on the ballot, got 2.2 percent of the vote.
If Ricketts is declared the winner, he will serve his first full six-year term in the U.S. Senate. The former two-time governor easily beat Omaha Democrat Preston Love Jr. in a 2024 special election to finish the final two years of former U.S. Sen. Ben Sasse, R-Neb., who resigned to lead the University of Florida.

Rep. Jack Bergman (L) and Callie Barr (R) | Office/courtesy photosDefying Democrats’ efforts to rally support in northern Michigan, U.S. Rep. Jack Bergman (R-Watersmeet) has won reelection in the state’s 1st Congressional District, defeating Traverse City attorney Callie Barr.
When the Associated Press called the race at 1:09 a.m., unofficial results showed Bergman had won 53.2% of the vote while Barr received 44.7%.
Bergman will serve his sixth term as Representative for Michigan’s 1st Congressional district, which includes the entirety of the state’s upper peninsula, and the northern portion of the lower peninsula.
Bergman and Barr previously faced off in 2024. Bergman prevailed, leading Barr by more than 20% of the vote.
In the lead-up to election night Bergman faced repeated criticisms for his participation in a taxpayer-funded program reimbursing representatives’ housing and meal expenses and was the subject of a Detroit News investigation which found he was living in a Washington, D.C. home sold to his daughter by campaign supporters, though Bergman’s campaign maintains he paid fair market value for his rent on the home “and is in full compliance with House Ethics.”
However, the negative press and attacks from his opponents were not enough to flip the northern Michigan district. 
In a statement shared to Facebook, Bergman thanked residents of the 1st Congressional for placing their trust in him once again.
“While tonight was a tough night for Republicans, there is no shortage of work ahead of us to get our Nation back on track,” Bergman said. “Americans are rightly frustrated with inflation, reckless government spending, and the direction of our Nation. They deserve leaders who will listen, stand firm, and deliver results.”

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Idaho voters reject abortion rights initiative Prop 1
description: Idaho voters rejected Proposition 1, the ballot initiative that sought to legalize abortion in the state up to fetal viability or in emergencies, and would have enumerated rights to other types of reproductive healthcare. The Associated Press called the race at 12:35 a.m. early Wednesday.  The voter-led ballot initiative received 44.6% of the vote, or […]
text:
A "Stop Prop 1" sign leans up against the wall during an election night watch party on Nov. 3, 2026, held at the Boise Centre in Downtown Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)Idaho voters rejected Proposition 1, the ballot initiative that sought to legalize abortion in the state up to fetal viability or in emergencies, and would have enumerated rights to other types of reproductive healthcare. The Associated Press called the race at 12:35 a.m. early Wednesday. 
The voter-led ballot initiative received 44.6% of the vote, or 268,311 votes in the 2026 general election, as of 12:41 a.m. on Wednesday. More than 55% voted against it. The proposition needed a simple majority of votes to pass. 
Idahoans United for Women and Families, the group formed to author and support the initiative, conceded that it did not pass in a press release sent just after 12:20 a.m. 
Idahoans United for Women and Families Executive Director Melanie Folwell speaks about Proposition 1 at the Oct. 17, 2026, No Kings rally at the Idaho Capitol in Boise. (Photo by Jim Max for the Idaho Capital Sun)
“This is a tremendous, frankly gutting, loss, especially for the women, families, and physicians of Idaho,” Melanie Folwell, executive director of Idahoans United for Women and Families, said in a press release. “We will see more doctors leave the state as a result of this election. And, most urgently, women will continue to suffer needlessly under one of the most cruel abortion bans in the nation.”
Election officials were still counting ballots early into Wednesday morning. Idaho’s election results do not become official until they are certified by the Idaho State Board of Canvassers, which meets Nov. 24.
The initiative would’ve repealed Idaho’s strict abortion ban, which outlaws nearly all abortions, except to prevent the death of the mother or in cases of rape and incest in the first trimester when a police report is provided. Idaho’s ban carries felony prison sentences and licensing penalties for doctors who perform abortions outside of the exemptions, as well as possible civil lawsuits for a minimum of $20,000. 
Opponents of the ballot initiative argue that it is the state’s prerogative to protect fetuses’ lives, and that Idaho’s exemptions are sufficient to protect the mother’s life. The Idaho GOP, the Salt Lake City-based Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, and Roman Catholic Diocese of Boise strongly opposed the initiative. Opponents formed a group called Stop Prop 1 in response to the proposed initiative. 
“The people of Idaho have spoken,” Stop Prop 1 communications director Mary Strow said in a press release. “They saw through the smokescreen of deception and barrage of out-of-state funded ads that sought to rewrite our laws and reshape our values. Idaho is and will always be a state that values life and protects the unborn.”
Idahoans United for Women and Families formed in 2024 to explore ways to restore abortion access in the state in response to the U.S. Supreme Court overturning Roe v. Wade in 2022, which triggered Idaho’s bans. 
Idahoans United in July turned in nearly 110,000 signatures to the Idaho Secretary of State’s Office to qualify for the 2026 general election ballot. In Idaho, to qualify for the general election, supporters must collect signatures from at least 6% of the registered voters statewide and from at least 6% of the registered voters in at least 18 of Idaho’s 35 legislative districts. To achieve the 6% statewide total, supporters needed 70,725 verified signatures. 
Its supporters argued Idaho’s laws were overreaching and potentially dangerous for pregnant women, and led to the state losing OB-GYNs. The petition to get the initiative on the ballot included signatures from Idaho voters across party lines. 
Since the U.S. Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade in 2022, voters in 17 states have voted on ballot measures regarding abortion, KFF reported. Since 2022, ballot measures to restore access to abortion failed in three states — Florida, Nebraska and South Dakota. Similar measures passed in 11 other states, and measures to curtail abortion access failed in three states. 
The campaigns for and against the proposed ballot measure collected millions of dollars. Idahoans United for Women and Families political action committee collected more than $5.8 million and spent more than $2 million to support the measure, state campaign finance data showed as of Tuesday. 
Opponents of the initiative formed the PAC Too Extreme for Idaho, which raised nearly $4.7 million and spent more than $4.2 million, campaign finance reporting showed Tuesday.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Banks, Miguez to meet in 6th District runoff
description: Chauna Banks, a Black Democrat, finished first Tuesday in the 6th Congressional District primary, a district that had to be redrawn after the U.S. Supreme Court ruled its previous version was a racial gerrymander.
text:
Former East Baton Rouge Parish Metro Council member Chauna Banks, left, will meet state Sen. Blake Miguez in a runoff for the 6th Congressional District. (Louisiana Legislature photos)Chauna Banks, a Black Democrat, finished first Tuesday in the 6th Congressional District primary, a district that had to be redrawn after the U.S. Supreme Court ruled its previous version was a racial gerrymander.
Only 665 votes separated Banks from the second-place finisher, state Sen. Blake Miguez, who as a Republican will be heavily favored defeat her in a Dec. 12 runoff election.
Miguez finished less than 1,000 votes ahead of the candidate in third place, state Sen. Rick Edmonds, R-Baton Rouge. in a contest with nearly 262,000 total votes cast. It wasn’t until after more than 90% of ballots had been counted that Banks, a former East Baton Rouge Parish Metro Council member, surged from third place to the lead.
Banks and Miguez are vying to replace U.S. Rep. Cleo Fields, a Black Democrat from Baton Rouge who decided not to seek reelection after the Supreme Court’s decision in Callais v. Louisiana. The plaintiffs, a group of white voters, challenged the lines of the 6th District that state lawmakers had drawn in 2024, successfully arguing that the underlying Voting Rights Act principles were unconstitutional.
The 2024 map gave Louisiana a second Black-majority district out of its six U.S. House seats to account for the 31% of state voters who are Black.
The Callais decision crumpled up that map and led Gov. Jeff Landry to revise the state’s election calendar so the Republican-led legislature could update Louisiana’s congressional district lines. The governor’s executive order halted the May 15 party primaries for U.S. House seats after absentee ballots had already been filed.
Eight other states also reconfigured their U.S. House maps in response to the Callais decision.
In addition to running in a predominantly white and Republican district, Banks will also face a distinct campaign finance disadvantage against Miguez. He raised more than $7.7 million for his congressional bid, according to Federal Elections Commission data. 
The agency had no records on Banks’ campaign.
The runoff winner will represent a district that includes much of East Baton Rouge Parish and portions of Ascension, Assumption, Iberville, Lafourche, Pointe Coupee, St. John the Baptist, St. Martin and West Baton Rouge parishes.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Eli Savit wins attorney general election, keeping state’s top law enforcement role with Democrats
description: DETROIT – Democratic nominee and Washtenaw County Prosecutor Eli Savit has won the race for Michigan Attorney General, defeating Republican nominee Eaton County Prosecutor Doug Lloyd by a margin of 51.8% to 45.5% as of 2:28 a.m. Wednesday, the time at which the Associated Press called the race.  “This campaign started 18 months ago, fueled […]
text:
Eli Savit shares a victory speech, declaring his win for Michigan Attorney General at the Michigan Democratic Party's election night event in the early hours of Nov. 4, 2026. (Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance)DETROIT – Democratic nominee and Washtenaw County Prosecutor Eli Savit has won the race for Michigan Attorney General, defeating Republican nominee Eaton County Prosecutor Doug Lloyd by a margin of 51.8% to 45.5% as of 2:28 a.m. Wednesday, the time at which the Associated Press called the race. 
“This campaign started 18 months ago, fueled by conversations on college campuses and with young people who were concerned about their future and who wanted an attorney general who would represent the people and not the powerful, and that is what we are going to get to work on doing from day one. to stand,” Savit said in a speech while declaring victory.
According to unofficial results, third-party candidates Jason Dye of the Libertarian Party, John Ludtke of the U.S. Taxpayers Party, Jeff Polonowski of the Green Party and Doug Dern of the Natural Law Party received 1.3%, 0.7%, 0.5% and 0.3% of the vote respectively.
Savit declared victory around 2 a.m. on Wednesday at the election watch party hosted by the state Democratic Party. He will succeed current Attorney General Dana Nessel, who is term-limited.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Late October polling showed Savit with around a 5-point lead over Lloyd, but also showed about 15% of those polled were undecided. With neither candidate benefiting from significantly more name recognition than his opponent, Savit benefited from an overall good environment for Democratic candidates in 2026. 
Savit, a progressive candidate, was nominated by the Michigan Democratic Party at their April convention, defeating a more moderate candidate in Oakland County Prosecutor Karen McDonald. He will succeed the term-limited current attorney general, Dana Nessel, who endorsed Savit.
Savit’s win completes the Democratic sweep of Michigan’s executive offices, following wins by Jocelyn Benson for governor and Garlin Gilchrist for secretary of state. The Democratic Party has maintained a hold on those offices since 2018.
It also follows a declaration of victory by Democrats in the Michigan House and Senate, setting up another trifecta similar to what the party enjoyed after the 2022 election, but before Republicans won the House in 2024.
This is a developing story and will be updated as more information becomes available.

text:
(Photo by Getty Images)Iowa’s state treasurer race was a dead heat between Republican incumbent Roby Smith and Democratic challenger John Norwood early Wednesday, with most of the vote counted.
Roby Smith, the Iowa state treasurer, is a Republican from Davenport. (Photo courtesy of the Iowa Legislature)
Smith had 50.5% of the vote to 49.5% percent for Norwood in unofficial results, with 96% of precincts reporting.
Democrat for Iowa Treasurer John Norwood, Aug. 15, 2026 at the Des Moines Register Political Soapbox. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch)
Tuesday’s election saw Democrats sweep most of the top-of-ticket races, including the governor’s office, U.S. Senate, and three of the four congressional districts. Republican incumbents were leading in several of the other statewide races, including secretary of agriculture and secretary of state, but the open state auditor’s race was neck-and-neck and Republican Attorney General Brenna Bird was trailing Democrat Nate Willems.
Smith, a former banker and former state senator from Davenport, touted breaking an “all-time record” in collecting interest on the state’s $10 million “idle money fund,” as well as managing record assets under the $7.25 billion ISAVE 529 program. He said his priority would be to expand on those results.
Norwood, a financial advisor who ran for Iowa secretary of agriculture in 2022, has said if elected, he would prioritize investing state dollars at local banks and credit unions, and supporting new crop markets. He also said he believed the Iowa Public Employees’ Retirement System (IPERS) CEO should be selected by a board rather than by the governor.
