name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Voters reject measure that could have triggered repeal of Medicaid expansion in South Dakota
authors: Seth Tupper, Meghan O'Brien, Makenzie Huber
description: South Dakota voters rejected a ballot question Tuesday that could have triggered a repeal of the state’s Medicaid expansion mandate. When The Associated Press called the race at 1:22 a.m. Wednesday, 56% of the votes were against Amendment I and 44% were in favor. Over 80% of votes statewide had been counted. Amendment I would […]
text:
The federal government's website for Medicaid, a health insurance program for people with low incomes. (Photo by South Dakota Searchlight)South Dakota voters rejected a ballot question Tuesday that could have triggered a repeal of the state’s Medicaid expansion mandate.
When The Associated Press called the race at 1:22 a.m. Wednesday, 56% of the votes were against Amendment I and 44% were in favor. Over 80% of votes statewide had been counted.
Amendment I would have repealed the Medicaid expansion requirement in the state constitution if the expansion’s federal funding share fell below 90%. The Republican state lawmakers who sent Amendment I to the ballot said expanded Medicaid would be too expensive for the state in that scenario.
One of those lawmakers is Rep. Will Mortenson, R-Fort Pierre, who said Tuesday night that “fiscal policy is a tough sell on the ballot.” He said South Dakota’s schools and nursing homes, and the state’s balanced budget, could be imperiled if the state has to shoulder a bigger share of expanded Medicaid costs in the future.
“I hope the Legislature keeps an eye on this issue going forward,” said Mortenson, who did not seek reelection this year.
Some healthcare officials spoke out against Amendment I. Tim Rave is a Republican former legislator who’s now president and CEO of the South Dakota Association of Healthcare Organizations.
“I think South Dakotans want to make sure that their fellow South Dakotans are taken care of, and they don’t want to face those medical debt challenges,” Rave said Tuesday night.
1,213 South Dakotans could lose Medicaid as federal work requirements take effect, department says

Medicaid is a federal-state health insurance program for people with low incomes. During the administration of President Barack Obama, the federal government offered to cover 90% of states’ costs to expand eligibility. South Dakota’s Republican-dominated Legislature declined the offer.
In 2022, South Dakota voters approved a citizen-initiated state constitutional amendment. It required an expansion covering adults with incomes up to 138% of the poverty level, adding them to traditional low-income coverage groups such as children, elderly people and people with disabilities.
Among the roughly 143,000 South Dakotans covered by Medicaid, about 31,000 are enrolled through the expansion.
Deb Fischer-Clemens is a nurse, a Democratic former state lawmaker and former senior vice president of Avera’s Center for Public Policy. She’s currently president of the South Dakota Nurses Association. She said Tuesday night “by rejecting Amendment I, voters chose to protect healthcare access for more than 30,000 hard-working South Dakotans and their families.”
Since the expansion’s implementation through the end of the last state fiscal year in June, the state had spent a total of $76 million on it and received $870 million in federal expansion funding, according to the state Department of Social Services.
The broad tax and spending law that President Donald Trump signed in 2025 established work, school or community service requirements that are expected to take effect next year for Medicaid expansion enrollees.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Forstag rides a ‘blue wave’ to victory in House race
description: MISSOULA —The second floor of the historic Florence Hotel erupted in cheers just before 11 p.m., when the first Missoula County vote results were released, and again 30 minutes later when Gallatin County made its first drop — both heavily favored Democrat Sam Forstag. In a statement released at 11:48, Forstag’s campaign declared victory in […]
text:
Scenes from the a watch party for Sam Forstag, Democratic candidate for Montana’s western congressional district, for the 2026 midterm election at the Florence Building in Missoula on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. (Ben Allen Smith/Lee Enterprises)MISSOULA —The second floor of the historic Florence Hotel erupted in cheers just before 11 p.m., when the first Missoula County vote results were released, and again 30 minutes later when Gallatin County made its first drop — both heavily favored Democrat Sam Forstag.
In a statement released at 11:48, Forstag’s campaign declared victory in the race for Montana’s western congressional race.
The Associated Press had not called the race as of midnight, but Aaron Flint has called Forstag and conceded the race.
Flint’s campaign did not respond with further comment.
Montana will send send Democrat to D.C., after two years of an all-Republican delegation and for the first time in the U.S. House since Forstag was born.
“This win is the work of thousands of Montanans who are sick of a politics that puts working people last, and who are ready to send one of our own to Washington to make it work for us,” Forstag said in his statement.
In Montana’s most competitive federal race, Forstag and Republican Aaron Flint have been locked in a tight race since polls closed at 8 p.m., with Flint gaining a lead when conservative Flathead County began reporting in his favor.
But as of 11:45 p.m., Missoula’s reported 43,000 votes broke 71%-to-27% for Forstag, and Gallatin’s 37,00 votes are reported at 61%-to-37% for Forstag.
Speaking to his supporters, Forstag said they were making a statement with each reported vote drop.
He talked about the feeling of helplessness he felt when the “other party” took power two years ago and began gutting sections of the government, hurting his fellow U.S. Forest Service workers and wildland firefighters.
“When a lot of people were hurting and a lot of promises were being gone back on, we had some folks come out here, and we talked about the fact that right now it feels like we’re fighting a hell of a fire,” Forstag told the crowd of around 200. “We are fighting greed, burning out of control, and we talked about the fact that it’s just like on a wildfire when you are 17 hours into a shift, swinging a tool or running a chainsaw, and that local engine or hotshot crew shows up. They’re not just bringing manpower or water; they’re bringing the kind of hope it’s going to take to fight this thing.
“And friends, we just took another swing at winning this thing.”
The New York Times estimates fewer than 70,000 votes are left to be tallied in the state and is forecasting the race to go to Forstag.
“Like we have said at 80-plus town halls and meet-and-greets across the state, like a Russian smokejumper said in National Geographic many years back: Well, what smokejumping is? It’s for three minutes, fly like eagle, for three weeks, dig like mole,” Forstag said, surrounded by his campaign team and family on stage. “And friends, we’ve been digging for a long time, but tonight, let’s fly.”
Scenes from the a watch party for Sam Forstag, Democratic candidate for Montana’s western congressional district, for the 2026 midterm election at the Florence Building in Missoula on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. (Ben Allen Smith/Lee Enterprises)

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Democrat holds a narrow lead in the race for auditor of state
description: Democrat Taylor Wettach was leading Republican Lt. Gov. Chris Cournoyer by a slim margin early Wednesday in the contest to replace Rob Sand as the state auditor. With 96% of the vote counted, the Associated Press had yet to declare a winner. Unofficial results showed Wettach had claimed 50.9% of the vote, to 49.1% for […]
text:
Taylor Wettach spoke to Iowa State Fair attendees and reporters during the Des Moines Register Political Soapbox on Aug. 22, 2026. (Photo by Brooklyn Draisey/Iowa Capital Dispatch)Democrat Taylor Wettach was leading Republican Lt. Gov. Chris Cournoyer by a slim margin early Wednesday in the contest to replace Rob Sand as the state auditor.
With 96% of the vote counted, the Associated Press had yet to declare a winner. Unofficial results showed Wettach had claimed 50.9% of the vote, to 49.1% for Cournoyer.
Wettach had campaigned on a pledge to continue the work of Sand, who opted not to seek reelection and instead run for governor.
At the Des Moines Register Political Soapbox in August, Wettach said his career as a lawyer would aid him in holding people and institutions accountable even with limitations that Republican state lawmakers have been placed on the auditor’s office.
“I have experience and understanding to look into those financials, and then as a lawyer, I have experience and understanding to make sure that where there are problems that we do find, we can do something about it,” Wettach said. “So I’m excited to take that background and leverage it.”
In his work as an attorney, Wettach said he’s negotiated complex financial matters involving millions of dollars and has worked “with some of the best auditors in the country.” He said he resigned from Simpson Thacher & Bartlett LLP, his former firm, in protest of pressure from the Trump’s administration to “cut a deal to do $125 million worth of free work in support of their priorities.”
The state auditor’s office is supposed to be an “independent watchdog” in service of Iowans and their tax dollars, Wettach said, a role he added Sand has filled successfully despite efforts from the state to restrict access the office has to information.
Wettach has indicate he intends to continue Sand’s support for the Public Innovation Efficiencies program, as well as Sand’s efforts to maintain the auditor’s independence.
Wettach said one of his priorities is addressing Education Savings Accounts program that routes public money to non-public schools. He also wants to support the auditor’s efforts to assist citizens fighting  corruption in rural areas.
Cournoyer, currently serving as Iowa’s lieutenant governor under Gov. Kim Reynolds represented Senate District 35 in the Iowa Legislature from 2019 to 2024. Previously, she served as a member of the Pleasant Valley School Board and as a reserve sheriff’s deputy in Scott County. She holds a bachelor’s in computer science from the University of Texas.
Cournoyer has promised that as auditor she would prioritize “transparency, efficiency, and results over headlines and partisanship.” She called her campaign an effort to secure “the next critical victory for Iowa conservatives” and said she had dedicated her entire career to stopping government waste and reducing the associated burden placed on Iowa taxpayers.
Cournoyer has been critical of Sand’s term as auditor, arguing he was using the office to pursue a politically driven agenda. Sand and Democratic lawmakers have said Republican-backed legislation has curtailed the auditor’s office access to information and ability to go to court.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Voters say yes to South Dakota Investment Council management of unclaimed property money
description: South Dakota voters approved a ballot question Tuesday that will allow the state Investment Council to manage the money in an unclaimed property trust fund. With 87% of the votes counted statewide by about 1:15 a.m. Central on Wednesday, 61% of the votes were in favor of Amendment K, and 39% were against it. State […]
text:
South Dakota Treasurer Josh Haeder appears in a video encouraging people to reclaim their unclaimed property from his office. (South Dakota Searchlight photo)South Dakota voters approved a ballot question Tuesday that will allow the state Investment Council to manage the money in an unclaimed property trust fund.
With 87% of the votes counted statewide by about 1:15 a.m. Central on Wednesday, 61% of the votes were in favor of Amendment K, and 39% were against it.
State lawmakers have begun transitioning unclaimed property proceeds into the fund and withdrawing only a portion each year to use in the state budget. The fund earns minimal interest, and lawmakers needed voter approval of Amendment K to place the fund under the management of the state Investment Council. The council will invest the money for higher returns, like it does for the state’s public employee retirement system and other trust funds benefiting schools, healthcare and the state budget.
State Sen. Taffy Howard, R-Rapid City, sponsored a bill that state lawmakers unanimously approved to send Amendment K to voters, with the support of the state’s Bureau of Finance and Management and the State Treasurer’s Office.
“I’m just happy to see that it’s passing easily,” Howard said Tuesday evening. “I would have loved to have seen it be 100%, obviously. It did pass the Legislature unanimously. But just as long as it passes and we can earn more money for the citizens of the state, that’s what really matters.”

Sen. Taffy Howard, R-Rapid City, speaks in the state Senate at the Capitol in Pierre on Feb. 11, 2026. (Photo by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)

State Treasurer Josh Haeder also praised the outcome as it was becoming clear Tuesday night.
“I couldn’t be prouder of the people of South Dakota for showing their support for Amendment K and helping us, what looks like, getting across the finish line in a positive way,” Haeder said.
Unclaimed property consists of an array of abandoned or forgotten private assets, such as bank accounts, stocks, life insurance payouts, uncashed checks and the contents of safe deposit boxes. The property is transferred to the state after three years if banks or other holders can’t find the owners.
The state continues trying to connect owners with their property, including on a searchable website. Many of them never make a claim, and much of the unclaimed money formerly went into the state budget.
Annual unclaimed property receipts surged to new highs in recent years — including more than $300 million during the 2025 fiscal year — due to factors including a glut of private assets left behind during pandemic-motivated relocations and Bancorp moving its national headquarters to Sioux Falls.
With so much growth in unclaimed property, some state lawmakers began to worry about the size of the potential liability facing the state. Rightful owners or their heirs can claim their money at any time, even if the state has already spent it. State lawmakers approved two bills last year to protect the state against that liability and bring more predictability to the amount of unclaimed property revenue available for the state budget.
One of those bills became a state law transitioning all unclaimed property revenue into the trust fund and limiting the amount withdrawn to fund the state budget. The money in the fund is available for future claimants while also generating interest to be used for the state budget. The other bill sent Amendment K to the ballot seeking voter approval for the Investment Council to manage the fund.
No ballot-question committees materialized to raise or spend money for or against Amendment K, resulting in little to no campaigning on the ballot question.

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Democrats flip statewide offices up and down the ballot in Georgia; state House is in play
description: Tuesday night was a clean sweep for Georgia Democrats, with voters electing Democrats to every statewide office that was on the ballot.  Voters reelected U.S. Sen. Jon Ossoff by a wide margin and elected former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms to be not just the first Democratic governor in Georgia in more than two decades […]
text:
Democrat Penny Brown Reynolds delivers her victory speech in Georgia's secretary of state race on Nov. 3, 2026. Maya Homan/Georgia RecorderTuesday night was a clean sweep for Georgia Democrats, with voters electing Democrats to every statewide office that was on the ballot. 
Voters reelected U.S. Sen. Jon Ossoff by a wide margin and elected former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms to be not just the first Democratic governor in Georgia in more than two decades but also the first elected Black woman governor to ever serve in the country. 
But Georgia voters didn’t stop there. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Democrats won three other open statewide seats that were seen as competitive going into Tuesday: attorney general, secretary of state and lieutenant governor. And they also ousted Republican incumbents in downballot races for labor commissioner, insurance commissioner, agriculture commissioner and state school superintendent, with the Democrats in those races leading by 7 points or more late Tuesday night.  
Starting in January, Democrats will also control a state board that regulates utilities, such as Georgia Power, for the first time in decades. Some congressional races were tighter than expected. 
And as of late Tuesday night, Republicans in the state House of Representatives also appeared to be at risk of losing their hold on a chamber they have controlled since 2004. Unofficial results from the secretary of state’s website showed Democratic candidates leading in 13 districts held by Republicans early Wednesday morning. House Democrats need a net gain of 10 seats to become the majority party.
State Sen. Josh McLaurin, who is the Democratic nominee for lieutenant governor, speaks at a press conference on the first day of Georgia’s special legislative session held in June. Jill Nolin/Georgia Recorder
“Georgia Democrats were bigger than just a party tonight,” said state Sen. Josh McLaurin, who is the lieutenant governor-elect, in a speech Tuesday night. “We are now the new governing coalition of the state of Georgia. It’s bigger than party, and it’s bigger than one moment. It’s the future, and I’m so proud of you.”
McLaurin is poised to be the first Democrat to preside over the Senate chamber since Mark Taylor, who served from 1999 until 2007. He will succeed Republican Lt. Gov. Burt Jones, who served one term as Senate president before launching an unsuccessful bid for governor this year. His opponent, Republican Sen. Greg Dolezal, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
In several races, winning Democratic candidates also made history. 
Democratic state Rep. Tanya Miller will be the first woman and the second Black person to ever serve as attorney general. In a victory speech, Miller pledged to use her position as the Peach State’s top prosecutor to protect people who have felt ignored by the system.
“Tonight I want every young girl watching, every young person who has ever been underestimated, every parent working two jobs to make ends meet, and every Georgian who has ever felt invisible to the institutions meant to protect you, I want you to hear me,” she said. “You matter. Your voice matters. Your vote matters, and your future matters. There is room for you in the promise of Georgia.”
She defeated Republican Brian Strickland, a lawyer and Republican state senator who has served in the Legislature since 2013.
Former Fulton County Judge Penny Brown Reynolds will become the first Black person in Georgia to be elected to the position of secretary of state.
In an interview, she said she felt humbled to receive such a decisive victory. Brown Reynolds had a more than 11-point lead as of late Tuesday night. 
“It’s very significant that the people of Georgia, from all walks of life, all ZIP codes, made a decision that I would be the person to represent them, not because I am the first Black woman — first Black period — but because I was the most qualified person,” she said. “I believe that they wanted somebody who really loves and cares for the people and understands the value of that vote.”
Brown Reynolds defeated Republican Tim Fleming, a two-term state lawmaker and the former deputy secretary of state during Gov. Brian Kemp’s tenure as the state’s top election official. Fleming could not be reached for comment on election night.
Democratic superintendent candidate Lydia Powell speaks to the press after an Oct. 13 debate. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder
Educator Lydia Powell is poised to become Georgia’s first Democratic state school superintendent in more than 30 years. She is set to become the first Black woman to lead Georgia’s public school system, which includes more than 1.7 million students across more than 180 districts.
Powell defeated incumbent Superintendent Richard Woods, who has served for more than a decade as the schools chief. Woods first took office in 2015 and won re-election in 2018 and 2022.
“Tonight the Lord has chosen to close this chapter of my life,” Woods wrote on social media Tuesday night. “I wish to congratulate Dr. Powell on her election win and pray for her success as Georgia’s next state school superintendent.”
Nikki Porcher led Labor Commissioner Bárbara Rivera Holmes, who was appointed to the role, by about 9 points. Keisha Sean Waites had an 8-point lead over Insurance Commissioner John King. And Katherine Juhan-Arnold was beating Agriculture Commissioner Tyler Harper by nearly 8 points. 
“Unfortunately, tonight has not gone our way,” Rivera Holmes said in a statement. “I want to congratulate Nikki Porcher on a hard-fought campaign and her victory in this race. I’m wishing her well and offering her my family’s prayers.”
The Georgia Republican Party put out an unsigned statement after the results started to roll in.
Nina Lee, a 35-year-old writer and film director, said she was excited to see Georgia flip blue for the first time in her life. (Maya Homan/Georgia Recorder)
“Tonight’s outcome is not what our candidates worked so hard to achieve. We respect the will of Georgia’s voters, and we hope those elected will serve all of Georgia,” the statement read in part. “Our next chapter begins with that responsibility. We will strengthen our local parties, welcome new voices and develop leaders who understand that public service starts with showing up and listening.
“To everyone disappointed tonight: take heart. We will never stop fighting for a Georgia that puts faith, families, and freedom first,” the statement also said. 
But back over at the Democrats’ election night party, attendees were elated. 
Atlanta attorney Michelle Augustine celebrated the historic string of wins for Black women at Bottoms’ Atlanta rally Tuesday night, waving a sign that read “Black women lead Georgia.”
“We have Judge Penny Brown Reynolds, we have Tanya Miller,” she said. “This sign means everything. This sign means everything, because Black women for sure lead Georgia.”
“I’m gonna be able to tell my children, my children will be able to tell their children, that I was actually here and made part of history,” she added.
Nina Lee, a 35-year-old writer and film director who attended the Democratic Party of Georgia’s watch party at the Hyatt Regency Atlanta, said she was excited to see Georgia flip blue for the first time in her life. 
Beverly Burks, the mayor of Clarkston, celebrates Democrats’ victory up and down the ballot in Georgia. Maya Homan/Georgia Recorder
“It’s wild,” she said. “I’m from here. I’ve lived here. I never thought I’d see the day.” 
Beverly Burks, the mayor of Clarkston, called the Democrats’ sweep of the state’s top offices “telling,” adding that the results are a sign that Black women can be elected statewide. 
As the first Black woman to serve as Clarkston’s mayor, Burks added, she’s no stranger to the acclaim — and challenges — that come with barrier-breaking politics. 
“I know what it means to be the first in terms of African American women elected to that role,” she said. “But that’s just a nice title, right? The work is what you do every day to make a difference for our Georgians who are suffering and need support.”
Georgia Recorder Deputy Editor Ross Williams contributed to this report.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: New faces, new leaders and a few more Democrats will shape North Dakota’s next Legislature
description: Democrats made small gains in North Dakota’s Legislature Tuesday, flipping some seats in Fargo and Grand Forks to boost their tiny minority. Republicans will keep their longtime control of the Legislature by supermajorities in the House and Senate. Seventy-five of 141 seats were on the ballot. Two incumbents, both Republicans, lost election. District 43 Sen.[...]
text:
The North Dakota Democratic-NPL Party holds its midterm election watch party at Kingpinz Entertainment Center in Fargo on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Dan Koeck/For the North Dakota Monitor)Democrats made small gains in North Dakota’s Legislature Tuesday, flipping some seats in Fargo and Grand Forks to boost their tiny minority.
Republicans will keep their longtime control of the Legislature by supermajorities in the House and Senate. Seventy-five of 141 seats were on the ballot. Two incumbents, both Republicans, lost election.
District 43 Sen. Jeff Barta, R-Grand Forks, lost reelection to Democrat Mary Adams, a Realtor who served in the House from 2018-2022 and lost House bids in 2022 and 2024.
Democrats Tyler York and Lucas Maughan won the district’s two open House seats, besting Republicans Jill Chandler and Mike Holmes. The House seats were open after Democratic Rep. Zac Ista declined to run again and Republican Rep. Eric Murphy lost his primary. Ista has been the House minority leader since 2023.
From the left, Democratic-NPL state House candidate Tyler York, Democratic-NPL state Senate candidate Mary Adams and Democratic-NPL state House candidate Lukas Maughan. (Photo courtesy of Dem-NPL State Party)
Democrat Nicole Derenne defeated Republican Connie Osowski in a special election for the two years remaining on a District 42 House seat in Grand Forks.
Republican Emily O’Brien held the seat from 2016-2025, when she resigned to become deputy commissioner of the state Health and Human Services Department. Republican Dustin McNally replaced her by appointment, but lost his primary to Osowski, whose husband, Republican Doug Osowski, holds the district’s other House seat.
In Fargo, Democrats Chris Tiongson and Stacy Heidenreich beat Republicans Jennifer Benson and Rich Slagle for two open District 41 House seats, though only 33 votes separated Heidenreich and Benson.
Republican Reps. Jorin Johnson and Karen Grindberg did not run. Lt. Gov. Michelle Strinden, a Republican, held one of the seats from 2018-2024.
Voters approve North Dakota governor’s first appointees, reelect all Republican incumbents

One of the Legislature’s few rural Democrats defeated a fellow incumbent to hang on to her seat in complete but unofficial results Tuesday.
Rep. Alisa Mitskog, D-Wahpeton, won a fourth term for Richland County’s District 25 over Rep. Kathy Skroch, R-Lidgerwood. Skroch previously served from 2016-2022. She was appointed last year to fill out the remaining term of Rep. Cindy Schreiber-Beck, R-Wahpeton, who died in May 2025. Skroch also lost to Mitskog in 2022.
Skroch and Barta were the only incumbents in the Legislature to lose election Tuesday.
Mitskog, a chiropractor, serves on the powerful House Appropriations Committee.
Republican Terry Goerger won the other District 25 House seat as the top vote getter.
Goerger and House Republican nominees Blaine DesLauriers and Tim Mihalick of Minot-area District 3 and Steve Sauter of Bismarck-area District 7 – all of whom won Tuesday – were the subjects of a court case challenging their primary paperwork based on alleged errors. Three Republican officials sought to have their potential victories overturned and the seats filled by appointment. The state Supreme Court denied the case.
Democrat Anastassiya Andrianova has been elected to succeed Rep. Gretchen Dobervich in Fargo’s District 11, according to unofficial results. Republican Doug Sharbono appeared to win the other open House seat in the district by 160 votes. Sharbono defeated independent candidate Cara Cody-Braun as they vied to succeed Rep. Liz Conmy after the lawmaker’s death earlier this year. 
Around two dozen North Dakota lawmakers chose not to seek reelection or were defeated in their primaries earlier this year. Three state reps ran unopposed for the Senate. Adams in Grand Forks and Republican Roger Brabandt of Minot-area District 5 are former lawmakers who will return.
Rep. Bob Martinson, R-Bismarck, who has served 50 years noncontinuously in the House as the most tenured incumbent lawmaker, won reelection to a final House term.
Rep. Bob Martinson, R-Bismarck, watches results during an election night watch party in Bismarck on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Martin/For the North Dakota Monitor)
Democrats haven’t been in the majority since the 1980s and 1990s. They have mostly lost seats over the years, down to as few as four Senate seats in 2023.
Most of the Democrats’ seats are ones representing districts in Fargo, which leans further to the left than most of North Dakota, and tribal reservations, where Native Americans tend to vote for Democrats.
Three seats for a joint legislative district encompassing the Spirit Lake and Turtle Mountain reservations also were on the ballot. A federal judge ordered the joint district in early 2024 after finding the Legislature’s 2021 redistricting map violated the Voting Rights Act for Native American voters. The case went all the way to the U.S. Supreme Court, which sent it back to a lower court earlier this year. Three Democrats ran unopposed for the seats.
Legislative term limits, which voters approved in 2022, won’t turn out any incumbents until 2028. North Dakota lawmakers are limited to eight years in the House and eight years in the Senate.
Due to retirements, House Republicans will choose a new majority leader, and the powerful House Appropriations Committee, which writes state budgets, will have a new chair.
Democrats also will elect new House and Senate minority leaders because those incumbents chose not to run again.
Lawmakers will be in Bismarck as soon as next week for two days of summaries of interim studies, followed by the Legislature’s three-day organizational session in early December. That’s when the House will elect a speaker, members will be sworn in and Gov. Kelly Armstrong will present his budget blueprint.
Lawmakers take office Dec. 1. The regular biennial session begins in early January.




North Dakota Monitor reporter Jacob Orledge contributed to this story.
Reach Monitor reporter Jack Dura at jdura@northdakotamonitor.com.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Democrat Chris Jones concedes agriculture secretary race to incumbent Mike Naig
description: Republican Mike Naig was expected to keep his job as Iowa Secretary of Agriculture as unofficial results from the Associated Press late Wednesday showed him leading Democratic challenger Chris Jones. Results late Tuesday showed a lead from Naig of less than 1%, but by early Wednesday morning, as a greater share of rural precincts submitted […]
text:
As of early Wednesday, the race for Iowa's Secretary of Agriculture had not been called, though Republican incumbent Mike Naig, pictured here in November 2025, maintained a slim lead, according to the Associated Press. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch)Republican Mike Naig was expected to keep his job as Iowa Secretary of Agriculture as unofficial results from the Associated Press late Wednesday showed him leading Democratic challenger Chris Jones.
Results late Tuesday showed a lead from Naig of less than 1%, but by early Wednesday morning, as a greater share of rural precincts submitted vote counts, Naig led with 53% of the vote to 47% for Jones, with an estimated 96% of the vote reported, according to the AP. 
Jones, who ran on a platform of improving water quality and dramatic shifts in the farm economy, conceded the race earlier in the night and said change for Iowa’s water quality isn’t going to happen if people just “nudge it.” Speaking at watch party in Des Moines’ East Village, Jones said a “big complex” system like Iowa’s agriculture changes with a flip. 
“So we really need to have grassroots demands here that this is gonna change, that we’re gonna ask for change, we’re gonna demand for change,” Jones said. “Change can happen. We should not be disbanded or despair … I did my best to make it happen. I tried to make words matter.”
Naig has been the head of the Iowa Department of Agriculture and Land Stewardship since 2018, and he has started programs like Choose Iowa, a state brand for local products, and championed the Farm-to-Faucet legislation in 2026 that provided greater state support for conservation practice adoption and water treatment infrastructure.
In a victory statement early Wednesday, Naig said he was grateful for the trust of Iowans who voted for him to serve in the role again.
“Tonight, Iowans rejected divisive rhetoric and attacks on our farming community, choosing instead a positive vision for the future of Iowa agriculture,” Naig said.
Jones is known for his Substack column and book, “The Swine Republic” where he has criticized the current agricultural system in Iowa that relies on large-scale farms growing mostly corn and soybeans and, he argues, contributes to Iowa’s poor water quality.
Naig said he was proud of the work he has done in the role so far and looks forward to “building” on that progress.
“We’ll continue to strengthen Iowa agriculture by building markets internationally, domestically, and locally, working together to improve water quality, protecting our food supply, and ensuring our farms remain strong for the next generation,” Naig said in the statement.
Democrat Chris Jones gives remarks during his watch party at the Iowa Tap Room in Des Moines. (Photo by Joanna Schroeder for Iowa Capital Dispatch)
 Throughout his campaign Jones said his candidacy should be considered a “referendum” on Iowa’s water quality. Before retiring, Jones was a research engineer at the University of Iowa. 
He has pitched dramatic shifts in Iowa agriculture, including taxpayer-supported off ramps for producers who want to transition their operations to grow oats, for example, instead of corn and soybeans. He has also called for the state to require a certain share of locally produced foods in school lunches, and to support new crop markets to move away from ethanol. 
Iowa has had a Republican secretary of agriculture since 2007, when Patty Judge left the role. 
Jones said that when he launched his campaign in January, he was one of the few candidates talking about water quality, but by the end of the campaign, “every candidate in the state was running on this.”
“We can only hope that maybe some of these people we see on the screen tonight are going to be the second people, that can take it up and take the ball over the goal line,” Jones said.
Joanna Schroeder contributed to this article.

title: Republican Kurt Alme declares victory, independent Seth Bodnar concedes
description: Republican Kurt Alme declared victory Tuesday for the U.S. Senate seat in Montana. “From the bottom of my heart, thank you to every Montanan who put their trust in me to serve as your next U.S. Senator,” Alme said in a statement. “Montana is my home, and as your Senator, I will fight to make […]
text:
Republican Kurt Alme declared victory in the U.S. Senate race Tuesday. He's pictured here at an event in Belgrade, Montana, on Monday, Oct. 26, 2026. (Jordan Hansen/Daily Montanan)Republican Kurt Alme declared victory Tuesday for the U.S. Senate seat in Montana.
“From the bottom of my heart, thank you to every Montanan who put their trust in me to serve as your next U.S. Senator,” Alme said in a statement. “Montana is my home, and as your Senator, I will fight to make life more affordable, make our communities safer and always protect our Montana way of life.”
Independent candidate Seth Bodnar conceded just before midnight.
“I want to congratulate Kurt Alme and wish him and his family the best,” Bodnar said. “This isn’t the result we worked so hard for, but I’m deeply grateful for my family and our campaign team, and I am proud of what we accomplished. We left it all on the field.”
Alme won 47% of the vote, and Bodnar had 39% around midnight.
Alani Bankhead, the Democratic nominee, earned 12%. Libertarian Kyle Austin earned 2%.
Alme, former U.S. Attorney for Montana, was tapped to run by Republican U.S. Sen. Steve Daines, who withdrew his candidacy at the last minute.
The move gave Alme, a first-time political candidate for federal office, a leg up.
Democrats and left-of-center voters split support between Bankhead, a political newcomer and military veteran, and Bodnar, the well-funded independent and former president of the University of Montana.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Nebraska poised for new approach to elections as Petersen ahead in secretary of state race
description: LINCOLN — Omaha businessman Scott Petersen was outpacing three other candidates early Wednesday for an apparent win as Nebraska secretary of state, likely cinching a new direction for state elections. Petersen, as of 12:30 a.m., had 52% of the votes compared to Democrat and small business owner Sarah Slattery’s 42%. He will succeed Republican Bob […]
text:
Scott Petersen of Omaha was ahead in the general election race for Nebraska secretary of state. Here he shown in Grand Island, Nebraska, on Oct. 5, 2026, before President Donald Trump spoke at a midterms rally. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — Omaha businessman Scott Petersen was outpacing three other candidates early Wednesday for an apparent win as Nebraska secretary of state, likely cinching a new direction for state elections.
Petersen, as of 12:30 a.m., had 52% of the votes compared to Democrat and small business owner Sarah Slattery’s 42%. He will succeed Republican Bob Evnen, who was seeking his third four-year term as the state’s top elections official before Petersen comfortably beat him in the May GOP primary election.
Other opponents in the general election were former state senator Bob Krist, of the America First Party, and Douglas County special project manager Paul Rumbaugh of the Working People Party. Each had about 3% of the votes.
Petersen earlier described his upset victory against incumbent Evnen as a referendum on election integrity issues raised by President Donald Trump and supporters. 
He has argued that voting by mail should be restricted and has promised to conduct full hand counts of races. Petersen also questioned whether state ballot-counting machines can access the internet and be hacked, a threat that county election officials say is not possible.
The new secretary of state will be paid $85,000. 
The office was among four constitutional officer posts up for election besides the governor and lieutenant governor.
Another feisty race pitted incumbent Mike Hilgers against Democrat Jocelyn Brasher for Nebraska attorney general. As of early Wednesday, Hilgers had garnered 54% of the vote and Brasher had 46%.
The job of primary lawyer for the state  pays $95,000.
Brasher, a former deputy Dodge County attorney who previously worked five years in the Nebraska AG’s Office, had said Hilgers, a former state lawmaker, was leading in the “wrong direction.” She said he was legislating based on his personal political views.
For state auditor, Mike Foley of Lincoln, a Republican, toppled challenger John Knight of Clay Center for the America First Party. 
Foley, in securing 74% of the vote as of midnight, won his fourth nonconsecutive term as the independent watchdog for state and local government finances. The annual salary is $85,000.
He had been running unopposed until Sept. 1, when Knight, an engineer and senior program manager, joined the race. 
For Nebraska state treasurer, Joey Spellerberg, a Republican, had garnered 57% of the vote as of early Wednesday, ahead of Daniel Ebers, a Democrat who works in hotel management and who said he ran to give voters a choice. 
Spellerberg had been mayor of Fremont for five years when Gov. Jim Pillen appointed him as treasurer in November 2025. The post that monitors the flow of public dollars for the state pays an annual salary of $85,000.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Garlin Gilchrist wins secretary of state election, maintaining Democratic control of office
description: Democratic nominee and Lt. Gov. Garlin Gilchrist II has won the race for Michigan Secretary of State, defeating Republican nominee and Macomb County Clerk Anthony Forlini by a margin of nearly eight percentage points as of 2:00 a.m., the time at which the Associated Press called the race.  “The biggest difference between us and them, […]
text:
Lt. Gov. Garlin Gilchrist II shares a victory speech in his win for Michigan Secretary of State with the Michigan Democratic Party's election night event in the early hours of Nov. 4, 2026. (Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance)Democratic nominee and Lt. Gov. Garlin Gilchrist II has won the race for Michigan Secretary of State, defeating Republican nominee and Macomb County Clerk Anthony Forlini by a margin of nearly eight percentage points as of 2:00 a.m., the time at which the Associated Press called the race. 
“The biggest difference between us and them, the biggest difference between Michigan and the rest of the country, the biggest difference between Democrats and those who vote against Democrats, is we have a place for everyone,” Gilchrist said in a victory speech. “Our vision is big enough to include everyone. Their vision is so small, so narrow, so weak that everybody can’t live. But Michigan, my arms are wide enough. I’m tall enough to bring everybody in the big picture.”
Unofficial election results show Gilchrist received 52.1% of the vote, while Forlini pulled in 44.4%. Third-party candidates Scott Aughney of the U.S. Taxpayers Party, Eric Borregard of the Green Party and Christine Sloan of the Libertarian Party received 0.6%, 0.4% and 1.7% of the vote respectively.
Two late October polls showed Gilchrist with a distinct lead over Forlini — he held a nine-point lead in one poll and an eleven-point lead in the other, both outside their respective margins of error. As a current statewide executive, Gilchrist benefited from broader name recognition than Forlini, as well as an overall positive environment for Democratic candidates in 2026. 
Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson won the gubernatorial election, and Washtenaw County Clerk Eli Savit claimed victory in the Michigan attorney general race, maintaining Democratic control in the three main elected statewide executive positions — a boost to the Democratic agenda with single-party control.
This is a developing story and will be updated as more information becomes available.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Blue wave erodes margins in Pennsylvania’s GOP strongholds
description: Democrats now dominate Pa.'s congressional delegation 11-6 and captured higher vote shares than the 2022 midterm, even in races they lost.
text:
Pennsylvania's Congressional District Map. (Pennsylvania Department of State)Incumbents have held onto their seats in a dozen of Pennsylvania’s congressional districts, leaving the state’s delegation favoring Democrats  by 11-6,  due to four “toss-ups” among at least 25 seats the party flipped across the country. 
Thirteen seats in the commonwealth were considered safe – but races in those districts held by Republicans were closer than the last midterm election in 2022, according to an analysis of results by the Capital-Star. The analysis didn’t include two districts – the 13th and 14th – where Republican incumbents John Joyce and Guy Reschenthaler ran unopposed in 2022. 
Among the most dramatic changes for GOP-held districts was the 9th, which encompasses six counties and parts of three others stretching through the state’s coal region into the northern tier. 
Republican Congressman Dan Meuser won a fifth term, getting 62% of votes to the 38% cast for Rachel Wallace, the Democrat challenging him. The results are unofficial.
Meuser, who was heavily favored to win, expressed gratitude for his constituency’s “overwhelming support … and the trust they have placed in me to continue representing them.”

Democrat Brooks ousts incumbent Mackenzie in Lehigh Valley’s 7th Congressional District


“Once again, voters in the 9th Congressional District have rejected the failed ideology of authoritarian socialism and reaffirmed the values Americans have spent 250 years defending: freedom, opportunity, and the promise of the American Dream,” he said in a statement. 
Meuser’s 24-point margin, while dramatic, does break his pattern of increasing them with each election. He won with 70 percent of votes in 2024, up from 60 percent of votes captured in his first win in 2018. 
That was the last time he faced a challenger in the primary election for the GOP nomination. 
Wallace was considered Meuser’s strongest opponent since then, out-fundraising him in some campaign finance reporting periods – but  overall, he raised about twice as much. 
She also brought in more money than challengers in the 12 other “safe” districts: As of Tuesday, her campaign had reported nearly $1.2 million versus the next highest total of $334,000 raised by Democrat Nancy Mannion in the 11th District covering Lancaster County and part of York County. 
Mannion came within 10 points of  U.S. Rep. Lloyd Smucker, who’s in his sixth term in Congress. That’s 13 points closer than in 2022 when Mannion also challenged him. 
Wallace was 14 points closer to Meuser (with 91 percent of votes counted) than his opponent in 2022, according to the Capital-Star’s analysis of results. 
Wallace’s campaign didn’t respond to requests for comment after the race was called.
A big issue early in the campaign was the federal government’s acquisition of two warehouses in the district for conversion to immigration detention centers – something Meuser says caught him by surprise. 
After those plans were scrapped, they all but dropped out of the dialogue. Like other candidates in other races this cycle – Meuser and Wallace’s topics of focus included healthcare, data centers, affordability and the impact of Trump’s tariffs on agriculture and small businesses. 

Democrat Bob Harvie defeats five-term Congressman Brian Fitzpatrick in Philly suburbs


Democratic incumbents expanded their victory margins, according to the Capital-Star’s analysis. 
In Philadelphia and the collar counties, it was Brendan Boyle (2nd District), Madeleine Dean (4th District), Mary Gay Scanlon (5th District) and Chrissy Houlahan (6th District) as well as the Pittsburgh region’s Summer Lee (12th District) and Chris Deluzio (17th District).
Scanlon and Houlahan – like Joyce, Meuser and Reschenthaler – each won another term Tuesday after first being elected in 2018. 
That year’s blue wave coincided with an off-cycle redistricting in Pennsylvania ordered by the state Supreme Court when it found the commonwealth’s prior congressional map was an unconstitutional partisan gerrymander – though some analyses have shown the resulting paritsan split likely could have been the same with the old boundaries in place.
Philadelphia state Rep. Chris Rabb won the Democratic primary in the deep blue city in May for the 3rd district, which cuts from the Northwest through West Philly, much of Center City and into South Philly. 
Rabb made it official Tuesday night with a 92-point victory over Independent Dennis Mahoney. His win holds significance apart from typical general elections in the Democratic stronghold because he’s among a slate of candidates ascending to Congress who ran as or closely aligned with the Democratic Socialists of America, which Rabb has said he joined this year. 
Rabb succeeds former U.S. Rep. Dwight Evans, who before serving in Congress was a state representative for 25 years. Evans announced his retirement last year after nearly a decade in the U.S. House starting in 2016. 
Elected in 2008, Republican Glenn “G.T.” Thompson remains the longest-serving of the delegation. Thompson, who heads the House Agriculture Committee, also represents the commonwealth’s largest congressional district at nearly 13,000 square miles enveloping most northern tier counties and stretching deep into the heart of the state.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: Republican re-elected as SC’s K-12 schools chief
description: Ellen Weaver has been head of the state Department of Education since 2022, when she won in a crowded primary election.
text:
South Carolina Education Superintendent Ellen Weaver speaks to supporters during an election night GOP watch party on Nov. 3, 2026, in Columbia, South Carolina. (Photo by John A. Carlos II/Special to the SC Daily Gazette)COLUMBIA — Republican Ellen Weaver won a second term Tuesday as South Carolina’s state superintendent for K-12 public schools.
Weaver received 51% of the vote against Democrat Sylvia Wright; 56,000 votes separated the two, according to unofficial results from the state Election Commission.
Baba Amin Ojuok, running for the United Citizens Party, received about 1% of the vote.
Weaver again defeated a teacher to continue overseeing policy at the state’s 72 public school districts. Wright, a teacher before moving into administration, most recently worked as a district coordinator for Dorchester 4.
For most districts, the job does not entail direct oversight over districts. The exceptions include rural Allendale, Marlboro and Jasper counties, where the state Department of Education is attempting to correct problems. The state also maintains some control over Williamsburg County schools — a takeover that, like Allendale, predates Weaver’s tenure.
Weaver previously led the conservative education-focused think tank Palmetto Promise Institute, the state’s leading advocate for school choice legislation. As state superintendent, she continued to advocate for expanding parents’ options.
Weaver has overseen implementation of the Education Scholarship Trust Fund, a taxpayer-funded program that provides money to parents for private K-12 tuition and other education-related expenses. Initially approved in 2023, five months after Weaver took office, the program was partially halted by a state Supreme Court ruling in September 2024. A second law approved eight months later reinstated parents’ ability to use the money for private tuition and expanded who qualified.
Weaver also points to improvements in student performance during her tenure. Teacher vacancies have also decreased amid salary increases approved by the Legislature.
Wright’s campaign centered around improving early childhood education. She wanted to build better pathways between pre-kindergarten and later grades, establish statewide training for district leaders, and put a halt on the K-12 scholarships Weaver wants to expand.
Weaver ran unopposed for the Republican nomination in June, a stark difference from the field of six Republicans on the ballot in 2022.
Wright defeated the Democratic nominee from four years ago, longtime teacher Lisa Ellis, for the party nomination.
It’s been 20 years since voters elected a Democrat as state superintendent. In 2006, Jim Rex won with fewer than 500 votes.
In 2018, voters soundly rejected the idea of letting the governor choose the education superintendent.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Republicans win races for South Dakota statewide offices, including secretary of state
description: Republicans won all the races Tuesday for South Dakota’s lesser-known statewide offices: secretary of state, attorney general, public utilities commissioner, auditor, treasurer, and commissioner of school and public lands. The Associated Press called the secretary of state race at 1:33 a.m. Wednesday for Republican Heather Baxter, who had 59% of the votes to[...]
text:
Rep. Heather Baxter, R-Rapid City, speaks in the state House of Representatives on Feb. 10, 2026. Baxter is this year's nominee for South Dakota secretary of state and built a large lead in partial returns. (Photo by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)Republicans won all the races Tuesday for South Dakota’s lesser-known statewide offices: secretary of state, attorney general, public utilities commissioner, auditor, treasurer, and commissioner of school and public lands.
The Associated Press called the secretary of state race at 1:33 a.m. Wednesday for Republican Heather Baxter, who had 59% of the votes to defeat Democrat Terrence Davis, 36%, and Libertarian Tamara Lesnar, 5%. About 90% of the votes had been counted statewide.
The secretary of state’s responsibilities include overseeing elections, campaign finance reporting, lobbyist registrations, business corporate filings and concealed pistol permits.
One of the main issues in the race was the candidates’ positions on election security. Baxter’s campaign website said she supports “improved hand-counting” methods. While serving as a legislator, she cosponsored an unsuccessful bill to prohibit the use of machines to count votes. 
Baxter told South Dakota Searchlight in an interview earlier this month that, if elected, she would focus on ensuring counties comply with state and federal requirements, while giving county auditors greater local control over their elections.
“The biggest misconception is that I’m going to go in and just completely get rid of these machines when I don’t even have that in my wheelhouse of what I’m allowed to do,” Baxter said.
Davis took the opposite approach, saying the state’s election system is sound and that Baxter was motivated by “the whole situation surrounding the 2020 election,” a reference to President Donald Trump’s false claim that the election was fraudulent.
Baxter is a small-business owner from Rapid City and state representative who focused on the secretary of state race after losing a legislative primary in June. Davis is a former state trooper from Sioux Falls. Lesnar, of Grenville, formerly served as a compliance officer at the Chicago Mercantile Exchange.
In other partial returns for lower-profile South Dakota statewide races Tuesday:

Republican Lance Russell was unopposed for attorney general.
Republican Don Haggar, 61%, beat Democrat Frank Kloucek, 39%, in the race for one of three seats on the Public Utilities Commission.
Republican Catherine Barranco, 63%, beat Democrat Tom Cool, 37%, in the race for state auditor.
Republican Melissa Hull, 63%, beat Democrat Margaret Kuipers, 37%, in the race for state treasurer.
Republican incumbent Brock Greenfield, 62%, beat Democrat Raeann Mettler, 38%, for commissioner of school and public lands.

Republicans also won the governor, U.S. Senate and U.S. House races Tuesday in South Dakota. Republicans have held every statewide office in South Dakota since Tim Johnson, a Democrat, decided not to seek reelection in 2014 and left the U.S. Senate in 2015.

text:
Yee Leng Xiong speaks at the state Democratic Party convention in June. (Photo by Baylor Spears/Wisconsin Examiner) Democratic candidate Yee Leng Xiong was elected the next Wisconsin state treasurer Tuesday, edging out Republican incumbent John Leiber. 
With 98% of the votes counted, AP called the race at 12:40 a.m. Wednesday.  Xiong led with just under 52% of the vote to just over 48% for Leiber.
Leiber had been the only Republican to win statewide office, other than Sen. Ron Johnson, in Wisconsin’s 2022 election.
The state treasurer is a relatively low-visibility office, but is included in the Wisconsin Constitution. An amendment that would have eliminated the office failed in 2018.
Besides signing state checks (technically done by machine), the primary duty of the treasurer is serving with the secretary of state and the attorney general on the state Board of Commissioners of Public Lands.
In his reelection campaign, Leiber emphasized focusing on the job of treasurer as it was outlined in the state constitution and statutes. He prided himself on not expanding the duties of the office and instead simply focusing on the job of treasurer as it was outlined in the state constitution and statutes.
Xiong campaigned saying he would seek to act as a watchdog over state finances, serving as “an independent voice for taxpayers and to make sure Wisconsin’s money is managed responsibly, transparently, and in the public interest.”
He cited his experience as a member of the Marathon County Board as well as a local school board treasurer. 
A Wausau native and the son of Hmong refugees from Southeast Asia, Xiong is the first person of Hmong descent to hold statewide office in Wisconsin.

title: Republicans win SC’s top accounting, investment banking roles
description: Republicans Curtis Loftis and Mike Burkhold won their races for South Carolina’s two top financial offices.
text:
South Carolina's next comptroller general, Mike Burkhold, speaks to supporters during an election night GOP watch party on Nov. 3, 2026, in Columbia, South Carolina. Behind him are Superintendent Ellen Weaver, Secretary of State Mark Hammond, Treasurer Curtis Loftis, and soon-to-be Agriculture Commissioner Cody Simpson. (Photo by John A. Carlos II/Special to the SC Daily Gazette)COLUMBIA — Republicans took South Carolina’s two top financial offices Tuesday.
Incumbent Treasure Curtis Loftis won a fifth term over Democrat Vincent Coe to remain the state’s chief banker. And Mike Burkhold, the founder of a healthcare technology company, beat out Democrat Tiffany Boozer, an accountant and auditor, to become the state’s lead accountant.

State Treasurer Curtis Loftis speaks to supporters during an election night GOP watch party on Nov. 3, 2026, in Columbia, South Carolina. (Photo by John A. Carlos II/Special to the SC Daily Gazette)

Loftis received 52.5% of the vote. And Burkhold won with 52% of the vote, according to unofficial results from the state Election Commission.
Burkhold takes over for Gov. Henry McMaster’s former budget director, Brian Gaines. The governor appointed Gaines in 2023 following previous Comptroller General Richard Eckstrom’s resignation amid a multibillion-dollar accounting error.
The two Republicans’ victories come as the state remains under a federal securities investigation launched in the wake of those accounting problems.
The issues stemmed from a decade-long changeover from the state’s legacy accounting system to a new one.
In 2023, it became public that a computer coding glitch in the comptroller’s office mistakenly double-counted public colleges’ revenue for more than a decade in the state’s annual financial report provided to Wall Street investors.
That error ended the tenure of Eckstrom, who had been the state’s comptroller since 2003.
Then in 2024, the focus of a Senate investigation into the matter shifted to the state Treasurer’s Office after more accounting errors made it appear the state had $1.8 billion sitting untouched in a fund with no record of its origins.
Investigators ultimately determined that the errors were all on paper and all but $200 million never actually existed.
Of all the state financial officials in office at the time, Loftis is the only one who remains, despite a Senate-led attempt at impeachment.

title: Gov. Shapiro  and Democrats on the brink of a sought-after trifecta in Harrisburg
description: For the first time since 1993, Democrats may have control over the governor’s office and the General Assembly.  Gov. text:
The Pennsylvania Capitol dome. (Photo by Peter Hall/Capital-Star)For the first time since 1993, Democrats may have control over the governor’s office and the General Assembly. 
Gov. Josh Shapiro, a Democrat, easily won reelection against Republican state Treasurer Stacy Garrity, while House Democrats appear on track to grow their majority in the House.
But Republicans’ 32 years leading the Senate appeared to come to an end Tuesday, with Democratic candidates claiming victory in a handful of critical races. 
As of 1:30 a.m., The Associated Press had not called the Senate or dozens of House races. 
Gov. Josh Shapiro cruises to a second term in Pennsylvania

Having control of both chambers could shore up Shapiro’s credentials if he decides to run for president in 2028, allowing him to potentially pass his top priorities without having to negotiate with Republicans. 
“For the first time in decades, Pennsylvanians used their power tonight to flip the state Senate so that we can deliver even more results for our communities,” Shapiro said in a statement just after midnight. 
“Now, with a Democratic trifecta, we’ll be able to get even more stuff done — from raising the minimum wage and lowering costs, to giving survivors their day in court, to building more housing and codifying abortion rights,” he continued. “I look forward to having them as strong partners in getting stuff done in Harrisburg and making real progress for all Pennsylvanians.”
All 203 House seats were on the line as well as 25 senators, but only a handful in either chamber were considered competitive. 
Going into the elections, Republicans held 27 seats in the Senate. Majority Leader Joe Pittman (R-Indiana) told reporters in September that he believed his party would grow their majority by one member, likely referring to Lancaster County’s Senate District 36.
Sen. James Malone, a Democrat, flipped the seat in a 2025 special election by 529 votes, but Rep. Tom Jones brought the district back into GOP control Tuesday. The Associated Press called the race at 1:29 a.m.

A Democratic pickup in Berks and Montgomery counties canceled out the GOP gain, however, when Democrat Chris Thomas defeated incumbent Republican Sen. Tracy Pennycuick. 
Democrats also prevailed in two other seats on the GOP radar: Senate District 14 (Lehigh and Northampton), held by Sen. Nick Miller; and Senate District 38 (Allegheny), held by Sen. Lindsey Williams. These were the only two competitive Senate races called by The AP as of publication. 
Democrats claimed to pick up three more seats, but The Associated Press had not called them in the early hours of Wednesday morning. They are:

Senate District 6 (Bucks), where Bucks County Clerk of Courts Eileen Hartnett Albillar challenged incumbent Republican Sen. Frank Farry. 
Senate District 16 (Bucks and Lehigh), where Lehigh County Controller Mark Pinsley challenged incumbent Republican Sen. Jarrett Coleman.
Senate District 40 (Lackawanna, Monroe and Wayne), where Brian Wrightson challenged incumbent Republican Sen. Rosemary Brown.

 House Democrats increase their majority

Democrats had a three-seat majority going into Tuesday following a special election in House District 12 earlier this year. But Rep. Brandon Dukes’ (D-Butler) time in the legislature appeared to be over, with Republican Scott Timko likely winning the rematch. 
Despite the loss, Democrats seemed poised to grow their majority, with a handful of candidates declaring victory well ahead of Associated Press calls. 
As of 1:30 a.m., AP had called four flips in favor of Democrats in House District 18 (Bucks), House District 44 (Allegheny), House District 160 (Chester and Delaware) and House District 137 (Northampton).
Democrats also claimed to flip House District 142 (Bucks), where Democrat Kristin Egan challenged incumbent Republican Rep. Joe Hogan.
The party also appeared to be in the lead in another five races over seats currently held by Republicans. 
Another three lawmakers — two Democrats and one Republican — opted to retire before this year’s elections. The AP projected a Democratic sweep, with wins in House District 45 (Allegheny), House District 121 (Luzerne) and House District 88 (Cumberland).

The AP called the elections for Idaho’s Congressional District 1 at 9:43 p.m. Tuesday for incumbent U.S. Rep. Russ Fulcher.

Independent U.S. Senate candidate Todd Achilles (second from right) chats with supporters at his election night watch party in Garden City on Nov. 3, 2026. Achilles challenged GOP U.S. Sen. Jim Risch in the general election. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)
Independent challenger Todd Achilles trailed with 35.7%, followed by independent Natalie Fleming and Libertarian Matt Loesby with 7% and 2 .9%, respectively. 
Risch, 86, is in his third, six-year term in the U.S. Senate. He is chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee and serves on the Energy and Natural Resources, Small Business and Entrepreneurship, Intelligence, and Ethics committees. He was first elected to the U.S. Senate in 2008. 
Achilles, 58, is a former Democratic state legislator from Boise who left the party and Statehouse seat to run for the U.S. Senate as an independent in 2025. His campaign outraised any recent U.S. Senate challenger in Idaho, collecting more than $1.8 million. During the campaign, Achilles publicly promised to not caucus with either party if elected, and to resign after two terms. 
Risch’s closest general election contest for U.S. Senate was in 2008, when he won with 57.7% against Democratic former Congressman Larry LaRocco, independent Rex Rammell, Libertarian Kent Marmon, and the independent candidate who legally changed his name to Pro-Life, according to the Idaho Secretary of State elections database. 
In the 2014 and 2020 general elections, Risch won with 65% and 63% of the vote, respectively. 
 Russ Fulcher wins fifth term as 1st Congressional District US House representative

Russ Fulcher
Voters on Tuesday chose Idaho Republican U.S. Rep. Russ Fulcher to serve a fifth term representing Idaho’s 1st Congressional District in the U.S. House. Fulcher received 62.5%, or 173,708 ballots, in his favor, preliminary results as of 11:37 p.m. show. 
He was followed by Democrat Kaylee Peterson, who had 30.58% of the vote, and independent Sarah Zabel with 6%. Constitution Party candidate Brendan Gomez had .88% of the vote. Gomez in September pleaded guilty to possession of child sex abuse material, but remained on the ballot because the deadline to withdraw had passed and felony convictions do not disqualify candidates from federal office under the U.S. Constitution. 
Fulcher, 64, was first elected in 2018. He sits on the House Committee on Energy and Commerce and the House Committee on Natural Resources.  
 Republican US House Rep. Mike Simpson leads in race to represent Idaho’s 2nd Congressional District

Mike Simpson (Photo courtesy of Mike Simpson)
Republican U.S House Rep. Mike Simpson, 76, was leading in his race as of about 11:40 p.m. Tuesday, but the race had not yet been called. 
Simpson is in his 14th, two-year term in Congress representing Idaho’s 2nd Congressional District. The incumbent had 49.88% of the vote, or 126,503 votes, against four challengers, results showed at 11:40 p.m.  
Simpson was trailed by Democrat Ellie Gilbreath, who had 42%, followed by independent Tripp Hutchinson with 3.45%, independent Emre Houser with 2.32%, and Libertarian Will Johanson with 2.13%. 
Simpson was first elected to the U.S. House in 1998. He serves as chairman of the House Interior and Environment Subcommittee on Appropriations.

Pate was seeking a fifth consecutive term in the office after previously serving a term from 1995-1999. He’s a former state senator and former mayor of Cedar Rapids, as well as the owner of Pate Asphalt.

text:
Abdul El-Sayed addresses supporters in Detroit early Wednesday, Nov. 4, 2026, as he declared victory over Republican nominee Mike Rogers in the U.S. Senate race. (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance)DETROIT — The progressive wave sweeping the nation reached its crest in Michigan early Wednesday as Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic U.S. Senate nominee, declared victory Republican former U.S. Rep. Mike Rogers.
“We just showed them that a movement of the people, by the people, and for the people will ultimately win,” El-Sayed told supporters gathered in Detroit. “They tried to confuse you. So let me just set the record this straight. I love America. I know exactly what America gave to me. Michiganders believe in Michigan, and I believe in Michiganders, and I am so honored that Michiganders believed in me.”
Unofficial results reported by the Associated Press show that with 80% of the vote counted, El-Sayed was leading Rogers 51.8% to 46.2% as of 1:50 a.m. The AP, however, had yet to officially call the race.
If confirmed, El-Sayed’s election would be historic: He would become the first Muslim U.S. senator when he takes office in January.
El-Sayed will succeed retiring U.S. Sen. Gary Peters (D-Bloomfield Township). It would also be the second loss in as many years for Rogers, who also lost in 2024 to now-U.S. Sen. Elissa Slotkin.
As a progressive closely associated with U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-New York) and U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vermont), El-Sayed will bring to Washington a focus on expanding the Affordable Care Act into a Medicare for All system, ending the war in Iran and renegotiating the U.S. relationship with Israel.
Throughout his political career, including the 2026 U.S. Senate campaign, El-Sayed has accused Israel of committing genocide against Palestinians during its war with Hamas in Gaza. While that determination remains controversial, it is supported by multiple international organizations including Amnesty International, Doctors Without Borders and a United Nations commission.
His victory comes in spite of the GOP narrative that Democratic Jewish voters were divided over El-Sayed as seen in polling conducted on behalf of The Jewish Majority, in which he “significantly underperformed Jocelyn Benson among Jewish early voters, receiving just 57% of the vote compared with 78% for Benson, a gap of more than 21 percentage points.”
Additionally, the polling, which was conducted October 25–31 among 482 Michigan Jewish early voters, said 99% of self-identified Jewish Democrats who did not vote for El-Sayed said they would have been likely to support a different Democratic nominee.
Although El-Sayed has fashioned himself as a capitalist concerned with ending corporate greed and allocation of wealth to the top 1% of earners, several of his campaign policies have been espoused or championed by democratic socialists. El-Sayed is not a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, but two of his closest allies, Ocasio-Cortez and U.S. Rep. Rashida Tlaib (D-Detroit), are associated with the organization and have praised his platform.
Working with Sanders in the Senate and Ocasio-Cortez in the House, El-Sayed aims to bring structural change to current U.S. policy if he can convince his fellow Democrats in the political center aisle to go further left.
The extent of that influence remains to be seen, but El-Sayed’s six-year Senate term could push Democrats toward policies many of their voters have advocated, particularly in Michigan. 
This is a developing story and will be updated as more information becomes available.

title: Arkansans approve 3 of 4 proposed ballot measures
description: Arkansans narrowly rejected a proposed constitutional amendment to create local economic development districts Tuesday, but approved three other ballot measures related to noncitizen voting, gun rights and water project funding. Issue 3 would have amended the state constitution to allow for local governments to create economic development districts and offer[...]
text:
Voters cast their ballots at the Pulaski Heights United Methodist Church in Little Rock, Arkansas, on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Katie Adkins/Arkansas Advocate)Arkansans narrowly rejected a proposed constitutional amendment to create local economic development districts Tuesday, but approved three other ballot measures related to noncitizen voting, gun rights and water project funding.
Issue 3 would have amended the state constitution to allow for local governments to create economic development districts and offer tax incentives to attract new business to the area. Nearly 50.7% of voters opposed the measure, according to results from secretary of state’s office. 
Supporters of the measure said it’s needed to make Arkansas more competitive, while opponents voiced concerns about being asked to approve a program whose rules would be developed by lawmakers at a later date.
Arkansas amendment would allow local economic development districts 

Meanwhile, voters approved Issue 1 and Issue 2 by wide margins. The measures earned 69% and 70% of the vote, respectively. 
Issue 1 adds language to the state constitution to explicitly prohibit noncitizens from voting in local and state elections. Arkansas’ constitution already requires voters to be U.S. citizens, and federal law prohibits noncitizens from voting in federal elections.
While no such laws exist in Arkansas, there are municipalities across the country that permit noncitizens to vote in local elections, such as school board elections. Proponents say this allows all citizen children to have a voice in their school district’s elected officials. However, Issue 1 supporters argue only citizens should be allowed to vote in elections.
Issue 2 amends Arkansas’ constitution, which already allows the right to bear arms, to expand that right to include the possession and use of ammunition and firearm accessories. It also makes the right to keep and bear arms “a natural, fundamental, and individual right that shall not be infringed.”
The measure’s sponsors say it’s needed to better protect the right to keep and bear arms, while critics argue it would make it more difficult to implement gun safety regulations.
Both constitutional amendments will go into effect Jan. 1. 
Arkansans also approved Issue 4, which authorizes the state to issue up to $500 million in general obligations bonds to pay for water, waste disposal, water pollution control, abatement and prevention, drainage, irrigation, flood control and wetlands and aquatic resources projects. 
The measure also allows bonds to be used to refinance previous bond issues.  
Voters approved the proposals with 56.4% of the vote, according to results from the secretary of state.
