Turnout is brisk, but voting is generally smooth, observers say


By Marty Schladen -  4:24 pm





With the exception of a bomb threat and scattered technical glitches, voting has been busy but smooth in Ohio, a coalition intended to ensure a trustworthy election reported Tuesday afternoon.
The Ohio Voter Rights Coalition has 1,100 volunteers for the heavily watched midterm. Most are working as poll monitors, but some are on call to quell disputes and others are attorneys available to settle legal questions.
Petee Talley of the Ohio Coalition on Black Voter Participation said there was an early afternoon bomb threat at a polling place located in Beverly Elementary School in Toledo. She said she hurried to the scene when she heard about it.
[Voter Guide: 2026 Ohio General Election Voter Guide: Races, deadlines, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
“People had ballots in their hands when they were evacuated,” Talley said.
It took about an hour for police to ensure the building was safe so voting could resume. Some voters waited, while others said they couldn’t, Talley said.
WTVG reported that some voting machines were moved outside so people could vote there while the building was closed.
Talley said she and poll workers collected the phone numbers they could, so they could call people who were forced to leave after the location reopened.
Steve David, state director of All Voting is Local, said that his group has heard a few complaints that votes registered differently on printouts from what voters said they touched on voting screens. 
“Make sure you check your ballot before you feed it into the tabulator,” he said. 
Maria Bruno of Ohioans Against Extremism said her group dispatched poll monitors who have spotted U.S. Justice Department personnel at voting locations in three counties. Dspite pre-election fears from some that they might try to intimidate voters, Bruno’s group hadn’t received any such complaints, she said.
Jen Miller of the League of Women Voters said her group has fielded hundreds of calls from people with limited mobility who want to vote curbside.
“They do not need to leave their car,” Miller said, adding that people should call their local board of elections for curbside assistance.
If you have questions or complaints about today’s voting, call the Election Protection Hotline 866-OUR-VOTE (866-687-8683.)
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.









Election monitors say few issues at Ohio polls, stand at the ready


By Susan Tebben -  12:02 pm





Members of the Ohio Voter Rights Coalition and its nonpartisan Election Protection program said there have been long lines at polling locations across Ohio, but the lines are moving and the few issues that have been seen are being resolved.
“In general, the strong turnout that we’ve seen during the early vote period has carried over to election day,” said Steve David, of All Voting is Local.
In a call with press on Tuesday morning, the coalition said there were no “significant disruptions” being reported at polling locations. The biggest activity has to do with changes to polling locations, an issue local boards of election and poll monitors with the coalition are helping voters handle.
“We’ve been getting folks out in the field to supplement the work that our BOEs have been doing, to provide additional signage and context to voters, encouraging them to check that they are at their correct polling location,” David said.
[Voter Guide: 2026 Ohio General Election Voter Guide: Races, deadlines, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
More than 1,000 people were trained by the election protection program to be poll monitors, peacekeepers, or legal monitors, according to Catherine Turcer, head of voting rights group Common Cause Ohio.
A new aspect of the coalition’s work this year has been organizing legal help before, during, and after Election Day.
“We are, to the degree humanly possible, doing our best to record and document everything that comes up on election day so that we are well-positioned for any legal fights that come subsequent to election day,” said Maria Bruno, a legal organizer for the coalition.
Poll monitors are also keeping an eye on U.S. Department of Justice representatives coming to counties in Ohio. The federal agency announced they would have monitors in Cuyahoga, Franklin, and Medina counties. This is not unusual; the Justice Department has monitors every election.
According to the announcement, monitors were placed in every state “checking for compliance with the federal voting rights statutes that fall within the jurisdiction of the Division.”
Bruno said voters should not engage with them, “but we definitely want to know if, in anyone’s voting experience, they are coming across any DOJ people.”
“Hopefully they should not be interfering with voting in any way, shape, or form, and they should not be broaching that 100-foot barrier around the polling location, so if anyone witnesses anything to that effect, we want to know immediately,” Bruno said.
Overall, voters have seemed enthusiastic when talking with poll monitors.
“We asked voters when they came out of the polling location, ‘how was the experience,'” said Petee Talley, of the Ohio Coalition on Black Civic Participation. “Most of them, if not all of them, had a very positive experience.”
Voting rights advocates also mentioned 100,000 absentee ballots that are currently outstanding in Ohio, ballots that will need to be dropped in a drop box or delivered directly to local boards of elections. Because the deadline for absentee ballots has changed to election day itself, mailing the ballots on Tuesday will likely mean they won’t be received in time to be counted.
While the poll monitors have not reported significant problems with photo identification requirements Ohio has in place, coalition members said the primary showed that the strictness of the law caused more than 700 provisional ballots to be thrown out.
“This is a persistent issue and we see the real impacts of that choice that the Ohio legislature made to pass that law,” David said.
Ohioans are required to present a valid photo ID, such as an unexpired drivers license, to the polls to verify identity. If voters don’t have a identification, they can vote using a provisional ballot (ballots that are counted after election day), and can bring proper identification to their local board of election within 4 days to ensure the ballot is counted.

Presidential years often see higher turnout than midterm election years such as 2026.
In 2022, the last midterm election year where statewide offices were up, 4.2 million Ohioans voted out of about 8 million registered, for a turnout rate of 52%.
In 2018, the last midterm election year where all statewide offices were up as open seats with no incumbents eligible to run due to term limits, nearly 4.5 million Ohioans voted, for a turnout rate of nearly 56%.
In 2014, just over 40% of registered Ohio voters cast ballots, and in 2010, just under 50% of registered Ohio voters cast ballots.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Democrats win US Senate, ending Republican dominance by harnessing voters’ frustration with Trump
authors: By Jill Colvin, Mary Clare Jalonick and Will Weissert,  Associated Press
description: Democratic Senate candidate Texas state Rep. James Talarico speaks at an election night event in Austin, Texas, Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026.
text:
WASHINGTON — Democrats won control of the U.S. Senate and were getting closer to taking a House majority on Tuesday night, delivering a shockingly decisive rebuke of Republican governance in Washington and ushering in a new era of congressional resistance to President Donald Trump.
The midterm elections displayed voters’ deep frustration with high prices, the war in Iran and concerns about government corruption.
Even Republican Sen. Susan Collins of Maine, a battle-tested survivor of difficult elections, lost to Democrat Troy Jackson.
The results from across the country were a major blow to Trump, who spent nearly every day of the last month holding rallies to energize his supporters but was unable to stop a wipeout.
Democrats have signaled they’ll use a foothold in Congress to ensure Trump’s final two years in office feature a series of investigations against top members of his administration and deeper scrutiny of how he’s enriched his family. In celebratory events Tuesday night, Democratic Senate Leader Chuck Schumer called it a “generational remake of the Senate map.” Democratic House Leader Hakeem Jeffries said “the American people are crying out for transformational change.”
Trump immediately sought to shift blame for his party’s losses, posting on his social media site before polls even closed on the West Coast that he wasn’t on the ballot — even though he spent weeks asking voters to pretend like he was. He vowed to veto Democrat-controlled legislation, sharing a picture of a red baseball cap with “veto” stenciled in the style of his trademark “Make America Great Again” campaign swag.
In a late-night phone interview with Fox News, Trump said he didn’t consider the elections to be a personal defeat. Voters, he said, “didn’t like the candidates.”
Democrats had braced for Trump to again try to undermine the results if they won after he warned that noncitizens would cast ballots en masse and filed lawsuits in Alaska and California. Instead, he said on Fox that he would accept them.
Still, the Republican-controlled Congress had acted as a rubber stamp to much of Trump’s agenda. While the president has proven adept at steamrolling efforts to rein him in, Democrats will seek to reshape the remainder of his term. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and tech titan Elon Musk, a former top Trump adviser, are among possible targets for investigations.
Despite the results, Senate Majority Leader John Thune wrote on X that “Senate Republicans will not stand idly by as the far-left, socialist wing of the Democrat Party attempts to unwind everything we’ve done.” He said they will work with Trump “to stop the worst impulses of Democrat extremism.”
Democrats charted an extraordinary path to Senate victory
Midterm elections are typically difficult for the president’s party, but Republicans had originally expected that their Senate majority was safe. Instead, Democrats marched through some of the most conservative states in the nation.
Josh Turek defeated Rep. Ashley Hinson in Iowa, while Adam Hamilton ousted Sen. Roger Marshall in Kansas to become the state’s first Democratic senator since 1932. A cascade of surprising Democratic victories included James Talarico defeating Ken Paxton in Texas, Annie Andrews upsetting Darline Graham in South Carolina, Sherrod Brown topping Sen. Jon Husted in Ohio and Roy Cooper taking an open North Carolina seat.
Trump played an outsized role in the Texas, North Carolina and South Carolina races. He endorsed Paxton and helped him defeat incumbent Sen. John Cornyn in the Texas primary. He sharply criticized North Carolina Republican Sen. Thom Tillis, who opted not to seek reelection. He also supported Graham, despite concerns about her candidacy.
Georgia Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff of Georgia walks out during an election night event, Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026, in Atlanta.  Credit: AP Photo/Mike Stewart
Less of a surprise was Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff winning reelection in Georgia, defeating Rep. Mike Collins. Rep. Chris Pappas also won a Senate race in New Hampshire, defeating former Sen. John Sununu to replace retiring Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen.
In the House, defeated Republicans included Rep. Tom Kean of New Jersey, who missed four months of votes in Washington this year as he underwent treatment for depression — a diagnosis he did not disclose until his return. Democrats who won included Jamie Ager over Jennifer Capps Balkcom in North Carolina and Lindsay James over Joe Mitchell in Iowa.
South Carolina Democratic Senate candidate Dr. Annie Andrews takes the stage at an election night event in Charleston, S.C., Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. Credit: AP Photo/Mic Smith
Bracing for a tough night, Republicans had spent the campaign’s final stretch pumping tens of millions of dollars into states and districts that Trump won handily two years ago, as Trump campaigned in heavily red areas. But even Republicans’ money advantage didn’t stem the Democratic tide.
“I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!” Trump wrote on his social media site.
The electorate is frustrated and unhappy
Voters were sour heading into Tuesday, with the midterm electorate deeply unhappy with the country’s direction and pessimistic about the future, according to The AP Voter Poll.
Most said they feel frustrated, with about three-quarters saying they feel “angry” or “dissatisfied” with the country’s current trajectory. Dissatisfaction was particularly high in blue states, but even in red states, a majority of voters were at least “dissatisfied.”
The economy was key to Trump’s White House comeback two years ago. But the poll found that three-quarters of voters say the economy is “not so good” or “poor.” About 8 in 10 say inflation has caused a “severe” or “moderate” financial hardship for their households.
Government corruption was also a big issue with voters. Roughly half cited it and the cost of living as “crucial” to their vote for Congress — higher than immigration enforcement policies, the war in Iran and artificial intelligence data centers. About 6 in 10 voters said Trump prioritizes his own personal interests more than the country’s interests.
Despite their relative advantage on issues, the Democratic Party is not much more popular with voters than the Republicans. Just under half of voters have a “somewhat” or “strongly” favorable view of the Democratic Party, while about 4 in 10 view Republicans positively.
Republicans tried to buck historical midterm precedent with an aggressive redistricting effort aimed at creating a more favorable congressional map. But in Florida and Texas, where Republicans hoped to pick up as many as nine seats, the plan looked to be falling short, with Democrats picking up targeted districts.
The GOP could still notch some key Senate wins
Outstanding Senate battlegrounds include Alaska, where the Trump administration filed a lawsuit to block certification of Senate results if Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan loses the race, citing the presence of a second candidate named Dan Sullivan on the ballot.
Republicans also hoped to pick up Michigan, where Mike Rogers faces progressive Abdul El-Sayed — one of a crop of left-wing candidates who prevailed in Democratic primaries. El-Sayed’s former primary opponent, Haley Stevens, upended the race by endorsing Rogers, renewing focus on tensions over Israel and the party’s direction.
Beyond Washington, 36 states elected governors. Democrats Josh Shapiro in Pennsylvania, JB Pritzker in Illinois, Wes Moore in Maryland, Maura Healey in Massachusetts and Kathy Hochul in New York all won reelection. In a stunning upset in Texas, Gina Hinojosa defeated Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, who was seeking a fourth term.
In Ohio, Republican Vivek Ramaswamy lost to Democrat Amy Acton after his campaign faced backlash for an ad featuring Acton’s estranged mother, who lost custody of Acton decades ago after her husband, Acton’s stepfather, was indicted for raping Acton as a child.
Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms of Georgia will be the first Black female governor of any state. In neighboring Florida, Byron Donalds became the nation’s first Black Republican to be elected governor.
Georgia Democratic gubernatorial candidate Keisha Lance Bottoms speaks at an election night event, Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026, in Atlanta. (AP Photo/Brynn Anderson)
House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York, in line to make history as the nation’s first Black speaker of the House if his party sweeps to power, has outlined a 100-day agenda focused on lowering the cost of living and aggressively overseeing the Trump administration.
The especially strong showing for Democrats could boost the party’s large crop of potential presidential candidates. It may also complicate the paths of Vice President JD Vance and other Republicans who may have been looking to turn their loyalty to Trump into momentum.
___
Associated Press journalists Joey Cappelletti, Lisa Mascaro, Linley Sanders, Aaron Kessler and Ali Swenson in Washington; Cody Jackson in Palm Beach Gardens, Fla.; and Allen Breed in Raleigh, N.C., contributed.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Democrats win control of Wisconsin Legislature, cementing first Democratic trifecta in 16 years
description: Democrats won control of the Wisconsin Senate and Assembly Tuesday night, along with the governor’s race — cementing Democratic trifecta control of state government for the first time in over 16 years. Democratic candidates won the majority of their targeted seats — claiming open seats and ousting longtime Republican incumbents. Democratic Senate Leader Dian[...]
text:
Newly elected Gov. David Crowley and Lt. Gov. Sarah Godlewski alongside Sen. Dianne Hesselbein, Rep. Greta Neubauer and Democratic Party of Wisconsin Chair Devin Remiker celebrate after winning the 2026 election. (Photo | Isiah Holmes/Wisconsin Examiner)Democrats won control of the Wisconsin Senate and Assembly Tuesday night, along with the governor’s race — cementing Democratic trifecta control of state government for the first time in over 16 years.
Democratic candidates won the majority of their targeted seats — claiming open seats and ousting longtime Republican incumbents.
Democratic Senate Leader Dianne Hesselbein declared victory in a statement a little before 10 p.m.
“For two years we’ve said that the Wisconsin Senate was the most flippable chamber in the country, and tonight voters across the state proved that to be true,” Hesselbein said. “We’re grateful that Wisconsinites have placed their trust in Senate Democrats to deliver progress in our state; now it’s time to get to work cutting costs and building a stronger future for our hardworking men and women.”
Assembly Democrats declared victory a little after 11 p.m. Democratic Leader Greta Neubauer (D-Racine) said in a statement that she was proud of everyone who stepped up to run for the Assembly. 
“They understood that this would be hard, that they would have to knock on doors every single day, face millions of dollars in attack ads, have to take time away from their families, and potentially face threats or violence. But they did it anyway, because they understood that this was our best shot in decades — our shot to win the Democratic trifecta, our shot to set Wisconsin on a new path. Our candidates and our members believe the people of our state deserve better,” Neubauer said. “And Wisconsin does deserve better. With this trifecta, we will end decades of Republican obstruction and build great schools, help families feel financially secure and to save for retirement. We will hold big tech accountable, protect our rights and freedoms, and make Wisconsin a state where everyone can thrive.” 
Democrats have not held control of the state Senate or Assembly since 2010, but new legislative maps helped put the Legislature in play this year. The maps, which were passed by the Republican-led Legislature and signed by Gov. Tony Evers, were adopted in 2024 after Wisconsin’s previous legislative maps were found by the state Supreme Court to be an unconstitutional gerrymander.
In the 2024 election, Democrats flipped 10 Assembly seats, slashing the Republican majority from 64 seats to 54 seats and the state Senate went from a 22-seat Republican supermajority to an 18-seat Republican majority. The close margin increased Democrats’ influence on issues including the state budget over the last two years. 
Headed into the election, Democrats were optimistic about their chances of taking control. 
The Democratic-led Legislature will work alongside Democratic Governor-elect David Crowley, who defeated Republican Tom Tiffany. 
“We know that people will be counting on us to deliver, and we will deliver. Alongside Governor David Crowley and our Democratic colleagues in the Senate, we will show that government can be a force for good and that things can be different with Democrats in charge,” Neubauer said. “Tonight we celebrate, tomorrow we get to work.” 
Chair of the Democratic Party of Wisconsin Devin Remiker said in a statement that voters had sent “a resounding message that they are tired of a broken political system, where politicians put billionaires, special interests, and their own self-interest ahead of working families.”
“They saw Republicans in the Legislature gerrymander themselves into power, block Governor Evers at every turn, and sit on their hands while costs went up. They saw three billionaires try to buy the governor’s office for Tom Tiffany. And they chose a different direction,” Remiker said. “Now it’s time to deliver. Governor-elect David Crowley, Lieutenant Governor-elect Sarah Godlewski, Senate Democratic Leader Dianne Hesselbein, and Assembly Democratic Leader Greta Neubauer will work together to lower costs, make healthcare more affordable and accessible, invest in our public schools, and build an economy that works for all Wisconsinites.” 
Here are the results in districts that were decisive in determining control:

In Senate District 31, The Associated Press called the race for Sen Jeff Smith (D-Brunswick). He defeated a challenge from Republican Michele Magadance Skinner, an Eau Claire County board member to win another term in office. The district covers Eau Claire County and parts of Dunn, Trempealeau and Chippewa counties. With more than 95% reporting, Smith brought in 58% of the vote while Skinner brought in 42%. 
In Senate District 5, state Rep. Robyn Vining (D-Wauwatosa) defeated Republican Mike Roberts, a businessman and healthcare professional from Pewaukee. The race for the seat, which covers Wauwatosa and other parts of Milwaukee County, was open after Sen. Rob Hutton opted not to run for reelection. With 94% reporting according to The Associated Press, Vining had brought in 57% of the vote and Roberts had brought in 43%. 
In Senate District 21, Democrat Trevor Jung, the former Racine transit and mobility director, defeated Republican businessman Jim Croft. This southeast district that includes part of Racine and Milwaukee Counties was open due to Sen. Van Wanggaard (R-Racine) retiring. With 90% reporting, Jung had brought in 58% of the vote while Croft had brought in 42%.
In Senate District 17, state Rep. Jenna Jacobson (D-Oregon) was leading state Sen. Howard Marklein (R-Spring Green) a little before 11 p.m. With more than 95% reporting according to The Associated Press, Jacobson had brought in 53% of the vote and Marklein had brought in 47%. The district represents Iowa, Lafayette, Green, Crawford and Grant counties as well as parts of Dane County.
In Assembly District 21, Democrat Daniel Bukiewicz, the mayor of Oak Creek, defeated Dylan Pfaffenbach, a Republican student at Carroll University. The race for the seat was open following the retirement of Rep. Jessie Rodriguez, a longtime Republican incumbent. With 84% reporting according to the Associated Press, Bukiewicz brought in 60% of the vote while Pfaffenbach brought in 40%.


In Assembly District 30, incumbent Rep. Shannon Zimmerman (R-River Falls), who was first elected in 2016, lost his reelection bid to Democratic challenger Kevin Knoke, a veteran and educator from Hudson. Zimmerman was first elected in 2016 and served on the Joint Finance Committee. With more than 95% reporting according to the Associated Press, Knoke brought in 53% of the vote while Zimmerman brought in 47%. 
In Assembly District 51, Rep. Todd Novak (R-Dodgeville) lost to Democratic challenger Ben Gruber, a conservation warden in Wisconsin who is member of AFSCME Local 1215. With 92% reporting according to the Associated Press, Gruber brought in 55% of the vote while Novak brought in 43%. 
In Assembly District 53, Republican David Daniels lost to Democrat Becky Nichols, a former Menasha city council member. The race was open due to the retirement of incumbent Rep. Dean Kaufert (R-Neenah). With more than 95% reporting according to the Associated Press, Nichols brought in 55% of the vote while Daniels brought in 39%.
In Assembly District 61, Rep. Bob Donovan (R-Greenfield) lost his reelection bid to Democratic challenger Ben Brist, an army veteran. With 88% reporting according to the Associated Press, Brist brought in 56% of the vote while Donovan brought in 44%. 
In Assembly District 85, Rep. Patrick Snyder (R-Weston) lost his reelection bid to challenger Democrat John Kroll, a Marathon county board supervisor. Snyder, who was first elected in 2016, ran his campaign by emphasizing his work across the aisle. With more than 95% reporting according to the Associated Press, Kroll brought in 54% of the vote while Snyder brought in 46%.
In Assembly District 88, Rep. Benjamin Franklin (R-De Pere) lost his reelection bid to Democrat Brandy Tollefson, a De Pere school board member. With more than 95% reporting according to the Associated Press, Tollefson brought in 54% of the vote while Franklin brought in 46%.
In Assembly District 89, Rep. Ryan Spaude (D-Ashwaubenon) fended off a challenge from Republican challenger Bobby Lindsey, a retired law enforcement professional and a Marine Corps veteran.  With more than 95% reporting according to the Associated Press, Spaude brought in 56% of the vote while Lindsey brought in 44%.
In Assembly District 92, Rep. Clint Moses (R-Menomonie) lost his bid for reelection to Democratic challenger Jeremiah Fredrickson, a fish farmer from Elk Mound. With more than 95% reporting according to the Associated Press, Fredrickson brought in 53% of the vote while Moses brought in 47%.
In Assembly District 94, Democratic Rep. Steve Doyle defeated Republican challenger Keith Purnell, an Army veteran. Doyle was first elected to the Assembly during a May 2011 special election and has been reelected since. With more than 95% reporting according to the Associated Press, Doyle brought in 57% of the vote while Purnell brought in 43%.

title: Nebraska voters appear to say ‘no’ to legalizing online sports betting
description: Though margins were still slim late Tuesday night, Nebraska voters were on track to reject a pair of ballot measures looking to legalize and regulate online sports betting, according to unofficial results. Initiative Measures 440 and 441 would together amend the Nebraska Constitution and state law, respectively, to legalize and regulate online sports wagers.[...]
text:
A row of slot machines stands at Harrah's casino in New Orleans. Three temporary casinos are now open in Nebraska with other communities, including Ogallala and Bellevue, seeking state permission to build. (Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)Though margins were still slim late Tuesday night, Nebraska voters were on track to reject a pair of ballot measures looking to legalize and regulate online sports betting, according to unofficial results.
Initiative Measures 440 and 441 would together amend the Nebraska Constitution and state law, respectively, to legalize and regulate online sports wagers. Initiative 440 had 239,331 votes “for” and 285,520 “against,” while Initiative 441 had 241,599 votes “for” and 283,159 “against” as of midnight.




Initiative sponsor Jordan McGrain said it was tough to make a call on either ballot measure, but acknowledged that the results as of midnight seemed to be “pretty clear.” He said similar measures that passed in other states succeeded by slim margins; however, he also said Nebraska voters did not appear to respond to the same arguments.
In 2020, Nebraskans authorized casino gambling at the state’s existing five racetracks. Under current state law, annual gaming revenue is taxed at 20%, and 70% of that amount is directed to property tax relief credits.
Since then, there have been multiple attempts in the Nebraska Legislature to legalize online sports betting, but all have been foiled. The repeated failures prompted a petition drive to put the issue on the ballot, under the group Tax Relief Nebraska.
Supporters largely argued that Nebraskans would participate in online wagering regardless of state law, which sends the tax revenue to other states like Iowa that have legalized the practice. Critics have long argued that the possible revenue benefits do not outweigh the social costs of the state effectively encouraging gambling.
Tax Relief Nebraska’s campaign was loudly opposed by a collection of advocacy groups and state officials, and the opposition continued to intensify once the petitions garnered enough signatures to qualify for the ballot. This included a dedicated opposition campaign called Save Nebraska Sports, which included backers such as State Auditor Mike Foley and Treasurer Joey Spellerberg.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
Spellerberg celebrated the initiatives’ apparent failure during his victory speech for the state treasurer’s race Tuesday night. He described the gambling battle as a “David and Goliath” matchup, saying Save Nebraska Sports was outspent 20-1 by Tax Relief Nebraska.
Spellerberg said the results were a sign that Nebraskans didn’t want the harmful impacts of gambling in their state. Despite the advertising claims that legalizing online sports betting would help cut property taxes, Spellerberg said, he believed voters understood that the actual tax benefits would be negligible.
“Voters in Nebraska looked right past that,” Spellerberg said.

Voters cast their ballots at the Pulaski Heights United Methodist Church in Little Rock, Arkansas, on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Katie Adkins/Arkansas Advocate)
Arkansas voters have approved one constitutional amendment explicitly banning noncitizens from voting in state and local elections, and another expanding the right to bear arms in the state’s constitution.
The Associated Press announced voters’ passage of Issue 1 and 2 around 9 p.m. Tuesday. These are two of the four measures included on the ballot.
Issue 1 adds language to the state Constitution to explicitly prohibit noncitizens from voting in local and state elections. Arkansas’ constitution already requires voters to be U.S. citizens, and federal law prohibits noncitizens from voting in federal elections.
While no such laws exist in Arkansas, there are municipalities across the country that permit noncitizens to vote in local elections, such as school board elections. Proponents say this allows all citizen children to have a voice in their school district’s elected officials. However, Issue 1 supporters argue only citizens should be allowed to vote in elections.
Issue 2 amends Arkansas’ constitution, which already allows the right to bear arms, to expand that right to include the possession and use of ammunition and firearm accessories. It also makes the right to keep and bear arms “a natural, fundamental, and individual right that shall not be infringed.”
The measure’s sponsors say it’s needed to better protect the right to keep and bear arms, while critics argue it would make it more difficult to implement gun safety regulations.

Candidate for Arkansas Secretary of State Sen. Kim Hammer (R) answers questions at the debate aginst opponents Kelly Grappe (D), and Michael Pakko (L) on Thursday, Oct. 15, 2026 at the Arkansas TV studios in Conway, Arkansas. (Photo by Katie Adkins/Arkansas Advocate)Republican state Sen. Kim Hammer, who sponsored laws restricting Arkansas’ ballot initiative process and requiring an anti-abortion monument on Capitol grounds, was elected secretary of state Tuesday.
Hammer defeated Democrat Kelly Grappe and Libertarian Michael Pakko in the race to be the state’s top election official. Hammer won with nearly 56% of the vote, according to results from the secretary of state’s office.
Hammer succeeds Republican Secretary of State Cole Jester, who defeated Libertarian Christopher Olson for state land commissioner in Tuesday’s election.
Hammer, who has served in the state Legislature since 2011, sponsored several laws restricting the initiative process that have been the subject of legal challenges. A federal judge has blocked several of the laws and ruled them unconstitutional, including ones requiring all canvassers to be Arkansas residents and paid canvassers working on a statewide initiative petition or referendum to be residents living in the state. That ruling has been appealed to the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals. 
Grappe and Pakko criticized Hammer over his work on the initiative changes, saying it hurt the direct democracy process. Hammer has said the measures ensure the security of the state’s election process.
Hammer is also the sponsor of the 2023 law that requires the state to allow a privately-funded anti-abortion monument on the Capitol grounds. Arkansas would be the first state with such a monument on state grounds.
Hammer won the race as Republican President Donald Trump has tried to exert more federal control over elections. The president earlier this year said Republicans should nationalize elections, and the GOP has been pushing for more voting restrictions at the federal level.
Hammer has said he doesn’t believe federal involvement was warranted and that Arkansas’ elections are already secure. 
Arkansas has one of the lowest voter turnout rates in the country, a distinction that all three candidates said they hoped to address if elected. Hammer has said he wants to expand voter outreach efforts with schools, community groups and others throughout the year, not just close to Election Day.
Hammer’s also said he wants to address a lack of parking at the state Capitol and that a long-term solution may need to be a parking deck for visitors and employees.

Russo told a crowd at the Ohio Democratic Party’s election night party that voters chose “a picture that is rooted in fairness, accessibility, and transparency, and I am […]
text:
Ohio Secretary of State-elect Allison Russo gives her victory speech. (Photo by Megan Henry, Ohio Capital Journal). Ohio Democratic lawmaker Allison Russo won election as the next Ohio Secretary of State on Tuesday, following a concession by opponent and current Ohio Treasurer Robert Sprague.
Russo told a crowd at the Ohio Democratic Party’s election night party that voters chose “a picture that is rooted in fairness, accessibility, and transparency, and I am so deeply honored and profoundly humbled to stand before you tonight as your next secretary of state.”
Russo said the office of secretary of state “touches the core of our daily lives.”
“And tonight, Ohioans have sent a very, very clear message, and that is that you want election systems that are secure, efficient, accessible, transparent for every eligible voter, not matter where they live or how they vote,” she said.
Just days before Election Day, a non-partisan election forecaster called Sabato’s Crystal Ball, which is at the University of Virginia’s Center for Politics, said the race was no longer leaning toward a Republican win, but was considered a toss-up.
Russo is currently in the Ohio House, and spent time during her tenure there as House Minority Leader. Sprague was also in the Ohio House before coming into statewide office.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
In his concession speech on Tuesday night, Sprague said every Republican on the ballot “knew going into this election that we were going to face significant headwinds, and they turned out to be stronger than any of us understood.”
“This was a national wave, and there are a number of good, Republican public servants who deeply love Ohio who were swept away tonight,” Sprague said.
He congratulated Russo, and said the Republican Party has “some soul searching ahead of us.”
The secretary of state has been a Republican since 2011, when current GOP Ohio U.S. Sen. Jon Husted took over from Democrat and current Ohio Supreme Court Justice Jennifer Brunner.
Husted was followed in 2019 by the current Republican, Secretary of State Frank LaRose.
Before Brunner was in office, Republicans Ken Blackwell and former governor Bob Taft had the seat. Taft took over for Democrat Sherrod Brown, who went on to become a U.S. senator, a position he won back from Husted in Tuesday’s unofficial results.
Megan Henry contributed to this article.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Democrats flip 16 Missouri House seats, ending Republican supermajority
description: The blue wave reached the steps of the Missouri Governor’s Mansion Tuesday when Democrats won the state House seat representing downtown Jefferson City on their way to flipping 16 seats from Republicans across the state. Republican Gov. Mike Kehoe’s official residence will be represented by Suzanne Luther, a former member of the Jefferson City Board […]
text:
Democrats won 17 seats in the Missouri House on Tuesday, breaking the Republican supermajority (Tim Bommel/Missouri House Communications).The blue wave reached the steps of the Missouri Governor’s Mansion Tuesday when Democrats won the state House seat representing downtown Jefferson City on their way to flipping 16 seats from Republicans across the state.
Republican Gov. Mike Kehoe’s official residence will be represented by Suzanne Luther, a former member of the Jefferson City Board of Education who defeated Republican Shane Kampeter.
Tuesday’s results broke the Republican’s two-thirds supermajority, which has been in place since 2012. And it was almost a mirror image of the Republican’s biggest night this century, when the GOP won 17 seats in 2010. 
The House will have 95 Republicans and 68 Democrats when it convenes in January.
“It feels really, really good to look towards the next General Assembly and not be a member of a super minority party,” said state Rep. Ashley Aune of Kansas City, the House Democratic floor leader. “It’s really exciting and I’m very, very heartened by the results so far tonight.”
In addition to taking seats they targeted, Democrats scored surprising victories in safe Republican seats in Cass County, where Stacy Czar of Belton defeated Steve Baker for the open 56th District seat. Democrats also won three seats in St. Charles County, where they had been shut out for 20 years.
Republicans did not flip any Democrat-held seat.
Notable Republican losses include state Rep. Brad Christ of St. Louis County in the 96th District, who was seeking a leadership position, and Maryellen Murphy, who was seeking to replace her husband James Murphy in the 94th District.
When Tuesday began, Republicans were assured five seats and Democrats were sure to win 32 in districts where the candidate was unopposed or faced only minor party opposition.
Both parties fielded candidates in 87 districts considered safe for the incumbent party, and those districts are where Republicans had the advantage that sustained their majority.
Only nine of those districts are safe Democratic seats, while Republicans held 78 seats considered safe.
Statewide, The Independent rated 39 districts as less than safe for the incumbent party. Of those, the national Democratic Legislative Campaign Committee targeted 12, including 11 held by Republicans.
The House Republican Campaign Committee focused on defending 13 seats, including 10 on the Democrats’ list, while targeting a single Democrat for defeat.
Democrats won almost every seat they targeted that was held by Republicans and held every seat they were defending.
The safe seats — and a huge fundraising advantage — were the GOP’s firewall to keep the majority even if the supermajority was lost.
Including the committees each party maintains to help members generally, candidates and incumbents on Tuesday’s ballot for the Missouri House raised $24.9 million since the start of 2025. The last full reports, covering the period up to Oct. 22, showed $11.1 million had been spent and $6.6 million had been passed on as contributions to other committees.
Republican candidates, their affiliated PACs and the House Republican Campaign Committee raised $17.7 million. Republicans spent $6.5 million and passed $5.8 million on to other committees, much of it going to the HRCC.
Democratic candidates and PACs, and the House Democratic Action Fund, raised $7.1 million. Candidates and the HDAF spent $4.6 million and reported making $767,000 in contributions.
Whether the shift is a part of a longer-term move to the Democrats will be seen in future elections. Voters are slow to change the party in power in Jefferson City.
Democrats won a Missouri House majority in every election from 1954 to 2000 and Republicans have won it in every election since. Democrats last won a supermajority in 1986.
Newly elected members from both parties will gather in Jefferson City Wednesday and Thursday to select leaders for the upcoming session.

title: Yes votes lead for Iowa constitutional amendment limiting income tax increases
description: Iowa lawmakers are likely to need a supermajority vote to increase personal and corporate income taxes after approval for a proposed constitutional amendment took the lead Tuesday night. Amendment 1 had received 55% yes votes to 45% no votes with 84% of votes counted as of 12:05 a.m., according to unofficial results from the Associated […]
text:
Amendment 1 would amend Iowa's constitution to require a supermajority vote of state lawmakers to raise personal or corporate income taxes. (Photo illustration with Capitol photo by Iowa Capital Dispatch and background via Getty Images)Iowa lawmakers are likely to need a supermajority vote to increase personal and corporate income taxes after approval for a proposed constitutional amendment took the lead Tuesday night.
Amendment 1 had received 55% yes votes to 45% no votes with 84% of votes counted as of 12:05 a.m., according to unofficial results from the Associated Press.
The amendment would require a two-thirds majority of both the Iowa House and Senate to increase personal or corporate income taxes.
Supporters, mostly Republicans, said imposing the restriction in the state constitution would preserve GOP-backed tax policies, including 3.8% flat-rate income tax approved in 2025. They argue that lawmakers could still raise the income tax as a last resort but would need broad, bipartisan support.

Democrats and other opponents of the amendment said it would lock in unsustainable tax cuts that largely benefitted Iowa’s highest income earners while creating a billion-dollar state budget deficit. They argue that needed revenue increases would fall on sales taxes and fees that disproportionally affect lower-income Iowans, while spending cuts would hit public schools and services that aid vulnerable residents.
Changing Iowa’s constitution is a multiyear process.  A resolution proposing a constitutional amendment must pass two consecutive general assemblies in identical form before going to voters in a general election.
Amendment 1 would be Iowa’s 52nd constitutional amendment.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Wisconsin voters pass two of three constitutional amendments
description: Wisconsin voters approved two of the three constitutional amendments on the ballot on Tuesday.  Over the last eight years, the Republican-controlled Legislature has frequently used the state’s constitutional amendment process to circumvent the veto pen of Democratic Gov. Tony Evers. Tuesday’s results give the Republicans a nine for 15 record in those efforts[...]
text:
A handmade sign outside a Madison home urges no votes on Wisconsin's three proposed constitutional amendments. (Photo by Henry Redman/Wisconsin Examiner)Wisconsin voters approved two of the three constitutional amendments on the ballot on Tuesday. 
Over the last eight years, the Republican-controlled Legislature has frequently used the state’s constitutional amendment process to circumvent the veto pen of Democratic Gov. Tony Evers. Tuesday’s results give the Republicans a nine for 15 record in those efforts. 
Under state law, a proposal to amend the state Constitution must be passed in two consecutive legislative terms and then approved by the voters. 
Anti-equity 
Voters approved an amendment that will prohibit state and local governments from discriminating against or granting preferential treatment to any groups based on race, sex, color, ethnicity, or national origin in public employment, public education, public contracting, or public administration. 
Of the three amendments on the ballot, this one passed the most easily, with voters approving the measure with 57% of the vote, as of 12:30 a.m.
The amendment is the product of Republican antagonism against diversity, equity and inclusion policies in recent years. GOP lawmakers have pointed to money spent by county governments on diversity programs as an expense that the amendment will put a stop to. 
Republicans have said government spending decisions should be based on merit instead of membership of a specific group. 
Opponents of the amendment argued that the state and federal constitutions already prohibit discrimination. They’ve also pointed to popular programs across state and local government that could now be considered illegal — including women’s health initiatives and childcare programs such as Head Start — and made the case that the government should be allowed to address disparities such as the high rate of Black maternal mortality in Wisconsin. 
Places of worship 
With a 52% margin, Wisconsin voters narrowly rejected a proposed amendment that would have prohibited the government from shutting down places of worship during a state of emergency. 
The proposal was introduced by Republican lawmakers angry that government orders during the COVID-19 pandemic closed churches across the state. Those closures sparked widespread protests from conservatives in the state. 
Opponents of the amendment had argued the state needs tools to protect public health in the event of an emergency. 
Partial veto 
Voters narrowly approved a constitutional amendment that will limit the governor’s partial veto authority, preventing its use to introduce new taxes or fees. The measure passed with 51% of the vote. 
The amendment was proposed after Gov. Tony Evers used his veto pen to change the 2023-25 biennial budget to allow schools to raise revenue limits by $325 per pupil per year for the next 400 years. Republicans across the state have frequently complained about the “400-year tax,” including Tom Tiffany, who made repealing the veto a major part of his run for governor. 
Governors of both parties have used the partial veto to extend provisions for hundreds of years. Republican Gov. Scott Walker used the power to extend a one-year moratorium on school referendum requests for energy efficiency projects, transforming it into a 1,000-year moratorium.
The partial veto authority of Wisconsin’s governor has been rolled back several times through the courts and the constitutional amendment process during the state’s history. Opponents of the amendment compared it to previous actions by Republican lawmakers to limit the authority of the governor after Evers, a Democrat, took office.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Benson wins key victory over James as Michigan’s next governor, continuing Dem control
description: Democratic nominee and Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson has declared victory in Michigan’s gubernatorial election, addressing supporters early Wednesday in Detroit. “This election, from the western reaches of the Upper Peninsula to downtown Detroit, voters sent a clear message: They want leaders who will fight for them, fight to lower costs, fight to grow o[...]
text:
Jocelyn Benson addresses supporters in Detroit in the early morning hours of Wed., Nov. 4, 2026 after declaring victory in the Michigan gubernatorial race. (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance)Democratic nominee and Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson has declared victory in Michigan’s gubernatorial election, addressing supporters early Wednesday in Detroit.
“This election, from the western reaches of the Upper Peninsula to downtown Detroit, voters sent a clear message: They want leaders who will fight for them, fight to lower costs, fight to grow our economy, fight the corruption that too often protects the powerful and hurts the people. And in this election, we showed the nation that in our democracy, the power of the people will always rule the day,” Benson said.
The Associated Press officially called the race for Benson at 1:45 a.m., with unofficial results showing her out ahead of James 53.7% to 44.6%. Benson has already launched a website with information about the transition and opportunities to join the incoming administration.
GOP gubernatorial nominee John James leaves the stage with his wife Elizabeth after talking to supporters in Detroit on Nov. 3, 2026. (C-SPAN Screenshot)
 
Benson held a convincing lead in the majority of polls and outraised James throughout the election, though he received an influx of money in the final days from major donors.
Benson’s victory is historic in a number of ways — it would be the first time in more than 50 years a party has retained control of the Michigan governor’s office after an incumbent governor finished their term. The last time was 1969 when Republican William Milliken succeeded incumbent Republican Gov. George Romney.
With her running mate, Senate Majority Leader Winnie Brinks (D-Grand Rapids), Benson and Brinks will also be the first all-female governing duo in Michigan.
Gov. Gretchen Whitmer congratulated Benson on the victory.
“I know that Governor-elect Benson will always put Michigan first. She will work with anyone to get things done and won’t let anyone mess with Michigan. She’s a tough, principled leader who doesn’t back down from hard fights, and Michigan is lucky to have her as our next governor,” Whitmer said in a statement.
This is a developing story and will be updated as more information becomes available.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Idaho amendment giving state Legislature sole power to regulate drugs fails
description: Idaho voters rejected a proposed amendment to the Idaho Constitution that would have taken away Idahoans’ rights to legalize marijuana or other drugs, according to the Associated Press. The Associated Press called the race at 10:39 p.m. Mountain time Tuesday. House Joint Resolution 4, or HJR4, would have made it so that only the Idaho […]
text:
People register to vote in the South Hills Middle School gymnasium on Election Day in Twin Falls, Idaho, Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Andrew Eakin for the Capital Sun)Idaho voters rejected a proposed amendment to the Idaho Constitution that would have taken away Idahoans’ rights to legalize marijuana or other drugs, according to the Associated Press.
The Associated Press called the race at 10:39 p.m. Mountain time Tuesday.
Idaho constitutional amendment to declare English as state’s official language passes

House Joint Resolution 4, or HJR4, would have made it so that only the Idaho Legislature has the authority to legalize any drug or psychoactive substance – including medical or recreational marijuana.  
Passing HJR 4 would have removed the authority for Idahoans to run a ballot initiative to legalize medical or recreational drugs. 
“Idaho voters clearly understood that HJR4 was never about drugs; it was always about the right of Idaho voters to make their voices heard through the ballot initiative process,” Reclaim Idaho Executive Director Luke Mayville said in a written statement late Tuesday night.
“As we traveled the state in recent months and engaged with voters across Idaho, we found Republicans, Democrats and independents united in their view that this resolution was nothing more than a power grab by the Idaho Legislature,” Mayville added. “The defeat of HJR 4 is a big win for Idahoans and a big win for ballot-initiative rights.”
Voters in Idaho’s neighboring states of Washington, Oregon, Montana and Nevada used the ballot initiative process to legalize marijuana in their states. 
In Idaho, a ballot initiative is a form of direct democracy where the voters of Idaho decide whether to pass a proposed law.
As of 11:55 p.m. Mountain time Tuesday, 364,020 voters or 66.7%, voted against HJR 4. Meanwhile 181,580 voters, or 33.3%, voted for HJR4. 
Republicans in the Idaho Legislature passed HJR 4 and sent it onto voters, saying they didn’t want out-of-state interest groups spending big and “deceiving” Idaho voters into approving marijuana. 
But David Adler, president of the nonprofit Alturas Institute in Idaho Falls, said passing HJR4 would have meant voters would voluntarily giving up their own rights and freedoms. Adler has taught courses on government and the Constitution at all three of Idaho’s public universities. 
Election officials were still counting ballots late into the night Tuesday. Idaho’s election results do not become official until they are certified by the Idaho State Board of Canvassers, which meets Nov. 24.
All forms of marijuana and cannabis are illegal in Idaho and remain illegal. 
With voters rejecting HJR 4 voters will retain their power to run a ballot initiative to legalize marijuana during a future election. 
The most recent effort to qualify a ballot initiative to legalize medical cannabis in Idaho failed earlier in 2026 after organizers failed to meet the signature gathering requirements necessary to qualify for an election.

title: Democrat Willems declares victory in race for Iowa attorney general
description: Democratic challenger Nate Willems declared victory late Tuesday over GOP incumbent Brenna Bird in the race for Iowa attorney general. Unofficial results showed that with 85 percent of the vote counted, Willems had claimed 53% of the vote in unofficial results, while Bird had claimed 47% of the ballots. The Associated Press had yet to […]
text:
Iowa Attorney General candidate Nate Willems speaks at the Des Moines Register Political Soapbox at the Iowa State Fair on Aug. 21, 2026. (Photo by Brooklyn Draisey/Iowa Capital Dispatch)Democratic challenger Nate Willems declared victory late Tuesday over GOP incumbent Brenna Bird in the race for Iowa attorney general.
Unofficial results showed that with 85 percent of the vote counted, Willems had claimed 53% of the vote in unofficial results, while Bird had claimed 47% of the ballots. The Associated Press had yet to project a winner in the race.
Nate Willems. (Photo courtesy of the Nate Willems campaign)
Willems, who represented District 29 in the Iowa House of Representatives from 2009 to 2013, is an attorney who campaigned on his experience in labor and employment law. He said she wanted the attorney general’s office to “adopt the mindset and the mentality that it goes to work every day for regular Iowans, workers, consumers and seniors and is not focused on Washington politics and political lawsuits.”
Speaking at the Iowa State Fair in August, Willems said that over the past 18 years he has represented “tens of thousands of Iowans” and recovered tens of millions of dollars doing “work that the attorney general’s office could be doing but does not.”
On environmental enforcement, Willems said Bird imposed minimal fines on companies found to be polluting Iowa air and water, calling it a “slap on the wrist.”
Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird. (Photo courtesy of Brenna Bird)
Bird’s campaign characterized Willems as a “far-left liberal with a dangerous and radical record.” She said she had doubled the number of prosecutors in the attorney general’s office assigned to prosecute murderers, rapists and child molesters, and had improved victim services throughout Iowa.
At the Iowa State Fair in August, Bird said she and Willems didn’t “see eye to eye” on a number of issues, including “stand your ground” laws and voter-ID laws that she supports.
Bird promoted her efforts to initiate lawsuits tied to transgender participation in women’s sports, the launch of a cold case unit, and her opposition to what she called “woke mandates” such as California’s Proposition 12 that would impose production standards for certain types of livestock.
Bird, the first Republican to serve as the state’s attorney general since 1979, defeated then-incumbent Tom Miller in 2022 by a narrow margin of 51% to 49%. Before serving as attorney general, Bird served as Guthrie County Attorney and Fremont County Attorney.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Kansas governor’s race deadlocked between Republican Ty Masterson, Democrat Cindy Holscher
description: With most of the Kansas vote counted, the race for Kansas governor between Democrat Cindy Holscher and Republican Ty Masterson was too close to call.
text:
Cindy Holscher, the Democratic candidate for Kansas governor, closes her Nov. 3, 2026, election watch party in Lenexa with a hopeful speech before the close race can be called. (Photo by Baya Burgess for Kansas Reflector)WICHITA — Democrat Cindy Holscher and Republican Ty Masterson battled to an unofficial draw Tuesday in the Kansas governor’s race, leaving anxious voters without a resolution in the high-stakes battle to determine who follows departing Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly.
Preliminary results mirrored campaign polling that suggested the outcome would be tight. The latest numbers issued shortly after midnight by the Kansas Secretary of State’s Office had Holscher with 546,523 votes for 50.3% of the total. Out of 1.08 million votes cast in the race, Masterson held 540,651 votes, or 49.7%. There were two remaining precincts to be counted, along with provisional ballots and mail ballots that arrive by Friday.
Holscher told supporters in Johnson County that she was confident that she would win the election when all ballots were finally tabulated.
“There are just a few more votes that need to be counted, but we are confident that once all the votes are counted, we will win,” Holscher said.
“We knocked on doors in every corner of this state. We made the calls. We showed up, no matter the weather or the circumstances. And because of you, we feel really, really good about where we are right now,” she added.
In Wichita, Masterson told a crowd of GOP supporters the contest was too close to call. He pulled the plug on festivities at a downtown hotel, but indicated he might come out on top if he landed 55% of the outstanding vote.
“Oh, man,” Masterson said. “It’s just way to close to call. I just wanted to close this down tonight because there’s obviously not going to be either a concession speech or a victory speech. What I’m afraid is we’re gonna have lawyers involved in this thing.”
Masterson, the Andover Republican and president of the Kansas Senate, didn’t break away from Holscher despite President Donald Trump’s personal intervention at pep rallies to drive MAGA loyalists to the ballot box. Masterson easily won the won the GOP nomination in August after Trump anointed his candidacy.
Masterson counted on the massive voter registration advantage among Kansas Republicans to propel his candidacy. With Trump’s approval rating in retreat and affordability the defining principle of the midterm campaign, it appeared conservative GOP enthusiasm faltered as stakes in the race inspired a surge in interest among Democratic voters. That left the outcome in doubt.
GOP nominee for governor Ty Masterson addresses the crowd at a GOP watch party Nov. 3, 2026, in Wichita, where he says the race is too close to call. (Photo by Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)
Holscher, an Overland Park state senator who didn’t initially receive the endorsement from Kelly, said the goal was to parlay voter outrage about the escalating cost of everything from ground beef to diesel fuel to claim a come-from-behind victory. In the primary, Kelly endorsed state Sen. Ethan Corson. After Holscher won the primary, Kelly pivoted to endorse the Johnson County Democrat.
At midnight, Holscher had yet to celebrate triumph or acknowledge defeat at her headquarters in Johnson County.
“I’m going to lower property taxes and bring down the cost of living for Kansans,” Holscher said in a preelection rally. “I’m going to fully fund our schools. That’s how every kid gets the same shot I had. I’m going to protect our seniors, stand up for our farmers. I’m going to expand Medicaid.”
“I want to work to make college more affordable, because students shouldn’t be graduating with a mountain of debt. I’ll work to legalize cannabis, because that’s what Kansans support,” she said.
For more than 50 years, Kansas voters elected governors from the political party opposite that of their immediate predecessors. In this instance, Masterson’s election would continue that history. The pivoting between Republican and Democratic governors could be broken if Holscher was elected to follow Kelly, the two-term Democrat.
Kelly grappled throughout her governorship with a Republican-dominated Legislature, and Holscher would have to do the same. House Democrats have sought to dispatch enough Republicans to erase the GOP’s two-thirds majority in that chamber. The Kansas Senate won’t be up for reelection until 2028.
The election of Holscher would break an extraordinary drought in Kansas elective politics. Her lieutenant governor running mate, Rep. KC Ohaebosim of Wichita, became the first Black person elected to statewide office since 1884.
Former Democratic Lt. Gov. Lynn Rogers, Holscher’s campaign treasurer, said Kansas Republicans underestimated how effective Holscher would be as a statewide candidate. There was a belief among some Kansas GOP operatives that Holscher’s failure to secure Kelly’s endorsement in the primary campaign would drag down her general election effort, he said.
Kelly did endorse Holscher after she defeated the governor’s preferred candidate, state Sen. Ethan Corson of Johnson County.
“I think the Republicans said she was the weaker candidate coming out because she didn’t have the original endorsement,” he said Tuesday from Holscher’s watch party.
He said the Holscher campaign reached out to young people and to voters concerned about the future of abortion rights, public schools. The campaign emphasized Masterson’s association with former Gov. Sam Brownback and passage in 2012 of huge income tax cuts that cratered the state budget, he said.
“We really tried hard with our younger voters because we knew how key that was,” Rogers said. “And, particularly young women voters because they knew that, again, if Masterson was elected, we’d go backwards on both of the constitutional amendments (on abortion) that we overwhelmingly rejected, and I think that was a big, big difference. We had to remind the younger people what Brownback did to our schools and our roads.”

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: Ayotte survives Democratic surge to defeat Warmington in race for NH governor
description: Gov. Kelly Ayotte won a second term as New Hampshire governor Tuesday, defying a national midterm backlash against Republicans across the country and New Hampshire.  But the New Hampshire the governor will lead for the next two years will be different from the one she won in 2024. Results early Wednesday morning indicated that Democrats […]
text:
Gov. Kelly Ayotte addresses supporters in Salem, an hour before the Associated Press declared she had won reelection, Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Ethan DeWitt, New Hampshire Bulletin)Gov. Kelly Ayotte won a second term as New Hampshire governor Tuesday, defying a national midterm backlash against Republicans across the country and New Hampshire. 
But the New Hampshire the governor will lead for the next two years will be different from the one she won in 2024. Results early Wednesday morning indicated that Democrats would likely gain control of the state House, Senate and Executive Council, creating high barriers to future Republican priorities.
Ayotte positioned herself as a moderate leader and waged a blistering campaign against her opponent’s past ties to the opioid industry.
The governor did not deliver remarks after the Associated Press projected the victory just before 1 a.m. Wednesday morning. But New Hampshire Republican Party Chairman Scott Maltzie said in a statement, “She ran a fantastic campaign and has consistently demonstrated that she understands what Granite Staters need.”
The victory continues a New Hampshire tradition of a moderate Republican holding onto the corner office in the era of President Donald Trump, even when Democrats in other races in the state won.
But it also came after an unusually personal campaign by the governor, fueled by fears that a national Democratic “blue wave” could sweep up Ayotte before she could solidify her tenure as a new governor. 
In her first reelection campaign, Ayotte ran on a message of affordability, touting laws she championed and signed to overhaul local zoning and encourage more housing construction, as well as her opposition to a statewide sales or income tax.
Warmington also centered her campaign on affordability, but attempted to castigate Ayotte and tie her to high costs in New Hampshire. Specifically, the Democrat pointed to increasing housing costs in the state, high prescription drug prices, spikes in New Hampshire electric rates and rising property taxes. 
Warmington said those crises were directly caused by a lack of state investment by Ayotte and New Hampshire Republican lawmakers, and said as governor, she would prioritize that spending. Warmington also criticized state funding of public schools in Republican budgets, and stood against the education freedom account program, which allows parents to use state education funding toward private schools or homeschools. 
To drive home that argument, Warmington devoted her first television ad to attacking Ayotte’s statement that she had “kept New Hampshire moving in the right direction.” 
“What planet is she on?” Warmington responded in the ad.
It was a critique that might have landed in a different race. As gas prices and inflation have both climbed, Democrats across the country have capitalized on affordability concerns to gain an edge over Republicans. 
But week after week, Warmington’s affordability argument failed to overcome a simple, memorable and devastating label levied by Ayotte and other New Hampshire Republicans: “Cinde Warmington: Opioid Lobbyist.” 
The phrase, splashed on billboards and road signs for months, sought to draw attention to Warmington’s past as a lobbyist for Purdue Pharma, the maker of OxyContin, in 2001 and 2002, and work as a lawyer representing the state pain care clinic PainCare. The wide prescribing of OxyContin and its representation by Purdue Pharma that it was not addictive helped fuel an opioid addiction crisis that crashed over New Hampshire for decades.
Warmington has consistently said she did not know Purdue Pharma was misleading patients and doctors at the time she worked for them, and she has said she regretted her work. In October, she released a television ad labeled “Had Enough,” in which she briefly expressed regret for her past roles but then argued Ayotte was using that past to deflect from her own leadership.
But Republicans hammered the point home. In a June ad, Ayotte used an attack ad originally run by Democrat Joyce Craig in her primary campaign, which also criticized Warmington’s opioid lobbying past.
In the candidates’ final debate before WMUR Oct. 29, Ayotte read aloud Warmington’s statements from 2002 calling Oxycontin a “miracle drug” with “very few side effects.” The association proved difficult for the Democrat to dislodge.
Both candidates attempted positive messaging, too. Warmington vowed support for public schools, while Ayotte vowed further reforms to decrease the cost of housing.
In brief remarks to a room of supporters in Salem Tuesday night around 11:30, before the race was called, Ayotte thanked her family members, campaign volunteers and staff, and husband. She did not mention the apparent Democratic legislative majorities.
“It has been a privilege to serve the people of New Hampshire over the last two years,” she said.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Alaska US Sen. Sullivan, in fight to keep his seat, makes new accusations against Peltola
description: U.S. Sen. Dan Sullivan, in a tough fight to keep his seat, took time after casting his vote at the Alaska Zoo in Anchorage on Tuesday to blast his Democratic opponent. “We are witnessing the biggest election cheating scandal in the history of the state of Alaska, one of the, maybe one of the biggest […]
text:
Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska, talks to reporters after casting his vote at the Alaska Zoo on Tuesday. Next to him is his wife, Julie Fate Sullivan. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)U.S. Sen. Dan Sullivan, in a tough fight to keep his seat, took time after casting his vote at the Alaska Zoo in Anchorage on Tuesday to blast his Democratic opponent.
“We are witnessing the biggest election cheating scandal in the history of the state of Alaska, one of the, maybe one of the biggest in the US Senate’s history,” the two-term Republican told a large crowd of reporters assembled at the zoo, a designated polling site for two South Anchorage precincts.
The scandal, Sullivan said, is the campaign to put a different candidate who shares his name onto the ballot.
Dan J. Sullivan of Petersburg, a retired teacher and longtime resident of that Southeast Alaska island community, is one of the candidates in a high-stakes race that could determine which party controls the U.S. Senate.
“Unfortunately, the scheme is working,” the senator told reporters gathered at a far end of the zoo parking lot, away from the polling site. “The decoy is on the ballot. Thousands, likely, of Alaskans are going to mistakenly throw away their vote. There’s no one voting for this guy on purpose.”     
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 

Sullivan used the impromptu news conference to make more accusations against his main opponent, Democratic candidate Mary Peltola and her campaign.
“I think we’re just touching the tip of the iceberg here,” he told reporters. “There’s now circulating, certainly in Alaska, this idea that there’s hush money paid to make the campaign manager drop her lawsuit and (recant) her story. Who knows who paid that hush money, if it’s true. But the truth is that they undertook the most outrageous election cheating scandal in Alaska history, and I think Alaskans are very upset about that.”
The Alaska Supreme Court already ruled that Dan Sullivan of Petersburg has the legal right to be on the ballot, and there is no law against convincing anyone to run for office for any reason unless bribery is involved.
Republican Gerald Heikes is the fourth candidate in the race. 
Still, the idea of two Dan Sullivans on the Alaska ballot has drawn national attention – and much more so since the New York Times published a story describing efforts by Democratic operatives connected to Peltola’s former staffers to convince the Petersburg Sullivan to run.
The tactic, called “ballot stacking,” is generally legal, and both parties have used it in Alaska elections.
 

Mary Peltola and Bill Hill wave to passing motorists on Election Day, Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026 in Midtown Anchorage. (Photo by Loren Holmes/Alaska Beacon)
 

	President Donald Trump, who already spent considerable time criticizing the Petersburg Sullivan as a “fake,” ratcheted up his rhetoric after the New York Times story ran and called for Peltola to be stripped from the ballot and the Alaska election to be overturned if she won.
The U.S. Justice Department, at Trump’s direction, is now involved. U.S. Attorney Michael Heyman, in an Anchorage news conference on Friday, said federal and state law enforcement officials are investigating the election for potential civil and criminal violations.
Heyman said the Justice Department is aware of allegations that the Peltola campaign and national Democrats “orchestrated a sprawling conspiracy to recruit, prop up Dan. J Sullivan as a sham candidate, and we are taking that extremely seriously.”
A federal judge on Sunday dismissed the Justice Department’s lawsuit seeking to block the state from declaring a winner in the U.S. Senate race if Peltola winds up on top. The Trump administration plans to appeal that decision.
On Tuesday, after casting his ballot, Sen. Sullivan referred to that national attention that the race has attracted.
“The whole country’s watching this,” he said.
The large crowd of reporters at the zoo supported that claim.
Before listening to his comments in the parking lot, the national reporters and photographers trailed Sullivan as he entered the zoo building, picked up his ballot, marked it, turned it in and picked up his “I Voted” sticker. He opted for the moose design.
Despite the senator’s claims that thousands of Alaskans could be deceived, several Alaska voters that spoke with the Alaska Beacon on Tuesday dismissed the controversy and the idea that there would be any confusion.
They noted that the ballot clearly identifies the senator as the incumbent, and they also pointed to the state’s ranked-choice voting system, which allows for both Sullivans to be chosen.
Ella Wheeles, 18, born and raised in Anchorage and now a freshman at the University of Alaska Anchorage, said Tuesday was her first time voting in a General Election. On the state’s high-profile U.S. Senate race, Wheeles said she doesn’t see any issue or confusion with two candidates on the ballot named Dan Sullivan.
 

Petersburg resident Barry Bracken, who donated money to fellow Petersburg resident Dan J. Sullivan’s U.S. Senate campaign, speaks at a Nov. 2, 2026, news conference in front of the Anchorage headquarters of the Federal Bureau of Investigation. Bracken spoke about how he was visited in Petersburg by two FBI agents who quizzed him about his donation. At the news conference, he criticized the Trump administration’s actions concerning the Senate race. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
 

	“If you know what the word incumbent means, it should not be a problem,” she said. “I think it’s pretty self-explanatory. And if you are an informed voter — which you always should be — it’s not hard to understand who’s who. And looking into their platforms isn’t hard, they’re everywhere. So, I think it’s unnecessarily being posed as confusing.”
TJ Smith, a resident of Anchorage for more than 30 years, cast his vote at the Loussac Library in Anchorage on Tuesday morning and said Alaskans have been hearing about the two Dan Sullivans on the ballot for months, and likely know who they want to vote for. “The judge did a really good job making it very clear who the incumbent is, who the incumbent isn’t, so it made it really simple,” he said.
Another Anchorage voter, Brandon Harker, said Tuesday after voting accompanied by his young daughter, that he thought the issue was “blown out of proportion.”
“So I think that’s kind of a non-issue, and I think yeah, with the ranked choice voting system, it kind of eliminates some of that as well,” he said. “You know, even if there is some confusion there, still, I think that kind of negates any potential for that to really affect the outcome.”
Also taking issue with the idea of voter confusion was Petersburg resident Barry Bracken, a longtime friend of fellow Petersburg resident Dan J. Sullivan, whom he described as “a very, very, very nice man.”
Bracken, speaking Monday at a news conference held by the left-leaning 907 Initiative and the Alaska AFL-CIO, the state’s largest union, said he got a visit by two Federal Bureau of Investigation agents on Friday who quizzed him about the donation he made to the Petersburg Sullivan.
The FBI agents asked if he contributed to the correct Sullivan, Bracken said at the news conference, held outside the FBI’s Anchorage office.
“And I said, ‘Well, as far as I’m concerned, I contributed to the right Dan Sullivan, because I wouldn’t give a nickel to the other guy.’ Which is maybe a little bit snarky, but that’s exactly the way I felt about it,” Bracken said at the news conference.
The idea that voters would confuse the two Dan Sullivans got ridiculed last week by the proprietor of Sew Yup’ik, a Native artist who occasionally posts spoof videos acting as the character “Uncle Nick.”
Nikki Corbett, in an “Uncle Nick” persona she has used for Facebook videos, says voters have been inundated with more than enough campaign information to distinguish the two Dan Sullivans.
“We already know. We get ‘m every day: phone call, text message, email, Facebook post, ad, door-knockers, door-kickers, door-skippers. All of them. We already know. So what?” she said in her “Uncle Nick” persona. “You don’t think we know how to read? It already says it: ‘Incumbent.’”
