title: Cavanagh, Hood victories preserve 6-1 Democratic majority on Michigan Supreme Court
description: Democratic-nominated incumbents Michigan Supreme Court Chief Justice Megan Cavanagh and Noah Hood have won reelection. The race was called just after 1 a.m. Wednesday by the Associated Press, at which point Cavanagh and Hood won 33.8% and 29.1% of the vote, respectively. While the race is nonpartisan on the ballot, political parties nominate candidates. Expe[...]
text:
Michigan Supreme Court Justice Noah Hood and Chief Justice Megan Cavanagh embrace on stage at a watch party for Michigan Democrats in Detroit on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance)Democratic-nominated incumbents Michigan Supreme Court Chief Justice Megan Cavanagh and Noah Hood have won reelection. The race was called just after 1 a.m. Wednesday by the Associated Press, at which point Cavanagh and Hood won 33.8% and 29.1% of the vote, respectively.
While the race is nonpartisan on the ballot, political parties nominate candidates. Experts said going into the election that, without parties listed on the ballot, incumbents hold a strong advantage. Cavanagh and Hood defeated Republicans Casandra Morse-Bills and Michael Warren, and U.S. Taxpayers Party nominees Thomas Howe and Jody White.
Speaking to the Michigan Democratic Party watch party just after 10 p.m., Cavanagh and Hood both thanked campaign volunteers and staff.
“We talked about what it means to vote justice first, not politics first, not special interests first, not personal agendas first. Justice first,” Cavanagh said. “Tonight, results tell me that this message resonated with people around this state because the people in this state believe our court should remain places where every person is treated fairly, heard respectfully, and judged according to the law.”
Michigan Supreme Court Chief Justice Megan Cavanagh celebrates her re-election to the court at a watch party for Michigan Democrats in Detroit on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance)
Cavanagh said that beginning her new eight-year term, she would do so “with humility and a deep sense of responsibility.”
“The trust the voters have placed in me is not something I take lightly,” she said. “I will continue to approach every case with an open mind, respect for the law, and dedication to equal justice under the law.”
Hood, the newest member of the Michigan Supreme Court, was elected to his first full term on the court. 
“Tonight, I am grateful to the wisdom and forethought of our governor to appointing me to this position, I am grateful for the wisdom and forethought of our party for nominating me to stay on, and I am grateful for the wisdom and forethought of every single one of you for voting and keeping me in office,” he said. 
Michigan Supreme Court Justice Noah Hood celebrates his re-election to the court at a watch party for Michigan Democrats in Detroit on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance)
Hood also reflected on working at the Frank Murphy Hall of Justice in Detroit seven years ago, about a quarter-mile from the watch party.
“Tonight I promise you the same thing that I promised every person that came into my courtroom: that you will get even-handed justice, and that you will not walk out of the courtroom confused. That is the best that I can offer,” he said.
Michigan Democratic Party Chair Curtis Hertel also released a statement, following the victories.
“Our democracy calls for three branches of government, each with integrity. It’s more important than ever that those who run our judicial system respect and uphold the rule of law. That’s why Michigan Democrats celebrate the election of Chief Justice Cavanagh and Justice Hood to our state’s Supreme Court — they have and will continue to defend and uphold our state’s Constitution and the democracy it protects,” Hertel said.

name: WyoFile
title: No new property tax cut: Wyoming voters defeat Proposition 1
description:
Result comes after opponents warned citizens initiative would decimate local budgets for counties, special districts and education. 
The post No new property tax cut: Wyoming voters defeat Proposition 1 appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Wyoming voters on Tuesday defeated Proposition 1, a sweeping tax relief ballot initiative that opponents warned would devastate budgets for local county governments, special districts and education. 
Though it came to the ballot with more than 30,000 signatures, the measure’s defeat illustrates the appetite for drastic property tax cuts did not extend to a majority of voters on Election Day. 
Proposition 1 would have exempted 50% of a primary residence’s assessed value from property taxation, resulting in annual property tax revenue decreases estimated at anywhere from $92.6 million to $124.8 million. 
The measure needed approval from more than 50% of those voting in the general election to pass. Ballots left blank counted as no votes.
As of 11:15 p.m. Tuesday, AP results showed that with two-thirds of the vote counted, 55% of voters opposing Prop 1, with 42% backing the measure. Laramie and Sweetwater counties were not included in that total, but results in those counties showed Prop 1 failing by similar or larger margins.
A yard sign photographed Oct. 29, 2026 in Lander urges people to vote against Proposition 1. (Katie Klingsporn/WyoFile)
Its loss comes on the heels of a well-funded and organized movement to defeat Proposition 1. Opponents ranged from organizations such as the Wyoming Hospitals Association and the Wyoming Education Association to prominent figures like former Gov. Dave Freudenthal, a Democrat, and Republican Gov. Mark Gordon. 
“The voters have spoken and tonight was a big win for the hard-working families of Wyoming,” Kim Amen, chair of the Vote No on Prop 1 Coalition, said in a statement. “We hope and trust that state lawmakers will listen to the will of the voters, who said loudly that critical services like our public schools, first responders, road repairs, and libraries should receive the funding they need and that Wyoming families deserve.”
The Wyoming Taxpayers Association — which bills itself as Wyoming’s “tax watchdog” — was among critics. That’s because Proposition 1 would have weakened Wyoming’s economy, disproportionately hurt counties not rich in minerals and forced reductions in essential services, the association said in campaign materials.
If Proposition 1 had passed, counties like Lincoln, Park and Fremont would have faced revenue cuts of more than 40%, according to the association.  
“Prop 1 is not sound fiscal policy,” reads a post from the association’s website. 
Homeowner relief vs. local budgets
Proposition 1 was among a raft of efforts to relieve property owners after COVID-era real estate trends pushed up residential values. That resulted in spiking tax bills for many Wyoming homeowners; increases varied by county. In Park County, the average homeowner saw their tax bills jump over 60% in three years. 
In October of 2023, two-time gubernatorial candidate Brent Bien, along with his former campaign manager Rich Weber and former Wyoming Republican Party state committeewoman Cheryl Aguiar, secured approval to begin collecting signatures to get a 50% exemption on the ballot, with no cap on the value.
Secretary of State Chuck Gray certified the initiative in January 2025 after verifying more than 30,000 signatures. 
The numbers indicated high interest — at least when the signature collecting was happening between late 2023 and early 2025. Wyoming lawmakers also passed several property tax relief measures after signature collecting began, including five bills in 2024 and a 2025 bill that created a 25% exemption on the first $1 million of a primary residence’s fair market value.

Some condominiums at Teton Village, the base of Jackson Hole Mountain Resort, are valued at more than $7 million and subject to annual property taxes of almost $50,000. (Angus M. Thuermer Jr./WyoFile)

That 25% exemption shrank revenue pools for public education, municipalities and special districts such as hospitals. Some county governments implemented hiring freezes and mandated departmental budget cuts. Some closed libraries, others stopped maintaining parks and many dipped into reserves. 
These results were cast as cautionary tales — examples of painful consequences brought on by property tax cuts. Over the last year, a chorus of opposition has swelled against Proposition 1 — voices that include county treasurers, fire chiefs, education advocates and perhaps most notably, prominent Republicans. 
If Proposition 1 passed, they say, the damages would have spiralled out of control. 
The “Vote No on Prop 1” PAC was well-resourced. Campaign finance filings show nearly $2 million in contributions; the National Education Association has donated $1.4 million. Bien, Weber and Aguiar’s PAC, BCR Voter Initiatives, meanwhile, reported contributions of less than $4,000.
Proposition 1’s supporters, including many who align with the far-right Wyoming Freedom Caucus, said misinformation capitalizing on fear blew the impact of the tax reduction out of proportion. Opponents ignored important nuances of the measure and used a “chicken little” strategy of predicting calamity, Prop 1 supporters argued. 
The loss is another blow to the Freedom Caucus. After years of consolidating power in Wyoming’s Legislature, the bloc in the August primaries lost majority control of the House and backslid in the Senate.

name: National
title: Democrats set to win majority of governorships for the first time in 16 years
description: Democrats are poised to control the majority of governor’s offices for the first time in 16 years after the GOP racked up major losses across the country. Democrats flipped governorships in Iowa, Ohio, Georgia and Texas and defended competitive races in Maine and Wisconsin, according to unofficial results from The Associated Press and Decision Desk […]
text:
Dr. Amy Acton speaks at a campaign rally in Cleveland ahead of her successful campaign for Ohio governor. Acton will become the first Democrat elected to lead Ohio in 20 years during a midterm election cycle that saw huge Democratic gains in states.
(Photo by Nick Evans, Ohio Capital Journal)Democrats are poised to control the majority of governor’s offices for the first time in 16 years after the GOP racked up major losses across the country.
Democrats flipped governorships in Iowa, Ohio, Georgia and Texas and defended competitive races in Maine and Wisconsin, according to unofficial results from The Associated Press and Decision Desk HQ.
Midterms are always tough for the party that holds the White House, but high prices and growing disapproval of President Donald Trump delivered even stronger than expected results for Democrats Tuesday.
“It’s a blue wave that was bigger than anyone had expected, and it’s having consequences across the country, including here in Texas,” said Mark Jones, a political science professor at Rice University in Houston. “Overall, Donald Trump has single-handedly turned many red states blue — or at least purple.”
By late Tuesday, Democrats had won races for attorney general and lieutenant governor for the first time in decades and were well on their way to flipping the Texas House.
“One of the real questions will be what do Democrats do with this power, and will they be able to retain it,” he said. “This has effectively opened a door for Democrats across the country.”


Gubernatorial races proved historic for both Democrats and Republicans on Tuesday with the election of the nation’s first Black woman governor and the first Black Republican governor.
But the Democratic party made major gains coast to coast, particularly in reliably conservative states, that could reshape state policy for years to come.
In Iowa, the election of Democrat Rob Sand ends more than a decade of Republican control of the legislature and the governor’s office.
In Ohio, Democrat Dr. Amy Acton’s win marks the first time in 20 years that Ohio voters have selected a Democrat to lead the Buckeye State.
Former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms will become Georgia’s first Democratic governor since 2002. 
While governors were on ballots in 36 states, the nonpartisan Cook Political Report with Amy Walter only identified a dozen races for governor as competitive. Those included: Alaska, Georgia, Florida, Iowa, Kansas, Michigan, Nebraska, Nevada, Ohio, Oregon, Texas and Wisconsin.
Republicans have controlled a majority of state governments since 2010. Before Tuesday’s election, Republicans boasted a 26-24 gubernatorial advantage over Democrats. But the GOP’s state legislative advantage was even stronger, with Republicans controlling 28 state legislatures and Democrats controlling 18 with divided control of chambers in three states, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures.
By 12:30 a.m. Wednesday, Democrats had notched  major legislative wins. Democrats broke the GOP supermajority in Florida, flipped control of the Wisconsin state Senate and flipped the North Carolina state House.
In Pennsylvania, Democrats won the GOP-held state Senate, seizing  a trifecta – control of the governor’s office and both chambers of the legislature – in Harrisburg.
“Tonight’s earth-shattering victory is undeniable proof that voters are fed up with the MAGA agenda,” Heather Williams, president of the Democratic Legislative Campaign Committee, said in a news release.
In Arizona, Democrats declared victory in a yearslong effort to win control of the legislature, proclaiming that Republicans would be in the minority at the state Capitol for the first time in 60 years.
Stateline reporter Kevin Hardy can be reached at khardy@stateline.org.

text:
Pierre residents fill out ballots at a polling place in South Dakota's capital city on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Meghan O'Brien/South Dakota Searchlight)South Dakota voters approved a state constitutional amendment Tuesday specifying that non-U.S. citizens are disqualified from voting.
The Associated Press called the race at 12:05 a.m. Wednesday with 62% of the votes in favor of Amendment J and 38% against it. About 72% of statewide votes had been counted.
The state constitution already affirms the right of U.S. citizens to vote, while state laws criminalize noncitizens voting. Opponents said the amendment is unnecessary because of those existing provisions.
Supporters of Amendment J — including the Republican state lawmakers who placed it on the ballot — said the lack of an explicit ban in the state constitution is a loophole that local governments could exploit to allow noncitizen voting. In recent years, 21 local governments in California, Maryland and Vermont, as well as Washington, D.C., have allowed noncitizens to vote in some local elections, such as for school boards.
South Dakota is among six states this year with voter citizenship requirements on the ballot. Between 2018 and last year, states put 15 such measures on their ballots, and voters approved all 15.

title: Ballot Measure 2, repeal of Alaska’s election system, trails with many votes uncounted
authors: James Brooks, Corinne Smith, Yereth Rosen
description: This article is developing and will be updated. A ballot measure seeking to repeal Alaska’s open-primary and ranked-choice election system is trailing in early vote counting, according to preliminary results posted Tuesday evening by the Alaska Division of Elections. With 45 of 400 precincts reporting results Tuesday night, “no” on repeal led “yes” by 56.7% [...]
text:
An attendee of President Donald Trump's rally on Tuesday, Oct. 13, 2026, in Wasilla, holds up a sign urging a yes vote on Ballot Measure 2. (James Brooks photo/Alaska Beacon)This article is developing and will be updated.
A ballot measure seeking to repeal Alaska’s open-primary and ranked-choice election system is trailing in early vote counting, according to preliminary results posted Tuesday evening by the Alaska Division of Elections.
With 45 of 400 precincts reporting results Tuesday night, “no” on repeal led “yes” by 56.7% to 43.3%.
In 2024, a similar repeal measure led on Election Day but as more absentee and early votes were counted, the no-repeal side took the lead and won, preserving the system for this year’s election.
If Ballot Measure 2 passes this year, it would repeal the state’s current system of elections, in which all candidates for an office run together and the top four vote-getters advance from the primary to the general election, which uses ranked-choice voting.    
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 

In place of that system, Alaska would return to party-run primaries, where political parties set the rules for who may participate. One candidate from each party would advance to the general election, and ranked choice voting would not be used.
In addition, the state would no longer have a law requiring third-party political donors to disclose the source of their money; contributors would be able to give money anonymously.
Because of a conflict with Ballot Measure 1, passed during the August primary election, enacting Ballot Measure 2 likely also would eliminate a limit on direct financial donations to governor candidates, allowing donors to give unlimited amounts of money in governor races. A final ruling on that elimination would take place after the election.
Both sides of the issue were principally funded by out-of-state donors. Advocates of Ballot Measure 2 raised about $2.5 million, less than one-quarter of the amount raised by supporters of the existing system.

name: Washington State Standard
title: Rough election night for Republicans in WA Legislature
description: Buoyant Democrats were on course Tuesday to strengthen their grip on power in the Washington state House. But the caucus is poised to lose its longest-serving member, and a series of intraparty battles could unseat incumbents in both legislative chambers. Meanwhile several incumbent Republicans are staving off stiff challenges. Numerous races deserve a close[...]
text:
Washington state Democrats gather in Seattle's Capitol Hill neighborhood and await the midterm results. (Photo by Jacquelyn Jimenez Romero/Washington State Standard)Buoyant Democrats were on course Tuesday to strengthen their grip on power in the Washington state House.
But the caucus is poised to lose its longest-serving member, and a series of intraparty battles could unseat incumbents in both legislative chambers. Meanwhile several incumbent Republicans are staving off stiff challenges. Numerous races deserve a close eye through the week as votes continue to be counted.
Democrats are seeking to widen their majorities in Olympia. They already run the show with a 59-39 majority in the House and 30-19 in the Senate. But this election will help them inch closer to a two-thirds supermajority, at least in the lower chamber. All 98 House seats and 24 of the 49 Senate positions were on the ballot this year.
The magic number for the Democrats to get a two-thirds supermajority of 66 seats in the House is seven pickups from Republicans.
And Democratic political consultant Dean Nielsen expects his party to flip at least seven state House seats.
“What should I wear for the funeral for the Washington State Republican Party?” he said in a text message.
On the other side, state Republican Party Chair Jim Walsh sees the Democrats picking up a couple, but falling short of the seven they’d need.
Statewide, more than 2 million ballots have been counted. More will be tallied in the coming days, so results could change. 
Democratic pickups?
House Democrats fancy a sweep in southwest Washington where four incumbent Republican lawmakers trail their Democratic challengers in the early vote tally. 
In the 17th District, Republican Reps. Kevin Waters of Stevenson and David Stuebe of Washougal are losing to Democrats Ben Christly and Diana Perez, both of Vancouver, respectively. 
Next door, in the 18th District, GOP Reps. Stephanie McClintock and John Ley, both of Vancouver, are behind Democrats Randi Knott and Deken Letinich.
Democrats may have solidified their turn of the 26th District away from split representation. Renee Hernandez Greenfield is ahead of Katy Cornell, a Republican pastor who found herself in hot water recently over inflammatory comments in resurfaced videos of sermons. Hernandez Greenfield is up nearly 10 points on Cornell.
The initial results for those five races were mostly expected among pundits. But others indicate nearly the worst night Republicans in the state could imagine when it comes to the Legislature. 
GOP Rep. Michael Keaton is trailing David Berg in a tight race in the Puyallup-area 25th District. Keaton’s seatmate, Rep. Cyndy Jacobsen has a narrow lead of 109 votes on Jenn Marie Strickling.
In a state Senate race that represents a rare opportunity for a Democratic pickup this cycle, Carolina Mejia, the Democrat, is leading incumbent Republican Drew MacEwen in the 35th District, which covers Mason County as well as parts of Thurston and Kitsap counties. Mejia has a 3-point lead, which amounts to 1,380 votes of 43,000 counted so far. Republican state representatives in this district have narrow leads.
In the Yakima Valley’s 14th District, two incumbent Republicans, Gloria Mendoza and Deb Manjarrez, are trailing their Democratic challengers, Chelsea Dimas and Ezequiel Morfin. They’re each losing by over 10 percentage points in the Latino-heavy district.
Republican state Rep. Brian Burnett is showing weakness in the 12th District, which covers Chelan County and crosses the Cascades into eastern King and Snohomish counties. He trails Stacy Willoughby, his Democratic opponent, by 3 points on election night. His seatmate, GOP Rep. Mike Steele, meanwhile, is up handily.
Democrats appeared poised to hang onto the Senate seat in the 42nd District in Whatcom County. Democrat Michael Shepard, a port commissioner, has a comfortable lead over Republican psychologist Erika Creydt in the race to replace Democratic Sen. Sharon Shewmake. 
Walsh said his party isn’t giving up on this race, despite Creydt facing a nearly 13-point deficit.
Democratic infighting
Only 17 votes separated Rep. Amy Walen of Kirkland and Jessica Forsythe of Redmond in the August primary. 
Tuesday’s results showed Forsythe up over Walen by 1,051 votes, with more than 25,000 counted in the 48th District. Forsythe is running to Walen’s left after the incumbent voted against the high-earners income tax the Legislature approved this year.
Kelabe Tewolde, a progressive Democrat, defeated Rep. Sharon Tomikos Santos, who has been in the Legislature since 1999 and chairs the powerful House Education Committee. She trails Tewolde by 24.5% on election night, likely an insurmountable margin.
Despite a drunk driving arrest in August, progressive Democrat Krista Perez is leading by over 3 percentage points in her bid to unseat Democratic Rep. Melanie Morgan in Pierce County’s 29th District. Morgan, like Walen, has faced criticism from progressives for voting against the income tax.
It’s a tight race in the 32nd District in north King and south Snohomish counties, where Democratic Sen. Jesse Salomon aims to retain his seat against progressive state Rep. Cindy Ryu. Ryu leads by 352 votes, or less than 1 point.
Longtime Rep. Gerry Pollet, a Seattle Democrat, had a whopping 30-point lead over former federal prosecutor Will Dreher, a fellow Democrat who ran on a platform focused on regulating artificial intelligence. Pollet declared victory Tuesday night. 
“Thank you to every one of my constituents who took the time to speak to me on their doorsteps, at the grocery store, or at the park, to tell me what the legislature can do for them,” Pollet said in a statement. “I’ll be taking your stories with me, and I want to keep hearing from you. See you again soon.”
Rep. Tarra Simmons, the first formerly incarcerated Washington state lawmaker, leads fellow Democrat Daria Ilgen by fewer than 500 votes with nearly 49,000 counted. Simmons has been embroiled in various ethics complaints in the past year.

description: North Carolina voters approved all three constitutional amendments on the ballot Tuesday. The amendments authorize lawmakers to impose limits on local governments’ power to raise property taxes, cap the state income tax, and require photo ID for all voters — not just those voting in person. The controversial, Republican-backed property tax amendment was appr[...]
text:
North Carolina voters approved all three constitutional amendments on the ballot Tuesday.
The amendments authorize lawmakers to impose limits on local governments’ power to raise property taxes, cap the state income tax, and require photo ID for all voters — not just those voting in person.
The controversial, Republican-backed property tax amendment was approved with 60% of voters casting votes in favor and 40% against the measure. 
Supporters had predicted voters feeling burdened by local property tax increases would approve the amendment, which GOP lawmakers said is a response to excessively high property taxes. Seniors in particular are cost-burdened by high taxes, they complained.
“Families are getting ripped off as some, but by no means all, local governments rake in billions more than inflation and population growth warrant,” state House Speaker Destin Hall, R-Caldwell, said in the spring.
The amendment gives lawmakers the authority to set a limit on local governments’ ability to increase property taxes by creating a levy limit. But it doesn’t specify how or how much the limit would be. Legislators would work out the details and set the levy limit later, likely in 2027.
Local government officials, progressive advocacy groups and Democratic lawmakers who oppose the measure say state lawmakers already have the authority to do this without a constitutional amendment.
They worry that limiting the amount of tax revenue local governments can collect could have dire consequences for local governments, which could be forced to cut services. Local property taxes help pay for vital needs like public safety, education, and public health.
State income tax amendment
The state income tax amendment was approved with 62% of voters casting votes in favor and 38% against. The amendment establishes a maximum income tax rate of 3.5%. It keeps North Carolina’s income tax rate from being raised higher than 3.5% for personal and corporate income taxes in the future. 
North Carolina’s personal income tax rate stands at 3.99% and it’s slated to fall to 3.49% in 2027.
Supporters of the Republican-backed amendment argued that a higher state income tax makes North Carolina less competitive in attracting business and jobs. 
Sen. Ralph Hise, R-Mitchell, noted that Tennessee, which borders North Carolina, does not have a personal income tax.
Critics argued that the legislature could lower the income tax rate without enshrining the policy in the state constitution.
House Democratic leader Robert Reives of Chatham County said even if the cap on the personal income tax rates passes, costs are still going to be passed on to North Carolinians through fees and sales taxes.
“You’re still getting taxed,” he said in May. “It’s just not coming through personal income tax.”
Photo ID amendment
The photo ID amendment was approved by 60% of voters with 40% voting against.
All voters in the state are already required to show ID when voting in person and by mail, but the photo requirement for mail-in voters was not in the constitution. The amendment enshrines the requirement in the constitution, which makes it more difficult for future legislators to overturn it.
Supporters argued that the Republican-backed amendment creates one standard for all voters, provides an additional identity safeguard and allows lawmakers to enact laws that may include exceptions to the photo ID law.
But critics argued that the amendment is unnecessary because state law already requires a photo ID for mail ballots.
“Really, what this is an effort to make more permanent a commitment to limiting access to the ballot for eligible voters,” Alexander Sirota, executive director of the N.C. Budget and Tax Center, told NC Newsline.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Berman defeats Steil to flip Wisconsin’s 1st Congressional District
description: Democrat Mitchell Berman defeated Republican U.S. Rep. Bryan Steil in Wisconsin’s 1st Congressional District Tuesday night in a race to become the first Democrat in the seat in more than three decades.  The Associated Press called the race for Berman at 11:48 p.m. With 95% of the ballots counted, Berman had more than 52% of […]
text:
Mitch Berman, the Democratic candidate elected Tuesday to represent Wisconsin's 1st Congressional District, greets supporters at his watch party in Elkhorn Tuesday night. (Photo by Heather Asiyanbi)Democrat Mitchell Berman defeated Republican U.S. Rep. Bryan Steil in Wisconsin’s 1st Congressional District Tuesday night in a race to become the first Democrat in the seat in more than three decades. 
The Associated Press called the race for Berman at 11:48 p.m. With 95% of the ballots counted, Berman had more than 52% of the vote to Steil’s share of just under 48%.
Berman’s victory breaks Steil’s four-term winning streak that began with the incumbent’s first election in 2018 and a Republican winning streak for the 1st District seat that began with the 1994 election.
In his victory speech, Berman gave a nod to Wisconsin’s recent World Series championship team.
“I have to give a special shout out and a special thank you to the Milwaukee Brewers for reminding the entire country what Wisconsin can do when we set our minds to it,” he said.
Berman harkened to his job as a nurse and the themes of affordability and healthcare that have been central to his campaign, along with his message focusing on working-class representation in Congress.
“As an ER nurse, I’ve seen patients rationing their medication because they didn’t know they’d be able to afford their next refill. I’ve seen working families, including my own, do everything right and still get squeezed to the ground. And I came into this race to fight for them,” Berman said. “This is about working-class communities coming together to advocate for change.”
The 1st District, which stretches from Lake Michigan to South Central Wisconsin, has been on Democrats’ congressional wish list for most of the last three decades, but it has been out of reach that whole time despite periodic attempts to flip the seat. It covers Kenosha, Racine and most of Walworth counties along with the eastern half of Rock County and the southern third of Milwaukee County. 
Republican and former U.S. House Speaker Paul Ryan easily won 10 terms. Steil, a corporate lawyer and former Ryan aide, embarked on a similar trajectory, winning by nine or 10 percentage points in 2024 and 2022 and even wider margins in his two previous elections. 
After Berman won a crowded Democratic primary in August, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee added the district to its list of seats targeted to flip from Republican to Democrat. In the final weeks of the campaign, Berman’s campaign pointed to polling showing the two candidates tied or Berman slightly ahead. 
Steil entered the general election with a significant fundraising advantage. Federal campaign reports through Oct. 14 showed Steil had raised approximately $6.4 million, compared with about $2 million for Berman.
Berman, an emergency room nurse who worked for 11 years at the Veterans Administration, entered the race in August 2025, saying his experiences with patients who could not afford basic medical care had helped convince him to run.
Berman, a resident in the Racine County town of Raymond, had previously been involved in local government disputes, including organizing a recall effort against two Raymond School Board members and filing an open meetings lawsuit against the school district in 2024.
U.S. Rep. Bryan Steil talks to a raucus crowd during his in-person listening session at Elkhorn High School in Elkhorn, Wisconsin, Thursday evening July 31, 2025. (Copyright Mark Hertzberg/for Racine County Eye)
Despite Steil’s election track record, there were signs more than a year ago of voter discontent, when several hundred voters at a noisy listening session in Elkhorn frequently shouted him down while he sought to defend the sweeping Republican tax and spending bill that President Donald Trump signed into law in July 2025.
Berman accused Steil of abandoning commitments to protect Medicaid by supporting the 2025 bill, which included tax cuts that largely favored the wealthy and corporations and made cuts to Medicaid and other safety-net programs over the next decade.  Steil defended the legislation as a measure to lower taxes, strengthen border security and tighten Medicaid eligibility requirements.
Berman focused his campaign on rising costs, particularly in healthcare, and with a message that portrayed Steil as out of touch with the needs and concerns of voters in the district. He also criticized Steil for supporting tariffs that Trump imposed early in his second term, charging that they were contributing the rising prices for consumers. 
Steil campaigned on his legislative record, highlighting Republican tax cuts, efforts to strengthen election security and legislation aimed at restricting stock trading by members of Congress. Steil defended the 2025 law, which included a temporary break in federal income taxes on qualifying tips and overtime pay and expanding tax deductions for seniors. 
He also highlighted his work as chairman of the House Administration Committee on legislation requiring proof of citizenship to register to vote in federal elections, and his Stop Insider Trading Act, which passed the House but stalled in the Senate.
 The Berman campaign contrasted Steil’s stock trading proposal with tougher legislation that has stalled in Congress.
Berman talked about treating underinsured and uninsured patients during his emergency room shifts. He also highlighted connections between Steil donors in banking, crypto currency, industries involved in data center development and housing investment with his votes on bills that benefited those industries.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Idaho Gov. Brad Little re-elected, state GOP incumbents lead on Election Day
description: Idaho Republican Gov. Brad Little was reelected in Tuesday’s general election and will serve a third term as the Gem State’s governor, according to the Associated Press.  The Associated Press called the race for Little at 10:36 p.m. Tuesday.  Little, a Republican from Emmett, was projected to beat his two closest challengers, Democrat Terri Pickens […]
text:
Idaho Gov. Brad Little speaks to supporters at a Republican election night watch party at the Boise Centre in Downtown Boise on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)Idaho Republican Gov. Brad Little was reelected in Tuesday’s general election and will serve a third term as the Gem State’s governor, according to the Associated Press. 
The Associated Press called the race for Little at 10:36 p.m. Tuesday. 
Little, a Republican from Emmett, was projected to beat his two closest challengers, Democrat Terri Pickens and independent John Stegner.
As of 10:45 p.m. Mountain time Tuesday, Little had received 195,0981 votes, or 53.1%, while Pickens was in second place with 132,912 votes, or 35.9%. Stegner was in third place, with 30,539 votes, or 8.2%.
Several other candidates ran for governor as well. 
Libertarian Paul Sand received 5,710 votes, or 1.5%. A Constitution Party candidate who changed his name from Marvin Richardson to Pro-Life received 3,967 votes, or 1%. And an independent named Jacob Burnett ran as a write-in candidate and had received 34%.  
Little will serve his third, four-year term as Idaho’s governor. He was first elected governor in 2018, having previously served as lieutenant governor and a member of the Idaho Senate.
In addition to Little, each of Idaho’s statewide incumbent Republican officials was also leading their re-election bids Tuesday night, according to partial unofficial election results released Tuesday by the state. 
The Associated Press also called the race for Idaho secretary of state in favor of Republican Secretary of State Phil McGrane at 10:31 p.m. Wednesday.
Lt. Gov. Scott Bedke, Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador, Idaho State Controller Brandon Woolf, Idaho State Treasurer Julie Ellsworth and Idaho Superintendent of Public Instruction Debbie Critchfield were leading their re-election bids as well. 
 Idaho Lt. Gov. Scott Bedke leads Democrat Eric Myricks

Idaho’s lieutenant governor serves as president of the Idaho Senate but only votes in cases of a tie vote. The lieutenant governor also serves as acting governor while the governor is out of the state or unable to perform the duties of office.
Bedke, a Republican from Oakley, held a large lead over Democratic challenger Eric Myricks of Nampa.
As of 10:45 p.m. Tuesday, Bedke has received 220,419 votes, or 59.3%. Myricks had received 152,947 votes, or 40.1%.
Bedke is running for his second four-year term as lieutenant governor. He previously served as the longtime speaker of the Idaho House of Representatives. 
 Idaho Secretary of State Phil McGrane beats Democrat Shawn Keenan

Idaho’s secretary of state is the state’s top elected official in charge of elections and is responsible for overseeing business filings, campaign finance and lobbying. 
As of 10:50 p.m. Tuesday, Secretary of State Phil McGrane, a Republican from Ada County, had received 246,710 voters, or 64.8%. Democrat Shawn Keenan had received 137,388 votes, or 35.5%
McGrane will serve his second four-year term as secretary of state.
 Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador leads Democrat Lori Hickman

The attorney general is the state’s chief legal officer, responsible for representing the state and its agencies in court and enforcing consumer protection laws. 
As of 10:55 p.m. Tuesday, Attorney General Raúl Labrador, a Republican, had received 215,891 votes, or 55.4%. Lori Hickman, a Democrat, had received 173,413 votes, or 44.5%.
Labrador is running for his second four-year term as attorney general. He previously served as a member of Congress, a member of the Idaho Legislature and as an immigration attorney. 
 Idaho State Controller Brandon Woolf leads Democrat Rakesh Mohan

The Idaho state controller is the chief fiscal officer for the state and responsible for paying all of the state’s bills and payroll.
As of 10:55 p.m. Tuesday, Woolf, a Republican, had received 239,872 votes, or 62.3%. Democrat Rakesh Mohan had received 144,768 votes, or 37.6%
Woolf is running for his fourth, four-year term as state controller. Woolf was first appointed Idaho state controller in 2012.
 Idaho State Treasurer Julie Ellsworth leads Democrat Kevin Jones

The Idaho state treasurer serves as the banker for the state and is responsible for investing idle state funds. 
As of 10:55 p,m. Tuesday, State Treasurer Julie Ellsworth, a Republican, had received 237,059 votes, or 61.7%.
Democratic challenger Kevin Jones had received 146,860 votes, or 38.2%.
Ellsworth is running for her third, four-year term as state treasurer. Ellsworth was first elected treasurer in 2018. She previously served as a member of the Idaho Legislature. 
 Idaho Superintendent of Public Instruction Debbie Critchfield leads Democrat Becky Sundin Mitchell and Constitution Party candidate Teresa Roundy

The Idaho superintendent of public instruction is the state’s top elected education official, oversees Idaho’s K-12 public education and has a seat on the Idaho State Board of Education. 
As of 10:55 p.m. Tuesday, Idaho Superintendent of Public Instruction Debbie Critchfield, a Republican, had received 224,093 votes, or 58%. 
Democrat Becky Sundin Mitchell had received 149,376 votes, or 38.7%.
Independent Teresa Roundy had received 12,432 votes, or 3.2%.
Critchfield is seeking her second, four-year term as superintendent of public instruction. Critchfield previously served as the president of the Idaho State Board of Education. 
State officials continued to count ballots late into the night on Tuesday. 
Idaho’s election results do not become official until after they are certified by the Idaho State Board of Canvassers, which meets Nov. 24.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Republican Brent Taylor claims victory; Justin Pearson does not concede US House race
description: Republican Memphis state Sen. Brent Taylor claimed victory in the race for Tennessee’s 9th Congressional District Tuesday, a district that was redrawn months before the election to give Republicans the upper hand. Taylor narrowly clinched the seat with 111,968 votes (49.63%), about 2,500 votes ahead of Democratic Memphis state Rep. Justin J. Pearson, accordi[...]
text:
State Rep. Justin J. Pearson takes the stage in Memphis on Nov. 3, 2026, with his wife, Oceana, at his right. (Photo by Brad Vest for Tennessee Lookout)Republican Memphis state Sen. Brent Taylor claimed victory in the race for Tennessee’s 9th Congressional District Tuesday, a district that was redrawn months before the election to give Republicans the upper hand.
Taylor narrowly clinched the seat with 111,968 votes (49.63%), about 2,500 votes ahead of Democratic Memphis state Rep. Justin J. Pearson, according to final unofficial counts reported by the Tennessee Secretary of State.
Taylor claimed victory in a social media post just after 11 p.m.
“Thank you Middle and West Tennessee! I won’t let you down!” he wrote.
But Pearson said he will wait for the race to be officially called before conceding. As of 11:55 p.m., the Associated Press had not yet called the race.
“At this point, we want everybody’s ballots to be counted,” he said. Pearson said his campaign has not made a decision on whether they may appeal the results. He will continue to serve as a state Rep. for Memphis if the race does not land in his favor.
“This is probably the most impressive race happening in the United States of America, for the simple fact that it was drawn so nothing near like this could be possible,” Pearson said. “I’m really excited about the fact that we’re going into these counties, we’re making inroads, we’re building relationships and connections that are going to outlast a single campaign. We’ve got a lot more work to do, and I’m just 31, so I’m ready to do it.”
Tennessee’s 9th District used to encompass nearly all of Memphis and had been represented by Democrats for more than 40 years. It was the state’s last Democratic-leaning U.S. House seat after Tennessee’s Republican supermajority split Davidson County into three districts in 2022.



Quotation







At this point, we want everybody’s ballots to be counted.


– Rep. Justin J. Pearson.


Tennessee Republicans held a special session in May to redraw the 9th District after the U.S. Supreme Court struck down a portion of the 1965 Voting Rights Act in Louisiana v. Callais.
The resulting map divided Memphis into three districts, diluting the power of Democratic votes in the majority-Black city. The new L-shaped 9th District stretches from the Memphis airport along the southern edge of rural West Tennessee before reaching up into Middle Tennessee to include part of wealthy Williamson County, typically a Republican stronghold.
Taylor entered the race for the newly drawn district almost immediately and gained endorsements from President Donald Trump and U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn.
Pearson launched his campaign for the 9th District in October 2025, challenging longtime U.S. Rep. Steven Cohen. Cohen, 77, ended his campaign soon after, refusing to compete for any of the three gerrymandered Memphis seats.
Nonpartisan election forecaster Cook Political Report rated the new 9th District “Solid Republican” with a plus-9 lean. It’s the weakest Republican advantage of the state’s nine congressional districts.
Taylor repeatedly called Pearson a Democratic Socialist, echoing rhetoric embraced by Republicans on the national level. Taylor’s campaign hit a snag the week before the election after the Nashville Scene published a story about allegations that Taylor sent unsolicited nude pictures to someone in 2021. 
Pearson made national headlines after Tennessee’s Republican supermajority expelled him from the Legislature in 2023 for protesting gun violence on the state House floor. The Shelby County Commission quickly reappointed Pearson to his seat. The ouster vaulted him to national prominence and allowed Pearson to raise money from donors throughout the country.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: Goehring hangs on to North Dakota agriculture commissioner seat
description: North Dakota Agriculture Commissioner Doug Goehring was reelected Tuesday after an active campaign by Democratic challenger Vern Thompson.  Goehring, a Republican, pulled in about 63% of the vote in complete but unofficial results. That percentage tracked with other Republicans in statewide races. Thompson had 37% of the vote. Goehring said Tuesday night he [...]
text:
Republican Agriculture Commissioner Doug Goehring speaks during an election night party in Bismarck on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Martin/For the North Dakota Monitor)North Dakota Agriculture Commissioner Doug Goehring was reelected Tuesday after an active campaign by Democratic challenger Vern Thompson. 
Goehring, a Republican, pulled in about 63% of the vote in complete but unofficial results. That percentage tracked with other Republicans in statewide races. Thompson had 37% of the vote.
Goehring said Tuesday night he tried to focus during the campaign on ag issues such as research and foreign trade. He said North Dakota doesn’t have a lot of control over federal tariff policies but the state still needs to pursue ag exports for North Dakota commodities.
“You put your head down and work through this,” he said. 
Goehring has been ag commissioner since being appointed in 2009. 
Thompson, a former farmer and state legislator, organized several community forums across the state during the campaign season, largely focused on data centers and their impact on rural areas. 
The North Dakota Department of Agriculture does not regulate data centers. But the agriculture commissioner has a seat on the three-person Industrial Commission, which plays a role in energy development, with data centers needing large amounts of power. 
Vern Thompson, left, North Dakota agriculture commission candidate, attends an election night party with other Democrats in Fargo on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Dan Koeck/For the North Dakota Monitor)
Thompson said he respected the results and the voters of North Dakota. 
“When I woke up this morning, I was at peace because our team, our campaign did everything we could,” he said late Tuesday. 
Thompson has said the state has not provided leadership on the controversial data center issue and should do more to protect affected landowners and provide guidance to local governments. 
Goehring, who farms at Menoken, has said the state should not interfere with landowners who could benefit from working with the developer of a data center or other projects. He has said it is important for North Dakota to develop its energy resources. 
Agriculture remains a dominant industry in North Dakota, but farmers in recent years have been stressed by shifting trade policies, drought, severe storms and the rising costs of inputs such as fuel and fertilizer. 
Thompson, who runs a trucking company in Fargo, said North Dakota leaders have been slow to react. Goehring has pointed to programs that have provided farmers with low-interest loans to rebuild from natural disasters and keep farming until the farm economy improves.

title: Alaska Republican incumbent Rep. Nick Begich III has big lead for state’s lone US House seat
authors: James Brooks, Corinne Smith, Yereth Rosen
description: This article is developing and will be updated. Republican incumbent Rep. Nick Begich III took a significant lead in early vote-counting for Alaska’s lone U.S. House seat, but stood just barely short of the threshold needed to avoid a ranked choice runoff. With 209 of 401 precincts reporting results Tuesday night, Begich had 49.3% of […]
text:
Independent U.S. House candidate Bill Hill waves to passing motorists on Election Day, Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026 in Midtown Anchorage. (Photo by Loren Holmes/Alaska Beacon)This article is developing and will be updated.
Republican incumbent Rep. Nick Begich III took a significant lead in early vote-counting for Alaska’s lone U.S. House seat, but stood just barely short of the threshold needed to avoid a ranked choice runoff.
With 209 of 401 precincts reporting results Tuesday night, Begich had 49.3% of Alaskans’ first-choice votes, while independent challenger Bill Hill had 40.9%.
Federally imprisoned Democratic candidate Eric Hafner had 7.1% of the vote, and Libertarian Jim McDermott had 2.6%.
With Hafner acting as a potential spoiler, Hill had trailed in pre-Election Day polling despite having the endorsement and backing of the Alaska Democratic Party. 
On Election Day, national results favored Democratic candidates across the country, and Hill appeared to benefit from the “blue tsunami” washing over the United States.
But as more votes were counted in Alaska, Begich reversed an initial Hill lead and now has a large advantage. 



How does Alaska’s election system work?
In Alaska, all candidates for an office run in a single primary election. The four who get the most votes — or everyone, if there are four or fewer candidates — advance to the November general election.
In that election, voters rank the candidates in order of preference.
If a candidate gets at least 50% of the first-preference votes, they win.
If none have 50%, the candidate with the fewest first-choice votes is eliminated. Voters who picked them have their votes go to their second choice.
The eliminations continue until only two candidates are left, and the person with the most votes wins.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Primary election reform backers concede as ballot measure falls short
description: Voters rebuffed an attempt to inject more competition into the state’s low-energy elections by shuttling all candidates through a single primary contest, regardless of their party affiliation.
text:
MASSACHUSETTS VOTERS on Tuesday rebuffed a proposal to dramatically upend the way the state conducts primary elections, declining to translate their frustrations with Beacon Hill into a change that opponents argued could do more harm than good by further boosting well-funded candidates. 
Bay Staters rejected a ballot measure that would have eliminated the state’s separate Democratic and Republican primaries in state elections and replaced them with a single, nonpartisan primary from which the top two candidates advance regardless of party. 
Proponents had hoped voters would be in the mood for a major shakeup, arguing that Beacon Hill has become ossified by a top-heavy power structure and a lack of competition. But a majority of voters concluded they would prefer to keep primary elections as they are instead of shifting to a model already in place in only a handful of other states. 
Campaign leaders conceded defeat around 11 p.m. The race had not yet been officially called, but with somewhat fewer than half of votes counted, the “no” side was leading by a wide margin. 
“Change can be difficult, no matter how uncomfortable the status quo is,” the Coalition for Healthy Democracy, which led the charge for the measure, said in a statement. “We are used to a system where most races are settled before November and most voters never get a real choice. The familiar can feel safe, even when the familiar isn’t working. And when you throw grit into the gears of a political machine, the machine fights back. The people who benefit most from the way things are fought hard for this result.” 
“On this question and others, every voter in Massachusetts got a real choice and a real contest. That’s how every election should feel,” the group concluded. “We’ll keep working until it does.” 
It’s a disappointing end for a well-funded operation helmed by Danielle Allen, a political scientist who ran for governor four years ago and pitched the primary elections overhaul as a way to generate much-needed competitiveness.  
The system, versions of which are in place in California, Washington state, and Alaska, would have placed all candidates onto a single primary election ballot and allowed the top two finishers to advance.  
In deep-blue Massachusetts, some sitting Democrats who for years cruised to reelection in races effectively decided in lower-turnout primaries might have ended up facing a fellow Democrat in the higher-turnout general election. Theoretically, one party could also have found itself shut out of the final contest if too many of its candidates split the primary vote and allow others to squeak through to the top spots. 
Unlike many other ballot measures, the debate around primary election reforms scrambled traditional partisan alignment. Backers stretched across the political spectrum, including former Democratic Gov. Deval Patrick, former Republican Gov. Charlie Baker, and former MassGOP chair Jennifer Nassour. On the other side, the opposition campaign stitched together an unusual alliance between the state Democratic Party, the state Republican Party, many progressive groups, and some labor unions. 
Some of those entities are satisfied with the status quo and are wary of losing the power they currently wield. Others agree that electoral politics in Massachusetts are in desperate need of reform, but argued the all-party primary proposal would exacerbate existing problems by benefitting wealthier candidates who have more resources to burn en route to the top two spots in a primary election. 
While the corner office has changed hands between Republicans and Democrats over the years, the state’s congressional delegation and Legislature have been dominated by one party for decades. Both US senators, all nine US representatives, 131 of 160 state representatives, and 35 of 40 state senators heading into Tuesday’s election were Democrats.  
In fact, Massachusetts is one of only three states this cycle where the party in power is guaranteed to retain a veto-proof supermajority in both legislative chambers. 
Competition, especially in the state House and Senate, has long been hard to come by. About three in five legislative districts featured a single candidate on any ballot this election season. And according to Ballotpedia, only one state’s elections are less competitive than those in Massachusetts, an upgrade after the Bay State landed dead last in the prior five cycles.  
“Without competition, elected officials don’t have to listen to voters, and then everybody feels stuck, and nothing is changing,” Allen said last month at a CommonWealth Beacon debate. “We don’t get movement on housing and affordability and other issues that we need.” 
Now, election reform activists will need to go back to the drawing board and come up with new methods to encourage more challengers to run for office. 
The proposal was not the only action Tuesday aimed at catalyzing changes on Beacon Hill nor the only vote dealing with election reform. 
Voters also approved a ballot measure subjecting the Legislature and the governor’s office to the state’s public records law, which requires government officials to make many documents and communications available upon request, starting in 2027. Most state agencies and local governments are already required to comply, but the Legislature is entirely exempt and governors in both parties have traditionally considered themselves mostly exempt with occasional exceptions. 
“What voters said is that government must be accountable to the people it serves,” said Mary Connaughton, director of government transparency at the Pioneer Institute think tank. 
Top Democrats in the Legislature have chafed at the ballot measure — which is also the latest front in Auditor Diana DiZoglio’s crusade to probe Beacon Hill — and could move in the closing weeks of the term to replace what voters approved with a less expansive records access law.  
DiZoglio has already pledged legal action to challenge such an outcome, which could place a major voter-backed transparency measure in the domain of the state’s courts for the second election in a row. A 2024 ballot question voters approved empowering DiZoglio’s office to audit the Legislature still has not been implemented amid an ongoing debate over its constitutionality. 
Another ballot question in the mix would allow eligible citizens to register to vote, or change their voter registration address, on Election Day itself. That race had not yet been called by midnight, but votes counted at that point showed yes with a lead. 
Secretary of State Bill Galvin led the charge to place the measure directly before voters after similar proposals repeatedly died in the House over the past two decades.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Rebecca Cooke flips Wisconsin’s 3rd Congressional District for Democrats
description: Democrat Rebecca Cooke has defeated Republican U.S. Rep. Derrick Van Orden in Wisconsin’s 3rd Congressional District, notching a win in one of the Democratic party’s highest priority House districts.  AP called the race at 11:48 p.m. with 90% of the vote counted. Cooke led Van Orden 52.4% to 45.8%. Cooke, who lost in the Democratic […]
text:
Rebecca Cooke greets supporters and delivers her victory speech at Mogie’s Pub in Eau Claire after winning the Democratic primary in the 3rd Congressional District (Henry Redman/Wisconsin Examiner)Democrat Rebecca Cooke has defeated Republican U.S. Rep. Derrick Van Orden in Wisconsin’s 3rd Congressional District, notching a win in one of the Democratic party’s highest priority House districts. 
AP called the race at 11:48 p.m. with 90% of the vote counted. Cooke led Van Orden 52.4% to 45.8%.
Cooke, who lost in the Democratic primary for the seat in 2022 and narrowly lost to Van Orden in 2024, ran as a moderate — staking out a number of positions counter to progressive priorities — but benefited from the support of U.S. Sens. Tammy Baldwin and Bernie Sanders as well as the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee. 
Cooke’s seven point victory, at the time the race was called shortly before midnight, was driven by winning large margins in the district’s bigger cities of Eau Claire and La Crosse while keeping Van Orden’s margins small enough in the rest of the largely rural district. 
Rebecca Cooke’s election night watch party at the Westgate Sportsman’s Club in Eau Claire. (Photo courtesy of William Garcia)
Cooke won by more than 20 points in both Eau Claire and La Crosse counties while keeping it close enough in the more rural counties — which had driven Trump’s wins in the state after the district voted for former President Barack Obama twice. Under a map in which Van Orden had to run up the score among rural voters, as of 11:45 p.m. on Tuesday evening, he was leading only a single county, Adams, by more than 20 points.
A former political consultant, Cooke has also previously run a non-profit, owned a small business and worked as a waitress. During the campaign, Van Orden had attempted to raise questions about Cooke’s authenticity while tying her to left-wing ideas, frequently referring to her as “commie Cooke.” 
But Van Orden, whose aggressive temperament and frequent scandals had made him a divisive figure among voters in the district, ran on embracing the first two years of President Donald Trump’s second term. He appeared at campaign events with more than a dozen high ranking Trump administration officials while defending his support of Trump’s tariffs and war in Iran, which voters in the district had blamed for increasing costs. 
The district has been hit hard by several of the Trump administration’s most unpopular policies. Hospitals have closed; farmers have struggled to keep up with rising diesel prices and the burden of tariffs and last winter Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s Operation Metro Surge in the Twin Cities extended into western Wisconsin as far as Eau Claire.
At the only debate of the campaign in October, Cooke argued that she was the only candidate of the two who would actually put “America first.” 
Cooke’s win brings Democratic control back to the district, which voted for Trump three times but was represented by former Democratic Rep. Ron Kind from 1997 to 2023.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Democratic candidate elected secretary of state in 3-way contest
description: A former state Assembly member and current Milwaukee alder won the race for Wisconsin secretary of state Tuesday, becoming the first Latina elected to statewide office. The AP called the race for JoCasta Zamarripa at 11:38 p.m. Tuesday. With 91% of the ballots counted, Zamarripa led with just over 50% of the vote.  Republican candidate […]
text:
JoCasta Zamarripa, elected Wisconsin secretary of state Tuesday, will be the first Latina elected to statewide office. (Wisconsin Examiner photo)A former state Assembly member and current Milwaukee alder won the race for Wisconsin secretary of state Tuesday, becoming the first Latina elected to statewide office.
The AP called the race for JoCasta Zamarripa at 11:38 p.m. Tuesday. With 91% of the ballots counted, Zamarripa led with just over 50% of the vote. 
Republican candidate Jay Schroeder had just over 46%, and Pete Karas of the Green Party had just under 4%.
JoCasta Zamarripa, Milwaukee alder and Wisconsin Secretary of State hopeful. (Campaign photo)
Zamarripa released a statement Tuesday thanking her supporters and vowing to “uphold our democracy, protect the right to vote, and keep partisan politics out of our everyday governing.”
The Wisconsin Secretary of State’s current duties include maintaining a variety of state records, affixing the state seal to acts of the governor, certifying certain documents for people going overseas, certifying the state’s votes for U.S. President and U.S. Senate, and sitting on the Board of Commissioners of Public Lands.
The public lands board, which also includes the state treasurer and the state attorney general, makes loans for public projects to local governments and distributes the revenues from the public lands timber sales to public schools through the state’s common schools fund.
“I will do the real work this office demands for Wisconsin families, and I will be a voice for every community that has too often felt unseen,” Zamarripa said.
Schroeder, the Republican candidate, made his central campaign issue a call to return election administration to the secretary of state’s office more than 50 years after it had been transferred to an independent agency. He won the Republican primary in August with a platform that focused almost entirely on taking over the election process, which would require a change in state law.
On the weekend before Election Day, the race was roiled by an allegation that Schroeder had impersonated Karas’ campaign with text messages in support of the Green Party candidate. Karas filed a complaint with the Wisconsin Elections Board Monday charging Schroeder with violating a state law against election misrepresentation.
Karas and Zamarripa both said the messages appeared to be aimed at pulling support from the Democratic candidate’s campaign — dividing voters who opposed Schroeder and in the process enabling the Republican to prevail.
Schroeder’s argument for bringing election administration back to the secretary of state’s office rests on claims about the elections commission’s operation and practices that current and former state elections officials and the other candidates have all rejected.
Schroeder was the Republican candidate for secretary of state in 2018 and also ran unsuccessfully in the Republican primary for the office in 2022. During that race, he indicated he would not have certified Wisconsin’s electoral votes for Joe Biden in 2020.
In an interview earlier this year he did not deny the earlier remark but distanced himself from it and said that he accepted Biden’s election as president that year.
Schroeder has campaigned as an “authentic MAGA activist” and a “MAGA aligned candidate on election integrity,” but in an interview also sought to downplay those characterizations.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins leading in Alaska’s gubernatorial race in early results
description: This article is developing and will be updated. Alaska is on course to have its first Democratic governor since Tony Knowles left office almost a quarter-century ago. According to incomplete, preliminary results published Tuesday night by the Alaska Division of Elections, Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins had 55.3% of the vote among four people competing to replace Re[...]
text:
Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins speaks with a reporter before voting on Election Day, Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026 at the University of Alaska Anchorage. (Photo by Loren Holmes/Alaska Beacon)This article is developing and will be updated.
Alaska is on course to have its first Democratic governor since Tony Knowles left office almost a quarter-century ago.
According to incomplete, preliminary results published Tuesday night by the Alaska Division of Elections, Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins had 55.3% of the vote among four people competing to replace Republican Gov. Mike Dunleavy, who is term-limited and unable to run for re-election this year. 
Only 45 of 400 precincts were reporting results from Election Day, and tens of thousands of early and absentee votes remain to be counted in coming days.
Kreiss-Tomkins and three Republicans — Bernadette Wilson, Dave Bronson and Treg Taylor — are all seeking to replace incumbent Gov. Mike Dunleavy, who is term-limited and unable to run for re-election this year.
Wilson, the leading Republican candidate, received the endorsement of President Donald Trump during an October rally in Wasilla. She has 27.5% of the vote according to the latest update, with Bronson at 10.8% and Taylor at 6.2%. 
Earlier in the day, Kreiss-Tomkins spoke with reporters before casting his ballot in his home precinct at the University of Alaska Anchorage Student Union on Tuesday morning. 
“We’re really proud of the campaign that we’ve built — a lot of hard work, very much a team effort across Alaska,” he said. “No matter the outcome, I feel great about the process to get here.”
He said after ten months of campaigning and speaking with thousands of Alaskans his No. 1 takeaway was how difficult it is for many Alaskans to get by. He said he’s made a “very, very long list” of issues he wants to tackle, and he’s committed to work across partisan divides for Alaskans, including with the Trump administration.  “I’m excited to work with anyone and everyone — Trump administration to the House and Senate and the Legislature to all other partners in and out of government, for I mean potentially some really big wins for Alaska.”

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Democrats appear to win the NC House majority and gain seats in the Senate
description: In a huge upset Tuesday night, Democrats appeared to win the majority in the North Carolina House, with Democratic candidates scoring stunning victories in districts held by influential, veteran Republicans. Democrats have not controlled a chamber of the General Assembly since 2010, when Republicans won majorities in both the House and Senate.  At the Democr[...]
text:
North Carolina voters will decide on a number of important races on Nov. 3, 2026 as well as a flurry of bond issues and constitutional amendments. (Photo: Clayton Henkel/NC Newsline) In a huge upset Tuesday night, Democrats appeared to win the majority in the North Carolina House, with Democratic candidates scoring stunning victories in districts held by influential, veteran Republicans. Democrats have not controlled a chamber of the General Assembly since 2010, when Republicans won majorities in both the House and Senate. 
At the Democrats’ victory party Tuesday night, Rep. Robert Reives of Chatham, who is the House Democrat leader, was introduced as the next House Speaker. 
“We have the power to make this state better,” he told the jubilant crowd. . 
All returns are unofficial until county boards of election certify the results. 
In one of the biggest upsets of the night, Democrat Jen Wiles defeated seven-term GOP Rep. Donny Lambeth in his Forsyth County House district.  Lambeth is a senior House budget writer and was an early Republican champion of Medicaid expansion. Wiles won 53.97% of the vote to Lambeth’s 46.03%, according to unofficial returns. 
Democrats ended the Republican’s veto-proof majority in the Senate, flipping seats held by powerful Republicans. 
Democrat Jessica Bichler defeated Republican incumbent Sen. Michael Lee in Senate District 7. With all precincts reporting in the New Hanover district, Bichler was leading 52.64% to 47.36%. Lee was considered a front-runner to replace Sen. Phil Berger as Senate leader.
In an eastern North Carolina district, Democrat Jess Rivera was leading incumbent Republican Sen. Buck Newton, 51.07% to  48.93%, with all precincts reporting. Newton is in his fifth term and co-chairs the Senate Finance and Judiciary committees. 
In a closely watched Senate race, Democratic former House member James Gailliard defeated Republican incumbent Sen. Lisa Barnes in Senate District 11, which includes Nash, Franklin and Vance counties. Gailliard leads with 51.37% of the vote to Barnes 46.28%, with all precincts reporting. 
House District 117, the district Rep. Jennifer Balkcom gave up to run for Congress, flipped from Republican to Democrat in unofficial returns, with Democrat Lynne Russo defeating Republican Chelsea Walsh, 51.74% to 48.26%.
In another House flip, Democrat LeVon Barnes defeated seven-term incumbent Rep. Dennis Riddell in District 64 in Alamance County, 52.73% to 47.27%, with all precincts reporting. 
In another mountain district, Democrat Charlie Wallin was leading incumbent Republican Ray Pickett with all precincts counted. The margin was in recount territory, with Wallin leading 50.30% to 49.70%. Candidates for the legislature who appear to have lost can request a recount if the difference in votes is 1% or less of total votes cast. 
In another flipped Senate seat, Democrat April Cook defeated Republican Kevin Crutchfield in District 34 in Cabarrus County. Cook was ahead 57.66% to 42.34%, with all precincts reporting. Crutchfield defeated the Republican incumbent in the GOP primary. 
Unofficial results show Democrats defeating GOP incumbents in urban Wake and Mecklenburg, and in more rural counties such as Nash and Wilson. 
Here’s what happened in some of the closely watched races.  
In Mecklenburg’s House District 105, Democrat Ken McCool defeated incumbent Republican Tricia Cotham, 57.11% to 42.89% with all precincts reporting. This is the second election cycle where Democrats put a special focus on defeating Cotham. She switched parties in 2023 to give House Republicans the veto-proof majority they needed to cancel vetoes of abortion, elections, and education bills. With a McCool victory, the entire Mecklenburg House delegation is Democratic. 
Two Democratic challengers defeated Republican incumbents in Wake County. With all precincts reporting, Democrat Winn Decker defeated GOP Rep. Erin Pare with 54.72% of the vote to her 45.28% in the southern Wake district.  In northern Wake County, Democratic challenger Evonne Hopkins defeated Republican incumbent Mike Schietzelt, 54.95% to 45.05% with all precincts reporting. 
And in northern Wake’s Senate district, Democratic incumbent Haseeb Fatmi defeated Republican Chris Stock 54.77% to 42.79%.  Fatmi was appointed to the seat this year to replace former Sen. Terence Everitt, who resigned in April.  
Wake County’s entire legislative delegation will be Democratic next year.   
Beyond North Carolina’s big metro areas, Democrat Lorenza Wilkins defeated incumbent Republican Rep. Allen Chesser, with all precincts reporting, 52.67% to 44.73%. The race was a rematch of the 2024 contest, which Chesser won by less than one point.  House District 25 includes most of Nash County, which is considered a bellwether for the state. Libertarian Nick Taylor received 2.61% of the vote in House District 25.
In House District 32, Democratic incumbent Rep. Bryan Cohn defeated Republican Frank Sossamon. Sossamon was trying to win back the seat that includes Granville and Vance counties that he narrowly lost to Cohn in 2024. Cohn holds a comfortable lead this year, with 55.39% of the vote to Sossamon’s 44.61%
In a House district that includes Wilson County and a bit of Nash, Democrat Dante Pittman, an incumbent in his first term defeated Republican Blake Boykin, chair of the Wilson County Board of Education, 58.26% to 41.74%, with all precincts reporting.
Registered Democrats built a substantial edge during the early voting period, which also saw higher than usual turnout by unaffiliated voters. With 2.8 million votes having been cast during the early voting period that ended Saturday, Republicans needed significant Election Day turnout to win in closely contested races. 
County boards of election must still count provisional ballots, some absentee ballots, and military ballots, which don’t have to be in until 5 p.m. Nov. 12.
Voters and candidates may also file election protests alleging illegalities or irregularities. 
County boards of election are scheduled to meet on Nov. 13 to certify election results. 
County boards of election must still consider provisional ballots. The apparent losers in some close contests may request recounts.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: Voters approve North Dakota governor’s first appointees, reelect all Republican incumbents
description: North Dakota voters on Tuesday approved Gov. Kelly Armstrong’s first appointments to statewide offices, giving green lights to Public Service Commissioner Jill Kringstad and State Superintendent Levi Bachmeier to keep serving two more years. Voters also reelected all other Republican state officeholders. No Democrat has won a statewide election in North Dako[...]
text:
Public Service Commissioner Jill Kringstad, a Republican, gives a speech at an election night party in Bismarck on Nov. 3, 2026. Kringstad won her race. (Photo by Kyle Martin/For the North Dakota Monitor)North Dakota voters on Tuesday approved Gov. Kelly Armstrong’s first appointments to statewide offices, giving green lights to Public Service Commissioner Jill Kringstad and State Superintendent Levi Bachmeier to keep serving two more years.
Voters also reelected all other Republican state officeholders. No Democrat has won a statewide election in North Dakota since Heidi Heitkamp’s 2012 U.S. Senate victory.
Armstrong appointed Kringstad to the regulatory panel in January 2025 to fill the vacancy left by Julie Fedorchak when she resigned to take North Dakota’s single seat in the U.S. House. Kringstad was previously the PSC’s director of business operations.
North Dakota sends Fedorchak back to DC

She defeated Democrat Scot Kelsh, a former state lawmaker, by a margin of about 62% to 38%, according to complete but unofficial results.
Kringstad said she enjoyed the experience of campaigning and traveling the state to hear the concerns of North Dakotans.
“I’m just really grateful to the people of North Dakota for the trust they have put in me,” said Kringstad, who will need to run for a full six-year term in 2028 to keep the seat.
Armstrong appointed Bachmeier in October 2025 to replace Kirsten Baesler, who resigned her post as North Dakota’s top K-12 schools official to join the U.S. Department of Education. Bachmeier was previously the business manager for West Fargo Public Schools.
He defeated longtime educator Tracy Foss by a margin of about 63% to 37%.
The position is nonpartisan, but Bachmeier is a Republican and Foss received support from the Democratic-NPL Party. Bachmeier will have to run for a full four-year term in 2028 to keep serving.
Voters handily reelected statewide Republican officeholders.
Governor predicts good results for Republicans in North Dakota but maybe not everywhere else

Attorney General Drew Wrigley won a rematch against Democrat Tim Lamb, a Grand Forks attorney who challenged him in 2022 and also ran unsuccessfully for state auditor in 2024.
Secretary of State Michael Howe defeated Democratic state Sen. Ryan Braunberger of Fargo for another four years as the state’s top election official. Braunberger is in the middle of his four-year Senate term and will serve in the 2027 Legislature.
Agriculture Commissioner Doug Goehring was reelected over Democrat Vern Thompson, a former lawmaker.
Tax Commissioner Brian Kroshus defeated Democrat Mark Nelson, a retired Rugby-area farmer, to continue serving. 
Public Service Commissioner Sheri Haugen-Hoffart won a full six-year term on the PSC against Democrat John Pederson, a Mayville State professor.
Supreme Court Justice Jerod Tufte was reelected to a 10-year term over challenger Ariston Johnson, a Watford City attorney.
Justice Douglas Bahr, whom former Gov. Doug Burgum appointed in 2023, won an eight-year term on the court. He ran unopposed. 
North Dakotans cast more than 239,000 ballots during the 2026 general election, a 39.8% turnout, the lowest voter turnout for a general election in 50 years, according to the Secretary of State’s Office. The previous low was 43% set in 2022.
“I am incredibly grateful for the 3,000 poll workers who stepped forward to make democracy happen,” Howe in a statement. “While the voter turnout is disappointing, I am hopeful more North Dakotans will become civically engaged and vote in future elections.”
Reach North Dakota Monitor reporter Jack Dura at jdura@northdakotamonitor.com.
