name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri voters approve constitutional protections for county sheriffs
description: Missouri voters narrowly approved Amendment 8 on Tuesday, giving county sheriffs constitutional protection and restricting who can seek their removal from office. The measure, which garnered 51% of the vote, writes into the Missouri Constitution the existing requirement that counties elect a sheriff every four years, along with certain duties already establi[...]
text:
Sen. Jill Carter, a Republican from Granby, studies the day's business on the first day of the 2024 legislative session (Annelise Hanshaw/Missouri Independent).Missouri voters narrowly approved Amendment 8 on Tuesday, giving county sheriffs constitutional protection and restricting who can seek their removal from office.
The measure, which garnered 51% of the vote, writes into the Missouri Constitution the existing requirement that counties elect a sheriff every four years, along with certain duties already established in state law.
The change means lawmakers can no longer eliminate the office of sheriff or change those constitutional duties without voter approval.
It also gives the state attorney general exclusive authority to initiate legal proceedings to remove a sheriff from office, a provision that drew opposition from some Republican and Democratic lawmakers.
Under current law, a county prosecutor or the attorney general can initiate a legal action known as quo warranto seeking a sheriff’s removal. Amendment 8 reserves that authority to the attorney general, with a court ultimately deciding whether a sheriff should be removed.
The amendment does not apply to St. Louis city, St. Louis County or St. Charles County.
Amendment 8 follows a four-year push by Republican lawmakers, led by state Sen. Jill Carter of Granby, to give sheriffs constitutional status.
Carter had the backing of the Missouri Sheriffs’ Association, led by Osage County Sheriff Michael Bonham.
Bonham told The Independent in October that more than 30 states already enshrine the sheriff’s authority in their constitutions and argued that Missouri should do the same.
“It is a pure motive to be able to protect the legitimate office of the sheriff in the state of Missouri,” he said, “that legislators can’t come in and [say] ‘We’re mad at the sheriffs’ and that’s it. We’re going to make a state police.”
The legislation lawmakers passed in May was narrower than earlier versions, which sought to give sheriffs authority to oversee federal and state investigations.
Those provisions were removed, but the debate surrounding Amendment 8 continued to reflect a broader political movement that sees county sheriffs as a check on government overreach.
The final version does not give sheriffs new authority to oversee federal or state investigations. Instead, it places several existing responsibilities into the Constitution, making them more difficult for future legislatures to change.
Opponents questioned some of those duties, particularly language requiring sheriffs to “apprehend and commit to jail all felons and traitors.”
The provision already exists in Missouri statute, but putting it in the Constitution means lawmakers can no longer change it without voter approval.
During House debate in May, several Democrats raised concerns about the wording, particularly the reference to “traitors.”
Democratic state Rep. Aaron Crossley of Independence noted that the word “traitor” is not defined in state statute.
“Is a traitor a protester?” he said. “Is it a political dissenter? Is it someone who disagrees with whoever is in power? I’m already uncomfortable with it being a statute, but putting it in our constitution where it can never be changed – or it can be but with a lot of hassle – I think that we’re really treading down a dangerous, dangerous road.”
Supporters maintained that the amendment was about preserving the elected office of sheriff, not expanding its authority.
Its passage now places that office and its constitutional duties beyond the reach of ordinary legislation, while concentrating the authority to seek a sheriff’s removal in the hands of one statewide elected official.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Republican Scott Fitzpatrick wins second term as Missouri state auditor
description: Republican State Auditor Scott Fitzpatrick won a second term Tuesday, defeating Democratic challenger Quentin Wilson in Missouri’s only statewide candidate race. Fitzpatrick won 50% of the vote to Wilson’s 47%. Libertarian Dustin Coffell won 3%. The victory keeps Republicans in control of all six statewide elected offices despite a historically bad Election [...]
text:
State Auditor Scott Fitzpatrick (photo submitted).Republican State Auditor Scott Fitzpatrick won a second term Tuesday, defeating Democratic challenger Quentin Wilson in Missouri’s only statewide candidate race.
Fitzpatrick won 50% of the vote to Wilson’s 47%. Libertarian Dustin Coffell won 3%.
The victory keeps Republicans in control of all six statewide elected offices despite a historically bad Election Day that saw them  lose their supermajorities in the Missouri House and Senate and a congressional seat in the St. Louis suburbs.
Fitzpatrick ran on his record of uncovering waste, fraud and abuse, particularly in local governments, and warning lawmakers about Missouri’s increasingly precarious financial outlook. The win gives him another four years to oversee the independent watchdog agency responsible for reviewing how state and local governments spend taxpayer money.
Wilson, who held leadership positions in several state agencies over two decades, argued the auditor should take a more proactive approach to helping government operate efficiently and save taxpayers money.
The contest drew relatively little attention compared with the high-profile ballot measures that dominated Missouri’s election.
But an August poll from Saint Louis University and YouGov suggested the race could be closer than expected, with Fitzpatrick leading Wilson 45% to 43%, within the margin of error.
Republicans have dominated statewide elections in Missouri for years. The last Democrat to hold statewide office was former Auditor Nicole Galloway, who left office in January 2023 after Fitzpatrick defeated her handpicked successor in the 2022 election.
 Expanding the watchdog role

Fitzpatrick, a former state treasurer and chairman of the Missouri House Budget Committee, has emphasized expanding his office’s authority to investigate local governments.
In2024, he successfully pushed for legislation giving his office greater discretion to launch audits when whistleblower complaints uncover evidence of wrongdoing.
Previously, the auditor generally needed a petition from residents or an invitation from local officials to conduct an audit. The new law allows the office, under certain circumstances, to move directly from an investigation to an audit and use subpoena power during the investigative stage.
The legislation passed unanimously in both chambers.
Fitzpatrick pointed to an audit of the city of Arnold as an example of how the expanded authority has strengthened his office.
The audit released in April, found that city officials abused transportation development district laws to collect millions in sales taxes without giving residents a vote.
The report also found conflicts of interest and improper spending of district revenue on city development projects.
“The city of Arnold had basically turned this into like a forever tax or a forever district,” Fitzpatrick previously told The Independent, “where they just kind of wanted to have an open-ended list of projects that they could use this money on.”
His office also used its subpoena power to compel testimony and obtain records during the investigation.
Fitzpatrick has highlighted his office’s investigation of Jackson County’s troubled 2023 property assessments.
An audit released Friday found widespread failures in the county’s assessment process, including inadequate notification of property owners and a failure to follow state law.
Separate litigation brought by the state ultimately resulted in a settlement worth up to $250 million for affected property owners.
Fitzpatrick said he initially expected to spend most of his time auditing state agencies. Instead, his office has increasingly focused on local governments, where he said investigators have uncovered most of their fraud cases.
Missouri has more than 4,000 political subdivisions, giving auditors far more potential targets than they have resources to investigate.
“There’s always going to be more things that need our attention than we have capacity to manage at any given time,” he said.
 A looming budget challenge

Fitzpatrick’s second term will also come as Missouri faces increasingly difficult budget decisions.
In a report released in December, he warned that state spending was outpacing revenue growth and could exhaust Missouri’s general revenue reserves by fiscal 2028 if existing trends continued.
The report found that the state’s general revenue balance, which peaked at $5.8 billion in 2023, had fallen to approximately $4.3 billion by the end of fiscal 2025.
“I do not see any prospects of a federal bailout coming to soften the blow of what’s about to happen this time,” Fitzpatrick told The Independent. “I think what we’re getting ready to encounter is unprecedented.”
Wilson agreed that Missouri faced serious budget problems but argued Fitzpatrick’s approach did not go far enough.
He proposed restructuring the auditor’s office to operate more like the federal Government Accountability Office, examining not only whether public money was spent properly but also whether government programs could operate more efficiently.
Wilson claimed that approach could save taxpayers as much as $1 billion annually.
He also criticized Fitzpatrick’s audits for sometimes taking too long and questioned whether the Republican incumbent was sufficiently independent of other GOP officeholders.
Fitzpatrick rejected those criticisms, arguing his office had demonstrated its willingness to scrutinize government officials regardless of party affiliation.
He also maintained that the auditor’s responsibility is to identify problems and recommend solutions, not make spending decisions.
“That’s between the legislature and the governor,” Fitzpatrick said, “and I’m neither one of those.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: Mississippi Senate election is too close to call Tuesday night
description: Candidates for Mississippi's U.S. Senate seat in the 2026 midterms are, from left, Ty Pinkins, Cindy Hyde-Smith and Scott Colom.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith and Democratic challenger Scott Colom were locked in a tight race late Tuesday, with each trying to reassure nervous supporters as vote counting continued in a state where Republicans have had a lock on U.S. Senate seats for decades.
Hyde-Smith led Colom slightly, but The Associated Press had not declared a winner as midnight approached. Independent Ty Pinkins was pulling about 2% of the vote. 
While the race remained too close to call, the narrow margin reflected what some onlookers called a “bluenami,” with Democrats notching stunning victories in Republican strongholds such as South Carolina and Texas. Most forecasters had rated the Mississippi Senate race as safe Republican. But as results began trickling in, it soon became clear the race would be anything but safe for the GOP, with Colom overperforming in many counties compared to Democrats in other recent races. 

Shortly before 11 p.m., Hyde-Smith spoke to a crowd of supporters at a watch party in Flowood. She nearly declared victory but stopped just short, saying that she would emerge as the winner by Wednesday morning. 
Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, left, with her daughter Anna-Michael Smith and husband Mike Smith, speaks to supporters during her watch party held at the Sheraton Flowood The Refuge Hotel & Conference Center, Tuesday, Oct. 3, 2026, in Flowood. Credit: Vickie D. King/Mississippi Today
“This is a much longer night than we thought it would be,” Hyde-Smith said. ”But we’re in a good lead right now.”
Hyde-Smith said there was record turnout on the Republican side, despite problems at some polling locations in traditionally Republican areas. She praised her campaign’s efforts, but acknowledged Democrats had given her a challenge she didn’t expect.
“I’ll tell you the Democrats got out and worked, they really got out and worked, and a lot of them showed up today. But not enough of them. I’ll just tell you that right now,” Hyde-Smith said. “I assure you I will continue to be your U.S. senator.”
Gerard Henderson, Colom’s campaign manager, told a crowd at Colom’s party in downtown Jackson that Tuesday was going to be a “long night.” 
“This is not over,” Henderson said. “We’re going to fight til the end.” 
Colom briefly visited with his supporters, hugging some of them and saying, “God bless you.” 
Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Scott Colom speaks to his supporters during his election watch party at the Ice House in Jackson on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
State Republican Party Mike Hurst said he expected Hyde-Smith to pull off a victory and overcome a disastrous performance for Republicans around the country. 
“I think if you look across the country, you see a number of things happen, a number of people responding to whatever the president has done, what Republicans have done,” Hurst said. “And I think you see that in Mississippi as well. At the end of the night, though, we are a Republican state. Mississippians are Republican individuals who are going to vote Republican.”
The Colom campaign estimated that around 10,000 or 15,000 affidavit ballots remained outstanding. The Hyde-Smith campaign said its internal numbers showed the incumbent would win. 
Brandon Presley, the Democratic nominee for governor in 2023, was at Colom’s watch party and crunching numbers with several supporters. He told Mississippi Today that Colom was in a better position on Tuesday night than he was on election night at this point in the gubernatorial election three years ago. 
Mississippi has no runoff in federal general elections, and the winner needs only a plurality. Colom is a Democratic district attorney in north Mississippi, and Hyde-Smith is seeking a second full term. 
The Mississippi Democratic Party filed a lawsuit against the DeSoto County circuit clerk shortly after polls closed at 7 p.m. The party argued in court documents that some polling precincts opened late and some ran out of ballots. 
The party asked for certain precincts to stay open an additional hour, but as of Tuesday night, well after polls had closed, a judge had not been assigned to the case.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Democrats sweep Triangle area legislative races
description: Strong Democratic turnout turned the Triangle’s legislative delegation solid blue Tuesday night, unseating two Republican House members and a Republican senator in a neighboring county. Voters in southern Wake County opted to flip House District 37, electing newcomer Winn Decker and sending home Republican Rep. Erin Paré after three terms. The Associated Pre[...]
text:
Republican Rep. Erin Paré, R-Wake, and Democrat Winn Decker faced off in a closely watched race to represent House District 37 in Wake County. (Photos: NCGA and Decker campaign) Strong Democratic turnout turned the Triangle’s legislative delegation solid blue Tuesday night, unseating two Republican House members and a Republican senator in a neighboring county.
N.C. HOUSE 37
Voters in southern Wake County opted to flip House District 37, electing newcomer Winn Decker and sending home Republican Rep. Erin Paré after three terms.
The Associated Press projected Decker as the winner, capturing nearly 55% percent of the vote, according to unofficial election results from the N.C. Board of Elections. Paré won 45% of the vote.
Decker, an education policy expert who formerly worked at The Hunt Institute, ran a campaign centered on affordability. Decker said on his website that as Wake County continues to grow, the district needs leadership committed to strengthening public education, improving infrastructure, and expanding economic opportunity.
Decker said his decision to run was based on his belief that the Republican-controlled legislature was not being responsive to the rising costs of housing, health care, groceries, and taxes.
Paré had hoped to win a fourth term in the House where she serves as a chair of the House Committee on Appropriations and chairs the House Select Committee on Property Tax Reduction and Reform. She advocated higher teacher pay and touted her background as a military spouse and small business owner.
The district covers the towns of Fuquay-Varina and parts of Holly Springs.
N.C. HOUSE 35
In her second attempt to win House District 35 in northern Wake County, Democrat Evonne Hopkins successfully defeated Republican incumbent Rep. Mike Schietzelt.
The Associated Press projected Hopkins as the winner, capturing 56% percent of the vote, according to unofficial election results from the N.C. Board of Elections. Schietzelt earned 44% of Tuesday’s vote.
Hopkins, a family law specialist, focused her campaign on lowering the cost of living, protecting access to Medicaid, and ensuring quality, affordable healthcare. In addition to paying teachers more, Hopkins advocated for more counselors, nurses, and special-education professionals in the state’s public schools. Hopkins was recognized for her work in child custody cases in 2024 with Legal Aid of North Carolina’s Pro Bono Hero Award.
Schietzelt, who came up short on Tuesday amidst very strong Democratic turnout, tried to lean into the affordability message. He called for higher pay for educators and worked to block a plan to turn Capital Boulevard into a toll road. More recently, Schietzelt said he would focus on rising housing and healthcare costs if elected to another term in the legislature.
N.C. SENATE 11
James Gailliard will return to the North Carolina legislature, this time in the state Senate. Gailliard, a Democratic former member of the North Carolina House of Representatives, defeated Republican incumbent Senator Lisa Stone Barnes. Barnes has represented Franklin, Nash and Vance counties in the Senate since 2021.
The Associated Press projected Gailliard as the winner, capturing 51% percent of the vote, according to unofficial election results from the N.C. Board of Elections. Barnes earned 46% of Tuesday’s vote.
Gailliard focused much of his campaign on education funding. Gailliard has been a vocal supporter of providing students with their constitutionally mandated right to a “sound basic education.” He also supports expanding the N.C. Teaching Fellows Program, universal pre-K and wraparound services such as mental health support, nutrition programs and after-school care.
Gailliard also proposes down-payment assistance for first-time home buyers, state funding for community development and affordable housing partnerships, and emergency rental assistance and eviction-prevention programs.
Barnes leaned into reducing taxes and controlling government spending. Senate Leader Phil Berger tapped Barnes to co-chair the new Select Committee on Property Tax Reform in September.
N.C. SENATE 18
Sen. Haseeb Fatmi, D-Wake, who was appointed to the N.C. Senate in May 2026 to replace Sen. Terence Everitt, won the support of voters Tuesday and will continue to represent Senate District 18. The district covers northern Wake County including Wake Forest and Rolesville and all of Granville County.
The Associated Press projected Fatmi as the winner, capturing 56% percent of the vote, according to unofficial election results from the N.C. Board of Elections.  Republican challenger Chris Stock earned more than 41% of Tuesday’s vote.
Fatmi, an attorney and former Wake Forest town commissioner, focused his campaign on tax relief for working families and lowering energy and healthcare costs.
Stock, who worked for state Sen. Brent Jackson, said on his website that he learned how to “craft efficient budgets” through his time at the General Assembly and would use that experience to lower costs for families, seniors, and small businesses.
The race also featured Libertarian Brad Hessel, former executive director of the Libertarian Party of North Carolina, who captured 2% of the vote.

text:
Democrat Mary Peltola waves to passing motorists on Election Day, Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026 in Midtown Anchorage. (Photo by Loren Holmes/Alaska Beacon)This article is developing and will be updated.
Alaska is on course to elect its first Democratic U.S. senator since 2008 in a closely watched race that will help determine whether Republicans or Democrats control the U.S. Senate.
With 45 of 401 precincts reporting results Tuesday night, Peltola had 54.1% of voters’ first-choice votes. Republican incumbent Sen. Dan S. Sullivan had 42.8% of the vote.
Independent challenger Dan J. Sullivan had 1.5%, and Republican challenger Gerald Heikes had 1.3%. 
Peltola’s lead follows a series of Democratic victories in U.S. Senate races across the country Tuesday night. If she prevails, she is expected to be the 55th or 56th Democratic senator in a large Democratic majority. 
In addition, Peltola and U.S. Sen.-elect Peggy Flanagan, D-Minnesota will be the first female Indigenous Senators in American history.
Some Republican officials said before the first results that they would challenge the legality of a Peltola victory, citing New York Times reporting that found Democratic campaigners recruited independent candidate Dan J. Sullivan in an attempt to siphon votes from the incumbent Dan S. Sullivan.
But late Tuesday, President Donald Trump — who ordered civil challenges against Peltola — told the Times he would not challenge the results of the election.

title: Democrat Sarah Trone Garriott defeats incumbent Zach Nunn in Iowa’s 3rd District
description: Iowa’s 3rd Congressional District will have a Democratic representative as state Sen. Sarah Trone Garriott won the district over Republican incumbent Zach Nunn, according to preliminary results from the Associated Press. Preliminary results from the AP show Trone Garriott pulled in 55% of the vote to 45% for Nunn, with 92% of precincts reporting. Trone […]
text:
Sarah Trone Garriott joined Rob Sand and other Democrats at an event Nov. 1, 2026 in Des Moines. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch)  Iowa’s 3rd Congressional District will have a Democratic representative as state Sen. Sarah Trone Garriott won the district over Republican incumbent Zach Nunn, according to preliminary results from the Associated Press.
Preliminary results from the AP show Trone Garriott pulled in 55% of the vote to 45% for Nunn, with 92% of precincts reporting.
Trone Garriott, who joined Iowa Democrats at a watch party in Des Moines, said that Iowans have “so much common ground” and she plans to “build on that common ground for a strong future.” 
“We are bringing change for everyone,” Trone Garriott said. “To restore healthcare, to lower costs, to stop these tariffs, to end this war. We did this to take on the corruption that is at the heart of the problem costing us so much, and make Washington accountable to the people, because we know that powerful things are possible when we show up on our common ground and we work really hard and we work together.” 
Trone Garriott, a pastor and state senator since 2020, thanked Nunn for his service to the country and to the state of Iowa. 
She said there are “significant” challenges ahead, but “the hope we have is stronger; the love we have for our neighbors is so much more powerful.”
Trone Garriott has said her priorities include lowering healthcare costs for Iowans by undoing portions of the Republican-led “One Big Beautiful Bill” Act and by working to restore expired tax subsidies for the Affordable Care Act. 
Speaking at the Iowa GOP watch party in Des Moines, Nunn said he is proud of the accomplishments he made while in office and for winning the “hardest district in the state.”
U.S. Rep. Zach Nunn stands with his wife, Kelly, his family and his staff following unofficial election results that he will not be reelected. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch)
Nunn defeated Democratic incumbent Cindy Axne in 2022. Trone Garriott’s win returns the district with Iowa’s most populous city to Democratic representation. 
Nunn highlighted legislation he advanced while in office to help military families and access to housing, along with funding he secured for infrastructure like rural water systems, streets and bridges.
Nunn, who is a combat veteran from the Des Moines area, and continues to serve as a Colonel in the U.S. Air Force Reserve, thanked his family repeatedly for their support.
“There are certain things I’m going to miss about fighting for Iowa, but I’m not going to miss being gone three or four times a week,” Nunn said while looking to his family on stage.
Nunn said he called Trone Garriott to congratulate her on the win. 
“Across the board, we have helped deliver for our community, for our families, and most importantly, for our country,” Nunn said. “And I challenge anybody else who takes this seat to do just as good, and hopefully better – but I’m proud of the very high bar we set.”

name: National
title: Voters across the country reject data centers
description: In local elections across the country, Americans voted overwhelmingly to restrict the buildout of data centers in their communities. Late Tuesday evening, 33 ballot measures to restrict data centers were passed by voters or were leading in ongoing vote counts, according to the tracking website Data Centers on the Ballot. Roughly a dozen similar measures […]
text:
People participate in a protest against the CoreWeave AI data center outside the municipal building on October 21, 2026, in Kenilworth. New Jersey. (Photo by Stephanie Keith/Getty Images)In local elections across the country, Americans voted overwhelmingly to restrict the buildout of data centers in their communities.
Late Tuesday evening, 33 ballot measures to restrict data centers were passed by voters or were leading in ongoing vote counts, according to the tracking website Data Centers on the Ballot. Roughly a dozen similar measures were on the ballot in communities where vote totals had not yet been announced.
The measures included outright prohibitions, temporary moratoriums, limitations on energy use, mandating voter approval before construction and advisory measures urging local officials to restrict data centers.
Only one measure, in North Dakota, resulted in a victory for voters who supported the construction of data centers.
The national backlash to data centers has become a major political issue. Residents in Republican and Democratic cities alike have pushed back on tech companies’ plans to aggressively build data centers to power their artificial intelligence platforms. Local and national activists have raised concerns about energy costs, pollution, water use, noise and conversion of farmland and other open spaces.
According to an NBC exit poll, 56% of voters said AI and data centers played a “crucial or major factor” in their vote for Congress.
In some communities, including 21 municipalities in Ohio, residents turned to local ballot measures or referendums in an effort to block the construction of proposed data centers. In nearly every result so far, voters overwhelmingly backed new restrictions or declined to approve measures that affirmed the buildout of such facilities.
Conserve Ohio, a campaign seeking to block data center development, worked with leaders in many of those communities to help draft ballot language.
“It’s one of the most beautiful things I’ve ever seen, people coming together across communities, putting partisan differences aside and uniting (to oppose data centers),” Nick Owens, an attorney with the group, told Stateline last month.
A poll published by UMass Amherst earlier this year found that only 11% of Americans would support the construction of an AI data center in their community.
Stateline reporter Alex Brown can be reached at abrown@stateline.org

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Elliott declares reelection victory in Indiana treasurer race, with comptroller vote tight
description: Republican Daniel Elliott will continue serving as Indiana treasurer, one of the state's top financial officers.
text:
Indiana Treasurer Daniel Elliott delivers a victory speech at the Intercontinental Hotel in downtown Indianapolis Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Mackenzi Klemann/Indiana Capital Chronicle.)Republican Daniel Elliott will continue serving as Indiana treasurer, one of the state’s top financial officers.
The race for state comptroller remained too close to call as votes continued to be tallied into early Wednesday.
Elliott claimed a three-point lead over Democratic challenger Coumba Kebe with 91% of votes reporting.
“This is possible because of the hard work that you have done,” Elliott told supporters at the Intercontinental Hotel. “Republicans up and down this state have made sure that we keep Indiana in a strong position. They want people who pay attention to them. They want people who understand how to focus on them, people who know how to take our dollars and focus on how we can make it work for Hoosiers—not for big corporations, not for institutions, but for people.”
The treasurer is Indiana’s chief financial officer, responsible for managing the state’s investments and savings programs.
First elected to the office in 2022, Elliott leaned on his experience on the campaign trail, boasting of the state’s $1.8 billion in investment earnings.
His opponent Kebe, a healthcare executive from Noblesville, campaigned for greater transparency and accessible reporting about state holdings, investment performance and fees, and to use the office to advocate for changes to Medicaid and childcare policy.
She received 48.5% of the vote in the incomplete tallies.
Supporters cheer on Indiana Treasurer Daniel Elliott, the first statewide victory for the GOP Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Mackenzi Klemann/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
Elliott acknowledged the tough election coutcomes for Republicans, telling supporters “the battle is not done.”
“We have a job to do,” he said. “We have things to get done. And this next four years, we are going to be focusing even more on the people of Indiana and making sure we get conservative principles out there.”
With Democrats breaking the Republican supermajority hold in the Indiana House, Elliott said he’s focused on continuing to generate money for Indiana.
“My goal as state treasurer is keep doing what I’ve been doing: raising money for the state of Indiana, running the best, the most high-tech 911 program in the state, in the country actually, and focusing on things like helping local governments with their infrastructure through Indiana Bond Bank.”
The race for comptroller, Indiana’s other top financial officer, remained tight into early Wednesday with incumbent Elise Nieshalla trailing Democratic challenger Jessica Bailey by 1.7 percentage points with 91% of votes reported.
Libertarian candidate John Schick followed in third with 3% of the vote.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Idaho constitutional amendment to declare English as state’s official language passes
description: Idaho voters widely approved amending the Idaho Constitution to declare English as the state’s official language. The Associated Press declared at 10:32 p.m. Wednesday that the amendment, which was proposed by the Idaho Legislature last year, passed. The amendment received support from 58.86% of Idaho voters, with about 200,000 votes, while 41.14% of voters [...]
text:
An election worker speaks to a voter in South Hills Middle School gymnasium on Election Day in Twin Falls, Idaho, Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Andrew Eakin for the Idaho Capital Sun)Idaho voters widely approved amending the Idaho Constitution to declare English as the state’s official language.
The Associated Press declared at 10:32 p.m. Wednesday that the amendment, which was proposed by the Idaho Legislature last year, passed.
The amendment received support from 58.86% of Idaho voters, with about 200,000 votes, while 41.14% of voters opposed it, with roughly 140,000 votes, according to unofficial election results from the Idaho Secretary of State’s Office at 10:43 p.m. Tuesday. Half of Idaho’s 44 counties were fully reporting election results by then.
State law already lists English as the state’s official language. Some critics say it’s unclear whether the amendment will end broader exceptions in state law that allowed governments to communicate in other languages, such as in law enforcement and public health situations. 
Here’s how the amendment will look in the Constitution: “The English language shall be the official language for the state of Idaho. Except as required by federal law, English shall be used in all public proceedings, public documents, public instruction, and any other public acts of any public institution in the state of Idaho.”
Thirty states have declared English as their official language, according to Ballotpedia. In 2025, President Donald Trump declared English as the nation’s official language in an executive order. 
In Idaho, Hispanics make up about 13% of the state’s population, and the state has welcomed thousands of refugees in recent years. Over the last decade, the state’s Hispanic population grew faster, by 25%, than the state’s overall population, which rose by 10%, according to statistics from the Idaho Commission on Hispanic Affairs. About 11% of Idahoans speak a language other than English at home, according to the U.S. Census Bureau. 
To pass, Idaho’s amendment needed support from at least 50% of voters.
Tuesday’s general election results won’t become official until the State Board of Canvassers certifies the election results. The canvass is scheduled to occur in the coming weeks. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
 How the amendment would work

The amendment’s legislative sponsor, Republican Rep. Dale Hawkins, said the amendment is intended to encourage people to learn English. But in Idaho, an agricultural state with a high population of Hispanic people, some worry that the lack of clarity around the amendment could make it harder for some residents to run their businesses, know what’s going on in their children’s schools or to stay up to date about what’s happening in their communities.
Hawkins said lawmakers had worked on the proposed Idaho amendment with the Trump administration.
“One of the things that unites us all as a culture, as a country, as a state, is language. And we see more and more people that are moving to the United States …” Hawkins said in an October interview. “And what used to be the desired effect, which was assimilation — learn the language, learn the culture, learn the history — those things have slipped away. And we don’t see assimilation anymore. And I believe that if we have a common language, then our culture will survive.”
The proposed constitutional amendment’s only exception allows the government to use other languages when required by federal law, such as in schools and, in some cases, election administration. 
University of Idaho law professor Richard Seamon previously told the Idaho Capital Sun that the amendment’s impact is not clear.
“If it said ‘only English,’ then I think it would clearly, pretty clearly, override these exceptions, and eliminate them,” Seamon said. “But it doesn’t say only … So I think that leaves room for discussion about the extent to which these exceptions will still apply.”
Hawkins said the proposed amendment is written to be more restrictive than the state law on purpose, and that it should override the state law.
Hawkins said whether some of the law’s exceptions would remain, such as the use of other languages by law enforcement soliciting tips to find a missing child or health officials informing the public about an infectious disease outbreak, should be handled on a case-by-case approach.
“Each one of those exceptions would have to be, for lack of a better term, studied and to make sure that we’re not creating loopholes so that we have no effect,” Hawkins said.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Strong Democratic turnout flips at least 5 US House seats across North Carolina
description: In unofficial results from election night, North Carolina voters appear to have ousted half of North Carolina’s Republican U.S. House delegation in a string of upset elections in what were drawn to be safe Republican seats. Rep. Richard Hudson, 9th Congressional District incumbent and National Republican Congressional Committee chairman, narrowly lost his se[...]
text:
Rep. Richard Hudson, 9th Congressional District incumbent and National Republican Congressional Committee chairman, left, appears to have narrowly lost his seat to Democrat Richard Ojeda, right. (Photos courtesy of campaigns) In unofficial results from election night, North Carolina voters appear to have ousted half of North Carolina’s Republican U.S. House delegation in a string of upset elections in what were drawn to be safe Republican seats.
Rep. Richard Hudson, 9th Congressional District incumbent and National Republican Congressional Committee chairman, narrowly lost his seat to Democrat Richard Ojeda, a former West Virginia state representative and veteran.
With all precincts reporting, Ojeda won 51% of the vote to Hudson’s 49%.
“The people of NC-09 looked at the guy running the entire Republican money machine, and they fired him,” Ojeda said in a statement. “This win belongs to every teacher, every nurse, every veteran, every family at Fort Bragg and every working person who’s sick and tired of watching the billionaire class take everything.”
Democrat and political newcomer Paul Barringer defeated Republican Rep. Brad Knott in the 13th Congressional District. With all precincts reporting, Barringer won 51% to Knott’s 48%.
“Even with such an uphill battle, this campaign and our supporters stood up and made it clear that our community wants a representative who will fight to lower costs, stand up to corruption, and help protect access to health care,” Barringer said in a statement.
Democrat and High Point Mayor Cyril Jefferson ousted 6th Congressional District incumbent Republican Addison McDowell in a Triad area race. As of midnight Tuesday night, Jefferson had 51% to McDowell’s 49% with all precincts reporting.
Congressman and longtime former N.C. House Speaker Republican Tim Moore lost his 14th Congressional District seat to opponent Democrat Lakeshia Womack. With all precincts reporting, Womack won 51% to Moore’s 49%.
Democrat Jamie Ager flipped the 11th Congressional District, formerly held by Republican Rep. Chuck Edwards, who ended his reelection campaign amid scandal. He defeated Edwards’ replacement on the ballot, Republican state Rep. Jennifer Balkcom, 57% to 41% with all precincts reporting.
And Republican incumbent Virginia Foxx in the 5th District was down by 99 votes to Democrat Chuck Hubbard with all precincts reporting, while incumbent Rep. Greg Murphy in the 3rd District was ahead by less than one percentage point. Both are subject to a recount.
These districts were all drawn as safe Republican seats. But this wasn’t a normal year.
Democrats banked a strong lead in early voting, which was up 36% overall over 2022. Black early voter turnout across the state reached roughly 584,000, up 52% compared to 2022, according to an analysis by the Southern Coalition for Social Justice. Unaffiliated voters also turned out in unprecedented numbers for a midterm.
In the meantime, the president’s approval ratings sank into the high 30s in the state as gas prices and inflation surged. The Associated Press’ Voter Poll found that North Carolina voters’ two top issues this year were the economy and “the state of democracy,” tied for first place at 35%. Immigration and crime, the issues GOP candidates most frequently campaigned on, ranked far lower, at 12% and 4% respectively.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Democratic county commissioner defeats five-term Congressman Brian Fitzpatrick in Philly suburbs
description: Fitzpatrick faced Harvie, who is vice-chair of the Bucks County Board of Commissioners and a former educator, in one of four Pennsylvania congressional races targeted by national Democratic groups as the party worked to win a majority in the U.S. House.
text:
U.S. Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick, left, and Bucks County Commissioner Bob Harvie. (Campaign photos)(This story has been updated with quotes from DNC Chair Ken Martin and Gov. Josh Shapiro.)
Challenger Bob Harvie toppled five-term Republican U.S. Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick to win a key congressional seat in the Philadelphia suburbs for Democrats.
According to the Associated Press, which called the race for Harvie at 12:37 a.m., 53% to 47% lead over Fitzpatrick. Democratic National Committee Chair Ken Martin congratulated Harvie, the state Democratic Party and his campaign organizers.
“As an educator and twice-elected Bucks County commissioner, Bob has been a consistent champion for working families in his community,” Martin said. “In the House, he will be a steadfast fighter for Pennsylvania’s 1st Congressional District while fighting to lower costs, protect healthcare, support workers, and make life more affordable.”
Harvie is a native of Bucks County who focused on the kitchen table issues that mattered to voters, Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee Chair Suzan DelBene said in a statement.
“Everyone loves an underdog story, and tonight Bob proved that a guy from Bristol Borough and a former public school teacher can make it to the halls of Congress thanks to his relentless focus on fighting for the community that raised him,” she said. “Bob is going to shake up a broken Congress and work with anyone to restore the American Dream.”
Fitzpatrick faced Harvie, who is vice-chair of the Bucks County Board of Commissioners and a former educator, in one of four Pennsylvania congressional races targeted by national Democratic groups as the party worked to win a majority in the U.S. House.
The 1st Congressional District includes all of Bucks County and a narrow strip of neighboring Montgomery County, each of which includes part of the Philadelphia suburbs and stretches into rural areas north of the city. 
“Tonight, Bucks County showed up to reject the chaos, cruelty, and corruption in Washington — and to vote for a public servant who knows what it means to show up, deliver for his community, and get things done,” Gov. Josh Shapiro said in a statement.
Harvie defeated former congressional science advisor Lucia Simonelli to win the Democratic nomination in the primary election. While he’s trailed Fitzpatrick in polls for most of the year, a recent New York Times/Siena University poll gave him a 2-point advantage over the incumbent. The non-partisan Cook Political Report, meanwhile, changed its rating for the race on Friday from “leans Republican” to a “toss up.”
Together, the candidates raised more than $11.4 million, while outside groups poured nearly $17 million into the race, including more than $9 million opposing Fitzpatrick,
As a Bucks County native who grew up in blue-collar Bristol and taught at Bucks County Technical High School, Harvie campaigned on deep roots in the community and an understanding of the challenges some residents face.
He said his experience as a commissioner and a township supervisor taught him that public service is about delivering for constituents and not about politics. He touted his record of bipartisan success as a member of the three-member board of commissioners improving housing affordability and navigating the COVID-19 pandemic.
Harvie has criticized Fitzpatrick for supporting the Trump administration’s policies and for taking contributions from corporate PACs, while pledging not to accept any himself. 
Fitzpatrick, a retired FBI special agent, won re-election in 2024 against Democratic challenger Ashley Ehasz by a 13% margin. 
Fitzpatrick has long been a target of Democrats, as was his older brother Mike Fitzpatrick who held the seat before him. The district has remained red since the elder Fitzpatrick defeated former U.S. Rep. Patrick Murphy in 2010, even as other districts in the once-staunchly Republican Philly suburbs went to Democrats.  
In the campaign against Harvie, Fitzpatrick cast himself as an independent voter, touting his role in a bipartisan Problem Solving Caucus that has tackled election reform and accountability in Congress. Fitzpatrick’s campaign also notes he was one of two House Republicans to vote against the Trump administration’s Big Beautiful Bill, which contained massive cuts to Medicaid and food assistance.
He said he opposes President Donald Trump’s “blanket and indiscriminate tariffs,” but also voted “yes” on procedural measures that blocked the House from considering resolutions to end the emergency declaration Trump used to enact them.
His campaign has attacked Harvie as “divisive” and a “hack,” while a PAC aligned with Fitzpatrick ran ads alleging Harvie is the subject of an FBI investigation into political corruption. Harvie’s campaign sent a cease and desist letter to Fitzpatrick in July stating that the claims are false and defamatory. 
The following month, Harvie sued the Defending America PAC and Chris Pack, a Republican consultant, for defamation.  
Harvie told the Philadelphia Inquirer last month that he has never been under investigation and that he appeared as a witness in 2022 before a federal grand jury in a probe into Falls Township, where he served as a supervisor from 2003 to 2020.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Threshold for South Dakota constitutional amendments should remain a simple majority, voters decide
authors: Seth Tupper, Joshua Haiar, John Hult
description: South Dakotans rejected a ballot question Tuesday that would have raised the threshold for voter approval of state constitutional amendments from a simple majority to 60%. When The Associated Press called the race at 11:24 p.m. Central time, 58% of the votes were against Amendment L and 42% were in favor. About 64% of statewide votes […]
text:
Campaign material from L-No, a South Dakota ballot question committee, urges a vote against a measure that would require 60% voter approval to change the state constitution. (Photo by John Hult/South Dakota Searchlight)South Dakotans rejected a ballot question Tuesday that would have raised the threshold for voter approval of state constitutional amendments from a simple majority to 60%.
When The Associated Press called the race at 11:24 p.m. Central time, 58% of the votes were against Amendment L and 42% were in favor. About 64% of statewide votes had been counted.
The Republican-dominated Legislature sent Amendment L to the ballot. Sponsoring lawmakers said a higher threshold for voter approval of constitutional amendments would protect the constitution from policies that don’t belong in it, while preserving it for fundamental elements like the structure and function of government.
Opponents said Amendment L was an attempt by Republican lawmakers to block voters from approving policies such as Medicaid expansion, which voters put in the constitution four years ago, or abortion rights, which petitioners have unsuccessfully attempted to place in the constitution.
One of the Amendment L opponents was Chase Jensen, a senior organizer with the nonprofit Dakota Rural Action. He said “South Dakota spoke clearly.”
“We are not going to willingly give up our rights or diminish the value of our vote,” Jensen said.
South Dakota voters rejected similar attempts in past elections to raise the threshold for voter approval of ballot questions.
In 2018, voters defeated Constitutional Amendment X, which would have raised the threshold for constitutional amendments to 55%. Constitutional Amendment C failed in 2022. It would have required 60% voter support for ballot questions that increase taxes and fees, or require the state to spend $10 million or more in a measure’s first five years of implementation.
Reynold Nesiba, a Democratic former legislator from Sioux Falls who has worked on previous ballot questions, said Amendment L represented the Republican Party in South Dakota “whittling away at direct democracy” and engaging in “sour grapes” against approved amendments like Medicaid expansion.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Progressive Democrat Matt Little wins U.S. House seat in south suburban district
description: Matt Little won the election to represent Minnesota’s 2nd Congressional District in the U.S. House, defeating state Sen. Eric Pratt, R-Prior Lake, leading by a wide margin, according to the Minnesota Secretary of State’s unofficial results Tuesday evening. Little, a 41-year-old attorney, served as the mayor of Lakeville for two terms and a state senator […]
text:
Matt Little, Democratic candidate for Minnesota’s 2nd congressional district, talks to supporters at a fundraising event at New Market Township Hall in Lakeville, Minnesota Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)Matt Little won the election to represent Minnesota’s 2nd Congressional District in the U.S. House, defeating state Sen. Eric Pratt, R-Prior Lake, leading by a wide margin, according to the Minnesota Secretary of State’s unofficial results Tuesday evening.
Little, a 41-year-old attorney, served as the mayor of Lakeville for two terms and a state senator in the south metro for one term, before losing to state Rep. Zach Duckworth, R-Lakeville in 2020.
Little won the DFL endorsement in the three-way Aug. 11 primary and presented himself as a more progressive successor to U.S. Rep. Angie Craig, who left the state’s most competitive congressional district for an unsuccessful Senate bid.
His election represents a leftward shift for the swing district that had a streak of voting red until choosing Craig, a moderate Democrat, in 2018. The 2nd Congressional District is purple but leans Democrat, according to the nonpartisan Cook Political Report’s pre-election ratings.
Little’s win also signals the possibility that Operation Metro Surge has led to enduring changes in the attitudes of suburban, exurban and even rural Minnesotans on the issue of immigration enforcement in response to President Trump’s deportation efforts.
During the surge, Little posted videos of himself following immigration agents, joining thousands of Minnesotans who sought to disrupt the operation that had become infamous for racial profiling and the killing of two Americans.
Race for Minnesota’s 2nd Congressional District tests how much south suburbs have shifted left

Little’s stated policy priority is Medicare for All, under which the government would insure all Americans for medically necessary healthcare instead of private health insurance companies. In several public debates leading up to his Nov. 3 win, Little clashed with Pratt, his mild-mannered opponent, on the war in Iran, healthcare, Social Security and data centers, among other issues.
Little has said that he’d vote to end the Iran war; to remove the cap on the Social Security tax; and to enact a one-year moratorium on data centers so that municipal governments can create regulations in their communities. He’s said he would fight for an “Anti-ICE Bill of Rights” that cuts U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement funding to pre-Trump levels and replaces ICE with another federal immigration agency.
Little has a private law firm where he sues assisted living homes for abuse and neglect, among other personal injury cases.
The last time Little lived in D.C., he was in his early 20s and working for the letter carriers union.
“My vantage point and my leverage at that time was minimal,” Little said in a Reformer interview weeks before the election. “This time, I’d like to build as many relationships as I can within the party, but also try and find some room to work with any Republicans.”
Pratt was first elected to the state Senate in 2012 and is the top Republican on the Minnesota Senate Finance Committee. He touted his experience in finance and banking as proof that he’ll effectively cut spending and prevent fraud in government programs, a central issue in Minnesota politics following revelations of widespread fraud in the state’s safety net programs.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Nebraska on track to add gender-based school sports requirements to state Constitution
description: Voters appeared to agree to cement sex-separate school sports requirements into the Nebraska Constitution with Tuesday’s approval of the Fairness for Girls ballot measure. Initiative Measure 442 had 318,439 yes votes to 160,626 no votes, as of 11:30 p.m. Tuesday, with 69% of the vote counted. The proposal would make permanent part of a 2025 […]
text:
Former Dunbar state Sen. Julie Slama speaking at the Capitol about the Fairness for Girls' ballot measure on June 30, 2026. (Juan Salinas II/Nebraska Examiner)Voters appeared to agree to cement sex-separate school sports requirements into the Nebraska Constitution with Tuesday’s approval of the Fairness for Girls ballot measure.
Initiative Measure 442 had 318,439 yes votes to 160,626 no votes, as of 11:30 p.m. Tuesday, with 69% of the vote counted. The proposal would make permanent part of a 2025 state law requiring public K-12 schools, colleges and universities, and any private schools or colleges in the state playing against those schools, to designate sports and teams as male, female or coed. Male students couldn’t play on female-only teams.


The ballot measure would not define “sex” in the constitution. State law defines sex as whether someone “naturally has, had, will or would have, but for a congenital anomaly or intentional or unintentional disruption, the reproductive system that at some point produces, transports and utilizes” either eggs (female) or sperm (male) for fertilization.
The measure faced multiple court challenges based on critics arguing the ballot language was too broad. The court battle led up to the Nebraska Supreme Court, which upheld the ballot measure’s validity in an October ruling.
Julie Slama, former state senator and sponsor of the Fairness for Girls campaign, started the night feeling optimistic, as she said she had heard consistent support for the initiative while she traveled across the state.
Slama described the measure as a “commonsense” issue that bypassed partisan lines. For an election that favored Democrats nationwide, the fact that the initiative passed by a wide margin indicated that Democrat voters supported the measure alongside Republicans, Slama said.
“Nebraskans are sick and tired of watching politicians in the Capitol turn things into a political football,” Slama said. “Opportunities for our daughters and granddaughters should never be a political football.”

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: Voters defeat free school meal ballot measure in North Dakota
description: North Dakota voters have rejected a proposed constitutional amendment that sought to guarantee free school meals to all K-12 students in the state.  Measure 2 was rejected by nearly 51% of voters, according to complete but unofficial results published by the North Dakota Secretary of State’s Office.   The measure’s margin of defeat was about 2,900 […]
text:
Miranda Jochim of Mandan serves lunch to students at Roosevelt Elementary School in Bismarck on Nov. 2, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)North Dakota voters have rejected a proposed constitutional amendment that sought to guarantee free school meals to all K-12 students in the state. 
Measure 2 was rejected by nearly 51% of voters, according to complete but unofficial results published by the North Dakota Secretary of State’s Office.  
The measure’s margin of defeat was about 2,900 votes. 
Measure 2 was a proposed amendment to the North Dakota constitution that would require schools to provide free lunch and breakfast to K-12 students and be reimbursed by the state for the expense. 
Voters reject higher bar to amend North Dakota’s constitution

The initiated measure was placed on the ballot by a group of sponsoring citizens after the North Dakota Legislature rejected similar proposals in recent legislative sessions. 
The program was estimated to cost $124.3 million to $134.3 million every two years starting in 2027-29, according to the Department of Public Instruction. 
Supporters argued the constitutional requirement will eliminate school meal debts, benefit students’ academic performance and provide financial relief to families across the state.
Opponents including Gov. Kelly Armstrong argued the measure was inappropriate for the state constitution, which is more difficult to change. 
Lawmakers have added state funding to expand how many students qualify for free or reduced lunch, bolstering the federal program. In 2025, lawmakers expanded the free lunch program to include families at 225% of the federal poverty level.
Some lawmakers have raised concerns that the state will lose out on federal dollars if families no longer fill out paperwork for the federal program. A state official has said many students automatically qualify because their families are eligible for other federal programs.
A 2023 law already requires North Dakota schools to provide a meal to students if they request one, even if they don’t have the money to pay, and prohibits any shaming of the student. 
But schools still charge for the meals if the student isn’t signed up for free and reduced lunch programs. Families can face consequences for the debt, such as being referred to debt collection agencies.
School meals are likely to be the subject of debate again during the 2027 legislative session. Some lawmakers have said they prefer a more targeted approach, such as the state paying off school meal debt at the end of a school year. 
Sen. Paul Thomas, R-Velva, has said he plans to propose initiatives ranging from larger portion sizes for school meals and more nutritious options, to trying to help students who go without sufficient meals on the weekends.

title: LePage, Dunlap race for Maine’s 2nd District still too close to call, likely headed to runoff
description: The race for Maine’s 2nd Congressional District is still too close to call, and appears likely to end up in a ranked-choice runoff later this week.  As of 12:37 a.m., former Republican Gov. Paul LePage and Democrat Matt Dunlap were neck and neck, each with 49.4% with 71% votes counted, according to initial totals from […]
text:
Paul LePage, the former Republican governor running for Congress in Maine's 2nd District, talks with supporters at the GOP watch party on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Emma Davis/ Maine Morning Star)The race for Maine’s 2nd Congressional District is still too close to call, and appears likely to end up in a ranked-choice runoff later this week. 
As of 12:37 a.m., former Republican Gov. Paul LePage and Democrat Matt Dunlap were neck and neck, each with 49.4% with 71% votes counted, according to initial totals from the Bangor Daily News, which gathered totals from municipalities and partnered with Decision Desk HQ to make the call. 
The Associated Press had also yet to call the race, but at 12:30 a.m. reported 72% of votes counted, with LePage leading with 51% of votes and Dunlap 49% of votes.
Both candidates called it a night, departing their respective election night events a before midnight. A spokesperson for LePage’s campaign said the results “generally look good but it is too early.” 
Dunlap’s campaign did not immediately respond to a request for comment. 
Matt Dunlap, the Democratic nominee for Maine’s 2nd Congressional District, arrives at a watch party in Old Town. (Photo by Andrew Clark/ Maine Morning Star)
With a declared write-in candidate in the race, one of the candidates must get more than 50% of total votes to be named the winner. If no candidate reaches that threshold, the race will go to a ranked-choice runoff — and Maine Secretary of State Shenna Bellows said last month she thinks a runoff in the district is likely. 
However, the Secretary of State’s Office said Tuesday they would not be making any official announcement about the runoff on election night.
It’s not an unprecedented situation for the 2nd District. In 2018, Democrat Jared Golden defeated incumbent Republican U.S. Rep. Bruce Poliquin in the nation’s first congressional election to use ranked choice voting to determine the winner. Since then, Golden has repeatedly defended his seat through the runoff process, mostly recently in the 2024 election against Republican Austin Theriault, which went to a ranked-choice runoff and then a recount.
Golden currently holds the seat, but announced last November that he would not seek reelection. LePage had already announced his campaign, and faced no Republican primary challengers. Dunlap had intended to challenge Golden, and went on to defeat three other candidates in a ranked-choice runoff in the June primary. 
Nationally, Democrats are poised to take over control of the U.S. House of Representatives and Senate after many previously Republican-held districts flipped in their favor in response to President Donald Trump’s declining approval.
.In September, the Cook Political Report had shifted their rating for the 2nd District race in Democrats favor, ultimately rating the district as leaning Republican. Looking ahead to the tabulations, last-place candidates will be eliminated first and votes will then be redistributed to a voter’s next choice. That’s repeated until one candidate receives more than 50% of votes. Write-in votes for people who were not declared write-in candidates are counted as blanks. 
Based on how long ranked-choice tabulations have taken in the past, Bellows said a runoff could go until Friday of next week.

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Colorado graduated income tax measure clings to slight lead; TABOR cap increase on track to pass
description: Colorado voters on Tuesday appeared on the verge of adopting the most sweeping set of changes to the state’s tax code in 34 years, with a ballot measure to raise the constitutionally-mandated revenue cap well ahead in preliminary results, and another to gradually hike income taxes on Coloradans earning over $500,000 a year holding on […]
text:
Election workers organize ballot envelopes at the Adams County clerk and recorder's office in Brighton on Tuesday. (Photo by Andrew Fraieli/Colorado Newsline)Colorado voters on Tuesday appeared on the verge of adopting the most sweeping set of changes to the state’s tax code in 34 years, with a ballot measure to raise the constitutionally-mandated revenue cap well ahead in preliminary results, and another to gradually hike income taxes on Coloradans earning over $500,000 a year holding on to a slim lead.
Meanwhile, a conservative countermeasure to block the latter proposal with a cap on income tax rates appeared headed for defeat.
Amendment 87, the graduated income tax measure, was the closest of the trio of tax-related ballot measures. As of 10 p.m., it led with 50.6% support, with 49.4% opposed. Unlike other constitutional amendments on the ballot this year, because it only repeals, rather than amends, language in the state constitution, it needs only a simple majority to pass.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Proposition 136, which would block Amendment 87 by capping the state’s income tax rate at 4.4%, stood at 47% support, short of the majority needed to pass. If both measures were to pass, the conflicting provisions within them would be resolved according to which received more yes votes.
Results showed Proposition NN, a legislatively referred measure to raise the state’s constitutionally-mandated revenue cap, on track to pass with 55% of voters in support and 45% opposed.
Amendment 87 proposes to hike corporate and individual income tax rates to 7.4% for income above $500,000 and gradually increase the rate to 8.4% for income above $1 million. Those higher rates would apply to the top 3% of earners, while the 97% of Coloradans who earn less than $500,000 per year would see a slight income tax reduction. A fiscal analysis by nonpartisan state legislative staff estimated that the measure would raise $2 billion in additional revenue for the state by the 2027-28 fiscal year.
State analysts projected Proposition NN, by raising the revenue cap set by the Taxpayer’s Bill of Rights, would increase the revenue the state is allowed to keep by about $500 million a year. The measure would likely eliminate TABOR refunds, the money returned to Colorado taxpayers in years when the revenue cap is exceeded, for the foreseeable future.
Proposition 136 was backed by conservative “dark money” group Advance Colorado, which aimed to block Amendment 87 by capping state income tax rates at their current level of 4.4%, preventing the amendment’s higher rates on higher earners from taking effect.

text:
Shortly after polls closed, U.S. Sen. Susan Collins thanked her family and staff, and prepared the crowd gathered at the GOP watch party in Bangor. (Photo by Emma Davis/ Maine Morning Star)This is a breaking story that will be updated.
Democrat Troy Jackson declared victory in the U.S. Senate race after five-term incumbent Republican U.S. Sen. Susan Collins conceded the race.
“It has been the honor of my life to serve the people of Maine in the United States Senate. I’m proud of all I have been able to accomplish for our state and for our country in the past 30 years,” Collins said in a release shortly before 12:30 a.m.
She said she called Jackson “to congratulate him and to assure him that my staff and I will work to ensure a smooth transition.”
His win is a major victory for the Democratic Party, which viewed Collins’ seat as a key pickup opportunity in their efforts to gain more control in the U.S. Senate. Though, with other states’ races called earlier, Democrats were already projected to flip the upper chamber. 
As of 12:18 a.m., Jackson had secured 52% of votes and Collins had 48% with 69% of votes counted, according to The Associated Press.
Jackson’s victory comes despite his late entry. A former logger and Maine Senate president from Allagash, Jackson secured his party’s nomination in late July, replacing former Democratic nominee Graham Platner, who dropped out earlier that month after an accusation of sexual assault, which he denied. 
Meanwhile, Collins’ loss comes after she faced accusations of corruption. That included ProPublica reporting that found the FBI had been looking into the senator’s alleged involvement in a pay-for-play scheme in recent years, until Trump’s purge of the bureau ended the inquiry. Collins has denied any wrongdoing.  
The U.S. Senate race was the most expensive in state history, with the tens of millions of dollars raised by the candidates being far surpassed by the hundreds of millions in outside spending.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: Voters reject higher bar to amend North Dakota’s constitution
description: North Dakota voters Tuesday rejected a higher bar to amend the state constitution. “No” votes for Measure 1 led “yes” votes by a margin of about 56% to 44%, according to complete but unofficial results. Measure 1 was for a 60% threshold for voters to approve future constitutional amendments.  The measure’s defeat is a blow […]
text:
Voters mark their ballots in the gymnasium at Grimsrud Elementary School in Bismarck on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Jack Dura/North Dakota Monitor)North Dakota voters Tuesday rejected a higher bar to amend the state constitution.
“No” votes for Measure 1 led “yes” votes by a margin of about 56% to 44%, according to complete but unofficial results. Measure 1 was for a 60% threshold for voters to approve future constitutional amendments. 
The measure’s defeat is a blow to North Dakota’s Republican-led Legislature, which put the measure on the ballot.
Lawmakers for years have tried to make it harder to change the constitution. They met with little success until June, when voters approved a single-subject requirement for future amendments.
Supporters, including Republican Gov. Kelly Armstrong, said North Dakota’s constitution is too easy to change, citing out-of-state organizations with lots of money to spend on whatever ballot initiative they support. Armstrong also said constitutionally mandated spending concerns him.
House Speaker Robin Weisz, who sponsored the measure in the Legislature, said he is disappointed and not surprised by Measure 1’s defeat, citing the money spent in opposition.
“My personal opinion – many of the ads were quite deceptive and confusing to the voters,” said Weisz, R-Hurdsfield.
Measure 1 saw millions of dollars in spending from both sides. The major players were the Washington, D.C.-based Fairness Project, which contributed more than $1.9 million in opposition, and the Armstrong-aligned StrongND Fund, which spent more than $1.5 million in support.
Opponents said the higher threshold would make it harder for voters to enact changes they want, and would effectively hand a veto to a minority of voters as small as 40% plus one vote.
A simple majority to amend the state constitution has worked for more than 100 years, said League of Women Voters of North Dakota President Kathy Tweeten, who opposed the measure. 
“The Legislature has tried to change that several times, and I think the people have spoken again,” Tweeten said.
The vast majority of constitutional amendments in recent years have passed with more than 60% support, such as ones creating the Legacy Fund, gubernatorial and legislative term limits and a congressional age limit. Some measures have even had more than 80% support.
Some anti-abortion proponents said the 60% threshold would be a roadblock to a potential future abortion rights initiative they say the Fairness Project or another outside organization would support. 
The Fairness Project has no plans to run an abortion rights initiative in North Dakota in 2028, Executive Director Hannah Ledford said in a statement Tuesday.
Voters in neighboring South Dakota had a similar 60% measure. 
Reach North Dakota Monitor reporter Jack Dura at jdura@northdakotamonitor.com.
