name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Indiana Democrats gain congressional seat; GOP incumbents lead elsewhere
description: Democrats gained a seat in Indiana’s congressional delegation Tuesday, while eight incumbent U.S. House members held leads in their reelection races. Election Day results pointed toward a six-to-three Republican advantage in Indiana’s congressional delegation, down from the GOP’s previous seven-to-two edge. The biggest upset appeared to be in central Indiana[...]
text:
U.S. Rep. André Carson delivers an election night victory speech on Tuesday. Nov. 3, 2026, in Indianapolis. (Photo by Tom Davies/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Democrats gained a seat in Indiana’s congressional delegation Tuesday, while eight incumbent U.S. House members held leads in their reelection races.
Election Day results pointed toward a six-to-three Republican advantage in Indiana’s congressional delegation, down from the GOP’s previous seven-to-two edge.
The biggest upset appeared to be in central Indiana’s 5th Congressional District, where Democratic state Sen. J.D. Ford declared victory over three-term Republican U.S. Rep. Victoria Spartz in one of the state’s most closely watched contests.
Elsewhere, the AP called races for Democratic U.S. Reps. Frank Mrvan and André Carson, both headed for additional terms in Northwest Indiana and Indianapolis, respectively.
Republican Reps. Marlin Stutzman, Jim Baird, Jefferson Shreve, Mark Messmer and Erin Houchin also secured additional terms, according to AP race calls. Republican U.S. Rep. Rudy Yakym maintained a lead in the 2nd Congressional District, which had not yet been called.
The races were part of a national fight for control of the U.S. House, where Republicans entered Election Day holding a narrow majority. The outcome will shape the Trump administration’s ability to advance its agenda on taxes, immigration, federal spending and other priorities.
Nationally, Democrats were making gains in congressional races across the country, with control of the U.S. House still undecided shortly after midnight. Democrats also made significant gains in Senate races, including Republican-held seats, as both parties awaited the final balance of power in Congress.
Ford declares victory over Spartz
In central Indiana’s 5th Congressional District, Ford declared victory over Spartz in a contest that drew national attention in the months leading up to Election Day.
With 98% of votes reporting shortly after midnight, Ford led with 134,476 votes, or 51.66%, according to the AP. The race had not yet been called.
If his lead holds, Ford will move from the Indiana Senate to Washington after eight years in the state legislature. Spartz, first elected to Congress in 2020, had sought a fourth term.
Democrat J.D. Ford declares victory over Victoria Spartz in major upset for Indiana’s 5th District

The district stretches from Hamilton County’s northern suburbs into communities including Anderson, Muncie, Marion and Kokomo.
A Ford victory would mark a reversal from 2024, when Spartz won reelection by more than 18 percentage points. The district had become more reliably Republican after state lawmakers redrew Indiana’s congressional boundaries in 2021.
Both candidates emphasized health care costs and government accountability, but offered different approaches to addressing those concerns.
Spartz campaigned on reducing federal spending, balancing the budget and increasing transparency and competition in health care. Ford pressed for protecting Medicaid funding, preserving rural hospitals, reproductive rights and addressing household costs.
The candidates also took opposing positions on the unsuccessful congressional redistricting effort. Spartz supported the proposed new boundaries, while Ford voted against them in the state Senate.
Mrvan, Carson win additional terms
In Northwest Indiana’s 1st Congressional District, Democratic U.S. Rep. Frank Mrvan won reelection over Republican Barb Regnitz, a Porter County commissioner seeking to return the seat to Republican control.
Mrvan had received 131,581 votes, or 62.58%, with 85% reporting shortly after midnight, according to AP results.
A Hammond native and former North Township trustee, Mrvan won a fourth term in Congress. His campaign emphasized federal infrastructure investments, union jobs, reproductive rights and reducing prescription drug costs.
Regnitz, whose professional background includes software engineering and financial planning, campaigned on stronger border enforcement, reducing federal spending and supporting law enforcement.
The National Republican Congressional Committee added Regnitz to its MAGA Majority program in July, giving her campaign additional national Republican support.
The candidates also offered different approaches to household affordability, with Mrvan emphasizing federal investment and health care savings while Regnitz argued that spending restraint and reducing inflation would improve families’ purchasing power.
The district, which includes communities along Lake Michigan and the Chicago metropolitan area, has remained in Democratic hands even as Republicans consolidated their hold on much of the rest of Indiana’s congressional delegation.
In the Indianapolis-based 7th Congressional District, Democratic U.S. Rep. André Carson won another term, defeating Republican Patrick McAuley and Libertarian James Sceniak.
Carson had received 145,719 votes, or 76.52%, with 94% reporting shortly after midnight, according to the AP.
Carson, Indiana’s longest-serving current U.S. House member, has represented the district since winning a special election in 2008 following the death of his grandmother, former U.S. Rep. Julia Carson.
His campaign emphasized affordability, infrastructure and equality, while criticizing Trump’s tariffs and reductions in federal assistance programs.
McAuley, who works in commercial real estate, focused on public safety, housing, homelessness and expanding career opportunities. Sceniak, a behavior therapist and previous Libertarian congressional candidate, emphasized privacy protections, lower taxes and veterans’ health care.
Republicans retain northern and central Indiana seats
In north-central Indiana’s 2nd Congressional District, Republican U.S. Rep. Rudy Yakym held a narrow lead over Democrat Jamee Decio in a three-way contest that also included Libertarian William Henry.
Yakym had received 95,216 votes, or 51.86%, with 86% reporting shortly after midnight, according to the AP. The race had not yet been called.
Yakym, who has held the seat since 2022, campaigned on lower taxes, limited government, reduced regulation and border security.
Decio, a South Bend lawyer and former Elkhart County deputy prosecutor, emphasized lowering everyday costs, protecting Medicaid and Social Security, and requiring data center developers to pay for their own infrastructure needs.
Henry, a military veteran and communications professional, advocated reducing federal spending and regulation, improving veterans’ health care and protecting medical privacy.
The district includes South Bend, Elkhart, Goshen and Warsaw, where the region’s manufacturing economy and the effects of federal trade policy have been campaign issues.
Reps. Erin Houchin, left, and Rudy Yakym pose with their contributions to the congressional time capsule. (Photo courtesy of Rep. Rudy Yakym’s X account)
In northeast Indiana, Republican U.S. Rep. Marlin Stutzman won another term, defeating Democrat Kelly Thompson in the 3rd Congressional District.
Stutzman received 109,692 votes, or 54.88%, with 96% reporting, according to the AP’s tally shortly after midnight.
Stutzman, a farmer and business owner from Howe, returned to Congress after winning the seat in 2024. He previously represented the district before an unsuccessful U.S. Senate campaign in 2016.
His reelection platform focused on reducing federal spending, strengthening border security, protecting gun rights and limiting federal involvement in education.
Thompson, a concrete contractor and nonprofit founder from North Webster, campaigned on health care access, wages, housing and government accountability. Her proposals included Medicare for All and prohibiting members of Congress and the president from trading stocks.
The two also differed over congressional redistricting. Stutzman supported another attempt to redraw Indiana’s boundaries. Thompson opposed it.
Farther west, Republican U.S. Rep. Jim Baird won a fifth term in the 4th Congressional District, defeating Democrat Drew Cox, a Purdue University music instructor.
Baird received 112,408 votes, or 54.17%, with 96% reporting shortly after midnight, according to the AP.
Baird, a farmer, small-business owner and Vietnam veteran, emphasized lowering costs, reducing federal regulation, securing the border and supporting energy independence.
Cox campaigned on health care access, workers’ rights, veterans’ services and reducing the influence of money in politics. He also supported overturning the U.S. Supreme Court’s Citizens United decision, which struck down restrictions on independent political spending by corporations and unions.
The district includes Lafayette, Crawfordsville and Greencastle, along with surrounding west-central Indiana communities.
GOP incumbents win in southern Indiana
In the 6th Congressional District, Republican U.S. Rep. Jefferson Shreve won a second term, defeating Democrat Cynthia “Cinde” Wirth in a rematch of their 2024 contest.
Shreve had received 99,497 votes, or 55.96%, with 87% reporting shortly after midnight, according to the AP.
Shreve, a former Indianapolis city-county councilor and businessman, won their previous matchup with 63.9% of the vote.
His campaign priorities included affordability, border security, reduced government spending, infrastructure and support for farmers and small businesses.
Jefferson Shreve addresses supporters at a rally ob Oct. 26, 2024, in Greenwood, Indiana. (Photo by Casey Smith/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
Wirth, a Columbus-based small-business owner, scientist and former high school teacher, campaigned on public education, affordable health care, environmental protection and support for working families.
The district includes communities south of Indianapolis and extends east to Richmond.
In southwestern Indiana, Republican U.S. Rep. Mark Messmer defeated Democrat Mary Allen in the 8th Congressional District.
Messmer received 117,503 votes, or 55.24%, with 94% reporting shortly after midnight, according to the AP.
Messmer, a former Indiana state senator and Senate majority leader, was first elected to Congress in 2024 after winning the seat previously held by Republican Larry Bucshon.
Allen, an at-large Evansville City Council member, small-business owner and Army Reserve veteran, campaigned on protecting Medicaid and Medicare, preserving rural hospitals, increasing affordable housing and reducing the cost of essential goods.
The district, which was once known for competitive elections and changes in party control, has been held by Republicans since 2010.
In the 9th Congressional District, Republican U.S. Rep. Erin Houchin won a third term, defeating Democrat Brad Meyer and Libertarian Tonya Hudson.
Houchin received 120,835 votes, or 54.14%, with 93% reporting shortly after midnight, according to the AP.



Quotation







I will continue working to hold government accountable, lower the cost of healthcare, secure our elections, strengthen our communities, and make sure Washington works for Hoosiers.


– Republican U.S. Rep. Erin Houchin


Houchin, a former state senator from Salem, campaigned on border security, reduced federal spending, abortion restrictions and parental involvement in education.
Meyer, a Bloomington electronics engineer, supported Medicare for All, higher wages, stronger collective bargaining rights and reducing housing and education costs.
Hudson, a real estate broker from Mitchell, called for abolishing the Internal Revenue Service, moving toward a sales-tax-based system and reducing federal regulations.
The district includes Bloomington and communities along the Ohio River, including New Albany.
“Tonight, I am thinking about the families, farmers, small-business owners, veterans, and citizens across Southern Indiana who inspire my service. Every conversation, every handshake, and every vote is a reminder of why I entered public service: to fight for the people of Indiana,” Houchin said in a late Tuesday statement.
“I do not take this responsibility lightly,” she continued. “I will continue working to hold government accountable, lower the cost of healthcare, secure our elections, strengthen our communities, and make sure Washington works for Hoosiers.”
Indiana’s delegation and the next Congress
If the remaining leads hold, Indiana’s nine-member U.S. House delegation would include three Democrats and six Republicans when the next Congress convenes in January.
Indiana’s two U.S. senators, Republicans Todd Young and Jim Banks, were not on the ballot this year.
The next Congress will confront decisions over federal spending, health care programs, immigration and the Trump administration’s legislative priorities.
The results also follow nearly a year of political conflict in Indiana over congressional redistricting.
Hoosier voters chose representatives under the same boundaries used in the previous two elections after an unsuccessful effort last year by Trump and other Republicans to redraw the state’s political boundaries ahead of the midterms.
The Indiana Senate rejected the proposed map in December on a 31-19 vote, with 21 Republicans joining all 10 Democrats to block a plan designed to give the GOP a chance at winning all nine seats.
The decision meant candidates ran under the same district boundaries approved by state lawmakers in 2021.

name: Washington State Standard
title: Gluesenkamp Perez cruising toward win over Braun in WA’s 3rd Congressional District

text:
Democratic U.S. Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez, D-Skamania, speaks to supporters at an election night party in Vancouver, Washington on Nov. 3, 2026. Results released Tuesday showed Gluesenkamp Perez leading Republican state Sen. John Braun in the 3rd Congressional District contest  (Photo by Taylor Balkom/The Columbian)Democratic U.S. Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez enjoyed a comfortable lead over Republican state Sen. John Braun on Tuesday, as she pursues a third term and her party seeks the House majority.
Gluesenkamp Perez led Braun by a margin of 55% to 44.1%, a sign she had not lost support of progressive Democrats who shunned her in the August primary. Her performance comes amid a cascade of Democrat wins nationwide that secured the House majority for her party heading into next year.
“It’s clear we’re going to win this race,” she said in a statement. “Thank you to everybody who knocked on doors in wet socks, who made the calls, wrote the postcards, and had the difficult conversations with their neighbors.”
Meanwhile, Republican Yakima County Commissioner Amanda McKinney was handily beating Democrat John Duresky in central Washington’s 4th Congressional District. McKinney garnered 54.1% of votes counted Tuesday and appeared on her way to succeed retiring U.S. Rep. Dan Newhouse of Sunnyside.
The match-up between Gluesenkamp Perez and Braun in southwest Washington’s 3rd Congressional District drew national attention as an electoral battleground that would help decide which party controls the U.S. House. 
The district encompasses Clark, Cowlitz, Lewis, Pacific, Wahkiakum, and Skamania counties and a small part of Thurston County.
President Donald Trump won it in all three of his presidential runs. But Republicans lost the congressional seat in 2022 when Gluesenkamp Perez, co-owner of an auto repair and machine shop, beat Republican Joe Kent, a former Army Special Forces soldier who Trump backed.
Her win thinned the ranks of Republicans in Washington’s 12-member congressional delegation from three to two. She defeated Kent in their rematch in 2024.
Gluesenkamp Perez is a co-chair of the centrist Blue Dog Coalition and has been successful in part by positioning herself as a moderate, touting her willingness to work across party lines, at times angering those in her party.
Some of that frustration emerged in the August primary when Brett Hennrich, a more progressive Democrat, ran to her left and garnered 16.7% of the vote. He later said he wouldn’t vote for the congresswoman on Tuesday. However, given Tuesday’s results, many of those who sided with Henrich, cast their lot with the congresswoman Tuesday.
Republican congressional candidate John Braun waves to supporters at a rally on Oct. 21, 2026 in in Chehalis, Washington, as House Speaker Mike Johnson (center) extols attendees to get Republicans to vote. (Photo by Jerry Cornfield/Washington State Standard)
Braun, of Centralia, isn’t cut from the same GOP cloth as Kent. In his four Senate terms, he’s worked with Democrats writing budgets and funding special education. He has legislative experience and electoral know-how, and hoped his brand of Republicanism would win over  Republican moderates and independent voters turned off by Kent.
He is president of Braun Northwest, a family-owned company specializing in building emergency vehicles at a facility in Chehalis. He campaigned as a pro-business, anti-tax, social conservative and cast Gluesenkam Perez as an ineffective member of Congress who only managed to pass one bill in four years.
But Braun couldn’t escape Trump’s shadow, which hung over midterm contests nationwide. This in spite of House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-Louisiana  campaigning with Braun three times.
Gluesenkamp Perez repeatedly sought to tie him to Trump’s agenda, including the president’s ‘Big Beautiful’ tax and spending reform bill and the war in Iran. In the final weeks, she also targeted the safety record of Braun’s business and his relationship with the family of a man killed in a workplace accident in 2024.
Gluesenkamp Perez garnered 61% of votes cast in Clark County, which is home to the largest bloc of Democratic voters. She also led in Skamania and Pacific counties. Braun was leading in the other four counties.
Collective spending by the candidates, their party’s campaign operations and independent political committees eclipsed $30 million.
Gluesenkamp Perez had spent nearly $9.3 million to Braun’s $2.6 million as of mid-October, according to filings with the Federal Election Commission. 
The Congressional Leadership Fund, a super PAC dedicated exclusively to electing Republicans to the U.S. House of Representatives, and No Going Back, a political action committee aligned with Trump’s MAGA Inc., had combined to spend in excess of $10 million million opposing the incumbent entering the last weeks of the campaign.
Braun has been the target of $8 million in spending by the House Majority PAC, the super PAC focused on electing Democrats to the House. The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee and Gluesenkamp Perez campaign have jointly spent several million dollars in opposition ads. 
“They wanted this seat back. They thought they could buy it, but they don’t understand how we work here,” Gluesenkamp Perez said. “This seat is not for sale. Everyday people doing the quiet, necessary work to build community: that’s how we push back against powerful people who think a seat in Congress is something you can buy.”
4th District
Nine of the state’s 10 members in the U.S. House sought reelection this year. The one vacancy is in the 4th District, where Newhouse is exiting after six terms.
McKinney, a county commissioner since 2019, had endorsements from Trump and Speaker Johnson.
Duresky, of West Richland, is a retired Air Force officer who also worked at the Hanford nuclear cleanup site. He is trying to become the first Democrat to win the House seat since former Gov. Jay Inslee did so in 1992. Inslee lost reelection after one term to Doc Hastings, a Republican, who held the seat until retiring in 2015.
This story was updated at 10 p.m. on Nov. 3, 2026 with comments from U.S. Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Letlow holds off Davis to keep Louisiana US Senate seat in GOP hands
description: Republican Congresswoman Julia Letlow survived a closer-than-expected challenge from Democrat Jamie Davis to claim Louisiana’s open seat in the U.S. Senate.
text:
U.S. Rep. Julia Letlow, R-Baton Rouge, speaks to supporters Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026, at the University of Louisiana at Monroe after winning Louisiana's U.S. Senate race against Democrat Jamie Davis. (Photo by Julia O'Donoghue/Louisiana Illuminator)Republican Congresswoman Julia Letlow survived a closer-than-expected challenge from Democrat Jamie Davis to claim Louisiana’s open seat in the U.S. Senate.
The Associated Press did not call the race for Letlow until 99% of votes had been counted. She prevailed with 50.9% support to Davis 49.1%, despite strong turnout among Black voters and Democrats in the early voting period.
Letlow’s win Tuesday caps a string of victories this year that included displacing incumbent U.S. Sen. Bill Cassidy in the May GOP primary and besting state Treasurer John Fleming in the June runoff for the party nomination.
Letlow is Louisiana’s first Republican woman to win a U.S. Senate race and the state’s second woman ever elected to the office. 
The political ascension of Letlow has unfolded at a breakneck pace, who just six years ago was an administrator at the University of Louisiana at Monroe. Her husband, Luke Letlow, won the 2020 election for the 5th Congressional District to succeed U.S. Rep. Ralph Abraham, for whom he served as chief of staff. 
But just five days before he was to be sworn into office, Luke Letlow died from complications related to COVID-19. Three months later, Julia Letlow won a special election to fill the vacancy and was re-elected twice. Through redistricting in 2024, the 5th District was shifted to pull more Baton Rouge voters into its boundaries, and Julia Letlow relocated to the capital the following year with her two young children. 
Letlow’s name by then had emerged among prominent Republicans who could unseat Cassidy, who was marked for ouster by President Donald Trump after he voted to convict him in his impeachment trial for his role in the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the U.S. Capitol. Trump used his social media platform to strongly suggest Letlow enter the Senate race just days before she announced her candidacy, and he officially endorsed her four days later.  
The president’s backing of Letlow did little to dissuade Cassidy and Fleming from touting their connections to the president during the GOP primary campaign. All three candidates featured Trump prominently in their television commercials and billboards. 
But since her party-runoff win, Letlow has made few public appearances in the run-up to Nov. 3. Trump had no involvement in the Louisiana race until he staged a “tele-rally” for Letlow on the eve of the election, pulled together just days before when it became evident Davis was making the race more competitive than anticipated.
Davis, a third-generation farmer from Tensas Parish, vaulted to the Democratic nomination with only minimal political experience. He was a member of Tensas Parish Police Jury from 2016-19, sits on the Democratic State Central Committee and lost a state legislative race in 2023.
The strong showing for Davis resulted from momentum among Black voters that started to build soon after a landmark U.S. Supreme Court decision in April in a Louisiana redistricting case. Conservative justices ruled that the Republican-led state Legislature could redraw the state’s U.S. House districts to remove one of Louisiana’s two majority-Black congressional districts in a case that significantly reduced protections for racial minority voters nationwide
At his election night party in Baton Rouge, Davis signaled to the state’s Republican leader that Democrats intend on putting up a serious challenge to his re-election bid next year.
“Jeff Landry, you’re on notice, buddy,” Davis said.
Jamie Davis, the Democratic candidate in Louisiana’s U.S. Senate race, addresses supporters at his election night party Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026, in Baton Rouge. (Photo by Piper Hutchinson/Louisiana Illuminator)
In-person and absentee voting totals from the early voting showed 34% participation from Black voters, a new high for a congressional midterm election in Louisiana, and 17,000 more Democrats than Republicans casting ballots statewide.
Davis also repeatedly pushed a hot-button bipartisan issue during his campaign: the growing trend among elected officials in Louisiana to sign non-disclosure agreements related to economic development. He reminded voters Letlow had signed an NDA involving the massive Meta Hyperion data center campus being built in Richland Parish, and that she purchased stock in companies involved in the project without disclosing those transactions as required by federal law. 
Letlow has played down those investments, claiming she was unaware her financial advisers were buying the stocks in question. 
A poll the Davis campaign paid for showed him in a dead heat with Letlow as of Friday, and national election trackers began to signal the Republican Party could be vulnerable in Louisiana. Davis also erased nearly all of Letlow’s fundraising edge, drawing within $2 million of the $7 million her campaign had amassed as of mid-October.
Davis received more than 720,000 votes, the most ever for a Black candidate in a statewide election in Louisiana, surpassing Cleo Fields (565,861) in the 1995 runoff for governor that he lost to Mike Foster.
This is a developing story.

Bohannan received 54% of their district constituents’ votes, with Miller-Meeks garnering 43% of the vo[...]
text:
Democratic candidate Christina Bohannan, running in Iowa's 1st Congressional District, attacks her Republican opponent's history of fighting against abortion in a speech on Aug. 10, 2024, at the Iowa State Fair. (Photo by Jack O'Connor/Iowa Capital Dispatch)Democrat Christina Bohannan has won the seat for Iowa’s 1st Congressional District after Iowans cast their election ballots Tuesday, the Associated Press has projected, unseating incumbent Republican Mariannette Miller-Meeks on her third run for the office.
Bohannan received 54% of their district constituents’ votes, with Miller-Meeks garnering 43% of the vote in unofficial results with 97% of votes counted. Independent candidate Michael Bridgford received 4% of the vote.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Miller-Meeks and Bohannan faced off against each other in 2022 and 2024 for the 1st District seat, which covers southeastern Iowa. Miller-Meeks won by more than 20,000 votes in 2022 and just 798 votes in 2024, confirmed through a recount that narrowed the gap even more than the 802 difference first counted.
Both candidates focused on lowering costs for Iowans in their campaigns, Miller-Meeks through Trump administration-backed policies like the “One, Big Beautiful Bill,” and Bohannan through reversing policies put in place by the current administration.
“Serving this district has been the honor of my life. The results tonight are disappointing, but I am grateful to every Iowan who put their trust in me, to our volunteers, to my staff, and to my family,” Miller-Meeks said in a statement. “Our country is at a crossroads, and our fight isn’t over.”

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico reelects Vasquez in closely watched Congressional District 2 race
description: Democrat Gabe Vasquez wins reelection in New Mexico's 2nd Congressional District against Republican Greg Cunningham.
text:
U.S. Rep. Gabe Vasquez (D-N.M.) announced the birth of his first son with his fiancee on Nov. 1, and won reelection to the 2nd Congressional District on Nov. 3. He Facetimed with his fiancee Nikki at his victory party in Las Cruces. (Photo by Leah Romero for Source NM)Following a campaign with national interest and millions of special interest dollars, incumbent Democratic U.S. Rep. Gabe Vasquez on Tuesday night held on to his seat representing New Mexico’s 2nd Congressional District.
Vasquez, now reelected to his third term, won the race by 57.9 % against Republican Greg Cunningham, a former Marine and Albuquerque police officer. The Associated Press called the race for Vasquez shortly after 10 p.m. with an estimated 80% of votes counted.
The incumbent’s victory in the 2nd Congressional District comes after individual donors and outside political action committees spent upwards of $21 million on the closely watched race. 
The National Republican Congressional Committee saw flipping the seat as important to its goals of keeping control of the U.S. House of Representatives. In recent weeks, President Donald Trump’s super PAC and others pumped millions of dollars toward television and other ads, many of which sought to cast Vasquez as soft on crime. 
Trump also endorsed Cunningham in the race, and House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) visited the state twice to stump for him. 
On the Democratic side, super PACs backed by Democratic Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker and others purchased advertising saying Cunningham, if elected, would fall fully in line with President Donald Trump’s agenda. 
The 2nd Congressional District race has been the most competitive New Mexico congressional race in recent years and has flipped multiple times over the last decade. Republican Yvette Herrell held the seat between 2020 and 2022, before narrowly losing to Vasquez by just over 1,200 votes. 
Redistricting in 2021 gave Democrats a better shot at winning the seat, including by carving a portion of Albuquerque’s Democrat-heavy South Valley into what was previously a predominately southern New Mexico district. 
State Republicans sued over the new boundaries, but a judge ultimately upheld them, noting that the seat remained competitive despite the changes and contained a roughly equal share of Republicans.
Earlier in the evening, Vasquez spoke to reporters from his election party in Las Cruces, saying the country “is at a verge of a breaking point. Economically, New Mexico families are not doing well, so we need to change course in Washington. We need to end this corruption. We need to give working families in this district a chance. We need to make sure that we protect our democracy, our voting rights, and restore dignity and decency to this country and end the rampant corruption in Washington.”
Source NM asked Vasquez what he’d found surprising on the campaign trail and he said that people “are very upset with the current economic policies of this Trump administration, but more than just that, they’re upset with both parties. They’re tired of inaction in Congress. They are tired of what they consider to be policies that haven’t benefited their personal life. And I think that is a referendum in this election.:
Vasquez announced on Nov. 1 that he and his fiancée, Nikki, announced they welcomed their first son to the world. On election night, he said he’d had about 12 hours of sleep over the previous 48 hours.
“Having an Election Day baby is a little bit stressful, but I am still proud and it’s actually renewed my commitment now being a parent for the first time to make sure that every family, including my own son, has a bright future ahead of them. It’s been a lot of swaddling and learning how to be a new dad, and I’m very proud of that.”
In his victory speech, Vasquez spoke about the Trump administration saying: “In the last two years, we’ve seen the transformation of the American dream turn into the American nightmare. We’ve seen seen politics at its worst. And I’m convinced now that we’ve secured the U.S. House majority and the U.S. Senate, the time for real accountability and reform is finally here. The day of reckoning for the corrupt Trump administration has come.
“Over the last two years, MAGA has governed in smoke filled rooms in Washington, with lobbyists and billionaires enriching themselves at our expense, writing the bills and the executive orders that have taken away our healthcare, our access to food, our access to affordable housing, our dignity as immigrants in this country, our civil rights as Americans, and the future away from a new generation. But this dark cloud of corruption has hovered over Congress and over the White House for far too long. And tonight the fog breaks, folks.”

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Republican Charlie Hatcher defeats Molder to win Tennessee’s 5th Congressional District
description: Former Tennessee Agriculture Commissioner Charlie Hatcher, a Republican, won Tennessee’s 5th Congressional District Tuesday, defeating Chaz Molder, the Democratic mayor of Columbia. Hatcher replaces outgoing U.S. Rep. Andy Ogles in the 5th District. He defeated Ogles in the primary, despite President Donald Trump’s endorsement of Ogles. The president endorse[...]
text:
.

Photograph  by John Partipilo/Tennessee LookoutFormer Tennessee Agriculture Commissioner Charlie Hatcher, a Republican, won Tennessee’s 5th Congressional District Tuesday, defeating Chaz Molder, the Democratic mayor of Columbia.
Hatcher replaces outgoing U.S. Rep. Andy Ogles in the 5th District. He defeated Ogles in the primary, despite President Donald Trump’s endorsement of Ogles. The president endorsed Hatcher after his primary victory, and he joined the president at a rally held in Clarksville in the final weeks of the campaign.
Hatcher received 51.7% of the vote over Molder’s 46.7% when The Associated Press called the race at 11:17 p.m.
Tennessee Republicans redrew the state’s U.S. House map in May, after the U.S. Supreme Court made it harder to challenge racially discriminatory voting maps.
In a special redistricting legislative session, GOP lawmakers changed the 5th District’s lines for the second time this decade. In 2022, state Republicans divided Nashville across the three congressional districts, successfully flipping the 5th from Democratic control to the GOP.
Ogles won the new seat that year, becoming the first Republican to win Tennessee’s 5th Congressional District seat since Reconstruction. 
In the most recent redrawing, the seat changed from incorporating a third of Nashville to including a third of Memphis. It now runs from the outskirts of Columbia, creating an upside-down L-shape that includes most of northwest and far-west Tennessee rural counties.
Both Hatcher and Molder entered the race for the 5th District before it was redrawn. 
Hatcher previously served as Tennessee commissioner of agriculture under Gov. Bill Lee before stepping down to run for Congress. Hatcher is a fifth-generation Williamson County dairy farmer, livestock veterinarian and operates Hatcher Family Dairy.
Molder is in his second term as the Columbia mayor, and received significant backing from the national Democratic Party and moderates like Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear. He initially entered the campaign when the 5th District included his hometown and the partisan lean was less extreme. 
Molder initially built his campaign around Ogles, a member of the Freedom Caucus in the U.S. House, which includes the GOP’s most conservative members. 
Hatcher ran as a moderate in the primary, using his “hire a farmer” slogan to paint himself as a less extreme Republican than Ogles. 
Hatcher and Molder held a joint general election forum in the final weeks of the campaign, a rarity among Tennessee candidates for office. 
Hatcher said in the forum he agreed with Trump’s tariffs and that the president shouldn’t end his war in Iran without the condition of no nuclear weapons in the country. He also supported U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, even though he thought there were “instances” where they went too far. 
“They’ve backed off since,” Hatcher said. “I think we’re in a good spot now.”

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Peggy Flanagan wins Minnesota U.S. Senate seat in historic victory
description: Minnesota Democrat Peggy Flanagan made history Tuesday as the first Native American woman elected to the U.S. Senate, a distinction she may share with Alaska Democrat Mary Peltola if she wins her race.  The two-term lieutenant governor beat out Republican Michele Tafoya, a former NFL sideline reporter and conservative podcaster, on a progressive economic pla[...]
text:
Lieutenant Governor Peggy Flanagan took the stage at the First Avenue Rally, Monday July 20, 2026. (Photo by Glen Stubbe/Minnesota Reformer)Minnesota Democrat Peggy Flanagan made history Tuesday as the first Native American woman elected to the U.S. Senate, a distinction she may share with Alaska Democrat Mary Peltola if she wins her race. 
The two-term lieutenant governor beat out Republican Michele Tafoya, a former NFL sideline reporter and conservative podcaster, on a progressive economic platform and promise to “rip ICE apart” following the incursion of some 3,000 federal immigration agents to the state earlier this year that left two Americans dead. 
Republicans tried to make the election a referendum on fraud in state-run programs that grew into a crisis under Gov. Tim Walz and led him to drop his bid for a third term.
Flanagan denied any responsibility for failing to stop fraud sooner, repeatedly citing the governor’s statement that the “buck stops” with him. She then redirected voters’ attention to reports of President Trump and his family enriching themselves through crypto, international real estate and mineral deals, defense contracts and presidential pardons. 
Flanagan, who supports Medicare for All, universal childcare and raising the minimum wage to $17 an hour, was backed by lefty icons including Sen. Bernie Sanders, and her victory is a win for the left flank of the Senate Democratic caucus. By winning the seat vacated by Sen. Tina Smith and previously held by progressive standard-bearers Paul Wellstone and Al Franken, Flanagan will continue a decades-long legacy.
Flanagan’s victory is something of a comeback after a rocky few years when she was sidelined during the Walz administration — tension between Walz and Flanagan spilled into the open after the governor returned from his vice presidential run in 2024 — and faced a tough Democratic-Farmer-Labor primary opponent in U.S. Rep. Angie Craig. 
The election of Flanagan, an enrolled member of White Earth Nation, is highly symbolic for Native Americans. Just four enrolled tribal members have served in the country’s most powerful legislative body, all men. 
But her ascension to the Senate goes beyond representation. Flanagan brings deep experience working with tribal governments that promises to make her a powerful advocate for the 575 federally recognized tribes. 
As lieutenant governor, Flanagan helped reshape state government’s relationship with the 11 tribal nations in Minnesota. The Walz-Flanagan administration expanded consultation with tribal leaders, restored thousands of acres of land, protected tribal gambling interests, supported an emerging tribal cannabis industry and established the first state office of Missing and Murdered Indigenous Relatives. 
Flanagan’s election is not surprising in a state that hasn’t elected a Republican senator since 2002, especially given Trump’s deep unpopularity and voters’ frustration with tariff-fueled inflation and higher gas prices that are the result of the war Iran. Still, nonpartisan polls largely showed a tight race leading up to Election Day, raising fears among Democrats that Minnesota could swing right while reddish states swung left. 
Minnesota Republicans, who haven’t won a Senate race since 2002, saw Tafoya as their best chance in years to win a statewide seat. Tafoya is well known and brought strong communication skills from her years on television, and she presented herself as an independent thinker willing to challenge Trump and a moderate on issues such as abortion. 
Flanagan graduated Phi Beta Kappa with a major in child psychology and a minor in American Indian studies from the University of Minnesota. She took a job at the Division of Indian Work in south Minneapolis before joining Wellstone Action, the nonprofit dedicated to carrying on the legacy of Sen. Paul Wellstone by training political organizers and candidates.
She served on the Minneapolis School Board and led the Children’s Defense Fund of Minnesota, and then won a seat in the state House in 2015. Walz tapped her to join his ticket for governor in 2017 and they were elected the next year.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Louisiana voters approve 7 of 10 constitutional amendments
description: Half of the ballot items involved property taxes that help pay for many parish governments, sheriffs and public schools.
text:
A sign directs voters to the polling location at the East Baton Rouge Public Library Branch in Zachary on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Elise Plunk/Louisiana Illuminator)A ballot with 10 amendments to the Louisiana Constitution was placed before voters statewide on Tuesday’s ballot, and they gave their approval to seven of the proposals.
Half of the ballot items involved property taxes that help pay for many parish governments, sheriffs and public schools.
The voting margins listed were as of 11:15 p.m. Tuesday
Amendment 1: YES – 75%
Amendment 1 gives surviving spouses of deceased disabled veterans to transfer a property tax exemption to a new house. It is expected to affect only a small group of people as just 229 people claimed the existing exemption last year, according to a legislative fiscal analysis.
Amendment 2: NO – 58%
The rejection of Amendment 2 denies local governments the power to remove real estate value assessment deadlines. It would have allowed local governments to keep property tax rates lower for a longer period of time. Under the current system, local officials have said they feel pressure to sometimes raise rates prematurely because if they don’t, they lose the ability to do so in the future. Opponents argued the proposal would create more uncertainty for taxpayers about when their property tax bills would be raised and by how much. 
Amendment 3: YES – 68%
Voters chose to remove the power of judges to grant bail to defendants convicted of certain crimes with minors as victims. The applicable offenses include kidnapping, human trafficking, rape and other sex crimes. Post-conviction bail can be granted at a judge’s discretion before a convicted person reports to prison, such as when their case is on appeal or they are awaiting sentencing. Judges can grant bail except when someone is charged with a crime punishable by death, and there is a high degree of evidence of their guilt. 
Amendment 4: YES – 56%
The provisions of Amendment 4 apply to only two living former Louisiana governors — Democrat John Bel Edwards and Republican Bobby Jindal — and any future holders of the state’s highest office. The amendment prohibits any governor from running for office again once they serve more than one and a half terms, equal to six years. Neither Edwards nor Edwards has expressed interest in running for the office again. 
Amendment 5: NO – 62%
The proposition would have given the Louisiana Legislature the authority to prioritize how the state pays off the debt of its retirement systems when there are surplus funds in the state budget. The existing law that stays in effect requires surplus dollars to go toward the oldest debt first. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Amendment 6: YES – 64%
Local governments can now increase the homestead exemption for many people 65 and older. Voters in the tax jurisdiction must also approve a tax break for seniors through a separate, local ballot initiative. 
Amendment 7: YES – 65%
The statewide vote clears the way for New Orleans to use $152 million in federal funds to replace lead pipes in its drinking water delivery system. Voter approval was needed because there were concerns a state law prohibits the use of that money on private property, though an opinion from Attorney General Liz Murrill had given the go-ahead to do so. The $152 million represents only a small fraction of the $1 billion-plus cost to remove lead pipes from the New Orleans water system. The city is under a 2037 federal deadline to complete the work. 
Amendment 8: YES – 63%
Several states have enacted laws that prohibit a “foreign adversary” or their representative from acquiring or expropriating property. Louisiana is the first to place the prohibition in its state constitution. A state law already prevents these nations from taking over property near military bases as well as buying or leasing any land or immovable property.   
The list of applicable countries currently includes China, Cuba, Iran, North Korea, Russia and the former Maduro regime in Venezuela. 
Amendment 9: YES – 59%
Voters approved an increase to the income threshold for people who qualify for a property tax freeze from $100,000 to $150,000. Impacted people are those 65 or older, disabled veterans, other residents who are totally and permanently disabled, and the spouses of military members killed or missing in action. The threshold will be adjusted to match inflation rates in future years. 
Amendment 10: NO – 53%
Voters statewide declined to give their approval for local governments to adopt property tax exemptions for owners who rehabilitate blighted properties. Improvements to derelict homes could have received a tax break of up to 75% of the property’s renovated assessed value for 20 years, and a 25% exemption would have been for remediating vacant land next to a home or business property.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: US Rep. Don Davis defeats Republican Laurie Buckhout in rematch for NC’s 1st Congressional District
description: Democratic U.S. Rep. Don Davis is headed back to Washington after defeating Republican challenger Laurie Buckhout in the most expensive U.S. House race in general election history.  With all 290 precincts reporting, Davis received just under 50% of the vote to Buckhout’s 47%, according to preliminary unofficial results from the North Carolina State Board of [...]
text:
U.S. Rep. Don Davis (left) and Republican challenger Laurie Buckhout (right) (Photos courtesy of campaigns)Democratic U.S. Rep. Don Davis is headed back to Washington after defeating Republican challenger Laurie Buckhout in the most expensive U.S. House race in general election history. 
With all 290 precincts reporting, Davis received just under 50% of the vote to Buckhout’s 47%, according to preliminary unofficial results from the North Carolina State Board of Elections. Libertarian challenger Tom Bailey received 3% of the vote. 
“To our volunteers, to every supporter who gave your all to help us on this campaign,” Davis said in his victory speech. “Thank you with all of my heart.”
In her concession speech to supporters, Buckhout said she called to congratulate Davis on his win.
“Tonight the voters of eastern North Carolina made their choice, and I respect it,” she said. “When he succeeds for this district, we all do. But we will hold him accountable.”
The race drew national attention as Republicans looked to expand their majority in the U.S. House and Democrats sought to regain control of the chamber. About $53 million has been poured into the district for ad buys and reservations. 
Democrats committed $29.6 million to support Davis, while Republicans spent $23.3 million backing Buckhout.
Buckhout and Davis faced off in 2024, when Davis defeated Buckhout by 6,307 votes, making it one of the year’s most competitive races. 
But the district is different this election cycle. In 2025, at the urging of President Donald Trump, Republican state lawmakers redrew North Carolina’s congressional maps, shifting the 1st District to include more Republican-leaning voters in hopes of unseating Davis.
The district stretches from the Virginia border north of the Triangle to the Outer Banks. It includes Rocky Mount, New Bern, Roanoke Rapids and Kill Devil Hills. 
Davis, an Air Force veteran and former six-term state senator, was first elected to Congress in 2022.  
During his campaign, he emphasized his work securing federal funding for eastern North Carolina communities, expanding access to health care and addressing the rising cost of living.
Buckhout is a retired Army colonel and defense consultant. She campaigned on lowering costs, securing the border and supporting eastern North Carolina’s farmers and fishermen. 
She also sought to tie Davis to national Democrats and criticized his opposition to President Donald Trump’s legislation. 
Bailey, the Libertarian candidate, offered voters a third option outside the two major political parties. A Vietnam War veteran, Bailey campaigned on voting rights and changes to the federal tax system.
He previously challenged Davis and Buckhout in 2024. In that election, Bailey received about 9,949 votes, more than the margin separating Davis and Buckhout.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: SC secretary of state wins 7th term leading office for business filings
description: South Carolina’s longtime secretary of state, Mark Hammond, won a seventh term in office.
text:
Secretary of State Mark Hammond, a Republican, won reelection. Here's Hammond pictured on the Statehouse grounds in Columbia, S.C. on Monday, Oct. 13, 2026. (Photo by Katharine Wilson/SC Daily Gazette) COLUMBIA — South Carolina’s longtime secretary of state won a seventh term in office Tuesday.
Republican Mark Hammond defeated Jason Belton, a Democrat and union organizer, with 53% of the vote, according to unofficial results from the state Election Commission.
South Carolina’s secretary of state leads the 30-person office where businesses, corporations, and charities file their paperwork. Other duties of the agency include regulating professional fundraisers and approving notaries.
Hammond, in his campaign, pledged to take more noncompliant charities to court to suspend their fundraising abilities and to use artificial intelligence to aid business owners with the registration process.
Voters first elected Hammond, 62, in 2002. He succeeded Jim Miles, the first Republican to win the job since Reconstruction, after Miles left to make an unsuccessful bid for governor.
It’s been 40 years since South Carolinians elected a Democrat to the office.

text:
Alabama Republican gubernatorial nominee Tommy Tuberville speaks to supporters after declaring victory during an election night watch party at The Hotel at Auburn University on Nov. 3, 2026. Democratic gubernatorial nominee Doug Jones did not immediately concede the contest. (Larry Robinson for Alabama Reflector)AUBURN — Republican U.S. Sen. Tommy Tuberville declared victory Tuesday in the race for Alabama governor, but Democrat Doug Jones did not concede in what appeared to be the closest gubernatorial contest in Alabama in 24 years.
As of 10:58 p.m., Tuberville, Alabama’s senior U.S. senator, had 778,000 votes (52.5%) in unofficial returns, according to The Associated Press. Jones had 703,000 (47.5%). The AP had not made a call in the race as of 11:17 p.m., with 80% of the vote counted.
Speaking to a crowd of more than 400 supporters in Auburn, Tuberville declared victory with less than 70% of ballots counted, according to the AP.
“Winning is not an accident, it is a decision,” Tuberville said to supporters in Auburn Tuesday evening. “Tonight, Alabama decided to win.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The Associated Press estimated that about 40% of Jefferson County’s ballots had not been counted as of 11 p.m. Speaking in Birmingham to about 200 supporters Tuesday, Jones said that “there are probably at least 100,000 votes in Jefferson County alone” and that a concession would be premature. 
“Seriously, we’ve been watching all of this unfold tonight,” he said. “It has been a slow process. You know, it dribbles in and dribbles out. But the fact of the matter is, there’s still a hell of a lot of votes out there.”
Jones added that “it’s not going to be easy with this, but there is a path there. We believe that we can absolutely do it, but we may not.”
The race was the most high-profile gubernatorial contest since 2018. Polling of the race was limited, but Tuberville showed leads in two polls conducted by Republican-leaning firms and a smaller one done by a Democratic firm. Tuberville had a financial advantage over Jones throughout the race. 
Jones, however, managed to hold his own in fundraising and campaigned around the state, holding over 20 town halls around the state, tapping into Democratic enthusiasm and drawing hundreds and sometimes thousands of people to his events. 
Democrats across the country made gains in seats that Republicans have held for years, gaining control of both chambers of Congress. Tuberville, declaring victory, said Alabama stood up to the “Blue wave.”
“In the face of blue waves, which we’ve had tonight unfortunately, this staff has stood up to the pressure and said, ‘Not in my Alabama,'” he said. “I guarantee you this: I and we will not let you down. The folks who didn’t vote for me, listen, I’m going to be your governor too. A lot of you didn’t vote for me. I don’t understand why. But honestly, at this point, I don’t care who you voted for, because we have to work and a lot of work to do.”
The two candidates’ platforms contrasted sharply. Tuberville ran on a mix of social conservative policies, promising to expand the CHOOSE Act, the state’s voucher program; to cut the state’s income and grocery taxes and to reduce the size of state government. 
“We’re all in it together, because the measure of a good economy isn’t what somebody announces at the podium. It’s how much money an Alabama family has to spend and then save for the future. Now, I’m going to promise you perfection. We’re not going to do that,” Tuberville said Tuesday. “We’re going to be accountable. Every goal we set will go on a public scoreboard.”
Tuberville released a “playbook” that covers all his policy goals for the former football coach’s first term. He plans to reduce the state workforce, bring more private jobs to Alabama, protect rural hospitals and audit every government agency, and more.
Jones called for a cut to the grocery tax as part of a broader effort to improve affordability in the state. The Democratic nominee also said he would work for Medicaid expansion, affordable housing, constitutional protections for in-vitro fertilization and constitutional reform. 
The candidates differed on data centers. Jones called for a one-year moratorium on new data center construction to give the Legislature a chance to develop regulations over the facilities. Tuberville’s message on the issue wavered. At a meeting of sheriffs in July, Tuberville praised data centers and called concerns about them “bullcrap.” In early September, Tuberville said he would work to give local communities power to reject data centers and require them to pay for power and water usage.
When Jones ran for reelection to the U.S. Senate in 2020, Tuberville won by 20 points. Jones’ performance, if it holds in official returns, would be the best by a Democratic gubernatorial nominee since former Gov. Don Siegelman narrowly lost to Republican Bob Riley in 2002. No subsequent Democratic gubernatorial nominee received more than 42% of the statewide vote before Jones on Tuesday.

title: Republican Kurt Alme leading in US Senate race, independent Seth Bodnar still hopeful
description: Republican Kurt Alme was leading on election night, but the U.S. Senate race had yet to be called around 10 p.m. Alme, whom political analysts had projected to win, had 50% of the vote, and independent Seth Bodnar, who outraised Alme by almost a couple of million, had 36%. Alani Bankhead, the Democratic nominee, had […]
text:
Republican Kurt Alme was leading on election night, but the U.S. Senate race had yet to be called around 10 p.m.
Alme, whom political analysts had projected to win, had 50% of the vote, and independent Seth Bodnar, who outraised Alme by almost a couple of million, had 36%.
Alani Bankhead, the Democratic nominee, had 12%. Libertarian Kyle Austin had 2%.
But most precincts had yet to fully report.
Montana has had an all-Republican congressional delegation since 2025, after U.S. Sen. Jon Tester, a Democrat, lost his seat to U.S. Sen. Tim Sheehy in the 2024 election.
This year’s Senate race has been bitter among Democrats and left-of-center Montanans. 
Bodnar supporters repeatedly urged Bankhead to drop out to consolidate support for the independent.
Bankhead stressed she was the nominee and would stay in the race.
She faced fierce headwinds, including significant money for Bodnar and what she described as a lack of support from the leader of the Montana Democratic Party, who later resigned to endorse Bodnar.
Bodnar is the former University of Montana president who resigned to make a run for the U.S. Senate.
Alme, is a former two-time U.S. Attorney for the District of Montana, as well as being part of two Republican governor’s administrations.
Bankhead is a retired lieutenant colonel who served in the U.S. Air Force.
Austin is a pharmacist who owns pharmacies in Butte and Billings.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Blue wave crashes over CT General Assembly
description: Democrats project majorities of at least 30-6 in the Senate and 111-40 in the House, with other races too close to call.
text:
Republicans lost at least five seats in the Connecticut Senate and nine in the House, with some races still to be determined early Wednesday morning, leaving the GOP with its smallest-ever presence in the upper chamber.
Democrats project majorities of at least 30-6 in the Senate and 111-40 in the House, with House Speaker Matt Ritter, D-Hartford, saying if other close races fall their way the advantage could be as much as 115-36. 
In the Senate, races involving three other Republican incumbents, including Senate Minority Leader Stephen Harding of Brookfield, were too close to call. 
Democrats said they definitely unseated three incumbents: Sen. John Kissel of Enfield, a state senator for 34 years, lost to David Kiner in the 7th District; Sen. Heather Somers of Groton lost to Joe de la Cruz in the 18th; and Sen. Jeff Gordon of Woodstock lost to Ethan Werstler in the 35th.
Democrats also won two open seats in Fairfield County. Rob Blanchard of Newtown won the 28th District seat that had been held by Sen. Tony Hwang, R-Fairfield, and Democrat Jill Oberlander of Greenwich captured the 36th District seat held by Sen. Ryan Fazio, the GOP nominee for governor.
The Republican base in Fairfield County continued to erode Tuesday, with Democrats also flipping state House seats in Newtown and Shelton, Democrats said.
House Democrats claimed early victories in the 106th and 113th House district, with Michelle Embree Ku unseating Rep. Mitch Bolinsky of Newtown and Bryan Lizotte winning the open seat in Shelton.
Democrats did not lose a seat in either chamber.
According to Democrats, other Republican incumbents to lose included Rep. Cara Pavalock-D’Amato of Bristol, Rep. Steve Weir of Hebron and Rep. Greg Howard of Stonington.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: NJ Democrats beat expectations, swipe 2 House seats from the GOP
description: New Jersey Democrats flipped two of the state’s three GOP-held House seats in what is largely seen as a rebuke of President Trump.
text:
From left, Lily Zeitz, Angela Zeitz, and Carol Simon Levin applaud at Bridgewater Manor on Nov. 3, 2026, as Rebecca Bennett takes the lead in the 7th District House race. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)New Jersey Democrats swept federal races Tuesday night, returning Republicans to a single-seat minority in the state’s 12-person congressional delegation for the second time under a Trump presidency.
Though Democrats were expected to perform well Tuesday, their vote totals — buoyed by an outsized lead in preelection ballots even before polls opened Tuesday — swelled beyond that expectation to flip GOP-held seats in the 2nd and 7th Congressional Districts while guarding all nine of their own.
“This is the moment we, as a district, as a state, and as a country, Democrats, independents, and Republicans, stood together and demanded better, demanded change,” said Rebecca Bennett, who ousted Rep. Tom Kean Jr. (R) in the 7th District. “We are demanding an end to the vast corruption in DC, and a focus on actually solving the problems we are facing as a country.”
Bennett, a healthcare executive and former U.S. helicopter pilot, defeated Kean, a member of a storied New Jersey political dynasty and the son of the popular former governor, by a wide margin, capturing 57% of the vote to Kean’s 41%.
Rep.-elect Rebecca Bennett (D) speaks during her victory party in Bridgewater on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)
In South Jersey’s 2nd District, Cape May City Mayor Zack Mullock (D) pushed through traditionally Republican ground to oust four-term Rep. Jeff Van Drew (R), a former state lawmaker who was elected to the House as a Democrat in 2018 but joined the GOP a year later. Mullock won 51% of the vote, and Van Drew nabbed 48%.
“I am so humbled, I can’t believe this is happening,” Mullock told supporters. “This is all about you. I think you all know I couldn’t have done this without you. We didn’t have enough money to do it without you. This was a grassroots campaign and I cannot thank you enough.”
The Democratic victories will again leave Rep. Chris Smith (R) the state’s lone Republican representative in Congress. He took that mantle for the first time in 2019, after a similar Democratic wave drove Democrats to victory in four GOP-held seats.
Many Democrats said the wins are voters’ response to the excesses of the second Trump administration.
“If there’s anything we’re seeing in America right now, it is a wave of change going through our nation, and mark my words: Results are not in, but this is going to be one of the greatest rebukes of a sitting president in the history of the United States of America,” Sen. Cory Booker (D), who won a third full term on Tuesday, said at his victory party in Hasbrouck Heights.
Those excesses ranged from masked federal agents in unmarked cars whisking people off the street or out of churches or schools, a war of choice in Iran that has choked global energy markets and surged gas prices, and tariffs that had enflamed tensions with allies and increased Americans’ cost of living, Booker said.
Booker won 63% of the vote to Republican challenger Justin Murphy’s 35%.
Though New Jersey Republicans have privately blamed Trump for the dour political environment they faced coming into Election Day, Van Drew declined to do the same in his concession speech.
“Sometimes life is bumpy. It’s not always easy, and you have challenges before you, and you can’t blame other people for that,” he said. “I’m not going to blame Donald Trump. I’m not going to blame the speaker. I’m not going to blame anybody. I made decisions in my life, and I’m proud of them.”
It remains to be seen how the Republican Party navigates the coming weeks and months and how closely its officials align with a president roundly rejected by the state’s voters and by voters nationwide. Democrats are expected to take control of the House and Senate after Tuesday’s results.
State Sen. Jon Bramnick (R-Union), a moderate who has long opposed Trump, urged his fellow Republicans to reject Trump in favor of the Republican values of yesteryear.
“No more excuses. We must return to our traditional principles and reject the hateful politics that has no place in our state,” he said in a social media post, later adding, “The voters have spoken.”
Democrats looking ahead also had to look past Trump, Booker said. Though the Democrats must pursue accountability for the Trump administration, they must also look to bridge income inequality and ensure residents have a pathway to the American dream, he said.
“The mission is bigger than him. He is not the main character of our story. The main character of our story is the American people, and the job of our generation is to redeem the dream of America,” Booker said.

Former poll worker explains voting can help the disconnect between citizens and the government


By Emma Johnson -  5:58 pm





Huntington City Hall is one of several voting precincts in Huntington, West Virginia, on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Emma Johnson for West Virginia Watch)
HUNTINGTON, W.Va — Payton Hunter, a life-long resident of Huntington, West Virginia, has experienced multiple elections as a voter and election poll worker. 
Hunter said going to vote is something she is very passionate about. 
“As a woman, I believe it is especially important for me to exercise my right to vote for the women who fought so hard for me to be able to,” Hunter said. 
Hunter also said voting in West Virginia is important because “our needs are often forgotten about in Washington.” 
“No matter if you vote or not in the election, everyone will feel the effects of this election, whether it be at the grocery store, the gas pump, or even at your place of work,” Hunter said. “This is another reason I chose to vote, because at least I know my vote counted in some way.” 
When asked if voting in every election was important Hunter said every election should be treated as an important election no matter what. 
“l believe everyone should get out and use their right to vote in every election,” Hunter said. “All elections are important and we are privileged to have the right to even vote at all, as a poll worker I’ve witnessed many people who seem to forget that.”
Hunter said as a West Virginian, voting helps address issues within the state at a national level.
“Generally West Virginia tends to see less government support nationally, which creates an obvious disconnect between national candidates and lower-level candidates,” Hunter said. “This is especially true on issues like the southern water crisis and data centers.” 
Hunter also said even the midterms matter, because “delegates and senators, even in our small state, tend to strongly influence whether a president can truly deliver on campaign promises”.
As a former poll worker, she said she encourages everyone to do their own research when it comes to voting for candidates. 
“I think it is so important for voters to do their research on the candidates they are voting for, especially in a digital world where campaign ads are shown everywhere,” Hunter said. “The political climate is constantly changing, and it is up to you as a voter to stay informed.”
Hunter said she also encourages younger people to get out and vote more so that their generation’s needs can also be met. 
“I would highly encourage all young adults to get out and vote because if more young people do not vote, their needs are not always going to be met,” Hunter said. “It’s better to start voting young, because those who do start voting at a younger age tend to continue to vote once they get older, that’s why I’m here voting.” 









U.S. Department of Justice monitors election in Kanawha County


By Lori Kersey -  5:44 pm





Representatives from the U.S. Department of Justice are monitoring the midterm election at precincts in Kanawha County on Tuesday.
Donald Kersey, chief of staff for the West Virginia Secretary of State’s Office, said the federal government notified the office last week that six election monitors would be in Charleston Tuesday.
The DOJ did not disclose which polling locations they planned to observe, but based on reports they are roving around the city rather than observing a single polling place all day, Kersey said.
The Department of Justice said in a statement Tuesday it was sending approximately 1,000 election monitors to all 50 states for the first time ever to check for compliance with federal voting rights statutes.
Monitors are coordinated by the DOJ’s Civil Rights Division, and include personnel from the Civil Rights Division, other DOJ divisions and components, U.S. Attorney’s Offices and federal observers from the Office of Personnel Management, the statement said.
“Election integrity has been one of the top priorities for this Administration and this Division,” Assistant Attorney General Harmeet K. Dhillon of the Civil Rights Division at the Department of Justice said in a statement. “I am very proud we are deploying the largest monitoring effort in DOJ history, and pursuing transparency for elections in an assertive and nondiscriminatory manner.”
In a social media post Tuesday, the American Civil Liberties Union of West Virginia noted that “federal election monitors are routinely sent to polling places.”
“It’s also important to note that monitors may NOT interfere with your right to vote in any way,” the organization said.
The ACLU advised voters to contact its Election Protection Hotline at 304-355-5123 to report election interference.









College students urge other young voters to use their right to vote


By Emma Johnson -  4:23 pm





Residents head to the polls to vote at First Presbyterian Church in Huntington, West Virginia, on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Emma Johnson for West Virginia Watch)
HUNTINGTON, W.Va — College students in Huntington, West Virginia, are showing up to polling locations throughout the city to cast their votes this election in hope to bring positive changes to the state and city.
Marshall University student Emily Grady said with West Virginia being a state that is “forgotten or seen as less,” voting could help change that outlook. 
“We are statistically one of the poorest, most depressed states with very high addiction rates and very low healthcare rates,” Grady said. “Due to those stats, we as West Virginia residents should want to vote even more to make change possible.” 
Grady said she is “tired” of people complaining about leadership, but doing nothing to help create a change in leadership. 
“I hear people, especially younger people, say they are unhappy with how things in the area are handled, but if you don’t like something regarding our government, speaking up by voting is how you fix that,” Grady said. “Thats why I’m out casting my vote today.” 
Another Marshall University student, Allison Mannon, said as a college student and young adult, she feels more inclined to vote in this election to make her voice heard.
“I think a lot of younger people forget that these changes being made in the government affect us too,” Mannon said. “I think we forget that even though we are young adults, our voices should be heard too.”
Mannon also said it is important to know who you are voting for by doing research on the candidates before just casting a vote. 
“Every voter should be doing their research on who and what they are voting for,” Mannon said. “Don’t just vote for someone because they sent you a text, piece of mail or you saw one of their billboards.” 

 Last updated: 4:26 pm 







Children seeing the voting process is important


By Katie Shaver -  4:08 pm





Johnson Elementary School in Bridgeport, West Virginia, serves as a polling place on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Katie Shaver for West Virginia Watch)
BRIDGEPORT, W.Va. — Leigha Trippett, an educator in Harrison County, brought her daughter to vote with her at Johnson Elementary School in Bridgeport, West Virginia.
Trippett said children seeing the voting process is important because they learn to use their voice and express their opinion on issues that affect them at an early age.
“It’s important for her to see that, to vote one day and stand up for what you believe in, especially as a woman,” Trippett said. “It’s just a day to see people in your community, and it’s important for her to see that.”
Trippett’s daughter asked to come today because she enjoys casting votes for her favorite characters on the children’s ballot.

 Last updated: 4:09 pm 







First-time voter stresses importance of research


By Katie Shaver -  3:30 pm





Johnson Elementary School in Bridgeport, West Virginia, serves as a polling place on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Katie Shaver for West Virginia Watch)
Brynn Radabaugh, a West Virginia University student, came back to her hometown of Bridgeport, West Virginia, to cast her first-ever vote.
Radabaugh said she looked through a voting website to find out who the candidates were personality-wise and what their campaign was built around.
Each gave a personally written description of the candidate, their job titles, and what main issues they were focused on.
“I felt that kind of helped me (see) character and learn what they were wanting to do,” she said.
Radabaugh was surprised by the levies present on the ballot, but after reading through them, felt they were a great idea to support. 
“I’m all for keeping up funding with stuff that’ll help other people, historical attractions and keeping the public libraries afloat.”

 Last updated: 3:34 pm 







Retired teacher, former poll volunteer urges all voters to show up


By Samuel Felinton -  3:05 pm





Voters go to University High School in Morgantown, West Virginia, to cast their ballots on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Samuel Felinton for West Virginia Watch)
MORGANTOWN, W.Va. — Jill Thacker has seen Election Day from both sides of the table. A retired teacher and former polling station volunteer, she came to University High School on Tuesday as a voter.
When asked about what she wanted to share from her perspective as a former poll volunteer, Thacker emphasized that background doesn’t matter; everyone needs to participate.
“I don’t care what your background is, what party you belong to, or who you’re supporting; you just have to get out here and have your voice heard,” Thacker said. “Every single person in this community deserves a seat at the table, but you only get it if you show up.”
When asked what brought her out to vote this year, Thacker said she was looking for a candidate who would stand up for older West Virginians.
“I came out to vote today because I’m looking for someone who can look at older folks on fixed incomes and actually promise us a fighting chance,” Thacker said. “We’ve worked hard our whole lives, and we just want to know that someone is going to go to bat for our healthcare and our benefits when it matters most.”









Voters question the motive behind proposed amendment to end noncitizen voting


By Katie Shaver -  2:51 pm





Johnson Elementary School in Bridgeport, West Virginia, serves as a polling place on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Katie Shaver for West Virginia Watch)
BRIDGEPORT, W.Va. — A proposed amendment to the West Virginia Constitution is on today’s ballot. 
The amendment aims to change the wording regarding citizens’ voting rights from “citizens of the state shall be entitled to vote” to “only citizens of the state who are citizens of the United States are entitled to vote.”
Brynn Radabaugh, a first-time voter, in Bridgeport, West Virginia, felt the amendment was unnecessary.
“I don’t see the point of it really,” Radabaugh said. “If you’re a West Virginia citizen, I think you’re a U.S. citizen.”
Christa Shafer said she is concerned about what this amendment means for the future of voting rights.
“I’m concerned about the amendment with some sneaky stuff put in there that would, down the line, have the ability to change voting rights,” Shafer said.
Radabaugh understands the concerns that led to the amendment, but does not think the wording change will matter much down the line.
“I know kind of why they’re doing it; they don’t just want anybody to come into West Virginia and vote, but I just don’t know why anybody would ever do that.”
Shafer agreed, saying that citizens already have the right to vote and proof of citizenship is already required at the polls. 









Out-of-town students return to Morgantown to vote


By Samuel Felinton -  2:13 pm





Mountaineer Middle School in Morgantown, West Virginia is one of several voting precincts in the city on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Samuel Felinton for West Virginia Watch)
MORGANTOWN, W.Va. — Not everyone voting at Mountaineer Middle School on Election Day was a West Virginia University student. Two friends came in from other campuses just to cast their ballots.
Thaddeus Watkins, a student at the University of Pittsburgh, and Jacob Sterling, a student at West Virginia Wesleyan College, drove to Morgantown to meet up and vote together. They said they hope it becomes a tradition, at least until they get their footing somewhere else.
“I want us to keep doing this every couple of years, just to have an excuse to see each other and do something that matters,” Watkins said.
Neither lives in Morgantown year-round anymore, but both said coming back to vote is important to them.
“It doesn’t matter if I’m only here for the holidays or a few months out of the summer, my voice belongs where my roots are,” Sterling said. “No matter where my classes are, I still call Morgantown home.”
When going into vote, their biggest issues were Flock cameras and data centers, which Sterling said “are moving into our neighborhoods faster than the regulations can keep up, and nobody is asking the community how we feel about the surveillance.”









How to report ‘election irregularities’


By Leann Ray -  6:30 am





To report suspicious election irregularities, you can call the West Virginia Secretary of State Investigations Division at 877-FRAUD-WV. The caller may remain anonymous.
For polling place concerns that do not involve potential fraud or cheating, such as a poll book error, contact your county clerk.

The American Civil Liberties Union of West Virginia has an Election Protection Hotline, which can be reached at 304-355-5123.
Anyone with questions about the voting process is encouraged to contact the hotline., said ACLU-WV Executive Eli Baumwell. Voters may also use the hotline to report concerns like electioneering at a polling place or voter intimidation tactics.
The hotline is staffed by attorneys and law students trained in election laws, and helps residents answer questions before, during and after an election.
