title: Early results show support for Colorado ballot measures led by anti-LGBTQ organization
description: Preliminary election night results show two Colorado ballot measures that would restrict the rights of transgender children are polling ahead, and a third measure to increase penalties for human trafficking has passed. As of 9:45 p.m., Proposition 134, which aims to prevent transgender children from participating in school sports, had 52% of Coloradans in fa[...]
text:
Adams County residents drop off ballots outside the Adams County clerk and recorder's office in Brighton on Tuesday. (Photo by Andrew Fraieli/Colorado Newsline)Preliminary election night results show two Colorado ballot measures that would restrict the rights of transgender children are polling ahead, and a third measure to increase penalties for human trafficking has passed.
As of 9:45 p.m., Proposition 134, which aims to prevent transgender children from participating in school sports, had 52% of Coloradans in favor and 48% against. The Associated Press estimated 70% of votes in the race were counted.
Proposition 135, which would prohibit health care professionals from knowingly performing any surgery on a minor “for the purpose of altering biological sex characteristics,” had just under 52% of Coloradans in favor and just over 48% against. The Associated Press estimated 70% of votes in the race were counted.
Proposition 133, which mandates that anyone convicted of child sex trafficking be sentenced to life in prison without parole, had just under 62% of Coloradans in favor and just over 38% opposed. The Associated Press called that race shortly after 9 p.m. Tuesday.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
All measures were backed by Protect Kids Colorado, an organization led by prominent anti-LGBTQ+ activist Erin Lee. Families Not Politics, the issue committee that opposed both anti-trans ballot measures, is led by LGBTQ+ advocacy organizations including One Colorado, Rocky Mountain Equality, the Transgender Law Center and Inside Out Youth Services, as well as Planned Parenthood of the Rocky Mountains and Cobalt, an abortion-rights organization. 
Organizations including Cobalt, an abortion-rights organization, and the Colorado Coalition Against Sexual Assault opposed Proposition 133.
Proposition 134 would add language in state statute to define boys and girls based on physical anatomy, excluding transgender people. The measure would restrict which teams students play on based on their “biological reproductive system.” Sports teams sponsored by schools or athletic associations would be required to expressly designate teams for men, women or co-ed participation. Schools and their athletic departments would be required to adopt policies implementing the requirements of the initiative by Jan. 1.
Opponents say Proposition 134 could result in all children being subjected to whatever verification process schools select.
Proposition 135 would prohibit state and federal funding including Medicaid from being used to pay for gender-affirming procedures. 
Opponents say Proposition 135 could result in the inability for trans children to receive any kind of surgery if discussion of their gender identity arises in conversation with a doctor. A 2024 Harvard study found that higher rates of cisgender people, both minors and adults, received the surgeries that transgender and gender diverse individuals receive for gender-affirming purposes. For example, it found that 97% of breast reduction procedures performed on teenagers were for cisgender boys. 
Proposition 133 will increase the current sentencing range for anyone convicted of child sex trafficking from the current range of between 8 and 48 years. Opponents warned it could be used by anti-abortion activists to target anyone who helps a minor obtain abortion care, and puts victims who were coerced to commit crimes at risk spending their lives in prison.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico voters approve paying state legislators
description: New Mexico voters on Nov. 3, 2026, approved Constitutional Amendment 4, allowing legislators to be paid for the first time in state history.
text:
The Roundhouse pictured Oct. 1, 2025, the opening day of the special legislative session. (Photo by Patrick Lohmann/Source NM)New Mexico lawmakers will have the option to receive salaries starting in 2029, following voter approval of Constitutional Amendment 4.
According to preliminary voting totals from the New Mexico Secretary of State’s Office, 62% of voters cast ballots in favor of the amendment, compared to 38% who were opposed. 
“New Mexicans today have rejected the status quo, and opened the door to a government that reflects their lived experience and the challenges they face every day. This vote is a historic step toward a more representative and accountable Legislature,” Eli Cuna, Vote for Change campaign manager said in a statement. “By tying lawmakers’ pay to New Mexico’s median household income, we’re creating a stronger connection between the people making decisions in Santa Fe and the families those decisions affect. This victory belongs to working families all across New Mexico who are eager to have a seat at the table and represent their communities to build a thriving state.”
New Mexico Election 2026: Constitutional Amendment 4

The amendment question asked voters whether they were for or against allowing New Mexico lawmakers to receive compensation equal to the state’s median household income, which is currently $67,800, according to U.S. Census figures. For 112 state lawmakers, the annual cost to taxpayers will be about $7.6 million.
Advocates pushed the amendment in a yearslong effort, saying the lack of salary means that qualified, community-oriented individuals can’t financially justify running for office. They said paying lawmakers salaries could make lawmakers less beholden to well-financed lobbyists offering expensive meals or other perks. 
The coalition also sees paying salaries as a key step in a broader “modernization” push at the Legislature, along with changes such as hiring paid district legislative aides, which state lawmakers began doing in 2024, and extending the legislative session beyond 30 days or 60 days.
Opponents, however, said the proposed salary is too high and were not convinced the money would actually lead to better policy. According to the National Conference of State Legislatures, the  proposed New Mexico salary is higher than the national average salary for lawmakers at  $44,320. Lawmakers in New Mexico’s neighboring states of Texas, Colorado and Arizona also receive salaries of significantly less than what New Mexico lawmakers would receive.
While New Mexico lawmakers do not receive a salary, they do receive per diem payments for costs associated with the annual legislative session and committee meetings in the interim. Lawmakers are also eligible to receive pensions after leaving office. 
The question’s victory on the November ballot marks the final step in a yearslong effort. The Legislature at the session earlier this year voted largely along party lines to approve House Joint Resolution 5, which puts the question of legislative salaries before voters.

name: Washington State Standard
title: Washington voters embracing income tax on high earners
description: Voters on Tuesday were upholding Washington’s new income tax on households earning more than a million dollars a year, a threshold opponents argued would eventually be lowered to apply to everyone. Initiative 645 to repeal the high-earners tax was failing by an overwhelming margin, 58% to 42%. It lacked support in the state’s most populous […]
text:
Washington state Sen. Jamie Pedersen of Seattle celebrates defeat of an initiative to repeal the income tax on high earners that he wrote and pushed through the Legislature. (Photo by Jacquelyn Jimenez Romero/Washington State Standard)Voters on Tuesday were upholding Washington’s new income tax on households earning more than a million dollars a year, a threshold opponents argued would eventually be lowered to apply to everyone.
Initiative 645 to repeal the high-earners tax was failing by an overwhelming margin, 58% to 42%. It lacked support in the state’s most populous counties on both sides of the state.
In King County, the state’s largest and home to the greatest concentration of Democrats, nearly 67% were voting it down. It was also getting turned down by voters in Skamania, Pacific, Mason and Okanogan counties.
This is a resounding political victory for Democratic Gov. Bob Ferguson, whose public embrace of the tax last December was a catalyst for its eventual passage by the Democrat–controlled Legislature.
It also will be a legacy success for Senate Majority Leader Jamie Pedersen, D-Seattle, an original architect of the tax, who withstood slings and arrows of opponents as he led efforts to massage the content to secure votes up to the final days of session.
“Tonight’s victory is momentous, but there is still more work to do. Defeating I-645 will avoid deep future budget cuts, but in the near term, until the Millionaires Tax is in place, there will still be very difficult decisions ahead in the upcoming legislative session for the governor and legislators,” said Erik Houser, spokesman for the No on 645 campaign.
“But tonight, by saying no to I-645, voters said yes to fiscal responsibility.They said yes to funding core services. They said yes to reforming our upside down tax code to make it more fair for Washington families,” he said.
It is a hard loss for Let’s Go Washington, the conservative political committee founded and funded by hedge fund manager Brian Heywood. His group launched a massive signature-gathering drive to get the initiative on the ballot after the Legislature blocked voters’ ability to erase it with a referendum.
“If the income tax doesn’t get repealed, for the next two years, every job creator that leaves this state, every entrepreneur who doesn’t set up shop in Washington, every employee who is concerned that tax will be lowered to them, that is on Governor Ferguson. This is his income tax,” Heywood said Tuesday night.
Washington voters have been asked 11 times over nearly a century to approve personal or corporate income taxes. The first vote, in 1932, was successful. But a 5-4 state Supreme Court decision in 1933 struck the measure down. Later measures failed, most recently in 2010 when the income thresholds were $200,000 for individuals and $400,000 for joint filers.
The income tax is a 9.9% tax on individual and household wage income above $1 million a year.  The state’s chief economist estimates the income tax will generate $3.5 billion from 25,000 filers in 2029, the first year of collections.
In addition to the ballot battle, there’s a pending lawsuit challenging the constitutionality of the tax. That case has effectively been on hold to see what voters do. Ferguson, a former three-term state attorney general, has consistently expressed confidence that courts would uphold the levy.
Just two years ago, Let’s Go Washington, the conservative political committee behind Initiative 645, qualified an initiative barring the state and local governments from taxing income. The Legislature adopted the measure only to set it aside earlier this year to allow for this income tax.
Washington’s tax system has long been considered among the most regressive in the country, meaning lower earners pay proportionally more of their income in taxes than wealthier households. This is largely due to the state’s heavy reliance on sales taxes and the lack of an income tax, according to policy experts. 
Until this year, Washington was one of only nine states nationwide that did not tax individual wage and salary income.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The disputed income tax was created by Senate Bill 6346, which the Legislature passed in March. It takes effect Jan. 1, 2028. The first dollars would start to arrive in 2029. 
Only a few paragraphs in the 110-page piece of legislation actually concern the income tax. Most of the text deals with how the money will be spent.
For example, the new law eliminates sales tax on diapers, personal hygiene products like soap and toothpaste, and some over-the-counter drugs. It also will repeal sales and use taxes for retail services, except advertising services, and expand a tax credit program for lower-income families. All this would happen in 2029 and the costs are to be covered from income tax collections.
Initiative 645 sought to repeal the income tax while preserving those elements.
Initiative foes forecast near ruination of the state’s social safety net and its ability to care for the most in need should those tax collections not materialize. They say the situation is already challenging with federal support for Medicaid and a host of social services getting cut.
They predicted the Legislature and governor would be forced to make deep cuts in all areas of state government to make ends meet.
Backers of the initiative countered that critics were trying to scare voters. They said because the first dollars would not arrive until 2029, the governor and lawmakers had time to find other ways to pay for the new commitments, or abandon them. 
The potential for the income threshold to drop below $1 million was an ongoing flashpoint.
Pro-initiative forces argued throughout the campaign that Democratic lawmakers would eventually levy the tax on households earning far less than $1 million because they will need the money. “Everybody knows it’s coming to that,”  Heywood said at a forum last month.
Late in the campaign, I-645 backers asserted retirees would see their pensions taxed because the law removed a prohibition on taxing pensions.
Ferguson has repeatedly vowed to veto any legislation that would lower the threshold.
The No on 645 campaign reported spending nearly $12.7 million as of Monday. Its biggest donors are the Service Employees International Union ($3.5 million), Washington Education Association ($3 million), Washington Federation of State Employees ($2.5 million), and National Education Association ($1 million).
Supporters had two primary committees pushing for passage of the initiative. 
One was Let’s Go Washington, which raised and spent more than $4 million. That sum included expenses to qualify the measure and separate initiatives concerning a ban on transgender girls’ participation in girls sports and parents rights.
The other committee was Vote Yes Repeal the Income Tax which reported $3.4 million in spending as of Monday. Lawrence Hughes, a retired businessman, is the largest donor at $750,000.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Amy Klobuchar elected Minnesota’s first woman governor
description: Amy Jean Klobuchar became the first woman elected Hennepin County attorney in 1998, the first woman U.S. senator from Minnesota in 2006, and on Tuesday she became the first woman to be elected Minnesota’s governor. Klobuchar, 66, prevailed over Republican House Speaker Lisa Demuth as Democrats secured the Democratic-Farmer-Labor Party’s hold on the governor’[...]
text:
Sen. Amy Klobuchar spoke to reporters at the Democratic-Farmer-Labor's watch party before the governor's race was called on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)Amy Jean Klobuchar became the first woman elected Hennepin County attorney in 1998, the first woman U.S. senator from Minnesota in 2006, and on Tuesday she became the first woman to be elected Minnesota’s governor.
Klobuchar, 66, prevailed over Republican House Speaker Lisa Demuth as Democrats secured the Democratic-Farmer-Labor Party’s hold on the governor’s office for a fifth consecutive term.
As a U.S. senator for 20 years, a 2020 presidential candidate and now Minnesota’s next governor, Klobuchar has cemented her place as one of the most-talked-about and written-about Minnesotans in state history. Her name has become practically synonymous with Minnesota itself, and now, having broken the glass ceiling of Minnesota politics, she enters the history books. The Associated Press called the race for Klobuchar late Tuesday.  
“Minnesota, you showed up like you have all year. You inspire me. And as your next governor, I will work my heart out for you. I promise that I will be a transformative governor for this state,” Klobuchar said in her victory speech at the Democratic-Farmer-Labor’s election night party. “In Minnesota, trust is not given — it is earned. It comes with expectations, and … results. And we will deliver results that you can see and feel in your life.”
Klobuchar’s homecoming and historic win should give her a considerable honeymoon with Minnesotans, but she’s also got a major to-do list. She inherits protracted challenges once she takes office in January — a test of the political prowess she’s become famous for over nearly three decades in public office.
Amy Klobuchar has already told us who she is

The aftermath of the rampant fraud in Minnesota’s social safety net programs continues — authorities executed search warrants on several early autism treatment providers just days ago. Klobuchar has promised to audit state government as soon as she takes office. Student test scores released last month were again stagnant. Younger Minnesotans cannot afford starter homes. The state’s population is barely growing, and the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown has stymied a key influx of workers in important industries like agriculture and construction.
Klobuchar will need to appoint a cabinet and staff her administration. Then she has until the third Tuesday in February to craft a two-year budget and submit it to the Legislature, according to state statute. That’s about 15 weeks from her election win. Minnesota’s spending is rising faster than revenue, creating a structural imbalance beginning in July.
The state still has a massive rainy day fund, but rising healthcare costs, cuts from the federal government and slow economic growth could push the Legislature to dip into the funds.
Klobuchar has said she will not raise taxes and root out fraud in state government. During her victory speech, Klobuchar cautioned that some of her decisions may not be popular.
“Spoiler alert: You may not like every single thing I do,” Klobuchar said.
Demuth, whose rapid rise to House speaker and Republican gubernatorial candidate has now stalled, gave up her seat in the Legislature to run for governor.
Amy to the rescue 
Klobuchar rescued Minnesota Democrats from potential disaster by jumping into the governor’s race in January at the behest of DFL Gov. Tim Walz, who dropped his third-term bid amid increasing scrutiny on fraud in Minnesota’s social safety net programs.
Republicans ran on the fraud scandal — the Trump administration’s stated rationale for sending thousands of immigration officials to the state during Operation Metro Surge — and made it their top issue, arguing it was a failure of Democratic governance.
Democrats had worried for months that Walz’s name at the top of the ticket would hand Republicans the governorship for the first time in 16 years and sink Democrats’ prospects down the ballot.
But Klobuchar — Minnesota’s most accomplished vote-getter and fundraiser — gave the DFL, with an assist from President Donald Trump’s sagging approval ratings, fresh energy.
Klobuchar early on in her campaign distanced herself from Walz, promising to get rid of the fraud, create a “growth agenda” for the state and build back trust in the government.
“I’m going to clean up this mess,” Klobuchar said in one of her latest ads.
Steeped in politics
Klobuchar grew up in Plymouth. Her father was a Star Tribune columnist and her mother an elementary school teacher. She was schooled in politics thanks to her father’s work, and went on to graduate from Yale and the University of Chicago Law School.
She worked in the private sector for over a decade, carving a niche for herself at a major Minneapolis firm working in telecommunications law. Klobuchar served as the Hennepin County attorney for eight years, where she was known as a tough-on-crime prosecutor.
In the Senate, Klobuchar has mastered popular issues and has often built relationships with Republicans. During her first year in office, she worked quickly after the deadly I-35W bridge collapse in 2007 to secure federal funding for a replacement. She helped make America’s pool drains safer for children, expanded broadband access and worked on numerous farm bills.
The senior senator is known as policy wonk who works long into the night poring over details. This got her into trouble during her presidential run, as reports of her tyrannical behavior toward her staff leaked. Her demanding boss persona is now well-known, and during her campaign, Klobuchar made the argument that Minnesota needs a hands-on governor who will get the details right.
Staffing a government
Klobuchar will be in charge of 50,000 state employees, and she has said she wants to start fresh with new staff, presumably ditching Walz’s personnel.
“Who you bring in matters, people with management experience. And especially when you’re trying to change a culture in a workplace and have people reporting to you more about things and coming forward with what the problems are. That’s going to be very important to me,” Klobuchar told WCCO radio Monday.
Klobuchar’s transition will have $162,000, according to state statute, with which to staff a transition team, rent out office space and recruit new employees.
Alongside the budget, a key task will be to hire new commissioners, poring over resumes and conducting thorough interviews and background checks. Walz during his transition launched a website through which people could submit applications for open positions, and his team worked out of the Capitol’s third floor.
Part of Klobuchar’s transition will be to turn the promises she made during the campaign into real policy. Klobuchar promised to help the construction industry build 100,000 new housing units, ban cell phones from schools, create a state tax credit if Congress fails to pass health insurance subsidies and streamline permitting processes that companies say slows the pace of construction.
Regarding Klobuchar’s U.S. Senate seat, if she resigns before her inauguration, Walz would appoint her successor. But Walz can and most likely would defer to Klobuchar, who would then appoint her own successor. Some potential appointees include Secretary of State Steve Simon and U.S. Rep. Kelly Morrison.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Republican US senator defeats independent challenger in South Dakota
description: A well-funded challenge by an independent fell short Tuesday as Republican U.S. Sen. Mike Rounds of South Dakota won reelection. Rounds led Brian Bengs 62% to 38% when The Associated Press called the race at about 11 p.m. Central time with 58% of statewide votes counted. Another six-year term for the 72-year-old Rounds will be […]
text:
U.S. Sen. Mike Rounds, R-South Dakota, left, was challenged by independent candidate Brian Bengs in the Nov. 3, 2026, general election. (Photos courtesy of U.S. Senate committee livestream and South Dakota Public Broadcasting)A well-funded challenge by an independent fell short Tuesday as Republican U.S. Sen. Mike Rounds of South Dakota won reelection.
Rounds led Brian Bengs 62% to 38% when The Associated Press called the race at about 11 p.m. Central time with 58% of statewide votes counted.
Another six-year term for the 72-year-old Rounds will be his third in the Senate, after he served eight years as governor and 10 years in the Legislature.
Nationally, Bengs was one of four independent candidates for Senate in Tuesday’s election who were the main opponents of Republican senators. The others were in Nebraska, Montana and Idaho — states like South Dakota where President Donald Trump has won and Democrats have struggled.
Bengs is a 56-year-old Hot Springs resident who served in the Navy and as an attorney in the Air Force, and later worked as a college professor and park ranger. He previously ran as a Democrat for Senate four years ago, when he lost to Republican Sen. John Thune by 44 points.
Since then, the number of voters registered as independent or non-politically affiliated has surpassed the number of Democrats in the state, while Republicans have built a 2-to-1 registration advantage over Democrats.
Bengs became the only challenger to Rounds when this year’s Democratic nominee, Julian Beaudion, dropped out in August. Beaudion said at the time that he was pressured by Bengs and some Democrats to withdraw, an allegation Bengs denied.
The situation left South Dakota Democratic voters with a choice to make, including 46-year-old Democrat Heather Reed of Sioux Falls, who declined to say Tuesday at her polling place whether she voted for Rounds or Bengs.
“It was complicated,” Reed said. “I didn’t feel like there was a good choice for somebody that I believe has full integrity and maturity and will stand up for people who are marginalized. I’m not sure that either of the candidates will do that.”
Yet Bengs attracted campaign contributions from across the country and help from outside groups, who sensed a rare opportunity to compete with a Republican incumbent in a Republican-leaning state. Rounds was also well-funded, and total spending on the campaign approached $10 million earlier this month, according to campaign finance reports.

Brian Bengs, independent South Dakota candidate for U.S. Senate, speaks to reporters on Sept. 3, 2026, at the Old Courthouse Museum in Sioux Falls. (Photo by John Hult/South Dakota Searchlight)

Anti-Rounds advertising from outside groups characterized him as complicit in Trump policies, including higher tariffs and the war in Iran, which have contributed to rising prices for fuel and consumer goods. Bengs criticized Rounds’ ties to the tech industry, including a Rounds senior adviser, Rob Skjonsberg, who has served as a state-level lobbyist for Facebook parent company Meta.
“South Dakotans deserve to know that the people who work for them aren’t using public service as a revolving door to lucrative lobbying jobs,” Bengs said during the campaign.
Bengs also highlighted contributions to Rounds’ campaign committee or associated political action committees, verified by South Dakota Searchlight, from people and political action committees tied to tech-company investors and major tech companies.
Rounds co-chairs the Senate Artificial Intelligence Caucus and has sponsored or cosponsored several bills impacting the tech industry. He responded to Bengs’ criticisms earlier this month in a Searchlight interview.
“Does anybody see where I would make a vote that would be different based upon individuals participating in funding my campaign or anybody else’s campaign?” Rounds said. “Everything that we do is reported. Everything that we do is done in accordance with Senate ethics rules and campaign rules. And the reason why folks support me is because they agree with me on my positions.”
Beyond those exchanges through the media, Bengs had difficulty inducing Rounds to engage. Bengs challenged Rounds to debates, but Rounds declined.
Rounds’ campaign focused on issues including his opposition to abortion, his support of military spending, and his A+ rating (compared to Bengs’ F) from the National Rifle Association.
South Dakota Searchlight’s John Hult contributed to this report.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Mike Mazzei, with Trump’s backing, continues GOP dominance in Oklahoma governor win
description: OKLAHOMA CITY – Mike Mazzei will be Oklahoma’s next governor after a grueling race that saw the Republican contribute a record amount of his own money. Mazzei, a Republican from Tulsa, defeated House Minority Leader Cyndi Munson, D-Oklahoma City, and three independents on Tuesday.   “It’s a tough night for Republicans across the country, but thank […]
text:
Republican Mike Mazzei gives a victory speech at the Arvest Convention Center in Tulsa on Nov. 3, 2026, after winning the general election for Oklahoma governor. (Photo by Ace Cuervo/For Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY – Mike Mazzei will be Oklahoma’s next governor after a grueling race that saw the Republican contribute a record amount of his own money.
Mazzei, a Republican from Tulsa, defeated House Minority Leader Cyndi Munson, D-Oklahoma City, and three independents on Tuesday.  
“It’s a tough night for Republicans across the country, but thank the Lord for Oklahoma,” Mazzei said, apparently referencing a series of high-profile GOP election losses in other parts of the U.S.
His supporters gathered at a watch party in Tulsa, which was briefly interrupted by a fire alarm. 
Mazzei, who once served as Gov. Kevin Stitt’s budget secretary, praised the legacy outgoing governor will leave. Stitt is in the final year of his second term and couldn’t run again due to term limits. 
Supporters cheer at Mike Mazzei’s campaign watch party Nov. 3, 2026, at the Arvest Convention Center in Tulsa after he won the general election for Oklahoma governor. (Photo by Ace Cuervo/For Oklahoma Voice)
“The sign of great leaders, everyone, is leaving things better off than you found it,” Mazzei said, adding that Stitt and his wife, Sarah, have done that.
Mazzei thanked his supporters and family.
“I want to applaud Representative Cyndi Munson,” Mazzei said. “She is a kind person and has worked incredibly hard and I thank her for serving our state as a legislator for the past 11 years.”
Mazzei was buoyed by an early endorsement by President Donald Trump and the record-setting $13 million Mazzei contributed. Mazzei previously told Oklahoma Voice that he did not know how he was going to repay the loans.
The new governor will earn $185,000 a year. 
Trump’s recent waning popularity in Oklahoma, where he won all 77 counties each of the three times he was on the ballot, didn’t appear to hurt Mazzei, despite complaints of high grocery and fuel prices. 
Trump in October campaigned for Mazzei and other Republicans at a rally in Durant.
Cyndi Munson, Democratic candidate for governor, gives her concession speech during her election watch party at the OKC Farmers Public Market in Oklahoma City, Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Nate Billings/For Oklahoma Voice)
Mazzei defeated Oklahoma Attorney General Gentner Drummond by a little more than 2,000 votes in the Aug. 25 Republican primary runoff.
Oklahoma and Tulsa counties, which are the state’s two most populous, both supported Munson, but Mazzei performed better in other areas of the state.
Mazzei is a former state senator and works as a financial adviser. 
In the Senate, Mazzei chaired the Finance Committee and championed elimination of ineffective tax preferences. 
His Senate service was hampered by a car accident in 2008, causing him to miss a significant number of votes. He broke his back and sustained nerve damage.
“I am definitely a walking miracle,” Mazzei said, adding that his story is one of triumph over tragedy.
Mazzei campaigned on elimination of the income tax, increasing student literacy, and lowering property taxes for seniors and veterans.
Munson had hoped to turn Trump’s declining popularity into votes in a state where Republicans outnumber Democrats 2-1 with nearly 500,000 independents.
She campaigned on affordability issues, healthcare and education. She supports abortion rights.
Her supporters gathered at a watch party in Oklahoma City.
“Unfortunately, tonight things did not go our way,” Munson said.
She said her campaign has a lot to be proud of and a lot to celebrate.
Munson previously worked at nonprofits and went to college on Oklahoma’s Promise, a scholarship program that provides lower-income students with free tuition.
Munson was raised by a single-father while Mazzei came from a military family.
Mazzei will be sworn into office in January as the state’s 29th governor.

title: U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn ekes out Tennessee governor’s seat
description: U.S. Sen. Final unofficial reports from the Tennessee Secretary of State showed Blackburn, a former Tennessee lawmaker who also served as a U.S. House […]
text:
U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn takes the stage before supporters at The Pinnacle in downtown Nashville on Nov. 3, 2026. Blackburn eked out a narrow win to become Tennessee's first woman governor. (Photo by John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout) U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn scratched out a victory Tuesday to become the first woman governor in Tennessee history, claiming a mandate to govern conservatively even though she failed to capture a majority vote.
Final unofficial reports from the Tennessee Secretary of State showed Blackburn, a former Tennessee lawmaker who also served as a U.S. House member before winning the Senate seat in 2018, picked up 45.6% of the vote to 43% for Democrat Jerri Green and 9.3% for independent David Hatley, an upper East Tennessee businessman targeted by the Blackburn campaign and dark-money groups with a barrage of negative TV ads. 
Blackburn claimed victory at 10 p.m. 
Blackburn’s campaign barely mentioned Green in the runup to Tuesday’s vote as Hatley nearly played spoiler in the race in spite of revelations that he was convicted of bank fraud decades ago and only recently had his voting rights restored.
“Tennessee did not just elect a governor, it chose a direction,” Blackburn said Tuesday night at The Pinnacle in downtown Nashville where she held her victory party with a crowd of several hundred who warmed up for the night with drinks and country music.
Blackburn did not mention the close margin of the election’s outcome, but said it is clear Tennesseans want a governor who will “govern on conservative principles.” She noted she will fight against socialist and Islamic policies and will put more money in people’s pockets, though she didn’t mention specifics, other than trying to lower property taxes.
In addition, Blackburn said she will focus on affordable housing, fighting crime, safe elections and making sure children have educational choices. Citing a familiar refrain, she mentioned keeping boys out of girls’ locker rooms.
U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn, who won the Tennessee governor’s race in a narrow victory, embraces conservative talk show host Clay Travis at her Nov. 3, 2026 Election Night party. Blackburn’s husband, Chuck, is at right. (Photo by John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)
Blackburn also said that Tennessee voters agree with the death penalty. 
In picking up the narrow win, Blackburn captured nearly all of Tennessee’s rural areas while Green carried the state’s urban counties, Hamilton, Knox, Davidson and Shelby.
President Donald Trump declined to endorse Blackburn during her primary race against U.S. Rep. John Rose of Cookeville but supported her in an Election Day statement in which he criticized Green and said Blackburn would “fight tirelessly” to grow the economy, cut taxes and regulations and unleash American energy dominance. Trump didn’t mention Hatley in his social media post.
Blackburn overlooked Green during the general election campaign and began hammering Hatley shortly after the Republican primary, starting a website called deadbeatDave.com with pictures of him wearing prison clothing and pointing out his bank fraud convictions. 
Two dark-money groups spent nearly $10 million attacking Hatley in the runup to the vote, including the Tennessee Freedom Fund and a pro-Blackburn PAC called Team Tennessee that poured in $3 million, and the Choose Freedom Fund, a group linked to MAGA Inc., which spent $6.5 million blasting the independent candidate.
Hatley, though, said he had been open about his past indiscretions in a biography, writing that he was convicted of writing bad checks when he was trying to start his business in his early 20s.
“This was just one battle for our state and it was not the end of the fight,” said Democratic gubernatorial nominee Jerri Green, conceding the race to U.S.Sen. Marsha Blackburn on Nov. 3, 2026, in Chattanooga. (Photo by Ben Sessoms for Tennessee Lookout)
Calling himself a conservative candidate, Hatley poured $12 million into his campaign and spent a good deal of energy driving home the claim that he couldn’t be bought by dark money or outside forces. During a forum last week, he said he would end “pay for play.”
Blackburn refused to participate in debates during the Republican primary and didn’t attend a gubernatorial forum at Middle Tennessee State University last week.
Green, a public defender and Memphis City Council member, said during the forum that she was the only person on the stage who had a path to election. Hatley and independent Lauren Pinkston also attended, but Green previously called on Pinkston to drop out of the race and accused Hatley of trying to buy the office.
From her Election Night event in Chattanooga, Green conceded the race shortly before 11 p.m. 
“Tonight isn’t the result we wanted,” Green said. “I know and understand this hurts.”
“Tonight I didn’t win for you but I want you to know that I’m not going anywhere, that you are not going anywhere, that we are not going anywhere.”
She raised $1.5 million for the campaign and brought in another $600,000 in the final reporting period, for a little more than $2 million. Green said, if elected, she would seek Medicaid expansion, issue an executive order to allow doctors to practice women’s healthcare without the threat of prosecution under the state’s anti-abortion laws and end the Tennessee Highway Patrol’s cooperation with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. She also wanted to stop the renewal of private prison contracts, eliminate the state grocery tax and cut tax rebates to big businesses.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Joseph Cao wins right to fill remaining BESE District 1 term
description: Joseph Cao, the former Republican congressman who Gov. Jeff Landry picked as a placeholder on the state school board late last year, won the right to take over the job for good in Tuesday’s election.
text:
Joseph Cao, a former one-term congressman from Harvey, will return to  elected office after winning a seat on the state Board of Elementary and Secondary Education. (Cao campaign photoJoseph Cao, the former Republican congressman who Gov. Jeff Landry picked as a placeholder on the state school board late last year, won the right to take over the job for good in Tuesday’s election.
Cao defeated Democrat Angela Hershey, a retired teacher from Madisonville, to clinch the District 1 seat on the Board of Elementary and Secondary Education. He received 64% of the votes from the district that includes parts of Jefferson, Orleans, St. Tammany and Tangipahoa parishes.
The governor chose Cao, an attorney from Harvey, as interim representative for District 1 after its elected officeholder, Paul Hollis of Mandeville, stepped down in December when President Donald Trump named him director of the U.S. Mint. 
Hollis’ unfinished term ends in January 2028, meaning Cao would have to run again next year if he wants to keep the District 1 seat.
This is Cao’s first election victory since he won in the 2nd Congressional District in 2008, becoming the first Republican to accomplish that feat in 180 years. Cao ousted 18-year incumbent William Jefferson, who was in the midst of a federal investigation that would end with his conviction for bribery and racketeering in 2009.
The 2nd District seat returned to Democratic hands after Cedric Richmond defeated Cao outright in a 2010 open primary. 
Cao’s most notable moment from his time in Congress came when he was the only Republican to vote in favor of President Barack Obama’s signature legislation, the Affordable Care Act.
Cao qualified for the Louisiana attorney general’s race in 2011 but dropped out of the race before the election to leave Buddy Caldwell unopposed for re-election.
The next attempt at elected office for Cao was the 2016 U.S. Senate race, in which he finished well behind open primary winners John Kennedy and Foster Campbell.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: GOP stronghold remains in WV Senate, but Democrats flip seats to gain 4 members
description: While the state Senate remains firmly under GOP control, Democratic candidates gained three seats in the Upper Chamber. The wins included flipping two seats to Blue in areas with West Virginia's last Democratic strongholds.
text:
Emblem of the West Virginia Senate in the state Capitol in Charleston, West Virginia.
(Photo by Will Price/West Virginia Legislative Photography)While the state Senate remains firmly under GOP control, Democratic candidates gained three seats in the Upper Chamber. The wins included flipping two seats to Blue in areas with West Virginia’s last Democratic strongholds.
Nineteen Senate seats were on ballots across the state, and 16 of those were won by Republicans.
The GOP will hold 30 seats in the 34 member Senate in 2027.
But, in Morgantown, John Williams added to the Democrat’s ranks after defeating long-time politician and incumbent Sen. Mike Oliverio, R-Monongalia, to claim the District 13 seat. 
Williams, who is currently in the House of Delegates, won with 55% of the votes when 99% of precincts were called by the Associated Press. Oliverio received 41.4% of the votes. 
“I think the totals show that we were ready for a change in Marion and Monongalian counties,” Williams said in a phone interview shortly after polls closed. He knocked more than 5,000 doors in the district, running on a campaign focused on affordability issues and pushing back on data centers development. 
“The results reflect that, and I’m excited to roll my sleeves up and get to work in the Senate on the issues that I advocated for,” Wiliams said.
DuRon Jackson, a Democratic candidate in Huntington, defeated Chris Miller to keep the District 5 seat Blue. 
The seat is currently held by long-serving state Sen. Mike Woelfel, a Democrat, who declined to run again.
Richie Robb defeated incumbent Sen. Anne Charnock, R-Kanawha, in District 17. Gov. Patrick Morrisey appointed Charnock to the district in early 2025 after Eric Nelson resigned.
In District 1, Sen. Laura Chapman, R-Ohio, was able to keep her seat against a significant challenge from Democratic candidate Shawn Fluharty.
Chapman won with around 53% of the vote with 98% of votes counted, according to the AP. Fluharty received 46.7% of the vote at the same time. 
In a phone interview, Chapman said she “wasn’t too worried” about Fluharty’s challenge due her focus on serving her Northern Panhandle constituents. 
“I’ve always been in the community and delivered for my constituents. I’ve probably given out my phone number to what feels like the entirety of the Northern Panhandle, and people do call me,” Chapman said. 
“I’ve been very successful in getting great things for the Northern Panhandle … delivering on infrastructure projects, roads, sewers, bridges (and) water,” she said. “I’m just so thankful that the voters have trusted me for another four years.”
This was Chapman’s first re-election campaign. A political action group linked to Morrisey spent six figures against Fluhary; Chapman is an ally of the governor. 
Sen. Tom Takubo, R-Kanawha, held onto his Kanawha County Senate seat after being targeted in the May primary. He faced a challenge on Tuesday night from Democratic candidate Wes Holden in Charleston’s strong Blue voting base.
Takubo received 52.9% of the votes with 99% of precincts reporting, according to the AP. Holden received around 47% of the votes. 
“It’s been really tough over the past 12 months,” Takubo said in a phone interview. “It’s sad to see what has happened to politics in the state of West Virginia.”
With the election in the rearview, the Senate remains deeply divided after a contentious Senate president race and bitter GOP primary in May.
Senate President Randy Smith, R-Preston, defeated Takubo and Sen. Eric Tarr, R-Putnam for the top position. The race split the Senate into factions — those aligning with Takubo and others siding with Smith. 
Takubo wants the Senate to focus on education, jobs, and reversing the state’s population decline. The Senate needs to get away from “divisive social issues,” he said. 
“We only got 34 people to make a lot of really important decisions,” Takubo said. “Each Senate member represents about 105,000 West Virginians, and every one of those voices should be heard. Now, will they be heard? You know, time will tell.”

name: Washington State Standard
title: Democrat-backed WA Supreme Court candidates win elections, except for one close race
description: All but one of the slate of five Washington state Supreme Court candidates backed by Democratic leaders led their races handily after the initial vote count Tuesday night in an election that will transform the court. Two recent appointees of Gov. Bob Ferguson, a new face to the high court and its chief justice all […]
text:
The Washington state Supreme Court building in Olympia. (Photo by Aspen Ford/Washington State Standard)All but one of the slate of five Washington state Supreme Court candidates backed by Democratic leaders led their races handily after the initial vote count Tuesday night in an election that will transform the court.
Two recent appointees of Gov. Bob Ferguson, a new face to the high court and its chief justice all were ahead, with more votes to count in the coming days. 
Their four opponents were backed by the state Republican Party.
The one Republican-backed candidate having some success is King County Superior Court Judge Sean O’Donnell, who leads the tightest race of the bunch over Democrat-endorsed appeals court Judge Ian Birk by 2 percentage points. This was the most closely watched of the five races.
These races garnered more attention this year for several reasons. Four justices are leaving the court, creating a rare opportunity to change its makeup. Conservatives have been unhappy with its decisions in recent years. 
The high-earners income tax, which voters are deciding on in this election via Initiative 645, is sure to land before the court, setting the stage for a decision on its constitutionality and whether to overturn nearly century-old precedent.
The court decides on appeals from lower courts on both civil and criminal matters. It also guides the work of lower courts. For example, the justices last year slashed caseload limits for the state’s overstretched public defender workforce.
Combined, the 10 candidates raised well over $3 million, far more than these sleepy campaigns usually draw. Millions more were spent by outside groups vying for their favored candidates. 
Public sector unions like the Washington Federation of State Employees, Washington Education Association and Service Employees International Union 775 backed a group called Beware the Attack on Our Courts, which supported candidates seen as left leaning.
The business-funded Concerned Taxpayers of Washington State and Citizens for Working Courts spent money on behalf of the more conservative slate of Supreme Court hopefuls.
The issue of justices arriving to the court via gubernatorial appointment as others retire early frustrates Republicans, who feel voters aren’t getting a fair shot to choose as the appointees arrive on the ballot as incumbents. 
Over 2 million ballots have been counted so far. The next tally is expected late Wednesday afternoon.
The results
In the most expensive race on the state Supreme Court slate, O’Donnell holds a 50.9% to 48.7% lead over Birk. The margin amounts to 36,500 votes.
Partisanship is uncommon in judicial campaigns. That wasn’t the case in this race, as Birk drew a lot of fire for calling O’Donnell, who has support from the state GOP but hasn’t drawn attention to it, a closet Republican. O’Donnell notes he has support from both sides of the political spectrum, including U.S. Rep. Adam Smith, state Public Lands Commissioner Dave Upthegrove and former Govs. Christine Gregoire and Gary Locke.
Ferguson and Brown endorsed Birk. 
Birk and O’Donnell raised more money for their campaigns than any other Supreme Court candidate this year. Birk brought in $625,000, while O’Donnell’s war chest totaled $573,000.
The winner will replace Justice Charles Johnson, who is retiring due to the state constitutional requirement to step away at age 75.
Justice Colleen Melody, who joined the court this year upon Gov. Bob Ferguson’s appointment, leads tax attorney Scott Edwards comfortably by a vote of 60% to 39.7%. 
Before joining the court, Melody, who had no prior judicial experience, led the state attorney general’s Civil Rights Division under Ferguson and Nick Brown. Edwards, who has led unsuccessful legal efforts to defeat progressive taxes, promised to be an independent voice who would restore trust in the Supreme Court, while Melody vowed a focus on the swath of issues the court oversees outside of deciding appeals, like court system accessibility.
The winner of this race will serve the final two years of retired Supreme Court Justice Mary Yu’s term. Normal terms are six years.
In the race for Position 3, King County Superior Court Judge Jaime Hawk is ahead of Mason County Superior Court Judge David Stevens 57.7% to 41.9%. 
Hawk, a former attorney for the American Civil Liberties Union, boasts endorsements from Ferguson and Brown, the attorney general, while Stevens is backed by the state Republican Party.
The winner of the race will replace Justice Raquel Montoya-Lewis, the first Native American elected statewide. She is retiring from the court.
Like Melody, new Justice Theo Angelis is ahead in his election bid after being appointed this year by Ferguson. Angelis leads retired Federal Way Municipal Court Judge Dave Larson, another Republican-backed candidate, 55.4% to 44.3%. 
Angelis, with no prior judicial experience joined the court earlier this year to replace longtime Justice Barbara Madsen. He came from the firm K&L Gates, where he once worked with Ferguson. 
Larson has run for Supreme Court several times, and came very close to winning in 2024.
The winner will serve two years before needing to be on the ballot again.
In the final race on the ballot, Chief Justice Debra Stephens is well ahead of attorney and veteran Todd Bloom. Stephens has 63.8% to Bloom’s 35.9%, the widest margin of the bunch.

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Democrats gain control of Georgia board that regulates utilities for first time in decades
description: Voters have handed Democrats control of the Georgia Public Service Commission, a little known but important regulatory board that influences how much Georgians pay for energy. Democrats Peter Hubbard, who is already on the commission, and Shelia Edwards, who was competing for an open seat, were both candidates leading by more than 10 points as […]
text:
Democrats Peter Hubbard, who won a full term to the Public Service Commission, and Shelia Edwards, who flipped the previously Republican-held seat, pictured at debates organized by the Atlanta Press Club. Photo credit: J Glenn Photography, courtesy of the Atlanta Press Club and Ross Williams/Georgia RecorderVoters have handed Democrats control of the Georgia Public Service Commission, a little known but important regulatory board that influences how much Georgians pay for energy.
Democrats Peter Hubbard, who is already on the commission, and Shelia Edwards, who was competing for an open seat, were both candidates leading by more than 10 points as of late Tuesday night, according to unofficial results from the secretary of state’s office. 
“I want to thank the people of Georgia for their votes and prayers! The voters have spoken and I am ready to go to work on their behalf,” Edwards said in a statement.
Hubbard had more pointed words about the direction the commission is headed in under a Democratic majority.
“I look forward to helping fulfill Southern Company’s goal of net zero emissions by 2050,” Hubbard said in a statement.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The commission came under public scrutiny last year after the formerly all-Republican commission voted to approve six rate increases over the last few years, resulting in an estimated average increase of about $500 per year for the average household. Those concerns coupled with the rapid influx of data centers made the debate around energy affordability and regulation a top issue for voters in 2026. While the commission does not control whether data centers come to Georgia, they have approved a massive expansion of energy infrastructure to support data centers. 
Hubbard, who flipped the District 3 seat in a 2025 special election, won his reelection bid to represent the Atlanta-area seat with 56% of the vote as of late Tuesday night.
Hubbard defeated former Republican commissioner Fitz Johnson, who was appointed to the seat in 2021 by Gov. Brian Kemp and lost the seat to Hubbard last year. Johnson did not respond to a request for comment Tuesday night.
Edwards, the Democratic nominee for District 5, is a community advocate and business owner based in Cobb County. She defeated Republican Josh Tolbert, a mechanical engineer, with 55% of the vote as of late Tuesday night.
Tolbert in a statement congratulated Edwards on her victory and said that despite the results not being in his favor, he’s “deeply grateful to everyone who supported (his) campaign and for the opportunity to meet so many wonderful Georgian.”
“I also want to applaud my fellow Republican candidates for their willingness to step forward and serve our state, and thank their families, supporters and volunteers for the tremendous sacrifices they made along the way,” Tolbert said.
With three of the five seats, Democrats will have a majority on the commission for the first time in 20 years starting next year. This is a monumental shift for the board that is responsible for regulating Georgia Power, which is the state’s largest electric utility. The commission became an all-Republican board in 2007 after incumbent Democrat David Burgess, who was the first Black official in the board’s history, was defeated by Republican Chuck Eaton in 2006.
Democrats regained spots on the commission last year when Hubbard and Alicia Johnson flipped two seats in a 2025 special election that was seen as a potential bellwether for the 2026 midterms. Hubbard and Johnson campaigned on making energy costs more affordable by prioritizing clean energy sources. They both defeated Republican incumbents who had voted to approve six rate increases over two years, resulting in an estimated average increase of about $500 per year for the average household.
Hubbard and Edwards continued to campaign on the promise of bringing down energy costs, but Hubbard shifted his focus to describing what the commission could do with a Democratic majority.
“What I’m looking to do with the majority on the commission is to work to lower folks’ power bills using clean energy and make sure that we’re holding data centers accountable,” Hubbard said at a debate organized by the Atlanta Press Club.
Edwards ran on being an advocate on the board for Georgians who are concerned about their power bills, saying that the PSC has acted too favorably toward Georgia Power in regulatory hearings. At the Atlanta Press Club debate, Edwards said that if she’s elected and Democrats get a majority, they “can turn the commission into a consumer-focused commission versus a utility-focused commission.”

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: Democrat fired by Trump administration narrowly leads in 1st District contest
description: South Carolina’s 1st Congressional District appears headed for an automatic recount with results that could mark a major victory for Democrats in a seat that was supposed to be safe for Republicans. With 98% of votes counted at midnight Tuesday, Democrat Nancy Lacore had a 0.7 percentage point lead over Republican Jenny Costa Honeycutt. Less […]
text:
Jenny Costa Honeycutt, left, and Nancy Lacore, right, won their runoff elections Tuesday, June 23, 2026. (Photos courtesy of Jenny Costa Honeycutt and Nancy Lacore)South Carolina’s 1st Congressional District appears headed for an automatic recount with results that could mark a major victory for Democrats in a seat that was supposed to be safe for Republicans.
With 98% of votes counted at midnight Tuesday, Democrat Nancy Lacore had a 0.7 percentage point lead over Republican Jenny Costa Honeycutt. Less than 2,400 votes separate the two, according to unofficial results. In South Carolina, results within a one-point margin require a recount.
If Lacore is declared the winner, it would make the second flip for South Carolina, following Democrat Annie Andrews winning the U.S. Senate seat.
In South Carolina’s other U.S. House districts, GOP incumbent Reps. Sheri Biggs in the 3rd District, William Timmons in the 4th District and Russell Fry in the 7th District won their re-election bids. And state Sen. Wes Climer, R-Rock Hill, will replace outgoing U.S. Rep. Ralph Norman in the 5th District.
As of midnight, The Associated Press also had yet to call a winner in the 2nd District, where GOP U.S. Rep. Joe Wilson led by 1.4 percentage points.
However, U.S. Rep. Jim Clyburn, who has been the only Democrat in South Carolina’s congressional delegation, sailed to another term in the 6th District.
Whether Lacore will join him on Capitol Hill has yet to be determined. It could mark the district’s third flip in eight years.
Republicans held control of it for nearly 40 years until Joe Cunningham flipped the district in 2018. Cunningham narrowly lost two years later to Republican U.S. Rep. Nancy Mace, who gave up the seat this year for an unsuccessful bid for governor.
Lacore’s lead is especially significant after legislators redrew the district to more heavily favor Republicans after the 2020 census. That map moved Democrat-heavy precincts into the 6th District, the only one in the state that votes reliably blue.
Proving the area’s GOP muster, Mace defeated Andrews, who won a statewide race Tuesday, by nearly 14 percentage points in 2022, then trounced her 2024 opponent by nearly 17 points.
Throughout this election cycle, polls showed the coastal district moving closer to the middle, until the nonpartisan Cook Political Report considered it a “toss-up” for Tuesday night. That turned out to be spot on.
Nationwide, voters have shown strong enthusiasm for Democrats.
Lacore and Honeycutt won their parties’ nominations in crowded primaries. Lacore defeated six other Democrats, and Honeycutt won out over nine other Republicans.
Lacore, a retired vice admiral and political newcomer, moved to South Carolina last year, after Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth removed her from her job as chief of the Navy Reserve with no reason given several months prior. That move, which came as part of a larger pattern of the Trump administration targeting perceived critics of the president, drew national interest and major donations.
As of Oct. 14, the end of the last reporting period, Lacore had raised more than $4.8 million, according to reports to the Federal Election Commission. Honeycutt, in comparison, had raised close to $1.3 million. Both spent nearly everything they had.
Honeycutt, a member of the Charleston County Council and a lifelong resident of the state, often criticized Lacore for not having spent long in the state.
Lacore pointed to her experience in government as qualification enough for Congress. She started her career as a Navy pilot, before joining the part-time reserve to raise her six children and work as a defense contractor. As head of the reserve, Lacore oversaw about 59,000 sailors and often worked with Congress for resources, including securing new airplanes, she previously said.
Honeycutt, a mother of three, runs a James Island law firm, where she specializes in representing construction companies, including resolving contract and payment disputes, as well as navigating government regulations. She worked as a clerk for then-Gov. Mark Sanford while attending law school at the University of South Carolina.
Both candidates’ campaigns focused on affordability, though they differed on the reasons for rising prices. While Honeycutt has said she wanted to cut government spending and reduce the national debt, Lacore pointed to President Donald Trump’s tariffs and the war in Iran as reasons for inflation.
Libertarian Bill Reeside was also on the ballot. Unofficial results show him with 1.6% of the vote.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Maybe we’re finally done hating on Connecticut
description: In 2018, I wrote a column called “Let’s Stop Hating on Connecticut.” It began with a colleague telling me he loved our state. I was so surprised that I asked, essentially, what was wrong with him. I had grown up here. Complaining about Connecticut was practically a local custom. We complained about the taxes, the […]
text:
In 2018, I wrote a column called “Let’s Stop Hating on Connecticut.” It began with a colleague telling me he loved our state. I was so surprised that I asked, essentially, what was wrong with him.
I had grown up here. Complaining about Connecticut was practically a local custom. We complained about the taxes, the roads, the weather, the cost of living. Then we complained that everybody else complained. My colleague, who wasn’t from here, couldn’t understand why people who lived somewhere beautiful seemed so determined to talk it down.
Nearly a decade later, I think he might have company.
I still hear the complaints. I make some of them myself. But I also meet more people who are proud to be here, and more people who have stopped waiting for someone else to fix what bothers them. New people are joining local boards and bringing new ideas with them. That matters in a state where so much of what affects our daily lives is decided by our towns. More people are starting businesses, too. According to CTData Collaborative, annual net business formations have climbed considerably since I wrote that first column.
Transit offers another example. Residents have spent years organizing and speaking up for better service. Now Connecticut has committed funding to increase Shore Line East service and is extending local transit pilots, including XtraMile. Those changes took people who cared enough to keep showing up.
That feels like a change.
It would be easy to call this a turnaround and credit one governor or one good budget. Connecticut doesn’t work that way. Governor Dannel Malloy took on long-neglected fiscal problems, including pension obligations and the structure of state government. Lawmakers from both parties adopted budget rules that helped the state save and pay down debt. Gov. Ned Lamont and the legislature have carried that discipline forward while making room for new investments.
The results are beginning to show up in everyday life. This school year, Connecticut began offering breakfast at no cost to public school students. The state has put more money toward education, including special education, and committed funding to improve transportation. We’re paying down obligations that earlier generations left behind while finding ways to serve the next one.
None of this means the state’s finances are permanently fixed. It means the hard choices of one decade can give us more choices in the next. That is what slow and steady is supposed to look like.
There are other reasons to appreciate where we live. We have had damaging storms, and climate change poses serious risks to our coastline. But as major disasters become more frequent elsewhere, Connecticut’s relative stability is something we appreciate more than we might have eight years ago. It gives us a good reason to protect the place we have.
The federal government feels less dependable, too. Connecticut cannot make up for every loss of federal support for critical services. But our state has stepped in to help protect residents when those services are threatened. It is reassuring to live somewhere whose people expect government to keep showing up.
And, yes, there is pizza. We have finally learned to say out loud that Connecticut is the pizza state. We should. We should also brag about the restaurants worth driving across the state for, the local farms supplying them, and the farmers markets that give our towns a reason to gather on a Saturday morning. Sometimes pride is simply telling a friend where to get a great pie.
Of course, there is one reliable way to identify a native Nutmegger: Say something nice about Connecticut and wait for the reply, “Yeah, but it’s so expensive.”
It is. Housing costs are shutting people out of communities they grew up in and making it harder for young families to put down roots. The state has begun to change its housing laws, but passing a law is only the start. We have to build homes people can afford, in communities across Connecticut. So many people want to live here; let’s make room for them.
Maybe some of this new affection comes from people who arrived from New York and Boston during the pandemic. Newcomers have always seemed quicker to notice what we take for granted. Perhaps they’ve helped us see it again. Or maybe we’re finally realizing that complaining is the easy part.
Back in 2018, I asked Connecticut residents to stop hating on our state and get involved. I hoped we could become the kind of people who love a place enough to improve it. I think more of us have.
Improving Connecticut takes work. It is also extremely rewarding. The work is far from finished, but for the first time in a long time, I’m hearing less about jumping ship and more about what we can build here. For the Land of Steady Habits, that’s real momentum.
Blaize Levitan lives in Guilford.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: What Louisiana’s 4 US House incumbents raised and spent to keep their seats
description: The four sitting members of Congress from Louisiana successfully fended off longshot challengers in Tuesday’s election
text:
U.S. House Majority Leader Steve Scalise raised more than $11 million and spent  
$12.4 million in his 2026 re-election campaign.
(Photo by Greg LaRose/Louisiana Illuminator)The four sitting members of Congress from Louisiana successfully fended off longshot challengers in Tuesday’s election, setting up the strong likelihood that the state will add a fifth Republican for its six U.S. House seats.
Yet House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-Benton, and Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-Jefferson, will have to cede control of their chamber after Democrats gained a majority of seats in the congressional midterm election.
The Associated Press declared wins for Johnson, Scalise, U.S Reps. Clay Higgins, R-Lafayette, and Troy Carter, D-New Orleans, with most of the votes counted Tuesday night. 
The two remaining U.S. House seats, the 5th and 6th districts, are expected to require runoffs in December.
The following campaign finance data from the Federal Elections Commission reflect contributions and spending in the 2025-26 election cycle as of mid-October. 
U.S. House Speaker Mike Johnson

Raised: $24.58 million
Spent: $19.32 million

Johnson scored a 4th Congressional District win over Democrats Conrad Cable of Farmerville and Matt Gromlich of Greenwood and Republicans Gordon Heslop of Natchitoches and Mike Nichols of Pitkin. He will keep the seat in Congress he has held since 2017. 
Cable was the top-funded candidate opposing Johnson, with more than $1.8 million collected. 
Grow the Majority, a political action committee Johnson started to back Republican candidates, has contributed more than $5 million to his own campaign. The Johnson Leadership Fund added another $1.85 million.
Almost $5.8 million of Johnson’s campaign spending has been with Convergence Media in Alexandria, Virginia, for digital advertising. He’s also given $1.4 million to the National Republican Congressional Committee, which disperses its funding to other GOP candidates. 
As House speaker, Johnson set a record this election cycle by raising more than $150 million for GOP congressional members and candidates. He said on Oct. 8 that his speaker’s super PAC was expected to add another $300 million toward Republican efforts to retain the GOP House majority. 
House Majority Leader Steve Scalise

Raised: $11.17 million 
Spent:  $12.39 million

Scalise, who took over the 1st Congressional District seat in 2008, won his race against Metairie Democrat Lauren Jewett, fellow Republican Randall Arrington of Ponchatoula and unaffiliated candidate Liddy Glass of Metairie. 
Scalise’s best-funded challenger, Jewett, raised $716,000. 
The Team Scalise PAC put $5.85 million in his campaign, and the Scalise Leadership Fund added almost $1.9 million. 
The largest single recipient of Scalise’s campaign spending was the National Republican Congressional Committee at $3.77 million. He also spent $1.85 million with the consulting firm Strategic Advance Services.
U.S. Rep. Clay Higgins, R-Lafayette

Raised: $904,294
Spent: $662,390

Higgins will hold on to the 3rd Congressional District seat he first won in 2016. He drew challenges from Democrats John Day of Lake Charles, Priscilla Gonzalez and Caleb Walker of Lafayette, Republican Kate Cotten of Lake Charles and no-party candidate Tia LeBrun of Sulphur. Day, the Louisiana Democratic Party’s endorsed candidate in the 3rd District, amassed the most of any of Higgins’ opponents with $222,000. Political action committees backing Higgins nearly matched that amount, putting $205,000 behind his re-election. 
The congressman’s PAC, the Higgins Victory Committee, put $486,000 into his campaign.
His largest single expenditure this cycle was a $40,000 donation to the National Republican Congressional Committee.
U.S. Rep. Troy Carter, D-New Orleans

Raised: $1.9 million
Spent: $1.82 million

Carter did not face opposition in the 2nd Congressional District within his own party, giving him an easy path to victory against Republican Peter Williams of Lettsworth, Libertarian Lisa Ballay of New Orleans and unaffiliated candidates Rocky Beach of Gonzales and Renata “Honey” Collins of New Orleans. 
None of his opponents reported significant campaign donations to the Federal Elections Commission.  
The Troy Carter Victory Fund was the largest single contributor to his campaign with two checks totaling just more than $40,000. Other than that money from his PAC, each of the remaining 1,174 contributions to Carter’s campaign over the two-year election cycle totaled $5,000 or less. Labor unions and corporate PACs made up the lion’s share of those donations.
The largest portion of Carter’s campaign spending — more than $309,000 — went to Angerholzer Broz Consulting, a Washington, D.C., firm that specializes in fundraising.  
The congressman also made two $50,000 donations to the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, a group dedicated to building a party majority in the legislative branch.

Several more Republican incumbents appeared in danger of losing their seats as vote-counting continued late Tuesday. This includes House Speaker Todd Huston, who was trailing his opponent Democrat Lauren Cole with 99% reporting.
Incumbent Democrats in uncalled races, meanwhile, had comfortable leads.
They scored big wins in the rapidly purpling suburbs north of Indianapolis, capitalizing on widespread discontent to surpass the four-seat margin required to break the two-thirds GOP hold on the chamber and wield greater influence.
Democratic challenger Tiffany Stoner thrashed Rep. Becky Cash, the Republican from Zionsville she’d lost to by just 64 votes two years ago. The margin was 59% to 41% as of 9:27 p.m., more than an hour after the AP’s 8:10 p.m. race call. House District 25 covers parts of Boone and Hendricks counties.
Next door, Democratic challenger Racheal Bleicher bested former Indianapolis Colts punter and Rep. Hunter Smith of Zionsville. She had 53% of the vote to the first-term represenative’s 47%, with 99% of ballots counted shortly after the AP’s 9:33 p.m. race call. House District 24 includes parts of Carmel, Sheridan, Westfield and Zionsville.
In Madison County, located northeast of Indianapolis, Democrat Kimberly Townsend garnered nearly 55% of the vote to the 45% posted by GOP Rep. Kyle Pierce of Anderson as of 11:02, when the race was called. The incumbent had represented House District 36 since 2022.
Directly west of Indianapolis, in Hendricks County, Democrat William Colteryahn easily defeated longtime Republican Rep. Greg Steuerwald, who has served in the House since 2007. Colteryahn had earned nearly 55% of the vote to Steuerwald’s 45% shortly after the race was called at 10:26 p.m.
Further south, Democrat Amy Huffman Oliver crushed Rep. Dave Hall, a Republican from Norman. She’d garnered 59% of the vote to his 41% as of 10:14 p.m., when the race was called. District 62 covers all of Brown County, plus bits of Monroe and Jackson counties.

text:
The door to the old Supreme Court Chamber at the Montana Capitol. (Micah Drew/Daily Montanan)At 9:45 p.m., nearly two hours after polls closed in Montana, the Secretary of State’s office showed 171,000 votes for Constitutional Initiative 132 — a measure to enshrine nonpartisan judicial races in the state constitution.
Preserving the nonpartisan judiciary led 69%-31% in the early results, one of the strongest leads of any Montana races this early.
Nonpartisan courts have been part of Montana’s judicial branch for nearly 100 years, but recently the state’s Republican Party has sought to change the system to allow for judges to run with partisan tags, saying it would help educate voters. 
Supporters of the nonpartisan judiciary — comprising existing judges, lawyers groups and a cross-partisan coalition of elected officials — say keeping politics out of one branch of government is essential for balancing out one-party majority rule. Currently, the top five “constitutional” officers in Montana, which includes the governor, attorney general and secretary of state, are Republican, as is the state’s entire Congressional delegation.

description: Missouri voters rejected Amendment 7 on Tuesday, turning down a proposal to create a state investment fund that supporters hoped could eventually generate enough money to eliminate state taxes. text:
(Iuri Gagarin/Getty Images).Missouri voters rejected Amendment 7 on Tuesday, turning down a proposal to create a state investment fund that supporters hoped could eventually generate enough money to eliminate state taxes.
The measure would have established the Show-Me Prosperity Fund, a permanent public endowment overseen by the state treasurer. Lawmakers could have invested state money in the fund, allowing earnings to compound over generations until they were sufficient to replace revenue from state taxes.
Unlike other high-profile ballot measures proposed by the General Assembly, Amendment 7 had no major funded campaign promoting its passage.
“There are no donors behind this. There is no think tank, no lobbyist that’s going to produce it. So there’s not going to be any money for it,” Republican state Sen. Adam Schnelting told The Independent in September. “It is one of those things where folks will have to do their due diligence and go online and look it up.”
Schnelting, a Republican from St. Charles who sponsored the legislation placing Amendment 7 on the ballot, said the idea was inspired by investment accounts he created for his children.
“When we do these calculations on the power of compounding, it is enormous,” he said. “So I just thought one day, why don’t we use the power of compound interest to ensure that we provide for future generations as far as our tax revenue is concerned?”
His legislative staff estimated that an initial investment of $250 million could grow large enough in 125 years to cover the state’s expenses, assuming sufficient investment returns over that period.
“We have to be willing to say, ‘This is not about me. This is not about you. It’s not even about our children. It’s about our grandchildren, our great grandchildren, our great grandchildren and Missourians going forward for hundreds of years,’” Schnelting said during Senate debate on the proposal. “It is about us creating a new model of how we fund government operations and getting away from the old model.”
Other states have similar funds, though they operate differently from Schnelting’s proposal.
Texas’ Permanent School Fund invests revenue from land sales and oil royalties to support public education. The Alaska Permanent Fund uses oil and mineral revenues to help pay for government services and distributes some of its earnings to residents through annual dividends.
Missouri’s proposal, by contrast, would have relied on money lawmakers chose to appropriate, along with donations and other contributions.
And while many states established sovereign wealth funds during periods of prosperity, Missouri lawmakers are facing declining revenues and mounting pressure to cut spending.
“We do not have a lot of general revenue that is going to be left on the bottom line this year, and even less next year,” state Sen. Maggie Nurrenbern, a Kansas City Democrat, said during Senate debate.
The measure received support from all but eight Republicans in the legislature, while Democrats opposed it.
Critics questioned whether Missouri could afford to set aside money for a fund that could not be used for state services until its investment earnings were sufficient to replace state tax revenue.
Under the proposal, the fund’s money would have been invested in exchange-traded funds tracking the S&P 500. Withdrawals would have been prohibited until the state treasurer determined that the earnings could replace state tax revenue and lawmakers approved that determination.
Schnelting acknowledged that Missouri’s financial circumstances could make an initial investment difficult. But he argued that lawmakers could find savings in the state budget to establish the fund, or simply leave the framework in place until the state’s finances improved.
“We could revisit it in a better time if that was required of us,” he said. “But I don’t foresee it being an issue actually funding the fund with an initial one-time investment. But again, that’s all based on whether or not the voters will approve Amendment 7 at the ballot box.”
