text:
Iowa Rep. Josh Turek, who is running for the U.S. Senate seat in 2026 against U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson, held a roundtable discussion Sep. 25, 2026 in Des Moines about rising fuel costs. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)Josh Turek defeated Republican Ashley Hinson in the U.S. Senate race Tuesday, the Associated Press has projected, becoming the first Democrat since former U.S. Sen. Tom Harkin was in office.
Unofficial results show Turek with nearly 51% of the vote and Hinson with 46% with 92% of Iowa’s precincts reporting.
Turek will join longtime U.S. Sen. Chuck Grassley, a Republican, in the Senate, filling the seat left by U.S. Sen. Joni Ernst, who chose not to seek a third term in office.
Though early political forecasts showed Hinson, a U.S. representative, having a strong lead in Iowa, the race gained more attention — and investment — as the election drew near. President Donald Trump rallied for Hinson and other GOP candidates in Iowa twice ahead of Election Day. According to an analysis by KCCI, the race was drawing roughly $4.6 million in political spending per day near the end of the election cycle.
Attacks against Hinson claimed that the Republican had enriched herself during her time in Washington, D.C. representing Iowa’s 2nd Congressional District, and criticized her public commitment and votes on banning members of Congress from stock trading while retaining private stock in an insurance company founded and sold by her husband. The candidate said she and her husband sold their publicly traded stocks after she first took office in 2021.
Many of opposition run against Turek, a state representative, focused on him missing votes during his time in the Iowa Legislature. An analysis of voting records, Turek missed 58% of Iowa House votes this year, but his campaign said he took 81% of votes since first taking office in 2023. While Turek has presented himself as a moderate, many ads also claimed he aligned closely with Democrats on issues relating to transgender youth and athletes, as well as immigration — claims Turek denied in his own ads.
Before serving in the Iowa House representing Council Bluffs, Turek was a two-time Paralympic gold medalist, winning in 2016 and 2020 as a member of the U.S. wheelchair basketball team. Turek, who was born with spina bifida, became the first permanently disabled member of the Iowa Legislature as he won election in 2022 by a margin of 6 votes after a recount.
Hinson has represented northeast Iowa in the U.S. House since her first victory in 2020. Before her time in federal office, she served as a state representative from 2017 to 2021, and was previously a news anchor for KCRG-TV. She has two sons and has presented herself as a “minivan-driving mom” on the campaign trail.
Thomas Laehn, a Libertarian currently serving as Greene County Attorney, was also on the ballot for the U.S. Senate seat. Laehn received just over 3% of votes in the race, according to preliminary results.

title: Republican Gov. Larry Rhoden wins four more years leading South Dakota
description: After a whirlwind three elections in five months, South Dakota Gov. Larry Rhoden has won his own four-year term. The Republican was leading Democratic challenger Dan Ahlers 64% to 36% on Tuesday when The Associated Press called the race at about 10:45 p.m. Central time with 52% of the votes counted statewide. Rhoden’s win caps […]
text:
South Dakota Gov. Larry Rhoden delivers his annual budget address to lawmakers at the Capitol in Pierre on Dec. 2, 2025. (Photo by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)After a whirlwind three elections in five months, South Dakota Gov. Larry Rhoden has won his own four-year term.
The Republican was leading Democratic challenger Dan Ahlers 64% to 36% on Tuesday when The Associated Press called the race at about 10:45 p.m. Central time with 52% of the votes counted statewide.
Rhoden’s win caps a political rise that began with his elevation from lieutenant governor when then-Gov. Kristi Noem resigned in January 2025. Noem joined President Donald Trump’s administration, leaving Rhoden to serve the final two years of her second term.
When Rhoden launched a campaign last November to keep the job, poll results showed him as an underdog to U.S. Rep. Dusty Johnson, who chose to run for governor instead of reelection to Congress.
Yet it was a political newcomer, Aberdeen businessman Toby Doeden, who swooped in to finish first in the June 2 Republican primary while spending $5 million of his own money on his campaign. Rhoden advanced to a top-two runoff by finishing second while Johnson fell to third, and state Speaker of the House Jon Hansen finished fourth.
Rhoden turned the tables on Doeden in the July 28 runoff, trouncing him by 42 points.
There was little suspense after that for Rhoden in a state where Republicans outnumber Democrats 2-to-1. Ahlers, a 52-year-old businessman and former legislator from Dell Rapids, struggled to gain a statewide foothold as his campaign’s minimal fundraising allowed him to spend only $164,000 by the Oct. 19 reporting deadline. Rhoden’s fundraising committee spent more than $3 million throughout the campaign.

South Dakota Democratic nominee for governor Dan Ahlers delivers his concession speech at a Democratic Party election results watch party in downtown Sioux Falls on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)

The defeat for Ahlers and his running mate, former legislator Steven McCleerey, extends a long losing streak for their party. The last time the state elected a Democratic governor was 52 years ago in 1974.
Rhoden is a 67-year-old rancher, custom welder and former legislator from rural Union Center who ran on his record from nearly two years as governor, including his work with legislators and his lieutenant governor, Tony Venhuizen, to sign several major bills into law.
Those include laws capturing revenue from sales tax increases to reduce homeowner property taxes, a law banning the use of a legal procedure known as eminent domain to gain land access for carbon capture pipelines, and a law funding construction of a $650 million replacement for the oldest parts of the state’s 145-year-old penitentiary.
“Good policy makes good politics,” Rhoden said while launching his campaign.
Rhoden could choose to run again four years from now for what would amount to a third term. Term limits in the state constitution say “no person shall be elected to more than two consecutive terms as governor,” but Rhoden served his first two years through the line of succession rather than direct election to the job.

description: Kentucky Democrats flipped a few seats in the statehouse Tuesday, though Republicans’ supermajority in the General Assembly was unchanged in this General Election.  Many races were left uncontested and the balance of power remained largely unchanged in the 100 House races and the 19 Senate races.   But there were some surprises. Tim Hall, a Louisville […]
text:
Kentucky's General Assembly will have plenty of races on Election Day on Nov. 3, 2026.  (Kentucky Lantern photo by Arden Barnes)Kentucky Democrats flipped a few seats in the statehouse Tuesday, though Republicans’ supermajority in the General Assembly was unchanged in this General Election. 
Many races were left uncontested and the balance of power remained largely unchanged in the 100 House races and the 19 Senate races.  
But there were some surprises.
Tim Hall, a Louisville Democrat, defeated Rep. Susan Witten, who has been in the statehouse since 2023. Witten notably sponsored the 2024 law that made animal torture a felony in Kentucky. Rep. Stephanie Dietz, R-Edgewood, was beaten by Democrat Aaron Currin.
And Sen. Lindsey Tichenor, part of the Liberty caucus, lost to Democrat Christian Furman.
As of 11:30 p.m., some high profile races weren’t yet called by the Associated Press:

The Secretary of State’s website showed Majority Whip Jason Nemes behind his Democratic challenger, Jennifer Hardin, by about 530 votes.
Sarah Cole McIntosh, a former Jefferson County Board of Education member and teacher, was about 2,000 votes ahead of incumbent Sen. Julie Raque Adams, R-Louisville.
Republican Tanner Hesterberg had a hefty lead over Democrat Johnny Ray Turner — about 3,000 votes. 
Democrat Suhas Kulkarni was up by about 800 votes in his bid to unseat Rep. Ken Fleming, R-Louisville.

Here are how some of the most-watched races played out: 
State House District 45: Incumbent Adam Moore versus Republican Killian Timoney 
In the 45th legislative district, incumbent Rep. Adam Moore, D-Lexington, defeated former Republican representative Killian Timoney, who held the purple district seat from 2021-2025. 
Timoney was previously defeated in the 2024 primary election by Liberty Republican candidate Thomas Jefferson. 
At that time, GOP voters criticised his vote against an anti-transgender law restricting medical treatment for youth and public schools. 
Timoney previously said his departure from the legislature felt “abrupt and it was premature.” 
Moore, who received an endorsement from Gov. Andy Beshear, ran on a platform focused on affordable health care, data center regulation and “strong public schools.” 
“I’m not someone who’s out there throwing bombs or trying to be a culture warrior, but just trying to actually, I think, restore faith in politics and government, and I think that’s been received very well,” Moore previously told the Lantern. 
State Senate District 6: Incumbent Lindsey Tichenor versus Democrat Christian Furman 
Democratic challenger Christian Furman ousted incumbent Sen. Lindsey Tichenor, R-Smithfield. 
Tichenor has notably worked on legislation to limit diversity, equity and inclusion initiatives in public schools and regulate “explicit” drag performances, among other issues. 
Furman, who was endorsed by Beshear, ran on a public safety and affordability platform. She previously told the Lantern she believed her experience as a doctor prepared her for the Senate. 
“I listen to the patient first of all. I listen to other doctors. I listen to their family,” Furman, a Prospect City Council member, said. “I collaborate with the whole healthcare team, and together we come up with a care plan, and that same skill set of being a doctor translates to being a senator.”

name: WyoFile
title: Voters send Chuck Gray to represent Wyoming in the US House
description:
Former state lawmaker from Casper who’s served as secretary of state since 2023 defeated Democrat Lisa Kinney.
The post Voters send Chuck Gray to represent Wyoming in the US House appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Wyoming voters on Tuesday elected Republican Chuck Gray to replace Harriet Hageman as the state’s lone congressman in the U.S. House of Representatives. 
Gray’s victory is the culmination of a 10-year rise from state lawmaker to secretary of state and now congressman-elect. He is an outspoken Trump supporter who advocated for a slew of changes to Wyoming’s election system that he said were needed for the system’s integrity, but his critics called them unnecessary and burdensome. 

Hageman was elected to an open U.S. Senate seat Tuesday, creating the House vacancy. Wyoming’s entire congressional delegation backed Gray, whose name was checked on 57% of ballots by the time the Associated Press called the race at 9:40 p.m. with 54% of the vote counted.

Democrat Lisa Kinney answers a question from the panel during a U.S. House debate on Thursday, Oct. 15, 2026, in Riverton. (Carl Cote/County 10)

Gray faced former state senator Democrat Lisa Kinney, Constitution Party candidate Jeffrey Haggit and Libertarian Shawn Johnson in Tuesday’s election. 
In Wyoming, where Republicans have been elected to Congress since 1976, when Teno Roncalio was reelected over Republican Larry Hart, many viewed the primary election as more pivotal than the general election in determining the state’s next congressman. 
Gray won that nine-person race in August, but there was never a crystal-clear frontrunner. He likely had the greatest name recognition, having held a statewide seat, secretary of state, for four years. The race was marked by big spending by candidates. There were several, the victor included, who spent seven figures on their candidacies.
Gray ultimately won with 25% of the vote — five points more than runner-up Steve Friess.
Rep. Chuck Gray, left, reads a bill during the 2017 general session. (Andrew Graham/WyoFile)
Gray has been seen as a firebrand in Wyoming politics. As secretary of state, he butted heads frequently with Gov. Mark Gordon. He was aligned with the Wyoming Freedom Caucus — a Republican faction that collapsed during the primary election — during his time as a state representative. 
Gray has fashioned himself as an acolyte of President Donald Trump. Although Trump didn’t endorse him during the primary election, he did so in advance of Tuesday’s general election, calling Wyoming’s incoming congressman a “true friend of MAGA.” 
“Chuck Gray has my Complete and Total Endorsement to be the next U.S. Representative from Wyoming — HE WILL NEVER LET YOU DOWN!,” the president’s Truth Social account posted.

title: Montana favoring initiative seeking to limit ‘dark money’
description: Montanans appeared on track to support an initiative seeking to limit political spending by corporations, nonprofits and other organizations in elections on Tuesday night. The vote received approval from 67% of voters in early returns, while 33% said no. About 128,000 ballots have been counted as of 9:30 p.m. Called “The Montana Plan,” the initiative […]
text:
A No Kings rally attendee holds a Transparent Election Initiative sign during a No Kings event on Saturday, Oct. 17, 2026 at the Montana State Capitol in Helena, MT. (Jordan Hansen / Daily Montanan)Montanans appeared on track to support an initiative seeking to limit political spending by corporations, nonprofits and other organizations in elections on Tuesday night.
The vote received approval from 67% of voters in early returns, while 33% said no. About 128,000 ballots have been counted as of 9:30 p.m.
Called “The Montana Plan,” the initiative is based upon the concept that corporations are regulated by states, and that Montana could limit corporate powers when it comes to contributing to elections, candidates and political parties. 
The plan grew out of frustrations about large sums of money flowing into political campaigns, as well as dissatisfaction with the “Citizens United” decision which equates campaign donations with political speech. That, in turn, affords it the highest protection by the First Amendment of the U.S. Constitution. That frustration reached a zenith during the 2024 election when the race between former U.S. Sen. Jon Tester, a Democrat was challenged by Tim Sheehy, a Republican. More than $250 million was dumped into that Senate race, even though the state only counts a little more than 1 million residents. 
There has been some opposition to the plan, including the Montana Chamber of Commerce and industrial interests such as the Montana Mining Association. The state Republican Party has also added opposition to it to its platform.
Those concerns stemmed from worries it would allow businesses to not be able to band together as easily, and that a wealthy individual with an agenda could buy an election.
Supporters of the initiative, however, said it leveled the playing field between large and small businesses. Hawai’i became the first state to pass similar legislation when its state lawmakers passed a measure to limit corporate spending in politics earlier this year.

name: WyoFile
title: Republicans sweep Wyoming’s statewide elected offices
description:
Robert Short will become the next secretary of state. Steve Harshman will serve as superintendent of public instruction.
The post Republicans sweep Wyoming’s statewide elected offices appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Republicans once again swept the field of Wyoming’s statewide elected offices in Tuesday’s general election. While two incumbents will remain in their current offices, newcomers will fill the secretary of state and state superintendent of public instruction posts in January. 
Short, who far outspent opponents, clinches secretary of state post
Republican Robert Short, a Converse County commissioner, will become Wyoming’s next secretary of state. He faced two opponents — former Republican state representative Tamara Trujillo, who ran as a Constitution Party candidate, and Worland Democrat Bryan McCarty.  
“I said I was going to be the short guy on the ballot, and apparently people actually remembered that,” Short, who is tall, said Tuesday night at a Casper election party hosted by Sen. Eric Barlow, who won the race to be Wyoming’s next governor. 
“I’m going to make the office boring again.”
Secretary of state candidate Robert Short talks at a watch party on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026, at the Wyo Sports Ranch in Casper. (Dan Cepeda for Oil City News and WyoFile)
In the Republican primary, Short spent nearly 10 times more than his competitors. Notable figures like former Wyoming Secretary of State Max Maxfield, former Wyoming GOP Chairman Diemer True and billionaire philanthropist Molly Hughes donated to Short’s campaign. Short beat out three Republican candidates, including Wyoming Freedom Caucus Chair Rep. Rachel Williams, in the primary election. 
The secretary of state oversees elections, registers businesses, records and maintains many state records and sits on various boards. The secretary is also the first in line for gubernatorial succession.
Current Secretary of State Chuck Gray didn’t run for reelection, choosing instead to seek Wyoming’s lone U.S. House seat. 
Longtime educator and lawmaker will be next state superintendent
Steve Harshman, a Casper Republican and educator who has served in the Legislature since 2003, clinched the vote to become Wyoming’s next State Superintendent of Public Instruction. He faced Democrat Ana Cordova. 
State superintendent candidate Steve Harshman is emotional while speaking at a watch party on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026, at the Wyo Sports Ranch in Casper. (Dan Cepeda for Oil City News and WyoFile)
Harshman has decades of experience as a high school history and physical education teacher, and more than 40 years as a football, wrestling and track coach. As state superintendent, Harshman will lead the Wyoming Department of Education. 
At Barlow’s Tuesday night election party in Casper, Harshman described a moment on the campaign trail when he and his wife, Becky, were driving back to Casper from Shoshoni one evening as the sun set. 
“She goes, ‘You know, this campaign has really kind of renewed my faith in our state and our country.’ And I just thought, you know, there’s so much noise out there,” Harshman said. “But when you actually talk to Wyoming people, it was just so refreshing. People are so good, so generous in this state. And so it was really a blessing to run for this office, so I appreciate that.”



Harshman said he traveled to all 48 school districts, putting 16,000 miles on his car in the process.
The current superintendent, Megan Degenfelder, ran for governor but lost to Barlow in the August Republican primary.  
Incumbents take treasurer and auditor
Republicans Curt Meier and Kristi Racines, Wyoming’s current state treasurer and state auditor, respectively, will both serve another four years. They were unopposed in the general election. 
Meier served 23 years in the Wyoming Senate before running for treasurer in 2018. He beat Lingle Rep. Scott Smith, a Wyoming Freedom Caucus member, in the Republican primary election. As treasurer, Meier has played a key role in making investment returns Wyoming’s top source of revenue. 
“We want to bring professionalism back all the way into our office and have professionals, not politicians, make the decisions that we have with oversight and guidance,” Meier said Tuesday night at Barlow’s election party.
The state auditor acts as the state’s head of accounting. First elected auditor in 2018, Racines debuted a website — WyOpen.gov — that provides state expenditure data to the public. The website was enshrined into law in 2025. Racines thanked the people gathered at Barlow’s election night party for their “support, for caring, for believing in Wyoming, for believing in a process that is messy, sometimes gross, sometimes unpleasant, but you cared enough to do it.” 
WyoFile reporter Maggie Mullen contributed to this story.

title: Bayh puts Indiana Democrats back in winning column with secretary of state victory
description: A new generation of the Bayh family is a winner again for Indiana Democrats. Beau Bayh prevailed in the secretary of state’s race with about 51.4% of the vote in Tuesday night’s vote tallies over Republican candidate Max Engling’s 43%. About 90% of the vote had been counted statewide. “Today, Hoosiers voted for change,” Bayh […]
text:
Democrat Beau Bayh celebrates his upset victory for secretary of state on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Tom Davies/Indiana Capital Chronicle)A new generation of the Bayh family is a winner again for Indiana Democrats.
Beau Bayh prevailed in the secretary of state’s race with about 51.4% of the vote in Tuesday night’s vote tallies over Republican candidate Max Engling’s 43%. About 90% of the vote had been counted statewide.
“Today, Hoosiers voted for change,” Bayh told a jubilant crowd of Democrats in Indianapolis. “For too long, the people of our state have been taken for granted. Too many decisions have been made behind closed doors by insiders. Too many families have played by the rules, while the people in the halls of power have played by a different set.”
The victory by the 30-year-old attorney and Marine Corps veteran is the first statewide win for a Democratic candidate since the 2012 election. 
Bayh’s success makes him the standard bearer among Indiana Democrats, following in the footsteps of his father, former governor and U.S. Sen. Evan Bayh, and late grandfather, U.S. Sen. Birch Bayh.
“Tonight, we said enough is enough. I did not run to join that system. I ran to fight against it. I’m not here to answer to party bosses, big donors, or the state house insiders. I’m here to answer to you. Hoosiers work hard for their money, and they deserve to know how every dollar is spent,” Bayh said.

Former Republican Indianapolis Mayor Greg Ballard, running under the Lincoln Party banner, received 3.6% of the vote — giving the new party enough support to clinch four-year automatic ballot status for its nominees in what was a goal to help what he called “independent-minded candidates.”
Libertarian Lauri Shillings pulled in 2% to maintain the party’s ballot status that it has held since the 1994 election.
Engling spoke to a subdued crowd at the Republican event.
“The voters have made their decision, and it’s not what we wanted. It’s not what we’re pushing for, but we fully respect that decision,” he said.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Democrat Fred Wellman ousts Republican Ann Wagner in Missouri congressional upset
description: Republican lawmakers redrew Missouri’s 2nd Congressional District to make U.S. Rep. Ann Wagner’s seat safer. On Tuesday, Democrat Fred Wellman won it anyway. Wellman, a retired military officer, was outspent by Wagner and her Republican allies. But he outraised her in the crucial final months of the campaign, making increasingly large ad buys as the […]
text:
Democrat Fred Wellman, who defeated U.S. Rep. Ann Wagner, a seven-term Republican, to flip the 2nd Congressional District (photo submitted).Republican lawmakers redrew Missouri’s 2nd Congressional District to make U.S. Rep. Ann Wagner’s seat safer. On Tuesday, Democrat Fred Wellman won it anyway.
Wellman, a retired military officer, was outspent by Wagner and her Republican allies. But he outraised her in the crucial final months of the campaign, making increasingly large ad buys as the election approached.
Wellman won his victory in St. Louis County, where he defeated Wagner by 14%. That was enough to cover Wagner’s majorities in Franklin, Warren and St. Charles counties, where Wellman cut deeply into Wagner’s margins from 2024.
In St. Charles County, where Wagner won by 16,000 votes in 2024, Wellman narrowed the margin to 4,000 votes. Overall, Wellman took 51.4% of the vote.
With the victory, Missouri will send a delegation of five Republicans and three Democrats to Washington in January. The loss compounds the GOP’s defeat in an effort to redraw district boundaries to flip the 5th District, a map change that would have put more rural Republican voters in Wagner’s district.
The 2nd District is the only one in Missouri that was listed at the start of 2025 as less than solidly safe for the incumbent party. Wagner won re-election in 2022 and 2024 with about 55% of the vote while other incumbents were winning with 60% or more.
In the two elections prior to redistricting for the 2020 census, Wagner had won with just 51% of the vote.
Wagner spent nearly $6 million defending her seat, including nearly $1.5 million on broadcast ads. Wagner’s allies from the Congressional Leadership Fund purchased $628,500 of broadcast ads attacking Wellmann and Protect our Family Values Action spent $220,000 backing Wagner.
Wellman raised $2.2 million and spent almost $500,000 on broadcast ads. He had independent support from VoteVets, which spent more than $500,000 in the district.
In Missouri’s other seven districts, voters retained the incumbent party. 
In northern Missouri’s 6th District, Republican nominee Chris Stigall will replace U.S. Rep. Sam Graves, a Tarkio Republican retiring after 26 years in Congress. Stigall defeated Democratic opponent Josh Smead and LIbertarian Andy Maidment, taking 66% of the vote
In the six districts with incumbents seeking re-election, the results are:

U.S. Rep. Wesley Bell, a St. Louis Democrat, easily won reelection in the 1st District, covering St. Louis and part of St. Louis County. He defeated Paul Berry III, a Republican who never formed a campaign committee, with 82% of the vote.
U.S. Rep. Bob Onder of Lake Saint Louis won his second term in the 3rd District, which runs from Central Missouri to St. Charles and Jefferson Counties. His margin narrowed in a  rematch of the 2024 contest against Democrat Bethany Mann of Saint Peters. Onder took 56% of the vote, compared to 61% in 2024.
U.S. Rep. Mark Alford of Kansas City won his third term in the 4th District, which runs west from Central Missouri to the Kansas border and includes Whiteman Air Force Base and Fort Leonard Wood. Alford defeated Democratic nominee Jordan Herrera of Kansas City and Libertarian Thomas Holbrook of Warrensburg. Alford took 64% of the vote, down from his 71% share in 2024.
U.S. Rep. Emanuel Cleaver will become the senior member of the Missouri delegation with his easy re-election in the 5th District in Jackson and Clay counties. The Kansas City Democrat filed for re-election when it was uncertain whether he would have to run in a district drawn to elect a Republican. State Sen. Rick Brattin, who won the GOP nomination for the gerrymandered district, put up only a token effort in the district used on Tuesday as Cleaver took 69% of the vote, up more than 8 percentage points from 2024.
The 7th District in southwest Missouri returned U.S. Rep. Eric Burlison, a Springfield Republican, to Washington for his third term. Burlison easily won a rematch with Democratic candidate Missi Hesketh of Forsyth, taking 69%
The 8th District of Southeast Missouri was again won by U.S. Rep. Jason Smith, who defeated Chris Reichard, taking 68% of the vote.

title: Republican McGowan claims in Iowa’s 4thCongressional District seat, AP projects
description: Republican Chris McGowan has won the race to represent Iowa’s 4th Congressional District against Democrat Dave Dawson, the Associated Press has projected.  Dawson will take the place of U.S. Rep. Randy Feenstra, who did not run for reelection due to an attempted run for governor. While the district has been redrawn several times during the […]
text:
Chris McGowan, the Republican running for Iowa's 4th Congressional District in 2026, spoke before Vice President JD Vance at a rally in Council Bluffs Sep. 18, 2026. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)Republican Chris McGowan has won the race to represent Iowa’s 4th Congressional District against Democrat Dave Dawson, the Associated Press has projected. 
Dawson will take the place of U.S. Rep. Randy Feenstra, who did not run for reelection due to an attempted run for governor. While the district has been redrawn several times during the period, the northwest Iowa region has solidly elected Republicans since the late 1990s. 
McGowan had nearly 60% of the vote to 42% for Dawson, with 78% of precincts reporting, according to unofficial figures from the AP. 
McGowan is a veteran and currently serves as president of the Siouxland Chamber of Commerce. Dawson served as a state representative from 2013-2017 and was previously a prosecutor at the Woodbury County Attorney’s Office. 
The candidates have differed on policies around the war in Iran, with McGowan saying he’d need more information to decide if it was a conflict the U.S. should remain involved in, and Dawson calling for the U.S. to end the conflict. 
McGowan has suggested the U.S. complete the Keystone XL pipeline, which has been delayed over environmental concerns, to help lower fuel costs in the country. 
Both candidates said they would support nationwide, year-round access to E15 fuels and completing a farm bill. 
Dawson’s top priorities included expanding healthcare options, investing in rural communities and raising incomes in Iowa.
McGowan, who has children serving in the military, has emphasized his commitment to national security and on securing the U.S. borders. McGowan, who lives on a small farm in Plymouth County according to his campaign website, has also said he would be a “reliable ally and advocate” for farmers.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Preliminary results: Utah’s 3 Republican incumbents lead in bids to return to U.S. House
description: Republican incumbents running to represent Utah’s three right-leaning congressional districts took the lead Tuesday just after the polls closed, according to initial results.
text:
People line up outside a polling location at the Main Library in Salt Lake City on Election Day, Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)Republican incumbents running to represent Utah’s three right-leaning congressional districts took the lead Tuesday just after the polls closed, according to initial results. 
Under a court-ordered redraw of the state’s congressional map, all three representatives — Blake Moore, Mike Kennedy and Celeste Maloy — are vying for different seats in the U.S. House than they’re currently representing. 
The new Utah boundaries are the culmination of a yearslong legal battle over redistricting in the state. They’ve also carved out a safe blue district centered in Salt Lake County, with Democrats expected to send a candidate to Congress for the first time in years. 
Nationally, forecasters said Democrats were on track to win control of the U.S. House and possibly the Senate as voters have grown frustrated with rising costs, States Newsroom reported.
In the race for northern Utah’s 2nd Congressional District, Moore led Democratic challenger Peter Crosby 50 % to 44% in a race where issues of the proposed Stratos data center and the drying Great Salt Lake factored large.  
Moore, who holds a leadership position as vice chair of the House Republican Conference, was the lone member of Utah’s House delegation to back former Wyoming Rep. Liz Cheney when she broke with Trump and condemned the Jan. 6 attack on the U.S. Capitol. 
Pointing to September polling commissioned by the Utah Debate Commission, the Utah Democratic Party has said Crosby is  “within striking distance” — five points — behind Moore. 
In response, Moore said last month he’s confident in his campaign, although he acknowledged third-party candidates and undecided voters can create some wild cards in polling. 
Hannah Petzinger uses Lauren Pierce’s back as a writing surface as she fills out a registration form at a polling location at the Main Library in Salt Lake City on Election Day, Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)
In the contest for the sprawling 3rd District covering more than half the state, Maloy pulled ahead of Democratic nominee Kent Udell with 59% to Udell’s 35%.
Maloy, an attorney and former congressional staffer, has pitched herself as a problem-solver and touted her role as chair of the large Congressional Western Caucus as she seeks a second full term in the House. 
And while Maloy supported Trump’s orders slashing Grand Staircase-Escalante and Bears Ears national monuments in Utah, Udell has condemned those decisions. He’s also called for more study of nuclear energy’s promise as he’s made his case to voters. 
In his bid for a second term in the U.S. House, freshman Kennedy led Democrat Jonny Larsen 53% to 41% for the 4th District. 
Kennedy has said he’s “just getting started making Washington smaller and Utah stronger” during his first term in the House, while Larsen cast himself as a moderate Democrat focused on issues of fiscal responsibility and national security.
Each of the three incumbents received a fresh show of support from President Donald Trump a day earlier on social media as Trump sought to give a boost to Republicans across the country in the final hours of their campaigns. 
In the post on X Monday, Trump encouraged Utahns to “GET OUT AND VOTE for these Great Patriots! They have my Complete and Total Endorsement and will never let you down!”
Left off of Trump’s Utah endorsements was Riley Owen, the moderate Republican and former White House staffer from his first term going up against former Democratic Rep. Ben McAdams in the new 1st District.

text:
Rep. Jeff Hurd, left, and Democratic challenger Dwayne Romero, right. (Photos by Lindsey Toomer, left, and Chase Woodruff, right/Colorado Newsline)Republican U.S. Rep. Jeff Hurd of Grand Junction and his Democratic challenger, Dwayne Romero, were in a close race Tuesday night, with Romero holding a narrow lead as county clerks across Colorado’s sprawling 3rd Congressional District continued to process ballot returns.
As of 9 p.m., Romero led by fewer than 6,000 votes, with 49.7% of the vote to Hurd’s 47.4%.
The 3rd District is Colorado’s largest congressional district by area, stretching from the greater Pueblo area across the San Luis Valley and much of the Western Slope.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Romero would be the first Democrat elected to represent the 3rd District since former Rep. John Salazar of the San Luis Valley, who served three terms before losing reelection in 2010.
In 2023, Hurd, an attorney, was recruited to run for Congress in a primary challenge against Rep. Lauren Boebert, a controversial far-right Republican who had come within 600 votes of losing the 3rd District to Democratic challenger Adam Frisch a year earlier. Months later, Boebert moved across the state to run in the more heavily Republican 4th District instead. Hurd went on to win the 3rd District GOP primary, and defeated Frisch in the 2024 general election by 5 percentage points.
Romero, an Army veteran and small business owner, launched his campaign relatively late in the 2026 election cycle, and won a head-to-head primary over financial executive Alex Kelloff.
As polls showed midterm voters turning against President Donald Trump and Republicans over the cost of living, the war in Iran and other issues, Hurd billed himself as a “voice of independence,” highlighting disagreements with Trump over his denial of disaster aid and a February vote against some of the president’s tariffs. That vote led Trump to briefly pull his endorsement from Hurd and back a primary challenger, before he reversed himself a month later and endorsed Hurd again.
To Democrats, Hurd’s occasional breaks with Trump meant little compared to his votes in favor of Republicans’ 2025 tax and spending law, which included steep cuts to Medicaid, food assistance and other social programs, along with the Iran war and most of the rest of Trump’s domestic and foreign policy agenda.
Until late October, Hurd and his supporters, including several deep-pocketed Republican super PACs, had massively outspent Romero and Democratic campaign groups in the 3rd District race. But Romero benefited from a late infusion of $2.5 million in outside spending on his behalf by the House Majority Project, the main Democratic House super PAC, beginning in the final week of October.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Democrat Betsy Fogle flips Missouri Senate seat Republicans held for more than 80 years
description: Democratic state Rep. Betsy Fogle defeated Republican state Rep. Melanie Stinnett on Tuesday, flipping a Springfield-based Missouri Senate seat that Republicans have held for more than 80 years. The Democratic win in Springfield, along with state Rep. Keri Ingle’s win in a Jackson County race, means Democrats have broken the GOP supermajority in the Missouri[...]
text:
State Rep. Betsy Fogle, D-Springfield, speaks on the Missouri House floor April 23 (Tim Bommel/Missouri House Communications).Democratic state Rep. Betsy Fogle defeated Republican state Rep. Melanie Stinnett on Tuesday, flipping a Springfield-based Missouri Senate seat that Republicans have held for more than 80 years.
The Democratic win in Springfield, along with state Rep. Keri Ingle’s win in a Jackson County race, means Democrats have broken the GOP supermajority in the Missouri Senate.
Fogle will succeed term-limited Republican state Sen. Lincoln Hough in the 30th District, which lies almost entirely within Springfield. Libertarian Cecil Ince was also on the ballot.
The victory marks a significant breakthrough for Missouri Democrats, who targeted the district as one of their best opportunities to chip away at Republican control of the state Senate.
The race drew millions of dollars in campaign contributions and spending as both parties fought for the seat. By the final week of the campaign, Fogle and Stinnett had each raised nearly $1.5 million between their campaign committees and supporting political action committees.
The contest was closely watched in part because of signs of voter dissatisfaction with Republican-backed policies.
In August, more than 80% of Greene County voters rejected two constitutional amendments proposed by Republican lawmakers. One would have made it harder for citizens to change the state constitution, while the other would have allowed lawmakers to expand sales taxes as part of a plan to eliminate the state income tax.
Fogle opposed both proposals, while Stinnett voted to place them on the ballot.
Their differences became a central issue in the campaign, with organizations supporting Fogle criticizing Stinnett for backing efforts to overturn voter-approved policies.
Stinnett voted for legislation repealing a paid sick leave law approved by voters in 2024 and for a proposed constitutional amendment that would restore Missouri’s abortion ban.
Melanie Stinnett and Betsy Fogle square off in competitive Missouri Senate race in Springfield

Fogle, meanwhile, emphasized her support for the initiative petition process and for protecting state services as Missouri faces difficult budget decisions.
She told The Independent before the election that she would welcome a shift of power from elected officials back to voters.
Both candidates entered politics after careers in health care, and both made improving services for people with disabilities a priority.
Fogle began her career at Jordan Valley Community Health Center, where she helped low-income patients navigate government programs and find access to medical care, transportation, child care and other services.
She has described that experience as formative to her political career, particularly witnessing the consequences when patients could not obtain the services they needed.
Fogle was first elected to the Missouri House in 2020 and has served on the House Budget Committee since 2021. She was the committee’s ranking Democrat in 2025 and 2026.
Her work on the budget has included helping restore $80.7 million in cuts proposed by Gov. Mike Kehoe to Medicaid services that allow people with disabilities to remain in their homes and communities.
Stinnett also worked to restore that funding, though the two lawmakers often differed over broader budget priorities.
Fogle has warned that declining state revenues could put Medicaid and public education at risk in the coming legislative sessions. She has linked those financial pressures to Republican efforts to reduce state taxes.
“You have to have dollars to pay your bills,” she told The Independent.
Stinnett, a speech-language pathologist who chairs the House Health and Mental Health Committee, emphasized her work expanding access to health care and services for people with disabilities.
She helped advocate for a 2019 law expanding insurance coverage for children with developmental or physical disabilities and worked on legislation in 2023 expanding Medicaid eligibility for employed people with disabilities.
The race also attracted spending from interests outside Springfield.
Legio XIII PAC, established by an Illinois-based company seeking to legalize video lottery terminals in Missouri, purchased radio advertisements opposing Fogle. Other political action committees and party organizations poured money into the contest.
Fogle’s victory ends a long Republican winning streak in the district.
Hough won reelection in 2022 with nearly 58% of the vote. Four years earlier, he defeated Democrat Charlie Norr with about 53% of the vote.
The district’s increasingly competitive elections made it an attractive target for Democrats, though the party still faced the challenge of winning over voters who have consistently elected Republicans to the Senate.
Fogle will enter the Senate as lawmakers face declining revenues, difficult budget choices and debates over funding for schools, health care and other state services.
Her victory gives Democrats another seat in a chamber long dominated by Republicans, but her ability to advance legislation will depend in part on working with members of the majority party.
Fogle has pointed to her years on the House Budget Committee as evidence that lawmakers from both parties can work together to protect programs they consider essential.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: State Question 847, which sought to limit property tax growth, fails Oklahoma general election vote
description: OKLAHOMA CITY — Oklahoma voters on Tuesday rejected a state question that would have limited increases in property taxes. State Question 847 proposed a 1.75% cap on yearly growth in the taxable assessed value of a homestead or agricultural property. Other properties’ value could be assessed at no more than 4% more than the year […]
text:
Voters fill out ballots for the midterm election at the Millwood Field House on Tuesday in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Emma Murphy/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY — Oklahoma voters on Tuesday rejected a state question that would have limited increases in property taxes.
State Question 847 proposed a 1.75% cap on yearly growth in the taxable assessed value of a homestead or agricultural property. Other properties’ value could be assessed at no more than 4% more than the year before. This would have slowed how much property owners’ taxes increased over time.
Similar limits on property value growth, ranging from 0.35% to 1.75%, would have applied to Oklahomans over age 65 who earn too much income to qualify for a “senior freeze” that halts property tax increases.
The state Legislature put SQ 847 on the ballot to offer some amount of relief from rising costs, particularly for homeowners also struggling with skyrocketing home insurance premiums.
Critics have said the state question would deal a blow to funding for school districts and other public services without offering a way to replace the lost money.
The Oklahoma Tax Commission estimated local tax jurisdictions would have lost $45.78 million in expected property tax revenue over the first year had SQ 847 passed.
House Speaker Kyle Hilbert, R-Bristow, said concerns about the cost of property taxes were “very loud at the state Capitol” this year.
The state currently allows homesteads and agricultural land to increase by no more than 3% in assessed value per year and other properties to grow in valuation by no more than 5% annually. State lawmakers proposed the ballot measure to let voters choose whether they wanted to lower those caps.
“It looks like the voters of Oklahoma tonight said no,” Hilbert said at a GOP election watch party in Oklahoma City on Tuesday night. “They don’t want to see changes to property taxes, and so moving forward, we’ll take that into consideration.”

text:
Troy Downing smiles during a political rally featuring President Donald Trump in Bozeman on Aug. 9, 2024. Downing won re-election on Nov. 3, 2026 (Photo by Blair Miller, Daily Montanan).U.S. Representative Troy Downing cruised to victory on Tuesday night in a race to retain his seat, and the Republican will be elected to his second term in Congress.
“Congressman Troy Downing is grateful to the people of Montana’s Second Congressional District for placing their trust in him for another term,” Keegan Bittner, a Downing spokesperson wrote in a statement. “Tonight’s victory reflects the hard work of our team and the support of Montanans across the district.”
The Associated Press called the race at 9:18 p.m. Downing led from the start and was heavily favored to win.
Downing took 53% of the vote in early returns, well ahead of Democrat Brian Miller’s 37%, Independent Michael Eisenhauer’s 9%, and Libertarian Patrick McCracken’s 2%. Miller and Eisenhauer did not immediately return comments, either.
Downing, a veteran, won by more than 30 points in the 2024 election. Prior to his terms in Congress, Downing was the state auditor.
He campaigned on lowering taxes and reducing government regulation. Downing raised about $2.7 million during the election, far more than Eisenhauer’s $348,000. Miller raised less than $50,000.
Downing was endorsed by President Donald Trump and unopposed in the Republican primary.
“The Congressman is proud of what he accomplished during his first term and looks forward to continuing his work on behalf of Montana’s families and communities,” Bittner wrote. “He remains committed to delivering results and ensuring central & eastern Montana have a strong voice in Washington.”

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: Former ag adviser to the governor elected SC’s next commissioner
description: Cody Simpson, who had the president's endorsement before announcing his candidacy, was elected to lead agriculture department.
text:
Democrat DeShawn Blanding (left) and Republican Cody Simpson (right) ran to be South Carolina's next agriculture commissioner. (Photos courtesy of the Blanding and Simpson campaigns)COLUMBIA — President Donald Trump’s pick for agriculture commissioner won election Tuesday.
Cody Simpson, a fifth-generation farmer who advised the governor on agricultural issues, won with about 52% of the vote. He defeated Democrat DeShawn Blanding, with 46%, according to unofficial results from the state Election Commission.
“I want to thank you on a very personal note from Home Branch, South Carolina, my family’s farm, where we’ve been farming since 1904,” Simpson told supporters at the GOP election night party at the State Fairgrounds.
“We have now shown the entire world that the American dream is alive and well,” he said. “South Carolina state is strong, and I am so grateful for the unity that we have in this room. We are so proud. I could not be more proud being a South Carolinian than I am right now.”
Also on the ballot were Libertarian Michael Sullens of Anderson and Chris Nelums of Columbia, who ran in the United Citizens Party.
Simpson will be the first new commissioner of agriculture in the state in 22 years. Longtime Commissioner Hugh Weathers, also a Republican, decided to retire this year.
Under the commissioner’s leadership, the Department of Agriculture is responsible for promoting agribusiness, keeping the food supply safe and inspecting all places that sell food, including restaurants and cafeterias.
The commissioner of agriculture is also the state’s topmost advocate for farms, which number more than 22,600 statewide. Agribusiness, which includes agriculture and forestry, remains the state’s top industry, with more than 260,000 jobs, according to the agency.
Simpson grew up in a single-wide trailer outside Manning, on the row crop farm his family has owned and operated since 1904. A longtime supporter of Gov. Henry McMaster, he joined the governor’s office in 2018 and stayed there until 2025, when the Trump administration appointed him as the U.S. Department of Agriculture Farm Service Agency’s executive director for South Carolina.
Simpson preferred to call himself “President Trump’s farmer in South Carolina.”
He left that position in February to run for office, following surprise preliminary endorsements from both McMaster and Trump. He won a four-way primary contest following a runoff vote.
Blanding ran unopposed for the Democratic nomination. He was the first Democrat to seek the office in 16 years.
As agriculture commissioner, Simpson has said he wants to put licensing and permitting systems online, create an office dedicated to disaster preparedness and recovery, and help farmers get USDA certifications that allow them to sell their products in more markets.
Blanding also hails from rural Clarendon County.
Originally from Manning, Blanding spent a stint in Washington, D.C., working for the agriculture committees in both the U.S. House and U.S. Senate. He also worked for two nonprofits, the Union of Concerned Scientists and the Rural Coalition.
In 2024, Blanding moved back to South Carolina to care for his family and restart his family’s former farm, which his parents sold after his grandfather’s death in the 1990s. He also founded consulting firm AgQuity Solutions.
Blanding had hoped to use the position as commissioner of agriculture to help historically disadvantaged farmers, including Black farmers and those with small farms.
Reporter Katharine Wilson contributed to this report.

text:
U.S. Rep. Tony Wied (R-De Pere) represents the 8th District covering Northeast Wisconsin. (Official U.S. House photo)Republican U.S. Rep. Tony Wied defeated his Democratic challenger, former Green Bay school board member and U.S. Army veteran Rick Crosson in Wisconsin’s 8th Congressional District. AP called the race at 10:01 p.m. with 72% of the vote counted. Wied won by a margin of 55.3% to 44.7% 
The Green Bay area district has been under Republican control since 2011, and this year it received less attention and investment from the national parties than Wisconsin’s more competitive 1st and 3rd CDs.
Two years ago, the seat was open after U.S. Rep. Mike Gallagher left Congress. Democrats put significant resources into the campaign of Dr. Kristin Lyerly, an OB-GYN and an outspoken proponent of abortion rights. Lyerly lost to Wied by 15 points.
Wied, the former owner of gas stations in the Green Bay area, presented himself during his reelection campaign as a good-tempered representative who has worked to improve the lives of people in northeast Wisconsin through his constituent services. He has also been a reliable supporter of  President Donald Trump’s agenda in the House of Representatives. 
Wied acknowledged in an Oct. 22 debate that gas and diesel prices have risen because of the war Trump started in Iran, but said that “decisive action” in Iran was needed. He also defended his vote in favor of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which cut billions in federal healthcare spending. He argued that the Affordable Care Act is responsible for pushing up medical costs and that he and other Republicans fought to bring federal money to rural hospitals. (The money sent to fund Wisconsin’s rural hospitals, but it’s far less than the shortfall they will face because of  the broader cuts to Medicare and Medicaid.)
As a member of the House Agriculture committee, Wied pointed to his work to get schools serving whole milk again and the passage of a 2026 farm bill by the House of Representatives as actions that he’s taken to help area farmers. 
Crosson accused Wied during the debate of avoiding his constituents by not holding any in-person town halls since he was elected. Wied responded that holding telephone town halls has helped him reach more constituents. He also said that holding town halls in person brings out a “left-wing mob.”

description: Incumbent mayors in Kentucky’s two biggest cities won their reelection bids in Tuesday’s General Election.  Louisville Mayor Craig Greenberg and Lexington Mayor Linda Gorton will both continue in their roles after nonpartisan elections.  As of 10:30 p.m. Greenberg received more than 130,670 votes and had claimed victory; Gorton received more than 56,000. In [...]
text:
Louisville Mayor Craig Greenberg won his bid for reelection. Nov. 3, 2026. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Sarah Ladd) Incumbent mayors in Kentucky’s two biggest cities won their reelection bids in Tuesday’s General Election. 
Louisville Mayor Craig Greenberg and Lexington Mayor Linda Gorton will both continue in their roles after nonpartisan elections. 
As of 10:30 p.m. Greenberg received more than 130,670 votes and had claimed victory; Gorton received more than 56,000.
Louisville 
In Louisville, Greenberg defeated Shameka Parrish-Wright, who received more than 37,000 votes in the primary. Greenberg won nearly 75,000 votes in the primary, putting the two face to face in the nonpartisan general election. In the General Election, Parrish-Wright received more than 96,000 votes. 
Parrish-Wright, a Louisville Metro councilwoman, ran on a platform that emphasized accessible housing, public restrooms, an audit of the city’s compliance with the Americans with Disabilities Act and more. 
Greenberg, who had Gov. Andy Beshear’s backing, ran on his first-term record, and said he wanted to make “early childhood education a reality for all 3 and 4 years olds in Louisville.” 
Recently, Greenberg faced criticism from opponents of data centers who have said the city needs to ban all data center construction. During a September debate between Greenberg and Parrish-Wright, the two also disagreed on police funding: Greenberg said the Louisville Metro Police Department “should have the best officers, and they should be the best paid.” Parrish-Wright said she wants to “level off the funding to make sure we do a forensic audit of LMPD and this previous administration’s spending of the budget.” 
In his Tuesday night victory speech, Greenberg said he had a lot left to accomplish for the city.
“I’m so proud of what we’ve accomplished, but I want you and everyone in Louisville to know something. I’m not satisfied — not even close — because as much progress as we’ve made, I know we can do so much more,” Greenberg said. “This election wasn’t just about what we’ve accomplished over the past four years. Tonight and every day and night moving forward is about what we’re going to accomplish over the next four years.”  
Lexington 
Linda Gorton, who has been the Lexington mayor since 2019, warded off challenger Raquel Carter in the nonpartisan race. 
Carter ran, according to her campaign website, because “Lexington needs new leadership.” 
“Under Linda Gorton, Lexington’s become unaffordable,” Carter’s site states. “Gorton was totally unprepared for the winter storms that shut down Lexington for weeks. Kids missed school, workers missed paychecks, and the damage to our roads has caused irreparable harm to working families.” 
In the May primary election, Gorton received 46% of the vote while Carter received 28% — a lead less striking than previous years when Gorton won in 2019 with 63% of the vote and in 2022 with 71% of the vote. 
Among many issues listed on her website, Gorton stressed the importance of affordability and the city’s Affordable Housing Program 
“As we attract more citizens to the many opportunities Lexington has to offer, we must assure that we also offer housing stock that they can afford,” her site states. “I believe we need a dedicated funding stream to support our program — something that currently is lacking. As your mayor, I will strengthen our partnerships with developers, while seeking a dedicated funding source to amplify the program. My goal is to create a reliable funding mechanism for our Affordable Housing Program, reducing the costs for developers as they boost our housing stock.”

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Voters change Indiana’s Constitution — twice
description: Hoosiers easily approved two constitutional amendments Tuesday, including one that will allow judges to hold more criminal defendants without bail. Public Question 1 — the bail change — passed with 59% of the vote. A second question allowing city and town judges to live outside the jurisdiction also passed with 63%. That was with 84% […]
text:
(Getty Images)Hoosiers easily approved two constitutional amendments Tuesday, including one that will allow judges to hold more criminal defendants without bail.
Public Question 1 — the bail change — passed with 59% of the vote. A second question allowing city and town judges to live outside the jurisdiction also passed with 63%. That was with 84% of the votes tallied.
Defendants are guaranteed the right to bail under the Indiana Constitution except in cases of murder or treason — even when a judge believes the defendant may reoffend while awaiting trial.
Now judges will be able to deny bail to any defendant if the state proves they cannot be safely released.
Supporters say the amendment is needed to detain defendants who repeatedly commit violent crimes while on bail, while critics worry it jeopardizes due process rights for defendants who may spend months in jail without a conviction.
Two successive general assemblies  approved the proposed amendment: in 2023 and 2026. Now it goes to the people on the Nov. 3 ballot.
The Indiana Criminal Justice Institute found 7% of defendants released on bail or their own recognizance statewide last year were rearrested and charged with a new offense while awaiting trial.
To hold someone accused of a crime without bail a judge must find the defendant poses a “substantial risk to any other person or the community” and that the proof in the case “is evident or the presumption strong” of their guilt. The state would then need to prove “by clear and convincing evidence” no other release conditions would “reasonably” protect public safety.
Defendants are entitled to an attorney and a hearing if the state asks to deny them bail, as well as the right to appeal the court’s decision.
Opponents are concerned that some accused of misdemeanor or low-level felonies might be held with no bail, but lawmakers turned back attempts to limit the law.
Public Question 2 was much simpler. It allows the judge of a city or town court to reside in the county where the court is located or the bordering county closest to the city of town in which the court is located.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri voters approve Amendment 6, curbing lawmakers’ power to overturn citizen laws
description: A constitutional amendment that sharply limits the power of state lawmakers to overturn laws enacted directly by voters won overwhelmingly on Tuesday, fundamentally changing the balance of power between citizens and their elected representatives. Amendment 6, which garnered roughly 60% of the vote on Tuesday, requires at least 80% of both the Missouri House [...]
text:
Laura Mitchell of Columbia, center, campaigns outside a polling station Tuesday as part of a final effort to pass a proposal limiting legislative power (Rudi Keller/Missouri Independent).A constitutional amendment that sharply limits the power of state lawmakers to overturn laws enacted directly by voters won overwhelmingly on Tuesday, fundamentally changing the balance of power between citizens and their elected representatives.
Amendment 6, which garnered roughly 60% of the vote on Tuesday, requires at least 80% of both the Missouri House and Senate to agree before lawmakers can propose changes to voter-approved initiatives. Even then, the changes must be approved in another statewide election.
The measure also makes the initiative petition process a fundamental constitutional right, prohibits lawmakers from weakening it and gives courts greater authority to rewrite misleading ballot language.
Its passage represents a significant victory for advocates of direct democracy who spent years accusing Missouri’s Republican-controlled legislature of ignoring election results when voters approved policies lawmakers opposed.
But the amendment’s future could also depend on the courts, with opponents raising questions about whether its protections can constitutionally extend to ballot measures approved more than a decade ago.
The vote comes after a series of confrontations between lawmakers and voters over policies ranging from abortion rights and the minimum wage to marijuana legalization and legislative redistricting.
Amendment 6 would remake balance of power between Missouri voters and lawmakers

Perhaps the clearest example came in 2025.
Six months after voters approved a minimum wage increase and guaranteed paid sick leave for many workers, Republican lawmakers passed legislation repealing the sick leave requirement and eliminating future inflation adjustments to the minimum wage.
Gov. Mike Kehoe signed the bill into law in July 2025, prompting outrage from supporters of the original ballot measure.
Under Amendment 6, lawmakers could no longer make such changes on their own. They would first need overwhelming bipartisan support to put the changes before voters.
The amendment does not automatically restore the sick leave provisions lawmakers repealed. Its restrictions govern legislative action going forward, although they also protect initiatives approved as far back as Jan. 1, 2010.
In 2010, voters approved regulations on puppy mills, only for lawmakers to repeal key provisions the following year. The episode helped convince initiative supporters to pursue constitutional amendments rather than ordinary statutes, which lawmakers could easily change.
The amendment’s reach back to 2010 could become the focus of a new legal battle.
Republicans have argued that applying the new restrictions to previously approved initiatives violates the Missouri Constitution and said he expects the amendment to face a court challenge.
The measure has already survived one major legal fight. In August, Secretary of State Denny Hoskins refused to certify it for the November ballot, arguing that it violated constitutional limits on initiative petitions.
The Missouri Supreme Court unanimously reversed that decision in September, rejecting objections that the proposal violated the constitution’s single-subject and single-article requirements. But the court also said other questions about the amendment’s constitutionality could not be decided before voters approved it.
Those questions could now return to court, including whether its restrictions impermissibly constrain future legislatures or can be applied to initiatives approved before the amendment took effect.
The proposal includes a severability clause intended to preserve the remaining provisions if a court invalidates part of the amendment.
Voter-approved constitutional amendments were already more difficult to undo because changes required another statewide election. But lawmakers needed only a simple majority in each legislative chamber to put a competing amendment on the ballot.
Amendment 6 raises that legislative threshold to 80% for proposals that would change citizen-initiated constitutional amendments, just as it does for voter-approved statutes.
In the 163-member House, that would require 131 votes. In the 34-member Senate, it would take 28.
The amendment also restricts lawmakers from enacting legislation similar in effect to laws rejected through the referendum process without meeting the same requirements.
Supporters argued those protections were necessary to ensure that legislative majorities could not simply disregard decisions voters made at the ballot box.
Opponents warned the proposal went too far.
The Missouri Chamber of Commerce and Industry opposed Amendment 6, arguing that it would leave lawmakers unable to easily correct unintended consequences of voter-approved laws, particularly those affecting businesses.
Republican lawmakers raised similar objections, arguing that initiative petitions lack the hearings, negotiations and opportunities for revision that accompany legislation.
Those concerns extend to relatively small changes. Even technical corrections to a citizen-approved law could face the amendment’s extraordinary legislative threshold.
But proponents maintained that lawmakers’ ability to rewrite citizen initiatives had become an invitation to disregard the electorate.
The campaign attracted support across party lines, including former Republican U.S. Sen. Jack Danforth, former Democratic Secretary of State Jason Kander, former Republican state Sen. Bob Johnson and the Missouri AFL-CIO.
Organized labor provided substantial financial support, as did other organizations seeking stronger protections for the initiative petition process.
The vote also came just three months after Missourians overwhelmingly rejected a Republican-backed constitutional amendment that would have required citizen initiatives to win a majority statewide and in each of Missouri’s eight congressional districts.
Amendment 6 preserves the existing statewide majority requirement and signature thresholds while prohibiting lawmakers from imposing additional restrictions that weaken citizens’ initiative or referendum powers.
It also requires ballot summaries to be clear, unbiased and accurate, and ensures courts can rewrite language found to be misleading.
Missouri voters established the initiative and referendum process in 1908 to give citizens a way to make or reject laws without relying entirely on the legislature.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Democrats set to pick up more seats in the West Virginia House
description: The Associated Press results indicate Democrats may have up to 20 seats when the Legislature convenes in January.
text:
The empty chamber of the West Virginia House of Delegates in the state Capitol in Charleston, West Virginia. (Photo by Perry Bennett/West Virginia Legislative Photography)As Ogden reporter Steven Allen Adams opined on MetroNews on Monday, “Whenever you have a blue wave, you’re going to get splashed.” 
And in the West Virginia House of Delegates, that splash came, with Democrats being poised to pick up six seats, according to the unofficial results posted by the Associated Press as of 10:46 p.m. Tuesday.
However, AP results indicate Democrats may have up to 20 seats when the Legislature convenes in January. 
Del. Sean Hornbuckle, D-Cabell, is the House minority leader. He said the wins are part of a strategy hatched in the wake of losses in the 2024 election. 
“Our game plan has been to focus on the issues that matter the most to people and we are seeing the fruits of that,” he said. “Even the folks who didn’t win ran a hell of a campaign. And I’m excited as hell to be working with these new members.” 
Del. Josh Holstein, R-Boone, chairman of the West Virginia Republican Party, said the losses were to be expected, and some races came in closer than initially expected. But he said the Republican Party still remains firmly in control of the House of Delegates. 
“We still have an overwhelming supermajority, one of the biggest in the nation,” he said. “I think this shows that the Republican Party is still the choice party for voters in West Virginia.” 
The wins were concentrated in urban areas of the state — Monongalia, Kanawha and Cabell counties. And more wins appear to be coming from the Eastern Panhandle. 
The House of Delegates currently comprises 91 Republicans and nine Democrats, one of the biggest supermajorities in the country. 
In the Legislature, an 80 seat majority allows the party in charge to suspend the constitutional rule that a bill must be read on three separate days. If Democrats are able to capture 21 seats, then Republicans won’t be able to do that. 
“Those days are gone,” Hornbuckle said. “I believe this will lead to a better product in our government.” 
Holstein downplayed the effect on having this power usurped. 
“Even if we aren’t able to suspend constitutional rules, we will still be able to easily pass our agenda,” he said. 
This year, the Democratic Party fielded 88 candidates in the general election, with 79 challenging either incumbent Republicans or open seats. In 2024, the party only fielded 58 total candidates in the general election. 
During the primary, at least 60 women signed up to run as Democrats, many making it to the general. West Virginia currently has some of the lowest female participation in the Legislature in the country. 
Nine Republicans and four Democrats ran uncontested. 
Third party challengers also had strong showings in the campaigns, filling the void where a major party candidate would’ve run unopposed.  
Del. Evan Hansen, D-Monongalia, defended a challenge from Mountain Party candidate Paige Reiring, while Democrat Olivia Miller saw a challenge from Constitution Party candidate Melissa Ann Deserio. 
Over on the GOP side, Del. Erica Moore in Roane was challenged by Libertarian candidate Tye Ward and Del. Mike Hornby, of Berkeley County, beat back a challenge from Constitution Party candidate Tara B. McCoy.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Democrats escape their superminority status in the Florida House
description: Florida Democrats stepped out of the struggle of being in the superminority in the state House Tuesday.  Republicans won 65 seats while Democrats won 49 seats, with six seats still to be called Tuesday night. That means Republicans will not reach the 80-seat threshold to retain the supermajority status they’ve held since 2022. Going into […]
text:
The Florida Capitol building on March 11, 2026. (Photo by Jay Waagmeester/Florida Phoenix)Florida Democrats stepped out of the struggle of being in the superminority in the state House Tuesday. 
Republicans won 65 seats while Democrats won 49 seats, with six seats still to be called Tuesday night. That means Republicans will not reach the 80-seat threshold to retain the supermajority status they’ve held since 2022. Going into election day, the GOP held 82 seats in the House. Four seats were vacant, all previously held by Republicans. Democrats held 34 seats pre-election.
The 49 seats Democrats won are 15 more than the party held before the election. They picked up one seat in the Florida Senate, too. With one vacancy in that body and one Independent, the Democrats could be out of superminority status in the Senate, too, come session. 
Supermajority status gave Republican lawmakers power to override rules regarding procedure and debate inside the chambers and override the governor’s veto pen.
A party needs 27 senators to hold a supermajority. As of Tuesday night, the Senate had 13 Democrats and 22 Republicans, with four seats to still be called, but in which Republicans were leading and one seat subject to a still-to-be-scheduled special election. It had been held by Bryan Avila, who was elected lieutenant governor to Byron Donalds Tuesday.
“Since the August primary, our coordinated campaign has knocked on more than 1.2 million doors and made 5.25 million calls to voters across Florida,” Florida Democratic Party Chair Nikki Fried said Tuesday. “That work helped drive a nearly 20-point swing toward Democrats statewide compared to the 2022 midterms, with Democratic turnout surpassing even 2018 levels.”
Fried applauded the state-level effort to elect Democrats, “We did all of this without major national investment in Florida,” she added. 
“Imagine what we could accomplish with the national support and investment this state deserves,” Fried, the last statewide-elected Democrat to serve on the Florida Cabinet, said. 
Senate Democratic Leader Tracie Davis was “thrilled” to welcome the new Democratic senators. Five of the 13 Democrats are new to the body.
“Last session, Senate Democrats led the way on some of the most important fights Floridians faced, from the affordability crisis to healthcare access to corruption in our state government,” Davis said in a news release. “I know this group of public servants will be ready to continue the fight this term.”
While Republicans maintained control of the governor’s mansion, and still hold majority status in both legislative chambers, Democrats will have more members on committees and voices for debate.
“Florida Democrats will now have more leverage to fight against the extreme Republican leadership in the state,” the Democratic Legislative Campaign Committee, a national organization, posted to social media Tuesday night.
The Florida Democratic Party sent a message to Rep. Hillary Cassel, who lost Tuesday. Cassel won the 2024 election as a Democrat but switched her party after the election to Republican.

Republicans gained back one seat they’d lost in a special election earlier this year, House District 87, which is home to President Donald Trump’s Mar-a-Lago.
