title: Missouri voters reject Trump-backed congressional map, dealing GOP redistricting defeat
description: A  Republican-drawn congressional map designed to give the GOP another seat in the U.S. House was soundly rejected by Missouri voters Tuesday, rebuffing President Donald Trump’s effort to reshape the state’s political boundaries in his party’s favor. The defeat of Proposition A means Missouri will retain the congressional districts established in 2022, prese[...]
text:
Supporters of a referendum on Missouri's gerrymandered redistricting map rally at the state Capitol Building on May 12 after the Missouri Supreme Court heard arguments on two cases involving the redistricting map (Rudi Keller/Missouri Independent).A  Republican-drawn congressional map designed to give the GOP another seat in the U.S. House was soundly rejected by Missouri voters Tuesday, rebuffing President Donald Trump’s effort to reshape the state’s political boundaries in his party’s favor.
The defeat of Proposition A means Missouri will retain the congressional districts established in 2022, preserving a Kansas City-based district that Republicans sought to redraw to improve their chances of defeating Democratic U.S. Rep. Emanuel Cleaver.
The outcome deals a setback to Trump and Missouri Republican leaders, who spent more than a year trying to impose new congressional boundaries and prevent voters from having the final say.
It also marks a victory for People Not Politicians, the political action committee that collected more than 300,000 signatures to force a statewide referendum on the legislature’s redistricting plan.
But whether the vote ends Missouri’s mid-decade redistricting fight remains uncertain.
Some Republican lawmakers have already suggested they could return to the issue in 2027, potentially drawing an even more aggressive map aimed at winning all eight of Missouri’s congressional seats.
For now, the vote means the boundaries used in Tuesday’s election will remain in place for the 2028 congressional races, unless the legislature passes another redistricting plan.
The defeated map would have divided Kansas City among three congressional districts, combining heavily Democratic neighborhoods with Republican-leaning communities across northern and central Missouri and the Ozarks.
The goal was to transform the 5th Congressional District, which Cleaver has represented since 2005, into a Republican stronghold.
Under the 2022 boundaries, Democratic presidential nominee Kamala Harris carried the district with roughly 61% of the vote in 2024. Trump would have won the redesigned district with about 58%.
That shift could have helped Republicans capture seven of Missouri’s eight congressional seats, despite the state’s population and congressional delegation remaining unchanged.
 A national political battle

Missouri’s redistricting fight began in 2025 as Trump urged Republican-controlled states to redraw congressional districts ahead of the 2026 midterm elections.
Republicans pursued new maps in states including Texas, while Democrats sought to counter those efforts elsewhere, including California.
In Missouri, Republican lawmakers approved a new map during a September 2025 special session, arguing that the state’s congressional boundaries should better reflect its increasingly Republican electorate.
Supporters also maintained the new districts were more compact and kept more counties intact.
Opponents described the effort as a partisan gerrymander intended to dilute Democratic voting strength in Kansas City and give Republicans another congressional seat without changing voters’ political preferences.
People Not Politicians responded by organizing a petition drive to put the map before voters.
The group gathered more than 300,000 signatures, but Secretary of State Denny Hoskins refused to certify the referendum, arguing that congressional redistricting was not subject to Missouri’s constitutional referendum process.
The Missouri Supreme Court unanimously rejected that position Sept. 3, ruling that the referendum was legal, sufficient and timely.
The court also concluded the new congressional map had never legally taken effect, requiring the state to return to boundaries approved in 2022.
After weeks of conflicting federal court orders, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled Sept. 25 that the 2022 map must govern the November election.
That decision ended the immediate fight over which districts voters would use, leaving the longer-term question to Proposition A.
 Money and political momentum

The final campaign was lopsided.
People Not Politicians reported at least $5.4 million in large contributions since mid-September, financing advertising and voter outreach to defeat the Republican map.
Put Missouri First, the political action committee that fought to prevent the referendum, spent roughly $2.9 million during the earlier battle but reported no large contributions after July.
Republican officials continued to endorse the map, but their organized campaign to persuade voters to approve it largely vanished.
The ballot language emphasized that the new congressional districts would keep more counties intact. It did not mention the potential partisan consequences of the proposed boundaries.
And because Proposition A was a referendum on a law already approved by the legislature, opponents of the map had to vote “no” to defeat it.
Voters ultimately rejected the redistricting plan despite Republican control of every statewide elected office and supermajorities in both chambers of the legislature.
 Another map in 2027?

The vote leaves open the possibility of another confrontation over Missouri’s congressional boundaries.
Minutes after the Missouri Supreme Court blocked the 2025 map in September, Republican state Sen. Nick Schroer posted “8-0 2027” on social media, signaling interest in a new plan intended to give Republicans all eight congressional seats.
Hoskins has also said he could envision lawmakers revisiting redistricting next year.
Whether Republicans could pursue another map may depend on Amendment 6, another measure approved by voters on Tuesday’s ballot.
That constitutional amendment will prohibit lawmakers from passing legislation similar in effect to a law rejected through referendum unless 80% of both legislative chambers agree to send the proposal back to voters.
Legal experts have said the provision could make another mid-decade congressional redraw extraordinarily difficult if Amendment 6 is approved. But the amendment does not define what constitutes legislation “similar in effect,” leaving room for additional court battles.
Even without Amendment 6, the Missouri Supreme Court’s September ruling established that congressional redistricting laws can be challenged through the referendum process. That means another Republican-drawn map could face another petition drive seeking to suspend it and put the question back before voters.

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: Goodlander wins reelection to New Hampshire’s 2nd Congressional District
description: U.S. Rep. Maggie Goodlander defeated Republican challenger Lily Tang Williams in the race to represent New Hampshire’s 2nd Congressional District Tuesday.  The Associated Press called the contest at 11:05 p.m., with Goodlander holding 60% of the vote with 61% of votes counted. Williams had 37% of the vote when the race was called. Independent candidate […]
text:
From left: Rep. Maggie Goodlander greets poll observer Sue Donaldson and Concord Supervisor of the Checklist Elizabeth Corell before casting her ballot on Tuesday, Nov. 3. "These incredible people, these nonpartisan, patriotic poll observers and election officials are doing the Lord's work to make this democracy happen today," Goodlander said later in the day. (Photo by Molly Rains/New Hampshire Bulletin)U.S. Rep. Maggie Goodlander defeated Republican challenger Lily Tang Williams in the race to represent New Hampshire’s 2nd Congressional District Tuesday. 
The Associated Press called the contest at 11:05 p.m., with Goodlander holding 60% of the vote with 61% of votes counted.
Williams had 37% of the vote when the race was called. Independent candidate Robbie Mahrou had 2%. 
Speaking in Concord earlier in the day, Goodlander listed priorities including lowering costs, rolling back tariffs imposed by President Donald Trump and bringing an end to the Iran War.
On Tuesday evening, as results began to trickle in, Goodlander addressed supporters.
“Whether you voted for me or not, I will work for you, all of you, with all my heart and everything I’ve got,” she said. 
This will be a second term for the Nashua native, who was first elected to Congress in 2024. Goodlander previously worked in intelligence with the U.S. Naval Reserve and as a law clerk, an attorney for the House Judiciary Committee, a foreign policy adviser for the late U.S. Sens. John McCain and Joe Lieberman, and with the U.S. Department of Justice during the administration of President Joe Biden.
Speaking outside the Christa McAuliffe School earlier Tuesday after casting her ballot, Goodlander said the election would come down to affordability and disapproval of the Iran war.
“The housing affordability crisis, the healthcare crisis, the childcare crisis, all these come down to really fundamental work that can be done and that must be done by Congress to lower the sky-high cost of living,” she said.
She went on to criticize Trump for the war and higher prices in New Hampshire. 
“There is a very clear reason why we see the cost of gas, the cost of diesel, the cost of home heating fuel through the roof: It’s the president’s decision to launch this war in Iran. We’ve got to end this war,” she said. 
Lily Tang Williams lost a bid to represent New Hampshire’s 2nd Congressional District to incumbent Democrat Maggie Goodlander on Nov. 3. (Photo by Molly Rains/New Hampshire Bulletin)
Williams has run for Congress before, most recently challenging Goodlander for the seat in 2024, when she lost with 47% of the vote. She also ran in the 2020 primary but failed to secure the Republican nomination. Williams moved to New Hampshire from Colorado as part of the libertarian Free State Project. Though she has previously been seen as a far-right candidate, this election cycle she sought to portray herself as more moderate, telling the Bulletin she was focused on kitchen-table issues like affordability. 
Attendees at her Tuesday night watch party, hosted at Concord’s Grappone Conference Center, said they supported her dedication to individual freedom, including the right to bear arms, and her vocal opposition to socialism and communism.
“She supports the Second Amendment, when (Goodlander) seems to want laws against it,” said Marty Mullen, of Pittsfield, at the party. 
New Hampshire’s 2nd Congressional District covers much of Western and Northern New Hampshire, including the cities of Concord, Nashua, Salem and Hanover.

title: Warner wins fourth term, Luria ousts Kiggans in VA-02, Taylor triumphs in VA-01
description: U.S. Sen. Mark Warner, D-Va., won a fourth term in Tuesday’s midterm elections, defeating Republican challenger Bert Mizusawa, a retired U.S. Army major general, 60% to 40%, with 3.1 million votes cast by 11 p.m., according to unofficial results from the Virginia Department of Elections.  Voters also approved three constitutional amendments protecting reprod[...]
text:
U.S. Sen. Mark Warner speaks to Virginians at his re-election celebration in Alexandria on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Nathaniel Cline/Virginia Mercury)U.S. Sen. Mark Warner, D-Va., won a fourth term in Tuesday’s midterm elections, defeating Republican challenger Bert Mizusawa, a retired U.S. Army major general, 60% to 40%, with 3.1 million votes cast by 11 p.m., according to unofficial results from the Virginia Department of Elections. 
Voters also approved three constitutional amendments protecting reproductive rights, guaranteeing marriage equality and automatically restoring voting rights after incarceration.
Virginians protect gay marriage, voting rights and reproductive rights in state Constitution

Former U.S. Rep. Elaine Luria declared victory late Tuesday night in her 2nd District rematch against Republican U.S. Rep. Jen Kiggans of Virginia Beach. The race was officially called in Luria’s favor at 11:47 p.m. by the Associated Press. 
The 1st Congressional District remained too close to call until Wednesday morning, when results data from the Virginia Department of Elections showed Democrat Shannon Taylor won the race. Taylor declared victory in the contest against incumbent U.S. Rep. Rob Wittman, R-Westmoreland, Tuesday night. 
There was no clear winner in the 5th District until Wednesday morning, when state elections data revealed U.S. Rep. John McGuire, R-Goochland, scratched out a narrow win over Democrat Tom Perriello, who had hoped to return to Congress.  Independent Cooke Harvey was also on the ballot. 
Democrats entered the election holding six of Virginia’s 11 congressional seats and had targeted several districts as potential pickups. The races were fought under the existing congressional maps after the Supreme Court of Virginia struck down the redistricting referendum that voters had approved in April. 
Democrats had hoped the proposed map would help them win as many as 10 seats this election cycle. 
 U.S. Senate

Warner, a former governor first elected to the Senate in 2008, campaigned on his experience and willingness to work across party lines. He also pledged to challenge President Donald Trump’s economic and healthcare policies and has said his next six-year term would be his last. 
The vice-chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee called for a public health insurance option, restoring enhanced Affordable Care Act premium subsidies and federal standards for data centers.
“This is my last campaign, but this is not the end of the road,” Warner said at his campaign victory party in Alexandria. “I start tomorrow on the next seven years, I start tomorrow in making sure this agenda becomes a reality. I start tomorrow … and I said to my friends before, you think (you know) Mark Warner so far? Wait till you see an untethered Mark Warner.”
 1st District

Taylor, Henrico County’s commonwealth’s attorney, conquered Wittman with 51.03% to 48.72% with about 406,243 votes tallied by 10:30 a.m. Wednesday. 
Taylor campaigned on restoring Medicaid funding and enhanced ACA subsidies while criticizing Wittman’s support for the Republicans’ sweeping federal tax-and-spending law.  
The 1st District stretches from Richmond’s suburbs to the Northern Neck, Middle Peninsula and Williamsburg area, with major population centers in Henrico, Chesterfield, Hanover and James City counties. Trump carried it in 2024, but Democratic Gov. Abigail Spanberger won 51% of the district’s vote last year. 
 2nd District

Luria reclaimed the 2nd District seat she lost in 2022, earning 51.51% of the vote compared to Kiggans’ 46.14%. A total of  303,901 voted had been tallied by 11:55 p.m. Independents Matt Baker and Bishop Staten received 1.42% and 0.80%, respectively. 
Both major party candidates are U.S. Navy veterans. Their rematch focused on accountability, healthcare and national security in a district with Virginia’s largest concentration of military personnel. 
Centered in Virginia Beach, the district also includes part of the Eastern Shore, Suffolk, Franklin and Isle of Wight County and part of Chesapeake. 
Luria campaigned on restoring ACA subsidies and expanding prescription drug savings. Kiggans defended her record in Congress and her support for the Republican tax-and-spending package.
 3rd District 

U.S. Rep. Bobby Scott, D-Newport News, defeated Republican Edwin Rivera 71.76% to 24.67%. Independents Makiba Gaines and Steve Woll received 1.73% and 1.62%, respectively, with 175,675 votes cast in the district by 11 p.m.   
Scott has represented the Hampton Roads district since 1993. It includes Newport News, Hampton and Norfolk, has a large Black population and an economy closely tied to military installations and shipbuilding. 
 4th District

U.S. Rep. Jennifer McClellan, D-Richmond, won another term with 69.35% of the vote, defeating Republican Robert Murray, who received 29.02%, and independent Joan Bell, who took 1.39%. A total of 266,880 votes were cast in the race as of 11 p.m. 
The district stretches from Richmond through Petersburg into Southside Virginia, encompassing urban neighborhoods and rural communities. Black residents account for more than two-fifths of its population. 
 5th District 

McGuire narrowly defeated Perriello in the 5th District, 50.21% to 47.99%, with roughly 360,146 voters tallied by 10:30 a.m. Wednesday. Independent Cooke Harvey had 1.60%. 
The district stretches from Charlottesville through Lynchburg and Danville, combining university communities, Richmond-area suburbs and rural Southside. Perriello previously represented the district for one term after winning the seat in 2008. 
 6th District

U.S. Rep. Ben Cline of Botetourt County, the Republican incumbent, defeated Democratic challenger Beth Macy 55.49% to 44.31%. The contest drew 292,415 votes by 11 p.m.. 
The heavily Republican district follows the Shenandoah Valley from the Winchester area toward Roanoke, encompassing agricultural communities and small cities. Macy, a former Roanoke Times reporter, is the author of “Dopesick,” which examined the opioid epidemic. 
 7th District

U.S. Rep. Eugene Vindman, D-Woodbridge, won a second term, defeating Republican Douglas Ollivant 59.65% to 37.80%. Independents Alaha Ahrar, Josh Ertle, Taner Lopez and Randall Terry received 0.94%, 0.24%, 0.82% and 0.37%, respectively. At the time of reporting, 319,769 votes were cast in the district. 
The 7th includes Prince William County suburbs, Fredericksburg-area communities and rural counties. It has substantial Black and Hispanic populations, along with many military families and federal workers. 
 8th District

After successfully fending off a primary challenge in August, U.S. Rep. Don Beyer, D-Alexandria, defeated Republican Tony Sabio 79.38% to 17.82%. Independents Shelly Arnoldi and Timothy Sharman received 1.22% and 1.29%, respectively, out of 283,146 votes cast by 11 p.m. 
The Northern Virginia district includes Arlington, Alexandria, Falls Church and part of Fairfax County. It has a highly educated population, a large contingent of federal workers and sizable Hispanic and Asian communities. 
 9th District

Republican U.S. Rep. Morgan Griffith of Salem defeated Democrat Joy Powers 65.13% to 34.67%, with 263,462 votes cast by reporting time. 
The heavily Republican Southwest Virginia district includes coalfield communities, rural Appalachian counties and the New River Valley, including Blacksburg and Radford. 
 10th District

U.S. Rep. Suhas Subramanyam, D-Loudoun, won reelection against Republican Dave Beckwith with 61.39% to 36.55%. Independent Ahsen Malilk received 1.86%. At 11 p.m., the race had drawn 326,793 votes. 
The district includes Loudoun, Fauquier and Rappahannock counties, Manassas, Manassas Park and portions of Fairfax and Prince William counties. It has substantial Asian and Hispanic populations. 
 11th District 

Democratic U.S. Rep. James Walkinshaw of Fairfax won his first full term with 72.78% of the vote, defeating Republican Arthur Purves, who received 25.43%. Dianne Blais of the Green Party took 1.42%, with 232,662 votes cast in the contest by 11 p… 
The Fairfax-centered district has a highly educated population and a large Asian community. Walkinshaw first won the seat in a September 2025 special election following the death of longtime U.S. Rep. Gerry Connolly. 
Editor’s note: This story was updated Wednesday morning with fresh data from the Virginia Department of Elections.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri voters reject Amendment 3, preserving abortion rights approved in 2024
description: Two years after becoming the first state to overturn an abortion ban at the ballot box, Missouri voters overwhelmingly rejected an attempt Tuesday to reinstate the ban, preserving the reproductive rights protections they approved in 2024. The defeat of Amendment 3, which won only 44% of the vote,  leaves in place a constitutional right to […]
text:
Mallory Schwarz, xecutive Director of Abortion Action Missouri, celebrates the defeat of Amendment 3 on Tuesday (Anna Spoerre/Missouri Independent). Two years after becoming the first state to overturn an abortion ban at the ballot box, Missouri voters overwhelmingly rejected an attempt Tuesday to reinstate the ban, preserving the reproductive rights protections they approved in 2024.
The defeat of Amendment 3, which won only 44% of the vote,  leaves in place a constitutional right to abortion up to the point of fetal viability, rejecting an effort by Republican lawmakers to reverse the narrow abortion rights victory two years ago.
The proposed amendment would have banned nearly all elective abortions, with exceptions for medical emergencies, fetal anomalies and pregnancies resulting from rape or incest if an abortion was sought within the first 12 weeks.
It also would have placed a constitutional ban on gender-affirming care for minors.
“The anti-abortion politicians did not like the way we voted in 2024 …” Tori Schafer, a spokesperson for the Stop the Ban campaign, said during a canvassing event in September. “Amendment 3 is a power grab, one that takes the power away from you and me to make medical decisions with our families and our doctors and puts politicians and lawyers in charge of our decisions.”
The result is a setback for Missouri’s anti-abortion movement, which spent two years rebuilding its campaign after narrowly losing the 2024 vote.
This time, unlike in 2024, the effort to reinstate an abortion ban had significant and organized support from Republican lawmakers, Gov. Mike Kehoe’s office and many of the state’s largest churches.
Kehoe, who campaigned across Missouri for Amendment 3 on Monday, told supporters during a stop in Chesterfield that its defeat would be “a sad day for Missouri.”
But the proposal also faced opposition from some anti-abortion activists who argued its exceptions went too far.
Among them was Republican state Sen. Mike Moon, who publicly criticized the amendment for allowing abortions in cases of rape, incest and medical emergencies.
The campaign supporting Amendment 3, Her Health, Her Future, raised more than $7 million, but was significantly outspent by abortion rights advocates.
Ahead of Election Day, Stop the Ban had raised more than $27 million.
The abortion rights campaign drew small donations from thousands of Missourians, but much of its financial support came from wealthy out-of-state donors and progressive nonprofit organizations that are not required to disclose their donors.
Among them was the Fairness Project, a Washington, D.C.-based nonprofit and the campaign’s largest contributor.
Tuesday’s vote preserves the reproductive rights amendment that Missourians approved in 2024 with support from 51.6% of voters.
That measure overturned the near-total abortion ban Missouri enacted in 2022, immediately after the U.S. Supreme Court struck down Roe v. Wade.
Missouri was the first state to enact a trigger law banning nearly all abortions following the Supreme Court’s ruling.
Thousands of Missouri women subsequently traveled to clinics in Illinois and Kansas to obtain abortions. Others ended pregnancies using medication obtained through telehealth providers in states where abortion remained legal.
The 2024 reproductive rights amendment reached the ballot through a citizen-led initiative petition effort spearheaded by organizations including the ACLU of Missouri, Abortion Action Missouri and local Planned Parenthood affiliates.
Following its passage, abortion access slowly returned to Missouri. A handful of Planned Parenthood clinics resumed providing the procedure amid ongoing litigation over dozens of abortion restrictions that were later found unconstitutional under the reproductive rights amendment.
In 2025, the Republican-controlled legislature voted to place another abortion amendment on the ballot, seeking to reverse the decision voters had made the previous year.
The campaign to pass Amendment 3 also focused heavily on gender-affirming care for minors, which has been restricted under state law since 2023.
The statutory ban on puberty blockers and cross-sex hormones is scheduled to expire in 2027, while the prohibition on gender-affirming surgeries for minors is permanent.
Proponents argued a constitutional prohibition was necessary to make those restrictions permanent. Opponents said the proposal was designed to attract voters who supported restrictions on gender-affirming care but might otherwise oppose an abortion ban.
By rejecting Amendment 3, voters also turned down the proposed constitutional ban on gender-affirming care for minors. The existing statutory restrictions remain in place.
In the final weeks of the campaign, Stop the Ban released a television advertisement featuring Michael Wolff, a former chief justice of the Missouri Supreme Court and dean emeritus at Saint Louis University School of Law, who called the amendment’s language “misleading.”
“Don’t let politicians fool us into banning abortion again,” he said.
National anti-abortion leaders had pointed to Missouri’s amendment as a possible model for reinstating abortion bans in other states by pairing abortion restrictions with a ban on gender-affirming care for minors.
“What happens in Missouri, right here, this year in this election, is not going to stay just in Missouri,” David Bereit, executive director of the Virginia-based Life Leadership Conference, said during a virtual fundraising event in October. “When Missouri wins, every other state will learn that these bad amendments can be reversed and undone. But if it loses, no other state will likely try this again for a long time, perhaps for a generation.”
This story will be updated.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: State Reps. Pat Moore, Gabe Firment advance to 5th District runoff
description: A glut of Monroe-area Republicans on the 5th Congressional District ballot opened the door for a Democrat from the city and a Central Louisiana lawmaker to claim the top two spots in Tuesday’s primary election.
text:
State Reps. Pat Moore, D-Monroe, left, and Gabe Firment, R-Pollock will meet in the Dec. 12, 2026, runoff for Louisiana's 5th Congressional District. (Louisiana Legislature photos)A glut of Monroe-area Republicans on the 5th Congressional District ballot opened the door for a Democrat from the city and a Central Louisiana lawmaker to claim the top two spots in Tuesday’s primary election.  
State Rep. Pat Moore, who received and then lost the Louisiana Democratic Party’s endorsement in the race, led the nine-candidate field with 18% of the vote. Her Louisiana House colleague, Rep. Gabe Firment, finished second with 17% to earn the other spot in the Dec. 12 runoff.  
The winner will represent a district anchored in Northeast Louisiana that reaches into the central part of the state, down along the Mississippi border and into portions of East Baton Rouge and the Florida Parishes.
Moore and Firment were both elected to the Louisiana Legislature in 2019, and both have backgrounds in the insurance business. Moore, who was on the Ouachita Parish Police Jury from 2007-19, is retired, while Firment owns a claims consulting business.
Notably falling short in the race were two other Monroe candidates: Misti Cordell, the Board of Regents chair who Gov. Jeff Landry endorsed, and state Rep. Michael Echols, who served a term on the Monroe City Council before being elected to the legislature the same year as Moore and Firment. 
Echols, by far, led the field in fundraising at $3.9 million and spent $2.3 million on the election, according to Federal Election Commission figures. Both figures are five times more than Cordell, who had the second largest war chest, reported.
The Democratic State Central Committee mistakenly gave Moore its endorsement before realizing she didn’t receive the majority backing from its members. The party then voted again and backed Antonio Wilson, a contractor from Tallulah.
Moore’s anti-abortion views also created friction within the party.

[…]
text:
President Donald Trump endorsed Michael Alfonso, the son-in-law of Department of Transportation Sec. Sean Duffy, in the Republican primary for Wisconsin’s 7th Congressional District Tuesday evening. (Alfonso headshot courtesy of campaign) Republican Michael Alfonso, 26,  the son-in-law of U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, won by a margin of 56.1% to 43.9% over Democrat Fred Clark, a conservationist and former state lawmaker, in the election for an open seat in Wisconsin’s 7th Congressional District. 
AP called the race at 10:03 p.m. with 86% of the vote counted.
The district, which covers much of the northern part of Wisconsin, is currently represented by U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany, the 2026 Republican candidate for governor.
Alfonso, whose father-in-law previously represented the 7th CD, received President Donald Trump’s endorsement during the primary. 
During the campaign, Alfonso faced criticism over his lack of work experience. After he went to college, he worked for as a producer on Dan Bongino’s podcast in Florida for about a year. He said during the Republican primary that he has worked as an accountant for a church since moving back to Wisconsin.
The district has been represented by a Republican for the last 16 years. Prior to Tiffany and Duffy, the seat was held from 1969 to 2011 by Democrat Dave Obey, the longest serving U.S. House member in Wisconsin history.
Alfonso ran as a strong supporter of the construction of a new segment of the Enbridge Line 5 pipeline, which he said would create jobs in the district. He also advocated for cutting taxes and regulations, especially on homebuilding. 
Throughout the campaign, he tied himself closely to President Trump and embraced Trump’s efforts to eliminate the Department of Education. During a candidate debate, he criticized “these ridiculous public universities that do nothing but indoctrinate our students” and called for taking away funding from them and putting it towards trade schools.

name: VTDigger
title: Vermonters vote to approve 2 constitutional amendments
description:
The public referendums were the final steps in ratifying the new items, which fortify collective bargaining rights and guarantee Vermonters equal protection under the law regardless of a number of characteristics.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermonters vote to approve 2 constitutional amendments.
text:
A ballot in the Vermont General Election on November 3, 2026. Photo by Noel Clark/VTDigger
Vermonters decisively approved two amendments to the state constitution Tuesday. The public referendums were the final steps in ratifying the new items, which fortify collective bargaining rights and guarantee equal protection under the law regardless of a number of characteristics.
The complex, yearslong amendment process requires legislative support in two consecutive bienniums. Voters last ratified constitutional changes in 2022, approving an explicit ban on slavery and landmark language affirming “an individual’s right to personal reproductive autonomy.”
Proposal 3, or Prop 3, enshrines the right to collective bargaining for employees, and prevents lawmakers from easily passing legislation that “interferes with, negates, or diminishes” that guarantee. The language explicitly protects labor agreements in which union membership becomes a condition of employment at a company, outlawing “right-to-work” legislation in the future.
The measure received strong bipartisan support in both of Vermont’s legislative chambers, passing 29 to zero in the Senate and 125 to 15 in the House last year.
The item’s proponents have argued the change is a necessary stand against what they see as nationwide, decades-long efforts to restrict the influence of unions in the U.S. Vermont labor leaders looked to Illinois, which is the only other state to have similarly robust constitutional labor protections, as a model.
Critics have argued that the restrictions on “right-to-work” laws will lock Vermont into an undesirable status quo and that the provision could cost Vermonters financially in the long term by giving unions too much power. One constitutional scholar also said the language would likely provide organizing protections to a broader set of employees in the state than is currently covered by statute — including farmworkers. 
Proposal 4, or Prop 4, is designed to guarantee people equal protection under the law, regardless of “race, ethnicity, sex, religion, disability, sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression, or national origin.” A majority of states have a similarly aimed provision in their constitutions.
This amendment proposal too enjoyed robust support among lawmakers, passing 128 to 14 in the House and without opposition in the Senate.
Supporters have said the measure will build on the protections afforded by the 14th Amendment to the U.S. Constitution, with part of the new item’s stated purpose being to shield the rights of historically marginalized communities in Vermont. The new language would likely strengthen the state’s legal foundations for some anti-discrimination lawsuits, according to constitutional experts.
Some of those same experts raised concerns about the “list” approach this language takes, which includes some characteristics but leaves others out — such as age. Other critics argued the item’s stated purpose was essentially redundant with existing federal protections, and might create legal uncertainty in the future.
Both proposed amendments have seen robust lobbying for and against them. A campaign supporting Prop 3 notably spent nearly $800,000 this election cycle, with contributions from an arm of the International Brotherhood of Teamsters.
As of just after 11 p.m., 74.05% of counted ballots had been in favor of Prop 3, with 25.95% against, according to the Associated Press. Prop 4 had received the support of 79% of tallied votes, with 21% opposed, the AP reported.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Democrat Rob Sand wins election to become Iowa governor, AP projects
description: Democrat Rob Sand will be Iowa’s next governor, the Associated Press projected Tuesday, ending more than a decade of a Republican trifecta of control at the Iowa Capitol with his defeat of Republican Zach Lahn. The race has received significant attention as it represented a chance for Democrats to break up GOP control over the […]
text:
Democratic State Auditor Rob Sand, joined by other Democratic candidates, urged union workers and volunteers to get out the vote at a rally and canvassing event with state and federal labor organizers at IBEW Local 347 in Ankeny Oct. 31, 2026. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)Democrat Rob Sand will be Iowa’s next governor, the Associated Press projected Tuesday, ending more than a decade of a Republican trifecta of control at the Iowa Capitol with his defeat of Republican Zach Lahn.
The race has received significant attention as it represented a chance for Democrats to break up GOP control over the Iowa state government for several years. It is also the first time in more than a decade that Iowa’s gubernatorial race was an open competition, as Gov. Kim Reynolds, the incumbent Republican, announced she would not seek reelection.
Unofficial results show Sand with 57.7% of the vote and Lahn with 42.3%, with 76% of precincts reporting.
Though Sand is a Democrat, he continually distanced himself from the Democratic Party during the campaign cycle, stating he was a moderate and independent of party control. But he also stated the need for Iowans to put a check on Republicans’ power in Iowa. Sand has argued Republicans’ decade of one-party control in Iowa has led more corruption and less accountability in state government.
Democrats had a relatively quick path uniting behind Sand as the party nominee after he launched his campaign in May 2025. But the path to find Reynolds’ potential successor was more complicated for Republicans. There were five candidates competing in June to become the GOP gubernatorial nominee, including U.S. Rep. Randy Feenstra, who received President Donald Trump’s endorsement in the primary and was considered by some to be the establishment pick. 
But Lahn, who centered his primary campaign on issues of water quality, cancer and support for “Make America Healthy Again” efforts, emerged as the victor. With more attention on Lahn as the nominee, more information about his background came to light — particularly regarding his previous residency in Kansas. 
Republican gubernatorial candidate Zach Lahn spoke in the rain to a crowd gathered at the Des Moines Register Political Soapbox at the Iowa State Fair Aug. 14, 2026. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)
The Kansas Reflector reported he registered to vote in Iowa in 2024, but had previously lived in and been a registered voter in Kansas, where he launched a private pre-K through 12th-grade school named Wonder financed by the Koch family. More reporting found Lahn frequently flew his personal aircraft from Iowa to Kansas, which Lahn said was because he has a “blended family” with some children based out of Wichita, Kansas. 
Sand has talked about Lahn’s former residency in Kansas on the campaign trail, often referencing a Lahn campaign ad where his opponent said “Iowa jobs are for Iowans” — which Sand says includes the job of Iowa governor. But Lahn has said the campaign ads and statements about his residency were an attack on his children and family.
Republicans also brought up Sand’s family connections during the campaign season, criticizing the Democrat for receiving money from the family of his his wife, Christine Lauridsen Sand, the CEO of the Lauridsen Group, Inc., a business that operating several food and health products companies.
When a member of the Lauridsen family died in October, Walter E. Lauridsen II, Lahn and other Republicans offered condolences to the family. The Lahn campaign said they were supportive of the Democrat’s decision to withdraw from a debate following his brother-in-law’s death, saying in a statement, “some things are bigger than politics.”

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Utah Supreme Court Justice Jill Pohlman on track to keep her place on the bench
description: Preliminary election night results show Utah Supreme Court Associate Chief Justice Jill Pohlman got nearly 79% of the vote, putting her on track to keep her seat on the state’s highest court. Pohlman, first appointed in 2022 by Utah Gov. Spencer Cox, was the only Utah Supreme Court justice up for retention election this year […]
text:
Jay Jorgensen (left) greets Utah Supreme Court Associate Chief Justice Jill Pohlman after a news conference announcing Cox's appointment of Jorgensen and Stephen Dent to the Utah Supreme Court at the Utah Capitol in Salt Lake City on June 2, 2026. (Katie McKellar/Utah News Dispatch)Preliminary election night results show Utah Supreme Court Associate Chief Justice Jill Pohlman got nearly 79% of the vote, putting her on track to keep her seat on the state’s highest court. 
Pohlman, first appointed in 2022 by Utah Gov. Spencer Cox, was the only Utah Supreme Court justice up for retention election this year after former Justice Diana Hagen resigned amid controversy earlier this year. 
Pohlman is also one of two remaining women on the court — which flipped from a female majority to a minority after the Utah Legislature revamped it, expanding it from five to seven seats. 
The court has also seen dramatic turnover in the past year, not only due to Hagen’s resignation but also because of the retirements of former Chief Justice Matthew Durrant and former Associate Chief Justice John Pearce. 
Senate confirms 2 more Utah Supreme Court justices, capping off era of change for the court

Utah Gov. Spencer Cox and the Republican-supermajority Utah Senate filled all of those openings on the bench — plus the two expanded seats — with five men. 
Pohlman was targeted by the Utah Republican Party and other conservative organizations this election season for joining in rulings against the GOP-controlled Legislature in two high-profile cases over redistricting and abortion. 
One was an anti-gerrymandering lawsuit over Utah’s 2018 voter-approved ballot initiative that banned partisan gerrymandering and created an independent redistricting process. That case has resulted in this year’s court-ordered congressional map. 
The other, brought by Planned Parenthood Association of Utah, has so far blocked the state’s near-total abortion ban from taking effect. 
During the Utah GOP’s nominating convention in April, party Chair Rob Axson urged state delegates to vote against retaining both Pohlman and Hagen — before Hagen resigned while under pressure from state leaders calling for an independent investigation into previously dismissed allegations that she had an affair with an attorney representing plaintiffs in the redistricting lawsuit. 
“We’re coming for you,” Axson said during the convention in April. “Justice Hagen and Justice Pohlman, go find a job in the private sector. We don’t want you anymore.”
The July 2024 Utah Supreme Court opinion in the redistricting case that has caught Republican legislators’ ire remanded the previously dismissed lawsuit back to district court, making clear that the Legislature’s power to change “government reform” ballot initiatives has limits. 
That 2024 opinion was unanimous, with all five justices, including Pohlman, ruling against the Legislature. 
Earlier this month, on Oct. 20, the conservative Utah Eagle Forum — which advocates against abortions — sent an email urging supporters to vote against Pohlman due to how she ruled in the lawsuit brought by the Planned Parenthood Association of Utah. 
Ex-Utah Supreme Court justice urges voters to retain judges amid push to unseat her former colleague

After Roe v. Wade (the landmark U.S. Supreme Court decision that established a constitutional right to an abortion) was overturned, the Utah Legislature’s “trigger” near-total abortion ban became law — until Planned Parenthood sued and a district court judge issued an order that temporarily blocked it from taking effect while the lawsuit played out in court. Since then, abortion in Utah has remained legal up to 18 weeks gestation. 
“When the case reached the Utah Supreme Court, the Justices, including Jill Pohlman, voted to uphold the injunction, and babies continued to die,” the Utah Eagle Forum email said. “JUDGE POHLMAN AGREED WITH PLANNED PARENTHOOD.”
In that 4-1 opinion in the abortion case issued in July 2024, Pohlman and three other justices affirmed the district court’s decision to block enforcement of the ban while the challenge was litigated. Former Chief Justice Matthew Durrant authored a dissenting opinion. 
In the face of campaigns against her, Pohlman has stayed silent. Utah judicial rules prohibit judges from campaigning for themselves. 
But Hagen, in the weeks leading up to the election, spoke out on social media urging voters to retain judges in order to preserve an “independent, non-political judiciary.” 
“Some people want judges to behave like politicians,” Hagen said in a video posted on LinkedIn. “They want them to make decisions based on their political views instead of based on the law. And those people are going to vote ‘no’ on the judges on their ballot, in the hopes that the next judge who’s appointed will do what they want them to do rather than what the law requires.” 
The Utah State Bar earlier this year issued a statement urging Utah voters to rely on evaluations from the Utah Judicial Performance Evaluation Commission, noting the state’s judges operate in a “merit-based” rather than political system. 
“Judges are bound by ethical obligations to apply the law as written, even when doing so may be unpopular,” Bar Executive Director Elizabeth Wright said in a statement in April. “Disagreement with a specific ruling should not be the basis for removal. A fair court system depends on judges who apply the law consistently for all, without being swayed by public or political pressure.”
Is Utah’s new 3-judge panel unconstitutional? Utah Supreme Court hears arguments

Pohlman’s retention election comes during a time of ongoing tension between the judiciary and the GOP-controlled Utah Legislature, which reached boiling point in the wake of the abortion and redistricting rulings and prompted the Legislature to pass several laws to make changes to the courts. 
In addition to expanding the Utah Supreme Court from five to seven seats, lawmakers have removed justices’ ability to choose their own chief justice and instead put that decision in the hands of the governor and the Utah Senate. 
The Legislature also created a new three-judge panel meant specifically to hear constitutional challenges to state laws — leading to legal fights over whether that court structure itself is unconstitutional. 
That question is being tested in three cases — over redistricting, abortion and fossil fuel development. Earlier this month, the newly expanded Utah Supreme Court heard arguments in those cases over the three-judge panel. It has not yet issued a decision.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Shomari Figures wins reelection in AL-02, overcoming Republican gerrymander
description: U.S. Rep. Shomari Figures, D-Montgomery, won reelection Tuesday to Alabama’s 2nd Congressional District, defeating Alabama Rep. Rhett Marques, R-Enterprise, and overcoming a legislative gerrymander meant to favor a Republican candidate. According to the Associated Press, as of 9:55 p.m., Figures had over 125,000 votes (55%). Marques had over 105,000 votes (4[...]
text:
U.S. Congressman Shomari Figures, D-Montgomery, addresses the crowd during his Election Night watch party in Montgomery on Nov. 3, 2026. Figures won re-election to Alabama's 2nd Congressional District Tuesday night. (Andrea Tinker/Alabama Reflector) U.S. Rep. Shomari Figures, D-Montgomery, won reelection Tuesday to Alabama’s 2nd Congressional District, defeating Alabama Rep. Rhett Marques, R-Enterprise, and overcoming a legislative gerrymander meant to favor a Republican candidate.
According to the Associated Press, as of 9:55 p.m., Figures had over 125,000 votes (55%). Marques had over 105,000 votes (45%). Marques conceded in the race Tuesday night.
The victory was a rebuke to the GOP-dominated Legislature’s move in May, at the behest of President Donald Trump, to redraw the state’s congressional maps after the U.S. Supreme Court weakened the Voting Rights Act in its Louisiana v. Callais decision. Following a special session of the Legislature this spring and a Supreme Court order, Alabama’s 1st, 2nd, 6th and 7th Congressional Districts were altered, allowing the state to use a 2023 Legislature-approved congressional map instead.
The new map reduced the Black Voting Age Population in the district from about 49% to just under 40% and was widely considered to be a GOP pick-up.
Addressing a crowd of at least 100 people Tuesday night, Figures said “we had the deck stacked against us.”
“I stood in a Senate committee hearing room that bears my father’s name, and I pleaded with the state legislature to not do what they ultimately did,” he said. “And we know what they did, but as anyone who has ever been part of a sibling relationship knows, that at some point, someday, whether by deed or by action, you make the point that we ain’t kids anymore. … And Montgomery tonight, we made that point loud.”
Figures ran on affordability issues as well as improving access to healthcare. He cited his work in Congress to keep Jackson Hospital in Montgomery open and a bill that would cover the full cost of higher education tuition, fees and books and job training opportunities for the dependents of educators, first responders and social workers who have at least 20 years of qualifying service.
Figures also tapped into Democratic anger over the U.S. Supreme Court’s Callais decision, weakening the Voting Rights Act, and subsequent redistricting, which drove Black turnout around the South.
Marques ran on affordability, pledging to lower taxes and create safe communities while touting his endorsement from President Donald Trump, promising to be an ally of the president if elected. 
Marques said in a statement Tuesday night while the results aren’t what he hoped for, “we are proud of the campaign we ran on Alabama common sense.”
“Alabama values will always be worth fighting for, and Christina and I are deeply grateful to everyone who supported, prayed for and worked alongside us throughout this campaign,” the statement said.
The two candidates traded barbs throughout the election. Figures attacked Marques’ vote to raise the gas tax in the state as part of the Rebuild Alabama Act, which had broad support in the Legislature, and criticized his ties to Trump telling al.com that “he’s in trouble because gas is high and he’s part of the reason why.”
Marques criticized Figures for voting against the One Big Beautiful Bill Act and taking money from out-of-state donors. 
Both candidates received outside money during the race, according to federal campaign finance records. Marques received nearly $4.9 million from political action committees and Figures received more than $1.9 million from PACs.
In a statement last year following the passage of the One Big Beautiful Bill, Figures said he voted against it because it was “nothing more than a handout for the rich” and “if we are going to spend more money, it should be to help Americans across the country keep a roof over their heads, clothes on their backs, and food on their tables.”
According to federal campaign finance reports, Figures raised $2.7 million and spent $1.5 million through Oct. 14. Marques raised $1.7 milion and spent $1.5 million through Oct. 14.
As of 10:34 p.m., four of Alabama’s five U.S. House incumbents — Figures; U.S. Rep. Mike Rogers, R-Saks; U.S. Rep. Robert Aderholt, R-Haleyville; U.S. Rep. Dale Strong, R-Madison;  and U.S. Rep Terri Sewell, D-Birmingham — had been re-elected. Jerry Carl, won re-election to the Alabama’s 1st Congressional District, which he represented from 2021 to 2025. AP had not called Alabama’s 6th Congressional District, where U.S. Rep. Gary Palmer, R-Hoover, was challenged by former Pelham City Council President Maurice Mercer.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Nebraska voters soundly reject proposal to extend legislative term limits
description: Nebraska’s state senators will remain limited to two consecutive four-year terms after voters rejected a constitutional amendment that would extend them. Constitutional Amendment 1 was on track to be rejected at the ballot box as of 10 p.m. Tuesday night, with 69,100 yes votes against 290,202 no votes, according to unofficial results. The measure would […]
text:
State Sen. Robert Dover of Norfolk holds a stack of binders containing the budgetary work spearheaded by the Legislature's Appropriations Committee. March 12, 2024. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)Nebraska’s state senators will remain limited to two consecutive four-year terms after voters rejected a constitutional amendment that would extend them.
Constitutional Amendment 1 was on track to be rejected at the ballot box as of 10 p.m. Tuesday night, with 69,100 yes votes against 290,202 no votes, according to unofficial results. The measure would have increased term limits in the state Legislature to a maximum of three consecutive terms instead of two.


Nebraskans implemented the current limits of two four-year terms for state senators via a voter-led initiative in 2000. It passed with 55.8% of the vote. Senators can sit out one term after being term-limited and run again.
The ballot measure came from Legislative Resolution 19CA, which state Sen. Rob Dover of Norfolk introduced in 2025. The resolution passed 39-10 in the Legislature, which put the proposal on the 2026 ballot.
Dover and other supporters of the amendment argued that eight years is too short for lawmakers to get a full grasp on how best to approach the job. Because Nebraska’s legislative sessions usually run 60-90 days each year, Dover said, eight years in office translates to about two-and-a-half years in session.
Several term-limited senators have noted that their last year in office is when they finally understand everything they need to do to accomplish their goals.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
From the beginning, supporters of the amendment knew getting voter approval would be an uphill battle. Dover said last week that he believed the current political environment isn’t welcoming to ideas of increasing political term limits, and said he believes most Nebraska voters don’t fully understand all the benefits.
“You wouldn’t pick a young quarterback Husker … and just when they’re starting to make some plays, kick them out,” Dover said. “That’s exactly what’s going on.”
Dover said given the current president and the public mindset against career politicians, he believes Nebraska lawmakers have been lumped in with the negativity. He argued that most Nebraskans don’t realize that shorter term limits in the Legislature have drawbacks, as the group of people who understand the inner workings of the Legislature are in the minority among state voters.
Despite his pessimism at the measure’s chances at the ballot box, Dover said he doesn’t regret introducing the constitutional amendment. Even if it fails, he said the vote count will give lawmakers more information about how current voters feel about term limits.
“I did my job to make Nebraska a better place and give the people’s voice a better chance at not being limited,” Dover said.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Republican US Sen. Tom Cotton wins reelection to seat in Arkansas
description: Republican U.S. Sen. Tom Cotton won reelection to his Arkansas seat Tuesday, fending off a challenge from Democrat Hallie Shoffner who focused on how tariffs and rising fuel prices were hurting the state’s farmers.  Cotton defeated Shoffner and Libertarian Jeff Wadlin, winning a third term to the Senate. The Associated Press called the race at […]
text:
Arkansas Republican U.S. Sen. Tom Cotton takes a few questions from media at Republican Party headquarters in downtown Little Rock Tuesday evening after being declared winner of his party’s primary. (Photo by John Sykes Jr./Arkansas Advocate)Republican U.S. Sen. Tom Cotton won reelection to his Arkansas seat Tuesday, fending off a challenge from Democrat Hallie Shoffner who focused on how tariffs and rising fuel prices were hurting the state’s farmers. 
Cotton defeated Shoffner and Libertarian Jeff Wadlin, winning a third term to the Senate. The Associated Press called the race at 9:40 p.m. 
With 84% of the vote counted, Cotton had a 12-point lead over Shoffner with nearly 396,000 votes. Shoffner received nearly 307,000 votes and Wadlin received more than 22,000.
In a statement, Cotton said he will “continue fighting for good jobs, safe streets, secure borders, and a strong military.”
“Tonight, Arkansans voted to defend the conservative values of faith, family, and freedom that have made our state great,” Cotton said.
Cotton, the chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee and the chamber’s third-ranked Republican, was elected to the U.S. House in 2012 and unseated Democratic U.S. Sen. Mark Pryor in 2014. 
Cotton easily won reelection in 2020 against only a Libertarian opponent after the Democratic candidate dropped out after the filing period.
Arkansas U.S. Senate candidate Hallie Shoffner waves at cars at Broadway and 9th Streets in Little Rock, Arkansas on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Katie Adkins/Arkansas Advocate)
A close ally of President Donald Trump, Cotton has been a vocal supporter of strict immigration enforcement and the ongoing war in Iran. He has also touted his support for the growth of Arkansas’ defense industry, including an upcoming multibillion-dollar artillery ammunition plant in Pine Bluff.
Cotton and Republican allies had heavily outspent Shoffner in the race, with ads portraying her as soft on immigration and too closely allied with national Democrats like former Vice President Kamala Harris.
Most political forecasters predicted Cotton’s win, though the Almanac of American Politics moved Arkansas’ U.S. Senate race from safe to “likely” Republican in October. Democrats have not won a statewide or U.S. House race in Arkansas since 2010.
“The people in Arkansas are worth fighting for,” Shoffner posted on Facebook Tuesday night. “Believe in Arkansas.”
Shoffner chose to challenge Cotton after she closed her family’s 150-year-old Jackson County soybean farm due to tariffs imposed by the Trump administration. Pitching herself as an everyday Arkansan without ties to special interest groups, Shoffner’s campaign gained national attention for her social media presence and her focus on her rural background.
Shoffner has regularly criticized Cotton’s past votes against the Farm Bill, the federal agriculture spending and policy package that Congress regularly renews. Cotton has said past versions of the bill allocated too much money to food aid programs such as the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program.
Senate Democrats have opposed the current Farm Bill recently endorsed by the Senate Agriculture Committee because of SNAP cuts, but Shoffner said she would have voted to advance the bill to give farmers financial aid.
SNAP will face spending cuts and higher administrative costs as of Jan. 1 thanks to the One Big Beautiful Bill Act of 2025. The sweeping federal tax and spending legislation, which Cotton supported and Trump signed last year, will also cut Medicaid spending starting in 2027. Medicaid serves more than 800,000 low-income and disabled Arkansans.
During their campaigns, Shoffner and Wadlin portrayed Cotton as uninterested in the needs of everyday Arkansans and criticized his absence from two debates hosted by nonpartisan TV outlets in October.
Cotton and Shoffner had agreed to a debate hosted by Salem Media Group, a conservative Christian outlet, before it retracted the offer in October.
Wadlin said he was not invited to the Salem Media debate.
Cotton had distanced himself from Trump on some issues, including opposing the president’s plan to allow more foreign beef imports.
Trump also criticized Cotton for opposing a bill that would make daylight saving time permanent. The president posted Cotton’s cellphone number in a post on his Truth Social account over the dispute.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Utah Amendment B to set 60% bar for ballot initiatives that increase taxes on track to fail
description: Preliminary election night results show Utahns rejecting the Utah Legislature’s proposed constitutional amendment to make it harder for ballot initiatives that come with tax increases to pass into law.  Amendment B — which would require certain citizen-proposed laws to be approved by at least 60% of voters instead of a simple majority as currently required [[...]
text:
Protesters hold up signs against amendments A and B during the No Kings protest at the Utah Capitol on Saturday, Oct 17, 2026. (Photo by Marco Lozzi for Utah News Dispatch)Preliminary election night results show Utahns rejecting the Utah Legislature’s proposed constitutional amendment to make it harder for ballot initiatives that come with tax increases to pass into law. 
Amendment B — which would require certain citizen-proposed laws to be approved by at least 60% of voters instead of a simple majority as currently required in the Utah Constitution — had only 37% approval after polls closed at 8 p.m. Tuesday night. About 63% voted to reject it.
If approved, Amendment B’s 60% threshold requirement would apply to ballot initiatives that increase taxes, either by creating a new tax, expanding an existing tax, hiking an existing tax rate, or changing a property tax rate in a way that results in a smaller decrease in the property tax rate than would occur under existing law. 
Another proposed constitutional amendment lawmakers put on this year’s ballot was Amendment A, which would strip out the explicit requirement for all other future proposed constitutional amendments to be published in newspapers before an election, instead replacing it with a more flexible rule that would be set by lawmakers. 
Amendment A was on track to pass, with nearly 60% voting in favor.
What’s up with amendments A & B? Lawmakers are asking voters to change the Utah Constitution (again)

Election results aren’t final until county and state canvasses are completed in two weeks. 
Of the two amendments, Amendment B stirred the most controversy — and attracted more than $3 million in spending in an effort to shoot it down.  
Critics launched a political issues committee, Utahns Protecting Our Constitution, to finance a multimillion-dollar campaign urging Utah voters to vote down Amendment B. 
Groups that joined that effort included Better Boundaries, which successfully sponsored an anti-gerrymandering ballot initiative in 2018 that created an independent redistricting process. 
They argued Amendment B would be an “unnecessary and permanent rewrite of Utah’s founding document that would weaken one of the most important tools citizens have to hold government accountable.” Democrats also opposed it, arguing it would allow legislators to have more power by requiring voters to face stricter rules than the Legislature itself. 
Under Amendment B’s increased approval threshold, Utahns’ 2018 ballot initiatives expanding Medicaid and legalizing medicinal cannabis would have failed.
Amendment B’s supporters, including the Utah Republican Party, GOP legislators and the Utah Taxpayers Association, argued the change would help protect taxpayer money, and it should be harder for ballot initiatives that raise taxes to pass at the ballot box. 
Barret Peterson drops off his ballot in a drop box outside the Main Library in Salt Lake City on Election Day, Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)
Jason Perry, director of the University of Utah’s Hinkley Institute of Politics, told KUER that Amendment B’s fate hinges on how Utah voters feel about the balance of power between themselves and their Legislature — and if the Legislature should have more power over certain issues, like tax increases, than the people.
“It’s about our elected officials and the amount of power the people are willing to give them,” he said. “When it comes to raising taxes, should there be a higher threshold or not? Keep in mind our constitution is very clear that the powers … are co-equal between the people and the Legislature. And this amendment kind of gets to what kind of power the people would like our Legislature to have. And also, for the people themselves, for certain issues relating to taxes, whether or not there should be a higher threshold for things like that. That’s really what’s at the heart of this.” 
If Amendment B fails, Perry said “it’s a reminder that the voters can make distinctions” about how far they want their Legislature’s power to go.
“They can trust their elected representatives to make policy decisions, but they will intervene at some point if they get to a position where they don’t like the direction,” Perry said. “It’s not one that can just be taken for granted. They can trust their elected officials. They can even like them, but it doesn’t mean they’re not interested in preserving their own ability to make change on their own.”
Ahead of Election Day, a poll conducted by Noble Predictive Insights indicated Amendment B was headed for trouble. It showed 56% opposed it, 34% would vote in favor, and 10% were undecided. 
That survey was conducted Oct. 26 and 27 of 527 likely general election voters, with a margin of error of plus or minus 4.27 percentage points. 
A voter uses a drive up ballot box outside the Main Library in Salt Lake City on Election Day, Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)People line up outside a polling location at the Main Library in Salt Lake City on Election Day, Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)
In response to those poll results, Utah GOP Chair Rob Axson issued a statement saying “Utah public opinion has consistently shown that Utahns oppose higher taxes,” and that the survey comes “after efforts by special interests with hidden liberal agendas to confuse and complicate the discussion” over Amendment B. 
Utahns Protecting our Constitution spent more than $3.1 million on the campaign opposing Amendment B, which included radio and TV ads, mailers and social media efforts, according to the group’s campaign finance disclosures.
Of the more than $3.1 million contributed to Utahns Protecting Our Constitution, the Fairness Project, based in Washington, D.C., contributed about $1.6 million toward the effort.
That group has launched ballot measure campaigns in states across the country, including efforts to oppose abortion restrictions, raise the minimum wage, expand Medicaid, reform redistricting and “protect the ballot measure process against attempts to diminish voters’ rights to use direct democracy,” the Fairness Project’s website says. 
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
Axson argued those out-of-state donations thumbed the scale toward “liberal” special interests rather than Utahns’ best interests.
“Amendment B puts families first by requiring broad public support before new taxes can be imposed,” Axson said. “Utah’s future should be decided by Utah voters, not deep-pocketed national interest groups.”
A spokesperson for Utahns Protecting our Constitution said in a statement in response to the poll results and Axson’s comments that “Utahns are recognizing Amendment B for what it is, another attempt by the Legislature to usurp their power as citizens. We continue to encourage Utahns to vote and reject this power grab.”
“This campaign has been led by Utahns, for Utahns,” Utahns Protecting or Constitution said. “More than 80% of our donors are from within the state, and that doesn’t even account for the countless hours Utahns have spent knocking doors, spreading the word online, and talking with friends and family. Time and time again, Utahns are showing up to protect their power and preserve their ability to keep politicians in check.”

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Attorney general of South Dakota wins election to US House
description: South Dakota’s Republican attorney general was elected to the state’s only U.S. House seat on Tuesday. Marty Jackley led his Democratic opponent, Nikki Gronli, 65% to 35% when The Associated Press called the race at 10:03 p.m. with 43% of the votes counted statewide. Jackley will take over in January for the departing Republican Rep. […]
text:
South Dakota Attorney General Marty Jackley talks to reporters on June 23, 2026, outside the federal courthouse in Rapid City. (Photo by Seth Tupper/South Dakota Searchlight)South Dakota’s Republican attorney general was elected to the state’s only U.S. House seat on Tuesday.
Marty Jackley led his Democratic opponent, Nikki Gronli, 65% to 35% when The Associated Press called the race at 10:03 p.m. with 43% of the votes counted statewide.
Jackley will take over in January for the departing Republican Rep. Dusty Johnson, who unsuccessfully sought the Republican nomination for governor in the June primary election.
The 56-year-old Jackley has been attorney general since 2022 and previously served as attorney general from 2009 to 2019, following a stint as U.S. attorney for South Dakota. When he leaves the Attorney General’s Office in January, he’ll be succeeded by Republican Lance Russell of Hot Springs, who ran unopposed for attorney general on Tuesday.
Gronli previously served as director of rural development for the U.S. Department of Agriculture during President Joe Biden’s administration and as vice chairperson of the South Dakota Democratic Party.
Polling commissioned by South Dakota News Watch and the Chiesman Center for Democracy showed 61% of likely voters still did not recognize Gronli’s name as of three weeks ago, while 60% recognized Jackley from his many years in statewide office. Jackley also out-fundraised and outspent Gronli, and had a built-in advantage with Republican voter registrations that outnumber Democrats 2-to-1.

Sept. 30, 2025 | Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan AdvanceState Rep. Donavan McKinney (D-Detroit) will succeed U.S. Rep. Shri Thanedar to represent Michigan’s 13th Congressional District. 
McKinney defeated Republican T.P. Nykoriak with 75.5% of the vote, according to unofficial results shared by the Associated Press, which called the race at 10:33 p.m..
Michigan Democratic Party Chair Curtis Hertel congratulated McKinney on his victory in a statement.
“As a labor organizer and state representative, Donavan has the values and experience we need to fight and deliver for Detroiters in the halls of Congress. His leadership will be key to making the wealthy pay their fair share, expanding access to healthcare and housing, and making sure every Michigander has a fair shot, no matter their zip code.”
The Working Families Party, a minor political party backing progressive candidates, also cheered McKinney’s victory.
“WFP champion Donavan McKinney defeated a sitting Congressman in the primary, despite millions in spending from corporate and crypto interests,” Branden Snyder, state director for the Michigan Working Families Party, said in a statement. “ Now he’s heading to Congress to fight for the community that raised him. We know that Donavan will fight with everything he has to protect the rights of workers and unions, stand up to corporate greed, and bring back investments to Michigan’s 13th Congressional District.”
This is a developing story and will be updated as more information becomes available.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: A victorious Rebecca Bennett says voters can soon ‘turn the page on the Trump era’
description: Rep.-elect Rebecca Bennett (D) celebrated Tuesday night in front of jubilant supporters in a packed Bridgewater ballroom after she ousted GOP Rep. Tom Kean Jr.
text:
Rep.-elect Rebecca Bennett (D) speaks during her victory party in Bridgewater on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)Democrat Rebecca Bennett defeated Republican Rep. Tom Kean Jr., the scion of one of New Jersey’s most famous political dynasties, in Tuesday’s midterm elections, riding a “tsunami of blue” that Democrats say was set in motion by growing public disgust with President Donald Trump and his administration’s policies.
Bennett, a former Navy helicopter pilot and healthcare executive making her first run for office, went into Election Day favored to win by a narrow margin. Instead, she walloped Kean, with voters giving her 58% of the vote to Kean’s 40%.
“Something remarkable is happening here in New Jersey and across the country,” Bennett told jubilant supporters in a packed ballroom at Bridgewater Manor. “This is the moment we begin to turn the page on the Trump era!”
Leroy Jones, the Democratic state chairman, took the stage shortly after 9 p.m. It was nearly an hour before the race was officially called, but already, his voice was hoarse from celebrating as Republican incumbents around the country fell to Democratic challengers. In New Jersey alone, two of three GOP House incumbents — Kean and Rep. Jeff Van Drew in South Jersey — lost their bids for re-election.
“This is a tsunami of blue, and it’s all because of you!” he wheezed at the cheering crowd. “I’m not trying to rhyme here. I’m no poet, but I’m just a Democratic chairperson who’s in his glory tonight because the people have spoken and they said yes to humanity, no to Donald Trump, yes to Rebecca Bennett! The 7th District has spoken loudly, and we are going to bask in that glory!”
Somerset County Democratic Chairwoman Peg Schaffer put it more succinctly.
“We’re kicking ass all over the country!” Schaffer shouted.
Bennett took the stage just before 10 p.m. and said she’d talked to Kean by phone — and that he’d conceded gracefully.
“He congratulated me on our victory, and he expressed his commitment to the peaceful transition of power,” Bennett said.
Kean, whose father was governor from 1982 to 1990 and whose ancestor was New Jersey’s first elected governor, closed his watch party to the press and public. His team had not issued any public statements as of Tuesday night.
Bennett took the stage with a sunny smile and spoke for about 10 minutes, sticking to the script and the overriding message she has repeated to voters throughout the campaign: “No one is coming to save us.”
“With corruption in the White House, a war in Iran, and a nation more divided than ever, we have real challenges ahead of us to solve,” she said. “But I believe our best days as a nation are yet to come. Tonight we have sent a message that we are not giving up on this country that we love! We are getting to work!”
She credited a groundswell of grassroots support with helping mobilize voters to the polls, saying almost 2,000 volunteers knocked on more than 200,000 doors and made a half million calls during her campaign.
Earlier, Gov. Mikie Sherrill — “the other Navy helicopter pilot,” she joked — congratulated supporters for delivering the district a win that’s expected to help Democrats flip the House.
“It is not OK to have a president of the United States who is corrupt and lining his own pockets. It is not OK in the richest country in the world to have working people struggling so hard. And so you knew, New Jersey 7, that you wanted a leader. You wanted somebody who was going to find a way, or make one. You wanted a badass,” she said. “You guys won it!”
During the campaign, Bennett had promised to focus on improving affordability, healthcare access, national security, and veterans’ services if she made it to Congress. She also frequently accused Trump and his administration of corruption. At her victory party, she vowed to work on banning members of Congress from trading stocks and getting dark money out of politics.
Sue Altman was all in.
Altman challenged Kean in 2024 and lost, so she was eager to see Bennett prevail. She described Bennett’s victory as a referendum on Trump, with voters rejecting America’s “downward spiral” since his second term began.
“I know Rebecca will be a brilliant member of Congress,” Altman said.
Jones was looking even further ahead.
“If the trend continues, folks, the Senate will be blue!” he shouted. “There will be a firewall up. Donald Trump will be down, and the people of America can once again say that our tomorrow is bright and shiny. But we will continue to fight through ’27 and ’28, because we are going to take back the White House as we’ve taken back Congress tonight! Tonight is a good night!”

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Denise Powell becomes the first Democrat in a decade to represent Nebraska’s 2nd District
description: Powell will serve two years in the U.S. House. She is the first Latina and first woman to be elected from the 2nd District.
text:
2nd Congressional District Democratic nominee Denise Powell speaks at a campaign event in North Omaha on Oct, 29. 2026. (Photo by Juan Salinas II/Nebraska Examiner)OMAHA — Democrat Denise Powell easily won against Republican Brinker Harding to represent Nebraska’s 2nd Congressional District, the state’s most politically divided and diverse district.
Harding conceded the race around roughly 9:03 p.m. Tuesday. The Associated Press called the race for her shortly before 11 p.m., when Powell led with 57.7% of the vote to Harding’s 40%, with 72% of votes counted.
“Tonight they chose common sense over chaos,” Powell told a hall of fist-bumping supporters when she delivered her victory speech about 9:25 p.m. “You helped send a clear message to 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue.”
Powell, who co-founded a group that coached local women how to run for office, was able to win a Democratic nomination in the heated May primary. The race to represent the slightly red-leaning 2nd District saw the two campaigns trying to paint each other as extreme throughout the campaign. In the last few weeks of the race, the two candidates have accused each other of benefiting from PAC spending and making late tax payments.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The 2nd District is a swing district that typically draws national attention. Notable Democrats and Republicans have campaigned there. Former U.S. Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg campaigned for Powell; House Speaker Mike Johnson visited the district for Harding.
Harding told the audience at his watch party that Powell “is gonna get more votes than we do. You might notice too, if you’ve been looking at the returns, we’re seeing a lot of this happen across the country.”
“It is truly an honor, and for all of you here tonight, you know, this was a fight we all took together. You are the rest of this team, and I’m sorry that I couldn’t lead the team to a better result,” Harding said. “But as I said, we have other races to win, and you will help us in that regard, I hope, in the next endeavor.”
Libertarian Eric Michael Foreman received 2.4% of the vote, according to unofficial results. 
Powell will serve two years in the U.S. House. She is the first Latina and the first woman to be elected to federal office in Nebraska.
