title: Democrat Sherrod Brown defeats Republican Jon Husted in Ohio US Senate race, AP projects
description: Former Ohio Democratic U.S. Sen. Sherrod Brown will again represent Ohioans in the U.S. Senate, after defeating Republican incumbent U.S. Sen. Jon Husted. The Associated Press projected the Brown victory at 11:11 p.m. Brown, 73, was projected the winner Tuesday in a special election. Husted was appointed by Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine to fill Vice […]
text:
Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Sherrod Brown speaks during a campaign rally at UAW 1250 on November 01, 2026 in Cleveland, Ohio. (Photo by Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images)Former Ohio Democratic U.S. Sen. Sherrod Brown will again represent Ohioans in the U.S. Senate, after defeating Republican incumbent U.S. Sen. Jon Husted. The Associated Press projected the Brown victory at 11:11 p.m.
Brown, 73, was projected the winner Tuesday in a special election. Husted was appointed by Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine to fill Vice President JD Vance’s seat at the start of 2025. 
The call came in the midst of what appeared to be a big night for Democrats amid voter anger at President Donald Trump, a Republican.
Husted has served a 25-year career in Ohio politics. But in the 2026 midterm, he ran in a highly nationalized election. 
Husted voted in support of unpopular measures such as tax cuts for the rich, cuts to healthcare, against releasing the Epstein files, in support of the Iran war, and to protect Trump’s tariffs, which many economists say made inflation worse.
Brown also painted Husted as “the face of data centers,” and Brown highlighted Husted’s involvement in a scandal in which an Akron-based FirstEnergy paid $61 million in bribes to get a $1.3 billion ratepayer bailout.
Brown said Husted was an out-of-touch tool of wealthy interests.
“They say you’re the company you keep,” Brown said at a rally on Monday night. “I want to talk about the kind of people Jon Husted surrounds himself with. Jon Husted had to testify in a criminal trial in defense of the indicted FirstEnergy utility executives in the state’s largest bribery scandal ever.”
While Brown again poised to carry Ohio, he failed to do it with new support from rural voters, said Lee Hannah, a political scientist at Wright State University.
“From what I can tell, Sherrod Brown is not doing better in rural Ohio,” Hannah said. “But in some of these suburban counties and some of the cities, he’s up about 5% if those margins hold. My guess is that he didn’t convert a lot of people in rural areas, but turnout wasn’t as high there.”
He said Brown has only two years before he has to run again, but he could work as a senator to gain support from rural Ohio.
“I would love to see a scenario where they don’t just investigate President Trump, but they also turn around some of these affordability issues,” Hannah said. “If he shows that he is delivering, we can see a turn in some of those numbers.”
As is the case in so many races Republicans didn’t expect to lose, Trump played a central role in the Ohio U.S. Senate contest.
First, he picked then-Sen. JD Vance to be his 2024 running mate. That required the state to conduct a special Senate election when Vance still would have had four years left in his term. So there wouldn’t have even been an Ohio Senate election on Tuesday.
In addition, then0-Lt. Gov. Husted and then-Ohio Attorney General Dave Yost had long been jockeying for the governorship after current Gov. Mike DeWine retired in January. But Trump endorsed Cincinnati billionaire Vivek Ramaswamy, clearing them from the field.
That left DeWine to appoint Husted to the Senate seat vacated by Husted, and set up Tuesday’s loss for Republicans. In the end, Husted and Ramaswamy lost in what had been an increasingly Republican state.
Brown, 73, was born in Mansfield. He holds an undergraduate degree from Yale University and a master’s from Ohio State. He was a state representative from 1975 to 1982, Ohio secretary of state from 1983 to 1991, and a congressman from 1993 to 2007.
Then-Sen. Mike DeWine was the Republican incumbent in 2006 — another midterm year when the Republican president was unpopular.
So from the time Brown entered the race this year, both parties had reason to know it would be a squeaker. They have spent accordingly.
With more than $500 million dropped on ads and ad reservations by the end of October, the Ohio Senate race is the second-most expensive this cycle and one of the 10 most expensive non-presidential races in U.S. history, The Hill reported last week.

title: Fayette Circuit judge beats Beshear-backed opponent for Court of Appeals seat
description: A Fayette Circuit Court judge has defeated a judge appointed by Gov. Andy Beshear in a Kentucky Court of Appeals race.  Voters in the 5th Appellate District backed Judge Lucy VanMeter over Court of Appeals Judge Will Moynahan Tuesday evening by a margin of 51%. Beshear had appointed Moynahan in 2025 after Justice Pamela Goodwine […]
text:
Lucy VanMeter being sworn in as a circuit judge by former Chief Justice John Minton. Her husband, former Chief Justice Laurance VanMeter holds the Bible. (Photo courtesy Lucy VanMeter campaign)A Fayette Circuit Court judge has defeated a judge appointed by Gov. Andy Beshear in a Kentucky Court of Appeals race. 
Voters in the 5th Appellate District backed Judge Lucy VanMeter over Court of Appeals Judge Will Moynahan Tuesday evening by a margin of 51%.
Beshear had appointed Moynahan in 2025 after Justice Pamela Goodwine was elected to the Kentucky Supreme Court. 
A watchdog group, the Kentucky Judicial Campaign Conduct Committee, questioned increasing partisan activity in the race as judicial races have long been nonpartisan in state history. The committee issued a statement in June saying it was wary of Beshear’s involvement in fundraising for Moynahan. Later, the committee’s chairman, Charles Boteler, told Kentucky Public Radio Democratic and Republican involvement in the race was concerning. KPR found more than a dozen GOP state lawmakers donated to VanMeter, including members of leadership. 
VanMeter was elected to the Fayette Circuit Court in 2018. Before that, she was part of law firm toll Keenon Ogden. She has degrees from DePauw University and the University of Kentucky College of Law. She is married to former Kentucky Supreme Court Chief Justice Laurance VanMeter. 
The 5th Appellate District includes Fayette, Madison, Franklin, Scott, Jessamine, Woodford, Clark and Bourbon counties.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison elected to third term
description: Minnesota voters re-elected Democratic Attorney General Keith Ellison to a third term Tuesday, handing him another four years to pursue his pledge to be a check on the Trump administration and large corporations.  Ellison beat out Republican patent lawyer and conservative activist Ron Schutz, who ran a largely sleepy campaign that included few public events [...]
text:
Attorney General Keith Ellison speaks after being endorsed at the 2026 DFL State Convention Friday, May 29, 2026 in Rochester, Minnesota. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)Minnesota voters re-elected Democratic Attorney General Keith Ellison to a third term Tuesday, handing him another four years to pursue his pledge to be a check on the Trump administration and large corporations. 
Ellison beat out Republican patent lawyer and conservative activist Ron Schutz, who ran a largely sleepy campaign that included few public events and just one news conference without taking questions from reporters. 
The race still drew big outside spending, totaling more than $12 million. Republicans tried to persuade voters to oust Democratic leaders over the sprawling scandal of fraud in state-run safety net programs that has come to light in recent years.  
Ellison defended his record on fighting fraud, boasting that his Medicaid fraud unit has won more than 350 convictions during his tenure. His office issued a flurry of news releases about cracking down on fraudsters. 
The Attorney General’s Office has served as a bulwark against the Trump administration, particularly for funding cuts to healthcare, education and food assistance. Ellison’s office has filed or joined 80 lawsuits against the Trump administration since the start of the second term, challenging tariffs, executive orders limiting birthright citizenship, Operation Metro Surge and more. 
Ellison ran with the slogan “afford your life,” a phrase he’s used long before affordability entered the national discourse. Ellison touted his record going after big corporations like John Deere and Ticketmaster as well as lesser known businesses for defrauding consumers, stealing workers’ wages and exploiting tenants. 
Ellison’s victory keeps alive major litigation against Big Oil. Ellison’s office has accused Exxon Mobil and other oil interests of defrauding Minnesotans by concealing what they knew about fossil fuel’s impact on the environment and global warming specifically. 
Schutz promised to be apolitical and lean on his experience as a trial lawyer to combat fraud and prosecute violent crime, even though the vast majority of crime is prosecuted by county attorneys, not the attorney general. He mostly avoided criticizing the Trump administration, but he also would not say if he opposed any of the lawsuits Ellison’s office filed. 
For Schutz, there is one significant upside to losing: He won’t have to relinquish control of his vast stock portfolio, which he committed to doing after the Reformer reported on his potential conflicts of interest.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: With McAdams ahead as the polls close, Utah is poised to send Democrat to Congress
description: Utah is poised to flip its 1st Congressional District blue as former U.S. House Rep. Ben McAdams leads on election night with 72% of votes, according to preliminary results posted after the polls closed Tuesday. Republican Riley Owen had 25% of votes. Libertarian Jesse West got 2% of votes, unaffiliated candidate Elias Henry Montgomery had […]
text:
Candidate for Utah’s 1st Congressional District Democrat Ben McAdams participates in a debate at Salt Lake Community College, Tuesday, Sept. 29, 2026, in Salt Lake City. (Pool photo by Erin Hooley/Deseret News)Utah is poised to flip its 1st Congressional District blue as former U.S. House Rep. Ben McAdams leads on election night with 72% of votes, according to preliminary results posted after the polls closed Tuesday. Republican Riley Owen had 25% of votes.
Libertarian Jesse West got 2% of votes, unaffiliated candidate Elias Henry Montgomery had 1%, and nonpartisan Babak “Bobby” Darvish, a last-minute write-in candidate, had less than one percent of votes.  
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
This is the first time a Democrat is set to be elected to represent Utah in Congress since McAdams lost his reelection bid in 2020 by tight margins. McAdams’ return comes at a moment when democrats are poised to reclaim the U.S. House, according to CNN. 
Utah’s election results aren’t final until county and state canvasses are completed in two weeks.
At a joint Utah Democratic Party event with candidates including Salt Lake County District Attorney Sim Gill and Democratic state Reps. Verona Mauga and John Arthur, who are seeking reelection, all eyes were on McAdams.
About 30 minutes before the results were announced, a handful of partygoers surrounded McAdams for photos, or to briefly discuss out-of-state results in which Democrats prevailed. Energy was high and smiles were big as they mentioned Georgia and North Carolina big wins.
The flip comes after a yearslong anti-gerrymandering legal fight in Utah that resulted in new congressional maps, decided in court. That included new boundaries for the 1st Congressional District, representing Salt Lake County, the state’s most populous area and a blue dot in a deep red state.
One of Utah’s hottest Democratic races shows how far left voters are willing to go 

The challenges to Utah’s congressional maps are not expected to be over any time soon. But for now, the court victory has deeply energized Democrats. McAdams’ nomination was decided in a packed primary that tested how far left voters were willing to go.
During his time in office, McAdams was considered one of the most conservative Democrats in Congress. But being “moderate” isn’t a label he’s ashamed to carry, though McAdams prefers to call himself “pragmatic.”
“Ultimately, I think the people who are counting on me, they don’t care what I say. They don’t care where I fall on the political spectrum. They care (about) what changes and makes their lives better,” McAdams told reporters after a September debate. “That’s what drives me as a public servant, is to make hard decisions, and work with people who sometimes I don’t like, certainly I don’t agree with, but to sit down with them to make the decisions, implement the policies that are going to make their lives better.”
During that debate McAdams and Owen, a naval officer and former White House staffer toward the end of President Donald Trump’s first term, agreed on some policy questions with Owen often splitting from the Trump administration’s agenda. 
Owen, however, later told reporters that what he believes to be the biggest distinction between him and his opponent, is that McAdams wants “bigger government,” while he wants more market-based incentives.
Owen was the only Utah Republican candidate Trump didn’t endorse in a social media post ahead of the election.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Republicans hold onto 2 of Arkansas’ 4 US House seats
description: Two Republicans representing deep red parts of Arkansas held onto their seats Tuesday, handily dispatching their Democratic challengers — though two of the state’s four congressional races still remain uncalled. The Associated Press called the 1st and 4th Congressional Districts for their incumbents early in the night, granting Reps. Rick Crawford and Bruce [...]
text:
U.S. Congressional District 2 candidates Democrat Chris Jones and incumbent Republican Rep. French Hill shake hands after the debate at the Arkansas TV studios in Conway, Arkansas on Thursday, Oct. 15, 2026. (Photo by Katie Adkins/Arkansas Advocate)Two Republicans representing deep red parts of Arkansas held onto their seats Tuesday, handily dispatching their Democratic challengers — though two of the state’s four congressional races still remain uncalled.
The Associated Press called the 1st and 4th Congressional Districts for their incumbents early in the night, granting Reps. Rick Crawford and Bruce Westerman a ninth and seventh term, respectively. 
The AP still has not called the 2nd Congressional District, where Republican Rep. French Hill is locked in a tight battle to represent central Arkansas with Democrat Chris Jones. The 3rd Congressional District, currently represented by Republican Rep. Steve Womack, lagged behind the other districts in reporting vote results and also remains uncalled.
Westerman, who has represented large swaths of south, west and north Arkansas since 2015, outraised and outspent his opponent James Russell by large margins.
The licensed forester from Hot Springs ran on his record as the chairman of the House Natural Resources Committee, where he has pushed for changes to the National Environmental Policy Act, as well as his support for the One Big Beautiful Bill Act that he says will help address affordability concerns stemming from the ongoing war in Iran.
Westerman, a former state legislator, defeated his 2024 Democratic opponent, Risie Howard, with more than 72% of the vote. 
“I’m honored to once again have the trust of the people of Arkansas’s Fourth Congressional District,” Westerman said in a statement provided by a spokesperson. “I’m grateful for the opportunity to continue serving and remain committed to working for Arkansas in Washington, D.C.”
 His 2026 opponent, Russell, offered Westerman congratulations after the race was called.
Crawford, who represents the 1st District, fended off both Democratic and Libertarian challengers Tuesday.
Crawford chairs the House Intelligence Committee, campaigned on supporting more infrastructure for his district covering parts of east, south and north Arkansas, as well as additional domestic fertilizer production to help his district’s agriculture-heavy economy.
Crawford won in a district that voted for Republican President Donald Trump by more than 45 percentage points in 2024. Crawford won reelection that year against Democrat Rodney Govens with nearly 73% of the vote.
Representatives for the Crawford campaign did not immediately provide comment.
Meanwhile, in the 2nd District, Jones hoped to capitalize on the sour national mood toward Republicans, with voters deeply unhappy about the cost of living and stubbornly high gas prices amid the war in Iran.
The 2nd Congressional District is the bluest of Arkansas’ four House seats, covering central Arkansas, including most of Little Rock. Redistricting by the majority-Republican state Legislature in 2021 made the map more favorable to Hill, who won reelection in 2024 with 59% of the vote.
Democrats have tried for years to unseat Hill, who first took office in 2015, but have not succeeded so far. Polling from Hendrix College and Talk Business and Politics found Jones with a slim lead over Hill in August, though the results were within the poll’s margin of error. 
The matchup in the 3rd Congressional District between Womack, Libertarian Bobby Wilson and Democrat Robb Ryerse is an amalgamation of previous elections. Wilson was Womack’s opponent in the general election in 2024, while Ryerse was defeated when challenging Womack during the Republican primary in 2018.
Womack, a self-described “institution guy,” was known for having a decade and a half long unbroken congressional voting streak. It was the longest active streak in Congress when it was broken in November 2025 due to a family emergency that prevented Womack from attending a vote. 
Womack stoked speculation in 2023 that he would retire after venting about Republican infighting in a Washington Post interview. He later called the speculation overblown and told the Advocate this year that he still had the energy and passion to represent the district in Congress.

name: California
title: Governor-elect Becerra must quickly confront state budget mess Newsom left behind
description: Xavier Becerra has won California's race for governor. Just days after he is inaugurated in January, he will have to submit a new budget. He faces a stark choice.
text:
The most fundamental — and arguably most important — duty of a California governor is managing the state budget.
Xavier Becerra, the former attorney general who won the governorship Tuesday, must submit a new budget to the Legislature just days after his inauguration in January. Outgoing Gov. Gavin Newsom is leaving him with a fiscal mess.
Newsom, who will likely launch a presidential campaign, insisted in June that the 2026-27 budget he signed was not only balanced but would remain so during his predecessor’s first year.
Not by a long shot.
During Newsom’s second term, he and the Legislature routinely enacted general fund budgets that spent billions of dollars more than the state’s tax system was producing, covering the gaps with accounting gimmicks, by draining emergency reserves and incurring on- and off-the-books loans.
A chart in the back pages of the 2026-27 budget reveals that during Newsom’s eight years of managing the budget, the state took in $1.4 trillion in general fund revenue but spent $1.7 trillion, averaging $37 billion in overspending each year. Among other things, the spending spree increased the state’s payroll by 100,000 positions.
Newsom leaves the state with what Gabe Petek, the Legislature’s budget analyst, describes as a $29 billion “wall of debt” that must eventually be repaid, echoing a term that former Gov. Jerry Brown coined in 2010.
Becerra faces a stark choice.
He could continue the deficit spending, running up even more debt — the governmental equivalent of a family maxing out its credit cards to finance its lifestyle. Or he could do what Brown did when he began his second governorship and faced a $35 billion “a wall of debt” from the effects of the Great Recession.
After his 2010 election, Brown engaged in a very public discussion about what it would take to balance the budget and whittle down its debts. He settled on a mixture of spending reductions and temporary sales and income tax increases, plus creating “rainy day” reserves to cushion future revenue drops.
During Brown’s governorship, general fund income and outgo closely matched, the aforementioned chart confirms. He bequeathed a healthy budget to Newsom.
It would take political courage for Becerra to adopt the face-the-music attitude that Brown displayed in 2011. Politically, the easier path would be to emulate Newsom, who was content to overspend revenues while shunning any major tax increases to cover the gaps.
Becerra has been very reluctant to reveal any policy intentions, but in an interview late last month, he indicated that he may be willing to increase taxes — unlike Newsom.
Becerra told Ashley Zavala, of Sacramento’s KCRA-TV, that he’s interested in raising taxes on high-income Californians, taxing employers whose low-paid workers qualify for Medi-Cal health benefits, closing corporate tax loopholes and adopting a mileage-based tax on electric cars.
Although Becerra opposed Proposition 40, the billionaire wealth tax on Tuesday’s ballot, he told Zavala that increasing taxes on high-income Californians would hinge on “if we can prove that you’re not paying your fair share,” adding “to me, that’s pretty basic. If you’re a billionaire and you’re paying at a lower tax rate than a firefighter or a teacher or a nurse, you’re not paying your fair share.”
Under legislation passed this year, the state is already exploring taxation of employers whose workers qualify for Medi-Cal, but it and the other taxes Becerra mentions would be a hard sell.
Overall, Californians already have one of the nation’s highest tax burdens, which is a factor in the state’s recent losses of population and corporate headquarters. Increases probably would have to be paired with spending cuts to make them palatable, and those reductions would face opposition as well.
Nobody ever said governing California is easy.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Democrats poised to keep CT’s constitutional offices
authors: Keith M. Phaneuf and P.R. Lockhart
description: The Democratic incumbents benefitted from campaigns that prioritized affordability and opposing many policies of President Donald Trump.
text:
Democrats were poised to sweep the races Tuesday night for constitutional offices that made up Connecticut’s underticket.
The incumbents each held leads of roughly 20 percentage points as results continued to trickle in. Around 10 p.m., the speeches began, although the Democrats were careful not to call them victory speeches as they addressed a sizable crowd gathered at Hartford’s Dunkin’ Park for Gov. Ned Lamont’s watch party, an event that doubled as state Democrats’ election night headquarters. 
William Tong will serve a third term as attorney general while Sean Scanlon, Stephanie Thomas and Erick Russell secured their second four-year stints as comptroller, secretary of the state and treasurer, respectively.
On a night when Connecticut Democrats fared well across the board, underticket candidates benefitted from campaigns that prioritized affordability and opposing many policies of President Donald Trump.
“It’s people not being fooled by what they’ve seen by this [Trump] administration,” said Russell, of New Haven, who beat Fred Wilms, a banking executive from Norwalk and former GOP state representative.

Treasurer Erick Russell appears during an election night party on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026 at Dunkin’ Park in Hartford. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

Russell has greatly improved returns on state pension benefits and brokered a compromise to launch Connecticut’s “Baby Bonds” program to combat generational poverty.
Russell called attention to the history of civil rights struggles that have informed his time in office, saying that the current political moment will require action. 
“This is our moment as a generation to take back our country,” he said to applause. 
After leaving the stage, Russell went to call his opponent to discuss the race. 
Russell and Scanlon, a Guilford Democrat, both campaigned on the huge state surpluses Connecticut has used to temper big federal cutbacks in healthcare and human services programs.
Scanlon, who defeated former Westport First Selectwoman Jennifer Tooker, ran on reforms made to pension systems and audits designed to curb wasteful spending in the Connecticut State Colleges and University system. But the comptroller also noted his key role in helping Lamont, a fiscally moderate-to-conservative Democrat, find middle ground with more progressive Democrats on spending issues.
“I guess I’m forever somebody who likes to find consensus, like I did as a legislator,” said Scanlon, who served four terms in the House before becoming comptroller.

Comptroller Sean Scanlon gives a victory speech during an election night party on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026 at Dunkin’ Park in Hartford. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

The comptroller made sure to emphasize that he was not giving a victory speech Tuesday evening but still framed the night as a sign that voters in the state supported calls for change both in Connecticut and nationally. 
“I think we have a mandate in this country and in this state to keep doing the work we’re doing but also to go beyond what we have been doing,” Scanlon told The Connecticut Mirror after leaving the stage. “And now that we’re finally in a better fiscal position, we can start to do the big things we’ve always wanted to do.”  
He specifically cited affordable healthcare as a goal he supports. 
Before results came in, both Wilms and Tooker said they felt good about their campaigns, which focused on the top issues facing those offices.
The Democratic-controlled General Assembly has called increasingly for Connecticut to ease budget caps that have generated huge surpluses since 2017 and helped shrink the state’s pension debt by $11 billion over the past seven years, Tooker said.
But Connecticut, which struggled with poor savings habits for seven decades prior to 2011, still ranks as one of the most indebted states per capita in the nation, carrying about $80 billion in bonded debt and unfunded retirement benefit liabilities.
“Once you start with that statement, people start to listen,” Tooker said.
Wilms, a banking executive and former state legislator, noted Connecticut’s failure to secure strong returns on its pension investments for decades before reforms began. And he called for a dramatic overhaul of the treasurer’s office.
Rather than leaving most investment authority in the hands of one elected official, voters should elect a treasurer who serves in conjunction with eight investment experts appointed by state leaders, he argued. Only collectively would they oversee billions in state assets.
“Is it right to have such power in the hands of an individual, personally?” Wilms said, repeating a question he often asked voters. “People got that intuitively.”
Thomas, a Norwalk Democrat who outpolled Fairfield real estate investor Peter Lumaj in the race for secretary of the state, said she worked hard to counter a recurring Trump message that states’ elections are severely susceptible to fraud.
Thomas said she often reminded voters that Connecticut municipalities have one registrar from each major party who work in conjunction with the secretary of the state’s office to organize elections and ensure both physical and cyber security. “We are protecting not only the integrity of the vote but the election workforce as well,” she added.
The secretary of the state noted that she could not speak much as the results of her race had not been decided yet but emphasized to the crowd that she wants to continue to create space for civic engagement within the state. 
In comments to the CT Mirror, Thomas added that should a second term become official, she wants to modernize the election system while continuing to build on other reforms made in the state. 
“We need more and more people learning how to engage with government so that they can have a voice,” she said. “So there’s a lot more to do.” 
Lumaj could not be reached for comment.

Attorney General William Tong speaks during an election night party on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026 at Dunkin’ Park in Hartford. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

And Tong, a Stamford Democrat who won his third term as attorney general, said he showed his office could safeguard families’ budgets despite numerous national policies that have driven up the cost of living.
Tong took legal action and reached agreements to combat price-fixing involving prescription drugs, concert and other event tickets, and even eggs.
“There’s a lot of talk about affordability, to the point where it’s almost not clear what the word means anymore,” Tong said. “I mean, what’s more important to people at the grocery store than buying a dozen eggs?”
Tong was fired up as he addressed the crowd, vowing to continue to use his position to pursue legal action against large corporations, specifically calling attention to social media companies. 
“We must continue to use our sovereign power in court to stop the monopolies and cartels from driving up prices,” he said. “We must stop the tech bros and the billionaires from extracting ever more from us and hoarding their wealth.”
The attorney general also said that he would continue to pursue aggressive action on artificial intelligence and data centers, issues that have fueled anxieties in communities around the state. 
His GOP opponent, Westport attorney John Bolton, had argued Tong used the office more for political gain than to assist those in need.
Bolton said Connecticut needs to do more to shield thousands of residents with out-of-state employers from the threat of double taxation, and to curb the polluting actions of neighboring states.
“I think the office [of attorney general] really needs to be returned to the people of Connecticut,” he said.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Sarah Huckabee Sanders wins second term as Arkansas governor
description: Republican Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders defeated Democratic state Sen. Fred Love and Libertarian Colt Shelby Tuesday night in her bid for a second term as Arkansas governor.  The Associated Press called the race around 9:43 p.m.  Sanders, the daughter of former Arkansas Gov. Mike Huckabee, earned national attention as President Donald Trump’s White House pres[...]
text:
Arkansas Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders speaks to supporters at her election watch party on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Katie Adkins/Arkansas Advocate)Republican Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders defeated Democratic state Sen. Fred Love and Libertarian Colt Shelby Tuesday night in her bid for a second term as Arkansas governor. 
The Associated Press called the race around 9:43 p.m. 
Sanders, the daughter of former Arkansas Gov. Mike Huckabee, earned national attention as President Donald Trump’s White House press secretary. She became the first woman elected Arkansas governor in 2022. 
Education was a major focus of Sanders’ first term, which saw the passage of the LEARNS Act, a wide-ranging education bill that increased Arkansas’ minimum teacher salary and created a school voucher program that allows state funds to be used for certain education expenses, including private school tuition. 
The growing cost of the program, which is now open to all Arkansas students, has faced bipartisan pushback. Earlier this year, lawmakers approved a state budget that includes $309 million for the program. They also set aside an additional $70 million in surplus funds to support anticipated growth of the program. 
Love said he would sign an executive order to halt the program if elected. 
Sanders’ time in the White House and as a Fox News commentator elevated her national profile as Arkansas governor. Shortly after taking office in 2023, she delivered Republicans’ response to President Joe Biden’s State of the Union Address. 
During Sanders’ first term as governor, she focused on culture war issues that included efforts to ban “indoctrination” in classrooms, banning the use of the term “Latinx” and signing laws restricting the rights of transgender students.
Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders addresses guests of a Get-Out-the-Vote rally in Rogers on Nov. 2, 2026 as (from left) First Gentleman Bryan Sanders, Republican U.S. Sen. John Boozman and state Sen. Bart Hester listen. (Photo by Antoinette Grajeda/Arkansas Advocate)
Sanders will begin her second term in January, which is also when lawmakers will convene for the legislative session. Sanders previously told the Advocate she expects healthcare to dominate the session, and that she wants to ensure access to quality affordable care. 
A major topic of discussion will likely be the future of the state’s Medicaid expansion program, which provides health coverage to nearly 209,000 Arkansans. The state requested a two-year extension after the Trump administration rejected its request to renew the program this summer. 
Arkansas’ program doesn’t meet a provision in a new federal law that requires it to not cost the federal government more than would be projected without the program.  
Sanders has said conversations are underway about “the best path forward” for the program, but has not specified what approach she’d prefer regarding the program’s delivery. 
In addition to healthcare access, Sanders told the Advocate during her campaign that tax cuts would also be a priority during her second term. 
Arkansas lawmakers approve $192M tax cut legislation, end session 

Lawmakers approved four rounds of income tax cuts and eliminated the state’s grocery tax during Sanders’ first term. The governor said she wants to continue “responsibly” phasing out the state’s income tax so people can keep more of their money and spend it how they want.
As governor, Sanders faced pushback from the majority-Republican Legislature over her announced plans for a 3,000-bed prison in Franklin County. The prison project was placed on hold following resistance from the local community and legislators.
Sanders also faced questions from lawmakers in her first term over the purchase of a $19,000 lectern that prompted a legislative audit, though a local prosecutor declined to pursue charges.
During Sanders’ campaign for a second term, the NAACP and some conservative influencers criticized her ad touting new work requirements for Medicaid recipients. The NAACP said the ad unfairly stereotyped the poor, while some GOP commentators complained about a white actor portraying a Medicaid recipient.
The Republican governor has been mentioned as a potential 2028 presidential hopeful, and her gubernatorial victory comes a week before a book she’s written is set to be released.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Democrat flips NEPA congressional seat, a key pick-up in battle for control of US House
description: Scranton Mayor Paige Cognetti handily won the race to represent Northeastern Pennsylvania in Congress, ousting first-term incumbent U.S. Rep. Rob Bresnahan.  The Associated Press called the race for Cognetti, a Democrat, at 10:41 p.m. when she had 55.2% of the vote. “Tonight, Northeastern Pennsylvania sent an unmistakable message. We’re tired of big corporat[...]
text:
U.S. Rep. Rob Bresnahan and Scranton Mayor Paige Cognetti (Photos from the U.S. House and Cognetti's campaign) Scranton Mayor Paige Cognetti handily won the race to represent Northeastern Pennsylvania in Congress, ousting first-term incumbent U.S. Rep. Rob Bresnahan. 
The Associated Press called the race for Cognetti, a Democrat, at 10:41 p.m. when she had 55.2% of the vote.
“Tonight, Northeastern Pennsylvania sent an unmistakable message. We’re tired of big corporations and wealthy donors calling the shots and rigging the system against the rest of us. And we’re tired of being told that this is just how Washington works,” she said. “We are ready to take on Washington corruption and build a government that works as hard as the people it’s supposed to serve.”
“To everyone who voted for me, thank you for putting your trust in me. And to the people who didn’t vote for me, I’m going to work just as hard for you,” Cognetti added. “Because whether you’re a Democrat, a Republican, or an Independent, whether you live in Scranton, Wilkes-Barre, Hazleton, the Back Mountain, the Poconos, Hawley or Dingman’s Ferry, you deserve a representative who listens to you, respects you, and fights for you. That’s the kind of congresswoman I intend to be. This is a victory for everyone who believes our government should belong to the people.”
The 8th Congressional District includes Lackawanna, Pike and Wayne counties as well as a portion of Luzerne County.
Bresnahan, a supporter of President Donald Trump, flipped the seat in 2024 with just over 50% of the vote, snagging the seat from longtime former U.S. Rep. Matt Cartwright, a Democrat. 

The latest updates from the 2026 election in Pennsylvania


But he soon came under fire for his “prolific” stock trading, which tracker Quiver Quantitative puts at $8.47 million.The multimillionaire now says he has “consistently” supported banning such activities and appears to have halted the money-making moves.
The vulnerable Republican was identified early as an opportunity for Democrats seeking to retake control of the U.S. House, along with three others in Pennsylvania. 
Polls and other data predicted a “blue wave” this midterm cycle as presidential approval ratings plummeted and voter sentiment soured on Republicans. The keyword for nearly every campaign — and a focus for both Cognetti and Bresnahan — was affordability, with gas, daily necessities and home energy prices stubbornly high.
Cognetti has raised more than $7.5 million since Jan. 1, 2025, compared to Bresnahan’s $6.5 million. Candidates and outside groups have bought more than $28 million in advertising, making it one of the most expensive national contests.
Cognetti won Scranton’s mayoral special election in 2019 as an independent, later changing her party affiliation. She has vowed to tackle high healthcare costs, halt Trump administration tariffs and end the war in Iran.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Democrat Keri Ingle defeats House Speaker Jon Patterson, flips Missouri Senate seat
description: Democratic state Rep. Keri Ingle defeated Republican House Speaker Jon Patterson on Tuesday, flipping a Missouri Senate seat in eastern Jackson County that Republicans have held for decades. Ingle, a former social worker from Lee’s Summit, will succeed Republican state Sen. Mike Cierpiot in the 8th District, which includes the suburbs of Lee’s Summit and […]
text:
State Rep. Keri Ingle, a Lee's Summit Democrat, heads to the State Senate, flipping the 8th district seat blue (photo submitted). Democratic state Rep. Keri Ingle defeated Republican House Speaker Jon Patterson on Tuesday, flipping a Missouri Senate seat in eastern Jackson County that Republicans have held for decades.
Ingle, a former social worker from Lee’s Summit, will succeed Republican state Sen. Mike Cierpiot in the 8th District, which includes the suburbs of Lee’s Summit and Blue Springs. She won 55% of the vote on Tuesday. Her victory, along with a Democratic win in Springfield, means Republicans have lost their supermajority in the Missouri Senate.
“The people of this district have trusted me to represent them in the Missouri Senate,” Ingle said in a statement Tuesday evening. “That means I’ll have a say in decisions that affect their lives. I owe them good judgment, hard work and the willingness to stand up for them, even when it’s difficult.”
Patterson, also from Lee’s Summit, outspent every other state Senate candidate this election cycle. As of the week before the election, he had spent $2.7 million between his campaign and political action committee. Ingle’s campaign and PAC spent $616,000, according to Missouri Ethics Commission filings.
The race was one of two Senate contests Democrats targeted as potential pickups, drawing attention and financial support from partisan organizations on both sides.
“We have been working for this moment for years. First with me flipping my house seat in 2018,” Ingle told The Independent in a pre-election interview. “So it is really fun and really gratifying to be in this particular moment.”
When campaigning door-to-door, Ingle emphasized her experience as a “social worker and mom of two.”
“I am always looking out for the little guys,” she told a mom in Lee’s Summit during one evening of door knocking in late September.
Before entering the legislature, Ingle worked in child welfare for the Jackson County Children’s Division. The job revealed systemic problems, and Ingle hoped to pass legislation to address them.
Missouri Senate battleground pits Jon Patterson against Keri Ingle in Jackson County

“It is really important to me that vulnerable populations were advocated for using good, sound, evidence-based practices,” Ingle said. “A lot of times legislators have really, really great intent when they file legislation…. But intent and impact are two very different things. So it’s really important that we look at what evidence tells are the best practices instead of just like, ‘Well, this sounds good. Let’s make this a law.’”
During her time in the House, she has supported bipartisan efforts, including a bill that would create tax credit programs designed to make child care more accessible. The legislation passed the House this year but stalled in the Senate, continuing a yearslong effort to expand access to child care.
“When it comes to issues around child welfare, survivors of sexual assault and crime prevention, I work in a very, very bipartisan manner,” she said. “I want to work with anyone who is willing to move the needle on those issues and do what is right for the people of the state.”
In 2021, Ingle co-sponsored a bill with state Rep. Rudy Veit, a Republican from Wardsville, to bring more oversight to unlicensed boarding schools. The legislation was signed into law with nearly unanimous legislative support.
“I am really proud of the work that I’ve been able to accomplish as a member of the super minority in the House,” she said. “I have also been able to advocate for and get money back for my district through the budget process, so I’m really proud of that work.”
Ingle is bracing for budget battles when lawmakers return to Jefferson City in January, with the state’s revenue falling behind projections. She said she will keep a close watch on any proposed cuts to social services and education.
“The budget is going to be our biggest lift over the next couple of years,” she said. “I am going to be an advocate for the most vulnerable people in this state because their services are always the ones that are first on the chopping block.”
She pointed to Gov. Mike Kehoe’s January budget proposal, which called for cutting $80.7 million from programs serving adults with developmental disabilities. Lawmakers ultimately restored the funding after bipartisan opposition to the proposed cuts.
Before cutting funding for these programs, Ingle would rather see lawmakers scale back the MOScholars program, which provides scholarships for private school tuition and other educational expenses through state tax credits.
This year’s budget underfunds the formula that determines state aid for public schools by $190 million, and the burden is not shared equally among districts. Provisions built into the public school funding law allow some school districts to keep the amount of state aid they receive flat even as enrollment declines.
The 8th District’s largest school systems, the Lee’s Summit and Blue Springs school districts, have seen their state aid reduced by 5% to 6% this year.
The Lee’s Summit School District has projected a $7 million to $10 million revenue shortfall for the 2026-27 school year, citing reductions in state funding and changes at the local and federal levels. In September, its board voted to reverse part of a voluntary property tax rate rollback to make up for lost revenue.
“The reality is that decisions made at the county level and some by some of our elected officials in Jefferson City have created a situation where our students, our staff and our community are paying the price,” board Vice
President Erica Miller said during the meeting. “Our district has been tasked with trying to make sense of a broken system.”
Weeks later, Miller endorsed Ingle in a video posted on Ingle’s campaign social media accounts, saying Ingle “will fight for our kids, our schools and our community.”


10:05 pmThis article was updated to include a statement from Ingle.

name: Daily Montanan
title: First results from western Montana house district shows tight race
description: MISSOULA — Polls in Montana closed at 8 p.m. and the Secretary of State’s office has shown results trickling in from a handful of counties in the hour since with Democrat Sam Forstag and Republican Aaron Flint in a closely matched battle for the state’s first congressional district.  Forstag’s campaign is hosting an election watch party […]
text:
Democrat Sam Forstag (left) faces off in a debate against Republican Aaron Flint during the 2026 election. The race is one of the most competitive in the country, and has been tabbed by pollsters as the one race in the state that could tilt toward the Democrats. (Screenshot, used with permission)MISSOULA — Polls in Montana closed at 8 p.m. and the Secretary of State’s office has shown results trickling in from a handful of counties in the hour since with Democrat Sam Forstag and Republican Aaron Flint in a closely matched battle for the state’s first congressional district. 
Forstag’s campaign is hosting an election watch party at Missoula’s Florence Hotel, while Flint’s campaign is in the Flathead Valley.
Speaking to supporters just before polls closed, Forstag said he’s optimistic about the night but proud of the campaign no matter the results.
“I’m feeling that special kind of optimism,” Forstag said. “I’m feeling like we can change this country again.”
With around 48,000 votes processed, by 9 p.m., the two candidates were separated by about 2,000, with Flint leading. He drew voters from the Bitterroot Valley by a 16-point margin., while Forstag earned twice as many votes from union-heavy Silver Bow County.
The district’s most populous counties — Missoula, Gallatin and Flathead — have reported no votes yet.
This is the third time Montana’s western district has held an election since it was created following the 2020 census. 
Incumbent Republican Rep. Ryan Zinke won and held the seat with a 3% and 8% margin the last two elections, but is retiring, leaving it open. 
Flint, a veteran and former talk radio host, was picked as a preferred successor and easily won the Republican primary. His conservative talk show was broadcast out of Billings for numerous years, making him a known figure among Republicans. He has benefitted from visits by President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance in recent weeks. 
Forstag is a political newcomer who has worked as a wildland firefighter and smokejumper in recent years, and spent two legislative sessions as a lobbyist in Helena. He won the Democratic primary with more progressive messaging, featuring high-profile endorsements from U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Sen. Bernie Sanders.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Crowley wins election, becoming Wisconsin’s first Black governor
description: In a historic victory Tuesday night, David Crowley was elected as Wisconsin’s first African American governor. Crowley, who became Milwaukee’s first Black county executive in 2019, defeated Republican U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany in a contentious race.  The Associated Press had not yet called the race for Crowley at 9:57 p.m with 72% of the vote […]
text:
David Crowley, Milwaukee County Executive during his run for governor. (Photo by Isiah Holmes/Wisconsin Examiner)In a historic victory Tuesday night, David Crowley was elected as Wisconsin’s first African American governor. Crowley, who became Milwaukee’s first Black county executive in 2019, defeated Republican U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany in a contentious race. 
The Associated Press had not yet called the race for Crowley at 9:57 p.m with 72% of the vote counted. Crowley had 53.9% of the vote to Tiffany’s 46.1%.
Tiffany is conceded in the race at around 9:45 p.m. “While we have our differences, we both love this great state,” Tiffany said. “And I wish him and his family the very best.” One person in the crowd at Tiffany’s victory party started heckling Crowley. Tiffany responded: “We’re gonna be magnanimous tonight.”
Tuesday night concluded a dynamic campaign for Crowley. During the Democratic primary, Crowley initially dropped out due to low polling numbers and endorsed Lt. Gov. Sara Rodriguez. 
Just days after Crowley endorsed Rodriguez, however, she also dropped out due to financial mismanagement within her campaign. This left state Rep. Francesca Hong (D-Madison), who ran as a democratic socialist, with a significant double digit lead over her remaining opponents. Crowley re-entered the race stating that many people, including Gov. Tony Evers, had urged him to run. 
After Crowley restarted his campaign, Evers — who had previously refrained from making an endorsement  — pitched Crowley as the only candidate capable of beating Tiffany. 
Crowley pushed back against claims that he re-entered the race because of Evers, or that he was the establishment candidate. He narrowly defeated Hong in the primary. 
The general election featured attack ads paid for by dark money groups that accused Crowley of raising sales and property taxes. Some ads urged viewers not to let Crowley make the rest of Wisconsin look like Milwaukee. 
Republicans tried to portray Crowley as a corrupt politician who funneled  money into a non-profit where his wife worked. Ads also focused on immigration, listing crimes committed  by non-citizens and re-played a clip of Crowley vowing to support immigrant communities by saying “I’m an accomplice.” 
Late in the race, an  ad originating from a GOP-linked group masquerading as a left-wing progressive outfit accused Crowley of being too pro-law enforcement, while other Republican attacks accused him of being soft on crime. 
Crowley focused on pitching his record of governing Milwaukee County. Pro-Crowley ads promised to make life more affordable and increase housing and slammed Tiffany as being more loyal to President Donald Trump than to Wisconsin. 
During the only candidate debate  in October, Crowley described Tiffany as in the pocket of the billionaires funding his campaign. Just three billionaires, Beloit resident Dianne Hendricks and Illinois residents Richard and Liz Uihlein contributed about 90% of the funds raised by the Tiffany campaign, directed to the Republican Party of Wisconsin and then transferred to the candidate.

name: VTDigger
title: Republican Phil Scott wins record 6th term as Vermont’s governor
description:
Scott overcame a well-funded challenge from Democrat and Progressive Amanda Janoo and has now been elected governor more times than anyone else in state history. 
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Republican Phil Scott wins record 6th term as Vermont’s governor.
text:
Gov. Phil Scott leaves the House of Representatives chamber after delivering his state of the state address at the Statehouse in Montpelier in Jan. 2026. File photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
MONTPELIER — Vermont’s Republican Gov. Phil Scott won reelection to a sixth term on Tuesday, defeating Democrat and Progressive Amanda Janoo in a race that proved more competitive than most voters would have imagined when Scott announced he would run again.
Janoo, an economist from Burlington running her first-ever political campaign, conceded in a speech at her campaign’s election night party in Burlington around 10:50 p.m. 
The Associated Press had not yet called the race for Scott at that point. 
Scott, who is 68 and lives in Berlin, has now been elected governor more times than anyone else in Vermont history, surpassing the previous record of five wins held by Democrat Howard Dean. 
As of the time Janoo conceded, however, Scott’s win looked on track to be his narrowest in years. 
Polling released ahead of Election Day suggested his favorability had taken a hit, especially among Democrats, many of whom reliably voted for him in the past. Scott has acknowledged that his vision for education reform and his decision to make state employees return to regular in-person work made him less popular with some voters. 
Janoo also raised more money than Scott over the last two months of the race and generated more excitement for her campaign than any other Democratic candidate for governor in years. 
But she had a significant disadvantage: Before this year, she was virtually unknown to voters. Scott made the case on the campaign trail that voters, to the contrary, knew him well and could trust his leadership, reminding them that he was in office during the Covid-19 pandemic and the devastating floods of 2023 and 2024. 
He also made the case that even though he is a Republican, he’s stood up to President Donald Trump’s administration when he thought federal actions would hurt the state, which is something many Democratic voters have rewarded him for.
Scott also likely benefited from a large infusion of cash into the race on his behalf — $950,000 as of last week, according to campaign finance reports — from the Republican Governors Association. The national organization donated to a Vermont-based super PAC that ran pro-Scott and anti-Janoo advertising on TV and online in recent weeks. 
Looking ahead, Scott said during the campaign that he would tackle the state’s affordability issues with a package of tax cuts or credits and pushing for more deregulatory reforms to the state’s healthcare system. He also wants the state government to continue on the path his administration set out over the last two years toward a consolidated education system with larger, regional districts.
It remains to be seen, though, how much support he’ll get for those ideas from lawmakers next year.
This story will be updated.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Luke Bronin declares victory as CT Democrats anticipate sweep in U.S. House races
description: Democratic candidates in CT's U.S. House races declared victory on Tuesday night as the party made widespread gains nationally.
text:
Democratic candidates in Connecticut’s U.S. House races were declaring victory on Tuesday night as the party made widespread gains nationally, likely retaking control of the House, in an election cycle dominated by an unpopular president.
Connecticut’s House delegation appeared all but guaranteed to remain all blue next year, with four Democratic incumbents holding their seats. One new member — Luke Bronin — celebrated a win in Connecticut’s 1st Congressional District seat based in Hartford, where Democrat Rep. John Larson had served since 1999. 
Just after 10 p.m., the Democrats were all leading their races by more than 20 points, with less than half of votes counted, according to the Associated Press.
Bronin was poised to defeat Republican challenger Amy Chai, a physician who previously ran for Congress in a different district. He joined statewide elected officials Tuesday night at Hartford’s minor league baseball stadium Dunkin’ Park, including Gov. Ned Lamont, Lt. Gov. Susan Bysiewicz and the constitutional officers who all appeared to have won their bids for reelection. U.S. Sen. Richard Blumenthal, who was not on this year’s ballot, also attended the party.
Speaking to supporters, Bronin began with words of appreciation for the absent U.S. Sen. Chris Murphy, who suffered a stroke over the weekend, and he thanked Larson for his service in Congress.
As the newest member, Bronin will join a congressional delegation with decades of seniority in Congress. He said the task for Democrats now is to use the opportunity given to them to win the American people’s trust and lay the groundwork for retaking the White House in 2028.
“Donald Trump’s entire presidency has been a con, and today, we can say the American people have stopped falling for it,” Bronin said.
Bronin, who served as an intelligence officer in the U.S. Navy Reserve and was deployed to Afghanistan, went into Tuesday’s election as the heavy favorite. He was poised to defeat Chai and Green Party nominee Mary Sanders, who was also on the ballot.
Chai said her views don’t fit neatly inside a political ideology and she described herself as an “open book.” She was either unaffiliated or part of the Libertarian Party until last year.
To the west, U.S. Rep. Jahana Hayes appeared on the verge of winning a fifth term to Connecticut’s 5th Congressional District over Republican opponent Chris Shea, a firefighter and retired Navy SEAL. The seat remains the most competitive in the state, but it got significantly less national attention and outside money than previous years.
Elsewhere in Connecticut, there were few surprises as races were called for U.S. Reps. Joe Courtney, D-2nd District, and Jim Himes, D-4th District. Rosa DeLauro, D-3rd District held strong leads as results trickled in. All three will be vying for top roles on their committees if Democrats take back the House.
In Waterbury, a lively crowd gathered at the same downtown hotel where Hayes held her last two election night watch parties. Thunderous applause and cheers broke out as a local news station provided an update on the 5th District race, showing Hayes with a sizable lead over Shea.
Before the race was called, Hayes entered the hotel ballroom around 10:20 p.m. to massive applause. She embraced supporters and danced before she took the stage. She said it’s rare she gets to attend the party and address supporters early in the night.
U.S. Rep. Jahana Hayes greeted supporters at her election night party from Waterbury on Tuesday, Nov. 3. She faced a challenge from Republican Chris Shea in Connecticut’s 5th Congressional District. Credit: Lisa Hagen / CT Mirror
Hayes said Shea called her five minutes earlier “conceding that the numbers do not look good for him.”
“I just want to say that this cycle was different. It was nastier. The attacks started earlier. They were more personal and there was more at stake. But we just kept working through it,” Hayes told supporters. “We kept turning out voters in every part of this district, and we crushed it in places that they said we would never get.
“And tomorrow, we get back to work,” she continued. “We get back to doing the work so that we can right size this government and put a check on this administration.”
Shea, a first-time candidate, gathered with supporters at the VFW in Oakville. He wanted to bring change to a district that’s been elusive to Republicans for years. Shea campaigned on his experience serving in the military and at the Pentagon.
Hayes’ closest reelection race was in 2022, which she won by a little over 2,000 votes. But she’s won every other race by more comfortable margins. Election analysts had rated this year’s race much closer to Democrats than recent years, particularly in a midterm election that was trending away from Republicans.
In the eastern part of the state, Courtney bested Republican opponent George Austin in the 2nd Congressional District.
When Courtney first ran for office in 2006, he was part of the blue wave that swept Democrats back into the majority — but in his own race, he flipped a Republican-held seat by eking out a victory with an 83-vote margin. Two decades later, the congressman has easily won reelection through a coalition of voters that cuts across party lines.
Austin is a business owner and works in construction. He noted local Republicans haven’t “put up a blue-collar candidate in a long time.” The district is the most rural one in the state and home to defense contractors like General Dynamics Electric Boat.
From her New Haven-based district, DeLauro declared victory in a historic 19th term representing the 3rd Congressional District. She faced a challenge from Republican Chris Lancia. Thomas Egan, a lawyer who ran unsuccessfully for elected office, was also on the ballot as the Independent Party nominee.
Lancia is a Coast Guard veteran and former federal law enforcement officer who works as a manager at TNI, a provider of fiber networks. He was a first-time candidate and former Democrat who said he believed it was time for a fresh face representing the 3rd District.
At the congresswoman’s Election Night party, at New Haven’s Schubert Theater, attendees wore hot pink buttons that read, “Fight Like Hell.” Around 9 p.m., DeLauro made an entrance, wearing an iridescent dress and matching scarf and lipsynching to “Proud Mary” as it played over the speakers.
U.S. Rep. Rosa DeLauro mingles with supporters at the Schubert Theater in New Haven, Conn. after declaring victory in her race for reelection to the House of Representatives on Nov. 3, 2026. Credit: Maia Nehme / CT Mirror
In a speech to her supporters, DeLauro thanked her family and her campaign team and congratulated the four other Democratic congressional candidates on the ballot. “We don’t have the final numbers, but they’re all winners,” she said.
“When I get back, and I get the gavel of the Appropriations Committee…” she said, before being interrupted by chants from the crowd of “Ro – sa! Ro – sa!” 
“I want that gavel!” she quipped, pledging that she’d use the chairmanship to “restore the power of the purse to the Congress.”
And from the southwestern corner of the state, Himes won another term to Connecticut’s 4th Congressional District against Republican Michael Goldstein and Independent Party nominee Benjamin Wesley. The AP called the race for Himes at 9:55 p.m.
The seat was a Republican stronghold for 40 years and was represented by more liberal Republicans. That changed in 2008 when Himes first ran and flipped the seat during the first election of Barack Obama. Himes defeated Chris Shays, a moderate Republican who would often buck his own party.
Since then, the 4th District has been reliably blue. Himes has some theories about what happened, pointing to changes in the Republican Party and less about the electorate itself.
It’s the third time that Goldstein, a doctor and attorney, ran for the seat. He lost the Republican primary in 2022 but became the nominee in 2024, eventually losing to Himes. Wesley, a mechanical engineer, was also running for the second time.
In the lead up to Tuesday’s elections, Republican congressional candidates bemoaned the lack of support they received from their own party. Republicans haven’t had a member of Congress represent Connecticut since 2009, but they hope the party reinvests in them at the federal level.
“I think that a more engaged Republican Party would probably be much better for the candidates,” Goldstein said in an interview weeks before Tuesday’s elections. “But this has been this way for a while. I don’t see it changing soon.”
Outside of Connecticut, Democrats were having a strong night in the overall battle for control of the House — and possibly even the Senate. In 2006, Democrats had a wave year, capturing both chambers of Congress in the midterm elections of George W. Bush’s second term as an unpopular war waged on.
Connecticut’s lawmakers could gain considerable influence if Democrats take back the majority in one or both chambers of Congress. They see potential majorities as a way to put a check on the last two years of the Trump administration.
As she said in her victory speech, DeLauro is hoping to reclaim the gavel of the House Appropriations Committee. She has served as the ranking member since 2023 of the influential panel that crafts spending bills, allocates money and funds the government. She previously served as chair for two years starting in 2021.
Courtney hopes to ascend leadership on the Seapower and Projection Forces Subcommittee, which is part of the House Armed Services Committee. And Himes wants to secure the chairmanship of the secretive House Intelligence Committee.
Hayes, meanwhile, will run in Democrats’ contested leadership race for the top spot on the House Committee on Education and the Workforce.
There’s a common theme in their prospective committee leadership plans: oversight of the Trump administration.
“Connecticut, for a really small delegation, we’re going to punch well above our weight, and most of that is due to Rosa DeLauro’s likely appropriations chairmanship,” Himes said in a recent interview. “From the standpoint of the power of the purse, I think it is going to be a really powerful check and balance.”
CT Mirror reporters Maia Nehme and Theo Peck-Suzuki contributed to this story.

name: Source New Mexico
title: AP declares Democrat Deb Haaland as first female, Native American governor in US
description: Deb Haaland, a former U.S. interior secretary who previously represented New Mexico in Congress, made history Tuesday night as the first Native American woman in the nation to be elected governor. The Associated Press declared Haaland the winner in the race with an estimated 41% of the vote counted. Haaland, a member of Laguna Pueblo, […]
text:
Former U.S. Interior Secretary and Democratic candidate for New Mexico governor Deb Haaland on May 28, 2026, addressed participants at Grand Summit Recovery and Workforce Development in Albuquerque about the importance of sobriety before marching across Central Avenue with them to an early voting location. (Joshua Bowling/Source NM)Deb Haaland, a former U.S. interior secretary who previously represented New Mexico in Congress, made history Tuesday night as the first Native American woman in the nation to be elected governor.
 The Associated Press declared Haaland the winner in the race with an estimated 41% of the vote counted.
Haaland, a member of Laguna Pueblo, watched results come in at the Route 66 Casino Hotel in Albuquerque along with supporters, fellow candidates and Democratic Party of New Mexico officials after polls closed at 7 p.m. Unofficial results from the New Mexico Secretary of State’s office reported she had earned 57% of the vote by 8:49 p.m. in her contest against Republican Gregg Hull, the former mayor of Rio Rancho.
Democratic gubernatorial nominee Deb Haaland and her running mate, New Mexico Commissioner of Public Lands Stephanie Garcia Richard, embrace as they prepare to announce victory over the Republican ticket of former Rio Rancho Mayor Gregg Hull and Sen. David Gallegos (R-Eunice). (Photo by Joshua Bowling/Source NM)
Haaland soundly defeated her primary opponent, Bernalillo County District Attorney Sam Bregman, in the June primary election and handily outfundraised Hull. Her campaign finance reports often contained so many donors that the documents, which were routinely thousands of pages, at times crashed the New Mexico Secretary of State’s website.
While Haaland and Hull ran a relatively cordial contest, Hull criticized her for backing out of a televised debate before Election Day. Haaland at the time said that KOB-TV’s preferred date conflicted with a prior obligation she made to meet with farmers in southern New Mexico.
Haaland, who served in President Joe Biden’s cabinet, on the campaign trail often vowed to be a staunch opponent of President Donald Trump. She campaigned on boosting affordability, creating a public option healthcare plan and overhauling the state’s troubled child welfare agency.
In September, she pledged to sign an executive order immediately upon taking office that would enact a statewide moratorium on new large-scale data center projects until the Legislature can pass a bill that places guardrails on the developments.
Haaland is set to replace Democratic Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham, who is term-limited after first winning election to the seat in 2018. Haaland previously succeeded Lujan Grisham when she was elected to U.S. Congress to represent New Mexico’s 1st Congressional District, and became one of the first of two Native American women elected to that political body.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Democrat Anita Earls wins reelection to the NC Supreme Court
description: North Carolina voters reelected Democrat Anita Earls to the state Supreme Court Tuesday. She defeated Republican challenger Sarah Stevens, a former state lawmaker and longtime attorney. At the same time, three Court of Appeals contests helped determine whether Republicans would further consolidate their control over the state’s appellate courts. Democrats ap[...]
text:
Justice Anita Earls (left) and Republican challenger Sarah Stevens (right).North Carolina voters reelected Democrat Anita Earls to the state Supreme Court Tuesday. She defeated Republican challenger Sarah Stevens, a former state lawmaker and longtime attorney.
At the same time, three Court of Appeals contests helped determine whether Republicans would further consolidate their control over the state’s appellate courts. Democrats appeared to have won each open seat.
Earls appears to have won by double digits with 92% of precincts reporting Tuesday evening, according to unofficial election results from the N.C. Board of Elections. 
“You have spoken, and your voices have been heard. A majority of you have decided to return me to the court,” Earls said during her victory speech. “You have decided you want a court that will fight to protect your rights and protect our children’s rights. Thank you for sharing our vision and working so hard to get us closer to where we need to be.”
Republicans currently hold a 5-2 majority on the state Supreme Court. Earls’ win maintains one of the two Democratic seats on the bench.
Earls has served on the Supreme Court since 2019. Before joining the bench, she spent more than three decades practicing civil rights law, including serving in the U.S. Department of Justice’s Civil Rights Division and founding the Southern Coalition for Social Justice.
Her tenure on the court has included several high-profile disagreements with Republican justices over redistricting, voting rights and public education funding.
Stevens, who represented Surry County in the North Carolina House from 2009 until 2026, practiced family law for more than 30 years and served as the chamber’s speaker pro tempore from 2017 to 2025.
Her campaign emphasized judicial restraint and interpreting the law as written. Stevens criticized Earls’ previous rulings on redistricting and voter identification, arguing that judges should not rewrite laws or substitute their own policy preferences for those of lawmakers.
The Supreme Court race was one of four statewide contests for seats on North Carolina’s appellate courts.
Voters also decided three seats on the 15-member Court of Appeals, which reviews decisions from lower courts and administrative agencies. Cases are generally heard by rotating panels of three judges.
In the first contest, Democratic incumbent Judge John Arrowood of Charlotte defeated Republican Michael Byrne of Cary. 
Arrowood appears to have won by a double-digit margin with 92% of precincts reporting, according to unofficial election results from the N.C. Board of Elections. 
Byrne is an administrative law judge with the state’s Office of Administrative Hearings. Arrowood has served on the Court of Appeals since 2017 and previously worked as an attorney and staff member for the court.
In the second contest, Democratic incumbent Judge Toby Hampson defeated Republican George Cooper Bell. Hampson appears to have won by double digits with 92% of precincts reporting, according to unofficial election results from the N.C. Board of Elections.
Bell, who lives in Cornelius, is a Mecklenburg County Superior Court judge who has presided over felony cases, including first-degree murder trials. Hampson of Raleigh has served on the Court of Appeals since 2019.
The third contest was for an open seat previously held by Democratic Judge Allegra Collins, who did not seek reelection. 
Republican Craig Collins, a Gaston County Superior Court judge, faced Democratic candidate Christine Walczyk, a Wake County District Court judge who has served on the bench since 2007. Walczyk defeated Collins by a double-digit margin with 92% of precincts reporting.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Republicans will add to their Public Service Commission majority
description: Democrats are losing the District 5 seat covering North Louisiana that they have held since 1974 when it was created in a revised Louisiana Constitution
text:
A row of energy transmission towers carries electricity along a highway outside of LaPlace, on July 1, 2024. (Wes Muller/Louisiana Illuminator)Republicans were on pace to win the two open seats on the Louisiana Public Service Commission in Tuesday’s election, which would expand the party’s majority to four on the five-member body that regulates power utilities, telecommunications and transportation companies in the state.
Democrats are losing the District 5 seat covering North Louisiana that they have held since 1974 when it was created in a revised Louisiana Constitution, which expanded the Public Service Commission from three to five districts.
The history-making Republican is John Atkins, who defeated Shreveport City Councilman James Green with 60% of the vote from the 24 parishes in the district with 90% of votes counted. 
Atkins, a Shreveport businessman in the timber and investment industries, won a six-year term and will take over in January from Foster Campbell. The conservative Democrat has represented District 5 since 2003 and was grandfathered in when voters approved term limits for the Public Service Commission in 2008.
The other Republican winner was Stephanie Hilferty in District 1, which covers six full parishes and parts of four others.  She had amassed 60% of the vote with nearly 90% of precincts reporting. She defeated Chris Justin, an engineer and small business owner from New Orleans with no party affiliation, and Democrat Connie Norris, a retired educator from Slidell.
Hilferty is a state representative who’s represented portions of Orleans and Jefferson parishes since 2016. She will take over from Eric Skrmetta, a Metairie Republican who’s reached his term limit on the commission and was a reliable vote for the state’s major electric utilities. Since July, Skrmetta has been an undersecretary with the U.S. Department of Energy.
After qualifying to run in February, Atkins promised not to accept contributions from the utility companies he will regulate. State campaign finance records show Atkins loaned his campaign $640,000, accounting for the vast majority of his funding for the election. The largest of his few donors was the political action committee of the Environmental Defense Fund, a group that typically gives to Democratic candidates.
Green, who was the Louisiana Democratic Party’s endorsed candidate in District 5, never had more than $15,000 in his campaign account.
Campaign finance records show Hilferty accepted $27,000 in campaign donations from power and telecommunications companies and their political action committees, Verite News reported. She has insisted these contributions will not influence her decisions as a PSC member.
Hilferty’s voting record in the legislature features a strong moderate streak, as she frequently aligned with the rest of the New Orleans delegation composed almost exclusively of Democrats.
She and Atkins join fellow Republicans Mike Francis of Crowley and Lafayette’s Jean-Paul Coussan. Davante Lewis of Baton Rouge is the lone Democrat on the commission.
The six-year terms of PSC members are staggered, with elections every two years. Francis and Lewis face re-election in 2028, and Coussan will have to run again in 2030.
