name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Democrat Amy Acton wins race for Ohio governor, the Associated Press projects
description: Democrat Dr. Amy Acton has won Ohio’s race for governor according to unofficial election results. The Associated Press called the race at 10:49 p.m. Acton’s win marks the first time in 20 years that Ohio voters have selected a Democrat to lead the state. The political newcomer will likely have her work cut out for […]
text:
Democratic nominee for governor Amy Acton at a rally in Cleveland. (Photo by Nick Evans, Ohio Capital Journal.)Democrat Dr. Amy Acton has won Ohio’s race for governor according to unofficial election results. The Associated Press called the race at 10:49 p.m.
Acton’s win marks the first time in 20 years that Ohio voters have selected a Democrat to lead the state. The political newcomer will likely have her work cut out for her. Despite a broadly positive night for her party, Acton will still be working with a Republican-controlled legislature.
Acton rose to statewide prominence at the outset of COVID-19 pandemic. In daily briefings alongside Gov. Mike DeWine, she distinguished herself as a communicator.
While Acton’s tenure as Ohio’s health director tipped her for a future in politics, it was also a source of ammunition for her opponent. Republican candidate Vivek Ramaswamy criticized her relentlessly — although not factually — as “Dr. Lockdown.” Gov. Mike DeWine has insisted the decision to close Ohio businesses was his and his alone.
Acton’s campaign didn’t get bogged down re-litigating the pandemic. Instead, she stayed focused on issues of affordability. Acton promised a “working families tax cut,” pairing a new earned income credit with a child tax credit. She committed to bringing down utility costs and starting a program to forgive medical debt.
Acton also called for a gas tax holiday a few hours before Ramaswamy embraced the idea.
The ad
In the closing weeks of the campaign, it appeared Acton might be on track to win the race as voters nationally soured on Republican leadership. But then an advertisement started circulating online, featuring Acton’s estranged mother Donna Arthur calling her a liar. Within hours, Ramaswamy’s campaign went from issuing a statement that didn’t deny they made the ad to acknowledging it was theirs.
The ad drew widespread condemnation and seems to have irreparably damaged Ramaswamy’ campaign.
Arthur sided with her husband and Acton’s stepfather, Cledith Arthur, when Acton accused him of raping her as a child. Cledith had already faced accusations of incest and pedophilia from a prior marriage. After a Mahoning County grand jury indicted Cledith in the case involving Acton, he and Donna skipped bail and fled the state. Acton said the last time she saw her mother was at the courthouse nearly 50 years ago.
Ramaswamy stood by the ad. He insisted Acton had lied about him, and “that deserves to be corrected.” Vice President JD Vance defended it, too, admonishing GOP critics to “quit whining.”
Speaking in Bexley Tuesday morning after she cast her ballot, Acton criticized Ramaswamy for running the ad. But she refused to credit it with putting her over the top.
“We were by all indications inching out ahead all along,” she said, noting her polling advantage with independents and the number of GOP voters who told her they were supporting her.
“It’s what we’ve seen on the ground,” she said. “It just hasn’t known party.”
“I do know and believe that my opponent crossed the line,” she added. “Five living governors on both sides denounced what he did. I have felt all along that there’s no low he won’t go to. I think he is out of touch. He’s out for himself, and I’ve always felt he was a danger to our state.”

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Democrat Killin ahead of Rep. Crank, early Colorado election results show
description: Early election night results show Democrat Jessica Killin has an early lead over Republican U.S. Rep. Jeff Crank in Colorado’s 5th Congressional District.  Killin had 52% of the vote over Crank’s 45% as of 8:30 p.m. The Associated Press estimated 74% of votes were counted as of 7:44 p.m. Democratic voters have outpaced Republican voters […]
text:
Republican U.S. Rep. Jeff Crank, left, and Democrat Jessica Killin, right. (Courtesy photos)Early election night results show Democrat Jessica Killin has an early lead over Republican U.S. Rep. Jeff Crank in Colorado’s 5th Congressional District. 
Killin had 52% of the vote over Crank’s 45% as of 8:30 p.m. The Associated Press estimated 74% of votes were counted as of 7:44 p.m.
Democratic voters have outpaced Republican voters in early ballot returns across the state, making it possible more votes for Crank will be counted later on. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The 5th District centers around Colorado Springs and has historically favored Republicans, though national Democrats named the district as a top priority to flip this election. The 5th District is the only district in Colorado that has never sent a Democrat to Congress. 
Killin, an Army veteran former chief of staff to second gentleman Doug Emhoff, has drawn massive support from national Democrats who saw her candidacy as an opportunity to flip the seat. 
Crank is a first-term member of Congress who won his seat in 2024 after former Republican Rep. Doug Lamborn retired. He won the seat with about 54.7% of the vote, continuing the perfect record of the district electing a Republican representative. 
Crank worked as a political consultant and radio show host and a former executive with the free-market organization Americans for Prosperity. He has aligned with President Donald Trump’s agenda, supporting landmark legislation including the tax and spending bill H.R. 1. 
Killin’s campaign has focused on Crank’s loyalty to Trump. She ran an ad featuring the family members of one of the most prominent survivors of Jeffrey Epstein to speak out about late convicted sex offender. Sky and Amanda Roberts, brother and sister-in-law of Virginia Roberts Giuffre, live in the 5th District and said Crank’s office declined to meet with them while some members of the House tried to force release of the Epstein files. Crank’s campaign defended his vote in support of releasing the files. 
Crank’s campaign has characterized Killin as a lobbyist immersed in Washington, D.C., and not focused on Colorado.

title: Early results show Eddy ahead in Montana Supreme Court race
description: It’s too early to call the nonpartisan race for an open seat on the Montana Supreme Court, but the Montana Secretary of State’s Office, which show 59,360 ballots have been processed statewide as of 8:45 p.m. In the race to replace outgoing Justice Beth Baker, Amy Eddy and Dan Wilson were separated by 12,000 ballots […]
text:
Flathead County District Court Judges Amy Eddy and Dan Wilson are facing off in the race for an open seat on the Montana Supreme Court. (contributed photos)It’s too early to call the nonpartisan race for an open seat on the Montana Supreme Court, but the Montana Secretary of State’s Office, which show 59,360 ballots have been processed statewide as of 8:45 p.m.
In the race to replace outgoing Justice Beth Baker, Amy Eddy and Dan Wilson were separated by 12,000 ballots in early returns, with Eddy leading.
There are seven seats on the Montana Supreme Court, including the chief justice. All positions for the state’s highest court, and only appellate court, are elected statewide, rather than by district, and are nonpartisan. 
Both candidates in the race for the open seat are currently district court judges in Flathead County
Eddy was appointed to the bench in 2015, and was also selected to preside over the state’s asbestos claims court. 
Wilson is a former prosecutor who has served as a Flathead District Court Judge for 10 years. He ran for the state Supreme Court in 2024, losing by 14 points. 
Both candidates declared the need for independence in the judicial branch during the campaign, but took different approaches, with Wilson aligning with the state Republican Party in a show of partisanship for the nonpartisan race. 
Voters are also deciding whether to support a constitutional amendment, CI-132, to keep Montana judicial races nonpartisan.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Democrat Janelle Stelson topples GOP Rep. Scott Perry in Pennsylvania’s 10th District
description: The race was one of the most expensive and competitive congressional contests in the state.
text:
Democrat Janelle Stelson addresses supporters after the polls closed on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Ian Karbal/Pennsylvania Capital-Star) In one of the most competitive Congressional districts in the country, Democrat Janelle Stelson defeated seven-term incumbent Rep. Scott Perry, a staunch Trump supporter and a longtime target for her party.
The race was a rematch. Stelson unsuccessfully challenged Perry in 2024, losing by roughly 5,100 votes, or just over 1% of the vote. But Democrats were hopeful that, in a year where political tailwinds appeared to be on their side, she could overcome that hurdle in this year.
While Stelson held a slight edge in polling throughout much of the campaign, one of the last polls of the election had the two in a virtual tie.
Perry, the former chair of the House Freedom Caucus, is one of President Donald Trump’s staunchest supporters in congress. He has been a vocal advocate for some of his administration’s most controversial policies, including its decision to go to war in Iran and enact sweeping cuts to the Medicaid program.
He was also a key ally in Congress during Trump’s unprecedented attempts to overturn the results of the 2020 election. Despite no evidence of widespread fraud, Perry voted not to certify Democrat Joe Biden as the winner after rioters temporarily forced Congress from its chambers on Jan. 6, 2021.
Stelson, a former Republican and WGAL news anchor, pitched herself as a moderate Democrat. She ran on bringing down the cost of living, repealing the Trump administration’s tariffs, ending the war in Iran, and protecting abortion access. She also criticized “far-left members of the Democratic Party who support open borders and defunding police.”
The 10th District includes all of Dauphin and parts of Cumberland and York Counties, encompassing the state capital Harrisburg and the city of York.
The race drew national attention and became one of the most expensive in the state. About a week ahead of the election, the candidates’ campaigns had collectively raised around $16 million, with Stelson having a roughly $2.4 million edge. Though the difference was made up in outside spending. 
As of Oct. 24, according to the nonpartisan money-in-politics tracker Opensecrets, over $12.2 million had been spent opposing Stelson or supporting Perry, compared to over $9.6 million supporting Stelson or opposing Perry.
In a race seen as potentially decisive in determining partisan control of Congress, both candidates drew support from high profile members of their party. Stelson campaigned with Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro. Perry was joined at a rally by U.S. House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.).
The final weeks of the campaign were marked by viscous and dubious messaging. Perry’s campaign ran ads misleadingly accusing Stelson of engaging in public nudity. The allegation was sourced to one of Stelson’s neighbors, though neither she nor the Perry campaign provided proof.
Reporting on the unproven claims led several TV stations in the district to pull the ad.
Perry also attempted to connect Stelson to an undocumented immigrant who was arrested and charged with indecent exposure and disorderly conduct. He pleaded guilty to the latter. 
According to a Department of Homeland Security press release, the man, Chimaobim Ibojekwe, was arrested for exposing himself in public while working as a canvasser for Stelson’s campaign.
Stelson’s campaign denied employing the man and said his name never appeared in their volunteer database. Federal campaign finance records confirm he was never paid by the campaign.
The nonprofit watchdog organization Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington accused DHS of violating the Hatch Act, a federal law that prohibits public officials from using their offices to influence elections, by publicizing the event and connecting it to Stelson’s campaign.
Stelson will be sworn in on Jan. 3, 2027.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: SC elects first Democrat to US Senate in 28 years in stunning win over Trump’s pick
description: Dr. Annie Andrews will be South Carolina’s next U.S. senator, becoming the first Democrat in 28 years to win the statewide office. When The Associated Press called the race at 10:40 p.m., the Lowcountry pediatrician had 50.6% of the votes over appointed Sen. Darline Graham. Andrews accomplished what many thought impossible a few months ago, […]
text:
Bill and Susan Taylor, of Chapin, and Sue Kreines of Ladson, cheer numbers coming in for Democrat Annie Andrews at her watch party at the Charleston Marriott in downtown Charleston, S.C., on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Jessica Holdman/SC Daily Gazette)Dr. Annie Andrews will be South Carolina’s next U.S. senator, becoming the first Democrat in 28 years to win the statewide office.
When The Associated Press called the race at 10:40 p.m., the Lowcountry pediatrician had 50.6% of the votes over appointed Sen. Darline Graham.
Andrews accomplished what many thought impossible a few months ago, as she took the majority of votes even in counties normally deeply red.
She was slated to face 24-year incumbent U.S. Lindsey Graham until he died July 11 from a ruptured aorta at age 71, resulting in a GOP sprint to replace him on the ballot.
As Alan Wilson, the state’s next governor, put it last Thursday, “No one had that on their bingo card when they began 2026.”
The late senator’s younger sister, Darline Graham, was appointed to the seat as an expected placeholder. She jumped into the special GOP primary to replace him on the ballot with the encouragement and endorsement of President Donald Trump.
That ultimately helped Andrews’ arguments that she alone was the candidate willing to buck Washington. It also ignited a GOP feud.
Graham emerged the winner in August of a 10-way contest, thanks partly to a Trump rally ahead of the runoff. But her nomination angered many Republicans — particularly supporters of U.S. Rep. Ralph Norman, who have long criticized Lindsey Graham as not conservative enough and saw this as their chance to elect a hardline Freedom Caucus Republican.
Andrews played into that frustration, likening Graham’s win to Trump handpicking a successor who will answer to him instead of South Carolinians. She invited Republicans to join her in a rejection of the Washington “swamp,” echoing Trump’s “drain the swamp” slogan.
“This Senate seat belongs to South Carolina. It does not belong to one family,” Andrews said at a rally in Columbia on Oct. 16.
And supporters of Norman, who tripled down on his refusal to campaign with Graham, encouraged upset conservatives to write his name on the ballot, potentially indirectly helping Andrews. His son, Warren Norman, publicly endorsed her. Ultimately, the number of write-ins weren’t enough to make a difference.
But many Republicans clearly split their ticket, as Wilson and other Republicans won.
Andrews focused on the pocketbook issues that are causing Trump’s support to sag even in South Carolina — where he won by 18 percentage points two years ago.
A pediatrician, she traveled the state talking about making healthcare more accessible and affordable, and ending the war in Iran to bring gas prices down.
Republicans painted her as a radical liberal, pointing to her previous advocacy at the Statehouse over transgender issues and her own social media posts as proof. They also pointed to her work over the last two years for the nation’s largest gun safety group to warn she wanted to ban guns and take them away.
But the allegations didn’t stick. She pledged to work for South Carolinians and stand up to her own party when she disagreed.
“I don’t know what’s so radical about thinking every county in South Carolina should have an OB-GYN or thinking that hardworking South Carolina families shouldn’t have to worry about putting food on the table, paying for their prescription drugs, and that if you’re sick in South Carolina, that you should be able to afford to see a doctor and be able to find a doctor in your community,” she told reporters last month when asked to respond to Trump’s accusations. “I don’t know what’s so radical about all that.”
With polls showing an increasingly tight contest, some as a statistical tie, Trump returned to South Carolina twice in the last two weeks to boost her support.
“I got you into this thing,” Trump said to her from the stage in Rock Hill last Thursday.
Before her brother’s death, Graham worked 30 years in state government. For the last seven, she led the state’s Commission for the Blind.
Both Andrews and Graham’s fellow Republicans criticized her throughout the campaign for her lack of political experience.
During the only runoff debate with Norman, she flubbed a foreign policy question. Asked whether Taiwan is a national security issue for the United States, Graham blanked, eventually acknowledging that “national security is not my thing, not my area of expertise.”
She said she’s not a polished politician and was just being honest. Critics on the left and right called it evidence that she’s woefully unprepared.
Andrews brought up the flub during their only debate last month.
Amid the infighting, other Republican nominees stepped up calls for unity in the last few weeks. Others joining Graham on the campaign trail recently to convince wary conservatives included former state Rep. Adam Morgan of Greenville. The founding chair of the uber-conservative Freedom Caucus in the Statehouse, which Norman helped launch in 2022, was also Norman’s running mate in his unsuccessful bid for governor earlier this year.
Graham also signaled to her brother’s critics on the right that she’s more conservative than him.
“On border security, I love my brother dearly. I love Lindsey,” she said on stage in Rock Hill. “But when it comes to illegal immigration. I take a tougher stance. If you come here illegally, you have to go.”
Many conservatives still faulted Lindsey Graham for his work in the bipartisan “Gang of Eight” and the failed effort in 2013 to overhaul America’s immigration laws, which gave him the nickname Grahamnesty.
Flipping that around, Darline Graham said Andrews supports amnesty.
Republicans painted Andrews as a radical liberal, while Graham would have Trump’s back.
For Democrats in South Carolina, the accusations coming from Republicans about Andrews only increased their enthusiasm.
Mari Shari of North Charleston said her response to the many ads calling Andrews “radically left” was “oh, that sounds good to me.”
“We need change,” said the 49-year-old accountant. “I just want a strong middle class and for everyone to be treated fairly.”
This is a developing story. Check back for updates.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Democrat Brooks ousts incumbent Mackenzie in Lehigh Valley’s 7th Congressional District
description: Democrats, who hoped to pick up four seats nationwide to win control of the House, targeted Mackenzie as one of four vulnerable Republican U.S. representatives in Pennsylvania.
text:
(This story will be updated through the night.)
Democrats flipped a Republican-held U.S. House seat Tuesday in Pennsylvania’s 7th Congressional District as firefighters union president Bob Brooks defeated first-term incumbent Rep. Ryan Mackenzie.
The Associated Press called the race for Brooks with 57% of the vote against Mackenzie’s 43% at 10:27 p.m., when about 80% of ballots had been counted.
The race pitted Brooks, a former firefighter and president of the state firefighters union, against Mackenzie, a first-term congressman and former state lawmaker. Mackenzie defeated three-term incumbent Democratic Rep. Susan Wild by a 1-point margin in 2024.
The 7th District lies in eastern Pennsylvania’s Lehigh Valley, encompassing Carbon, Lehigh and Northampton counties and the commonwealth’s third-largest metro area, with Allentown at its heart. Its dense urban core and expansive rural areas help make the district among the most swingy in the nation, according to political observers.
Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee Chair Suzan DelBene said Brooks demonstrated in the campaign that he knows what a hard day’s work and serving his community looks like. “That’s why he’s going to Congress,” she said.
“After 20 years putting out fires in the city of Bethlehem, 30 years coaching youth baseball, and a lifetime of hard work, the voters of the Lehigh Valley put their trust in Bob because they know he will fight for them,” DelBene said. “Bob is going to help put out the fire in Washington D.C. and build something better from the ashes.”
Democratic National Committee Chair Ken Martin congratulated Brooks and the Pennsylvania Democratic Party and local organizers for the victory.
“As a local firefighter and an advocate for first responders, Bob always fought to protect working families and keep his community safe. He will take this fight to Congress while lowering costs, expanding access to healthcare, standing up for workers, and making life more affordable,” Martin said.
Brooks emerged as the winner of a four-way race for the nomination in the Democratic primary in May. A Muhlenberg College Institute of Public Opinion poll released shortly before Election Day gave Brooks a 49% to 43% advantage over the incumbent.
Democrats, who hoped to pick up four seats nationwide to win control of the House, targeted Mackenzie as one of four vulnerable Republican U.S. representatives in Pennsylvania. 
Mackenzie and Brooks collected about $13.4 million in combined campaign contributions, making it one of the most costly in Pennsylvania, according to the campaign finance tracking group OpenSecrets. Outside spending accounted for another $23.5 million, including $4 million in support of Brooks and about $9 million opposing each of the candidates.
Mackenzie, an ally of President Donald Trump, touted his support for the administration’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act and the tax cuts it encompassed, including an increase in the child tax credit and credits for tips and overtime. 
He took credit for breaking with Republicans when he voted for an extension of the Affordable Care Act tax credits that helped reduce the cost of health and for voting in support of federal housing affordability measures. Mackenzie was also a co-sponsor of the Ratepayer Protection Act, a bipartisan measure that passed the House this fall with the aim of ensuring consumers don’t get stuck with energy costs associated with data centers. 
Brooks talked up his everyman credentials and experience as a firefighter, with campaign ads showing him driving a plow truck for his landscaping business and extinguishing a flaming dumpster standing in for the Washington, D.C., establishment. 
He said his experience as a union leader promoting legislation in Harrisburg and Washington to help firefighters and first responders give him the credentials to serve in the House. He vowed to work to end the war in Iran and hold corporations accountable for high prices and fight corruption. 
Among his victories, Brooks counts the addition of workers’ compensation benefits for first responders suffering from post-traumatic stress injuries. He’s also worked with state lawmakers to pass a bill that would ban a group of chemicals known as PFAS from firefighters’ turnout gear  and firefighting foam. Gov. Josh Shapiro signed the bill into law last month.
In Washington, Brooks claims credit for the Social Security Fairness Act, which repealed provisions of federal law that limited or eliminated Social Security benefits for firefighters, police and other public employees across the country.
Brooks attacked Mackenzie as “a career politician who has voted with Trump nearly 100% of the time in Washington” and told voters it’s time to “send one of us” to Washington to “shake things up.” 
In its final weeks, the race between Brooks and Mackenzie turned increasingly ugly, with the campaigns trading cease and desist letters over commercials each claimed was defamatory.
Throughout the race, Mackenzie and outside groups opposing Brooks hammered him in commercials, questioning his suitability for Congress because of a Northampton County lawsuit over a $130,000 debt to his former mother-in-law. Brooks and his ex-mother-in-law Carol Wiley settled the case in September. 
Last month Brooks’ campaign demanded that Mackenzie cease airing an ad that accused Brooks of “violating state law” by canceling the workers’ compensation insurance for employees of his landscaping business. Brooks’ lawyer said the claim is demonstrably false because the business had no employees when the policy expired.
Brooks withdrew from the only debate scheduled with Mackenzie, citing months of “outright lies … that go completely outside of the bounds of acceptable campaign rhetoric.” Mackenzie refused to take down the ad.
Days later, lawyers for Mackenzie’s campaign demanded that Brooks’ take down an ad claiming Mackenzie had fought legislation to provide workers’ compensation for first responders suffering from post-traumatic stress disorder. The bill was signed into law in 2024 after several failed attempts.
The ad featured state Rep. Jennifer O’Mara (D-Delaware), who sponsored the legislation after experiencing the loss of her father, a Philadelphia firefighter, to suicide while struggling with the condition. “Ryan Mackenzie fought us the whole time,” she said in the ad. Brooks’ campaign refused to stop airing the commercial.

text:

Mark Pocan and Gwen Moore were both reelected Tuesday. | Official photosWisconsin’s incumbent Democratic U.S. Reps Gwen Moore (D-Milwaukee) and Mark Pocan (D-Black Earth) cruised to early reelection victories Tuesday evening as Democrats across the nation gained momentum in more competitive races, setting up a likely Democratic takeover of the House of Representatives.

A small business owner, union member, and advocate for progressive causes, he serves on the powerful House Appropriations Committee and is co-chair of the Equality Caucus, co-chair of the Labor Caucus, and chair emeritus of the Congressional Progressive Caucus.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Rhode Island voters reject two bond questions, approve $450 million in borrowing
description: Rhode Islanders OK’d three of five bond measures on Tuesday’s ballot, approving a combined $450 million in borrowing to fund projects in higher education, housing and environmental projects, while rejecting $150 million for economic development and historic preservation.  The bond package was the biggest ever put before Rhode Islanders at the ballot box. Acc[...]
text:
Rhode Island College students study inside Adams Library on Monday, Nov. 2, 2026. The library stands to receive $50 million in renovations and a consolidated student success and career readiness center now that voters approved Question 1 on Tuesday's ballot. (Photo by Michael Salerno/Rhode Island Current)Rhode Islanders OK’d three of five bond measures on Tuesday’s ballot, approving a combined $450 million in borrowing to fund projects in higher education, housing and environmental projects, while rejecting $150 million for economic development and historic preservation. 
The bond package was the biggest ever put before Rhode Islanders at the ballot box. 
According to unofficial results from the Rhode Island Board of Elections as of 10:19 p.m., the five measures fared as follows:

 Question 1: Higher education, $275 million. 59.82% of voters approved.
 Question 2: Housing, $120 million. 61.12% of voters approved.
 Question 3: Economic development, $100 million. 52.47% of voters rejected.
  Question 4: Cultural economy, $50 million. 50.79% of voters rejected.
 Question 5: Green economy, $55 million. 66.92% of voters approved.

The state issues general obligation bonds for the authorized measures. These bonds are then repaid with interest through future state budgets. 
Approval of the bond questions does not mean the state borrowing begins immediately. 
The state’s voter information guides estimated the total costs of the loans, modeling 5% interest and a 20-year repayment plan for each loan. Under those assumptions, the three approved measures would cost approximately $722 million in principal and interest, compared with roughly $963 million had voters approved all five.
The defeat of Questions 3 and 4 — which sought to fund economic development and create a State History Center, respectively — represents the first time voters in the Ocean State have defeated a bond measure since 2006, when they rejected a $4 million bond for Newport’s Fort Adams. Before Tuesday, every bond put before Rhode Islanders in the intervening two decades had won approval.
Katherine MacGregor, 45, of Middletown, an attorney and registered Democrat, said she voted yes on four of the five ballot questions Tuesday morning.
The only one she rejected was Question 3, the $100 million economy bond for site development at the Quonset Business Park in North Kingstown and the I-195 District in Providence along with infrastructure enhancements. The bond question, which did not specify which projects would benefit from the bond money, was supported by the RI Ports Coalition. 
“It was a little unclear I thought in the description what they were developing,” MacGregor said. “It was not sufficiently detailed.”
MacGregor was interviewed outside the polling site at Thompson Middle School in Newport where she accompanied her significant other Brian Russell, 57, who voted there. 
Russell said he voted yes on four of the five ballot questions too. But he voted no on Question 4, which sought a total of $50 million with $45 million for a new state history center across from the State House in Providence and $5 million for the state program providing matching grants to municipalities looking to preserve historic and culturally significant properties.
The state already has sufficient resources devoted to historic preservation, he said.
“It just seemed to be $50 million for something that I felt was kind of covered,” Russell said.
Here’s a breakdown of the bonds voted on Tuesday. 
Question 1: $275 million for higher education
The largest bond measure approved provides $275 million for construction and renovations at Rhode Island’s three public institutions of higher education.
More than half the package — $165 million — will go to the University of Rhode Island (URI) for a new Integrated Health Building on its Kingston campus. The new building will be near White Hall, which currently houses URI’s nursing education program.
URI spokesperson Dawn Bergantino told Rhode Island Current in a recent email that the facility would strengthen existing programs in nursing, pharmacy and health sciences by modernizing teaching and clinical training spaces. Spending on construction for this project would continue through fiscal year 2031, the university expects.
Another $60 million will fund a 44,000-square-foot Workforce Innovation Center at the Community College of Rhode Island’s (CCRI) Knight Campus in Warwick.
A rendering of the Workforce Innovation Center envisioned for the Community College of Rhode Island’s Knight Campus in Warwick. (Courtesy of Rhode Islanders for Higher Education)
CCRI’s Chief of Staff Amy Kempe said via email that the center will expand the college’s existing offerings and increase training opportunities in skilled trades — some of which currently lack dedicated facilities, including plumbing, HVAC and welding.
Kempe cited a recent partnership with Senesco Marine in which CCRI needed to use the company’s welding space to train prospective workers. Similar training opportunities could now be provided on campus with the new workforce center, Kempe said. She noted that more than 22,000 square feet of the building would be devoted to laboratories and workshops. 
The remaining $50 million will go toward Rhode Island College (RIC), which wants to use the money to renovate the Adams Library and its Student Success and Career Readiness Center. 
Academic advising, tutoring and career services are already offered in the Adams Library. But school spokesperson John Taraborelli said in a recent email that these services are “housed deep within the lower levels of an outdated building, working in space that was not designed for their purposes.”
“Despite some minor updates and renovations throughout the years, Adams Library is still very much the same building it was when it opened in 1963,” Taraborelli wrote.
The renovations would modernize the building and make student support services more central and accessible.
Question 2: $120 million for housing and homeownership
Voters decided to authorize $120 million for housing construction and redevelopment, echoing their approval from two years ago, when Rhode Islanders approved the same amount in a similar bond.
Like the 2024 bond, the version approved by voters Tuesday is intended to support new construction, rehabilitation, property acquisition and infrastructure improvements.
At least $25 million is allotted to help increase the supply of housing intended for homeownership. Up to $10 million could support public housing development.
The latest bond approval comes amid scrutiny of the effectiveness of previous state investments in housing. A May report by the Rhode Island Public Expenditure Council questioned the cost and pace of state subsidized housing production. The council’s analysis found that $52.2 million in public funding had financed 200 new rental units, for an average development cost of more than $512,000 per unit.
State housing officials disagreed with that assessment and argued that the report overlooks the costs and complications associated with subsidized housing. Housing Secretary Deborah Goddard said in October that the state’s actual subsidy per unit was much lower, while some developments incur additional costs because of additional support services for residents, or because of environmental cleanup needed for certain sites. 
Projects funded through the Question 2 bond money are expected to begin in 2028, with completion anticipated between 2029 and 2032.
Quonset Terminal 5 at the Port of Davisville. (Photo by Quonset Development Corporation)
Question 3: $100 million for economic development
Voters rejected $100 million in financing for industry and infrastructure development. 
The investments, which were intended to jumpstart business development, would have included $55 million for land acquisition, environmental cleanup, utility installation and other improvements at sites such as Quonset Business Park and Providence’s I-195 Redevelopment District.
Another $45 million was meant to support infrastructure including defense, ocean technology, life sciences and cybersecurity. Projects which could potentially receive funding included underwater testing facilities, research and production sites, and investments supporting businesses in the life sciences. 
No specific projects were earmarked for the funding, however.
The measure was a scaled-down version of Gov. Dan McKee’s original $115 million proposal, which lawmakers reduced over the course of the legislative session earlier this year.
An architectural rendering shows what a Rhode Island State History Center could look like across from the State House in Providence.(Rendering by LLB Architects/courtesy of the Rhode Island Department of State)
Question 4: $50 million for history and cultural preservation
The rejection by Rhode Island voters set back Secretary of State Gregg Amore’s longstanding goal to build a dedicated place to host Rhode Island’s historical artifacts in Providence.
The defeated measure would have authorized up to $45 million for a two-story, 24,600-square-foot State History Center across from the State House and next to the Department of Administration. Another $5 million in supporting grants would have gone toward preserving historic and cultural properties statewide.
The State History Center, which would have tentatively opened in 2030, was designed to feature exhibits including Rhode Island’s colonial Royal Charter and one of the state’s copies of the Declaration of Independence. Tuesday’s rejection leaves the project without the proposed bond financing.
But the State History Center has survived setbacks before. Amore’s original proposal in 2024 would have cost $102 million, but lawmakers never approved its funding and it never made it into the budget that year nor was it put before voters.
Beachgoers are shown at Goddard Memorial State Park in Warwick in July 2025. (Photo by Laura Paton/Rhode Island Current)
Question 5: $55 million for the green economy
The final measure provides $55 million for climate resilience, environmental restoration and recreational improvements. Most of the projects have an expected five-year timeline for completion.
The biggest portion of the funding, $25 million, goes toward the Resilient Rhody Infrastructure Fund, meant to assist municipalities for projects that address flooding, coastal erosion and other climate-related hazards.
Other funding allocations include:

$12 million for improvements at state parks, beaches and campgrounds
$7 million for Narragansett Bay and watershed restoration
$3 million each for brownfield cleanup, farmland preservation and open-space conservation
$2 million split between local recreation projects and marine infrastructure improvements, such as boat launches and docks.

text:
Democratic gubernatorial nominee Hannah Pingree speaks in Deering Oaks park in Portland on October 17 as part of the national No Kings day of action. (Photo by Jim Neuger/ Maine Morning Star)This is a breaking story that will be updated.
Democrat Hannah Pingree has been declared the winner in Maine’s gubernatorial election, according to an initial call by the Bangor Daily News and Decision Desk HQ. 
The former speaker of the Maine House of Representatives defeated Republican Bobby Charles and independent Rick Bennett in the three-way contest to succeed Gov. Janet Mills. 
As of 10:30 p.m., Pingree had secured 48.8% of votes while Charles had 43% and Bennett had 8.2% with 29% of votes counted, according to initial totals from the Bangor Daily News, which gathered totals from municipalities and partnered with Decision Desk HQ to make the call. The Associated Press has yet to call the race.
Pingree had been seen as the frontrunner in the race and her campaign raised more money than both of her opponents combined. According to the Maine Ethics Commission, the Democrat raised more than $4.9 million. Charles has raised just over $2 million, and as of last week Bennett has raised slightly below a million dollars.
The results mean Democrats will continue to control the Blaine House for the next four years. Pingree previously served under Mills as the inaugural head of the Governor’s Office of Policy, Innovation and the Future.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Mississippi reelects all four of its US House members
description: Voters fill out their ballots at Briarwood Presbyterian Church in Jackson during the midterm elections on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Mississippi’s four U.S. House incumbents easily won new two-year terms Tuesday. 
Democrats are attempting to reclaim a majority in the lower chamber of Congress, and they looked poised to do so as early results from around the country began pouring in. But Mississippi’s House incumbents, three of whom are Republicans, were all re-elected. 
1st Congressional District
In the 1st District in northern Mississippi, Republican Rep. Trent Kelly won a seventh term, defeating attorney Cliff Johnson, director of the MacArthur Justice Center and a professor at the University of Mississippi School of Law. 
The Associated Press declared Kelly as the winner, leading with 64% of the vote in incomplete and unofficial totals, and Johnson receiving 34.6%. Johnny Baucom, a Libertarian candidate from Columbus, trailed both with 1.4%. 
The historically conservative district stretches from northeast Mississippi to the populous DeSoto County on the northwestern side of the state.

Kelly serves on the House Armed Services Committee and chairs the Seapower and Projection Forces Subcommittee. He is the vice chair of Intelligence and a member of the Agriculture Committee. He has been a staunch defender of President Donald Trump, particularly the president’s defense and national security decisions.
Before becoming a law school professor, Johnson worked for five years as an assistant U.S. attorney during the Clinton administration. He had been hoping to become the first Democrat to represent Mississippi’s 1st District in Congress since Travis Childers won in 2008.  
Kelly first won a special election in 2015 to fill the seat after the death of former Rep. Alan Nunnelee. He has since been reelected to a full term six times.
2nd Congressional District
In the 2nd District in central and western Mississippi, longtime Rep. Democrat Bennie Thompson defeated Republican challenger Ron Eller, a cardiac physician’s assistant from Jackson.  
The Associated Press declared Thompson as the winner with incomplete and unofficial results, leading with 65.5% and Eller receiving 32%. Bennie Foster, an independent candidate from Jackson, trailed both with a little over 2%.
A native of Bolton, Thompson has represented the 2nd District covering Jackson and the Delta since 1993. He is the current ranking member and former chairman of the Homeland Security Committee.
A civil rights leader and former chair of the House Select Committee investigating the Jan. 6 Capitol attack, Thompson is a towering figure in state and national politics. That status has made him the prime target of Republican state leaders, who are poised to redraw his seat through redistricting after the U.S. Supreme Court’s Callais decision that gutted the Voting Rights Act earlier this year.
Thompson, the lone Democrat and lone Black member of Mississippi’s congressional delegation, has dominated his reelection contests ever since first entering Congress. 
3rd Congressional District 
In the 3rd District in central Mississippi, four-term Rep. Republican Michael Guest defeated Democratic challenger Michael Chiaradio, a farmer and entrepreneur from Shubuta.
The district covers central portions of the state, such as the GOP stronghold of Rankin County, and stretches from the Louisiana border in the west to rural Alabama border towns in the east.
Guest serves as chair of the House Ethics Committee, and also serves on the Homeland Security and Appropriations committees. He ran a steady, low-profile campaign, appearing at local events hosted by the Mississippi Federation of Republican Women and with U.S. Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith.
Chiaradio, a first-time candidate for Congress originally from New Jersey, is a former baseball player turned farmer living in rural Mississippi. He told Mississippi Today that he believed a localized message built around economic frustration could unite both disaffected conservatives and a fractured Democratic Party. 
4th Congressional District
In the 4th District in southern Mississippi, Republican Rep. Mike Ezell won a third term, defeating Democratic state lawmaker Jeffrey Hulum. 
The Associated Press declared Ezell as the winner, leading with 57.7% and Hulum receiving 39.5% with. Carl Boyanton, an independent candidate from Diamondhead, trailed both with 2.8%.
A native of Pascagoula, Ezell was formerly sheriff of Jackson County. He entered Congress after defeating former Republican U.S. Rep. Steven Palazzo in 2022. Before that, Ezell was the Jackson County sheriff. He serves on the Natural Resources Committee and the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee. 
Ezell has said he wants to introduce legislation that rolls back unnecessary federal regulations at the Federal Emergency Management Agency to make it easier for state and local governments to receive relief after natural disasters damage Mississippi communities. 
Hulum had been attempting to become the first Democrat to win the southern district since 2008. He currently represents Gulfport in the Mississippi House of Representatives, and he served in the U.S. Army for 22 years, retiring as a sergeant major. If elected, Hulum would have been be the first Black person to represent the 4th Congressional District.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: Alan Wilson declares victory in SC governor’s race; Johnson concedes
description: COLUMBIA — South Carolina’s four-term GOP attorney general is moving to the Governor’s Mansion. Voters elected Republican Alan Wilson as South Carolina’s next governor and state Sen. Mike Reichenbach as lieutenant governor.  When Democratic state Rep. Jermaine Johnson conceded at 10:31 p.m., Wilson was leading with 52% of the vote, with 90% of votes counted,[...]
text:
South Carolina Republican Party Chairman Drew McKissick addresses the crowd at the GOP election night watch party on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026, at the Moore Building on the South Carolina State Fairgrounds in Columbia. (Photo by John A. Carlos II/Special to the SC Daily Gazette)COLUMBIA — South Carolina’s four-term GOP attorney general is moving to the Governor’s Mansion. 
Voters elected Republican Alan Wilson as South Carolina’s next governor and state Sen. Mike Reichenbach as lieutenant governor. 
When Democratic state Rep. Jermaine Johnson conceded at 10:31 p.m., Wilson was leading with 52% of the vote, with 90% of votes counted, according to unofficial results. 
Johnson said he spoke to Wilson, who said he needed Johnson’s help to unite South Carolina. When he gets home, he’ll pray for Wilson, Johnson said.
“I believe that when we wish our leaders to fail, we are wishing our own selves to fail,” Johnson said at his election night party at Brookland Baptist Church in West Columbia “So, I don’t want him to fail. I want him to be the best governor this state has ever seen.”
The results were much closer than expected. The Associated Press had yet to call the race when Johnson conceded.
Wilson will take the helm from his former boss, Gov. Henry McMaster, South Carolina’s oldest and longest-serving governor in state history. Wilson was an assistant attorney general when McMaster was the state’s chief prosecutor.
Wilson, whose 31 years in the Army National Guard includes a combat tour in Iraq, campaigned as a career prosecutor and career soldier who will “continue to fight for the state of South Carolina.”
His platform included familiar GOP pledges to push for lowering taxes, expanding school choice, and continuing to “back the blue.”
He’s touted working with local, state and federal law enforcement officers in a tenure that spanned two Democrats and one Republican in the White House.
“I earned the respect of a large majority of the sheriffs and law enforcement in this state because they trust me to fight for you,” Wilson said last Thursday during a GOP rally in Rock Hill ahead of President Donald Trump taking the stage. 
“I’m honored that they have my back, and I’m going to have their back because they’ve got your back. And I’ve also got Donald Trump’s back because he has your back.” 
He’s gone to court repeatedly to combat the Obama and Biden administrations and support the Trump administration. Last year alone, Wilson’s office announced joining other Republicans or declared victory on more than 60 multi-state lawsuits.
Inside Alan Wilson’s historic GOP primary victory over Pamela Evette

Yet, he didn’t initially have Trump’s endorsement.
The president instead backed Lt. Gov. Pamela Evette ahead of a contentious, five-way GOP primary in June, propelling her into a first-place finish heading into the runoff, though by less than 3 percentage points. With Wilson showing momentum and picking up endorsements from their former competitors, Trump endorsed Wilson too — saying voters couldn’t go wrong with either candidate.
Wilson then trounced Evette by 37 percentage points, a historic margin, to become the GOP nominee.
Wilson, a native of Lexington County, noted during the runoff debate that Evette, the lieutenant governor since 2018, moved to South Carolina from Ohio 20 years ago.
He was the first gubernatorial candidate of either party to pick a running mate. He chose a Pee Dee legislator with a common bond: Like Wilson, the adopted son of U.S. Rep. Joe Wilson, Reichenbach was adopted as a child.
The Florence Republican, first elected to the state Senate in a 2022 special election, becomes the first Black lieutenant governor since Reconstruction.
His role is largely up to Wilson. The job of lieutenant governor has no official duties in state law, other than stepping up if something happens to the governor.
When Wilson announced his pick in January, Reichenbach said he hopes to use the job as a metaphorical megaphone to advocate for issues that are deeply personal for him, such as making adoptions easier and more affordable.
Johnson campaigned on a “New SC,” arguing that the Republican dominance over state politics hasn’t delivered for residents. 
South Carolina hasn’t elected a Democrat to the governor’s office since 1998, when state-Rep. Jim Hodges ousted David Beasley. It’s been 20 years since a Democrat won any statewide office.
It was the first open gubernatorial race since 2010, when state Rep. Nikki Haley became the state’s first female and first minority governor. Mid-way through her second term, Haley became Trump’s first United Nations ambassador, allowing then-Lt. Gov. McMaster to ascend to the job in January 2017.
In South Carolina, governors can’t be elected to more than two consecutive terms. But McMaster was in office for nearly two years before voters first elected him, giving him 10 total years.

Voters returned U.S. Rep. Scott Fitzgerald in the 5th District to his seat in the U.S. House of Representatives Tuesday.
With 77% of the ballots counted, the AP called the 5th District race for Fitzgerald (R-Juneau) at 9:14 p.m. Fitzgerald defeated Democrat Andy Beck of West Bend, winning a fourth term in office.
The 5th District covers all of Jefferson and Washington counties, most of Waukesha County and a portion of Dodge County.
Beck, who has worked in healthcare sales, marketing and customer service for a variety of firms, ran a grass-roots campaign. He raised a little less than $15,000 as of June 30, according to Federal Election Commission filings.  
Fitzgerald, a former state senator who was first elected to Congress in 2020, raised more than 10 times that amount, $1.7 million in the 2025-26 cycle, spending more than $1.3 million in the same period, Open Secrets reports.

title: Hoosiers reject a possible casino in northeast Indiana
description: A new casino won’t be coming to northeast Indiana after voters in those counties rejected a referendum to add gaming Tuesday. Public Question No. 3 in Allen, DeKalb and Steuben counties asked, “Shall inland casino gambling be permitted in (your) county?” According to the Fort Wayne Journal Gazette, more than 58% — or 6,234 votes […]
text:
Gaming operators from around the nation can now bid to build a new casino in XXXX. (Getty Images)A new casino won’t be coming to northeast Indiana after voters in those counties rejected a referendum to add gaming Tuesday.
Public Question No. 3 in Allen, DeKalb and Steuben counties asked, “Shall inland casino gambling be permitted in (your) county?”
According to the Fort Wayne Journal Gazette, more than 58% — or 6,234 votes – voted no in Steuben County, according to unofficial final results. Nearly 65% – or 7,374 voters – opposed the casino in DeKalb County.
Allen County results were still coming in, but 59% of the votes were opposed with 98% reporting.
Business groups in Allen County backed the project as an economic development tool while opponents criticized gambling as a predatory enterprise that would be bad for Hoosiers.
An Indiana Gaming Commission study projected that an Allen County casino could generate $204 million in revenue and $61 million in annual state taxes. Steuben County Economic Development Corp. released a feasibility study in April with its own case for a casino there.
Lawmakers left Indianapolis off the list because it would take away business from two existing casinos in Shelbyville and Anderson. Some also preferred the unserved northeast Indiana corner because it would draw patrons from Ohio and Michigan.
House Enrolled Act 1038, approved earlier this year, authorizes a new license for an inland casino in one of the three northeast counties and knocks off one unused “racino” license for horse-racing wagering with slot machines.
Casino developers were to submit applications to the Indiana Gaming Commission by Dec. 1. If they reject the casino idea, the law provides, “a second public question under this section may not be held in that county.”
Whichever developer is selected would be required to invest at least $500 million across the prospective casino and non-gambling amenities, with at least 60% spent within two years of the license authorization.  The rest must be invested — and the development completed — within five years of when operations begin.
They’d also pay a fee to the state: $100 million for the license and $50 million to support former host communities hurt by casino closures. Additional payments to the host community or state could be part of the deal, too.

text:
Jon Echols, Oklahoma's next attorney general, speaks during the GOP Election Night Watch Party, Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026, at Skirvin Hotel in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Kyle Phillips/For Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY — Republican Jon Echols is set to be Oklahoma’s next attorney general.
Echols will succeed Attorney General Gentner Drummond who launched an unsuccessful bid for governor rather than seek a second term. 
He won the election over Democrat Nick Coffey. Echols said Coffey is a “good man” who ran a “valiant race.”
“This is just the end of our race, but this is the start of our mission,” Echols said during his victory speech at the Skirvin Hotel in Oklahoma City. “We campaigned on a simple platform, and that is that we are going to create: a safer, freer, stronger Oklahoma.”
He said as the next attorney general, he will ensure the law applies equally to all regardless of party affiliation.  
Echols, 46, served in the Oklahoma House for 12 years and was the majority floor leader for eight of them. He holds a law degree from Oklahoma City University.  
Echols lives in Oklahoma City where he practices law in civil litigation, regulatory compliance and consumer protection. 
He’s also owned healthcare and construction companies.
As attorney general, Echols has said he wants to protect the freedoms of Oklahomans and uphold Judeo Christian values, protect landowners from foreign interests and stand with President Donald Trump.
Echols will be sworn in as attorney general Jan. 11.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Democrat J.D. Ford declares victory over Victoria Spartz in major upset for Indiana’s 5th District
description: Hoosier Democrat J.D. Ford declared victory in a major political upset Tuesday night, unseating three-term Republican U.S. Rep. Victoria Spartz in Indiana’s 5th Congressional District and flipping a seat the GOP had held for years. Ford, a two-term state senator from Indianapolis, defeated Spartz in a closely watched contest that became one of Indiana’s most[...]
text:
Republican U.S. Rep Victoria Spartz, left, speaks with Democratic state Sen. J.D. Ford following a news conference about flooding damage in Carmel, Indiana, on Aug. 31, 2026. (Photo by Tom Davies/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Hoosier Democrat J.D. Ford declared victory in a major political upset Tuesday night, unseating three-term Republican U.S. Rep. Victoria Spartz in Indiana’s 5th Congressional District and flipping a seat the GOP had held for years.
Ford, a two-term state senator from Indianapolis, defeated Spartz in a closely watched contest that became one of Indiana’s most competitive congressional races as Democrats sought to gain ground in the U.S. House.
With 93% of votes counted as of 10:15 p.m., Ford had received 51.6% of the vote to Spartz’s 48.4%, according to the Associated Press. Nearly 255,000 votes had been tallied at that point.
The victory marks a notable political shift in a district that stretches from Indianapolis’ northern suburbs into north-central Indiana, including Carmel, Fishers, Noblesville, Anderson, Muncie and Marion.
It also ends Spartz’s six-year tenure in Congress and sends Ford, Indiana’s first openly gay state legislator, to Washington after eight years in the Indiana Senate.
“Tonight, Hoosiers made history, and they sent a message that will be heard far beyond Indiana’s 5th District,” Ford said in a statement. “This victory belongs to every person who has felt ignored by Washington, every family struggling to make ends meet and every voter who refused to believe that change was impossible. Hoosiers are demanding leaders who put people ahead of powerful interests and deliver results that make their lives better. I’m truly honored that Hoosiers have trusted me to be the person who fights for that change, and that’s exactly what I intend to do.”
Spartz won reelection two years ago by more than 18 percentage points, and she carried the district by an even wider margin in her race before that. Her first congressional victory, in 2020, was much narrower, before Republican lawmakers redrew Indiana’s congressional boundaries the following year.
Ford’s win gives Democrats a pickup in Indiana as both parties compete for control of the U.S. House.
A competitive race in Republican territory
Ford’s challenge to Spartz drew growing attention from national Democrats in the months leading up to Election Day.
The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee added Indiana’s 5th District to its list of competitive races in August, targeting a seat that had become more reliably Republican after the 2021 redistricting process.
An internal poll commissioned by Ford’s campaign over the summer showed Spartz leading 48% to 46%, within the survey’s margin of error. A separate poll released in October by House Majority PAC, a Democratic-aligned super PAC, put a generic Republican candidate at 48% and a Democrat at 47%.
The race also drew increased scrutiny from national election analysts.



Quotation







Hoosiers are demanding leaders who put people ahead of powerful interests and deliver results that make their lives better.


– Democrat congressional candidate J.D. Ford


Just days before the election, the Cook Political Report moved the contest from “Likely Republican” to “Leans Republican,” as the race grew more competitive.
Spartz acknowledged the political challenges ahead of the election.
In an October interview with State Affairs, the congresswoman described an “extremely difficult political environment,” pointing to economic concerns, population changes in the district and the possibility of lower Republican turnout in a midterm election.
“So the political environment is challenging, and we are not taking this election for granted,” Spartz said.
Ford’s victory adds to recent Democratic gains in Hamilton County and the surrounding Indianapolis suburbs, where Republicans have traditionally been dominant.
Competing messages on costs and accountability
Ford, who was first elected to the Indiana Senate in 2018 after defeating Republican incumbent Mike Delph, built his congressional campaign around household affordability, healthcare and government accountability.
He criticized President Donald Trump’s tariffs and their effects on Indiana families, farmers and businesses, while promising to challenge federal policies he said were driving up everyday expenses.
“All across the 5th district, I hear families talk about the high cost of groceries, utilities and gas,” Ford said in a statement to State Affairs before the election. “I will always listen to what matters to the people of the 5th district, and I will always fight to make life more affordable.”
His campaign also called for protecting Medicaid funding, preserving rural hospitals and lowering prescription drug costs.
On housing, Ford proposed restricting purchases by large corporations and international investors. He also supported requiring data centers to cover their own utility and water costs rather than shifting those expenses onto existing customers.
Sen. J.D. Ford, D-Indianapolis, questions Sen. Scott Alexander, R-Muncie, about his bill, which would regulate paid political influencers as lobbyists. (Photo by Leslie Bonilla Muñiz/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
The Democratic challenger pledged to hold regular town halls and strengthen congressional oversight of federal agencies.
Spartz, meanwhile, campaigned on her record of seeking federal spending reductions, healthcare changes and a more accountable federal government.
The Ukrainian-born congresswoman, a certified public accountant and former Indiana state senator, argued that another term would allow her to continue work on federal budget reforms and reducing the national debt.
“I want to finish major reforms I have started, particularly fixing healthcare, addressing our unsustainable national debt and overhauling Congress’s broken budget process,” Spartz said in October.
She also advocated stronger border enforcement, changes to legal immigration and expanded healthcare price transparency.
The campaign grew increasingly contentious in its final weeks, with the candidates trading accusations over Spartz’s family stock transactions, campaign advertising and their respective records.
Ford questioned Spartz’s financial disclosures and transactions involving her famil. Spartz disputed the allegations and accused her opponent of misleading voters.
The candidates also clashed over the terms of a potential debate. Ford called for a public event before constituents and Spartz proposed a televised discussion focused on policy.
From the Indiana Senate to Congress
Ford’s victory follows two terms in the Indiana Senate, where he has represented District 29 since 2018.
His first election was itself a notable upset. Ford defeated longtime Republican state Sen. Mike Delph, becoming the first openly gay member of the Indiana General Assembly.
He won reelection in 2022 with 51.7% of the vote.
In the legislature, Ford has been a prominent Democratic voice on LGBTQ+ rights, education, healthcare and government accountability.
Republican Rep. Victoria Spartz takes questions from a hostile crowd during a town hall on Friday, March 28, 2025, in Westfield. (Casey Smith/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
His election to Congress will also create an opening in his Indiana Senate district, which includes portions of Marion and Hamilton counties.
Spartz, who previously served in the Indiana Senate, first won election to Congress in 2020 after Republican Susan Brooks opted against seeking another term.
Her time in Washington included a shifting relationship with Trump, repeated calls for federal spending restraint and a high-profile reversal of her initial decision not to seek reelection in 2024.
She ultimately ran again that year, surviving a contested Republican primary before winning another term in November.
Ford will take office in January for a two-year term.
“Tonight, voters proved that no seat belongs to a political party. It belongs to the people,” Ford said. “Whether you voted for me or not, I will fight for you. I will listen, show up and never forget who sent me to Washington. To every voter, volunteer and supporter who made this historic victory possible, thank you. Tonight, we celebrate what Hoosiers made possible. Tomorrow, we begin the work of delivering the change they voted for.”

name: National
title: In historic night, voters elect first Black woman, first Black Republican as governors
description: Georgia voters elected the nation’s first Black woman governor on Tuesday while neighbors to the south in Florida became the first to elect a Black Republican governor. Former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms will be the first Democrat to occupy Georgia’s top office in more than two decades. In Florida, Republican U.S. Rep. Byron Donalds […]
text:
Byron Donalds speaks at a rally in Tallahassee a week before Tuesday’s midterm election. Donalds made history becoming the nation’s first Black Republican elected to governor and the first Black candidate to win statewide office in Florida. (Photo by Jay Waagmeester/Florida Phoenix)Georgia voters elected the nation’s first Black woman governor on Tuesday while neighbors to the south in Florida became the first to elect a Black Republican governor.
Former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms will be the first Democrat to occupy Georgia’s top office in more than two decades. In Florida, Republican U.S. Rep. Byron Donalds became the first Black person ever elected to statewide office there and the nation’s first elected Black Republican governor.
Those historic victories were called early during Tuesday’s high-stakes midterm elections, when Democrats hoped to claw back state power from Republicans, who have controlled a majority of governorships and state legislatures for the last 16 years.
A total of 36 gubernatorial elections were held Tuesday. As of 10:45 p.m. Eastern time, Democrats had won ten of those contested races and Republicans had secured three, according to The Associated Press.  
For the first time ever, at least three Black governors will serve simultaneously in the United States, according to Tuesday’s unofficial results. Lance Bottoms and Donalds will join Maryland Gov. Wes Moore, a Democrat, who easily won reelection Tuesday.
Before Moore, only two other Black governors had ever been elected: Deval Patrick in Massachusetts and L. Douglas Wilder in Virginia, both Democrats.
The only Black Republican ever to serve as governor was Pinckney Benton Stewart Pinchback, appointed to lead Louisiana during Reconstruction beginning in 1872.
Of the 36 gubernatorial elections on the ballot Tuesday, only a dozen were identified as competitive by the nonpartisan Cook Political Report with Amy Walter, which ranks the competitiveness of state and national races. Those included Alaska, Georgia, Florida, Iowa, Kansas, Michigan, Nebraska, Nevada, Ohio, Oregon, Texas and Wisconsin.
Currently, Republicans boast a 26-24 gubernatorial advantage over Democrats nationally. Aided by mounting disapproval of Republican President Donald Trump, Democrats hope to gain a national advantage for the first time since 2010.
Democrats are also aiming to flip hundreds of state legislative seats this cycle. Republicans currently boast control of 28 state legislatures and Democrats control 18, while three states have divided control of chambers, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures.
Democrat Deb Haaland will become the nation’s first Native American woman to serve as governor after the former Interior Secretary won election in New Mexico. Haaland is an enrolled member of the Pueblo of Laguna.
New Mexico will be the second state to be led by a Native American governor following Oklahoma, where current Republican Gov. Kevin Stitt is an enrolled member of the Cherokee Nation and former Gov. Johnston Murray was a member of the Chickasaw Nation.
In Texas, state Rep. Gina Hinojosa could become the nation’s third Latina governor. The Democrat leads the Republican Gov. Greg Abbott by a significant margin with 56% of the state’s votes counted, according to The Associated Press.
Only two other Latino women have ever served as governor, both in New Mexico: Current Democratic Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham and former Republican Gov. Susana Martinez.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Virginians protect gay marriage, voting rights and reproductive rights in state Constitution
description: On Election Day, Virginians approved three amendments to enshrine reproductive, marriage and voting rights for former felons into the state’s constitution, the culmination of a multi-year journey through the state legislature galvanized by lawmakers, advocates and major federal shifts.  Over sixty-one percent of voters answered yes to Ballot Question 1 as of[...]
text:
Virginians For Reproductive Freedom campaign director Han Jones gives a victory speech and cheers on supporters after Virginia voter opted to enshrine reproductive rights into the state Constitution on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Charlotte Rene Woods/Virginia Mercury)On Election Day, Virginians approved three amendments to enshrine reproductive, marriage and voting rights for former felons into the state’s constitution, the culmination of a multi-year journey through the state legislature galvanized by lawmakers, advocates and major federal shifts. 
Over sixty-one percent of voters answered yes to Ballot Question 1 as of 10 p.m. Tuesday, according to unofficial results from the Virginia Department of Elections. It asked if access to contraception, fertility treatment and abortions access should be protected. 
On Ballot Question 2, which asked if a defunct ban on same-sex marriage should be removed from the constitution, 56% of voters replied affirmatively.
The third ballot question asked whether the voting rights restoration process for formerly incarcerated people should become automatic or remain petition-based. 55% of voters said yes. 
The mood was optimistic and festive throughout the night at a watch party in Richmond hosted by Virginians For Reproductive Freedom, the coalition of advocacy groups that spearheaded outreach about the first of the three amendments. By the time results were called just past 9 p.m. for the referendum, glasses were raised, excited screams were had, and then dancing continued. 
 Reproductive rights amendment  

The first amendment  drew the most debate from lawmakers, healthcare professionals, advocates and the public — with tears, shouting, and a call of “out of order” on the day it first cleared the legislature in 2025 and increasingly intense campaigns for and against it this year. 
“Never again will our reproductive rights be a political football in Virginia,” said Han Jones, campaign manager for Virginians For Reproductive Freedom said Tuesday shortly after victory was declared. “It takes multi-year concerted work, but as you can see in Virginia, it’s paying off.” 
Constitutional amendments have to pass the General Assembly two years in a row before making it to ballots. The reproductive rights amendment received pushback each step of the way and opposition from every Republican member of the General Assembly while the two other amendments saw slim bipartisanship.
Proponents had sought the measure because Virginia is the only southern state without deep restrictions or bans on abortion. 
After federal protections were overturned by the U.S. Supreme Court in 2022, Justice Clarence Thomas suggested reviewing contraception next. 
That, paired with state-level cases challenging in vitro fertilization, prompted Virginia lawmakers’ holistic approach to protecting reproductive rights. 
It is now Virginians’ right to obtain birth control medication or devices as well as fertility treatments. 
People can also get abortions for any reason through their second trimester and a single physician — instead of three, as in previous years — will need to approve late-term abortions. 
 Same-sex marriages protected

The second amendment voters approved will lift a technical ban on gay marriage and affirm “that two adults may marry regardless of sex, gender, or race.” These unions must receive equal protection under the law. 
Since 2006, Virginia has technically banned gay marriage. 
The prohibition has been rendered moot since the Supreme Court ruled on Obergefell v. Hodges, which has upheld such unions nationally since 2015. 
But after federal abortion protections were removed by the Supreme Court, Virginia lawmakers set to work enshrining state-level protections moving forward. 
“Tonight’s victory belongs to generations of Virginians who organized, advocated and fought for equality, often without knowing whether they would live to see this day,” said Narissa Rahaman, Executive Director at Equality Virginia. 
 Voting rights will be restored to former felons

Virginians also approved the amendment granting automatic voter rights restorations to people with felony convictions who have completed their sentences. 
Historically, the state has disenfranchised people convicted of felony crimes unless they are pardoned by a governor or successfully petition one for restoration. 
The subjective process has not always been clear and restorations have ebbed and flowed across gubernatorial administrations. 
Numbers of grantees dropped under former Gov. Glenn Youngkin’s administration and applicants noted lack of clarity or guidance on the process.
Gov. Abigail Spanberger has restored more than 60,000 people this year.
Proponents of the measure argued that taking it out of the hands of governors will ensure clarity and that people who want to participate in democracy can do so. 
Though a largely Democrat-led initiative, Del. Mike Cherry, R-Colonial Heights, had carried a past version of the bill and voted with his Democratic colleagues to get it to ballots. 
“If a judge didn’t give you a life sentence, we shouldn’t give you a life sentence as a society,” he said in a recent call with The Mercury. “Once you’ve been adjudicated for your crime and you’ve served your time, then your right should be restored.” 
 Reproductive, marriage amendments face legal challenges

A circuit court judge has set a hearing date for Nov. 13 in a case that seeks to strike the reproductive rights amendment down. 
Filed by the Founding Freedoms Law Center, the legal arm of conservative advocacy group the Family Foundation, the case argues the ballot language was “misleading” and that proper procedure for amending the constitution was not followed. 
Founding Freedoms Law Center also recently filed a case on behalf of a pastor in Prince William County challenging the marriage amendment.  
“This fight is not over. It moves today to the courtroom and the Capitol,” Family Foundation president Victoria Cobb said in a statement. “When the blue wave that swept up these amendments recede, voters will see what’s been left in our Constitution.”
