name: WyoFile
title: Wyoming Supreme Court allows major wind turbine project to advance
description:
State’s high court disagrees with lower court ruling that the proposed clean energy project near Glenrock must connect to the power grid.
The post Wyoming Supreme Court allows major wind turbine project to advance appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
The Wyoming Supreme Court ruled Tuesday to allow the Pronghorn H2 wind project on state trust land near Glenrock to move forward.
The court ruled that the Wyoming State Board of Land Commissioners’ approval of the Pronghorn H2 wind lease south of Glenrock could advance to the Industrial Siting Council, even though the court also found that neighboring landowner Michael Stephens and Stephens Land and Livestock have standing to sue.
The Wyoming Supreme Court, with no judges dissenting, reversed Douglas District Court Judge F. Scott Peasley’s decision to toss the deal. Peasley threw out the lease because the project did not connect to the power grid, interpreting the “wind energy leasing” rule as requiring a grid connection. The supreme court disagreed.
At the same time, the state’s high court also found that the petitioners have standing to sue because of their proximity to the project, calling the harms to views and property values “substantial, immediate and pecuniary.”
The justices rejected the other challenges to the project, regarding how much money it would raise for the state, future mineral interests and impacts to wildlife. The court found that the land board is allowed to set rates on a case-by-case basis, and that companies could still lease the minerals on the state land, provided they cannot unreasonably get in the way of the wind farm. 
The Pronghorn H2 project still has to go through the Industrial Siting Council permitting process, which can take several years and may address other concerns the plaintiffs have.
“These decisions were never political, they were made to ensure the highest and best value for our state lands, buttressed by the legal and contractual obligations made by the state,” Gov. Mark Gordon said in a statement. “Today’s Supreme Court decision affirms the original vote made by the State Board of Land Commissioners granting this lease.”
The plaintiffs can file within the next 15 days for a rehearing, although these requests are rarely granted.
There are about 1,500 wind turbines spinning in Wyoming with a generating capacity of approximately 3,700 megawatts — that’s about 25% of the state’s total electrical generation capacity, according to multiple sources compiled in April by WyoFile.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico voters (mostly) ready to make history in governor’s race
authors: Joshua Bowling, Patrick Lohmann, Matt Mondschein, Leah Romero
description: Source New Mexico headed to the polls in Albuquerque, Española, Las Cruces, Rio Rancho, Santa Fe and Santo Domingo Pueblo to talk with voters about the issues and candidates that brought them to the polls on Nov. 3, 2026.
text:
Voters cast ballots on Election Day, Nov. 3, 2026, at Mesilla Town Hall. (Photo by Leah Romero for Source NM)By 5 p.m. in New Mexico, 672,450 registered voters had cast ballots — approximately 48% of the state’s 1.4 million voters had cast ballots, according to the Secretary of State’s Office, which will next report voter turnout after the polls close.
In 2022, New Mexico had a 52.3% voter turnout in the November midterm.
Nearly 49% of the voter casting ballots so far are registered Democrats, followed by Republicans at 32.4% and unaffiliated voters at just under 18%.
Overall, Democrats make up 39.6% of the state’s voters, followed by Republicans at 30.4% and unaffiliated or Decline to State voters at 28.1%.
New Mexico’s high Democratic turnout echoed the national trend of record turnout and expectations that Democrats might win back control of Congress and curtail the Trump administration’s policy agendas.
Across the Albuquerque and Rio Rancho areas Tuesday morning, voters said they were backing the candidates and ballot measures they believed would push back against the Trump administration’s policies.
Voters in the area overwhelmingly told Source NM they hoped their votes would counter federal efforts to implement cuts to services such as Medicaid and SNAP. 
As news regarding the federal government’s efforts to monitor polling places nationwide spread ahead of Election Day and as immigration advocates prepared for the possibility of federal interference, Albuquerque resident Jessica Queen said she felt like voting in Albuquerque was a calm spot in an otherwise turbulent national political landscape.
“I’m grateful to be in blue New Mexico,” she said.
Polling spot Carlos Gilbert Elementary in Santa Fe on Election Day, Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Matt Mondschein/Source NM)New Mexico voters fill out ballots at Carlos Gilbert Elementary in Santa Fe on Election Day, Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Matt Mondschein/Source NM)New Mexico voters fill out ballots at Carlos Gilbert Elementary in Santa Fe on Election Day, Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Matt Mondschein/Source NM)Voters cast ballots on Election Day, Nov. 3, 2026, at Mesilla Town Hall. (Photo by Leah Romero for Source NM)The line to vote at the Sandoval County Administration Building on Nov. 3, 2026, wound around the lobby and stretched to the entrance during the noon lunch hour. (Photo by Joshua Bowling/Source NM)Philip Dodge, a 73-year-old Rio Rancho resident, said he discussed the issues on Tuesday’s general election ballot with his family before coming to the Sandoval County Administration Building to vote. (Photo by Joshua Bowling/Source NM)Jane Fleenor of Rio Rancho told Source NM the governor’s race was the most important issue on her ballot Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Joshua Bowling/Source NM)Mark Rodriguez and Aramea Atencio, left and right, made a date out of voting together at Carlos Gilbert Elementary in Santa Fe on Election Day, Nov. 3, 2026. The couple said they were most excited to vote for Democratic gubernatorial candidate Deb Haaland and added that Trump administration immigration policy motivated them to vote. (Photo by Matt Mondschein/Source NM)New Mexico U.S. Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández (D-N.M.), alongside state Rep. Tara Lujan (D-Santa Fe), wave to cars outside the Rodeo de Santa Fe Fairgrounds on Election Day, Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Matt Mondschein/Source NM)
Jim Libbin voted at the Las Cruces Village Independent Living Social Center. (Photo by Leah Romero for Source NM)Zane James of Albuquerque cast his ballot Tuesday morning, Nov. 3, 2026, at Eldorado High School. (Photo by Joshua Bowling/Source NM)Michael Quintana, a Santo Domingo Pueblo member and gas station general manager, said Nov. 3, 2026, that Democratic gubernatorial nominee Deb Haaland, if elected as the state's first Indigenous governor, would finally give pueblos "a voice." (Photo by Patrick Lohmann/Source NM)Matthew Thomas, left, voted Tuesday morning, Nov. 3, 2026, at the Doña Ana County government building. (Photo by Leah Romero for Source NM)Juan Velasquez of Albuquerque said he got a ride to the nearest polling place on Nov. 3, 2026, vote “MAGA all the way.” (Photo by Joshua Bowling/Source NM)New Mexico supporters of Republican gubernatorial candidate Gregg Hull outside the Rodeo de Santa Fe Fairgrounds on Election Day, Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Matt Mondschein/Source NM)Jolyne Marshall of Albuquerque said her top priority was “stopping the descent into fascism.” (Photo by Joshua Bowling/Source NM)Joseph Calabaza, 70, said rising gasoline prices were at the top of his mind Tuesday when he walked into the Santo Domingo Pueblo to vote for Democrats up and down the ballot. (Photo by Patrick Lohmann/Source NM)Joann Crespin, Santo Domingo Pueblo member and retired special education teacher, said she wanted to vote for Democrat Deb Haaland in the governor's race and in support of school bonds on Election Day, Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Patrick Lohmann/Source NM) New Mexico Democratic gubernatorial nominee Deb Haaland, second from left, joined Santo Domingo Pueblo Gov. Raymond Aguilar, Jr., second from right, in the pueblo during her first Election Day stop on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Patrick Lohmann/Source NM)
Further north, at the Sandoval County Administration Building, Rio Rancho residents told Source NM they were similarly excited to vote for Haaland.
Philip Dodge, a 73-year-old Rio Rancho resident, said he discussed the issues on Tuesday’s general election ballot with his family before coming to the Sandoval County Administration Building to vote. (Photo by Joshua Bowling/Source NM)
Philip Dodge, a 73-year-old U.S. Navy veteran, said he voted for “anything non-Republican.” He took exception with federal cuts to programs such as Medicaid, which he said his son depends on. And he said he was outraged at the way U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth is “disrespecting the military.”
When asked if he voted for Hull, who was the longest-serving mayor in Rio Rancho’s history, Dodge shook his head to say “no.”
“I see the way the roads are around here,” he said.
Regardless of political parties, every Albuquerque and Rio Rancho voter who spoke with Source NM after leaving the polls Tuesday said they voted in favor of Constitutional Amendment 4, which would let state lawmakers collect an annual salary for their work for the first time.
Juan Velasquez, an Albuquerque Republican who said he voted “MAGA all the way” Tuesday, said he backed the proposal to pay lawmakers.
He said he voted for Republicans all down the ballot because he believes their policies are better for the economy, particularly in a state like New Mexico that routinely ranks among the poorest in the nation.
To him, paying lawmakers is another way to address that problem.
“This is a poor state to begin with, then you go into politics and you’re still poor,” he said. “I think they should all get paid. Why shouldn’t they?”
Nearly every voter Source NM spoke with in Albuquerque and Rio Rancho also said they wanted to see Deb Haaland, the former U.S. Interior Secretary running as New Mexico’s Democratic gubernatorial nominee, make history Tuesday evening by becoming the nation’s first woman Native American governor.
“I’m pulling for Auntie Deb,” Albuquerque resident Queen said after casting her ballot at the Bernalillo County Clerk’s Office.
Haaland starts day on Santo Domingo Pueblo
New Mexico Democratic gubernatorial nominee Deb Haaland, second from left, joined Santo Domingo Pueblo Gov. Raymond Aguilar, Jr., second from right, in the pueblo during her first Election Day stop on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Patrick Lohmann/Source NM)
Haaland, an enrolled Laguna Pueblo member, began Election Day on Tuesday morning visiting the Santo Domingo Pueblo, which has around 2,300 enrolled members and sits between Albuquerque and Santa Fe.
The Pueblo is one of four that has endorsed her campaign for governor and also endorsed her for her first congressional campaign in 2017, when she became one of the first Native Americans elected to the U.S. House.
Haaland, who also made history as the first Indigenous cabinet secretary under President Joe Biden, told Source NM she hadn’t dwelled too much on the historic nature of her candidacy before Election Day, but she did say representation matters in politics. 
“It mattered when I became one of the first Native women in Congress. It mattered when President Biden nominated me, and it’ll matter here,” she said. “Lots of Native people all across the country [are] running. So, I feel grateful that, perhaps in some small way, I might have inspired them to believe that they could run for office, too.”
Source NM spoke to 10 voters outside the Pueblo’s community center, all of whom said they had voted for Haaland. Most of them said Haaland being Indigenous at least partially influenced their decision to vote for her, though others said her success as a former Interior Department Secretary and their former congressional representative heavily factored in, as well. 
“She’s a strong lady, and we can always depend on her,” said Sammy Garcia, a tribal council member. “We’re proud of her, what she has done for us, and now we’re depending on Deb Haaland to see if we can help our tribe.”
Eliana Bailon, a 22-year-old Santo Domingo Pueblo member, said she hopes Haaland’s candidacy counteracts stereotypes on tribal land and shows that women can be strong leaders in what are often “patriarchal” societies.
“Her being a woman, it gives us women more power,” she said. “As you may know, most pueblos don’t really have women leaders, so I think it’s really important that she could be at a higher position.”
Bailon arrived at the polls Tuesday afternoon with her partner, Derek Masawiestewa, a 23-year-old, Santa Ana Pueblo member who had never voted before. She urged him to cast a ballot, including for Haaland.
“She was like, it’s very important,” Masawiestewa told Source NM. So he put in an application Tuesday for same-day registration. “I’m just hoping I can make a difference.”
Governor’s race, Trump policies resonate at Santa Fe, Española polls
The governor’s race between Democrat Haaland and Republican Hull also dominated discussion at various polling spots in Santa Fe.
Mark Rodriguez and Aramea Atencio, left and right, made a date out of voting together at Carlos Gilbert Elementary in Santa Fe on Election Day, Nov. 3, 2026. The couple said they were most excited to vote for Democratic gubernatorial candidate Deb Haaland and added that Trump administration immigration policy motivated them to vote. (Photo by Matt Mondschein/Source NM)
For Aramea Atencio and Mark Rodriguez, a couple who voted at Carlos Gilbert Elementary, the prospect of electing the first Native American woman governor brought them out to vote. 
“That was my main motive — to support women, support indigenous peoples,” Atencio said. “This is their land and everything else follows after that.”
Arthur Montoya, voting at the Rodeo de Santa Fe Fairgrounds, also prioritized the governor’s race and said he was casting a ballot for Hull. 
He told Source NM that the most important issue for him this election was voting for candidates that “show up for every New Mexican” and are not “influenced by outside forces.” 
He added that federal policies set by the Trump administration did not affect his ballot, saying that he’s focused on New Mexico and that he’s “not really concerned about Washington. It’s about us.”
The opposite held true for Steve Montoya, a Navy veteran who voted down the ballot for Democrats at the Dan Roybal Community Center in Española. When asked what the top issue was for him when he cast his ballot, he told Source NM, “The Republicans got everything so screwed up right now that we need to get back on track.” 
He added that the Trump administration’s foreign policy in particular was a cause of concern because “what they have done to our reputation around the world. That is the biggest thing.”
On the eve of the U.S. elections, the Trump administration again launched military strikes against Iran after starting the war in February. Since then, gas and oil prices have increased, which U.S. Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández told Source NM motivated the high voter turnout this midterm election. 
“I think the key issues that New Mexicans are voting on is they are tired of the division. They’re tired of the corruption. They’re tired of the cost,” Leger Fernández said outside the Rodeo de Santa Fe Fairgrounds. When asked about concerns about possible election interference, she added that when voters show up in “overwhelming force,” then “Trump and Republicans who want to overturn our elections, who want to suppress our vote, they have a very hard time doing it. We’re not going to let them do it.”
Rodriguez echoed the sentiment after voting at Carlos Gilbert Elementary in Santa Fe, telling Source NM he cast his vote today to be “a thorn in [Trump’s] side, trying to vote against him at all costs.” 
Ready for change in Las Cruces
More than 60 people stood in line at Corbett Center Student Union on New Mexico State University’s main campus in Las Cruces Tuesday morning. (Photo by Leah Romero/Source NM)
Polling locations also were busy in Las Cruces the morning of Election Day, with several voters telling Source NM that they voted Democrat down the ballot because they were tired of Republican corruption, particularly at the federal level.
“The past few years of every time I opened my phone it’s just, from the top down from our government, it’s just pedophilia, and racism and fascism and it’s a lot of doom scrolling everywhere you go,” Las Crucen Matthew Thomas told Source NM. “So I thought I needed to do something to combat that.”
He added that he voted against state constitutional amendment 4 that proposed paying state legislators because he feels that lawmakers already receive money from outside sources. “I thought, why do they need our money when they’re already getting paid under the table from who knows how many sources,” Thomas said.
Jim Libbin told Source that he also voted against the constitutional amendment this time because he would like to see legislators convene in Santa Fe more often. 
“It just seems like a pretty good salary for a 30-day session every other year,” Libbin said. “I know they work all year long, but if they’re going to increase salaries then it seems to me they ought to have a longer session and do their work there.”
Libbin, however, said he voted Republican on the “major issues” on the ballot this election because he believes it is time for change in Democratic-led state, in which the majority party has control of both legislative chambers and the governor’s office. 
“We’ve been dominated by the Democratic Party for so long and we end up at the bottom of the heap in everything,” he said.
Mesilla Park resident and educator Roberta Madrid told Source that while she has voted for candidates on both sides of the aisle in the past, she supported Democratic candidates Tuesday because the Republican Party is “kind of cuckoo right now and we can’t let our country die.”
Madrid previously lived in Arizona for 20 years, a Republican-leaning state, and believes they’ve passed policies harmful to public education. “New Mexico has its issues, but they truly support public education,” Madrid said. She added that New Mexico’s gubernatorial race was particularly important to her and she voted for Deb Haaland, hoping to see a Native American woman elected to the office.
Manuel Jimenez, a third-year New Mexico State University student studying secondary education, told Source that Tuesday was his first time voting in an election. Immigrant rights were what motivated him to cast his ballot. 
He said he hasn’t seen his mother and other family for a long time because they live in Mexico and fear their visas will be taken away if they try crossing into the U.S. from Ciudad Juárez.
“Seperation is a big problem, not only for me, but I’m sure for a lot more people that come from Mexico and other places around the world,” Jimenez said, adding that he wants to see policies past that would help immigrants feel safer across the entire country.
“I just thought it would be important to vote right now, knowing that I can do it and have an impact in the smallest way,” he said. “Knowing that my vote also will help not only me, but a lot more people, one way or another.”

title: Incumbents Rogers, McGarvey cruise to easy victories in Congressional races
description: Two incumbents, one Republican, one Democrat, crushed their opponents early on election night with plus 40 point victory margins. Incumbent 5th District Congressman Hal Rogers crushed his Democratic opponent Ned Pillersdorf  with a 44 point margin when the Associated Press called the race at 7 p.m. Rogers, the longest serving House member at 88 who […]
text:
U.S. Rep. Hal Rogers talk to reporters at the 2026 SOAR Summit in Corbin. (Kentucky Lantern photo by McKenna Horsley)Two incumbents, one Republican, one Democrat, crushed their opponents early on election night with plus 40 point victory margins.
Incumbent 5th District Congressman Hal Rogers crushed his Democratic opponent Ned Pillersdorf  with a 44 point margin when the Associated Press called the race at 7 p.m.
Rogers, the longest serving House member at 88 who is also known as the Dean of the House, has served Eastern and South Kentucky since 1981. He is known for bringing projects and funding to one of the poorest regions of Appalachia.
“It is a tremendous honor to earn the continued confidence of the people of Southern and Eastern Kentucky. I will continue to listen to my constituents and fight for the conservative values that make this nation so great,” Rogers said in a statement. “Our work together has never slowed down. In fact, we are working hard every single day to create a brighter future in Kentucky’s Appalachian region. Southern and Eastern Kentucky is a special place to call home and I’ll continue to give my all for the people I serve whether I’m here or echoing their voice in Washington.”
Democrat Ned Pillersdorf of Prestonsburg, hoped to make issues out of a lack of affordability and changes to Medicaid and SNAP that will hurt many families in Eastern Kentucky. But name recognition and incumbency apparently won out.
U.S Rep. Morgan McGarvey of the 3rd District in Jefferson County beat Republican Maria Teresa Rodriguez by a 52 point margin.
U.S. Rep. Morgan McGarvey of the 3rd District, gives a victory speech at the Galt House on Tuesday night. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Sarah Ladd)
In his victory speech, delivered before a crowd of some 200 gathered at the Galt House in downtown Louisville, Democratic U.S. Rep Morgan McGarvey said the results are the result of failed policies out of Washington D.C. 
“I want to be really clear-eyed for a second about what this means,” he said. “This is a big night, but this is not about party. This is certainly not about me. This is about us. This is about decency over division. This is about compassion over cruelty. It’s about cohesion over corruption.” 
He said “this election is about not looking back to those times” when the country was segregated and other “hard times” in the United States’ history. 
“This is about gas being over $4 a gallon and diesel being over $6.50 a gallon right here in Kentucky because our president chose to go to an unjust war with Iran, putting our troops at risk and our country less safe,” McGarvey said. “And of course, he’s driving our costs up while he and his friends do nothing but get richer. This is about stopping the corruption we see coming right out of the White House. But I will tell you, as dark as it seems today, we have been through hard times in this country before. We’ve been through worse.”

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: Affordability takes center stage as New Hampshire voters head to the polls
authors: Ethan DeWitt, Molly Rains, William Skipworth, Maya Mitchell
description: There was a common refrain at the New Hampshire polls on Tuesday: frustration with high prices.  The issue of affordability dominated a contentious midterm election cycle marked by clashes over candidates’ relationships to President Donald Trump, the Iran war, and concern over rising costs for childcare, healthcare, groceries and more.  Amid record turnout p[...]
text:
A voter emerges from a voting booth in New London during the November 2026 midterm elections. (Photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)There was a common refrain at the New Hampshire polls on Tuesday: frustration with high prices. 
The issue of affordability dominated a contentious midterm election cycle marked by clashes over candidates’ relationships to President Donald Trump, the Iran war, and concern over rising costs for childcare, healthcare, groceries and more. 
Amid record turnout predicted by Secretary of State David Scanlan last week, voters formed snaking lines in front of schools and city halls. At stake are control of the New Hampshire governor’s office, a U.S. Senate seat, two U.S. House of Representatives seats, and control of the New Hampshire House and Senate. 
Also to be determined are two ballot measures: One to eliminate a defunct state official position and another that would cap school districts’ property taxes.
As they filed into the polls earlier today, voters from across the state outlined the concerns and goals shaping their decisions at the ballot box.
At Winnacunnet High School in Hampton, many voters said they were bringing affordability worries to the polls. (Photo by Molly Rains/New Hampshire Bulletin)
Focus on affordability
At Winnacunnet High School in Hampton on Tuesday morning, multiple voters identified affordability as the central concern driving them to the polls.
David Burns, a Democrat who said he had lived in Hampton for 25 years, said the rising prices of groceries, healthcare, insurance and gas were among his main concerns. He said he voted for all Democrats in hopes they would lower costs. 
“My line of thinking is, the mansions should pay more, and you’ve got to support your schools,” he said. 
Also at the polls Tuesday was Robert Gagalis, who said the economy, high taxes and housing costs were his main motivators.
“It’s always an issue,” he said. 
John and Jane Romps of Manchester said that in the current economy, they were “OK.” The two retirees said they “couldn’t take any more politics” but were thinking about inflation when they were voting. 
Others recognized rising prices but said it did not win them over to Democrats.
In Hooksett, Chris Babelcastro called affordability “a big concern.” But speaking of Democrats, he added: “My belief is they kind of got us into this to begin with.”
Nearby, Mike Weinman also said high prices were a problem, but he did not attribute them to a particular party. He was voting Republican to support Trump’s actions and policies against “diversity, equity and inclusion” efforts. “I think some things over this president’s tenure have changed for the positive,” he said. 
Affordability was a motivator for Al Bertocci, of Tilton, who also voted Republican.
“When’s the last time any one of these clowns on either side have gone in a grocery store?” he asked.
“I Voted” stickers, designed by New Hampshire fourth and fifth graders, line the railings outside the Webster Elementary School in Manchester. (Photo by Maya Mitchell/New Hampshire Bulletin)
Corruption concerns
Bertocci voted straight-ticket Republican because he believes Democrats are taking corrupt kickbacks feeding into an affordability crisis. Still, he said he was frustrated with both parties.
“I just don’t like both parties fighting constantly and getting nothing done,” he said. “They don’t do anything.”
Bertocci, 73, thinks Pappas epitomizes that.
“He hasn’t done jack s—t,” he said of the Democratic Senate candidate. He said Pappas’ husband has been a lobbyist for Uber, Amazon and other companies, but Pappas still voted on bills affecting those companies
Bertocci, a retiree who moved from Massachusetts to Danbury seven years ago and then to Tilton a year ago, said he was a Democrat “for many, many years” but said he believes the party leaders are only in it for themselves these days.
“It’s not our parents’ or grandparents’ Democratic Party anymore,” he said.
Zoe Hill (right), a candidate for state representative and the child of Executive Councilor Karen Liot Hill, holds signs in support of Democrats alongside a fellow support at the Lebanon City Hall polling location during Election Day, Nov. 3. (Photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)
Health costs
Two years ago, Scott Stafford split his ticket the New Hampshire way: by voting for Democrats up and down the ballot but choosing Republican Kelly Ayotte for governor.
On Tuesday outside Londonderry High School, Stafford’s ballot was completely marked for Democrats, including Democrat Cinde Warmington for governor. He voted for candidates he said would support older people. Specifically: Medicare.
A Kaiser Family Foundation study found that the average Medicare Advantage beneficiary in the U.S. had a choice of 35 plans for 2027 compared to 39 plans on 2026, ahead of open enrollment in October, as insurers retreat from certain markets amid rising costs. Stafford said he had heard worries about reduced choice from many older friends this year.
“I spoke with the woman that set mine up and — pretty slim pickings here in Rockingham County,” he said. “There’s only very few choices out there this year. Last year was great.”
He added: “This year, I got to get all new doctors.”
Stafford said he isn’t precisely sure how that situation might be improved, but he expects Democrats will have a better plan than Republicans. “I had to make sure I voted all the right people,” he said. 
Driven by the tax cap
Voters statewide were also asked a hyperlocal budget question. Question 2 asked voters whether they wanted a two-year tax cap on their school district that would bar school boards from proposing budgets that raise constituents’ school property taxes more than the value of inflation and any new construction in town. If adopted, the cap could be overridden by a 60% vote at the district’s annual meeting. 
Should 60% or more of voters approve in any school district, the measure will pass.  
Some voters said the tax cap question was an animating reason to vote Tuesday. 
Dan Hebert poses for a photo after voting in the Concord Heights neighborhood. Hebert voted for a tax cap because he was upset with the Concord School District’s recent fiscal decisions. He’s also concerned about how property taxes affect people on a fixed income like himself. (Photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)
In the Concord Heights, Dan Hebert voted for a tax cap, and he said his vote was motivated by whats going on locally.
“I think every town is different,” he said.
He stressed that he respects the teachers and the work they do. However, he wants Concord School District and the state to seek other forms of revenue because of how hard property taxes hit people on fixed incomes, like himself. (Hebert receives benefits for his disability.)
“I also think that the property tax, being the only tax, is benefiting a certain group of people, ” he said. “And it’s not my people.”
Hebert usually votes absentee because his disability, which requires him to use a power wheelchair to move around, prevents him from getting into a standard voting booth. However, this year, he came in person because he saw a lot of politicians disparaging mail-in voting and was concerned his vote wouldn’t be counted. 
Randy Stevens, 36, of Manchester, voted against a tax cap, even if it may impact his taxes.
Stevens has children in Manchester schools, and said that he does not “mind paying more taxes to take care of my community.” 
Supporters hold signs for Republican candidates outside of Webster Elementary School in Manchester. (Photo by Maya Mitchell/New Hampshire Bulletin)
“I think it’s really important, and I also recognize that cost of living is going up for me and for everyone else, and that we have to continuously adjust and provide the level of education that our children need to be successful when they grow up and they’re adults into our community,” he said. “I really don’t know the minutia and the details. But if it means investing into my community and my educational system, I’m going to do that.”
Stevens said he always votes for candidates who “care about the people” he serves as executive director of Hope Recovery New Hampshire. He said human service problems are always top of mind when entering the voting booth. 
Candidate quality
For some voters, it was more about the candidates than the issues.
Linda and Gene Rosenthall pose for a photo after voting in New London during the November 2026 midterm elections. Each split their ballot between Republican Gov. Kelly Ayotte and Democratic congressional candidates Chris Pappas and Maggie Goodlander. (Photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)
Husband and wife duo Gene, 60, and Linda Rosenthall, 63, of New London, said they both voted for Republican Gov. Kelly Ayotte to be reelected but chose Democrats Chris Pappas and Maggie Goodlander in the two congressional races.
Ayotte is counting on split-ticket voters like the Rosenthalls to bring her her first reelection victory. It’s a formula set by previous governors in the historically purple state that prides itself on independence. Her predecessor, Chris Sununu, also a Republican, swept through four consecutive elections while Democrats won in every single congressional race during that time. A September St. Anselm College poll found that 13% of voters planned to split their ballot between the two parties.
The Rosenthalls said the biggest motivators for them was putting a check on the Trump administration, which they vehemently oppose. Gene, a retired airline pilot, called the president an “embarrassment” to the country on the global stage.
Kirk Ballard, 55, voted at Lebanon City Hall Tuesday. He said he was sad to see Jeanne Shaheen retiring instead of running for reelection, but thought that Pappas “looks like a good guy.” He voted for Warmington, he said, because “I’m never going to vote for a Republican governor.”
He had a unique motivation behind some of his local votes. For county sheriff, Ballard wrote in his own name as a protest vote.
“Because I was arrested on, what I would call, in my opinion, from my perspective, an illegitimate domestic dispute charge, and I was sent to the Grafton County jail for two months without bail,” Ballard said. “… I don’t agree with the way the Corrections Department works. I don’t believe in the way that the police department, here at least, responded.”
Other voters brought personal experience into the Pappas-Sununu contests. 
Andy Desrosiers was a teacher at Salem High School when John E. Sununu and his siblings attended. “Comes from a great family,” Desrosiers said outside the polls in Windham. 
When Gov. Chris Sununu was on the ballot for eight years, Desrosiers voted for him. 
But that goodwill didn’t earn John Sununu Desrosiers’ vote Tuesday. Frustrated by a litany of decisions by President Donald Trump, from attacking Iran to imposing military-style crackdowns on undocumented people, Desrosiers is voting for change, and John Sununu was not the candidate to bring it, he said.
John Sununu’s opposition to abortion — he voted for multiple federal abortion restriction bills from 2002 to 2008 and earned a 100% rating from the National Right to Life Committee in 2006 — was also a dealbreaker for Desrosiers.
As he talked, Denise Dolloff came up beside Desrosiers. “My former student!” Desrosiers said.
Dolloff knows John Sununu too; she was his classmate at Salem High. And on Tuesday, she voted for him. 
“Christine was my sister’s closest friend in high school. And I think Peter worked for my parents for their business when he was a teenager,” Dolloff said, naming two other Sununu siblings. “There was a Sununu for almost every grade at one point in time,” she added. 
While she and John Sununu live in different towns today, he gives her a hug every time she sees him, Dolloff says. “He never forgot his roots,” she said. “He came to an event last St. Patrick’s Day in Salem and he went around shaking hands and remembering so many people’s names.”
And while he differs from his brother Chris — such as not being as comfortable on camera — there’s a hardworking, earnest side to John that might not translate in an interview, she said. Dolloff, a Trump supporter, argued it would allow him to separate himself from the president when needed. 
Desrosiers was less sure.
“Right now, his association with anything Trump would give me a reason to not vote for him,” he said.

title: Voters sail through a mostly smooth Election Day, despite fears of federal interference
description: America voted.After the Trump administration pressured election officials, after concerns that armed federal agents would deploy to the polls, after fears U.S. Department of Justice election monitors would intimidate voters — ballots were cast by the millions Tuesday, mostly without incident.Across the United States, voters headed to their polling places. At[...]
text: America voted.After the Trump administration pressured election officials, after concerns that armed federal agents would deploy to the polls, after fears U.S. Department of Justice election monitors would intimidate voters — ballots were cast by the millions Tuesday, mostly without incident.Across the United States, voters headed to their polling places. At churches, schools and community centers, they rendered their verdict on the direction of the country and those who lead it.As the votes are counted, what comes next is uncertain.President Donald Trump has long put forward false allegations of election fraud and baseless conspiracy theories to undermine results he doesn’t like. Ahead of Tuesday, polling suggested voters may give Democrats control of Congress and usher in a new era of divided government in Washington, D.C.Days or weeks of courtroom battles could lie ahead if Trump deploys the machinery of the federal government to advance claims of a stolen election. His 2020 election loss set off a host of unsuccessful lawsuits that tried to overturn election results in battleground states, part of a campaign that culminated in a mob of his supporters storming the Capitol.But on Tuesday, American democracy passed a crucial test — voters voted.“What we’re seeing today could have looked a lot different,” Andrew Walchuk, policy director and counsel for the nonpartisan watchdog group Common Cause, told reporters. “We could have seen a lot of different scenarios based on what the administration wanted to get away with.”Over the past year, the Trump administration filed dozens of election-related lawsuits on everything from voter rolls to ballot counting. Federal courts halted nearly all of these efforts, including a demand that California set aside the ballots of 20,000 people the Trump administration alleged were suspected noncitizens.Trump and his allies have said they’re focused on preventing noncitizen voting, which they say cancels out the votes of U.S. citizens. The U.S. Department of Homeland Security has arrested dozens of alleged noncitizen voters in recent weeks, and the president continues to call on Congress to pass the SAVE America Act, which would require voters to prove their citizenship.“We are going to continue our yearslong fight on Election Integrity,” Trump wrote in a Saturday social media post.Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin issued multiple warnings against illegal voting on Tuesday. On social media he wrote that if ineligible voters cast a ballot, DHS “will find you, hunt you down, and you will be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law.”In the statesWhatever happens next, on Tuesday states administered elections under their own rules as laid out in the U.S. Constitution.In Albuquerque, New Mexico, Jolyne Marshall, who said her top priority was “stopping the descent into fascism,” said she had heard talk about the potential for voter suppression, such as federal agents at polling places. On Tuesday, she said she had a seamless voting experience.The Rev. Suzanne Parker Miller spent Election Day as a poll chaplain in Raleigh, North Carolina, for Faith United to Save Democracy, a nonpartisan, multi-faith group. She said she had been told to anticipate some type of federal presence in the area.“I didn’t know what to expect today, which is just always a little unnerving,” Parker Miller said. “But I’ve done this in the past and what I came in expecting today was to also have a very peaceful and fair and free election.”The Justice Department deployed about 1,000 election monitors across the country and in addition to DOJ personnel, drew upon federal law enforcement agents typically not assigned to the polls. The makeup of the monitors raised concerns among Democrats and voting rights leaders that they could be used to intimidate voters.The Michigan Department of Attorney General said it was following up on reports that monitors in Flint had improperly asked poll workers about the details of their training and in Dearborn had asked for copies of training materials. State officials said they had contacted the Justice Department’s election monitor coordinator for Michigan about the activity.“That coordinator confirmed that this activity that the monitors were engaging in is not consistent with how the monitors were trained,” Angela Benander, a spokesperson for the Michigan Department of State, told reporters.Leaders with the League of Women Voters in Ohio and Pennsylvania said during a news conference that monitors in their states were wearing plain clothes and staying out of the way.“They’re really just asking short questions of voters when they come out, sometimes,” Jen Miller, executive director of the League of Women Voters of Ohio, told reporters.Usual election problemsAcross the country, election officials said the challenges they encountered on Tuesday centered on typical problems — the weather, power outages and technical issues — and not federal interference.The most significant problem appeared in Westchester County, New York, where voting machines were unable to accept paper ballots. The New York State Board of Elections said in a statement that an update to the county’s election programming caused the issue.Election officials emphasized that voting continued and that ballots were being kept in secure bags, though the problem could affect the speed of results. The area includes the district of Republican Rep. Mike Lawler, who faces Democrat Cait Conley in a closely watched toss-up race.Westchester County Executive Ken Jenkins, a Democrat, said in a statement that the county had fallen short of the standard of providing a fair, secure and seamless election process. He promised to convene a bipartisan team to review the decisions and failures that led to “this debacle.”“The voters deserve better, and I intend to make sure they get it,” Jenkins said.Lawsuit after lawsuitDespite isolated problems, the relative smoothness of voting across the country stood in stark contrast to the frenetic pace of legal challenges that played out in the months, days and hours before Tuesday.As Election Day approached, the Justice Department sued Alaska and California. In Alaska, the Trump administration sought to preemptively pause certification of the U.S. Senate election, an effort a federal judge quickly dismissed.In California, Justice Department lawyers raised the possibility that election officials could face prosecution if they tabulated the ballots of noncitizens. A federal judge blocked the Trump administration from issuing threats, but that order was halted Tuesday by an en banc panel of the U.S. 9th Circuit Court of Appeals — a rare election-related legal victory for the president.“The rule of law prevails. Separation of powers does not allow judges to take control of core executive branch powers. We will conduct our criminal investigations without fear or favor,” Bill Essayli, first assistant U.S. attorney for the Central District of California, wrote on social media.The Justice Department alleged in a lawsuit that Homeland Security had identified 20,000 suspected noncitizen voters registered in the state. It demanded California set aside the ballots of anyone on the list. State and local election officials raised concerns about the accuracy of the list and said the demand encroached on their authority over elections.A district court judge and an appeals court both rejected the demand. And on Monday, the Supreme Court rejected the Trump administration’s request in a one-sentence order that election legal experts said spoke volumes. In a statement, the Justice Department said it was disappointed in the decision but that the court loss wasn’t the end of its efforts. In addition to deploying monitors and charging noncitizen voters, the department said it would “pursue other legal avenues to ensure that only eligible American citizens vote.” David Becker, a former Justice Department Voting Section attorney who leads the nonpartisan Center for Election Innovation & Research, on a press call noted that the Supreme Court had issued its order without any dissents or explanation.“Just a complete smackdown,” Becker said, adding that the justices were sending a message that “they’re not going to credit any future efforts to impose federal fiat on the states as they manage their elections.”Joshua Bowling of Source New Mexico, Clayton Henkel of NC Newsline and Jon King of Michigan Advance contributed reporting.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Signs don’t vote: Tennessee state Senate candidates in Chattanooga push for last-minute votes
description: CHATTANOOGA, Tenn. — Signs don’t equal votes, state Sen. Bo Watson said Tuesday, standing among dozens of political posterboards in front of a polling location on Signal Mountain in Hamilton County.  The Republican has spent two decades in the state Senate and is running for re-election to District 11, which covers northern Chattanooga in Hamilton […]
text:
Photographed on Nov. 3, 2026 outside a Signal Mountain poll, state Sen. Bo Watson says he feels confident state Republicans will have a good Election Day result. (Photo by Ruby Rayner for Tennessee Lookout)CHATTANOOGA, Tenn. — Signs don’t equal votes, state Sen. Bo Watson said Tuesday, standing among dozens of political posterboards in front of a polling location on Signal Mountain in Hamilton County. 
The Republican has spent two decades in the state Senate and is running for re-election to District 11, which covers northern Chattanooga in Hamilton County, including a portion of the city proper, as well as Collegedale and Red Bank. Democratic challenger and first-time candidate Tim Roberts aims to take the long-held seat. 
Watson said he remembers when he first ran for state office in 2004, he went out and bought campaign signs after seeing a local candidate with tons. The candidate with all the signs ended up losing by a wide margin, Watson said. 
Watson said after that election he was told ‘signs don’t vote; people do.’
And, in this election, people have. Early voting in Hamilton County exceeded both 2022 and 2018 turnout, according to the Hamilton County Election Commission. 



Quotation







I think that Republicans and the Republican ideology reflects the majority of Tennesseans' view and Tennessee's view of America.


– Sen. Bo Watson, R-Hixson


“I think any political person would say, ‘Well, I’m encouraged that people are voting because that is an important privilege that we have in this state and in this country, and you know you’re excited to see people exercise that privilege,’” Watson said.
Despite having an opponent, Watson said he isn’t running against an individual but rather an environment where Democrats are energized and are campaigning. 
“We’ve basically been running against the Democrat(ic) Party here locally,” he said.
Polling predicts a strong night for the Democratic Party nationwide, but Watson said he is confident that Tennessee will elect Republicans up and down the ballot.
“I think that Republicans and the Republican ideology reflects the majority of Tennesseans’ view and Tennessee’s view of America,” Watson said.



Quotation







There's communities you can work with that have been underserved for years, and just if you have a voice, you can bring attention to that.


– Tim Roberts, Democratic nominee


Republicans hold a supermajority at the state level, and President Donald Trump won the state by nearly 30 percentage points in 2024. 
Watson’s Senate seat is one of seven held by Republicans that have a partisan lean of less than 60% toward the GOP, which historically have a higher chance of flipping in a wave election. 
In this kind of climate, you obviously want to protect against that,” Watson said about his seat flipping. “I feel really good about the campaign we’ve run. I feel really good about our chances.”
Watson said he feels confident, but he’s not taking a win for granted and so has run a hard campaign.
Democratic opponent Roberts said he’s told people the race is like looking for a rock on a sandy beach. He said he doesn’t know about a blue wave touching Tennessee, but high early voting turnout shows there is surely excitement. 
Roberts said he ran because he thinks people should have options, would like to see the supermajority broken up, and disagreed with a Watson bill that ultimately failed, that would have allowed public schools to deny education to students without legal documentation.
From governor to Congress to Senate speaker, how the Lookout is following TN’s midterm election

“If I win today, I’m ready to get to work,” Roberts said. “If I don’t win, I mean that’s fine too. I mean it’s there you shouldn’t lose hope. There’s always ways to do things. There’s communities you can work with that have been underserved for years, and just if you have a voice, you can bring attention to that.”
Watson didn’t say whether he would vote to make Senate Majority Leader Jack Johnson Speaker.
Watson, who has received money from Johnson’s political action committee in this election, could be a key vote among the 14 required to win Johnson the position, which also serves as lieutenant governor.
“I have to win my race first, so I am really a one step at a time person,” Watson said. “There are 27 members — at least currently. So again, Bo Watson has to take care of Bo Watson first, and I’ll worry about those things on Wednesday.” 
Johnson and Sen. Paul Bailey, a Sparta Republican, are vying for the chance to succeed Lt. Gov. Randy McNally, who is retiring after nearly four decades in office. 
Johnson’s Political Action Committee, JACK PAC, contributed $15,400 directly to Watson and spent another $30,413.88 on advertising for Watson, according to the PAC’s pre-general expenditure filings.

name: California
title: California accepts big broadband money from Trump — but not the terms and conditions
description: California accepted $1.4 billion in federal broadband funding while saying it will stand behind state net neutrality laws the program forbids.
text:
In summary
California accepted $1.4 billion in federal broadband funding while saying it will stand behind state net neutrality laws the program forbids.


The state of California has agreed to accept $1.4 billion in federal funding to bring broadband internet access to 270,000 people while simultaneously challenging conditions attached to the funding.
Those conditions would stop the state from enforcing broadband laws that reduce costs and guarantee equal access for internet destinations.
California is the last state to accept money from a broadband program created in 2021 as part of an infrastructure bill passed during the Biden administration. 
Under terms updated by the Trump administration one year ago, states that accept funding from the Broadband, Equity, Access, and Deployment program must stop enforcing net neutrality rules, which ensure equal connection speeds for every app and website, as well as any rules that influence broadband internet costs. California enjoys the strongest net neutrality laws in the nation. 
In recent weeks, digital access advocates argued that if the state accepts the money without meaningfully challenging the terms, it could endanger communities reliant on internet access for emergency services and raise costs for low-income Californians who receive internet subsidies. Through 2040, accepting the terms could cost Californians up to $16 billion, according to an estimate from open internet advocacy group Public Knowledge. 
Gov. Gavin Newsom’s office said it is both taking the federal money and maintaining its access rules. In a written statement shared with CalMatters, Anthony Martinez, a spokesperson for the governor, said that “Connecting these communities is the goal, and so is protecting them. California’s laws, including our net neutrality protections, still stand.”
The president of the California Public Utilizes Commission, the agency chosen by Newsom to administer the program, provided the federal agency that administers the program with both a signed notice that California will accept the funding and a letter that calls the terms vague and outside of the commission’s legal authority. The letter sent Monday also acknowledges that the state will not distribute program funding to companies like Comcast, Pacific Bell, SpaceX, and Verizon until disagreements about the terms are resolved. 
“The CPUC cannot be bound by any terms or conditions that are unconstitutional or not authorized by law and it expressly does not waive or concede any arguments or challenges concerning the legality, interpretation, or applicability of any term or condition,” wrote CPUC president John Reynolds in the letter.
Stephen Yusko, a spokesperson for the National Telecommunications and Information Administration within the Department of Commerce, responded to the letter today by saying that the terms and conditions of the award constitute the entire agreement between his agency and the utilities commission.
“No part of the letter outlining CPUC’s concerns is incorporated into or made part of the award,” he said in a statement provided to CalMatters.
Last month a group of law professors who work on issues related to internet freedom and access urged the utilities commission and governor’s office not to accept the money without challenging the terms in court. Stanford University professor Barbara van Schewick told CalMatters that “only a court, or NTIA agreeing in writing, can take [the access terms] out of California’s award, and neither has happened.”
But she said she’s happy to see the letter makes clear that the state will not sign agreements with companies getting the federal broadband funding until the utilities commission and federal government resolve their disagreement over the terms. It also preserves a strong legal argument that the utilities commission lacks the authority to prevent other state entities from enforcing the law.
“The real test comes the first time a BEAD provider blocks a competitor’s app, throttles firefighters, or walks away from a price commitment,” she told CalMatters. “If the state enforces its laws when that happens, the letter will have protected Californians.”
She added: “If the state looks the other way, [the terms] will have worked exactly as the providers intended, without a single court ever ruling on it.”
Phil Grosse is a member of the California Democratic Party Rural Caucus. In recent weeks Grosse and dozens of community leaders along the Russian River in Sonoma County urged the governor to challenge the broadband funding terms in court before accepting the money. He believes the terms would end phone service guarantees and backup battery power for cellular towers, endangering the lives of rural Californians.
“We can’t accept the money without all kinds of poisoned pills attached to it, and I’m glad the CPUC acknowledged that, and that they are bound to follow state laws and regulations,” he said, adding that he anticipates the whole ordeal will end up in court. “I’m hopeful the Trump administration will see the wisdom in the CPUC’s letter but I’m rather doubtful.”

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Former delegate to plead guilty in child rape case
description: A disgraced, former assistant majority leader in the House of Delegates is expected to plead guilty in federal court to charges relating to the sexual assault of a teenager.
text:
Former Del. Elliott Pritt addresses the House of Delegates on the last night of the 2026 legislative session. Pritt, who faces a federal charge, plans to plead guilty. (Photo by Perry Bennett | West Virginia Legislative Photography)A disgraced, former assistant majority leader in the House of Delegates is expected to plead guilty in federal court to charges relating to the sexual assault of a teenager. 
Lawyers for David “Elliott” Pritt, 36, filed Tuesday for motion to cancel a scheduled bond modification hearing because their client had signed a guilty plea agreement with the federal government. 
U.S. Magistrate Court Judge Omar J. Aboulson issued an order Tuesday to cancel the bond hearing, but has not scheduled a hearing for a guilty plea. 
Pritt represented Fayette County in the House of Delegates after being elected in 2022 as a Democrat. He switched to the Republican in 2023 and rose to the ranks as assistant majority leader, a position that is rotated out from session-to-session. 
The West Virginia Republican Party took the extraordinary step of expelling Pritt, the first in the party’s history. 
Pritt faces charges of enticement of a minor, production of child sexual abuse material and witness tampering. He could serve up to life in prison. 
However, while his attorneys have said Pritt is willing to plead guilty, a judge must still accept his deal with the government in order to proceed. 
Pritt previously pleaded not guilty before Judge Aboulson.
Since his arrest on July 22, Pritt has been held in a correctional facility in Kentucky.
An investigation this summer revealed Pritt, who worked as a public school teacher at the time of arrest, allegedly sexually assaulted a teenage girl.
A criminal complaint said that Pritt allegedly began communicating with the girl when she was in eighth grade in 2024 through the online game Roblox then later on Snapchat. Pritt later allegedly initiated a physical relationship with the minor and requested that she meet him in his classroom at Oak Hill High School to engage in sexual activity at least five to 10 times.
Last month, Pritt asked to be released on bond for mental health treatment at a veterans medical center in Martinsburg while awaiting adjudication, WCHS reported.
Federal prosecutors opposed Pritt’s release for reasons that included safety of the community.
The federal prosecutors also cited a love letter written by Pritt to the minor girl earlier this year as reason he should not be moved to a less-strict mental health facility.
Pritt previously removed himself from the ballot since he was seeking reelection to the House.

name: VTDigger
title: Who checks the software’s work?
description:
Training workers to catch what automation misses should be part of every manufacturing apprenticeship.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Who checks the software’s work?.
text:
Dear Editor,
A recent report published by VTDigger on a Brattleboro manufacturing roundtable described employers and educators working to strengthen the talent pipeline. One missing measure is whether beginners learn to spot problems that automated systems overlook.
In a recent employment study, Anthropic reported that the share of its technical hires who were junior fell from 27% to 9% as artificial intelligence agents took on more work. Vermont manufacturers face different conditions, but the question is timely: Who will teach workers sound judgment when software increasingly handles routine preparation?
The Windham Regional Career Center and employers should jointly design supervised, paid practice in checking automated output. Give a trainee a simulated production order with conflicting specifications. Ask them to find the mismatch, consult the authoritative drawing and bring a recommended correction to a qualified supervisor. Never make actual safety decisions part of an unsupervised exercise.
Vermont’s registered apprenticeship system already combines classroom instruction with work alongside experienced professionals. Employers can add short error-detection exercises and document when each apprentice can handle ordinary exceptions without prompting.
Count placements and certificates, certainly. Also report how many apprentices demonstrate reliable verification skills and remain employed after training. That would tell Windham County whether its manufacturing pipeline builds the competence employers need.
Gleb Tsipursky
Columbus, Ohio

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: No major issues reported in Milwaukee so far on Election Day
description: Voters in Milwaukee streamed to the polls amidst overcast skies and rainy weather on Election Day. Some polling sites reported high turnout while several police departments in the Milwaukee area said there were minimal reported incidents.  At Milwaukee’s South Division High School, located on the predominantly Latino South Side, voters arrived and checked in[...]
text:
South Division High School in Milwaukee as a polling location in 2026. (Photo | Isiah Holmes/Wisconsin Examiner)Voters in Milwaukee streamed to the polls amidst overcast skies and rainy weather on Election Day. Some polling sites reported high turnout while several police departments in the Milwaukee area said there were minimal reported incidents. 
At Milwaukee’s South Division High School, located on the predominantly Latino South Side, voters arrived and checked in. The polling site’s chief election worker said shortly before noon that 63 people had arrived. Outside, poll chaplains standing with umbrellas who were there to make sure voters could cast their ballots without interference said that there had been no issues so far, an observation echoed by the chief poll worker. 
In the leadup to the midterm elections, anxiety was high that federal agents would be deployed to polling locations in certain neighborhoods, including those with large numbers of immigrant families. Milwaukee is one of two cities in Wisconsin where the Department of Homeland Security sent election monitors for the midterms, in an effort pro-democracy groups criticized for targeting Democratic strongholds and minority communities..
In a statement sent shortly before 2 p.m., the Milwaukee Police Department told the Wisconsin Examiner that the department had responded to three incidents related to the election. Milwaukee officers responded to a high school — the department did not specify which one — where there were complaints about election signs being stolen. Officers determined that the signs had been placed in a right of way where they were not allowed, and no arrests were made. 
Officers also responded to a college campus in Milwaukee following a report that individuals were possibly too close to the entrance of a polling location with election materials. When officers arrived the individuals were no longer at the scene. The third incident was a motor vehicle crash involving a city vehicle conveying election workers who were transporting ballots. The workers had just dropped off the ballots and were involved in the accident as they were leaving. Two election workers were transported to a local hospital, as well as the driver of the vehicle that struck them. 
When asked whether things were quiet, Waukesha Police Capt. Dan Baumann said in an emailed statement to the Examiner “we don’t use that ‘Q’ word,” adding, “I’m knocking on wood as I type but all things are going well on the home front.” Lt. Nicholas Wenzel of the Waukesha County Sheriff’s Department also said that he had not heard of any election-related incidents. The Wauwatosa and West Allis Police Departments did not respond to a request for comment. 
WISN 12 News reported that multiple polling locations had reported technical issues, including the Saveland Park Pavilion on the South Side. By 10:22 a.m. the issue, involving 100 ballots which could not be read into the machine, had been resolved. Milwaukee Election Commissioner Patricia Ruiz-Cantú said the issues with machines were resolved easily, and mentioned that one location had ballots without Voter ID numbers. Ruiz-Cantú said that the ballots were audited and found to be eligible voters casting legitimate ballots and that this was the result of a clerical error. 
Over 462,000 Wisconsinites had cast their ballot during in-person absentee voting by the time polling locations opened Tuesday morning. Nearly 797,000 ballots have been returned to the Milwaukee municipal clerk to be counted today.

name: VTDigger
title: When the last Holocaust survivors are gone, who will teach their history?
description:
The responsibility to bear witness is passing to survivors’ children and grandchildren, but families can’t do it alone.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  When the last Holocaust survivors are gone, who will teach their history?.
text:
This commentary is by Debora Steinerman, co-founder of the Vermont Holocaust Memorial.
I recently attended the 36th Annual World Federation of Jewish Holocaust Survivors and Descendants Conference in Philadelphia — perhaps one of the last gatherings to include several Holocaust survivors. Those survivors were very young children when the Nazi persecution of European Jews began. Today, they fear that when their voices are gone, their stories will be forgotten.
As a founder of the Vermont Holocaust Memorial, a child of Holocaust survivors and descendant of its victims, I feel a profound responsibility to preserve their legacy. I attended with my daughter, a member of the third generation, who is now carrying the mantle of remembrance in her own community. Watching her generation step forward gives me hope, but the urgency of their mission was unmistakable.
Throughout the conference, participants spoke of growing antisemitism, Holocaust denial and false equivalencies that distort history. They worry that the Holocaust will become a footnote in history books rather than a defining lesson about the consequences of hatred, dehumanization and indifference.
Eighty-one years after the end of World War II, its effects continue to haunt survivors and their descendants. Conference sessions explored intergenerational trauma, survivor guilt and a particularly poignant question: “Are we allowed to be happy?” The Holocaust did not end emotionally when the war ended. Its losses reverberate through families, shaping identities and leaving absences that can never be filled.
As we commemorate the 88th anniversary of Kristallnacht, the “Night of Broken Glass,” on Nov. 9-10, I am reminded that history is not something that happened only to others. I grew up with the knowledge that my grandfather, aunts, uncles and cousins had been murdered simply because they were Jewish. I never had the opportunity to get to know them. Before the war, they were ordinary people: shopkeepers, businesspeople, homemakers, students and playful children. They had dreams and futures that were violently taken away.
Their life stories are part of my inheritance. Descendants of Holocaust survivors and victims carry that legacy, whether they recognize it or not. We inherit the memories, the silences and the responsibility to ensure that those who were murdered are remembered as individuals, not merely as statistics.
Yet remembrance must also inspire hope. At the conference, the third-generation participants spoke with resilience, confidence and joy. They are finding new ways to preserve history, using technology and social media to share their experiences and stand proudly in their Jewish identities. Their voices are a breath of fresh air. They reminded us that honoring the past does not mean surrendering the future.
But hope alone is not enough. We must act.
Vermont remains one of the very few states without a requirement to teach the Holocaust in its secondary schools. Although many dedicated Vermont educators ensure that students learn this history, education should not depend on an individual teacher’s initiative or a school’s priorities.
Every student deserves to learn about Jewish life before, during and after the Holocaust, what happened and how a so-called enlightened society descended into genocide. Students must understand the roles of perpetrators, bystanders and those who resisted. They need historically accurate, carefully vetted resources that help them recognize antisemitism, challenge propaganda and distinguish historical fact from deliberate distortion.
The Vermont Holocaust Memorial supports educators through annual professional development workshops, exhibits, projects and a speakers bureau. These efforts are invaluable, but they cannot substitute for a consistent statewide commitment.
When Holocaust education is not required, students may graduate without meaningful understanding of one of history’s most consequential atrocities. That allows room for ignorance, denial and the normalization of prejudice. We cannot leave such an essential responsibility to chance. If it is not in the curriculum, it can be said that it never happened.
As survivors die, the obligation to bear witness falls to their children, their grandchildren, educators and communities. Our task is not simply to preserve their testimony but to ensure that the lessons remain relevant to each new generation. It is about equipping students with the knowledge to recognize where hatred leads and the courage to challenge it.

READ MORE

Vermont must make Holocaust education a priority by establishing a statewide requirement and ensuring that teachers have the proper training and resources to teach it responsibly. 
I left the conference encouraged by my daughter’s generation but also mindful of what is at stake. When the last of the Holocaust survivors are gone, the world will still need witnesses. Vermont must ensure that future generations are prepared to carry the responsibility forward.

title: Michigan officials flag improper interactions between DOJ election monitors and poll workers

Kim Bush, a spokeswoman for Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel,[...]
text:
Voters wait in line on Nov. 3, 2026, at Bethlehem Lutheran Church in Lansing, Mich., one of several local polling places in Ingham County. (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance)Michigan election officials say they contacted the U.S. Department of Justice on Tuesday after receiving reports that federal election monitors in Dearborn and Flint had questioned poll workers about their training, conduct which state officials said was outside the monitors’ legal authority.
Kim Bush, a spokeswoman for Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel, said DOJ monitors in Dearborn asked poll workers for copies of their training materials, while monitors in Flint asked questions about how poll workers were trained.
The Michigan Department of State and Attorney General’s Office contacted the DOJ’s Michigan election monitor coordinator, who acknowledged the reported conduct was inconsistent with the monitors’ training and said the department would speak directly with monitors to clarify what they are permitted to do.
“That coordinator confirmed that this activity that the monitors were engaging in is not consistent with how the monitors were trained. and that they would follow up with the monitors on the ground in Dearborn to remind them of what they are not permitted to do and what they are permitted to do,” Angela Benander, spokesperson for the department of state, told reporters. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
A request for comment was sent by Michigan Advance to the DOJ, but has yet to be returned. This story will be updated when a response is received.
Under Michigan law, DOJ monitors are generally limited to observing election procedures. They cannot question poll workers about their training or handle election materials. They also cannot enter a polling location without permission from the local clerk.
State officials said they had also received reports of DOJ monitors speaking with voters in Lansing but had no concerns about those interactions. The law permits monitors to speak with voters outside polling locations after they have cast their ballots, provided voters are told they are not required to participate, which the monitors reportedly did.
As of Tuesday afternoon, state officials said they had received no additional reports of concerning conduct by DOJ or congressional election observers and had not identified any significant problems beyond routine Election Day issues, such as equipment malfunctions.
“We have, it sounds like, pretty consistently high turnout,” Benander said during a 3 p.m. briefing. “But at this time, the report that we have to share is that things are running smoothly.”
Seventy-one DOJ monitors were assigned to polling locations in Detroit, Dearborn, Hamtramck, East Lansing, Grand Rapids, Flint and Warren.

name: WyoFile
title: Defense questions poisoning evidence in UW grad student’s attempted murder case
description:
The case against Aili Wang, a University of Wyoming microbiology graduate student, will advance. She faces charges for attempted second-degree murder and aggravated assault and battery.
The post Defense questions poisoning evidence in UW grad student’s attempted murder case appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
LARAMIE—Aili Wang appeared on a courtroom screen wearing a black shirt and glasses with her hair tied back. She sat at a desk in a brightly lit white cinderblock room at the Albany County Detention Center. With her arms extended before her, she fiddled with a pen and looked blankly into the camera. A pair of deputies put a phone in front of her. Just as the hearing began, Wang lifted the phone from its cradle and held it to her ear. 

Aili Wang (Mark Gomelsky via UW)

Wang, who was studying microbiology at the University of Wyoming as a graduate student from China, is charged with attempted second-degree murder and aggravated assault for allegedly poisoning a fellow student. She faces the possibility of life behind bars. On Oct. 6, authorities arrested Wang at the Los Angeles International Airport, where prosecutors allege she was attempting to flee the country and return to China, court records show. 
Several law enforcement officers and reporters sat in the sunlight-filled courtroom for Wang’s preliminary hearing Tuesday. People directly connected to the case, including one person who appeared to be the alleged victim, also filled the audience until Deputy County and Prosecuting Attorney Joel Defebaugh asked for them to leave the hearing, noting that they may eventually be called as witnesses during trial. 
Police began investigating in September after the alleged victim, another international graduate student in Wang’s office who’s identified in court records as “K.T.,” started having symptoms of possible poisoning. During Tuesday’s preliminary hearing in Albany County Circuit Court, University of Wyoming Police Department Chief Joshua Holland elaborated that the relationship between the two was initially “collegial” but “soured” following accusations of “sabotage” related to research experiments. Holland didn’t go into detail Tuesday about these accusations or who made them. 
At the Tuesday hearing, Defebaugh said he had received new information that Wang worked previously in China for a company pursuing the same research as K.T.
K.T. became suspicious after tasting a “bitter” flavor in a cup of tea he made with a coffee maker on his desk, Holland said. He tasted the bitterness again about a week later in mid-August. K.T. also began experiencing tiredness, inability to sleep, tingling and other symptoms, the Associated Press reported. The alleged victim and his wife tested water from the coffee maker and found the neurotoxin acrylamide, which can be acutely toxic in high doses. 
Holland said that K.T.’s blood samples showed elevated levels of iron — an indication of liver damage that could be a result of acrylamide poisoning. K.T. continues to get medical care for his symptoms, Holland stated. 
According to the police account, Wang used her university email over the summer to buy acrylamide twice on eBay and later requested the site to delete her order history and account. She was also recorded on a surveillance camera going through the alleged victim’s desk, “taking photos and manipulating notebooks” and rinsing out his mug with a liquid from her own mug. But Linda Devine, Wang’s attorney, noted during the Tuesday hearing that none of the video footage showed Wang actually putting anything in K.T.’s coffee pot. 
As part of the investigation, Holland said he had consulted with a toxicologist about the potential hazards of acrylamide. The expert, he said, told him that the “dose is the poison” when it comes to acrylamide’s bodily impact, but acknowledged that, at this time, authorities haven’t quantified the amount of acrylamide that was in the alleged victim’s coffee pot. A lab is now testing samples, according to Holland. He said authorities searched Wang’s car and home but didn’t find acrylamide. 
Devine said that knowing how much acrylamide was allegedly in K.T.’s coffee pot “is key” to understanding whether the substance could have caused bodily harm. “In order to determine if it’s poisonous, we need to know what the dose is,” Devine said. 
Albany County Circuit Court Judge Robert Sanford found sufficient probable cause to move both charges over to district court, where the case could continue to a trial. 
While the court originally set a $200,000 bond for Wang, Sanford subsequently granted prosecutors’ request to increase the amount to $1.5 million cash-only. He denied Devine’s two requests to reduce that bond amount. 
Wang will likely return to court in several weeks for her arraignment, where she’s expected to enter a formal plea to the charges.
The post Defense questions poisoning evidence in UW grad student’s attempted murder case appeared first on WyoFile .

title: U.S. Department of Justice monitors election in Kanawha County
description: Representatives from the U.S. Department of Justice are monitoring the midterm election at precincts in Kanawha County on Tuesday.
text:
The U.S. Department of Justice is monitoring the midterm election at precincts in Charleston, West Virginia, on Nov. 3, 2026, according to the Secretary of State's Office. A polling station at Edgewood Summit in Charleston, West Virginia, during the 2024 primary election. (Photo by Lori Kersey/West Virginia Watch)Representatives from the U.S. Department of Justice are monitoring the midterm election at precincts in Kanawha County on Tuesday.
Donald Kersey, chief of staff for the West Virginia Secretary of State’s Office, said the federal government notified the office last week that six election monitors would be in Charleston Tuesday. 
The DOJ did not disclose which polling locations they planned to observe, but based on reports they are roving around the city rather than observing a single polling place all day, Kersey said. 
The Department of Justice said in a statement Tuesday it was sending approximately 1,000 election monitors to all 50 states for the first time ever to check for compliance with federal voting rights statutes. 
Monitors are coordinated by the DOJ’s Civil Rights Division, and include personnel from the Civil Rights Division, other DOJ divisions and components, U.S. Attorney’s Offices and federal observers from the Office of Personnel Management, the statement said.
“Election integrity has been one of the top priorities for this Administration and this Division,” Assistant Attorney General Harmeet K. Dhillon of the Civil Rights Division at the Department of Justice said in a statement. “I am very proud we are deploying the largest monitoring effort in DOJ history, and pursuing transparency for elections in an assertive and nondiscriminatory manner.”
In a social media post Tuesday, the American Civil Liberties Union of West Virginia noted that “federal election monitors are routinely sent to polling places.” 
“It’s also important to note that monitors may NOT interfere with your right to vote in any way,” the organization said. 
The ACLU advised voters to contact its Election Protection Hotline at 304-355-5123 to report election interference.
