name: Mississippi Today
title: MBI accidentally released a report about the fatal shooting of Kohen Wiley. Here’s what we know.
description: A new set of records mistakenly released to a local news outlet by the Mississippi Bureau of Investigation provides the most detailed look yet at how the agency investigated the police shooting death of 1-year-old Kohen Wiley in a Walmart parking lot this summer.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Mukta Joshi is an investigative reporter at Mississippi Today. She is spending a year as a New York Times Local Investigations fellow examining immigration and criminal justice issues. She can be reached at mukta.joshi@nytimes.com.
A new set of records mistakenly released to a local news outlet by the Mississippi Bureau of Investigation provides the most detailed look yet at how the agency investigated the police shooting death of 1-year-old Kohen Wiley in a Walmart parking lot this summer. 
In response to a public records request, TVMO News Network received 65 unredacted pages – including summaries of witness statements – that the MBI had not intended to make public. 
After the mistake was brought to MBI’s attention, officials shared a redacted copy with the outlet with names and sensitive information removed, and requested that version be used instead. 
You can access that copy here:
CLICK TO DOWNLOAD 
The documents provide a first look at how the officers involved recounted what happened in June, when they chased two women accused of shoplifting diapers and baby clothes and surrounded their car as they began to flee. Previously released video of the incident shows Hunter Foster, then a sergeant with the Senatobia Police Department, stepping in front of the car and pointing his gun as it backed up, and then firing as it approached him.
Mississippi’s attorney general, Lynn Fitch, determined in October that Foster was justified in firing at the car and announced the state would not pursue charges against him.
While the documents include some details that had not previously been made public, there are no major revelations that explain, or call into question, the reasoning behind the attorney general’s decision not to pursue charges. The report does not include any conclusions investigators may have drawn about the officers’ actions.
Alex Gibert, a spokesperson for MBI, said the agency’s investigation remains open and active, despite Fitch’s decision not to prosecute Foster. Gibert declined to comment on the specifics of what or whom officials were investigating. 
The document, titled “Report of Investigation,” does not appear to be a complete record, because it references several attachments that are not included.
Here are some key takeaways from the released records:

How many officers, if any, were struck by the fleeing car has been a point of contention. In their statements, four officers said that the car struck at least one of the officers who had surrounded the car. No more than two officers were struck, the statements indicate. 


Foster told investigators that the vehicle was “already striking” him and the sheriff’s deputy to his right before he could get out of its path. 
Colson Sims, a Senatobia officer, said he observed Foster “buckled over the hood of the vehicle” due to “being struck.” 
Nathan Noe, a Tate County sheriff’s deputy, said the vehicle struck his left thigh as it reversed, and then again struck him and Foster as it accelerated forward.
Marshall Scott, another Tate County sheriff’s deputy, said the car struck Noe as it reversed.

MBI’s first official statement about the incident, issued in June, said the car had “almost” struck one officer. Multiple experts who reviewed body-worn camera footage and surveillance video of the incident said there was no definitive evidence that any of the officers were struck, although the car came close to several of them, making it difficult to determine. 

Martin Zummach, Foster’s lawyer, recently said during a television interview that his client had no idea who he was chasing and he wouldn’t have fired at the car had he known they were accused only of shoplifting diapers. The footage released by MBI so far showed a Walmart loss prevention employee only saying, “Two girls running,” before officers sprinted out of the store. 

But the officers may have had more information about the women than was previously known. In their statements, they made several references to the women being accused of shoplifting.

Noe’s statement referenced a conversation with a Walmart employee, who had told officers he was going to confront two Black women who had been shoplifting. Noe said the employee later came back to tell officers the women were running. That led Foster and the other officers to chase them to their car.
Sims told investigators that the loss prevention employee said “two shoplifters” were running from them.
Foster’s statement refers to suspects “who had just shoplifted” when describing the women entering their vehicle.


A central question not addressed by state authorities is whether officers at the scene ever saw Kohen in his mother’s arms before Foster fired at the car. None of the officers said in their statements that they saw a child, or knew one was present. Shaquille Moore, one of the Senatobia officers involved in the chase, said in his statement they only learned about the child after the injuries were reported.
Experts have raised concerns about Foster’s decision to shoot, in part because at least one officer was standing near the driver and could have been hit. Moore told investigators he did not fire at the driver for that reason. 
The report’s incident summary says charges are pending against both Kohen’s mother, Vellesiya Wiley, and the driver of the car, Latoya Ferrell. It does not mention the nature of the charges, or describe whether they are related to shoplifting or other actions taken by the women.

title: Delaware voter turnout reaches 292,000 by mid-afternoon; Democrats lead in numbers and rate
description: Nearly 36% of registered voters had cast ballots by 2:53 p.m., with Election Day voting continuing until polls close at 8 p.m. DOVER, Del. — More than 292,000 Delawareans had cast ballots by mid-afternoon Tuesday, pushing statewide turnout to about 36% with several hours of Election Day voting remaining. The state’s Election Voted List showed 292,484 ballots[...]
text:
Nearly 36% of registered voters had cast ballots by 2:53 p.m., with Election Day voting continuing until polls close at 8 p.m.
DOVER, Del. — More than 292,000 Delawareans had cast ballots by mid-afternoon Tuesday, pushing statewide turnout to about 36% with several hours of Election Day voting remaining.
The state’s Election Voted List showed 292,484 ballots cast as of 2:53 p.m. Nov. 3, including early, absentee and Election Day voting.
The party figures reflect voters’ registration, not which candidates they supported.
Registered Democrats accounted for 147,714 ballots, or about 44.4% of registered Democrats statewide. Republicans had cast 82,800 ballots, representing about 41.5% of registered Republicans.
Another 61,970 ballots came from unaffiliated voters and those registered with other parties, representing about 22.3% of that group.
Democrats make up roughly 41% of Delaware’s registered voters but accounted for slightly more than half of ballots cast through mid-afternoon. Republicans were turning out at a rate relatively close to Democrats, while turnout among unaffiliated and minor-party voters remained substantially lower.
How Delawareans have voted
Absentee voting accounted for 20,298 ballots: 12,915 Democrats, 3,899 Republicans and 3,484 voters registered as unaffiliated or with other parties.
Early voting, which ended Sunday, produced 129,584 ballots: 66,540 Democrats, 37,456 Republicans and 25,588 other voters.
Election Day polling places had recorded 142,602 ballots by mid-afternoon, including 68,259 Democrats, 41,445 Republicans and 32,898 other voters.
That brought the statewide totals to:

Democrats: 147,714
Republicans: 82,800
Unaffiliated and other parties: 61,970

Total: 292,484
Election Day voting accelerates
Polling-place voting had grown rapidly Tuesday, rising from roughly 55,000 ballots earlier in the day to more than 142,000 by 2:53 p.m.
Early in-person voting closed Sunday with 129,584 ballots cast.
Absentee ballots were also continuing to be received Tuesday.
County totals
New Castle County led the state with 145,875 ballots cast through mid-afternoon.
Sussex County had recorded 98,771 ballots, while Kent County had recorded 47,838.
Sussex County has generated particularly strong early and absentee participation relative to its population, while New Castle County was accounting for much of the Election Day voting volume.
Turnout approaching 2022 levels
Delaware’s 2022 midterm general election finished with turnout of about 42.7% of registered voters.
With turnout already near 36% by mid-afternoon Tuesday, Delaware was approaching that level with several hours of voting remaining.
The final turnout percentage will depend on the remainder of Election Day participation and the final absentee count.
The figures should not be interpreted as an indication of how Democratic, Republican or unaffiliated voters cast their ballots. Candidate preferences will only become clear as election results are reported.

text:
Ballots are about to be removed from his ballot drop box in Tacoma, Washington on Oct. 29, 2026. (Photo by Jerry Cornfield/Washington State Standard)
Election Day is here in Washington and the nation. Numerous pivotal races will be decided. 
There are three conservative-backed initiatives, on the state’s new income tax for high earners, the participation of transgender girls in girls’ school sports and parental rights of public school students. There’s a momentous election for the state Supreme Court, with five of the nine positions on the ballot. 
All 98 seats in the state House are up for grabs, and 24 of the 49 in the state Senate are on the ballot, as well. All of Washington’s seats in the U.S. House will be decided, as well, though most won’t be competitive.
We’ll have reporters in the field and will be tracking the results as they roll in. 
The first vote count is expected to start posting tonight around 8 p.m. More vote tallies will continue in the coming days, as mail ballots trickle in. Voters have until 8 p.m. to return their ballots.
Follow along here for updates throughout the day and night.



Key Events


Nov. 3, 2026 1:43 pm
Taking the partisan out of politics in Snohomish County


Nov. 3, 2026 1:39 pm
No issues with DOJ election monitors in King County


Nov. 3, 2026 1:35 pm
Will Pierce County dump its sheriff?










Taking the partisan out of politics in Snohomish County


By Jerry Cornfield - Tuesday November 3, 2026 1:43 pm





A local measure in Snohomish County would erase political party labels for elected county offices and the people running to serve in them.
Under Proposition 3, “all candidates for a Snohomish County elected office appear on the ballot without a political party designation and that all elected county offices be non-partisan offices.”
Several Snohomish County offices are already nonpartisan. These include treasurer, auditor, assessor, sheriff and clerk.
This one would affect those on the County Council and in the county executive job. If passed, it would apply next year when two council seats and the county executive’s position are on ballots. It would apply for the other three council seats when they are up for election in 2029.
The King County Council is nonpartisan. But don’t tell the Democratic and Republican parties as they seem to do battle in each election as they always have.









No issues with DOJ election monitors in King County


By Jake Goldstein-Street -  1:39 pm





Federal election monitors from the U.S. Department of Justice visited several voting centers this morning in Washington state’s King County, which includes Seattle.
As of 12:30 p.m., they’d been to Federal Way, Bellevue, Kenmore and Kent, said Halei Watkins, spokesperson for King County Elections. They’re expected to stop by every voting center in the state’s most populous county by day’s end.
“There haven’t been any issues with monitors, they’ve been following the rules just fine,” Watkins said.
The monitors so far just observed the process and could be checking for disability access and translated election materials. Watkins said they’ve been asked to check in with staff when they arrive at voting centers so their presence is known.
They’re also slated to be in Yakima County on the east side of the state, but county election officials haven’t heard from them.
“At this point we have no idea if they are in the area or not,” Auditor Charles Ross said in an email around 1:30 p.m.
Before the election, local and state election officials said they expected no problems with the monitors, though the Justice Department is ramping up these efforts this year. Federal monitors haven’t been in King County since 2008.









Will Pierce County dump its sheriff?


By Jerry Cornfield -  1:35 pm





Voters elected Keith Swank as sheriff of Pierce County in 2024. Today, they are considering a local ballot measure that if passed would evict him with two years to go in his term.
Charter Amendment 53 would make the sheriff an appointed position rather than an elected one. Swank, who was narrowly elected, would be out of office on Jan. 1, 2027, if it passes. Right now, King County is the only county in the state with an appointed sheriff.
Swank, a mercurial public servant, isn’t about to get appointed to the job given the number of times he’s clashed with other elected Pierce County leaders, including County Executive Ryan Mello. 
Even if Swank keeps his job, he could face added scrutiny. Charter Amendment 54 would create a new Public Safety Ombuds Office to provide independent oversight of the sheriff and sheriff’s department.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: The latest updates from the 2026 election in Pennsylvania
description: The Capital-Star is providing the latest updates on the 2026 election in Pennsylvania.
text:
(Getty images)This story will updated throughout the day and night. 
‘Here as polling observers and peacekeepers’ in Harrisburg
4:38 p.m.
Anjel Scarborough, 62, an Episcopal priest at All Saints Episcopal Church in Hershey, is spending most of her day at the 11th precinct polling place in Harrisburg. 
She’s with a left-leaning organization called Changing the Conversation Together that’s been canvassing and working to get out the vote in underserved neighborhoods nearby.
“We’re here as polling observers and peacekeepers, and helping people exercise their right to vote,” she said about their role on election day.
Anjel Scarborough, a priest at All Saints Episcopal Church in nearby Hershey, was greeting voters outside the 11th Precinct polling place in Harrisburg, as part of a left-leaning organization called Changing the Conversation Together. (Photo by Ian Karbal/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)
Scarborough said she herself supports any candidate opposing the Trump administration. She said President Donald Trump’s agenda has been “harming the most vulnerable populations in our country,” pointing in particular to Project 2025, a comprehensive policy playbook authored by the conservative think tank, the Heritage Foundation. While Trump denied any affiliation with the project during the 2024 election, some of its key architects now serve critical roles in his administration.
“I think the theologian Karl Barth said it well, who said ‘You should preach with the bible in one hand and a newspaper in the other,’” she said. “For me it’s the bible in one hand and a smartphone in the other. You need to know how to really look at the ethics of our faith, and how do we apply those ethics towards evaluating candidates by their character.”
While her congregation is in one of the more affluent areas of central Pennsylvania, she said many of the members work or used to work at the Penn State Hershey Medical Center.
“I have a lot of doctors and medical people who saw the devastation firsthand of the COVID-19 pandemic, and they’re also living and dealing with, firsthand, the rise in measles and the public health policies that have been implemented by the Trump administration.”
She said many of her members are concerned about the looming impacts of Medicaid cuts that were enshrined into law as part of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. While the bill was signed into law in 2025, it was authored so policies that are expected to lead to the steepest cuts, like new work-requirements for Medicaid enrollees, will go into effect after the midterms.
The nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office estimated that work requirements alone could lead to over 5 million people losing Medicaid coverage by 2034. Limited studies have shown that, in states that when Arkansas implemented work requirements for Medicaid, little impact was made on overall employment, but thousands lost coverage. 
The changes are estimated to save around $325 billion over 10 years, largely because of an expected drop in the number of Americans covered. Advocates have warned the policy will likely lead to eligible workers losing Medicaid coverage, in part because of stringent new paperwork requirements.
The 11th Precinct polling place had served 330 voters as of around 3:20 p.m., and is on track to see higher turnout than the 2022 midterm elections.
— Ian Karbal
Chester County reports mail-in ballot processing moving smoothly 
4:15 p.m.
Chester County Board of Elections employee Karen Butala sorts ballots Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026, in West Chester, Pa. (Photo by Peter Hall/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)
Mail-in ballot processing moved smoothly Tuesday in Chester County, where a foreign object in a ballot envelope forced election workers to evacuate the building last week.
After polls opened Tuesday, the first shift of county employees who volunteered to open and prepare ballots for scanning began work. 
They included people from the county’s Public Defender’s Office, Finance Department, Assessment Office and other agencies who stepped up to aid election officials in processing more than 59,000 mail ballots received through Monday, with more to come in the mail and drop off boxes around the county.
Before the ballots can be electronically scanned to record the votes, they must first be checked for signatures and dates, removed from their envelopes, sorted and flattened. None of the work can begin until polling places open on Election Day. 
“Things are going well. No news is good news,” said Kevin Seeling, a technical administrator for the county Board of Elections. He added the process was on pace to have the mail ballots tallied by the time polls close.
On Friday, the building was locked down after a worker identified a “non-liquid substance” inside a ballot envelope by feeling the outside. The Chester County Hazardous Materials Response Team was able to render the building safe within 90 minutes.
Preliminary testing directed by the FBI revealed there was no biohazard inside the envelope
County officials announced Tuesday morning that voting hours would be extended for 30 minutes in three precincts due to issues setting up voting machines. 
At Susan W. Starkweather Elementary School a few miles away, volunteers reported a slow, but steady flow of voters to the polls inside. 
On the ballot, voters had to choose between incumbent Republican state Rep. Craig Williams and Democratic challenger Elizabeth Moro in addition to the gubernatorial and congressional races. It’s one of a handful of districts where Democrats hope to flip the seat to retain and deepen their majority in the state House of Representatives.
But those who spoke with a reporter said they had broader issues than the state legislature on their minds. 
An election volunteer speaks with a voter Nov. 3, 2026, outside the Sarah W. Starkweather Elementary School in Westtown Township, Pa. Maureen Samara, an employee of Chester County’s Pocopson Home for seniors, sorts ballots on Election Day, Nov. 3, 2026, in West Chester, Pa. (Photo by Peter Hall/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)
Kenny Gill, a math professor at LaSalle University in Philadelphia, said he has voted in every election recently and on Tuesday selected all Democrats.
“I voted a mixed ballot before … I feel like everything has gotten so radicalized. You know, there was a once upon a time where both the parties were kind of moderate,” Gill said. “There’s a lot of common ground, and I just feel like everything’s gotten so extreme. It’s not a new thing for the last five or 10 years, at least.”
Describing the federal government as “a clown show,” Gill said he’s disturbed by the Trump administration’s “purely punitive” policies and the tactics police and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement are using across the country.
“There’s so much being funneled into defense and increasing security and funding more and more cruel devices for ICE agents to use against people, like those gloves that shock people,” he said.
Meanwhile, cuts to the federal budget have targeted programs that help people.
“Then we’re going to put billions into spending on this crap to torment our own citizens. Right? Things are ridiculous,” Gill added.
Kristin Grandzol said she voted because she wants Democrats to take control of the U.S. House of Representatives.
“With Trump in office, I just want anything that can help counterbalance some of his decisions,” she said.
The war in Iran, with no clear resolution in sight, was her biggest motivator to come to the polls.
“All this money is going to the war in Iran, and we have people here who can’t eat and get health care,” Grandzol said.
Nick Bonkoski brought his three daughters with him when he voted. Their futures were on his mind as he cast his ballot, he said.
“Raising three children these days, there’s a lot of things that are affecting the way that we look at what’s going on in politics around the world,” he said, adding that the cost of fuel and groceries were also a big concern with five mouths to feed. 
Latisha Johnson said she votes “every single year” and said the economy and women’s rights were her main motivators in this election. She voted for all Democrats.
“I think that the underserved are being severely underserved with this presidency,” she said. “We live in a really nice, affluent area here. And I think as Americans, it’s our responsibility to take care of everyone, including and most importantly those that are underserved.”
— Peter Hall
